Implement a tiny event dispatcher using a table of handlers.
typedef void (*Handler)(void *ev, void *ctx);
Handler table[N];
void dispatch(int type, void *ev, void *ctx) {
    if ((unsigned)type < N && table[type])
        table[type](ev, ctx);
}
Registration is just table[type] = fn;. This replaces a growing switch and lets modules self-register.
How do you emulate a virtual method / interface in C?
Put function pointers in a struct (“ops” / vtable). Each “object” carries a pointer to its ops table plus its own data: struct shape { const struct shape_ops *ops; ... }; s->ops->area(s);. Different concrete types supply different ops tables.
What breaks if you cast a void(*)(int) to void(*)(void) and call it?
Calling a function through a pointer of incompatible type is undefined behaviour. It may happen to work with a compatible calling convention on one ABI and crash or pass garbage on another. Keep the pointer type matching the function.

Advanced deep

POSIX dlsym returns void * but you need a function pointer. Is the cast legal?
ISO C says object and function pointers need not be interconvertible, so strictly it's implementation-defined. POSIX explicitly requires the conversion to work and documents the idiom; the portable-looking workaround is *(void **)&fn = dlsym(...) to dodge a compiler warning, but on any real POSIX platform a direct cast is fine and defined by POSIX itself.
How does a function-pointer dispatch table compare to a switch for a bytecode interpreter, performance-wise?
A dense switch often compiles to a jump table already, so raw dispatch cost is similar. The interpreter-specific win is computed goto / “threaded code” (a GCC label-pointer table), where each opcode handler ends by jumping directly to the next opcode's handler. That spreads the indirect branch across many sites, improving branch-predictor accuracy versus one hot switch dispatch point. A struct-of-pointers table is also more extensible at run time; a switch is faster to write and lets the optimiser see all cases.
Can you store a pointer to a function with C linkage in a variable typed for C++ linkage (or vice versa)?
Language linkage is part of a function type in C++. A pointer to an extern "C" function has a different type from a pointer to an ordinary C++ function, and mixing them is technically ill-formed (many compilers allow it). When registering C++ callbacks with a C API, declare the callback extern "C" so its type matches what the C library expects.

Variadic Functions (<stdarg.h>)

How printf accepts any number of arguments — and why writing your own is a minefield of promotions and missing type information.

Notes

A variadic function is declared with ... after at least one named parameter and can be called with a varying number of trailing arguments (printf, scanf, execl, logging helpers). At run time the function has no way to ask how many arguments it received or what their types are, so the caller must encode that somehow — a count, a sentinel value, or a format string. This page covers the <stdarg.h> mechanism (va_list, va_start, va_arg, va_end, va_copy), the default argument promotions that make va_arg(ap, float) undefined, how to forward the arguments to vprintf-style functions, the loss of type safety and how compilers help, and when to reach for a struct or array instead.

The mechanism: <stdarg.h>

What / how. Declare the function with a trailing ... after one or more real parameters. Inside, use a va_list and four macros: va_start to initialise it (pass the last named parameter), va_arg to fetch the next argument (you supply its type), va_end to finish, and va_copy if you need to traverse the list twice.

#include <stdarg.h>

int sum_n(int count, ...) {           // 'count' tells us how many follow
    va_list ap;
    va_start(ap, count);              // anchor just past 'count'
    int total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++)
        total += va_arg(ap, int);      // pull the next int, advance the cursor
    va_end(ap);                       // mandatory cleanup
    return total;
}

sum_n(3, 10, 20, 30);              // 60

There is no argument count at run time

What / why. The callee cannot discover how many arguments it got or their types — va_arg just reads whatever bytes come next as the type you name. So the interface has to carry that information. Three standard designs:

  • Explicit count — sum_n(3, a, b, c). Simple; the caller can lie.
  • Sentinel — a terminating value the loop stops on, e.g. a NULL-terminated list of strings. Pitfall: the terminator must have the right type. Bare NULL (or 0) may be passed as an int, which is narrower than a pointer on LP64, so va_arg(ap, char*) reads garbage. Pass (char *)NULL, and mark the function __attribute__((sentinel)) so the compiler checks.
  • Format string — the string encodes the number and types of the following arguments (printf("%d %s", n, s)). Most flexible, zero redundancy, but a mismatch is UB.
// sentinel style
void print_all(const char *first, ...) {
    va_list ap; va_start(ap, first);
    for (const char *s = first; s != NULL; s = va_arg(ap, const char *))
        fputs(s, stdout);
    va_end(ap);
}
print_all("a", "b", "c", (char *)NULL);   // cast the terminator!

Default argument promotions apply to the variadic part

What. Because there is no prototype for the ... arguments, each is subject to the default argument promotions: float is promoted to double, and any integer type narrower than int is promoted to int / unsigned int. Consequence. You must retrieve the promoted type or it is undefined behaviour:

va_arg(ap, float);        // ALWAYS UB -- the value was promoted to double
va_arg(ap, double);       // correct
va_arg(ap, char);         // UB -- promoted to int
va_arg(ap, short);        // UB -- promoted to int
va_arg(ap, int);          // correct for char/short/bool/enum args
va_arg(ap, unsigned);     // use for unsigned char/short after promotion (if unsigned int)

This is also why printf has no %f-for-float vs %lf-for-double distinction on input: a float argument is already a double by the time printf sees it.

Forwarding to vprintf-style functions

What / why. You cannot pass ... along to another variadic function — there is no syntax for it. The standard library therefore provides v* variants that take a va_list: vprintf, vfprintf, vsnprintf, vsscanf, … This is how you wrap printf in a logger.

void log_msg(const char *level, const char *fmt, ...) {
    fprintf(stderr, "[%s] ", level);
    va_list ap;
    va_start(ap, fmt);
    vfprintf(stderr, fmt, ap);        // hand the whole list over
    va_end(ap);
    fputc('\n', stderr);
}
// need the list twice? (e.g. measure length then format)
va_list ap, ap2;
va_start(ap, fmt);
va_copy(ap2, ap);                     // ap is consumed by the first pass
int need = vsnprintf(NULL, 0, fmt, ap);
char *buf = malloc(need + 1);
vsnprintf(buf, need + 1, fmt, ap2);
va_end(ap2); va_end(ap);

Type safety, compiler help, and alternatives

  • No checking: printf("%s", 42) and printf("%d") (missing argument) compile and are UB. Add __attribute__((format(printf, 2, 3))) (GCC/Clang; the numbers are the format-string parameter position and the first variadic position) to your own printf-like functions so -Wformat checks call sites.
  • va_list is opaque and on some ABIs an array type — you can’t assign it, and a helper that needs to advance the caller’s list must take va_list *. Always match every va_start/va_copy with a va_end, even on error paths.
  • Prefer a fixed interface for your own APIs: a struct of options (with designated initialisers), or a pointer + count array. They keep full type checking, allow default values, and don’t promote. C11 _Generic can do type-directed dispatch without varargs.
  • Security note: never pass user input as the format string (printf(user_str)) — that’s the classic format-string vulnerability (%n writes memory, %s/%x leak it). Always printf("%s", user_str).
Cheat Sheet
  • Declare: T f(T1 named, ...) — at least one named parameter is required before ....
  • <stdarg.h>: va_list ap; → va_start(ap, last_named); → va_arg(ap, TYPE) repeatedly → va_end(ap);. va_copy(dst, src) to traverse twice.
  • The callee can’t know arg count/types — pass a count, a sentinel (cast it: (char*)NULL), or a format string.
  • Default argument promotions hit the variadic args: float→double, char/short/bool→int. So va_arg(ap, float) and va_arg(ap, char) are UB — request double / int.
  • Can’t forward ...; use the v* functions: vprintf, vfprintf, vsnprintf, vsscanf. Logger pattern = va_start → vfprintf → va_end.
  • No type checking — annotate your printf-likes with __attribute__((format(printf, fmt_idx, first_var_idx))); keep -Wformat.
  • Prefer a struct of options or array + count for new APIs — type-safe, supports defaults, no promotions.
  • Never printf(user_input) — format-string vulnerability. Use printf("%s", user_input).
Q&A
How does a variadic function know how many arguments it received?
It doesn’t — there is no run-time mechanism. The caller has to encode it: an explicit count parameter, a sentinel value the loop stops on, or a format string that describes the following arguments. va_arg blindly reads the next slot as whatever type you name; if you over-read, you get garbage and undefined behaviour.
Why is va_arg(ap, float) always wrong?
Arguments in the ... part undergo the default argument promotions, which convert float to double. So a float you passed is actually stored as a double; asking va_arg for a float reads the wrong size and desynchronises the cursor — undefined behaviour. Always retrieve double. Likewise char/short/_Bool arguments must be retrieved as int.
You want to write void mylog(const char *fmt, ...) that prepends a timestamp and calls printf. How?
You can’t pass ... to printf directly. Use the va_list-taking variant: va_list ap; va_start(ap, fmt); vfprintf(stdout, fmt, ap); va_end(ap); (print the timestamp before the vfprintf). If you need the formatted length first (to allocate a buffer), va_copy the list, call vsnprintf(NULL, 0, fmt, ap) for the size, then vsnprintf(buf, size+1, fmt, ap_copy), ending both lists. Add __attribute__((format(printf, 1, 2))) so the compiler validates every mylog(...) call.
What’s wrong with print_all("a", "b", NULL) for a NULL-terminated variadic function on a 64-bit system?
If NULL expands to a bare 0 (an int), it’s passed as a 4-byte int, but the function does va_arg(ap, char *) expecting an 8-byte pointer. The read is misaligned/oversized and the “terminator” may not compare equal to NULL, so the loop runs off the end. Fix: pass (char *)NULL (or (char *)0) so a full-width null pointer is on the argument list, and declare the function with __attribute__((sentinel)) so missing/incorrect terminators are diagnosed.
When should you not use a variadic function?
For your own APIs, almost always — they lose type checking, force the promotions on you, and make defaults awkward. Prefer a struct of parameters filled with designated initialisers (f((opts){.timeout = 5})), or a const T *items, size_t n array, or C11 _Generic for type-directed behaviour. Reserve variadics for (a) implementing a printf-family function where a format string is genuinely the interface, and (b) matching an existing C ABI (execl, open’s optional mode).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Name the four <stdarg.h> macros and what each does.
va_start(ap, last_named) — initialise the va_list. va_arg(ap, TYPE) — return the next argument as TYPE and advance. va_end(ap) — finish (required). va_copy(dst, src) — duplicate a partially-used list so it can be traversed again.
Can a function be declared with just ... and no named parameters?
No (in C). There must be at least one named parameter before the ..., because va_start needs the name of the last fixed parameter as its anchor. (C++ relaxes this; C does not.)

Intermediate core

Implement a type-safe-ish int max_of(int count, ...) and explain each risk you’re accepting.
int max_of(int count, ...) { va_list ap; va_start(ap, count); int m = INT_MIN; for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) { int v = va_arg(ap, int); if (v > m) m = v; } va_end(ap); return m; }. Risks accepted: (1) the caller must pass count correctly — too high reads past the arguments (UB), too low silently ignores some; nothing enforces it. (2) All arguments must actually be int — passing a long or a pointer and reading it as int is UB and gives nonsense; the compiler can’t check because there’s no prototype for the variadic part. (3) count == 0 returns INT_MIN — a sentinel result you have to document. (4) No promotion protection: if someone passes a short it’s promoted to int so that’s fine, but char/short retrieved as anything else would be UB. A safer design is int max_of(const int *a, size_t n) — full type checking, obvious empty case, and the count can’t disagree with the data.
Explain the __attribute__((format(printf, m, n))) annotation and give a case it catches.
It tells GCC/Clang that this function takes a printf-style format string as parameter m and that the variadic arguments start at parameter n (use n = 0 for vprintf-style functions that take a va_list instead of ...). With it, the compiler applies its normal -Wformat checking to every call of your function: mismatched specifier and argument type (mylog("%d", "hello")), wrong count (mylog("%d %d", x)), non-literal format strings (mylog(userInput) → -Wformat-security), and %n in a writable format. Without it, those bugs compile clean and are undefined behaviour at run time. It costs one line and turns a whole class of latent crashes/vulnerabilities into compile errors.

Advanced deep

Design a logging library’s public API. Compare a variadic printf-style interface against alternatives, covering type safety, performance, extensibility, and misuse.
Option A — variadic printf-style (log_info(const char *fmt, ...)): familiar, compact call sites, one function per level. Implement over vsnprintf into a stack buffer (fall back to heap if truncated), then hand the finished line to the sink. Add __attribute__((format(printf, 1, 2))) so call sites are checked, and -Werror=format -Werror=format-security in the build so a non-literal format or a %n can’t merge. Costs: still zero type safety without the attribute; the format string is parsed at run time on every call (measurable in hot paths); structured fields (key/value) are awkward — you end up formatting them into the message text, which loses machine-parseability. Misuse risk: log_info(msg) where msg is user data — the attribute + -Wformat-security is your only guard. Option B — explicit builder / structured (log_ev(LOG_INFO, "user login", KV_STR("user", u), KV_INT("attempt", n), KV_END) or a fluent le = log_begin(...); log_kv_str(le, ...); log_end(le);): fully type-checked (each KV_* is a real function/macro with a typed argument), emits structured records natural for JSON/logfmt and downstream querying, extensible (new value types = new KV_*), and no format-string parsing or vulnerability. Costs: more verbose call sites; the KV_* varargs terminator still needs a sentinel discipline (or use a compound-literal array); a tiny per-call allocation unless you pool. Option C — compile-time formatting (C doesn’t have std::format/constexpr checks like C++20, but you can get partway with _Generic dispatch for common types and a small set of typed log_str/log_int/log_ptr primitives, or code-generation): best type safety, no run-time format parsing, but limited flexibility and more machinery. Recommendation: expose both — a printf-style front for ad-hoc human messages (with the format attribute and hardened warnings), and a structured builder for events that will be queried/alerted on; internally normalise both to the same record type before the sink. Cross-cutting: make the level check a cheap early-out macro (if (log_enabled(LOG_DEBUG)) log_debug(...), or a wrapper macro that short-circuits) so disabled levels don’t even evaluate arguments; keep the formatting off the caller’s critical path (enqueue the raw fields / pre-rendered line to a background writer); bound message size and truncate safely; make the API async-signal-safe or provide a separate signal-safe path (no malloc, no vsnprintf with %f) for signal handlers; and never let the format string come from untrusted input. Net: variadic is fine for the human-message convenience layer if hardened with the format attribute and warnings; use a typed/structured API for anything you’ll machine-process, and unify them below the public surface.

The Preprocessor & Macros

A text-substitution pass that runs before the compiler — powerful, and full of foot-guns.

Notes

The preprocessor is a text-substitution pass that runs before the compiler sees your code — it handles #include, #define, and #if. It is genuinely useful for header guards, configuration, and small code generation, but because it works on tokens with no knowledge of C’s grammar or types, careless macros introduce subtle bugs. This page covers where it sits in the build, the macro pitfalls (missing parentheses, double evaluation, the dangling else), stringize and token-paste, include-guard strategies, the useful predefined macros, and the X-macro pattern.

Where it sits in the build

The preprocessor is the first stage. It transforms your .c file (plus everything it #includes) into one big self-contained translation unit of pure C, which the compiler proper then parses. It works purely on tokens — it knows nothing about types, scopes, or C grammar.

// what you write:
#define N 3
#include <stdio.h>
int a[N];

// $ gcc -E file.c     (stop after preprocessing) shows pure C:
//   ... hundreds of lines pasted in from <stdio.h> ...
//   int a[3];         <- N replaced, #define line gone, no types checked yet

Macro pitfalls

// 1. missing parentheses
#define SQ(x) x*x
SQ(a+b)        // -> a+b*b   ... wrong
#define SQ(x) ((x)*(x))   // fix: parens around params AND whole body

// 2. double evaluation of arguments with side effects
#define MAX(a,b) ((a)>(b)?(a):(b))
MAX(i++, j)    // i incremented once or twice depending on branch

// 3. dangling-else / multi-statement macros
#define DBG(x) printf("%d\n",x); log(x)   // breaks after an if without braces
#define DBG(x) do { printf("%d\n",x); log(x); } while (0)  // fix

# stringize and ## token paste

#define STR(x)  #x            // STR(foo)  -> "foo"
#define XSTR(x) STR(x)         // expands x first: XSTR(__LINE__) -> "42"
#define CAT(a,b) a##b          // CAT(var,3) -> var3

You need the extra indirection layer (XSTR) because # and ## suppress expansion of their operands.

Include guards vs #pragma once

#ifndef MYLIB_FOO_H
#define MYLIB_FOO_H
/* declarations */
#endif

Standard, portable, and works even if the same file is reachable by two paths. #pragma once is shorter and widely supported but not in the standard.

Useful predefined macros

__FILE__, __LINE__, __func__ (actually a variable, C99), __DATE__, __STDC_VERSION__, and compiler-specific ones like __GNUC__. assert is a macro that expands to nothing when NDEBUG is defined.

// A logging macro that stamps every message with its source location:
#define LOG(msg) \
    fprintf(stderr, "[%s:%d %s] %s\n", __FILE__, __LINE__, __func__, msg)

void work(void) {
    LOG("starting");           // -> [work.c:42 work] starting
}

#if __STDC_VERSION__ >= 201112L
    // safe to use C11 features (_Static_assert, _Generic, ...)
#endif

X-macros

A single list macro drives multiple generated tables (enum + names + handlers) so they can't drift out of sync:

#define COLORS  X(RED) X(GREEN) X(BLUE)
enum Color { #define X(c) c, COLORS #undef X };
const char *name[] = { #define X(c) #c, COLORS #undef X };
Cheat Sheet
  • Wrap every macro parameter and the whole body in parentheses.
  • Multi-statement macro → do { ... } while (0).
  • Never pass side-effecting expressions to a macro that may use the arg twice.
  • Prefer static inline functions, const, and enum over macros where possible — they have types and scope.
  • #x stringizes; a##b pastes; both need a helper layer to expand args first.
  • Header guard: #ifndef UNIQUE / #define UNIQUE / ... / #endif.
  • #if defined(X) && X > 2 for version checks; undefined names in #if count as 0.
  • assert() vanishes under -DNDEBUG — never put required side effects inside it.
  • -E (gcc/clang) dumps preprocessed output for debugging expansions.
Q&A
Why parenthesise macro bodies and parameters?
Because expansion is textual: without parentheses the surrounding operators bind differently than intended (SQ(a+b) → a+b*b).
Why do { } while(0) around a multi-statement macro?
It makes the macro a single statement that still needs a terminating semicolon and behaves correctly after an if without braces.
Difference between #include <x> and #include "x"?
" " searches the current file's directory (and user paths) first, then the system paths; < > searches only the system/include paths. Use quotes for your project headers.
What does # do in a function-like macro?
Stringizes the argument — turns the token(s) into a string literal, with special handling of embedded quotes/backslashes.
Macro vs inline function — which to prefer?
inline (or static inline): it's type-checked, scoped, debuggable, and evaluates arguments once. Reach for a macro only when you need textual tricks (stringize, paste, generic-over-type without _Generic, compile-time constants).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What phase does the preprocessor run in, and does it understand C types?
It runs before compilation proper, operating on the token stream. It has no knowledge of types, scope, or expressions — it only does inclusion, macro substitution, and conditional compilation.
Write a safe MIN(a,b) macro.
#define MIN(a,b) ((a) < (b) ? (a) : (b)) — parens around each parameter and the whole expression. (Still evaluates one argument twice; document that or use a GCC statement-expression / an inline function.)
What's a header include guard?
An #ifndef NAME / #define NAME / ... / #endif wrapper that prevents the header's contents being processed more than once per translation unit.
What does #undef do?
Removes a current macro definition, so the name reverts to being an ordinary identifier (or can be redefined differently).

Intermediate core

Why does STR(__LINE__) give "__LINE__" and how do you fix it?
The # operator stringizes its argument without expanding it first. Add an indirection: #define STR(x) #x and #define XSTR(x) STR(x), then XSTR(__LINE__) expands __LINE__ to the number, which STR then stringizes.
Give a concrete bug from passing arr[i++] to MAX(a,b).
MAX(arr[i++], x) expands to ((arr[i++]) > (x) ? (arr[i++]) : (x)). If the first branch is taken, i is incremented twice and a different element is returned than the one compared — and the double modification of i without a sequence point is itself UB.
What is an X-macro and what problem does it solve?
A macro that lists items once (#define LIST X(a) X(b) X(c)); you then #define X differently and re-expand LIST to generate several parallel constructs (an enum, a name array, a jump table). It keeps those tables in sync because they're all generated from one source list.
How do you conditionally compile code only on GCC ≥ 7?
#if defined(__GNUC__) && (__GNUC__ > 7 || (__GNUC__ == 7 && __GNUC_MINOR__ >= 0)). Undefined identifiers evaluate to 0 in #if, so the defined() guard prevents a false match on other compilers.

Advanced deep

Explain the preprocessor's argument prescan and when it does not happen.
When a function-like macro is invoked, each argument is fully macro-expanded (“prescanned”) before being substituted into the body — unless that parameter is an operand of # or ## in the body, in which case it's used raw. That's the whole reason two-level STR/XSTR and CAT/XCAT wrappers exist: the outer macro expands the argument, the inner one applies #/##.
How can you build a variadic macro that forwards __VA_ARGS__ and handles the zero-argument case?
#define LOG(fmt, ...) fprintf(stderr, fmt, __VA_ARGS__) breaks when called with just a format. C99 workaround: GCC's , ##__VA_ARGS__ deletes the comma when empty; C++20 / C23 provide __VA_OPT__(,) for a portable version: #define LOG(fmt, ...) fprintf(stderr, fmt __VA_OPT__(,) __VA_ARGS__).
Why can't the preprocessor implement true recursion, and how do libraries fake counting/iteration?
A macro is “painted blue” (marked non-replaceable) while its own expansion is being rescanned, so it cannot call itself. Metaprogramming libraries (Boost.Preprocessor) simulate recursion by pre-defining a finite ladder of differently-named macros (REPEAT_1, REPEAT_2, ... up to a fixed limit) and deferring expansion with EMPTY()/DEFER tricks so an outer rescan pass performs the next step.

const, volatile, static, extern & Linkage

How names, definitions, and translation units fit together — and how headers should be written.

Notes

This topic is about names: how a definition in one .c file becomes visible to — or is deliberately hidden from — the others, and what static, extern, const, and inline each do to that visibility and to the object itself. Get it wrong and you hit “multiple definition” link errors, silent duplicate globals, or a header that cannot be included twice. This page covers translation units and the one-definition idea, the three kinds of linkage, the correct declare-in-header / define-in-one-.c pattern, const at file scope, C’s surprising inline semantics, and tentative definitions.

Translation units and the one-definition idea

Each .c file plus everything it #includes is a translation unit (TU), compiled independently to an object file. The linker then joins the object files, matching each use of an external name to its one definition. A name with external linkage may be declared in many TUs but must be defined exactly once across the whole program (the "one definition rule").

// math.h
int square(int);           // DECLARATION -- may appear in every TU that includes this

// math.c
int square(int n) { return n * n; } // DEFINITION -- exactly one across the whole program

// main.c
#include "math.h"          // gets the declaration; linker binds the call to math.o
int main(void) { return square(7); }

Linkage

LinkageMeaningHow to get it
ExternalOne entity shared across all translation units.File-scope function/variable with no static.
InternalOne entity private to this translation unit.static at file scope.
NoneA fresh entity each time the declaration is seen.Locals, function parameters, typedef, most block-scope names.
// ---- util.c ----
int shared = 1;             // EXTERNAL: other .c files can link to 'shared'
static int hidden = 2;      // INTERNAL: name is private to util.c
static void helper(void) { }   // INTERNAL: won't clash with a 'helper' elsewhere
void api(void) {
    int local = 3;          // NO linkage: a fresh object each call
}

// ---- main.c ----
extern int shared;           // OK: resolves to util.c's definition
// extern int hidden;         // LINK ERROR: 'hidden' has internal linkage

extern and the header pattern

// config.h
extern int g_verbosity;          // declaration -- promise it exists
void set_verbosity(int);

// config.c
#include "config.h"
int g_verbosity = 0;             // the single definition

Put declarations (not definitions) in headers. A bare int g; in a header included by several .c files gives multiple definitions — a link error under modern -fno-common defaults.

const and linkage

In C, a file-scope const still has external linkage by default (unlike C++, where it's internal). So const int K = 10; in a header included twice is a redefinition; use static const or (better) put the definition in one .c and extern const in the header, or use an enum/#define for true compile-time constants.

// shared.h -- included by several .c files
// const int K = 10;         // BAD in C: external linkage -> duplicate symbol at link
enum { K = 10 };               // GOOD: compile-time constant, no symbol, header-safe
static const int TIMEOUT = 30;    // OK: internal linkage, a private copy per TU
extern const char *VERSION;       // OK: declare here, define once in a .c

inline in C (differs from C++)

C99 inline without static or extern provides an inline definition that does not emit an external symbol; you must supply one extern inline (or normal) definition in exactly one .c for the address/non-inlined calls. The simple, portable choice for header helpers is static inline.

// vec.h -- safe, portable header helper
static inline int clampi(int v, int lo, int hi) {
    return v < lo ? lo : (v > hi ? hi : v); // each TU gets its own inlinable copy
}
// Plain `inline int clampi(...)` here would need ONE `extern inline int clampi(...);`
// in some .c file, or you get "undefined reference to clampi" at link time.

Tentative definitions

int x; at file scope is a tentative definition. Multiple tentative definitions of the same variable in one translation unit collapse into one, initialised to zero. Across translation units they're still multiple definitions.

// ---- one .c file ----
int x;                     // tentative definition
int x;                     // another tentative -- fine, they merge
int x = 5;                 // the real definition wins; x starts at 5
// int x = 6;              // ERROR: two initialised definitions

// Put `int x;` in a header included by 2+ .c files -> multiple-definition link error.
Cheat Sheet
  • Translation unit = one .c + its includes → one .o.
  • Declare in headers, define in exactly one .c.
  • static @ file scope → internal linkage (file-private).
  • extern → “defined elsewhere”; needed to share a global via a header.
  • C const at file scope has external linkage (unlike C++).
  • Header constants: enum, #define, or static const / extern const + one definition.
  • Header helpers: static inline (simplest correct choice).
  • -fno-common (modern default) turns duplicate globals into link errors — good.
  • Function default linkage is external; add static for internal helpers.
Q&A
Declaration vs definition?
A declaration introduces a name and its type; a definition also allocates storage (variables) or provides the body (functions). You can declare many times, define once.
What does static do to a global?
Gives it internal linkage — other translation units cannot see or link to it, avoiding name clashes.
How do two .c files share one global correctly?
Define it once (int g = 0;) in one .c; declare it (extern int g;) in a header both include.
Why did const int MAX = 100; in a shared header cause a link error in C but not C++?
C keeps file-scope const at external linkage, so each including .c defines the same symbol. C++ makes it internal by default, so each unit gets its own private copy.
Safest way to put a small helper in a header?
static inline — each including file gets its own inlinable copy with no duplicate-symbol risk.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What is a translation unit?
A single source file after preprocessing — the .c file with all its #includes pasted in and macros expanded. It's the unit the compiler turns into one object file.
Where should function declarations live, and where their definitions?
Declarations (prototypes) go in a header shared by callers and the implementer. The definition (body) goes in exactly one .c file.
What linkage does a local variable have?
None — each entry into its scope creates a distinct object; the name isn't visible to the linker at all.
How do you make a helper function invisible to other files?
Mark it static at file scope — internal linkage.

Intermediate core

You get “multiple definition of `g`” at link time. Likely cause and fix?
A real definition (int g; or int g = ...;) sits in a header that's included by more than one .c, so every unit defines g. Fix: header gets extern int g; only; put int g = 0; in exactly one .c. (Historically the “common” model hid this; modern compilers default to -fno-common.)
What's a tentative definition?
A file-scope declaration like int x; with no initialiser and no extern. If no other definition of x with an initialiser appears in the translation unit, the compiler emits one zero-initialised definition. Several tentative definitions of the same name in one unit are fine and merge.
Explain C99 inline and why static inline is usually recommended.
A plain inline function definition in a header is an “inline definition” that emits no standalone symbol; you must place exactly one extern (or ordinary) definition in some .c to satisfy address-of and non-inlined calls — easy to forget and get a link error. static inline sidesteps that: every translation unit gets its own internal copy, inlinable, no external symbol, no coordination needed.
Does const on a global let the compiler put it in read-only memory?
Yes, a const object with static storage duration and no volatile can be placed in .rodata. Attempting to cast away const and write it is undefined behaviour and typically faults.

Advanced deep

How does -fno-common change behaviour, and why is it now the default?
With the old “common” model, an uninitialised file-scope variable became a common symbol; the linker merged same-named commons from different objects into one, silently. That hid bugs (accidental global name collisions) and interacted badly with link-time optimisation and shared libraries. -fno-common makes each such variable a normal definition, so duplicates become multiple-definition errors, forcing the correct extern-in-header pattern. GCC 10 / modern Clang made it the default.
What is the difference between visibility (__attribute__((visibility("hidden"))) and linkage?
Linkage is a C-language concept about name sharing between translation units at static link time. Symbol visibility is an ELF/shared-library concept controlling whether an external-linkage symbol is exported from a .so for dynamic linking. A function can have external linkage (visible to other .os in the same library) yet hidden visibility (not part of the library's public ABI), which shrinks the dynamic symbol table and speeds load time.
Two libraries both define a static function helper(). Any conflict?
No. static gives internal linkage, so each helper is private to its own translation unit; the linker never compares them. The symbols may not even appear in the global symbol table. This is exactly why library-internal helpers should be static.

Bit Manipulation Tricks

Masks, shifts, and the handful of idioms that come up in almost every low-level interview.

Notes

Bit manipulation means treating an integer as a row of individual bits and using &, |, ^, ~, and shifts to set, clear, test, or extract them. It shows up in flag and permission masks, hardware registers, compact data structures, hashing, and a whole genre of interview puzzles. This page covers the mental model, the four fundamental operations, the idioms worth memorising (lowest set bit, power-of-two test, count / toggle / swap), packing values into fields by hand, and the shift gotchas — signed shifts, shifting by ≥ the type width, and integer promotion.

Think of a value as a row of bits

Bit n has place value 2n, numbered from the right (the least significant bit is bit 0). A mask is a value with 1s exactly where you want to act; the bitwise operator then decides what "act" means.

unsigned x    = 0x45;      // 0100 0101  -- bits 0, 2, 6 are set
unsigned mask = 1u << 3;    // 0000 1000  -- a "1" exactly at bit 3

x = x | mask;                // SET   bit 3 -> 0x4D
x = x & ~mask;               // CLEAR bit 3 -> 0x45 again
x = x ^ mask;                // TOGGLE bit 3 -> 0x4D
int b3 = (x >> 3) & 1u;       // TEST  bit 3 -> 1

The four fundamental operations

x |  (1u << n)     // set bit n
x & ~(1u << n)     // clear bit n
x ^  (1u << n)     // toggle bit n
(x >> n) & 1u       // test bit n  (0 or 1)

Use unsigned types and 1u/1UL so the shift can't hit signed overflow or shift into the sign bit (both UB). Shifting by ≥ the type width is also UB.

Common idioms

GoalExpression
Is power of two (x>0)(x & (x - 1)) == 0
Clear lowest set bitx & (x - 1)
Isolate lowest set bitx & (-x)
Set lowest clear bitx | (x + 1)
Round up to next power of twofill bits down then +1
Count set bits (popcount)Kernighan: loop x &= x - 1
Swap without tempa ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b; (a ≠ b)
Absolute value (branchless)(x ^ (x>>31)) - (x>>31) (32-bit)
// Kernighan popcount: loops once per set bit
int popcount(unsigned x){ int c=0; while(x){ x &= x-1; c++; } return c; }

In practice, prefer compiler intrinsics: __builtin_popcount, __builtin_clz (count leading zeros), __builtin_ctz (trailing), or C23 <stdbit.h>. They map to single instructions.

Masks & fields

// extract bits [hi:lo] of x
(x >> lo) & ((1u << (hi - lo + 1)) - 1)
// insert value v into field [hi:lo]
x = (x & ~(mask << lo)) | ((v & mask) << lo);

Shift gotchas

  • Right shift of a negative signed value is implementation-defined (usually arithmetic / sign-extending).
  • 1 << 31 on 32-bit int is UB (overflows INT_MAX); use 1u << 31.
  • Shift count must be 0 ≤ n < width. x << 32 for 32-bit x is UB, not 0.
  • Operands narrower than int are promoted first, so (uint8_t)0xFF << 8 is computed in int.
unsigned u = 1u << 31;      // OK: 0x80000000
// int s = 1 << 31;          // UB: signed overflow
// unsigned bad = u << 32;   // UB: shift count == width, NOT defined as 0

int neg = -8;
int r = neg >> 1;           // impl-defined: -4 on GCC/Clang (arithmetic shift), don't rely on it

uint8_t byte = 0xFF;
int wide = byte << 8;      // byte promotes to int first -> 0xFF00 (65280), no truncation
Cheat Sheet
  • set x|=1u<<n · clear x&=~(1u<<n) · toggle x^=1u<<n · test (x>>n)&1u
  • power of two: x && !(x & (x-1))
  • x & (x-1) drops lowest set bit; x & -x isolates it.
  • popcount / clz / ctz → use __builtin_* or C23 <stdbit.h>.
  • Always shift unsigned; suffix the literal (1u, 1ull).
  • Shift by ≥ width or into/of the sign bit → UB.
  • XOR swap is a party trick — fails when the two operands alias; just use a temp.
  • Field insert: x = (x & ~(m<<lo)) | ((v & m) << lo);
  • a ^ b ^ b == a — basis of XOR checksums, the “single number” trick, and XOR linked lists.
Q&A
How to check if an integer is a power of two?
x > 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0. A power of two has exactly one set bit; subtracting 1 flips that bit and sets all lower ones, so the AND is zero.
What does x & -x give?
The lowest set bit of x as a value (two's complement negation flips all bits above the lowest set bit and leaves it). Useful in Fenwick trees.
Why use 1u instead of 1 when shifting?
1 is a signed int; shifting into the sign bit or past it is undefined. 1u (or wider) makes the operation well-defined modulo the width.
Fastest way to count set bits?
A hardware POPCNT via __builtin_popcount / std::popcount / C23 stdc_count_ones. Kernighan's loop is the portable fallback; table lookup is another.
Is right-shifting a negative number safe?
It's implementation-defined (nearly always arithmetic shift, preserving sign). For portable, predictable behaviour, shift unsigned values.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

How do you set, clear, and toggle bit n of x?
Set: x |= 1u << n;. Clear: x &= ~(1u << n);. Toggle: x ^= 1u << n;.
How do you test whether bit n is set?
(x >> n) & 1u (yields 0 or 1), or (x & (1u << n)) != 0.
What is x << 3 equivalent to arithmetically?
Multiplying by 8 (2^3), for unsigned or non-overflowing values. x >> 3 is integer division by 8 for non-negative values.
Swap two integers without a temporary.
a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b; — but only if a and b are different objects. If they alias, this zeroes the value. A temp variable is clearer and just as fast.

Intermediate core

Given an array where every value appears twice except one, find the single value in O(n)/O(1).
XOR all elements together. Pairs cancel (v ^ v == 0), leaving the unique value. long r = 0; for (i) r ^= a[i]; return r;.
Round x up to the next power of two (32-bit).
x--; x|=x>>1; x|=x>>2; x|=x>>4;
x|=x>>8; x|=x>>16; x++;
This smears the highest set bit down through all lower positions, then +1 carries to the next power of two. Handle x == 0 and overflow separately.
Extract bits [12:4] of a 32-bit register value r.
Width is 12 - 4 + 1 = 9 bits: (r >> 4) & ((1u << 9) - 1), i.e. (r >> 4) & 0x1FF.
Why is uint16_t a = 0xFFFF; uint32_t b = a << 16; a trap on some code, and safe here?
a is promoted to int before the shift. If int is 32-bit, 0xFFFF << 16 sets bit 31 of a signed int — that's signed overflow / UB. It's only safe if you cast first: (uint32_t)a << 16. So the given line is actually the trap; the fix is the cast.

Advanced deep

Implement branchless abs(int x) and explain why it works.
int mask = x >> (sizeof(int)*8 - 1); return (x ^ mask) - mask;. For x ≥ 0, mask is 0: result is x. For x < 0, arithmetic right shift makes mask all-ones (-1): x ^ -1 is ~x, then - (-1) adds 1, giving ~x + 1 == -x. Caveat: relies on arithmetic right shift (implementation-defined) and still overflows for INT_MIN.
How would you reverse the bits of a 32-bit word efficiently?
Divide-and-conquer swaps: exchange adjacent 1-bit groups, then 2-bit, 4-bit, 8-bit, 16-bit, each with a mask and shifts — 5 steps, O(1): 
x = ((x&0x55555555)<<1)|((x>>1)&0x55555555);
x = ((x&0x33333333)<<2)|((x>>2)&0x33333333);
x = ((x&0x0F0F0F0F)<<4)|((x>>4)&0x0F0F0F0F);
x = (x<<24)|((x&0xFF00)<<8)|((x>>8)&0xFF00)|(x>>24);
Or use a byte lookup table, or __builtin/ARM RBIT.
What's the trick behind a Fenwick (binary indexed) tree's i & -i?
i & -i isolates the least-significant set bit, which equals the size of the range that node i is responsible for. To move to the parent in an update you add it (i += i & -i); to move to the previous responsible node in a prefix query you subtract it (i -= i & -i). This gives O(log n) update and query with O(n) space and almost no constant factor.

Undefined Behaviour & Classic Pitfalls

The interviewer isn't testing trivia — they want to know you won't ship a time bomb.

Notes

Undefined behaviour (UB) is any operation the C standard places no requirements on — signed overflow, out-of-bounds access, use-after-free, data races, and dozens more. It matters because the compiler is allowed to assume UB never happens and optimise on that basis, so a program containing UB can work for years and then miscompile, crash, or turn into a security hole after an unrelated change or a compiler upgrade. This page classifies the flavours (undefined / unspecified / implementation-defined), tours the greatest hits, explains why “it works on my machine” proves nothing, and lists the tools and habits that catch it.

The three flavours

  • Undefined behaviour (UB) — the standard imposes no requirements. The compiler may do anything: crash, corrupt data, or (worse) optimise your code away assuming UB can't happen.
  • Unspecified behaviour — several outcomes are allowed, no choice documented (e.g. order of evaluation of function arguments).
  • Implementation-defined — allowed to vary, but the implementation must document its choice (e.g. sizeof(int), right shift of negatives, char signedness).
int a = INT_MAX + 1;            // UNDEFINED: anything may happen, at any -O level
printf("%d %d\n", f(), g());     // UNSPECIFIED: f or g may run first (no set order)
int n = sizeof(int);           // IMPLEMENTATION-DEFINED: 4 here, 2 on some MCUs -- but documented

The greatest hits

UBExample
Signed integer overflowINT_MAX + 1; also -INT_MIN, INT_MIN / -1
Out-of-bounds accessa[n] on a[n]; even forming a + n + 1
Use after free / danglingreading a freed block or a returned local's address
Null / wild dereferenceunchecked malloc, uninitialised pointer
Strict aliasing violationreading an int object through a float *
Data racetwo threads, one writes, no synchronisation
Modifying an object twice with no sequence pointi = i++;, a[i] = i++;
Shift out of range / into sign bit1 << 31, x << 32, x << -1
Reading uninitialised automatic storageint x; printf("%d", x);
Bad printf format/arg mismatchprintf("%d", 3.0), %s with an int
Calling a function through a wrong-type pointersee Function Pointers topic
int a[4];
a[4] = 0;                  // OOB write: index 4 is past the last valid index (3)

int i = 0;
i = i++ + 1;               // UB: i modified twice with no sequence point between

int x;
printf("%d\n", x);          // UB: reading uninitialised automatic storage

printf("%d\n", 3.0);        // UB: %d with a double -- format/arg mismatch

Why “it works on my machine” is not a defence

Modern optimisers actively assume UB never happens and rewrite your code on that basis. If you dereference p, the compiler is entitled to conclude p can't be null and delete any later if (p == NULL) as unreachable. Signed-overflow assumptions turn x + 1 > x into a constant true.

// WRONG -- check is after the deref, so -O2 may delete it entirely:
int first_wrong(int *p) {
    int v = *p;                // compiler now "knows" p != NULL
    if (!p) return -1;         // provably-false -> removed as dead code
    return v;
}
// RIGHT -- guard before the first dereference:
int first_ok(int *p) {
    if (!p) return -1;
    return *p;
}

Sequence points / sequencing (C11 model)

Between two sequence points (the ;, &&, ||, ?:, comma operator, end of a full expression), an object may be modified at most once, and a value read only to compute the new value. i = i++ violates this; i = i + 1 is fine.

int i = 1;
i = i + 1;         // FINE: one modification, read is only to compute the new value
// i = i++;        // UB: two modifications of i, unsequenced
// a[i] = i++;     // UB: which i indexes a[] -- old or new? unsequenced
foo(), bar();      // comma operator IS a sequence point: foo() fully done before bar()
if (p && *p) { }    // && sequences: *p only runs after p is known non-null

Defences

  • Compile with -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic, treat warnings as errors.
  • Run tests under -fsanitize=address,undefined (ASan + UBSan) and Valgrind.
  • Use -fno-strict-aliasing only as a stopgap; fix the aliasing.
  • Static analysis (clang-tidy, Coverity, cppcheck).
# build with every warning, warnings are errors, sanitizers on:
gcc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror \
    -fsanitize=address,undefined -g app.c -o app
./app                 # ASan/UBSan print file:line + a diagnosis on the first violation
valgrind --leak-check=full ./app   # catches leaks / invalid reads a sanitizer build missed
Cheat Sheet
  • UB = anything allowed, retroactively. Unspecified = pick from a set. Impl-defined = documented choice.
  • Signed overflow is UB; unsigned overflow wraps (well-defined mod 2^N).
  • No modifying an object twice between sequence points (i = i++;).
  • Argument evaluation order is unspecified — don't rely on it.
  • OOB, use-after-free, null deref, uninitialised read = classic UB.
  • Type-pun via memcpy or union, never a raw incompatible pointer cast.
  • UB can make the optimiser delete checks — bugs appear only at -O2, far from the cause.
  • Tooling: -Wall -Wextra, ASan, UBSan, Valgrind, static analysers.
Q&A
Signed vs unsigned overflow?
Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2^N — fully defined. Signed overflow is undefined behaviour; the compiler may assume it never happens.
Is a[i] = i++; defined?
No. The read of i to index and the modification of i are unsequenced — UB. Split it into two statements.
What's wrong with printf(user_string)?
If the string contains % specifiers, printf reads non-existent arguments — a crash or an info-leak / write (%n) vulnerability. Use printf("%s", user_string).
Does UB only affect the offending statement?
No. The standard puts no bound on the effects; optimisers propagate the “can't happen” assumption backward and forward, so earlier or later code can be transformed or removed.
How do you catch UB you can't see?
Run the test suite under UBSan/ASan, use Valgrind, enable all warnings, and add static analysis in CI.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Define “undefined behaviour”.
A construct for which the C standard imposes no requirements at all. A conforming compiler may produce any result, including one that looks correct, and is entitled to optimise on the assumption that it never occurs.
Give three everyday examples of UB.
Reading an uninitialised local, indexing an array out of bounds, dereferencing a pointer after free, signed integer overflow, dividing by zero, dereferencing NULL — any three.
Is unsigned integer overflow undefined?
No. Unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap modulo 2^N. Only signed overflow is UB.
What flag turns on the runtime UB checker in GCC/Clang?
-fsanitize=undefined (UBSan), usually paired with -fsanitize=address.

Intermediate core

Why might the compiler remove if (ptr == NULL) return; that appears after *ptr = 0;?
Dereferencing ptr is UB if it's null, so the compiler is allowed to assume ptr is non-null from that point on. The later null check is therefore “provably false” and gets deleted as dead code. The fix is to check before dereferencing.
Explain the strict aliasing rule with an example that breaks.
float f = 1.0f;
unsigned bits = *(unsigned *)&f;   // UB: reading a float object as unsigned
The compiler assumes an unsigned * and a float * never alias, so it may reorder or cache across the access and produce a wrong bits. Use memcpy(&bits, &f, sizeof bits).
What is unspecified (not undefined) about f(g(), h())?
The order in which g() and h() are called is unspecified — the compiler picks, and may differ between calls/builds. It's not UB (nothing catastrophic), but code that depends on the order is non-portable and fragile.
Is INT_MIN % -1 safe?
No — like INT_MIN / -1, the mathematical result (or the division it implies) overflows int, which is UB. Guard division/modulo when the divisor could be -1 and the dividend could be the minimum value.

Advanced deep

How can signed-overflow UB cause a loop to become infinite under optimisation?
for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) where n == INT_MAX: the compiler may assume i + 1 never overflows (signed), conclude i <= n is always true, and turn the exit test into a constant “true”. It's entitled to because reaching the overflow would be UB. Using an unsigned or size_t counter (defined wraparound) or a < bound avoids it.
What does the “as-if” rule permit, and how does UB interact with it?
The compiler may transform the program however it likes as long as the observable behaviour (I/O, volatile accesses, program termination) of a conforming program is preserved. If the program has UB it is not a conforming program for that input, so the as-if constraint is void — the compiler owes you nothing, which is why UB-based optimisations are legal even when they change what you expected.
You must reinterpret a buffer of bytes as a struct received off the wire. How do you do it without aliasing UB?
Don't cast the buffer pointer to struct T * and dereference. Instead memcpy the bytes into a real struct T object (the compiler treats memcpy as changing the effective type), and account for endianness and padding explicitly — ideally parse field by field from the byte array rather than relying on struct layout at all. Access as unsigned char * is also always allowed.

File I/O & Standard Library Essentials

FILE* vs file descriptors, buffering, and the str* / mem* functions you'll be asked to reimplement.

Notes

C offers two layers of I/O: buffered streams (FILE *, fopen, fread, printf) built on top of raw OS file descriptors (int, open, read). Knowing which layer you are on explains buffering surprises, why output can be lost on a crash, and how to mix the two safely. This page covers both layers and the buffering modes, how to read lines without overflowing a buffer, how the library reports errors (errno, return values, feof/ferror), and the str* / mem* functions you are often asked to reimplement.

Two layers of I/O

C stdio (<stdio.h>)POSIX (<unistd.h>)
HandleFILE *int file descriptor
Openfopenopen
Read/writefread/fwrite, fgets, fprintfread/write
BufferingYes — in user spaceNo — each call is a syscall
PortableISO C, everywherePOSIX only

stdio wraps a descriptor with a user-space buffer to cut syscall count. Get the underlying fd with fileno(fp); wrap an fd with fdopen.

// Layer 1: ISO C stdio -- buffered, portable
FILE *fp = fopen("data.txt", "rb");
if (!fp) { perror("fopen"); return 1; }
char buf[64];
size_t got = fread(buf, 1, sizeof buf, fp); // may return short at EOF
fclose(fp);                             // flushes + closes

// Layer 2: POSIX -- unbuffered, one syscall per call
int fd = open("data.txt", O_RDONLY);
if (fd < 0) { perror("open"); return 1; }
ssize_t n = read(fd, buf, sizeof buf);   // n == -1 on error, 0 at EOF
close(fd);
// FILE *via = fdopen(fd, "r");          // wrap an fd in a buffered stream

Buffering modes

  • Fully buffered — flushed when the buffer fills. Default for files and non-tty pipes.
  • Line buffered — flushed on '\n'. Default for stdout when it's a terminal.
  • Unbuffered — each write goes straight out. Default for stderr.

This is why interleaved printf/fprintf(stderr,...) can print out of order, and why a crash can “lose” the last printf — the buffer wasn't flushed. Force it with fflush(stdout), setvbuf, or a trailing '\n' on a tty. Streams are flushed on normal exit() / return from main, but not on _exit, abort, or a signal.

printf("progress...");      // sits in the buffer if stdout is a pipe/file (no '\n')
fflush(stdout);              // force it out now (e.g. before a long computation)

char big[65536];
setvbuf(stdout, big, _IOFBF, sizeof big); // full buffering with a bigger buffer
setvbuf(stderr, NULL, _IONBF, 0);          // _IONBF = unbuffered (stderr's default)

abort();                    // does NOT flush -- any buffered printf output is lost

Reading lines safely

char buf[256];
while (fgets(buf, sizeof buf, fp)) {
    buf[strcspn(buf, "\n")] = '\0';   // strip newline if present
    ...
}
// POSIX getline() handles arbitrary length via realloc

Return values & errors

  • fopen returns NULL on failure and sets errno; print with perror / strerror.
  • fread/fwrite return the count of elements transferred; a short count means EOF or error — disambiguate with feof/ferror.
  • fgetc/getchar return int (so EOF, which is negative, is distinguishable from any unsigned char). Storing the result in a char is a classic bug.
FILE *fp = fopen(path, "r");
if (!fp) { perror(path); return -1; }   // NULL + errno -> "path: No such file..."

int c;                        // MUST be int, not char --
while ((c = fgetc(fp)) != EOF) // ...so EOF (-1) can't be confused with byte 0xFF
    putchar(c);

if (ferror(fp)) fputs("read error\n", stderr); // short read: error vs clean EOF?
fclose(fp);

The string/memory functions

FunctionNote
strlenO(n) scan for \0.
strcpy / strcatNo bounds check — caller guarantees room.
strncpyPads with \0; may not terminate. Not a “safe strcpy”.
snprintfBounded, always terminates; returns needed length.
memcpyUB if regions overlap — use memmove then.
memsetFills bytes; can't portably zero a pointer/float to a valid value on exotic targets (fine on mainstream).
strtokMutates its input, keeps hidden state, not reentrant — prefer strtok_r/strsep.
atoiNo error reporting; use strtol and check endptr/errno.
char dst[8];
snprintf(dst, sizeof dst, "%s", src); // bounded + always terminated (unlike strcpy/strncpy)

char ov[4] = "abcd";               // note: no room for '\0'
memmove(ov + 1, ov, 3);              // overlapping -> memmove, NOT memcpy (that would be UB)

// robust string-to-number: detect "not a number" and trailing junk
const char *in = "42x";
char *end;
errno = 0;
long v = strtol(in, &end, 10);
if (end == in || *end != '\0' || errno == ERANGE)
    fputs("bad integer\n", stderr);   // here *end == 'x' -> rejected (atoi would return 42 silently)
Cheat Sheet
  • FILE* = buffered ISO C; fd = raw POSIX syscalls. Bridge with fileno/fdopen.
  • stdout: line-buffered on a tty, fully buffered to a pipe/file. stderr: unbuffered.
  • A crash before fflush loses buffered output. exit() flushes; _exit/abort/signal don't.
  • getchar() returns int — store in int, compare to EOF.
  • fread/fwrite return element counts; check with feof/ferror.
  • Reading lines: fgets + strip \n, or POSIX getline for unbounded.
  • snprintf over sprintf; memmove when ranges overlap.
  • strtol/strtod (check endptr + errno) over atoi/atof.
  • strtok is stateful & destructive — use strtok_r.
  • Always fclose (it flushes); check its return for write errors.
Q&A
Difference between FILE * and a file descriptor?
A file descriptor is a small integer index into the kernel's open-file table; each read/write is a syscall. FILE * is a stdio structure that adds a user-space buffer and formatting on top of a descriptor, reducing syscalls.
Why did my printf output not appear before the crash?
stdout was fully or line buffered and the buffer wasn't flushed before the abnormal termination. Add \n (on a tty), call fflush(stdout), or set unbuffered with setvbuf.
Why must getchar()'s result be stored in an int?
It returns every possible unsigned char value plus a distinct negative EOF. In a char, either EOF is indistinguishable from a valid byte (0xFF) or the comparison never matches.
memcpy vs memmove?
memcpy is undefined if source and destination overlap; memmove handles overlap correctly (as if via a temporary). Use memmove for arr-shifting.
Why prefer strtol to atoi?
atoi has no way to report overflow or “not a number” — it returns 0 for garbage. strtol reports the first unparsed character via endptr and range errors via errno == ERANGE.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does fopen return on failure?
NULL, with errno set. Always check before using the stream; report with perror("open failed").
Which stream is unbuffered by default?
stderr, so error messages appear immediately even if the program crashes. stdout is line-buffered to a terminal, fully buffered otherwise.
How do you read a line of unknown length portably-ish?
fgets into a fixed buffer in a loop (detect the missing \n to know it was truncated), or POSIX getline(), which reallocs the buffer to fit.
What does fclose do besides releasing the handle?
Flushes any buffered output first. Its return value can report a deferred write error, so it's worth checking for files you wrote.

Intermediate core

A program's stdout looks fine on the terminal but is reordered when redirected to a file. Why?
On a terminal stdout is line-buffered, so lines appear promptly and roughly in order with stderr (unbuffered). Redirected to a file it becomes fully buffered — large chunks flush at once, so its output can land after stderr text that was actually produced later. Fix with setvbuf, explicit fflush, or stdbuf.
Implement strlen.
size_t my_strlen(const char *s) {
    const char *p = s;
    while (*p) p++;
    return (size_t)(p - s);
}
O(n), no bounds check (matches the standard). Real libc versions read word-at-a-time with bit tricks.
Why is char buf[64]; fread(buf, 1, 64, fp); printf("%s", buf); risky?
fread doesn't null-terminate. If it read 64 bytes with no \0, printf("%s") runs off the end of buf. Read into buf[65], capture the return count n, and set buf[n] = '\0'.
How do you distinguish EOF from a read error after fgets returns NULL?
Call feof(fp) (true → clean end of input) versus ferror(fp) (true → an I/O error occurred, check errno). fgets alone can't tell you which.

Advanced deep

You fork() a process that has buffered but unflushed stdout. What can go wrong?
The child inherits a copy of the not-yet-flushed buffer. If both parent and child later flush (e.g. at exit), the buffered text is written twice. Standard practice: fflush(NULL) before fork, and have the child use _exit (which skips stdio cleanup) after an exec failure so it doesn't double-flush.
When is raw read()/write() preferable to stdio, and what must you handle that stdio hid?
For large bulk transfers, non-blocking/async I/O, sockets with poll, or when you need exact syscall control (O_DIRECT, sendfile, precise lseek). You must then handle short reads/writes (loop until the full count is done), EINTR retries, and your own buffering — all of which stdio did for you.
Why can zeroing a struct with memset(&s, 0, sizeof s) not be assumed to make its pointer members NULL or its floats 0.0 — and why is it fine in practice?
The C standard only guarantees that all-bits-zero is a valid representation for integer types. A null pointer or 0.0 need not be all-bits-zero on exotic architectures, so strictly you should assign NULL/0.0 explicitly (or use {0} initialisation, which does the right thing). In practice every mainstream platform (x86, ARM, IEEE-754, null == 0) makes memset-to-zero produce null pointers and zero floats, so it's a portability pedantry point rather than a real bug on normal targets.

Error Handling: errno, Return Codes & Cleanup

C has no exceptions — just return values, a thread-local errno, and the discipline to check every call and unwind every resource.

Notes

C provides no try/catch and no built-in result type. The universal convention is: a function’s return value says whether it succeeded (0 vs non-zero, a valid pointer vs NULL, ≥ 0 vs -1), and the global errno (an int, thread-local since C11 and POSIX) carries a code explaining why it failed. Handling errors well in C is mostly mechanical rigour — check every return, capture errno before it’s clobbered, and release every acquired resource on every exit path. This page covers the errno rules, perror/strerror, the EINTR retry loop, the goto cleanup idiom for multi-resource functions, setjmp/longjmp and its traps, how to design your own error-reporting API, and where assert fits (and doesn’t).

The return-value + errno convention

What. A function signals failure through its return value; the reason lands in errno (declared in <errno.h> as a modifiable lvalue, thread-local in modern C). Why. It’s what the entire C standard library and POSIX do, so you must read and follow it — and doing so consistently is what makes C code robust.

FILE *f = fopen(path, "r");
if (f == NULL) {              // check the RETURN VALUE first
    int e = errno;            // capture errno immediately
    fprintf(stderr, "open %s: %s\n", path, strerror(e));
    return -1;
}

ssize_t n = read(fd, buf, len);
if (n < 0) { perror("read"); ... }   // perror = "read: " + strerror(errno) + "\n"

The errno rules that trip people up

  • It is not a failure flag. A successful call is allowed to change errno, and many do. Detect failure from the return value; consult errno only after a return value that the function’s docs say means error.
  • It gets clobbered. The very next library call — including fprintf, malloc, or strerror itself — may overwrite it. Copy it to a local the instant you see the error: int e = errno;.
  • Some functions need a reset. strtol/strtod return 0/LONG_MAX both legitimately and on error, so the pattern is errno = 0; v = strtol(s, &end, 10); if (errno != 0 || end == s) { ...error... }.
  • Reporting: perror("ctx") prints ctx: message\n to stderr; strerror(e) returns the message string (classic strerror isn’t thread-safe — use strerror_r POSIX or strerror_s C11 Annex K in threaded code). Don’t hand-roll an errno→string table.

EINTR — the interrupted-syscall retry loop

What / why. A blocking system call (read, write, wait, connect, nanosleep…) can be cut short by signal delivery, returning -1 with errno == EINTR having done no work. Robust code retries rather than treating it as a real failure.

ssize_t r;
do {
    r = read(fd, buf, len);
} while (r < 0 && errno == EINTR);
if (r < 0) { /* a real error */ }

// or install handlers with SA_RESTART so the kernel auto-restarts eligible calls
struct sigaction sa = { .sa_handler = on_sig, .sa_flags = SA_RESTART };

Cleanup on error paths — the goto cleanup idiom

What / why. A function that acquires several resources (allocate, open, lock, connect) must release them — in reverse order — on every failure exit. Duplicating the teardown at each early return is where leaks and double-frees creep in. The idiomatic C solution is a single exit reached by goto to a ladder of labels.

int process(const char *path) {
    int   rc  = -1;          // pessimistic default
    FILE *f  = NULL;
    char *buf = NULL;
    int   fd  = -1;

    f = fopen(path, "r");
    if (!f)            goto out;            // nothing acquired yet

    buf = malloc(BUFSZ);
    if (!buf)          goto out_file;       // undo fopen

    fd = open("/tmp/scratch", O_WRONLY | O_CREAT, 0600);
    if (fd < 0)       goto out_buf;        // undo malloc + fopen

    /* ... real work; set rc = 0 on success ... */
    rc = 0;

    close(fd);
out_buf:  free(buf);
out_file: fclose(f);
out:      return rc;
}

Labels are named for what they clean up; each falls through to the next, so the teardown runs in exactly reverse order. Initialise every handle to a “nothing” value so the ladder is safe to enter at any point.

setjmp/longjmp — non-local jump, use sparingly

What. setjmp(env) records the current execution point and returns 0; a later longjmp(env, val) from anywhere below on the call stack makes setjmp “return again”, this time with val. It’s the closest C has to throwing an exception. Why / when. Deeply recursive parsers, interpreters, and a few error frameworks use it to bail out of many stack frames at once. Traps.

jmp_buf env;
if (setjmp(env) != 0) {          // control returns here after longjmp
    // handle the "exception"
} else {
    deep_parse(env);              // somewhere inside: longjmp(env, 1);
}
  • Local variables changed between setjmp and longjmp are indeterminate unless declared volatile.
  • It runs no cleanup — any resources acquired in the skipped frames leak; you must track and free them yourself.
  • longjmping into a function that has already returned is undefined behaviour.
  • Not async-signal-safe in general; use sigsetjmp/siglongjmp if a signal handler is involved.

Designing your own error API, and where assert fits

  • Pick one convention and hold it. Either return an int status (0 = OK; negative errno-style or a project error enum) with results in out-parameters, or return the object and report via a separate bool *ok / error out-param. Never “-1 sometimes, NULL other times, sets errno occasionally.”
  • For a library, prefer your own error enum plus a const char *lib_strerror(int) over hijacking the global errno — it’s clearer and doesn’t collide with libc.
  • Document for every function: what the failure return is, whether it sets errno, and whether partial work / partial output can happen on failure.
  • assert() is for programmer bugs — impossible states, violated preconditions the caller is contractually required to meet. It is compiled out by -DNDEBUG, so it must never guard a real runtime condition like “file not found”, “malloc failed”, or “bad user input” — those need actual handling. Rule: assert checks things that can only be false if the code is wrong; error handling deals with things that can be false because the world is imperfect.
Cheat Sheet
  • No exceptions in C. Convention: return value = success/failure; errno (thread-local, <errno.h>) = the reason.
  • Detect failure from the return value only. errno is meaningful after a documented error return; a successful call may still change it.
  • Any later call can clobber errno — do int e = errno; immediately, before fprintf/malloc/anything.
  • strtol/strtod: set errno = 0; first, then check errno and the end pointer.
  • Report: perror("ctx") → ctx: msg\n; strerror(e) string (use strerror_r/strerror_s when threaded). Don’t roll your own table.
  • EINTR: wrap blocking syscalls in do { r = call(); } while (r < 0 && errno == EINTR);, or use SA_RESTART.
  • goto cleanup ladder for multi-resource functions: rc = -1; default, handles init’d to “nothing”, labels release in reverse order, single return rc;.
  • setjmp/longjmp: last resort; non-volatile locals indeterminate, no automatic cleanup, don’t jump into a returned function, use sigsetjmp with signals.
  • assert() = programmer-bug checks, compiled out by NDEBUG — never for runtime errors (missing file, alloc failure, bad input).
  • Your APIs: one convention, results via out-params, document the failure return and whether errno is set.
Q&A
Why can’t you use errno itself to decide whether a call failed?
Because a successful call is permitted to set errno to a non-zero value, and many library functions do (as a side effect of internal work). The standard only guarantees that errno holds a meaningful code after a function returns a value its documentation defines as an error indicator. So you check the return value to know if it failed, then read errno to know why. Testing errno != 0 after a call that succeeded can give a false positive.
Why save errno into a local variable right after a failed call?
Because almost any subsequent library call — fprintf(stderr, ...), strerror(), malloc(), even locale functions — can overwrite the global errno with its own (possibly successful) result. If you print an error message first and read errno afterward, you may report the wrong reason. The pattern is: on seeing the error return, do int e = errno; as the very next statement, then use e for logging, cleanup decisions, and the eventual return code.
What is the goto cleanup idiom and why is it considered good C style here?
A function that acquires N resources uses a single exit point reached by goto to a ladder of labels, each of which frees one resource and falls through to the next, so teardown happens in reverse acquisition order exactly once. It’s preferred over nested ifs or repeated cleanup at every early return because those duplicate the teardown (drift → leaks/double-frees) and get unreadable past two resources. It’s the standard pattern in the Linux kernel and system libraries. The keys: a pessimistic rc default, every handle initialised to a “nothing” sentinel (NULL, -1) so entering the ladder early is safe, and labels named for what they undo.
Your program reads a config file with fgets and it sometimes returns short or fails under load. You suspect signals. What’s going on and how do you fix it?
A blocking call underneath (read) can be interrupted by a delivered signal and return early with errno == EINTR, before completing. Fix options: (1) retry loop — while ((r = read(...)) < 0 && errno == EINTR) ; — around the low-level I/O; (2) install signal handlers with SA_RESTART so the kernel automatically restarts interruptible syscalls (note: not all calls are restartable even with the flag — read on a socket with a timeout isn’t); (3) block signals during the critical I/O with pthread_sigmask and handle them at a safe point. For stdio specifically, also check ferror/feof to distinguish a real error from EOF, and be aware that a partial fread is normal — loop until you have the bytes you need or hit real EOF/error.
When is assert() the wrong tool?
Whenever the condition can be false because of the environment rather than a bug in your code: malloc returning NULL, a file not existing, a network peer disconnecting, user input out of range, a config value missing. assert is compiled out entirely when NDEBUG is defined (typical for release builds), so any check you actually depend on at run time vanishes — and worse, if the asserted expression has side effects, the behaviour changes between debug and release. assert is for “this can only be false if I wrote the code wrong” (invariants, postconditions, caller-contract preconditions). Real errors get real handling: check, report, clean up, and return or exit deliberately.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

How does a C function typically report both “it failed” and “why”?
The return value indicates failure (e.g. NULL, -1, or a non-zero status), and the thread-local global errno holds a code (like ENOENT, EACCES) explaining the reason. perror/strerror turn the code into text.
What does perror("open") print if errno is EACCES?
open: Permission denied followed by a newline, written to stderr. It’s shorthand for fprintf(stderr, "%s: %s\n", "open", strerror(errno)).

Intermediate core

Write (describe) a function that opens a file, mmaps it, parses it, and must not leak on any failure. What’s the structure?
Single-exit with a goto ladder. Declare int rc = -1; and every handle at its “nothing” value: int fd = -1; void *map = MAP_FAILED; struct parsed *p = NULL;. Then: fd = open(path, O_RDONLY); if (fd < 0) goto out; — capture errno if you want to propagate the reason. fstat to get the size (goto out_fd on failure). map = mmap(NULL, size, PROT_READ, MAP_PRIVATE, fd, 0); if (map == MAP_FAILED) goto out_fd;. p = parse(map, size); if (!p) goto out_map;. Do the work, set rc = 0. Then the ladder: out_map: munmap(map, size); out_fd: close(fd); out: return rc; (and note you can close(fd) right after mmap succeeds since the mapping keeps its own reference — then the ladder only needs munmap). Each label undoes exactly one acquisition, in reverse order, once. If any step needs the real reason returned, save int e = errno; at the failing branch and errno = e; (or set a field) just before return, because munmap/close in the ladder can overwrite it.
Compare returning -1/errno, returning a project error enum, and setjmp/longjmp for a medium-sized C library.
-1 + errno: matches libc/POSIX so it’s familiar and composes with syscalls; downsides are the tiny value space of standard errno codes (you can’t express domain-specific failures well), the global-state footguns (clobbering, must-save-immediately), and thread-local storage cost. Fine for thin wrappers over the OS. Project error enum (functions return lib_status, 0 = OK, results via out-params, plus const char *lib_strerror(lib_status)): explicit, greppable, extensible to your domain, no hidden global, easy to log and to map to HTTP/gRPC codes at a boundary; costs a little verbosity and an out-param discipline. This is the best default for a library’s public API. You can still translate OS errors into your enum at the lowest layer. setjmp/longjmp: lets deeply nested code (a recursive-descent parser, a bytecode interpreter) abandon many frames at once, which the return-code style makes tedious. But it bypasses all cleanup, so every allocation in the unwound region must be tracked in an arena/pool you can reset at the landing pad, non-volatile locals across the setjmp are unreliable, it doesn’t compose across library boundaries (a caller doesn’t expect your function to longjmp), and it’s not signal-safe. Reasonable internally for one self-contained subsystem with arena allocation; never expose it across the public API. Recommendation: project error enum + out-params as the public contract; OS-error translation at the bottom; optionally setjmp+arena inside one recursive module, with the boundary function converting a caught jump into a normal enum return so callers never see it.

Advanced deep

Design an error-handling strategy for a long-running C service (network daemon): API conventions, resource safety, partial failures, logging, and behaviour under malloc failure and signals.
API conventions: one status type across the codebase — an enum (or int) where 0 = OK and negatives are categorised (transient vs permanent, client-fault vs server-fault), results always via out-parameters, and a const char *err_str(int). Every function documents its failure return and whether output params are touched on failure (prefer “untouched unless OK”). At the OS boundary, translate errno immediately into the project code (and log the raw errno). Keep a per-request/per-connection error context struct so a deep failure can attach a message and a code that bubbles up without a global. Resource safety: goto-cleanup ladders everywhere multiple resources are held; RAII-style helper macros (__attribute__((cleanup)) on GCC/Clang) for the common cases (auto-free, auto-close, auto-unlock) so early returns are safe; per-connection arena/pool allocators so tearing down a connection frees everything in one call and a mid-request failure can’t leak. Bound every buffer; check every write/read for short results and EINTR. Partial failures: decide and document idempotency — on a failed request, either fully roll back (transactional: stage work, commit last) or return a precise “processed N of M” so the client can resume; never leave a half-applied state with an ambiguous success code. For multi-step pipelines, checkpoint and make each step retry-safe. Logging: structured, leveled, rate-limited; log the project code, the raw errno/OS detail, a request id, and enough context to reproduce — but never secrets. Distinguish “expected” errors (client sent bad input — info/warn, counter++) from “unexpected” (invariant broken — error, alert). Emit metrics per error category so you alert on rate, not on individual lines. malloc failure: decide policy explicitly. For most request-scoped allocations, treat OOM as a request failure — return a “resource exhausted” status, free the request arena, keep serving others; use calloc/overflow-checked sizes so you never under-allocate. For startup/critical structures, fail fast and exit with a clear message. Consider a small pre-allocated emergency reserve so you can still log and shed load under memory pressure. Never abort() on a normal allocation failure in a service that should degrade gracefully — but do abort() (or a controlled crash + supervised restart) on a detected memory-corruption/invariant violation, because continuing is worse. Signals: handlers do the minimum — set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag or write a byte to a self-pipe/eventfd; the event loop notices and does the real work. Only async-signal-safe functions in handlers (no malloc, no printf, no strerror). Wrap blocking syscalls in EINTR retry loops or rely on SA_RESTART where semantics allow; use signalfd/pselect/epoll_pwait to fold signals into the loop. Install a fatal-signal handler (SIGSEGV/SIGABRT) that writes a minimal breadcrumb (async-safe) and re-raises so a core dump / supervisor restart happens. Supervision: run under a supervisor (systemd, k8s) that restarts on exit; make startup idempotent and fast; drain and finish in-flight work on SIGTERM (graceful shutdown), then exit 0. Testing: fault injection — a wrapper allocator that fails the Nth malloc, a syscall shim that injects EINTR/ENOSPC/short writes, and fuzzing of the parser — run under ASan/UBSan in CI so cleanup-path bugs surface. Net: one status convention + error-context struct, goto/cleanup-attribute + per-connection arenas for leak-proof teardown, explicit partial-failure semantics, structured rate-limited logging with per-category metrics, graceful degradation on OOM (fail the request, not the process) but fail-fast on corruption, minimal self-pipe signal handlers with EINTR-safe I/O, and fault-injection testing to prove the error paths actually work.

From Source to Executable: the Toolchain

What actually happens between gcc hello.c and a process running main.

Notes

This page follows one .c file through every stage of the toolchain — preprocess, compile, assemble, link, load — to the moment the CPU is executing main. Understanding the pipeline turns cryptic errors into obvious ones: a preprocessor error, a compile error, an “undefined reference” from the linker, and a “cannot open shared object” from the loader are four different problems at four different stages. It covers what each stage consumes and produces, the command to stop at each one, and how static and dynamic linking differ.

The whole pipeline at a glance

“Compiling” is really four programs run in sequence, then a fifth step by the OS at run time. Each stage consumes the previous stage's output and produces a lower-level form.

# run each stage by hand -- normally `gcc hello.c` does all of it:
