cpp    hello.c        -o hello.i    # 1 preprocess -> expanded C
gcc -S hello.i        -o hello.s    # 2 compile    -> assembly text
as     hello.s        -o hello.o    # 3 assemble   -> relocatable object (ELF)
ld ... hello.o -lc    -o hello      # 4 link       -> executable (ELF)
./hello                             # 5 OS loads & runs it

Stage 1 — Preprocess (.c → .i)

Pure text manipulation: #include pastes headers, #define macros are expanded, #if/#ifdef branches are resolved, comments are stripped, and #line markers are inserted. Output is one big self-contained translation unit of C with no directives left. (Covered in depth in the Preprocessor topic.)

// hello.c
#include <stdio.h>
#define GREETING "hi"
int main(void) { puts(GREETING); }   // comment -- will be stripped

// after `gcc -E hello.c`  (hello.i):
//   ...<hundreds of lines from stdio.h>...
//   extern int puts(const char *);
//   int main(void) { puts("hi"); }   <- macro expanded, comment gone, no #directives

Stage 2 — Compile (.i → .s)

  • Front end: lexing → parsing → semantic analysis (type checking, name lookup) → an intermediate representation (GCC GIMPLE, LLVM IR).
  • Optimiser: works on the IR — constant folding, dead-code elimination, inlining, loop transforms, register allocation planning. This is where -O0…-O3/-Os act, and where the compiler exploits the absence of undefined behaviour.
  • Back end: instruction selection + register allocation + scheduling → target assembly text for one CPU/ABI.
// add.c
int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

# gcc -O2 -S add.c  -> add.s (x86-64):
#   add:
#       lea     eax, [rdi + rsi]   ; args arrive in edi, esi per the SysV ABI
#       ret                        ; return value goes in eax
# still TEXT -- no machine-code bytes, no final addresses yet.

Stage 3 — Assemble (.s → .o)

The assembler turns mnemonics into machine-code bytes and writes a relocatable object file (ELF on Linux). It is not runnable: addresses of anything defined in another file, and even some addresses within this file, are left as relocations to be patched later.

Stage 4 — Link (.o + libraries → executable)

The linker does three jobs:

  1. Section merging / layout — concatenate all .text from every input into one, all .data into one, etc., and assign each a final virtual address.
  2. Symbol resolution — for every undefined symbol, find the one input that defines it. Missing → undefined reference. Two definitions → multiple definition.
  3. Relocation — now that final addresses are known, walk the relocation records and patch the code/data.

Static vs dynamic linking

Static (.a, -static)Dynamic (.so, default)
When resolvedAt link time — library code copied into a.outAt load time by ld.so
Executable sizeLarge (self-contained)Small
MemoryEach process has its own copyOne libc.so mapped, shared read-only across all processes
UpdatesMust relink to pick up a library fixReplace the .so, all programs benefit
StartupFastSlight cost: ld.so resolves symbols & relocations

Dynamic executables are usually position-independent (PIE / -fPIC): the code can be loaded at any address. Calls to functions in another .so go through the PLT (procedure linkage table), whose entries are resolved on first call ("lazy binding") by updating the GOT (global offset table). LD_BIND_NOW=1 forces eager resolution; ldd a.out lists the needed .sos; LD_LIBRARY_PATH / rpath / ldconfig control the search.

gcc hello.c -o dyn           # default: dynamic
ldd dyn                      # =>  libc.so.6 => /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6
ls -l dyn                    # ~16 KB -- libc is NOT inside it

gcc -static hello.c -o stat  # copy every used libc routine into the exe
ldd stat                     # =>  "not a dynamic executable"
ls -l stat                   # ~900 KB -- self-contained, runs with no libc.so present

Stage 5 — Load & run

execve("./a.out", argv, envp) makes the kernel: read the ELF header, create a fresh address space, mmap the PT_LOAD segments (.text r-x, .rodata r--, .data/.bss rw-), set up the initial stack with argv/envp/auxv, and jump to the ELF entry point. For a dynamic executable the entry point is the dynamic linker (/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2), which maps the needed shared libraries, performs relocations, then jumps to the program's real entry.

#include <stdio.h>

__attribute__((constructor)) static void setup(void) {
    puts("1: runs from .init_array, BEFORE main");
}
__attribute__((destructor)) static void teardown(void) {
    puts("3: runs from .fini_array, on normal exit");
}
int main(void) {
    puts("2: main");
    return 0;              // _exit() here would SKIP teardown() and the stdout flush
}

Diagnostic commands

gcc -save-temps -O2 hello.c   # keep hello.i / hello.s / hello.o
gcc -E / -S / -c              # stop after preprocess / compile / assemble
file a.out                    # ELF type: relocatable / executable / shared, PIE?
nm hello.o                    # symbols: T defined text, U undefined, D data, B bss
objdump -d -r hello.o         # disassembly + relocation entries
readelf -h -S -l a.out        # ELF header, sections, program (load) segments
ldd a.out                     # shared libraries needed
LD_DEBUG=all ./a.out          # trace the dynamic linker
Cheat Sheet
  • Pipeline: preprocess (.c→.i) → compile (.i→.s) → assemble (.s→.o) → link (.o+libs→a.out) → load & run.
  • gcc -E/-S/-c stop after 1/2/3; -save-temps keeps all intermediates.
  • A .o is relocatable: sections + symbol table (defined / undefined) + relocation records ("patch this address later").
  • Linker: merge sections → resolve symbols (missing = undefined reference, dup = multiple definition) → relocate.
  • Static (.a): copied in, big exe, per-process copy, relink to update. Dynamic (.so): resolved by ld.so at load, small exe, one shared read-only copy, update in place.
  • PIE/-fPIC code is address-independent; cross-.so calls go via PLT→GOT (lazy binding; LD_BIND_NOW = eager).
  • Run: execve → kernel maps PT_LOAD segments → ld.so → _start → __libc_start_main → .init_array → main → exit → .fini_array/atexit → _exit.
  • Inspect: nm, objdump -dr, readelf -hSl, ldd, file, LD_DEBUG.
Q&A
Why do you get "undefined reference to foo" only at link time, not compile time?
Each .c is compiled in isolation. The compiler only needs a declaration of foo to emit a call with an unresolved reference. It's the linker, seeing all the object files together, that must find a definition — and errors if none of them (or the linked libraries) provides one. Common causes: forgot to link the .o/-l library, library listed before the object that uses it, name mangling mismatch (C vs C++).
What is a relocation?
A record in an object file saying "at this offset in this section, once you know the final address of symbol X, write it here (in this format)". The assembler emits them because it can't know final addresses; the linker (for static addresses) and the dynamic linker (for load-time addresses / shared libs) consume them.
What's in .bss and why does it make the executable smaller?
.bss holds zero-initialised and uninitialised globals/statics. The ELF file only records its size, not its bytes, because the loader just maps zero-filled pages. .data (non-zero initial values) stores the actual bytes on disk.
Static vs dynamic linking — one advantage each?
Static: a single self-contained binary with no runtime dependency surprises and slightly faster startup. Dynamic: one copy of libc in RAM shared by every process, and a security fix ships by replacing one .so instead of rebuilding every program.
What does ld.so do?
The dynamic linker/loader. For a dynamic executable the kernel transfers control to it first. It maps every needed shared object (following DT_NEEDED, the search paths, and rpath), applies their relocations, resolves symbols (possibly lazily via the PLT/GOT), runs their initialisers, and only then jumps to the program's entry point.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Name the four build stages and their output extensions.
Preprocess (.i), compile (.s), assemble (.o), link (executable, e.g. a.out).
Which stage produces the "undefined reference" error?
Linking. The compiler is happy with a declaration; the linker needs a definition.
What does gcc -c do?
Compile and assemble to a .o object file, but stop before linking.

Intermediate core

You link gcc main.o -lm and get "undefined reference to sqrt"; gcc -lm main.o works. Why?
Traditional linkers process inputs left to right and pull a member out of an archive (.a, and -lm is libm.a/libm.so handling) only to satisfy an already-seen unresolved symbol. With -lm first, nothing is unresolved yet, so libm is skipped; then main.o introduces sqrt as unresolved and there's nothing left to satisfy it. Put libraries after the objects that use them (gcc main.o -lm), or use --start-group/--end-group for mutually dependent archives. Shared libraries are less order-sensitive but the rule still holds for archives.
A global int counter; appears (no extern) at file scope in two .c files. It used to link, now it fails. What changed and what's correct?
Historically C compilers treated an uninitialised file-scope definition as a tentative definition that became a "common" symbol; the linker merged multiple commons into one, so it linked (fragile, non-standard). GCC/Clang now default to -fno-common, so each is a real definition and you get "multiple definition of counter". Correct pattern: exactly one .c has the definition (int counter = 0;) and a shared header has the declaration (extern int counter;) which every other .c includes.

Advanced deep

Walk through lazy binding: what happens the first time a dynamically-linked program calls printf, and every time after.
The compiler emits call printf@plt — a jump to this program's PLT stub for printf, not to printf itself (whose address isn't known until load time and varies by ASLR). First call: the PLT stub does an indirect jump through the corresponding GOT slot. Initially that slot points back into the PLT (to a small trampoline) which pushes an identifying index and jumps to the dynamic linker's resolver (_dl_runtime_resolve). The resolver looks up printf in the symbol tables of the loaded shared objects (respecting symbol interposition / LD_PRELOAD order), writes the real address into the GOT slot, and tail-calls printf. Every later call: the PLT stub's indirect jump through the GOT now lands directly on printf — one extra indirection, no resolver. This "resolve on first use" amortises startup cost across only the functions actually called. Controls: LD_BIND_NOW=1 or linking with -z now resolves everything at load (slower start, but the GOT can then be made read-only via RELRO — -z relro -z now — a hardening measure against GOT-overwrite attacks). -fno-plt makes calls go straight through the GOT, skipping the PLT stub. For data symbols there is no lazy option — the GOT entries for variables are always resolved at load time.
What is position-independent code, why is it needed for shared libraries, and what does it cost?
Why: a shared library must work when mapped at an address chosen at load time (different per process under ASLR, and different libraries can't all get their "preferred" base). So its code cannot contain hard-coded absolute addresses of its own functions/globals. How (-fPIC): the code addresses its own global data relative to the instruction pointer or through the GOT — a per-module table, filled in by the loader, holding the real addresses of globals and imported symbols. A reference to a global becomes "load the address from GOT[n], then dereference" instead of "load from absolute address". Function calls within the module can be PC-relative; calls to other modules go via the PLT. The GOT/PLT themselves are the only parts patched at load time, so .text stays shared read-only across processes. Cost: an extra indirection (and a register tied up for the GOT pointer on some ABIs) for global-data access and cross-module calls — usually a few percent, more in globals-heavy code; historically worse on x86-32 (scarce registers, no PC-relative addressing) than on x86-64 (RIP-relative addressing makes PIC nearly free for local data). Modern distros compile executables as PIE too (so the main program also benefits from ASLR), accepting the same small cost. -fPIE is the executable variant; fully static non-PIE binaries avoid it entirely but lose ASLR on the main image and can't use dlopen of PIC libs cleanly.

Memory Management & Every Segment

How a process gets memory from the kernel, what every region of its address space is for, and how malloc is actually built.

Notes

This is the deep version of the memory story: how a process actually obtains memory from the kernel (brk, mmap), what every region of its virtual address space is for, and how a general-purpose allocator like glibc’s malloc is built on top. It answers the questions behind everyday symptoms — why RSS does not drop after free, why one huge allocation behaves differently from many small ones, what fragmentation is, and how the stack and thread-local storage are laid out. Useful for performance work, debugging, and any interview that goes below the malloc API.

The complete address space

A 64-bit Linux process has a huge virtual address space carved into regions with different permissions and lifetimes. Reading /proc/self/maps shows the real thing; conceptually, low→high:

RegionContentsPermsLifetime / notes
.textMachine coder-xWhole run; shared read-only between processes running the same binary.
.rodataString literals, const globals, jump tablesr--Writing here faults.
GOT / PLT / .init_arrayDynamic-link fixups, constructor listrw- then r-- (RELRO)Made read-only after startup with -z relro -z now.
.dataGlobals/statics with a non-zero initialiserrw-Bytes stored in the file.
.bssZero / uninitialised globals/staticsrw-No file bytes; loader zero-fills. Also thread-local .tbss.
Heapmalloc/calloc/realloc blocks (small/medium)rw-Grown/shrunk with brk; contiguous just above .bss.
mmap areaShared libraries, large mallocs, mmap'd files, thread stacks, TLS blocksvariesIndependent mappings; freed with munmap.
StackCall frames: locals, saved registers, return addresses, spilled argsrw-Grows down; a guard page faults on overflow. Default 8 MB (ulimit -s).
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
const char *lit = "x";          // "x" -> .rodata ; lit -> .data
int g_zero;                     // .bss
int g_init = 1;                 // .data
int main(void) {
    int loc;                    // stack
    void *hp = malloc(1);         // heap (small) -- just above .bss
    void *big = malloc(1<<20);     // mmap region (>= ~128 KB)
    printf("text %p\nrodata %p\ndata %p\nbss %p\nheap %p\nmmap %p\nstack %p\n",
           (void*)main, (void*)lit, (void*)&g_init,
           (void*)&g_zero, hp, big, (void*)&loc);
    // then: system("cat /proc/self/maps");  // see the real ranges + perms
    free(hp); free(big);
}

How the process gets memory from the kernel

User code never talks to physical RAM. It asks the kernel to add mappings to its virtual address space; physical pages are attached lazily on first touch (demand paging).

#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/mman.h>

void *lo = sbrk(0);              // current program break (top of heap)
sbrk(64 * 1024);                 // move it up 64 KB -- this is roughly what small malloc does
void *hi = sbrk(0);              // hi - lo == 65536

// a big block: its own anonymous region, RAM attached only on first write
size_t n = 4 * 1024 * 1024;
char *p = mmap(NULL, n, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE,
              MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0);
p[0] = 1;                       // NOW one 4 KB page is faulted in (demand paging)
munmap(p, n);                    // returned to the OS immediately (unlike brk memory)

Inside malloc (glibc / ptmalloc style)

  • The allocator manages the heap as a list of chunks. Each chunk has a small header: its own size (with the low bits reused as flags — e.g. "previous chunk in use"), and for free chunks, forward/back pointers fd/bk stored in the user area. So a freed 24-byte allocation and an in-use one look different in memory.
  • malloc(n) rounds n up (for alignment — 16 bytes on x86-64 — and the header) and searches bins: fastbins and tcache (per-thread, LIFO, for small sizes, very fast), then small/large bins (size-segregated free lists), then the unsorted bin, then splits the top chunk (the "wilderness" at the end of the heap), then sbrk/mmap for more.
  • free(p) puts the chunk back in a bin and coalesces it with adjacent free chunks (using the neighbouring headers) to fight fragmentation. Fastbin/tcache chunks are not immediately coalesced (speed).
  • realloc: if the next chunk is free and big enough it grows in place; otherwise it mallocs a new block, memcpys, and frees the old — which is why the pointer can move.
  • Arenas: to reduce lock contention, glibc gives each thread its own arena (its own heap + bins, up to ~8×cores); the main arena uses brk, others use mmap.
// tcache is per-thread and LIFO: free then malloc the same size -> same address
void *a = malloc(32); free(a);
void *b = malloc(32);        // b == a  (came straight back off the tcache bin)

// realloc moves when it can't grow in place:
char *p = malloc(16);
char *q = malloc(16);        // q sits right after p, blocking in-place growth
char *r = realloc(p, 4096);  // r != p: new chunk allocated, 16 bytes copied, old p freed
free(q); free(r);
size_t before = mallinfo2().uordblks;  // bytes currently handed out
char *a = malloc(100);
printf("%zu\n", malloc_usable_size(a)); // often 104-120: rounding + header = internal frag
char *keep = malloc(16);            // small live block...
free(a);                          // ...sits between freed space and the top -> heap can't shrink
// RSS stays high here: free() gave bytes back to the allocator, not the kernel
malloc_trim(0);                    // ask glibc to return free space at the top of the heap
free(keep);

Fragmentation & why RAM doesn't drop after free

  • Internal fragmentation: you asked for 100 bytes, got a 112-byte chunk — 12 wasted inside the block (rounding + header).
  • External fragmentation: total free space is plenty, but it's scattered in small gaps between live blocks, so a large request still fails / needs new OS memory.
  • free returns memory to the allocator, not usually to the OS. The heap can only shrink from the top (via sbrk down), so one live chunk near the top pins the whole heap. Only mmap'd chunks (large ones) are munmap'd back immediately. malloc_trim(0) asks glibc to give back free top space.
// External fragmentation in action:
void *blocks[1000];
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) blocks[i] = malloc(64);
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i += 2) free(blocks[i]); // free every other one
// ~32 KB is now free, but in 500 scattered 64-byte holes:
void *big = malloc(4096);        // still needs fresh memory -- no single 4 KB gap exists

The stack in detail

  • Per call: return address, saved frame pointer (rbp), callee-saved registers, local variables, and space for arguments to further calls. Set up by the function prologue, torn down by the epilogue.
  • The red zone (x86-64 SysV): 128 bytes below rsp a leaf function may use without adjusting rsp.
  • A guard page below the stack turns overflow into SIGSEGV instead of silently clobbering the mmap region. Large local arrays / alloca / VLAs can jump past the guard page — compilers add stack probing to prevent that.
  • Each thread gets its own stack (default 8 MB, in the mmap area) and its own guard page. alloca/VLA memory is freed at function return, not scope exit.
void g(int *p) { *p = 42; }

void f(int n) {
    int local;              // carved out by the PROLOGUE (sub rsp, N)
    int *vla = alloca(n * sizeof int); // grows rsp NOW; freed at f()'s return, not scope exit
    g(&local);
    g(vla);
}                          // EPILOGUE (mov rsp, rbp; pop rbp; ret) drops the whole frame at once
// recursion with no base case -> frames march past the guard page -> SIGSEGV

Thread-local storage (TLS)

_Thread_local / __thread variables get one instance per thread. Initialised ones live in a template section .tdata, zero ones in .tbss; on thread creation the runtime allocates a per-thread block from that template and points the thread's TLS register (fs on x86-64) at it. Access compiles to "fs-relative load", not a normal global load.

#include <threads.h>

_Thread_local int errno_like = 0;   // one independent copy per thread (template in .tdata)
static _Thread_local char scratch[64]; // per-thread buffer -- no lock needed, no sharing

int worker(void *arg) {
    errno_like = 7;               // does NOT affect any other thread's errno_like
    return 0;                    // compiles to an fs-relative store on x86-64
}

Tools

cat /proc/$$/maps          # every mapping: range, perms, file
pmap -x PID                # mappings with RSS/dirty sizes
size a.out                 # text / data / bss sizes
valgrind --tool=massif ./a # heap usage over time
./a with -fsanitize=address # overruns, UAF, double free, leaks
mallinfo2() / malloc_stats()/ malloc_info()  # allocator introspection
mallopt(M_MMAP_THRESHOLD, ...) # tune brk-vs-mmap cutoff
Cheat Sheet
  • Low→high: NULL guard, .text r-x, .rodata r--, GOT/PLT (RELRO), .data rw-, .bss rw-, heap ↑, big gap, mmap area (libs, big mallocs, thread stacks, TLS) ↓, guard page, stack ↓, argv/env/auxv.
  • Get memory: brk/sbrk move the one heap's top; mmap(MAP_ANON) makes an independent region. Pages backed by RAM only on first touch.
  • malloc: round up (align 16 + header) → search tcache/fastbins → small/large bins → unsorted → split top chunk → sbrk/mmap. Big requests (≥ ~128 KB) go straight to mmap.
  • A chunk = header (size + flags) + user area; free chunks store fd/bk in the user area and get coalesced with free neighbours.
  • realloc may move the block (malloc + memcpy + free) if it can't grow in place.
  • Arenas = per-thread heaps + bins to avoid lock contention.
  • Fragmentation: internal (waste inside a block) vs external (scattered free gaps). free gives memory to the allocator, not the OS; heap shrinks only from the top; only mmap'd chunks are returned on free.
  • Stack: per-call prologue/epilogue frames, red zone (128 B), guard page; per-thread 8 MB stacks. TLS = per-thread copy of .tdata/.tbss, reached via the fs register.
  • Inspect: /proc/PID/maps, pmap -x, size, ASan, massif, malloc_stats.
Q&A
Difference between brk and mmap for allocation?
brk/sbrk adjust a single "program break" pointer, growing or shrinking the one contiguous heap segment that sits just above .bss. mmap creates a brand-new, independently-sized anonymous mapping somewhere in the address-space gap. malloc uses brk for small/medium blocks (cheap, reuses freed space) and mmap for large ones (so a huge free returns the memory to the OS at once, and one giant block doesn't pin the whole heap).
Where does malloc store its bookkeeping?
In a header immediately before the pointer it returns (chunk size + flags), and for free chunks, in the user-data area itself (the fd/bk free-list links). It also keeps global bin arrays in the arena. This is why writing one byte before p[0] or past p[n-1] corrupts the allocator, and why the crash surfaces later inside malloc/free.
Why doesn't my program's RSS go down after I free a lot of memory?
free returns chunks to the allocator's free lists, not to the kernel. The brk heap can only be trimmed from its top, so any still-live allocation near the top keeps the whole region mapped. Only large, mmap-backed allocations are munmap'd immediately. You can call malloc_trim(0), or design to allocate big transient buffers so they're mmap'd, or use an allocator like jemalloc/tcmalloc with different return policies.
Internal vs external fragmentation?
Internal: space wasted inside an allocated block because the allocator rounded your request up (to an alignment/size class, plus its header). External: enough total free memory exists, but it's split into many small non-contiguous holes, so a large contiguous request can't be met. Coalescing adjacent free blocks fights external fragmentation; size classes trade a little internal fragmentation for speed.
What is a stack guard page?
An unmapped page placed just past the end of a stack. If recursion or a large local array pushes the stack pointer into it, the access faults (SIGSEGV) instead of silently overwriting whatever mapping is adjacent. Because a single huge local can leap over a one-page guard, compilers emit "stack probes" that touch each page as the frame grows.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which direction does the heap grow, and which way the stack?
Heap grows toward higher addresses (up); the stack grows toward lower addresses (down).
Which segment holds an uninitialised global int, and does it take space in the executable file?
.bss. It takes no file space — only its size is recorded; the loader zero-fills it.
What syscall grows the classic heap?
brk / sbrk (move the program break). Large allocations use mmap instead.

Intermediate core

A loop does p = malloc(100) then free(p) a million times and memory stays flat; changing it to malloc(1 MB) each time also stays flat but is slower. Explain both.
The 100-byte case: each free puts the chunk into tcache/a fastbin, and the next malloc(100) pops that exact chunk straight back — no syscall, no growth, effectively a hot cache. Memory is flat because the same chunk is reused. The 1 MB case: 1 MB is above the mmap threshold, so each malloc is an mmap syscall (kernel sets up a fresh zero-filled mapping, page tables, etc.) and each free is a munmap syscall. Memory is still flat (returned to the OS every iteration) but the per-iteration cost is two syscalls plus page-fault handling on first touch — far slower than a free-list pop. Lesson: reuse large buffers instead of reallocating them in a loop.
You malloc 1000 blocks, free every other one, then try to malloc a block twice the size. It fails or extends the heap despite ~half the heap being free. Why?
External fragmentation. The freed blocks are interleaved with live ones, so the free space is a sequence of small holes, none individually large enough for the big request, and they can't be merged because live chunks sit between them (coalescing only joins adjacent free chunks). The allocator therefore either finds nothing suitable and grows the heap (sbrk/mmap), or fails. Mitigations: allocate objects of similar lifetime together (pool/arena allocators), use size classes so same-size frees are reusable, compact by copying (not possible in place in C), or over-allocate large buffers up front. This pattern is exactly why long-running C servers use custom pool allocators.

Advanced deep

Trace a malloc(48) in a multithreaded glibc program from the call to the returned pointer, naming every structure it touches.
(1) Size adjustment: request 48 → add the chunk header and round to the 16-byte alignment and the minimum chunk size → an internal request size (e.g. 64). (2) tcache (per-thread cache, glibc ≥ 2.26): index by size class; if tcache->entries[idx] is non-empty, unlink the head (a single-linked LIFO), do the tcache integrity/count check, and return it — no lock, a handful of instructions. (3) If tcache is empty for that class, take the arena: the thread has a cached arena pointer; arena_get tries to lock it, and if contended may spin up or reuse another arena (up to ~8×ncores; extra arenas are mmap-based). (4) With the arena locked, check fastbins for that size (singly-linked LIFO, no coalescing) — if hit, possibly refill tcache from it, return one. (5) Else consolidate fastbins into the unsorted bin, then scan the unsorted bin: exact fit → return; otherwise sort each entry into its small bin (exact size classes) or large bin (ranges, kept sorted). (6) Try the appropriate small/large bin for a fit or a chunk to split (return the front, put the remainder back as a "last remainder"). (7) Else carve from the top chunk (the wilderness at the current end of the heap): split off 64 bytes, shrink the top. (8) If the top chunk is too small, extend the heap: main arena calls sbrk (or mmap if sbrk fails / arena is mmap-based); a non-main arena grows its mmap'd heap or maps a new one. (9) The chunk's size field low bits are set (PREV_INUSE etc.), the next chunk's prev_size/flags updated, the arena unlocked, and the address of the user area (header + 16 bytes in) returned. Structures touched: the tcache struct (thread-local), the arena/malloc_state (bins arrays, top, fastbins, mutex), individual malloc_chunk headers, and possibly sbrk/mmap. A request ≥ M_MMAP_THRESHOLD (~128 KB, adaptive) skips almost all of this and goes straight to a dedicated mmap.
Explain how the same physical page can appear in many places, using: shared libraries, fork, .bss, and calloc.
The MMU maps virtual pages to physical frames, and the kernel is free to point many virtual pages (in one process or many) at one frame, marking it read-only or copy-on-write to keep them consistent. Shared libraries: libc.so's .text is mapped file-backed and read-only into every process that uses it — all of them share the same physical frames; only the per-process GOT/PLT and writable data get private copies. fork: the child's entire address space is created by pointing its page tables at the parent's frames, all marked copy-on-write. Reads in either process hit shared frames; the first write to a page triggers a fault, the kernel copies that one page, and the two diverge. This is why fork is cheap and why a child that immediately execves copies almost nothing. .bss and fresh mmap(MAP_ANONYMOUS): the kernel maps every page to a single shared, read-only zero page. Reads anywhere in a 1 GB .bss cost zero physical RAM; the first write to a page faults and gets a private zeroed frame. calloc: when it obtains memory via mmap, that memory is already zero-page-backed, so calloc can skip the memset entirely — the "zeroing" is lazy, per-page, on first write. (When calloc instead reuses a chunk from the free list, it does have to memset.) Common thread: physical memory is allocated on write, not on map, and the kernel aggressively shares frames until someone dirties them — which also means a program's committed virtual size (VSZ) can hugely exceed its resident size (RSS).

Shell Basics, the Shebang & Execution Model

What actually happens between pressing Enter and the command running.

Notes

A shell is both an interactive command interpreter and a scripting language: it reads lines, expands them (variables, globs, substitutions), and runs the result as programs or built-ins. This page covers the execution model — the difference between sh (the POSIX standard) and bash (a superset with extras), running a script in a child process vs sourcing it into the current shell, the #! shebang line and why #!/usr/bin/env bash is preferred, how the shell finds a command (built-in → function → $PATH search), and $?, the exit status of the last command.

What a shell is

A shell is both an interactive command interpreter and a programming language. Common ones: bash (the usual Linux default), dash (a small, fast POSIX sh — often /bin/sh on Debian/Ubuntu), zsh (macOS default), ksh. Scripts that must be portable target POSIX sh; scripts that use [[ ]], arrays, local, etc. require bash.

# which shell am I in, and is it interactive?
echo "$0"              # -bash (login), bash, /bin/sh ...
echo "$BASH_VERSION"   # set only under bash; empty under dash/sh
case $- in *i*) echo interactive;; *) echo script;; esac

# portable POSIX sh vs bash-only feature:
if [ "$x" = "y" ]; then :; fi      # works everywhere
if [[ $x == y* ]]; then :; fi        # bash/zsh/ksh only ([[ ]], globbing)

Three ways to run a script

InvocationWhat happens
./script.shNeeds the execute bit (chmod +x) and a shebang. The kernel reads #! and runs the named interpreter with the script as an argument. Runs in a new process.
bash script.shRuns explicitly under bash; execute bit and shebang are ignored. New process.
source script.sh / . script.shExecutes each line in the current shell — no subprocess. Variable assignments, cd, and function definitions persist. Used for env setup (. ~/.bashrc).
# goto.sh contains:  cd /var/log ;  FOO=bar
./goto.sh                 # runs in a child shell...
pwd; echo "$FOO"         # ...your shell: unchanged dir, FOO empty

. ./goto.sh               # source: runs in THIS shell
pwd; echo "$FOO"         # /var/log  and  bar

bash goto.sh              # explicit interpreter: no +x bit or shebang needed

The shebang

#!/usr/bin/env bash   # find bash via PATH -- portable across distros/macOS/Homebrew
#!/bin/bash           # exact path -- predictable, no PATH games (safer for root/cron)
#!/bin/sh             # POSIX shell -- do not use bashisms

Only the first line, and only if it starts with the two bytes #!. On Linux you get at most one argument after the interpreter path, so #!/usr/bin/env bash -e is unreliable — put set -e in the script instead.

How a command name is resolved

bash looks in this order: alias → function → builtin (cd, echo, [, …) → executable found by scanning $PATH left to right (bash caches hits — hash -r clears it). Inspect with type -a name; get just the path with command -v name. Avoid which (an external program, not aware of builtins/functions, behaviour varies).

type -a echo        # echo is a shell builtin  /  echo is /usr/bin/echo   (all matches, in order)
command -v ls       # /usr/bin/ls        -- just the resolved path; use in `if` guards
command -v ll       # alias ll='ls -l'   -- reports aliases/functions too

if ! command -v jq >/dev/null; then
    echo "jq is required" >&2; exit 1   # dependency check, portable
fi
hash -r             # forget cached PATH lookups after installing/moving a binary

Exit status

Every command returns 0–255. 0 means success; non-zero means failure. $? holds the last command's status. A process killed by signal N reports 128 + N (so 130 = Ctrl-C / SIGINT, 137 = SIGKILL). true/: always succeed, false always fails.

grep -q root /etc/passwd
echo $?              # 0  -> found (success)
grep -q nobody___ /etc/passwd
echo $?              # 1  -> not found (failure, but not an error)

if mkdir /tmp/out; then            # `if` just tests the exit status
    echo "created"
else
    echo "mkdir failed with $?" >&2
fi
# sleep 5 then Ctrl-C -> $? == 130  (128 + SIGINT(2))

Startup files (interactive shells)

  • Login shell (SSH, console login, bash -l): reads /etc/profile then the first of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, ~/.profile.
  • Interactive non-login (a new terminal tab): reads ~/.bashrc.
  • Common practice: put everything in ~/.bashrc and have ~/.bash_profile source it.
  • Non-interactive scripts read neither — but honour $BASH_ENV if set.
# ~/.bash_profile  (login shells) -- make login behave like a normal terminal:
if [ -f ~/.bashrc ]; then . ~/.bashrc; fi

# ~/.bashrc  (interactive non-login) -- aliases, prompt, functions go here
alias ll='ls -alF'
export EDITOR=vim

# a cron/CI script reads NEITHER file -> set what you need explicitly:
#   PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin  at the top of the script
Cheat Sheet
  • ./s.sh & bash s.sh → subshell (changes don't leak). . s.sh / source s.sh → current shell (changes persist).
  • chmod +x s.sh is only needed for ./s.sh.
  • Shebang must be line 1, byte 0. #!/usr/bin/env bash for portability; #!/bin/sh = no bashisms.
  • Don't rely on flags in the shebang — use set -euo pipefail inside.
  • Resolution: alias → function → builtin → $PATH. Check with type -a, command -v.
  • $? = last exit code. 0 = ok. Signal N → 128+N (130 = Ctrl-C).
  • set -x trace, set -e exit on error, set -n parse only.
  • Login shell → ~/.bash_profile; new terminal → ~/.bashrc; script → neither.
Q&A
Difference between running ./script.sh and source script.sh?
./script.sh forks a new shell process; its cd, variable, and function changes vanish when it exits. source (or .) runs the lines in your current shell, so those changes stick. That's why you source an environment file but execute a normal script.
Why #!/usr/bin/env bash instead of #!/bin/bash?
env looks up bash on $PATH, so it works when bash lives in /usr/local/bin or /opt/homebrew/bin (macOS). #!/bin/bash is more predictable and is preferred for privileged/cron scripts where you don't want $PATH to influence which interpreter runs.
What does exit code 130 mean?
The process was terminated by SIGINT (signal 2) — typically the user pressed Ctrl-C. The convention is 128 + signal_number.
Script runs with bash script.sh but "permission denied" with ./script.sh. Why?
./script.sh needs the execute permission bit; bash script.sh only needs read. Run chmod +x script.sh.
Is sh script.sh the same as bash script.sh?
Not necessarily. On many systems /bin/sh is dash or bash-in-POSIX-mode, which rejects arrays, [[ ]], local, source, C-style for, and more.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What is a shebang and where must it appear?
The #! line at the very top of a script (first line, first character). It tells the kernel which interpreter to run the file with, e.g. #!/usr/bin/env bash. Without it, ./file is executed by the caller's shell (or fails).
How do you check a script's exit status?
Read $? immediately after it runs: ./job.sh; echo "exit=$?". 0 is success, anything else is failure.
Which file should custom aliases go in for a normal terminal?
~/.bashrc, which is read by interactive non-login shells (new terminal windows/tabs).
What does chmod +x script.sh do?
Adds the execute permission bit so the file can be run directly as ./script.sh.

Intermediate core

A script does cd /var/log and you want your shell to end up there. How do you run it?
Source it: source ./goto.sh or . ./goto.sh. Executing it normally runs the cd in a child process that then exits, leaving your shell's directory unchanged.
Why is which discouraged in scripts?
which is an external binary that doesn't know about shell functions, aliases, or builtins, and its output/exit-code conventions differ between systems. command -v name is a POSIX builtin that reports whatever the shell would actually run, and type -a name shows every match in order.
Explain the difference between a login shell and an interactive shell.
"Login" means the shell was started as part of authenticating a session (console login, SSH, su -) — it reads profile files. "Interactive" means it has a prompt and reads commands from a user — it reads ~/.bashrc. A shell can be one, both, or neither: an SSH session is both; a terminal tab is interactive non-login; a cron job is neither.
What's wrong with #!/usr/bin/env bash -euo pipefail?
On Linux the kernel passes everything after the interpreter as a single argument, so env receives the literal string "bash -euo pipefail" and fails to find that command. Put set -euo pipefail on the first line of the script body instead.

Advanced deep

Walk through exactly what the kernel and shell do when you type ls -l and press Enter.
The shell reads the line, performs expansions (none here), and splits it into words ls and -l. It checks: alias? function? builtin? — no — then searches $PATH, finds /usr/bin/ls (and caches it). It fork()s; the child execve("/usr/bin/ls", ["ls","-l"], environ) which replaces the process image. The parent wait()s. ls writes to fd 1, exits with a status; the shell stores it in $? and prints the next prompt.
How can a script detect whether it was sourced or executed?
In bash: compare ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} with $0 — if they're equal the file is being executed, if they differ it was sourced. A common guard: 
if [[ "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" == "${0}" ]]; then
    main "$@"   # only run when executed directly
fi
This lets a file act as both a runnable script and a sourceable library of functions.
Your cron job works interactively but fails under cron with "command not found". Why?
cron runs a minimal non-interactive, non-login shell with a bare PATH (often just /usr/bin:/bin) and none of your ~/.bashrc / ~/.profile environment. Tools in /usr/local/bin or a language version manager's shims aren't found. Fixes: use absolute paths, set PATH explicitly at the top of the script, or source the needed profile.

Variables, Quoting & Parameter Expansion

Ninety percent of shell bugs are a missing pair of double quotes.

Notes

Almost every shell bug is a quoting bug. The shell performs a fixed sequence of expansions on each word — parameter/variable expansion, command substitution, arithmetic, then word splitting (on $IFS) and pathname expansion (globbing) — and quoting is how you control which steps happen. This page covers single quotes (literal, no expansion) vs double quotes (expand, but no splitting/globbing), $VAR vs ${VAR}, the ${VAR:-default} / ${VAR:?err} / ${VAR:+alt} family, and why you almost always want "$VAR" and "$@" in double quotes.

Variables

No spaces around =: name=value (a space makes the shell try to run name as a command). Everything is a string. Read with $name or ${name}; use braces when the name touches other text: ${file}_bak. export name puts it in the environment of child processes; without export it's a shell-local variable.

name="Leo"             # no spaces around =
# name = "Leo"          # ERROR: shell tries to run the command `name`
echo "$name"           # Leo
file=report
echo "${file}_bak.txt" # report_bak.txt  -- braces separate the name from trailing text

greeting="hi"          # shell-local: children do NOT see it
export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"  # exported: every child process inherits a copy
API_KEY=secret ./deploy.sh    # set for just this one command's environment

The three quoting modes

FormBehaviour
'single'Completely literal. No expansion of anything. Cannot contain a '.
"double"Expands $var, $(cmd), `cmd`, and \ before $ ` " \ . Suppresses word-splitting and globbing. The default choice.
unquotedExpands and then word-splits on $IFS (space/tab/newline) and applies globbing (*, ?, []). Dangerous with data.
f="my file.txt"
rm $f          # runs: rm my file.txt   -> two args, wrong
rm "$f"        # runs: rm "my file.txt" -> one arg, correct
echo "$HOME"   # /home/leo
echo '$HOME'   # $HOME literally

Always quote expansions unless you have a specific reason not to. The main deliberate exception is when you want splitting, e.g. set -- $flags.

Word splitting and $IFS

After expansion, an unquoted result is split into words at any run of $IFS characters (default space, tab, newline). "$var" is not split; "$@" expands to the positional parameters each individually quoted (the one form you almost always want); "$*" joins them with the first $IFS char.

line="root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash"

# deliberate splitting: change IFS, let the shell split for you
IFS=: read -r user _ uid _ <<< "$line"
echo "$user $uid"       # root 0

# accidental splitting: the classic bug
files="a.txt b c.txt"
for f in $files; do echo "[$f]"; done   # [a.txt] [b] [c.txt] -- 3 words, not 1
for f in "$files"; do echo "[$f]"; done # [a.txt b c.txt] -- 1 word (quoted)

Parameter expansion (bash / POSIX)

ExpansionResult
${v:-default}Value of v, or default if unset/empty (doesn't assign).
${v:=default}Same, but also assigns default to v.
${v:?msg}Error out with msg if v is unset/empty.
${v:+alt}alt if v is set and non-empty, else empty.
${#v}Length of the value.
${v#pat} / ${v##pat}Strip shortest / longest matching prefix.
${v%pat} / ${v%%pat}Strip shortest / longest matching suffix.
${v/old/new} / ${v//old/new}Replace first / all (bash).
${v:offset:len}Substring (bash).
path="/var/log/syslog.1"
echo "${path##*/}"   # syslog.1   (basename)
echo "${path%/*}"    # /var/log   (dirname)
echo "${path%.*}"    # /var/log/syslog
Cheat Sheet
  • Assignment: x=1 — no spaces. Read: "$x" or "${x}".
  • Quote every expansion: "$var", "$(cmd)", "${arr[@]}", "$@".
  • '...' = fully literal. "..." = expand but don't split/glob. Unquoted = expand + split + glob.
  • "$@" = args as separate words (use this). "$*" = args joined into one string.
  • Defaults: ${v:-x} use x, ${v:=x} use & set x, ${v:?err} fail if empty, ${v:+x} x only if v set.
  • Trim: ${v#pfx} ${v##pfx} (front), ${v%sfx} ${v%%sfx} (back). Double = greedy.
  • Replace: ${v/a/b} first, ${v//a/b} all. Case (bash): ${v^^} upper, ${v,,} lower.
  • Length ${#v}; substring ${v:2:3}.
  • Unset vs empty: -/+ without the colon test only "unset"; with : they also treat empty as unset.
Q&A
When do single vs double quotes matter?
Single quotes are fully literal — use them for regexes, sed/awk programs, and passwords. Double quotes still expand $, ` `, $() but prevent word-splitting and globbing — use them around every variable reference.
What does "$@" give you that $@ or "$*" doesn't?
The positional parameters as separate words, each individually quoted, preserving spaces inside each argument. $@ unquoted splits each arg on whitespace; "$*" mashes them into a single string.
Difference between ${v-x} and ${v:-x}?
Without the colon, the fallback applies only when v is unset. With the colon, it also applies when v is set but empty.
How do you get the filename and directory from a path without calling basename/dirname?
"${p##*/}" for the filename, "${p%/*}" for the directory — pure parameter expansion, no subprocess.
Why did for f in $files break on a file called "budget report.xlsx"?
Unquoted $files is word-split on spaces, so the loop sees budget and report.xlsx separately. Store names in an array and iterate "${files[@]}".
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Why does x = 5 fail?
Shell assignment must have no spaces around =. With spaces, the shell parses x as a command name and = and 5 as arguments. Use x=5.
What's the difference between echo "$PATH" and echo '$PATH'?
Double quotes expand the variable and print its value; single quotes are literal and print the four characters $PATH.
How do you provide a default value for a possibly-unset variable?
${VAR:-default} — evaluates to default when VAR is unset or empty, without changing VAR. Use ${VAR:=default} if you also want to assign it.
What does ${#name} return?
The number of characters in the value of name (or the number of elements for ${#arr[@]}).

Intermediate core

Rewrite cp $src $dst to be safe, and explain why.
cp -- "$src" "$dst". Quoting stops word-splitting (so paths with spaces stay one argument) and globbing (so a literal * in a name isn't expanded). -- stops a name beginning with - being read as an option.
Extract 2024-01 from report-2024-01-final.csv using only parameter expansion.
f=report-2024-01-final.csv
t="${f#report-}"     # 2024-01-final.csv
echo "${t%-final.csv}"  # 2024-01
What does set -u change about unset variables, and how do you still allow optional ones?
With set -u (nounset), referencing an unset variable is an error that aborts the script — great for catching typos. For genuinely optional variables, give an explicit fallback: "${DEBUG:-}" or "${LEVEL:-info}".
Why is "$*" occasionally the right choice over "$@"?
When you deliberately want the arguments joined into a single display/log string, e.g. echo "Running with: $*". You can also set IFS first to control the separator: (IFS=,; echo "$*") prints them comma-separated.

Advanced deep

Explain the full order of expansions bash performs on a command line.
1. Brace expansion ({a,b}). 2. Tilde expansion (~). 3. Parameter/variable expansion, command substitution, arithmetic expansion — left to right. 4. Word splitting on $IFS (only on the results of step 3 that were unquoted). 5. Pathname expansion (globbing). 6. Quote removal. Crucially, word splitting and globbing happen after variable expansion, which is why "$var" (quoted) is safe from both, and why you can't glob using a pattern stored in a quoted variable.
You need to split a string on commas into an array. Show a robust way and its caveats.
IFS=, read -r -a parts <<< "$csv"
# parts=(a b c) for csv="a,b,c"
Caveats: this doesn't handle quoted fields or embedded commas (not a real CSV parser); a trailing , yields an empty last element; and setting IFS only for the read line (prefix form) avoids leaking it. For real CSV, use awk/python.
What is the difference between ${arr[@]} and ${arr[*]} inside vs outside double quotes?
Unquoted, both expand and then word-split, so they behave similarly (and unsafely). Quoted, "${arr[@]}" produces one word per element (spaces preserved) — the correct way to pass an array on. "${arr[*]}" produces a single word with elements joined by the first character of IFS. The same distinction as "$@" vs "$*".

Conditionals: test, [ ] and [[ ]]

Three test syntaxes, one of which you should almost always use.

Notes

Shell conditionals branch on a command’s exit status (0 = true/success, non-zero = false), not on a boolean type. This page covers the three test constructs — the test / [ ] POSIX builtin, bash’s [[ ]] (no word-splitting, =~ regex, &&/|| inside), and arithmetic (( )) — the string, numeric, and file-test operators, short-circuit && / || chaining, and case for pattern matching. It also covers the classic traps: unquoted variables in [ ], = vs -eq, and [ ] vs [[ ]].

if tests an exit status, not a boolean

if command; then ...; elif other; then ...; else ...; fi

if runs the command and branches on whether its exit status is 0. [ (a.k.a. test) and [[ are just commands that exit 0/1. So if grep -q foo file works with no brackets at all.

[ ] vs [[ ]]

[ ... ] / test[[ ... ]] (bash/ksh/zsh)
TypePOSIX builtin/commandbash keyword
Unquoted empty var[ $x = y ] → syntax error if x emptySafe — no word-splitting inside
&& / ||Not allowed inside; use -a/-o (fragile) or chain [ ] && [ ]Allowed: [[ a && b ]]
< >Must be escaped \< (string compare)Bare < > (string compare)
Pattern matchNo[[ $f == *.txt ]], and =~ for regex

Rule of thumb: in bash scripts use [[ ]]; in strict POSIX sh use [ ] with every variable quoted.

x=""
# [ $x = y ]            # -> `[ = y ]` -> "unary operator expected" (word-split)
[ "$x" = y ]              # POSIX-safe ONLY because of the quotes -> false, no error
[[ $x == y ]]            # bash: safe even unquoted; no splitting inside [[ ]]

f=archive.tar.gz
[[ $f == *.tar.gz ]] && echo "tarball"       # glob match -- [[ ]] only
[[ $f =~ \.([a-z]+)$ ]] && echo "${BASH_REMATCH[1]}" # regex -> gz
[[ -f $f && -r $f ]] && echo "readable file"       # && inside the brackets

Common test operators

StringsNumbersFiles
-z s empty
-n s non-empty
s1 = s2 / !=
s1 == pat (in [[ ]])		 -eq -ne
-lt -le
-gt -ge		 -e exists
-f regular file
-d directory
-r -w -x perms
-s non-empty
f1 -nt f2 newer

String vs numeric matters: [ "10" = "10.0" ] is false; [ "10" -eq "010" ] is true.

s="hello"
[[ -n $s ]]     && echo "string is non-empty"
[[ $s == h* ]]  && echo "starts with h"

a=10 b=9
[[ $a -gt $b ]]     && echo "numeric: 10 > 9"    # -gt/-lt/-eq = NUMBER compare
[[ $a > $b ]]       && echo "string: '10' sorts after '9'? no"  # > = LEXICAL compare (false!)

for p in /etc/passwd /nope; do
    [[ -f $p && -s $p ]] && echo "$p: exists and non-empty"
done

Arithmetic: (( ))

if (( count > 10 && count % 2 == 0 )); then ...; fi
(( i++ ))            # C-style, no $ needed on names
n=$(( (a + b) * 2 )) # arithmetic expansion -> string result

(( expr )) exits 1 when expr evaluates to 0 — a gotcha with set -e: (( flag = 0 )) "fails". Use : $(( ... )) or an if when that matters.

case

case "$1" in
    start|run)  do_start ;;
    stop)       do_stop ;;
    *.log)      rotate "$1" ;;
    *)          echo "usage: ..."; exit 2 ;;
esac

case uses glob patterns (not regex), is often clearer than an if/elif ladder, and ;;& (bash) falls through to test the next pattern too.

Cheat Sheet
  • if branches on exit status 0. Brackets are optional if you already have a command.
  • Prefer [[ ... ]] in bash: no word-split surprises, supports && || < > == globs, =~ regex.
  • POSIX [ ... ]: quote everything, use -a/-o sparingly (prefer [ ] && [ ]).
  • Strings: -z -n = !=. Numbers: -eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge. Never mix.
  • Files: -e -f -d -r/-w/-x -s -L (symlink) f1 -nt f2.
  • Arithmetic condition: (( n > 0 )). Arithmetic value: x=$(( a*b )).
  • (( )) returns non-zero when the result is 0 — watch out under set -e.
  • case $x in pat) ... ;; *) ... ;; esac — glob patterns, clean multi-way branch.
  • Regex: [[ $s =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; captured groups in ${BASH_REMATCH[@]}. Don't quote the pattern.
Q&A
Why prefer [[ ]] over [ ] in bash?
Inside [[ ]] there is no word-splitting or globbing, so [[ $x == foo ]] is safe even when x is empty or has spaces. It also supports &&, ||, unescaped </>, glob matching with ==, and regex with =~.
How do you compare numbers vs strings?
Numbers: [ "$a" -lt "$b" ] or (( a < b )). Strings: [ "$a" = "$b" ] or [[ $a == "$b" ]]. Using = on numbers compares them as text ("10" != "010").
What does if grep -q pattern file; then do without any brackets?
grep -q exits 0 if it found a match, 1 otherwise, and prints nothing. if branches on that status directly — brackets are only needed for test expressions.
How do you test that a variable is a non-negative integer?
[[ $n =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]. The pattern after =~ must be unquoted; quoting it makes it a literal string match.
Why did [ $answer = yes ] throw "unary operator expected"?
answer was empty, so after expansion the test became [ = yes ] — malformed. Quote it: [ "$answer" = yes ], or use [[ $answer == yes ]].
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does if actually test?
The exit status of the command that follows it. Zero → run the then branch; non-zero → skip to elif/else.
Which operator checks a string is empty?
-z: [[ -z "$s" ]] is true when s has zero length. -n is the opposite.
Write a test for "file /etc/passwd exists and is readable".
[[ -r /etc/passwd ]] (readable implies it exists), or explicitly [[ -e /etc/passwd && -r /etc/passwd ]].
How do you branch on several exact values of $1?
A case statement: case "$1" in a) ...;; b|c) ...;; *) ...;; esac.

Intermediate core

Give a concrete input where [ $x = "y" ] breaks but [[ $x == "y" ]] doesn't.
x="" (unset/empty) → [ = "y" ] is a syntax error ("unary operator expected"). x="a b" → [ a b = "y" ] is "too many arguments". [[ ]] doesn't word-split its operands, so both cases just evaluate to false.
Why can ((i--)) unexpectedly abort a script?
(( expr )) returns exit status 1 when the arithmetic result is 0. So when i goes from 1 to 0, ((i--)) yields the old-value semantics... actually it returns success/failure based on the value: post-decrement of 1 evaluates the expression to 1 (truthy) but ((--i)) or ((i=0)) evaluates to 0 and "fails". Under set -e that terminates the script. Safe forms: i=$((i-1)) or : $((i--)).
Match a filename ending in .tar.gz or .tgz in one condition.
[[ $f == *.tar.gz || $f == *.tgz ]], or with a case: case $f in *.tar.gz|*.tgz) ... ;; esac.
Extract the numeric version from v2.14.3-rc1 with a regex test.
if [[ $s =~ ^v([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+)\.([0-9]+) ]]; then
    major=${BASH_REMATCH[1]}; minor=${BASH_REMATCH[2]}; patch=${BASH_REMATCH[3]}
fi

Advanced deep

Why is [ "$a" = "$b" -a "$c" = "$d" ] considered unsafe, and what should you write?
With -a/-o, test receives many arguments and has to guess how to parse them; certain values (e.g. an operand that is itself =, !, or -n) make the parse ambiguous and the result is unspecified by POSIX. Chain separate tests instead: [ "$a" = "$b" ] && [ "$c" = "$d" ], or use [[ $a == "$b" && $c == "$d" ]] in bash.
What's the difference between [[ $x == $y ]] and [[ $x == "$y" ]]?
On the right side of ==/!= inside [[ ]], an unquoted value is treated as a glob pattern. So if y='*', [[ $x == $y ]] is true for any x, while [[ $x == "$y" ]] is true only when x is literally *. Quote the right side unless you specifically want pattern matching.
How would you emulate [[ ]]'s safety in a POSIX sh script that must run under dash?
Quote every operand, and defend against operands that look like operators by prefixing a constant: [ "x$a" = "x$b" ] or [ "${a}" = "${b}" ] with the leading-x trick for values that could start with -. Use case for pattern matching (case $f in *.txt) ... esac) since [ has no glob operator. For numeric work use [ "$a" -lt "$b" ] which is well-defined.

Loops: for, while, until

And the one correct way to loop over lines of a file.

Notes

Loops in the shell iterate over words, not lines by default — which is the source of most “it broke on a filename with a space” bugs. This page covers for x in … (and why for f in *.txt is safe but for f in $(ls) is not), C-style for ((;;)), while / until, the while IFS= read -r line idiom for reading a file or stream line by line, break / continue with levels, and piping into a loop vs the subshell-variable-scope gotcha it creates.

for

for host in web1 web2 db1; do ssh "$host" uptime; done
for f in *.log; do gzip -- "$f"; done       # glob; handles spaces
for i in {1..10}; do echo "$i"; done          # brace range (bash)
for ((i = 0; i < n; i++)); do ...; done          # C-style (bash)
for arg in "$@"; do process "$arg"; done     # iterate script args

If a glob matches nothing it stays literal by default (*.log as text). Guard with shopt -s nullglob (bash) so the loop body simply doesn't run.

while / until

while ! ping -c1 -W1 "$host" &>/dev/null; do sleep 2; done
until [[ -f /tmp/ready ]]; do sleep 1; done

while cond loops while cond succeeds; until cond loops until it succeeds.

Reading a file line by line — the correct idiom

while IFS= read -r line; do
    printf '%s\n' "$line"
done < input.txt
  • IFS= — don't trim leading/trailing whitespace.
  • -r — don't treat backslash as an escape.
  • redirect the file into the loop with <, not cat file |.
  • To also get the last line when the file has no trailing newline: while ... || [[ -n $line ]]; do.

Never for line in $(cat file) — it word-splits on spaces and globs, so lines with spaces or * break.

The subshell-in-a-pipeline trap

count=0
cat file | while read -r _; do ((count++)); done
echo "$count"    # prints 0 !

Each pipeline stage runs in a subshell, so count is incremented in a child and lost. Fixes: redirect instead of pipe (done < file), use a process substitution (done < <(cmd)), or in bash set shopt -s lastpipe (non-interactive only).

break / continue

break N and continue N act on the N-th enclosing loop.

for f in *.csv; do
    [[ -s $f ]] || continue          # skip empty files, go to next iteration
    grep -q FATAL "$f" && break         # stop the whole loop on the first bad file
    process "$f"
done

for dir in proj/*/; do
    for file in "$dir"*.log; do
        [[ $file == *skip* ]] && continue 2  # jump to the NEXT dir (2nd enclosing loop)
        echo "$file"
    done
done
Cheat Sheet
  • for x in a b c; do ...; done — iterate a word list / glob / "$@".
  • Glob that might not match: shopt -s nullglob first.
  • C-style: for ((i=0;i<n;i++)). Range: {1..10}, {0..20..5}.
  • Line-by-line: while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file.
  • NUL-delimited (filenames from find -print0): while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do ...; done < <(find ... -print0).
  • Never for line in $(cat file); never cat file | while read if you need vars afterwards.
  • Pipeline stages run in subshells → variable changes don't survive. Redirect or use < <(...).
  • break N / continue N target the N-th enclosing loop.
Q&A
Why is for line in $(cat file) wrong?
Command substitution output is word-split on $IFS (spaces, tabs, newlines) and then globbed, so you iterate over words, not lines, and any * expands to filenames. Use while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file.
Why does a counter incremented inside cmd | while read read back as unchanged?
The while loop on the right of the pipe runs in a subshell. Its variable updates are in that child process and disappear when it exits. Feed the loop with redirection or process substitution instead of a pipe.
What do IFS= and -r do in read?
IFS= stops read stripping leading/trailing whitespace from the line. -r stops it interpreting backslashes. Together they give you the raw line.
How do you loop over files safely, including names with spaces or newlines?
Use a glob directly (for f in ./*.txt) which is space-safe, or for recursive/complex selection use find ... -print0 piped into while IFS= read -r -d '' f.
Difference between while and until?
while c runs the body as long as c succeeds (exit 0). until c runs the body as long as c fails, stopping once it succeeds.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Print numbers 1 to 5.
for i in {1..5}; do echo "$i"; done (bash), or portably i=1; while [ "$i" -le 5 ]; do echo "$i"; i=$((i+1)); done.
Loop over every .conf file in /etc.
for f in /etc/*.conf; do echo "$f"; done. Add shopt -s nullglob beforehand so the loop is skipped if there are none.
How do you exit a loop early?
break leaves the innermost loop; continue skips to its next iteration. break 2 leaves two levels.
Read a file line by line — the recommended pattern?
while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file.

Intermediate core

Your loop over *.txt runs once with f set to the literal string *.txt. Why, and how do you prevent it?
No file matched the glob, and by default bash leaves an unmatched pattern unexpanded. Set shopt -s nullglob so an unmatched glob expands to nothing (loop body skipped), or shopt -s failglob to make it an error.
Rewrite grep ERROR log | while read l; do ((n++)); done; echo $n so n survives.
Use process substitution so the loop runs in the main shell: 
n=0
while IFS= read -r l; do ((n++)); done < <(grep ERROR log)
echo "$n"
Or just n=$(grep -c ERROR log).
Retry a command up to 5 times with a 3-second back-off.
for attempt in {1..5}; do
    curl -fsS "$url" && break
    echo "attempt $attempt failed" >&2
    sleep 3
done
Add an else-style check afterwards ([[ $attempt -eq 5 ]]) to detect total failure.
Iterate over find results that may contain spaces and newlines.
while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
    process "$f"
done < <(find . -type f -name '*.log' -print0)
-print0 / read -d '' use the NUL byte as the separator, the only character that can't appear in a filename.

Advanced deep

Explain shopt -s lastpipe and its limitations.
Normally every command in a pipeline runs in its own subshell. lastpipe makes bash run the last stage of a pipeline in the current shell instead, so cmd | while read ...; do ((n++)); done updates n in place. Limitations: it only takes effect when job control is off (i.e. in scripts, not interactive shells), it's bash-only, and only the final stage benefits. Redirection / < <(...) is more portable.
A while read loop that also runs ssh inside consumes only the first line. Why?
ssh (like ffmpeg, mysql, etc.) reads from stdin, and stdin for the loop body is the file you redirected in — so ssh slurps the rest of it. Fix: redirect ssh's stdin from /dev/null (ssh host cmd < /dev/null) or use ssh -n, or read the file on a different file descriptor: while IFS= read -r line <&3; do ...; done 3< file.
How do you parallelise a loop body across N workers in pure bash?
Background each job with & and cap concurrency with wait -n (bash 4.3+): 
max=8
for item in "${items[@]}"; do
    (( $(jobs -rp | wc -l) >= max )) && wait -n
    work "$item" &
done
wait
Or, more robustly, pipe the list into xargs -P "$max" -n1 or GNU parallel.

Functions & Positional Parameters

Functions return an exit code, not a value — internalise that and the rest follows.

Notes

A shell function is a named block that receives positional parameters exactly like a script does — $1, $2, $@, $# — not a named-argument list. This page covers defining and calling functions, "$@" (each arg preserved) vs "$*" (all args joined) and why the quoting matters, shift, local variables (functions otherwise mutate globals), returning information via exit status (return N, 0–255) vs stdout (echo + command substitution), and recursion.

Defining and calling

greet() {                 # POSIX form (preferred)
    local name="$1"       # 'local' is bash/ksh, not POSIX
    printf 'Hello, %s\n' "$name"
}
greet World               # call: no parentheses, args space-separated

Functions must be defined before they're called. They share the shell's environment; local keeps a variable scoped to the function (and its callees — dynamic scope).

Positional parameters

TokenMeaning
$0Script name (not affected by function calls).
$1 … $9, ${10}Arguments. Braces required past 9.
$#Number of arguments.
"$@"All args as separate quoted words. Use this to forward args.
"$*"All args as one string joined by first char of IFS.
shift [n]Drop the first n (default 1) args; $2 becomes $1, etc.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# call:  ./deploy.sh --env prod app1 app2
echo "script  : $0"      # ./deploy.sh
echo "count   : $#"      # 4
echo "first   : $1"      # --env

while [[ $1 == --* ]]; do
    case $1 in
        --env) env=$2; shift 2 ;;   # consume flag + value; $3 becomes $1
        *) echo "unknown: $1" >&2; exit 2 ;;
    esac
done
echo "env=$env, targets: $*"   # env=prod, targets: app1 app2
run_all "$@"                 # forward the REMAINING args, each intact

Inside a function, $1… are the function's arguments; $0 is still the script.

Returning results

  • Status: return N sets the exit code (0–255). With no return, the function's status is that of its last command.
  • Value: there is no value return. Either echo/printf the result and have the caller capture it with $(...), or write it into a variable the caller names (pass the name, assign with printf -v or a nameref).
max() { (( $1 > $2 )) && echo "$1" || echo "$2"; }
biggest=$(max 3 9)        # capture stdout

# by-reference (bash 4.3+ nameref)
parse() { local -n out=$1; out="parsed:$2"; }
parse result "data"; echo "$result"   # parsed:data

Gotchas

  • Capturing with $(...) runs the function in a subshell — side effects (variable changes, cd) don't persist.
  • Mixing echo "logging" with echo "result" pollutes the captured value — send logs to >&2.
  • return only takes 0–255; returning -1 becomes 255, and large numbers wrap mod 256.
  • local x=$(cmd) masks cmd's exit status (it becomes local's status, always 0). Split into two lines if you need $?.
count() { echo "counting..."; ls | wc -l; }   # BUG: log line goes to stdout
n=$(count)                # n = "counting...\n42"  -- polluted
count() { echo "counting..." >&2; ls | wc -l; } # FIX: log to stderr

get_id() { echo "$1"; return -1; }
get_id x; echo $?         # 255, not -1  (return wraps mod 256)

# local hides the exit status:
lookup() { local v=$(grep -q x file); echo $?; }  # always 0 (status of `local`)
lookup() { local v; v=$(grep x file) || return 1; }  # FIX: declare, then assign
Cheat Sheet
  • Define: name() { ...; }. Call: name arg1 arg2 (no parens, no commas).
  • $# count, $1..$9 / ${10} args, "$@" forward-all, shift to consume.
  • Return an exit code with return N (0–255). Return a value via stdout + $(func), or a nameref (local -n).
  • Send diagnostics to stderr (echo ... >&2) so they don't contaminate $(func).
  • local every function variable to avoid clobbering the caller (bash; POSIX has no local).
  • local x=$(cmd) hides cmd's failure — declare then assign on separate lines.
  • $(func) runs in a subshell: no persistent side effects.
  • $0 stays the script name even inside functions; there's no "function name" in $0 (use ${FUNCNAME[0]} in bash).
Q&A
How does a shell function "return" data?
It doesn't return a value. It prints to stdout and the caller captures it with command substitution, or it assigns to a variable whose name the caller passed in. return only sets the numeric exit status.
"$@" vs "$*" for passing arguments through?
"$@" — it preserves each argument as a distinct word, including embedded spaces. "$*" flattens everything into one string and is almost never what you want when forwarding.
What does shift 2 do?
Discards the first two positional parameters; what was $3 becomes $1, and $# drops by 2. Used to consume parsed options before handling the rest.
Why did result=$(myfunc); echo $? always show 0 even when myfunc failed?
If the assignment is local result=$(myfunc), $? reflects the local builtin (success), not the function. Without local, result=$(myfunc) does propagate the function's status. Declare and assign separately when in doubt.
Do variable changes inside x=$(myfunc) persist?
No. Command substitution runs the function in a subshell, so any variables it sets or directories it enters are gone once it returns.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

How do you pass and read arguments in a function?
Call it as fn a b c; inside, they are $1, $2, $3, with $# = 3 and "$@" = all of them.
What does return without a number do?
The function exits with the status of the last command it ran.
Why use local inside functions?
Without it, assignments modify (or create) global shell variables and can silently clobber the caller's state. local name confines the variable to the function.
How does the caller get a string result from a function?
The function echos it; the caller captures with x=$(func args).

Intermediate core

Write a die helper that prints a message to stderr and exits non-zero.
die() { printf '%s\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }
[[ -f $config ]] || die "config not found: $config"
Using >&2 keeps the message off stdout; "$*" lets you pass a multi-word message.
A function both logs progress and returns a computed path. How do you keep them separate?
Send all logging to stderr (echo "working..." >&2) and only echo the final path to stdout. Then p=$(compute_path) captures just the path while the log still shows on the terminal.
Forward all of a wrapper script's arguments to an inner command, unchanged.
exec real-tool --flag "$@" (or without exec if you need to run code afterwards). "$@" reproduces every argument exactly, including ones with spaces or globs.
How do you return a value by reference in bash without a subshell?
Pass the target variable's name and assign through it, either with a nameref (local -n ref=$1; ref=value, bash 4.3+) or printf -v "$1" '%s' "value". The caller sees the change because no subshell was involved.

Advanced deep

Explain dynamic scoping in bash functions and a bug it causes.
A local variable is visible not just in the declaring function but in every function it calls (unlike lexical scope). So a helper that reads $i can accidentally see a caller's loop variable i. Worse, a callee that does i=... without local mutates the caller's local i. Defence: local-declare every variable in every function, and give loop counters unlikely names in reusable helpers.
Why can return not signal "value 300", and how do people encode richer results?
Exit statuses are a single byte: return 300 yields 300 & 255 = 44. Conventions: reserve small codes for categories of failure (like curl/rsync do), print the real payload to stdout, or set well-known variables / a nameref. For structured data, emit JSON on stdout and parse with jq.
What's the difference between func() ( ... ) and func() { ... }?
Braces run the body in the current shell; parentheses run it in a subshell. The subshell form auto-isolates side effects: cd, set options, IFS changes, and variable assignments inside it don't leak out. Handy for a function that must cd somewhere to do its work, at the cost of a fork.

Arrays & String Manipulation

Real lists (not space-separated strings), and string surgery without sed.

Notes

Bash arrays and string operators let you avoid shelling out to sed/cut/expr for common manipulations. This page covers indexed arrays (arr=(a b c), "${arr[@]}", "${#arr[@]}") and associative arrays (declare -A), and the parameter-expansion toolkit: length ${#x}, substring ${x:off:len}, prefix/suffix strip ${x#pat} / ${x%pat} (and ## / %% greedy), substitution ${x/old/new} / ${x//old/new}, and case conversion ${x^^} / ${x,,}. All of it is builtin — no subprocess.

Indexed arrays (bash)

files=(a.txt b.txt "c d.txt")     # literal
files+=(e.txt)                    # append
files[10]="far.txt"              # sparse indices are fine
mapfile -t lines < input.txt      # read file into array, one line per element
readarray -t out < <(some-cmd)    # same, from a command
ExpressionResult
"${files[@]}"All elements, each a separate quoted word. Iterate with this.
"${files[2]}"One element.
"${#files[@]}"Number of elements.
"${!files[@]}"The list of indices (useful for sparse arrays).
"${files[@]:1:2}"Slice: 2 elements starting at index 1.

A bare $var where var is an array gives only element 0 — a common surprise.

Associative arrays (bash 4+)

declare -A color
color[apple]=red
color[lime]=green
for k in "${!color[@]}"; do echo "$k -> ${color[$k]}"; done

Must be declared with declare -A first. Iteration order is unspecified.

String operations via parameter expansion

GoalExpression
Length${#s}
Substring${s:7:4} (offset 7, length 4); negative offset ${s: -3} (mind the space)
Strip prefix / suffix${s#pre} ${s##*/}   ${s%suf} ${s%%.*}
Replace${s/old/new} first, ${s//old/new} all, ${s/#old/new} anchored start, ${s/%old/new} anchored end
Case (bash)${s^^} upper, ${s,,} lower, ${s^} first char up
Default / assign${s:-x} ${s:=x}
s="/opt/app/config.yaml"
echo "${s##*/}"   # config.yaml
echo "${s%.*}"    # /opt/app/config
echo "${s//\//_}"  # _opt_app_config.yaml

The patterns are globs, not regex (*, ?, [...]). For regex work, use [[ =~ ]], sed, or awk.

Building a command safely

args=(-v --output "$dst")
[[ $verbose ]] && args+=(--debug)
rsync "${args[@]}" "$src" "$remote"

Accumulate options in an array, not a string — a string can't carry an argument that contains spaces.

Cheat Sheet
  • Create: a=(x y z). Append: a+=(w). From file: mapfile -t a < f. From cmd: readarray -t a < <(cmd).
  • Iterate: for x in "${a[@]}". Count: ${#a[@]}. Indices: ${!a[@]}. Slice: ${a[@]:start:len}.
  • $a == ${a[0]} — a frequent bug.
  • Assoc: declare -A m; m[k]=v; "${m[k]}"; "${!m[@]}" keys. Order not guaranteed.
  • Substr ${s:off:len}; trim ${s#pfx} ${s##*/} ${s%sfx} ${s%%.*}; replace ${s//a/b}; case ${s^^} ${s,,}.
  • Anchored replace: ${s/#x/y} (start), ${s/%x/y} (end).
  • Patterns are globs, not regex.
  • Build argv as an array (cmd "${opts[@]}"), never as a flat string.
Q&A
Why store a list of paths in an array instead of a string?
A space-separated string can't distinguish a space inside one path from a separator between two. "${arr[@]}" expands to exactly one word per element, so spaces, tabs, and globs in a name are preserved.
What does $myarray give when myarray has 5 elements?
Just the first element (index 0). You need "${myarray[@]}" for all of them.
How do you read a file's lines into an array?
mapfile -t arr < file (or readarray -t arr < file). -t strips the trailing newline from each line.
Get the file extension from archive.final.tar.gz.
${name##*.} → gz (longest prefix up to the last dot). ${name#*.} → final.tar.gz.
Replace all slashes with dashes in a path variable.
${path//\//-} — the backslash escapes the slash so it's treated as a literal to match.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

How do you get the number of elements in array a?
${#a[@]}. (${#a} without [@] gives the string length of element 0.)
Correctly iterate over array a.
for x in "${a[@]}"; do ...; done — quotes and [@] both required so elements with spaces stay intact.
Uppercase a string in bash without tr.
${s^^} for all characters; ${s^} for just the first.
Strip a trailing / from $dir.
${dir%/} removes one trailing slash if present; ${dir%%/} is equivalent here. Use ${dir%"/"} to be explicit.

Intermediate core

Build an rsync command line where --exclude patterns come from a bash array.
excludes=(".git" "node_modules" "*.tmp")
cmd=(rsync -a)
for e in "${excludes[@]}"; do cmd+=(--exclude "$e"); done
"${cmd[@]}" "$src/" "$dst/"
Each --exclude and its pattern are separate array elements, so patterns with spaces or * survive.
Count word frequencies from a variable using an associative array.
declare -A n
for w in $text; do (( n[$w]++ )); done
for w in "${!n[@]}"; do printf '%s %d\n' "$w" "${n[$w]}"; done
(Unquoted $text is intentional here to word-split into tokens.)
Given ts=2024-06-15T09:30:00Z, extract the date and the time with parameter expansion only.
Date: ${ts%%T*} → 2024-06-15. Time: ${ts#*T} → 09:30:00Z, then ${_%Z} or ${time%Z} to drop the Z.
Why is arr=( $(cmd) ) risky and what's the fix?
The unquoted substitution is word-split on IFS and glob-expanded, so output containing spaces or * is mangled. Use mapfile -t arr < <(cmd) for line-based output, or set IFS and disable globbing deliberately if you really want field splitting.

Advanced deep

How do you deep-copy an array and pass an array into a function by name?
Copy: new=( "${old[@]}" ) (indices are renumbered from 0; use declare -A + a loop to preserve keys). By name (bash 4.3+): process() { local -n a=$1; echo "${#a[@]}"; } then process myarr. Pre-4.3 fallback: pass "${arr[@]}" and rebuild inside with local -a a=("$@").
Explain the difference between ${arr[@]:2} and ${arr[@]: -2} and a subtlety with the second.
${arr[@]:2} is all elements from index 2 onward. ${arr[@]: -2} is the last two elements. The space before -2 is mandatory: without it, :-2 is parsed as the "use default" operator (${arr[@]:-2} means "the array, or 2 if unset").
You need an ordered map (insertion order preserved) in bash. How?
Bash associative arrays don't preserve order, so keep two structures: an indexed array of keys in insertion order plus an associative array for lookups. On insert, append to the key list only if the key is new ([[ -v map[$k] ]] test), then set map[$k]. Iterate the key array to get ordered traversal. If this is getting complex, it's a sign the task belongs in awk or Python.

I/O Redirection, Pipes & Here-docs

Three fixed file descriptors, and the ordering rule that trips everyone up.

Notes

Every process starts with three open file descriptors — 0 stdin, 1 stdout, 2 stderr — and redirection rewires them to files, devices, or pipes before the command runs. This page covers > / >> / <, redirecting stderr, the order-sensitive 2>&1 (“make fd 2 a copy of wherever fd 1 points now”), /dev/null, here-documents (<<EOF) and here-strings (<<<), pipes and tee, and process substitution <(cmd) which hands a command’s output to something that expects a filename.

The standard descriptors

0 = stdin, 1 = stdout, 2 = stderr. Redirection rewires them for one command.

SyntaxEffect
> filestdout to file, truncating it (1> is the same).
>> filestdout appended to file.
2> filestderr to file.
> file 2>&1stdout to file, then stderr to "wherever fd 1 now points" (the file).
2>&1 > fileWrong order: stderr goes to the terminal (fd 1's value at that moment), then stdout goes to file.
&> file / >& filebash shorthand for > file 2>&1.
< filestdin from file.
2>/dev/nulldiscard stderr.
n>&-close fd n.
make > out.log 2>&1      # both stdout and stderr into out.log  (order matters)
make > out.log 2> err.log # split them into two files
rm -f nope 2>/dev/null   # run quietly: discard the error message
./gen >> results.txt      # append, don't truncate
sort < unsorted.txt      # stdin from a file

echo "debug: starting" >&2  # write to stderr so it stays off a captured stdout
x=$(./compute)           # ...so $x gets only the real result

Pipes

a | b connects a's stdout to b's stdin; stderr is not piped unless you add 2>&1 (or |& in bash). Exit status of the pipeline is the last command's, unless set -o pipefail (then it's the last non-zero). $PIPESTATUS (bash array) holds every stage's status. Each stage runs in its own subshell (see the Loops topic for why that matters).

make 2>&1 | tee build.log      # see output AND save it, incl. errors
grep -c ERROR < app.log         # prefer redirection to 'cat app.log |'

Here-documents and here-strings

cat <<EOF          # here-doc: expands $var and $(cmd)
user = $USER
host = $(hostname)
EOF
