cat <<'EOF'        # quoted delimiter -> NO expansion (literal)
$USER stays literal
EOF

cat <<-EOF         # <<- strips leading TAB indentation (tabs only!)
	indented with tabs
EOF

grep foo <<< "$text"   # here-string: feed one string as stdin

Custom file descriptors & process substitution

exec 3> audit.log          # open fd 3 for the rest of the script
echo "event" >&3
exec 3>&-                  # close it

diff <(sort a.txt) <(sort b.txt)   # <(...) is a filename that streams cmd output
tee >(gzip > out.gz) > out.txt      # >(...) streams into a command
Cheat Sheet
  • fds: 0 in, 1 out, 2 err. > truncate, >> append, < read.
  • Merge err into out: cmd > f 2>&1 — order matters, 2>&1 comes last. Shorthand &> f.
  • Discard: 2>/dev/null, everything: &>/dev/null.
  • Pipes don't carry stderr; use 2>&1 | or bash |&.
  • Pipeline status = last stage. set -o pipefail + ${PIPESTATUS[@]} to catch earlier failures.
  • Prefer cmd < file over cat file | cmd (no extra process, keeps vars in-shell).
  • Here-doc <<EOF expands vars; <<'EOF' is literal; <<-EOF strips leading tabs.
  • Here-string: cmd <<< "$var".
  • Process substitution: diff <(a) <(b), ... > >(consumer). bash/zsh only.
  • Persistent fd: exec 3>file ... echo x >&3 ... exec 3>&-.
Q&A
Why does cmd 2>&1 > file still print errors to the screen?
Redirections apply left to right. At 2>&1, fd 1 is still the terminal, so fd 2 is pointed there. Then > file moves fd 1 to the file — but fd 2 already has its own copy of the terminal. Correct order: cmd > file 2>&1.
How do you save a command's output and see it live?
Pipe to tee: cmd | tee out.log. Add 2>&1 before the pipe to include errors, and tee -a to append.
Difference between <<EOF and <<'EOF'?
Unquoted delimiter: the here-doc body undergoes variable and command substitution. Quoted ('EOF' or \EOF): the body is passed through literally — useful for embedding scripts or config with $ in them.
What's a here-string?
cmd <<< "word" feeds word (plus a trailing newline) to cmd's stdin. Handy: read a b c <<< "$line", bc <<< "2^10".
What does <(command) evaluate to?
A filename (like /dev/fd/63) that, when read, yields command's stdout. It lets tools that require file arguments consume a pipeline, e.g. diff <(cmd1) <(cmd2).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What are file descriptors 0, 1, and 2?
Standard input, standard output, and standard error.
Redirect both stdout and stderr of build to log.txt.
build > log.txt 2>&1 (portable) or build &> log.txt (bash shorthand).
Throw away all output of a noisy command.
noisy &>/dev/null, or portably noisy >/dev/null 2>&1.
Append instead of overwrite?
Use >>: echo line >> file.

Intermediate core

The last command in a | b | c succeeds but a failed. How do you detect that?
Set set -o pipefail so the pipeline's exit status is the rightmost non-zero one. Or inspect the bash array ${PIPESTATUS[@]} immediately after, which lists each stage's status.
Feed a multi-line block of literal config (containing $) into a file.
cat > app.conf <<'EOF'
password = $ecretPa$$
path = $HOME/data
EOF
Quoting the delimiter ('EOF') prevents any expansion, so the $ sequences are written verbatim.
Swap stdout and stderr of a command.
Use a spare fd as temporary storage: cmd 3>&1 1>&2 2>&3 3>&-. fd 3 saves the original stdout, stdout becomes stderr, stderr becomes the saved stdout, then fd 3 is closed.
Compare the sorted contents of two command outputs without temp files.
diff <(cmd1 | sort) <(cmd2 | sort) — process substitution gives each side a readable pseudo-file.

Advanced deep

Explain what exec 1> >(logger -t myapp) 2>&1 at the top of a script does.
exec with only redirections (no command) changes the script's own file descriptors for the rest of its run. Here stdout is redirected into a process substitution running logger, and stderr is merged into it. Net effect: everything the script and its children print goes to syslog, tagged myapp, with no per-command redirection. Caveat: the logger subprocess is reaped asynchronously, so the very last lines can race with script exit — sometimes you add a wait or a brief sleep.
Why can a background job in a script hang the terminal even after the script "finishes"?
The child inherited the script's stdout/stderr, which may be a pipe (e.g. script | tee). As long as the backgrounded child holds that write end open, the reader (tee, or the terminal's controlling process) sees the pipe as still active and doesn't get EOF. Fix: redirect the background job's fds away (daemon &>/dev/null &) or explicitly close them (daemon >&- 2>&- &), i.e. proper daemonisation.
What's the difference between cmd > file and cmd >| file?
Identical unless set -o noclobber is active. With noclobber, plain > refuses to overwrite an existing regular file (error), protecting against accidental clobbering; >| is the explicit "yes, truncate it anyway" override.

Command Substitution & Arithmetic

Capturing output, doing maths, and not losing exit codes in the process.

Notes

Command substitution captures a command’s stdout and splices it into the current command line; arithmetic expansion evaluates integer math. This page covers $(cmd) (nestable, clear) vs the legacy backtick form, why the result is subject to word-splitting unless quoted, how the exit status of $(…) propagates (and the local x=$(cmd) trap that hides it), $(( expr )) for arithmetic and the (( expr )) command form, let, and integer-only limitations (use awk or bc for floating point).

Command substitution

now=$(date +%s)                 # preferred
now=`date +%s`                  # legacy backticks -- avoid
files=$(ls)                     # fine to print; bad to parse (see caveats)

$(...) runs the command in a subshell, captures its stdout, and strips all trailing newlines. Prefer it over backticks: $() nests cleanly ($(a $(b))), and backslashes inside behave predictably.

  • The result is subject to word-splitting and globbing unless quoted: always write x="$(cmd)".
  • Only stdout is captured; stderr still goes to the terminal (add 2>&1 to capture it too).
  • Exit status: x=$(cmd) sets $? to cmd's status. But local x=$(cmd) / export x=$(cmd) set $? to the builtin's status (0). Declare then assign separately.
  • Trailing-newline stripping bites when you expected one: [[ "$(printf 'a\n\n')" == "a" ]] is true.

Arithmetic

FormUse
$(( expr ))Arithmetic expansion — yields a string. n=$(( (a+b)/2 )).
(( expr ))Arithmetic command — for side effects / conditions. (( i++ )), if (( x > 0 )).
let "expr"Older equivalent of (( )); quoting-heavy, prefer (( )).
expr a + bExternal command, POSIX, slow, finicky spacing. Last resort for strict sh.
a=7 b=2
echo $(( a / b ))        # 3   -- integer only, truncates
echo $(( a % b ))        # 1
echo $(( 2 ** 10 ))      # 1024
echo $(( 0x1F ))         # 31  -- base prefixes work
echo $(( 8#17 ))         # 15  -- base#number
(( total += price ))     # names used without $ inside (( ))
  • Integer only. For decimals use awk 'BEGIN{print 7/2}', bc -l <<<'7/2', or python3 -c.
  • A leading zero means octal: $(( 08 )) is an error. Strip it: $(( 10#$var )) forces base 10 — essential for values like "09" from date.
  • (( expr )) exit status is 1 when expr is 0 — can trip set -e.
  • Undefined variables in arithmetic are treated as 0 (even under set -u for bare names inside (( ))).

Capturing structured output: read and mapfile

What / why. Command substitution gives you one blob of text. When the command emits fields or lines you want as separate values, splitting that blob with $IFS is fragile (spaces in data, glob characters). read and mapfile parse the stream directly.

# split one line into named fields (no subshell, no word-split surprises)
read -r year month day <<< "$(date +'%Y %m %d')"

# iterate lines safely: -r keeps backslashes, IFS= keeps leading/trailing spaces
while IFS= read -r line; do
    printf 'got: %s\n' "$line"
done < file.txt

# slurp all lines into an array, one element per line (bash 4+)
mapfile -t lines < file.txt          # same as: readarray -t lines
printf '%s line(s)\n' "${#lines[@]}"

# field-split a known-delimited record
IFS=':' read -r user _ uid _ <<< "$(getent passwd \"$USER\")"
  • read returns non-zero at EOF — that is how the while read loop terminates; do not treat it as an error.
  • Piping into while read runs the loop in a subshell, so variables set inside are lost. Use < file or < <(cmd) (process substitution) instead of cmd | while ….
  • mapfile -t strips the trailing newline from each element; without -t they are kept.
Cheat Sheet
  • Capture: out="$(cmd)" — always quote; use $() not backticks.
  • $() strips trailing newlines and captures stdout only.
  • local x=$(cmd) loses cmd's exit code — use local x; x=$(cmd).
  • Maths value: n=$(( a + b )). Maths condition/side-effect: (( n > 0 )), (( n++ )).
  • Inside (( )) / $(( )), use bare names (no $), C operators, **, %, ternary.
  • Integer only. Decimals → bc -l, awk, python3.
  • Leading zero = octal. Force base 10 with $(( 10#$n )).
  • (( )) returns non-zero when result is 0 — guard under set -e.
  • $RANDOM (0–32767), $SECONDS, $(( RANDOM % 100 )) for a rough 0–99.
Q&A
Why prefer $(...) to backticks?
It nests without escaping ($(a $(b))), backslash handling inside is intuitive, and it's visually clearer. Backticks are only kept for very old sh compatibility.
Does command substitution capture stderr?
No, only stdout. Add 2>&1 inside: out=$(cmd 2>&1) to fold stderr in.
Difference between $(( )) and (( ))?
$(( )) is an expansion that produces the numeric result as text (use it where you need the value). (( )) is a command that evaluates the expression for its side effects and exit status (use it in if/while or for i++).
Why does x=$(( 08 + 1 )) error?
A leading zero makes bash parse 08 as octal, and 8 isn't a valid octal digit. Use $(( 10#08 + 1 )) to force base 10.
How do you do floating-point division in the shell?
Delegate: echo "scale=2; 7/3" | bc -l, or awk 'BEGIN{printf "%.2f\n", 7/3}'. Bash arithmetic is integer-only.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Store today's date in a variable.
today="$(date +%F)" — command substitution, quoted.
Add two variables a and b.
sum=$(( a + b )). Inside $(( )) you don't need the $ on the names.
Increment a counter i.
(( i++ )) or i=$(( i + 1 )).
What happens to trailing newlines in x=$(cmd)?
They're removed. x gets the output with all trailing \n stripped (internal newlines are kept).

Intermediate core

Why does if ! out=$(risky); then echo fail; fi work but if ! local out=$(risky) doesn't?
out=$(risky) propagates risky's exit status, so ! sees the real result. local out=$(risky) makes the overall status that of the local builtin, which almost always succeeds, so the failure is swallowed. Declare first: local out; out=$(risky) || { echo fail; return 1; }.
day=$(date +%d) then (( day + 1 )) fails on the 8th and 9th. Fix it.
date +%d yields 08/09, parsed as invalid octal. Force base 10: (( 10#$day + 1 )), or capture without the pad using date +%-d (GNU date).
Compute a percentage with one decimal place from done/total.
awk -v d="$done" -v t="$total" 'BEGIN{printf "%.1f%%\n", 100*d/t}', or bc -l <<< "scale=1; 100*$done/$total". Pure bash can only give the integer part: $(( 100 * done / total )).
Generate a random number from 1 to 6.
$(( RANDOM % 6 + 1 )). ($RANDOM has slight modulo bias for ranges that don't divide 32768 evenly; fine for a dice roll, not for cryptography — use /dev/urandom for that.)

Advanced deep

How do you capture stdout into a variable and still get the exit code and stderr separately?
One pattern using an extra fd and process substitution: 
{ out=$(cmd 2>/dev/fd/3); rc=$?; } 3>&1 1>&2 | ...   # tricky
More readable: send stderr to a temp file — out=$(cmd 2> err.txt); rc=$?; err=$(<err.txt) — or in bash 4+ capture both with a marker: out=$(cmd; printf "\n%d" "$?"); rc=${out##*$'\n'}; out=${out%$'\n'*}. The temp-file approach is the one most people use in practice.
Explain the performance cost of command substitution in a hot loop and how to avoid it.
Each $(...) does a fork + execve of an external program (unless it's a builtin) and sets up a pipe — on the order of a millisecond each, so a loop doing x=$(basename "$f") per file is dominated by process spawning. Replace with builtins/parameter expansion (x=${f##*/}), read data once into an array, or push the whole loop into a single awk/sed invocation.
What does $(< file) do and why is it better than $(cat file)?
It's a bash special case for command substitution containing only an input redirection: the shell reads the file's contents directly (still stripping trailing newlines) without forking cat. Same result, no external process. (mapfile is better still if you want the lines as an array with newlines intact.)

Exit Status, set -euo pipefail & trap

The "unofficial strict mode" — what it buys you, and where it bites.

Notes

Robust scripts fail loudly and clean up after themselves. This page covers the set flags — -e (exit on any unchecked failure, plus its many surprising exceptions), -u (error on unset variables), -o pipefail (a pipeline fails if any stage fails, not just the last) — the common set -euo pipefail preamble and its caveats, and trap for running handlers on EXIT (guaranteed cleanup), ERR, and INT/TERM, typically paired with mktemp for safe temporary files.

The strict-mode header

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'          # optional: safer word-splitting
OptionEffect
set -e (errexit)Exit immediately if a command returns non-zero (with many exceptions, below).
set -u (nounset)Referencing an unset variable is a fatal error. Use "${x:-}" for intentionally-optional vars.
set -o pipefailA pipeline fails if any stage fails, not just the last.
set -x (xtrace)Print each command (after expansion) before running — debugging.

Where set -e does not trigger

  • A command in an if/while/until condition, or on the left of && / ||, or negated with !.
  • Any command in a pipeline except the last (unless pipefail).
  • Inside a function called in such a context — set -e is suppressed for the whole function if the call is tested. This is the classic surprise.
  • local x=$(failing_cmd) — status is the local builtin's.

So set -e is a helpful safety net, not a guarantee. For critical steps, still check explicitly: cmd || die "cmd failed".

set -e

if grep -q x file; then :; fi   # grep failing here does NOT abort (it's a condition)
false || echo "handled"          # left of || -> not fatal
false | true                       # pipeline status is `true` -> not fatal (no pipefail)

check() { false; echo "still ran"; }  # set -e is DISABLED inside a tested function
if check; then echo ok; fi          # prints "still ran" then "ok" -- surprise!

deploy || { echo "deploy failed" >&2; exit 1; }  # explicit check = the real guarantee

trap — run code on signals and on exit

tmpdir=$(mktemp -d)
cleanup() { rm -rf "$tmpdir"; }
trap cleanup EXIT              # runs on ANY exit: normal, error, or signal
trap 'echo "interrupted"; exit 130' INT TERM
Pseudo-signalFires when
EXITThe shell exits, for any reason. Best place for cleanup.
ERRA command fails (same rules/exceptions as set -e). Good for logging context.
INTCtrl-C (SIGINT).
TERMkill default.
DEBUGBefore every command (bash) — profiling/tracing.

trap - EXIT removes a trap. Traps are per-shell: a subshell doesn't inherit them unless it's a function context. Keep handlers short and idempotent (an EXIT trap can run after a partial failure).

Safe temp files

tmp=$(mktemp)                       # unique file, mode 600
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d)                 # unique dir
trap 'rm -f "$tmp"; rm -rf "$tmpdir"' EXIT

Never use /tmp/myscript.$$ hand-rolled names — predictable, racy, a symlink-attack vector. mktemp creates atomically.

Cheat Sheet
  • Header: set -euo pipefail. Add set -x temporarily to debug.
  • -e exit-on-error, -u unset-is-error, pipefail any-stage-fails.
  • -e is skipped in if/while conditions, after !, before &&/||, and non-final pipe stages — and inside a function whose call is being tested.
  • For must-succeed steps: cmd || die "msg" — don't rely on -e alone.
  • Allow one command to fail under -e: cmd || true.
  • trap 'cleanup' EXIT — runs on normal exit, error, and signal. Put temp-file removal here.
  • trap 'handler' INT TERM for graceful Ctrl-C / kill.
  • trap - SIG resets; trap '' SIG ignores.
  • Temp files: mktemp / mktemp -d, never /tmp/$$.
Q&A
What do the three parts of set -euo pipefail do?
-e: abort on any unchecked command failure. -u: abort on use of an unset variable. pipefail: make a pipeline's status reflect the first failing stage, not just the last command.
Why is set -e not a substitute for real error handling?
It has many exemptions (conditions, negation, &&/|| chains, pipelines, tested function calls) and can be toggled off by a sourced file. Critical operations still need explicit || { ...; exit 1; }.
How do you guarantee cleanup even if the script is killed?
trap 'rm -rf "$tmpdir"' EXIT. The EXIT trap runs on normal completion, on set -e abort, and after the default action of most signals.
How do you let a single command fail without set -e killing the script?
Append || true (or || :), or wrap it: if ! cmd; then handle; fi.
Why use mktemp instead of /tmp/out.$$?
$$ is predictable, so an attacker can pre-create /tmp/out.PID as a symlink and redirect your writes. mktemp creates a fresh, unguessable name atomically with safe permissions.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does set -e do?
Makes the script exit as soon as any command (subject to several exceptions) returns a non-zero status, instead of plowing on.
What is a trap?
A handler you register for a signal or pseudo-signal (like EXIT): trap 'commands' SIGNAL. When that event occurs, the shell runs the commands.
Where should you delete temporary files?
In an EXIT trap, so they're removed however the script ends.
How do you see every command as it executes?
set -x (or run the script with bash -x script.sh). set +x turns it off.

Intermediate core

With set -e, this function doesn't abort on failure when called as if check; then. Why?
When a function (or any compound command) is used as the condition of if, &&, ||, or after !, errexit is disabled for the entire duration of that command — including inside the function. So an internal failing command won't stop it; only the function's final exit status is used. If you need internal failures to matter, don't test the call, or check explicitly inside.
Write a robust temp-dir + cleanup preamble.
set -euo pipefail
work=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT
trap 'echo "aborted" >&2; exit 130' INT TERM
The EXIT trap covers normal and error exit; the INT/TERM trap gives a clean message and a conventional code (and still triggers EXIT).
Why can grep pattern file under set -e abort your script unexpectedly?
grep exits 1 when it finds no match — a normal outcome, not an error, but set -e treats non-zero as failure. Guard it: grep pattern file || true, or handle both cases with an if.
How do you make an ERR trap print the failing line and command?
trap 'echo "ERR at line $LINENO: $BASH_COMMAND (rc=$?)" >&2' ERR
$LINENO and $BASH_COMMAND are set by bash at the point of failure; useful with set -o errtrace (-E) so the trap is inherited by functions and subshells.

Advanced deep

Your script spawns a long child; on Ctrl-C the script exits but the child keeps running. Fix it.
The child is in the same process group and also received SIGINT, but if it ignores it or is in its own session it survives; conversely a backgrounded child doesn't get the terminal's SIGINT at all. Track the PID and kill it from the trap: 
child_pid=
cleanup() { [[ $child_pid ]] && kill "$child_pid" 2>/dev/null; }
trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM
long-task & child_pid=$!
wait "$child_pid"
For a whole tree, kill -- -$$ (negative PID = process group) or start the child with setsid and kill its group.
Explain why set -e; a | b with b succeeding hides a's crash, and the two ways to catch it.
errexit only inspects the pipeline's exit status, which by default is b's. If b exits 0, the pipeline is "successful" regardless of a. Fix 1: set -o pipefail, making the pipeline status the last non-zero one. Fix 2: check ${PIPESTATUS[@]} right after the pipeline and act on any non-zero entry.
What's the difference between trap '' INT, trap - INT, and trap 'handler' INT in a script that also spawns children?
trap 'handler' INT installs your handler. trap '' INT makes the shell ignore SIGINT — and crucially, children started afterward inherit "ignored", so they can't be Ctrl-C'd either. trap - INT resets to the default disposition (terminate). A common bug: setting trap '' INT to protect a critical section and forgetting to restore it, leaving un-interruptible subprocesses.

Text Processing: grep, sed, awk, cut, sort, uniq

The classic pipeline toolkit — and when to reach for awk instead of chaining five tools.

Notes

The Unix philosophy is small tools composed by pipes over line-oriented text, and this page covers the core set. grep (filter lines by regex; -E, -o, -v, -c), sed (stream editor; s/old/new/g, address ranges, in-place), awk (field-aware mini-language; $1…$NF, patterns {action}, BEGIN/END, sums and lookups), and cut / sort / uniq / tr / wc / paste. The recurring idea: reach for awk when you need fields or accumulation, sed for straight substitution, grep to select.

The pipeline model

Each tool reads lines on stdin, transforms them, writes lines on stdout. A pipe chains them into a stream; stages run concurrently, not one-after-another.

# "top 5 client IPs causing 500s" -- each stage does one job on the line stream:
grep ' 500 ' access.log \
  | awk '{print $1}' \          # field 1 = client IP
  | sort \                       # group identical IPs together (uniq needs adjacency)
  | uniq -c \                    # count each run -> "  42 10.0.0.9"
  | sort -rn \                   # rank by count, highest first
  | head -5

# stages run concurrently: `head` closing early makes `grep` stop via SIGPIPE

grep — find lines

grep -E 'warn|error' app.log      # -E extended regex
grep -i -n -c foo file            # ignore case / line numbers / count
grep -v '^#' conf                  # invert: drop comment lines
grep -o '[0-9]\{3\}' file           # -o: print only the match
grep -rl TODO src/               # -r recurse, -l list filenames only
grep -q pattern file && echo hit  # -q: quiet, use the exit code
grep -F 'a.b.c' file               # -F fixed string, no regex

sed — stream edit

sed 's/old/new/' f          # replace first per line
sed 's/old/new/g' f         # all per line
sed -E 's/(-)?[0-9]+/N/g'   # -E extended regex + backrefs \1
sed -n '2,5p' f            # -n quiet; print only lines 2-5
sed '/^$/d' f              # delete blank lines
sed -i.bak 's/foo/bar/g' f  # edit in place, keep f.bak

Use a different delimiter when the pattern has slashes: sed 's#/usr/local#/opt#'.

awk — field-oriented mini-language

awk '{print $1, $3}' f            # fields 1 and 3 (default split on whitespace)
awk -F: '{print $1}' /etc/passwd  # -F sets the field separator
awk '$3 > 1000 {print $1}'        # pattern { action }
awk '{s += $2} END {print s}'      # sum a column
awk '!seen[$0]++'                 # de-dupe, preserving order
awk 'NR==1 || $1 ~ /^web/'        # NR = record number; ~ regex match
awk -v t="$threshold" '$2 > t'   # pass a shell var in with -v

Special vars: $0 whole line, $1..$NF fields, NF field count, NR line number, FS/OFS input/output separators. BEGIN{} / END{} blocks run before/after.

cut / sort / uniq / tr

cut -d, -f1,3 data.csv          # fields by delimiter (no quoting support)
cut -c1-8 file                  # by character position
sort -t, -k2,2 -n -r file       # by 2nd comma field, numeric, reverse
sort -u file                    # sort + drop duplicates
sort file | uniq -c | sort -rn  # frequency count, most common first
uniq -d                         # only lines that repeat (input must be sorted!)
tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]'       # translate/delete characters
tr -d '\r' < dosfile             # strip carriage returns

uniq only collapses adjacent duplicates — always sort first (or use awk '!seen[$0]++' to keep original order).

When to stop chaining

grep | awk | sort | uniq -c often collapses to a single awk program with an associative array. One process instead of four, and no "adjacent only" uniq trap.

# the 4-stage pipeline above, as ONE awk pass:
awk '$9 == 500 { count[$1]++ }
     END { for (ip in count) print count[ip], ip }' access.log \
  | sort -rn | head -5

# awk holds the tally in an associative array -- no external sort until the very end,
# no "uniq only sees adjacent lines" bug, one process instead of four.
Cheat Sheet
  • grep: -E regex, -F fixed, -i icase, -v invert, -o only-match, -c count, -n line#, -r recurse, -l files, -q quiet, -w word.
  • sed 's/a/b/g' replace-all; -n '5,10p' print range; '/re/d' delete; -i[.bak] in place; -E for ( ) + ? and \1.
  • awk 'COND {ACTION}'; fields $1..$NF, NF, NR, -F sep, -v k=v, BEGIN/END. Sum: {s+=$n} END{print s}. Dedup: !seen[$0]++.
  • cut -d DELIM -f LIST or -c CHARS — single-char delimiter, no quotes.
  • sort -k F,F -t SEP -n -r -u; stabilise with -s.
  • uniq needs sorted input; -c count, -d dups only, -u uniques only.
  • tr for char-level translate/-d delete/-s squeeze; no regex.
  • Frequencies: sort | uniq -c | sort -rn — or one awk pass.
  • Locale affects sorting/regex: prefix LC_ALL=C for byte-order, speed, and stable behaviour.
Q&A
Why must you sort before uniq?
uniq only removes duplicates that are adjacent. Sorting brings identical lines together. To dedupe without reordering, use awk '!seen[$0]++'.
grep -F vs grep -E?
-F treats the pattern as a literal fixed string (fast, no metacharacters) — good for searching for things like a.b[1]. -E enables extended regex (+, ?, |, () without backslashes).
How do you sum the third whitespace-separated column of a file?
awk '{s += $3} END {print s}' file.
Replace text in place with sed and keep a backup?
sed -i.bak 's/old/new/g' file — edits file, saves the original as file.bak. (BSD/macOS sed requires the extension argument: sed -i '' ... for no backup.)
Count how many times each status code appears in an access log's 9th field.
awk '{c[$9]++} END {for (k in c) print k, c[k]}' access.log | sort -n.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Print lines of file that contain error, case-insensitively.
grep -i error file.
Print the second column of a space-separated file.
awk '{print $2}' file (or cut -d' ' -f2, but cut mishandles runs of spaces — awk is more forgiving).
Replace every tab with a comma in data.tsv.
tr '\t' ',' < data.tsv, or sed 's/\t/,/g' data.tsv.
Show the 10 most frequent lines in a file.
sort file | uniq -c | sort -rn | head.

Intermediate core

From /etc/passwd, list usernames whose UID is ≥ 1000.
awk -F: '$3 >= 1000 {print $1}' /etc/passwd. The -F: sets the colon field separator; the pattern filters, the action prints field 1.
Extract all IPv4 addresses from a log with grep.
grep -Eo '([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}' file. -o prints just the matches; the regex is loose (doesn't validate 0–255) but fine for extraction. Pipe to sort -u for the unique set.
Print lines 20–30 of a large file efficiently.
sed -n '20,30p;30q' file — the 30q quits after line 30 so sed doesn't read the rest. Or awk 'NR>=20 && NR<=30; NR==30{exit}'.
Sum column 5 of a CSV grouped by column 1.
awk -F, '{sum[$1] += $5} END {for (k in sum) print k, sum[k]}' data.csv
One pass, an associative array keyed by the group column. (Assumes no quoted commas — use a real CSV parser otherwise.)

Advanced deep

Collapse cat access.log | grep 500 | awk '{print $7}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn into one process. Why bother?
awk '$9 == 500 {c[$7]++} END {for (u in c) print c[u], u}' access.log | sort -rn
One awk invocation instead of a cat + grep + awk + two sorts + uniq. Fewer forks and pipes (noticeable on big files), it filters on the real status field ($9) rather than any line containing "500", and it sidesteps uniq's adjacency requirement. Only the final ranking sort is genuinely needed.
Why can the same sort command give different results on two machines, and how do you make it deterministic?
Sort order depends on the locale (LC_COLLATE): a UTF-8 locale uses language-specific collation where case and punctuation interleave, while C/POSIX sorts by raw byte value. This also affects [a-z] ranges in grep/sed. Force reproducibility (and speed) with LC_ALL=C sort .... Also pin the field with -k2,2 (not just -k2, which sorts from field 2 to end of line).
Print each paragraph (blank-line-separated block) that contains the word "ERROR".
awk -v RS='' '/ERROR/' file — setting the record separator RS to the empty string puts awk in "paragraph mode", so each record is a whole block. The bare pattern /ERROR/ prints matching records. ORS='\n\n' if you want to preserve the blank-line separation on output.

find, xargs & Process Management

Selecting files by any criterion, running commands over them safely, and controlling jobs.

Notes

This page covers two related toolkits. find walks a directory tree and tests each entry (name, type, time, size, permissions) then acts — -print, -exec … \; (one process per file) vs -exec … + / xargs (batch), with -print0 / -0 to survive filenames containing spaces and newlines. Then process management: running jobs in the background with &, jobs / fg / bg, wait (and wait -n), kill and the signal numbers, and how subshells and pipelines spawn processes.

find

find . -type f -name '*.log' -mtime +7 -size +1M
find /var -type d -empty -delete
find . -newer ref.txt -not -path './.git/*'
find . -type f -perm -u+x
TestMeaning
-type f/d/lregular file / directory / symlink
-name / -inameglob on basename (case-insensitive)
-path / -regexmatch the whole path
-mtime +7 / -mmin -30modified >7 days ago / <30 min ago
-size +1M / -emptybigger than 1 MiB / zero bytes
-maxdepth N / -prunelimit recursion / skip a subtree

Combine with -a (implicit), -o, !/-not, and \( ... \) groups.

Running a command per result

find . -name '*.bak' -delete
find . -name '*.txt' -exec gzip {} \;        # one gzip per file
find . -name '*.txt' -exec gzip {} +          # batch args, few processes
find . -name '*.txt' -print0 | xargs -0 gzip   # same idea via xargs
find . -type f -exec sh -c 'mv "$1" "${1%.txt}.md"' _ {} \;   # per-file shell

Always pair -print0 with xargs -0 so filenames with spaces/newlines survive. Plain xargs splits on whitespace and treats quotes specially.

xargs

... | xargs -0 -n1 basename        # -n1: one arg per invocation
... | xargs -0 -P4 -n1 convert     # -P4: 4 parallel workers
... | xargs -0 -I{} cp {} /backup/ # -I{}: placeholder, implies -n1
... | xargs -r cmd                 # -r: don't run cmd if input is empty (GNU)

Job control & signals

long-task &            # run in background, $! holds its PID
jobs ; fg %1 ; bg %1   # list / foreground / background
wait                   # wait for all children
wait "$pid"            # wait for one; $? is its exit code
kill -TERM "$pid"      # polite stop (default). -KILL cannot be caught
kill -0 "$pid"         # no signal -- just test "is it alive / mine?"
nohup cmd &>out &      # survive terminal hangup
disown %1              # detach a job from the shell
SignalDefaultCatchable?
SIGINT (2)terminate (Ctrl-C)yes
SIGTERM (15)terminate (kill)yes
SIGKILL (9)terminate nowno
SIGHUP (1)terminate on hangupyes
SIGSTOP / SIGCONTpause / resumeSTOP no

Subshells & grouping

( cmds ) runs in a subshell — cd, set, variables don't leak out. { cmds; } groups in the current shell (note the spaces and trailing ;). Use (cd "$dir" && make) to build elsewhere without changing your directory.

pwd                       # /home/leo
( cd /tmp && tar xf pkg.tar )  # subshell: cd is local to the ( )
pwd                       # /home/leo  -- unchanged

# { } groups WITHOUT a subshell -- redirect several commands at once:
{ echo "=== report ==="; date; df -h; } > report.txt

# subshell to sandbox `set` options:
( set -e; risky_step_1; risky_step_2 )   # -e applies only inside the parens
Cheat Sheet
  • find PATH TESTS ACTION. Tests: -type, -name/-iname, -path, -mtime/-mmin, -size, -empty, -perm, -maxdepth, -prune.
  • Actions: -print, -print0, -delete, -exec cmd {} \; (per file), -exec cmd {} + (batched).
  • Safe pipeline: find ... -print0 | xargs -0 .... Never plain find | xargs.
  • xargs: -0 NUL-sep, -n1 one per run, -P N parallel, -I{} placeholder, -r skip-if-empty.
  • Background: cmd &, PID in $!. wait [pid], jobs, fg/bg %n, disown, nohup.
  • Signals: TERM = polite default, KILL(9) = uncatchable, HUP = terminal closed, INT = Ctrl-C.
  • kill -0 "$pid" tests existence/permission without signalling.
  • ( ... ) subshell isolates side effects; { ...; } groups in place.
Q&A
Why -print0 | xargs -0 instead of find ... | xargs?
Default xargs splits its input on any whitespace and honours quotes, so a file called my report.txt becomes two arguments and it's a file breaks. NUL is the only byte that can't occur in a path, so -print0/-0 delimit unambiguously.
Difference between -exec cmd {} \; and -exec cmd {} +?
\; runs cmd once per file (slow for many files). + appends as many filenames as fit onto one command line and runs cmd a handful of times — much faster, like xargs.
What's in $!?
The PID of the most recently backgrounded command. Save it right after cmd & to wait on it or kill it later.
Which signal can a process not catch or ignore?
SIGKILL (9) — and SIGSTOP. Everything else can be handled or blocked. Send SIGTERM first and give the process a chance to clean up; escalate to -9 only if it won't die.
How do you run 8 conversions in parallel over files from find?
find . -name '*.png' -print0 | xargs -0 -P8 -n1 optipng. -P8 keeps 8 workers busy, -n1 gives each one file.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Find all .tmp files under the current directory and delete them.
find . -type f -name '*.tmp' -delete.
Run a command in the background and get its PID.
mycmd & then read $! immediately: pid=$!.
What does wait with no arguments do?
Blocks until all background child jobs of the current shell have finished.
Politely ask a process to stop, then force it.
kill "$pid" (sends SIGTERM); if it's still alive after a grace period, kill -9 "$pid" (SIGKILL).

Intermediate core

Delete files older than 30 days in /var/log, but not directories, and not recursing into archive/.
find /var/log -type d -name archive -prune -o -type f -mtime +30 -print -delete. -prune stops descent into archive; the -o then handles the file case.
Rename every .jpeg to .jpg under a tree, handling spaces in names.
find . -type f -name '*.jpeg' -print0 |
  while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
    mv -- "$f" "${f%.jpeg}.jpg"
  done
Or: find . -name '*.jpeg' -exec sh -c 'mv -- "$1" "${1%.jpeg}.jpg"' _ {} \;.
Start a long job that keeps running after you log out.
nohup ./job.sh &> job.out & then optionally disown. nohup ignores SIGHUP and redirects the tty streams; & backgrounds it; disown removes it from the shell's job table so it isn't signalled on exit. (Or run it under tmux/screen/systemd-run.)
Why might xargs run your command with no arguments, and how do you stop that?
If the input is empty, classic xargs still runs the command once with no args (which can be destructive, e.g. rm with no files, or a compiler reading stdin). GNU xargs -r (--no-run-if-empty) suppresses that. BSD xargs does it by default.

Advanced deep

Implement a graceful shutdown: on SIGTERM, stop accepting work, let in-flight jobs finish, then exit.
pids=()
term=0
trap 'term=1' TERM INT
while (( ! term )); do
    next_item || break
    work "$item" & pids+=($!)
done
for p in "${pids[@]}"; do wait "$p"; done
exit 0
The trap just sets a flag; the loop checks it at a safe point rather than being interrupted mid-item, then waits out the workers. Real supervisors (systemd) send SIGTERM, wait TimeoutStopSec, then SIGKILL.
A backgrounded child becomes a zombie / an orphan. Explain both and how they're handled.
Zombie: the child exited but the parent hasn't waited, so the kernel keeps its exit status and a PID slot. In a script, wait (or the shell reaping jobs) clears it; a long-lived parent that never waits leaks zombies. Orphan: the parent exited first; the child is re-parented to init/PID 1 (or a subreaper), which waits for it when it dies. Orphans are harmless; zombies accumulate. nohup/disown deliberately create orphans that outlive the shell.
You need to kill a process and all its descendants. What are the options and trade-offs?
(1) Process group: start it with setsid or in its own job, then kill -TERM -- -$PGID (negative = whole group). Clean, but a child that calls setsid escapes. (2) pkill -P / walk /proc/*/stat for the PID tree recursively — racy if processes fork during the walk. (3) cgroups (systemd-run --scope, or a manual cgroup.kill): the kernel guarantees every task in the cgroup is included — the robust modern answer. (4) A PID-namespace (container): killing PID 1 in the namespace takes everything with it.

getopts, Debugging, Portability & Gotchas

Parsing options properly, finding bugs fast, and knowing what breaks under /bin/sh.

Notes

This page covers making a script a well-behaved, portable program. getopts parses -a -b value style options in a loop (POSIX, single-letter; contrast the external getopt for long options). Debugging: set -x (trace every expanded command), set -v, PS4 customisation, bash -n (syntax check without running), and ShellCheck as a linter. Portability: what is a bashism ([[ ]], arrays, local, <<<) vs POSIX sh, and how the shebang decides which rules apply.

Option parsing with getopts (POSIX builtin)

verbose=0 output=
while getopts ":vo:h" opt; do
    case $opt in
        v) verbose=1 ;;
        o) output=$OPTARG ;;
        h) usage; exit 0 ;;
        \?) echo "unknown option: -$OPTARG" >&2; exit 2 ;;
        :)  echo "-$OPTARG needs a value" >&2; exit 2 ;;
    esac
done
shift $((OPTIND - 1))     # drop parsed options; "$@" is now the operands
  • The optstring ":vo:h": a letter followed by : takes an argument (-o); a leading : enables "silent" error handling so you get \? and : cases yourself.
  • Handles -vo file, -v -o file, -ofile. Does not handle --long options — use getopt (the external GNU program) or hand-roll a case over "$1" for those.
  • OPTIND resets per shell, not per function — set local OPTIND if you parse options inside a function.

Debugging

ToolUse
bash -n scriptParse only — catches syntax errors without running.
bash -x script / set -xTrace each command after expansion. Scope it with set -x; ...; set +x.
PS4Prefix for xtrace lines: export PS4='+ ${BASH_SOURCE}:${LINENO}:${FUNCNAME[0]:-main}: '.
set -vEcho input lines as read (before expansion).
shellcheck scriptStatic analysis — catches quoting bugs, [ ] mistakes, useless cat, etc. Run it in CI.
trap '...' DEBUG / ERRHook every command / every failure.
bash -n deploy.sh          # syntax check only -- never runs a line
shellcheck deploy.sh      # static analysis: quoting bugs, SC2086, useless cat, ...

# rich xtrace: show file:line:function for every command
export PS4='+ ${BASH_SOURCE##*/}:${LINENO}:${FUNCNAME[0]:-main}: '
set -x
result=$(compute 2 3)
set +x                    # stop tracing here

# print a location + message on any failing command:
trap 'echo "FAILED at line $LINENO: $BASH_COMMAND" >&2' ERR

POSIX sh vs bashisms

Bash-onlyPOSIX sh alternative
[[ ... ]][ ... ] / test, quote everything
arrays, declare -Apositional params, or a different tool
local(none — use subshells or unique names; many shs do support it)
function f {}f() {}
source.
for ((;;)), {1..9}while + counter; seq
echo -e, echo -nprintf (portable, no flag ambiguity)
&>, |&>file 2>&1
${var^^}, ${var/a/b}tr, sed

If the shebang is #!/bin/sh, assume dash. Run checkbashisms or shellcheck -s sh. If you need bash features, use #!/usr/bin/env bash and own it.

#!/bin/sh                # => dash on Debian/Ubuntu: bashisms below all FAIL
# arr=(a b c)             # syntax error -- no arrays in POSIX sh
# [[ $x == a* ]]          # syntax error -- no [[ ]]
# echo -e "a\tb"          # prints the literal: -e   a\tb

# portable equivalents:
x=hello
[ "${x#h}" != "$x" ] && echo "starts with h"   # prefix test via ${x#...}
printf '%s\t%s\n' a b                          # printf, not echo -e
i=1; while [ "$i" -le 3 ]; do echo "$i"; i=$((i+1)); done

Classic gotchas (all covered elsewhere in this section)

  • Unquoted $var → word splitting + globbing.
  • for f in $(ls) / cat f | while read → broken on spaces / lost variables.
  • local x=$(cmd) → swallowed exit status.
  • Leading zero in arithmetic → octal.
  • 2>&1 before >file → wrong target.
  • set -e not firing inside tested functions / pipelines.
  • echo mangling -n, backslashes, leading - → prefer printf '%s\n'.
  • Parsing ls output → use globs or find.
n=010
echo $((n + 1))          # 9  -- leading zero => parsed as OCTAL (8), not 10
echo $((10#$n + 1))      # 11 -- force base 10

printf '%s\n' "-n"          # prints -n  (echo "-n" would print nothing)
Cheat Sheet
  • while getopts ":ab:c" o; do case $o in ...; esac; done; shift $((OPTIND-1)).
  • Optstring: x: = -x takes $OPTARG; leading : = you handle \? (unknown) and : (missing arg).
  • No --long support in getopts; use GNU getopt or a manual case "$1" in --foo) ...; shift;; esac loop.
  • In a function: local OPTIND before the loop.
  • Debug: bash -n (syntax), bash -x / set -x (trace), rich PS4, shellcheck in CI.
  • Portability: #!/bin/sh ⇒ no [[ ]], arrays, local*, source, {a..b}, C-for, echo -e/-n, &>.
  • Use printf not echo for anything non-trivial.
  • command -v to check a dependency exists; fail early with a clear message.
Q&A
What does shift $((OPTIND - 1)) accomplish after a getopts loop?
It removes all the option words that getopts consumed, so "$@" and $1… are now just the positional operands (e.g. the file arguments).
Does getopts handle --verbose?
No, only single-dash short options (and clustering like -abc). For long options use the external getopt (GNU) or parse manually with a while/case over $1.
Quick way to check a script for syntax errors without executing it?
bash -n script.sh. Pair with shellcheck script.sh for semantic issues.
Why prefer printf over echo in scripts?
echo's handling of -n, -e, and backslashes varies between shells and builds; a variable starting with - can be swallowed as an option. printf '%s\n' "$x" is unambiguous and portable.
How do you know if your script is safe to run under dash?
Set the shebang to #!/bin/sh and test with dash, run checkbashisms, or shellcheck -s sh. Common offenders: [[ ]], arrays, local, source, {1..10}, echo -e.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which builtin parses -a -b value style options?
getopts, used in a while getopts "ab:" opt; do case ...; done loop.
How do you dry-run a script for syntax errors?
bash -n script.sh — it parses but doesn't execute.
Name two things that work in bash but not in /bin/sh (dash).
[[ ... ]], arrays, local, source (vs .), {1..10}, C-style for, echo -e, &> — any two.
What tool lints shell scripts for common mistakes?
shellcheck.

Intermediate core

Write option parsing for a script taking -n NAME, -f (flag), and a trailing file argument.
name= force=0
while getopts ":n:f" o; do
  case $o in
    n) name=$OPTARG ;;
    f) force=1 ;;
    *) echo "usage: $0 [-n name] [-f] FILE" >&2; exit 2 ;;
  esac
done
shift $((OPTIND - 1))
file=${1:?FILE required}
You call getopts inside a function and the second call in the same script doesn't parse. Why?
OPTIND is a global that getopts advances and only auto-resets when the shell starts. After the first parse it's left pointing past the options. Declare local OPTIND (and optionally local OPTARG) at the top of the function, or manually OPTIND=1 before each loop.
Make xtrace output show file, line, and function.
export PS4='+ ${BASH_SOURCE##*/}:${LINENO}:${FUNCNAME[0]:-main}(): '
set -x
Now every traced line is prefixed with where it came from — invaluable in multi-file scripts.
Fail fast if a required external tool is missing.
for dep in jq curl git; do
  command -v "$dep" >/dev/null || { echo "missing: $dep" >&2; exit 1; }
done

Advanced deep

Compare getopts (builtin) with getopt (GNU program). When would you use each?
getopts is a POSIX shell builtin: portable, no subprocess, but short options only, no permutation of options after operands, and no long options. GNU getopt is an external binary that supports --long options, optional arguments, and reorders args so options can follow operands — but it's Linux-centric (the BSD/macOS getopt is the old dumb one) and needs the eval set -- "$(getopt ...)" idiom with careful quoting. Rule: getopts for portable scripts with simple short flags; GNU getopt (or a hand-written parser) when you need long options and can assume GNU userland.
Your script passes shellcheck and works on your machine but fails in the CI container. List plausible causes.
Different shell (/bin/sh = dash vs bash) if the shebang is sh or it's invoked as sh script; different tool versions (BSD vs GNU sed/date/getopt — e.g. sed -i syntax, date -d); a minimal PATH or missing packages; a different locale (LC_ALL) changing sort/regex; no TTY (so read, progress bars, or tput misbehave); read-only or absent /tmp; unset environment the script assumed; CRLF line endings from a Windows checkout. Pin the shebang, use absolute or checked tools, set LC_ALL=C, and test in the same container locally.
What are the trade-offs of IFS=$'\n\t' in the strict-mode header?
It removes the space from IFS, so unquoted expansions split only on newlines and tabs — which makes accidental word-splitting on space-containing values less catastrophic and makes iterating command output line-based by default. Downsides: it's non-standard behaviour that surprises readers; anything that legitimately relies on space-splitting (parsing "$flags", some read patterns, $* joining) now behaves differently; and it doesn't fix the real problem, which is missing quotes. Many style guides say: just quote everything and leave IFS alone.

References vs Pointers & C-with-Classes

The first thing a C++ interview checks: do you know what a reference actually is.

Notes

A reference is an alias — another name for an existing object, fixed to that object for its whole life and never null. A pointer is a separate object holding an address that you can retarget or set to null. Choosing between them (and knowing when C++ diverges from C) is the first real C++ design decision on every function signature. This page covers reference semantics and the const& parameter idiom, the dangling-reference traps, where C++ genuinely differs from “C with classes”, and a first look at RAII.

What a reference is

A reference is an alias for an existing object — another name for the same storage. It must be initialised, can never be rebound, and cannot be null (barring UB). The compiler usually implements it as a pointer, but semantically it is the object.

int x = 10;
int& r = x;      // r is x
r = 20;           // x is now 20
int& bad;         // error: must be initialised

int* p = &x;      // pointer: separate object holding an address
p = nullptr;      // can be reseated, can be null
ReferencePointer
NullableNoYes
ReseatableNoYes
Must initYesNo
ArithmeticNoYes
Extra storageOften none (optimised)Yes (a pointer variable)
Syntaxobj.memberptr->member

When to use which

  • Pass by const& for non-trivial read-only parameters — no copy, can't be null, can't be changed.
  • Pass by & (non-const) for an out/in-out parameter that always exists.
  • Pass by pointer when "no object" is a valid argument (optional), or when you need to reseat, or for arrays/C APIs.
  • Pass by value for small/cheap types (int, std::string_view) or when the function needs its own copy anyway (then move from it).
void print(const std::string& s);   // read-only, no copy, never null
void grow(std::vector<int>& v);       // in/out param that always exists
void attach(Node* opt);              // nullptr is a meaningful "no node"
int  square(int n);                  // small/trivial -> by value

std::string name = "Leo";
print(name);        // binds a reference -- no std::string copy made
grow(numbers);      // function mutates the caller's vector in place
attach(nullptr);    // legal: pointer parameter accepts "nothing"

Dangling references

const std::string& f() {
    std::string local = "hi";
    return local;          // UB: reference to destroyed local
}
auto&& r = std::vector<int>{1,2}[0];   // temp vector dies; r dangles

A const& bound to a temporary extends that temporary's lifetime to the reference's scope — but only for the immediate temporary, not sub-objects reached through it.

C++ vs C, briefly

  • Stronger typing: no implicit void* → T*; enum is its own type; function prototypes required.
  • struct and class can have member functions, constructors/destructors, access control (class defaults private, struct public).
  • new/delete (call ctors/dtors) instead of malloc/free.
  • References, function/operator overloading, templates, namespaces, RAII, exceptions, the STL.
  • nullptr not NULL; bool is built in; // comments (also in C99).
// C: this compiles. C++: error -- no implicit void* -> int* conversion
int* p = malloc(sizeof(int));      // C++ needs static_cast<int*>(...)

// C++ way: types carry behaviour, cleanup is automatic (RAII)
struct Timer {
    Timer()  { start(); }             // constructor -- runs on creation
    ~Timer() { stop();  }             // destructor  -- runs at end of scope, always
};
void work() {
    Timer t;                          // no malloc/free, no manual stop() call
    auto* buf = new int[64];          // new runs constructors; delete[] runs destructors
    delete[] buf;
}
Cheat Sheet
  • Reference = permanent alias: init required, no rebind, no null, no arithmetic.
  • Pointer = object holding an address: nullable, reseatable, supports arithmetic.
  • Read-only non-trivial param → const T&. Optional param → const T* or std::optional.
  • Small/trivially-copyable → pass by value. Strings you only read → std::string_view.
  • Never return a reference/pointer to a local.
  • const T& to a temporary extends the temporary's life to the ref's scope (immediate temp only).
  • T&& is an rvalue reference (see Move Semantics), not "reference to reference".
  • class members default private; struct default public. Otherwise identical.
Q&A
Can a reference be null or rebound?
No. It must be bound to a valid object at initialisation and refers to that same object for its whole life. If you need "maybe none" or "point somewhere else later", use a pointer.
Why prefer const std::string& over std::string for a read-only parameter?
It avoids copying the string on every call. const documents and enforces that the function won't modify the caller's object. (For strings specifically, std::string_view is often even better.)
Is a reference an object?
Not observably — it has no size of its own (sizeof(ref) gives the referent's size), you can't take "the address of the reference" (you get the referent's address), and you can't have an array of references. Implementations typically use a pointer under the hood.
What extends a temporary's lifetime?
Binding it directly to a named const& (or &&) reference. The temporary then lives as long as the reference. This does not apply to a reference returned from a function or to a temporary reached via a member access.
Default access in class vs struct?
class: members and base classes are private by default. struct: public. That's the only language difference.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Give three differences between a reference and a pointer.
A reference must be initialised and can't be reseated or null; a pointer can be uninitialised, reassigned, and null. A pointer supports arithmetic and has its own address/storage; a reference doesn't. Syntax: . vs ->.
How do you pass a large object to a function without copying it, read-only?
By const reference: void f(const BigThing& b).
What's wrong with returning int& to a local variable?
The local is destroyed when the function returns, so the caller holds a reference to freed stack memory — undefined behaviour on use.

Intermediate core

When is a pointer parameter the right choice over a reference?
When "no argument" is meaningful (an optional out-param you can pass nullptr for), when the callee must store or reseat what it's given, when interoperating with a C API, or when passing an array with a separate length. Otherwise a reference is clearer and can't be null.
Explain what happens: const std::string& s = std::string("x") + "y";
The + produces a temporary std::string. Binding it to the named const& extends its lifetime to match s's scope, so using s afterwards is valid. Without the reference (or with auto&& plus a member access) it would be destroyed at the end of the full expression.
What does int& f(int& x) { return x; } enable, and what's the risk?
Returning a reference lets the call be an lvalue: f(a) = 5; assigns to a. It's how operator[] and operator* work. The risk is returning a reference to something that won't outlive the call (a local, or a container element after the container is resized).

Advanced deep

Why does std::vector<bool> break the "references alias real objects" model?
It's a space-optimised specialisation that packs bits, so v[i] can't return a real bool& — it returns a proxy object that behaves like a reference. Consequences: auto x = v[i]; deduces the proxy, not bool; bool* p = &v[i]; doesn't compile; and generic code written for "container of T" can misbehave. This is the standard example of "don't use vector<bool> when you want a container of bytes-sized bools".
Does binding a temporary to a const& member in a constructor extend its lifetime?
No. Lifetime extension does not apply to reference members: the temporary is destroyed at the end of the constructor, leaving the member dangling. A class that stores a const T& member must be documented as non-owning and the caller must guarantee the referent outlives the object. If you need ownership, store a value or a smart pointer.
What is reference collapsing and where does it matter?
When references-to-references arise through templates or typedefs, they collapse by the rule "& wins": T& &, T&& &, T& && → T&; only T&& && → T&&. This is the mechanism behind forwarding references (template<class T> void f(T&& x)): an lvalue argument deduces T as U& so T&& collapses to U&, an rvalue deduces U so it stays U&& — enabling std::forward.

Classes, Constructors, Destructors & RAII

RAII is the single idea that makes C++ resource management sane. Know it cold.

Notes

A C++ class bundles data with the functions that maintain its invariants, and its constructor/destructor run automatically at the start and end of the object’s lifetime. RAII — Resource Acquisition Is Initialization — turns that into the core C++ resource-management technique: acquire in the constructor, release in the destructor, and cleanup becomes automatic and exception-safe. This page covers construction and member-initialisation order, member-init lists and delegating constructors, the RAII pattern itself, and explicit, = default, and = delete.

Object lifetime

Construction runs when an object comes into existence (declaration, new, element insertion); the destructor runs deterministically when it leaves scope, is deleted, or its container is destroyed. This determinism — unlike GC languages — is what RAII exploits.

struct Noisy {
    Noisy(const char* n) : n_(n) { std::cout << "+" << n_ << "\n"; }
    ~Noisy()                 { std::cout << "-" << n_ << "\n"; }
    const char* n_;
};
{
    Noisy a("a");            // +a
    Noisy b("b");            // +b
}                          // -b then -a  (destroyed in REVERSE order, deterministically)

Member initialisation

class Widget {
    int id_;
    std::string name_;
    const Config& cfg_;
public:
    Widget(int id, std::string name, const Config& c)
        : id_(id), name_(std::move(name)), cfg_(c) {}   // member init list
};
  • Members are initialised in declaration order, not the order in the init list — compilers warn if they differ.
  • Use the init list, not assignment in the body: const members, references, and members without a default ctor must be initialised there; others avoid a default-construct-then-assign.
  • Prefer default member initialisers (int id_ = 0;) for defaults.

Special member functions

FunctionPurpose
Default constructorT() — suppressed once you declare any other ctor.
Destructor~T() — release resources.
Copy ctor / copy assignValue-copy from another T.
Move ctor / move assignSteal resources from an rvalue T.

= default asks for the compiler's version; = delete forbids it (e.g. a non-copyable handle). Declaring a destructor or copy op suppresses the implicit move ops — see Rule of 5.

class FileHandle {
    std::FILE* f_;
public:
    explicit FileHandle(const char* p) : f_(std::fopen(p, "r")) {}
    ~FileHandle() { if (f_) std::fclose(f_); }   // release in the destructor

    FileHandle(const FileHandle&)            = delete;  // a file handle must not be copied
    FileHandle& operator=(const FileHandle&) = delete;
    FileHandle(FileHandle&&)                 = default; // but moving it is fine
    FileHandle& operator=(FileHandle&&)      = default;
};

RAII

Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation: wrap every resource (heap memory, file handle, lock, socket, DB transaction) in an object that acquires it in its constructor and releases it in its destructor. Then correctness is automatic — early return, exception, or normal exit all run the destructor.

{
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m);   // lock acquired
    std::ofstream out("log.txt");        // file opened
    if (bad) return;                     // dtors still run: file closed, mutex unlocked
    out << data;
}                                        // dtors run here on the normal path

Standard RAII types: std::unique_ptr/shared_ptr, lock_guard/unique_lock/scoped_lock, fstream, std::vector/string, std::jthread. Roll your own with a small wrapper class or std::unique_ptr with a custom deleter.

explicit

Mark single-argument constructors explicit to stop surprising implicit conversions (void f(Widget); f(42); silently building a Widget from 42). explicit on conversion operators too. Rule of thumb: single-arg ctors are explicit unless you deliberately want the conversion (like std::string from const char*).

struct Seconds {
    explicit Seconds(int s) : s_(s) {}   // remove `explicit` and the call below compiles
    int s_;
};
void wait(Seconds t);

wait(Seconds{5});   // OK -- intent is explicit
// wait(5);        // ERROR with `explicit`: no silent int -> Seconds conversion
Cheat Sheet
  • Dtor runs deterministically at scope exit / delete / container destruction — the basis of RAII.
  • Init members in the member initialiser list; they run in declaration order.
  • const members, references, and no-default-ctor members must use the init list.
  • Prefer default member initialisers (T x_ = 0;) for simple defaults.
  • Declaring any constructor removes the implicit default constructor.
  • RAII: acquire in ctor, release in dtor → exception-safe, leak-free, no manual cleanup.
  • Use standard RAII types; never raw new/delete, raw lock/unlock, raw fopen.
  • explicit on single-argument constructors and conversion operators by default.
  • = default / = delete to request or forbid a special member.
Q&A
What is RAII in one sentence?
Tie a resource's lifetime to an object's lifetime, so the destructor releases it automatically on every exit path.
In what order are class members constructed?
In the order they are declared in the class, regardless of the order in the constructor's initialiser list. Destructors run in reverse.
Why prefer the member initialiser list to assigning in the constructor body?
Body assignment first default-constructs the member then overwrites it (two steps, and impossible for const/reference/no-default-ctor members). The init list constructs it once with the right value.
What does explicit prevent?
Implicit conversions and copy-initialisation through that constructor/operator, so Widget w = 5; or passing 5 where a Widget is expected won't silently compile.
When does the compiler stop giving you a default constructor?
As soon as you declare any constructor of your own. Add T() = default; to get it back.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

When does a destructor run for a local object?
When control leaves the object's scope — by reaching the closing brace, return, break, or an exception propagating through. Always, on every path.
Name three standard RAII types.
std::unique_ptr / std::shared_ptr, std::lock_guard / std::scoped_lock, std::fstream, std::vector / std::string — any three.
What's the fix for a function that news an object and might throw before delete?
Don't use raw new. Hold it in a std::unique_ptr (or a value/container). Its destructor frees the memory whether the function returns normally or via an exception.

Intermediate core

Members declared a then b; init list says : b(1), a(b). What happens?
a is constructed first (declaration order) using b, which hasn't been initialised yet — so a gets garbage. Then b is set to 1. The init-list order is misleading; reorder the declarations or don't cross-depend.
Write a minimal RAII wrapper for a C FILE*.
class File {
    FILE* f_;
public:
    explicit File(const char* p) : f_(std::fopen(p, "r")) {
        if (!f_) throw std::runtime_error("open");
    }
    ~File() { if (f_) std::fclose(f_); }
    File(const File&) = delete;
    File& operator=(const File&) = delete;
    FILE* get() const { return f_; }
};
Or just std::unique_ptr<FILE, decltype(&std::fclose)> with fclose as the deleter.
Why should you generally not do real work in a constructor that can't signal failure?
A constructor has no return value, so the only way to report failure is to throw. If throwing isn't acceptable in your context, the object can end up half-constructed and invalid. Options: throw and let RAII clean up, use a factory function returning std::optional/expected, or a two-phase init() (least preferred — leaves a zombie state).

Advanced deep

What happens if a destructor throws, and what's the rule?
If a destructor throws while another exception is already propagating (stack unwinding), std::terminate is called — the program dies. Since C++11 destructors are implicitly noexcept, so a throw from one calls terminate anyway. Rule: destructors must not let exceptions escape. If cleanup can fail (e.g. close() on a buffered file), catch and log inside the destructor, and offer a separate close() method callers can use to handle errors explicitly.
Explain the order of operations when an exception is thrown from a constructor's body.
Any base-class subobjects and data members that were fully constructed before the throw are destroyed, in reverse order. The object's own destructor does not run (the object never finished construction). If the object was being created with new, the matching operator delete is called to free the raw storage. This is why a member that is itself RAII (like a unique_ptr) makes constructor bodies exception-safe for free.
You need "run this cleanup on scope exit" without writing a whole class. Options?
A scope-guard: a small template holding a callable and invoking it in its destructor (ScopeGuard g{[&]{ cleanup(); }};), with a dismiss() to cancel. This is std::experimental::scope_exit / gsl::finally / Boost.ScopeExit, and is standardised as std::scope_exit in C++23's library fundamentals. Useful for C-API resources and rollback logic where a dedicated RAII type would be overkill.

Initialization: {} vs (), Aggregates & the Vexing Parse

C++ has accumulated a dozen ways to give a variable its first value — and they don’t all mean the same thing.

Notes

Over the decades C++ has grown many initialisation syntaxes — T x;, T x = v;, T x(v);, T x{v};, T x{};, new T, new T() — and each triggers slightly different rules about which constructor runs, whether members are zeroed, and whether a narrowing conversion is allowed. Getting it wrong gives you an indeterminate value (undefined behaviour to read), a function declaration where you wanted an object (the “most vexing parse”), or a vector with two elements when you asked for ten. This page maps the kinds of initialisation, aggregate and designated initialisers, the std::initializer_list hijack, the vexing parse, brace-narrowing checks, member-initialisation order, and a rule of thumb for which syntax to reach for.

The kinds of initialization

FormNameWhat it does
T x;defaultClass: default ctor. Built-in at block scope: indeterminate (UB to read). At static scope: zero.
T x{}; / T x = T();valueScalars zeroed; class default-ctor’d; a class with no user-provided ctor gets all members zeroed.
T x(a, b);directOverload-resolve constructors; explicit ctors allowed.
T x = a;copyLike direct but explicit ctors are excluded; one user-defined conversion considered.
T x{a, b};list / braceinitializer_list ctor if viable, else aggregate init, else other ctors. Narrowing is ill-formed.
int  a;            // indeterminate -- reading it is UB
int  b{};          // 0
int  c(2.5);       // 2  (silent truncation)
int  d{2.5};       // ERROR: narrowing double -> int inside braces  (good)
std::string s = "hi";  // copy-init (explicit string ctors excluded here)

Aggregate & designated initialization

What. An aggregate is a class/array with no user-declared or inherited constructors, no private/protected non-static data members, no virtual functions, and no virtual/private/protected bases. It can be initialised member-by-member with braces, with no constructor involved. Why. Plain data structs (config, POD, coordinate types) get clean initialisation for free; C++20 designated initialisers make it self-documenting.

struct Point { int x, y, z; };
Point p1{1, 2, 3};
Point p2{1, 2};              // z is value-initialised -> 0
Point p3{.x = 1, .z = 3};       // C++20: y = 0; must be in declaration order, no reordering
Point p4{};                    // all members zeroed

struct Bad { int a; private: int b; };
// Bad b{1, 2};   // ERROR: not an aggregate (has a private data member)

The std::initializer_list hijack

What / why it bites. Any type with a std::initializer_list constructor has braces prefer that constructor, even when another constructor looks like a better match. The canonical trap is std::vector.

std::vector<int> v1(10, 1);   // ()  -> vector(size_type, const T&)  -> ten 1s
std::vector<int> v2{10, 1};   // {}  -> initializer_list ctor        -> the two elements 10, 1
std::vector<std::string> v3{3};  // initializer_list<string> not viable from int -> falls back to vector(3)
std::vector<int> v4{3};       // but here int IS a valid element -> one element {3}, NOT three 0s

Rule: when you want a sizing/positional constructor, use (); use {} only when you mean “these are the contents”.

The most vexing parse

What. If something can be parsed as a function declaration, it is. Widget w(); declares a function returning Widget; Rect r(Area()); declares a function taking a pointer-to-function. Fix. Use braces, or add parentheses.

Widget w();          // FUNCTION declaration, not an object!
Widget w{};          // object, default-initialised  (preferred fix)

Rect r(Area());      // function: Rect r(Area(*)())
Rect r{Area{}};      // object  (preferred)
Rect r((Area()));    // object  (extra parens disambiguate)

Member initialization order

  • Default member initialisers in the class body (int count = 0;) apply unless a constructor’s member-init list overrides them.
  • Members are initialised in declaration order, not the order you write them in the member-init list. Compilers warn (-Wreorder); a member that depends on another declared later reads it uninitialised.
  • Bases are initialised before members; a delegating constructor (Foo() : Foo(0) {}) runs the target constructor first.
  • Prefer brace-or-equals initialisers for every member so no constructor path can leave one indeterminate.
struct S {
    int n;
    std::vector<int> v;
    S(int k) : v(k), n(k) {}   // WARNING: n is declared first, so n runs BEFORE v(k);
                                //          harmless here, dangerous if v used n
};

Rule of thumb

  • Prefer {} for the narrowing check and because it can never be a vexing parse — except when you specifically want a non-list constructor (vector(n, val), string(n, ch)): then use ().
  • Use = value for simple copy-initialised scalars and strings where it reads naturally.
  • Always give class members a default member initialiser (= {} / = 0).
  • auto x{1} is int (C++17+); auto x = {1, 2} is std::initializer_list<int>; auto x{1, 2} is ill-formed.
Cheat Sheet
  • T x; — class: default ctor; built-in at block scope: indeterminate (UB to read); static scope: zero.
  • T x{}; / T x = T(); — value-init: scalars 0, members zeroed if no user ctor.
  • T x(a,b) direct (explicit ctors OK); T x = a copy (explicit ctors excluded).
  • T x{...} — tries initializer_list ctor first, then aggregate init, then other ctors; narrowing is an error.
  • vector<int> v{10,1} = two elements; vector<int> v(10,1) = ten 1s. Positional/sizing ctor → use ().
  • Most vexing parse: Widget w(); is a function decl. Fix with Widget w{}; or extra parens.
  • Aggregate (no user ctors, no private data members, no virtuals): brace member-by-member; C++20 designated {.x=1,.z=3} in declaration order.
  • Members initialise in declaration order, not member-init-list order (-Wreorder). Give every member a default initialiser.
  • auto x{1} → int; auto x = {1,2} → initializer_list<int>.
Q&A
Why does std::vector<int> v{10, 1}; not give you ten ones?
Because brace initialisation checks for a viable std::initializer_list constructor before any other, and vector has one. {10, 1} is a two-element initializer_list<int>, so you get the vector [10, 1]. To call vector(size_type count, const int& value) you must use parentheses: std::vector<int> v(10, 1);. This is the single most common brace-initialisation surprise.
What is the “most vexing parse” and how do you avoid it?
When a declaration could be read as either an object definition or a function declaration, C++ chooses the function. Widget w(); declares a function named w taking no arguments and returning Widget — not an object. Foo f(Bar()); declares a function taking an (unnamed) function pointer. Avoid it by using braces for value-initialisation (Widget w{};, Foo f{Bar{}};) or, if you must use parentheses, wrap the inner expression in an extra pair (Foo f((Bar()));).
What’s the difference between int x; at block scope and at namespace scope?
At namespace (or static) scope, x has static storage duration and is zero-initialised before the program starts, so it’s reliably 0. At block scope, x has automatic storage and default initialisation leaves it with an indeterminate value — reading it before assigning is undefined behaviour. For a class type, both call the default constructor. Use int x{}; at block scope when you want a guaranteed zero.
When is a class not an aggregate, and why does it matter?
It stops being an aggregate if it has any user-declared or inherited constructor, any private/protected non-static data member, any virtual function, or a virtual/non-public base. It matters because only aggregates support member-by-member brace initialisation (and C++20 designated initialisers) without writing a constructor. Add one explicit constructor to a plain data struct and S s{1, 2, 3}; stops compiling unless a matching constructor exists.
Your constructor’s member-init list is : b(a), a(x) and a linter complains. What’s wrong?
Members are initialised in the order they are declared in the class, regardless of the order in the member-init list. If a is declared before b, then a(x) runs first and b(a) second — fine. But if b is declared first, b(a) runs while a is still uninitialised, so b gets garbage. The fix is to write the member-init list in declaration order (which also silences -Wreorder) and to not have one member’s initialiser depend on another member’s value where the order is subtle.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does int x{}; give you, and how is it different from int x;?
int x{}; value-initialises x to 0. int x; at block scope leaves x with an indeterminate value (reading it is undefined behaviour). At namespace/static scope both end up 0.
Which initialisation syntax rejects narrowing conversions?
Brace initialisation: int x{2.5}; is a compile error, whereas int x(2.5); compiles and truncates to 2. That’s a reason to prefer braces for scalars.

Intermediate core

Explain the precedence rules for what T obj{args}; does, with an example where it surprises people.
Brace (list) initialisation resolves in this order: (1) if T has one or more std::initializer_list constructors and the braced list is convertible to one of them, that constructor wins — even over a “better” non-list constructor; (2) otherwise, if T is an aggregate, do member-by-member aggregate initialisation with no constructor call; (3) otherwise, do normal overload resolution over the remaining constructors. In all cases, narrowing conversions inside the braces make the program ill-formed. The classic surprise: std::vector<int> v{10, 1}; gives a two-element vector [10,1], not ten ones, because step (1) picks the initializer_list<int> constructor. std::vector<int> v(10, 1); uses parentheses, skips step (1), and calls vector(size_type, const int&) for ten ones. Another: std::vector<std::string> v{3}; — 3 can’t form an initializer_list<string>, so it falls to vector(size_type) = three empty strings; change the element type to int and {3} becomes a one-element list instead.

Advanced deep

You’re setting a team style guide for initialisation. What do you mandate, and what edge cases must the guide call out?
Default: brace-initialise (T x{...}), because it forbids narrowing, is immune to the most vexing parse, and works uniformly for scalars, aggregates, and class types. Explicit exception: use parentheses when you need a constructor that a braced list would shadow — container sizing constructors (std::vector<T> v(n), std::vector<T> v(n, value)), std::string(n, ch), std::make_unique<T[]>(n) — and add a comment saying why. Members: every non-static data member gets a default member initialiser (= {}, = 0, = nullptr) so no constructor path leaves it indeterminate; keep member-init lists in declaration order (enable -Werror=reorder). Plain data: keep POD/config structs as aggregates (no hand-written constructors) so designated initialisers work; if you need validation, prefer a factory function returning the aggregate over adding a constructor that breaks aggregate-ness. Edge cases to call out: (1) the initializer_list hijack — give examples for vector/map. (2) auto x{1} is int since C++17 but was initializer_list<int> before — forbid auto with braces except the single-element case, and forbid auto x{a, b} (ill-formed anyway). (3) T x = {…} (copy-list-init) forbids explicit constructors — know when that’s the behaviour you want (e.g. preventing std::vector<int> v = {1,2,3} from silently calling an explicit ctor). (4) empty braces vs empty parens for new: new T default-initialises (indeterminate scalars), new T() and new T{} value-initialise (zeroed) — always use one of the latter. (5) reference and const members must be initialised in the member-init list or with a default member initialiser — they can’t be assigned later. (6) guard against accidental aggregate-init reordering when adding a member in the middle of a struct that has positional {...} call sites — prefer designated initialisers at call sites for structs that evolve. Tooling: -Wall -Wextra, clang-tidy checks (modernize-use-default-member-init, cppcoreguidelines-pro-type-member-init, cppcoreguidelines-prefer-member-initializer), and -Werror=uninitialized / MSan in test builds to catch anything the rules miss.

Copy Semantics & the Rule of 3/5/0

If you write one of the special members, you probably need to think about all of them.

Notes

When a class owns a resource (heap memory, a file handle, a socket), the compiler-generated copy operations do the wrong thing — they copy the handle, not the resource, so two objects free the same thing. The Rule of 3/5/0 is the guidance for which of the special member functions (destructor, copy/move constructor, copy/move assignment) you must write together, or better, avoid writing at all. This page covers deep vs shallow copy, the copy constructor and assignment operator (including self-assignment), and why the Rule of Zero — own nothing raw, let members manage themselves — is the target.

Shallow vs deep copy

The compiler-generated copy constructor and copy assignment do a memberwise copy. For a class holding a raw owning pointer that means two objects pointing at the same buffer — a double-free and aliasing bug. You then need a deep copy that duplicates the buffer.

class Buf {
    int* p_; size_t n_;
public:
    Buf(const Buf& o) : p_(new int[o.n_]), n_(o.n_) { std::copy(o.p_, o.p_+n_, p_); }
    Buf& operator=(Buf o) { swap(*this, o); return *this; }  // copy-and-swap
    ~Buf() { delete[] p_; }
};

The rules

RuleStatement
Rule of 3If you define a destructor, copy ctor, or copy assignment, you almost certainly need all three.
Rule of 5C++11: add the move ctor and move assignment to that set.
Rule of 0Best: design classes that need none of them — hold resources in RAII members (vector, unique_ptr) so the compiler-generated versions are correct.
// Rule of 5: raw resource -> spell out all five
class Buffer {
    int* p_ = nullptr; size_t n_ = 0;
public:
    explicit Buffer(size_t n) : p_(new int[n]{}), n_(n) {}
    ~Buffer()                       { delete[] p_; }                 // 1 dtor
    Buffer(const Buffer& o)          : p_(new int[o.n_]), n_(o.n_) { std::copy(o.p_, o.p_+n_, p_); } // 2
    Buffer& operator=(Buffer o)      { swap(o); return *this; } // 3 (copy-and-swap covers 3+5)
    Buffer(Buffer&& o) noexcept       : p_(o.p_), n_(o.n_) { o.p_ = nullptr; o.n_ = 0; } // 4
    void swap(Buffer& o) noexcept     { std::swap(p_, o.p_); std::swap(n_, o.n_); }
};

// Rule of 0: same job, ZERO special members -- vector manages the resource
class Buffer0 { std::vector<int> data_; public: explicit Buffer0(size_t n) : data_(n) {} };

copy-and-swap

Take the parameter by value (invokes copy or move), then swap with *this. One implementation handles both copy and move assignment, is self-assignment safe, and gives the strong exception guarantee (the copy happens before any mutation).

Buffer& operator=(Buffer rhs) {   // rhs is a BY-VALUE copy (or move) of the argument
    swap(rhs);                    // take rhs's guts; rhs's dtor frees our old guts
    return *this;
}
Buffer a(4), b(8);
a = b;                // rhs = copy of b, then swap  -> a now owns a copy, no leak
a = std::move(b);     // rhs = moved-from b, then swap -> no allocation at all
a = a;                // safe: rhs is an independent copy before any mutation

Suppression rules

  • Declaring a destructor or any copy op ⇒ move ops are not generated (you silently get copies where you expected moves).
  • Declaring a move op ⇒ copy ops are deleted.
  • So: if you declare one special member, = default or = delete the rest explicitly.
struct Logged {
    std::vector<int> v;
    ~Logged() { std::cout << "destroyed\n"; }   // added just for a log line...
};
Logged a;
Logged b = std::move(a);   // ...now COPIES the vector -- move ctor was suppressed by ~Logged

struct Fixed {
