Techniques: lock striping (Java 7 ConcurrentHashMap — N segment locks, so writers to different segments don't contend); per-bucket / CAS-based updates (Java 8 — CAS to install the first node, synchronise only on the bucket head for chains, help with resize); fully lock-free designs using atomic pointers and a "resize in progress" forwarding marker; or RCU / epoch schemes where readers never block and writers publish new versions. Reads are usually wait-free. Trade-offs: memory overhead, weaker iteration guarantees (weakly consistent iterators), and size() becoming approximate or expensive.

Trees & Binary Search Trees

Traversals, the BST invariant, and why an unbalanced BST is just a slow linked list.

Notes

A tree is a hierarchy of nodes with one root and no cycles; a binary search tree (BST) is a binary tree that keeps the ordering invariant “everything in the left subtree < node < everything in the right subtree”, which makes search, insert, and delete O(height). This page covers tree terminology, the four traversals (in-, pre-, post-, level-order) and what each is good for, BST search/insert/delete, and why an unbalanced BST degenerates to a linked list — the problem that balanced trees solve.

Terminology

Root, parent/child, leaf, internal node, edge, depth (root to node), height (node to deepest leaf), subtree. A binary tree: each node has ≤ 2 children. Complete, full, perfect, balanced are distinct shapes.

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

def height(node):                   # edges on the longest downward path
    if not node: return -1            # empty tree: -1;  single node: 0
    return 1 + max(height(node.left), height(node.right))

def is_leaf(node):
    return node and not node.left and not node.right

Traversals

OrderVisitUse
In-order (L, N, R)left, node, rightBST → sorted output
Pre-order (N, L, R)node firstcopy/serialize a tree, prefix expression
Post-order (L, R, N)node lastdelete/free a tree, postfix expression, compute subtree aggregates
Level-order (BFS)by depth, using a queueshortest path in unweighted tree, printing by row

DFS traversals are naturally recursive (call stack) or iterative with an explicit stack; level-order needs a queue.

def inorder(node, out):
    if not node: return
    inorder(node.left, out)      # L
    out.append(node.val)         # N  -> for a BST this yields sorted order
    inorder(node.right, out)     # R

from collections import deque
def level_order(root):          # BFS, row by row
    q, rows = deque([root] if root else []), []
    while q:
        rows.append([n.val for n in q])
        q = deque(c for n in q for c in (n.left, n.right) if c)
    return rows

Binary Search Tree

  • Invariant: for every node, all keys in the left subtree are < the node's key, all keys in the right subtree are >.
  • search, insert, delete: O(h) where h is the height. Balanced → O(log n); degenerate (sorted insertions) → O(n).
  • Delete cases: leaf (remove), one child (splice), two children (replace with in-order successor/predecessor, then delete that).
  • In-order traversal yields keys in ascending order — a free sorted iteration.
def search(node, key):
    while node and node.val != key:
        node = node.left if key < node.val else node.right  # one comparison drops half the tree
    return node

def insert(node, key):
    if not node: return TreeNode(key)
    if key < node.val: node.left  = insert(node.left, key)
    elif key > node.val: node.right = insert(node.right, key)
    return node                  # depth of descent = O(h)

When BSTs degenerate

Inserting already-sorted (or reverse-sorted) data builds a path, not a bush → O(n) operations. Fixes: self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black — next topic), randomised insertion order, treaps, or just use a hash table if you don't need ordered iteration / range queries.

root = None
for k in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]:      # ALREADY SORTED input
    root = insert(root, k)      # every key goes right -> a linked list
# height(root) == 4 for 5 nodes  ->  search() is now O(n), not O(log n)

import random
keys = list(range(1, 6)); random.shuffle(keys)  # randomised order -> expected O(log n) height
Cheat Sheet
  • Height = longest root→leaf path; depth = node's distance from root.
  • In-order = sorted (for a BST). Pre-order = serialize. Post-order = free / bottom-up aggregates. Level-order = BFS with a queue.
  • BST invariant: left subtree < node < right subtree, recursively.
  • search/insert/delete = O(h): O(log n) balanced, O(n) degenerate.
  • Delete-with-two-children: swap with in-order successor (leftmost of right subtree), then delete that.
  • Sorted input into a plain BST → linked-list shape → use a self-balancing tree.
  • Use a BST/ordered map for range queries, floor/ceil, ordered iteration; use a hash map otherwise.
  • DFS recursion depth = tree height → risk of stack overflow on skewed trees; go iterative if needed.
Q&A
Which traversal prints a BST's keys in sorted order?
In-order (left, node, right).
Difference between height and depth of a node?
Depth is the number of edges from the root down to the node; height is the number of edges from the node down to its deepest descendant leaf. The tree's height is the root's height.
What's the time complexity of BST search, and what does it depend on?
O(h), the height. For a balanced tree h ≈ log₂n; for a degenerate (linear) tree h = n.
How do you delete a node with two children from a BST?
Replace its key with its in-order successor (the smallest key in the right subtree) or predecessor, then recursively delete that successor node, which has at most one child.
Why can inserting sorted data into a BST be a problem?
Each new key is larger than all previous, so it always goes to the far right — the tree becomes a straight chain of height n, and every operation is O(n). Self-balancing trees restructure to keep height O(log n).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What data structure does level-order traversal use?
A queue.
State the BST property.
For every node, all keys in its left subtree are smaller and all keys in its right subtree are larger than the node's key.
Maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height h (edges)?
2^(h+1) − 1 (a perfect tree).

Intermediate core

Validate that a binary tree is a BST.
Recurse with an allowed (min, max) range: each node's key must be strictly within its bounds; recurse left with max = node.key, right with min = node.key. Checking only node.left.key < node.key < node.right.key locally is wrong — it misses violations deeper down. Equivalent: an in-order traversal must be strictly increasing.
Find the k-th smallest element in a BST.
In-order traversal, counting nodes; return the k-th visited. O(k) with early stop, O(h + k) to reach it. If the tree stores subtree sizes (an order-statistics tree), it's O(h): at each node compare k with left-subtree size to go left, return, or go right with adjusted k.

Advanced deep

How do you do an iterative in-order traversal with O(1) extra space?
Morris traversal: for each node with a left child, find its in-order predecessor (rightmost node of the left subtree) and temporarily set that node's right pointer to the current node (a "thread"). Walk left; when you return via a thread, output the node, remove the thread, and go right. It mutates pointers during traversal but restores them, using no stack — O(n) time, O(1) space. Trade-off: not thread-safe / not usable on a shared immutable tree, and more complex to get right.
Serialize and deserialize a binary tree. What's the key design choice?
Choose a traversal and explicitly mark null children (e.g. pre-order with # for null). Pre-order + null markers lets deserialize rebuild recursively by consuming tokens in the same order. Level-order + null markers also works (LeetCode's format). Without null markers a single traversal is ambiguous — you'd need two (e.g. in-order + pre-order), which fails if keys aren't unique. Cost: null markers roughly double the token count for sparse trees.

Balanced Trees & Heaps

Keeping tree height O(log n), and the array-as-tree trick behind priority queues.

Notes

This page covers two structures that guarantee logarithmic operations by controlling shape. A self-balancing BST (AVL, red-black, B-tree) does rotations/splits on every update to keep the height O(log n), so ordered operations stay fast regardless of insertion order — this is what backs std::map, TreeMap, and database indexes. A binary heap is a complete binary tree kept in an array with a weaker “parent ≤ children” invariant, giving O(1) find-min and O(log n) insert/extract — the basis of the priority queue and heapsort. It covers the balancing ideas, heapify, and when to reach for each.

Self-balancing BSTs

TreeBalance ruleCharacter
AVLheights of the two subtrees differ by ≤ 1stricter balance → faster lookups, more rotations on write
Red-blackcolour rules keep the longest path ≤ 2× the shortestlooser → fewer rotations, favoured for general maps (std::map, Java TreeMap)
B-tree / B+treehigh branching factor, all leaves same depthdisk/SSD & DB indexes — one node = one page, minimises I/O

All give O(log n) search/insert/delete and, unlike a hash table, keep keys ordered (range queries, floor/ceil, sorted iteration). Balance is restored by rotations (local O(1) pointer rewires) after an insert/delete.

# a left rotation: the O(1) pointer rewire that fixes a right-heavy node
def rotate_left(x):
    y = x.right                  #     x               y
    x.right = y.left             #      \             / \
    y.left = x                   #       y    ->     x   T3
    return y                     #      / \           \
                                 #     T2  T3          T2   (order preserved, height drops)

# ordered ops a hash map can't do:
#   floor(k)  -> largest key <= k        ceil(k) -> smallest key >= k
#   range(lo, hi) -> all keys in [lo, hi] via an in-order walk

Binary heap

  • A complete binary tree stored in an array: node i's children are 2i+1, 2i+2; parent is (i-1)/2. No pointers.
  • Heap property: min-heap — every parent ≤ its children (root is the minimum). Max-heap is the mirror.
  • push: append, then sift up — O(log n). pop (min): swap root with last, shrink, sift down — O(log n). peek: O(1).
  • Build-heap from an unsorted array: sift down from the last internal node upward — O(n), not O(n log n).
h = []                          # array IS the tree
def push(x):
    h.append(x); i = len(h) - 1
    while i > 0 and h[(i-1)//2] > h[i]:      # sift up: swap with parent while smaller
        p = (i-1)//2
        h[i], h[p] = h[p], h[i]; i = p
# pop-min: move last to root, then sift down comparing to the smaller child

import heapq                    # in practice, use the stdlib min-heap
heapq.heappush(h, 5); heapq.heappop(h)  # O(log n) each; h[0] is the min in O(1)

Uses

Priority queue (Dijkstra, A*, task scheduling), heapsort (build max-heap, repeatedly pop), "top-k" (a size-k heap in O(n log k)), median maintenance (two heaps), merging k sorted lists.

import heapq
# top-k largest in O(n log k): keep a size-k MIN-heap, evict the smallest
def top_k(nums, k):
    h = nums[:k]; heapq.heapify(h)          # O(k)
    for x in nums[k:]:
        if x > h[0]: heapq.heapreplace(h, x)   # push+pop in one O(log k) op
    return h

# running median: max-heap of the low half, min-heap of the high half

Heap vs BST

A heap only gives you the min (or max) fast — no ordered iteration, no arbitrary search (that's O(n)). A balanced BST gives ordered operations but a larger constant and pointer overhead. Use a heap when you only ever want the extreme element.

h = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]; heapq.heapify(h)
h[0]                # 1  -> the min, O(1)
4 in h              # works but O(n) -- a heap is NOT a search structure
sorted(h)          # no cheap ordered iteration; you must fully sort or pop repeatedly
# need floor/ceil/range/ordered-iterate as well? use a balanced BST / TreeMap.
Cheat Sheet
  • AVL: tightly balanced, more rotations, fastest reads. Red-black: looser, fewer rotations, default for library maps.
  • B/B+ trees: wide fan-out, one node per disk page → database and filesystem indexes.
  • Balanced BST ops all O(log n); rebalancing = O(1) rotations per level.
  • Binary heap = complete tree in an array; children of i at 2i+1/2i+2.
  • push/pop O(log n) (sift up/down), peek O(1), build-heap O(n).
  • Heap = priority queue; no search, no ordered traversal.
  • Heapsort: build max-heap O(n), pop n times O(n log n), in-place, not stable.
  • Top-k with a min-heap of size k: O(n log k). Streaming median: max-heap (low half) + min-heap (high half).
Q&A
How is a binary heap stored without pointers?
As an array representing a complete binary tree level by level. For index i: left child 2i+1, right child 2i+2, parent (i-1)/2. The completeness guarantee is what makes this indexing valid.
Why is building a heap O(n), not O(n log n)?
You sift down from the bottom up. Most nodes are near the leaves and sift down only a level or two; the work is ∑ (nodes at height h) × h, which converges to O(n). Inserting one-by-one with sift-up would be O(n log n).
AVL vs red-black tree — when does each win?
AVL keeps stricter balance, so lookups are slightly faster — better for read-heavy workloads. Red-black does fewer rotations per update, so it's better for write-heavy workloads and is the common choice for standard-library ordered maps.
Can you search a heap for an arbitrary value efficiently?
No — O(n). The heap property only orders parents vs children, not siblings or cousins. If you need search, use a balanced BST or keep a side hash map of value→index.
Why do databases use B-trees instead of binary balanced trees?
Disk/SSD reads happen in pages (4–16 KB). A B-tree node fills a page and has hundreds of children, so the tree is very shallow (3–4 levels for millions of keys) — each level is one I/O. A binary tree would need ~log₂n ≈ 20+ I/Os for the same data.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What's at the root of a min-heap?
The smallest element. peek is O(1).
Insert and extract-min complexity for a binary heap?
Both O(log n) — sift up on insert, sift down after removing the root.
Does a self-balancing BST keep keys in sorted order?
Yes — in-order traversal is still sorted, which is why it supports range queries that a hash map can't.

Intermediate core

Find the k largest elements of an n-element array efficiently.
Maintain a min-heap of size k: push the first k, then for each remaining element, if it's larger than the heap's min, pop and push it. End with the k largest. O(n log k) time, O(k) space — better than sorting (O(n log n)) when k « n. (Quickselect gives O(n) average if you only need them unordered.)
Maintain the running median of a stream.
Two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half, a min-heap for the upper half, kept balanced in size (differ by ≤ 1). Insert into the appropriate heap, then rebalance by moving one element across if sizes diverge. Median is the top of the larger heap, or the average of both tops when equal. O(log n) per insert, O(1) query.

Advanced deep

Dijkstra with a binary heap is O((V+E) log V). What does a Fibonacci heap change, and why isn't it used much?
A Fibonacci heap gives amortised O(1) decrease-key and O(1) insert, with O(log n) extract-min, lowering Dijkstra to O(E + V log V) — asymptotically better for dense graphs. In practice it's rarely used: large hidden constants, poor cache locality (lots of pointer manipulation and node cutting), and complex implementation. Pairing heaps or just a binary heap with "lazy deletion" (push duplicates, skip stale pops) are simpler and faster on real inputs. It's a "great in theory" structure.
Why is heapsort O(n log n) worst-case and in-place, yet usually slower than quicksort in practice?
Heapsort's sift-down repeatedly jumps between array positions i and 2i+1/2i+2 — a scattered, cache-unfriendly access pattern — and it does more comparisons/swaps with worse branch prediction than quicksort's mostly-sequential partition scan. Quicksort's O(n²) worst case is avoidable (introsort: switch to heapsort when recursion goes too deep), so the standard library gets quicksort's speed with heapsort's guarantee. Heapsort shines when you need a hard worst-case bound and O(1) space, e.g. embedded or adversarial contexts.

Graphs: Representation & Traversal

Adjacency list vs matrix, BFS vs DFS, and the problems each traversal unlocks.

Notes

A graph is a set of vertices connected by edges — the model for networks, dependencies, maps, social connections, and state machines. The two representations (adjacency list vs adjacency matrix) trade memory for lookup speed, and the two traversals (BFS and DFS) are the foundation of almost every graph algorithm. This page covers representation trade-offs, BFS/DFS and their uses (shortest path in unweighted graphs, connected components, cycle detection), topological sort of a DAG, and the directed/undirected and weighted/unweighted distinctions that change which algorithm applies.

Representations

Adjacency listAdjacency matrix
SpaceO(V + E)O(V²)
Edge exists?O(degree)O(1)
Iterate neighboursO(degree)O(V)
Best forsparse graphs (most real graphs)dense graphs, or when you query specific edges a lot

Also: edge list (just pairs) — handy for Kruskal / Bellman-Ford. Store weights alongside.

from collections import defaultdict
adj = defaultdict(list)               # adjacency list: O(V+E) space
for u, v in edges:
    adj[u].append(v); adj[v].append(u) # undirected -> add both directions

mat = [[0]*V for _ in range(V)]         # adjacency matrix: O(V^2) space
for u, v in edges: mat[u][v] = mat[v][u] = 1
mat[u][v]                             # O(1) "is there an edge?" -- the matrix's one win

BFS

  • Queue-based, explores by distance from the source.
  • Gives the shortest path in an unweighted graph (fewest edges).
  • O(V + E). Track visited to avoid revisiting; store parent to reconstruct paths.
  • Also: bipartite check (2-colour), level/"minimum steps" problems, multi-source BFS.
from collections import deque
def shortest_unweighted(adj, src, dst):
    q, dist, parent = deque([src]), {src: 0}, {src: None}
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        if u == dst: break
        for v in adj[u]:
            if v not in dist:            # first time we reach v => via a shortest path
                dist[v] = dist[u] + 1
                parent[v] = u
                q.append(v)
    return dist.get(dst)                # hop count; walk `parent` back for the route

DFS

  • Stack/recursion, goes deep before wide.
  • O(V + E). Uses: cycle detection, topological sort (DAG), connected components, bridges/articulation points, strongly connected components (Tarjan/Kosaraju), maze/backtracking.
  • Edge classification (tree / back / forward / cross edges) — a back edge means a cycle.
def dfs(adj, u, seen):
    seen.add(u)
    for v in adj[u]:
        if v not in seen:
            dfs(adj, v, seen)          # recurse -> uses the call stack

def components(adj, nodes):
    seen, count = set(), 0
    for u in nodes:
        if u not in seen:
            dfs(adj, u, seen); count += 1  # each unseen start = one new component
    return count

Cycle detection

  • Undirected: DFS — a visited neighbour that isn't the parent means a cycle. Or union-find while adding edges.
  • Directed: DFS with three colours (white/grey/black) — an edge to a grey (in-progress) node is a back edge = cycle. Or Kahn's algorithm: if topological sort can't place all nodes, there's a cycle.
WHITE, GREY, BLACK = 0, 1, 2
def has_cycle(adj, nodes):
    color = {u: WHITE for u in nodes}
    def visit(u):
        color[u] = GREY                # on the current DFS path
        for v in adj[u]:
            if color[v] == GREY: return True   # back edge -> cycle
            if color[v] == WHITE and visit(v): return True
        color[u] = BLACK               # fully explored
        return False
    return any(visit(u) for u in nodes if color[u] == WHITE)

Topological sort

Linear ordering of a DAG so every edge points forward. Kahn's: repeatedly remove a node with in-degree 0. DFS: push nodes onto a stack on exit; reverse it. O(V + E). Used for build systems, task scheduling, dependency resolution.

from collections import deque
def kahn(adj, nodes):
    indeg = {u: 0 for u in nodes}
    for u in nodes:
        for v in adj[u]: indeg[v] += 1
    q = deque(u for u in nodes if indeg[u] == 0)   # no unmet dependencies
    order = []
    while q:
        u = q.popleft(); order.append(u)
        for v in adj[u]:
            indeg[v] -= 1
            if indeg[v] == 0: q.append(v)
    return order if len(order) == len(nodes) else None  # None => a cycle exists
Cheat Sheet
  • Adjacency list: O(V+E) space, sparse graphs (default). Matrix: O(V²), O(1) edge test, dense graphs.
  • BFS: queue, shortest path in unweighted graphs, level order, bipartite check. O(V+E).
  • DFS: stack/recursion, cycle detection, topological sort, components, bridges/SCC. O(V+E).
  • Always track visited; store parent to rebuild paths.
  • Directed cycle = back edge to a grey node (3-colour DFS) or Kahn's leftover nodes.
  • Undirected cycle = DFS hits a visited non-parent, or union-find sees both endpoints already joined.
  • Topological sort: Kahn (in-degree 0 queue) or DFS finish-time reverse; DAG only.
  • Weighted shortest path is a different tool (Dijkstra / Bellman-Ford — see Algorithms).
Q&A
When do you prefer an adjacency matrix?
Dense graphs (E ≈ V²), or when you frequently ask "is there an edge u→v?" and rarely iterate all neighbours. Otherwise the adjacency list's O(V+E) space wins for the sparse graphs that dominate practice.
Which traversal finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph, and why?
BFS. It expands nodes in non-decreasing order of distance from the source, so the first time it reaches a node is via a minimum-edge path.
How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph with DFS?
Mark nodes white (unvisited), grey (on the current DFS path), black (fully explored). If DFS finds an edge to a grey node, that's a back edge → there's a cycle.
What does topological sort require of the graph?
It must be a DAG (directed, acyclic). If a cycle exists, no valid linear ordering can exist.
Time and space complexity of BFS/DFS on an adjacency list?
O(V + E) time (each vertex and edge processed once). Space O(V) for the visited set plus the queue/stack (which can hold up to O(V)).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which structure backs BFS and which backs DFS?
BFS uses a queue; DFS uses a stack (explicit or the recursion call stack).
Space of an adjacency matrix for V vertices?
O(V²), regardless of how many edges exist.
Can topological sort be applied to a graph with a cycle?
No — only to a DAG.

Intermediate core

Count connected components in an undirected graph.
Iterate all vertices; each time you find an unvisited one, run BFS/DFS from it to mark its whole component and increment a counter. O(V + E). (Union-find also works: components = number of distinct roots after unioning every edge.)
Detect whether an undirected graph is bipartite.
BFS/DFS 2-colouring: colour the start, colour each neighbour the opposite. If you ever try to give a node a colour it already has that conflicts (a same-colour edge), it's not bipartite. Do this per component. O(V + E).
Implement Kahn's topological sort.
Compute in-degrees. Push all in-degree-0 nodes to a queue. Repeatedly pop a node, append to the order, and decrement each successor's in-degree, pushing any that hit 0. If the final order has fewer than V nodes, the graph has a cycle. O(V + E).

Advanced deep

Explain 0-1 BFS and when it beats Dijkstra.
When every edge weight is 0 or 1, use a deque: relax an edge of weight 0 by push_front, weight 1 by push_back. The deque stays sorted by distance in two "layers", so each node is finalised in O(1) amortised — total O(V + E), beating Dijkstra's O(E log V) and avoiding the heap entirely. Generalises to "0-k BFS" with k buckets (dial's algorithm) for small integer weights. Common in grid problems where moving costs 0 or 1.
How does Tarjan's algorithm find strongly connected components in one DFS pass?
During DFS it assigns each node a discovery index and tracks low[v] = the smallest index reachable from v's subtree via at most one back/cross edge to a node still on the stack. It keeps DFS-visited nodes on an explicit stack. When it finishes a node v with low[v] == index[v], v is the "root" of an SCC: pop the stack down to v — those nodes form one SCC. O(V + E), single pass, versus Kosaraju's two passes (DFS, transpose, DFS in finish order).

Union-Find & Tries

Two specialised structures: near-O(1) connectivity, and prefix-indexed strings.

Notes

Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union, DSU) maintains a partition of elements into disjoint sets and answers two questions in near-constant time: which set is this element in (find) and merge these two sets (union). With the two standard optimisations — union by rank/size and path compression — a sequence of m operations runs in O(m · α(n)), where α is the inverse Ackermann function (≤ 4 for any realistic n). This page covers the forest representation, both optimisations and why they work, and the applications: Kruskal’s MST, connected components, cycle detection in an undirected graph, and offline connectivity queries.

Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find)

Maintains a partition of elements into disjoint sets, supporting:

  • find(x) — representative ("root") of x's set.
  • union(x, y) — merge the two sets.
  • connected(x, y) — find(x) == find(y).

Backed by a parent[] forest. Two optimisations make it nearly constant time:

  • Union by rank/size — attach the smaller tree under the larger, keeping trees shallow.
  • Path compression — during find, point every node on the path directly at the root.

Together: O(α(n)) amortised per operation, where α (inverse Ackermann) is ≤ 4 for any practical n — effectively O(1).

int find(int x) { return parent[x] == x ? x : (parent[x] = find(parent[x])); }
void unite(int a, int b) {
    a = find(a); b = find(b);
    if (a == b) return;
    if (size[a] < size[b]) swap(a, b);
    parent[b] = a; size[a] += size[b];
}

Uses: Kruskal's MST, connected components in a stream of edges, cycle detection while adding edges, "number of islands II", equivalence classes, percolation.

Trie (prefix tree)

  • A tree where each edge is a character; a path from the root spells a prefix; nodes flagged as "end of word".
  • insert, search, startsWith: O(L) where L = key length — independent of the number of stored keys.
  • Space can be large (a child pointer per possible character); compress with a radix/Patricia trie (merge single-child chains) or use a hash map per node.
  • Uses: autocomplete, spell-check, IP routing (longest-prefix match), dictionary word games, replacing a hash set when you need prefix queries or lexicographic order.
class Trie:
    def __init__(self):
        self.kids = {}          # char -> Trie node (hash map: sparse-alphabet friendly)
        self.end = False       # True if a word ends exactly here

    def insert(self, word):
        node = self
        for ch in word:
            node = node.kids.setdefault(ch, Trie())  # descend, creating as needed -- O(L)
        node.end = True

    def _walk(self, prefix):
        node = self
        for ch in prefix:
            if ch not in node.kids: return None
            node = node.kids[ch]
        return node

    def search(self, word):      # whole word present?
        n = self._walk(word);  return bool(n) and n.end
    def starts_with(self, pre):  # any word with this prefix? (autocomplete)
        return self._walk(pre) is not None
Cheat Sheet
  • Union-Find ops: find, union, connected, over a parent[] forest.
  • Union by size/rank + path compression → O(α(n)) ≈ O(1) amortised.
  • Union-Find uses: Kruskal MST, dynamic connectivity, cycle detection on edge insertions, equivalence classes.
  • Can't efficiently split sets or enumerate a set's members (unless you keep extra structures).
  • Trie: edges = characters, mark word-ends. insert/search/prefix = O(key length).
  • Trie lookup time is independent of dictionary size; space is the cost.
  • Compress with radix/Patricia trie; or store children in a hash map for sparse alphabets.
  • Trie uses: autocomplete, longest-prefix match (routing), lexicographic iteration, prefix counting.
Q&A
What two optimisations make union-find near-constant-time?
Union by rank/size (attach the shorter/smaller tree under the taller/larger one) and path compression (flatten the find path toward the root). Together they give O(α(n)) amortised.
What is α(n) practically?
The inverse Ackermann function — it grows so slowly it's ≤ 4 for any n that fits in the universe. So union-find operations are effectively O(1).
Name a classic use of union-find.
Kruskal's minimum spanning tree: sort edges by weight, add an edge only if its endpoints are in different sets (no cycle), then union them.
What's the time complexity of trie search, and why is that notable?
O(L), the length of the search key — it doesn't depend on how many keys are stored, unlike a BST (O(L log n)) or even a hash set in the worst case.
When is a trie better than a hash set?
When you need prefix operations (autocomplete, "does any stored word start with X"), longest-prefix matching, sorted/lexicographic iteration, or counting words with a given prefix — things a hash set can't do without scanning everything.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does find(x) return in a disjoint-set structure?
The representative (root) element of the set containing x. Two elements are in the same set iff their find results are equal.
What does each edge in a trie represent?
A single character; the path from the root to a node spells out a string prefix.
Trie operation to check if any word starts with "pre"?
startsWith("pre") — walk the trie following p→r→e; success if all edges exist. O(3).

Intermediate core

Use union-find to detect a cycle while building an undirected graph from a list of edges.
For each edge (u, v): if find(u) == find(v), adding this edge creates a cycle — report it. Otherwise union(u, v). Processing all m edges is O(m · α(n)).
Why does path compression alone (without union by rank) still give good amortised bounds?
Path compression alone gives O(log n) amortised per operation, and with union by rank/size added it drops to O(α(n)). Either optimisation alone is decent; both together are what reach inverse-Ackermann. Union by rank alone (no compression) is O(log n) worst case per op.
Estimate a trie's memory for 100k English words vs a hash set.
A naive array-of-26-children trie allocates 26 pointers per node; with millions of nodes that's tens of MB — often several times the hash set, which stores each string once plus a small overhead. Mitigations: hash-map children (only allocate used slots), radix/Patricia compression (collapse non-branching chains, big win for real dictionaries), or a DAWG (merge identical suffix subtrees). The trie "pays" memory to buy O(L) prefix queries.

Advanced deep

How would you support union and find plus rollback (undo the last k unions)?
Use union by rank/size without path compression (compression makes changes hard to undo), and keep a stack recording each union's effect (which root got a new parent, and the old rank/size). To roll back, pop the stack and restore parent and rank/size. Ops become O(log n) instead of O(α), but you get persistence — used in "offline dynamic connectivity" and segment-tree-on-time / DSU-on-tree techniques. A weighted / partially-persistent variant supports full history queries.
What is a suffix trie / suffix automaton used for, and why not just a plain trie of all suffixes?
A trie of all n suffixes of a length-n string has O(n²) nodes — too big. A suffix tree (Ukkonen's algorithm, O(n)) path-compresses it to O(n) nodes and answers substring queries, longest repeated substring, longest common substring of two strings, etc. in O(pattern length). A suffix automaton is an even more compact O(n) DAG recognising all substrings, great for counting distinct substrings. Both trade implementation complexity for powerful linear-time string analytics that a plain trie or hashing can't match.

Range Queries: Prefix Sums, Fenwick & Segment Trees

Answer “aggregate over subarray [l, r]” thousands of times — with or without updates — in O(1) or O(log n) instead of O(n).

Notes

A common problem shape is “given an array, repeatedly ask for the sum / min / max / gcd over a range [l, r]”, sometimes with element updates in between. Recomputing each answer is O(n) per query. This page covers the four standard structures that make it fast: prefix sums (O(1) query, no updates), the Fenwick tree / BIT (O(log n) point-update and prefix-query, tiny constant), the segment tree (O(log n) for any associative operation, plus lazy propagation for range updates), and the sparse table (O(1) query for idempotent ops on a static array). It also covers how to choose between them and the difference/2-D variants.

Prefix sums — static, O(1)

What / why. Precompute cumulative sums; any range sum is a subtraction. The simplest and fastest when the array never changes.

pre = [0] * (n + 1)
for i in range(n):
    pre[i + 1] = pre[i] + a[i]        # O(n) build

def range_sum(l, r):                  # inclusive [l, r]
    return pre[r + 1] - pre[l]        # O(1)

# 2-D "integral image": pre[i+1][j+1] = a[i][j] + pre[i][j+1] + pre[i+1][j] - pre[i][j]
# any rectangle sum is then 4 lookups. Used in image processing and grid problems.

# Difference array: to add v to a[l..r] many times, then read once:
diff[l] += v; diff[r + 1] -= v            # O(1) per range update
# final a[i] = prefix sum of diff  -- O(n) once at the end

Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree) — point update + prefix query

What / why. An implicit tree stored in one array where index i is responsible for the range of length i & -i ending at i. Both update and prefix_sum walk O(log n) indices using the lowbit trick. Smallest code and constant of the update-capable structures; works for any invertible, associative operation (sum, xor).

class BIT:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        self.t = [0] * (n + 1)          # 1-indexed

    def update(self, i, delta):          # add delta at position i (1-indexed)
        while i <= self.n:
            self.t[i] += delta
            i += i & -i                   # jump to the next range that covers i

    def prefix(self, i):                 # sum of a[1..i]
        s = 0
        while i > 0:
            s += self.t[i]
            i -= i & -i                   # drop the lowest set bit
        return s

    def range_sum(self, l, r):
        return self.prefix(r) - self.prefix(l - 1)
# range-update + point-query: run a BIT over a difference array.
# range-update + range-query: keep two BITs (a classic trick).

Segment tree — any associative operation, plus range updates

What / why. A binary tree where each node holds the aggregate of its array range. A query splits [l, r] into O(log n) canonical nodes; a point update walks one root-to-leaf path. Unlike the BIT it works for non-invertible operations (min, max, gcd, “count of value > x”, custom struct merges), and with lazy propagation it does range updates (add v to [l, r]) in O(log n) too. Cost: 2–4× the memory and a bigger constant than a BIT.

# iterative sum segment tree, array-backed, 1-based leaves at [n, 2n)
class SegTree:
    def __init__(self, a):
        self.n = len(a)
        self.t = [0] * (2 * self.n)
        self.t[self.n:] = a
        for i in range(self.n - 1, 0, -1):
            self.t[i] = self.t[2 * i] + self.t[2 * i + 1]     # build O(n)

    def update(self, i, val):               # set a[i] = val
        i += self.n; self.t[i] = val
        while i > 1:
            i //= 2; self.t[i] = self.t[2 * i] + self.t[2 * i + 1]

    def query(self, l, r):                  # sum of [l, r)   -- O(log n)
        res = 0; l += self.n; r += self.n
        while l < r:
            if l & 1: res += self.t[l]; l += 1
            if r & 1: r -= 1; res += self.t[r]
            l //= 2; r //= 2
        return res
# swap '+' for min/max/gcd to get a different query; add a lazy[] array for range updates.

Sparse table — O(1) static idempotent queries

What / why. For an idempotent operation (min, max, gcd — where overlapping the two halves doesn’t change the answer), precompute the answer for every range whose length is a power of two: st[k][i] = op over a[i .. i + 2^k - 1]. A query [l, r] is then op(st[k][l], st[k][r - 2^k + 1]) with k = floor(log2(r - l + 1)) — two lookups, O(1). No updates.

K = (n).bit_length()
st = [[0] * n for _ in range(K)]
st[0] = a[:]
for k in range(1, K):
    for i in range(n - (1 << k) + 1):
        st[k][i] = min(st[k-1][i], st[k-1][i + (1 << (k-1))])   # O(n log n)

def range_min(l, r):                       # inclusive
    k = (r - l + 1).bit_length() - 1
    return min(st[k][l], st[k][r - (1 << k) + 1])

Choosing

NeedUse
Static array, O(1) sum queriesPrefix sums (2-D variant for grids)
Many range updates, one final readDifference array + one prefix pass
Point updates + prefix/range sum (invertible)Fenwick / BIT — least code, smallest constant
Range updates, or min/max/gcd/custom mergesSegment tree (+ lazy propagation for range updates)
Static array, O(1) range-min/max/gcdSparse table
Cheat Sheet
  • Prefix sums: pre[i+1]=pre[i]+a[i]; sum(l,r)=pre[r+1]-pre[l]. Build O(n), query O(1), no updates. 2-D for grids.
  • Difference array: range-update O(1) (d[l]+=v; d[r+1]-=v), then one prefix pass for the final values. Inverse of prefix sums.
  • Fenwick / BIT: point-update + prefix-query, both O(log n), tiny constant, ~n memory. Lowbit: i & -i. Invertible ops only (sum, xor). Two BITs → range-update + range-query.
  • Segment tree: node = aggregate of its range; query/update O(log n) for any associative op (sum, min, max, gcd, custom). Lazy propagation → range updates O(log n). ~2–4n memory, bigger constant.
  • Sparse table: build O(n log n), query O(1), static, idempotent ops only (min/max/gcd). Two lookups per query.
  • Decision: static+sum → prefix; point-update+sum → BIT; range-update / min-max / merges → segment tree; static RMQ → sparse table.
Q&A
When can you use a prefix-sum array and when can’t you?
Use it when the array is static (no element updates between queries) and the operation is invertible — sum, xor, product-over-a-group. Then every range query is O(1). You can’t use it when elements change (each update would cost O(n) to rebuild the suffix of pre) or when the operation is min/max/gcd (no inverse, so you can’t “subtract” the left part out). For updates use a Fenwick tree or segment tree; for min/max on a static array use a sparse table.
Fenwick tree vs segment tree — which and why?
Prefer the Fenwick tree when you only need point updates and prefix/range sums (or another invertible op): it’s ~10 lines, uses one array of size n, and has the smallest constant factor. Use a segment tree when you need any of: a non-invertible operation (min, max, gcd, “first index ≥ x”), range updates (with lazy propagation), or per-node auxiliary data / custom merge logic. The segment tree is strictly more general but costs 2–4× the memory and a larger constant, and more code.
What is lazy propagation and what does it buy you?
A technique for segment trees that defers range updates. When you apply “add v to [l, r]”, instead of touching every leaf, you update the O(log n) canonical nodes covering [l, r] and store a pending “+v for my whole subtree” tag on each. The tag is pushed down to children only when a later query or update actually needs to descend past that node. This makes range updates O(log n) instead of O(n), enabling problems like “add to a range, then query range sum/min” efficiently.
Why does a sparse table only work for min/max/gcd and not sum?
A sparse-table query combines two precomputed power-of-two ranges that overlap (unless the query length is itself a power of two). For an idempotent operation — min(x, x) = x, likewise max and gcd — counting the overlap twice doesn’t change the result. For sum, the overlap would be added twice, giving the wrong answer. Sum on a static array can still be O(1) with a plain prefix-sum array; sum with updates needs a BIT or segment tree.
You need range sum with both point updates and range updates. What structure?
A segment tree with lazy propagation handles both uniformly: a point update is a range update on [i, i]. Alternatively, the two-BIT trick supports range-update + range-query for sums in O(log n) with less memory: maintain BIT1 and BIT2 so that the prefix sum up to i is BIT1.prefix(i) * i - BIT2.prefix(i), and a range-add updates both. Use the segment tree if the operation isn’t a plain sum or you also need range-min/max.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Given a static array, how do you answer sum(l, r) in O(1)?
Build a prefix-sum array pre where pre[i] is the sum of the first i elements (pre[0] = 0). Then sum(l, r) (inclusive) is pre[r + 1] - pre[l]. Build is O(n), each query O(1).
What’s the time complexity of update and query in a Fenwick tree?
Both are O(log n) — each walks at most ⌈log₂ n⌉ indices by repeatedly adding or removing the lowest set bit (i & -i).

Intermediate core

Design a structure for “given an array, support add(i, x) and range_min(l, r)”. Walk through why each simpler option fails.
Prefix approach fails: min has no inverse, so you can’t compute min(l, r) from precomputed prefixes by “subtracting”. Sparse table fails: it gives O(1) range-min but only on a static array — there’s no efficient update. Fenwick tree mostly fails: a BIT can do prefix-min with point updates that only decrease a value, but a general add(i, x) (which can increase) breaks it, because a BIT node can’t recompute its min without rescanning its range. Segment tree works: build a segment tree where each node stores the minimum of its range (build O(n)). add(i, x): update leaf i, then walk up recomputing node.min = min(left.min, right.min) — O(log n). range_min(l, r): recurse, returning +∞ for ranges disjoint from [l, r], the node’s stored min for ranges fully inside, and the min of the two child results otherwise — O(log n) because at most two nodes per level are “partial”. If you additionally needed range_add(l, r, x), add lazy propagation: store a pending delta on each node, apply it to the node’s min, and push it to children on the way down.

Advanced deep

You’re building analytics over a stream of (timestamp, metric) events and need fast range aggregates (sum, count, p95) over arbitrary time windows, with late-arriving data. Design the data structures.
Bucketise time: fix a base granularity (say 1s or 1m) and accumulate events into fixed buckets keyed by floor(ts / g). Each bucket holds a small mergeable summary, not the raw events: for sum/count a scalar; for quantiles a mergeable sketch (t-digest or DDSketch — both merge associatively and answer p95 with bounded relative error in kilobytes). This makes every bucket an element of an associative monoid. Range aggregation: over the array of buckets, build a segment tree whose node type is that summary (merge = add sums/counts, merge sketches). A window query [t0, t1] becomes a segment-tree range query over the covered buckets — O(log B) merges, each O(sketch size). Point/bucket updates from new events are O(log B). For very long horizons, add a second, coarser layer (hour buckets) built by rolling up the minute layer, so old data is queried at lower resolution — a hierarchical / multi-resolution time-series structure; sparse tables or precomputed prefix summaries can serve the fully-immutable historical tail in O(1). Late-arriving data: because a bucket’s summary is a mergeable monoid, a late event is just another update(bucket, summary_of_one_event) that re-merges up the tree — O(log B), no rebuild. Bound lateness with a watermark: buckets older than the watermark are sealed and moved to the immutable prefix layer (and any event later than that goes to a small “corrections” side log surfaced separately). Concurrency / scale: shard buckets by time range or by series across nodes; each shard keeps its own segment tree; a query fans out and merges partials (the monoid makes this trivial and order-independent). Persist sealed buckets to columnar storage; keep the recent, mutable tail in memory. Why not raw prefix sums: they’d give O(1) sum/count but (a) can’t do quantiles, (b) can’t absorb a late event without an O(n) suffix rebuild. The segment-tree-of-sketches keeps updates logarithmic, handles non-invertible aggregates, and is naturally distributable. Net: fixed-granularity buckets holding mergeable summaries (scalars + t-digest/DDSketch), a segment tree over them for O(log B) windowed aggregates and O(log B) late-data updates, a coarser rollup layer plus O(1) prefix summaries for the immutable historical tail, and sharding with monoid merges for horizontal scale.

Probabilistic Structures: Bloom Filter, Count-Min, HyperLogLog

Trade a small, tunable error for tiny fixed memory and O(1) operations — the structures behind “maybe in the set”, “roughly how many”, and “how many distinct” at scale.

Notes

When an exact answer would need gigabytes, a probabilistic (sketch) data structure gives an approximate answer in a small, fixed amount of memory with a bounded error you choose in advance. This page covers the three that come up constantly in large-scale systems: the Bloom filter (approximate set membership — no false negatives, tunable false positives), the Count-Min sketch (approximate item frequencies / heavy hitters), and HyperLogLog (approximate count of distinct elements). For each: how it works, the error/space trade-off, that they’re mergeable (so they distribute), and where they’re used — plus when a wrong answer is unacceptable and you shouldn’t use them.

Bloom filter — approximate set membership

What / how. A bit array of m bits and k independent hash functions. add(x): set the k bits h₁(x) … hₖ(x). contains(x): return true only if all k of those bits are set. Guarantees. No false negatives (if you added it, all its bits are set). Tunable false positives (unrelated elements’ bits can collide to look present). Cannot delete (removing bits would create false negatives) — use a counting Bloom filter (small counters instead of bits) or a cuckoo filter (stores fingerprints, supports delete, often less space at low FPR).

FPR ≈ (1 - e^(-k·n/m))^k        # n = #elements inserted
optimal k = (m / n) · ln 2       # then FPR ≈ 0.6185^(m/n)
# rule of thumb: ~9.6 bits per element -> ~1% FPR ; ~14.4 bits -> ~0.1%

class Bloom:
    def __init__(self, m, k): self.b = bytearray((m + 7) // 8); self.m, self.k = m, k
    def _idx(self, x):
        h1, h2 = hash((0, x)), hash((1, x))
        return [(h1 + i * h2) % self.m for i in range(self.k)]   # double hashing
    def add(self, x):
        for i in self._idx(x): self.b[i // 8] |= 1 << (i % 8)
    def __contains__(self, x):
        return all(self.b[i // 8] >> (i % 8) & 1 for i in self._idx(x))

Uses. LSM-tree / SSTable “does this file maybe contain the key” (RocksDB, Cassandra, HBase, Bigtable) to skip disk reads; web-cache / CDN “have we seen this URL”; blocklist pre-check before an expensive exact lookup; crawler URL dedup; “one-time” email/coupon checks. Two Bloom filters over the same m, k merge by bitwise OR.

Count-Min sketch — approximate frequencies

What / how. A d × w grid of counters with d hash functions (one per row). add(x, c): for each row r, grid[r][h_r(x)] += c. count(x): min over the d rows of grid[r][h_r(x)] — the min cancels most of the over-count from other items colliding into the same cell. Guarantee. Never under-estimates; over-estimates by at most ε · N with probability 1 - δ, where w = ⌈e/ε⌉ and d = ⌈ln(1/δ)⌉.

# w controls the error size, d controls the confidence
w = ceil(e / eps);  d = ceil(ln(1 / delta))
# e.g. eps = 0.001, delta = 1e-6  ->  w ≈ 2719, d ≈ 14  ->  ~150 KB of counters
add(x): for r in range(d): C[r][h[r](x) % w] += 1
count(x): return min(C[r][h[r](x) % w] for r in range(d))

Uses. Heavy hitters / top-k (pair with a small heap), streaming rate-limiting and abuse detection, per-key traffic estimates in network monitoring, “trending” counts, feature frequency in ML pipelines. Count-Min sketches with the same dimensions/hashes merge by element-wise addition.

HyperLogLog — approximate distinct count

What / how. To count distinct elements: hash each element to a uniform bit string; use the first p bits to pick one of 2^p buckets, and in that bucket keep the maximum number of leading zeros seen in the remaining bits (+1). Intuition: seeing a hash with r leading zeros suggests you’ve processed roughly 2^r distinct values. Combine the buckets with a bias-corrected harmonic mean. Result. Standard error ≈ 1.04 / √(2^p) — e.g. p = 14 (16384 buckets, ~12 KB) gives ~0.8% error for cardinalities from a handful up to billions.

add(x):
    h = hash64(x)
    bucket = h >> (64 - p)
    rank = leading_zeros(h << p | (1 << (p - 1))) + 1
    M[bucket] = max(M[bucket], rank)

estimate():
    Z = 1 / sum(2.0 ** -M[i] for i in range(m))
    return alpha_m * m * m * Z          # + small/large-range corrections
# merge two HLLs: M_merged[i] = max(M_a[i], M_b[i])  -- trivially distributed

Uses. Unique visitors / unique devices / distinct search queries, Redis PFADD/PFCOUNT/PFMERGE, Presto/BigQuery/Redshift APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT, cardinality of set intersections/unions (via inclusion–exclusion). The bucketwise-max merge makes it ideal for map-reduce and per-shard aggregation.

When not to use them

  • A wrong answer is unacceptable (billing, security allow-lists where a false positive grants access, correctness-critical dedup) — or use the sketch only as a fast pre-filter before an exact check.
  • You need to enumerate the elements, or delete arbitrary elements (plain Bloom can’t; use counting Bloom / cuckoo filter), or get exact counts.
  • The data set is small enough that an exact hash set / hash map fits comfortably — then just use that.
  • You mis-size the structure: an over-full Bloom filter’s FPR climbs toward 1; a Count-Min with too few columns over-counts badly. Size from the expected n and the error you can tolerate, and monitor fill.
Cheat Sheet
  • Bloom filter = set membership. m bits, k hashes; add sets k bits; contains = all k set. No false negatives, tunable false positives. No delete (→ counting Bloom / cuckoo filter). Merge = OR. ~10 bits/elem → ~1% FPR; optimal k = (m/n)ln2.
  • Count-Min sketch = frequencies. d×w counters; add increments one per row; count = min over rows (kills collision over-count). Never under-counts. w=⌈e/ε⌉, d=⌈ln(1/δ)⌉. Merge = add. Pair with a heap for top-k.
  • HyperLogLog = distinct count. Bucket by hash prefix, track max leading-zeros per bucket, harmonic-mean combine. Error ≈ 1.04/√(2^p); p=14 → ~12 KB, ~0.8% error, works to billions. Merge = bucketwise max.
  • All three: fixed tiny memory, O(1) ops, one-directional bounded error, mergeable → distribute well.
  • Don’t use when a wrong answer is unacceptable (or use as a pre-filter), when you must enumerate/delete/get exact counts, or when an exact structure just fits.
Q&A
Can a Bloom filter give a false negative?
No. If an element was inserted, every one of its k bit positions was set, and bits are never cleared, so contains will always find them all set and return true. It can give a false positive — an element that was never inserted whose k positions happen to all have been set by other elements. So “absent” is definitive; “present” means “probably”.
Why do LSM-tree databases (RocksDB, Cassandra) put a Bloom filter on each SSTable?
A read may have to check many on-disk sorted files. Before doing a disk seek + binary search in a file, the engine checks that file’s in-memory Bloom filter: if it says “definitely not here”, the file is skipped entirely. Only files that say “maybe” are actually read. Since most files genuinely don’t contain a given key, this turns most point lookups from O(#files) disk reads into 1–2, at the cost of a few bits of RAM per key and an occasional wasted read on a false positive.
Why does Count-Min take the minimum across its rows?
Each row’s counter for x equals x’s true count plus the counts of every other item that hashed to the same cell in that row — so every row’s estimate is an over-estimate. Different rows use different hash functions, so the set of colliding items differs per row. The row with the fewest (or lightest) collisions gives the tightest over-estimate, and that’s the minimum. Taking the min never drops below the true count (no collisions can make it smaller) and usually gets close to it.
How does HyperLogLog count billions of distinct items in a few kilobytes?
It never stores the items. It hashes each to a uniform bit pattern and, per bucket, keeps only a small integer: the longest run of leading zeros observed. A uniformly random hash has a run of r leading zeros with probability 2^-r, so the longest run seen across N distinct hashes is about log₂ N — observing a run of 30 zeros suggests ~230 distinct values passed through. Using 2^p buckets and averaging (bias-corrected harmonic mean) reduces the variance to ~1.04/√(2^p). Total storage is 2^p small counters (6 bits each) — ~12 KB for p = 14.
You need “unique users per day” across 200 shards. Why is HyperLogLog a good fit and a plain hash set not?
A hash set of user IDs would need memory proportional to the number of distinct users and you’d have to ship all 200 shards’ sets to one place and union them — huge network and memory cost, and unioning is O(total size). HyperLogLog uses a fixed ~12 KB per shard regardless of user count, and merging is bucketwise max — associative, commutative, O(buckets), and lossless with respect to the estimate. So each shard maintains its own HLL, you merge the 200 tiny sketches, and read the count — with ~1% error, which is fine for a “unique users” metric. You also get unique-users-per-week for free by merging seven daily sketches.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does a Bloom filter answer, and what error can it make?
It answers approximate set membership: “is x in the set?”. It can return a false positive (says present when absent) with a tunable probability, but never a false negative (never says absent when present).
Which structure estimates the number of distinct elements in a stream?
HyperLogLog — approximate cardinality in ~kilobytes with ~1–2% error, and mergeable across shards by taking the bucketwise maximum.

Intermediate core

Design a duplicate-URL detector for a web crawler seeing billions of URLs. Exact vs Bloom vs hybrid — walk the trade-offs.
Exact hash set: correct, but billions of URLs × tens of bytes each = hundreds of GB — needs a distributed store or disk, and every “seen?” check is a lookup there. Works but expensive and slow. Pure Bloom filter: ~10 bits/URL → a few GB of RAM for billions of URLs at ~1% false-positive rate. Fast, O(1), fits in memory. The cost is that ~1% of new URLs are wrongly judged “already seen” and silently dropped — the crawler misses ~1% of pages. Also, a fixed-size Bloom filter degrades as it fills, so you must size it for the final n or use a scalable Bloom filter (a chain of filters, adding a new one as the current fills). No deletes (fine here — you never “unsee” a URL). Hybrid (recommended): Bloom filter as a fast in-memory pre-filter in front of an exact store. “Bloom says absent” (definitive) → it’s new, enqueue it and add to both. “Bloom says present” (maybe) → do one exact lookup to confirm; if the exact store also has it, skip; if not (a Bloom false positive), it’s new after all. This makes the common case (most URLs genuinely new or genuinely seen) hit only the Bloom filter, sends only the ~1% ambiguous cases to the exact store, and has zero false drops. Shard the exact store and the Bloom filter by URL hash; each shard’s Bloom filter is independent. Persist the Bloom filter periodically so a restart doesn’t lose dedup state. If memory is tight and a tiny miss rate is acceptable (some crawlers accept it), pure scalable Bloom is the pragmatic choice.

Advanced deep

Design the metrics layer for a large API platform: per-endpoint request rate, error rate, top-N noisy clients, and distinct users — all with bounded memory per node and cheap aggregation across nodes.
Model each metric as a mergeable sketch so per-node memory is bounded and cross-node aggregation is an associative merge. (1) Request & error rate per endpoint: exact counters are fine here — the number of endpoints is small (hundreds/thousands). Keep windowed counters (e.g. a ring of 1-second buckets) per (endpoint, status-class); merge across nodes by adding. Sketches aren’t needed unless you also want per-(endpoint×client×region) breakdowns, where the key space explodes — then use Count-Min per endpoint keyed by the sub-dimension. (2) Top-N noisy clients (heavy hitters over a huge, unbounded client-id space): a Count-Min sketch (sized for, say, ε=0.1% of total traffic, δ=1e-6 → ~150 KB) plus a small min-heap of the current top-N candidates. On each request: cms.add(client); if cms.count(client) exceeds the heap’s minimum, insert/update it in the heap. Per node this is O(1) and ~150 KB regardless of client count. Merge across nodes by adding the Count-Min grids and re-deriving the top-N from the union heap (or the Space-Saving / Misra-Gries algorithm if you want deterministic error bounds on the heap itself). (3) Distinct users per endpoint per window: a HyperLogLog per (endpoint, time-bucket), ~12 KB each at p=14, ~1% error. hll.add(user_id) per request. Merge across nodes and across time buckets by bucketwise max — so “distinct users this hour” is the merge of 60 one-minute sketches from every node, computed in O(nodes × buckets × 16384) with no data movement of raw IDs. Set intersection (“users who hit both A and B”) via inclusion–exclusion on HLLs, accepting the compounded error. (4) Latency percentiles (bonus, same pattern): a mergeable quantile sketch (t-digest / DDSketch) per (endpoint, bucket), few KB, merge associatively for p50/p95/p99 over any window/region. Pipeline: each node maintains its sketches in memory for the recent window, flushes serialized sketches (not raw events) to a collector every few seconds; the collector merges by key and stores the merged sketches in a time-series/columnar store; dashboards and alerts query merged sketches. Sizing & safety: pick each sketch’s parameters from the tolerable error and monitor fill/estimate-vs-exact on a sampled subset; keep exact counters for the handful of metrics where being off by 1% is unacceptable (billing, SLA reporting) — there, sample-and-extrapolate or full exact aggregation on a smaller key space. Why this shape: bounded per-node memory independent of cardinality, O(1) update on the hot path, and aggregation that is a commutative/associative merge — so it parallelises across nodes and time windows with no re-shuffling of raw data, which is exactly what a large platform needs.

Sorting Algorithms

Know the four that matter, their trade-offs, and when comparison sorts stop being optimal.

Notes

Sorting arranges elements in order, and the choice of algorithm is a set of trade-offs among worst-case time, average time, extra space, stability (does it preserve the relative order of equal keys), and adaptivity to already-sorted data. This page covers the comparison sorts you must know — insertion, merge, quicksort, heapsort — with their guarantees and when each is the right pick, the Ω(n log n) lower bound for comparison sorts, and the linear-time non-comparison sorts (counting, radix, bucket) and the constraints that let them beat it.

The comparison sorts

AlgorithmAvg / WorstSpaceStableNotes
QuicksortO(n log n) / O(n²)O(log n)NoFastest in practice; partition around a pivot. Worst case on bad pivots — use random / median-of-three.
Merge sortO(n log n) / O(n log n)O(n)YesPredictable; great for linked lists and external sorting; needs a buffer.
HeapsortO(n log n) / O(n log n)O(1)NoIn-place with a guaranteed bound; cache-unfriendly, so usually slower than quicksort.
Insertion sortO(n²) / O(n²)O(1)YesO(n) on nearly-sorted data; used as the base case for small subarrays inside quick/merge.

Introsort (C++ std::sort): quicksort, switch to heapsort when recursion goes too deep, insertion sort for tiny ranges — quicksort speed with an O(n log n) guarantee. Timsort (Python, Java objects): merge sort that exploits existing sorted "runs".

# quicksort: partition around a (randomised) pivot, recurse each side
import random
def quicksort(a, lo=0, hi=None):
    if hi is None: hi = len(a) - 1
    if lo >= hi: return
    a[lo], a[random.randint(lo, hi)] = a[random.randint(lo, hi)], a[lo]  # random pivot
    p, i = a[lo], lo
    for j in range(lo + 1, hi + 1):
        if a[j] < p:
            i += 1; a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]        # push smaller-than-pivot left
    a[lo], a[i] = a[i], a[lo]
    quicksort(a, lo, i - 1); quicksort(a, i + 1, hi)

Stability

A stable sort preserves the relative order of equal keys. Matters when you sort by one field after another (sort by name, then stably by department). Merge/insertion/Tim are stable; quick/heap are not (without extra work).

people = [("Ann", "Sales"), ("Bob", "Eng"), ("Cy", "Sales")]
people.sort(key=lambda p: p[0])       # 1) by name
people.sort(key=lambda p: p[1])       # 2) STABLE by dept -> Ann before Cy preserved within Sales
# [('Bob','Eng'), ('Ann','Sales'), ('Cy','Sales')]  -- an unstable sort could swap Ann/Cy

The Ω(n log n) lower bound

Any sort that only compares elements needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case (there are n! orderings; each comparison gives 1 bit; log₂(n!) ≈ n log n).

# a comparison sort is a decision tree: each internal node is "a[i] < a[j]?"
#   leaves           >= n!   (one per possible permutation)
#   tree height      >= log2(n!)  ~=  n*log2(n) - 1.44n   (Stirling)
#   worst-case comparisons = height  ->  Omega(n log n)
# counting/radix/bucket dodge this by NOT comparing -- they read key structure instead.

Non-comparison sorts (beat the bound with structure)

  • Counting sort — O(n + k) for integer keys in a small range k. Stable.
  • Radix sort — O(d · (n + b)) for d digits in base b; sorts fixed-width integers/strings by repeated stable counting sort per digit.
  • Bucket sort — O(n) expected for uniformly distributed reals in [0, 1).
# counting sort: keys are ints in [0, k)
def counting_sort(a, k):
    count = [0] * k
    for x in a: count[x] += 1          # tally each value -- O(n)
    out, i = [], 0
    for v in range(k):
        out += [v] * count[v]           # emit in value order -- O(n + k) total
    return out
# radix sort = counting-sort by the 1s digit, then 10s, then 100s ... (each pass stable)
Cheat Sheet
  • Quicksort: avg O(n log n), worst O(n²), in-place, not stable, fastest real-world. Randomise the pivot.
  • Merge sort: always O(n log n), stable, O(n) space, ideal for linked lists / external sort.
  • Heapsort: always O(n log n), O(1) space, not stable, cache-unfriendly.
  • Insertion sort: O(n²), but O(n) on nearly-sorted; small-array base case.
  • std::sort = introsort; Python/Java-objects = Timsort (adaptive, stable).
  • Comparison sorts can't beat Ω(n log n) worst case.
  • Small integer range → counting sort O(n+k); fixed-width keys → radix sort; uniform reals → bucket sort.
  • Need stability → merge / Tim / counting; not quick / heap.
Q&A
Why is quicksort usually faster than merge sort despite the same average complexity?
It sorts in place with a tight, cache-friendly partition loop and low constant factors; merge sort does extra data movement into and out of an O(n) buffer. Quicksort's downside is the O(n²) worst case, mitigated by randomised pivots / introsort.
What does "stable" mean and when do you need it?
Equal elements keep their original relative order. You need it for multi-key sorting done in passes (sort by secondary key, then stably by primary), or when equal keys carry associated data whose order is meaningful.
Why can't a comparison sort be faster than O(n log n)?
There are n! possible input orderings; a comparison yields one bit, so a decision tree distinguishing all of them has depth ≥ log₂(n!) ≈ n log n. Any algorithm restricted to comparisons hits this bound in the worst case.
When is counting/radix sort applicable and what's the catch?
When keys are integers (or fixed-width) in a bounded range. Counting sort is O(n + k); if k is huge (e.g. 64-bit values), that's worse than n log n. Radix sort handles large ranges by processing digit-by-digit but needs a stable per-digit sort and extra space.
Which sort would you use for a nearly-sorted array?
Insertion sort (O(n) when few elements are out of place) or Timsort, which detects and merges existing sorted runs.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Worst-case complexity of quicksort?
O(n²) — when the pivot is consistently the smallest or largest element (e.g. already-sorted input with a naive first-element pivot).
Which of merge sort and heapsort is stable?
Merge sort. Heapsort is not stable.
Which common sort is O(1) auxiliary space and always O(n log n)?
Heapsort.

Intermediate core

How does introsort avoid quicksort's O(n²) worst case?
It tracks recursion depth; if it exceeds ~2·log₂n (a sign of pathological pivots), it switches the current partition to heapsort, which is O(n log n) guaranteed. Small partitions are finished with insertion sort. So the common case runs at quicksort speed and the worst case is bounded.
You must sort 100 million 32-bit integers, memory permitting. What's fast?
LSD radix sort on the 4 bytes (four stable counting-sort passes, base 256) — O(4n) with a 256-entry histogram, typically beating comparison sorts for this size and key type. If memory is the constraint, an in-place MSD radix or introsort. If it doesn't fit in RAM, external merge sort.
Sort a large singly linked list. Which algorithm and why?
Merge sort. It needs only sequential access and O(1) extra pointers to split and merge (no random indexing, no shifting), it's stable, and it's O(n log n) worst case. Quicksort on a list is awkward (partitioning needs care) and heapsort needs random access.

Advanced deep

Explain how external merge sort handles data that doesn't fit in memory.
Phase 1 (run formation): read chunks that fit in RAM, sort each in memory (e.g. with quicksort/heapsort), write each as a sorted "run" to disk — producing ceil(N/M) runs for N records and memory M. Phase 2 (merge): do a k-way merge of the runs using a min-heap over the current front element of each run, streaming output to disk; k is bounded by how many input buffers fit in memory. If there are more runs than one merge pass can handle, merge in multiple passes (each pass reduces run count by factor k), giving O(N log_k(N/M)) I/O. Large sequential I/O and double-buffering are what make it practical.
Why does Timsort exist, and what real bug did its "galloping"/merge invariant have?
Real-world data has pre-sorted runs (appended logs, partially updated lists); Timsort finds ascending/descending runs, extends short ones with binary insertion sort to a minimum length, and merges runs while maintaining size invariants on a stack, using "galloping mode" (exponential search) when one run is consistently winning the merge. A 2015 formal-verification effort found the run-merging stack invariant was too weak, allowing the merge stack to exceed its preallocated size — a latent ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException for adversarial inputs. It was fixed by strengthening the invariant / enlarging the stack. Lesson: even widely-deployed, "obviously correct" library sorts had a subtle bound bug found only by proof.

Recursion, Backtracking & DP

From "solve it in terms of smaller subproblems" to "and remember the answers".

Notes

This page covers three related techniques. Recursion solves a problem in terms of smaller instances of itself, with a base case to stop; understanding the call stack is key to reasoning about it. Backtracking is recursion that explores a decision tree, undoing each choice before trying the next — the template for permutations, subsets, N-queens, and constraint puzzles. Dynamic programming applies when a recursion has overlapping subproblems: cache the results (memoisation) or build them bottom-up (tabulation) to turn exponential into polynomial. It covers the templates, how to spot DP, and the state/transition/order framework.

Recursion

  • A function that calls itself on smaller input. Needs a base case and progress toward it.
  • Each call uses a stack frame → recursion depth is bounded by the stack (~10k–100k frames). Deep or unbounded recursion → stack overflow — convert to iteration + explicit stack, or use tail recursion where the language optimises it.
  • Cost = (number of calls) × (work per call). Draw the recursion tree.
def factorial(n):
    if n <= 1: return 1          # BASE CASE -- without it: infinite recursion / stack overflow
    return n * factorial(n - 1)  # progress: argument strictly shrinks toward the base

# same thing iteratively, when depth could exceed the stack limit:
def factorial_it(n):
    r = 1
    for k in range(2, n + 1): r *= k
    return r

Backtracking

Systematically build candidates and abandon ("prune") a partial candidate as soon as it can't lead to a solution. Template:

def backtrack(state, choices):
    if is_solution(state): record(state); return
    for choice in choices:
        if valid(state, choice):
            apply(state, choice)          # choose
            backtrack(state, next_choices) # explore
            undo(state, choice)            # un-choose

Uses: permutations/combinations/subsets, N-Queens, Sudoku, word search, generating valid parentheses, graph colouring. Worst case is exponential; pruning is what makes it tractable.

Dynamic programming

Applies when a problem has optimal substructure (optimal answer built from optimal sub-answers) and overlapping subproblems (the same sub-answers recur). Two styles:

Memoisation (top-down)Tabulation (bottom-up)
Formrecursion + a cachefill a table in dependency order
Computesonly needed statesall states
Overheadrecursion + hashingtight loops, often O(1) space with rolling arrays

Steps: define the state, write the recurrence (transition), identify base cases, decide iteration order, optionally reduce space. Classics: Fibonacci, coin change, knapsack, longest common subsequence, edit distance, longest increasing subsequence, matrix-chain, grid paths.

# coin change (fewest coins for `amount`) -- bottom-up tabulation
def min_coins(coins, amount):
    dp = [0] + [float('inf')] * amount     # dp[x] = fewest coins to make x
    for x in range(1, amount + 1):
        for c in coins:
            if c <= x:
                dp[x] = min(dp[x], dp[x - c] + 1)  # take one coin c, then solve x-c
    return dp[amount] if dp[amount] != float('inf') else -1
# states = amount+1, transitions = len(coins)  ->  O(amount * len(coins))

# top-down equivalent: recursion + @lru_cache(None) on the same recurrence

DP vs greedy vs divide-and-conquer

Divide-and-conquer: subproblems are independent (merge sort). DP: subproblems overlap. Greedy: a locally optimal choice is provably globally optimal (needs a proof; fails for 0/1 knapsack, works for fractional knapsack / Huffman / MST).

# GREEDY works for fractional knapsack: take highest value/weight first
def frac_knapsack(items, cap):        # items = [(value, weight)]
    items.sort(key=lambda it: it[0]/it[1], reverse=True)
    take = 0.0
    for v, w in items:
        if cap >= w: take += v; cap -= w        # whole item
        else: take += v * (cap / w); break       # fraction -> optimal here
    return take
# the SAME greedy is WRONG for 0/1 knapsack (can't split) -> needs DP over (item, capacity)
Cheat Sheet
  • Recursion needs a base case + strict progress toward it. Depth ≤ stack size.
  • Convert deep recursion to an explicit stack loop to avoid overflow.
  • Backtracking = choose / explore / un-choose, with pruning; exponential worst case.
  • DP requires optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems.
  • Memoisation = recursion + cache (lazy). Tabulation = iterative table fill (eager, often O(1) space with rolling rows).
  • DP recipe: state → recurrence → base cases → evaluation order → space optimisation.
  • Overlapping subproblems → DP; independent subproblems → divide & conquer; provable local-optimal → greedy.
  • Time ≈ (number of states) × (transitions per state).
Q&A
What two properties must a problem have for DP to apply?
Optimal substructure (the optimal solution is composed of optimal solutions to subproblems) and overlapping subproblems (the same subproblems are solved repeatedly in a naive recursion).
Memoisation vs tabulation?
Memoisation is top-down: normal recursion with a cache, computing only the states you actually reach. Tabulation is bottom-up: fill a table in an order where each entry's dependencies are already done, often allowing O(1)-space rolling arrays. Same complexity; different constant factors and stack usage.
How is backtracking different from brute force?
Brute force enumerates all candidates fully. Backtracking builds candidates incrementally and abandons a partial path the moment it violates a constraint (pruning), cutting the search space dramatically.
When does greedy fail where DP succeeds?
0/1 knapsack: taking the highest value-per-weight item first can be suboptimal because you can't take fractions. DP considers all combinations. Coin change with arbitrary denominations is another (greedy fails for {1, 3, 4} making 6).
What limits recursion depth in practice?
The call stack size (often ~1–8 MB → tens of thousands of frames). Beyond that you get a stack overflow; rewrite iteratively with an explicit stack or use an explicit work queue.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What must every recursive function have?
A base case (a condition that returns without recursing) and recursive calls that move strictly toward it.
What does memoisation add to plain recursion?
A cache of already-computed results, so each distinct subproblem is solved once. Turns exponential recomputation into polynomial.
Three steps of the backtracking pattern?
Choose (apply a candidate), explore (recurse), un-choose (undo it before trying the next).

Intermediate core

Coin change (min coins for amount N, unlimited coins). Give the DP.
dp[0] = 0; for a from 1 to N: dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - c]) over all coins c ≤ a (infinity if none). Answer dp[N]. O(N × #coins) time, O(N) space. This is bottom-up tabulation; the state is "min coins to make amount a".
Why is naive recursive Fibonacci O(φⁿ) and how does DP fix it?
fib(n) calls fib(n-1) and fib(n-2), recomputing the same values exponentially — the call tree has ~φⁿ nodes. Memoise (cache fib(k)) or tabulate (loop keeping the last two values) to make it O(n) time, and O(1) space with the rolling-variable version.
Generate all subsets of a set. Recursion structure?
For each element, branch on "include it" or "exclude it", recursing on the rest; at the end of the list, emit the current subset. 2ⁿ leaves. Equivalent iterative form: for each of the 2ⁿ bitmasks, pick the elements whose bit is set.

Advanced deep

How do you reduce a 2-D DP (like edit distance) from O(nm) space to O(min(n, m))?
Each cell dp[i][j] depends only on dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1] — i.e. the current and previous row. Keep two 1-D arrays (prev row, current row), or even one array plus a saved "diagonal" scalar, iterating so you overwrite each entry only after its old value has been used. Space drops to O(m) (choose the shorter dimension as the row). The catch: you lose the ability to backtrack the actual alignment/path afterward — if you need the path, either keep the full table, or use Hirschberg's divide-and-conquer to recover it in O(nm) time and O(min(n,m)) space.
What is "DP on subsets" (bitmask DP) and its complexity, with an example?
State = a subset of up to ~20 items encoded as an integer bitmask, plus maybe a position. Transitions add/remove one element. Example: Travelling Salesman — dp[mask][i] = shortest path visiting exactly the set mask, ending at city i; transition dp[mask | (1<<j)][j] = min(dp[mask][i] + dist[i][j]). Complexity O(2ⁿ · n²), feasible for n ≤ ~20. Also used for assignment problems, "minimum number of groups", and Steiner-tree-style problems. The exponential factor is inherent (these are NP-hard); bitmask DP just makes small n practical and is far better than brute-forcing n! orders.

Recurrences & the Master Theorem

Turning "T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n" into "Θ(n log n)" without hand-waving.

Notes

A recurrence expresses an algorithm’s running time in terms of its cost on smaller inputs — e.g. merge sort is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n). Solving it turns that self-reference into a closed-form growth rate so you can compare algorithms. This page covers where recurrences come from (divide-and-conquer, recursive definitions), the Master Theorem and its three cases for T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), the recursion-tree method for building intuition, and the common recurrences that don’t fit the Master Theorem (uneven splits, subtract-and-conquer, the Akra–Bazzi cases).

Where recurrences come from

A divide-and-conquer algorithm that makes a recursive calls on inputs of size n/b, plus f(n) non-recursive work, has running time T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n).

def merge_sort(a):
    if len(a) <= 1: return a                 # base case
    mid = len(a) // 2
    l = merge_sort(a[:mid])                  # a = 2 recursive calls...
    r = merge_sort(a[mid:])                  # ...on inputs of size n/b, b = 2
    return merge(l, r)                       # f(n) = O(n) merge work
# => T(n) = 2*T(n/2) + n

The Master Theorem

Compare f(n) with the "watershed" n^(log_b a):

CaseConditionResult
1f(n) = O(n^(log_b a - ε)) (leaves dominate)T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a))
2f(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) · log^k n) (balanced)T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) · log^(k+1) n)
3f(n) = Ω(n^(log_b a + ε)) + regularity (root dominates)T(n) = Θ(f(n))
Merge sort:  T = 2T(n/2) + n    a=2,b=2 -> n^1;  f=n  -> case 2 -> Θ(n log n)
Binary srch: T = 1T(n/2) + 1    a=1,b=2 -> n^0;  f=1  -> case 2 -> Θ(log n)
Strassen:    T = 7T(n/2) + n^2  a=7,b=2 -> n^2.81; f=n^2 -> case 1 -> Θ(n^2.81)
Naive D&C:   T = 2T(n/2) + n^2  -> f dominates -> case 3 -> Θ(n^2)

When the Master Theorem doesn't apply

Unequal splits (T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n), varying subproblem count, subtractive recurrences (T(n) = T(n-1) + n → Θ(n²)), or gaps between the cases. Then use the recursion-tree method (sum the work per level × number of levels) or substitution (guess a bound, prove by induction). Akra–Bazzi generalises the Master Theorem to unequal splits.

# subtractive (NOT a T(n/b) form) -- unroll it instead of the Master Theorem:
#   T(n) = T(n-1) + n
#        = T(n-2) + (n-1) + n
#        = ...
#        = 1 + 2 + ... + n  =  n(n+1)/2  =  Theta(n^2)

# recursion-tree for T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n  (unequal split):
#   every level still sums to ~n of work; longest path has log_{3/2} n levels
#   => Theta(n log n)
Cheat Sheet
  • T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n); watershed = n^(log_b a).
  • Case 1: f smaller → Θ(n^(log_b a)). Case 2: f equal (×log^k) → add one log. Case 3: f bigger (+ regularity) → Θ(f(n)).
  • 2T(n/2)+n → n log n. T(n/2)+1 → log n. 2T(n/2)+1 → n. T(n-1)+1 → n. T(n-1)+n → n². 2T(n-1)+1 → 2ⁿ.
  • Recursion tree: (work at level i) × (number of levels). Geometric → dominated by biggest term.
