  • Substitution: guess, plug into the recurrence, prove by induction, fix constants.
  • Unequal splits → Akra–Bazzi or recursion tree, not the plain Master Theorem.
Q&A
Solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n).
Θ(n log n) — Master Theorem case 2 (a=2, b=2, watershed n^1, f(n)=n matches).
Solve T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1).
Θ(log n) — each level halves n and does constant work; there are log₂n levels. (Binary search.)
Solve T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n).
Θ(n²). It's not a Master-Theorem form (subtractive, not divisive); unrolling gives n + (n-1) + … + 1.
Why does the Master Theorem sometimes not give an answer?
There are "gaps" between the three cases (e.g. f(n) is polynomially larger than the watershed by less than any ε, like a log factor difference that case 3 doesn't cover), or the recurrence has unequal splits / varying a and b. Use a recursion tree or substitution.
What does the "regularity condition" in case 3 ensure?
That a·f(n/b) ≤ c·f(n) for some c < 1 — i.e. the work really does shrink geometrically down the tree so the root term dominates the sum. Without it, the top-level cost isn't necessarily the total.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What running time does T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n represent?
Θ(n log n) — the merge sort / balanced divide-and-conquer recurrence.
How many levels does a recurrence that divides n by b have?
About log_b(n).
What's the watershed function in the Master Theorem?
n^(log_b a) — you compare f(n) against it to pick the case.

Intermediate core

Use a recursion tree to solve T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n.
Level i has 3^i nodes each doing n/2^i work → level cost (3/2)^i · n. Summing a growing geometric series over log₂n levels is dominated by the last level: 3^(log₂n) = n^(log₂3) ≈ n^1.585. So T(n) = Θ(n^log₂3). (Master Theorem case 1 agrees: watershed n^1.585 > f(n)=n.)
Quickselect's average recurrence is T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n). Solve it and contrast with quicksort.
Θ(n) — one recursive call on ~half, linear partition work; the sum n + n/2 + n/4 + … = 2n. Quicksort makes two recursive calls (2T(n/2) + n) → n log n. Recursing on only one side is what drops selection from n log n to linear.

Advanced deep

The median-of-medians selection recurrence is T(n) = T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + O(n). Why is it O(n)?
The two recursive sizes sum to n/5 + 7n/10 = 9n/10 < n, a constant factor below n. A recursion tree then has per-level work forming a decreasing geometric series (ratio 9/10), so the total is O(n / (1 - 9/10)) = O(10n) = O(n). Substitution confirms: assume T(k) ≤ ck for k < n, then T(n) ≤ c(n/5) + c(7n/10) + an = (9c/10)n + an ≤ cn when c ≥ 10a. The key insight: any recurrence where the child sizes sum to (1-ε)n with linear extra work is linear — this is why the "5" in median-of-medians matters (groups of 3 would give sizes summing to ≥ n and break linearity).
State the Akra–Bazzi method and one thing it handles that the Master Theorem can't.
For T(n) = ∑ a_i T(b_i n + h_i(n)) + g(n) with 0 < b_i < 1, find the unique p with ∑ a_i b_i^p = 1; then T(n) = Θ(n^p (1 + ∫_1^n g(u)/u^(p+1) du)). It handles unequal split sizes (different b_i) and multiple different-sized subproblems — e.g. T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n, where solving (1/3)^p + (2/3)^p = 1 gives p = 1, and the integral contributes a log, yielding Θ(n log n). The plain Master Theorem requires all subproblems to be the same size n/b.

Binary Search & Search on the Answer

The algorithm everyone "knows" and half get wrong — plus its most powerful use.

Notes

Binary search finds a target in a sorted range in O(log n) by repeatedly halving the search interval. Its real power in interviews is “search on the answer”: if you can write a monotonic yes/no predicate over a numeric range (“can we do it with budget x?”), binary search finds the boundary even when there’s no array to search. This page covers a correct, off-by-one-free template, the lower_bound/upper_bound primitives and what they return, and the parametric-search pattern with worked examples.

Correct binary search

# find target in sorted a, or -1
lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
while lo <= hi:
    mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2      # avoids overflow in fixed-width langs
    if a[mid] == target: return mid
    elif a[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
    else: hi = mid - 1
return -1

Pitfalls: (lo+hi)/2 overflow; lo < hi vs ≤; forgetting mid±1 (infinite loop); wrong half on ties. Prefer the half-open invariant style below.

lower_bound / upper_bound (the useful primitives)

# first index i with a[i] >= x  (lower_bound)
lo, hi = 0, len(a)                 # half-open [lo, hi)
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if a[mid] < x: lo = mid + 1
    else: hi = mid
return lo

upper_bound uses a[mid] ≤ x. From these: count of x = upper - lower; insertion point; predecessor/successor.

Binary search on the answer (parametric search)

If you can write a monotonic predicate feasible(v) — false for small v, true for large v (or vice versa) — binary-search v over its range even if the data isn't sorted. The search space is the answer, not an array.

# min ship capacity to move all packages in D days
lo, hi = max(w), sum(w)
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if days_needed(w, mid) <= D: hi = mid   # feasible -> try smaller
    else: lo = mid + 1
return lo

Classic uses: "minimum largest sum" splits, Koko eating bananas, allocate books, sqrt/nth-root, "can we finish in T time", aggressive cows. Complexity: O(log(range) × cost(feasible)).

Cheat Sheet
  • Requires a sorted array (for value search) or a monotonic predicate (for answer search).
  • mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2 to dodge overflow.
  • Prefer half-open [lo, hi) with while lo < hi; return lo. Fewer off-by-one bugs.
  • lower_bound: first ≥ x (branch a[mid] < x). upper_bound: first > x (branch a[mid] ≤ x).
  • count(x) = upper_bound(x) − lower_bound(x).
  • Search on the answer when: answer is an integer/real in a known range, and feasible(v) is monotonic.
  • Complexity O(log n) for arrays; O(log(range) × check cost) for parametric search.
  • For floats, iterate a fixed ~100 times or until hi - lo < eps.
Q&A
Why write mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2 instead of (lo + hi) / 2?
In fixed-width integer languages, lo + hi can overflow when both are large; the subtraction form stays in range. (Famous bug in java.util.Arrays.binarySearch, fixed 2006.)
What does lower_bound return?
The index of the first element ≥ x (or end if all are smaller) — the position where x would be inserted to keep the array sorted, before any equal elements.
What must be true to "binary search on the answer"?
There's a predicate feasible(v) that is monotonic in v — once it becomes true (or false) it stays that way — so the boundary can be found by halving the value range.
Give a problem solved by parametric binary search.
"Split an array into k contiguous parts minimising the largest part sum": binary-search the answer S; feasible(S) = "greedily we can form ≤ k parts each with sum ≤ S", which is monotonic in S.
Time complexity of binary search on a range of size R with an O(n) feasibility check?
O(n log R).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Precondition for binary search on an array?
The array must be sorted (by the key you're searching on).
Complexity of binary search?
O(log n) comparisons.
How do you count occurrences of x in a sorted array in O(log n)?
upper_bound(x) - lower_bound(x).

Intermediate core

Find the minimum in a rotated sorted array (no duplicates).
Binary search on the "is this half sorted" property: if a[mid] > a[hi], the min is in (mid, hi] → lo = mid + 1; else it's in [lo, mid] → hi = mid. Loop while lo < hi; answer is a[lo]. O(log n). (Duplicates degrade it to O(n) worst case.)
Koko eats bananas: n piles, she eats k/hour, wants to finish in H hours. Minimum k?
Binary-search k in [1, max(pile)]. feasible(k) = sum(ceil(pile/k)) ≤ H, which decreases monotonically as k grows. Take the smallest feasible k. O(n log(max pile)).

Advanced deep

Find the median of two sorted arrays in O(log(min(m, n))).
Binary-search a partition of the shorter array at index i (so j = (m+n+1)/2 - i partitions the other). The partition is correct when A[i-1] ≤ B[j] and B[j-1] ≤ A[i] — then everything left of both cuts is the lower half. If A[i-1] > B[j], move i left; else move it right. Handle ±∞ sentinels at the ends. The median is derived from max(A[i-1], B[j-1]) and (for even total) min(A[i], B[j]). The search space is only the shorter array, hence O(log(min(m,n))).
When would you binary-search on a real-valued answer, and how do you decide the iteration count?
For continuous optimisation with a monotone feasibility test — minimum radius to cover points, minimum speed, geometric thresholds. You can't compare to an exact target, so loop either until hi - lo < ε (relative or absolute, chosen from the required output precision) or a fixed number of iterations. Each iteration halves the interval, so ~100 iterations shrinks a range of 10^9 to below 10^-21 — well past double precision — making a fixed count (60–100) a safe, loop-condition-free choice that also avoids infinite loops from floating-point rounding near the boundary.

Two Pointers & Sliding Window

Turning nested loops into a single linear pass over an array or string.

Notes

The two-pointer technique walks two indices through a sequence — from opposite ends, or one chasing the other — to solve in O(n) problems that look like they need O(n²) nested loops. The sliding window is the “fast/slow, same direction” variant for “best/longest/shortest contiguous subarray with property P”. This page covers the standard forms (opposite ends on a sorted array, fast/slow for cycle detection, fixed and variable windows), the invariant you maintain, and the conditions that make the technique valid (usually monotonicity or a sorted input).

Two-pointer forms

  • Opposite ends — l = 0, r = n-1, move inward. Sorted-array pair sum, container-with-most-water, palindrome check, reverse in place, 3-sum (fix one, two-pointer the rest).
  • Same direction / fast-slow — one pointer scans, another marks a boundary. Remove duplicates in place, partition, cycle detection (Floyd), nth-from-end of a list.
# pair summing to target in a SORTED array
l, r = 0, len(a) - 1
while l < r:
    s = a[l] + a[r]
    if s == target: return (l, r)
    elif s < target: l += 1
    else: r -= 1

Sliding window

  • Fixed size k — slide a window of width k, updating an aggregate in O(1) (sum, or a deque for max/min).
  • Variable size — expand right to include elements; while the window is invalid, shrink from left. Track the best valid window. "Longest substring without repeats", "smallest subarray with sum ≥ S", "min window substring".
left = 0; best = 0; seen = {}
for right, ch in enumerate(s):
    if ch in seen and seen[ch] >= left:
        left = seen[ch] + 1
    seen[ch] = right
    best = max(best, right - left + 1)

When it applies

The array/string is traversed once, the window's validity is monotonic (growing the window can only make it "more invalid", shrinking only "more valid"), and each element enters and leaves the window O(1) times → overall O(n).

# APPLIES: smallest subarray with sum >= S  (all positives -> monotonic)
left = tot = 0; best = float('inf')
for right, x in enumerate(a):
    tot += x
    while tot >= S:                  # window valid -> try to shrink it
        best = min(best, right - left + 1)
        tot -= a[left]; left += 1
# DOESN'T APPLY: array has negatives -> adding an element can DECREASE the sum,
# so shrinking isn't safe. Use prefix sums + a hash map / monotonic deque instead.
Cheat Sheet
  • Opposite-end pointers: sorted pair/triplet sums, palindrome, in-place reverse, two-way partition.
  • Fast/slow pointers: dedup in place, list cycle (Floyd), middle of list, nth-from-end.
  • Fixed window: slide, add the entering element, remove the leaving one; deque for window max/min.
  • Variable window: expand right; while invalid, advance left; record best when valid.
  • Each index moves forward only → O(n) time, O(1)–O(k) space.
  • Needs monotonic feasibility (shrinking always helps validity). Otherwise it doesn't work.
  • Unsorted "pair sum" → hash set, not two pointers (two pointers needs order).
Q&A
Why does the two-pointer pair-sum need a sorted array?
Movement decisions rely on order: if the sum is too small you must increase it, which (in a sorted array) means moving the left pointer right; too big → move the right pointer left. Without order, neither move is guaranteed to help.
Fixed vs variable sliding window?
Fixed: the window is always exactly k wide; you slide it and update an aggregate. Variable: the window grows and shrinks to stay valid under some constraint, and you track the largest/smallest valid window seen.
What's the complexity of the "longest substring without repeating characters" sliding-window solution?
O(n) time (each character is added and removed from the window at most once), O(min(n, alphabet)) space for the last-seen map.
When can't you use a sliding window for a "subarray with property P" problem?
When P isn't monotonic under window growth — e.g. subarrays with a target sum when negatives are allowed (extending the window can decrease the sum), so shrinking doesn't reliably restore validity. Use prefix sums + hash map instead.
How do fast/slow pointers find a linked-list cycle?
Advance slow by 1 and fast by 2; if they ever meet, there's a cycle; if fast hits null, there isn't. O(n) time, O(1) space (Floyd's).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Check if a string is a palindrome with two pointers.
l=0, r=len-1; while l < r: if s[l] != s[r] return false; l++, r--. Return true. O(n)/O(1).
Remove duplicates from a sorted array in place, returning the new length.
Slow pointer w=1; for r from 1: if a[r] != a[r-1], a[w++] = a[r]. Return w.
What structure gives O(1) window max for a fixed sliding window?
A monotonic deque of indices with decreasing values.

Intermediate core

Smallest subarray with sum ≥ S (positive integers).
Expand right, adding to a running sum; while sum ≥ S, record right - left + 1 and subtract a[left++]. O(n). Works because all elements are positive, so shrinking always reduces the sum monotonically.
3-sum: all unique triplets summing to 0.
Sort. For each i (skip duplicates), two-pointer l = i+1, r = n-1 for pairs summing to -a[i], skipping duplicate l/r values. O(n²) time, O(1) extra (excluding the sort).

Advanced deep

Minimum window substring (smallest window of s containing all chars of t, with multiplicity). Outline and complexity.
Count needed chars of t in a map; track required = distinct chars needed and formed = distinct chars currently satisfied in the window. Expand right, decrement the char's need; when a char's window count reaches its needed count, formed++. While formed == required, update the best window and shrink from left, incrementing needs and decrementing formed when a char drops below its requirement. Each pointer advances ≤ n times → O(n) (or O(n · alphabet) with array counts). The subtlety is only counting a char as "formed" when it hits exactly the required multiplicity, not on every occurrence.
"Subarrays with exactly K distinct integers" — why compute atMost(K) - atMost(K-1)?
A sliding window naturally counts subarrays with at most K distinct (expand right, shrink left while distinct > K, add right - left + 1 each step). "Exactly K" isn't directly windowable because shrinking to fix "too many distinct" also skips valid "exactly K" windows. But exactly-K = (at-most-K) − (at-most-(K−1)), and each at-most query is an O(n) window pass, so the whole thing is O(n). This "exactly = atMost(k) - atMost(k-1)" trick generalises to many counting-with-a-bound problems.

Greedy Algorithms

Take the best-looking option now — and be able to prove that never regrets.

Notes

A greedy algorithm builds a solution by repeatedly taking the choice that looks best right now, never reconsidering. It’s fast and simple when it works — but it only produces the optimum for problems with the right structure, and it’s wrong (sometimes subtly) for the rest. This page covers the idea and the risk, how to prove a greedy choice is safe (the exchange/“stay ahead” arguments), the classic problems where greedy is provably optimal (activity selection, Huffman coding, fractional knapsack), and cautionary cases where it fails (0/1 knapsack, general coin change).

The idea & the risk

Build a solution by repeatedly making the locally optimal choice, never reconsidering. Fast and simple — but only correct if the problem has the greedy-choice property (a globally optimal solution can be reached by greedy local choices) and optimal substructure. Otherwise greedy gives a wrong (but plausible) answer.

# activity selection: max non-overlapping intervals
def max_activities(intervals):        # intervals = [(start, finish)]
    intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])  # greedy KEY: earliest finish first
    count, last_end = 0, float('-inf')
    for s, f in intervals:
        if s >= last_end:             # fits after the last chosen one
            count += 1; last_end = f    # commit, never reconsider
    return count

Proving greedy correct

  • Exchange argument — take any optimal solution; show you can swap one of its choices for the greedy choice without making it worse; repeat until it is the greedy solution.
  • Stays-ahead — show that after each step the greedy partial solution is at least as good as any other on the relevant metric.
# Exchange argument for activity selection (sketch):
#   Let OPT be any optimal set. Let g = greedy's first pick (earliest finish).
#   Let o = OPT's first activity by finish time.  finish(g) <= finish(o).
#   Swap o -> g in OPT: g still doesn't overlap OPT's remaining activities
#   (they start after finish(o) >= finish(g)).  |OPT| unchanged, still optimal.
#   Recurse on the rest  =>  greedy matches an optimal solution.

Where greedy works

ProblemGreedy rule
Activity selectionalways pick the next activity with the earliest finish time
Fractional knapsacktake items by value/weight ratio, fractional last one
Huffman codingrepeatedly merge the two lowest-frequency nodes
Kruskal / Prim MSTadd the cheapest safe edge (cut property)
Dijkstrafinalise the closest unvisited node
Interval scheduling / mergingsort by start or end, sweep
Jump game / gas stationtrack the furthest reachable / running tank
# Kruskal MST: sort edges by weight, add each if it joins two components
def kruskal(n, edges):                # edges = [(w, u, v)]
    edges.sort()                      # greedy: cheapest edge first
    parent = list(range(n))
    def find(x):
        while parent[x] != x: parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]; x = parent[x]
        return x
    total = 0
    for w, u, v in edges:
        ru, rv = find(u), find(v)
        if ru != rv:                  # safe edge (no cycle) -> take it
            parent[ru] = rv; total += w
    return total

Where greedy fails

0/1 knapsack (can't take fractions → need DP), coin change with arbitrary denominations ({1,3,4}, target 6: greedy 4+1+1, optimal 3+3), longest path, most TSP variants.

# coin change, denominations {1, 3, 4}, target 6
def greedy_coins(coins, amount):
    coins.sort(reverse=True)
    n = 0
    for c in coins:
        n += amount // c; amount %= c
    return n
greedy_coins([1, 3, 4], 6)   # 3  ->  4 + 1 + 1   (WRONG)
# optimal is 2  ->  3 + 3.  Need DP (see min_coins) for arbitrary denominations.
Cheat Sheet
  • Greedy = locally optimal choice each step, no backtracking. Needs greedy-choice property + optimal substructure.
  • Prove with an exchange argument or stays-ahead; if you can't, greedy is probably wrong.
  • Most greedy solutions start by sorting by the right key (finish time, ratio, weight…).
  • Works: activity selection (earliest finish), fractional knapsack (best ratio), Huffman, Kruskal/Prim, Dijkstra, interval merge.
  • Fails: 0/1 knapsack, general coin change, longest path — use DP.
  • If a counterexample exists, one is usually tiny (3–4 elements) — try to find it before coding.
Q&A
What two properties justify a greedy algorithm?
The greedy-choice property (a locally optimal choice is part of some globally optimal solution) and optimal substructure (an optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems).
How do you prove a greedy algorithm correct?
Usually an exchange argument: assume an optimal solution differs from greedy at the first choice; swap in the greedy choice and show the solution is no worse; conclude greedy is optimal. Or "greedy stays ahead" of any alternative at every step.
Why does greedy work for fractional knapsack but not 0/1?
Fractional: you can always fill the remaining capacity exactly with the best-ratio item, so taking highest ratio first is safe. 0/1: a high-ratio item might crowd out two items that together are better; you can't split, so local choice isn't safe — DP is required.
Give a coin system where greedy fails.
Denominations {1, 3, 4}, amount 6: greedy takes 4 then 1 then 1 (3 coins); optimal is 3 + 3 (2 coins). Greedy is optimal only for "canonical" systems (like standard currency).
What's the greedy rule for activity selection?
Sort activities by finish time; repeatedly pick the earliest-finishing activity compatible with those already chosen. This maximises the count of non-overlapping activities.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does a greedy algorithm never do?
Reconsider or undo a choice it has made. It commits to the local optimum at each step.
First step of most greedy interval problems?
Sort the intervals — usually by end time (scheduling) or start time (merging).
Is greedy guaranteed optimal for the 0/1 knapsack?
No. Use dynamic programming.

Intermediate core

Merge overlapping intervals.
Sort by start. Walk through; if the current interval's start ≤ the last merged interval's end, extend that end to max(end, cur.end); otherwise append the current interval. O(n log n).
Gas station: can you complete the circuit? Return the start index or -1.
If total gas < total cost, return -1. Otherwise sweep once tracking a running tank; whenever it goes negative, reset the tank to 0 and set start = i + 1. The final start works. O(n). Correctness: if you run out going from start to i, no station in [start, i] can be a valid start.

Advanced deep

Prove the earliest-finish-time greedy is optimal for activity selection.
Exchange argument. Let greedy pick activities g₁, g₂, … (each the earliest-finishing compatible one). Let OPT be any optimal schedule o₁, o₂, … sorted by finish. Claim: finish(g₁) ≤ finish(o₁) since g₁ is the globally earliest finish. So replacing o₁ with g₁ in OPT keeps it valid (g₁ ends no later, so it can't conflict with o₂) and the same size. Induct on the remaining problem (activities starting after finish(g₁)). Hence some optimal solution starts with every greedy choice, so greedy achieves the optimal count.
What is a matroid and why does it matter for greedy?
A matroid is a set system (E, I) where I (the "independent sets") is non-empty, downward-closed, and satisfies the exchange property: if A, B ∈ I with |A| < |B|, some element of B\A can be added to A keeping it independent. Theorem (Rado–Edmonds): the greedy algorithm — sort elements by weight descending, add each if it keeps the set independent — finds a maximum-weight independent set exactly when the structure is a matroid. This explains why Kruskal's MST works (forests form a graphic matroid) and gives a principled test for "will greedy work here?" beyond ad hoc exchange arguments.

Divide & Conquer

Split into independent subproblems, solve each, combine — and analyse with a recurrence.

Notes

Divide and conquer solves a problem by splitting it into smaller independent subproblems, solving those recursively, and combining the results. It’s the pattern behind merge sort, quickselect, fast multiplication, and closest-pair, and its running time is analysed with a recurrence. This page covers the split/solve/combine template, the canonical algorithms and where the work happens (in the split, or in the combine), and how divide-and-conquer differs from dynamic programming — the subproblems here don’t overlap.

The pattern

  1. Divide the problem into a subproblems of size n/b.
  2. Conquer each recursively (base case for small n).
  3. Combine the sub-answers in f(n) work.
def max_subarray(a, lo, hi):          # classic D&C skeleton
    if lo == hi: return a[lo]            # CONQUER: base case
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    left  = max_subarray(a, lo, mid)      # DIVIDE: two independent halves
    right = max_subarray(a, mid + 1, hi)
    cross = cross_sum(a, lo, mid, hi)     # COMBINE: best span crossing the midpoint, O(n)
    return max(left, right, cross)
# T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)  ->  O(n log n)

Cost: T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n) — solve with the Master Theorem (see Recurrences topic). Key requirement: the subproblems are independent (no shared sub-answers — that's DP).

Canonical algorithms

AlgorithmDivide / CombineTime
Merge sortsplit in half / merge two sorted halvesΘ(n log n)
Quicksortpartition around a pivot / nothingΘ(n log n) avg
Quickselectpartition / recurse one side onlyΘ(n) avg
Binary searchcompare middle / recurse one halfΘ(log n)
Karatsuba multiply3 half-size multiplies / adds & shiftsΘ(n^1.585)
Strassen matmul7 half-size productsΘ(n^2.807)
Closest pair of pointssplit by x / check a thin stripΘ(n log n)
Count inversionsmerge sort, count cross pairsΘ(n log n)
# quickselect: k-th smallest in O(n) average -- recurse into ONE side only
import random
def quickselect(a, k):
    p = random.choice(a)
    lo  = [x for x in a if x < p]
    eq  = [x for x in a if x == p]
    hi  = [x for x in a if x > p]
    if k < len(lo):            return quickselect(lo, k)
    if k < len(lo) + len(eq):  return p        # found it, no further recursion
    return quickselect(hi, k - len(lo) - len(eq))
# T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n)  ->  O(n)  (vs O(n log n) if you recursed both sides)

D&C vs DP

Both break a problem down. D&C: subproblems don't overlap, so plain recursion is fine. DP: subproblems overlap, so you must cache (memoise) or build a table to avoid exponential recomputation.

# D&C is fine: merge_sort(left) and merge_sort(right) share NO subproblems.

# DP needed: naive fib recomputes the same calls exponentially
def fib(n):
    return n if n < 2 else fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)  # fib(n-2) computed by BOTH branches -> O(phi^n)

from functools import lru_cache
@lru_cache(None)                           # cache overlapping subproblems -> O(n)
def fib_dp(n):
    return n if n < 2 else fib_dp(n-1) + fib_dp(n-2)
Cheat Sheet
  • Divide into a subproblems of size n/b, conquer recursively, combine in f(n).
  • Analyse: T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n) → Master Theorem.
  • Subproblems must be independent (overlapping → that's DP).
  • Recurse on one side (binary search, quickselect) → often O(n) or O(log n) instead of O(n log n).
  • Combine step is usually where the cleverness is (merge, strip check, cross-inversion count).
  • Karatsuba/Strassen: fewer recursive multiplications at the cost of more additions.
  • Parallelises well — independent subproblems on different cores.
Q&A
What distinguishes divide & conquer from dynamic programming?
D&C's subproblems are independent — each is solved once, no overlap. DP's subproblems overlap, so it stores results to avoid recomputing them.
Why is quickselect O(n) average while quicksort is O(n log n)?
After partitioning, quickselect recurses into only one side (the one containing the target rank); quicksort recurses into both. The one-sided recurrence T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n) sums to O(n).
How does Karatsuba multiply two n-digit numbers faster than schoolbook?
Schoolbook needs 4 half-size multiplications (T = 4T(n/2) + n → n²). Karatsuba computes the middle term as (a+b)(c+d) - ac - bd, needing only 3 (T = 3T(n/2) + n → n^log₂3 ≈ n^1.585).
What's the combine step in counting inversions?
During the merge of two sorted halves, whenever you take an element from the right half before the left half is exhausted, every remaining left-half element forms an inversion with it — add len(leftRemaining) to the count.
Does divide & conquer parallelise well?
Yes — the subproblems are independent, so they can run on separate threads/cores; only the combine step needs synchronisation. Merge sort and many D&C algorithms have good parallel speedup.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Name the three phases of divide & conquer.
Divide, conquer (recurse), combine.
Which is D&C: binary search or Dijkstra?
Binary search (split, recurse one half). Dijkstra is greedy.
Recurrence for merge sort?
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) → Θ(n log n).

Intermediate core

Find the maximum subarray sum with divide & conquer.
Split in half. The answer is the best of: max subarray entirely in the left half (recurse), entirely in the right half (recurse), or crossing the midpoint (best suffix of left + best prefix of right, computed in O(n)). T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n log n). (Kadane's does it in O(n), but the D&C version is the classic teaching example.)
Quickselect: find the k-th smallest element.
Partition the array around a (randomly chosen) pivot. If the pivot lands at index k, return it. If k < pivot index, recurse on the left part; else recurse on the right with adjusted k. Average O(n); worst O(n²) unless you use median-of-medians for a guaranteed O(n).

Advanced deep

Closest pair of points in the plane in O(n log n). What makes the combine step O(n)?
Sort by x, split at the median x into L and R; recursively get the min distances d_L, d_R; let d = min(d_L, d_R). A closer pair straddling the split must lie within a vertical strip of width 2d around the median. Sort the strip's points by y (or keep a y-sorted list merged bottom-up). For each point in the strip, you only need to check the next ~7 points in y-order — a geometric packing argument shows no more than a constant number of points can be within d in a d × 2d box. So the strip check is O(n), giving T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n log n).
Why did Strassen's algorithm matter historically, and why is it rarely used for small matrices?
It broke the "obvious" Θ(n³) barrier for matrix multiplication in 1969, opening the field of fast matrix multiplication (current record ~n^2.37 via Coppersmith–Winograd descendants). Practically: the recursion has a large constant (7 multiplies but 18 add/subtracts of n/2 matrices), worse cache/vectorisation behaviour, and numerical stability concerns. Optimised BLAS uses the cubic algorithm with heavy blocking/SIMD for typical sizes and only switches to Strassen (with a cutoff to cubic at the base) for very large matrices. So it's a genuine asymptotic improvement whose crossover point is in the hundreds–thousands.

Number Theory & Modular Arithmetic

GCD, primes, and doing arithmetic “mod 1e9+7” without overflowing — the toolkit behind counting problems, hashing, and combinatorics.

Notes

A recurring class of problems needs a small set of number-theory tools: the greatest common divisor, listing or testing primes, and doing arithmetic modulo a large prime (usually 1_000_000_007) so answers stay in range — “count the arrangements, modulo M”, string hashing, modular inverses for combinations, cryptography-adjacent puzzles. This page covers Euclid’s GCD and its extended form, safe modular add/subtract/multiply and the overflow trap, fast (binary) exponentiation, modular inverse (Fermat and extended-Euclid), the Sieve of Eratosthenes and fast factorisation, and computing nCr mod p with precomputed factorials.

GCD, LCM, and extended Euclid

What / why. gcd(a, b) is the largest integer dividing both; Euclid’s algorithm computes it in O(log min(a, b)). The extended version also returns coefficients x, y with ax + by = gcd(a, b) — the basis of the modular inverse and the Chinese Remainder Theorem.

def gcd(a, b):
    while b: a, b = b, a % b
    return a

def lcm(a, b):
    return a // gcd(a, b) * b          # divide FIRST to avoid overflow

def ext_gcd(a, b):                     # returns (g, x, y) with a*x + b*y = g
    if b == 0: return (a, 1, 0)
    g, x1, y1 = ext_gcd(b, a % b)
    return (g, y1, x1 - (a // b) * y1)

Modular arithmetic — the overflow trap

  • Add / multiply then take % m. For subtraction, use (a - b + m) % m so the result is never negative (in C/C++/Java % can return a negative value for negative operands).
  • The #1 bug: a * b where a, b are near 1e9 overflows a 32-bit int long before you get to take the mod. Cast one operand to 64-bit: (long long)a * b % m. If m itself can be ~1e18, you need __int128 or a mulmod routine.
  • Division is not / under a modulus — it’s multiplication by the modular inverse.
add = (a + b) % m
sub = (a - b % m + m) % m
mul = a * b % m                    # in C: (int64_t)a * b % m
# "a / b mod m"  ==  a * inv(b) mod m   (requires gcd(b, m) == 1)

Fast exponentiation & modular inverse

def power(a, b, m):                   # a^b mod m in O(log b)
    a %= m; res = 1
    while b:
        if b & 1: res = res * a % m
        a = a * a % m
        b >>= 1
    return res

def inv(a, p):                        # p PRIME:  Fermat's little theorem
    return power(a, p - 2, p)

def inv_general(a, m):                # any m with gcd(a, m) == 1
    g, x, _ = ext_gcd(a % m, m)
    return x % m                       # (assert g == 1)

# inverses of 1..n in O(n):  inv[1] = 1;  inv[i] = -(m // i) * inv[m % i] % m

Primes: sieve and factorisation

def sieve(n):                         # all primes ≤ n, O(n log log n)
    is_p = bytearray([1]) * (n + 1); is_p[0] = is_p[1] = 0
    for i in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1):
        if is_p[i]:
            is_p[i*i :: i] = bytearray(len(is_p[i*i :: i]))
    return [i for i in range(n + 1) if is_p[i]]

# smallest-prime-factor sieve -> factorise any x ≤ n in O(log x):
#   spf[i] set during a linear sieve; then repeatedly divide x by spf[x].

def factorise(x):                     # trial division, O(sqrt x), no precompute
    f = {}
    d = 2
    while d * d <= x:
        while x % d == 0: f[d] = f.get(d, 0) + 1; x //= d
        d += 1
    if x > 1: f[x] = f.get(x, 0) + 1
    return f

For primality of a single large number use Miller–Rabin (deterministic for 64-bit with a fixed base set); for factoring a large number use Pollard’s rho.

Combinations modulo a prime

What / why. “How many ways … mod 1e9+7” almost always reduces to binomial coefficients. Precompute factorials and inverse factorials once; each nCr is then O(1).

MOD = 10**9 + 7
N = 200_005
fact = [1] * N
for i in range(1, N): fact[i] = fact[i-1] * i % MOD
inv_fact = [1] * N
inv_fact[N-1] = power(fact[N-1], MOD-2, MOD)
for i in range(N-2, -1, -1): inv_fact[i] = inv_fact[i+1] * (i+1) % MOD

def nCr(n, r):
    if r < 0 or r > n: return 0
    return fact[n] * inv_fact[r] % MOD * inv_fact[n-r] % MOD
# n huge, p small -> Lucas' theorem: nCr(n,r) mod p = prod of nCr(n_i, r_i) over base-p digits
Cheat Sheet
  • GCD: gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,a%b), O(log). LCM: a//gcd*b (divide first). ext_gcd → x,y with ax+by=g → inverse + CRT.
  • Modular: add/mul then %m; subtract via (a-b+m)%m. % can be negative in C/Java. a/b mod m = a*inv(b) mod m.
  • Overflow: (int64_t)a * b % m — int*int overflows well before 1e9+7. m ~ 1e18 → __int128 / mulmod.
  • Fast pow: square-and-multiply, O(log b). Powers modular inverse (Fermat, a^(p-2) mod p), nCr, matrix power, Miller–Rabin.
  • Modular inverse: exists iff gcd(a,m)=1. m prime → a^(m-2). General → ext_gcd. Inverses 1..n in O(n).
  • Sieve of Eratosthenes: primes ≤ n in O(n log log n); SPF sieve → O(log x) factorisation. Trial division to sqrt(x) otherwise. Big single number → Miller–Rabin / Pollard rho.
  • nCr mod p: precompute fact[] and inv_fact[], then O(1) per query. n huge, p small → Lucas.
  • Also handy: Euler totient φ(n), CRT, base conversion, digit DP.
Q&A
Why can’t you just write (a / b) % m?
Integer division discards the remainder, and there’s no reason b divides a exactly — and even if it did, (a/b) % m isn’t generally equal to the modular result you want. Under a modulus, “divide by b” means “multiply by the modular inverse of b” — the value b⁻¹ such that b · b⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod m). It exists iff gcd(b, m) = 1. If m is prime you get it from Fermat (b^(m-2) mod m); otherwise from the extended Euclidean algorithm.
What’s the classic overflow bug in modular multiplication and how do you fix it?
Computing a * b % m where a and b are 32-bit integers near 1e9: the product a * b can be ~1e18, which overflows a 32-bit int (max ~2.1e9) before the % m is applied — so you take the mod of a garbage value. Fix: promote one operand to 64-bit so the multiplication happens in 64-bit: (long long)a * b % m in C/C++, (long) a * b % m in Java. If m itself is up to ~1e18, even 64-bit overflows and you need __int128, a mulmod via __int128/long double, or Python’s arbitrary precision.
How does fast exponentiation compute a^b mod m in O(log b)?
Write b in binary. Maintain a running base that you square each step (so it becomes a, a², a⁴, a⁸, … mod m) and a result that you multiply by the current base whenever the corresponding bit of b is 1. Since a^b is the product of a^(2ⁱ) over the set bits i of b, and there are at most ⌈log₂ b⌉ bits, you do O(log b) multiplications instead of b. Every multiply is followed by % m.
When would you use a sieve versus trial division for factorisation?
Use trial division (up to √x) when you need to factor a few numbers, or numbers too large to sieve — it’s O(√x) per number, no preprocessing. Use a Sieve of Eratosthenes (or a smallest-prime-factor linear sieve) when you’ll test primality or factor many numbers all bounded by some n — O(n log log n) once, then O(1) primality checks and O(log x) factorisation per number. For a single very large number (say 10¹⁸), neither is practical: use Miller–Rabin for primality and Pollard’s rho for factoring.
You need nCr mod 1e9+7 for up to n = 2×10⁵, called a million times. What’s the setup?
Precompute, once, fact[i] = i! mod p for i up to the max n (O(n)), then inv_fact[maxN] = power(fact[maxN], p-2, p) via Fermat, and fill inv_fact downward with inv_fact[i] = inv_fact[i+1] * (i+1) % p (O(n), one modpow total). Then each query is nCr(n, r) = fact[n] * inv_fact[r] % p * inv_fact[n-r] % p in O(1), with a guard returning 0 for r < 0 or r > n. Total: O(n) preprocessing + O(1) per query. (If n could exceed the precompute bound but r is small, compute the falling factorial n·(n-1)…(n-r+1) directly times inv_fact[r].)
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does the extended Euclidean algorithm return that plain gcd doesn’t?
Coefficients x and y such that a·x + b·y = gcd(a, b) (Bézout’s identity). These give the modular inverse of a mod b (when gcd = 1, x is the inverse) and are used in the Chinese Remainder Theorem.
Under a modulus m, how do you compute “a divided by b”?
Multiply a by the modular inverse of b: a · b⁻¹ mod m, valid when gcd(b, m) = 1. For prime m, b⁻¹ = b^(m-2) mod m.

Intermediate core

Count the number of paths from the top-left to the bottom-right of an m×n grid moving only right/down, modulo 1e9+7. Derive the formula and the implementation.
Any such path makes exactly (m-1) down-moves and (n-1) right-moves in some order — a sequence of (m-1)+(n-1) moves, and the path is determined by which positions are the down-moves. So the count is C(m+n-2, m-1). Modulo a prime p = 1e9+7: precompute fact[k] = k! mod p for k up to m+n, compute inv_fact via one Fermat modpow of the largest factorial and a downward sweep, then return fact[m+n-2] * inv_fact[m-1] % p * inv_fact[n-1] % p. Total O(m+n) preprocessing, O(1) to answer. Watch: take the mod after every multiplication (three multiplies here), and use 64-bit for the products. If there were blocked cells you’d instead do an O(mn) DP with dp[i][j] = (dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]) % p; the closed form only works for a clear grid.

Advanced deep

Design a fast, collision-resistant string-hashing scheme for a system that does millions of substring-equality checks (e.g. a plagiarism / near-duplicate detector). Cover the maths and the failure modes.
Polynomial rolling hash: treat a string s as the polynomial ∑ s[i]·B^(L-1-i) evaluated modulo a large prime M, for a random base B in [2, M-1]. Precompute prefix hashes h[i] and powers B^i mod M; then the hash of any substring s[l..r] is (h[r+1] - h[l]·B^(r-l+1)) mod M in O(1) — the core primitive for the millions of equality checks. Comparing two substrings by hash is O(1). Modular arithmetic details: do the subtraction as (h[r+1] - h[l]*pw % M + M) % M to avoid negatives; compute h[l]*pw in 64-bit ((int64)h[l] * pw % M) — the classic overflow trap. Choose M a prime near 2^61 (so products fit in __int128) or use two independent 32-bit primes. Precompute powers with a loop, not pow per query. Collision analysis: for a single random base mod one prime M, two distinct strings collide with probability ≈ L / M per comparison (birthday-style over the number of comparisons Q: expected collisions ≈ Q² / (2M)). With Q = 10^6 comparisons and M ≈ 10^9, that’s ~500 expected collisions — unacceptable. Fixes: (a) double hashing — two primes / two bases, treat strings as equal only if both hashes match; collision probability multiplies to ~L²/(M₁M₂), negligible; (b) use a 61-bit Mersenne prime so M alone is huge; (c) on a hash match, do a real character comparison to confirm (turns collisions from silent errors into a rare slow path — the safe default for a correctness-sensitive tool). Adversarial failure: if B and M are fixed and public, an attacker can construct colliding inputs (Thue–Morse-style, or by solving the polynomial equation). For anything facing untrusted input, pick B (and ideally M from a small set) randomly at run time per process, and still verify matches. Other failure modes: base B ≤ alphabet size or B not coprime to M (weak mixing); using char values that can be negative (add an offset so digits are in [1, ...] — and never let a digit be 0, or leading zeros make "a" and "aa" collide depending on convention); forgetting that hash equality is necessary but not sufficient. System design: build a hash of every document’s k-gram (shingling), store (hash, doc, pos) in an index; near-duplicate detection then compares shingle-hash sets (Jaccard via MinHash on top of these hashes, or LSH banding) — the rolling hash is the cheap primitive that makes generating billions of shingle hashes feasible, and MinHash/LSH is the layer that turns exact-substring hashes into similarity. Net: prefix + power arrays for O(1) substring hashes, two large primes (or one 61-bit prime) with a randomised base, verify on match, offset the alphabet, and layer MinHash/LSH for the actual similarity search.

Dynamic Programming Patterns

The recurring shapes: knapsack, subsequences, intervals, grids, trees, bitmask.

Notes

Dynamic programming applies when a problem has optimal substructure (the answer is built from answers to subproblems) and overlapping subproblems (the same subproblem recurs), so caching subproblem answers turns exponential recursion into polynomial time. This page covers the workflow for deriving a DP (define the state, the transition, the base case, and the evaluation order), a catalogue of recurring patterns — 0/1 and unbounded knapsack, LCS / edit distance, LIS, interval DP, DP on trees, bitmask DP — and how to reason about and reduce the time and space.

The workflow

Define the state (what parameters identify a subproblem), write the transition (recurrence relating a state to smaller ones), fix base cases, choose an evaluation order (memoise top-down, or tabulate in dependency order), then optionally reduce space (rolling arrays).

# LCS length -- the five steps, made concrete:
def lcs(a, b):
    m, n = len(a), len(b)
    dp = [[0]*(n+1) for _ in range(m+1)]        # STATE: dp[i][j] = LCS of a[:i], b[:j]
    for i in range(1, m+1):                     # ORDER: prefixes small -> large
        for j in range(1, n+1):
            if a[i-1] == b[j-1]:
                dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1       # TRANSITION: extend the match
            else:
                dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
    return dp[m][n]                            # BASE CASE: row/col 0 already 0

The pattern catalogue

PatternStateExamples
0/1 knapsackdp[i][w] = best using first i items, capacity wsubset sum, partition equal sum, target sum
Unbounded knapsackdp[w], items reusablecoin change (min coins / #ways), rod cutting
Subsequence (2 strings)dp[i][j] over prefixesLCS, edit distance, shortest common supersequence
LISdp[i] = longest ending at i; or patience sortingO(n²) DP or O(n log n) with binary search
Interval DPdp[i][j] over a range, split at kmatrix-chain, burst balloons, palindrome partitioning
Grid DPdp[r][c] from top/leftunique paths, min path sum, maximal square
DP on treesdp[node][state], combine childrenmax independent set, tree diameter, house robber III
Bitmask DPdp[mask][...], mask = subset of ≤20 itemsTSP, assignment, "min groups"
Digit DPdp[pos][tight][...]count numbers ≤ N with a property
# 0/1 knapsack, 1-D rolling array -- capacity loop goes DESCENDING
def knapsack(weights, values, cap):
    dp = [0] * (cap + 1)              # dp[w] = best value at capacity w
    for wt, val in zip(weights, values):
        for w in range(cap, wt - 1, -1):  # descending -> each item used at most ONCE
            dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - wt] + val)
    return dp[cap]
# ascending instead -> unbounded knapsack (item reusable). Same code, one flip.

Space & time

Time ≈ (#states) × (transitions per state). Space = state table, often collapsible: a 2-D prefix DP needing only the previous row → two 1-D arrays or one with careful ordering. If you need the actual solution (not just its value), keep a parent/choice table or re-derive by walking the DP backward.

# LCS length in O(min(m,n)) space -- keep only two rows
def lcs_len(a, b):
    if len(b) > len(a): a, b = b, a       # iterate over the shorter -> smaller rows
    prev = [0] * (len(b) + 1)
    for ca in a:
        cur = [0] * (len(b) + 1)
        for j, cb in enumerate(b, 1):
            cur[j] = prev[j-1] + 1 if ca == cb else max(prev[j], cur[j-1])
        prev = cur                        # O(n*m) time, O(n) space
    return prev[-1]
Cheat Sheet
  • Recipe: state → transition → base cases → order → space reduction.
  • 0/1 knapsack: iterate capacity descending for the 1-D version; unbounded: ascending.
  • Two-string DP (LCS/edit distance): dp[i][j] from dp[i-1][j-1], dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]; O(nm) → O(min(n,m)) space.
  • LIS: O(n²) DP, or O(n log n) maintaining the smallest tail per length (binary search).
  • Interval DP: loop by increasing length, split point k inside; O(n³) typical.
  • Tree DP: post-order; each node returns state(s) computed from children.
  • Bitmask DP: O(2ⁿ · poly(n)); n ≤ ~20.
  • Time = states × transitions. Reconstruct via a choice table or backward walk.
Q&A
Why iterate capacity descending in the 1-D 0/1 knapsack?
So each item is only used once: dp[w] is updated from dp[w - weight], and going high-to-low ensures dp[w - weight] still reflects the previous item's row, not this item's. Ascending order would allow reusing the item (which is the unbounded knapsack).
What's the state for edit distance?
dp[i][j] = minimum operations to turn the first i chars of A into the first j chars of B. Transition: if chars match, dp[i-1][j-1]; else 1 + min(insert, delete, replace).
How does the O(n log n) LIS work?
Maintain an array tails where tails[k] is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. For each element, binary-search its position in tails and overwrite (or append). The length of tails at the end is the LIS length.
When do you need bitmask DP?
When a subproblem is identified by "which subset of a small set (≤ ~20 elements) has been used/visited" — TSP, assignment problems, "partition into groups". The state count is 2ⁿ.
Memoisation vs tabulation trade-off?
Memoisation computes only reachable states and is easy to write from the recurrence, but has recursion overhead and stack-depth limits. Tabulation visits all states in a fixed order, enabling tight loops and O(1)-row space, at the cost of sometimes computing states you don't need.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does dp[i][j] usually represent in a two-string DP?
The answer for the first i characters of one string and the first j of the other.
Time complexity of the classic 0/1 knapsack DP?
O(n × W) where n = items, W = capacity. (Pseudo-polynomial — exponential in the number of bits of W.)
Coin change "number of ways": iterate coins outer or inner?
Coins outer, amount inner — this counts combinations (order doesn't matter). Swapping the loops counts permutations.

Intermediate core

Longest common subsequence recurrence.
dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 if A[i-1] == B[j-1], else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Base: dp[0][*] = dp[*][0] = 0. O(nm) time; O(min(n,m)) space with rolling rows (but you lose easy reconstruction).
House robber on a binary tree (can't rob adjacent nodes). State & transition?
Post-order; each node returns a pair (rob, skip). skip = max(childL) + max(childR) (children free to do anything). rob = node.val + skip_of(L) + skip_of(R). Answer = max of the root's pair. O(n).

Advanced deep

Explain "burst balloons" (interval DP) — why the natural "which balloon to burst first" framing fails and the fix.
If you define dp by the first balloon burst in a range, the subranges become non-contiguous and coupled (bursting one changes the neighbours of others). The fix: define dp[i][j] for the open interval (i, j) and iterate over which balloon k is burst last in that interval. When k is last, its neighbours are exactly the fixed boundaries i and j, and the left and right sub-intervals (i, k) and (k, j) are independent. Transition: dp[i][j] = max over k of dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] + nums[i]*nums[k]*nums[j]. O(n³). The "think about the last operation, not the first" reframing is a recurring interval-DP trick (also matrix-chain, optimal BST).
How does digit DP count integers in [0, N] with some digit property?
Process the number left to right, digit position by position. State: (pos, tight, ...propertyState), where tight means the prefix built so far equals N's prefix (so the current digit is capped at N's digit; otherwise it can be 0–9). Memoise on (pos, tight=false, propertyState) — the tight=true path is a single chain and not cached. Add a started/leadingZero flag if leading zeros need special handling. At pos == len, return 1 if the property holds. Complexity O(len × 10 × #propertyStates). Handles "count numbers with digit sum S", "no two equal adjacent digits", "≤ K distinct digits", etc.

Graph Traversal Applications

What you can actually do once you can BFS and DFS a graph.

Notes

This page covers the algorithms that fall straight out of a BFS or DFS once you see a problem as a graph: flood fill and grid traversal, finding connected components, testing whether a graph is bipartite, detecting cycles in directed and undirected graphs, and using the DFS tree (discovery/finish times, back edges) to find bridges and articulation points. It’s about recognising the graph hiding in a problem and picking the right traversal.

Flood fill / grid as graph

Treat a grid cell as a node with up-to-4 (or 8) neighbours. BFS/DFS from a cell to fill a region, count islands, find the shortest path in a maze (BFS), or expand from multiple sources at once (multi-source BFS: seed the queue with all sources — "rotting oranges", "walls and gates", "01 matrix").

def count_islands(grid):
    R, C = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    def flood(r, c):
        if not (0 <= r < R and 0 <= c < C) or grid[r][c] != '1': return
        grid[r][c] = '0'                          # mark visited in place
        for dr, dc in ((1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)): # 4 neighbours = graph edges
            flood(r+dr, c+dc)
    n = 0
    for r in range(R):
        for c in range(C):
            if grid[r][c] == '1': flood(r, c); n += 1  # each new flood = one island
    return n

Connectivity

  • Connected components (undirected): loop vertices, BFS/DFS each unvisited one, count.
  • Strongly connected components (directed): Tarjan (one DFS, low-link) or Kosaraju (DFS, transpose, DFS by finish order).
  • Bipartite check: 2-colour via BFS/DFS; a same-colour edge → not bipartite.
def is_bipartite(adj, nodes):
    color = {}
    for s in nodes:
        if s in color: continue
        color[s], stack = 0, [s]
        while stack:
            u = stack.pop()
            for v in adj[u]:
                if v not in color:
                    color[v] = color[u] ^ 1       # opposite colour
                    stack.append(v)
                elif color[v] == color[u]:
                    return False                  # same-colour edge -> odd cycle
    return True

Cycle detection

  • Undirected: DFS — a visited neighbour that isn't the parent means a cycle. Or union-find.
  • Directed: 3-colour DFS (edge to a grey node = back edge = cycle), or Kahn's topological sort leaving nodes unplaced.
def undirected_has_cycle(adj, nodes):
    seen = set()
    def dfs(u, parent):
        seen.add(u)
        for v in adj[u]:
            if v == parent: continue          # the edge we came in on -- not a cycle
            if v in seen or dfs(v, u): return True
        return False
    return any(u not in seen and dfs(u, None) for u in nodes)

DFS tree structure

DFS classifies edges (tree / back / forward / cross) and computes disc[] (discovery time) and low[] (earliest reachable ancestor). From these:

  • Bridges — edge (u, v) is a bridge iff low[v] > disc[u].
  • Articulation points — removing them disconnects the graph; found via the same low-link condition (with a root special case).
timer = [0]; disc, low, bridges = {}, {}, []
def dfs(u, parent):
    disc[u] = low[u] = timer[0]; timer[0] += 1
    for v in adj[u]:
        if v == parent: continue
        if v not in disc:
            dfs(v, u)
            low[u] = min(low[u], low[v])
            if low[v] > disc[u]:            # v can't reach u or above without this edge
                bridges.append((u, v))
        else:
            low[u] = min(low[u], disc[v])   # back edge -> update reachability
Cheat Sheet
  • Grid problems: cell = node, 4/8 neighbours. BFS for shortest steps, DFS/BFS for region fill.
  • Multi-source BFS: push all sources first, then standard BFS → nearest-source distance for every cell.
  • Connected components: iterate + BFS/DFS unvisited; SCC via Tarjan (1 pass) or Kosaraju (2 passes + transpose).
  • Bipartite: 2-colouring; conflict edge → no.
  • Undirected cycle: DFS visited-non-parent, or union-find. Directed cycle: grey back-edge, or Kahn leftovers.
  • Bridges / articulation points: DFS with disc[] and low[]; low[v] > disc[u] → bridge.
  • Topological order (DAG): Kahn (in-degree queue) or DFS finish-time reverse.
  • All these are O(V + E) on an adjacency list.
Q&A
How do you count islands in a grid of land/water?
Scan cells; on each unvisited land cell, run BFS/DFS to mark its whole connected region, and increment a counter. O(rows × cols).
What is multi-source BFS and when do you use it?
BFS started from many sources simultaneously (all pushed into the queue before the loop). Every node's first visit gives its distance to the nearest source. Used for "how far is each cell from the closest exit/fire/gate".
How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph?
DFS with three states: unvisited, in-progress (on the current recursion path), done. An edge to an in-progress node is a back edge, so there's a cycle. Alternatively, if Kahn's topological sort can't place all V nodes, a cycle exists.
What is low[v] in bridge-finding?
The smallest discovery time reachable from v's DFS subtree using tree edges plus at most one back edge. If a child v of u has low[v] > disc[u], no back edge from v's subtree bypasses the edge (u, v), so it's a bridge.
Kosaraju vs Tarjan for SCCs?
Both are O(V + E). Kosaraju: DFS to get finish order, build the transpose graph, DFS in reverse finish order — two passes, conceptually simple. Tarjan: a single DFS maintaining a stack and low-links — one pass, less memory (no transpose), slightly trickier to implement.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which traversal gives shortest path in an unweighted maze?
BFS.
How do you check if a graph is bipartite?
Try to 2-colour it with BFS/DFS; if any edge connects two same-coloured nodes, it isn't bipartite.
Complexity of BFS/DFS on an adjacency list?
O(V + E).

Intermediate core

Course schedule: given prerequisites, can all courses be finished?
Build a directed graph course → dependent. Run Kahn's topological sort (or 3-colour DFS). If you can order all courses (no cycle), yes; a cycle means an impossible circular dependency. O(V + E).
Rotting oranges: minutes until no fresh orange remains (or -1).
Multi-source BFS from all initially-rotten oranges. Each BFS "level" is one minute; rot fresh neighbours and enqueue them. The answer is the number of levels processed; if any fresh orange is still unreached, return -1. O(rows × cols).

Advanced deep

Find all bridges in an undirected graph in one DFS. Give the core condition and an edge case.
DFS assigning disc[u] (entry time) and low[u] = min(disc[u], disc of nodes reachable via one back edge from u's subtree). For a tree edge (u, v): after returning from v, set low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]); if low[v] > disc[u], edge (u, v) is a bridge. Edge case: when relaxing, skip the immediate parent edge once (not all edges to the parent) — with parallel edges between u and its parent, the second such edge is a valid back edge and prevents both from being bridges. Track parent by edge id, not just node id. O(V + E).
Explain the 2-SAT → SCC reduction.
A 2-SAT formula (clauses of ≤ 2 literals) is satisfiable iff no variable x has both x and ¬x in the same strongly connected component of the "implication graph". Build the graph: each clause (a ∨ b) becomes two edges ¬a → b and ¬b → a (if a is false then b must be true, and vice versa). Run an SCC algorithm (Tarjan). If x and ¬x share a component → UNSAT. Otherwise assign each variable by comparing the SCC (in reverse topological / component order) of x vs ¬x — the literal whose component comes later is true. O(n + m). This turns a satisfiability problem into linear-time graph work.

Shortest Paths

Pick the algorithm by edge weights: unweighted, non-negative, negative, or all-pairs.

Notes

The shortest-path problem — least-cost route between vertices — has a different right answer depending on the graph: unweighted, non-negative weights, negative weights, or all-pairs. This page covers the decision table and then each algorithm: BFS (unweighted), Dijkstra (non-negative, with a priority queue), Bellman–Ford (handles negative edges, detects negative cycles), Floyd–Warshall (all pairs, O(V³)), and A* (Dijkstra guided by a heuristic). It covers why Dijkstra breaks on negative edges and how each one relaxes edges.

The decision table

SituationAlgorithmTime
Unweighted (or all equal weights)BFSO(V + E)
Weights 0/10-1 BFS (deque)O(V + E)
Non-negative weights, single sourceDijkstra (binary heap)O((V + E) log V)
Negative weights allowed, single sourceBellman-FordO(V · E)
All pairs, dense, small VFloyd-WarshallO(V³)
Goal-directed with a heuristicA*≤ Dijkstra in practice
def pick(graph):
    if graph.unweighted:      return bfs           # fewest edges, O(V+E)
    if graph.weights_0_1:     return zero_one_bfs   # deque: appendleft(0-edge), append(1-edge)
    if graph.min_weight >= 0:  return dijkstra      # non-negative only
    if graph.all_pairs:       return floyd_warshall # dense + small V
    return bellman_ford                              # negatives + cycle detection

Dijkstra

Grow a set of finalised nodes; repeatedly take the unfinalised node with the smallest tentative distance (min-heap), finalise it, and relax its outgoing edges. Correct only for non-negative weights — a negative edge could improve an already-finalised node. Use lazy deletion (push duplicates, skip stale pops) rather than decrease-key.

import heapq
def dijkstra(adj, src):                 # adj[u] = [(v, w), ...]
    dist = {src: 0}
    pq = [(0, src)]
    while pq:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        if d > dist.get(u, float('inf')): continue  # stale entry -> skip (lazy deletion)
        for v, w in adj[u]:
            nd = d + w
            if nd < dist.get(v, float('inf')):
                dist[v] = nd
                heapq.heappush(pq, (nd, v))   # relax
    return dist

Bellman-Ford

Relax all edges V - 1 times (the longest simple path has ≤ V-1 edges). A further relaxation that still improves something → a negative cycle reachable from the source. Slower but handles negatives and detects negative cycles.

def bellman_ford(n, edges, src):        # edges = [(u, v, w)]
    dist = [float('inf')] * n; dist[src] = 0
    for _ in range(n - 1):               # V-1 full passes
        for u, v, w in edges:
            if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w
    for u, v, w in edges:              # one more pass...
        if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
            raise ValueError("negative cycle")  # ...still improves => negative cycle
    return dist

Floyd-Warshall

for k in V:
  for i in V:
    for j in V:
      dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j])

k is "intermediate vertices allowed so far". Handles negative edges (no negative cycles); dist[i][i] < 0 afterward flags a negative cycle through i.

A*

Dijkstra with priority g(n) + h(n), where h estimates the remaining distance to the goal. If h is admissible (never overestimates) the result is optimal; if also consistent, no node is expanded twice. A good heuristic (e.g. straight-line distance on a map) massively prunes the search.

import heapq
def astar(adj, src, goal, h):           # h(n) = estimated cost from n to goal
    g = {src: 0}
    pq = [(h(src), src)]                 # priority = f = g + h
    while pq:
        _, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        if u == goal: return g[u]
        for v, w in adj[u]:
            ng = g[u] + w
            if ng < g.get(v, float('inf')):
                g[v] = ng
                heapq.heappush(pq, (ng + h(v), v))  # admissible h => optimal result
    return None
# h(n) = 0  ->  A* degenerates to Dijkstra.  h(n) = true distance  ->  straight to goal.
Cheat Sheet
  • Unweighted → BFS. 0/1 weights → 0-1 BFS (deque, push_front for 0).
  • Non-negative weights → Dijkstra + min-heap, O((V+E) log V). Lazy deletion over decrease-key.
  • Negative edges → Bellman-Ford, O(VE); extra relaxation succeeds → negative cycle.
  • All pairs → Floyd-Warshall O(V³) (or Dijkstra from each source for sparse graphs; Johnson's for sparse + negatives).
  • Dijkstra is wrong with any negative edge.
  • A* = Dijkstra with f = g + h; admissible h → optimal; consistent h → no re-expansion.
  • Reconstruct paths via a prev[] / parent array updated on each successful relaxation.
Q&A
Why does Dijkstra fail with negative edge weights?
It finalises the closest node and never revisits it. A negative edge encountered later could create a shorter path to that already-finalised node, which Dijkstra can't account for.
How does Bellman-Ford detect a negative cycle?
After V-1 rounds of relaxing all edges, shortest paths are final if no negative cycle exists. If a V-th round still relaxes some edge, a reachable negative cycle must exist.
What does the outer loop variable k mean in Floyd-Warshall?
"Consider paths whose intermediate vertices are all in {0, …, k}." After the loop finishes for all k, every vertex is allowed as an intermediate, so dist holds true shortest paths.
When is A* just Dijkstra?
When the heuristic h is 0 everywhere — then priority is just g(n), the known distance, which is Dijkstra.
Single-source shortest path on a DAG — anything faster than Dijkstra?
Yes: topologically sort, then relax edges in that order — O(V + E), and it handles negative weights (no cycles possible).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Best algorithm for shortest path with all edge weights = 1?
BFS — O(V + E), simpler and faster than Dijkstra.
Dijkstra's time complexity with a binary heap?
O((V + E) log V).
Which algorithm gives all-pairs shortest paths in O(V³)?
Floyd-Warshall.

Intermediate core

Implement Dijkstra with a min-heap and lazy deletion.
Push (0, source). While the heap is non-empty, pop (d, u); if d > dist[u] skip (stale). Otherwise for each edge (u, v, w), if dist[u] + w < dist[v], update dist[v] and push (dist[v], v). No need to remove old entries — the staleness check handles them. Heap can hold up to O(E) entries.
Cheapest flights within K stops (weighted graph, stop limit). Approach?
Bellman-Ford limited to K + 1 relaxation rounds — each round allows one more edge (stop). Crucially, relax from a snapshot of distances at the start of each round so a single round can't chain multiple edges. Or a BFS/Dijkstra-style search with state (node, stopsUsed).

Advanced deep

What is Johnson's algorithm and when does it beat Floyd-Warshall?
All-pairs shortest paths for graphs with negative edges but no negative cycles, on sparse graphs. Step 1: add a virtual node with 0-weight edges to all vertices; run Bellman-Ford from it to get h(v) for every vertex. Step 2: reweight each edge w'(u,v) = w(u,v) + h(u) - h(v), which is provably non-negative and preserves shortest paths. Step 3: run Dijkstra from every source on the reweighted graph, then subtract the offset. Total O(VE + V·E log V) = O(VE log V), which beats Floyd-Warshall's O(V³) when E « V².
Prove Dijkstra's correctness for non-negative weights (sketch).
Invariant: when a node u is popped/finalised, dist[u] is its true shortest distance. Suppose not — let u be the first finalised node with dist[u] > δ(s, u). Consider a true shortest path s → … → u; let y be the first node on it not yet finalised, with finalised predecessor x. Since x was finalised correctly, dist[y] ≤ dist[x] + w(x,y) = δ(s, y) (relaxed when x was processed). Because edge weights are non-negative, δ(s, y) ≤ δ(s, u) < dist[u]. So dist[y] < dist[u], meaning the heap would have popped y before u — contradiction. Non-negativity is essential in the δ(s,y) ≤ δ(s,u) step.

MST & Topological Sort

Cheapest connecting tree, and ordering a dependency graph.

Notes

Two classic graph results. A minimum spanning tree is the cheapest set of edges connecting every vertex of a weighted undirected graph; Kruskal’s (sort edges + union-find) and Prim’s (grow a tree with a heap) both find one, justified by the cut property. A topological sort is a linear ordering of a DAG’s vertices so every edge points forward — the basis of build systems, task scheduling, and dependency resolution. This page covers both algorithms for each, and how to detect that no topological order exists (a cycle).

Minimum Spanning Tree

A subset of edges connecting all V vertices with no cycle and minimum total weight (exactly V - 1 edges). Both standard algorithms are greedy, justified by the cut property: for any partition of the vertices, the lightest edge crossing it is in some MST.

KruskalPrim
Ideasort all edges; add the next lightest that doesn't form a cyclegrow a tree from a start vertex, always adding the lightest edge leaving it
Cycle checkunion-finda "visited" set
TimeO(E log E)O((V + E) log V) with a heap; O(V²) with an array (good for dense)
Best forsparse graphs, edge list givendense graphs
import heapq
def prim(adj, start):                   # adj[u] = [(w, v), ...]
    seen = {start}
    pq = list(adj[start])                # frontier edges leaving the tree
    heapq.heapify(pq)
    total = 0
    while pq:
        w, v = heapq.heappop(pq)
        if v in seen: continue          # stale frontier edge
        seen.add(v); total += w         # lightest edge leaving the tree = safe (cut property)
        for e in adj[v]: heapq.heappush(pq, e)
    return total

Topological sort

A linear order of a DAG's vertices such that every edge u → v has u before v. Not unique. Two methods:

  • Kahn's (BFS): repeatedly remove a vertex with in-degree 0, decrementing its successors. If fewer than V vertices come out → there's a cycle.
  • DFS: push each vertex onto a stack when its DFS finishes; the reversed stack is a topological order.

Uses: build systems (make), task/course scheduling, spreadsheet recalculation, package managers, resolving symbol dependencies at link time.

def topo_dfs(adj, nodes):
    seen, order = set(), []
    def visit(u):
        seen.add(u)
        for v in adj[u]:
            if v not in seen: visit(v)
        order.append(u)                  # append on FINISH
    for u in nodes:
        if u not in seen: visit(u)
    return order[::-1]                    # reverse -> every edge points forward

Related

Longest path in a DAG = topological order + DP relax (the general longest-path problem is NP-hard, but a DAG makes it linear). Lexicographically smallest topological order = Kahn's with a min-heap instead of a queue.

# longest path in a DAG: relax edges in topological order
def longest_path(adj, nodes, weight):
    order = topo_dfs(adj, nodes)
    dist = {u: 0 for u in nodes}
    for u in order:                     # u's predecessors are already final
        for v in adj[u]:
            dist[v] = max(dist[v], dist[u] + weight[(u, v)])
    return max(dist.values())            # O(V + E) -- only because it's a DAG
Cheat Sheet
  • MST: V-1 edges, connected, acyclic, minimum total weight. Greedy works via the cut property.
  • Kruskal: sort edges, add if endpoints in different DSU sets, union. O(E log E). Sparse / edge list.
  • Prim: heap of frontier edges, grow one tree. O((V+E) log V) heap or O(V²) array. Dense.
  • Both give the same total weight; the tree itself may differ if weights tie.
  • Topological sort needs a DAG; result not unique.
  • Kahn's: in-degree-0 queue; leftover vertices → cycle. DFS: reverse of finish order.
  • Lexicographically smallest topo order → Kahn's with a min-heap.
  • DAG longest/shortest path: process in topological order, relax — O(V + E).
Q&A
State the cut property.
For any cut (partition of vertices into two non-empty sets), the minimum-weight edge crossing the cut belongs to some MST. This is what makes greedily adding safe edges correct.
Kruskal vs Prim — when to use each?
Kruskal when the graph is sparse or given as an edge list (sort edges, union-find). Prim when the graph is dense (its O(V²) array version beats sorting O(V²) edges) or given as an adjacency structure.
What data structure makes Kruskal efficient?
Union-Find (disjoint set) — O(α(V)) per "are these connected / union them" check while scanning sorted edges.
Can topological sort be applied to any directed graph?
No — only a DAG. If the graph has a directed cycle, no valid linear order exists (and both Kahn's and DFS can detect that).
Is a topological ordering unique?
Generally no. It's unique iff at every step there's exactly one vertex with in-degree 0 (equivalently, the DAG has a Hamiltonian path).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

How many edges in an MST of a connected graph with V vertices?
Exactly V − 1.
Which algorithm pairs with union-find?
Kruskal's MST.
What does Kahn's algorithm start with?
All vertices that have in-degree 0.

Intermediate core

Implement Kruskal's algorithm.
Sort edges by weight ascending. Initialise a DSU over V vertices. For each edge (u, v, w) in order: if find(u) != find(v), add the edge to the MST and union(u, v). Stop when you've added V − 1 edges. O(E log E) dominated by the sort.
Return the lexicographically smallest valid course order.
Kahn's algorithm but with a min-heap of the currently-available (in-degree 0) vertices instead of a plain queue. Always take the smallest-numbered available vertex next. O((V + E) log V).

Advanced deep

How do you find a minimum spanning tree that must include a given edge, or exclude one?
Must include edge e: contract e (union its endpoints first / add it to the tree with weight treated as −∞), then run Kruskal/Prim on the rest. Must exclude e: run the MST algorithm skipping e. For "is edge e in every MST / some MST": e is in some MST iff it's a minimum-weight edge across some cut (equivalently, in the graph of edges with weight < w(e), its endpoints are in different components); e is in every MST iff it's the unique lightest edge across some cut (no alternative equal-weight edge closes the same cycle). These are the basis of MST sensitivity analysis.
Prove Prim's algorithm produces a minimum spanning tree.
Loop invariant: the set of edges chosen so far, A, is a subset of some MST. Initially A = ∅ — true. Inductive step: Prim adds the lightest edge (u, v) crossing the cut (S, V\S) where S is the current tree's vertices. By the cut property, this lightest crossing edge is in some MST T. If (u, v) ∈ T, A ∪ {(u,v)} is still a subset of T. If not, T ∪ {(u,v)} has a cycle containing another edge (x, y) crossing the cut; w(x,y) ≥ w(u,v), so swapping gives an MST T' containing A ∪ {(u,v)} with weight ≤ w(T). Either way the invariant holds. After V-1 edges, A is a spanning tree that is a subset of an MST — hence is an MST.

String Matching

Finding a pattern in text faster than the O(nm) nested loop.

Notes

String matching is finding all occurrences of a pattern P (length m) inside a text T (length n). The naive method is O(nm); the classic algorithms get to O(n + m) by never re-examining text characters they’ve already ruled out. This page covers Rabin–Karp (rolling hash — great for multiple patterns), KMP (the prefix/failure function that says how far to shift after a mismatch), and the Z-algorithm (Z-array of longest prefix-matches), with the preprocessing each one does and when to reach for it.

Naive

For each of the n - m + 1 alignments, compare up to m characters. O(nm) worst case (e.g. text aaaa…a, pattern aaa…ab). Fine for short patterns / small text.

def naive_search(text, pat):
    n, m = len(text), len(pat)
    for i in range(n - m + 1):        # every alignment
        if text[i:i+m] == pat:        # up to m comparisons each -> O(nm) worst
            yield i

Rabin-Karp (rolling hash)

  • Hash the pattern and each length-m window of the text; compare hashes, verify on match.
  • The rolling hash updates in O(1) as the window slides: h = (h - text[i]·b^(m-1))·b + text[i+m], all mod a large prime.
  • O(n + m) average; O(nm) worst case if many hash collisions (mitigate with a good modulus / double hashing).
  • Shines for multiple pattern search (hash all patterns, one text pass) and 2-D pattern matching.
def rabin_karp(text, pat, B=256, M=(1<<61)-1):
    n, m = len(text), len(pat)
    hp = ht = 0; power = pow(B, m-1, M)
    for i in range(m):                     # hash pattern + first window
        hp = (hp*B + ord(pat[i]))  % M
        ht = (ht*B + ord(text[i])) % M
    for i in range(n - m + 1):
        if hp == ht and text[i:i+m] == pat:  # verify -- hashes can collide
            yield i
        if i + m < n:                       # roll: drop text[i], add text[i+m], O(1)
            ht = ((ht - ord(text[i])*power)*B + ord(text[i+m])) % M

KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt)

  • Precompute the prefix function π[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix.
  • On a mismatch after matching k chars, don't restart — jump the pattern to π[k-1], reusing the known match.
  • The text pointer never moves backward → O(n + m) guaranteed, O(m) extra space.
# prefix function
π = [0]*m; k = 0
for i in 1..m-1:
    while k > 0 and p[i] != p[k]: k = π[k-1]
    if p[i] == p[k]: k += 1
    π[i] = k

Z-algorithm

Computes Z[i] = length of the longest substring starting at i that matches a prefix of the string. Run on pattern + separator + text; any Z[i] ≥ m in the text part is a match. O(n + m), often simpler to reason about than KMP.

def z_array(s):
    n = len(s); z = [0]*n; l = r = 0
    for i in range(1, n):
        if i < r: z[i] = min(r - i, z[i - l])  # reuse the earlier match ("Z-box")
        while i + z[i] < n and s[z[i]] == s[i + z[i]]:
            z[i] += 1
        if i + z[i] > r: l, r = i, i + z[i]
    return z

def search(text, pat):
    z = z_array(pat + "\x00" + text)          # separator can't appear in either string
    m = len(pat)
    return [i - m - 1 for i in range(m+1, len(z)) if z[i] >= m]  # Z[i] >= m -> full match
Cheat Sheet
  • Naive: O(nm) worst, O(1) space, fine for small inputs.
  • Rabin-Karp: rolling hash, O(n + m) average, great for many patterns / 2-D; verify on hash hit.
  • KMP: prefix function π, O(n + m) worst case, text pointer never backtracks.
  • Z-algorithm: Z[i] = prefix-match length at i; run on P + '#' + T; O(n + m).
  • Aho-Corasick: KMP generalised to a trie of many patterns — all matches in O(n + total pattern length + #matches).
  • Boyer-Moore (bad-char + good-suffix): sublinear average, used by grep; skips ahead from the end of the pattern.
  • Suffix automaton / suffix array: preprocess the text once, then answer many pattern queries fast.
Q&A
What does the KMP prefix function store?
π[i] = the length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix of it. On a mismatch it tells you how far you can shift the pattern without missing a match.
Why is KMP O(n + m) and not O(nm)?
The text index only ever moves forward. Each character is compared a bounded number of times because failed matches fall back via π rather than re-scanning the text.
What is a rolling hash?
A hash of a sliding window that can be updated in O(1) when the window shifts by one — subtract the outgoing character's contribution, multiply by the base, add the incoming character (all modulo a large prime).
Rabin-Karp's worst case and when it hits.
O(nm) — when the hash collides at (almost) every window so you keep doing full O(m) verifications. Rare with a good random modulus; adversarial input can force it, mitigated by double hashing or a secret modulus.
When would you choose Rabin-Karp over KMP?
Searching for many patterns at once (hash them all, one text pass), 2-D pattern matching, or when you need "any of these substrings" checks — the hash comparison generalises where KMP's single-pattern automaton doesn't.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Worst-case time of naive substring search?
O(nm) — text length n, pattern length m.
KMP's overall complexity?
O(n + m), guaranteed.
Which algorithm uses a rolling hash?
Rabin-Karp.

Intermediate core

Compute the prefix function for "ababaca".
Index: a b a b a c a → π = [0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1]. At index 4 ("ababa"), the longest prefix=suffix is "aba" (length 3); the "c" breaks it back to 0; the final "a" matches the prefix "a" (length 1).
Find the shortest palindrome by adding characters only to the front.
Build s + '#' + reverse(s) and compute its prefix function; the last value k is the length of the longest palindromic prefix of s. Prepend the reverse of s[k:]. O(n). (Same result via the Z-algorithm or Manacher.)

Advanced deep

Describe Aho-Corasick and its complexity for matching many patterns.
Build a trie of all patterns. Add failure links: from each node, a pointer to the longest proper suffix of the string-so-far that is also a trie node (computed by a BFS over the trie, exactly the multi-pattern generalisation of KMP's π). Also add output links so that when you land on a node you can enumerate every pattern that ends there or at a suffix. Then scan the text once, following child edges or failure links on mismatch, emitting matches. Total: O(Σ pattern lengths) to build + O(text length + number of matches) to search. It's what tools like fgrep -f patterns.txt, intrusion-detection signature scanners, and spam filters use.
How does a suffix array answer "does P occur in T" and how is it built efficiently?
