Avoid SO_LINGER-0 hacks — they skip TIME_WAIT's safety.

Advanced deep

How does BBR differ fundamentally from loss-based congestion control, and what problem does it solve?
Loss-based CC (Reno/CUBIC) increases the send rate until the network drops packets, then backs off — it deliberately fills buffers until they overflow. On modern paths with large router buffers ("bufferbloat"), this means TCP keeps queues full, adding hundreds of ms of latency even without loss, and it collapses on links with random (non-congestive) loss. BBR instead continuously estimates the bottleneck bandwidth (max delivery rate seen) and the minimum RTT (propagation delay without queuing), and paces sending to bandwidth × minRTT — operating at the "knee" where the pipe is full but the queue is nearly empty. Result: high throughput with low latency, and resilience to random loss. Trade-offs: BBRv1 could be unfair to CUBIC flows sharing a link and mis-estimate under heavy multiplexing; BBRv2/v3 add loss and ECN signals back in to address that.
Explain head-of-line blocking in TCP and why it matters for HTTP/2.
TCP delivers bytes strictly in order. If segment N is lost, segments N+1, N+2… that already arrived sit in the kernel buffer and are not handed to the application until N is retransmitted and received — everything behind the gap is blocked. HTTP/1.1 sidestepped this by opening ~6 parallel TCP connections. HTTP/2 multiplexes many logical streams over one TCP connection to save handshakes and enable prioritisation — but now a single lost packet stalls all streams, because they share one ordered byte stream. On lossy networks HTTP/2 can therefore be slower than HTTP/1.1. HTTP/3 fixes it by moving to QUIC, which tracks delivery per-stream over UDP, so loss on one stream doesn't block the others.

UDP & When to Use It

A thin wrapper over IP: ports and a checksum, nothing else — and why that's sometimes exactly right.

Notes

UDP is the thin option: it adds ports and a checksum to IP and nothing else — no connection, no handshake, no reliability, no ordering, no congestion control. That’s a feature when you want the lowest latency and are willing to handle loss yourself. This page covers exactly what UDP does and doesn’t give you, when it’s the right choice (DNS, real-time media, gaming, QUIC), how protocols build reliability and ordering back on top of it selectively, and the gotchas (fragmentation, no built-in congestion control, amplification attacks).

What UDP is (and isn't)

  • Adds to IP: source/destination port, length, checksum. 8-byte header (vs TCP's 20+).
  • No connection setup, no reliability, no ordering, no flow/congestion control. A datagram is sent once; it may be lost, duplicated, or reordered.
  • Message-oriented: each sendto is one datagram the receiver gets whole (or not at all) — unlike TCP's byte stream with no message boundaries.
int fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM, 0);   // SOCK_DGRAM = UDP; no connect(), no handshake

// one sendto = exactly one datagram; the peer recvfrom()s it whole or not at all
sendto(fd, "PING", 4, 0, (struct sockaddr*)&dst, sizeof dst);

char buf[1500];
ssize_t n = recvfrom(fd, buf, sizeof buf, 0, NULL, NULL);
// n could be 4, or this recvfrom could block forever -- the PING may simply be lost

When to choose UDP

Use caseWhy UDP
DNS queriestiny request/response; a retry is cheaper than a handshake
Real-time media (VoIP, video, games)a late packet is useless; better to skip it than stall for retransmission
QUIC / HTTP/3build a better transport in userspace on top of UDP
Multicast / broadcastTCP is point-to-point only
Metrics, logs, telemetry (statsd, syslog)lossy is acceptable; don't want backpressure on the app
Service discovery (mDNS, DHCP)broadcast to unknown peers
$ dig +short example.com          # DNS: one UDP datagram out, one back -- retry is cheaper than a handshake
$ dig +tcp example.com            # falls back to TCP only for big responses / zone transfers

# media: RTP-over-UDP -- a 40ms-late audio packet is useless, so it's dropped, not resent
$ ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -f rtp rtp://239.0.0.1:5004

Reliability on top of UDP

If you need some guarantees, you re-implement selectively: sequence numbers + ACKs for the messages that matter, forward error correction, your own pacing/congestion control (be a good network citizen!), and NAT keepalives. This is what QUIC, RTP/RTCP, DTLS, and game netcode do.

# minimal app-level reliability layered on UDP:
send({seq: n, data: chunk})
start_timer(n)
on_ack(k):    stop_timer(k)                 # peer confirmed receipt
on_timeout(n): send({seq: n, ...}); backoff()  # selective retransmit + your own pacing
# only mark the messages that MUST arrive as reliable; leave the rest fire-and-forget

Gotchas

  • Large UDP datagrams get IP-fragmented; a single lost fragment loses the whole datagram. Keep payloads under the path MTU (~1200 bytes is a safe internet default).
  • No congestion control means a misbehaving UDP app can cause congestion collapse — add your own.
  • Amplification: small spoofed request → large response (DNS, NTP, memcached) is a DDoS vector.
# fragmentation: a 4000-byte datagram is split into 3 IP fragments;
# lose ONE fragment -> the kernel discards the whole 4000-byte datagram.
#   fix: cap app payload at ~1200 bytes (safe internet MTU), or set DF and do PMTUD.

# amplification: 60-byte spoofed DNS query -> 3000-byte ANY response at the victim
#   ~50x gain. Mitigation: BCP38 source-address filtering, rate limiting, no open resolvers.
Cheat Sheet
  • UDP = IP + ports + checksum. 8-byte header. Connectionless, unreliable, unordered, no flow/congestion control.
  • Message-oriented: one sendto = one datagram delivered whole or not at all.
  • Use when: latency > reliability (media, games), tiny req/resp (DNS), multicast/broadcast, lossy-OK telemetry, or you're building your own transport (QUIC).
  • Add app-level reliability selectively: seq+ACK, FEC, your own pacing.
  • Keep datagrams < path MTU (~1200 B safe) to avoid fragmentation.
  • You must implement congestion control yourself — unbounded UDP is antisocial.
  • Spoofable + amplifiable → classic reflection-DDoS vector.
Q&A
Why does DNS use UDP?
Queries and answers are usually small (fit in one datagram), and setting up a TCP connection (handshake, teardown, TIME_WAIT) for each lookup would add latency and server load. If the response is too big or truncated, the resolver retries over TCP.
Why is UDP better for live video than TCP?
If a packet is lost, TCP stalls the whole stream retransmitting it — but by the time it arrives, that frame's moment has passed. UDP lets the app skip the loss and keep playing (concealing the gap), keeping latency low.
Does UDP guarantee a datagram arrives intact if it arrives at all?
Mostly — the checksum (mandatory in IPv6, optional-but-usual in IPv4) detects corruption, and datagrams are delivered whole or dropped. It does not guarantee delivery, non-duplication, or order.
What must you add if you build a protocol on UDP?
Whatever guarantees you need: sequence numbers and ACKs for reliability/ordering, retransmission timers, and — importantly — congestion control so you don't overwhelm the network. Optionally FEC and NAT keepalives.
What is a UDP amplification attack?
An attacker sends a small request with a spoofed source IP (the victim's) to a service that replies with a much larger response (open DNS resolver, NTP monlist, memcached). The victim is flooded with amplified traffic it never asked for.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Does UDP have a handshake?
No — it's connectionless. You just send datagrams.
Give two protocols that run over UDP.
DNS, DHCP, QUIC/HTTP-3, NTP, RTP, mDNS — any two.
TCP is a byte stream; UDP is a ___ stream?
Message (datagram) oriented — boundaries are preserved.

Intermediate core

You're sending 4 KB JSON blobs over UDP and losing many under load. Likely cause?
4 KB exceeds the ~1500-byte Ethernet MTU, so each datagram is IP-fragmented into ~3 packets; losing any one fragment discards the whole datagram, and fragment reassembly buffers can overflow under load. Keep datagrams under the path MTU (chunk the data yourself), or use TCP/QUIC for anything that big.
Why does QUIC build on UDP rather than being a new protocol number directly on IP?
Middleboxes (NATs, firewalls, load balancers) drop or mangle IP packets with unfamiliar protocol numbers — only TCP and UDP reliably traverse the internet ("protocol ossification"). UDP gives QUIC ports (for NAT traversal and demultiplexing) and universal reachability, while leaving QUIC free to implement its own reliability, encryption, and congestion control in userspace where it can be updated without OS changes.

Advanced deep

What congestion-control obligations does an application-layer UDP protocol have, and how does QUIC meet them?
An unresponsive UDP flow that ignores loss can drive a link into congestion collapse and starve TCP flows (which back off) — the IETF requires UDP apps sending significant volume to be "TCP-friendly" (roughly, use no more than a competing TCP flow would). QUIC implements a full congestion controller in userspace: by default a NewReno/CUBIC-equivalent (slow start, congestion avoidance, loss-based reduction), with pluggable BBR; it does per-packet ACK-based RTT sampling, packet pacing, and explicit loss detection with its own retransmission (re-sending the data in a new packet with a fresh packet number, avoiding TCP's retransmission ambiguity). It also handles the amplification risk: before validating the client's address, a QUIC server may send at most 3× the bytes it received, preventing the handshake from being used as a reflection amplifier.
How do you do reliable, ordered delivery of only some messages over UDP without reinventing TCP badly?
Use a proven layer rather than hand-rolling: QUIC streams (reliable, ordered, multiplexed, with unreliable DATAGRAM frames alongside for the "don't care" messages), SCTP (message-oriented, multi-streamed, partial reliability via "timed reliability"), or RTP + RTCP for media (RTP carries timestamped media unreliably; RTCP carries feedback). If you must build it: give each message a sequence number and a "reliability class"; ACK only the reliable classes with SACK-style bitmaps; retransmit on a small fixed number of RTOs then give up; run a real congestion controller (copy CUBIC or use a library); and cap in-flight bytes. The common failure is a naive stop-and-wait or fixed-timer scheme that either wastes bandwidth or congestion-collapses.

DNS Resolution

Turning api.example.com into an IP — the distributed, cached lookup that precedes almost every connection.

Notes

DNS is the distributed database that turns names like example.com into IP addresses (and much more). A lookup walks a hierarchy — root servers, then the TLD servers, then the domain’s authoritative servers — usually via a caching recursive resolver that does the walking for you. This page covers the hierarchy and the recursive-vs-iterative distinction, the steps of a resolution, the common record types (A/AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS, SOA), how caching and TTLs work (and why “DNS propagation” is really cache expiry), and modern additions (DNSSEC, DoH/DoT, anycast).

The hierarchy

The namespace is a tree: root (.) → TLD (.com, .org, .io) → authoritative servers for a domain (example.com). No single server has everything; resolution walks down the tree.

$ dig +trace www.example.com
.                       NS  a.root-servers.net.        # 1. root: "ask a TLD server"
com.                    NS  a.gtld-servers.net.        # 2. .com TLD: "ask the domain's NS"
example.com.            NS  a.iana-servers.net.        # 3. authoritative for example.com
www.example.com.  300   A   93.184.216.34             # 4. the answer, TTL 300s

A lookup

  1. App asks the OS stub resolver, which asks a configured recursive resolver (your ISP's, or 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1).
  2. If not cached, the recursive resolver does iterative queries: asks a root server (→ "ask the .com servers"), then a TLD server (→ "ask example.com's nameservers"), then the authoritative server (→ the answer).
  3. The recursive resolver caches the answer for its TTL and returns it to the client, which also caches it.
$ cat /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 1.1.1.1               # the recursive resolver the stub asks

$ dig www.example.com
;; QUESTION SECTION:
;www.example.com.        IN  A
;; ANSWER SECTION:
www.example.com. 276 IN  A   93.184.216.34    # 276 = seconds LEFT on the cached TTL (was 300)
;; Query time: 1 msec                          # 1ms = served from the resolver's cache

Record types

TypeMaps
A / AAAAname → IPv4 / IPv6 address
CNAMEname → another name (alias)
MXdomain → mail servers (with priority)
NSdomain → its authoritative nameservers
TXTarbitrary text (SPF, DKIM, domain verification)
SOAzone metadata (serial, refresh, TTLs)
PTRIP → name (reverse DNS)
$ dig +short example.com MX
10 mail.example.com.            # priority 10 -- lower is preferred
$ dig +short example.com TXT
"v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all"
$ dig +short -x 93.184.216.34   # reverse (PTR): IP -> name
$ dig +short www.example.com CNAME   # CNAME chains resolve to a final A/AAAA

Caching & TTL

Every record has a TTL (seconds) controlling how long resolvers may cache it. Low TTL = faster changes but more queries; high TTL = fewer queries but slow propagation. "DNS propagation delay" is really just old cached records expiring. Negative answers (NXDOMAIN) are cached too (per the SOA's minimum).

# migration playbook: drop TTL first, wait it out, then cut over
#  day -2:  set  www  A  <old-ip>  TTL 60      (was 3600)
#  day  0:  change to <new-ip>   -- caches expire within 60s, not an hour
#  day +1:  raise TTL back to 3600
$ dig +short www.example.com   # poll from several networks until all return the new IP

Modern DNS

DoH (DNS over HTTPS) / DoT (over TLS) encrypt queries against snooping and tampering. DNSSEC signs records so resolvers can verify authenticity (prevents cache poisoning) — but doesn't encrypt. DNS is also a load-balancing tool: multiple A records, GeoDNS, weighted responses.

$ curl -s -H 'accept: application/dns-json' \
    'https://1.1.1.1/dns-query?name=example.com&type=A'   # DoH: query over HTTPS, port 443

$ dig example.com +dnssec +short      # RRSIG present -> records are cryptographically signed

$ dig +short bigsite.com A            # multiple A records = DNS round-robin load spreading
203.0.113.10
203.0.113.11
Cheat Sheet
  • Hierarchy: root → TLD → authoritative. Recursive resolver does the walking; stub resolver just asks it.
  • Recursive query (client → resolver: "get me the answer") vs iterative (resolver → each server: "who's next?").
  • Records: A/AAAA (IP), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), NS (nameservers), TXT, SOA, PTR (reverse).
  • TTL controls cache lifetime; "propagation" = waiting for old cached records to expire. Lower TTL before a planned change.
  • NXDOMAIN (name doesn't exist) is also cached.
  • UDP/53 normally; falls back to TCP/53 for large responses or zone transfers.
  • DoH/DoT encrypt; DNSSEC authenticates (doesn't encrypt).
  • DNS-based load balancing: multiple A records, GeoDNS, weighting.
Q&A
Recursive vs iterative query?
In a recursive query the client asks a resolver to do all the work and return the final answer. In iterative queries (what the resolver then does), each server responds with either the answer or a referral to the next server down the tree.
What does a CNAME do, and what's a restriction?
It aliases one name to another (www.example.com → example.com). A CNAME can't coexist with other records at the same name, so you can't put a CNAME at a zone apex (example.com itself needs SOA/NS) — providers offer ALIAS/ANAME as a workaround.
Why does a DNS change take hours to "propagate"?
It doesn't push anywhere — resolvers worldwide keep serving the old record from cache until its TTL expires. Lowering the TTL a day before the change shrinks that window.
Why does DNS use UDP but sometimes TCP?
UDP for the common small query/response (cheap, no handshake). TCP when the response exceeds what fits/what the resolver accepts over UDP (the TC truncated flag triggers a retry over TCP), and always for zone transfers.
What does DNSSEC protect against, and what does it not do?
It cryptographically signs records so a resolver can verify they came from the real zone and weren't tampered with (defeats cache poisoning / spoofing). It does not encrypt the query or answer — that's DoH/DoT's job.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which record maps a hostname to an IPv6 address?
AAAA.
What controls how long a DNS answer is cached?
Its TTL (time to live), in seconds.
What's the first server type a recursive resolver contacts for an uncached name?
A root server (which refers it to the appropriate TLD servers).

Intermediate core

You're migrating a service to a new IP with minimal downtime. DNS plan?
Days ahead, drop the record's TTL to 60–300s so caches turn over fast. At cutover, update the A/AAAA record. Keep the old server serving until traffic drains (watch logs) — some resolvers ignore TTL. Once traffic is fully on the new IP, raise the TTL back up. Better still, put a load balancer / stable anycast IP in front so the app IP never changes.
How can DNS do geographic load balancing?
The authoritative server (GeoDNS) inspects the resolver's source IP (or EDNS Client Subnet), looks it up in a geo database, and returns the A record for the nearest data center. Combined with health checks it can also fail traffic away from a down region. Caveat: it sees the resolver's location, which for public resolvers (8.8.8.8) may be far from the user unless ECS is supported.

Advanced deep

Explain a DNS cache-poisoning attack (Kaminsky) and the mitigations.
Classic attack: when a resolver queries an authoritative server, the attacker races to send a forged response before the real one. To be accepted, the forgery must match the query name, the 16-bit transaction ID, and the source port. Pre-2008, the source port was often fixed and the ID predictable/incrementing, so guessing was feasible — and Kaminsky's insight was to attack many non-existent subdomains (1.bank.com, 2.bank.com…) so a failed guess doesn't matter and you get near-unlimited attempts, then include a poisoned NS/glue record for the whole zone. Mitigations: source-port randomisation (adds ~16 bits of entropy), 0x20 encoding (randomise the case of the query name, which the response must echo), DNSSEC (signatures make forgery infeasible), and running queries over DoT/DoH to an authenticated resolver.
What is the negative-caching and the "thundering herd on expiry" problem for a popular record, and how do resolvers handle it?
When a very popular record's TTL expires, every cache miss at a busy resolver triggers a fresh upstream lookup — potentially thousands simultaneously ("cache stampede"), hammering the authoritative servers. Resolvers mitigate with: request coalescing (in-flight de-duplication — one upstream query, many waiters); serve-stale (RFC 8767 — return the expired record immediately while asynchronously refreshing, so users never wait on a slow/down authoritative server); prefetching (refresh popular records shortly before expiry); and jittering effective TTLs slightly so many records don't expire in lockstep. Authoritative-side, anycast and generous TTLs on stable records reduce the load. Negative answers (NXDOMAIN) are cached per the zone's SOA minimum to blunt floods of queries for names that don't exist (a common DDoS pattern).

HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 & HTTP/3

Same semantics, three very different wire protocols — and the head-of-line problem driving the evolution.

Notes

HTTP is the request/response protocol of the web: a client sends a method + URL + headers (+ body); the server replies with a status code + headers (+ body). The semantics (methods, status codes, headers, caching, content negotiation) have been stable for decades; what changed across HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 is the wire format — each version attacking a different form of head-of-line blocking. This page covers the stable semantics and then what each version does differently and why (keep-alive, multiplexing, HPACK, QUIC over UDP).

Semantics (stable across versions)

  • Methods: GET (safe, cacheable), HEAD, POST, PUT (idempotent), PATCH, DELETE (idempotent), OPTIONS. Safe = no side effects; idempotent = repeating has the same effect as once.
  • Status classes: 1xx info, 2xx success (200, 201, 204), 3xx redirect (301 permanent, 302/307 temporary, 304 not-modified), 4xx client error (400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 429), 5xx server error (500, 502, 503, 504).
  • Headers: Content-Type, Cache-Control/ETag, Authorization, Accept, Host (required in 1.1). Stateless — each request self-contained; state via cookies/tokens.
PUT /users/7 HTTP/1.1              # idempotent: send it 3x, user 7 ends the same
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
Content-Type: application/json

{"name": "Ann"}

HTTP/1.1 200 OK                    # 201 if it created, 204 if no body, 409 on a conflict
ETag: "v4"                         # client can later send If-None-Match: "v4" -> 304

HTTP/1.1

Text protocol, one request/response at a time per connection. Keep-alive reuses the TCP connection; pipelining (send multiple without waiting) exists but is broken in practice. Browsers work around the serialisation by opening ~6 parallel connections per origin. Head-of-line blocking at the HTTP level: a slow response blocks the ones behind it on that connection.

$ curl --http1.1 -v https://api.example.com/a
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
< Connection: keep-alive           # TCP connection reused for the next request...
# ...but request B waits for A's full response first (HTTP-level head-of-line blocking)
# browsers dodge this by opening ~6 TCP connections per origin

HTTP/2

  • Binary framing; multiplexing many streams over one TCP connection (no more 6-connection hack).
  • Header compression (HPACK) — repeated headers cost almost nothing.
  • Stream prioritisation, server push (now deprecated/removed — ineffective in practice).
  • Still over TCP → TCP-level head-of-line blocking: one lost packet stalls all streams.
$ curl --http2 -v https://api.example.com/a & curl --http2 https://api.example.com/b
* Using HTTP/2, server supports multiplexing
* h2h3 [:method: GET] ... stream 1        # request A -> stream 1
* h2h3 [:method: GET] ... stream 3        # request B -> stream 3, SAME TCP connection, concurrent
# but a single dropped TCP segment stalls BOTH streams until it's retransmitted

HTTP/3

Runs over QUIC (over UDP). Per-stream reliability → a loss on one stream doesn't block others. Combined transport+TLS 1.3 handshake (1-RTT, 0-RTT on resume). Connection migration across IP changes. TLS is mandatory.

$ curl --http3 -v https://cloudflare.com/
* Connected to cloudflare.com ... via HTTP/3      # QUIC over UDP/443
< alt-svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400                    # servers advertise h3; client upgrades on the next visit
# loss on stream 1 does NOT block stream 3 -- QUIC recovers per-stream
# switch Wi-Fi -> cellular mid-download: connection ID survives, no reconnect
Cheat Sheet
  • Safe methods (no side effects): GET, HEAD, OPTIONS. Idempotent: those + PUT, DELETE (and ideally PATCH). POST is neither.
  • Status: 2xx ok, 3xx redirect (304 = use your cache), 4xx you erred (401 auth needed, 403 forbidden, 404 missing, 409 conflict, 429 rate-limited), 5xx server erred (502/503/504 = upstream/overload/timeout).
  • HTTP/1.1: 1 in-flight request per connection → browsers open ~6; app-level head-of-line blocking; needs Host.
  • HTTP/2: binary, multiplexed streams over 1 TCP conn, HPACK header compression — but TCP head-of-line blocking remains.
  • HTTP/3: over QUIC/UDP, per-stream loss recovery, faster handshake, connection migration, TLS required.
  • Caching: Cache-Control (max-age, no-store, private), ETag + If-None-Match → 304.
Q&A
Difference between safe and idempotent methods?
Safe = the request has no side effects on the server (GET, HEAD). Idempotent = making the request N times has the same server state as making it once (GET, PUT, DELETE). All safe methods are idempotent; PUT/DELETE are idempotent but not safe; POST is neither.
What problem did HTTP/2 multiplexing solve, and what did it leave unsolved?
It removed HTTP-level head-of-line blocking and the need for ~6 parallel connections by carrying many concurrent streams on one connection. It didn't solve TCP-level head-of-line blocking — a single lost TCP segment still stalls every stream until it's retransmitted.
301 vs 302 vs 307?
301 = permanent redirect (clients/search engines update their links; method may change to GET historically). 302 = found/temporary (ambiguous method handling). 307 = temporary, method and body preserved. 308 = permanent, method preserved. Prefer 308/307 for clarity.
How does a conditional GET save bandwidth?
The server sends an ETag (or Last-Modified) with the response. Next time, the client sends If-None-Match: <etag>; if unchanged, the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body and the client uses its cached copy.
Why is HTTP called stateless, and how do apps keep state?
Each request is independent — the server doesn't inherently remember previous requests from the same client. Applications layer state on top via cookies (a session id) or tokens (JWT) sent with every request.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What status code means "the resource hasn't changed, use your cache"?
304 Not Modified.
Which HTTP version introduced multiplexed streams over one connection?
HTTP/2.
Is PUT idempotent?
Yes — sending the same PUT repeatedly leaves the resource in the same state.

Intermediate core

Your API returns 200 with an error message in the body. Why is that bad?
Clients, proxies, caches, and monitoring all key off the status code. A 200 means "success" — caches may store it, retries won't trigger, dashboards show no errors, and generic client code won't branch to error handling. Use the right 4xx/5xx (400 for bad input, 409 for conflict, 422 for semantic validation, 503 for overload) with a structured error body.
On a lossy mobile network, HTTP/2 is slower than HTTP/1.1 for your site. Explain.
HTTP/1.1 spreads requests over ~6 TCP connections, so a lost packet only stalls one of them. HTTP/2 puts everything on one connection; a single lost segment triggers TCP head-of-line blocking that pauses all multiplexed streams until retransmission. With enough loss, the serialised stall outweighs the multiplexing benefit. HTTP/3 (QUIC) fixes this with per-stream delivery.

Advanced deep

Why was HTTP/2 Server Push added and then effectively abandoned?
Push let a server proactively send resources (CSS, JS) it knew the client would request after the HTML, aiming to save a round trip. In practice it was net-negative: servers pushed resources already in the client's cache (wasting bandwidth — the client can only send RST_STREAM after the push starts), prioritisation interactions were tricky, it competed with the critical HTML for bandwidth, and CDNs/frameworks struggled to know exactly what to push. Chrome removed support in 2022. The problem it targeted is better solved by 103 Early Hints (server sends Link: rel=preload hints before the full response, letting the client decide) and by good <link rel=preload> in the HTML itself.
Explain HPACK and the security consideration that shaped it (vs HTTP/1's plain headers and vs SPDY's gzip).
HTTP/2 headers repeat massively across requests (cookies, user-agent, accept). SPDY compressed them with gzip, but that enabled the CRIME attack: if attacker-controlled data and a secret (session cookie) are compressed together, the compressed size leaks whether the attacker's guess matches part of the secret — byte-by-byte extraction. HPACK is designed to resist this: it uses a static table of common header name/value pairs, a bounded dynamic table of recently-seen headers (indexed by reference), and Huffman coding of literals — but crucially it does not do context-mixing compression across the boundary between values, and it lets sensitive headers be marked "never indexed" so they're never placed in the shared dynamic table. This gives most of gzip's ratio on real header sets without the chosen-plaintext leak. (QPACK in HTTP/3 solves the same problem with the added complication of QUIC's out-of-order stream delivery.)

HTTPS & the TLS Handshake

Authenticated, confidential, tamper-evident channels — and how the keys get agreed.

Notes

TLS is the layer that makes HTTP into HTTPS: it authenticates the server (via a certificate signed by a trusted CA), negotiates keys, and then encrypts and integrity-protects everything. This page covers what TLS actually provides (confidentiality, integrity, authentication), the split between slow asymmetric crypto (used once, to agree a key) and fast symmetric crypto (used for the bulk data), certificates and the chain of trust, the streamlined TLS 1.3 one-round-trip handshake, and forward secrecy (a stolen server key can’t decrypt past traffic).

What TLS provides

  • Confidentiality — traffic is encrypted (symmetric cipher, e.g. AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305).
  • Integrity — an AEAD tag detects tampering.
  • Authentication — the server proves its identity with a certificate (mutual TLS adds client auth).
$ openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -brief
Protocol version: TLSv1.3
Ciphersuite: TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384      # AEAD = confidentiality + integrity in one
Verification: OK                         # authentication: cert chain trusted
Peer certificate: CN = example.com
# tamper with a byte in transit -> the GCM auth tag fails -> connection aborts

Symmetric vs asymmetric

Asymmetric crypto (RSA, ECDSA, ECDH) is slow but lets strangers agree on a secret / verify identity. Symmetric crypto is fast. So TLS uses asymmetric during the handshake to authenticate and to derive a shared symmetric key, then encrypts the bulk data symmetrically.

# handshake (asymmetric, ~once): ECDHE key agreement + a signature over the transcript
#   -> both sides now hold the same 32-byte session key

# bulk data (symmetric, per record): AES-GCM with that session key -- ~GB/s per core
#   asymmetric ops per connection: 1-2      symmetric ops: millions

Certificates & the chain of trust

A certificate binds a domain to a public key and is signed by a Certificate Authority. Your OS/browser ships a set of trusted root CAs. The server presents its cert plus intermediates; the client verifies the signature chain up to a trusted root, checks the domain matches (SAN), the validity dates, and revocation (OCSP stapling / CRL). Let's Encrypt made certs free and automated (ACME).

$ openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -showcerts </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
    | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
subject= CN = example.com
issuer=  C = US, O = Let's Encrypt, CN = R3        # leaf signed by an intermediate...
notAfter=Sep  1 12:00:00 2024 GMT                  # ...expiry checked by the client
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name: DNS:example.com, DNS:www.example.com  # must match the host
# chain: leaf  <-  Let's Encrypt R3  <-  ISRG Root X1 (in the OS trust store)

TLS 1.3 handshake (1-RTT)

  1. ClientHello: supported ciphers + a Diffie-Hellman key share (guessing the group).
  2. ServerHello: chosen cipher + its DH key share; then (encrypted) the certificate, a signature over the handshake, and "Finished".
  3. Both sides derive the same session keys from the DH exchange. Client sends "Finished"; application data can flow.

0-RTT resumption: on a repeat visit the client can send data in the first flight using a pre-shared key — fast, but replayable, so only for idempotent requests.

ClientHello   { ciphers, key_share=g^x }                 -->    # 1 flight from client
                        <-- ServerHello { key_share=g^y }, {EncryptedExtensions,
                                          Certificate, CertVerify, Finished}
{Finished}, {application_data}  -->                              # app data on the 2nd flight = 1-RTT
# resume:  ClientHello + early_data (0-RTT)  -- only safe for GET/idempotent (replayable)

Forward secrecy

Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE) means each session's keys are derived from fresh random values and discarded after. Stealing the server's long-term private key later does not let an attacker decrypt past captured sessions. TLS 1.3 makes this mandatory (removed static-RSA key exchange).

# each connection: server generates a fresh ephemeral key pair (x, g^x), uses it once, discards x
#   session key = KDF( (g^y)^x )   -- never sent, never stored

# attacker records ciphertext today, steals the server's cert private key next year:
#   static RSA (TLS <=1.2): private key decrypts ALL recorded past sessions   -- bad
#   ECDHE (TLS 1.3):        past sessions stay safe -- the per-session x is long gone
Cheat Sheet
  • TLS = confidentiality + integrity + authentication over TCP (or QUIC).
  • Asymmetric (RSA/ECDSA/ECDHE) authenticates + agrees a key; symmetric (AES-GCM/ChaCha20) encrypts the data.
  • Certificate binds domain → public key, signed by a CA; client verifies chain to a trusted root + domain match + dates + revocation.
  • TLS 1.3: 1-RTT handshake, all handshake after ServerHello encrypted, only AEAD ciphers, forward secrecy mandatory, static-RSA removed.
  • 0-RTT resumption: data in the first packet, but replayable → idempotent requests only.
  • Forward secrecy (ECDHE): past traffic stays safe even if the server key later leaks.
  • SNI tells the server which hostname's cert to present (one IP, many sites); Encrypted Client Hello hides it.
  • mTLS = client also presents a cert (service-to-service auth).
Q&A
Why does TLS use both asymmetric and symmetric cryptography?
Asymmetric is needed to authenticate a stranger and agree a secret over an open channel, but it's ~100× slower. So it's used only briefly in the handshake; the actual data is protected with a fast symmetric cipher using the key that was agreed.
What does a certificate authority actually attest?
That the entity controlling a given public key also controls the named domain(s) (for a DV cert). The CA signs the certificate; clients trust it because they trust the CA's root, which ships with the OS/browser.
What is forward secrecy and how is it achieved?
Compromise of the server's long-term key doesn't expose past sessions. Achieved with ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE): each session's keys come from fresh random values that are thrown away afterward, so there's nothing to recover later.
What's the risk with TLS 1.3 0-RTT data?
An attacker who captured the first flight can replay it. The server can't distinguish a replay from the original at that point, so 0-RTT must only carry safe/idempotent requests (a GET, not a "transfer $100").
What is SNI and why does it matter?
Server Name Indication — the client puts the target hostname in the ClientHello so a server hosting many domains on one IP knows which certificate to send. Historically it's sent in cleartext (a privacy leak); Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) addresses that.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Three properties TLS gives a connection?
Confidentiality (encryption), integrity (tamper detection), and authentication (server identity).
How many round trips does a TLS 1.3 full handshake take?
One (1-RTT); zero for a resumed session with 0-RTT data.
What signs a website's certificate?
A Certificate Authority (CA), whose root certificate is trusted by the client's OS/browser.

Intermediate core

A browser shows "certificate not trusted" but the cert is valid. Common causes?
The server didn't send the intermediate certificate(s), so the client can't build a chain to a trusted root (works in some browsers that cache intermediates, fails in others). Or: the system clock is wrong (cert appears expired/not-yet-valid), the root isn't in this device's trust store (private CA not installed), the hostname doesn't match a SAN entry, or the cert was revoked.
Why is HTTPS on a CDN edge still "end to end" secure — or is it?
It's TLS-terminated at the edge, so the connection user↔edge is encrypted and authenticated, but the CDN decrypts your traffic there. Edge↔origin is a separate TLS connection (should also be TLS, ideally with origin cert validation / mTLS). So it's secure against network eavesdroppers on both hops, but you are trusting the CDN with plaintext. True end-to-end (origin-only key) would defeat the CDN's ability to cache/compress/inspect; some setups use edge compute or field-level encryption for the most sensitive data.

Advanced deep

Walk through the TLS 1.3 key schedule and why the handshake is authenticated after keys are derived.
After ClientHello/ServerHello exchange ECDHE shares, both sides compute the shared secret and run it through HKDF to derive a chain of keys: early secret → handshake secret (→ client/server handshake traffic keys, used to encrypt the rest of the handshake) → master secret (→ application traffic keys) → and a resumption secret. The server then sends its Certificate and a CertificateVerify = a signature (with the cert's private key) over a transcript hash of every handshake message so far, followed by a Finished = an HMAC over the transcript keyed by a derived "finished key". The client verifies the signature (proves the peer holds the cert's private key and that the handshake wasn't tampered with — the transcript hash covers the cipher/version negotiation, defeating downgrade attacks) and the Finished MAC (proves both sides derived the same keys). Authentication comes after key derivation because TLS 1.3 encrypts the certificate itself for privacy, and because binding the signature to the full transcript is what makes the negotiation tamper-proof.
What is certificate transparency and what class of attack does it mitigate?
CT requires CAs to publish every certificate they issue to public, append-only, cryptographically-verifiable logs; browsers (Chrome, Safari) reject certs that aren't accompanied by signed proofs of log inclusion (SCTs). It mitigates mis-issuance: a CA that is compromised, coerced, or buggy issuing a valid cert for a domain it shouldn't (e.g. a government-compelled cert for google.com, or the 2011 DigiNotar breach). Before CT, such a cert could be used for MITM and the real domain owner would never know. With CT, the domain owner (or automated monitors like crt.sh) can watch the logs and detect an unexpected cert for their domain within hours, then get it revoked and the CA distrusted. It's detection, not prevention — but it makes covert mis-issuance essentially impossible to keep hidden.

Sockets & the Client/Server Lifecycle

The system-call sequence behind every network server.

Notes

A socket is the OS handle for one end of a network connection — the API your program uses to actually send and receive. This page covers the call sequence for both sides (socket / bind / listen / accept on the server, socket / connect on the client, then read/write), how ports and the 4-tuple identify a connection, blocking vs non-blocking I/O and why servers use epoll/kqueue, and the operational issues everyone hits (TIME_WAIT, EADDRINUSE, partial reads/writes, half-open connections).

The call sequence

SERVER                         CLIENT
socket()                       socket()
bind(addr:port)
listen(backlog)
accept()  <-------- 3-way ----- connect(addr:port)
   returns a NEW fd
read()/write() <-- data --> write()/read()
close()                        close()
  • socket() creates an endpoint (domain: AF_INET/AF_INET6; type: SOCK_STREAM=TCP, SOCK_DGRAM=UDP).
  • bind() assigns a local address/port (servers; clients usually let the OS pick an ephemeral port).
  • listen() marks it passive; backlog bounds the queue of completed-handshake connections waiting for accept().
  • accept() pops one connection and returns a new fd dedicated to that client; the listening fd keeps accepting.

Ports

0–1023 well-known (need privilege), 1024–49151 registered, 49152–65535 ephemeral (client source ports). A TCP connection is identified by the 4-tuple (src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port) — that's why one server port serves thousands of clients.

$ ss -tan
State   Local Address:Port    Peer Address:Port
LISTEN  0.0.0.0:443           0.0.0.0:*          # one listening socket
ESTAB   10.0.0.5:443          203.0.113.7:51002  # distinct 4-tuples,
ESTAB   10.0.0.5:443          203.0.113.7:51044  # same server ip:port -> both fine
ESTAB   10.0.0.5:443          198.51.100.9:40311
# the kernel demuxes incoming packets to a socket by the full (sip,sport,dip,dport)

Blocking vs non-blocking

  • Blocking: read() waits until data arrives. Simple; one thread per connection → doesn't scale to 10k+ connections (memory, context-switch cost).
  • Non-blocking + event loop: O_NONBLOCK + epoll/kqueue/IOCP — one thread watches many fds, handles whichever is ready. Basis of nginx, Node.js, Redis.
// blocking: this thread parks until bytes arrive (fine for a few connections)
int n = read(fd, buf, sizeof buf);

// non-blocking + epoll: one thread, thousands of fds
fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, O_NONBLOCK);
int ep = epoll_create1(0);
epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, fd, &(struct epoll_event){.events = EPOLLIN, .data.fd = fd});
struct epoll_event ev[64];
int k = epoll_wait(ep, ev, 64, -1);   // returns only the fds that are READY
for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) handle(ev[i].data.fd);  // read() now won't block

Common issues

  • bind: address already in use after restart → set SO_REUSEADDR (lets you rebind while old connections linger in TIME_WAIT).
  • Partial reads/writes: write(n) may send fewer than n bytes — loop.
  • EINTR: a syscall interrupted by a signal — retry.
  • A dead peer isn't noticed until you write (and get RST/EPIPE) or a keepalive fails — use SO_KEEPALIVE or app-level heartbeats.
int yes = 1;
setsockopt(fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &yes, sizeof yes);  // rebind despite lingering TIME_WAIT

// write() can be short -- always loop:
size_t off = 0;
while (off < len) {
    ssize_t w = write(fd, buf + off, len - off);
    if (w < 0) { if (errno == EINTR) continue;   // interrupted -> retry
                  if (errno == EPIPE) break;      // peer gone -> stop
                  return -1; }
    off += (size_t)w;
}
Cheat Sheet
  • Server: socket → bind → listen → accept (returns a new per-client fd) → read/write → close.
  • Client: socket → connect → read/write → close.
  • Connection identity = 4-tuple (src ip, src port, dst ip, dst port); one listening port, many clients.
  • backlog = queue of established connections awaiting accept.
  • Blocking = thread-per-connection (simple, doesn't scale). Non-blocking + epoll/kqueue = one thread, many fds (scales).
  • SO_REUSEADDR to rebind past TIME_WAIT; SO_REUSEPORT to let multiple processes accept on one port.
  • Always loop on read/write (partial I/O); retry on EINTR; handle EPIPE/ECONNRESET.
  • Ephemeral port exhaustion limits outbound connections from one host to one dest — pool/reuse.
Q&A
What does accept() return, and why a new fd?
A brand-new socket fd bound to that specific client connection. The original listening socket stays open to accept further connections. Read/write happen on the new fd.
How does one server port handle thousands of simultaneous clients?
Each connection is uniquely identified by the full 4-tuple (client IP + client port + server IP + server port). The server port is constant; the client side varies, so the kernel can demultiplex.
Blocking vs non-blocking sockets — the scaling difference?
Blocking needs a thread (or process) parked per connection; at 10k+ connections the memory and scheduler overhead dominates ("C10k problem"). Non-blocking sockets with an event notification mechanism (epoll) let one thread service thousands of connections, acting only on ready ones.
Why SO_REUSEADDR?
After a server restarts, its old connections may be in TIME_WAIT holding the port; without SO_REUSEADDR, bind() fails with "address already in use". It's standard for servers.
Your write() returned 500 when you asked to send 1400 bytes. Bug?
No — that's normal for stream sockets. The kernel accepted 500 bytes into the send buffer; you must loop, advancing the offset, until all 1400 are written (or handle EAGAIN on a non-blocking socket).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which call makes a socket passive (ready to accept connections)?
listen().
What socket type is TCP?
SOCK_STREAM. UDP is SOCK_DGRAM.
Does a client usually call bind()?
No — it lets the OS assign an ephemeral source port automatically during connect().

Intermediate core

What is the "C10k problem" and how is it solved?
Handling 10,000 concurrent connections on one server. Thread-per-connection collapses under memory (each thread's stack) and context-switch overhead. Solution: an event-driven model — non-blocking sockets plus a scalable readiness API (epoll on Linux, kqueue on BSD/macOS, IOCP on Windows) so a small thread pool handles all connections, doing work only for sockets that are ready. nginx, HAProxy, Node, Redis are built this way; modern systems also use io_uring for async I/O.
A load-balanced service can't open more outbound connections to the database. Error is about ports. Why?
Ephemeral source-port exhaustion: outbound connections from one host IP to one destination IP:port are limited to the ~28k–64k ephemeral port range, minus those in TIME_WAIT. Fix: use a connection pool (few long-lived connections, not one per request), widen ip_local_port_range, enable tcp_tw_reuse, or spread across multiple source IPs / destination ports.

Advanced deep

Explain level-triggered vs edge-triggered epoll and a bug edge-triggered invites.
Level-triggered (default): epoll_wait reports a fd as ready as long as there's data to read / space to write — you can read "some" and be told again next call. Edge-triggered (EPOLLET): you're notified only on the transition from not-ready to ready; if you don't drain the socket completely, you won't be notified again until more data arrives. The classic bug: an edge-triggered handler does one read(), gets 4 KB, processes it, and returns — leaving 60 KB in the socket buffer that epoll never re-signals, so the connection hangs. Correct edge-triggered code loops read() until it returns EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK (and similarly loops write()). Edge-triggered means fewer syscalls under high load but demands this discipline; level-triggered is more forgiving and usually fast enough.
How does SO_REUSEPORT change the accept model, and what problem does it solve over a shared listening socket?
Traditionally all worker processes/threads share one listening fd and race in accept() (or an epoll on it), which historically caused the "thundering herd" (all workers wake, one wins) and, even with modern wakeup-one behaviour, uneven load distribution and a single accept-queue bottleneck. SO_REUSEPORT lets multiple sockets bind the same IP:port; the kernel keeps a separate accept queue per socket and hashes incoming connections (by 4-tuple) across them. Each worker has its own listener and queue — no lock contention on accept, better multicore scaling, and load spread by the kernel. Caveats: connection distribution is by hash not by worker readiness, so a slow/blocked worker still gets its share (its queue can overflow and drop SYNs); and on graceful restart, removing a socket can drop its queued connections unless handled carefully. nginx, Envoy, and HAProxy use it for multicore accept scaling.

NAT, Proxies, Load Balancers & CDNs

The boxes between the client and your server, and what each one does to a request.

Notes

Between a browser and an application server sit a stack of intermediaries that the app usually can’t see: proxies, load balancers, and CDNs. This page covers forward vs reverse proxies (who they act on behalf of), load balancers at L4 (connection-level, fast, opaque) vs L7 (request-level, content-aware, can do TLS termination, routing, retries), health checks and sticky sessions, and CDNs — edge caches near users, fronted by anycast so the same IP routes each client to its nearest point of presence.

Proxies

Forward proxyReverse proxy
Sits in front ofthe clientthe server
Client knows?yes (configured)no (looks like the server)
Usescorporate egress filtering, caching, anonymity, bypassing geo-blocksTLS termination, load balancing, caching, compression, WAF, hiding backend topology
# forward proxy: the CLIENT is configured to use it
$ export https_proxy=http://proxy.corp:3128
$ curl https://example.com/            # request goes to proxy.corp, which fetches it

# reverse proxy (nginx): the client just sees "the server"
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name api.example.com;
    location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080; }   # TLS terminates here; app is plain HTTP
}

Load balancers

  • L4 (transport): forwards by IP:port, doesn't read the payload. Fast, protocol-agnostic, preserves the connection. Can't route by URL. (e.g. AWS NLB, IPVS.)
  • L7 (application): terminates the connection, reads HTTP — routes by host/path/header, does TLS termination, retries, sticky sessions, request rewriting. (nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, ALB.)
  • Algorithms: round-robin, least-connections, weighted, consistent hashing (for cache affinity), IP hash.
  • Health checks remove unhealthy backends; sticky sessions pin a client to one backend (needed only if the backend holds session state — better to externalise it).
# HAProxy: L7 path routing + least-connections + health checks
frontend web
    bind :443 ssl crt /etc/ssl/site.pem
    use_backend api  if { path_beg /api/ }      # route by URL -> needs L7
    default_backend  web

backend api
    balance leastconn                           # or roundrobin / source (IP hash)
    option httpchk GET /healthz
    server a1 10.0.1.11:8080 check              # 'check' -> ejected when /healthz fails
    server a2 10.0.1.12:8080 check

CDN

A globally distributed set of edge caches near users. Serves static assets (and increasingly dynamic/API responses) from the nearest POP, reducing latency and origin load. Also provides: DDoS absorption, TLS termination, compression, edge compute (Workers/Lambda@Edge), and origin shielding. Cache control via Cache-Control, ETag, surrogate keys, and explicit purge/invalidation.

$ curl -sI https://cdn.example.com/app.abc123.js
cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable   # hashed filename -> cache forever
age: 84213                                            # seconds this object has lived in the edge cache
x-cache: HIT, cloudfront                              # served from the POP, origin not touched

$ curl -sI https://cdn.example.com/index.html
cache-control: no-cache          # revalidate every time (ETag), so deploys show immediately
x-cache: MISS from edge          # fetched from origin (or the origin shield) this time

Anycast

The same IP announced from many locations; BGP routes each client to the topologically nearest one. Used by DNS roots, CDNs, and DDoS scrubbing to spread load and shorten paths.

$ dig +short one.one.one.one         # 1.1.1.1 -- one IP...
1.1.1.1
$ mtr -r 1.1.1.1                     # ...but from London you land in a London PoP,
                                     #    from Sydney a Sydney PoP -- same IP, ~5ms each
# the CDN announces 1.1.1.1 from hundreds of sites via BGP; routers pick the shortest AS path
Cheat Sheet
  • Forward proxy = in front of clients (egress control, caching, anonymity). Reverse proxy = in front of servers (TLS, LB, caching, WAF).
  • L4 LB: routes by IP:port, payload-blind, fast, connection-preserving. L7 LB: reads HTTP, routes by host/path/header, TLS termination, retries.
  • LB algorithms: round-robin, least-connections, weighted, consistent-hash, IP-hash.
  • Health checks eject bad backends; sticky sessions pin clients — avoid by keeping backends stateless.
  • CDN: edge caches near users → lower latency, less origin load, DDoS absorption, edge compute.
  • Cache keys/TTL via Cache-Control/ETag; invalidate via purge or versioned URLs.
  • Anycast: one IP, many sites, BGP picks the nearest — DNS, CDNs, scrubbing.
  • X-Forwarded-For / Forwarded carry the real client IP through proxies (trust only from known proxies).
Q&A
Forward vs reverse proxy?
A forward proxy acts on behalf of clients (they're configured to use it) — egress filtering, caching, anonymity. A reverse proxy acts on behalf of servers (clients think it is the server) — TLS termination, load balancing, caching, security.
L4 vs L7 load balancing — key trade-off?
L4 is faster and protocol-agnostic but can only route on IP/port. L7 understands HTTP so it can route by URL/host/header, terminate TLS, retry failed requests, and rewrite — at higher CPU cost and by terminating the connection.
When do you actually need sticky sessions?
Only when a backend holds per-user state in local memory (session, upload progress, a websocket). The better fix is to externalise that state (Redis, JWT, DB) so any backend can serve any request — then you don't need stickiness and can scale/deploy freely.
What does a CDN give you besides caching static files?
Lower latency (edge near the user), reduced origin bandwidth/load, DDoS absorption at the edge, TLS termination, automatic compression, HTTP/2-3, and edge compute for personalisation/routing.
How does anycast route a user to the nearest node?
The same IP is advertised via BGP from many locations; each router forwards toward whichever announcement has the shortest AS path / lowest metric, so packets naturally flow to the topologically closest node.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which type of proxy hides the backend servers from clients?
A reverse proxy.
Which load balancer can route /api and /images to different servers?
A layer-7 (application) load balancer — it reads the HTTP path.
What header commonly carries the original client IP through a proxy?
X-Forwarded-For (or the standard Forwarded).

Intermediate core

Users are being logged out randomly after you added a second app server. Cause and fix?
Sessions are stored in each server's local memory; the load balancer sends the user's next request to the other server, which doesn't have their session. Fixes: move sessions to a shared store (Redis/DB) or switch to stateless tokens (signed JWT/cookie); as a stopgap, enable sticky sessions on the LB. Stateless backends are the right long-term answer.
Why use consistent hashing for load balancing in front of a cache tier?
So a given key routes to the same cache node most of the time, maximising hit rate. With plain modulo hashing, adding/removing one node reshuffles almost every key (mass cache misses / stampede on the origin). Consistent hashing (with virtual nodes) only moves ~1/N of keys when a node changes, keeping the cache mostly warm.

Advanced deep

Compare direct server return (DSR) with a standard reverse-proxy load balancer.
In a normal L7 proxy, both request and response flow through the LB — simple, enables TLS termination and response inspection/manipulation, but the LB must handle the full bidirectional bandwidth (often the bottleneck for high-throughput / large-download workloads). DSR (a.k.a. direct routing, used by IPVS, some hardware LBs): the LB forwards only the inbound packets to a backend (rewriting L2 MAC, or via tunnelling, keeping the original destination IP), and the backend replies directly to the client, bypassing the LB entirely. Since responses are usually far larger than requests, the LB's bandwidth need drops enormously and it scales further on cheap hardware. Costs: it's L3/L4 only (no TLS termination, no HTTP routing, no response rewriting), every backend must be configured with the VIP on a loopback and suppress ARP for it, health checking is trickier, and it doesn't work across L3 boundaries without tunnelling. Used where raw throughput matters more than L7 features (video, large file serving, game traffic).
What is "origin shielding" / a tiered CDN cache, and what failure does it prevent?
Without shielding, every CDN edge POP that has a cache miss goes straight to your origin. For a global CDN with 100+ POPs, a newly-published (or just-expired) popular object can trigger ~100 near-simultaneous origin fetches — and a purge across all POPs causes a synchronised stampede. Origin shield designates one mid-tier cache (usually a POP near the origin) that all other edges fetch through: edges miss → ask the shield → shield makes at most one origin request and fans the result back out. This collapses N origin requests into 1, smooths purge storms, and lets you firewall the origin to accept traffic only from the shield. Cost: an extra hop of latency on shield misses, and the shield is a concentration point that needs its own redundancy.

Firewalls, NAT & Packet Filtering

Deciding which packets are allowed, and letting many private hosts share one public address — two stateful middleboxes on every real network path.

Notes

Two related jobs sit on the packet path of almost every network. A firewall decides which packets are allowed through, based on rules matching addresses, ports, protocol, and — if it’s stateful — whether the packet belongs to a connection it already permitted. NAT rewrites addresses and ports so that many hosts behind one public IP can reach the internet (and, with port forwarding, so external clients can reach a chosen internal host). This page covers stateless vs stateful filtering and the Linux netfilter model, SNAT/PAT and DNAT, why NAT breaks peer-to-peer and how STUN/TURN/ICE work around it, CGNAT and IPv6, and firewall types from packet filter to WAF.

Packet filtering: stateless vs stateful

  • Stateless: each packet is judged alone against rules matching the 5-tuple (src IP, dst IP, src port, dst port, protocol) plus interface/flags. To allow a TCP conversation you must permit both directions explicitly (e.g. allow out dst 443 AND allow in src 443) — brittle and over-permissive.
  • Stateful: the firewall tracks connections in a conntrack table. You allow the first packet of a permitted flow; the return traffic is then matched as ESTABLISHED (or RELATED for things like FTP data / ICMP errors) and allowed automatically. This is the default everywhere now (Linux netfilter, cloud security groups, host firewalls).
  • DROP vs REJECT: drop silently discards (a black hole — slows port scanners, hides the host); reject sends back an ICMP “administratively prohibited” or a TCP RST (faster failures for legitimate clients). Most perimeters drop; internal segments often reject.

The Linux model (netfilter / iptables → nftables)

# hooks a packet passes through:
  PREROUTING → [routing decision] → INPUT (to local) | FORWARD (through) → POSTROUTING
                                        OUTPUT (from local) → POSTROUTING
# tables: filter (accept/drop), nat (SNAT/DNAT), mangle (edit fields), raw (skip conntrack)

# a minimal stateful host firewall (nftables idea)
default policy: INPUT drop, FORWARD drop, OUTPUT accept
accept  ct state established,related
accept  iif lo
accept  ip protocol icmp
accept  tcp dport { 22, 443 } ct state new
# everything else on INPUT is dropped

NAT: SNAT / PAT and DNAT

  • SNAT (source NAT) / MASQUERADE: rewrite the private source IP:port to the router’s public IP:port on egress; store the mapping; reverse it on the return. PAT / NAPT (“overloading”): many internal hosts share one public IP, disambiguated by the translated source port. This is what every home router does.
  • DNAT (destination NAT): rewrite the destination. Port forwarding (203.0.113.1:8080 → 192.168.1.10:80) exposes one inside service; load balancers use DNAT to spread connections across a pool. 1:1 / static NAT maps a whole public IP to a private one. Hairpin NAT lets inside hosts reach the inside server via its public IP.
  • NAT breaks anything that embeds addresses in the payload (old FTP, SIP) — needs an ALG (application-layer gateway) or a NAT-aware protocol.

NAT traversal for peer-to-peer

The problem. A NATed host has no inbound mapping until it sends out first, so two NATed peers can’t directly connect. The toolkit (used by WebRTC, VoIP, games):

  • STUN: the peer asks a public STUN server “what source IP:port do you see from me?” — learning its public mapping to advertise.
  • UDP hole punching: both peers send packets to each other’s public mapping at the same time; each outbound packet creates a return mapping, so the next inbound packet gets through. Works for full-cone / address-restricted NATs; fails for symmetric NAT (a different mapping per destination).
  • TURN: when direct fails, both peers relay through a public TURN server — always works, costs bandwidth and latency.
  • ICE: gather all candidate paths (host, STUN-reflexive, TURN-relayed), try them in priority order, use the first that connects.

Firewall types, CGNAT, and IPv6

  • Layers of firewall: packet filter (5-tuple) → stateful (connections) → application-layer / proxy / WAF (understands HTTP — blocks SQLi/XSS, rate-limits, inspects TLS after terminating it) → next-gen (app identification, IDS/IPS, threat intel).
  • Deployment: network firewall at the perimeter/between segments; host firewall on the machine; cloud security group (stateful, default-deny, attached to an instance/ENI) and network ACLs (stateless, subnet-level).
  • CGNAT (carrier-grade NAT): ISPs put many customers behind one IPv4 — saves addresses but exhausts ports, breaks inbound connections and geolocation, and creates a logging/abuse-attribution burden.
  • IPv6 gives every device a globally routable address, so NAT is unnecessary — but a stateful firewall (default-deny inbound) is still essential; the address is reachable, the policy is what protects it.
  • DDoS-relevant: SYN floods → SYN cookies (don’t allocate state until the handshake completes); connection-rate limiting; and note the conntrack table itself is a finite resource an attacker can try to exhaust.
Cheat Sheet
  • Stateless filter: judge each packet on the 5-tuple; must allow both directions. Stateful: allow the first packet, conntrack auto-allows the ESTABLISHED,RELATED return. Default: stateful, default-deny inbound.
  • DROP = silent black hole (stealth, slows scanners); REJECT = ICMP/RST (fast failure). Perimeter drops, internal often rejects.
  • Linux: netfilter hooks PREROUTING/INPUT/FORWARD/OUTPUT/POSTROUTING; tables filter/nat/mangle/raw; iptables or nftables; conntrack table.
  • SNAT/MASQUERADE = rewrite private src→public on egress; PAT/NAPT = many hosts share one IP by port. DNAT = rewrite dst = port forwarding / LB.
  • Unsolicited inbound has no NAT mapping → dropped. P2P traversal: STUN (learn your public mapping), hole punching (both send out at once), TURN (relay), ICE (try all candidates). Symmetric NAT defeats hole punching.
  • Firewall layers: packet filter → stateful → app-layer/WAF (HTTP-aware, TLS-terminating) → NGFW (IDS/IPS). Deploy as perimeter / host / cloud security group (stateful) + network ACL (stateless).
  • CGNAT: ISP shares one IPv4 across customers — port exhaustion, no inbound, attribution pain. IPv6: no NAT needed, still needs a default-deny stateful firewall.
Q&A
What does “stateful” mean for a firewall, and why is it better than stateless?
A stateful firewall tracks connections in a table (conntrack): when it permits the first packet of an allowed flow, it records the flow, and thereafter it recognises the return packets as belonging to that established connection and allows them without a separate rule. A stateless firewall judges every packet in isolation, so to permit a simple outbound HTTPS request you’d need a rule allowing outbound to port 443 and a rule allowing inbound from port 443 — the second rule is broad (any host, any time) and easy to abuse, and it can’t distinguish a real reply from an unsolicited packet that just has source port 443. Stateful is both tighter (return traffic only for connections you actually initiated) and simpler to write.
Explain SNAT vs DNAT with a concrete example of each.
SNAT (source NAT): your laptop at 192.168.1.20:52000 connects to a web server. The home router rewrites the packet’s source to <public IP>:41000, remembers the mapping, and forwards it. The server replies to <public IP>:41000; the router looks up the mapping and rewrites the destination back to 192.168.1.20:52000. This is how many devices share one public address (with port overloading, it’s PAT). DNAT (destination NAT): you run a game server on 192.168.1.50:25565 and want friends to reach it. You add a port-forward rule: packets arriving at <public IP>:25565 have their destination rewritten to 192.168.1.50:25565 and are forwarded inside; replies are un-NATed on the way out. Load balancers do the same thing, rewriting the destination to whichever backend they pick.
Why can’t two computers behind different home routers connect directly, and how does WebRTC solve it?
Each is behind NAT with default-deny inbound: there is no port mapping for an unsolicited incoming connection, so a packet from the other peer is dropped. WebRTC uses ICE to work around it. Each peer uses STUN to learn the public IP:port its NAT assigns to an outbound flow (its “server-reflexive candidate”) and exchanges all its candidate addresses with the other peer via the signalling channel. Then both peers simultaneously send packets to each other’s public candidates — UDP hole punching: each outbound packet opens a return path in that peer’s NAT, so the incoming packet from the other side now matches an existing mapping and gets through, establishing a direct path. If the NATs are symmetric (a different external port per destination, so the STUN-learned mapping doesn’t match what the peer will hit) or otherwise uncooperative, ICE falls back to a TURN relay: both peers connect out to a public server that forwards packets between them — always works, at the cost of that server’s bandwidth and added latency.
If IPv6 doesn’t need NAT, does that mean IPv6 hosts are less secure?
Not inherently. NAT was never designed as a security control — its “protection” is a side effect of there being no inbound mapping by default. With IPv6, every host has a globally routable address, so the address is reachable, but a properly configured stateful firewall with a default-deny inbound policy (on the CPE / host / cloud security group) provides exactly the same “only return traffic and explicitly-allowed services get in” behaviour — and does it as an explicit, auditable policy rather than an accident of address translation. IPv6 also removes NAT’s downsides (broken P2P, ALG hacks, port exhaustion, ambiguous logging). The security requirement is the same on both: run a stateful firewall; don’t rely on NAT.
What’s the difference between a cloud “security group” and a “network ACL”?
A security group is stateful and attached to an instance/interface: you typically write only allow rules for inbound (and often for outbound), and return traffic for an allowed connection is permitted automatically; it’s default-deny. A network ACL is stateless and attached to a subnet: it evaluates each packet independently (so you must allow ephemeral return ports explicitly), supports both allow and deny rules evaluated in order, and applies to all traffic crossing the subnet boundary. Best practice is to do the fine-grained per-service policy in stateful security groups and use network ACLs sparingly as a coarse subnet-level guardrail (e.g. block a bad CIDR).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does NAT let you do?
Let many hosts on a private network share a single public IP address for outbound internet access (source NAT / PAT), and expose a chosen internal service to the outside via port forwarding (destination NAT).
In a stateful firewall, what rule allows the response to an outbound request?
A rule that accepts packets matching connection state ESTABLISHED (and usually RELATED). You only need an explicit rule for the first, NEW packet of an allowed connection; the return path is then automatic.

Intermediate core

Write the rule set (conceptually) for a public web server: SSH from the office only, HTTP/HTTPS from anywhere, everything else denied, and it can reach a database on a private subnet.
Default policy: INPUT drop, FORWARD drop, OUTPUT accept (or also restrict OUTPUT for a hardened box). INPUT chain, in order: (1) accept ct state established,related — return traffic for anything the server initiated (DNS, package updates, DB replies). (2) accept iif lo — loopback. (3) accept ip protocol icmp icmp type { echo-request, dest-unreachable, time-exceeded } — ping and, importantly, Path-MTU ICMP. (4) accept tcp dport 22 ip saddr <office CIDR> ct state new — SSH only from the office; optionally rate-limit new SSH (limit rate 6/minute) to blunt brute force. (5) accept tcp dport { 80, 443 } ct state new — web from anywhere. (6) everything else falls through to the default drop (silent, so scanners get no feedback). OUTPUT (if restricting): accept to the DB subnet on the DB port, to DNS resolvers on 53, to the package mirrors / update endpoints on 443, plus established,related and lo; drop the rest. Reaching the private DB: this is normal outbound traffic from the web server to 10.0.2.0/24:5432 — allowed by the OUTPUT rule (or by default-accept OUTPUT), and the DB’s own firewall / security group should accept tcp dport 5432 only from the web server’s IP (and established,related). No inbound rule is needed on the web server for the DB; the replies match established. Extras: log-and-drop the final catch-all at a low rate for visibility; use fail2ban/CrowdSec on the SSH and web logs; and if it’s behind a cloud LB, the “from anywhere” for 80/443 becomes “from the LB’s security group / health-check ranges” instead.

Advanced deep

Design the perimeter for a multi-tier web application in the cloud: segmentation, north-south and east-west controls, NAT for egress, and DDoS considerations.
Segmentation: a VPC with subnets per tier and per AZ — public (load balancers, NAT gateways), app-private (web/API instances), data-private (databases, caches), and a management subnet. Only the public subnet has a route to an internet gateway; private subnets route egress through a NAT gateway in the public subnet (so instances have no public IP and can’t receive unsolicited inbound, but can pull updates / call third-party APIs). Data subnet has no egress route at all if possible (or egress only to specific endpoints via a proxy / VPC endpoints). North-south (inbound): everything public enters through a managed edge — a CDN + WAF in front, then an L7 load balancer. The WAF does app-layer filtering (OWASP rules, bot management, per-IP/token rate limits, geo rules), request-size limits, and TLS termination. The LB’s security group allows 443 from the CDN/WAF egress ranges only (not 0.0.0.0/0), and health-check ranges. The web tier’s security group allows its app port only from the LB’s security group. East-west (between tiers): security groups reference each other by ID, not CIDR — app SG allows the DB port from the web SG; DB SG allows only that; cache SG allows only the app SG. Default-deny everywhere; no tier can reach another except on the one required port. A stateless network ACL per subnet as a coarse backstop (e.g. deny known-bad CIDRs, deny inter-AZ management traffic). Optionally a firewall appliance / cloud network firewall for centralised egress filtering and IDS/IPS on the inspection path. Egress control: route all outbound through the NAT gateway and an egress filtering proxy or DNS/domain allow-list so a compromised instance can’t exfiltrate to arbitrary hosts or pull C2; block the cloud metadata IP (169.254.169.254) except where an instance legitimately needs a scoped role, and use IMDSv2. Use VPC endpoints (private links) for cloud services so that traffic never traverses the internet or the NAT gateway. Management: no direct SSH from the internet — a bastion / SSM Session Manager / VPN into the management subnet, MFA, short-lived credentials, all access logged. DDoS: volumetric absorption at the CDN/edge (the provider’s anycast scrubbing network) so raw floods never reach the VPC; the L7 LB + WAF handle L7 floods (slowloris, HTTP request floods) with connection limits, timeouts, and rate limiting keyed by IP/ASN/token; SYN-flood protection is built into the managed LB; autoscaling with sane max limits and per-client quotas so a flash crowd or attack degrades rather than collapses, and circuit breakers so the app sheds load before the DB does. Watch the conntrack/flow-table and NAT-gateway port limits as finite resources. Observability: VPC flow logs to a SIEM (alert on unexpected east-west flows, egress to new destinations, spikes in denied traffic), WAF and LB logs, and per-security-group change alerts. Net: private-by-default subnets with egress via NAT + filtering proxy, all inbound through CDN/WAF/L7-LB with SG-to-SG references enforcing least-privilege east-west, no public IPs on workloads, bastion-only management, VPC endpoints for cloud services, and layered DDoS handling from edge scrubbing down to app-level rate limits — with flow logs feeding detection.

Cookies, Sessions, CORS & WebSockets

The browser-side mechanics of stateful, cross-origin, real-time web apps.

Notes

This page covers the browser-side plumbing that web applications depend on. Cookies and their security attributes (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite) and how they enable sessions — contrasted with stateless token (JWT) auth. The same-origin policy and how CORS deliberately relaxes it (simple requests vs preflight). And real-time delivery: the progression from polling to long-polling to Server-Sent Events to WebSockets (the HTTP Upgrade handshake to a full-duplex connection).

Cookies

Small key/value pairs the server sets via Set-Cookie; the browser attaches them to matching future requests automatically. Attributes:

  • HttpOnly — not readable by JS (mitigates XSS token theft).
  • Secure — only sent over HTTPS.
  • SameSite=Strict/Lax/None — controls sending on cross-site requests (CSRF defence; Lax is the modern default).
  • Domain, Path, Max-Age/Expires.
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Set-Cookie: sid=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=86400
//  HttpOnly -> document.cookie can't read it (XSS can't steal it)
//  Secure   -> never sent over plain http
//  SameSite=Lax -> not sent on cross-site POST (CSRF defence), IS sent on top-level GET nav

// every later request to the same site carries it automatically:
GET /account HTTP/1.1
Cookie: sid=abc123

Session vs token auth

Server sessionToken (JWT)
Statesession store on server; cookie holds only an idself-contained signed token; server keeps nothing
Revocationdelete the session — instanthard — valid until expiry (needs a blocklist / short TTL + refresh)
Scalingneeds shared session storestateless, easy to scale
# server session: cookie is just a key into Redis
sid = random_token()
redis.setex("sess:" + sid, 3600, user_id)      # revoke = redis.del(...), instant

# JWT: signed, self-contained, server stores nothing
token = base64(header) + "." + base64({sub: 7, exp: now + 900}) + "." + hmac_sha256(...)
# verify = recompute the HMAC; no DB hit. But you CAN'T revoke it before exp=900s
# -> short access token + a revocable refresh token

Same-origin policy & CORS

Origin = scheme + host + port. By default JS can send a cross-origin request but can't read the response. CORS lets a server opt in: it returns Access-Control-Allow-Origin (and friends). "Non-simple" requests (custom headers, PUT/DELETE, JSON content-type) trigger a preflight OPTIONS request that the server must answer with the allowed methods/headers before the real request is sent. CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server — it's not a server-side security control.

# preflight (browser sends this automatically for a non-simple request):
OPTIONS /api/orders HTTP/1.1
Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT
Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type

# server must approve BEFORE the real PUT is allowed to run:
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, PUT, DELETE
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: content-type
# NOTE: curl / server-to-server calls ignore all of this -- CORS is a browser-only guard

Real-time: polling → WebSockets

TechniqueHow
Short pollingclient requests every N seconds — simple, wasteful, latency ≈ N
Long pollingserver holds the request open until data or timeout, then client re-requests
Server-Sent Eventsone-way server→client stream over HTTP (text/event-stream), auto-reconnect
WebSocketfull-duplex; starts as an HTTP Upgrade, then a persistent framed TCP channel
// WebSocket: one HTTP Upgrade, then a persistent 2-way channel
GET /chat HTTP/1.1
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZQ==

HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols          // after this, no more HTTP -- framed messages both ways

// SSE (simpler, server -> client only, auto-reconnect):
const es = new EventSource("/stream");
es.onmessage = e => render(e.data);       // server sends: "data: {...}\n\n"

WebSockets suit chat, live dashboards, multiplayer, collaborative editing. Considerations: they bypass normal HTTP caching/LB semantics, need sticky routing or a pub/sub backplane (Redis) for multi-server fan-out, and their own auth (usually a token in the connect URL or first message).

Cheat Sheet
  • Cookie flags: HttpOnly (no JS), Secure (HTTPS only), SameSite (CSRF: Lax default, Strict, None+Secure for cross-site).
  • Server session: revocable, needs shared store. JWT: stateless, scales, but hard to revoke — use short expiry + refresh tokens.
  • Origin = scheme + host + port. Same-origin policy blocks JS from reading cross-origin responses.
  • CORS = server opt-in via Access-Control-Allow-*; preflight OPTIONS for non-simple requests. Enforced by the browser only.
  • Real-time: short poll (simple/wasteful) < long poll < SSE (one-way, HTTP) < WebSocket (full-duplex, Upgrade).
  • WebSockets need sticky sessions or a Redis/pub-sub backplane for multi-server broadcast; auth via token on connect.
  • CSRF: state-changing requests need a token or SameSite cookies; CORS does not prevent CSRF.
Q&A
What does SameSite=Lax do?
The cookie is sent on same-site requests and on top-level cross-site navigations (clicking a link) but not on cross-site subrequests (an image, an XHR/fetch, a form POST from another site) — blunting CSRF while keeping normal navigation working. It's the browser default now.
Is CORS a security feature that protects my server?
No. The browser enforces it to protect users from a malicious site reading responses from another origin they're logged into. Your server still receives and processes the request; non-browser clients ignore CORS entirely. Server-side auth/authorization is still mandatory.
When does a CORS preflight happen?
For "non-simple" cross-origin requests: methods other than GET/POST/HEAD, custom headers, or a Content-Type other than form/urlencoded/plain/multipart (so JSON POSTs preflight). The browser sends OPTIONS first; the real request proceeds only if the server allows it.
JWT vs server-side session — main trade-off?
JWTs are stateless (no session store, easy horizontal scaling) but can't be easily revoked before expiry. Sessions are instantly revocable and can hold arbitrary server state, but need a shared, fast session store. Common compromise: short-lived JWT access tokens + a revocable refresh token.
SSE vs WebSocket?
