One mutex, two condition variables (notFull, notEmpty). put: lock; while (size == capacity) notFull.wait(lock); enqueue; notEmpty.signal(); unlock. take: lock; while (size == 0) notEmpty.wait(lock); dequeue; notFull.signal(); unlock; return. The while loops handle spurious wakeups and multiple waiters; signalling the other condition after each operation wakes a blocked counterpart.
Why can notify() (signal one) instead of notifyAll() cause a deadlock in some designs?
If threads wait on the same condition variable for different predicates (e.g. a bounded buffer where producers and consumers share one condvar), notify() might wake a thread whose predicate is still false; it re-checks, goes back to sleep, and the thread that could have proceeded was never woken — the system stalls with work available. Fixes: use separate condition variables per predicate, or always notifyAll() (correct but can cause a thundering herd).

Advanced deep

How does a futex-based mutex avoid a syscall in the uncontended case?
The lock is a plain integer in shared user memory. Lock: atomically CAS it from 0→1 in userspace; if that succeeds (uncontended), you're done — no kernel involvement at all. Only if the CAS fails (someone holds it) does the thread call futex(FUTEX_WAIT), passing the address and expected value; the kernel double-checks the value (avoiding a lost-wakeup race) and, if it still matches, sleeps the thread on a kernel wait queue keyed by that address. Unlock: atomically set to 0; if the old value indicated waiters, call futex(FUTEX_WAKE) to wake one. So the fast path (the overwhelmingly common case) is a single atomic instruction, and the kernel is touched only under real contention. glibc's mutex uses a 3-state variant (0 free, 1 locked-no-waiters, 2 locked-with-waiters) so the unlock fast path also skips the syscall when there are no waiters.
Compare lock-based synchronisation with RCU (read-copy-update) for a read-mostly data structure.
A reader/writer lock still has readers taking and releasing the lock (atomic ops, cache-line bouncing on the lock word across cores) and can starve writers or readers. RCU: readers take no lock and pay essentially nothing — they just mark a lightweight "read-side critical section" (on Linux, often just disabling preemption) and dereference the pointer. Writers make a copy of the node, modify the copy, then atomically swap the pointer; old readers keep using the old version. The writer then waits for a grace period — until every CPU has passed through a quiescent state (context switch / idle / user mode), guaranteeing no reader still holds the old pointer — before freeing the old node. Wins: near-zero reader overhead, perfect reader scalability, no reader/writer contention. Costs: writers are more expensive and serialised among themselves (still need a lock), reclamation is deferred (memory lingers for a grace period), and it only suits structures where readers can tolerate seeing a slightly stale but consistent version (linked lists, routing tables, config). It's heavily used in the Linux kernel.

Deadlock: Conditions, Prevention, Avoidance

When everyone is waiting for everyone else — the four conditions and the four responses.

Notes

Deadlock is a set of threads each waiting for a resource another holds, so none can proceed — and it requires all four Coffman conditions to hold simultaneously (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait). This page covers those conditions and how breaking any one prevents deadlock, the four handling strategies (prevention, avoidance via the banker’s algorithm, detection-and-recovery, and deliberately ignoring it), what real systems actually do (lock ordering), and the related failures livelock and starvation.

The four Coffman conditions (all needed for deadlock)

  1. Mutual exclusion — a resource is held by at most one process.
  2. Hold and wait — a process holds resources while waiting for more.
  3. No preemption — a resource can't be forcibly taken; only released voluntarily.
  4. Circular wait — a cycle of processes each waiting for a resource the next holds.

Break any one and deadlock is impossible.

// all four conditions present -> classic deadlock
// T1:                              T2:
pthread_mutex_lock(&A);   //        pthread_mutex_lock(&B);   -- mutual exclusion
/* ...work... */                 //        /* ...work... */          -- hold and wait
pthread_mutex_lock(&B);   //        pthread_mutex_lock(&A);   -- circular wait, no preemption
// T1 holds A waits B, T2 holds B waits A -> both blocked forever

The four strategies

StrategyHow
PreventionStructurally negate a condition: acquire all resources at once (no hold-and-wait); impose a global lock order (no circular wait); allow preemption / rollback.
AvoidanceGrant a request only if the resulting state is "safe" (there exists an order in which all processes can finish). Banker's algorithm — needs max-claims up front.
Detection & recoveryLet deadlocks happen; periodically look for a cycle in the wait-for graph; recover by killing a victim or rolling back.
OstrichIgnore it — deadlocks are rare, and the cost of prevention isn't worth it. What general-purpose OSes (and most apps) actually do.
// PREVENTION by lock ordering: always take the lower-addressed lock first
void transfer(Account *a, Account *b, long amt) {
    Account *first  = a < b ? a : b;
    Account *second = a < b ? b : a;
    pthread_mutex_lock(&first->m);
    pthread_mutex_lock(&second->m);      // every thread agrees on the order -> no cycle
    a->bal -= amt; b->bal += amt;
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&second->m);
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&first->m);
}

// PREVENTION by try_lock + backoff: don't hold-and-wait
while (1) {
    lock(&A);
    if (try_lock(&B) == 0) break;   // got both
    unlock(&A); usleep(rand() % 100);  // release everything, retry
}

In practice

The overwhelmingly common real-world fix is consistent lock ordering: number your locks and always acquire them in increasing order. Also: keep critical sections short, use try_lock with backoff, avoid calling out to unknown code while holding a lock, and use a single coarse lock where the concurrency isn't worth the risk. Databases use detection (wait-for graph) + victim abort.

# the DB does detection + victim abort for you:
mysql> SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G
LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK
*** (1) WAITING FOR ... lock on `accounts` ...
*** (2) HOLDS THE LOCK(S) ...
*** WE ROLL BACK TRANSACTION (2)          # app gets error 1213 -> just retry the txn

Livelock & starvation

Livelock: processes keep changing state in response to each other but make no progress (two people stepping aside in a corridor). Starvation: a process is perpetually denied a resource (always lower priority, or unlucky in lock acquisition).

// LIVELOCK: both retry forever in lockstep (no deadlock -- they're "busy")
while (1) {
    lock(&A);
    if (try_lock(&B)) break;
    unlock(&A);                 // both threads back off at the exact same time, repeat
}
// fix: RANDOMISED backoff (usleep(rand()...)) so they desynchronise

// STARVATION: a writer never runs because readers keep arriving on an RW lock
//   fix: writer-preferring rwlock, or FIFO ticket lock
Cheat Sheet
  • Coffman conditions (need all 4): mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait.
  • Prevention = negate one structurally (all-at-once acquisition; global lock ordering; allow preemption).
  • Avoidance = only grant if the new state is safe; Banker's algorithm (needs max claims).
  • Detection = find a cycle in the wait-for graph, then kill/roll back a victim (databases do this).
  • Ostrich = ignore; what general-purpose OSes do.
  • Practical fix: consistent global lock order; short critical sections; try_lock + backoff; don't call unknown code under a lock.
  • Livelock = active but no progress. Starvation = perpetually denied (fix with ageing/fair locks).
Q&A
List the four conditions necessary for deadlock.
Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. All four must hold simultaneously.
What's the simplest practical way to prevent deadlock among multiple locks?
Impose a total order on the locks and always acquire them in that order everywhere. A cycle in the wait-for graph then becomes impossible, so circular wait is broken.
Deadlock avoidance vs prevention?
Prevention removes the possibility by design (negating a Coffman condition). Avoidance allows the conditions but checks each allocation request at runtime and only grants it if the system stays in a "safe" state where all processes can still complete (Banker's algorithm).
What does the "ostrich algorithm" mean and why is it common?
Ignoring deadlocks entirely. Prevention/avoidance impose real costs (resource under-utilisation, up-front declarations, overhead), and deadlocks in practice are rare and often recoverable by killing a process. So most general-purpose OSes just don't handle it.
Livelock vs deadlock?
In deadlock, processes are blocked and doing nothing. In livelock, they're actively running and changing state in response to each other but never making forward progress — e.g. two threads that both back off and retry in lockstep forever.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which Coffman condition does "acquire all locks at once, or none" eliminate?
Hold-and-wait.
What does the Banker's algorithm require processes to declare?
Their maximum possible resource needs, up front.
How do databases typically deal with deadlock?
Detection — they build a wait-for graph, find cycles, and abort a victim transaction (which is then retried).

Intermediate core

Two threads: T1 locks A then B; T2 locks B then A. Show the deadlock and two fixes.
Interleaving: T1 locks A, T2 locks B, T1 waits for B (held by T2), T2 waits for A (held by T1) — circular wait, both stuck. Fix 1: consistent order — make T2 also lock A then B. Fix 2: try_lock B after locking A; if it fails, release A, back off a random interval, retry (breaks "no preemption"). Fix 3: a single lock covering both A and B if the extra concurrency isn't needed.
Why is deadlock avoidance rarely used in real systems?
It needs every process's maximum resource claim declared in advance, which is often unknown or wildly conservative; the safety check runs on every allocation (overhead); and it under-utilises resources by refusing requests that would probably be fine. It fits constrained, well-characterised systems (some embedded/real-time), not general-purpose ones.

Advanced deep

Explain "lock ordering" enforcement tools like Linux's lockdep.
Lockdep builds, at runtime, a graph of observed lock-acquisition orders: whenever lock B is taken while lock A is held, it records an edge A→B for the lock classes (not instances — e.g. "inode→mutex" as a class). If it ever sees the reverse order (B held, A taken) it reports a potential deadlock immediately, even if the actual timing that triggers it never occurs in this run — because the two orderings existing anywhere in the codebase means an interleaving can deadlock. It also validates rules like "no sleeping lock taken in IRQ context", recursive locking, and irq-safe/irq-unsafe consistency. This shifts deadlock discovery from rare production hangs to CI/testing. The cost is significant runtime overhead (it's a debug-kernel feature), and it needs correct "lock class" annotations to avoid false positives/negatives when the same code path legitimately locks two instances of the same class in a defined order (handled with nesting subclasses).
Dining philosophers: give a solution that is deadlock-free and starvation-free, and explain why each property holds.
One clean solution: a central "waiter"/arbitrator (a mutex or semaphore initialised to N−1) that limits the number of philosophers simultaneously trying to eat to N−1. Deadlock-free: with at most N−1 philosophers contending for N forks, at least one philosopher can always get both forks (pigeonhole) — circular wait is broken because the cycle can't fully form. Starvation-free if the arbitrator and the fork mutexes use FIFO / fair queuing, so every philosopher's request is eventually served. Alternative: asymmetric ordering — odd philosophers pick up the left fork first, even philosophers the right first; this breaks the uniform circular wait (deadlock-free) but needs fair mutexes to also be starvation-free. The resource-hierarchy solution (number the forks, always pick up the lower-numbered first) is deadlock-free but the highest-numbered philosopher can be starved without additional fairness.

Inter-Process Communication

Isolated processes need channels — and each channel makes a different speed/scope trade.

Notes

Inter-process communication is how separate processes — which by design don’t share memory — exchange data and signals. The mechanism you choose trades throughput, latency, direction, whether it crosses machines, and how much the kernel is involved. This page covers pipes and FIFOs, message queues, shared memory (fastest, but you supply the synchronization), Unix-domain and network sockets, and signals — with the strengths, limits, and classic gotchas of each.

The mechanisms

MechanismShapeNotes
Pipe (anonymous)unidirectional byte streamrelated processes only (shared fd via fork); the shell's |
Named pipe / FIFObyte stream via a filesystem pathunrelated processes on the same host
Message queuediscrete messages, optionally prioritisedpreserves boundaries; POSIX (mq_*) or SysV
Shared memorya region mapped into multiple processesfastest (no copy through the kernel); needs your own synchronisation (semaphore/mutex)
Unix domain socketstream or datagram, bidirectionallocal, fast, supports passing fds and credentials; same API as network sockets
Signala single async notification (number)no payload (bar sigqueue); for events/termination, not data
Memory-mapped fileshared memory backed by a filepersistent, and OS syncs to disk
eventfd / futex / pidfdlightweight kernel-assisted signallingmodern Linux building blocks
// anonymous pipe: parent -> child stream (the shell's `|`)
int fds[2]; pipe(fds);
if (fork() == 0) { close(fds[1]); read(fds[0], buf, n); }   // child reads
else              { close(fds[0]); write(fds[1], msg, n); }  // parent writes

// shared memory: the fastest -- no kernel copy, but YOU add the lock
int shm = shm_open("/ring", O_CREAT | O_RDWR, 0600);
ftruncate(shm, SZ);
void *p = mmap(NULL, SZ, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_SHARED, shm, 0);
// both processes see *p; guard it with a sem_t in the shared region

Choosing

  • Need max throughput / big data → shared memory (+ a lock or lock-free ring).
  • Need message boundaries and simple flow → message queue or datagram socket.
  • Local RPC, fd passing, auth → Unix domain socket.
  • Simple parent→child stream → pipe.
  • Across machines → TCP/UDP sockets (only option).
  • Just "wake up" / "please stop" → signal / eventfd.
# local RPC + fd passing + peer credentials -> Unix domain socket
srv = socket(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0); bind(srv, "/run/app.sock"); listen(srv, 8);
# pass an open fd to another process via SCM_RIGHTS; check SO_PEERCRED for uid/pid

# big streaming data, same host -> shared-memory ring beats a socket (no copy)
# cross-machine -> you have no choice: TCP/UDP
# "reload your config" -> a signal:  kill -HUP $(pidof app)

Gotchas

Pipes have limited buffer (default 64 KB) — a full pipe blocks the writer; a reader closing early makes the writer get SIGPIPE/EPIPE. Shared memory has no built-in synchronisation — races are on you. SysV IPC objects leak if not removed (ipcrm).

$ yes | head -1              # head exits -> `yes` gets SIGPIPE and dies (that's intended here)

$ ipcs -m                    # SysV shared memory segments -- these LEAK past process exit
key        shmid  owner  bytes   nattch
0x00000000 98304  leo    4194304 0        # nattch 0 and still here -> orphaned
$ ipcrm -m 98304             # must clean up manually (POSIX shm_unlink is friendlier)
Cheat Sheet
  • Pipe: unidirectional stream, related processes (shell |). FIFO: same via a pathname, unrelated processes.
  • Message queue: discrete, boundary-preserving, prioritised messages.
  • Shared memory: fastest (zero-copy); you provide the synchronisation.
  • Unix domain socket: local, bidirectional, fast, can pass fds + peer credentials.
  • Signal: async notification, essentially no payload; for events/termination.
  • mmap'd file: shared memory that persists and syncs to disk.
  • Cross-machine → network sockets only.
  • Watch: pipe buffer full → writer blocks; reader gone → SIGPIPE; SysV objects persist until ipcrm.
Q&A
Why is shared memory the fastest IPC?
Data isn't copied into and out of the kernel — both processes map the same physical pages and read/write directly. Other mechanisms copy through kernel buffers (at least once, often twice).
What's the catch with shared memory?
It provides no synchronisation. Concurrent access is a data race unless you add your own mutex/semaphore (often placed in the shared region) or use a lock-free structure.
Anonymous pipe vs named pipe (FIFO)?
An anonymous pipe exists only as file descriptors shared via fork() — only related processes can use it. A FIFO has a name in the filesystem, so any process that can open that path can connect, related or not.
What can a Unix domain socket do that a TCP socket to localhost can't?
Pass open file descriptors between processes (SCM_RIGHTS) and the peer's verified credentials (SO_PEERCRED), with lower overhead (no TCP/IP stack, checksums, or loopback routing).
Can you send data with a signal?
Barely — a plain signal carries only its number. sigqueue() with a real-time signal can attach one integer/pointer value. Signals are for notification ("child exited", "please reload config", "terminate"), not data transfer.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What IPC mechanism does the shell's | use?
An anonymous pipe.
Which IPC needs you to add your own locking?
Shared memory.
Which IPC works across different machines?
Network sockets (TCP/UDP). The others are host-local.

Intermediate core

Two processes exchange millions of small records per second on one host. Design the IPC.
A shared-memory ring buffer (SPSC: single-producer, single-consumer) with atomic head/tail indices and acquire/release ordering — no locks, no per-message syscall. Use a semaphore or eventfd only for "wake the consumer when it was idle" (with a batched/coalesced signal) to avoid busy-waiting. Pad head and tail to separate cache lines to prevent false sharing. Fall back to a Unix domain socket if you need boundary framing and flow control without writing the ring yourself.
A writer process hangs when its pipe reader is slow. Why, and options?
The pipe's kernel buffer (default 64 KB) filled up, so write() blocks until the reader drains it — this is backpressure, often desirable. Options: make the writer's pipe fd non-blocking and handle EAGAIN (drop or buffer in userspace); increase the pipe capacity with fcntl(F_SETPIPE_SZ); use a larger-buffered mechanism (socket with a big SO_SNDBUF, or a message queue); or fix the real problem — the slow reader.

Advanced deep

How does passing a file descriptor over a Unix socket actually work, and why is it useful?
You send a normal message with sendmsg() that carries an ancillary data block of type SCM_RIGHTS containing one or more fd numbers. The kernel intercepts this: on the receiving side it installs new fd entries in the receiver's fd table that refer to the same underlying open-file description (same offset, same file, incremented refcount) — the numeric fd value differs, but it's the "same handle". This lets a privileged process open a resource the unprivileged one can't (a low port, a device, a file outside a sandbox) and hand it over; lets a listener process accept connections and distribute the connected sockets to worker processes (systemd socket activation, some load balancers); and underpins privilege-separation designs where one tiny trusted process owns all the dangerous opens. The security model: the receiver gets exactly the access the sender had on that description, nothing more.
Compare the copy costs of pipe, Unix socket, and shared memory for a 1 MB transfer, and how zero-copy techniques change it.
Pipe / Unix socket: write() copies from the sender's buffer into a kernel buffer (copy 1); read() copies from the kernel buffer into the receiver's buffer (copy 2) — ~2 MB of memory traffic plus two syscalls, for 1 MB of payload. Shared memory: the sender writes 1 MB into the shared region (copy 1, unavoidable unless it produced the data there directly), the receiver reads it in place (copy 0) — ~1 MB traffic, no per-transfer syscall. Zero-copy paths: splice()/vmsplice() move pages between a pipe and a file/socket by reference (page "stealing"), avoiding the userspace bounce; sendfile() streams a file to a socket entirely in the kernel; MSG_ZEROCOPY lets the kernel DMA directly from user pages for large socket sends (with an async completion notification, since the buffer must stay stable). For local bulk transfer the winning designs are: put the producer's output directly in shared memory (true zero-copy), or use memfd + fd-passing so the receiver mmaps the sender's buffer.

I/O, Interrupts & DMA

How the CPU actually moves data to and from disks and network cards — and why interrupts, DMA, and async I/O exist.

Notes

Everything outside the CPU and RAM — disks, SSDs, network cards, keyboards — is a device the OS talks to through a driver. This page covers the mechanisms: how the CPU learns a device is ready (polling vs interrupts), how bulk data moves without the CPU copying every byte (DMA), the layered path a disk read takes through the kernel (page cache → filesystem → block layer → driver → device → completion interrupt), the difference between blocking, non-blocking, and truly asynchronous I/O (epoll, io_uring), and the interrupt-rate problems that show up at high throughput (interrupt storms, coalescing, NAPI, IRQ affinity).

Device types & how the CPU addresses them

  • Character devices: an unstructured byte stream, accessed sequentially — terminals, serial ports, /dev/random, sound.
  • Block devices: fixed-size blocks with random access — disks, SSDs. The filesystem and page cache sit on top.
  • Network devices: packet-oriented, not a file in /dev; accessed through the socket API and the network stack.
  • Memory-mapped I/O: the device’s control/status registers appear at physical memory addresses; the driver reads/writes them like memory (with barriers). Port-mapped I/O (x86 legacy): separate address space via in/out instructions.

Polling vs interrupts

What / why. Polling: the CPU repeatedly reads a status register until the device is ready. Simple and low-latency, but burns CPU while waiting — only sensible for devices that are almost always ready (very fast NVMe under heavy load, some real-time contexts). Interrupts: the device asserts an IRQ line; the CPU finishes the current instruction, saves minimal state, jumps to the registered interrupt service routine (ISR), which acknowledges the device and returns. The thread that was waiting is later made runnable. Interrupt handling is deliberately split:

  • Top half (the ISR): runs with interrupts disabled, must be tiny — read a status word, acknowledge, copy nothing heavy, schedule the rest.
  • Bottom half (softirq / tasklet / workqueue on Linux): runs later with interrupts enabled — the actual packet processing, block-request completion, waking waiters.

DMA — moving data without the CPU

What / why. A DMA engine transfers data directly between a device and RAM. The CPU programs the transfer (physical source, destination, length, direction), the device and DMA controller do the movement, and the CPU gets one interrupt when the whole transfer completes — instead of copying every word through a register (“programmed I/O”). Scatter-gather DMA handles a list of non-contiguous buffer fragments in one operation. An IOMMU sits between devices and RAM to translate and permission-check DMA addresses (isolation, and letting a device see contiguous virtual buffers). Cache coherence must be handled — the driver flushes/invalidates CPU caches for the DMA region, or the platform is DMA-coherent.

The block I/O path (Linux)

read() syscall
  → VFS  →  page cache lookup   [HIT: copy to user buffer, done]
  → filesystem: map file offset → device blocks (extents / indirect)
  → block layer: build 'bio' requests, merge & sort them
  → I/O scheduler (mq-deadline / BFQ / kyber / none) via blk-mq per-CPU queues
  → device driver: submit to the hardware queue; DMA set up
  → device performs the transfer
  → completion interrupt → bottom half marks the request done
  → wake the sleeping thread; data now in the page cache and the user buffer

I/O schedulers trade throughput (merge/sort for sequential access), latency (deadline caps), and fairness (BFQ) — on fast NVMe, none (just the multi-queue plumbing) is often best.

Blocking, non-blocking, and async

ModelBehaviour
Blockingread() sleeps the thread until data is ready. Simple; one thread per concurrent I/O.
Non-blocking + readinessO_NONBLOCK + epoll/kqueue: the kernel tells you which fds are readable/writable; you then do a non-blocking op. One thread, many sockets. Great for network I/O; doesn’t truly work for regular files (they’re “always ready” but the read still blocks on disk).
Asynchronous completionSubmit an operation, get told when it’s finished (not just ready). POSIX AIO (weak, often thread-pool emulated); Linux io_uring — shared submission/completion ring buffers, batched syscalls, real async for storage and network, zero-copy options.

Interrupt-rate problems at scale

  • Interrupt storm: at millions of packets/sec, one IRQ per packet melts a core. NAPI: after the first interrupt, disable further NIC interrupts and poll the ring in the bottom half until it drains, then re-enable — interrupt at low load, poll at high load.
  • Interrupt coalescing: the NIC fires one interrupt per N packets or per T microseconds — fewer interrupts, slightly more latency.
  • IRQ affinity: pin a device’s interrupts to specific cores so cache stays warm and one core isn’t swamped. MSI-X gives a device many interrupt vectors (one per queue); RSS hashes flows across NIC queues so receive processing spreads over cores.
Cheat Sheet
  • Device types: character (byte stream), block (random-access blocks, under the FS + page cache), network (packets, via sockets). Registers via memory-mapped I/O (or x86 port I/O).
  • Polling: CPU spins on a status register — low latency, wastes CPU; only for near-always-ready devices. Interrupts: device raises IRQ → ISR runs.
  • ISR is split: top half (tiny, IRQs off, acknowledge + schedule) and bottom half (softirq/tasklet/workqueue — the real work).
  • DMA: CPU programs (src, dst, len); controller moves data device↔RAM; one completion interrupt. Scatter-gather for fragmented buffers; IOMMU for translation/isolation; handle cache coherence.
  • Block path: syscall → VFS → page cache (hit = done) → FS → block layer (bio, merge) → I/O scheduler (blk-mq: mq-deadline/BFQ/kyber/none) → driver + DMA → device → completion IRQ → wake thread.
  • I/O models: blocking (thread sleeps), non-blocking + epoll (readiness, one thread many sockets, not for disk), async completion (io_uring — submit/complete rings, batched, real async for storage + net).
  • High rate: NAPI (interrupt→poll under load), coalescing (1 IRQ per N/T), IRQ affinity + MSI-X + RSS to spread across cores.
Q&A
Why is DMA essential rather than just an optimisation?
Without it, the CPU must copy every word of every transfer from/to a device register (“programmed I/O”). For a modern SSD (gigabytes/sec) or a 10/40/100 GbE NIC, that copying alone would consume one or more full CPU cores, leaving nothing for actual work — and the memory-bus contention would still bottleneck. DMA lets the CPU program a transfer (addresses + length) and then do useful work while the DMA engine moves the data, receiving a single interrupt at the end. Bulk I/O at line rate simply isn’t possible on general-purpose CPUs without it.
What is the top-half / bottom-half split in interrupt handling and why does it exist?
The top half is the interrupt service routine that runs immediately when the IRQ fires — with interrupts disabled (at least that line), preempting whatever was running. It must be as short as possible: acknowledge the device, grab a status word or descriptor, and schedule the rest of the work. The bottom half (Linux softirq, tasklet, or workqueue) runs slightly later with interrupts re-enabled and does the substantial processing — parsing packets, completing block requests, waking waiters. The split exists because long work in the top half would block all other interrupts (missed timer ticks, dropped packets, worse latency for every device) and can’t safely sleep or take normal locks. Keep the top half tiny; defer everything else.
Why doesn’t epoll help with regular file I/O the way it helps with sockets?
epoll reports readiness — “this fd won’t block if you read now.” For a socket, data either has arrived or hasn’t, so readiness is meaningful. A regular file is always considered readable (there’s always “data” at the current offset, even if it’s on a slow disk), so epoll immediately says “ready” and the subsequent read() still blocks on the actual disk I/O. To get non-blocking file I/O you need true asynchronous submission: Linux io_uring (submit a read, get a completion event when the data is actually in your buffer) or a thread pool doing blocking reads. O_NONBLOCK on a regular file has essentially no effect.
Your server drops packets under high load and one CPU is pegged at 100% in soft IRQ. What’s happening and what do you tune?
The NIC is firing an interrupt per packet (or close to it), and all of that receive processing is landing on a single core, which saturates in softirq context and can’t keep up — the ring buffer overflows and the NIC drops packets. Tuning: (1) ensure NAPI is active (it is by default in modern drivers) so the driver switches to polling the ring under load instead of taking an interrupt per packet. (2) Enable/raise interrupt coalescing (ethtool -C) to batch interrupts. (3) Spread the load across cores: enable multi-queue with MSI-X and RSS so different flows hash to different NIC queues, each with its own interrupt, and set IRQ affinity (or use irqbalance / explicit /proc/irq/*/smp_affinity) to pin each queue’s IRQ to a distinct core; also RPS/RFS to spread softirq work if hardware queues are limited. (4) Grow the NIC ring buffers (ethtool -G). (5) If it’s userspace that can’t drain fast enough, that’s a separate app-side fix (more worker threads, bigger socket buffers, or a kernel-bypass stack like DPDK/AF_XDP for extreme rates).
What does io_uring change compared with the older read/write + epoll model?
It replaces “one syscall per operation” and “readiness then a blocking op” with two shared ring buffers between the app and the kernel: a submission queue where the app posts operations (read, write, accept, send, fsync, …) and a completion queue where the kernel posts results. The app can batch many operations and submit them with a single io_uring_enter (or with SQPOLL, zero syscalls — a kernel thread polls the ring). Operations are truly asynchronous, including file I/O (which epoll can’t do). It supports linked operations, fixed buffers/files to skip per-call setup, and zero-copy send. The result is far fewer syscalls and context switches at high I/O rates, and one uniform async interface for storage and network. Costs: newer API, a learning curve, and a history of kernel security issues that led some environments to restrict it.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What’s the difference between polling and interrupt-driven I/O?
Polling: the CPU repeatedly checks a device status register until it’s ready — simple but wastes cycles. Interrupt-driven: the device signals the CPU (an IRQ) when it’s ready, so the CPU can do other work meanwhile and only handle the device on the interrupt.
In one sentence, what does a DMA controller do?
It transfers a block of data directly between a device and RAM without the CPU copying each word, raising a single interrupt when the whole transfer is complete.

Intermediate core

Compare thread-per-connection blocking I/O with an epoll event loop for a server handling 50,000 idle-ish connections.
Thread-per-connection blocking: each connection has a thread that blocks in read(). Simple to write (linear code, no state machine), but 50,000 threads means ~50,000 stacks (even at 64 KB each that’s ~3 GB), heavy scheduler load, and lots of context switches when many wake at once — the classic C10K problem. Fine for hundreds of connections, not tens of thousands. epoll event loop: one (or a few, one per core) threads call epoll_wait, which returns only the handful of fds that are actually ready; the loop does a non-blocking read/write on each and dispatches to per-connection state. Memory is a small buffer + state struct per connection (kilobytes, not a stack), and the kernel does O(ready) work, not O(total). This scales to hundreds of thousands of mostly-idle connections on modest hardware. Costs: the code becomes callback/state-machine style (mitigated by async/await or coroutines that compile to the same thing), you must handle partial reads/writes and backpressure explicitly, and CPU-bound work in a handler stalls the whole loop (offload to a worker pool). For the described workload (many connections, little activity each), the epoll loop is clearly right; a hybrid (epoll for I/O readiness + a bounded worker pool for request processing) is the common production shape. For a small number of very busy connections doing heavy per-request CPU work, threads can be simpler and fast enough.

Advanced deep

Design the I/O architecture for a storage service that must sustain millions of small random reads per second from NVMe with low tail latency. Cover the data path, threading, interrupts, and the syscall interface.
Goal: keep the per-request path short and predictable; eliminate syscalls, copies, context switches, and cross-core traffic on the hot path. Device path: NVMe with many hardware submission/completion queues — one queue pair per worker core, so submissions and completions for a core never touch another core’s queue (no locks, no cache-line bouncing). Use polled completions for the completion queues under load (NVMe polling / io_uring IOPOLL) instead of interrupts — at millions of IOPS an interrupt per completion is pure overhead and adds jitter; a core that’s always busy polls its CQ with near-zero latency. Fall back to interrupt mode when idle to save power. Threading: a fixed pool of pinned worker threads, one per dedicated core, each owning: its NVMe queue pair, its slice of connections, its buffer pool, and its portion of any in-memory index/cache. Shared-nothing — a request is hashed to the owning core and handled entirely there; cross-core work only for the rare cases (rebalancing, replication) via explicit message passing, not shared mutable state. Housekeeping (GC, compaction, metrics) on separate non-hot cores. Syscall interface: io_uring per worker, with registered fixed buffers and fixed file descriptors (skip per-call refcount/lookup), SQPOLL so submissions need no syscall at all (a kernel thread drains the SQ), and batched submit/complete. This collapses “syscall + copy + wait + wakeup” per read into “write an SQE, read a CQE from a ring in user memory.” Consider SPDK (full userspace NVMe driver, kernel bypass) if you can dedicate the device — it removes the block layer and page cache entirely and gives the tightest, most predictable path, at the cost of reimplementing caching/scheduling/failure handling yourself. Memory / copies: pre-allocated, huge-page-backed buffer pools per core; DMA directly into the response buffer; zero-copy from that buffer to the network (io_uring zero-copy send, or sendfile-style). Align buffers to the NVMe LBA and to 4 KB. Avoid the page cache for this workload (O_DIRECT or SPDK) since random reads over a huge dataset get near-zero cache hit and the cache just adds a copy and reclaim pressure — keep an explicit application cache sized to the working set instead. Interrupts / IRQ: MSI-X vectors mapped one-per-core-queue with affinity pinned to that core; isolcpus/nohz_full/no irqbalance on the worker cores so nothing steals cycles or causes jitter; move all other device IRQs and kernel threads off those cores. Tail latency: bound the queue depth per core so a burst can’t build an unbounded backlog (little’s law: latency = depth / throughput); use hedged/tied requests to a replica for the slow 0.1%; separate read and write paths so a compaction write burst can’t stall reads (or rate-limit background writes with token buckets); watch for NVMe device-side latency spikes (garbage collection) and steer around a misbehaving drive. Backpressure: when a core’s in-flight limit is hit, shed or delay new requests explicitly rather than letting queues grow. Observability: per-core histograms for submit→complete and end-to-end latency, CQ poll efficiency, ring-full events, and per-drive latency — all lock-free per-core counters aggregated off the hot path. Net: shared-nothing pinned workers, one NVMe queue pair per core, polled completions with io_uring/SQPOLL (or SPDK kernel bypass), O_DIRECT with per-core huge-page buffer pools and an explicit app cache, MSI-X affinity + core isolation to kill jitter, and per-core bounded queue depth plus hedging for the tail.

System Calls & the Kernel Boundary

How user code asks the kernel for something — and why crossing that line costs.

Notes

A system call is the controlled entry point from an unprivileged user program into the kernel to request a privileged service (open a file, send on a socket, map memory). It’s deliberately expensive — a hardware trap that switches privilege level and mode — which is why batching and avoiding syscalls matters for performance. This page covers the user/kernel space split, exactly what happens on a syscall (trap, mode switch, dispatch, return), the vDSO shortcut for a few hot calls, and monolithic vs microkernel design.

User space vs kernel space

The CPU runs at a privilege level. User mode can't touch hardware, other processes' memory, or privileged instructions. Kernel mode can. A system call is the controlled doorway: user code executes a special instruction (syscall on x86-64, svc on ARM) that traps into a fixed kernel entry point.

// user code CANNOT do this directly -- it must ask the kernel
*(volatile uint8_t*)0xB8000 = 'A';   // write to VGA memory -> SIGSEGV in user mode
outb(0x3F8, 'A');                    // privileged I/O instruction -> #GP fault

// the sanctioned doorway: a syscall
write(1, "A", 1);                    // libc wrapper -> `syscall` instruction -> kernel does the I/O

What happens on a syscall

  1. libc wrapper puts the syscall number in a register and arguments in others, executes syscall.
  2. CPU switches to kernel mode, jumps to the kernel's entry handler, switches to the kernel stack.
  3. Handler validates the number, copies/validates user pointers (copy_from_user — never trust a user address), dispatches via the syscall table.
  4. Does the work (maybe blocking → scheduler runs something else).
  5. Puts the return value / -errno in a register, switches back to user mode.

Cost: ~100–500 ns direct, more with mitigations (Spectre/Meltdown page-table isolation). Not free — hence batching (readv, io_uring, sendmmsg) and the vDSO.

$ strace -T -e trace=write ./app
write(1, "hi\n", 3)  = 3 <0.000004>      # <time> = ~4 us here incl. the terminal

# x86-64 calling convention: nr in rax, args in rdi,rsi,rdx,r10,r8,r9
mov  rax, 1          # __NR_write
mov  rdi, 1          # fd
mov  rsi, msg
mov  rdx, 3          # len
syscall             # trap; kernel returns result (or -errno) in rax

vDSO

A small shared library the kernel maps into every process so hot, read-only calls like gettimeofday()/clock_gettime() can be served in user space from a kernel-updated memory page — no mode switch at all.

$ cat /proc/self/maps | grep vdso
7ffe...000-7ffe...000 r-xp 00000000 00:00 0   [vdso]   # kernel-mapped code page

# clock_gettime() reads a kernel-updated timestamp page in USER mode -> no syscall
$ strace -e trace=clock_gettime ./ts_loop     # prints (almost) nothing: the calls never trap
$ ltrace ./ts_loop                            # but ltrace still sees the libc call

Kernel architectures

MonolithicMicrokernel
In-kernelscheduler, MM, drivers, filesystems, network stackonly scheduler, MM, IPC; drivers/FS are user-space servers
Speedfast (direct calls)slower (IPC between servers)
Reliabilitya driver bug can crash the kernela driver crash is a restartable service
ExamplesLinux, *BSD (modular monolithic)QNX, seL4, MINIX 3; macOS/Windows are hybrids
# Linux monolithic-but-modular: a driver is a function call away, and can panic the box
$ lsmod | head -3
Module        Size  Used by
nvme         57344  3
ext4        901120  1
$ sudo rmmod nvme        # unload a driver from the running kernel (no reboot)

# microkernel (QNX/seL4): that same nvme driver is a user process;
# if it crashes, a supervisor restarts it and the kernel never notices
Cheat Sheet
  • User mode = restricted; kernel mode = privileged. Syscall = the guarded transition (a trap instruction).
  • Flow: set syscall number + args → syscall/svc traps → kernel entry, validate, copy_from_user → dispatch via syscall table → return value/-errno → back to user mode.
  • Cost ~100–500 ns (+ KPTI overhead) → batch calls (io_uring, readv/writev, sendmmsg).
  • vDSO serves clock_gettime/getpid-class calls in user space — no mode switch.
  • Kernel must never trust user pointers — always validate + copy.
  • Monolithic (Linux): everything in kernel, fast, driver bug = crash. Microkernel: minimal core + user-space servers, robust, IPC overhead.
  • Interrupts/exceptions also enter kernel mode but aren't syscalls.
Q&A
Why can't user code just call kernel functions directly?
They run at different privilege levels in separate address spaces. The only way in is a trap instruction that switches the CPU to kernel mode and jumps to a fixed, validated entry point — so the kernel controls exactly what user code can trigger and can check every argument.
What is the vDSO and why does it exist?
A kernel-provided shared object mapped into every process. It lets frequently-called, safe, read-only operations (getting the time, the PID) run entirely in user space against a kernel-maintained data page — eliminating the mode-switch cost for the hottest "syscalls".
Why must the kernel copy user-supplied buffers with copy_from_user?
A user pointer might be invalid, unmapped, point into kernel memory, or be concurrently unmapped by another thread. copy_from_user checks the address range is legitimately user memory and handles faults gracefully, preventing a malicious or buggy program from making the kernel read/write arbitrary memory.
Monolithic vs microkernel — core trade-off?
Monolithic keeps drivers, filesystems, and the network stack in kernel space: fast (plain function calls) but a bug anywhere can take down the whole system. Microkernel runs those as isolated user-space servers: a crash is contained and restartable, at the cost of IPC overhead on every cross-component interaction.
How does io_uring reduce syscall overhead?
It sets up shared submission and completion ring buffers between user space and the kernel. The app writes many I/O requests into the submission ring and can process many completions from the completion ring, amortising or eliminating per-operation syscalls (with SQPOLL, a kernel thread polls the ring so the app makes no syscall at all).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What CPU state change does a system call cause?
A switch from user mode to kernel (privileged) mode, via a trap, and back on return.
Is printf a system call?
No — it's a libc function that may eventually invoke the write system call (after formatting and buffering).
Where do device drivers live in a microkernel?
In user space, as separate server processes; the kernel only mediates IPC and basic scheduling/memory.

Intermediate core

A program reading a file byte-by-byte with read(fd, &c, 1) is extremely slow. Why and fix?
Every byte is a full syscall (mode switch + kernel work) — hundreds of ns each, millions of times. Fix: read in large blocks (read(fd, buf, 65536)) and parse from the buffer, or use buffered stdio (fread/getc over a FILE*, which does big read()s under the hood), or mmap the file and access it as memory.
Why did Meltdown/Spectre mitigations make syscalls measurably slower?
Kernel Page-Table Isolation (KPTI) gives user mode and kernel mode separate page tables, so a syscall/interrupt must switch CR3 on entry and exit — adding TLB flushes (partly mitigated by PCID) and page-table reloads that a syscall previously didn't need. Retpolines / IBRS for Spectre add indirect-branch overhead in the kernel. Net effect: syscall-heavy workloads (databases, high-connection servers) saw single-digit to ~30% regressions depending on call rate, which is why syscall batching (io_uring) got more important.

Advanced deep

Trace a write(fd, buf, n) from the instruction to the return, including the security checks.
The libc wrapper loads the syscall number for write into rax, fd→rdi, buf→rsi, n→rdx, and executes syscall. The CPU saves the user rip/rflags, switches to ring 0, and jumps to the address in the LSTAR MSR — the kernel's entry stub. The stub switches to the kernel stack for this thread, saves the full user register set, (with KPTI) switches to the kernel page tables, and runs any entry-time mitigations. It bounds-checks rax against the syscall table size and calls sys_write. That resolves fd through the process's fd table to a struct file (returns -EBADF if invalid or not opened for writing), checks the file's write permission and any LSM (SELinux/AppArmor) hook, then calls the file's write operation. For a regular file that means copy_from_user(kernel_page, buf, n) — which verifies [buf, buf+n) lies in user address range and handles a fault by returning -EFAULT rather than oopsing — then copies into the page cache, marks pages dirty, updates the file offset, and returns the byte count. Back in the stub: the return value goes in rax, mitigations run, page tables/stack switch back, registers restore, sysret returns to just after the syscall instruction in user mode. libc checks for a negative value in [-4095, -1], and if so sets errno = -rax and returns -1.
Why are hybrid kernels (macOS XNU, Windows NT) neither purely monolithic nor microkernel, and what did they keep from each?
Both started with microkernel ambitions (XNU wraps the Mach microkernel; NT was influenced by microkernel design) but found the IPC cost of running performance-critical subsystems — the filesystem, network stack, and especially the graphics/window server — as separate user-space servers unacceptable for a desktop OS. So they pulled those back into kernel space for speed, while keeping microkernel-style structure and interfaces internally: XNU keeps Mach's message-passing, ports, and memory-object abstractions and layers a BSD "personality" (POSIX syscalls, sockets, VFS) on top, all in one kernel address space; NT keeps a layered "executive" of subsystems communicating through well-defined interfaces, with the microkernel-ish core ("kernel layer") handling scheduling and synchronisation, but drivers and file systems run in kernel mode. The result: the modularity, portability, and clean internal APIs of a microkernel, with the in-address-space call performance of a monolith — and the monolith's downside that a bad kernel-mode driver can still crash the system (hence Windows' driver signing and, later, moving some drivers back to user mode via UMDF).

Races & the Critical Section

Why count++ from two threads loses increments — and the vocabulary for it.

Notes

A race is when a program’s result depends on the unpredictable timing of concurrent operations. This page distinguishes two things people conflate: a data race (two threads access the same memory, at least one writing, with no synchronization — undefined behaviour in C/C++/Java/Go) and a race condition (a logic bug where a correct-looking sequence can interleave badly). It covers the classic lost-update bug, the critical section (the code that must run atomically), TOCTOU (time-of-check to time-of-use) races, and why you reason in terms of the invariant that must always hold.

The classic bug

// two threads run this; count starts at 0, ends at... maybe 1, not 2
count = count + 1;
//   load count -> reg      (both read 0)
//   add 1                  (both compute 1)
//   store reg -> count     (both write 1)  -- one increment lost

The read-modify-write isn't atomic; a thread switch between the load and the store loses an update. This is a data race: two threads access the same location, at least one writes, with no synchronisation and no defined ordering — undefined behaviour in C/C++/Java's model.

Data race vs race condition

  • Data race — the concrete "unsynchronised concurrent access" defect above. Tools (TSan) detect these.
  • Race condition — a broader logic bug where correctness depends on timing/ordering, even with each individual operation synchronised (e.g. check-then-act on shared state).
// DATA RACE (TSan flags it): two threads, no sync, one writes
int total;
void *w(void*_) { total += 1; return NULL; }   // $ clang -fsanitize=thread

// RACE CONDITION with NO data race: each op is atomic, the SEQUENCE is wrong
if (map.contains_key(k))          // thread A passes...
    v = map.get(k);               // ...thread B removes k here -> A gets null / throws
// fix: map.get_or_default(k), or hold the lock across check+use

Critical section

A region of code that accesses shared state and must run atomically with respect to other threads — only one thread inside at a time. Protect it with a lock (or make the operation a single atomic instruction, or avoid sharing).

void deposit(Account *a, long amt) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&a->m);        // enter -- only one thread past this point
    a->balance += amt;                // CRITICAL SECTION: keep it SHORT
    a->txn_count += 1;
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&a->m);      // leave
}
// don't do network / disk / malloc inside the lock -- widens contention

TOCTOU

Time-of-check to time-of-use: if (!exists(f)) create(f); — another thread/process can create f in the gap. Fix with an atomic operation (open(O_CREAT|O_EXCL), putIfAbsent, CAS) that checks and acts as one step.

// RACY: gap between the check and the create
if (access("/tmp/lock", F_OK) != 0)      // "doesn't exist"...
    fd = open("/tmp/lock", O_CREAT | O_WRONLY, 0600);  // ...someone else created it here

// ATOMIC check-and-act: O_EXCL fails if the file already exists
fd = open("/tmp/lock", O_CREAT | O_EXCL | O_WRONLY, 0600);
if (fd < 0 && errno == EEXIST) { /* someone else holds it */ }

Invariants

A critical section usually exists to keep an invariant true (a doubly-linked list's forward and backward pointers agree; an account's debits and credits balance). Mid-update the invariant is temporarily broken — which is exactly why no other thread may observe that state.

// invariant: node->next->prev == node   for every node
lock(&list->m);
n->next = cur->next;
cur->next = n;                // <-- HERE the invariant is broken: n->next->prev still points past n
n->next->prev = n;
n->prev = cur;               // invariant restored
unlock(&list->m);            // no other thread could see the half-updated state
Cheat Sheet
  • x++ is load + add + store — not atomic; concurrent increments lose updates.
  • Data race = unsynchronised concurrent access, ≥1 writer → UB. Race condition = timing-dependent logic bug (superset).
  • Critical section = code that must execute atomically w.r.t. other threads; guard with a lock / atomic / no-sharing.
  • TOCTOU = check-then-act with a gap; fix with an atomic check-and-act (O_EXCL, compare_exchange, putIfAbsent).
  • Shared mutable state is the root cause — prefer immutability, confinement (thread-local), or message passing.
  • "Works on my machine" proves nothing — races are nondeterministic and load-dependent.
  • Keep critical sections short; hold the lock only while the invariant is being read/repaired.
Q&A
Why can two threads doing count++ a million times each leave count less than 2 million?
count++ compiles to load, increment, store. If thread B loads count after thread A loaded but before A stored, both compute the same new value and one store overwrites the other — that increment is lost.
Data race vs race condition?
A data race is a specific defect: concurrent access to the same memory with at least one write and no synchronisation. A race condition is any bug where the outcome depends on the relative timing of operations — you can have a race condition even when every individual access is properly locked (e.g. releasing a lock between "check" and "act").
What is a critical section?
A block of code accessing shared data that must not be executed by more than one thread at a time, so that partial updates (a broken invariant) are never observed by another thread.
Give a TOCTOU example and its fix.
if (!file_exists(p)) fd = open(p, O_CREAT) — a race between the check and the create lets two processes both "win". Fix: open(p, O_CREAT | O_EXCL), which atomically fails if the file already exists.
Best way to avoid races entirely?
Don't share mutable state: use immutable data, confine state to one thread (thread-local, an actor's mailbox), or communicate by passing messages/ownership instead of sharing memory.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Is x++ atomic?
No — it's a read, a modify, and a write. Use an atomic type / atomic increment, or a lock.
What are the conditions for a data race?
Two or more threads access the same memory location concurrently, at least one access is a write, and there's no synchronisation ordering them.
How many threads may be inside a critical section at once?
One.

Intermediate core

A cache uses if (map.get(k) == null) map.put(k, compute(k)); from many threads. What's wrong?
Check-then-act race: two threads can both see null and both call compute (wasteful, and wrong if compute has side effects or must be single). Fix with an atomic operation: map.computeIfAbsent(k, this::compute) or putIfAbsent on a concurrent map, or hold a lock across check-and-put.
Two threads each acquire a lock, increment a shared counter, release — and the total is still wrong sometimes. What could it be?
Likely they're locking different lock objects (e.g. a per-instance lock when the counter is static, or a freshly-created lock each call), so the mutual exclusion never actually applies. Or the counter is read outside the lock elsewhere. The lock must be the same object guarding every access to that state.

Advanced deep

Why is a benign-looking data race on a bool stop flag still undefined behaviour, and what actually goes wrong?
In the C/C++/Java memory model, any data race is UB — the compiler is allowed to assume no other thread touches the variable. Concretely: the compiler may hoist the read of stop out of the worker's loop (it "can't change"), so the loop never sees the update and spins forever; it may reorder the write of stop relative to other writes the worker depends on; a non-atomic write can tear on some architectures; and the value may sit in a register/cache and never become visible. Marking it volatile (Java) or std::atomic<bool> with at least relaxed ordering (C++) tells the compiler and CPU it's shared, forcing an actual memory access each time and preventing the reordering — that's the minimum correct fix.
Explain sequential consistency as a correctness model and why real hardware/languages don't give it by default.
Sequential consistency (Lamport): the result of any execution is as if all threads' operations were executed in some single global interleaving that respects each thread's program order. It's the intuitive model programmers reason with. Hardware doesn't provide it for free because store buffers, out-of-order execution, and cache-coherence protocols let a core's writes become visible to different cores at different times, and its own later reads can bypass the store buffer — so thread 1 can see its own write before thread 2 does. Compilers also reorder independent memory ops for scheduling/register allocation. Enforcing SC everywhere would mean a full memory barrier on essentially every shared access — a large, usually-wasted cost. So languages expose a relaxed model with explicit ordering primitives (acquire/release, seq_cst fences, synchronized) and guarantee SC only for data-race-free programs ("SC-DRF"): if you synchronise all conflicting accesses, you get to keep reasoning as if it were sequentially consistent.

Mutexes & Condition Variables

Locking correctly, and waiting for a condition without missing the wakeup.

Notes

A mutex enforces mutual exclusion — only one thread holds it at a time — so it protects a critical section. A condition variable lets a thread wait for a predicate to become true without spinning, and be woken when another thread changes the state. This page covers using a mutex correctly (RAII/scoped locking, always releasing on every path), lock granularity (coarse = simple but contended, fine = scalable but deadlock-prone), the wait/notify pattern and why you must re-check the predicate in a loop (spurious and stolen wakeups), and mutex reentrancy.

Using a mutex

  • Guard every access (read and write) to the shared state with the same mutex.
  • Use RAII / scope guards (std::lock_guard, synchronized, with lock:) so the lock is released on every exit path, including exceptions.
  • Hold it for as short a time as possible; never do I/O or call unknown callbacks while holding it (deadlock / latency risk).
class Counter {
    std::mutex m_;
    long n_ = 0;
public:
    void incr() {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m_);   // RAII: unlocks on return OR exception
        n_++;                                // nothing slow in here
    }
    long get() {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m_);   // READS need the same lock too
        return n_;
    }
};

Lock granularity

CoarseFine
Locksone big lock for everythingmany small locks (per bucket, per node)
Prossimple, no deadlock, easy to reasonmore parallelism
Conscontention bottleneckdeadlock risk, overhead, complexity

Start coarse; refine only where profiling shows lock contention.

// COARSE: one lock for the whole map -> every op serialises
std::mutex big; std::unordered_map<K,V> m;

// FINE: shard into N stripes -> N threads can write concurrently to different keys
struct Shard { std::mutex m; std::unordered_map<K,V> m2; };
Shard shards[16];
Shard& s = shards[hash(k) % 16];
{ std::lock_guard lk(s.m); s.m2[k] = v; }   // only contends with same-shard writers

Condition variables

lock(m);
while (!predicate())      // WHILE, not if
    cv.wait(m);           // atomically unlocks m + sleeps; relocks on wake
// predicate() is true here, m is held
consume();
unlock(m);
  • Spurious wakeups: wait can return without a signal — the while re-checks.
  • Lost wakeup: if you signal before the waiter is waiting, it's missed. Prevented by holding the mutex while changing the predicate and signalling, and by the waiter checking the predicate before waiting.
  • notify_one vs notify_all: use all when waiters wait on different predicates; one is enough (and cheaper) when any waiter can make progress.

Reentrancy

A plain mutex deadlocks if the same thread locks it twice. Recursive mutexes allow it but usually signal a design smell — restructure so the lock is taken once at the top.

// SELF-DEADLOCK: public method locks, then calls another public method that locks again
void add(int x)      { lock(m); total += x; addAll_(x); unlock(m); }
void addAll(int x)   { lock(m); /* ... */ unlock(m); }   // add() -> addAll() -> lock(m) HANGS

// FIX: split into a locked public shell + an unlocked private core
void add(int x)      { lock(m); add_(x); unlock(m); }
void add_(int x)     { total += x; addAll_(x); }   // assumes caller holds m
Cheat Sheet
  • Same mutex guards every read and write of the state.
  • RAII lock guards → released on all exit paths (exceptions included).
  • Short critical sections; no I/O / callbacks / blocking under a lock.
  • Start with one coarse lock; split only where contention is measured.
  • Condvar idiom: hold mutex → while (!pred) cv.wait(m) → act → unlock.
  • Always while not if (spurious wakeups); change predicate + signal under the mutex (lost-wakeup).
  • notify_all when waiters have different conditions; notify_one when any can proceed.
  • Plain mutex is non-reentrant — don't re-lock on the same thread.
Q&A
Why check the predicate in a while loop, not an if?
Spurious wakeups (the thread wakes with no signal) and the possibility that another thread changed the state back between the signal and this thread reacquiring the lock. Re-checking guarantees the predicate actually holds before proceeding.
What is a lost wakeup and how is it prevented?
A signal sent before the consumer starts waiting is never seen, so the consumer sleeps forever with data available. Prevented by: holding the mutex while you both change the predicate and signal, and having the waiter check the predicate under the mutex before calling wait (which atomically releases the mutex and sleeps).
Why not do network I/O while holding a mutex?
The I/O can take arbitrarily long (or block), during which no other thread can enter the critical section — a huge contention stall — and if the I/O path itself tries to acquire another lock, you risk deadlock. Copy what you need out under the lock, release, then do the I/O.
Coarse vs fine-grained locking trade-off?
Coarse (one lock) is simple and deadlock-free but serialises everything. Fine-grained (many locks) allows concurrent operations on disjoint data but adds overhead and deadlock risk from multi-lock acquisition. Refine only where contention is proven.
notify_one vs notify_all?
notify_one wakes a single waiter — correct and efficient when any waiter can handle the new state. notify_all wakes everyone — needed when waiters are blocked on different conditions and you don't know which one(s) can now proceed; costs a thundering herd.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does a condition variable's wait do to the associated mutex?
Atomically releases it and puts the thread to sleep; reacquires it before wait returns.
Why use RAII lock guards?
They release the lock automatically when the scope ends — on normal return, early return, or an exception — so you can't forget to unlock.
Is a standard mutex reentrant?
No — re-locking it on the same thread deadlocks. Use a recursive mutex only if you truly must.

Intermediate core

Two mutexes, and you sometimes need both. How do you avoid deadlock?
Always acquire them in a fixed global order (e.g. by address or an assigned id), everywhere. Or use a deadlock-avoiding lock of both at once (std::scoped_lock(m1, m2) / std::lock), which uses a back-off algorithm. Or a try_lock on the second with release-and-retry on failure.
A worker sometimes hangs on a condvar even though the producer clearly signalled. Diagnose.
Classic lost wakeup: the producer changed the predicate and/or signalled without holding the mutex, or the consumer checked the predicate and then called wait in two separate locked regions with a gap. Fix: producer sets the predicate and signals while holding the same mutex the consumer uses; consumer does lock; while(!pred) wait(m); ... ; unlock as one locked region.

Advanced deep

Compare "Mesa" and "Hoare" condition-variable semantics and why real systems use Mesa.
Hoare semantics: signal immediately transfers control (and the mutex) to a waiting thread, which runs before the signaller continues — so the predicate is guaranteed true on wake and an if would suffice. But it requires precise scheduler cooperation, extra context switches, and careful handling of the signaller's suspended state. Mesa semantics (used by pthreads, Java, C++, C#): signal just marks a waiter runnable; the signaller keeps the lock and runs on; the woken thread competes for the lock later, by which time another thread may have consumed the condition. Hence you must re-check in a while. Mesa is chosen because it's far simpler to implement, imposes no scheduling constraints, composes with multiple signallers/waiters, and the while-loop discipline also transparently handles spurious wakeups. The cost is that discipline — forgetting the loop is a common bug.
When is a reader-writer lock actually slower than a plain mutex, despite allowing concurrent readers?
An RW lock has more internal state (reader count + writer flag/queue) so its lock/unlock fast path does more atomic work and more cache-line contention than a simple mutex — every reader still performs a synchronised update to the shared reader count, bouncing that cache line between cores. If critical sections are very short (a few reads), that bookkeeping overhead can exceed the time saved by parallelism, so a plain mutex (or better, an atomic/seqlock/RCU) wins. RW locks pay off only when read critical sections are long enough that reader parallelism dominates, reads vastly outnumber writes, and reader-count contention isn't itself the bottleneck. Also watch for writer starvation (reader-preferring implementations) or reader starvation (writer-preferring) depending on the fairness policy.

Read-Write Locks, RCU & Seqlocks

Read-mostly data doesn’t need a plain mutex serialising every reader — these primitives let readers run in parallel (or pay almost nothing) and only serialise writers.

Notes

A huge fraction of shared state is read-mostly: a config object, a routing table, a feature-flag map, a cache index — read thousands of times per write. A plain mutex forces those reads to happen one at a time for no reason. This page covers the read-optimised alternatives: the read-write lock (many concurrent readers or one writer), the optimistic read (StampedLock) that lets a reader validate afterwards instead of locking, the seqlock (a parity counter — writers never wait for readers), and RCU (readers pay essentially nothing; writers copy, swap a pointer, and defer freeing the old version past a grace period). It also covers the costs each one hides and how to choose.

Read-write lock (shared / exclusive)

What / why. rdlock can be held by many threads at once; wrlock is exclusive. Use it when reads dominate and the read critical section is long enough that running readers in parallel actually helps. Costs to know:

  • Acquiring a read lock still writes a shared reader-count word, so multiple readers bounce that cache line between cores — for a tiny critical section a plain mutex is often faster.
  • Writer starvation: a steady stream of readers can keep a writer waiting forever unless the lock is write-preferring or fair. Most production rwlocks let you choose.
  • Not free of deadlock: a thread that holds a read lock and then tries to upgrade to a write lock can deadlock with another doing the same.
std::shared_mutex m;                       // C++17
{ std::shared_lock lk(m); read(data); }    // many of these run concurrently
{ std::unique_lock lk(m); write(data); }   // exclusive
// Java: ReentrantReadWriteLock, or StampedLock (below)
// pthread_rwlock_t with PTHREAD_RWLOCK_PREFER_WRITER_NONRECURSIVE_NP to avoid writer starvation

Optimistic read (StampedLock)

What / why. A reader takes a cheap stamp, reads the data without any lock, then asks “did a writer run in the meantime?”. If not, it did a genuinely contention-free read (no shared write at all). If yes, it retries or falls back to a real read lock. Best when writes are rare and the read is short and can be safely re-done.

StampedLock sl = new StampedLock();
long stamp = sl.tryOptimisticRead();
int a = x, b = y;                 // read into locals
if (!sl.validate(stamp)) {        // a writer intervened
    stamp = sl.readLock();
    try { a = x; b = y; } finally { sl.unlockRead(stamp); }
}
use(a, b);
// StampedLock is NOT reentrant and has no condition support -- know its limits.

Seqlock (sequence lock)

What / how. A version counter guards the data. The writer: increment the counter (now odd ⇒ “write in progress”), write the data, increment again (now even). The reader: read the counter (spin while it’s odd), read the data, read the counter again — if it’s unchanged (and even) the read was consistent; otherwise retry. Writers never block for readers; readers never block writers.

// reader
do {
    seq = load_acquire(&s.seq);
    if (seq & 1) continue;         // writer active
    x = s.x; y = s.y;                  // may be torn -- that's ok, we recheck
} while (load_acquire(&s.seq) != seq);   // changed? retry

// writer (needs its own mutex vs other writers)
s.seq++;  store_release;
s.x = ...; s.y = ...;
s.seq++;  store_release;
  • Perfect for small, hot, rarely-written data — the kernel uses it for jiffies and the timekeeping data behind gettimeofday/vDSO.
  • Caveats: readers can observe a torn intermediate state, so the data must be safely re-readable — no pointers you would dereference mid-read. Not for large structures (the retry cost grows). Writer–writer still needs a real lock.

RCU (Read-Copy-Update)

What / why. Readers pay almost nothing — no lock, no atomic RMW, no write; they just delimit a “read-side critical section” (in the classic kernel form this is little more than disabling preemption). A writer makes a private copy of the node to change, modifies the copy, then atomically swaps the pointer so new readers see the new version. Existing readers may still be traversing the old version, so the old node is freed only after a grace period — a point by which every read-side critical section that started before the swap has finished (synchronize_rcu() to wait, or call_rcu(cb) to defer the free).

  • Ideal for read-mostly pointer-based structures: linked lists, hash tables, radix trees, routing tables — updates rare, reads on the hot path.
  • The hard part is the reclamation infrastructure (grace-period detection, deferred callbacks). Userspace: liburcu. Related schemes: hazard pointers and epoch-based reclamation solve the same “when is it safe to free” problem for lock-free code.
  • Not a fit when writes are frequent (copy + grace-period cost per update) or readers need a fully consistent multi-item snapshot.

Choosing

SituationUse
Tiny critical section, any read/write mixplain mutex (rwlock overhead isn’t worth it)
Reads » writes, non-trivial read sectionrwlock (write-preferring) or StampedLock optimistic read
Small POD struct, very hot reads, rare writesseqlock
Read-mostly pointer structure (list/tree/hash), rare updatesRCU (or hazard pointers for lock-free)
Counters / stats updated by many threadsper-CPU / sharded counters — avoid the shared line entirely
Cheat Sheet
  • rwlock (std::shared_mutex, ReentrantReadWriteLock, pthread_rwlock): many readers or one writer. Reads still write a shared counter (cache-line bounce); risk of writer starvation → use write-preferring. Not worth it for tiny sections. Never upgrade a held read lock.
  • StampedLock optimistic read: tryOptimisticRead() → read into locals → validate(stamp); on failure retry or take a real read lock. Contention-free when no writer ran. Not reentrant, no conditions.
  • seqlock: writer increments a counter to odd, writes, increments to even; reader reads counter (retry if odd), reads data, re-reads counter (retry if changed). Writers never wait for readers. Only for small re-readable POD; readers can see torn data; no pointers to deref mid-read; writer–writer needs its own lock. (kernel jiffies, vDSO time.)
  • RCU: readers do ~nothing (mark a read section); writer copies node, modifies, atomically swaps pointer; free the old copy only after a grace period (synchronize_rcu/call_rcu). Best for read-mostly pointer structures; bad when writes are frequent. liburcu; cousins = hazard pointers, epoch reclamation.
  • Decision: tiny section → mutex; reads»writes + real work → rwlock/optimistic; hot small struct → seqlock; read-mostly list/tree → RCU; hot counters → shard per-CPU.
Q&A
You replaced a mutex with a read-write lock for a read-heavy structure and it got slower. Why is that possible?
Two common reasons. (1) The critical section is tiny. Acquiring a read lock still performs an atomic read-modify-write on a shared reader-count word, so every reader on every core writes the same cache line and it ping-pongs between caches — more expensive than a short mutex acquire/release, and there was no real parallelism to gain because each reader was only in the section for a few nanoseconds. (2) Reader/writer bookkeeping and fairness logic in the rwlock implementation adds branches and, for fair/write-preferring modes, extra synchronization. Rwlocks pay off when readers genuinely overlap for a meaningful duration (holding the lock across a non-trivial computation or I/O). For hot, tiny reads, a plain mutex, a seqlock, RCU, or sharded/per-CPU data is usually faster.
How does a seqlock let writers proceed without ever waiting for readers?
The writer doesn’t coordinate with readers at all — it just bumps a version counter to an odd value (signalling “in progress”), writes the data, and bumps it to the next even value. It never checks for or blocks on readers. The reader does all the work of detecting a conflict: it snapshots the counter, copies the data into locals, and re-reads the counter; if the counter is odd or has changed, a write overlapped its read, so the data it copied might be torn/inconsistent and it simply retries. This is only safe because the reader never acts on the possibly-torn data until it has confirmed consistency, and because the data is plain values it can harmlessly re-read (dereferencing a pointer read mid-write would already be a bug).
What is a “grace period” in RCU and why is it necessary?
When an RCU writer swaps the pointer to a new version of a node, threads that were already inside a read-side critical section may still be holding and dereferencing the old pointer. The writer therefore can’t free the old node immediately. A grace period is an interval guaranteed to be long enough that every read-side critical section that was in progress at the moment of the swap has since completed — after which no thread can possibly still reference the old node, so it’s safe to free. The writer either blocks in synchronize_rcu() until a grace period elapses, or registers a callback with call_rcu() that the RCU machinery invokes after one. Detecting grace periods cheaply (typically: every CPU has passed through a quiescent state such as a context switch) is the core of an RCU implementation.
When is RCU the wrong choice?
When writes are frequent: every update copies the node and incurs grace-period / deferred-free overhead, and a burst of writers can pile up pending callbacks (memory pressure) — a rwlock or fine-grained locking is better for balanced read/write. When readers need a consistent snapshot across multiple items (RCU gives you a consistent view of a single pointer dereference, not an atomic multi-node read) — you’d need a seqlock-style version over the whole structure or an actual lock. When the data isn’t naturally pointer-swappable (large in-place structures). And when the reclamation infrastructure isn’t available or the added complexity isn’t justified by the measured contention on a simpler lock.
What’s the risk of allowing a thread to upgrade a read lock to a write lock?
Deadlock. If two threads each hold the read lock and each then requests an upgrade to write, neither can get exclusive access until the other releases its read lock — and neither will, because each is waiting for the upgrade. That’s a classic circular wait. Most rwlock APIs therefore either forbid upgrades, or provide a single non-blocking tryUpgrade that fails (so you drop the read lock and re-acquire as a writer, re-validating state), or a dedicated “upgradable read lock” that only one thread may hold at a time.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does a read-write lock allow that a mutex doesn’t?
Multiple threads to hold the lock for reading at the same time (only writers are exclusive). A plain mutex serialises everything, readers included.
In RCU, who pays the synchronization cost — readers or writers?
Writers. Readers do essentially nothing (mark a read-side section, no locks or atomics). Writers copy, atomically swap a pointer, and defer freeing the old version until a grace period passes.

Intermediate core

You have a routing table read on every packet (millions/sec) and updated a few times a minute. Compare mutex, rwlock, seqlock, and RCU for this.
Plain mutex: every packet lookup serialises on one lock — the lock itself becomes the bottleneck at millions of ops/sec across cores (cache-line contention on the lock word). Unusable at this rate. rwlock: readers can overlap, but each still does an atomic RMW on the shared reader count, so that cache line ping-pongs across every core doing lookups — better than a mutex but still a scalability wall at high core counts, and the lookup section is short so the parallelism gain is small. seqlock: works if the routing entry you read is small POD you can copy and re-read; readers do no shared writes, writers never block. But a routing table is usually a pointer-based structure (trie / radix), and a seqlock reader mustn’t dereference a pointer that could be freed mid-read — so a whole-table seqlock is awkward here. Fine for a single small fixed record, not a trie traversal. RCU: the right tool. Lookups enter an RCU read section (near-zero cost) and traverse the current trie via rcu_dereference; they never block and never write shared memory, so lookup throughput scales linearly with cores. An update builds the new/changed nodes, publishes them with an atomic pointer swap (rcu_assign_pointer), and frees the replaced nodes via call_rcu after a grace period — a few times a minute, so the copy/grace-period cost is irrelevant. This is exactly why the Linux kernel’s routing and many lookup tables are RCU-protected. Answer: RCU (or an equivalent epoch/hazard-pointer scheme if you’re in userspace without liburcu); mutex and rwlock don’t scale to per-packet reads, and a plain seqlock doesn’t suit pointer traversal.

Advanced deep

Design the concurrency for a config store: a nested config object read on nearly every request, hot-reloaded occasionally from disk, needing a consistent snapshot per request. Cover the read path, the reload path, and reclamation.
Model the whole config as one immutable value behind a single atomic pointer. The config is a deeply-immutable object graph (frozen maps/structs); nothing inside is ever mutated after construction. A global atomic<shared_ptr<const Config>> (C++), AtomicReference<Config> (Java), or atomic.Value / a pointer guarded by RCU (Go/kernel-style) holds the current version. Read path: at the start of handling a request, do one atomic load of the pointer into a local (auto cfg = g_config.load()). Use that local for the entire request. This gives a consistent snapshot for free — the request sees one coherent version even if a reload happens mid-request, because it holds its own reference to that immutable version.
