Cost is a single atomic load (and, with shared_ptr, one refcount increment) per request — effectively free, and fully parallel across cores. No rwlock, no seqlock retry, no per-field locking. Reload path: a background thread (triggered by a file watcher / SIGHUP / poll) reads the new config from disk, fully constructs and validates a new immutable Config object off to the side, and only on success does one atomic store to publish it (compare-and-set if you want to detect concurrent reloads). If parsing/validation fails, log and keep the old version live — readers never see a half-built config. Reloads are rare, so the full-rebuild cost is irrelevant; the atomic publish is a single instruction. Reclamation: this is the part the primitive choice decides. With shared_ptr/GC: automatic — the old Config is freed when the last in-flight request that captured it drops its reference; the only cost is the atomic refcount traffic on the control block (acceptable at request granularity; if it ever shows up in profiles, shard the pointer per-core or use hazard_ptr/RCU). With a raw pointer + RCU: readers take an RCU read-lock for the duration they use cfg (or just capture it and exit the section if the object is guaranteed alive via the scheme), and the reload thread frees the old object with call_rcu after a grace period — zero reader-side atomics, at the cost of the RCU infrastructure. With epoch-based reclamation: readers pin an epoch, the writer retires the old object, and it’s freed once all readers have advanced past that epoch. Extras: expose a getConfigSnapshot() accessor so no code path forgets and re-loads the atomic mid-request (which would reintroduce inconsistency); version-stamp each Config and log “now serving config v#N” on publish for observability; if some subsystems need to react to changes (reopen a connection pool, resize a cache), fire change callbacks from the reload thread after the publish, passing old and new. Why not rwlock/seqlock: a rwlock read still contends a shared line on every request and doesn’t give you a snapshot that survives a mid-request reload without holding the lock the whole request (blocking reloads); a seqlock can’t protect a pointer-rich nested object a reader dereferences. The immutable-value-behind-an-atomic-pointer pattern (a.k.a. RCU-style publish) is the standard answer: near-free parallel reads, atomic publish, and snapshot consistency by construction.

Semaphores & Classic Problems

Counting resources, and the three textbook problems every interview draws from.

Notes

A semaphore is a counter with atomic wait (decrement, block at 0) and signal (increment, wake a waiter) — a binary semaphore acts like a lock, a counting semaphore limits concurrent access to N units of a resource. This page uses semaphores to solve the textbook synchronization problems that every real system is a variant of: the bounded-buffer producer–consumer, readers–writers (and its starvation trade-offs), and dining philosophers (deadlock and how to break it).

Semaphore

An integer with two atomic operations: acquire/wait/P (decrement; block if it would go negative) and release/signal/V (increment; wake a waiter).

  • Counting semaphore(N) — up to N threads may proceed; models "N units of a resource" (a connection pool, N parking spots).
  • Binary semaphore(1) — acts like a lock, but with no owner: any thread can release, which enables using it for signalling between threads.
sem_t slots;
sem_init(&slots, 0, 3);          // counting(3): at most 3 concurrent downloads

void *worker(void *_) {
    sem_wait(&slots);              // P: take a permit (blocks if 0 left)
    download();
    sem_post(&slots);             // V: return a permit -- ANY thread may do this
    return NULL;
}
// binary(0) as a one-shot signal: thread A sem_wait()s, thread B sem_post()s when ready

Producer–consumer (bounded buffer)

sem empty = N;   sem full = 0;   mutex m;
producer: empty.acquire(); m.lock(); buf.push(x); m.unlock(); full.release();
consumer: full.acquire();  m.lock(); x=buf.pop();  m.unlock(); empty.release();

empty counts free slots, full counts items; the mutex protects the buffer itself. Acquire the counting semaphore before the mutex to avoid holding the mutex while blocked.

Readers–writers

Many readers concurrently, or one writer exclusively. Naive "reader-preference" starves writers; "writer-preference" starves readers; a fair version bounds waiting for both. Usually solved with an RW lock or by a "turnstile" semaphore that new readers must pass, which a waiting writer can hold.

mutex rc_lock; int readers = 0; sem resource(1);

read():
    lock(rc_lock)
    if (++readers == 1) resource.acquire()   // first reader locks out writers
    unlock(rc_lock)
    ... read ...
    lock(rc_lock)
    if (--readers == 0) resource.release()   // last reader lets a writer in
    unlock(rc_lock)

write():
    resource.acquire(); ... write ...; resource.release()   // exclusive
// this is READER-preference: a steady reader stream starves writers -> add a turnstile

Dining philosophers

5 philosophers, 5 forks, each needs both neighbouring forks to eat. Grab-left-then-right by all → deadlock. Fixes: limit to 4 seated at once (a counting semaphore); asymmetric order (odd grabs left first, even grabs right first); pick up both forks atomically under a mutex; or a waiter/arbitrator.

// deadlock: everyone grabs left, then waits forever for right
philosopher(i):
    fork[i].acquire()
    fork[(i+1)%5].acquire()      // all 5 stuck here

// FIX 1: asymmetric order -- the last philosopher grabs right first, breaking the cycle
if (i == 4) { right.acquire(); left.acquire(); }
else        { left.acquire();  right.acquire(); }

// FIX 2: cap concurrent diners at 4 with a counting semaphore
sem seats(4);
seats.acquire(); left.acquire(); right.acquire(); /* eat */ ; right.release(); left.release(); seats.release();
Cheat Sheet
  • Semaphore = atomic counter; acquire (P, dec/block), release (V, inc/wake). No ownership.
  • Counting(N) = N concurrent permits (resource pool). Binary(1) = lock-like but any thread can release → good for signalling.
  • Producer–consumer: empty=N, full=0, plus a mutex for the buffer; acquire the count semaphore before the mutex.
  • Readers–writers: many readers XOR one writer; watch for starvation — use a fair RW lock.
  • Dining philosophers deadlock fix: cap concurrent diners at N−1, asymmetric fork order, atomic two-fork grab, or an arbitrator.
  • Prefer higher-level constructs (blocking queues, RW locks, Semaphore classes) to hand-rolled P/V.
Q&A
Counting vs binary semaphore?
Counting allows up to N threads through (N units of a resource). Binary is initialised to 1 and behaves like a lock — but unlike a mutex it has no owner, so any thread can release it, which is what makes it usable for one thread signalling another.
In bounded-buffer producer–consumer, what do the two semaphores count?
empty counts free slots (starts at N), full counts filled slots (starts at 0). A producer waits on empty, a consumer waits on full; a separate mutex protects the buffer data structure.
Why acquire the counting semaphore before the mutex, not after?
If you locked the mutex first and then blocked on a full/empty semaphore, you'd hold the mutex while sleeping — no one else could touch the buffer, and the counterpart thread that would unblock you can't get in. Acquire the resource count first, then briefly take the mutex only to mutate the buffer.
What causes deadlock in dining philosophers and one fix?
Every philosopher picks up their left fork, then all wait forever for the right (held as someone's left) — circular wait. Fix: allow at most 4 to attempt eating simultaneously (a semaphore initialised to 4), so at least one can always get both forks.
What's the starvation risk in readers–writers?
A steady stream of readers can keep the resource read-locked forever, so a writer never gets exclusive access (reader preference). The mirror problem gives writers priority and starves readers. Fair implementations queue requests so both make progress.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does acquire() (P) do when the semaphore is 0?
Blocks the calling thread until another thread calls release().
Which classic problem models "many readers or one writer"?
The readers–writers problem.
Semaphore to limit concurrent access to 3 printers?
A counting semaphore initialised to 3.

Intermediate core

Implement a rate limiter allowing N concurrent requests, blocking the rest.
A counting semaphore initialised to N. Each request does sem.acquire() before proceeding and sem.release() in a finally when done (even on error/exception). When N are in flight, the N+1th blocks until one finishes. For a per-second rate (not concurrency), use a token bucket instead: refill tokens on a timer, acquire a token per request.
Solve dining philosophers without deadlock and without a global arbitrator.
Asymmetric acquisition: philosophers with an even id pick up the right fork first then the left; odd id pick up left first then right. This breaks the uniform cycle — at least one philosopher's acquisition order is "reversed" relative to a neighbour, so a full circular wait can't form. Combine with fair fork mutexes (FIFO) to also guarantee no individual philosopher starves.

Advanced deep

Why is a semaphore easy to misuse compared to a mutex + condition variable?
A semaphore conflates two roles — mutual exclusion and counting/signalling — and carries no association with the data it protects or the predicate it represents. Common errors: forgetting a release on an error path (permanent permit leak, eventual deadlock); calling release more times than acquire (silently raising the count, letting too many threads in); using one semaphore for two different conditions (a wake meant for condition A satisfies a waiter for condition B); and the count drifting out of sync with reality after an exception. A mutex+condvar makes the invariant explicit (the predicate is re-checked in a while), the mutex has a clear owner, and RAII guards the release. Dijkstra's semaphores are a minimal primitive; higher-level constructs (blocking queues, latches, barriers, CompletableFuture) encode the intent and are harder to get wrong.
Design a fair readers–writers lock and prove neither side starves.
Use a single FIFO queue of waiters (a ticket lock / a Semaphore with fairness, or a condvar with an explicit queue). State: activeReaders, activeWriter (bool), and the FIFO wait queue. A thread joins the tail of the queue; it may proceed when it reaches the head and the lock's state permits it (reader: no active writer; writer: no active readers or writer). Crucially, a reader at the head does not jump ahead of a writer that's queued earlier — that's what makes it fair. No writer starvation: once a writer is enqueued, only readers already ahead of it in the queue (a bounded set) can go first; new readers queue behind it, so the writer waits for a bounded number of predecessors. No reader starvation: symmetrically, a queued reader waits only for the bounded set of earlier writers plus at most one in-progress writer. Bounded waiting on both sides ⇒ both make progress. The cost vs a reader-preference lock is slightly lower read throughput under heavy read load, since readers can't all barge in past a waiting writer.

Message Passing: Channels, CSP & the Actor Model

Instead of sharing memory and guarding it with locks, threads communicate by sending messages — and whole classes of races simply can’t occur.

Notes

The alternative to “shared mutable state + locks” is message passing: concurrent units keep their state private and coordinate by sending each other values. If nothing is shared, nothing can be raced on — the bug you fix isn’t “forgot a lock” but “designed the message flow wrong”. This page covers the two main flavours: channels (the CSP model — a first-class typed conduit, buffered or unbuffered, with select) as in Go, and the actor model (isolated entities with a mailbox, processing one message at a time, with supervision) as in Erlang/Akka. It covers the trade-offs, the standard patterns (pipeline, fan-out/fan-in, request/reply), and how deadlock still shows up.

Channels (CSP)

What / how. A channel is a typed pipe. A send blocks and a receive blocks according to the buffering:

  • Unbuffered: a rendezvous — the sender blocks until a receiver is ready and vice versa. Data transfer and synchronization happen together.
  • Buffered (capacity N): a bounded FIFO — the sender blocks only when the buffer is full, the receiver only when empty. This is backpressure: a slow consumer eventually stalls a fast producer.
  • select waits on several channel operations at once and proceeds with whichever is ready (with an optional default for non-blocking).
  • Closing a channel signals “no more values” to every receiver (a broadcast); receiving from a closed channel returns the zero value immediately.
// Go: fan-out workers reading one channel, writing results to another
jobs := make(chan Job, 100)      // buffered: up to 100 queued
results := make(chan Result)

for i := 0; i < 8; i++ {         // 8 workers
    go func() {
        for j := range jobs {       // loop until jobs is closed and drained
            results <- process(j)
        }
    }()
}
go func() { for _, j := range allJobs { jobs <- j }; close(jobs) }()

for range allJobs { collect(<-results) }   // gather
// request/reply: put a reply channel INSIDE the message
type Ask struct{ key string; reply chan Value }

The actor model

What / how. An actor is an object with (1) private state no one else can touch, (2) a mailbox, and (3) a behaviour that, for each received message, may: update its state, send messages to other actors (by address), spawn child actors, or change its behaviour for the next message. Because it handles messages one at a time, its state needs no locks. Actors are location-transparent — an address might be local or on another node — which is why the model underpins distributed frameworks. Erlang/OTP, Akka, Elixir, Microsoft Orleans, Ray.

  • Supervision: actors are arranged in trees; a parent supervises its children and, on a child crash, restarts it (or escalates). “Let it crash” — don’t defensively handle every error inside the actor; let it die clean and be restarted to a known-good state.
  • No shared state means a message is (conceptually) copied; large payloads cost serialization, so you pass references/handles for big data.

Channels vs actors

Channels (CSP)Actors
The primitiveThe conduit — first-class, many senders/receivers, selectThe entity — addressable identity, state + mailbox + behaviour
Concurrency unitLightweight thread / goroutine (anonymous)The actor (has a name/address)
Natural fitData-flow pipelines, worker pools, coordinationStateful entities, distributed systems, fault-tolerant services
Failure modelYou handle it (closed channels, contexts)Built-in: supervision trees, restart strategies

Trade-offs & the ways it still goes wrong

  • Wins: no data races (nothing shared), local reasoning per unit, backpressure falls out of bounded buffers/mailboxes, the same model scales to multiple machines.
  • Costs: copying / serialization; you can just relocate the bug — deadlock becomes “A waits for a message from B, B waits for a message from A”; there is no global order across independent channels/actors; message-flow bugs are harder to see in a stack trace.
  • Unbounded mailboxes / channels are a memory-blowup risk under load — bound them and decide the policy when full (block = backpressure, drop, or fail).
  • Deadlock still happens: sending on an unbuffered channel with no receiver, cyclic channel dependencies, or every goroutine blocked (Go’s runtime panics with “all goroutines are asleep — deadlock!” only when the whole program is stuck).
Cheat Sheet
  • Idea: don’t share memory and lock it — keep state private and send messages. No shared mutable state → no data races.
  • Channel: typed conduit. Unbuffered = rendezvous (both block until handoff). Buffered(N) = bounded queue = backpressure. select for multiway wait; close broadcasts “done”.
  • Actor: private state + mailbox + behaviour; processes one message at a time (no internal locks); addressable; location-transparent; supervision trees + “let it crash”.
  • Channels = the conduit (Go, core.async, Rust mpsc/crossbeam). Actors = the entity (Erlang, Akka, Elixir, Orleans, Ray).
  • Patterns: pipeline (stages + channels), fan-out/fan-in (worker pool), request/reply (embed a reply channel in the message), pub/sub, token-bucket rate limit.
  • Still fails: cyclic waits (deadlock as “everyone waiting for a message”), no global ordering, unbounded mailbox → OOM. Bound queues and pick a full-policy.
Q&A
“Don’t communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating.” What does that mean in practice?
Instead of putting data in a shared variable and coordinating access with a mutex, you give ownership of the data to one goroutine/actor and pass it around via channels/messages. At any moment exactly one unit “has” the data and can mutate it freely with no lock; when it sends the data on, it conceptually gives up ownership. The synchronization is the message send/receive itself. This removes the entire category of “forgot to lock” / “locked the wrong thing” bugs, at the cost of designing the ownership/message flow deliberately.
Unbuffered vs buffered channel — when do you want each?
Unbuffered when you need the send and receive to be a synchronization point — the sender must know the receiver actually took the value (handoff of ownership, a “done” signal, lock-step coordination). Buffered when you want to decouple producer and consumer speeds and get bounded queuing: a small buffer absorbs bursts, and a full buffer provides backpressure that stalls the producer instead of letting an unbounded queue grow. Size the buffer to the burst you want to absorb, not “big enough that it never blocks” — that just hides overload until you run out of memory.
How can a message-passing program still deadlock?
By constructing a cycle of waits with messages instead of locks: A does a blocking send to B and then waits for B’s reply; B does a blocking send to A and waits for A’s reply — neither can receive because both are blocked in send. Or: a single goroutine sends on an unbuffered channel with no other goroutine ever receiving. Or all workers are blocked receiving from a channel that will never get another value because the only producer already exited without closing it. The Coffman conditions still apply; you’ve just changed “resource” from “lock” to “channel operation”. Fixes are analogous: avoid cyclic send dependencies, prefer select with timeouts/cancellation, close channels to release ranged receivers, and make at least one side non-blocking.
What does “let it crash” mean and why is it considered good practice in the actor model?
Rather than wrapping every operation in an actor in defensive error handling that tries to limp on in a possibly-corrupt state, you let the actor throw and die on an unexpected error. Its supervisor then restarts it — recreating it with fresh, known-good initial state — or escalates if restarts keep failing. This works because actors are isolated (one crashing doesn’t corrupt others) and cheap to create, and because most transient failures (a bad message, a downstream blip) are cleared by a clean restart. The result is systems that self-heal from unanticipated faults, with error-handling logic concentrated in the supervision strategy instead of smeared through business code. It complements — doesn’t replace — handling expected errors (validation, retries) explicitly.
You have a worker pool reading jobs from a channel. How do you shut it down cleanly?
The producer closes the jobs channel when there are no more jobs. Each worker’s for job := range jobs loop then exits naturally once the channel is drained. To wait for all workers to finish, use a sync.WaitGroup (increment per worker, Done when its loop exits, Wait in the shutdown path), then close the results channel. For early cancellation (shutdown before jobs are exhausted), pass a context.Context and have workers select on both ctx.Done() and the jobs channel, returning promptly on cancellation. Don’t close the jobs channel from a worker or from multiple places (closing a closed channel panics; the sender owns the close).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What’s the core promise of message passing over shared-memory-plus-locks?
No shared mutable state means no data races — there is nothing for two threads to concurrently read/write without synchronization, because the synchronization is the message send/receive.
Why does an actor not need locks around its own state?
It processes exactly one message at a time from its mailbox, so there is never concurrent access to its state — the serialization is built into the model.

Intermediate core

Design a bounded, backpressured pipeline: stage A reads from a source, stage B transforms, stage C writes to a sink, each stage parallelised. How do channels give you flow control?
Connect the stages with buffered channels of small capacity: src→chAB (cap m)→B workers→chBC (cap n)→C workers→sink. Each stage is a set of goroutines doing for x := range inCh { out <- f(x) }. Flow control is automatic: if the sink (C) is slow, chBC fills, so B’s workers block on out <- ..., so they stop draining chAB, so it fills, so A blocks reading the source — the whole pipeline throttles to the slowest stage with a bounded amount of in-flight work (roughly the sum of the buffer capacities plus one item per worker). Choose buffer sizes to absorb short bursts (a few times the number of workers), not to “never block”. Shutdown: A closes chAB when the source is exhausted; B’s workers exit their range loops, and a WaitGroup for stage B closes chBC after the last B worker returns; C’s workers then drain and exit, and a WaitGroup for C signals “pipeline done”. Cancellation / errors: thread a context.Context through every stage; workers select on ctx.Done() alongside their channel ops so a failure anywhere (or a caller cancel) tears the whole pipeline down promptly without goroutine leaks; propagate the first error out on a dedicated 1-buffered error channel. This is the canonical Go pipeline pattern and it needs no mutexes at all.

Advanced deep

Compare shared-memory + locks, CSP channels, and the actor model for building a concurrent in-memory key-value store with range queries and TTL expiry. Which would you pick and why?
Shared-memory + locks: the store is a concurrent map (sharded, or a lock-free / RCU structure for reads) plus a background sweeper for TTL. Pros: lowest latency and highest throughput for point reads/writes — a read is a hash lookup under a read lock or lock-free; no message hop. Range queries need a sorted structure (skip list / B-tree) with its own concurrency scheme (fine-grained locks, optimistic, or RCU) — doable but this is exactly where locking gets subtle (iterator vs concurrent modification). TTL sweep is a scan under locks or per-shard. Cons: correctness burden is on you; range-scan-while-mutating and “expire during read” are classic race sources; scaling requires careful sharding to avoid a hot lock. CSP channels: a single owner goroutine holds the data structure; all operations are messages (Get{key, reply}, Put, Range{lo, hi, reply}, tick for expiry) on one request channel; the owner processes them serially, so no locks and trivially correct. Pros: dead simple to reason about, no data races, easy to add features (transactions = just don’t yield between messages). Cons: that owner goroutine is a serialization bottleneck — every operation, including concurrent reads, queues behind it; a long range query blocks all other ops. Mitigate by sharding into many owner goroutines by key range (now range queries within a shard are fine, cross-shard need scatter-gather and lose snapshot consistency) — at which point you’ve rebuilt sharded locking with channels and extra copying. Actor model: essentially the sharded-CSP design with identity and supervision — one actor per shard (or per key-range), a supervisor that restarts a shard actor on a bug, and the TTL sweeper as another actor sending expiry messages. Pros: the fault tolerance is free (a corrupt shard restarts from a snapshot/WAL), and it extends naturally to a distributed KV store (shard actors on different nodes, consistent hashing for placement) — this is basically how Orleans/Akka-based stores and Riak work. Cons: same serialization-per-shard bottleneck as CSP, plus mailbox/backpressure management, and range queries spanning shards are a distributed scatter-gather with weak consistency. Pick: if it must be a single-process, latency-critical cache — sharded shared-memory with a read-optimised structure (RCU/optimistic reads) for the point-lookup hot path and a concurrent sorted index for ranges; accept the complexity and lean on TSan + stress tests. If it needs to be fault-tolerant and/or distributed, or the team values obvious correctness over peak throughput — the actor-per-shard model, with a WAL/snapshot per shard for restart, consistent-hash placement, and range queries as bounded scatter-gather with documented consistency. CSP-with-one-owner is the right choice only for a small store or a prototype where simplicity dominates. A common real design is a hybrid: shared-memory lock-free reads for the hot point-lookup path, and an actor/channel control plane for expiry, rebalancing, and admin operations.

Deadlock, Livelock & Starvation

Three ways a concurrent system can stop making progress — and how to design them out.

Notes

This page covers the three ways concurrent progress can fail. Deadlock: threads each hold a resource the other needs and wait forever — it needs all four Coffman conditions, and lock ordering is the standard fix. Livelock: threads keep changing state in response to each other but make no progress (two people stepping aside in a corridor). Starvation: a thread is perpetually denied a resource it needs because others keep winning. It also covers priority inversion — a low-priority lock holder blocking a high-priority thread — and its fix, priority inheritance.

Deadlock

Threads permanently blocked, each waiting for a resource another holds (the four Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait — see the OS Deadlock topic). Practical prevention in application code:

  • Consistent global lock ordering — assign every lock a rank; always acquire in increasing rank.
  • Lock-both-at-once — std::scoped_lock(a, b) / tryLock-both with back-off.
  • Don't call out under a lock — no user callbacks, no acquiring a second subsystem's lock, no blocking I/O.
  • Coarser locking — one lock can't deadlock with itself.
  • Timeouts — tryLock(timeout) converts a deadlock into a detectable, recoverable failure.
// C++17: lock BOTH atomically -- scoped_lock uses a deadlock-avoiding algorithm
std::scoped_lock lk(a.m, b.m);        // no matter the order callers pass a, b

// or tryLock + timeout turns a hang into a handled error
if (!mtx.try_lock_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(500))) {
    metrics.inc("lock_timeout");
    return ERR_BUSY;                  // recoverable, not a permanent freeze
}

Livelock

Threads are running and changing state but making no progress — e.g. two threads that each detect contention, release everything, and retry in lockstep forever. Fix: randomised exponential back-off so the retry timing desynchronises, or a priority/tie-breaker so one thread wins.

int attempt = 0;
while (!try_acquire_both()) {
    release_all();
    int backoff = (1 << std::min(attempt++, 6)) * 10;   // 10,20,40,...,640 ms
    std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(backoff + rand() % backoff));
    // the RANDOM jitter is the point -- it desynchronises the two threads
}

Starvation

A thread is perpetually denied progress though the system as a whole advances: always lower priority, always loses the lock race, or a stream of readers blocks a writer. Fixes: fair locks (FIFO), ageing (raise priority with wait time), bounded-waiting guarantees.

// unfair: whoever the scheduler wakes wins -> an unlucky thread may never get in
std::mutex m;                         // no ordering guarantee

// fair: FIFO ticket lock -- served strictly in arrival order
std::atomic<int> next{0}, serving{0};
int my = next.fetch_add(1);         // take a ticket
while (serving.load() != my) cpu_relax();  // wait my turn
/* critical section */
serving.fetch_add(1);               // call the next ticket

Priority inversion

A high-priority thread waits on a lock held by a low-priority thread that a medium-priority thread keeps preempting — the high thread is effectively blocked by the medium one. Fix: priority inheritance (the lock holder temporarily runs at the waiter's priority) or a priority ceiling.

// the Mars Pathfinder bug: low-prio task holds a lock a high-prio task needs,
// medium-prio tasks keep preempting the low one -> high task misses its deadline -> watchdog reboot

// FIX: enable priority inheritance on the mutex
pthread_mutexattr_t a;
pthread_mutexattr_init(&a);
pthread_mutexattr_setprotocol(&a, PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT);  // holder inherits waiter's priority
pthread_mutex_init(&m, &a);
Cheat Sheet
  • Deadlock = permanently blocked cycle. Livelock = busy but no progress. Starvation = one party perpetually denied.
  • Deadlock prevention: global lock order; lock-multiple atomically; no callbacks/I-O under a lock; coarser locks; tryLock + timeout.
  • Livelock fix: randomised exponential back-off; a deterministic tie-breaker so someone always wins.
  • Starvation fix: fair (FIFO) locks, ageing, bounded-waiting.
  • Priority inversion fix: priority inheritance or priority ceiling on the lock.
  • Detect deadlocks in prod: thread dumps / jstack, watchdog timers on lock acquisition, lock-order checkers (TSan, lockdep).
Q&A
Deadlock vs livelock?
In deadlock the threads are blocked and idle. In livelock they're actively executing — typically retrying an operation — but their actions keep cancelling each other out so no useful work completes.
Simplest reliable way to prevent lock-ordering deadlocks?
Define a total order over all locks (by id/address) and always acquire them in that order. A cycle in the wait-for graph then can't form.
How does randomised back-off cure livelock?
Livelock usually comes from threads reacting in perfect synchrony. Adding a random delay before each retry breaks the symmetry, so one thread arrives first, acquires what it needs, and makes progress while the other waits.
What is priority inversion?
A high-priority thread is blocked on a resource held by a low-priority thread, which itself is preempted by unrelated medium-priority threads — so the high-priority thread waits on the medium ones indirectly. Priority inheritance fixes it by boosting the holder to the waiter's priority.
How do you detect a deadlock in a running JVM service?
Take a thread dump (jstack, kill -3, or a profiler). The JVM annotates detected deadlocks explicitly ("Found one Java-level deadlock") showing which threads hold and wait for which monitors. Watchdogs that alert when a lock acquisition exceeds a threshold catch it proactively.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which is running-but-stuck: deadlock or livelock?
Livelock — the threads are executing but not progressing. Deadlock threads are blocked.
Name a lock-ordering-free way to acquire two mutexes safely.
std::scoped_lock(m1, m2) / std::lock(m1, m2) — it uses a deadlock-avoidance algorithm (try/back-off).
What fixes writer starvation in a readers–writers lock?
A fair (FIFO) policy or bounding how long a writer can be made to wait — e.g. blocking new readers once a writer is queued.

Intermediate core

Your service occasionally freezes; a thread dump shows two threads each holding one lock and waiting for the other. Fix approach?
It's a lock-ordering deadlock. Identify the two locks and every code path that takes both; impose one consistent acquisition order and refactor all paths to follow it. Where a natural order doesn't exist, switch to std::scoped_lock/tryLock-with-backoff, merge the two locks into one, or restructure so only one is held at a time (copy data out under lock A, release, then take lock B).
A retry loop with while(!tryLock(a) || !tryLock(b)) { unlockAll(); } spins forever under load. Why and fix?
Livelock: two threads keep grabbing one lock, failing the other, releasing, and retrying in sync. Fix: after a failed attempt, sleep(random exponential backoff) before retrying, so the threads desynchronise; or give threads a priority so one consistently wins; or use std::lock, which is designed to acquire multiple locks without livelock.

Advanced deep

How does priority inheritance actually work, and what's its cost / a subtlety with nested locks?
When a high-priority thread H blocks trying to acquire a mutex held by low-priority thread L, the runtime raises L's effective (scheduling) priority to H's, so L is scheduled promptly, finishes its critical section, releases the mutex (at which point L's priority drops back and H acquires it). With nested locks it must be transitive: if L is itself blocked on a mutex held by even-lower thread K, K must also be boosted to H's priority — the boost propagates down the whole chain. Costs and subtleties: each block/unblock updates a priority-inheritance chain (bookkeeping, and the scheduler must re-evaluate run queues); the boost is per-mutex, so a thread holding several PI mutexes runs at the max of its waiters' priorities and must recompute on each acquire/release; there's a risk of "priority inheritance chains" causing latency spikes; and it only helps if the mutex implementation supports it (pthreads needs PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT set explicitly — the default doesn't, which is the Mars Pathfinder bug). Priority ceiling avoids the chains by pre-boosting on acquire, at the cost of needing to know the max waiter priority per lock up front.
Give a definition of lock-freedom and starvation-freedom and explain why a lock-based algorithm can't be lock-free.
Lock-free: at any point, some thread is guaranteed to make progress within a bounded number of steps of the whole system (individual threads may still stall or retry forever). Wait-free (stronger): every thread completes its operation in a bounded number of its own steps — no starvation. Starvation-free (a liveness property applicable to lock-based code too): every thread that wants to enter its critical section eventually does. A mutex-based algorithm cannot be lock-free because if the thread holding the lock is descheduled (or crashes) inside the critical section, every other thread that needs the lock is blocked indefinitely — no thread makes progress, violating the lock-free guarantee. Lock-free algorithms achieve their guarantee by using atomic RMW (CAS) with retry: a stalled thread's incomplete operation doesn't block others because there's no held lock — others just win the CAS and proceed. The trade-off is complexity, the ABA problem, and reclamation difficulty (see the Lock-free topic).

Atomics & Compare-and-Swap

Lock-free updates built from one hardware primitive — and the ABA trap.

Notes

Atomic operations read-modify-write a single variable indivisibly, with no lock — fetch_add, exchange, and the fundamental one, compare-and-swap (CAS): “if this location still holds expected, set it to new, atomically, and tell me if it worked.” CAS in a retry loop is how you build lock-free counters, flags, and data structures. This page covers what hardware guarantees atomicity for, the CAS loop pattern, when atomics genuinely beat a mutex (and when they don’t), and the ABA problem that bites naive lock-free code.

Atomic operations

An atomic read-modify-write completes indivisibly — no other thread sees a partial state. Hardware provides: atomic load/store, fetch_add/fetch_sub, exchange, and the universal primitive compare-and-swap (CAS):

// atomically: if (*p == expected) { *p = desired; return true; } else { expected = *p; return false; }
bool compare_exchange(p, &expected, desired);

The CAS loop

old = x.load();
do {
    new = f(old);                    // compute the update
} while (!x.compare_exchange_weak(old, new));  // retry if someone changed x

This implements any atomic transformation without a lock: read, compute, and swap only if nothing changed in between. Under low contention it's a single successful CAS; under high contention threads retry (which can livelock-ish — add back-off).

When atomics beat locks

  • Single-word updates: counters, flags, statistics, sequence numbers, a lock-free stack/queue head.
  • No blocking → no deadlock, no priority inversion, resilient to a thread being descheduled mid-operation.
  • But: multi-word invariants, complex data structures, and anything needing several coordinated updates still want a lock (or a carefully-designed lock-free algorithm).
// hot counter: atomic beats a mutex (no context switch, no contention on a lock word)
std::atomic<long> requests{0};
requests.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);   // stats: ordering doesn't matter

// lock-free stack push via CAS on the head
void push(Node *n) {
    n->next = head.load();
    while (!head.compare_exchange_weak(n->next, n)) { }   // retry if head moved
}
// but a lock-free MAP with resize? -> use a real library, this is expert territory

The ABA problem

A CAS on a pointer sees the value is still A and succeeds — but between your read and your CAS, another thread changed it A → B → A (freed A, reused the address). Your CAS wrongly thinks nothing happened. Fixes: a tagged pointer (pointer + version counter, CAS the whole double-word), hazard pointers / epoch-based reclamation to prevent premature reuse, or LL/SC (load-linked/store-conditional) which fails if the location was written at all.

// T1: reads head -> A, plans head = A->next  (call it X)
// T2: pop A ; pop X ; free both ; push a NEW node that malloc reuses A's address
// T1: CAS(head, A, X)  -> SUCCEEDS (address matches!) but X is freed memory -> corruption

// FIX: version-tagged head, CAS the whole {ptr, counter} pair
struct Tagged { Node *ptr; uint64_t tag; };
std::atomic<Tagged> head;   // every push/pop bumps tag -> A@tag5 != A@tag9, CAS fails correctly
Cheat Sheet
  • Atomic RMW = indivisible read-modify-write; hardware gives fetch_add, exchange, and CAS (the universal one).
  • CAS loop: load → compute → compare_exchange; retry on failure — lock-free single-word transform.
  • compare_exchange_weak may fail spuriously (cheaper on LL/SC archs) — fine inside a loop; use _strong for a one-shot.
  • Use atomics for counters/flags/single-pointer updates; use locks for multi-word invariants.
  • Atomics: no deadlock, no priority inversion, robust to preemption — but retries under contention.
  • ABA: value goes A→B→A, CAS falsely succeeds. Fix: version-tagged pointer, hazard pointers / epochs, or LL/SC.
  • Contended atomics still bounce a cache line between cores — not free at scale; consider sharding/striping counters.
Q&A
What does compare-and-swap do?
Atomically: check whether a memory location still holds an expected value; if so, write a new value and report success; if not, report failure (and typically load the current value). It's the building block for lock-free updates.
Why is CAS used in a loop?
Between reading the current value and attempting the swap, another thread may have changed it, so the CAS fails. You recompute the new value from the fresh current value and retry until the CAS succeeds — meaning your update was applied to an unchanged base.
When would you use an atomic instead of a mutex?
For a single-word operation — incrementing a counter, flipping a flag, swapping a pointer — where a lock would be pure overhead and a source of contention/blocking. Multi-variable invariants still need a lock or a dedicated lock-free design.
What is the ABA problem?
Your CAS expects value A and succeeds because the location currently reads A — but it was changed to B and back to A (often via free-and-reuse of a pointer) in between, so "unchanged" is an illusion and your logic acts on stale assumptions (e.g. reattaching a freed node).
How do you defend against ABA?
Attach a monotonically increasing tag/version to the value and CAS the {value, tag} pair as one wide word; or use a memory-reclamation scheme (hazard pointers, epoch-based, RCU) so an address can't be reused while any thread might still CAS on it; or use LL/SC hardware, which detects any intervening write.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which atomic operation is considered "universal" for building lock-free structures?
Compare-and-swap (CAS) — or its LL/SC equivalent.
How do you atomically increment a shared counter without a lock?
atomic<int>::fetch_add(1) (C++), AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() (Java), atomic.AddInt64 (Go).
Does an atomic operation block?
No — it completes without waiting. Contended CAS loops may retry, but no thread is put to sleep.

Intermediate core

Implement a lock-free push onto a singly linked stack.
node->next = head.load();
while (!head.compare_exchange_weak(node->next, node)) { }
// on failure, compare_exchange reloads node->next to the current head, then retry
Pop is symmetric (head.compare_exchange(old, old->next)) but is where ABA and reclamation bite — another thread may free the node whose next you're about to read.
A heavily contended atomic counter is a bottleneck. Options?
The single cache line ping-pongs between all cores. Options: striped/sharded counters — N sub-counters on separate cache lines, each thread increments counter[threadId % N], sum them on read (Java's LongAdder). Per-thread counters aggregated periodically. Or accept approximate counts and batch updates. The read cost rises (sum N cells) but writes stop contending.

Advanced deep

Why does compare_exchange_weak exist alongside _strong, and when do you use each?
On architectures using LL/SC (ARM, PowerPC, RISC-V), the store-conditional can fail spuriously — not because the value changed, but because of an interrupt, a context switch, or another (even unrelated, same-cache-line) access between the load-linked and store-conditional. compare_exchange_weak is allowed to report such spurious failures, which lets the compiler emit the bare LL/SC pair with no retry wrapper — the cheapest possible code. compare_exchange_strong must not fail spuriously, so on LL/SC it wraps the pair in its own internal retry loop. Rule: use _weak when you're already in a loop (the classic CAS loop) — a spurious failure just costs one extra harmless iteration, and you get the faster codegen. Use _strong for a one-shot CAS not in a loop (e.g. "try once to claim this slot, otherwise take a different path"), where a spurious failure would incorrectly send you down the fallback path. On x86 (which has a real CAS instruction, cmpxchg) there's no spurious failure and the two compile identically.
Explain hazard pointers as a solution to safe memory reclamation in lock-free code.
The core problem: in a lock-free pop, thread T1 reads pointer p to a node it's about to dereference/CAS; thread T2 concurrently removes and frees that node — T1 now has a dangling pointer. Hazard pointers: each thread has a small set of single-writer, multi-reader "hazard" slots. Before dereferencing p, a thread publishes p into one of its hazard slots and then re-validates that p is still reachable (still the head, etc.). When a thread retires a node (logically removes it), instead of freeing immediately it adds the node to a per-thread "retired" list; periodically it scans all threads' hazard slots and frees only retired nodes that appear in nobody's hazard set. Guarantees: a node in use by some thread is always protected (its pointer is in that thread's hazard slot, so the scanner skips it), and memory is bounded (each thread retires at most a constant per operation, and reclaims once hazards clear). Costs: a store + fence to publish a hazard pointer on the read path (cheaper than a lock, pricier than nothing), an O(threads × hazards) scan amortised over reclamation, and API intrusiveness. Alternatives with different trade-offs: epoch-based reclamation (lower read-path cost, but a stalled thread can pin memory indefinitely) and RCU (near-zero read cost, deferred bulk reclamation).

Memory Models & Ordering

Why one thread's writes appear out of order to another — and how to pin the order down.

Notes

A memory model defines what one thread is guaranteed to observe about another thread’s memory writes — because compilers and CPUs freely reorder operations, so “the code runs top to bottom” is only true for a single thread in isolation. This page covers the reorderings that happen, the happens-before relation that synchronization establishes, the C++/Java-style memory orders (relaxed, acquire/release, seq_cst) and what each buys you, why volatile is not a concurrency tool in C/C++, and where explicit fences fit.

Reordering

Compilers reorder independent memory operations for optimisation; CPUs reorder via store buffers and out-of-order execution. Within one thread this is invisible (program order is preserved for that thread's own view). Across threads, another thread can observe the writes in a different order — unless you add synchronisation.

// famous: BOTH threads can print 0 on x86, and freely on ARM -- store buffers
int x = 0, y = 0, r1, r2;
// thread 1              thread 2
x = 1;          //      y = 1;
r1 = y;         //      r2 = x;
// r1 == 0 && r2 == 0 is a legal outcome: each store sits in a buffer, not yet visible
// fix: make x,y std::atomic (seq_cst) OR add a full fence between the store and the load

Happens-before

The formal ordering guarantee: if action A happens-before B, then A's effects are visible to B. It's established by program order within a thread, and across threads by matched synchronisation: unlock→lock of the same mutex, a release store→an acquire load of the same atomic, thread start/join, etc. No happens-before edge between two accesses to the same data → data race → UB.

Payload data;
std::atomic<bool> ready{false};

// producer
data = compute();                          // (1)
ready.store(true, std::memory_order_release);  // (2) publishes (1)

// consumer
if (ready.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) // (3) if this sees true...
    use(data);                             // (4) ...(1) happens-before (4): data is fully visible

The memory orders (C++ / similar)

OrderGuarantee
relaxedAtomicity only — no ordering w.r.t. other memory. Fine for counters/stats.
acquire (on a load)No reads/writes after it can be reordered before it. Pairs with a release.
release (on a store)No reads/writes before it can be reordered after it. Publishes prior writes.
acq_relBoth, for a RMW.
seq_cst (default)Acquire/release plus a single total order all threads agree on. Simplest to reason about, most expensive.

The release/acquire pair is the workhorse: thread A writes data then does a release store to a flag; thread B does an acquire load of the flag and, if it sees the new value, is guaranteed to see all of A's prior writes.

counter.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);  // stats: atomic, but ordering is nobody's concern

// spinlock built from acquire/release:
void lock()   { while (flag.exchange(true, std::memory_order_acquire)) cpu_relax(); }
void unlock() { flag.store(false, std::memory_order_release); }  // publishes the critical section

// seq_cst (the default): needed when multiple atomics must share ONE global order
x.store(1);  // plain x.store(1) == x.store(1, memory_order_seq_cst)

volatile is not atomic

In C/C++, volatile prevents the compiler eliding/reordering accesses to that variable (for memory-mapped I/O, signal handlers) but gives no atomicity, no cross-thread ordering, no CPU barrier. It is not a threading tool. (Java's volatile is different — it does provide acquire/release semantics.)

// WRONG: volatile gives no atomicity and no cross-thread visibility guarantee
volatile bool stop = false;
volatile int count = 0;
count++;                       // still load/add/store -- races just like a plain int

// RIGHT: std::atomic gives both
std::atomic<bool> stop{false};
std::atomic<int> count{0};
count.fetch_add(1);
// volatile's real job: MMIO -> volatile uint32_t *reg = (uint32_t*)0x40000000;

Fences

atomic_thread_fence(memory_order) imposes ordering without being tied to a specific variable — used to separate groups of relaxed atomics, or in lock-free algorithms.

// publish several relaxed writes with ONE fence instead of a release on each
a.store(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
b.store(2, std::memory_order_relaxed);
std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_release);  // nothing above moves below
ready.store(true, std::memory_order_relaxed);

// consumer side:
if (ready.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) {
    std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_acquire);  // nothing below moves above
    use(a, b);                                             // a==1, b==2 guaranteed
}
Cheat Sheet
  • Compilers + CPUs reorder memory ops; a thread sees its own order, other threads may not.
  • Happens-before: A hb B ⇒ A's effects visible to B. Established by program order + matched sync (unlock/lock, release/acquire, start/join).
  • Data-race-free program ⇒ you may reason as if sequentially consistent (SC-DRF).
  • Orders: relaxed (atomic only) < acquire/release (pairwise publish/consume) < seq_cst (global total order, default, priciest).
  • Publish pattern: write data → store(flag, release); reader load(flag, acquire) then read data.
  • C/C++ volatile ≠ atomic: no atomicity, no ordering, no barrier. Use std::atomic. (Java volatile does give acquire/release.)
  • Prefer seq_cst unless profiling shows the barrier cost matters; relax carefully with a written argument.
Q&A
Why can thread B see thread A's writes in a different order than A performed them?
Compiler reordering of independent operations, and CPU features (store buffers, out-of-order execution, per-core cache visibility) mean A's stores can become visible to other cores at different times. Only synchronisation establishing happens-before forces an observable order.
What is happens-before?
A partial order on memory operations. If A happens-before B, B is guaranteed to see A's effects. It comes from program order within a thread plus cross-thread edges like unlock→lock of the same mutex or release-store→acquire-load of the same atomic.
Explain the release/acquire pattern.
Writer: set up data, then do a release store to a flag. Reader: acquire load of the flag; if it observes the flag's new value, all writes the writer did before the release are visible. It's a one-way barrier pair — cheaper than full sequential consistency.
Is volatile enough for a thread-shared flag in C++?
No. It stops the compiler optimising away accesses but provides no atomicity and no memory ordering/barriers, so other writes around it can still be reordered and the value can tear. Use std::atomic<bool>. (In Java, volatile does give the needed acquire/release semantics.)
When is memory_order_relaxed acceptable?
When you need atomicity but not ordering relative to other memory — e.g. a statistics counter, or an id generator, where no other data's visibility depends on it. If any "if I see this, I must also see that" reasoning is involved, you need acquire/release or stronger.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which memory order is the default for std::atomic operations?
memory_order_seq_cst (sequential consistency).
Does C++ volatile make a variable safe to share between threads?
No. It's for memory-mapped I/O and signal handlers, not threading.
A release store pairs with what kind of load?
An acquire load of the same atomic variable.

Intermediate core

Thread A: data = 42; ready = true; Thread B: if (ready) print(data); — can B print 0?
Yes, with plain variables (data race, UB) or with relaxed atomics: B can see ready == true while data is still stale, because the two stores can be reordered / become visible independently. Fix: make ready a std::atomic<bool>, store it with release, load it with acquire; then seeing ready == true guarantees data == 42.
Why is a seq_cst atomic store more expensive than a release store on x86?
A release store on x86 is essentially a plain mov (x86's memory model already gives release semantics for stores). A seq_cst store additionally needs to be globally ordered with respect to seq_cst loads on other variables, which requires draining the store buffer — emitted as an xchg or a trailing mfence. That full barrier stalls the pipeline until pending stores are visible, costing tens of cycles.

Advanced deep

Explain the "IRIW" (independent reads of independent writes) litmus test and what it distinguishes.
Four threads: T1 does x = 1; T2 does y = 1; T3 reads x then y; T4 reads y then x. Question: can T3 see x=1, y=0 while T4 sees y=1, x=0 — i.e. the two reader threads disagree on the order in which the two independent writes happened? Under sequential consistency (and under C++ seq_cst on all four accesses), this outcome is forbidden: there's a single global order, so T3 and T4 must agree. Under weaker models — C++ acquire/release (not seq_cst), or POWER/ARM hardware — it is allowed, because write propagation isn't required to be multi-copy atomic: T1's store to x can reach T3's core before T4's, and independently for y. IRIW is the canonical test that separates "release/acquire is enough" from "you actually need seq_cst": release/acquire gives you per-pair ordering and cache coherence per-location, but not a single total order across different locations that all threads observe identically. x86-TSO happens to forbid IRIW (it's "multi-copy atomic"), which is why code that's buggy-in-theory often passes on Intel and fails on ARM.
What is memory_order_consume, why was it deprecated in practice, and what replaced it?
consume was meant to be a weaker, cheaper acquire: instead of ordering all subsequent reads after the load, it would order only those data-dependent on the loaded value (following the pointer you just loaded). On weakly-ordered hardware like ARM/POWER, dependent loads are already ordered by the hardware's respect for data dependencies — so consume could compile to a bare load with no fence, ideal for RCU-style "load a pointer, then dereference it" patterns. In practice, no compiler implemented it correctly: tracking the "dependency chain" through arbitrary code (across function calls, through the optimiser which loves to break dependencies by turning p + (x - x) into p, etc.) proved intractable. Every compiler silently promoted consume to acquire, giving correctness but not the performance win. C++17 discouraged it, and work continues on a redesigned dependency-ordering facility (std::dependency-style, or marking pointer types). For now: use acquire; the Linux kernel gets the consume effect via rcu_dereference plus a documented rule that you must not break the dependency chain.

Lock-free & Wait-free Basics

Progress guarantees, a lock-free stack, and why it's usually not worth it.

Notes

A lock-free algorithm guarantees that some thread always makes progress, even if others are suspended — no lock to hold, so no deadlock, no priority inversion, no “holder got descheduled” stall. This page covers the progress hierarchy (obstruction-free < lock-free < wait-free), builds a lock-free stack (Treiber’s algorithm) with a CAS loop, explains the hard part — safe memory reclamation (hazard pointers, epochs) and the ABA problem — and, importantly, when a lock-free structure is not worth the complexity.

Progress guarantees (weakest to strongest)

PropertyGuarantee
BlockingA stalled thread (holding a lock) can block everyone.
Obstruction-freeA thread running in isolation (others paused) finishes in bounded steps.
Lock-freeSome thread always makes progress system-wide; individual threads may starve.
Wait-freeEvery thread finishes in a bounded number of its own steps. No starvation. Hardest to build.
// BLOCKING: if this thread is preempted right here, everyone waiting on m stalls
lock(m); x += 1; unlock(m);

// LOCK-FREE: a preempted thread just makes its peers retry once -- the SYSTEM progresses
do { old = x.load(); } while (!x.compare_exchange_weak(old, old + 1));

// WAIT-FREE: fetch_add ALWAYS completes in O(1) of THIS thread's steps -- no loop, no starvation
x.fetch_add(1);

Lock-free stack (Treiber)

push(n): do { n->next = head; } while (!CAS(&head, n->next, n));
pop():   do { old = head; if (!old) return null; nx = old->next; }
         while (!CAS(&head, old, nx));
         // ... now safe to reclaim 'old'?  -- this is the hard part

The algorithm is short; safe memory reclamation is the real work — another thread may still be reading old when you free it (and ABA if you reuse the address). Solutions: hazard pointers, epoch-based reclamation, RCU, or a garbage-collected runtime (which is why lock-free is much easier in Java/C#/Go).

When is it worth it?

  • Yes: extreme contention on a hot single-word structure (a counter, a queue head), hard real-time (can't tolerate a lock holder being descheduled), signal handlers / interrupt context (can't take a lock).
  • Usually no: a well-designed lock with short critical sections is simpler, easier to verify, and often faster under realistic contention. Lock-free code is notoriously hard to get right (ordering, ABA, reclamation) and hard to test.

Prefer proven library structures (ConcurrentLinkedQueue, folly::MPMCQueue, Go channels) over rolling your own.

// signal handler: CANNOT take a lock (handler may run while main thread holds it -> deadlock)
volatile sig_atomic_t got_sigint = 0;
void handler(int) { got_sigint = 1; }        // lock-free flag, the one safe pattern here

// everything else: reach for the library, not a hand-rolled Treiber stack
//   Java:  new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>()
//   C++:   moodycamel::ConcurrentQueue  /  folly::MPMCQueue
//   Go:    ch := make(chan T, 1024)
Cheat Sheet
  • Blocking < obstruction-free < lock-free (some thread progresses) < wait-free (every thread progresses, bounded).
  • Lock-free = no mutex; built from CAS-retry loops; a descheduled thread can't block others.
  • Treiber stack / Michael-Scott queue: the algorithm is easy; reclamation + ABA is the hard part.
  • Reclamation: hazard pointers, epochs, RCU, or a GC runtime.
  • Worth it for: hot single-word contention, real-time, interrupt/signal context.
  • Not worth it for: general data structures — a short-critical-section lock is simpler, verifiable, often faster.
  • Use battle-tested library implementations; don't hand-roll.
Q&A
Lock-free vs wait-free?
Lock-free guarantees that the system makes progress — at least one thread completes an operation in bounded steps — but a particular thread could keep losing CAS races and never finish. Wait-free guarantees every thread completes in a bounded number of its own steps, so no starvation. Wait-free is much harder and rarer.
Why can't a mutex-based algorithm be lock-free?
If the thread holding the lock is descheduled (or crashes) inside the critical section, every other thread that needs the lock is stuck — no thread makes progress, violating the definition.
What's the hardest part of a lock-free linked structure?
Safe memory reclamation: knowing when it's safe to free a node that was unlinked, given another thread may still hold a pointer to it — plus avoiding ABA when addresses are reused. The CAS-based linking itself is a few lines.
When is lock-free genuinely the right choice?
Hard real-time or interrupt/signal context where you can't afford a lock holder being preempted or can't sleep; and extreme contention on a tiny hot structure where lock overhead dominates. Otherwise a well-scoped lock is usually simpler and competitive.
Why is lock-free easier in Java/Go than C++?
The garbage collector solves reclamation for free — you never explicitly free a node, so "another thread still has a pointer" is fine and ABA-via-reuse largely disappears. In C++ you must add hazard pointers / epochs / RCU yourself.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Does "lock-free" mean no thread ever waits?
No — it means the system as a whole always progresses. An individual thread can retry indefinitely (that's wait-freedom, which is stronger).
What primitive is a lock-free stack built from?
Compare-and-swap (CAS) on the head pointer, in a retry loop.
Name one memory-reclamation technique for lock-free structures.
Hazard pointers, epoch-based reclamation, or RCU.

Intermediate core

Your lock-free queue works in tests but crashes under load in production. Likely cause?
Use-after-free / ABA in the reclamation path: a node is dequeued and freed while another thread is mid-way through reading its next pointer or CASing on it. Tests don't hit the exact interleaving; production load does. You need a reclamation scheme (hazard pointers / epochs), or switch to a well-tested library queue, or a lock-based bounded queue if the contention doesn't actually warrant lock-free.
Why might a lock-free queue be slower than a mutex-guarded one under moderate contention?
Every operation does one or more CAS retries, each an atomic RMW that bounces the head/tail cache line between cores; under contention the retry rate climbs and threads burn CPU spinning. A mutex with a very short critical section does one atomic to lock, a few instructions, one to unlock, and blocks (yielding the CPU) when contended rather than spinning. Lock-free wins at the extremes (either near-zero contention where the single CAS is cheap, or pathological contention where blocking's context-switch cost dominates), and loses in the messy middle.

Advanced deep

Sketch the Michael-Scott lock-free queue and the role of its "helping" mechanism.
It's a singly linked list with atomic head and tail pointers and a dummy first node. Enqueue: read tail and tail->next; if tail is still the last node (next == null), CAS tail->next from null to the new node; then CAS tail forward to the new node. Dequeue: read head, tail, head->next; if the queue isn't empty, read the value from head->next, CAS head to head->next, then reclaim the old dummy. The "helping": because enqueue is two CAS steps (link the node, then swing tail), another thread can observe a "half-finished" enqueue where tail->next != null. Instead of blocking, that thread helps complete the operation — it does the second CAS (swing tail forward) itself before proceeding. This is what makes the queue lock-free rather than merely obstruction-free: no thread's stall between the two CAS steps can block others, because anyone who notices will finish the job. Every lock-free multi-step algorithm needs some form of this cooperative completion.
What is the theoretical significance of CAS having "consensus number infinity"?
Herlihy's consensus hierarchy ranks synchronisation primitives by the maximum number of threads for which they can solve wait-free consensus (all threads agree on one value, each finishing in bounded steps). Atomic registers (plain reads/writes) have consensus number 1 — they can't solve consensus for even 2 threads wait-free. test-and-set, fetch-and-add, and swap have consensus number 2. CAS (and LL/SC) have consensus number ∞ — they can solve wait-free consensus for any number of threads. The practical consequence: CAS is universal — any sequential object has a wait-free concurrent implementation built from CAS (Herlihy's universal construction). That's why every modern architecture provides a CAS-class instruction and why lock-free/wait-free data structures are all ultimately CAS loops: nothing weaker is expressive enough, and nothing stronger is needed.

Thread Pools & Work Queues

Reuse a fixed set of threads to run a stream of tasks — and size it right.

Notes

A thread pool keeps a fixed set of worker threads pulling tasks from a queue, so you pay thread-creation cost once and cap concurrency deliberately — instead of spawning a thread per task and letting the scheduler thrash. This page covers why pools exist, their anatomy (workers + a task queue + a submit/shutdown API), how to size the pool for CPU-bound vs I/O-bound work, work stealing (per-worker deques to cut contention), backpressure when the queue fills, and graceful shutdown that drains in-flight work.

Why pools

Creating a thread per task is expensive (stack allocation, kernel setup) and unbounded (a spike of tasks spawns thousands of threads → memory blow-up, scheduler thrash). A pool caps concurrency, amortises thread creation, and gives a place to apply backpressure.

// ANTI-PATTERN: a thread per request -> 50k requests = 50k threads = OOM
for (Request r : incoming) new Thread(() -> handle(r)).start();

// pool: reuse N threads, cap concurrency, apply backpressure when saturated
ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    8, 8, 0L, MILLISECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1000),                 // BOUNDED queue
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());     // full -> submitter runs it -> natural throttle

Anatomy

  • N worker threads, each looping: take a task from the queue, run it, repeat.
  • A bounded task queue (blocking or with a rejection policy) so a producer flood can't OOM you.
  • A rejection / backpressure policy when full: block the submitter, drop, run on the caller's thread, or fail fast.
// the worker loop, conceptually:
void worker() {
    while (running) {
        Task t = queue.take();          // blocks until a task is available
        try { t.run(); }
        catch (Throwable e) { log(e); }   // one bad task must not kill the worker
    }
}

Sizing

WorkloadPool size
CPU-bound≈ number of cores (or cores + 1)
I/O-boundhigher — roughly cores × (1 + wait_time / compute_time); often set empirically
Mixedseparate pools per workload class so slow I/O tasks don't starve CPU tasks
int cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors();   // e.g. 8
ExecutorService cpu = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(cores);          // hashing, compression
// I/O-bound: each task waits ~90 ms, computes ~10 ms -> factor (1 + 90/10) = 10
ExecutorService io  = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(cores * 10);     // remote calls
// keep them SEPARATE: a burst of slow HTTP calls must not block the CPU pool

Work stealing

Each worker has its own deque; it pushes/pops its own tasks from one end (cache-friendly, no contention), and when idle steals from the other end of a random busy worker's deque. Great for recursive divide-and-conquer (fork/join) where task counts are uneven. Used by Java's ForkJoinPool, Go's scheduler, Rust's Rayon, .NET TPL.

// fork/join: each recursive split becomes a task; idle workers steal the subtasks
class SumTask extends RecursiveTask<Long> {
    protected Long compute() {
        if (hi - lo <= 1000) return serialSum();
        int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
        SumTask l = new SumTask(lo, mid);  l.fork();   // push to THIS worker's deque
        SumTask r = new SumTask(mid, hi);
        return r.compute() + l.join();          // idle worker may have stolen l
    }
}
new ForkJoinPool().invoke(new SumTask(0, n));

Shutdown

Graceful: stop accepting new tasks, let in-flight and queued tasks drain, then join workers (with a timeout → force). Never just kill worker threads — tasks may hold locks or leave state half-updated.

pool.shutdown();                                   // stop accepting new tasks; keep draining the queue
if (!pool.awaitTermination(30, SECONDS))         // wait for in-flight + queued to finish
    pool.shutdownNow();                            // timed out -> interrupt workers (last resort)
// shutdownNow() just interrupts -- tasks must actually check Thread.interrupted()
Cheat Sheet
  • Pool = fixed workers + a task queue; caps concurrency, amortises thread creation, enables backpressure.
  • Always use a bounded queue + an explicit rejection policy (block / caller-runs / drop / fail).
  • Size: CPU-bound ≈ #cores; I/O-bound ≈ cores × (1 + wait/compute); measure.
  • Separate pools per workload class — don't let blocking I/O tasks starve CPU tasks (or deadlock via task dependencies).
  • Work stealing: per-worker deque + steal-when-idle — best for fork/join / recursive tasks.
  • Graceful shutdown: stop intake → drain → join with timeout → force. Never kill workers mid-task.
  • Beware: submitting a task that waits on another task in the same bounded pool → deadlock.
Q&A
Why use a thread pool instead of creating a thread per task?
Thread creation/teardown is costly, and an unbounded task rate would create unbounded threads (memory exhaustion, scheduler overhead, cache thrash). A pool bounds concurrency, reuses threads, and provides a queue where you can apply backpressure.
How big should a CPU-bound pool be?
About the number of hardware cores (sometimes cores + 1 to cover the occasional page fault / brief block). More than that just adds context-switching without more parallelism.
Why bound the task queue?
An unbounded queue silently converts a load spike into unbounded memory growth and ever-rising latency until an OOM. A bounded queue plus a rejection policy makes overload visible and controllable (block the producer, shed load, or fail fast).
What is work stealing and when does it shine?
Idle workers take tasks from busy workers' local deques instead of a single shared queue. It minimises contention and balances load automatically — ideal for fork/join workloads where subtasks are spawned recursively and unevenly.
What's the danger of submitting a task that blocks waiting on another task in the same pool?
If the pool's threads are all occupied by tasks waiting on queued tasks that can't be scheduled, you deadlock the pool. Use a separate pool for the dependent work, or a design that doesn't block a pool thread on another pool task (e.g. continuation-based / async).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What sits between task submitters and worker threads in a pool?
A task queue (ideally bounded).
Rough pool size for pure number-crunching on an 8-core box?
About 8 (cores), maybe 9.
What technique lets idle workers grab work from busy ones?
Work stealing (per-worker deques).

Intermediate core

Java's Executors.newCachedThreadPool() caused an OOM under load. Why, and what to use instead?
It has an unbounded implicit queue (SynchronousQueue handoff) and an effectively unbounded max thread count — a burst of submissions spawns a thread each, until memory is exhausted. Use a ThreadPoolExecutor with a fixed core/max pool size, a bounded ArrayBlockingQueue, and an explicit RejectedExecutionHandler (CallerRunsPolicy for natural backpressure, or fail-fast with alerting).
Estimate the pool size for tasks that spend 90ms on I/O and 10ms on CPU, on 4 cores.
Target: keep the 4 cores busy. Each task uses a core only 10% of its wall time, so you need ~10 tasks in flight per core to saturate it: 4 × (1 + 90/10) = 4 × 10 = 40 threads. In practice you'd verify empirically and cap it, and prefer async I/O (which needs far fewer threads) if the platform supports it.

Advanced deep

How does a work-stealing deque avoid locks between the owner and thieves?
The owner operates on the bottom of its deque (push/pop) and thieves on the top (steal), so they touch opposite ends and only conflict when the deque has 0–1 elements. The classic Chase-Lev design uses a growable circular array with atomic top and bottom indices: push is a plain store of the element then a relaxed store of bottom+1 (owner only, no CAS); pop decrements bottom, and only if it's now racing a thief for the last element does it CAS top to resolve the tie; steal reads top, reads the element, then CASes top forward — failing (and retrying) if another thief or the owner won. So the common case (non-empty deque, owner pushing/popping) is lock-free and CAS-free for the owner, thieves pay one CAS, and the only contended point is the last element. Subtleties: memory fences between the bottom decrement and the top read to prevent reordering, and safe reclamation / ABA handling on the underlying array when it grows.
What is "thread pool induced deadlock" via task dependencies, and how do fork/join frameworks avoid it?
If task A, running on a pool thread, submits subtasks B and C to the same bounded pool and then blocks waiting for their results, it occupies a pool thread while needing pool threads. With enough such A's, every pool thread is a blocked A and no B/C can ever run — deadlock. Fork/join frameworks (Java ForkJoinPool) avoid it with join-time work donation / continuation: when a worker calls join() on a subtask that isn't done, instead of blocking it executes other pending tasks from its own or others' deques (including possibly the very subtask it's waiting on), so the thread stays useful and the dependency graph always makes progress as long as it's acyclic. It may also spin up a compensation thread temporarily to maintain target parallelism when a worker genuinely must block (managed blockers). The general lesson: never block a pool thread on work that must run in the same pool — use a separate pool, or an async/continuation style where "waiting" doesn't hold a thread.

Futures, Promises & async/await

Representing "a value that isn't ready yet" and composing work without blocking a thread.

Notes

A future (or promise) is a handle to a value that isn’t ready yet; async/await is syntax that lets you write sequential-looking code that actually suspends at each await and lets an event loop run other tasks meanwhile. This page covers the future/promise model and composition, how the single-threaded event loop achieves concurrency without threads, the cardinal sin of calling a blocking operation inside async code (it freezes every other task), and structured concurrency — scoping child tasks so they can’t outlive or leak from their parent.

Future / Promise

  • A future is a read handle to a result that will exist later; a promise is the write handle the producer uses to fulfil it (or fail it with an exception).
  • You can get() (block until ready), poll isDone(), or — better — attach a continuation (then/thenApply/.then()) that runs when the value arrives, so no thread blocks waiting.
  • Composition: thenCompose/flatMap (chain a dependent async step), thenCombine (join two), allOf/anyOf (fan-in / race).
// producer holds the promise (write), consumer holds the future (read)
CompletableFuture<int> f = new CompletableFuture<>();
executor.submit(() -> f.complete(slowComputation()));   // fulfil later

// DON'T: f.get() blocks this thread. DO: attach a continuation
f.thenApply(x -> x * 2)
 .thenCompose(x -> fetchAsync(x))     // dependent async step
 .thenAccept(System.out::println)
 .exceptionally(e -> { log(e); return null; });   // always handle the failure path

CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b, c).join();   // fan-in: wait for all three

async / await & the event loop

async functions return a future; await suspends the function until the awaited future completes, without blocking the underlying thread — the runtime saves the continuation and runs other ready work on the event loop. When the awaited operation finishes (an I/O completion, a timer), the continuation is scheduled and the function resumes. One or a few OS threads can drive thousands of concurrent async operations.

async def fetch(url):
    async with session.get(url) as r:   # suspends HERE -- the loop runs other tasks
        return await r.text()

async def main():
    # 1000 concurrent fetches on ONE thread
    results = await asyncio.gather(*[fetch(u) for u in urls])
asyncio.run(main())

The cardinal sin: blocking in async code

Calling a synchronous blocking operation (a blocking socket read, Thread.sleep, a lock wait, CPU-heavy work) inside an async function ties up the event-loop thread, so every other task on that loop stalls. Offload blocking/CPU work to a dedicated thread pool (run_in_executor, Task.Run, tokio::spawn_blocking).

async def handler():
    time.sleep(2)                    # BUG: freezes the loop -> ALL requests stall 2s
    hash = bcrypt(password)          # BUG: 100ms of CPU also blocks the loop

async def handler_ok():
    await asyncio.sleep(2)             # yields to the loop
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    hash = await loop.run_in_executor(pool, bcrypt, password)   # CPU work off-loop

Structured concurrency

Child tasks are scoped to a block: the scope doesn't exit until all children complete, an error in one cancels the siblings, and cancellation propagates down. Prevents "fire and forget" leaks and orphaned tasks. Kotlin coroutine scopes, Java's StructuredTaskScope, Python's TaskGroup, Trio's nurseries, Swift task groups.

async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:   # Python 3.11+
    t1 = tg.create_task(fetch(a))
    t2 = tg.create_task(fetch(b))
# the `with` block does not exit until BOTH finish.
# if fetch(a) raises -> fetch(b) is CANCELLED, the error propagates out. No orphans.
print(t1.result(), t2.result())
Cheat Sheet
  • Future = read side of a pending result; Promise = write side (fulfil / reject).
  • Prefer continuations (then/await) over blocking get().
  • Compose: thenCompose/flatMap (dependent), thenCombine (join), allOf/anyOf (fan-in / first-wins).
  • await suspends the coroutine, not the thread — the event loop runs other tasks meanwhile.
  • Never block (sync I/O, sleep, locks, CPU crunch) on an event-loop thread — offload to a thread pool.
  • Always handle a future's failure path; an unobserved failed future can swallow exceptions.
  • Structured concurrency: scope child tasks, propagate cancellation + errors, no leaked tasks.
  • Cancellation should be cooperative — check a token / catch CancelledError and clean up.
Q&A
Difference between a future and a promise?
They're two ends of the same one-shot channel: the future is the consumer's read-only handle to the eventual value; the promise is the producer's handle used to set the value (or an error). The consumer gets the future; the producer keeps the promise.
What does await block — the thread or the task?
Only the async task/coroutine. The underlying OS thread is released back to the event loop to run other ready tasks; the awaiting task resumes later when its awaited future completes.
Why is time.sleep(5) (blocking) a bug inside an async handler?
It blocks the event-loop thread for 5 seconds, during which no other coroutine on that loop can run — all concurrent requests stall. Use the async sleep (await asyncio.sleep(5)) which yields to the loop.
How do you run CPU-bound work from async code without stalling the loop?
Hand it to a separate thread or process pool: loop.run_in_executor(pool, fn) / await Task.Run(...) / spawn_blocking, and await that. The loop stays free while the pool thread does the heavy work.
What problem does structured concurrency solve?
"Fire and forget" tasks that outlive their logical parent, leak resources, swallow exceptions, or can't be cancelled together. Structured concurrency ties child task lifetimes to a lexical scope, propagates cancellation and errors, and guarantees no task is left running when the scope exits.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does an async function return?
A future/promise/task representing the eventual result — not the value directly.
Better than calling future.get() and blocking?
Attach a continuation/callback (then/await) that runs when the value is ready, freeing the thread meanwhile.
How many OS threads does an event-loop server typically use to handle thousands of connections?
One per core (or just one), plus a small pool for blocking/CPU offload.

Intermediate core

Fetch three URLs concurrently and combine the results, in async style.
