Start all three without awaiting individually, then await them together: Python a, b, c = await asyncio.gather(f(u1), f(u2), f(u3)); JS const [a,b,c] = await Promise.all([f(u1),f(u2),f(u3)]); Java CompletableFuture.allOf(a,b,c).thenApply(...). Awaiting them one at a time (await f(u1); await f(u2); ...) would serialise them.
An async web service's latency spikes whenever one endpoint is hit. That endpoint parses a large file synchronously. Explain and fix.
The synchronous parse runs on the event-loop thread, monopolising it for the parse duration; every other in-flight request on that loop is frozen until it finishes — hence the correlated spikes. Fix: move the CPU-bound parse to a thread/process pool (run_in_executor / worker) and await it, so the loop keeps servicing other requests. Chunk the work if it must stay on the loop.

Advanced deep

What is "colored functions" and the async/await criticism it names?
From Bob Nystrom's essay: in languages with async/await, functions come in two "colors" — sync and async. An async function can only be meaningfully called from another async function (you need await, which needs an async context); a sync function can't await. So "async-ness" is viral: making one leaf function async forces every caller up the chain to become async too, you often need duplicate sync/async versions of libraries, and bridging (calling async from sync) requires blocking on the event loop or spawning one, which is awkward and deadlock-prone. Languages that avoid the split: Go (goroutines — every function can block cheaply because the runtime multiplexes; no await keyword), and Java's virtual threads (project Loom — blocking a virtual thread is cheap, so ordinary synchronous code scales without coloring). The trade-off: colored async makes suspension points explicit (you can see where interleaving happens, aiding reasoning about races and cancellation), whereas transparent lightweight threads hide them.
How does cooperative cancellation work in a coroutine runtime, and what are its failure modes?
Cancellation is a request, not a forced stop: the runtime marks the task cancelled, and at the next suspension point (await) the awaited operation throws a cancellation exception (Python CancelledError, Kotlin CancellationException, .NET OperationCanceledException via the token). The coroutine unwinds, running finally/defer blocks and with exits to release resources, then propagates. Failure modes: (1) a coroutine that never awaits (a tight CPU loop) is never cancellable — it must poll the token explicitly. (2) Swallowing the cancellation exception in a broad except Exception (Python distinguishes BaseException for exactly this reason) turns cancellation into a silent no-op. (3) Doing more awaits during cleanup after cancellation can re-raise or hang unless run in a shielded / non-cancellable scope. (4) Not awaiting the cancelled task means you don't know when (or whether) it actually stopped — structured concurrency fixes this by making the scope wait for cancelled children to finish unwinding.

Common Concurrency Bugs & Tools

The failure patterns that recur, and how to actually find nondeterministic bugs.

Notes

Concurrency bugs are the ones that pass every test run and then fail in production once a year. This page is a catalogue of the recurring ones — data races, deadlocks, lost/spurious wakeups, check-then-act races, publishing an object before it’s fully constructed, forgetting a memory barrier — plus double-checked locking done correctly, and the tools that actually find these bugs: thread/address sanitizers, stress and fuzz testing, deterministic replay, and model checkers.

The recurring bug catalogue

BugSignature
Data raceunsynchronised shared access; intermittent wrong values/crashes, worse under load
Deadlockthreads permanently blocked in a lock cycle
Livelockthreads busy, retrying, no progress
Atomicity violationeach op is locked but the sequence isn't (check-then-act)
Order violationcode assumes A runs before B; sometimes it doesn't
Lost wakeup / missed signalcondvar signalled before waiter waits
Broken double-checked lockingpublishing a partially-constructed object (needs a memory barrier / volatile)
Non-thread-safe library used concurrentlye.g. a shared SimpleDateFormat, Random, non-reentrant lib
// ATOMICITY VIOLATION -- each call is thread-safe, the pair isn't
if (!set.contains(x))     // thread A checks: absent
    set.add(x);           // thread B added x in between -> maybe added twice / logic wrong
// fix: set.putIfAbsent(x)  (one atomic op)  or hold a lock across both

// NON-THREAD-SAFE LIBRARY shared across threads
static SimpleDateFormat FMT = new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd");   // mutable internal state!
FMT.format(d);            // concurrent calls -> garbage output / exceptions
// fix: DateTimeFormatter (immutable), or a ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat>

Double-checked locking, done right

// BROKEN in old Java / naive C++: another thread can see 'instance' non-null
// but pointing at a not-yet-constructed object.
// FIX: the field must be volatile (Java) / std::atomic with acquire/release (C++),
// or just use a static local (C++11 thread-safe) / holder-class idiom (Java).

Tools

  • ThreadSanitizer (TSan) — instruments the binary, detects data races and some deadlocks at runtime with low-ish overhead. Run your test suite under it.
  • Helgrind / DRD (Valgrind) — race and lock-order detection, slower.
  • Go: go test -race. Java: jstack/thread dumps for deadlocks, jcstress for memory-model litmus tests, FindBugs/SpotBugs static checks.
  • Stress testing — run the concurrent code with many threads, randomised delays / yields / thread counts, for a long time, on varied hardware (weak-memory ARM surfaces bugs x86 hides).
  • Model checkers — CHESS, Loom (Rust), TLA+/PlusCal for the design — exhaustively explore interleavings for small models.
$ clang -fsanitize=thread -g race.c -o race && ./race
==================
WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race (pid=4123)
  Write of size 4 at 0x0000... by thread T2:
    #0 worker race.c:8
  Previous read of size 4 at 0x0000... by thread T1:
    #0 worker race.c:8            # exact lines + both stacks

$ go test -race ./...            # Go: race detector built in
$ jstack <pid> | grep -A5 deadlock   # Java: thread dump names the lock cycle

Prevention beats detection

Minimise shared mutable state; prefer immutability, confinement, and message passing; use high-level concurrent collections and structured concurrency; keep critical sections tiny; write down the locking discipline and enforce it in review / with a checker.

// SHARE by communicating, don't communicate by sharing (Go)
results := make(chan int)
for _, job := range jobs {
    go func(j Job) { results <- process(j) }(job)   // no shared mutable state
}
for range jobs { total += <-results }               // only this goroutine touches `total`

// or confine: give each worker its OWN accumulator, merge at the end (map-reduce)
Cheat Sheet
  • Common bugs: data race, deadlock, livelock, atomicity violation (check-then-act), order violation, lost wakeup, broken DCL, misused non-thread-safe library.
  • Double-checked locking needs a volatile/atomic field (or use a static local / holder idiom).
  • Detect races: TSan (-fsanitize=thread), Go -race, Valgrind Helgrind/DRD.
  • Detect deadlocks: thread dumps / jstack, lock-order checkers (lockdep), watchdog timers.
  • Stress test: many threads, randomised delays/yields, long runs, weak-memory hardware (ARM).
  • Design-level: model checkers (TLA+, Loom, jcstress) for interleavings.
  • Best defence: less shared mutable state — immutability, confinement, message passing, concurrent collections.
Q&A
Why are concurrency bugs so hard to reproduce?
They depend on a specific interleaving of thread execution, which varies with load, core count, scheduler decisions, and hardware memory model. A test can pass a million times and fail on the machine that matters. This is why deterministic tooling (sanitizers, model checkers) is essential.
What is an atomicity violation?
Individual operations are each synchronised, but a group of them that should be atomic isn't — e.g. if (list.contains(x)) list.remove(x) with a lock released between the two calls. Another thread can interleave and invalidate the check.
Why was the classic double-checked locking idiom broken?
Without a memory barrier, the write that publishes the singleton reference can become visible to another thread before the writes that initialise the object's fields, so a second thread sees a non-null but half-constructed instance. Marking the field volatile (Java 5+) or using acquire/release atomics fixes the ordering; simpler still is a lazily-initialised static.
What does ThreadSanitizer detect and how?
Primarily data races: it instruments every memory access and synchronisation operation, maintains a happens-before relation, and reports when two accesses to the same location (one a write) are not ordered by any happens-before edge. It also catches some lock-order inversions and misuse.
How do you stress-test concurrent code effectively?
Run it with far more threads than cores, insert randomised sleep/yield at suspected interleaving points, vary thread counts and iteration counts, run for minutes not milliseconds, and test on weakly-ordered hardware (ARM) as well as x86 — combined with running under TSan.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What flag runs Go tests with the race detector?
go test -race.
Name a tool that detects data races in C/C++ at runtime.
ThreadSanitizer (-fsanitize=thread), or Valgrind's Helgrind/DRD.
What one keyword fixes the classic Java double-checked-locking bug?
volatile on the instance field (Java 5+ semantics).

Intermediate core

A shared HashMap occasionally causes an infinite loop or corrupted reads under concurrent writes. Explain.
HashMap isn't thread-safe. Concurrent puts during a resize can corrupt the bucket linked lists — historically producing a cyclic list, so a later get spins forever; in newer JDKs you get lost entries or size inconsistencies instead. Fix: use ConcurrentHashMap, or guard every access with the same lock, or confine the map to one thread. Never "it seems to work" — it's UB in the library's contract.
You suspect a race but can't reproduce it. Systematic approach?
Build the test suite with TSan / run -race and exercise the concurrent paths. Add a targeted stress test (many threads, high iteration count, randomised yield/sleep at the suspected window). Run on ARM as well as x86. If it's a design question, model the protocol in TLA+ or jcstress. Once TSan flags it, the report gives you both stacks and the missing happens-before edge — add the synchronisation there.

Advanced deep

Why can't testing alone give you confidence in lock-free / weak-memory code, and what closes the gap?
The state space of interleavings is astronomically large and the scheduler explores a biased, tiny, hardware-dependent slice of it — a bug may require a 1-in-10⁹ interleaving plus a specific store-buffer state that only occurs on one microarchitecture. Passing tests sample that space almost not at all. What closes the gap: (1) exhaustive model checking of a reduced model — TLA+/PlusCal for the algorithm's design, or CHESS/rr-chaos/Loom(Rust)/jcstress which systematically enumerate or perturb interleavings for the actual code up to a bound, catching bugs that need N context switches. (2) Formal proof of the linearizability/memory-ordering argument (many published lock-free structures come with one; deviating from the paper invalidates it). (3) Weak-memory-aware tools: running under TSan (which models happens-before, not just observed order), and litmus-testing the specific access patterns against a formal hardware model (herd7, RMEM). (4) Preferring verified library implementations so you inherit someone else's proof. The pragmatic stance: only write lock-free code you can cite a proof for, keep it tiny, and gate it behind model-checked tests in CI.
Explain the "benign race" fallacy with a concrete miscompilation.
Developers often reason "this race is harmless — worst case a thread reads a slightly stale value". But in the C/C++/Java model any data race is UB, and the compiler optimises assuming races don't happen, producing outcomes no interleaving of the source could. Concrete: if (cfg != null && cfg.ready) use(cfg); racing with cfg = new Config(...). The compiler may (a) load cfg twice — once for the null check, once for .ready — so you null-check a non-null value then dereference null; (b) hoist the cfg read out of a loop so an update is never seen; (c) with x = shared; if (x==0) a(); if (x==0) b();, re-read shared for the second check and run a() but not b() though "x==0" was the condition for both — a state unreachable in any sequential execution ("out-of-thin-air"-adjacent). Real cases: the Linux kernel has hit compiler-introduced double-loads breaking security checks; hence READ_ONCE/WRITE_ONCE macros. The fix is never "it's probably fine" — it's to make the access atomic (even relaxed), which restores the "compiler must emit exactly one honest load/store" guarantee.

The File Descriptor Model

Three tables between an int and a file — and why that structure explains dup, fork, and pipes.

Notes

The three levels

process fd table          system open-file table          inode table
[0] -----------------> [ offset, flags, ref ] ----> [ inode: size, perms, data ]
[1] -----------------> [ offset, flags, ref ] ----> [ same or other inode ]
[3] --------------------------^ (dup: 2 fds -> 1 description)
  • fd — a small non-negative int, an index into the per-process fd table.
  • Open file description — system-wide, holds the current file offset and the open flags (O_APPEND, O_NONBLOCK). Shared when you dup() or inherit across fork().
  • inode — the file itself (metadata + data location). Multiple descriptions can point to one inode.

Consequences

  • dup(fd) / dup2 make a second fd sharing the same description — same offset. That's how shell redirection wires 1 to a file.
  • After fork(), parent and child fds share descriptions: a read in one advances the offset the other sees. (A fresh open() gets its own description — independent offset.)
  • close-on-exec (O_CLOEXEC / FD_CLOEXEC): the fd is auto-closed when the process execs a new program — prevents fd leaks into children. Set it by default on everything you open.
// shell "cmd > out.txt": redirect fd 1 to a file, then exec
int f = open("out.txt", O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0644);
dup2(f, 1);              // fd 1 now shares f's open file description (same offset)
close(f);
execlp("ls", "ls", (char*)NULL);   // ls writes to fd 1 -> lands in out.txt

// set close-on-exec so this fd does NOT leak into a child program
int fd = open(path, O_RDONLY | O_CLOEXEC);

fd 0, 1, 2 and "everything is a file"

0 stdin, 1 stdout, 2 stderr by convention. The same read/write/close API works on regular files, pipes, sockets, terminals, devices (/dev/null), eventfd, timerfd, signalfd, epoll fds — uniform interface, different backends.

$ ls -l /proc/self/fd
0 -> /dev/pts/3        # stdin  = the terminal
1 -> /dev/pts/3        # stdout
2 -> /dev/pts/3        # stderr
3 -> 'socket:[41221]'  # a TCP socket -- same read()/write()/close() API
4 -> anon_inode:[eventfd]
5 -> /var/log/app.log

Limits

Per-process fd limit (RLIMIT_NOFILE, ulimit -n) and a system-wide max. Servers raise the soft limit; "too many open files" (EMFILE) means a leak or an under-set limit. The lowest free fd is always returned, which enables the close(1); open(...) redirection trick.

$ ulimit -n
1024                              # soft limit -- often too low for a server
$ ulimit -n 65536                 # raise it (up to the hard limit)

$ ls /proc/$(pgrep -n server)/fd | wc -l
1023                              # near the cap -> next accept() fails with EMFILE
$ lsof -p $(pgrep -n server) | grep -c 'sock'   # find the leak: thousands of stuck sockets
Cheat Sheet
  • fd (int, per-process) → open file description (system-wide: offset + flags) → inode (the file).
  • dup/dup2 and fork share the description → shared offset. A new open gets its own.
  • Set O_CLOEXEC on everything — fds otherwise leak across exec.
  • 0/1/2 = stdin/stdout/stderr; open returns the lowest free fd.
  • Same read/write/close API for files, pipes, sockets, ttys, devices, eventfd/timerfd/signalfd/epoll.
  • RLIMIT_NOFILE caps open fds; EMFILE = leak or limit too low; raise with ulimit -n / setrlimit.
  • Redirection: dup2(file_fd, 1) makes writes to fd 1 go to the file.
Q&A
What are the three levels between an fd number and file data?
The per-process file descriptor table (fd → description), the system-wide open file description table (holds the offset and status flags), and the inode table (the file's metadata and data blocks).
Why does reading from an fd in a forked child advance the parent's file position?
After fork(), the child's fd entries point to the same open file descriptions as the parent's, and the offset lives in the description — so a read in either process moves the shared offset.
What does dup2(fd, 1) accomplish?
It makes fd number 1 (stdout) refer to the same open file description as fd. Anything the process writes to stdout now goes wherever fd points — the mechanism behind > file redirection.
What is O_CLOEXEC and why use it?
A flag marking an fd to be closed automatically when the process calls exec(). Without it, fds leak into every child program you spawn — a resource leak and a security issue (the child can read/write files it shouldn't know about). Set it on every open/socket/pipe2.
You get EMFILE ("too many open files") under load. Causes?
Either a file-descriptor leak (opening without closing, e.g. per-request connections never released) or RLIMIT_NOFILE set too low for the workload. Check ls /proc/PID/fd | wc -l over time; raise the limit with ulimit -n / LimitNOFILE=, and fix the leak.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What number does open() return on success?
The lowest-numbered file descriptor not currently in use by the process.
Where is a file's current read/write offset stored?
In the open file description (system-wide table), not in the fd or the inode.
What API do sockets, pipes, and regular files share?
read(), write(), close() (and fcntl, dup, poll) — "everything is a file".

Intermediate core

Two processes both open("log", O_WRONLY|O_APPEND) and write concurrently. Do writes interleave/corrupt?
Each has its own open file description, but O_APPEND makes each write() atomically seek-to-end-then-write in the kernel, so records don't overwrite each other — provided each write is a single write() call and within PIPE_BUF/filesystem limits. Without O_APPEND, both would use stale offsets and clobber each other. (This is also why shell >> from parallel processes is safe for line-sized appends.)
How does the shell implement cmd > out.txt?
fork(); in the child: fd = open("out.txt", O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, 0644), then dup2(fd, 1) (fd 1 now points at the file), close(fd), then exec(cmd). The exec'd program writes to fd 1 as usual, unaware it's a file.

Advanced deep

Explain the difference between dup()ing an fd and independently open()ing the same file, in terms of the three tables.
dup(fd) adds a new entry to the fd table pointing at the same open file description — so the two fds share the file offset and the status flags (setting O_NONBLOCK via one affects both), and closing one leaves the description alive (refcount > 0) until the other closes. A second open() of the same path creates a new open file description (new offset starting at 0 or end, its own copy of the flags) that happens to reference the same inode. So: same inode both ways, but shared vs independent offset/flags. This is why a library that dups stdin to save it can restore it exactly (same position), whereas re-opening /dev/stdin would reset the position.
What is the "lowest free fd" guarantee's role in fd-passing and privilege separation designs?
Because open/dup/accept always return the lowest available fd, a program can deterministically place an fd at a known number by closing that number first (close(3); dup2(sock, 3)), which is how systemd socket activation and inetd hand a listening socket to a service at fd 3 (SD_LISTEN_FDS_START). Privilege-separation designs exploit the same determinism: a privileged parent opens exactly the fds a sandboxed child is allowed (a config file, a log, a socket), places them at agreed numbers, sets everything else CLOEXEC, then execs the unprivileged child — which inherits precisely that fd set and can't name any other file (especially after a chroot/namespace/seccomp that blocks new opens). The fd becomes an unforgeable capability: possession of fd 3 is the permission to use that resource, nothing more.

File I/O, Short Reads & Locking

The raw syscalls, the loops you must write around them, and how (not) to lock a file.

Notes

The syscalls

  • open(path, flags, mode) — flags: O_RDONLY/O_WRONLY/O_RDWR, plus O_CREAT, O_EXCL (fail if exists — atomic create), O_TRUNC, O_APPEND, O_NONBLOCK, O_CLOEXEC, O_DIRECT, O_SYNC.
  • read(fd, buf, n) → bytes read (0 = EOF, −1 = error). May return fewer than n (signal, pipe, socket, EOF near end).
  • write(fd, buf, n) → bytes written. May be short (full pipe/socket buffer, signal).
  • pread/pwrite — read/write at an explicit offset without moving the file position (thread-safe for concurrent I/O on one fd).
  • lseek, ftruncate, fstat, close.
int fd = open("data.bin", O_RDWR | O_CREAT | O_CLOEXEC, 0644);

// two threads, one fd, no shared offset -> use pread/pwrite
char hdr[16];  pread(fd, hdr, 16, 0);        // read at offset 0, position unchanged
pwrite(fd, rec, reclen, 4096);            // write at offset 4096, thread B unaffected

// O_APPEND: the seek-to-end + write is ONE atomic step (safe for concurrent log writers)
int log = open("app.log", O_WRONLY | O_APPEND | O_CREAT, 0644);

The loops you must write

// full read
size_t done = 0;
while (done < n) {
    ssize_t r = read(fd, buf + done, n - done);
    if (r < 0) { if (errno == EINTR) continue; return -1; }
    if (r == 0) break;   // EOF
    done += r;
}

Same pattern for write. Never assume one call transfers everything.

Durability

  • write() returning doesn't mean "on disk" — it's in the kernel page cache. fsync(fd) forces data + metadata to stable storage; fdatasync skips non-essential metadata.
  • The atomic rename pattern for crash-safe file updates: write to file.tmp, fsync it, rename("file.tmp", "file") (atomic on the same filesystem), then fsync the directory.
// crash-safe atomic update of config.json
int fd = open("config.json.tmp", O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0644);
write_all(fd, data, len);
fsync(fd); close(fd);                          // data durably on disk...
rename("config.json.tmp", "config.json");      // ...atomic swap: readers see old OR new, never partial
int dir = open(".", O_RDONLY | O_DIRECTORY);
fsync(dir); close(dir);                        // persist the rename itself

File locking

  • flock(fd, LOCK_EX) — whole-file advisory lock, associated with the open file description. Simple; not great over NFS.
  • fcntl(F_SETLK) — POSIX byte-range advisory locks. Powerful but has a notorious flaw: locks are dropped when any fd to the file in the process is closed.
  • F_OFD_SETLK (Linux) — open-file-description locks: like POSIX ranges but tied to the description (survive unrelated closes, work across threads). Prefer these.
  • All of the above are advisory — only processes that also check the lock are constrained.
// single-instance guard: whole-file exclusive lock
int fd = open("/var/run/app.lock", O_CREAT | O_RDWR, 0644);
if (flock(fd, LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB) < 0) {
    fprintf(stderr, "already running\n"); exit(1);   // EWOULDBLOCK -> another instance holds it
}
// released automatically when fd closes / process exits

$ flock -n /var/run/app.lock ./app   # shell wrapper: same idea, from cron
Cheat Sheet
  • read/write can be short — always loop until done or EOF; retry on EINTR.
  • O_CREAT|O_EXCL = atomic "create only if absent". O_APPEND = atomic seek-to-end per write.
  • pread/pwrite for offset-explicit, position-independent, thread-safe I/O on one fd.
  • write() success ≠ durable. fsync/fdatasync to force to disk.
  • Crash-safe update: write tmp → fsync tmp → rename over the target → fsync the dir.
  • Locks are advisory: flock (whole file, per-description), fcntl F_SETLK (byte ranges, buggy close semantics), F_OFD_SETLK (ranges, sane — prefer).
  • O_DIRECT bypasses the page cache (DB engines); O_SYNC makes every write durable (slow).
Q&A
Why must you loop around read()?
It can legitimately return fewer bytes than requested — interrupted by a signal, reading from a pipe/socket with only some data available, or hitting EOF partway. Your code must accumulate until it has what it needs or sees EOF (return 0).
Does a successful write() mean the data is safely on disk?
No — it's in the kernel's page cache and will be flushed later. A crash before flush loses it. Call fsync(fd) (or fdatasync) when you need durability, and fsync the containing directory after creating/renaming files.
How do you atomically replace a config file so a reader never sees a partial write?
Write the new content to a temporary file in the same directory, fsync it, then rename() it over the original. rename is atomic within a filesystem, so a concurrent reader opens either the entire old file or the entire new file.
What's the classic bug with POSIX fcntl locks?
The lock is released as soon as the process closes any file descriptor referring to that file — not just the one it locked with. A library that opens the file, checks something, and closes its fd can silently drop your lock. Linux's F_OFD_SETLK (open-file-description locks) fixes this.
Are file locks enforced by the kernel?
The common ones (flock, fcntl F_SETLK, OFD locks) are advisory: they only coordinate processes that voluntarily check for the lock. Mandatory locking exists on Linux but is deprecated, unreliable, and rarely used.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does read() return at end of file?
0.
Which flag makes open() fail if the file already exists?
O_EXCL (combined with O_CREAT) — an atomic "create new".
Which call forces buffered file data to disk?
fsync() (or fdatasync() for just the data).

Intermediate core

A program copies a file with one read and one write and occasionally produces a truncated copy. Bug?
It assumes read fills the buffer and write flushes it in one call. Both can be short. Fix: loop — read in a loop until 0, and for each chunk write in a loop until the whole chunk is written, retrying on EINTR. Or use sendfile/copy_file_range which handle it in-kernel.
Two threads write to the same fd with write() after lseek(). Race?
Yes — the lseek and write aren't atomic together, so thread B can seek between A's seek and write, and both write to the wrong place. Use pwrite(fd, buf, n, offset), which takes the offset as an argument and doesn't touch the shared file position — atomic and thread-safe.

Advanced deep

Explain why "write tmp, rename over target" still needs a directory fsync, and the full crash-safe recipe.
rename() guarantees a reader sees either the old or new file — but only if both the new file's data and the directory entry change survive a crash. The recipe: (1) open target.tmp with O_CREAT|O_EXCL in the same directory (same filesystem, so rename is atomic); (2) write the full contents; (3) fsync(tmp_fd) — forces the data blocks and the file's own metadata to disk, so after a crash target.tmp isn't a zero-length or partially-written file; (4) rename("target.tmp", "target") — atomically swaps the directory entry; (5) fsync the directory fd — forces the directory entry change itself to disk, otherwise a crash right after rename can leave the directory still pointing at the old inode (or, worse with some filesystems/mount options, at a not-yet-durable new one). Skipping step 3 risks a valid directory entry pointing at garbage data; skipping step 5 risks losing the rename. Some filesystems (ext4 with auto_da_alloc) heuristically fsync data on rename-over-existing to protect naive apps, but you can't rely on it portably. fdatasync can replace fsync in step 3 if the file size is already correct.
When and why would a database engine use O_DIRECT, and what does it then have to implement itself?
O_DIRECT bypasses the kernel page cache: reads/writes DMA straight between the device and user buffers. A database (PostgreSQL optionally, MySQL/InnoDB and Oracle commonly) wants this because it maintains its own buffer pool tuned to its access patterns and doesn't want the data cached twice (double buffering wastes RAM) or the kernel's readahead/writeback heuristics fighting its own. What it must then do itself: (1) alignment — buffer address, file offset, and length must all be multiples of the device block size (typically 512 or 4096); unaligned I/O fails with EINVAL. (2) Its own caching / buffer pool with eviction policy. (3) Its own readahead / prefetching for scans. (4) Write ordering and durability — O_DIRECT doesn't imply O_SYNC; the write can still sit in the drive's cache, so you still need fsync/FUA or the drive's cache disabled for the WAL. (5) Often async I/O (io_uring / libaio) since direct I/O blocks the calling thread on the device. The payoff is predictable latency and no page-cache pressure; the cost is a lot of infrastructure and portability caveats.

fork, exec, wait & Daemons

Spawning processes the Unix way, reaping them, and detaching one from the terminal.

Notes

fork / exec / wait

  • fork() → COW copy of the process. Returns child PID to parent, 0 to child, −1 on error.
  • execve(path, argv, envp) (and wrappers execl, execvp…) → replaces the image; keeps PID and non-CLOEXEC fds. Only returns on failure.
  • wait(&status) / waitpid(pid, &status, opts) → reap a child, get its exit status. WIFEXITED/WEXITSTATUS, WIFSIGNALED/WTERMSIG. WNOHANG = non-blocking poll.
  • posix_spawn() — fork+exec in one safe call (preferred in threaded programs).
pid_t pid = fork();
if (pid == 0) {
    execlp("gzip", "gzip", "big.log", (char*)NULL);
    _exit(127);                       // only reached if exec FAILED
}
int st;
waitpid(pid, &st, 0);
if (WIFEXITED(st))   printf("exit %d\n", WEXITSTATUS(st));   // normal exit
if (WIFSIGNALED(st)) printf("killed by %d\n", WTERMSIG(st));   // e.g. SIGKILL = 9

Process groups & sessions

  • Process group — a set of related processes (a shell pipeline); a signal to -pgid hits all of them. Ctrl-C sends SIGINT to the foreground group.
  • Session — a collection of process groups with one controlling terminal and a session leader. setsid() starts a new session with no controlling tty.
$ sleep 100 | sleep 100 &             # a pipeline = one process group
$ ps -o pid,pgid,sess,cmd
  PID  PGID  SESS CMD
 4001  4001  3990 sleep 100           # both sleeps share PGID 4001
 4002  4001  3990 sleep 100
$ kill -TERM -4001                    # leading '-' -> signal the whole GROUP
# Ctrl-C in a terminal sends SIGINT to the foreground process group, not just one process

Daemonising (the classic double-fork)

  1. fork(), parent exits → child is orphaned, not a group leader.
  2. setsid() → new session, no controlling terminal.
  3. fork() again, first child exits → the daemon can never reacquire a tty.
  4. chdir("/"), reset umask, close/redirect 0/1/2 to /dev/null, optionally write a PID file.

Modern practice: don't hand-roll this. Let systemd (Type=simple), supervisord, or a container runtime run your process in the foreground and manage lifecycle, logging, and restart.

# the classic dance (DON'T write this today):
if (fork() != 0) exit(0);       # 1. parent exits
setsid();                        # 2. new session, drop the tty
if (fork() != 0) exit(0);       # 3. can't reacquire a controlling tty
chdir("/"); umask(0);
# dup2 /dev/null onto 0,1,2 ...

# TODAY: just run in the foreground, let the supervisor handle it
# /etc/systemd/system/app.service:
[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/bin/app
Type=simple
Restart=on-failure

PID 1 duties

In a container, your process is often PID 1 and inherits init's job: reap orphaned zombies and forward signals. If it doesn't, use a tiny init (tini, docker --init).

$ docker run myimg
$ docker exec ... ps               # <defunct> zombies piling up under PID 1 (your app)
                                   # app doesn't wait() for the children it spawns

$ docker run --init myimg          # inserts `tini` as PID 1: reaps zombies, forwards SIGTERM
# or in the Dockerfile:  ENTRYPOINT ["tini", "--", "/usr/bin/app"]
Cheat Sheet
  • fork → child (PID 0 in child, >0 in parent). exec* → replace image (returns only on failure). wait/waitpid → reap + status.
  • Decode status: WIFEXITED/WEXITSTATUS, WIFSIGNALED/WTERMSIG. WNOHANG to poll.
  • Prefer posix_spawn to fork+exec in multithreaded code.
  • Process group: signal -pgid hits the whole group (Ctrl-C → foreground group SIGINT).
  • Session: setsid() → new session, drops the controlling terminal.
  • Daemonise = fork/setsid/fork/chdir("/")/umask/redirect 0,1,2 — but really just run in foreground under systemd/supervisor/container.
  • Container PID 1 must reap zombies + forward signals → use tini / --init if your app doesn't.
Q&A
What does exec() return on success?
It doesn't return — the calling process's memory image is replaced. Any code after a successful exec never runs; code after it handles the failure case (and should _exit).
Why the double fork when daemonising?
The first fork + setsid detaches from the controlling terminal and makes a new session (the process becomes session leader). The second fork ensures the daemon is not a session leader, so it can never accidentally acquire a controlling terminal by opening a tty device.
How do you check whether a child exited normally or was killed?
From wait's status: WIFEXITED(status) true → use WEXITSTATUS; WIFSIGNALED(status) true → use WTERMSIG for the signal number.
What is a process group used for?
Delivering a signal to a set of related processes at once — e.g. the shell puts a pipeline in one group so Ctrl-C (SIGINT) or a kill -TERM - terminates every command in it.
Why does a containerised app sometimes accumulate zombies?
The app is PID 1 but doesn't wait() for children it didn't directly spawn (grandchildren re-parented to it). PID 1 is supposed to reap all orphans. Fix: run a proper init as PID 1 (tini, docker run --init) or make the app reap in a SIGCHLD handler.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does fork() return to the child?
0.
Which call reaps a terminated child and retrieves its exit code?
wait() / waitpid().
What does setsid() do?
Creates a new session with the calling process as leader, with no controlling terminal — a step in daemonising.

Intermediate core

Write the skeleton to run /bin/ls -l and print its exit code.
pid_t p = fork();
if (p == 0) { execl("/bin/ls", "ls", "-l", (char*)NULL); _exit(127); }
int st; waitpid(p, &st, 0);
if (WIFEXITED(st)) printf("exit %d\n", WEXITSTATUS(st));
else if (WIFSIGNALED(st)) printf("killed by %d\n", WTERMSIG(st));
Why is fork() then non-trivial work (before exec) dangerous in a multithreaded process?
Only the calling thread survives in the child; other threads vanish mid-operation, so any lock they held (including inside malloc, printf, the allocator) stays locked forever in the child. Between fork and exec you may only call async-signal-safe functions. Use posix_spawn (or vfork+exec), which avoids the window, or fork before creating threads.

Advanced deep

Why is "run in the foreground under a supervisor" now preferred over the double-fork daemon, point by point?
(1) Lifecycle: the supervisor knows the exact PID (it started the process) — no fragile PID files that go stale or get reused; it can reliably stop, restart with backoff, and enforce a stop timeout then SIGKILL. (2) Readiness: Type=notify / health checks let the supervisor know when the service is actually ready, vs "the parent exited so it must be up". (3) Logging: stdout/stderr are captured to the journal/log system with metadata; the daemon doesn't need to reimplement log rotation or syslog. (4) Resource control: the supervisor puts the process in a cgroup with memory/CPU/IO limits and can kill the whole process tree cleanly (no escaped grandchildren). (5) Reaping & signals: systemd as PID 1 (or a container init) reaps zombies and forwards signals correctly. (6) Security: User=, NoNewPrivileges=, seccomp, namespace isolation, read-only filesystem — declaratively, without the app dropping privileges by hand. (7) Simplicity/correctness: the double-fork dance has many easy-to-get-wrong steps (fd handling, umask, session leadership, signal masks inherited across exec). Foreground + supervisor moves all of that to well-tested infrastructure.
Explain the "self-pipe" / signal-forwarding pattern a container entrypoint needs.
An entrypoint script or wrapper that execs the real app is fine (the app becomes PID 1 directly). But if the wrapper must stay as PID 1 (to set up something, or run several processes), it has to: (a) install handlers for SIGTERM/SIGINT that forward the signal to the child's process group, so docker stop actually reaches the app instead of being ignored (PID 1 has no default signal dispositions — unhandled SIGTERM to PID 1 does nothing); (b) reap zombies via a SIGCHLD handler or a waitpid(-1, ..., WNOHANG) loop, since re-parented orphans land on PID 1; (c) exit with the child's status so the container's exit code is meaningful. The robust move is to not write this yourself — use tini as the entrypoint (or docker run --init, which injects tini), which does exactly signal-forwarding + reaping in ~200 lines of audited C, and exec your app so it's a direct child.

Signals & Signal Handlers

Asynchronous notifications with a tiny, treacherous execution environment.

Notes

What a signal is

An asynchronous notification delivered to a process (or thread). Each has a default action: terminate (SIGTERM, SIGINT), terminate + core dump (SIGSEGV, SIGABRT), ignore (SIGCHLD by default action is ignore-ish), stop (SIGSTOP), continue (SIGCONT). You can install a handler for most; SIGKILL and SIGSTOP can't be caught, blocked, or ignored.

$ kill -l                      # list signal names/numbers
$ kill -TERM 4201              # polite: process can catch it and clean up
$ kill -KILL 4201             # kill -9: uncatchable, no cleanup -- last resort
$ kill -STOP 4201; kill -CONT 4201   # pause / resume (also uncatchable STOP)

# default actions: SIGINT=term, SIGSEGV=term+core, SIGCHLD=ignore, SIGHUP=term
$ trap 'echo reloading; reload_config' HUP   # shells too: install a handler

Handlers run in a hostile environment

  • A handler can interrupt the program anywhere — mid-malloc, mid-printf.
  • You may only call async-signal-safe functions from a handler (a short whitelist: write, _exit, sig_atomic_t assignments, most raw syscalls). Not malloc, printf, most of libc, or anything that takes a lock — risk of deadlock/corruption.
  • Shared state: only touch a volatile sig_atomic_t flag (or a lock-free atomic). The main loop checks the flag.
// UNSAFE: printf/malloc may hold a lock the interrupted main code also holds -> deadlock
void bad(int s) { printf("got %d\n", s); }        // DON'T

// SAFE: the only fully portable thing to do is set a flag
volatile sig_atomic_t g_stop = 0;
void on_term(int s) { g_stop = 1; }               // (write(2,...) is also allowed)

The safe patterns

  • Flag + main loop: handler sets volatile sig_atomic_t stop = 1;; the event loop notices and shuts down cleanly.
  • Self-pipe: handler write(1 byte) to a pipe; the pipe's read end is in your select/epoll set, so signal delivery becomes a normal readable-fd event.
  • signalfd (Linux): read signals as bytes from an fd — no handler at all, integrates with epoll.
// signalfd: turn signals into readable-fd events, no handler, epoll-friendly
sigset_t mask; sigemptyset(&mask); sigaddset(&mask, SIGTERM); sigaddset(&mask, SIGHUP);
sigprocmask(SIG_BLOCK, &mask, NULL);        // block normal delivery
int sfd = signalfd(-1, &mask, 0);
// add sfd to your epoll set; when readable:
struct signalfd_siginfo si;
read(sfd, &si, sizeof si);
if (si.ssi_signo == SIGTERM) shutdown_gracefully();  // full libc allowed here -- it's the main loop

Interrupted syscalls

A blocking syscall interrupted by a signal returns -1 / EINTR. Either install the handler with SA_RESTART (kernel auto-restarts many syscalls) or wrap every blocking call in a retry loop. Note SA_RESTART doesn't cover everything (select, poll, certain timeouts).

ssize_t n;
do { n = read(fd, buf, len); } while (n < 0 && errno == EINTR);  // retry loop

// or ask the kernel to auto-restart:
struct sigaction sa = { .sa_handler = on_term, .sa_flags = SA_RESTART };
sigaction(SIGTERM, &sa, NULL);        // still doesn't cover poll/select/epoll_wait

SIGCHLD

Sent when a child stops or exits. Install a handler that waitpid(-1, &st, WNOHANG) in a loop to reap all available children (signals coalesce — two children exiting may deliver one SIGCHLD).

void on_sigchld(int s) {
    int saved = errno;
    while (waitpid(-1, NULL, WNOHANG) > 0)   // LOOP: 3 children may = 1 signal
        ;
    errno = saved;                          // handler must not clobber errno
}
// or the shortcut: signal(SIGCHLD, SIG_IGN) -> kernel auto-reaps, no zombies
Cheat Sheet
  • Signals: async notifications; default = terminate / core / ignore / stop / cont. SIGKILL/SIGSTOP uncatchable.
  • In a handler: only async-signal-safe calls (write, _exit, raw syscalls, sig_atomic_t). No malloc/printf/locks.
  • Communicate to main code via volatile sig_atomic_t flag, or a self-pipe, or signalfd.
  • Blocking syscall + signal → EINTR: use SA_RESTART or retry loops (SA_RESTART doesn't cover select/poll).
  • Use sigaction, not signal() (portable, defined semantics, SA_RESTART/SA_SIGINFO).
  • Block signals with sigprocmask/pthread_sigmask around critical regions; deliver to one dedicated thread.
  • SIGCHLD handler: while (waitpid(-1,&st,WNOHANG) > 0); — signals coalesce.
Q&A
Which two signals cannot be caught or ignored?
SIGKILL (9) and SIGSTOP.
Why can't you call printf from a signal handler?
The handler may have interrupted the main program inside printf (or malloc), which holds an internal lock. Re-entering it deadlocks or corrupts state. Only async-signal-safe functions (like write) are guaranteed re-entrant.
What's the safe way to shut down a server on SIGTERM?
The handler sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag (or writes a byte to a self-pipe). The main loop sees it, stops accepting new work, drains in-flight requests, and exits — all the real logic runs in normal code, not the handler.
What is EINTR and how do you deal with it?
A blocking syscall was interrupted by a signal before completing, so it returns −1 with errno == EINTR. Either register handlers with SA_RESTART (the kernel restarts many such calls automatically) or wrap the call in do { r = call(); } while (r < 0 && errno == EINTR);.
Why loop waitpid with WNOHANG in a SIGCHLD handler?
Signals don't queue — if three children exit close together you may get only one SIGCHLD. Looping waitpid(-1, ..., WNOHANG) until it returns 0 or −1 reaps all of them.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What signal does Ctrl-C send?
SIGINT (2), to the terminal's foreground process group.
Which function should you use to install handlers, signal() or sigaction()?
sigaction() — portable, well-defined semantics, and lets you set SA_RESTART, SA_SIGINFO, and a mask.
What type must a variable shared between a handler and main code be?
volatile sig_atomic_t (or a proper lock-free atomic).

Intermediate core

Describe the self-pipe trick and why it exists.
Create a pipe, set both ends non-blocking, add the read end to your select/epoll set. The signal handler does nothing but write(pipe_wr, "x", 1) (async-signal-safe). Now a signal shows up as a readable fd in your event loop, which you handle in normal code alongside sockets — no race between "check flag" and "block in select" (the classic pselect/ppoll problem), and no unsafe work in the handler. signalfd is the modern Linux replacement.
In a multithreaded program, which thread runs a signal handler, and how do you control it?
For a process-directed signal, the kernel picks an arbitrary thread that doesn't have it blocked. To make it deterministic: block the signal in all threads (pthread_sigmask at startup, before creating threads so they inherit the mask), then have one dedicated thread call sigwait()/sigwaitinfo() (or read a signalfd) to handle signals synchronously in normal code. This avoids the async-signal-safety minefield entirely.

Advanced deep

Why is pselect/ppoll's atomic signal-mask argument necessary, and what race does it close?
The naive pattern is: block SIGTERM, check if (!got_signal), then select() (unblocking SIGTERM so it can interrupt the wait). The race: a signal delivered after the check but before select blocks sets the flag and returns from its handler, but select then blocks forever — the wakeup was lost. pselect(..., &sigmask) takes a signal mask and atomically: replaces the mask (unblocking SIGTERM), waits, and restores the mask on return — as a single uninterruptible operation. So there's no window: if the signal arrives at any point, either it's still blocked (pending, and pselect returns immediately once unblocked) or pselect is already waiting and gets interrupted. The self-pipe / signalfd approaches sidestep the whole problem by turning the signal into a pipe write that the ordinary (already-blocking-on-a-fd) event loop notices — which is why they're now preferred over pselect gymnastics.
What exactly makes a function "async-signal-safe", and why is malloc not one despite "just bumping a pointer" sometimes?
Async-signal-safe means the function is either fully reentrant or the signal can't interrupt it in a state that a second concurrent invocation would corrupt — formally, POSIX publishes an explicit list, and the property must hold for every code path. malloc fails because its fast path still manipulates shared allocator data structures (free lists, arena bins, size-class caches) protected by a lock; if a signal arrives while the main thread holds that lock and the handler calls malloc, the handler's malloc either deadlocks waiting for a lock its own thread holds, or (in a lock-free arena) observes a half-updated free list and corrupts the heap. The occasional "just bump a pointer" case (allocating from a thread cache that happens to have a free chunk) doesn't help — safety must be guaranteed unconditionally, and you can't know which path you'll hit. The same reasoning rules out printf (stdio buffer + lock), syslog, getenv after setenv, and anything using errno without saving/restoring it. The safe set is basically raw syscalls plus a handful of string/`str`-free helpers.

Pipes, FIFOs & socketpairs

Kernel byte channels between processes — and the SIGPIPE that catches everyone once.

Notes

Anonymous pipe

  • pipe(fds) → fds[0] read end, fds[1] write end. Unidirectional byte stream, in-kernel buffer (default 64 KB, tunable via fcntl(F_SETPIPE_SZ)).
  • Only useful between processes that share the fds — i.e. related via fork(). The shell's |.
  • Each process should close the ends it doesn't use, or EOF/SIGPIPE semantics break (see below).
int fds[2]; pipe(fds);
if (fork() == 0) {
    close(fds[1]);                    // child: close the write end it won't use
    dup2(fds[0], 0); close(fds[0]);   // stdin now reads from the pipe
    execlp("wc", "wc", "-l", (char*)NULL);
}
close(fds[0]);                        // parent: close read end
write(fds[1], data, len);
close(fds[1]);                        // LAST write end closed -> child's read() returns 0 (EOF)

The two end-of-stream behaviours

  • Reader sees EOF (read returns 0) only when all write ends are closed. If the writing process forgot to close its copy of fds[1], the reader blocks forever.
  • Writer on a pipe with no readers gets SIGPIPE (default: terminate). If you ignore/handle SIGPIPE, write returns -1/EPIPE. Network servers routinely signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN) and check EPIPE.
signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN);          // don't die when the peer goes away
ssize_t n = write(sock, buf, len);
if (n < 0 && errno == EPIPE) {    // now write() reports it instead of killing us
    close(sock); drop_client();
}
// classic bug: child inherits fds[1], never closes it -> parent's read() never sees EOF

Atomicity

Writes of up to PIPE_BUF (≥ 512, usually 4096) bytes are atomic — they won't interleave with other writers' data. Larger writes can be split and interleaved.

$ getconf PIPE_BUF /             # 4096 on Linux

# many processes appending short lines to one pipe/FIFO -> each line stays intact
write(fifo, "[worker-3] done\n", 15);   // <= PIPE_BUF -> atomic, no interleaving

# a 1 MB write from two writers -> the kernel splits it, chunks interleave
# fix: keep messages < PIPE_BUF, or add length-prefixed framing + a lock

FIFO (named pipe)

mkfifo(path) creates a pipe with a filesystem name, so unrelated processes can connect by opening the path. open for read blocks until a writer opens it (and vice versa) — a rendezvous. Same byte-stream, SIGPIPE, and atomicity rules as anonymous pipes.

$ mkfifo /tmp/jobs
$ tail -f /tmp/jobs &              # reader; open() blocks until a writer appears
$ echo "process file-42" > /tmp/jobs   # unrelated process, connects by path
process file-42

# open(O_RDONLY) blocks for a writer; add O_NONBLOCK to return immediately (ENXIO if none)

socketpair

socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0, fds) → a bidirectional connected pair (both ends read and write). Also supports datagram mode (message boundaries) and, uniquely, passing file descriptors and credentials via sendmsg/SCM_RIGHTS. The go-to for a parent↔child two-way channel.

int sv[2];
socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0, sv);   // sv[0] <-> sv[1], BOTH read+write
if (fork() == 0) {
    close(sv[0]);
    write(sv[1], "hi parent", 9);      // child -> parent
    read(sv[1], buf, sizeof buf);       // parent -> child, same fd
} else {
    close(sv[1]);
    // send an open fd to the child via sendmsg + SCM_RIGHTS ...
}
Cheat Sheet
  • pipe(): [0] read, [1] write, unidirectional, ~64 KB buffer, related processes only.
  • Reader gets EOF only when all write ends are closed → close unused ends religiously.
  • Writing to a pipe with no readers → SIGPIPE (kills you) or EPIPE if ignored. Servers SIG_IGN it.
  • Writes ≤ PIPE_BUF (~4 KB) are atomic; larger can interleave/split.
  • mkfifo: named pipe for unrelated processes; open blocks for a rendezvous.
  • socketpair(AF_UNIX): bidirectional, stream or datagram, can pass fds (SCM_RIGHTS) & peer creds.
  • Full pipe → writer blocks (backpressure); empty pipe → reader blocks. Set O_NONBLOCK for EAGAIN.
Q&A
When does a pipe reader see EOF?
Only after every write-end file descriptor is closed — across all processes. A common bug: a child inherits the parent's copy of the write end and doesn't close it, so the reader never gets EOF.
What happens when you write to a pipe whose read end is closed?
The kernel sends SIGPIPE, which by default terminates the process. If you ignore or handle SIGPIPE, the write instead returns −1 with errno == EPIPE.
Anonymous pipe vs FIFO?
An anonymous pipe has no name; it's shared by passing the fds (so only related processes). A FIFO (mkfifo) has a pathname, so any process that can open that path can connect — related or not.
Why choose a socketpair over a pair of pipes for a two-way channel?
One socketpair gives you a full-duplex connection (each fd is read/write), versus needing two pipes for bidirectional communication. It also supports datagram framing and can carry file descriptors and credentials between the two ends.
Is a large write() to a pipe guaranteed not to interleave with another writer?
Only up to PIPE_BUF bytes (at least 512, typically 4096). Beyond that the kernel may split the write and another process's data can appear in between. Keep messages small or add your own framing/locking.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which index of pipe(fds) is the read end?
fds[0]. fds[1] is the write end.
What creates a named pipe?
mkfifo(path, mode) (or the mkfifo shell command).
How do most network servers avoid dying from SIGPIPE?
signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN) (or MSG_NOSIGNAL on send), then handle EPIPE from write/send.

Intermediate core

A parent creates a pipe, forks, the child execs a filter, and the parent's read from the pipe hangs forever. Likely cause?
The parent didn't close its own copy of the pipe's write end after forking. As long as any write-end fd is open anywhere (including in the parent itself), the reader never sees EOF. Both sides must close the ends they don't use immediately after fork (and mark them O_CLOEXEC so they don't survive the child's exec either).
Set up a bidirectional parent–child channel and explain the fd bookkeeping.
socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0, sv) gives sv[0], sv[1]. fork(). Parent: close(sv[1]), use sv[0] for both reading and writing. Child: close(sv[0]), use sv[1]. Each end is full-duplex, so no second channel is needed. When one side closes its fd, the other's read returns 0 (EOF) and its write gets EPIPE — clean teardown.

Advanced deep

How does splice() / vmsplice() achieve zero-copy pipe I/O, and what's the constraint?
A Linux pipe is internally a ring of page references, not a byte array copied twice. splice(fd_in, fd_out, len) moves data between a file/socket and a pipe by transferring page ownership — the kernel attaches the source's pages to the pipe buffer (or vice versa) without copying the bytes through userspace. So splice(socket → pipe) then splice(pipe → file) streams a socket to disk with no user buffer and no copy. vmsplice "gifts" user pages into a pipe similarly. Constraints/caveats: one end of a splice must be a pipe (it's the page-container); true zero-copy only happens when pages can be moved rather than copied (source must be page-cache-backed and aligned; sockets support it); with vmsplice(SPLICE_F_GIFT) you must not touch the gifted user pages again until they've been consumed, or you get a data race with the kernel (a known footgun). sendfile is the simpler file→socket special case built on the same machinery. io_uring now offers registered-buffer zero-copy sends that avoid the pipe intermediary entirely.
Explain the deadlock in a naive "write request, read response" over a single pipe pair, and the fix.
Two processes each write a large message to the other then read the reply, over pipes with finite (~64 KB) buffers. If both messages exceed the buffer: process A's write fills the pipe and blocks waiting for B to read; B's write fills its pipe and blocks waiting for A to read — but neither ever gets to its read. Classic buffer deadlock. Fixes: (1) bound message size below PIPE_BUF or the buffer size; (2) use non-blocking fds and an event loop (poll both directions, drain readable ends while writing writable ends); (3) dedicated reader/writer threads per direction; (4) a protocol where one side fully sends before the other replies (strict request/response with a size prefix so the reader knows when it's done). The same hazard appears with popen-style two-way filters and is why popen is one-directional and libraries like Python's subprocess.communicate() use threads/select internally.

I/O Multiplexing: select / poll / epoll

Watching thousands of file descriptors from one thread — the heart of every async server.

Notes

The problem

You have N sockets and want to act on whichever becomes readable/writable, without a thread per socket. You need the kernel to tell you "which of these fds are ready".

// DOESN'T SCALE: a thread blocked in read() per connection
for (;;) { int c = accept(srv, ...); pthread_create(&t, NULL, handle, &c); }
// 100k connections -> 100k threads -> ~100 GB of stacks, scheduler meltdown

// SCALES: one thread asks the kernel "which of my N fds can I touch now?"
// most of those 100k sockets are idle at any instant -> one thread is plenty

The three APIs

selectpollepoll (Linux)
fd limitFD_SETSIZE (~1024)nonenone
Per-call costO(n) — copy + scan the whole set every callO(n) — pass the whole array every callO(1) to wait; O(active) results. Interest set kept in the kernel.
PortableeverywherePOSIXLinux only (BSD/macOS: kqueue; Windows: IOCP)

epoll: epoll_create1(), epoll_ctl(ADD/MOD/DEL) to manage the interest set once, then epoll_wait() returns only the ready fds. This is why it scales to 100k+ connections.

int ep = epoll_create1(0);
epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, listen_fd,
          &(struct epoll_event){ .events = EPOLLIN, .data.fd = listen_fd });  // register ONCE

struct epoll_event ev[128];
for (;;) {
    int n = epoll_wait(ep, ev, 128, -1);      // O(1) to wait; returns only READY fds
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (ev[i].data.fd == listen_fd) accept_new(ep);
        else service(ev[i].data.fd);
    }
}

Readiness vs completion

select/poll/epoll are readiness models: "the fd won't block if you act now" — you still do the read/write. Windows IOCP and Linux io_uring are completion models: "your read already finished, here's the data". Completion models avoid the extra syscall and suit true async disk I/O (which has no "readiness").

// READINESS (epoll): 2 syscalls -- "is it ready?" then "do the read"
epoll_wait(ep, ev, n, -1);
read(fd, buf, len);

// COMPLETION (io_uring): submit the read, later collect the finished result -- 0 extra syscalls
struct io_uring_sqe *sqe = io_uring_get_sqe(&ring);
io_uring_prep_read(sqe, fd, buf, len, offset);
io_uring_submit(&ring);
// ... io_uring_wait_cqe(&ring, &cqe) -> cqe->res bytes already in buf

Level- vs edge-triggered

  • Level-triggered (default): reports an fd as ready while there's data. You can read part of it and be told again. Forgiving.
  • Edge-triggered (EPOLLET): reports only on the transition to ready. You must drain the fd (loop read/write until EAGAIN) or you'll never be notified again for that data. Fewer syscalls; easy to get wrong.
// EDGE-TRIGGERED: you get ONE notification for the transition -> you MUST drain fully
epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, fd,
          &(struct epoll_event){ .events = EPOLLIN | EPOLLET, .data.fd = fd });
for (;;) {
    ssize_t r = read(fd, buf, sizeof buf);
    if (r > 0) process(buf, r);
    else if (r < 0 && errno == EAGAIN) break;   // drained -- stop until the NEXT edge
    else break;                                // 0 = EOF, other = error
}
// leave one byte unread with EPOLLET and you never hear about this fd again -> stuck

Also useful

EPOLLONESHOT (re-arm explicitly — good for thread pools), eventfd/timerfd/signalfd to fold timers and signals into the same loop, EPOLLEXCLUSIVE to avoid thundering herd on a shared listener.

// one loop, everything as an fd:
int tfd = timerfd_create(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, 0);   // timers
int efd = eventfd(0, EFD_NONBLOCK);              // wake the loop from another thread
epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, tfd, &(struct epoll_event){ .events = EPOLLIN, .data.fd = tfd });
epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, efd, &(struct epoll_event){ .events = EPOLLIN, .data.fd = efd });
// EPOLLONESHOT: after epoll_wait reports fd once, it's disabled -> a worker thread
// can handle it without another thread also grabbing the same event
Cheat Sheet
  • select: portable, FD_SETSIZE cap (~1024), O(n) rebuild+scan every call.
  • poll: no fd cap, still O(n) array passed each call.
  • epoll: kernel keeps the interest set; epoll_wait returns only ready fds; scales to 100k+. Linux (macOS/BSD = kqueue, Windows = IOCP).
  • All three are readiness models (you still call read/write). io_uring/IOCP are completion models.
  • Level-triggered: notified while data remains (safe). Edge-triggered (EPOLLET): notified on transition only → must loop read/write to EAGAIN.
  • Non-blocking fds are mandatory with edge-triggered; recommended everywhere.
  • Fold signals/timers into the loop with signalfd/timerfd/eventfd.
Q&A
Why does epoll scale better than select/poll?
select/poll pass the entire fd set to the kernel on every call and the kernel scans all of them — O(n) per wait. epoll registers the interest set once with epoll_ctl; epoll_wait then just returns the fds that became ready, so the per-call cost is proportional to the number of active connections, not total.
Readiness vs completion notification?
Readiness (select/poll/epoll/kqueue): the kernel tells you an fd can be operated on without blocking, and you then do the read/write. Completion (IOCP, io_uring): you submit the operation and the kernel notifies you when it's done, with the result — no second syscall, and it works for disk I/O which has no meaningful "ready" state.
Level-triggered vs edge-triggered epoll?
Level-triggered keeps reporting an fd as ready as long as unread data exists. Edge-triggered reports only when the state changes to ready, so you must consume all available data (loop until EAGAIN) or you'll miss the rest until new data arrives.
Why must fds be non-blocking with edge-triggered epoll?
Because you must loop read/write until it returns EAGAIN to fully drain the fd. With a blocking fd, the loop's final call (when no data is left) would block the whole event-loop thread.
What's the portable alternative to epoll on macOS and Windows?
kqueue on macOS/BSD (similar readiness model, also handles timers/signals/file events), and I/O Completion Ports (IOCP) on Windows (a completion model). Cross-platform libraries (libuv, libevent, Boost.Asio) abstract over all of them.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Roughly what fd count does select break down at?
Around 1024 (FD_SETSIZE), and it degrades well before that due to the O(n) rescans.
Which call registers an fd with an epoll instance?
epoll_ctl(epfd, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, fd, &event).
Is epoll a readiness or completion API?
Readiness — it tells you an fd is ready; you still perform the read/write.

Intermediate core

An edge-triggered epoll server occasionally "loses" data on a busy connection. Bug?
The handler does a single read() per EPOLLIN event and returns. With edge-triggered mode, if more data was already in the socket buffer, no new event fires until additional data arrives (or never, if the peer is done sending) — the tail sits unread. Fix: loop read() until it returns EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK (and do the same for write() on EPOLLOUT). The fd must be non-blocking.
Multiple worker threads share one epoll fd watching a listening socket; on each connection they all wake. Fix?
Classic thundering herd. Options: add EPOLLEXCLUSIVE when registering the listener so the kernel wakes only one waiter per event; or use EPOLLONESHOT and re-arm from the thread that handled it; or give each worker its own epoll instance and use SO_REUSEPORT so the kernel load-balances incoming connections across per-worker listeners (no shared epoll at all).

Advanced deep

Why is io_uring a step beyond epoll, and what classes of work does it unlock?
epoll still requires one syscall to wait and then one or more syscalls (read/write/accept) per ready fd — syscall overhead grows with connection activity, worsened by Spectre/Meltdown mitigations. io_uring uses two shared ring buffers (submission + completion) mapped between user and kernel: the app writes many operation descriptors into the SQ and reads many results from the CQ, so a batch of I/O costs one io_uring_enter syscall — or zero with SQPOLL (a kernel thread polls the SQ). Crucially it's a true completion model that covers operations epoll never could: buffered and O_DIRECT disk reads/writes (which have no "readiness"), fsync, openat, statx, accept, connect, send/recv with registered buffers for zero-copy, and linked operations (do B only if A succeeds) and timeouts as SQEs. So a single loop can drive network + disk + filesystem-metadata work with minimal syscalls. Costs: newer/complex API (use liburing), a history of security CVEs (some hardened environments disable it), and completion-model programming is a bigger mental shift than readiness.
Explain the epoll "stale fd after close" hazard in a multithreaded reactor.
epoll registers an fd by number, but internally associates the interest with the underlying open file description. If thread A closes fd 7 and thread B (or the same thread later) opens a new socket that also gets fd number 7, a pending epoll_wait result or a not-yet-processed event for "fd 7" now refers to the wrong object — you read/write the new connection thinking it's the old one, or you epoll_ctl(DEL) the wrong registration. It gets subtler: if the fd was dup'd, closeing one copy does not remove it from epoll (the description is still open), so events keep firing for a "closed" fd. Mitigations: never close an fd that another thread might still be handling for this epoll loop — use a per-connection state object with a refcount / generation number, mark it "closing", let the loop drain outstanding events, then epoll_ctl(DEL) and close; or serialise all epoll_ctl + close operations onto the loop thread; or use EPOLLONESHOT so an fd can't have concurrent events in flight. libuv/libevent encapsulate exactly this bookkeeping.

mmap & Shared Memory

Mapping files and memory into the address space — for speed, sharing, and zero-copy.

Notes

mmap flavours

mmap(addr, len, prot, flags, fd, offset)
flagsEffect
MAP_PRIVATE + fdCopy-on-write view of a file. Writes stay in your process, never hit disk. Used for executables, shared libraries.
MAP_SHARED + fdWrites go through the page cache to the file and are visible to other mappers. File-backed shared memory.
MAP_ANONYMOUS + MAP_PRIVATEZero-filled memory not backed by a file — what malloc uses for big allocations.
MAP_ANONYMOUS + MAP_SHAREDAnonymous shared memory — inherited across fork, for parent/child sharing.

prot: PROT_READ/WRITE/EXEC. mprotect changes it later (guard pages, W^X). munmap to release; msync to flush a MAP_SHARED mapping to disk.

File I/O via mmap

  • Reading a file becomes dereferencing pointers; the kernel faults pages in on demand and caches them — no read syscall per chunk, no double-buffering.
  • Great for random access over a large file, or sharing a read-only dataset between processes (one copy in RAM).
  • Downsides: a fault on a network filesystem or a truncated file → SIGBUS; page-fault latency is unpredictable; not faster than a big sequential read for a linear scan.
// random access over a 4 GB index file, no read() per lookup
int fd = open("index.dat", O_RDONLY);
struct stat st; fstat(fd, &st);
const uint64_t *idx = mmap(NULL, st.st_size, PROT_READ, MAP_PRIVATE, fd, 0);
close(fd);                              // the mapping keeps its own reference

uint64_t v = idx[1'234'567];             // page fault pulls in ONE 4 KB page; cached after
madvise((void*)idx, st.st_size, MADV_RANDOM); // tell the kernel: don't read-ahead

POSIX shared memory between unrelated processes

fd = shm_open("/myseg", O_CREAT|O_RDWR, 0600);
ftruncate(fd, SIZE);
p = mmap(NULL, SIZE, PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE, MAP_SHARED, fd, 0);
// ... use *p ...   synchronise with a process-shared mutex/semaphore IN the segment
shm_unlink("/myseg");

(Older SysV: shmget/shmat. Linux also has memfd_create for an anonymous file you can pass by fd.)

Huge pages

MAP_HUGETLB or transparent huge pages back the mapping with 2 MB pages — fewer TLB entries per GB, big win for large in-memory data (databases, JVM heaps).

$ echo 1024 > /proc/sys/vm/nr_hugepages     # reserve 1024 x 2 MB = 2 GB

void *p = mmap(NULL, 2UL << 30, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE,
              MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS | MAP_HUGETLB, -1, 0);
// 2 GB now covered by ~1024 TLB entries instead of ~500,000 -> far fewer dTLB misses

$ grep Huge /proc/meminfo         # HugePages_Total / _Free / AnonHugePages
$ java -XX:+UseTransparentHugePages -Xmx8g App   # the JVM equivalent
Cheat Sheet
  • MAP_PRIVATE+fd = COW file view (exe/libs). MAP_SHARED+fd = writes go to the file + other mappers.
  • MAP_ANONYMOUS|MAP_PRIVATE = zeroed memory (big malloc). MAP_ANONYMOUS|MAP_SHARED = share across fork.
  • mmap a file → access as memory, demand-paged, page-cache-backed, no per-chunk syscall.
  • Fault on truncated/short file or NFS error → SIGBUS. Linear scans: plain read is as fast.
  • Unrelated processes: shm_open + ftruncate + mmap(MAP_SHARED); sync with a process-shared mutex/sem placed inside the segment; shm_unlink to remove.
  • msync to flush MAP_SHARED; munmap to release; mprotect to change perms / guard pages.
  • memfd_create for an anonymous fd-passable buffer; MAP_HUGETLB for 2 MB pages.
Q&A
MAP_PRIVATE vs MAP_SHARED for a file mapping?
MAP_PRIVATE is copy-on-write: your writes create private copies and never reach the file or other processes. MAP_SHARED: writes go through the page cache to the file and are visible to everyone else mapping it.
How does two processes sharing an mmap'd region synchronise access?
They must place a synchronisation primitive inside the shared region — a mutex created with PTHREAD_PROCESS_SHARED, or a POSIX unnamed semaphore — or use a named semaphore. Plain mutexes in each process's private memory don't coordinate anything.
When is mmap'ing a file not a win over read?
For a single linear pass: a large sequential read with readahead is just as fast and has predictable latency, while mmap adds per-page fault overhead and TLB pressure. mmap wins for random access, repeated access, or sharing the data between processes.
What causes SIGBUS on an mmap'd file?
Accessing a page that maps beyond the file's current length (the file was truncated after mapping, or you mapped past EOF), or an I/O error faulting the page in (e.g. a network filesystem going away).
How do two unrelated processes get shared memory?
shm_open("/name") to get an fd to a POSIX shared-memory object, ftruncate to size it, then both mmap it with MAP_SHARED. (Or SysV shmget/shmat, or pass a memfd_create fd over a Unix socket.)
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does malloc use mmap for?
Large allocations — an anonymous, zero-filled MAP_PRIVATE mapping returned to the program (and unmapped on free).
Which flag flushes an mmap'd file's dirty pages to disk?
Call msync(addr, len, MS_SYNC).
How is a shared library mapped into a process?
MAP_PRIVATE file mapping — code pages are shared read-only across processes; any writable data is copy-on-write.

Intermediate core

Two processes need a lock-free ring buffer in shared memory. Outline the setup.
Create a POSIX shm object (shm_open + ftruncate to sizeof(header) + N*slotsize), mmap(MAP_SHARED) in both. The header holds atomic head/tail indices (use C11 atomics / __atomic — they work across the shared mapping since it's the same physical memory). Producer does a release-store to advance tail after writing a slot; consumer does an acquire-load of tail before reading. No mutex needed for SPSC. Pad head and tail to separate cache lines. For MPSC/MPMC add CAS loops or an in-segment PTHREAD_PROCESS_SHARED mutex.
Why must a pthread_mutex shared between processes be initialised specially?
By default a mutex only works within one address space (it may store thread ids or point to per-process data). You must pthread_mutexattr_setpshared(&attr, PTHREAD_PROCESS_SHARED) and place the mutex object itself in the shared memory segment (not a copy in each process). Also consider PTHREAD_MUTEX_ROBUST so that if the process holding it crashes, the next acquirer gets EOWNERDEAD and can recover rather than deadlocking forever.

Advanced deep

Explain how mmap(MAP_SHARED) + the page cache gives "free" IPC and persistence, and the coherence guarantees.
When multiple processes mmap the same file region MAP_SHARED, the kernel maps the same page-cache pages into every process's page tables. A write by one process dirties that shared page; every other mapper sees the change immediately (same physical memory, subject to CPU cache coherence, which x86/ARM provide within a machine). The kernel's writeback thread later flushes dirty pages to the file, so the data also persists across process exits and (with msync/on clean shutdown) across reboots. So one mechanism gives you: shared memory IPC (no copy, no syscall per access), a persistent backing store, and crash-consistency you can tighten with msync. Guarantees/limits: coherence is guaranteed between processes on the same host; it is not coherent with concurrent write() calls to the same file on some systems and definitely not across NFS. Ordering between the shared write and the file being on disk is only what msync/fsync enforce — a crash can lose or reorder unflushed pages. And there's no notification: readers must poll or you must add a separate signal/eventfd. This pattern underlies LMDB, some message queues, and shared read-only datasets (one RAM copy for N workers).
Compare mmap-based file access with read/write for a database storage engine, including the failure modes that pushed some engines away from mmap.
Pro-mmap (LMDB, older MongoDB/MMAPv1, SQLite optional): no user-space buffer pool to build, the OS page cache is the cache, reads are pointer dereferences, and the same pages are shared with other processes for free. The problems (documented in "Are You Sure You Want to Use MMAP in Your Database?"): (1) No control over eviction — the OS may evict a page you're about to need, or keep cold pages, and you can't pin the hot working set; page-fault stalls are unpredictable and invisible to your latency accounting. (2) I/O errors become SIGBUS mid-instruction instead of a checkable return value — hard to handle gracefully; a bad sector can crash the process. (3) No async — a fault blocks the faulting thread; you can't overlap I/O with compute the way io_uring + a buffer pool can. (4) Dirty-page writeback is on the OS's schedule, not yours, so you lose control over write ordering needed for crash consistency (you end up calling msync constantly, negating the simplicity). (5) Transactional safety: single-copy pages make it hard to do copy-on-write MVCC without your own shadow paging. (6) TLB pressure and, historically, address-space limits on 32-bit. Modern engines (RocksDB, WiredTiger, Postgres) run their own buffer pool over pread/pwrite (or direct I/O + io_uring) precisely to get eviction control, error handling, async, and write scheduling — accepting the extra code. mmap remains great for read-mostly, single-writer, "let the OS handle it" designs like LMDB.

/proc, /sys, Environment & Limits

The kernel's introspection filesystems, plus the per-process knobs every program inherits.

Notes

procfs

A virtual filesystem exposing kernel + process state as files.

$ pid=$(pgrep -n nginx)
$ cat /proc/$pid/status | grep -E 'VmRSS|Threads'
VmRSS:   51200 kB
Threads: 4
$ ls /proc/$pid/fd | wc -l              # open-fd count -- rising = a leak
$ cat /proc/$pid/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '  # argv is NUL-separated
$ grep '' /proc/$pid/limits             # effective rlimits
$ cat /proc/loadavg                     # 0.52 0.44 0.39 2/431 40567
PathShows
/proc/PID/status, statstate, memory (VmRSS), threads, UIDs, signal masks
/proc/PID/fd/symlinks for every open fd (count them to find leaks)
/proc/PID/maps, smapsthe address-space layout (segments, libs, permissions)
/proc/PID/cmdline, environNUL-separated argv / env
/proc/PID/limitseffective rlimits
/proc/meminfo, loadavg, stat, net/*system-wide stats (what top, free, ss parse)
/proc/sys/*tunable kernel parameters (same as sysctl)

sysfs

/sys exposes the device model: buses, drivers, block devices (/sys/block), CPU topology and frequency, cgroup controllers (v2 under /sys/fs/cgroup), thermal, power. Writable attributes tune drivers/hardware.

$ cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/rotational   # 0 = SSD, 1 = spinning disk
$ cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cpufreq/scaling_governor
powersave
$ echo performance | sudo tee /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/scaling_governor
$ nproc; lscpu | grep -E 'Socket|Core|Thread'   # CPU topology (also under /sys)

Resource limits

getrlimit/setrlimit (shell: ulimit) cap per-process resources, each with a soft (current) and hard (ceiling) value:

  • RLIMIT_NOFILE — open fds (raise for servers).
  • RLIMIT_NPROC — processes/threads per user (fork-bomb guard).
  • RLIMIT_AS / RLIMIT_DATA — virtual memory.
  • RLIMIT_CORE — core-dump size (0 disables dumps).
  • RLIMIT_STACK, RLIMIT_CPU, RLIMIT_FSIZE.

cgroups (v2) are the modern, hierarchical way to limit CPU/memory/IO for a group of processes; systemd units set them declaratively.

$ ulimit -n            # 1024   (soft)
$ ulimit -Hn           # 1048576 (hard ceiling this user may raise to)
$ ulimit -c unlimited  # enable core dumps for this shell

# cgroup v2: cap a whole process tree, not just one process
$ systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=512M -p CPUQuota=50% ./job
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/job.scope/memory.current

Environment & argv

environ / getenv/setenv; inherited across fork, replaced or kept across exec. getopt/getopt_long for option parsing. Exit codes: 0 success, 1–125 app-defined, 126 not executable, 127 not found, 128+n killed by signal n.

$ FOO=bar ./child            # set in child's environment only
$ ./child; echo $?          # 0 ok
$ ./no-such-cmd; echo $?    # 127 = not found
$ /etc/hostname; echo $?    # 126 = found but not executable
$ sleep 5; # Ctrl-C ; echo $?   # 130 = 128 + SIGINT(2)

# the environment is just a NUL-separated blob:
$ cat /proc/self/environ | tr '\0' '\n' | head
Cheat Sheet
  • /proc/PID/: status/stat (state, RSS), fd/ (open fds — leak hunting), maps/smaps (address space), cmdline/environ, limits.
  • /proc/sys/* == sysctl tunables; /proc/meminfo, loadavg, net/* feed top/free/ss.
  • /sys: device model, block devices, CPU freq/topology, cgroup v2 (/sys/fs/cgroup).
  • rlimits (soft/hard) via ulimit/setrlimit: NOFILE (fds), NPROC, AS, CORE, STACK, CPU.
  • cgroups v2 for grouped CPU/mem/IO limits (systemd sets them).
  • Exit codes: 0 ok, 126 not executable, 127 not found, 128+n signal n.
  • Env inherited across fork; kept/replaced across exec (via envp).
Q&A
How do you see all the file descriptors a running process has open?
ls -l /proc/PID/fd (each entry is a symlink to the file/socket/pipe). lsof -p PID is the friendlier front-end. Watch the count over time to spot leaks.
What's the difference between soft and hard resource limits?
The soft limit is the value currently enforced; a process can raise its own soft limit up to the hard limit. Only a privileged process can raise the hard limit. ulimit -Sn / -Hn show them.
How do you change a kernel tunable like net.core.somaxconn at runtime?
sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=1024 or echo 1024 > /proc/sys/net/core/somaxconn; persist it in /etc/sysctl.d/.
Where do you read a process's resident memory size?
/proc/PID/status (the VmRSS line) or /proc/PID/statm (field 2 × page size). /proc/PID/smaps_rollup gives a finer breakdown (PSS, shared/private).
What does exit code 127 from a shell command mean?
"Command not found" — the shell couldn't locate the executable on $PATH. 126 means it was found but not executable; 128+n means it was killed by signal n.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What kind of filesystem is /proc?
A virtual (in-memory, kernel-generated) filesystem — the files don't exist on disk; reading them queries kernel state.
Shell command to raise the open-file limit for the current session?
ulimit -n 65536 (up to the hard limit).
Where does free get its numbers?
/proc/meminfo.

Intermediate core

A service crashes but produces no core dump. Checklist?
