Describe refactoring a "big ball of mud" module toward a clean design without a rewrite.
Work in small, safe steps under a growing test net — the "strangler fig" approach at module scale. (1) Characterisation tests first: pin the current behaviour (including its bugs) with tests at the module's boundary, so any refactor that changes observable behaviour fails loudly. Use approval/golden-master tests if the module is hard to assert on. (2) Find seams: identify the module's real inputs/outputs and introduce an interface at that boundary; route callers through it. Now you have a place to insert new implementations. (3) Extract the easy wins: pull pure functions out (no dependencies → trivially testable), then classes with a single clear responsibility, using automated refactorings (extract method/class) which are behaviour-preserving. (4) Break dependencies: where the tangle is a class that news up its collaborators / hits the DB / reads globals, apply "dependency-breaking" techniques (extract-and-override, parameterise constructor, wrap the static) to get it under test, then refactor its internals. (5) Introduce the new design alongside the old: build the clean version of a slice behind a feature flag or a routing switch; migrate one use case at a time; delete the old path once traffic is fully on the new one. (6) Package by feature as you go, so each extracted piece lands in a cohesive home. (7) Keep each commit shippable and reviewed — never a multi-week branch. The discipline: every step is small enough to verify, the module keeps working the whole time, and you can stop at any point with the codebase better than you found it. This is slower than a rewrite on paper but far less risky — rewrites of understood-badly systems routinely lose edge-case knowledge and take longer than estimated.

Interview Framework & Estimation

A repeatable structure for the 45 minutes, and the numbers to do capacity math in your head.

Notes

The structure

  1. Clarify (5 min) — functional requirements, non-functional (scale, latency, availability, consistency), and explicit non-goals. Nail down the 2–3 features you'll design.
  2. Estimate (3 min) — QPS (avg & peak), storage/year, bandwidth, and whether it fits on one machine. These numbers drive every later decision.
  3. API (3 min) — the handful of endpoints, their shapes.
  4. Data model (5 min) — entities, access patterns, then choose storage (SQL / KV / doc / column / blob) from the access patterns.
  5. High-level design (10 min) — boxes and arrows: clients → LB → stateless app tier → caches / DB / queue / object store. Walk the main read and write paths.
  6. Deep dive (10 min) — the interviewer picks 1–2 areas; go deep: sharding key, cache invalidation, fan-out, consistency.
  7. Bottlenecks & wrap (5 min) — single points of failure, hot spots, what breaks at 10× scale, monitoring.
# API sketch produced in step 3 — a few endpoints, explicit shapes
POST /v1/urls        {url}            -> 201 {shortCode}
GET  /{shortCode}                     -> 302 Location: <long url>
GET  /v1/urls/{code}/stats            -> 200 {clicks, createdAt}

# step 4: pick storage FROM the access pattern, not by habit
#   lookup is by exact key, read-heavy, tiny values -> KV store (not a JOIN-y RDBMS)

Latency numbers to know (order of magnitude)

Operation~Time
L1 / branch mispredict~1 ns / ~5 ns
Main memory reference~100 ns
Mutex lock/unlock~25 ns
Compress 1 KB~1–3 µs
SSD random read~16–100 µs
Datacenter round trip~0.5 ms
Read 1 MB sequentially from SSD~50–200 µs
Disk seek (HDD)~5–10 ms
Cross-continent round trip~100–150 ms
# Use them to reason about a design, e.g. "render needs 30 sequential DB reads":
#   30 x 0.5 ms datacenter RTT      = 15 ms   -> fine
#   30 x 100 ms cross-continent RTT = 3 s     -> must co-locate or batch
# and "serve 1 MB image from disk vs memory":
#   SSD seq read ~100 us  vs  RAM ~100x faster -> cache hot objects in RAM/CDN

Estimation shortcuts

  • 1 day ≈ 86,400 s ≈ 10⁵ s. So 1M requests/day ≈ ~12 QPS average; multiply by 2–10 for peak.
  • 1 char ≈ 1 byte; a "tweet" ~300 B; a small row ~1–2 KB; a photo ~1–5 MB; a minute of video ~10–50 MB.
  • Storage/year = writes/sec × bytes/write × 3×10⁷ s.
  • A modern server: ~tens of thousands of simple QPS, ~64–256 GB RAM, ~10–40 TB SSD, ~10–25 Gbps NIC.
# Worked example: Twitter-scale timeline
writes  = 500e6 tweets/day / 86400        # ~5,800 tweet writes/sec avg
peak_w  = writes * 3                       # ~17k/sec
reads   = 200e9 timeline views/day / 86400 # ~2.3M reads/sec  -> read:write ~400:1
storage = 500e6 * 300 * 365 * 3            # bytes/yr = count x size x days x replicas
        # ~= 164 TB/yr  -> does NOT fit one box -> shard + blob store for media
Cheat Sheet
  • Flow: clarify → estimate → API → data model → high-level (LB → stateless app → cache/DB/queue/blob) → deep dive → bottlenecks.
  • Always: functional + non-functional (scale, latency, availability, consistency) + non-goals.
  • Estimate QPS (avg & peak ×2–10), storage/year, bandwidth; check "fits on one box?".
  • 1M/day ≈ 12 QPS avg. Day ≈ 10⁵ s. Storage/yr = wps × bytes × 3×10⁷.
  • Memory ~100 ns, SSD read ~50 µs, DC RTT ~0.5 ms, cross-continent ~100 ms, HDD seek ~10 ms.
  • Choose storage from access patterns, not by default.
  • Keep the app tier stateless (state in DB/cache/session store) so it scales horizontally.
Q&A
Roughly how many QPS is 1 million requests per day?
~12 average (1M / 86,400). Design for peak, which is typically 2–10× the average depending on the traffic pattern — so plan for ~50–120 QPS.
What's the order-of-magnitude latency of a main-memory access vs a datacenter round trip?
~100 nanoseconds for memory; ~0.5 milliseconds (500,000 ns) for an in-datacenter RPC round trip — about 5000×. Cross-continent is ~100–150 ms, another ~300×.
Why estimate before designing?
The numbers decide the architecture: 10 QPS and 10 GB fits on one machine (design accordingly); 1M QPS and 100 TB/year forces sharding, caching, and async processing from the start. Designing without numbers leads to over- or under-engineering.
Why keep the application tier stateless?
So you can add/remove instances freely behind a load balancer without session affinity, and any instance can serve any request. Session/user state goes to a shared store (Redis, DB, or a signed token).
How do you pick a datastore in the interview?
From the access patterns: key lookups by id → KV; queries across fields / transactions → relational; whole-aggregate documents / flexible schema → document; huge write volume with known query shapes → wide-column; large binary objects → blob store; relationships / traversal → graph. State the pattern, then the choice.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

First step when given a system design prompt?
Clarify requirements — functional, non-functional (scale/latency/availability/consistency), and what's out of scope.
Seconds in a day, to one significant figure?
~90,000 (86,400) — often rounded to 10⁵ for mental math.
Where should user session state live in a horizontally scaled web tier?
In a shared store (Redis / DB) or a signed client token — not in an app instance's memory.

Intermediate core

Estimate storage for a service ingesting 5,000 events/sec, each ~500 bytes, retained 1 year.
5,000 × 500 B = 2.5 MB/s. × 86,400 s/day ≈ 216 GB/day. × 365 ≈ ~79 TB/year raw. Add ~1.5–3× for indexes/replication overhead → ~120–240 TB. Conclusion: doesn't fit one node → you need partitioning + a retention/compaction strategy (or tiered storage: hot in a fast store, cold in object storage / parquet).
A read-heavy service does 50k QPS, each request 1 DB query at 2 ms. How many DB connections/replicas roughly?
By Little's Law, concurrency = throughput × latency = 50,000 × 0.002 s = 100 in-flight queries at any instant. So you need ~100 usable connections (plus headroom, say 150–200) across the read replicas. If one replica sustains ~10k QPS of this query, you need ~5–6 replicas (plus one for redundancy). Caching the hot reads (say 90% hit rate) cuts DB QPS to ~5k → 1–2 replicas.

Advanced deep

How do you reason about the "does it fit on one machine?" question, and why does it matter so much?
Compare your estimated working set and throughput against a single modern server: ~128–512 GB RAM, ~10–40 TB NVMe, ~25–100 Gbps network, and — for the CPU — anywhere from a few thousand to hundreds of thousands of "simple" operations/sec depending on how much work each does (a Redis GET: ~100k+/s/core; a complex query with joins: dozens/s). Check four dimensions: (1) Does the hot dataset fit in RAM? If yes, you can serve reads from memory on one box and the design collapses to "one replicated node + backups". If no, you're doing disk I/O per read and need caching or sharding. (2) Does peak QPS × per-request CPU exceed one machine's cores? If yes, you need a horizontally scalable stateless tier. (3) Does storage/year exceed one machine's disk? If yes, sharding or object storage. (4) Does peak bandwidth exceed the NIC? (matters for media/CDN-shaped systems). It matters because the moment you can't fit on one machine, you inherit distributed-systems problems — partitioning, replication, consistency trade-offs, partial failure, cross-node coordination — which are an order of magnitude more design and operational complexity. A strong answer explicitly says "at this scale it fits on one primary with read replicas and we're done; at 100× we'd shard by X" — showing you scale the design effort to the actual requirements rather than reaching for Kafka and 20 microservices for 100 QPS.
What non-functional requirements do candidates most often forget to pin down, and how does each change the design?
(1) Consistency requirement per operation — "must a user see their own write immediately?" (read-your-writes), "can two users briefly see different values?" (eventual OK), "does money/inventory need strict serializability?". This decides single-primary vs multi-primary, sync vs async replication, whether you can use a cache freely, and whether you need distributed transactions or can use a saga. (2) Availability target — 99.9% (~8.8 h/yr down) vs 99.99% (~52 min) vs 99.999% changes whether you need multi-AZ, multi-region, active-active, and how much redundancy/failover automation. (3) Latency SLO and at which percentile — "p50 < 100 ms" is very different from "p99.9 < 200 ms"; tail latency drives timeouts, hedged requests, connection-pool sizing, and whether synchronous fan-out is acceptable. (4) Durability — "can we lose the last few seconds of writes on a crash?" decides sync vs async commit, replication factor, and whether an in-memory queue is acceptable. (5) Read:write ratio — 100:1 (cache everything, read replicas) vs 1:1 (caching helps less, write path is the bottleneck) vs write-heavy (LSM storage, batching, async). (6) Data retention & deletion — GDPR "delete on request", retention limits, and audit requirements change storage choice and add a deletion pipeline. (7) Traffic shape — steady vs spiky (flash sale, viral event) decides autoscaling, queue buffering, and pre-provisioning. (8) Cost sensitivity — sometimes a stated constraint. Asking about these early, and restating "so we're optimising for availability over consistency here, correct?", is a strong signal and prevents designing the wrong system confidently.

Load Balancing

Spreading traffic across servers, removing dead ones, and where the LB itself can fail.

Notes

L4 vs L7

L4 (transport)L7 (application)
Routes byIP + portURL path, Host, headers, cookies
Sees payloadnoyes (terminates the connection, often TLS)
Cost / featuresfast, cheap, protocol-agnosticretries, rewrites, path routing, WAF, canary — more CPU
ExamplesAWS NLB, IPVS, hardware LBsnginx, HAProxy, Envoy, ALB
# L7 (nginx): route by path, terminate TLS, retry idempotent failures
upstream api  { server 10.0.1.11:8080; server 10.0.1.12:8080; }
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    location /api/ {
        proxy_pass http://api;
        proxy_next_upstream error timeout http_502;   # retry a dead backend
    }
    location /static/ { root /var/www; }              # L7 can branch on the URL; L4 cannot
}

Algorithms

  • Round robin (+ weighted) — simple, good when requests are uniform.
  • Least connections / least response time — adapts to uneven request cost.
  • Consistent hashing — same key → same backend (cache affinity, sticky routing) with minimal remap on membership change.
  • IP hash — cheap client→backend stickiness.
# Consistent hashing: key -> point on a ring -> next node clockwise.
# Adding/removing 1 of N nodes remaps only ~1/N of keys (vs nearly all with key % N).
ring = sorted(hash(f"{node}#{v}") for node in nodes for v in range(150))  # 150 vnodes/node = balance

def route(key):
    h = hash(key)
    i = bisect.bisect(ring, h) % len(ring)
    return owner[ring[i]]                 # same key -> same backend -> cache stays warm

Health checks & failure

  • Active: LB probes each backend (/healthz) and ejects failing ones. Passive: mark a backend down after N consecutive request errors.
  • Distinguish "liveness" (process up) from "readiness" (can serve — DB connected, caches warm). Drain connections gracefully on deploy.
  • The LB is a SPOF → run it redundantly: a VIP with failover (keepalived/VRRP), an anycast address, or a managed LB across AZs. Global traffic uses DNS/GeoDNS/anycast to pick a region, then a regional LB.
# Two probe endpoints with different meaning:
GET /livez   -> 200 if the process is running          # fail => restart the pod
GET /readyz  -> 200 only if DB reachable AND caches warm  # fail => pull from LB, don't restart

# HAProxy: eject after 3 failed checks, re-add after 2 good ones
server s1 10.0.1.11:8080 check inter 2s fall 3 rise 2

Sticky sessions

Pin a client to one backend (cookie or IP hash). Needed only if the backend holds per-session state — the better fix is stateless backends (session in Redis / signed token) so any request can go anywhere, enabling free scaling and deploys.

// Stateful backend NEEDS stickiness (fragile):
Cookie: SRVID=server2            // server2 dies -> that user's session is gone

// Better: stateless backend, session lives in shared store -> no stickiness needed
session = redis.get("sess:" + cookie.sid)   // any backend can serve any request
// or a signed token the client carries: JWT / cookie with HMAC, server keeps nothing

Autoscaling

Scale the backend pool on a signal (CPU, request rate, queue depth, p99 latency). Scale out fast, in slowly (avoid flapping). Pre-warm for known spikes. The LB must pick up new instances automatically (service discovery / target groups).

# Kubernetes HPA: scale on CPU, out fast / in slow to avoid flapping
metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60 } }
behavior:
  scaleUp:   { stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0,   policies: [{ type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 30 }] }
  scaleDown: { stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300, policies: [{ type: Pods,    value: 1,   periodSeconds: 60 }] }
Cheat Sheet
  • L4: routes by IP:port, payload-blind, fast, connection-preserving. L7: reads HTTP, path/host/header routing, TLS termination, retries, canary.
  • Algorithms: round-robin / weighted (uniform), least-connections / least-latency (uneven cost), consistent-hash (cache affinity), IP-hash (cheap stickiness).
  • Health: active probe (/healthz) + passive ejection; separate liveness vs readiness; graceful connection draining on deploy.
  • LB is a SPOF → redundant (VIP+VRRP, anycast, multi-AZ managed LB). Global: DNS/GeoDNS/anycast → regional LB.
  • Sticky sessions only if backends are stateful — prefer stateless (session in Redis/token).
  • Autoscale on CPU / RPS / queue depth / p99; out fast, in slow; service discovery so the LB sees new instances.
Q&A
When do you need an L7 load balancer?
When routing decisions depend on request content — send /api and /static to different pools, route by Host for multi-tenant, do path-based canary/blue-green, terminate TLS centrally, or apply a WAF. If you only need "spread TCP connections across identical servers", L4 is faster and cheaper.
Liveness vs readiness health check?
Liveness = "is the process alive?" (restart it if not). Readiness = "can it serve traffic now?" (has DB connections, caches warm, not overloaded). The LB routes only to ready instances; an instance can be live but temporarily not ready (starting up, reconnecting).
Why is consistent hashing used for load balancing in front of caches?
It maps a key to the same backend most of the time, so cache hit rates stay high, and when a backend is added/removed only ~1/N of keys move — avoiding the mass cache-miss stampede that plain modulo hashing causes.
The load balancer is a single point of failure. How do you address that?
Run it redundantly: an active/standby pair sharing a virtual IP with fast failover (VRRP/keepalived), an anycast IP announced from multiple nodes, or a cloud managed LB that's inherently multi-AZ. For multi-region, DNS or anycast directs users to a region and a regional LB pair handles it from there.
How do you avoid needing sticky sessions?
Make the backends stateless — store session data in a shared store (Redis) or a signed/encrypted cookie/JWT the client sends each request. Then any instance can serve any request, so you can scale and deploy without worrying about affinity.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which LB layer can route by URL path?
Layer 7 (application).
Which algorithm adapts to backends handling requests of very different cost?
Least connections (or least response time).
What removes a crashed backend from rotation?
Health checks (active probing or passive error-based ejection).

Intermediate core

After a deploy, users get errors for ~30 s even though the new instances are healthy. Cause and fix?
Old instances were killed before the LB stopped sending them traffic, or new instances were added to rotation before they were actually ready (still warming caches / opening DB pools). Fix: on shutdown, first fail the readiness check (LB drains), wait for in-flight requests to finish (connection draining with a timeout), then exit. On startup, don't pass readiness until dependencies are connected and warm. Use rolling deploys with maxUnavailable small, and health-check grace periods.
Your service is behind one LB in one AZ. Design for AZ failure.
Run backends in ≥2 (ideally 3) AZs, and a cross-AZ load balancer (cloud managed LBs span AZs by default; for self-managed, an LB pair per AZ behind a global entry). The database needs a multi-AZ setup too (a standby in another AZ with automatic failover, or a quorum across 3 AZs). DNS/anycast at the top so if a whole region degrades you can shift traffic. Test with game days / chaos experiments that actually kill an AZ's instances.

Advanced deep

Why can "least connections" load balancing perform badly, and what's the modern alternative?
Classic least-connections works well only when every backend is identical and every request costs the same amount of the resource that matters. Failure modes: (1) a backend that's slow (GC pause, degraded disk, noisy neighbour) accumulates connections and, counterintuitively, attracts more under least-connections in some implementations, or is avoided so hard it never recovers — and "connection count" doesn't capture "this box is at 95% CPU". (2) In a large fleet behind multiple LB instances, each LB only sees its own connections, so global balance is poor. (3) Long-lived connections (HTTP/2, gRPC, websockets) break the model — connection count is nearly constant regardless of load. The modern approach: power of two choices (pick two backends at random, send to the less-loaded — provably close to optimal balance with O(1) state and no global coordination, used by Envoy, Finagle, NGINX Plus); latency-/EWMA-based weighting where each backend's recent response-time and error-rate feed a dynamic weight (Netflix's approach), so a degrading backend sheds load automatically; outlier detection (eject a backend that's returning 5xx or timing out at an anomalous rate, re-admit gradually); and for request-level fairness with expensive requests, concurrency limiting per backend (a token per in-flight request) plus load-based shedding. For gRPC/HTTP-2 you also need request-level LB (each RPC balanced independently) not connection-level, often via a client-side LB (xDS/Envoy) or an L7 proxy that de-multiplexes streams.
Explain how a large service actually routes a user request from their browser to a specific backend process, layer by layer.
(1) DNS: the browser resolves api.example.com; the authoritative DNS (often GeoDNS / a traffic manager like Route 53, NS1, Akamai) returns an IP for the nearest healthy region/PoP based on the resolver's location and per-region health, with a low TTL so it can shift traffic. Some providers return an anycast IP instead, and BGP routes the packets to the nearest edge. (2) Edge / CDN PoP: the anycast IP terminates at a CDN edge that may serve cached static content directly, or (for dynamic API traffic) terminates TLS and proxies onward over a warm, optimised backbone connection to the origin region. (3) Regional L4 LB: at the origin, a layer-4 load balancer (hardware, or IPVS/Maglev-style ECMP where routers hash flows across many LB nodes, each LB node consistently hashing the 4-tuple to a backend so connections stay pinned) spreads connections across the L7 proxy tier. Google's Maglev and Cloudflare's Unimog are examples — they give per-flow consistency without shared state so LB nodes are stateless and horizontally scalable. (4) L7 proxy tier (Envoy / nginx / a service mesh ingress): parses HTTP, does path/host routing, applies auth/rate-limit/WAF, picks the target service, and load-balances at the request level across that service's instances — using power-of-two-choices or EWMA weights, honouring outlier detection and per-instance concurrency limits, and re-resolving the instance list from service discovery (Consul, EDS/xDS, Kubernetes endpoints) as instances come and go. (5) Backend instance: the request lands on one process; if that process is itself multi-threaded/async, an internal work queue or thread pool assigns it to a worker. Cross-cutting: every hop has its own health checking and connection draining, timeouts are set to decrease at each inner layer (so an inner call times out before the outer one gives up), retries are budgeted (retry only at one layer, with a cap, to avoid retry storms), and the whole path is traced (a trace/span id propagated in headers) so you can see where a slow request spent its time.

Caching Strategies & Invalidation

Where to cache, which read/write pattern, and the two hard problems: invalidation and stampede.

Notes

Where

Client / browser → CDN edge → API gateway → in-process (per app instance) → distributed (Redis/Memcached) → database buffer pool. Cache as close to the client as the freshness requirement allows.

# Same value, cached at every layer — each with a shorter reach + its own TTL
Browser:  Cache-Control: private, max-age=60        # 1 user, 60 s
CDN edge: Cache-Control: public,  s-maxage=300       # all users in a region, 5 min
App L1:   Caffeine maxSize=10_000, expireAfterWrite=5s  # per instance, tiny + short
Redis L2: SET post:42 <json> EX 3600                 # shared across instances, 1 h
# rule: cache as close to the client as the freshness requirement allows

Read patterns

PatternHow
Cache-aside (lazy)app checks cache; on miss, reads DB, populates cache. Most common; cache only holds what's asked for.
Read-throughapp asks the cache; the cache library fetches from DB on miss. Same effect, logic in the cache layer.
# Cache-aside read: the app owns the miss path
def get_post(pid):
    key = f"post:{pid}"
    v = redis.get(key)
    if v is not None:
        return json.loads(v)            # hit
    row = db.query("SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id=%s", pid)   # miss -> source of truth
    redis.set(key, json.dumps(row), ex=3600)               # fill, always with a TTL
    return row

Write patterns

PatternTrade-off
Write-throughwrite DB + cache synchronously — cache always fresh, writes slower.
Write-back (write-behind)write cache, flush to DB async — fast writes, risk of loss on cache crash, DB lags.
Write-aroundwrite DB only, skip cache — avoids polluting cache with write-once data; next read is a miss.

Common combo: cache-aside reads + write-through-or-invalidate on writes. On a write, either update the cache entry or (safer) delete it so the next read repopulates — avoids stale-write races.

def update_post(pid, patch):
    db.execute("UPDATE posts SET ... WHERE id=%s", pid)  # 1. source of truth first
    redis.delete(f"post:{pid}")                        # 2. delete, don't set
    # why delete not set: two concurrent writers that each SET can interleave and
    # leave the OLDER value in cache. delete -> next read reloads the committed row.

The hard problems

  • Invalidation: keeping the cache consistent with the source. Options: short TTLs (accept bounded staleness), explicit delete on write, versioned keys (user:123:v7), or a change-data-capture stream that invalidates. "There are only two hard things… cache invalidation."
  • Stampede / dogpile: a hot key expires and thousands of requests all miss and hit the DB at once. Fixes: per-key single-flight (one request recomputes, others wait), probabilistic early expiry (refresh slightly before TTL), serve-stale-while-revalidate, or a lock in the cache.
  • Hot key: one key hotter than a single cache node can serve — replicate it to multiple nodes, or add a tiny local L1 with a 1–5 s TTL.
  • Thundering herd on cold start: a fresh/flushed cache means every request misses — warm it, or ramp traffic.
# Stampede fix: only ONE caller recomputes a hot expired key; the rest serve stale
def get(key, ttl, recompute):
    v, exp = redis.hmget(key, "v", "exp")
    if v and time.time() < float(exp):
        return v                                   # fresh
    if redis.set(key + ":lock", 1, nx=True, ex=10):  # won the lock -> refresh
        nv = recompute()
        redis.hset(key, mapping={"v": nv, "exp": time.time() + ttl})
        redis.delete(key + ":lock")
        return nv
    return v or recompute()                       # others: serve slightly stale, no DB pile-up
Cheat Sheet
  • Layers: client → CDN → gateway → in-process → Redis/Memcached → DB buffer pool.
  • Reads: cache-aside (app manages) or read-through (cache library manages). Cache-aside is the default.
  • Writes: write-through (fresh, slower), write-back (fast, lossy), write-around (skip cache for write-once).
  • On write: delete the cache key (repopulate on next read) — safer than update against races.
  • Invalidation: short TTL, explicit delete, versioned keys, or CDC-driven.
  • Stampede: per-key single-flight, early/probabilistic refresh, stale-while-revalidate, lock.
  • Hot key: replicate across nodes or add a short-TTL local L1. Cold cache: warm it / ramp.
  • Cache hit rate is the metric — watch it; a drop means wrong keys, too-short TTL, or churn.
Q&A
What is cache-aside?
The application checks the cache first; on a miss it reads the database, then writes the value into the cache before returning. The cache only ever holds data that's been requested. It's the most common pattern and keeps caching logic in the app.
On a write, should you update the cache entry or delete it?
Deleting is safer. Updating from the write path can race with a concurrent read that repopulates with a stale DB value, leaving the cache wrong. Deleting forces the next read to fetch fresh from the DB. (Update is fine if you have a single writer per key or a version check.)
What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?
When a popular key expires, many concurrent requests all miss and hit the backing store simultaneously, overloading it. Prevent with per-key single-flight (only one request recomputes; the rest wait for its result), refreshing the value slightly before it expires (probabilistic early expiration), or serving the stale value while one request refreshes in the background.
Write-through vs write-back?
Write-through updates the cache and the database synchronously on every write — the cache is always consistent but writes are as slow as the DB. Write-back updates the cache immediately and flushes to the DB asynchronously — writes are fast, but a cache crash can lose unflushed writes and the DB is temporarily behind.
How do you handle a "hot key" that's read more than one cache node can handle?
Replicate that key across multiple cache nodes (route reads randomly among them), or add a small in-process L1 cache on each app server with a very short TTL (1–5 s) to absorb the request volume, accepting a few seconds of staleness for that key.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

In cache-aside, who populates the cache on a miss?
The application — it reads the DB and writes the value into the cache.
Which write strategy risks losing data if the cache crashes?
Write-back (write-behind) — writes buffered in the cache aren't yet persisted.
Simple way to bound cache staleness?
A short TTL on entries.

Intermediate core

A profile page caches the user's data for 10 min. The user edits their name and it doesn't update for 10 min. Fix.
Invalidate on write: when the profile is updated, delete user:{id}:profile from the cache (and any derived keys like a rendered card), so the next read repopulates with fresh data. Keep a modest TTL as a backstop for missed invalidations. If the user must see their own change instantly even before propagation, do read-your-writes: after the write, either bypass the cache for that user's next read or write the new value into their session/local cache.
Your Redis cache node fails; the database immediately falls over. What went wrong and how do you prevent it?
The DB was sized assuming the cache absorbs, say, 95% of reads; losing the cache 20×'d its load instantly (cache-loss stampede). Mitigations: (1) run the cache as a replicated cluster so a single node loss only drops its shard, and clients fail over; (2) on cache miss/error, protect the DB with per-key single-flight and a concurrency limiter / circuit breaker so it degrades (higher latency, some 503s) rather than collapses; (3) keep a small local L1 on app servers so a cache outage still serves hot keys; (4) capacity-plan the DB for "cache cold" as a survivable-degraded mode, and load-test it; (5) warm the cache gradually on recovery rather than letting full traffic hit a cold cache.

Advanced deep

Design cache invalidation for a system where one source record feeds many derived, cached views (e.g. a product feeds search results, category pages, recommendation blocks, the product page itself).
Point invalidation from the write path won't scale — the writer would have to know every derived view. Use change-data-capture + a fan-out invalidation pipeline. (1) Every write to the product goes to the DB and emits a change event (via the transactional outbox pattern or a CDC connector like Debezium reading the WAL — so the event is guaranteed iff the write committed). (2) A consumer maps product:{id} changed to the set of affected cache keys. For directly-keyed views (product:{id}) that's a delete. For derived views (search results containing this product, category page N) you have choices: dependency tracking — when a view is cached, also record "this view depends on products [a,b,c]" in a reverse index, so an invalidation looks up dependents and deletes them (accurate, but the reverse index is extra state and can get large); or tag/generation-based — tag each cached search/category entry with a catalog-generation counter, bump the generation on any catalog change, and lazily treat older-generation entries as misses (cheap, but over-invalidates — one product change busts all category caches). A middle ground: coarse tags (per category, per brand) so a change busts only related views. (3) For high-churn source data, don't invalidate at all — use short TTLs + stale-while-revalidate on the derived views and accept seconds of lag; reserve precise invalidation for the product page itself and price/availability. (4) Make invalidation idempotent and retry-safe (deleting a key twice is fine) and monitor the pipeline lag — a stalled invalidation consumer silently serves stale data, so alert on consumer lag and have a periodic full TTL sweep as a backstop. (5) For CDN-cached HTML, use surrogate keys / cache tags (Fastly, Cloudflare) so one API call purges all edge copies tagged with product-{id}.
Explain the negative-cache and "cache penetration" problem, and how to defend a database from queries for keys that don't exist.
Cache penetration: requests for keys that don't exist in the DB always miss the cache (nothing to cache) and hit the DB every time — an attacker (or a buggy client) hammering random/enumerated ids can bypass the cache entirely and overload the database, even though the cache is "working". Defenses: (1) Negative caching — cache the "not found" result too, with a short TTL (e.g. 30–60 s), so repeated lookups for a missing key are served from cache. Keep the TTL short so a key that's later created isn't shadowed for long, or invalidate the negative entry on create. (2) Bloom filter (or cuckoo filter) in front of the cache/DB containing all valid keys: a lookup first checks the filter; a "definitely not present" answer short-circuits to 404 without touching cache or DB. The filter is small (a few bits per key), rebuilt/updated as keys are added, and its false-positive rate just means an occasional real lookup for a non-key (acceptable). This is what Redis/CDN edge configs and many read-heavy services use. (3) Input validation — reject malformed/out-of-range ids before they reach the cache layer. (4) Rate limiting per client on 404-heavy traffic. (5) For enumeration attacks, use non-sequential/opaque ids so an attacker can't just count up. The combination of a Bloom filter for the bulk "key doesn't exist" case plus short-TTL negative caching for the ones that slip through, behind a rate limiter, keeps the DB protected from both accidental and malicious penetration.

Database Scaling: Replication & Sharding

Scale reads with replicas, scale writes with shards — and pay for both in complexity.

Notes

The ladder (do these in order)

  1. Optimise: indexes, query rewrites, connection pooling, schema fixes. Buys a lot.
  2. Scale up: bigger box (more RAM = more of the working set cached). Simple; has a ceiling.
  3. Caching: offload reads to Redis/CDN (see Caching topic).
  4. Read replicas: async copies of the primary; route reads to them, writes to the primary.
  5. Functional partitioning: split by feature (users DB, orders DB, analytics DB).
  6. Sharding: horizontally split one dataset across many primaries by a shard key. Last resort — big complexity jump.
-- Rungs 1-2 first: an index often beats a bigger box
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
-- Seq Scan ... rows=2,000,000  (cost=0..48000)   <-- reads the whole table

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_time ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC);
-- Index Scan ... rows=20  (cost=0..1.2)          <-- now O(log n) + 20 rows

Replication

  • Async (default): fast writes, but replicas lag — a read right after a write may see stale data (replication lag). Handle with: read-your-writes routing (send that user's reads to the primary briefly), or wait-for-LSN.
  • Sync / semi-sync: primary waits for ≥1 replica to ack — no data loss on primary failure, higher write latency.
  • Failover: promote a replica when the primary dies (automatic with a coordinator; watch for split-brain — fence the old primary).
# Route reads to replicas, writes to primary — but read-your-writes for the author
def route(query, user):
    if query.is_write:
        return primary
    if now() - last_write_time[user] < 2.0:   # wrote in the last 2 s
        return primary                          # avoid showing them stale data
    return least_lagged(replicas)               # everyone else: replica (skip if lag > 1 s)

Sharding

  • Shard key choice is everything: it must spread load evenly and keep related data together. Range-based (easy scans, risk of hot ranges), hash-based (even spread, no range scans), or directory/lookup-based (flexible, extra hop).
  • Hotspots: a celebrity user, a "today" partition — mitigate with key salting, sub-sharding hot keys, or a separate tier.
  • Cross-shard queries & transactions are expensive (scatter-gather, 2PC/saga). Design so the common queries hit one shard.
  • Resharding (adding shards) is painful — use consistent hashing / virtual buckets from the start so you move ~1/N of data, and build it online (dual-write + backfill + cutover).
# Fixed virtual buckets decouple key placement from physical shard count
BUCKETS = 4096
def shard_for(key):
    b = crc32(key) % BUCKETS
    return bucket_map[b]        # {0..4095} -> physical shard; only this map changes on reshard

# co-locate a conversation's messages: shard by conversation_id, NOT message_id
#   shard_for(msg.conversation_id)   -> whole thread on one shard, single-shard reads
Cheat Sheet
  • Order: index/tune → scale up → cache → read replicas → functional split → shard. Don't skip to sharding.
  • Read replicas scale reads; sharding scales writes + storage.
  • Async replication → replication lag → stale reads. Fix with read-your-writes (route to primary) or LSN wait. Sync = no loss, slower writes.
  • Failover: promote a replica; fence the old primary to avoid split-brain.
  • Shard key: even distribution + co-locate related data. Hash (even, no ranges), range (scans, hot ranges), directory (flexible, extra hop).
  • Hotspots (celebrity, "today"): salt the key, sub-shard, or isolate.
  • Cross-shard joins/transactions are costly → design queries to hit one shard; use consistent hashing so resharding moves ~1/N.
  • Resharding online: dual-write + backfill + verify + cutover.
Q&A
Read replicas vs sharding — what does each solve?
Read replicas add read capacity (and read availability) by serving reads from async copies — but every replica still holds the whole dataset and all writes go to one primary, so write throughput and total storage aren't helped. Sharding splits the data across multiple independent primaries, so writes, storage, and working-set memory all scale — at a large jump in complexity.
What is replication lag and how do you deal with a "user edits then can't see the edit" bug?
Async replicas apply the primary's changes after a delay (ms to seconds under load). A read routed to a replica right after a write can miss it. Fixes: for a short window after a write, route that user's reads to the primary (read-your-writes); or have the write return the log position (LSN) and make the read wait until the chosen replica has applied at least that LSN; or cache the just-written value in the user's session.
What makes a good shard key?
It distributes both data volume and request load evenly (no hot shard), and it co-locates data that's queried together so common queries touch a single shard. E.g. shard a chat app by conversation_id so all messages of a conversation are together; sharding by message_id would scatter a conversation's history.
Why is resharding hard, and how do you make it less so?
Adding a shard with naive modulo hashing remaps almost every key, requiring a massive data move with the system live. Use consistent hashing or a large fixed number of virtual buckets mapped to physical shards, so adding capacity moves only ~1/N of the data. Do the migration online: dual-write to old and new locations, backfill historical data, verify, then flip reads and stop the dual-write.
How do you handle a cross-shard query like "all orders in the last hour across all users"?
Scatter-gather: query every shard in parallel and merge results in the app / a coordinator — acceptable if infrequent. For frequent cross-cutting queries, maintain a separate denormalized store (a search index, a time-series DB, or an analytics warehouse fed by CDC) optimised for that access pattern, rather than forcing the sharded OLTP store to serve it.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which scaling technique increases write throughput?
Sharding (horizontal partitioning across multiple primaries).
Where do writes go in a primary + read-replicas setup?
To the primary only. Reads can go to replicas.
What causes stale reads from a replica?
Replication lag — the replica hasn't yet applied the primary's latest changes.

Intermediate core

You shard users by hash(user_id). A query "get a user's 50 most recent orders" is now slow. Why, and fix?
Orders were probably sharded by order_id (or their own hash), so one user's orders are spread across all shards — the query becomes scatter-gather + merge + sort. Fix: co-locate — shard orders by user_id too (same shard function), so a user and all their orders live on one shard and the query is a single-shard indexed lookup. The trade-off: a query "all orders for product X" now scatters instead — you pick the shard key for the dominant access pattern and serve the other via a secondary index / search store.
Your primary DB is at 80% CPU, 95% reads. Cheapest effective next step?
Add read replicas and route reads to them — it directly offloads the 95%. Before that, verify indexes/queries are sane and add a cache for the hottest reads (which may drop primary load enough to need no replicas). Sharding would be premature here since it's a read problem, not a write/storage one.

Advanced deep

Walk through migrating a single-primary Postgres to a sharded setup with zero downtime.
(1) Choose the shard key from the dominant access pattern; decide on N logical buckets (e.g. 1024) mapped to a small number of physical shards, so future resharding just remaps buckets. (2) Introduce a routing layer in the app (or a proxy like Vitess/Citus) that computes bucket = hash(key) % 1024 → physical shard. Initially all buckets point at the existing DB — behaviour unchanged, but the indirection is in place. (3) Stand up the new shards (empty). (4) Dual-write: the app writes each row to both its current location and its target shard (in the same transaction where possible, or via the outbox so it's reliable). New data is now on both. (5) Backfill historical data to the target shards with a throttled batch job that reads by bucket range and copies, tracking progress; run it during low traffic, resumable. (6) Verify: a checksum/row-count comparison per bucket between old and new; reconcile discrepancies (usually rows changed mid-backfill — a second pass or a CDC-based catch-up). (7) Cut over reads bucket-by-bucket (or shard-by-shard): flip the routing so reads for migrated buckets go to the new shard; monitor error rate and lag; keep the ability to flip back. (8) Stop dual-writing to the old DB once all buckets are cut over and stable for a bake period. (9) Decommission the old DB (keep a backup). Throughout: feature-flag every step, migrate a canary bucket first, have a rollback for each phase, and watch replication lag, error rates, and query latency. The routing-by-bucket design means adding a 5th physical shard later is just "move ~1/5 of buckets" with the same dual-write/backfill/verify/cutover machinery, not another full migration.
What is a "hot shard" / "hot partition", give three real causes, and how do you fix each without a full reshard?
A hot shard receives disproportionate load, becoming the bottleneck while others idle. Cause 1: skewed key distribution — a few keys are far more active (a celebrity account with millions of followers, a viral post, a huge tenant on a multi-tenant DB sharded by tenant_id). Fix: sub-shard the hot key — split that one entity's data across multiple shards with a composite key (celebrity_id + bucket), fanning writes/reads across buckets and merging on read; or promote the hot entity to its own dedicated shard/instance. Cause 2: time-based key — sharding or a range index by timestamp means all current writes land on the "now" partition (append hotspot), classic in time-series and in DynamoDB/Cassandra with a monotonic partition key. Fix: salt the key with a random or hash prefix (shard = hash(id) % K combined with the day) so today's writes spread across K partitions; queries for a time range read all K and merge. Cause 3: pathological query pattern — a popular query (e.g. a leaderboard, a "trending" list, a global config row) that every request reads, all hitting the shard that owns that row. Fix: this is a caching problem, not a sharding one — cache the result aggressively (short TTL + stale-while-revalidate), replicate the row to every shard, or serve it from a dedicated read-optimised store. General mitigations that don't require resharding: per-key rate limiting to cap the damage, request coalescing/single-flight on the hot key, adaptive throttling on the hot shard so it sheds load rather than falling over, and a monitoring dashboard of per-shard QPS/CPU so hotspots are caught early (an unmonitored hot shard is how "the DB is slow" incidents start).

CAP & Consistency Models

What you give up during a partition, and the spectrum of "how fresh must a read be".

Notes

CAP, stated precisely

In a distributed store, during a network partition you must choose between Consistency (every read sees the latest write) and Availability (every request gets a non-error response). You cannot have both while partitioned. When there's no partition, you can have both.

  • CP: refuse requests on the minority side to stay consistent — etcd, ZooKeeper, HBase, Spanner.
  • AP: keep serving, reconcile later (eventual consistency) — Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak.
  • PACELC: extends it — if Partition then A or C; else trade Latency vs Consistency.
# Same request, two designs, during a partition of the replica set:

# CP store (etcd): write to the minority side is REJECTED
$ etcdctl put /lock/x "held"
Error: context deadline exceeded        # no quorum -> refuse -> caller must handle it

# AP store (Cassandra CL=ONE): write is ACCEPTED on whatever node is reachable
cqlsh> INSERT INTO cart (id, items) VALUES (42, [...]);   # succeeds, converges later
#   risk: a concurrent write on the other side -> conflict to reconcile (LWW / CRDT)

Consistency models (strongest → weakest)

ModelGuarantee
Linearizable / strongreads see the most recent completed write, as if one copy. Needs consensus / a leader.
Sequentialall clients see operations in the same order (not necessarily real-time).
Causaloperations that are causally related are seen in order; concurrent ones may differ.
Read-your-writesyou always see your own prior writes (others may lag).
Monotonic readsyou never see time go backwards on successive reads.
Eventualif writes stop, all replicas converge… eventually. Reads may be stale/out of order meanwhile.
// What each model rules out for the same history: write x=1, then write x=2
// linearizable : after the x=2 write returns, NO client can read x=1
// read-your-writes: the writer never reads x=1 again; another client still might
// monotonic reads : if you saw x=2 once, you never see x=1 afterwards
// eventual        : any client may read 1, 2, or (briefly) nothing, in any order

Quorums (Dynamo-style)

N replicas; a write waits for W acks, a read queries R. If W + R > N a read is guaranteed to see the latest write (overlap). Tunable per operation: W=N, R=1 (fast reads, slow/fragile writes), W=1, R=N (fast writes, slow reads), W=R=(N/2)+1 (balanced, majority). Doesn't give linearizability on its own (needs read-repair + anti-entropy, and it's still subject to concurrent-write conflicts).

# N = 3 replicas
W = 2; R = 2          # W + R = 4 > N = 3  -> read set and write set always overlap
                    # => a quorum read sees the latest quorum-acked write

W = 1; R = 1          # W + R = 2 < 3  -> fast, but a read can miss the newest write (stale)
W = 3; R = 1          # fast reads, but any one replica down -> writes fail

Choosing

Money, inventory, uniqueness → strong/linearizable (accept lower availability / higher latency). Feeds, likes, presence, analytics → eventual is fine (favour availability + latency). Often per-operation: strong for "reserve seat", eventual for "show seat map".

# Same feature, two consistency choices — pick per operation, not per system

# show the seat map: stale-by-a-few-seconds is fine -> eventual, hit a replica/cache
GET  /events/42/seats        -> replica read, Cache-Control: max-age=5

# reserve seat 12A: double-booking is unacceptable -> linearizable
POST /events/42/seats/12A/hold
   BEGIN; SELECT ... FOR UPDATE;                 # serialise on the leader
   INSERT hold WHERE NOT EXISTS(active hold);    # unique/conditional -> exactly one winner
   COMMIT;
Cheat Sheet
  • CAP: during a partition, pick C or A. No partition → can have both.
  • CP (etcd/ZK/Spanner) refuses on the minority side; AP (Cassandra/Dynamo) serves stale + reconciles.
  • PACELC: else, Latency vs Consistency.
  • Models: linearizable > sequential > causal > read-your-writes / monotonic reads > eventual.
  • Quorum: W + R > N ⇒ reads see latest write. Tune per op (W=N,R=1 / W=1,R=N / majority).
  • Strong needs consensus/leader (Raft/Paxos) → latency + reduced availability. Eventual = cheap + available.
  • Choose per operation: strong for money/inventory/uniqueness; eventual for feeds/likes/presence.
  • ACID consistency (constraints) ≠ CAP consistency (replica agreement).
Q&A
State CAP correctly.
When a network partition splits a distributed data store, it must sacrifice either consistency (some reads return stale/no data) or availability (some requests error). Without a partition, a system can provide both.
What does W + R > N guarantee in a quorum system?
That the set of replicas a read contacts (R) overlaps with the set the latest write reached (W) in at least one replica — so the read can observe the newest version (with versioning to pick it). It's necessary for strong-ish reads but not sufficient for linearizability (concurrent writes still need conflict resolution).
What is read-your-writes consistency?
A client is guaranteed to see the effects of its own previous writes on subsequent reads, even if other clients might still see stale data. Implemented by routing that client's reads to the primary (or a caught-up replica) for a window, or by including a version token.
Give an operation that needs strong consistency and one that doesn't.
Needs strong: reserving the last item in stock, transferring money, claiming a unique username — a stale read causes a real error. Fine with eventual: displaying a like count, a social feed, "user is online" — brief staleness is imperceptible and availability matters more.
Is a single-node database "CP" or "CA"?
CAP is about distributed systems; a single node isn't partition-tolerant at all. People loosely call it "CA", but really CAP doesn't apply until the data is replicated or partitioned across nodes.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

In CAP, what forces the C-vs-A choice?
A network partition — nodes can't communicate.
What does the E in PACELC stand for?
"Else" — the non-partition case (Latency vs Consistency trade-off).
Which is stronger: causal or eventual consistency?
Causal — it additionally guarantees causally-related operations are seen in order.

Intermediate core

A comment thread shows a reply before the comment it replies to. Which consistency model would prevent this, and how?
Causal consistency. The reply causally depends on the parent comment (it was written after reading it), so a causally-consistent store guarantees any client that sees the reply has already seen the parent. Implementation: attach causal metadata — a version vector or a "depends-on" set of the operations the writer had observed — and a replica only makes a write visible once it has applied that write's dependencies. Cheaper approximations: route a conversation's reads and writes through the same partition/replica (so ordering is naturally preserved), or on the client, buffer a reply until its parent is present.
You have N=3 replicas. What (W, R) for "writes must survive one node loss with no data loss, reads can be slightly stale"?
W = 2 (a write is acked by a majority, so it survives losing any one node — the surviving 2 always include at least one with the write). R = 1 is acceptable if slight staleness is OK and you rely on read-repair / anti-entropy to converge; if you want reads to see the latest confirmed write, use R = 2 so W + R = 4 > 3. The trade: R=1 gives faster, more available reads at the cost of occasionally serving a value that isn't the very latest.

Advanced deep

Why is "eventually consistent" not enough for a shopping cart, and what stronger-but-not-strong model do Dynamo-style systems actually provide?
Pure last-write-wins eventual consistency loses data: add item A on your phone, add item B on your laptop before replicas sync — LWW keeps only whichever write has the higher timestamp, and one item silently vanishes (Amazon's original Dynamo paper's motivating example). What you want is that concurrent updates merge rather than clobber. Dynamo provides causal consistency with conflict detection via version vectors: each object carries a vector clock; a write includes the version it read, so the store can tell whether a new write supersedes the current version (causally after — just replace) or is concurrent with it (neither dominates — keep both as sibling versions). On the next read the client gets all siblings and must reconcile — for a cart, "merge = union of items" (so A and B both survive; a removed item needs a tombstone or a per-item counter to not resurrect). This is strong eventual consistency: replicas that have received the same set of updates are in the same state, and the merge function is commutative/associative/idempotent so order and duplicates don't matter — the formalisation of which is CRDTs (a grow-only set, an OR-set for add/remove, a PN-counter for the quantity). The application pays with merge logic and metadata overhead, but never loses a user's action and stays available during partitions — the right trade for a cart, where "briefly showing an extra item" is far better than "dropped the thing they added".
How does Google Spanner claim to provide external consistency (linearizability) globally, seemingly beating CAP?
Spanner doesn't beat CAP — it's a CP system that chooses consistency and gives up availability during a partition (a minority partition can't serve reads/writes). What's notable is that it provides external consistency (a stronger-than-linearizable guarantee: if transaction T1 commits before T2 starts in real time, every observer sees T1 before T2) across data centres on different continents, which normally requires either coordinating on every operation (too slow) or accepting weaker consistency. It achieves this with TrueTime: a time API backed by GPS receivers and atomic clocks in every datacenter that returns an interval [earliest, latest] guaranteed to contain the true absolute time, with the uncertainty (ε) typically a few milliseconds. On commit, a transaction is assigned a timestamp s = TrueTime.now().latest, and Spanner then waits out the uncertainty ("commit wait") — it holds locks until TrueTime.now().earliest > s, i.e. until it's certain that real time has passed s everywhere — before making the write visible. This guarantees that any transaction that starts later (anywhere) gets a strictly higher timestamp, so timestamp order == real-time order == the serialization order. Reads at a timestamp are lock-free (MVCC snapshot reads) and can be served by any replica that's caught up to that timestamp. Underneath, each shard ("Paxos group") uses Paxos for replication and a leader; cross-shard transactions use 2PC across the Paxos leaders. The cost: commit latency includes ~2ε of commit-wait (so tightening clock sync directly improves latency — hence the atomic clocks), writes need a Paxos majority, and availability drops on partition. It's "CAP-compliant CP with unusually good latency and global linearizability, bought with special hardware for tight time bounds".

Message Queues & Async Processing

Decouple producers from consumers — and the delivery, ordering, and failure guarantees that follow.

Notes

What a queue buys you

  • Decoupling — producer doesn't know or wait for consumers.
  • Buffering / smoothing — absorb spikes; consumers work at their own rate (backpressure via a bounded queue / consumer lag).
  • Retry & durability — a failed message is redelivered; survives a consumer crash.
  • Fan-out — one event, many independent consumers (pub/sub).
# Synchronous: the request blocks on slow work (email + thumbnail + index)
def upload(file):
    save(file)
    send_email(...)          # 400 ms
    make_thumbnail(file)     # 900 ms   -> user waits ~1.4 s, fails if SMTP is down

# Decoupled: enqueue and return; workers do the rest at their own pace
def upload(file):
    save(file)
    queue.publish("media.uploaded", {"id": file.id})   # ~2 ms, returns 202
    # email-worker and thumb-worker consume independently; a spike just grows the backlog

Delivery semantics

SemanticMeaning
At-most-oncefire and forget; may be lost, never duplicated. OK for metrics.
At-least-onceredelivered until acked — may be duplicated. The common default; consumers must be idempotent.
Exactly-onceno loss, no dup. Only achievable end-to-end with idempotency/dedup or transactional processing (Kafka EOS within Kafka). Usually you engineer "effectively once" = at-least-once + idempotent consumer.
# "Effectively once" = at-least-once delivery + an idempotent consumer
def handle(msg):
    if seen.add(msg.id) is False:      # msg.id already processed
        return ack(msg)                  # dedup: no-op, just ack the redelivery
    with db.transaction():
        apply(msg)                       # the actual effect
        db.insert("processed", msg.id)     # commit effect + marker atomically
    ack(msg)                             # crash before ack -> redelivered -> marker catches it

Ordering

Global order is expensive/unavailable at scale. Most systems give per-partition (per-key) order: messages with the same key (userId, orderId) go to the same partition and are processed in order; different keys are unordered relative to each other. Choose the partition key so "must be ordered together" data shares one.

// Kafka: the partition key decides ordering scope
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("orders", order.userId(), event));
// all events for one userId -> same partition -> consumed in send order
// different users -> different partitions -> processed in parallel, no cross-user order

// WRONG key if per-user order matters:
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("orders", event.uuid(), event)); // scatters a user's events

Failure handling

  • Retry with backoff (+ jitter) for transient failures; cap attempts.
  • Dead-letter queue (DLQ): after N failures, move the message aside for inspection/replay — don't block the queue or drop it silently.
  • Poison message: one message that always fails can stall a partition — DLQ it.
  • Consumer lag is the key metric: rising lag = consumers can't keep up (scale out, or the messages are too expensive).
def consume(msg):
    try:
        process(msg)
        msg.ack()
    except TransientError:
        delay = min(2 ** msg.attempts + random.random(), 300)  # exp backoff + jitter, cap 5 min
        msg.retry(after=delay)
        if msg.attempts >= 5:
            dlq.send(msg)          # poison message -> set aside, inspect/replay later
            msg.ack()             # stop it blocking the partition

Kafka vs SQS/RabbitMQ (rough)

Kafka: partitioned log, high throughput, replayable (offset-based), ordered per partition, consumers track their own offset. Great for event streaming, CDC, fan-out to many consumer groups. SQS / RabbitMQ: classic queue, per-message ack/delete, easy autoscaling of consumers, built-in DLQ/visibility timeout, no replay. Good for task/job processing.

# Kafka: offset-based, REPLAYABLE, order per partition, N consumer groups read independently
$ kafka-consumer-groups --describe --group billing
  TOPIC   PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG
  orders  0          1_240_991       1_241_005       14
$ ... --reset-offsets --to-datetime 2026-08-29T00:00:00 --execute   # reprocess a day

# SQS: no offsets — per-message delete + visibility timeout, no replay
aws sqs receive-message --queue-url $Q --visibility-timeout 30   # hidden 30 s while you work
aws sqs delete-message  --queue-url $Q --receipt-handle $RH        # ack = delete
Cheat Sheet
  • Queue = decouple + buffer spikes + retry/durability + fan-out (pub/sub).
  • Delivery: at-most-once (lossy), at-least-once (dup-prone — default; make consumers idempotent), exactly-once (only "effectively once" via idempotency/dedup).
  • Ordering: per-partition/per-key only. Route "must be ordered together" data to the same key.
  • Retry with exponential backoff + jitter; cap attempts; then → DLQ (never silently drop; don't block on a poison message).
  • Watch consumer lag — rising = scale consumers or messages too heavy.
  • Kafka: partitioned replayable log, per-partition order, many consumer groups — streaming/CDC/fan-out.
  • SQS/RabbitMQ: per-message ack/delete, visibility timeout, easy consumer autoscaling, built-in DLQ — task queues.
Q&A
Why is "at-least-once" the common default, and what does it demand of consumers?
Because guaranteeing no loss is essential and cheap (redeliver until acked), while guaranteeing no duplicate end-to-end is hard. So a message can be processed more than once (consumer crashed after doing the work but before acking, or an ack was lost). Consumers must be idempotent — processing the same message twice has the same effect as once.
How do you get ordering in a partitioned queue?
You get order only within a partition. Assign a partition key such that all messages that must be ordered relative to each other (e.g. all events for one account_id) hash to the same partition; they're then delivered and processed in order. Cross-partition ordering isn't guaranteed.
What is a dead-letter queue for?
Messages that fail processing repeatedly (bad data, a bug, a permanently-unavailable dependency) are moved to a separate DLQ after N attempts, instead of being retried forever (blocking the queue) or dropped (losing data). You alert on DLQ depth, inspect the messages, fix the cause, and replay them.
What is consumer lag and why do you monitor it?
The gap between the latest produced message and the latest one the consumer has processed (in Kafka, the offset difference). Rising lag means consumers can't keep up — you're falling behind real time. It's the primary health signal for a queue-backed pipeline; you respond by scaling consumers, optimising the per-message work, or shedding load.
Kafka vs a traditional queue like SQS — when each?
Kafka when you need a replayable event log, per-key ordering at high throughput, and multiple independent consumer groups reading the same stream (event sourcing, CDC, analytics fan-out). SQS/RabbitMQ when you have discrete tasks/jobs, want simple per-message ack/delete and visibility timeouts, easy consumer autoscaling, and don't need replay.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which delivery semantic can produce duplicates?
At-least-once.
Where does a message go after exceeding its retry limit?
A dead-letter queue (DLQ).
What determines which partition a message lands in?
Its partition/message key (hashed).

Intermediate core

An order-processing consumer sometimes charges a customer twice. Root cause and fix?
At-least-once redelivery: the consumer processed the "place order" message, charged the card, then crashed (or its ack was lost) before committing the offset, so the message was redelivered and it charged again. Fix: make the charge idempotent — pass an idempotency key (the message id / order id) to the payment provider so a repeat call returns the original result instead of charging again; and/or record "processed message X" in the same transaction as the side effect (dedup table) and skip already-seen ids. Then redelivery is harmless.
Your queue consumers are keeping up on average but lag spikes badly during traffic bursts. Options?
The queue is already absorbing the spike (that's its job) but consumers drain too slowly. Options: (1) autoscale consumers on lag (or queue depth), scaling out fast; (2) increase per-consumer parallelism (more partitions so you can add more consumers — you can't have more active consumers than partitions in Kafka); (3) batch processing (process N messages per DB transaction / API call) to raise throughput; (4) make the work cheaper or move slow parts to a second downstream queue; (5) if some messages are lower priority, use separate queues so bursts of bulk work don't delay urgent messages. Set an alert on lag and a max-age so you know if you're falling behind SLA.

Advanced deep

Explain how Kafka provides "exactly-once semantics" and why it's still not truly exactly-once end-to-end.
Kafka EOS has three pieces: (1) Idempotent producer — each producer gets a producer id and monotonic sequence numbers per partition; the broker dedups retried sends, so a producer retry after a network blip doesn't create a duplicate in the log. (2) Transactions — a producer can atomically write to multiple partitions and commit its consumer offsets in one transaction, coordinated by a transaction coordinator with a two-phase commit to the partition leaders; consumers with isolation.level=read_committed only see messages from committed transactions. This enables the classic "consume → transform → produce" pipeline (Kafka Streams) to be exactly-once: reading input, producing output, and advancing the input offset all commit or all abort together, so a crash-and-restart reprocesses from the last committed offset and re-produces the same output atomically — no dupes, no loss, within the Kafka boundary. Why it's not truly end-to-end exactly-once: the moment your consumer does a side effect outside Kafka — charge a card, send an email, write to an external DB that isn't in the Kafka transaction — that external action can happen and then the offset commit fails, or vice versa. Kafka can't make a Stripe call and an offset commit atomic. So for external effects you're back to "at-least-once + make the external effect idempotent" (idempotency key, dedup table, upsert), which the industry calls effectively-once. Also: EOS adds latency (transaction coordination), reduces throughput, requires careful configuration (enable.idempotence, transactional.id, acks=all, replication), and a bug in transaction handling can stall consumers on a "hanging transaction". So Kafka EOS is genuinely useful for stream-processing topologies but "exactly-once" is a property of the Kafka-internal pipeline, not a magic wand for side effects.
Design the failure and ordering strategy for a payment events pipeline: events must be processed per-account in order, none lost, transient failures retried, permanent failures isolated, and a bad deploy must be recoverable.
Ordering: partition the topic by account_id so all of an account's events land on one partition and are consumed in order by one consumer; different accounts parallelise across partitions. Size partition count for peak parallelism (you can add partitions later but it changes key→partition mapping, so over-provision). Processing model: single-threaded per partition (or a per-account lock if you multiplex), commit the offset only after the side effect is durably done. Idempotency: each event has a stable id; the consumer records processed ids in a dedup table written in the same DB transaction as the effect, and skips seen ids — so at-least-once redelivery is safe. Transient failures (downstream 5xx, timeout): retry in-process with exponential backoff + jitter, a few attempts; if still failing, do not skip ahead (that would break ordering for the account) — either block that partition with bounded backoff (accepting lag on that account) or, better, move the whole account's stream to a per-account retry topic processed more slowly, and pause the main partition consumer for that key until it drains, preserving order. Permanent failures (malformed event, business-rule rejection): after N attempts, publish to a DLQ with full context (original event, error, stack, attempt count) and advance past it only if skipping is acceptable for that event type; if order integrity means you can't skip, DLQ it and halt that account's stream with an alert for a human to decide (replace, replay, or manually resolve). Alert on DLQ depth and on any halted partition. Bad deploy recovery: because Kafka is a replayable log, keep a generous retention (e.g. 7–30 days) and store the offsets the consumer group had committed. If a deploy processes events wrongly, stop consumers, roll back the code, reset the consumer group's offsets to just before the bad deploy started (or to a saved checkpoint), and reprocess — which is safe precisely because of the dedup table (already-applied events are skipped) and idempotent effects. For effects that can't be un-done or re-derived (an email already sent), the dedup table prevents re-sending; for external DB writes, use upserts keyed by event id. Also keep a "processing version" stamp so you can tell which events were touched by the bad version. Monitoring: per-partition lag, DLQ depth, retry-topic depth, dedup-table hit rate (a spike means heavy redelivery — investigate), and end-to-end event age SLO.

Idempotency, Retries & Exactly-Once

Networks fail mid-request, so everything gets retried — make the retry safe.

Notes

Why it matters

A client sends "charge $50", gets no response (timeout, dropped connection), and retries. Did the first one succeed? The client can't tell. Without protection you double-charge. Idempotency means processing the same logical request N times has the same effect as once.

# NOT idempotent: each retry moves money again
def charge(acct, amount):
    acct.balance -= amount          # timeout -> client retries -> charged twice

# idempotent: the operation carries its own identity, second apply is a no-op
def charge(acct, amount, op_id):
    if db.exists("charges", op_id): return db.get("charges", op_id)
    with db.transaction():
        acct.balance -= amount
        db.insert("charges", op_id, result)

Idempotency keys

  • The client generates a unique key per logical operation (a UUID) and sends it with every retry (Idempotency-Key header, Stripe-style).
  • The server, on first receipt, records (key → in-progress) atomically; does the work; stores (key → result). A retry with the same key returns the stored result without re-doing the work. A retry while still in-progress waits or returns 409.
  • Keys expire after a window (24h) — long enough to cover retries, short enough to bound storage.
POST /v1/payments HTTP/1.1
Idempotency-Key: 9f1c2b7a-...-e4       # client generates once, reuses on every retry
{ "amount": 5000, "currency": "usd" }

# server:
row = db.upsert_if_absent("idem", key, status="IN_PROGRESS")   # atomic claim
if row.existed:
    return row.status == "DONE" ? 200(row.response) : 409("in progress")
resp = do_charge(...)
db.update("idem", key, status="DONE", response=resp, ttl="24h")

Naturally idempotent designs

  • PUT /resource/{id} with the full state (vs POST which creates).
  • Upserts keyed by a business id; SET x = value (not x += 1).
  • Conditional writes: UPDATE ... WHERE version = N (optimistic concurrency — a stale retry does nothing).
  • Dedup table: record processed request/message ids, skip seen ones (do the insert + the effect in one transaction).
-- SET, not increment: replaying the same message lands on the same value
UPDATE inventory SET qty = 7          WHERE sku = 'A1';   -- idempotent
UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1     WHERE sku = 'A1';   -- NOT: double-apply undercounts

-- optimistic concurrency: a stale retry updates 0 rows and is safely ignored
UPDATE orders SET status='PAID', version=version+1
WHERE id=42 AND version=3;                        -- rowcount 0 => someone already advanced it

Retry hygiene

  • Exponential backoff + jitter — synchronised retries cause a thundering herd ("retry storm") that keeps a recovering service down.
  • Retry budget: cap retries as a fraction of total traffic; retry only at one layer (not client + gateway + service, which multiplies).
  • Only retry idempotent / safe operations, or ones with an idempotency key. Retry on transient errors (timeout, 503, connection reset), not on 400/401/404.
  • Circuit breaker: after a failure threshold, stop calling a dead dependency for a cool-off, then probe.
def call_with_retry(fn):
    for attempt in range(4):                       # capped attempts
        try:
            return fn()
        except (Timeout, Http503, ConnReset):    # transient only; NOT 400/404
            if attempt == 3: raise
            sleep(min(2 ** attempt, 10) * (0.5 + random.random()))  # backoff + jitter
# retry at ONE layer only — client OR gateway OR service, never all three (2*2*2 = 8x load)

The transactional outbox

To reliably "update the DB and publish an event", write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business change; a separate poller/CDC publishes outbox rows to the queue and marks them sent. No lost events, no phantom events, and the queue consumer's idempotency handles the at-least-once delivery.

-- One transaction: business change + the event to publish
BEGIN;
  INSERT INTO orders(id, status) VALUES(42, 'PLACED');
  INSERT INTO outbox(id, topic, payload, sent)
         VALUES(gen_uuid(), 'order.placed', '{"id":42}', false);
COMMIT;                       -- both commit or neither: no DB/queue divergence

# poller: SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE NOT sent -> publish -> UPDATE sent = true
# crash between publish and update -> re-published -> consumer dedup absorbs it
Cheat Sheet
  • Idempotent = same effect for 1 or N executions. Required because retries are unavoidable.
  • Idempotency key: client sends a UUID per logical op; server stores key→result, returns stored result on retry. Expire keys after ~24h.
  • Prefer naturally idempotent ops: PUT full state, upsert by business id, SET not +=, conditional WHERE version=N.
  • Dedup table: record processed ids in the same transaction as the effect; skip seen.
  • Retries: exponential backoff + jitter; retry at one layer only; retry budget (% of traffic); only transient errors; circuit breaker for dead deps.
  • DB write + event publish atomically → transactional outbox (+ CDC/poller), consumer idempotent.
  • "Exactly-once" in practice = at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing = effectively once.
Q&A
Why can't a payment API just "not process the same request twice" on its own?
It can't tell a genuine second payment from a retry of the first — the requests look identical and the network hid the first response. The client must supply an idempotency key that stays constant across retries of the same logical operation, so the server can recognise "I've already done this one" and return the original result.
How does an idempotency key work server-side?
On first receipt the server atomically inserts (key, status=in_progress); if that insert conflicts, it's a retry — return the stored result (or wait if still in progress). Otherwise it performs the operation and updates the row to (key, status=done, result=...). All retries with that key then get the stored result.
Which operations are naturally idempotent?
GET, PUT (set full state), DELETE; assignments like status = 'paid'; upserts keyed by a business identifier; conditional updates with a version check. Non-idempotent: POST that creates, counters (x = x + 1), appends, "send email".
What is a retry storm and how do you prevent it?
Many clients retry a failing service simultaneously, and because their retries are synchronised (same fixed delay), the load spikes in waves that prevent recovery. Prevent with exponential backoff plus jitter (randomise the delay), a cap on attempts, a retry budget (retry at most X% of requests), retrying at only one layer, and a circuit breaker that stops calls to a dependency that's clearly down.
What problem does the transactional outbox solve?
The dual-write problem: you can't atomically "commit a DB change" and "publish a message to a broker" — a crash between them loses the event or publishes one for a change that rolled back. The outbox writes the event into a table in the same DB transaction as the change; a separate process reliably relays outbox rows to the broker afterward.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Is PUT idempotent?
Yes — sending the same PUT repeatedly leaves the resource in the same state.
What do you add to a fixed retry delay to avoid synchronised retries?
Jitter (randomness).
Should you retry an HTTP 400 response?
No — it's a client error; the same request will fail again. Retry transient errors (timeouts, 503, connection resets).

Intermediate core

Design an idempotent "create order" endpoint.
Client sends POST /orders with an Idempotency-Key header (a UUID it keeps constant across retries). Server: INSERT INTO idempotency(key, status) VALUES (?, 'processing') — if it fails on the unique constraint, the key exists: return the stored response (200 with the original order) or 409 if still processing. If the insert succeeds, create the order in the same transaction, then update the idempotency row with the response body and status done, keyed for lookup. Set a TTL (24h) on idempotency rows. Now any number of retries yield exactly one order and the same response.
A microservice updates its DB then calls another service; sometimes the DB commit succeeds but the call is lost. Fix without distributed transactions.
Transactional outbox: in the same DB transaction as the update, insert a row into an outbox table describing the message to send. A separate relay (a poller on the outbox, or CDC on the WAL) reads unsent outbox rows and publishes them to a queue/calls the other service, marking them sent on success (with retries). The downstream is made idempotent (dedup on the message id). Now the message is sent iff the DB change committed, exactly-effectively-once, with no 2PC.

Advanced deep

Walk through the failure modes of an idempotency-key implementation and how to handle each.
(1) Concurrent duplicate requests (client fires two before the first responds): the second's INSERT ... key hits the unique constraint while the first row is still processing. Options: return 409 Conflict ("retry shortly"), or block/poll until the first finishes and return its result. Blocking is friendlier but ties up a connection — use a short timeout then 409. (2) Crash after the effect, before storing the result: the idempotency row is stuck at processing forever, so retries get 409 indefinitely even though the work was done. Mitigate with a processing lease/timeout: if a row has been processing longer than T, a retry may take it over — but then you might re-run the effect. So the effect itself must also be idempotent (dedup on the same key inside the payment provider / DB), making the idempotency row an optimisation, not the sole guarantee. (3) Same key, different request body (client bug: reused a key for a new operation): detect it — store a hash of the request payload with the key and reject (422) if a later request with that key has a different hash, rather than silently returning the old result. (4) Key expiry vs late retry: a retry arrives after the key's TTL → treated as new → double effect.
