Set the TTL well beyond the maximum realistic retry window (Stripe uses 24h), and ideally keep the effect idempotent independently. (5) Storage failure of the idempotency store: if the store is a separate system and it's down, you can't check — fail closed (reject) for money-moving ops, or fall back to the effect's own idempotency. (6) Partial results / multi-step operations: if "create order" does 3 things and crashes after step 2, storing "done" would be wrong. Either make the whole thing one DB transaction (so it's all-or-nothing and the idempotency row commits with it), or model it as a saga with its own per-step idempotency and a resumable state machine. The robust design: idempotency key as the fast-path dedup, plus the underlying effect being idempotent so a lease takeover or expired key can't cause a double.
Compare "at-least-once + idempotent consumer" with true two-phase-commit exactly-once, and explain why the industry overwhelmingly chooses the former.
2PC exactly-once: a coordinator runs prepare/commit across the message broker and the consumer's database (both must support XA/2PC), so consuming a message and applying its effect are one atomic transaction — no dupes, no loss, no consumer-side idempotency needed. At-least-once + idempotent consumer: the broker redelivers until acked (so no loss), and the consumer dedups (idempotency key / processed-id table / upsert) so redelivery is harmless. Why the industry picks the latter: (1) 2PC is a blocking protocol — if the coordinator dies after prepare, participants hold locks/resources until it recovers; this couples the availability of the broker and the DB and creates head-of-line blocking. (2) Not everything speaks XA — Kafka, most modern brokers, HTTP APIs, and many databases (and certainly external services like Stripe or an email provider) have no distributed-transaction support, so 2PC simply isn't an option across those boundaries. (3) Performance — 2PC adds round trips and coordination on every message; at-least-once is a single ack. (4) Operational complexity — a transaction coordinator is another stateful component to run, monitor, and recover; "hung transactions" are a known pain. (5) Idempotency is needed anyway — for retries at the API layer, for replay after bugs, for reprocessing after a bad deploy — so once your effects are idempotent, exactly-once delivery buys you little. The pragmatic result is effectively-once: cheap, non-blocking, works across heterogeneous systems, and degrades gracefully. The cost is that you must design every consumer's side effects to be idempotent (a real discipline: dedup tables, natural keys, upserts, conditional writes), and reason carefully about non-idempotent-by-nature effects (sending an email — dedup on a send-id before calling the provider). 2PC-style exactly-once is reserved for cases where both endpoints are in the same transactional system (Kafka Streams' EOS within Kafka) or a single database.

CDNs, Blob Storage & Static Content

Serving files and media at scale — edge caching, object stores, and presigned uploads.

Notes

Object / blob storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob)

  • Flat key→object store (the "folders" are just key prefixes). Massive scale, ~11 nines durability (erasure-coded across facilities), cheap, but higher per-request latency than a disk and eventual-ish listing.
  • Store the bytes here (images, video, backups, logs, build artifacts); store metadata (owner, tags, the object key) in your DB.
  • Presigned URLs: your backend signs a time-limited URL granting PUT (upload) or GET (download) directly to the object store — the large bytes never transit your servers. The client uploads straight to S3; your API just issues the URL and later records the metadata.
  • Lifecycle rules: auto-transition old objects to colder/cheaper tiers, expire after N days.
# Direct-to-S3 upload: the bytes never touch your API
# 1) client asks your backend for a signed PUT
url = s3.generate_presigned_url("put_object",
        Params={"Bucket": "uploads", "Key": f"u/{uid}/{uuid4()}.jpg"},
        ExpiresIn=900)                         # 15-min window
# 2) client: curl -X PUT --upload-file photo.jpg "$url"   -> straight to S3
# 3) S3 event -> your service records {key, owner, size} in the DB

CDN

  • A global mesh of edge PoPs that cache your content near users. Origin can be your object store or your app.
  • Cache key: usually URL + selected headers/query params. Be deliberate — caching on a param you didn't mean to (or a per-user cookie) either fragments the cache or leaks data.
  • TTL / Cache-Control: long TTLs for immutable assets; use content-hashed filenames (app.9f3a2c.js) so a new version = a new URL = instant "invalidation" with no purge.
  • Purge / invalidation: explicit for content that changes at a stable URL; surrogate keys / cache tags let one call purge all related objects. Purges take seconds–minutes to propagate.
  • Also provides: TLS termination, compression, HTTP/2-3, DDoS absorption, edge compute, and origin shielding (one mid-tier cache all edges fetch through, so the origin sees ~1 request per object).
# Immutable asset: cache "forever", new build = new URL (no purge call ever)
GET /static/app.9f3a2c.js
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

# Mutable at a stable URL: revalidate + tag it so one call purges related objects
GET /api/products/42
Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300
Surrogate-Key: product-42 catalog          # later: PURGE by key "product-42"

Hot objects & media

A viral video: the CDN absorbs it (that's the point). Within the CDN, popular objects are replicated across a PoP's servers. For live video / large VOD: chunked adaptive streaming (HLS/DASH) — segments are just cacheable static files; the manifest lists bitrates and the player picks based on bandwidth.

# HLS manifest: bitrate ladder; player picks a rendition, then fetches .ts segments
#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=800000,RESOLUTION=640x360
360p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=2800000,RESOLUTION=1280x720
720p/index.m3u8
# 720p/index.m3u8 -> seg_000.ts, seg_001.ts, ...  each a plain cacheable file
# a viral view spike = many GETs for the SAME segment keys -> CDN serves from edge, origin idle
Cheat Sheet
  • Object storage: flat key→bytes, huge scale, ~11 nines durability, cheap, higher latency. Bytes in S3, metadata in your DB.
  • Presigned URLs: client uploads/downloads directly to/from the object store; big bytes bypass your servers.
  • Lifecycle rules: tier down / expire old objects automatically.
  • CDN caches content at edge PoPs near users; cache key = URL + chosen headers/params (be careful).
  • Immutable assets: long TTL + content-hashed filenames → new version = new URL = no purge needed.
  • Mutable-at-stable-URL: explicit purge / surrogate keys; propagation takes seconds–minutes.
  • CDN also: TLS, compression, HTTP/2-3, DDoS absorption, edge compute, origin shielding.
  • Media: adaptive streaming (HLS/DASH) — segments are cacheable static files.
Q&A
Where do you store an uploaded profile photo — your database or object storage?
Object storage (S3/GCS) for the image bytes; your database stores only the metadata (user id, the object key, content type, size, upload time). Databases are bad at large blobs (bloat, backup size, buffer-pool pollution); object stores are purpose-built and cheap.
What is a presigned URL and why use one for uploads?
A time-limited, signed URL your backend generates that authorises the holder to PUT (or GET) a specific object directly against the object store. For uploads, the client sends the file straight to S3 using that URL — your servers never handle the megabytes, saving bandwidth and CPU and avoiding a proxy bottleneck.
How do you "invalidate" a JavaScript bundle on the CDN when you deploy a new version?
Don't invalidate — change the URL. Build with a content hash in the filename (bundle.[hash].js); the new deploy references the new filename, which is a cache miss and fetches fresh, while the old file stays cached for anyone still on the old HTML. Set a very long TTL since the content at a given URL never changes.
What's the risk of including a query parameter or cookie in the CDN cache key?
Including a param that varies per request (a tracking token, a session id) makes every request a unique key — near-zero hit rate. Worse, if a per-user response gets cached under a key that another user matches, you leak one user's data to another. Only key on params that genuinely change the response, and strip cookies for cacheable paths.
What is origin shielding?
Designating one CDN cache tier that all edge PoPs fetch through, so on a cache miss the origin gets a single request instead of one per PoP. It collapses cache-fill storms and purge storms, smooths origin load, and lets you firewall the origin to accept traffic only from the shield.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What lets a client upload a file directly to S3 without it passing through your server?
A presigned (pre-authorised, time-limited) URL.
How do you make a static asset cache "forever" yet still deploy new versions?
Content-hashed filenames — a new build produces a new URL, so the old cached file is simply never requested again.
What's the typical durability figure for cloud object storage?
~11 nines (99.999999999%) — via erasure coding across multiple facilities.

Intermediate core

Design the image upload flow for a social app.
Client calls POST /uploads → backend generates an object key (user/{id}/{uuid}.jpg), returns a presigned PUT URL (5–15 min expiry) + the key. Client PUTs the bytes directly to the object store. Client then calls POST /photos with the key + caption; backend verifies the object exists (HEAD) and its size/type, writes a photo row (owner, key, dimensions, status=pending). An async worker (triggered by an S3 event) generates resized variants / thumbnails, runs moderation/NSFW checks, extracts EXIF, and flips status to ready. Serving: images are fronted by the CDN with long TTLs and content-hashed or immutable keys; the app returns CDN URLs. Cleanup: a job removes objects with no matching ready row after 24h (abandoned uploads).
Your origin is getting hammered every time a popular file's TTL expires across the CDN. Fix?
Enable origin shielding so only one shield PoP revalidates with the origin per object; other PoPs fetch from the shield. Add stale-while-revalidate so edges serve the slightly-stale file while one background request refreshes it (no synchronized miss). Stagger/jitter TTLs so many objects don't expire in lockstep. For truly immutable content, use content-hashed URLs and a near-infinite TTL so there's no revalidation at all. And put the origin behind a firewall that only accepts the shield's IPs.

Advanced deep

Design video-on-demand delivery for a service with 100M users: upload, transcode, storage, and adaptive playback.
Upload: presigned multipart upload directly to object storage (large files, resumable, parallel parts). An upload-complete event kicks off processing. Transcode pipeline: a job splits the source into GOP-aligned chunks and fans out transcoding across a worker fleet (or a managed service like MediaConvert), producing a ladder of renditions (e.g. 240p/360p/480p/720p/1080p/4K at target bitrates) in a streaming container — segmented into 2–10 s HLS/DASH fragments — plus a manifest per rendition and a master manifest. Also generate: thumbnails/sprite sheets for scrubbing, captions, and per-title encoding (analyse the content to pick optimal bitrates per video rather than a fixed ladder — Netflix's approach, big bandwidth savings). Store all segments + manifests in object storage with a key scheme like video/{id}/{rendition}/seg-{n}.ts. Delivery: everything is static cacheable files, so put a CDN in front with long TTLs; segments are immutable (content-addressed keys), manifests get shorter TTLs (or are immutable per-version too). Popular titles are naturally hot in the CDN; origin shielding + a multi-tier cache keep origin fetches minimal; for the very biggest titles, pre-push (pre-warm) segments to PoPs before a release. Playback: the player downloads the master manifest, measures throughput and buffer level, and requests segments from the rendition that will keep the buffer full — ramping up/down as bandwidth changes (ABR). It fetches a few segments ahead. DRM (Widevine/FairPlay/PlayReady) wraps the segments with license servers gating keys. Live is the same but the manifest grows as segments are produced, with a short DVR window and lower-latency modes (LL-HLS/CMAF chunked transfer). Cost/scale levers: per-title encoding, AV1/HEVC for newer clients (smaller files), tiered storage (cold titles to cheaper storage), CDN offload ratio as the key metric, and regional origins. Metadata (catalog, availability, user watch history, recommendations) is a separate concern in your databases — the video-serving path is deliberately "just static files behind a CDN" because that's what scales to 100M users at reasonable cost.
How would you serve private user content (e.g. paid downloads, medical records) through a CDN without leaking it?
The core tension: a CDN caches responses by URL and serves them to anyone who requests that URL, but this content must only reach authorised users. Approaches, roughly in order of strength: (1) Signed URLs / signed cookies — the CDN validates a short-lived signature (HMAC over the path + expiry, sometimes + client IP) before serving; your app issues the signature only to authorised users. The object can still be cached at the edge (keyed on the path, ignoring the signature params), so you get CDN performance, but a leaked signed URL works until it expires — keep expiries short (minutes) and consider IP-binding. (2) Signed cookies for a whole path prefix (a user's media directory) so you don't sign every URL; good for apps that load many assets. (3) Edge auth / edge compute — run a function at the PoP (Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge) that checks a session token / calls an auth service before serving from cache; more flexible policy, small latency cost, and the origin stays protected. (4) Per-user cache keys — include the user id in the cache key so responses can't cross users; only viable if the per-user hit rate justifies it (usually not for unique downloads). (5) No CDN caching, CDN as pass-through — the CDN terminates TLS and proxies to origin with auth on every request; you lose edge caching but keep DDoS protection, TLS offload, and a warm backbone connection — fine for low-volume sensitive downloads. (6) Encrypt at rest, decrypt client-side — the CDN serves ciphertext; the client gets the key via an authenticated channel; the CDN never sees plaintext (used for the most sensitive data, adds client complexity and defeats server-side transforms). Never rely on "unguessable URL" alone (no expiry, no auth) — those leak via logs, referrers, browser history, and sharing. For regulated data (HIPAA/PCI), also ensure the CDN vendor is contractually covered (BAA), access-logged, and that cache TTLs for private content are short or zero.

Design a URL Shortener

The classic warm-up — key generation, the read-heavy redirect path, and scale.

Notes

Requirements & estimate

  • Functional: POST /shorten {url} → short code; GET /{code} → 301/302 redirect. Optional: custom alias, expiry, click analytics, user accounts.
  • Scale example: 100M new links/month ≈ ~40 writes/s; read:write ~100:1 → ~4000 redirects/s (peak ×several). 5 years → ~6B links.
  • Storage: ~6B × (short code + long URL + metadata) ≈ a few hundred GB — fits comfortably; the challenge is redirect latency and QPS, not size.
# Back-of-envelope that drives the design
writes  = 100e6 / (30 * 86400)     # ~39 links/sec  -> trivial
reads   = writes * 100             # ~3,900 redirects/sec avg, ~x5 peak ~20k/sec
rows_5y = 100e6 * 12 * 5           # 6e9 rows x ~500 B ~= 3 TB  -> one sharded table is fine
# conclusion: optimise the READ path (cache + cheap KV), not storage

Short code generation

ApproachNotes
Base62 of an auto-increment id7 chars = 62^7 ≈ 3.5×10¹² codes. Sequential → guessable/enumerable; needs a global counter (a DB sequence, or a range-allocator / Snowflake-style id).
Random code + collision checkgenerate 7 random base62 chars, insert with a unique constraint, retry on conflict. Unguessable; collision rate negligible until the space fills.
Hash(url) → take first N charssame URL → same code (dedup for free), but collisions between different URLs must be handled (append a disambiguator).
Offline key poola "key generation service" pre-generates unique codes into a table; the write path just pops one. Removes collision handling from the hot path.
ALPHABET = "0123..9a..zA..Z"          # 62 symbols
def encode(n):                        # base62 of a unique counter id
    s = ""
    while n:
        n, r = divmod(n, 62)
        s = ALPHABET[r] + s
    return s.rjust(7, "0")              # id 1_000_000_000 -> "15ftgG"

# random alternative: unguessable, no global counter
code = "".join(secrets.choice(ALPHABET) for _ in range(7))
db.execute("INSERT INTO urls(code,url) VALUES(%s,%s)", code, url)  # UNIQUE(code) -> retry on dup

Storage & the read path

  • A KV store or a simple table: code (PK) → long_url, created_at, expires_at, owner. Shard by code hash if needed.
  • Redirect path must be fast: GET /{code} → cache lookup (Redis / in-process LRU) → on miss, DB → cache it → return 301 (permanent, cacheable by browsers/proxies) or 302 (if you need to count every click / change targets). Most links are hit hard right after creation then decay — caching gives >95% hit rate.
  • Put the whole thing behind a CDN for the redirect (301s are cacheable) if analytics allow.
def redirect(code):
    url = local_lru.get(code) or redis.get(code)     # >95% stop here
    if url is None:
        url = db.get("urls", code)                     # cold miss
        if url is None: return 404
        redis.set(code, url, ex=86400)
    queue.publish("click", {"code": code, "ts": now(), "ref": req.referrer})  # async, off critical path
    return 302, {"Location": url}                   # 302: every hit reaches us so we can count

Analytics & extras

Emit a click event (code, timestamp, referrer, geo from IP, UA) to a queue → async aggregation (counts by day/country/referrer) in a separate store — never on the redirect's critical path. Custom aliases: reserve the code with a unique constraint; validate charset/length; block profanity/reserved words. Expiry: store expires_at, check on read, lazy-delete + background sweep.

-- click events land raw, then a job rolls them up (never query raw on the hot path)
INSERT INTO clicks_raw(code, ts, country, referrer) VALUES (...);

-- hourly aggregation job
INSERT INTO clicks_daily (code, day, country, n)
SELECT code, date_trunc('day', ts), country, count(*)
FROM clicks_raw WHERE ts >= now() - interval '1 hour'
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ON CONFLICT (code, day, country) DO UPDATE SET n = clicks_daily.n + EXCLUDED.n;
Cheat Sheet
  • API: POST /shorten → code; GET /{code} → redirect. It's read-heavy (~100:1).
  • Code: base62(id) (compact, but sequential/guessable + needs a counter) / random+unique-constraint+retry (unguessable) / hash(url) (dedup, handle collisions) / pre-generated key pool (no hot-path collision handling).
  • 7 base62 chars ≈ 3.5×10¹² — plenty.
  • Store: code → url + metadata in KV / small table; shard by code hash at scale. Size is small; QPS is the problem.
  • Redirect path: cache (Redis / local LRU, >95% hit) → DB on miss. 301 if cacheable / no per-click count needed; 302 if you must count or may change the target.
  • Analytics: fire a click event to a queue → async aggregation. Never on the redirect path.
  • Custom alias: unique constraint + validation + blocklist. Expiry: expires_at + lazy + sweep.
Q&A
Why is a URL shortener a read-heavy system, and how does that shape the design?
Each link is created once but redirected many times (often 100:1 or more). So the redirect path is optimised above all: an aggressive cache (Redis + per-instance LRU) fronting a simple key-value lookup, cacheable 301s, minimal work per request, and analytics pushed off to async. The write path can be comparatively heavy.
Base62 of an auto-increment id vs a random code — trade-offs?
Sequential base62 gives the shortest codes and is simple, but codes are guessable/enumerable (a competitor can crawl all your links) and you need a globally unique increasing id (a bottleneck or a distributed id scheme). Random codes are unguessable and need no global counter, at the cost of a uniqueness check (insert with a unique constraint, retry on the rare collision).
301 or 302 for the redirect?
301 (permanent) lets browsers, proxies, and CDNs cache the redirect — great for performance, but you then don't see most repeat clicks (bad for analytics) and can't change where the code points. 302 (found/temporary) means every click hits your server — you can count them and change the target — at higher load. Many services use 302 for analytics reasons.
How do you keep click analytics off the critical path?
On redirect, emit a lightweight click event (code, time, referrer, IP-derived geo, user agent) to a message queue and return the redirect immediately. Downstream consumers aggregate into counts/dimensions in a separate analytics store. The redirect never waits on analytics writes.
How do you support custom aliases without collisions?
Treat the alias as the primary key with a unique constraint; the create request fails if it's taken (return 409). Validate the charset and length, and reject reserved paths (api, login), profanity, and impersonation attempts. Custom and generated codes share the same key space and table.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

How many unique codes does 7 base62 characters give?
62^7 ≈ 3.5 × 10¹².
What's the dominant traffic pattern?
Reads (redirects) — far more than writes (shortening).
Where do you store the code→URL mapping?
A key-value store or a small indexed table, fronted by a cache.

Intermediate core

Two servers generate short codes concurrently from a shared counter. How do you avoid a bottleneck?
Don't have each write hit one global counter. Range allocation: each app instance claims a block of ids (say 10,000) from the counter service in one round trip, then hands them out locally; when the block runs low it grabs another. The central counter is touched once per 10k writes instead of every write. Alternatively use a distributed id scheme (Snowflake: timestamp + machine id + sequence) that needs no coordination at all, then base62-encode it — accepting slightly longer, time-ordered codes.
A few links go viral and their redirects overwhelm one cache/DB shard. Fix?
Hot-key problem. The links are already cacheable, so: add a small per-instance L1 cache with a short TTL so most viral hits never leave the app server; for a 301-eligible link, let the CDN cache the redirect so the edge absorbs it entirely; if using 302, replicate the hot entries across multiple cache nodes and route reads randomly. Since the value (a URL) is tiny and immutable, replication is cheap. Monitor per-code request rates so you can react.

Advanced deep

Design the system for global low-latency redirects (users on every continent) with the ability to update or delete links.
Redirect latency is dominated by the user→server round trip, so you must serve redirects from edge locations near the user, not one region. Architecture: (1) The code→URL mapping is small and read-mostly — replicate it globally. Options: a globally-distributed database (DynamoDB global tables, Spanner, CockroachDB) with a replica in each region, or push the mapping to edge KV stores (Cloudflare KV, DynamoDB + DAX, Fastly's config) that each PoP reads locally. (2) The redirect runs as edge compute (Workers / Lambda@Edge): read the code from the local edge KV, return the redirect — single-digit-ms, no origin hop for the hot path. (3) Writes (create/update/delete) go to a primary region's database; changes propagate to the edge KV asynchronously (seconds), which is fine because links rarely change and a brief propagation delay on an update is acceptable (the old target still works). For deletes that must be immediate (abuse/legal takedown), also maintain a small, fast-propagating denylist checked at the edge, or accept the propagation window and additionally return a takedown page from the primary. (4) Use 302 if you need per-click analytics or the ability to change targets; emit click events from the edge to a regional queue → central aggregation. Use 301 + long cache for links where analytics don't matter, letting browsers/CDN cache and cutting even the edge-KV read. (5) Consistency: creation should be read-your-writes for the creator (they get the code back and it works immediately) — achieved by writing to the primary and returning the code, while global visibility is eventual; a redirect for a brand-new code in a far region might 404 for a few seconds, mitigated by a fallback that, on edge-KV miss, does one origin lookup and populates. (6) Custom-alias uniqueness must be enforced at the primary (a global unique constraint), not at the edge, so alias creation is a single-region transaction even though reads are global. Trade-off summary: you get ~10 ms redirects worldwide and simple scaling because the data is tiny and read-mostly; you pay with eventual-consistency handling for updates/deletes and a single-region write path for uniqueness.
How do you prevent your URL shortener from being abused for phishing, malware distribution, and spam?
Shorteners hide the destination, which attackers love. Layered defences: (1) At creation — check the target URL against threat-intel feeds (Google Safe Browsing, PhishTank, commercial reputation APIs), block known-bad domains, newly-registered domains, and IP-literal URLs; rate-limit link creation per account/IP; require auth for bulk creation; disallow shortening URLs that already point at other shorteners (redirect chains). (2) Ongoing scanning — re-scan targets periodically (a link created clean can be repointed or the destination page changed after approval — "time-bomb" links); crawl/render high-traffic destinations to detect phishing kits and malware. (3) At redirect time — for links flagged as risky or unverified, show an interstitial warning page ("You are being redirected to example.com — proceed?") rather than an immediate redirect; block outright for confirmed-malicious. (4) Transparency — offer a preview endpoint (+ suffix, or /preview/{code}) so users and security tools can see the destination without visiting it; publish the destination in the response for scanners. (5) Abuse signals — watch for a link with a sudden traffic spike from spam-like sources, many links from one account to similar domains, or user reports; auto-suspend and review. (6) Takedown — a fast path to disable a code globally (the denylist from the previous answer), an abuse-report form, and cooperation with registrars/hosts. (7) Reputation — track per-account trust; new/untrusted accounts get interstitials and lower rate limits, established clean accounts get direct redirects. The unavoidable tension: interstitials and scanning add latency and friction that hurt legitimate use, so you tune aggressiveness by the link's and creator's risk score rather than applying it uniformly.

Design a News Feed / Chat System

Fan-out on write vs read, delivery, ordering, and the celebrity problem.

Notes

News feed: the core question is fan-out

Fan-out on write (push)Fan-out on read (pull)
On postwrite the post id into every follower's feed list (precomputed timeline in Redis)do nothing extra
On feed loadread the precomputed list — fast, O(1)-ishquery recent posts from everyone you follow, merge, sort — expensive
Costwrite amplification = follower count; wasteful for inactive followersread amplification = followee count; slow for users following thousands
Best formost users (few followers, read often)celebrities (millions of followers)

Hybrid (what Twitter/Instagram do): push for normal accounts; for a followed celebrity, don't fan out — pull their recent posts at read time and merge into the pushed feed. Threshold on follower count.

def on_post(author, post_id):
    if author.follower_count < 100_000:            # normal: fan-out on write
        for f in followers(author):
            redis.lpush(f"feed:{f}", post_id)
            redis.ltrim(f"feed:{f}", 0, 799)
    # else celebrity: write nothing; readers pull at load time

def load_feed(user):
    ids = redis.lrange(f"feed:{user}", 0, 49)          # pushed part, O(1)
    for c in celebrities_followed(user):
        ids += recent_posts(c, 10)                     # pull + merge
    return hydrate(sorted(set(ids), reverse=True)[:50])

Feed storage & ranking

  • Per-user timeline = a capped list (last ~800 post ids) in Redis, backed by a durable store for regeneration.
  • Chronological is simplest; ranked feeds add a scoring service (recency, affinity, engagement prediction) applied at read time over a candidate set.
  • New follower / cache miss: regenerate the timeline by pulling from followees (the pull path is the fallback).
# Ranked feed: cheap candidate gen, then score a bounded set at read time
candidates = pushed_ids(user, 300) + pulled_ids(user, 100)   # ~400 items max
def score(p):
    age_h = (now() - p.ts) / 3600
    return (1 / (age_h + 2)) * affinity(user, p.author) * predicted_engagement(user, p)
feed = sorted(candidates, key=score, reverse=True)[:50]   # only 400 scored, not the whole graph

Chat: the core question is delivery

  • Connection layer: clients hold a persistent connection (WebSocket) to a gateway server; a registry maps userId → gateway node (in Redis) so a message can be routed to the recipient's node, which pushes it down the socket. Offline → store and send a push notification.
  • Storage: messages in a store partitioned by conversation_id (all of a chat's messages together, ordered). Wide-column (Cassandra) or a sharded DB suits the write volume and access pattern ("last N messages of conversation X").
  • Ordering: per-conversation order via a monotonic sequence assigned by the conversation's owning partition (not client timestamps — clock skew). Clients sort by that sequence.
  • Delivery state: sent / delivered / read receipts are per-recipient status rows or a "last read sequence" per user per conversation.
  • Group chat: fan out the message to each member's delivery path; large groups have the same celebrity-style amplification problem — cap group size or pull for huge groups.
  • Presence: heartbeats to the gateway; publish online/offline transitions; presence is best-effort and eventually consistent.
# send a message: server assigns the order, routes to the recipient's gateway node
def send(conv_id, sender, body):
    seq = redis.incr(f"conv:{conv_id}:seq")          # server sequence, NOT client clock
    db.insert("messages", conv_id=conv_id, seq=seq, sender=sender, body=body)
    for uid in members(conv_id):
        node = redis.get(f"conn:{uid}")             # userId -> gateway node
        if node: rpc(node).push(uid, {"conv": conv_id, "seq": seq, "body": body})
        else:    push_notification(uid)          # offline -> stored; client syncs from last seq
Cheat Sheet
  • Feed: fan-out on write (precompute each follower's timeline — fast reads, write amplification) vs fan-out on read (merge followees' posts at read — slow reads, no write cost).
  • Hybrid: push for normal users, pull for celebrities (follower-count threshold), merge at read.
  • Timeline = capped list of post ids in Redis + durable backing store for regen on miss/new-follow.
  • Ranked feed = candidate set + scoring service at read time.
  • Chat: persistent WebSocket to a gateway; userId → gateway node registry in Redis for routing; offline → store + push notification.
  • Messages partitioned by conversation_id, ordered by a server-assigned per-conversation sequence (not client clocks).
  • Delivery/read state = per-user "last read sequence" per conversation.
  • Group chat / huge groups = fan-out per member; cap size or pull for very large groups. Presence = best-effort heartbeats.
Q&A
Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read for a news feed?
On write: when you post, the post is pushed into every follower's precomputed timeline, so loading a feed is a cheap list read — but a post by someone with 10M followers does 10M writes. On read: nothing happens at post time; loading a feed queries recent posts from everyone you follow and merges them — cheap writes, but slow for users following thousands. Most systems use a hybrid.
What is the "celebrity problem" and the fix?
Fan-out on write amplifies by follower count, so accounts with millions of followers make each post catastrophically expensive and flood inactive followers' timelines. Fix: for accounts above a follower threshold, don't fan out — fetch their recent posts at feed-read time and merge them into the reader's otherwise-pushed timeline.
How does a chat message reach a specific online user?
Each user's client holds a WebSocket to a gateway server; a registry (Redis) maps user id → which gateway node. To deliver, the system looks up the recipient's node and forwards the message to it (via a queue or direct RPC), and that node pushes it down the socket. If the user is offline, the message is stored and a push notification is sent.
How do you order messages in a conversation correctly?
Assign each message a monotonically increasing sequence number from the partition that owns the conversation (server-side), not the sender's clock — client clocks are skewed and untrustworthy. Clients display messages sorted by that sequence, and track a "last read sequence" per conversation for read receipts and unread counts.
Where do a user's feed timeline and a conversation's messages physically live?
The timeline is a capped list of post ids per user, cached in Redis (with a durable backing store to rebuild it). Conversation messages are stored partitioned by conversation id — all messages of one chat co-located and ordered — typically in a wide-column store or a sharded database sized for the write volume.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which fan-out strategy makes feed reads fastest?
Fan-out on write (push) — the timeline is precomputed.
What protocol do chat clients typically use for real-time delivery?
WebSocket (a persistent bidirectional connection).
What do you partition chat messages by?
conversation_id — so a chat's messages are co-located and ordered.

Intermediate core

A user follows 5,000 accounts and their feed load is slow under pure fan-out-on-read. What do you do?
Switch that user (and most users) to fan-out on write: maintain a precomputed timeline list so a feed load is one capped list read plus a batch fetch of the post bodies. Keep fan-out-on-read only for the celebrity accounts among those 5,000 — pull their recent posts at read time and merge. Cache the merged result briefly. Cap the timeline length (e.g. 800 entries) so it doesn't grow unbounded. For the initial timeline build (or after a cache miss), do a one-time pull-and-merge from all followees and store it.
How do you deliver a message to a user who's offline, then online on 3 devices?
On send, always persist the message to the conversation store with its sequence number. If the recipient has no live connection, enqueue a push notification. When the user comes online on a device, that device connects to a gateway, registers (userId, deviceId) → node, and does a sync: "give me all messages in my conversations after last-seen-sequence per conversation". Each device tracks its own last-seen watermark, so all three converge to the full history. New live messages are then pushed to every registered device for that user (fan-out over the user's device list). Read receipts update a per-user (not per-device) last-read sequence so "read" is consistent across the user's devices.

Advanced deep

Design the connection/gateway tier for a chat service with 50M concurrent WebSocket connections. How do connections, routing, and failure work?
Connection tier: a fleet of stateless-ish gateway servers, each holding maybe 100k–500k connections (tuned with epoll/kqueue, large fd limits, and careful memory per connection). 50M / 200k ≈ 250+ gateway nodes across regions/AZs. A layer-4 load balancer (or DNS + client-side selection) spreads new connections; connections are long-lived so LB just needs to balance counts, not requests. Routing registry: a distributed store (Redis Cluster / a purpose-built service) maps userId → {gatewayNode, connectionId} (a set, since multi-device). Updated on connect/disconnect with a TTL + heartbeat so stale entries expire if a node dies. Message delivery: sender's gateway (or an API server) receives a message, persists it, then looks up each recipient's gateway node(s) in the registry and forwards the message there — via an internal message bus (Kafka/NATS topic per gateway node, or direct gRPC). The recipient's gateway pushes it down the matching socket(s). For group chat, resolve the member list → their nodes → forward once per node (dedup) rather than once per member. Backpressure: a slow client's send buffer fills — the gateway drops the connection (client reconnects and re-syncs from its watermark) rather than buffering unboundedly. Failure: a gateway node crashes → its ~200k clients' connections drop; clients auto-reconnect (with jittered backoff to avoid a reconnect storm) to a new node via the LB, re-register, and sync missed messages by watermark — because the source of truth is the persisted conversation store, no messages are lost, only a brief delivery gap. To avoid a thundering herd when a big node dies, clients spread reconnects over tens of seconds and the LB steers them to underloaded nodes. Scaling: add gateway nodes; the registry and message bus scale independently. Regional: gateways in each region; cross-region messages route through the bus; presence and routing registries are regional with a global overlay for cross-region conversations. Metrics: connections per node, message fan-out latency, reconnect rate (spikes = a node problem), registry lookup latency, and per-node memory/fd headroom.
How would you rank a news feed (not chronological) at scale, and what are the failure modes?
Two-stage funnel. Stage 1 — candidate generation: assemble a few hundred to a few thousand candidate items cheaply — the user's pushed timeline (recent posts from followees), plus pulled recent posts from followed celebrities, plus optionally "recommended" items (posts from non-followees the user might like, from a separate retrieval model). This stage optimises for recall and speed, not precision. Stage 2 — ranking: score each candidate with a model predicting the probability of each valued engagement (click, like, comment, share, dwell time, "meaningful interaction", and negative signals like hide/report), combined into a single value score with tuned weights; also apply business rules (diversity — don't show 5 posts from one author; freshness decay; demote borderline/policy content; inject ads). Serve the top N. Where the compute goes: candidate generation and feature fetching (author affinity, user history, post features, real-time engagement counts) dominate; the model inference is batched. Feature freshness matters — engagement counts and the user's recent activity feed into the score, so there's a real-time feature store. Failure modes: (1) Feedback loops — the model learns "users engage with outrage/clickbait" and amplifies it; needs explicit negative-feedback signals, diversity constraints, and integrity classifiers in the loop. (2) Cold start — new users/posts have no engagement features; fall back to popularity + demographic priors, explore deliberately. (3) Filter bubble — pure engagement optimisation narrows the feed; inject exploration and source diversity. (4) Staleness — if the ranking pipeline lags, users see an old feed; have a chronological fallback and cap end-to-end latency. (5) Latency budget — ranking must complete in tens of ms for a feed load; if the model service is slow, serve a cheaper heuristic ranking rather than blocking. (6) Metric myopia — optimising short-term clicks can hurt long-term retention and wellbeing; teams add long-horizon and survey-based objectives. (7) Consistency — the same user refreshing shouldn't see a totally reshuffled feed; add position stability / seen-item suppression. The system is deliberately layered so each stage can degrade independently (skip recommendations, skip ranking → chronological) under load or failure.

The Object Model: Blob, Tree, Commit

Everything in Git is an object in a content-addressed store — understand this and the rest follows.

Notes

A content-addressed key-value store

At its core Git is a key-value database. You hand it content, it stores the content and returns a hash (SHA-1 historically; SHA-256 in newer repos). The hash is the key: the same content always produces the same hash, and any change to the content produces a completely different hash. Objects live in .git/objects/ (loose objects, then packed into .pack files for efficiency).

# content-addressed: the hash IS the key; same bytes -> same hash, always
$ echo 'hello' | git hash-object --stdin
ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a
$ printf 'hello' | git hash-object --stdin      # one byte different...
b6fc4c620b67d95f953a5c1c1230aaab5db5a1b0      # ...totally different hash
# so Git can't be fooled: any edit to a file changes its blob's name,
# which changes its tree, which changes the commit hash.

The four object types

TypeWhat it holds
blobThe raw contents of one file. No filename, no permissions, no history — just bytes. Two files with identical content anywhere in the repo share one blob.
treeA directory listing: a list of entries, each being (mode, type, hash, name). Entries point at blobs (files) or other trees (subdirectories). This is where filenames and the executable bit live.
commitA snapshot pointer: the hash of one root tree, zero or more parent commit hashes, author + committer (name, email, timestamp), and the commit message.
tag (annotated)A named, described pointer to another object (usually a commit) with its own author, message, and optional signature. Lightweight tags are just a ref, not an object.
# walk the types for the current commit
$ git cat-file -p HEAD
tree 9d1f2a...            # commit -> one root tree
parent 4c7b8e...         #        -> previous commit
author Leo <x@y> 172... +0000
    Fix parser

$ git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree}
100644 blob a1b2c3...  README.md      # tree -> (mode, type, hash, name) rows
040000 tree d4e5f6...  src            # ...pointing at blobs and subtrees
$ git cat-file -p a1b2c3             # blob = just the file bytes, no name

How a commit represents your whole project

A commit points to one tree — the root directory. That tree points to blobs and subtrees, which point to more blobs and subtrees, all the way down. So a single commit hash transitively names the exact content of every file and every directory. Git stores a full snapshot conceptually (not diffs); it just deduplicates via hashing, so unchanged files across commits reuse the same blob and unchanged directories reuse the same tree. Packfiles then delta-compress similar objects on disk, but that's a storage optimisation invisible to the model.

# unchanged files/dirs are REUSED, not re-stored: commit two versions,
# compare the tree of a subdir that didn't change
$ git rev-parse HEAD~1:docs
7f3ab9c0e2...
$ git rev-parse HEAD:docs
7f3ab9c0e2...          # identical -> same tree object -> zero extra storage
# only the path from the changed blob up to the root commit gets new hashes.

History = a DAG of commits

Each commit records its parent(s), so commits form a directed acyclic graph. A normal commit has one parent; the first commit has none (a "root commit"); a merge commit has two or more. Branches and tags are just named pointers ("refs") into this graph, stored as files under .git/refs/ (or in packed-refs). HEAD usually points at a branch ref.

# the DAG made visible: parents, branches (refs), and a merge (2 parents)
$ git log --graph --oneline --all
*   e1a2b3c (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'feature'
|\
| * 9f8e7d6 (feature) Add cache layer      # feature's commits
* | 4c5b6a7 Hotfix logging
|/
* 2b3c4d5 Base commit                      # common ancestor
$ cat .git/refs/heads/main                 # a branch is literally a file...
e1a2b3c9d0...                              # ...holding one commit hash

Inspecting objects

git hash-object -w file.txt      # store content as a blob, print its hash
git cat-file -t <hash>           # show an object's type
git cat-file -p <hash>           # pretty-print an object's content
git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree}      # dump the root tree of the current commit
git rev-parse HEAD               # resolve a ref/expression to a full hash
git count-objects -v             # loose vs packed object stats
Cheat Sheet
  • Git = content-addressed KV store; the SHA of the content is the key. Same content → same hash; any change → new hash.
  • blob = file contents (no name). tree = directory (entries: mode, type, hash, name). commit = one root tree + parent(s) + author/committer + message. annotated tag = named pointer object with message/signature.
  • A commit → a tree → blobs + subtrees: one hash names your entire project state.
  • Snapshots, not diffs — but unchanged blobs/trees are reused across commits; packfiles delta-compress on disk.
  • History is a DAG: 1 parent = normal, 0 = root commit, ≥2 = merge.
  • Refs (branches, tags) = files in .git/refs/ holding a commit hash. HEAD → current branch.
  • Poke around: git cat-file -p <hash>, git cat-file -t, git rev-parse, git hash-object -w.
Q&A
What are the four Git object types?
Blob (file contents), tree (a directory listing pointing at blobs and subtrees), commit (a pointer to one root tree plus parent commits and metadata), and annotated tag (a named pointer object with its own message/signature).
Does a blob store the filename?
No. A blob is just the file's bytes. The filename, path, and mode (e.g. executable bit) are stored in the tree entry that points at the blob. That's why two identically-named files with different content are different blobs, and two differently-named files with identical content are the same blob.
Does Git store diffs between commits?
Conceptually no — each commit is a full snapshot (a complete tree). Git avoids bloat by reusing unchanged blob and tree objects across commits (dedup via hashing) and by delta-compressing objects inside packfiles on disk. The model is snapshots; deltas are an invisible storage detail.
What is a branch, physically?
A tiny file (e.g. .git/refs/heads/main, or a line in packed-refs) containing a single 40-hex-character commit hash. "Moving a branch" just rewrites that file. This is why branching and deleting branches are instant.
Why is the commit hash different if I commit the same tree twice?
Because the commit object includes the committer timestamp (and usually a different parent). The tree hash would be identical, but the commit object's bytes differ, so its hash differs.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What is used as the key for a Git object?
A cryptographic hash of the object's content (SHA-1, or SHA-256 in newer repositories).
Which object type contains filenames?
The tree object — each entry is (mode, type, hash, name).
How many parents does the very first commit in a repo have?
Zero — it's a root commit.

Intermediate core

You copy config.yaml to config.bak without changing it and commit. How many new blobs are created?
Zero new blobs. The content is identical, so it hashes to the same blob that already exists; Git just adds a second tree entry (config.bak) pointing at that same blob hash. A new tree object (the directory now has an extra entry) and a new commit object are created, but no new blob.
Explain how one commit hash can guarantee the exact state of a 10,000-file project.
The commit points to a single root tree hash. That tree's bytes include the hashes of all its entries (files as blobs, subdirectories as subtrees). Each subtree in turn includes its children's hashes, recursively. Because every hash is derived from content, changing any byte of any file changes that blob's hash, which changes its parent tree's hash, which propagates up to the root tree hash, which changes the commit hash. So the commit hash is a Merkle-root over the entire directory structure — it cryptographically fixes every file and folder.
What's the difference between an annotated tag and a lightweight tag?
A lightweight tag is just a ref — a file under .git/refs/tags/ holding a commit hash, with no extra data. An annotated tag creates a real tag object containing a tagger name/email/date, a message, and optionally a GPG signature; the ref then points at that tag object, which points at the commit. Releases should use annotated (or signed) tags so there's a recorded author and message; lightweight tags are fine as private bookmarks.

Advanced deep

Git historically used SHA-1, which has known collision attacks. Why hasn't this broken Git, and what has been done about it?
Several reasons it hasn't been catastrophic: (1) Git hashes a type/length header plus the content, and for commits the object includes parent hashes and timestamps, so a useful collision must be a valid Git object of the right type that also fits the surrounding DAG — much harder than a raw SHA-1 collision. (2) The known attacks (SHAttered, 2017) are identical-prefix / chosen-prefix collisions requiring the attacker to craft both colliding blobs; they can't produce a collision for an existing object they don't control (no preimage attack on SHA-1 is known). (3) Git added a collision-detection library (sha1dc / "hardened SHA-1") that detects the SHAttered attack pattern and aborts, so those specific PDFs can't even be added. (4) The real fix is the SHA-256 object format: repositories can be created with --object-format=sha256, making all object names 256-bit. Interop with SHA-1 repos is still maturing (hosting support, a mapping between the two hashes), so migration has been gradual, but the transition design exists and new security-sensitive repos can opt in today.
What is a packfile, how does git gc build one, and what problem does it solve?
Storing every object as its own zlib-compressed file ("loose objects") wastes space (no cross-object compression) and inodes, and makes network transfer chatty. A packfile (.git/objects/pack/*.pack with a companion .idx) bundles many objects into one file and stores similar objects as deltas against a chosen base object (delta chains), then compresses. git gc (invoked automatically past thresholds, or manually) runs git repack: it walks reachable objects, groups likely-similar ones (heuristics on type, size, path/filename, and recency — newer objects are kept whole or shallowly-deltated for fast access), picks base objects, computes deltas up to a max chain length, and writes the pack plus an index for O(log n) lookup by hash. It also prunes unreachable loose objects older than the expiry (default 2 weeks, and only those not referenced by the reflog). The result: dramatically smaller repos, fewer files, and packs can be sent almost as-is over the wire ("thin packs" during fetch/push send deltas against objects the other side already has). Trade-off: deep delta chains cost CPU to reconstruct an object, so Git caps chain depth and keeps a delta cache.

The Three Trees: Working Tree, Index, HEAD

Almost every confusing Git command makes sense once you track which of the three trees it moves.

Notes

The three "trees" (states)

TreeWhat it is
HEADThe last commit on the current branch — the snapshot your next commit will be based on. "What I last committed."
Index (staging area / cache)A binary file (.git/index) listing the exact file contents (blob hashes) + metadata that will go into the next commit. "What I've proposed to commit."
Working treeThe actual files on disk you edit. "What I'm working on right now."
# one edit, seen in all three trees at once
$ echo 'x' >> app.py           # working tree changed only
$ git status --short
 M app.py                      # column 2 = worktree vs index
$ git add app.py
$ git status --short
M  app.py                      # column 1 = index vs HEAD (now staged)
$ git commit -m 'x'            # index written as a commit; all three match again

The basic workflow moves content between them

edit file        # working tree changes, index & HEAD unchanged
git add file     # copy working-tree version into the index
git commit       # write the index as a new commit; HEAD moves to it

After a clean commit, all three trees match. git status is essentially a diff report: "Changes to be committed" = index vs HEAD; "Changes not staged" = working tree vs index; "Untracked files" = in working tree, not in index.

reset moves things between the three trees

CommandHEADIndexWorking tree
reset --soft <c>→ cunchangedunchanged
reset [--mixed] <c>→ c→ cunchanged
reset --hard <c>→ c→ c→ c (discards changes)

So git reset --soft HEAD~1 "uncommits" but keeps everything staged; git reset HEAD~1 also unstages; git reset --hard HEAD~1 throws the work away entirely.

# squash the last 3 commits into one, keeping all their changes staged
$ git reset --soft HEAD~3      # HEAD -> 3 back; index + worktree untouched
$ git commit -m 'Combined feature'

# "uncommit" but keep edits to re-split them
$ git reset HEAD~1            # --mixed: HEAD + index back one; files still on disk, unstaged

# nuke local commits AND edits (no recovery except reflog)
$ git reset --hard origin/main

checkout / restore / switch

  • git checkout <commit> — moves HEAD (detaches it) and updates index + working tree to that commit; refuses if it would clobber uncommitted changes.
  • git checkout <branch> — same, but HEAD follows the branch (not detached).
  • git checkout -- <file> / git restore <file> — overwrite the working-tree file from the index (discard unstaged edits).
  • git restore --staged <file> — copy HEAD's version into the index (unstage), leaving the working tree alone. git restore --staged --worktree <file> resets both.
  • Newer split: git switch for branches, git restore for files — less overloaded than checkout.
# the one checkout did too many jobs; the split names the intent:
$ git switch feature            # change branch (was: git checkout feature)
$ git switch -c hotfix          # create + switch  (was: checkout -b)
$ git restore app.py            # discard unstaged edits, from the index
$ git restore --staged app.py   # unstage, from HEAD (worktree edit kept)
$ git restore --source=HEAD~2 app.py   # bring back an old version of one file

Other index operations

git add -p          # stage selected hunks interactively
git reset -p        # unstage selected hunks
git rm --cached f   # remove from index (stop tracking) but keep on disk
git diff            # working tree vs index
git diff --staged   # index vs HEAD  (aka --cached)
git diff HEAD       # working tree vs HEAD (both combined)
Cheat Sheet
  • HEAD = last commit. Index = next commit's staged content (.git/index). Working tree = files on disk.
  • add = working tree → index. commit = index → new commit, HEAD moves.
  • git status: "to be committed" = index vs HEAD; "not staged" = worktree vs index; "untracked" = not in index.
  • reset --soft = move HEAD only. reset --mixed (default) = HEAD + index. reset --hard = HEAD + index + working tree (destroys changes).
  • git restore <file> = discard unstaged edits (from index). git restore --staged <file> = unstage (from HEAD).
  • git diff = worktree vs index. git diff --staged = index vs HEAD. git diff HEAD = worktree vs HEAD.
  • git rm --cached = untrack but keep file. git add -p / reset -p = hunk-level staging.
Q&A
What is the index / staging area?
A file (.git/index) that holds the complete list of file paths and their blob hashes that will form the next commit. git add writes working-tree content into it; git commit turns it into a commit. It lets you build a commit incrementally and commit only some of your changes.
Difference between git diff and git diff --staged?
git diff (no args) shows working tree vs index — your unstaged changes. git diff --staged (or --cached) shows index vs HEAD — what you've staged and would commit. git diff HEAD shows everything (staged + unstaged) vs the last commit.
What do --soft, --mixed, and --hard control in git reset?
Which of the three trees get updated to the target commit. --soft: only HEAD moves (index and working tree untouched → your changes are left staged). --mixed (default): HEAD and index move (changes left unstaged in the working tree). --hard: all three move (working-tree changes are discarded — the only destructive one).
How do I unstage a file I accidentally git added?
git restore --staged <file> (modern) or git reset HEAD <file> (classic). Both copy HEAD's version of that path back into the index; your working-tree edits are preserved.
What's the difference between git rm and git rm --cached?
git rm file deletes it from both the index and the working tree (staged for deletion). git rm --cached file removes it only from the index — Git stops tracking it, but the file stays on disk. Use --cached when you committed something that should have been gitignored.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which command copies a change from the working tree into the index?
git add.
After a clean git commit with nothing else changed, how do the three trees compare?
All three (HEAD, index, working tree) are identical — git status reports "nothing to commit, working tree clean".
Which reset mode discards your uncommitted working-tree changes?
git reset --hard.

Intermediate core

You've made 3 commits that should really be 1. You want to keep all the changes staged and re-commit once. Which command?
git reset --soft HEAD~3. HEAD moves back 3 commits, but the index and working tree are untouched — so all the combined changes from those 3 commits are sitting staged, ready for a single new git commit. (git reset --mixed HEAD~3 would also work but leaves them unstaged, so you'd need to git add again.)
You run git checkout <some-old-commit> and Git warns about "detached HEAD". What does that mean and what's the risk?
Normally HEAD points at a branch name, and that branch points at a commit. In detached HEAD, HEAD points directly at a commit with no branch in between. You can look around and even make commits, but those commits aren't on any branch — if you then git checkout main, nothing references them and they become candidates for garbage collection (recoverable via the reflog for a while). To keep work done in detached HEAD, create a branch first: git switch -c new-branch.
What does git add -p do and when is it useful?
It walks through your unstaged changes hunk by hunk and asks, for each, whether to stage it (y/n/split/edit). It lets you separate unrelated changes that live in the same file into different commits — e.g. stage a bug fix now while leaving a half-finished refactor in the same file unstaged. It operates purely on the index; nothing is committed.

Advanced deep

Walk through exactly what git commit -a -m "msg" does in terms of the three trees, and name a case where -a silently does the wrong thing.
-a makes Git, just before committing, automatically stage modifications and deletions of already-tracked files (equivalent to git add -u) — it copies the current working-tree content of every tracked, modified path into the index. Then it commits the index as a new commit and advances HEAD. Sequence: (working tree → index) for tracked changes, then (index → new commit), then HEAD moves. Cases where it does the wrong thing: (1) New files are not tracked yet, so -a ignores them — you think you committed everything but new files were left out. (2) If you had carefully staged only some hunks with git add -p, -a overrides that by staging the entire current content of those files, silently including the hunks you deliberately left out. (3) A file you'd staged and then further edited: -a commits the newer working-tree version, not the version you reviewed and staged. So -a is a convenience for the "I edited tracked files and want all of it" case and a footgun whenever your index was intentionally different from your working tree.
Why is the index a performance feature, not just a UX feature? What metadata does it cache and how is that used?
The index is a flat, sorted binary file listing every tracked path with its blob hash and cached stat data from the last time Git saw that file: mtime, ctime, inode, device, size, and mode. On git status / git diff, Git doesn't re-hash every file in the repo — it lstat()s each path and compares the stat fields to the cached ones. If they match, Git assumes the content is unchanged and skips reading and hashing the file entirely. Only files whose stat data differs get their content hashed to confirm a real change. For a large repo this turns an O(total bytes) operation into O(number of files) syscalls. Extensions build on this: the untracked cache stores directory mtimes so Git can skip scanning unchanged directories for new files; the fsmonitor integration (Watchman / built-in) lets the OS tell Git which paths changed since last time, avoiding even the full lstat() walk; the split index and sparse index reduce the cost of writing and carrying the index itself. The "racy git" problem (a file modified in the same second the index was written, so mtime matches but content changed) is handled by treating entries with mtime ≥ index mtime as dirty and re-checking them.

Branches, HEAD & Fast-Forward

A branch is just a movable pointer — once that clicks, merges and rebases stop being mysterious.

Notes

A branch is a pointer, not a copy

A branch is a 41-byte file under .git/refs/heads/ containing one commit hash. Creating a branch writes that file; it does not copy any files. When you commit on a branch, Git creates the commit and then updates the branch file to point at the new commit. That's the whole mechanism — branches are cheap because they're one line of text.

# a branch really is just a file with a hash in it
$ git branch feature           # no files copied, instant, even on a huge repo
$ cat .git/refs/heads/feature
4c7b8e1f09a2c3...              # same hash as main right now
$ git commit -am 'work'        # commit, THEN this file is rewritten:
$ cat .git/refs/heads/feature
9d0e1a2b3c4d...               # advanced; main's file is untouched

HEAD

  • HEAD is a file (.git/HEAD) that normally contains ref: refs/heads/main — a symbolic reference to the current branch. "The current branch" is defined as whatever HEAD points to.
  • When you commit, Git follows HEAD → branch, and moves that branch.
  • Detached HEAD: HEAD contains a commit hash directly (from git checkout <hash> or git checkout v1.0). Commits you make advance HEAD but no branch — create a branch to keep them.
$ cat .git/HEAD
ref: refs/heads/main            # normal: symbolic ref to a branch
$ git checkout v1.0
$ cat .git/HEAD
a1b2c3d4e5...                  # DETACHED: a raw hash, no branch
# commits here are reachable only by hash; leaving loses them:
$ git switch -c keep-this      # attach a branch before switching away

Fast-forward vs true merge

Say main is at commit C and you branch feature, then add D and E on feature. main has not moved.

C ← D ← E   (feature, HEAD)
^
main

git checkout main; git merge feature: since main's commit C is an ancestor of feature's E, Git can just slide the main pointer forward to E. No new commit, no merge — a fast-forward. History stays linear.

Now suppose someone else committed F on main while you worked:

      D ← E   (feature)
     /
C ← F         (main)

The branches have diverged. A fast-forward is impossible. Git creates a merge commit M with two parents (E and F) that combines both lines. This is a "true" / "3-way" merge (it uses E, F, and their common ancestor C).

Controlling merge behaviour

git merge feature              # FF if possible, else a merge commit
git merge --no-ff feature      # always create a merge commit (keeps the branch visible)
git merge --ff-only feature    # only if it can FF, else fail (good for scripts / pulls)
git config pull.ff only        # make 'git pull' refuse to create surprise merge commits
git merge --squash feature     # stage the combined diff, no merge; you commit once, no link to feature

Everyday branch commands

git switch -c feature           # create + switch (old: git checkout -b)
git branch                      # list local branches (* = current)
git branch -vv                  # + upstream tracking + ahead/behind
git branch -d feature           # delete (refuses if not merged)
git branch -D feature           # force delete
git branch -m old new           # rename
git switch -                    # jump back to previous branch
git push -u origin feature      # push + set upstream tracking

Tracking branches & remotes

origin/main is a remote-tracking branch — Git's local cache of where main was on origin at your last fetch. It only moves when you fetch/pull. Your local main can be "ahead 2, behind 1" relative to it. git status reports this when your branch has an upstream set.

$ git fetch                     # updates origin/* only; your branches untouched
$ git status -sb
## main...origin/main [ahead 2, behind 1]   # measured against the cached ref
$ git branch -vv
* main  9d0e1a2 [origin/main: ahead 2, behind 1] local work
# reconcile: git rebase origin/main   (replay your 2 on top of their 1)
#        or: git merge  origin/main   (merge commit)   -- git pull does one of these
Cheat Sheet
  • Branch = file in .git/refs/heads/ holding one commit hash. Committing moves it. Creating/deleting is instant.
  • HEAD = symbolic ref to the current branch (ref: refs/heads/…). Detached HEAD = points straight at a commit.
  • Fast-forward: target branch's tip is an ancestor of the source → just slide the pointer, no merge commit, linear history.
  • True / 3-way merge: branches diverged → new merge commit with 2 parents, using the common ancestor.
  • merge --no-ff = always a merge commit. merge --ff-only = FF or fail. merge --squash = flatten, no parent link.
  • git switch -c new branch; git branch -d safe delete; -D force; switch - = previous branch.
  • origin/main = remote-tracking branch, a snapshot from your last fetch; "ahead/behind" is measured against it.
Q&A
What actually happens when you create a branch?
Git writes a new file under .git/refs/heads/ containing the current commit's hash. No files are copied, nothing is duplicated. Switching to it just updates HEAD to point at that ref and updates the working tree/index to match its commit.
What is a fast-forward merge?
When the branch you're merging into has not diverged — its tip commit is a direct ancestor of the branch you're merging from — Git doesn't need a merge commit. It simply moves the current branch pointer forward to the other branch's tip. History remains a straight line.
When is a fast-forward not possible?
When both branches have commits the other doesn't — they've diverged from a common ancestor. Git then performs a three-way merge and records a merge commit with two parents.
What does --no-ff achieve?
It forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward would be possible. Teams use it so that every feature branch leaves a visible "merge bubble" in history, making it easy to see which commits belonged together and to revert a whole feature with one git revert -m 1.
What is origin/main and why doesn't it update as I work?
It's a remote-tracking branch: a local, read-only pointer recording where main was on the remote origin the last time you communicated with it. It only advances on git fetch (or pull, which fetches then merges/rebases). Between fetches it's a stale-but-useful reference point for "ahead/behind" counts.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

How much data is copied when you run git branch new-feature?
Essentially none — Git writes one small file containing a commit hash.
What does HEAD normally point to?
The current branch (a symbolic ref like ref: refs/heads/main), not a commit directly.
Does a fast-forward merge create a merge commit?
No — it just moves the branch pointer forward.

Intermediate core

git branch -d feature fails with "not fully merged". What does that check, and when is -D safe?
-d refuses to delete a branch whose tip commit is not reachable from HEAD (or from its configured upstream) — i.e. it has commits that would become unreferenced. It's protecting you from losing work. -D (force) is safe when you know those commits are unwanted (an abandoned experiment), or when they are reachable another way — e.g. you already merged the branch with --squash or rebased its commits onto main under new hashes, so the original commits are redundant. Even after -D, the branch's old tip is in the reflog for a couple of weeks, so an accidental force-delete is recoverable.
Your teammate asks why git pull sometimes creates a weird "Merge branch 'main' of …" commit on their branch. What's happening and how do you prevent it?
git pull = git fetch + git merge origin/<branch> by default. If they have local commits and the remote also advanced, the two have diverged, so the merge can't fast-forward and Git records a merge commit right there on their branch — often with an ugly auto-generated message, and it clutters history with tiny merge bubbles. Prevention options: git config --global pull.ff only (pull refuses and tells them to decide) combined with git pull --rebase when they do have local work (replays their commits on top of the updated remote, keeping history linear); or set git config --global pull.rebase true to make rebase the default. For shared long-lived branches, merges are fine; for a personal feature branch, rebase-on-pull is usually what people want.

Advanced deep

Explain how Git computes "ahead 3, behind 2", and why that count can be misleading after a rebase or force-push.
Given your branch tip L and its upstream tip R, Git finds the merge base B (their most recent common ancestor) and counts commits on each side: "ahead" = commits reachable from L but not R (i.e. on B..L), "behind" = commits reachable from R but not L (B..R). It's literally git rev-list --left-right --count R...L. This is a graph comparison by commit identity (hash), not by content. After you rebase your branch, every one of your commits gets a new hash even though the diffs are identical. So if upstream hasn't changed, you'll now show "ahead N, behind N" — N brand-new commits ahead, and the N original pre-rebase commits (still reachable from origin/branch until you push) counted as "behind" — because Git sees two disjoint sets of commit objects that happen to represent the same changes. Similarly, after someone force-pushes a rewritten upstream, your local remote-tracking branch is stale and the ahead/behind numbers reflect the divergence between old and new histories, not real unmerged work. The fix is to fetch and then reconcile deliberately (reset your local branch to the new upstream, or rebase onto it), after which the counts become meaningful again. The lesson: ahead/behind answers "how do these two commit graphs differ?", which only equals "how does the work differ?" when no history rewriting has happened.
What is a symbolic ref, how does git symbolic-ref differ from a normal ref, and where else does Git use them besides HEAD?
A normal ref (.git/refs/heads/main) contains a 40-hex commit hash — it points at an object. A symbolic ref contains the text ref: refs/heads/<name> — it points at another ref, forming one level of indirection. HEAD is the canonical example: "current branch" is implemented as HEAD being a symbolic ref to a branch, so that committing updates the branch HEAD names, and detaching just means overwriting HEAD with a raw hash instead. git symbolic-ref HEAD reads it; git symbolic-ref HEAD refs/heads/other repoints it without touching the working tree (unlike switch, which also updates files). Other uses: refs/remotes/origin/HEAD is a symbolic ref recording the remote's default branch (what git clone checks out, and what a bare origin means in some commands) — you can retarget it with git remote set-head origin -a. During an interactive rebase or a merge, Git writes transient symbolic/plain refs like ORIG_HEAD, MERGE_HEAD, REBASE_HEAD to track state. Worktrees each get their own HEAD. The indirection is also why the reflog is per ref: HEAD's reflog records every value HEAD took (including branch switches), while main's reflog records only where main pointed.

Merge vs Rebase

Two ways to combine work — one preserves history as it happened, the other rewrites it to look tidy.

Notes

The setup

      D ← E     feature
     /
A ← B ← C       main

You want feature to include main's new commit C.

Merge

git checkout feature; git merge main creates a merge commit M with two parents (E and C):

      D ← E ← M     feature
     /       /
A ← B ← C ←--/     main
  • Nothing is rewritten. E, D, C keep their hashes.
  • M records "these two lines of development were joined here", with the exact state at that time.
  • History is truthful but can become a tangle of criss-crossing lines ("merge bubbles") on busy repos.

Rebase

git checkout feature; git rebase main takes your commits (D, E), sets them aside, moves feature to C, then replays D and E on top as brand-new commits D′ and E′:

A ← B ← C ← D′ ← E′     feature
        ^
        main
  • D′ and E′ have new hashes (new parent, new committer date) — the originals are now unreferenced.
  • History is linear: it looks like you started your work from C all along.
  • Each replayed commit can hit conflicts; you resolve, git rebase --continue, repeat.

The golden rule

Don't rebase commits that others have based work on (anything already pushed to a shared branch that teammates pulled). Rebasing rewrites hashes; when you force-push the rewritten branch, everyone else's history diverges from yours and they get painful conflicts. Rebase freely on your own unpushed / unshared commits.

# SAFE: branch is yours and unpushed
$ git log --oneline @{u}..     # commits not yet on the upstream -> free to rebase
$ git rebase -i main

# DANGER: teammate already pulled 'feature'
$ git rebase main && git push --force     # their 'feature' now diverges from yours
# if you must, use --force-with-lease so you don't clobber commits you haven't seen:
$ git push --force-with-lease

When to use which

Use mergeUse rebase
Integrating a shared/long-lived branchUpdating your local feature branch onto latest main
You want the true record of when things joinedYou want a clean, linear, reviewable history
The branch is public and others use itCleaning up your own commits before opening/merging a PR
Preserving context of parallel workAvoiding "Merge branch 'main'" noise commits
# typical solo feature branch: rebase to stay current, no merge noise
$ git switch feature
$ git fetch origin
$ git rebase origin/main        # replay my work on the latest main
$ git push --force-with-lease   # my branch only; nobody else is on it

# integrating a shared release branch: merge, keep the join recorded
$ git switch main
$ git merge --no-ff release/2.4

Related commands

git pull --rebase             # fetch, then rebase your local commits onto the new upstream
git rebase --onto A B feature # replay feature's commits that are after B, onto A
git merge --no-ff feature     # force a merge bubble even if FF is possible
git rebase -i main            # interactive: also reorder/squash/edit while replaying
git rebase --abort            # bail out, restore pre-rebase state
git config rerere.enabled true# reuse recorded conflict resolutions across replays

Semi-linear / "rebase and merge" workflows (common on GitHub/GitLab): rebase the feature branch onto main first, then merge with --no-ff — linear commits plus a merge commit marking the feature boundary.

Cheat Sheet
  • Merge: joins two branches with a 2-parent merge commit. Non-destructive, hashes unchanged, true history, can get tangled.
  • Rebase: replays your commits on top of another branch as new commits (new hashes). Linear history, "as if you started from latest". Rewrites history.
  • Golden rule: never rebase/rewrite commits others have already pulled from a shared branch.
  • Rebase conflicts are resolved per replayed commit: fix → git add → git rebase --continue (or --abort).
  • git pull --rebase avoids "Merge branch 'main'" noise on your feature branch.
  • Rule of thumb: rebase to update your branch onto main; merge to bring a finished branch into main (often --no-ff).
  • Enable rerere to auto-reapply conflict resolutions during long rebases.
Q&A
Core difference between merge and rebase?
Merge combines two branches by creating a new commit with both branch tips as parents — existing commits are untouched. Rebase moves your branch's commits so they replay on top of another branch, creating new commits with new hashes and discarding the originals — producing a linear history.
Why does rebase change commit hashes?
A commit's hash is derived from its content including its parent hash and committer date. Rebasing gives each replayed commit a different parent (and a new committer timestamp), so its bytes differ and it gets a new hash. The original commits still exist until garbage-collected but nothing points to them.
What is "the golden rule of rebasing"?
Never rebase commits that exist outside your local repo — i.e. that others may have pulled. Rewriting shared history forces everyone else into a divergent state and messy recovery. Only rebase private, unpushed (or unshared) work.
How are conflicts handled differently in merge vs rebase?
A merge resolves conflicts once, at the single merge commit. A rebase replays commits one at a time and can stop with a conflict on each commit; you fix each, git add, and git rebase --continue. It's more interruptions but each is smaller and localised to that commit's change.
What does git pull --rebase do?
It fetches the upstream, then instead of merging origin/<branch> into your local branch (which would create a merge commit when you have local commits), it rebases your local commits on top of the updated upstream. Result: linear history, no "Merge branch" commits on your branch.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which operation produces a linear history?
Rebase.
How many parents does a standard merge commit have?
Two (or more, for an octopus merge).
Is it safe to rebase commits you've already pushed to a shared main that colleagues pulled?
No — that violates the golden rule and forces everyone into a divergent history.

Intermediate core

Your feature branch is 20 commits behind main. Compare the review/history outcome of git merge main into it vs git rebase main.
merge main: one merge commit is added to your feature branch; your 20-behind situation is resolved in a single conflict-resolution pass; history now shows a merge bubble, and when the PR is eventually merged, reviewers see your original commits plus a "Merge branch 'main' into feature" commit mixed in. Diffs against main include the merge. rebase main: your feature commits are replayed on top of current main as new commits, so the branch becomes a clean linear series that applies directly to main's tip; the PR diff is exactly your changes with no merge noise; reviewers can read commit-by-commit.
