Mitigation: keep PRs small (then squash loses little); write a thorough squash-commit body summarising the key changes; link the PR (GitHub keeps the original commits on the PR page). (2) The main commit matches no real commit that was ever tested in isolation — though it is the exact state that CI tested as the PR head, so bisect on main is still sound. (3) Cherry-pick/backport granularity — you can't backport just one commit of the PR; you take all or nothing. Mitigation: split into separate PRs when parts need independent backporting. (4) Co-authorship / attribution can be lost unless Co-authored-by: trailers are preserved (GitHub does aggregate them into the squash message). (5) Rebasing dependent branches — a branch started off the pre-squash feature branch now sees its base commits "disappear" (replaced by one squashed commit), forcing a messy rebase; git rebase --onto main <old-base> fixes it but people trip on it. Mitigation: don't stack branches off unmerged feature branches, or coordinate the squash. (6) Revert asymmetry — reverting the squash is easy (one commit), but you can't revert just part of the feature. (7) Signed-commit policies — the squash commit is created by the platform, so it's signed (if at all) by the platform's key, not the author's; teams requiring author signatures use rebase-merge instead. (8) Merge metadata — you lose the record of when the branch was integrated and the two-parent link, so tooling that reasons about merge structure (e.g. --first-parent release notes) sees a flat list. Overall: squash is a good default when PRs are small and history readability matters most; switch to rebase-merge when every commit is valuable and must be individually signed/bisectable, and to merge-commits when preserving the exact integration history matters (large features, audit requirements).

Grafana Architecture & Data Sources

Grafana stores almost nothing about your metrics — it queries other systems and draws the result.

Notes

What Grafana is (and isn't)

Grafana is a visualization and alerting layer, not a database. It holds dashboards, users, data source definitions, alert rules, and annotations in its own small SQLite/MySQL/Postgres backend. The actual time series, logs, and traces live in data sources — Prometheus, Loki, Tempo, InfluxDB, Elasticsearch, Graphite, CloudWatch, a SQL database, etc. At render time each panel sends a query to its data source and plots what comes back.

# Grafana's own DB is tiny — it stores dashboards + config, not a single data point
sqlite> .tables
alert_rule   annotation   dashboard   data_source   org   user   ...
sqlite> SELECT count(*) FROM dashboard;      -- 214
# the metrics themselves? not here. a panel just holds a query string:
#   { "datasource": {"uid": "prom-prod"}, "expr": "rate(http_requests_total[5m])" }
# at render time Grafana forwards that to Prometheus and plots the response.

Data source plugins

  • Each data source type is a plugin (built-in or installed) that knows that backend's query language and API.
  • A configured data source instance has a URL, auth, and default settings. Panels reference it by UID (stable) — not by name — which is what makes dashboards portable.
  • The -- Mixed -- data source lets one panel pull from several sources at once; -- Dashboard -- reuses another panel's result; -- Grafana -- is the built-in one for annotations and test data.
# panels reference a data source by UID, never by display name -> portable JSON
{
  "targets": [
    { "datasource": { "type": "prometheus", "uid": "P1809F7CD0C75ACF3" },
      "expr": "up{job=\"api\"}" }
  ]
}
# import the same dashboard on another Grafana -> it prompts to map that UID
# to a local Prometheus. Rename the data source freely; the UID is stable.

Query path: proxy vs direct

ModePathImplication
Server (proxy) — defaultbrowser → Grafana server → data sourceData source needn't be reachable from the browser; credentials stay server-side; CORS is a non-issue.
Browser (direct)browser → data source directlyOnly for sources that support it; needs network + CORS from every user's browser; rarely used now.
# proxy mode (default): the query goes THROUGH the Grafana server
GET https://grafana.corp/api/datasources/proxy/uid/prom-prod/api/v1/query?query=up
#   -> Grafana adds the stored Authorization header, calls http://prometheus:9090
#   browser never sees the Prometheus URL or credentials, no CORS setup needed

# direct mode: browser calls http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/query itself
#   -> Prometheus must be reachable from every laptop + send CORS headers

Deployment shape

  • Stateless Grafana pods/instances behind a load balancer, all pointing at one shared config database → horizontal scale and HA.
  • Unified alerting needs the shared DB (and for HA, instances coordinate so a rule fires once).
  • Sessions are JWT/cookie; no sticky sessions required for the UI.
  • Grafana Cloud bundles hosted Prometheus (Mimir), Loki, and Tempo as the data sources.
# HA: N identical stateless Grafana replicas, ONE shared config DB
[database]
type = postgres
host = grafana-db.internal:5432        # all replicas read/write here

[unified_alerting]
enabled = true
ha_peers = grafana-0:9094,grafana-1:9094,grafana-2:9094   # gossip so a rule fires ONCE
# scale out = add a replica behind the LB; no sticky sessions (JWT/cookie auth)

Provisioning & config

Data sources, dashboards, alerting, and plugins can be defined as YAML files under conf/provisioning/ (or via Terraform / the HTTP API) so the whole Grafana setup is reproducible — see the Provisioning topic. grafana.ini / env vars (GF_*) control server settings.

# conf/provisioning/datasources/prod.yaml — checked into git, applied on boot
apiVersion: 1
datasources:
  - name: Prometheus
    uid: prom-prod            # stable UID dashboards reference
    type: prometheus
    url: http://prometheus:9090
    isDefault: true

# every grafana.ini key has an env override: [auth] disable_login_form=true
#   -> GF_AUTH_DISABLE_LOGIN_FORM=true
Cheat Sheet
  • Grafana = viz + alerting layer. Its DB holds dashboards/users/datasources/alerts/annotations only. Metrics live in data sources.
  • Data source = a plugin instance (URL + auth), referenced by UID for portability.
  • Special sources: Mixed (many at once), Dashboard (reuse a panel's data), Grafana (test data / annotations).
  • Server/proxy access (default): browser → Grafana → source; creds stay server-side. Browser access: direct, needs CORS.
  • HA = multiple stateless Grafana instances + one shared SQL config DB behind an LB.
  • Reproducible setup via conf/provisioning/*.yaml, Terraform, or the HTTP API; server config in grafana.ini / GF_* env vars.
Q&A
Does Grafana store your metrics?
No. It stores dashboards, data source configs, users, alert rules, and annotations in a small relational DB. The time series/logs/traces stay in the backend systems (Prometheus, Loki, etc.), which Grafana queries live for every panel refresh.
Why reference a data source by UID instead of name?
The UID is stable across renames and across environments. If a dashboard JSON hard-codes a data source name it breaks when imported somewhere the source is named differently; with a UID (or a dashboard variable of type datasource) the dashboard stays portable.
What's the difference between server and browser access mode?
Server (proxy) mode routes queries through the Grafana backend, so the data source only needs to be reachable from the server and credentials never reach the browser. Browser mode has each user's browser call the data source directly, which requires network reachability and CORS configuration on the data source; it's now uncommon.
How do you run Grafana highly available?
Run several stateless Grafana instances behind a load balancer, all sharing one external SQL database (MySQL/Postgres) for config. For alerting HA the instances use that DB plus a gossip/coordination channel so each alert notification is sent once, not once per instance.
What is the Mixed data source?
A pseudo-source that lets a single panel contain queries against multiple real data sources simultaneously — e.g. a Prometheus query and a CloudWatch query on the same graph. Each query row picks its own source.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Where does Grafana keep dashboards and users?
In its own relational database (SQLite by default, or MySQL/Postgres for production/HA).
What plots the data in a panel — Grafana or the data source?
The data source executes the query and returns data; Grafana renders it. Grafana does no storage of the series.
Which access mode keeps data source credentials off the client?
Server / proxy mode (the default).

Intermediate core

A dashboard exported from staging shows "Data source not found" when imported to production. What are the likely causes and fixes?
The dashboard JSON references a data source by a UID (or name) that doesn't exist in prod. Fixes: (1) Give the two environments' data sources the same UID (set it explicitly in provisioning YAML: uid: prometheus-main) so exported dashboards resolve everywhere. (2) Parameterise the dashboard with a datasource-type template variable so the panel's source is ${DS_PROM} and the importer picks it at import time (this is what "Export for sharing externally" does — it replaces concrete sources with __inputs). (3) Manage dashboards via provisioning/Terraform where the source UID is a known constant. Long term, standardise data source UIDs across environments.
Panels are slow and the Grafana server CPU spikes on dashboard load. How does the query path explain this and what do you tune?
In proxy mode every panel's query flows through the Grafana backend, which also does the response processing (transformations, field config, downsampling to the panel's pixel width via max data points and min step). A 30-panel dashboard on a short refresh hammers both Grafana and the data source. Tune: raise the dashboard refresh interval / min refresh; reduce panels per dashboard (overview + drilldowns); set sensible Max data points and Min interval so you don't fetch raw high-resolution data to draw 400 px wide; use $__rate_interval for Prometheus; enable query caching (Enterprise/Cloud) for repeated identical queries; use recording rules in Prometheus so heavy aggregations are precomputed; lazy-load panels (only render on scroll). Scale Grafana horizontally if it's genuinely CPU-bound on response processing.

Advanced deep

Design a multi-tenant Grafana setup where 20 teams each see only their own dashboards and data, with self-service dashboard editing but protected shared infrastructure dashboards.
Options, roughly in increasing isolation: (1) Single Grafana, folders + RBAC: one folder per team; team members get Editor on their folder, Viewer (or none) elsewhere; a central platform team owns a locked "Infra" folder (Editor = platform only, Viewer = everyone). Use Grafana Teams synced from your IdP groups (OAuth/SAML) so membership is automatic. Fine-grained RBAC (Enterprise) can also restrict data source usage per team. Data isolation is the hard part on a shared Prometheus: use label-enforced queries — a per-team data source pointing at Prometheus/Mimir with a X-Scope-OrgID header or an enforced namespace=~"team-a-.*" label matcher (Mimir/Cortex/Loki support per-tenant IDs; the "label enforcer"/PromQL rewrite proxies do it for vanilla Prometheus). Each team's data source is provisioned with their tenant/label baked in and they can't edit it. (2) Organizations: Grafana Orgs give separate dashboard/user/data-source namespaces in one instance — stronger separation, but Orgs are semi-deprecated in favour of folders+RBAC and are clumsy for users in many teams. (3) Instance per team (or Grafana Cloud stack per team): total isolation, highest ops cost; worth it only for hard security/compliance boundaries. Recommended: single instance, IdP-synced Teams, folder RBAC, provisioned per-team scoped data sources with enforced tenant/label, shared read-only Infra folder, and dashboards-as-code for the shared ones so "protected" means "changes go through a PR", while team folders stay click-to-edit. Add quotas (org/user/dashboard limits) and a provisioned org-wide default folder structure.
Grafana's config database is a single point of failure in your HA setup. Walk through failure modes and mitigations.
The shared SQL DB holds dashboards, users, data sources, API keys/service accounts, alert rules, alert state, annotations, and provisioning bookkeeping. Failure modes: (1) DB down → Grafana can't load dashboards or evaluate alerting state; existing rendered pages may partly work but refreshes fail, logins fail, and alert evaluation stalls (no new notifications, and on recovery you may get a burst). (2) DB slow / connection pool exhausted → UI latency, alert evaluation lag; a runaway annotations table (every alert state change writes annotations) is a classic cause. (3) Data loss / corruption → lose dashboards and alert rules not stored elsewhere. (4) Split brain on failover → duplicate alert notifications if two Grafana groups can't coordinate. Mitigations: run the DB itself HA (managed Postgres/MySQL with a replica and automatic failover, or Postgres with Patroni); keep Grafana's DB connection settings tuned (max_open_conn, max_idle_conn, conn_max_lifetime) and monitor pool saturation; set annotation retention (annotations.alerting.max_age, cleanup job) so tables don't bloat; **treat dashboards and alert rules as code** — provision them from Git so a DB rebuild is terraform apply / restart, not a restore; back up the DB regularly and test restores; for alerting HA configure the peer settings (ha_peers, ha_listen_address) correctly and use the DB-backed alertmanager state so dedup survives an instance loss; put Grafana behind health checks that fail the instance out if it can't reach the DB. On Grafana Cloud this is all managed; self-hosted, the DB's own HA and IaC-managed content are the two big levers.

Panels, Visualizations & Field Config

A panel is a query plus a visualization plus field config — know what each layer controls.

Notes

The anatomy of a panel

  1. Queries — one or more, each with a ref id (A, B, …), against a data source.
  2. Transformations — optional post-processing of the returned data frames (own topic).
  3. Visualization — how to draw it (time series, stat, gauge, bar gauge, table, state timeline, heatmap, …).
  4. Field config — units, decimals, min/max, thresholds, color scheme, display name, no-value text, links.
  5. Overrides — field config applied selectively (by name, by regex, by query, by type).
# the five stages, as they appear in panel JSON
{
  "targets": [ {"refId": "A", "expr": "rate(http_req_total[$__rate_interval])"} ],
  "transformations": [ {"id": "renameByRegex", "options": {...}} ],
  "type": "timeseries",                       // 3. visualization
  "fieldConfig": {
    "defaults": {"unit": "reqps", "min": 0,   // 4. field config
                 "thresholds": {"steps": [{"value": null,"color":"green"},
                                          {"value": 100,"color":"red"}]}},
    "overrides": [ {"matcher": {"id":"byName","options":"5xx"},   // 5. override one series
                    "properties": [{"id":"color","value":{"fixedColor":"red"}}]} ]
  }
}

Common visualizations and when to use them

VizUse for
Time seriesMetrics over time (the default). Lines/bars/points, stacking, multiple Y axes.
StatOne big number per series + sparkline; good for current value with thresholds coloring.
Gauge / Bar gaugeA value against a known range (0–100%, against SLO).
TableInstant queries, top-N lists, label inspection; supports cell coloring, sparklines, data links.
HeatmapDistribution over time — native for Prometheus histograms.
State timeline / Status historyDiscrete states (up/down, ok/warn/crit) over time.
LogsLog lines from Loki/Elasticsearch, with level coloring and dedup.
# match the query SHAPE to the viz:
sum(rate(http_req_total[5m])) by (le)   # range vector over time  -> Time series / Heatmap
sum(up{job="api"})                       # single instant scalar   -> Stat / Gauge
topk(10, sum by (route)(rate(err[5m])))  # instant, many rows      -> Table
max_over_time(up[$__interval])           # 0/1 discrete over time   -> State timeline

Units, thresholds, mappings

  • Unit: pick the real unit (bytes, seconds, percent (0–100), percent (0.0–1.0), req/s). Grafana then scales axes and tooltips (ms→s→min).
  • Thresholds: value bands with colors; drive Stat/Gauge coloring, time-series threshold lines/regions, and table cell colors. "Percentage" mode makes them relative to min/max.
  • Value mappings: map a raw value/range to text + color (0 → "Down" (red), 1 → "Up" (green)).
  • Standard options: Display name (with ${__field.labels.instance}), Min/Max, Decimals, No value.
// unit: raw seconds from Prometheus -> Grafana shows "1.4 s", "320 ms" automatically
"unit": "s"          // NOT "ms": the data is in seconds; the unit just formats it

// thresholds: colour a Stat panel by error-budget burn
"thresholds": { "mode": "absolute",
  "steps": [ {"value": null, "color": "green"},
             {"value": 2,    "color": "orange"},   // burn rate > 2x
             {"value": 10,   "color": "red"} ] }

// value mapping: 0/1 up-series -> readable state
"mappings": [ {"type":"value","options":{"0":{"text":"Down","color":"red"},
                                         "1":{"text":"Up","color":"green"}}} ]

Overrides — the key skill

Base field config applies to every series. An override targets a subset: "fields with name matching /error/" → color red; "field rx_bytes" → unit bytes, custom axis; "fields returned by query B" → right Y axis, dashed line. This is how you put two different units on one graph, or highlight one series.

# one graph, two units: latency (ms, left axis) + error rate (%, right axis)
"overrides": [
  { "matcher": {"id": "byFrameRefID", "options": "B"},        # query B = error rate
    "properties": [
      {"id": "unit", "value": "percent"},
      {"id": "custom.axisPlacement", "value": "right"},
      {"id": "custom.lineStyle", "value": {"dash": [8, 4]}} ] },
  { "matcher": {"id": "byRegexp", "options": "/5xx|error/i"},
    "properties": [ {"id": "color", "value": {"mode":"fixed","fixedColor":"red"}} ] }
]

Data links & drilldown

Field config can add data links — clickable URLs built from the value and its labels (${__field.labels.pod}, ${__value.raw}, ${__url_time_range}) that jump to another dashboard, an Explore query, or an external tool. Combined with template variables this makes overview→detail navigation.

# data link on a "pod" table -> open the pod-detail dashboard, same time range
{
  "title": "Inspect pod",
  "url": "/d/pod-detail/pod?var-pod=${__data.fields.pod}&${__url_time_range}",
  "targetBlank": false
}
# ${__value.raw}  = the numeric cell value
# ${__field.labels.namespace} = a label carried on the series
# ${__url_time_range} = expands to from=...&to=... so context follows the click
Cheat Sheet
  • Panel = queries (A,B,…) → transformations → visualization → field config → overrides.
  • Time series for over-time; Stat for one number + sparkline; Gauge/Bar gauge for value-in-range; Table for instant/top-N; Heatmap for histograms; State timeline for up/down.
  • Set the real unit so axes/tooltips auto-scale. percent = 0–100, percentunit = 0–1.
  • Thresholds color Stat/Gauge/table cells and draw lines on time series. Value mappings turn numbers into labelled states.
  • Overrides = field config scoped by name/regex/type/query — use for dual units, dual axes, highlighting one series.
  • Display name supports ${__field.labels.X}; data links support ${__value.raw}, ${__field.labels.X}, ${__url_time_range} for drilldown.
Q&A
How do you show two series with different units (e.g. latency in ms and error rate in %) on one time series panel?
Set a sensible base unit, then add field overrides: one override matching the latency field sets unit = milliseconds and axis = left; another matching the error-rate field sets unit = percent and axis = right (Placement: right). Overrides are how per-series axis/unit/color is done.
What's the difference between "Percent (0-100)" and "Percent (0.0-1.0)" units?
They tell Grafana how the raw value is expressed. If your query returns 0.87 meaning 87%, use percentunit (0.0–1.0). If it returns 87, use percent (0–100). Picking the wrong one shows 0.87% or 8700%.
When would you use a Stat panel vs a Gauge?
Stat shows the current (or last/min/max/mean) value as a large number, optionally with a sparkline and threshold-based background color — good when there's no meaningful fixed ceiling. Gauge draws the value on an arc between min and max — good when there is a known range (disk 0–100%, latency against a 500 ms budget).
How do you make a table panel link each row to a per-pod dashboard?
Add a data link in field config with a URL like /d/pod-detail?var-pod=${__data.fields.pod}&${__url_time_range}. The link is templated from the row's fields and the current time range, so clicking a row opens the detail dashboard scoped to that pod.
What does the "Percentage" threshold mode do?
It interprets threshold numbers as percentages of the field's min–max range rather than absolute values, so the same threshold config works across series with different scales.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which visualization is the default for metrics over time?
Time series.
What panel feature turns the number 0 into a red "Down" label?
A value mapping.
What scopes field config to just some series?
A field override (by name, regex, type, or query).

Intermediate core

A time series panel shows six pods but the legend just says "value" six times. How do you get meaningful names?
The series names come from the query's returned labels. For Prometheus, set the query's Legend format to something like {{pod}} (or {{namespace}}/{{pod}}). Alternatively, in field config set Display name to ${__field.labels.pod}. If a transformation stripped the labels (e.g. "Reduce" or a rename), fix that upstream. Using a Legend template is the usual answer for Prometheus/Loki.
You want a panel that's green when a service's success ratio ≥ 99.9%, yellow 99–99.9%, red below. Describe the config.
Query returns the success ratio. Set unit to percentunit (if it's 0–1) or percent (0–100). Visualization: Stat or Gauge. Add thresholds: base (red) at the bottom, a step at 99 (yellow), a step at 99.9 (green) — thresholds color everything from that value upward. For Stat, set "Color mode: background" so the whole tile changes color; "Graph mode: area" for a sparkline. For Gauge, set Min 95 / Max 100 so the arc is readable near the SLO. Optionally add a threshold line on a companion time series panel.

Advanced deep

Explain Grafana's data frame model and how "wide" vs "long" format affects which visualizations and transformations work.
Grafana normalises every data source response into data frames — a frame is a set of typed fields (columns) of equal length, with metadata (name, labels, config). A time series is a frame with a time field plus one or more numeric fields; each numeric field carries its own labels map. Wide format: one time column and N value columns side by side (one per series) — what most time series panels expect, and what lets the graph align points on a shared time axis. Long/tall format: a time column, one value column, and separate label columns (e.g. pod, status) where each row is one observation — this is how SQL sources and some others return data, and it's what "group by" style analysis wants. Consequences: (1) Time series panel needs wide (or a frame with labelled numeric fields); feeding it long data plots the label columns as if numeric or collapses everything into one line — you apply the "Prepare time series → Multi-frame / Wide" transformation, or in SQL pivot in the query. (2) Table panel is happy with long. (3) Transformations are format-sensitive: "Labels to fields" converts label metadata into columns (wide→long-ish); "Rows to fields" / "Fields to rows" pivot; "Merge" needs compatible frames; "Group by" produces aggregated frames. (4) Heatmap wants either a Prometheus histogram frame (buckets as series) or a "Heatmap" calculation. (5) Alerting reduces each frame to a single number per series via the reduce expression, so the frame's field labels become the alert instance's labels — if your query returns one unlabelled wide frame you get one alert instance, if it returns many labelled series you get multi-dimensional alerts. Knowing whether your source returns wide or long tells you which transformation to reach for and why a panel is "empty" or "weird".
A dashboard's panels each re-run nearly identical expensive queries. What Grafana features reduce the load, and what are their limits?
(1) Panels referencing another panel via the -- Dashboard -- data source: panel B uses "results of panel A" and then applies its own transformations/viz — A's query runs once. Limit: B can't change the query, only post-process; and it only works within one dashboard. (2) Query caching (Enterprise/Cloud): identical queries (same source, expr, time range rounded to an interval) served from a short-TTL cache shared across users and panels. Limit: needs Enterprise; TTL vs freshness trade-off; time-range rounding means "last 5m" may be a few seconds stale. (3) Recording rules in Prometheus/Mimir/Loki: precompute the expensive aggregation server-side on a schedule; panels query the cheap recorded series. Limit: fixed resolution, extra series/cardinality to store, and a lag equal to the rule interval; you maintain the rules. (4) Shared base query in Dashboard Studio-style setups / repeated panels with a single templated query. (5) Reduce work per query: correct Max data points / Min step / $__rate_interval so you're not pulling raw resolution; use $__interval. (6) Lazy loading: panels below the fold don't query until scrolled into view; a long dashboard therefore doesn't fire everything at once. (7) Increase the dashboard's min refresh and remove aggressive auto-refresh. The durable fix for genuinely heavy aggregations is recording rules; caching and panel-reuse cut duplicate work but don't make a single slow query fast.

Dashboards, Rows & Template Variables

Variables turn one dashboard into hundreds — per environment, per service, per pod.

Notes

Dashboard structure

  • A dashboard = panels laid out on a 24-column grid, optionally grouped into rows (collapsible; can repeat).
  • Dashboard settings: time options (default range, refresh list, timezone), variables, annotations queries, links, tags, and the JSON model.
  • Every dashboard has a UID (in the URL /d/<uid>/<slug>) — stable across renames, used by links and provisioning.
# top of the dashboard JSON model
{
  "uid": "api-overview",            // stable; /d/api-overview/... survives a title change
  "title": "API Overview",
  "templating": { "list": [ /* variables */ ] },
  "annotations": { "list": [ /* event overlays */ ] },
  "time": { "from": "now-6h", "to": "now" },
  "refresh": "30s",
  "panels": [ { "gridPos": {"h": 8, "w": 12, "x": 0, "y": 0}, ... } ]  // 24-col grid
}

Variable types

TypeWhat it is
QueryValues come from a data source query (e.g. label_values(up, job) for Prometheus). Refresh: on load / on time-range change.
CustomHand-typed comma list (prod,staging,dev).
ConstantHidden fixed value, often used by provisioned dashboards.
Data sourcePicks which data source instance the panels use — makes a dashboard portable across Prometheis.
IntervalTime buckets (1m,5m,1h) → used as $__interval-style step in queries.
Text boxFree user input.
Ad hoc filtersSpecial: adds arbitrary key=value label filters applied to all queries against a source (Prometheus/Loki/Elastic).
# Query variable (Prometheus): fill $job from live label values
label_values(up, job)                         # -> api, worker, cron, ...
label_values(up{job="$job"}, instance)        # $instance, scoped to the chosen job

# Custom variable: hand-typed
prod, staging, dev

# Interval variable "$step": 1m,5m,10m,1h   -> use as ...[$step] in rate()

Multi-value, "All", and formatting

  • Enable Multi-value and/or Include All. "All" can be a custom value (.*) or an auto-generated list.
  • In a Prometheus query use the regex form: pod=~"$pod" (not pod="$pod") so multi-select works.
  • Control interpolation with format functions: ${pod:regex}, ${pod:pipe}, ${servers:json}, ${var:csv}, ${var:singlequote}, ${var:sqlstring}. Raw is ${var} / [[var]] / $var.
# $pod is multi-select with values: api-1, api-2

sum(rate(cpu{pod="$pod"}[5m]))     # BROKEN: expands to pod="api-1,api-2"
sum(rate(cpu{pod=~"$pod"}[5m]))    # OK: pod=~"api-1|api-2"  (regex form)

# format functions pick the right syntax per target language:
${pod:regex}   -> (api\-1|api\-2)      # for =~
${pod:pipe}    -> api-1|api-2
${pod:json}    -> ["api-1","api-2"]    # for a JSON body
${pod:sqlstring} -> 'api-1','api-2'    # for an IN (...) clause

Chained (dependent) variables

A variable's query can reference another variable: label_values(kube_pod_info{namespace="$namespace"}, pod). Selecting a namespace narrows the pod list. Order matters; Grafana re-queries downstream variables when an upstream one changes.

# variable order in the list = dependency order (top drives bottom)
$cluster : label_values(kube_node_info, cluster)
$namespace : label_values(kube_pod_info{cluster="$cluster"}, namespace)
$pod : label_values(kube_pod_info{cluster="$cluster",namespace="$namespace"}, pod)
# pick a new $cluster  -> Grafana re-runs the $namespace query, then the $pod query

Repeating panels & rows

Set a panel (or row) to Repeat for a multi-value variable — Grafana clones it once per selected value (one graph per region, a row of panels per service). Great for "same view, N things" without hand-copying panels.

# one panel definition, cloned per value of a multi-value variable
"repeat": "region",              // $region = us-east, us-west, eu
"repeatDirection": "h",          // lay the clones out horizontally
"targets": [ {"expr": "sum(rate(req_total{region=\"$region\"}[5m]))"} ]
// render: 3 identical panels, each pinned to one region. Edit once, all update.

Built-in macros

$__interval / $__rate_interval (auto step), $__range, $__from / $__to (ms epoch; also :date variants), $__timeFilter() (SQL sources), $__searchFilter (type-ahead in a query variable), $__dashboard, $__user, $__org.

# Prometheus: let Grafana choose the rate window from panel width + scrape interval
rate(http_requests_total[$__rate_interval])

# SQL data source: bound the query to the dashboard's time picker
SELECT $__timeGroup(ts, '1m') AS time, avg(latency_ms)
FROM requests
WHERE $__timeFilter(ts)          -- expands to  ts BETWEEN '...' AND '...'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
Cheat Sheet
  • Dashboard = 24-col grid of panels, optional collapsible rows, a stable UID in /d/<uid>.
  • Variable types: Query, Custom, Constant, Data source, Interval, Text box, Ad hoc filters.
  • Prometheus values: label_values(metric, label). Reference in query as label=~"$var" (regex form) for multi-select.
  • Multi-value + Include All; format with ${var:regex}, ${var:json}, ${var:csv}, ${var:pipe}, ${var:sqlstring}.
  • Chained variables: downstream var query filters by $upstream; changing upstream re-queries it.
  • Repeat a panel or row per selected value for "same view, many things".
  • Macros: $__rate_interval, $__interval, $__range, $__from/$__to, $__timeFilter(), $__searchFilter.
Q&A
How do you populate a variable with the list of jobs from Prometheus?
A Query variable against the Prometheus data source with query label_values(up, job) (or label_values(job)). Set refresh to "On dashboard load" or "On time range change".
Why use pod=~"$pod" instead of pod="$pod" in the panel query?
With multi-value enabled, $pod interpolates to (a|b|c), which is a regex alternation. =~ is the regex-match operator, so it matches any of them; = would look for a literal pod literally named "(a|b|c)" and match nothing. For single-value it also works and future-proofs the panel.
What are chained variables?
Variables whose query references an earlier variable, e.g. label_values(kube_pod_info{namespace="$namespace"}, pod). The pod list depends on the selected namespace; Grafana re-evaluates the pod variable whenever namespace changes.
What does setting a row to "Repeat for" a variable do?
Grafana duplicates that entire row (and its panels) once for each selected value of the variable, substituting the value into each copy's queries and titles — e.g. one row of dashboards per Kubernetes namespace, generated automatically.
What is the Ad hoc filters variable?
A special variable that lets the viewer add arbitrary label = value (or =~, !=) filters from a dropdown, and Grafana automatically injects them into every query against the chosen data source. Good for exploratory dashboards where you don't know in advance which labels people will slice by.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which variable type makes a dashboard work across multiple Prometheus instances?
A Data source variable.
What Prometheus function is typically used in a Query variable to list label values?
label_values(<metric>, <label>).
What does the Repeat option on a panel do?
Clones the panel once per selected value of a multi-value variable.

Intermediate core

Selecting "All" for a 500-value pod variable makes queries huge and slow. What are your options?
(1) Set the "All" value explicitly to .* and use pod=~"$pod" so "All" becomes a single cheap regex rather than a 500-term alternation. (2) Disable "Include All" and require a real selection, or default to one value. (3) Add an upstream namespace variable and chain pod off it so the list is bounded. (4) Use an aggregating query that doesn't need per-pod selection for the overview panels, and only use $pod on drilldown panels. (5) Cap with Selection options → limit or a more selective label_values query. (6) Consider a recording rule so the "all pods" aggregate is precomputed.
You need a variable value passed into a Loki query as an exact string and into a URL as a slug. How do you control interpolation?
Use format specifiers. For the Loki label matcher you want the raw/regex-safe form: ${service:regex} (or plain ${service} inside service=~"..."). For the URL you want it URL-safe: Grafana URL-encodes variable values in link interpolation by default, or use ${service:percentencode}. Other handy ones: ${var:json} for a JSON array, ${var:csv} for comma-separated, ${var:pipe} for a|b|c (regex alternation), ${var:singlequote}/${var:doublequote}/${var:sqlstring} for SQL. The point: the same variable can be rendered differently per usage site.

Advanced deep

Design a single "service health" dashboard that works for 200 services across 3 environments and 4 regions, editable by service teams but consistent. Cover variables, layout, and how it's maintained.
Variables (ordered, chained): datasource (type datasource, so it maps to the right Prometheus per env) → env (custom: prod,staging,dev, or query if encoded in labels) → region (label_values(up{env="$env"}, region)) → service (label_values(http_requests_total{env="$env",region=~"$region"}, service)) → optional pod/instance chained off service. Add an ad hoc filters variable for exploratory slicing. Use $__rate_interval everywhere. Layout: top row = SLO/overview Stat panels (availability, error rate, p99 latency, saturation) using RED signals, colored by thresholds tied to the service's SLO; a "repeat row per region" section so multi-region selection fans out; drilldown rows (by endpoint, by dependency, by pod) collapsed by default and lazy-loaded. Every panel query filters by service=~"$service",env="$env",region=~"$region". Data links on panels jump to logs (Loki, same selectors), traces (Tempo), and the per-pod dashboard, carrying ${__url_time_range} and label values. Maintenance: the dashboard is code — a JSON/Jsonnet (grafonnet) or Terraform definition in Git, provisioned read-mostly into a shared "Platform" folder; service teams don't edit the golden one. If teams need custom panels, they "Save As" a copy into their own folder (editable) that still inherits the variable scheme, or the platform dashboard exposes a "team extensions" row sourced from a per-team library panel. Consistency comes from: one templated definition, standard variable names, SLO thresholds pulled from a config (per-service slo_target recording rule or a lookup), and CI that lints the dashboard JSON. Because it's driven by labels + variables, "200 services" is still one dashboard, and onboarding a service is just emitting the right labels.
How do template variables interact with dashboard caching, sharing, and permalinks? What breaks and how do you make links reproducible?
Variable state lives in the URL query string as var-<name>=<value> (repeated for multi-value), plus from/to for time and refresh. Implications: (1) Permalinks — "Copy link" with "Current time range" and current variables produces a URL that reproduces exactly what you see; without those options the recipient gets defaults. Use "Share → Link → Shorten URL" so the long var list becomes a stable short link stored in Grafana (survives even if defaults change). (2) Snapshots freeze the data and resolved variables into a static copy — good for incident write-ups, but detached from live data. (3) Query caching keys on the fully interpolated query, so two users with different var-pod get different cache entries; a user toggling "All" vs a specific value gets different entries — expected, but means cache hit rate depends on how varied people's selections are. (4) Default value drift — if a link omits a var- param, Grafana uses the variable's current default, which an editor may have changed; reproducible links must include every relevant var-. (5) Chained variables — a link that sets var-pod but not var-namespace may load with the pod value invalid until namespace resolves; include the whole chain. (6) Provisioned dashboards reset on redeploy, so user "favourite" variable states aren't persisted in the dashboard — rely on the URL. (7) Alerts and reporting: alert rule panels and scheduled PDF reports need explicit variable values baked in (report settings let you pin them). Best practice for a link you'll paste into an incident channel: Share → enable "Current time range", "Template variables", "Shorten URL".

Querying Prometheus (PromQL) in Grafana

The most common Grafana pairing — and the place people most often write subtly wrong queries.

Notes

PromQL data types

  • Instant vector — one sample per matching series at a single instant (http_requests_total).
  • Range vector — a window of samples per series (http_requests_total[5m]); only functions like rate(), increase(), *_over_time() take these.
  • Scalar and string.
http_requests_total                 # instant vector: {job="api"} 5231, {job="web"} 812
http_requests_total[5m]             # range vector: each series -> [(t1,v1)...(tn,vn)]
rate(http_requests_total[5m])       # range vector IN -> instant vector OUT
rate(http_requests_total)          # ERROR: rate() needs a range vector, got instant
2 * scalar(count(up))              # scalar

Instant vs range queries in Grafana

Range queryInstant query
Returnsa time series (value at each step across the panel's time range)one value per series (at range end)
Use fortime series graphsStat/Gauge/Table "current value", top-N
Toggle"Range" (default in graph panels)"Instant" checkbox in the query editor
# same expr, two API calls Grafana makes:

# Range  -> GET /api/v1/query_range?query=...&start=..&end=..&step=15s
#   result: a line with a point every 15s across the panel  -> Time series panel

# Instant -> GET /api/v1/query?query=...&time=<range end>
#   result: one number per series  -> Stat / Gauge / Table
topk(5, sum by (route)(rate(errors_total[5m])))   # only meaningful as Instant

Counters: always rate()

Counters only go up (and reset to 0 on restart). Graphing them raw is meaningless. Use rate(metric[window]) for per-second average rate (handles resets), or increase(metric[window]) for the total over the window. irate() uses only the last two samples — spiky, for fast-moving graphs only.

# raw counter: a ramp from process start + a cliff on restart -> useless
http_requests_total                     # 4.1M ... 4.1M ... 0 (restart) ... 12k

rate(http_requests_total[5m])           # ~820 req/s, and the restart is smoothed out
increase(http_requests_total[1h])       # ~2.95M requests in the last hour
sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) by (status)   # per-second, grouped by status code

The rate window and $__rate_interval

  • The [window] must cover at least 4 scrape intervals or rate() gets erratic / empty.
  • Grafana provides $__rate_interval = max($__interval + scrape_interval, 4 × scrape_interval) — use it as the rate window: rate(http_requests_total[$__rate_interval]). It adapts to zoom level and avoids gaps.
  • $__interval is the step Grafana computes from range width ÷ panel pixels; $__interval_ms is the numeric form.
# scrape_interval = 15s

rate(http_requests_total[1m])              # BAD: only ~4 samples, gaps when zoomed out
rate(http_requests_total[$__rate_interval]) # GOOD: >= 4x scrape, grows as you zoom out
#   zoomed in  (step 15s) -> $__rate_interval = 1m
#   zoomed out (step 10m) -> $__rate_interval = ~10m15s   no gaps at any zoom

Aggregation

sum(rate(http_requests_total[$__rate_interval])) by (status)      # group up
sum without (instance) (rate(http_requests_total[$__rate_interval])) # drop one label
topk(5, sum by (route) (rate(http_requests_total[$__rate_interval])))
histogram_quantile(0.95,
  sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[$__rate_interval])))

Note: aggregate the rate, never rate(sum(...)). For histograms you must keep the le label and sum by (le) before histogram_quantile.

Legend, format, and min step

  • Legend: {{status}} / {{instance}} {{job}} to name series.
  • Format: Time series / Table / Heatmap (Heatmap for _bucket series).
  • Min step stops Grafana asking for finer resolution than Prometheus stores.
  • Exemplars: toggle on to overlay trace-linked points on latency graphs (needs exemplar storage + a trace data source).
# query editor fields:
Legend format:  {{method}} {{status}}        # -> "GET 200", "POST 500" per line
Format:         Heatmap                        # for *_bucket series
Min step:       15s                            # never request finer than the scrape
# without a legend format you get the full {__name__="...", job="...", ...} label set

Query-type variables

label_values(metric, label), label_values(label), metrics(regex), query_result(<promql>) for a variable whose values come from an arbitrary expression.

label_values(node_cpu_seconds_total, instance)   # distinct values of one label
label_values(job)                                 # values of a label across all metrics
metrics(node_.*)                                  # metric names matching a regex
query_result(topk(5, sum by (pod)(rate(err[5m])))) # values built from a full expression
#   -> then use  regex  /pod="([^"]+)"/  to extract just the pod name for the dropdown
Cheat Sheet
  • Range vector metric[5m] → only for rate/increase/*_over_time. Instant vector → everything else.
  • Graph = Range query; Stat/Gauge/top-N = Instant query.
  • Counters → rate(metric[$__rate_interval]) (per-sec, reset-safe). Total over window → increase(). Spiky fast graph → irate().
  • Always rate() first, then sum by (...) — never rate(sum(...)).
  • p95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(x_bucket[$__rate_interval]))).
  • Use $__rate_interval for rate windows; $__interval for step. Legend {{label}} to name series.
  • Heatmap panel + query Format = Heatmap for _bucket series. Toggle Exemplars for trace links.
Q&A
Why is $__rate_interval preferred over a hard-coded [5m]?
It's computed as at least 4× the scrape interval and also grows with the panel's step when you zoom out, so rate() never has too few samples (which causes gaps or noise) and never wastes work at wide zoom. A fixed [5m] breaks if the scrape interval is 2m, and is suboptimal when you're looking at 30 days.
When do you use an Instant query?
When the panel needs a single current number per series rather than a line — Stat, Gauge, Bar gauge, and Table panels showing "right now" values or topk lists. It returns the value at the end of the dashboard time range.
What's wrong with rate(sum(http_requests_total)[5m])?
sum() produces one series by adding counters that reset independently; a single reset in any instance makes the summed series jump backwards, and rate() then misreads it. Correct order is sum(rate(http_requests_total[$__rate_interval])) — compute per-series rate (which handles each series' resets) first, then add.
How do you graph p95 request latency from a histogram?
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[$__rate_interval]))). You rate each bucket, sum by the le label to aggregate across instances while preserving buckets, then apply histogram_quantile.
Your time series panel has gaps between points. PromQL-side causes?
Rate window shorter than ~4 scrape intervals; scrape failures (target down) leaving no samples; a step larger than expected so sparse metrics don't land in every bucket; or querying a metric that only exists intermittently. Fixes: use $__rate_interval, set "Connect null values", check target health, or use <metric> or vector(0) where zero-filling is appropriate.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which PromQL function turns a counter into a per-second rate?
rate() (over a range vector).
Range query or instant query for a Stat panel showing the current value?
Instant query.
What Grafana variable should be the rate window?
$__rate_interval.

Intermediate core

A dashboard looks fine at "last 1 hour" but the same panels are empty at "last 30 days". Why, and how do you fix it without two dashboards?
At 30 days the panel step ($__interval) becomes large (say 20m). If the rate window is hard-coded [1m], each 20-minute step now contains at most one scrape per minute but the window only looks back 1 minute from each step point — often landing between scrapes → no data. Also Prometheus may have downsampled/expired raw data, or the query hits the 11,000-point result limit. Fixes: use rate(metric[$__rate_interval]) so the window scales with the step; ensure retention covers 30 days or query a downsampled/recorded series; set a reasonable "Max data points"; for very long ranges point at Thanos/Mimir with downsampling. One dashboard, adaptive query.
You need "error ratio per service" as a single Stat panel per service, red above 1%. Write the query and describe the panel.
Query (Instant): sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total[$__rate_interval])). This yields a value per service (0–1). Panel: visualization Stat (or Bar gauge for many services), unit percentunit, decimals 2, Legend {{service}}, thresholds: green base, red at 0.01. Enable "Repeat by variable" on $service if you want one tile each, or leave it multi-series. Add a data link to a per-service errors dashboard. Guard against divide-by-zero on low traffic with ... / clamp_min(sum by (service)(rate(http_requests_total[$__rate_interval])), 1) or by only alerting when denominator traffic is above a floor.

Advanced deep

Explain how Grafana decides the actual step and number of points for a Prometheus range query, and every knob that influences it.
Grafana issues a query_range call with start, end, and step. It computes step as: step = max(intervalMs, minStepMs) where intervalMs ≈ timeRange / maxDataPoints, then rounds to a "nice" interval. Inputs: (1) Panel width in pixels → default maxDataPoints (roughly the pixel width, capped). Overridable per query as Max data points. (2) Time range width. (3) Min step (query option) / Min interval (data source setting) / $__interval floor — prevents asking for finer than the scrape interval; if unset, defaults from the data source's "Scrape interval" field. (4) Prometheus itself rejects queries returning more than query.max-samples or more than 11,000 points per series — Grafana's step calc is partly to stay under that. (5) $__interval in the expression is set to this same computed step, and $__rate_interval derives from it plus the configured scrape interval. (6) The data source "Resolution" setting (1/1, 1/2, …) multiplies the step down. (7) For instant queries none of this applies — it's a single query at end. Consequences: a narrow panel or a low Max data points gives a coarse step (fast, less detail); zooming out coarsens the step (so hard-coded rate windows break — hence $__rate_interval); setting Min step below the scrape interval just wastes work (Prometheus has no data between scrapes) and can hit the point limit; setting Max data points very high on a wide range can make Prometheus refuse the query. The practical rule: leave Max data points default, set Min step = scrape interval, and use $__rate_interval for rates and $__interval for *_over_time windows.
A team wants Grafana panels to show data consistent with what their Prometheus alerts fire on, but the graph and the alert frequently disagree. What causes the mismatch and how do you reconcile them?
Sources of divergence: (1) Different evaluation model — a Prometheus alerting rule evaluates the expression at a fixed evaluation_interval as an instant query at "now", with for: requiring it to stay true; a Grafana graph runs a range query with a computed step and shows historical points. The alert sees values you can't see on a coarse graph. (2) Rate window — the alert rule likely hard-codes [5m]; the panel uses $__rate_interval which at wide zoom might be [20m], smoothing spikes away. Match them: either hard-code the same window in the panel for the "alert view" panel, or use recording rules that both consume. (3) Step vs raw — the panel downsamples to pixels, hiding a 30-second breach the alert caught. Lower Max data points won't help; instead add an annotation from the alert. (4) Alignment — alert evaluation timestamps aren't on the panel's step grid. (5) Grafana-managed alerts vs Prometheus alerts — if the alert is Grafana-managed it runs its own query + reduce + threshold with its own interval, independent of both. (6) Stale data / lookback delta differences. Reconciliation: (a) Build the alert from a recording rule (job:http_errors:ratio5m) and point both the alert and a dedicated panel at that exact series — now they can't disagree on the math. (b) Overlay the firing periods as annotations (Grafana can query the ALERTS metric: ALERTS{alertname="X",alertstate="firing"}) so the graph shows when it fired even if the line looks fine. (c) Add a panel that replicates the alert's exact instant expression with an Instant query and a threshold at the alert's value. (d) Document the rate window and evaluation interval on the panel. The core fix is a shared recording rule as the single source of truth.

Logs with Loki & LogQL

"Prometheus for logs" — index only labels, grep the rest, and derive metrics from log lines.

Notes

The Loki model

  • Loki indexes only a small set of labels (e.g. job, namespace, app, level) — not the log content. The raw lines are stored compressed in object storage, grouped by label set into streams.
  • This makes ingestion cheap and storage cheap, but content search is a brute-force scan of the matching streams — so you must first narrow by labels, then filter.
  • Keep label cardinality low. High-cardinality labels (user id, request id, path) create millions of tiny streams and destroy performance — put those in the line, extract at query time.
# a stream = one unique combination of INDEXED labels
{job="api", namespace="prod", level="error"}   -> one stream, all its lines appended

# BAD: user_id as a label -> ~1 stream per user -> millions of streams
{job="api", user_id="12345"}

# GOOD: user_id stays in the line; pull it out only when querying
{job="api"} | json | user_id="12345"

LogQL: two query kinds

Log queryMetric query
Returns log linesReturns a time series computed from logs
{app="api"} |= "error"sum(rate({app="api"} |= "error" [$__interval]))
# LOG query -> raw lines, for a Logs panel / Explore
{app="api", level="error"} |= "payment" | json | line_format "{{.msg}}"

# METRIC query -> a number over time, for a Time series / Stat panel / alert
sum(rate({app="api", level="error"} |= "payment" [5m]))
# same selector + filters; wrapping it in rate()/count_over_time() makes it a series

Log query pipeline

{namespace="prod", app="checkout"}          # 1. stream selector (indexed labels, required)
  |= "timeout"                              # 2. line filter: contains
  != "healthcheck"                          # line filter: not contains
  |~ "user_id=(42|43)"                      # line filter: regex match
  | json                                    # 3. parser: json / logfmt / pattern / regexp
  | duration > 500ms                        # 4. label filter on extracted fields
  | line_format "{{.method}} {{.path}} {{.duration}}"   # 5. reformat the line

Filters early = less data scanned. Parsers (json, logfmt, pattern `<ip> - - <_> "<method> <path>"`, regexp "...") turn line content into temporary labels you can then filter, aggregate, or format on.

Metric queries from logs

sum by (level) (rate({app="api"} | json | __error__="" [5m]))     # lines/sec by level
sum(count_over_time({app="api"} |= "panic" [1h]))                 # count in window
quantile_over_time(0.95,
  {app="api"} | json | unwrap duration_ms [5m]) by (route)       # p95 from a numeric field

rate/count_over_time count lines; unwrap pulls a numeric extracted field so sum_over_time, avg_over_time, quantile_over_time can do real math on it.

In Grafana

  • Logs panel for lines (level coloring, dedup, wrap, "show context", newest/oldest first).
  • Time series for metric queries; a common panel has a log-volume bar on top of the Logs panel (Explore does this automatically).
  • Derived fields (data source config): regex on the line to extract e.g. a trace ID and turn it into a link to Tempo — the basis of logs→traces navigation.
  • Loki as an alert source: metric LogQL queries can back Grafana-managed alert rules ("more than N errors in 5m").
# Derived field (Loki data source config) -> logs-to-traces link
name:          traceID
matcher regex: (?:trace_id|traceID)=(\w+)
url:           ${__value.raw}
internalLink:  Tempo                # clicking the extracted id opens the trace

# alert rule backed by a metric LogQL query
expr:  sum(count_over_time({app="checkout", level="error"} [5m])) > 20
for:   10m
Cheat Sheet
  • Loki indexes labels only; content is scanned. Always start with a tight {label="..."} selector, then filter.
  • Keep label cardinality low — no request/user/path IDs as labels.
  • Line filters: |= contains, != not, |~ regex, !~ not regex.
  • Parsers: | json, | logfmt, | pattern "...", | regexp "..." → create fields; then | field > 500ms to filter, | line_format to rewrite.
  • Metric queries: rate()/count_over_time() count lines; unwrap <field> + *_over_time for numeric math; quantile_over_time(0.95, ... | unwrap x [5m]).
  • Grafana: Logs panel for lines, time series for metrics, derived fields for logs→traces links, LogQL metric queries can drive alerts.
Q&A
How is Loki different from Elasticsearch for logs?
Elasticsearch builds a full inverted index over log content, enabling fast arbitrary text search at high storage/compute cost. Loki indexes only labels and stores compressed lines in object storage; queries brute-force-scan the label-selected streams. Loki is cheaper to run and pairs naturally with Prometheus labels, but content search must be preceded by a selective label filter.
Why is high label cardinality bad in Loki?
Each unique combination of label values is a separate stream with its own chunks. A label like request_id creates a stream per request — millions of tiny chunks, huge index, terrible query and ingestion performance, and often ingestion limits being hit. Such fields belong in the log line and are extracted at query time with a parser.
What does | json do in a LogQL pipeline?
It parses each (JSON) log line and promotes its fields to temporary labels for the rest of the pipeline, so you can then do | level="error", | duration > 1s, aggregate by a field, or line_format using it. It doesn't change what's stored.
How do you compute p95 of a latency value that's inside your JSON logs?
quantile_over_time(0.95, {app="api"} | json | unwrap duration_ms [5m]) by (route). unwrap tells Loki to treat the extracted duration_ms field as the sample value; quantile_over_time then computes the percentile over the window per route.
What are derived fields?
A Loki data source setting: a regex applied to each log line to extract a value (e.g. a trace ID) and render it as a clickable link, optionally to another data source (Tempo). This is how clicking a log line jumps to the corresponding trace.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What part of a log does Loki index?
Only the labels (the stream selector); the line content is not indexed.
Which LogQL operator is a regex line filter?
|~ (and !~ for "does not match").
What does count_over_time({app="x"} |= "error" [1h]) return?
The number of matching log lines in each 1-hour window — a metric series, not log lines.

Intermediate core

A LogQL query {cluster="prod"} |= "OutOfMemory" times out. How do you make it fast?
{cluster="prod"} selects every stream in the cluster — terabytes to scan. Narrow the label selector first: add namespace, app, and if you have it level="error" or container. Shorten the time range. Put the most selective |= filter immediately after the selector and before any parser (parsing is expensive; filter raw bytes first). If this is a recurring need, add a lower-cardinality label that captures the relevant dimension, or create a recording rule / alert that maintains a counter. Check Loki's split-by-time and parallelism settings so the query fans out across queriers. In Grafana, reduce "Max lines".
Build a Grafana panel showing error-log rate per service with the ability to click through to the raw errors.
Panel 1 (Time series): query sum by (service) (rate({env="prod"} | json | level="error" [$__rate_interval])), Legend {{service}}, unit "logs/s", thresholds for coloring. Add a data link on the panel: URL to Explore or a Logs dashboard with ?left=/var-service=${__field.labels.service} and ${__url_time_range}, so clicking a series opens the filtered log view. Panel 2 (Logs panel) on the same dashboard: {env="prod", service=~"$service"} | json | level="error", newest first, dedup by signature, "Enable log details" for label inspection. Wire a service template variable via label_values({env="prod"}, service). Optionally configure derived fields on the Loki source to linkify trace_id to Tempo for a third hop.

Advanced deep

Your org wants metrics, alerting, and dashboards driven partly from logs (no separate metrics pipeline for some legacy apps). Design it with Loki + Grafana and name the pitfalls.
Approach: (1) Structured logging first — get the legacy apps emitting JSON or logfmt with stable keys (level, route, status, duration_ms). Without structure, everything downstream is fragile regex. (2) Labels: only app, env, namespace, maybe level as Loki labels; everything else stays in the line. (3) Query-time metrics: dashboards use LogQL metric queries (sum by (route)(rate(... | json | status=~"5.." [$__rate_interval])), quantile_over_time(0.95, ... | unwrap duration_ms [5m])). (4) Recording rules: Loki's ruler evaluates LogQL metric queries on a schedule and writes the result to a Prometheus-compatible store (remote_write to Mimir/Prometheus). Now the expensive log scans happen once per interval, and dashboards/alerts read cheap real metric series — this is the key move for scale. (5) Alerting: alert on the recorded series (or directly via Loki ruler alerting rules) with for: and burn-rate logic. (6) Retention: short retention on raw logs, longer on the recorded metrics. Pitfalls: log-derived metrics are only as reliable as log delivery — dropped/rate-limited/late logs silently undercount, so you can't fully trust availability numbers computed from logs; a logging format change breaks the parser and thus the metric with no compile-time warning — version the pipeline and alert on "parser error rate" (__error__!=""); brute-force scans are costly, so unbounded ad-hoc queries can DOS Loki — enforce per-tenant limits and prefer recorded series; timestamps come from the log line or ingest time, both of which can skew; high-cardinality extracted fields used in by () clauses still blow up query memory even though they aren't stream labels; and exactly-once is impossible — treat log-based counts as approximate. Good for legacy/supplementary signals; not a replacement for a real metrics client on critical paths.
Explain how Loki executes a metric query across its architecture, and which Grafana-side settings interact with that.
Path: Grafana sends the LogQL query_range to the Loki query-frontend. The frontend splits the request by time (e.g. into per-hour sub-queries, split_queries_by_interval) and by shard (Loki can shard by the index's fingerprint space, querier.max-query-parallelism), producing many small sub-queries placed on an in-memory queue. Queriers pull sub-queries, each resolving the stream selector against the index (BoltDB-shipper / TSDB) to find matching chunks, fetching chunks from object storage (and recent data from ingesters via the write path), then running the pipeline (line filters → parser → label filters → unwrap) over the decompressed lines and computing partial aggregates. The frontend merges partials into the final series, optionally caches results (results_cache), and returns. Limits that bite: max_query_length, max_query_series, max_entries_limit_per_query, max_query_parallelism, per-tenant ingestion and query rate limits, chunk cache size. Grafana settings that interact: (1) The panel's step / Max data points becomes the LogQL range step — too fine over a long range multiplies sub-queries and can hit limits or time out. (2) Min step to floor it. (3) Max lines (data source) caps returned log lines (not metric queries). (4) Query timeout on the data source vs Loki's own query_timeout. (5) The time range vs max_query_length. (6) Whether the query is instant vs range — instant is a single point, far cheaper for "current error count". (7) Grafana's query caching (Enterprise) sits in front of Loki's own results cache. (8) Using a recording rule series instead of a raw LogQL metric query bypasses most of this. Practically: keep ranges bounded, step reasonable, selectors tight, and push heavy aggregations into the ruler.

Transformations & Mixed Data Sources

Reshape, join, and compute on query results in the panel — without changing the query.

Notes

What transformations are

A transformation runs in Grafana, after the query, before the visualization. It operates on the returned data frames: rename fields, filter rows, join two queries, compute a new column, pivot, reduce to a single value. They run in order, each consuming the previous one's output. Debug with the "Table view" toggle and the transformation's own preview.

// pipeline runs top-to-bottom, each stage eats the previous output
"transformations": [
  { "id": "joinByField",  "options": { "field": "time", "mode": "outer" } },
  { "id": "calculateField", "options": {                 // new column = A / B
      "mode": "binary",
      "binary": { "left": "errors", "operator": "/", "right": "total" },
      "alias": "error_ratio" } },
  { "id": "organize", "options": { "excludeByName": { "errors": true, "total": true } } }
]
// query stays untouched; toggle "Table view" to see the frame after each stage

The transformations you'll actually use

TransformationPurpose
Join by field (Outer/Inner)Merge query A and query B on a shared field (e.g. time, or instance) into one table — the basis of "A / B" math across data sources.
Add field from calculationNew field = binary op on two fields (A/B for a ratio), or a row-wise reduce, or a cumulative/window function.
Organize fieldsRename, reorder, hide fields (the usual "make the table readable" step).
Filter data by values / by name / by queryDrop rows or series you don't want to show.
Group byAggregate rows by one or more fields (sum/mean/count/last per group) — SQL-style.
ReduceCollapse each series to one number (last, max, mean…) — feed Stat/Table.
Labels to fields / Fields to rows / Rows to fieldsPivot between wide and long shapes.
MergeCombine multiple frames/series into one table aligned on shared fields.
Config from query resultsUse one query to set another's min/max/thresholds/display name dynamically (e.g. pull the SLO target and use it as the gauge max).
Partition by valuesSplit one frame into several series by a field's values.
# Goal: a Table of "pod | cpu | mem | restarts", one row per pod, from 3 queries
A: sum by (pod)(rate(container_cpu_seconds_total[5m]))
B: sum by (pod)(container_memory_working_set_bytes)
C: sum by (pod)(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total)

transforms:
  1. Join by field: pod                 # A+B+C -> one wide table keyed by pod
  2. Organize fields: rename A->cpu, B->mem, C->restarts
  3. Filter data by values: mem > 0     # drop empty rows

Mixed data source

  • Panel data source = -- Mixed -- lets each query row pick its own source (Prometheus + CloudWatch + a SQL DB in one panel).
  • Combine with Join by field on time and Add field from calculation to divide a metric from source A by a metric from source B.
  • Alignment matters: the two sources must produce points on comparable timestamps; use "Join" (outer) and be aware of null handling.
# panel datasource: -- Mixed --   (each row picks its own)
A  [Prometheus] sum(rate(app_requests_total[5m]))
B  [CloudWatch] ALBRequestCountPerTarget        # AWS-side count

transforms:
  1. Join by field: time            # align both series on the timestamp
  2. Add field from calculation: A / B  ->  "internal_vs_edge_ratio"
# only works if both emit points at comparable steps; outer join + null-as-zero

Gotchas

  • Transformations can be expensive on large frames — they run client/server-side on every refresh; prefer doing math in the query when the data source can.
  • Some panels ignore some transformations; order-dependence surprises people (filter before group, rename after join).
  • "Add field from calculation → Binary operation" needs the two fields in the same frame — usually you must Join first.
  • Alerting evaluates queries + expressions, not panel transformations — so a ratio built only via a transformation can't be alerted on; rebuild it as a query/expression.
# WON'T alert: ratio exists only as a panel transformation
panel: A=errors, B=total, transform: A/B -> error_ratio    # invisible to alerting

# WILL alert: rebuild the ratio in the query (or a Grafana "Math" expression)
expr: sum(rate(errors_total[5m])) / sum(rate(requests_total[5m])) > 0.05
# order also bites: Filter BEFORE Group; Organize/rename AFTER Join
Cheat Sheet
  • Transformation = post-query, pre-viz reshape of data frames; runs in order; debug with Table view.
  • Join by field (on time or a key) → then Add field from calculation (A / B) for cross-query/cross-source math.
  • Organize fields (rename/hide/reorder), Filter by name/value/query (drop series/rows), Group by (aggregate), Reduce (series → one number).
  • Pivot: Labels to fields, Rows to fields, Fields to rows. Combine frames: Merge.
  • Config from query: drive another panel's max/thresholds/name from a query result.
  • -- Mixed -- data source = per-query source selection in one panel.
  • Alerting ignores transformations — express ratios as queries/expressions, not transforms.
Q&A
Where do transformations run?
In Grafana, after the data source returns results and before the visualization renders. They manipulate the data frames (columns/rows), chained in the order listed.
How do you graph "metric from Prometheus divided by metric from a SQL database" in one panel?
Set the panel data source to -- Mixed --, add query A (Prometheus) and query B (SQL). Add a Join by field transformation on time to put both value columns in one frame, then Add field from calculation → Binary operation → A.value / B.value. Hide the source columns with Organize fields.
Why can't you alert on a value produced by a transformation?
Grafana's alerting pipeline evaluates the panel's queries and server-side expressions, not its visualization-layer transformations. If a ratio exists only as a transformation, the alert rule can't see it — you must recreate it as a math/reduce expression or as a query the data source computes.
What does "Config from query results" do?
It takes fields from one query and uses them as configuration for the panel — e.g. a query returns each host's capacity, and that becomes the per-series Max so a bar gauge shows utilisation against each host's own limit; or a query returns the SLO target and it becomes a threshold.
You joined two queries but the calculation column is all null. Likely cause?
The join key doesn't line up — timestamps from the two sources don't match exactly (different step or scrape offset), so the outer join produces rows where only one side has a value. Fix by aligning steps (same interval / min step), using an inner join if appropriate, or resampling one source; sometimes doing the division in the query language instead is simpler.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Do transformations change the query sent to the data source?
No — they only reshape the results after they come back.
Which data source lets one panel query Prometheus and CloudWatch together?
The -- Mixed -- data source.
Which transformation collapses each series to a single number?
Reduce.

Intermediate core

A table should show, per pod: CPU usage, memory usage, and restart count — each from a separate Prometheus query. How do you build it?
Three Instant queries (A: CPU, B: memory, C: restarts), each returning a value per pod. Add Join by field on pod (outer) to get one row per pod with three value columns. Organize fields to rename them "CPU", "Memory", "Restarts" and set order; set per-column units via field overrides (bytes, percent, short). Optionally Filter data by values to show only pods with restarts > 0, or add cell coloring via thresholds. Visualization: Table. If labels other than pod differ between queries, the join can fragment — strip extra labels in the queries with sum by (pod).
Explain the difference between "Group by", "Reduce", and "Merge", with a use case for each.
Group by: SQL-style aggregation — pick grouping field(s) and an aggregation per other field; many rows → one row per group. Use: raw per-request rows → count and mean latency per endpoint. Reduce: collapse each series/field across time to one value (last/max/mean/delta/…). Use: a time series panel's data → a Stat/Table showing each series' current or peak value. Merge: combine multiple frames into a single table by aligning on shared field values (e.g. same time or same label), interleaving rows/columns. Use: several queries each returning a small table keyed by instance → one unified table. Roughly: Group by = aggregate rows; Reduce = aggregate a series over time; Merge = stitch frames together without aggregating.

Advanced deep

When should logic live in the query language vs a Grafana transformation vs a server-side expression? Give the decision criteria.
Query language (PromQL/LogQL/SQL/…) — default for anything the data source can do: filtering, aggregation, rate/quantile, joins within one source, math on series. Reasons: it runs close to the data (less transferred), it's reusable by alerts and recording rules, it's cacheable, and it scales with the backend. Downside: cross-source math isn't possible, and complex reshaping can be awkward. Server-side expressions (Grafana's Math / Reduce / Resample / Classic condition, run in the alerting/backend engine) — use when you need to combine results from multiple queries or multiple data sources for alerting, or reduce a series to a scalar for a threshold. They're evaluated by both the alert path and the panel, so a ratio built as an expression can be alerted on. Downside: limited function set, evaluated in Grafana (data must be pulled back), can be slow on big frames. Transformations — use for presentation-layer reshaping that only matters for the panel: renaming/hiding columns, pivoting wide↔long for a specific viz, joining two queries for a table display, "config from query" to drive thresholds, filtering rows for readability. Downside: not visible to alerting, recomputed every refresh in Grafana, order-sensitive, can be expensive. Decision flow: Can the data source compute it? → do it in the query. Do I need it for an alert, or across sources, reduced to a number? → server-side expression. Is it purely how the table/graph looks? → transformation. And if a transformation is doing heavy lifting on large data every refresh, that's a smell — push it into a query or a recording rule.
A mixed-source panel that divides request count (Prometheus) by active users (BigQuery) is flaky: sometimes empty, sometimes spiky, slow to load. Diagnose and fix.
Causes: (1) Timestamp misalignment — Prometheus emits points on its scrape grid (e.g. every 30s aligned), BigQuery returns rows at query-defined buckets; an outer Join by time produces many rows where only one side has a value → the division yields null (empty gaps) or, where a lone late point lines up, a spike. Fix: make both sides emit the same bucket boundaries — in the BigQuery SQL, TIMESTAMP_TRUNC / GROUP BY to the panel's $__interval and align to the same epoch; on the Prometheus side use a matching step and maybe avg_over_time(...[$__interval]); then use an inner join or a Resample expression to a common interval before dividing. (2) Different resolution — if BigQuery is hourly and Prometheus is per-minute, resample Prometheus to hourly (recording rule or *_over_time) so the ratio is meaningful. (3) Slow / rate-limited BigQuery — each panel refresh runs a scan-heavy SQL query with cost and latency; cache it (materialised view / scheduled query into a small table that Grafana reads), lengthen the panel refresh, and use an Instant-style single-value query where possible. (4) Spiky because of divide-by-small — when active users dips near zero the ratio explodes; clamp_min the denominator or only show the ratio when users > threshold (Filter by value). (5) Nulls from the join — set "Connect null values" appropriately and decide whether missing = 0 or missing = gap. (6) Consider whether this belongs in a panel at all: precompute the ratio in a nightly job that writes a single "requests per active user" series to Prometheus/remote-write, and just graph that — removes the mixed-source fragility entirely and makes it alertable.

Grafana Unified Alerting

Rules produce alert instances; notification policies route them; contact points deliver them.

Notes

The pieces

ObjectRole
Alert ruleOne or more queries + expressions, a condition, an evaluation interval, and a for (pending) duration. Produces alert instances — one per series/dimension.
Evaluation groupRules in a group evaluate sequentially at the group's interval; groups live in a folder.
LabelsAttached to instances (from the data + rule); used for routing and grouping.
AnnotationsHuman text (summary, description, runbook_url, dashboard/panel links) — not used for routing.
Notification policy treeMatches instance labels → picks a contact point, grouping, timings, mute timings. Nested; "continue matching" optional.
Contact pointWhere to send: email, Slack, PagerDuty, Opsgenie, webhook, OnCall, … with a message template.
SilenceLabel-matcher-based suppression for a time window. Mute timing = recurring schedule (e.g. weekends).
# one rule, evaluated by series -> one alert INSTANCE per dimension
expr: sum by (service)(rate(http_5xx[5m])) / sum by (service)(rate(http_total[5m])) > 0.05
#   -> instance {service="checkout"}  FIRING
#   -> instance {service="search"}    NORMAL
# each instance carries labels (service=..., + rule labels like severity="page")
# labels route + group;  annotations (summary/runbook_url) are display-only

Rule types

  • Grafana-managed — evaluated by Grafana; can use any data source and multi-step server-side expressions (Query → Reduce → Math → Threshold). State stored in Grafana's DB.
  • Data-source-managed (Mimir/Loki/Prometheus recording & alerting rules) — Grafana edits rules that live and evaluate in that system's ruler. Single data source, PromQL/LogQL only, but scales with the backend and is the same rules your infra team manages as code.
# Grafana-managed: multi-source, multi-step (Query -> Reduce -> Math), state in Grafana DB
A [Loki]        count_over_time({app="api",level="error"}[5m])
B [Prometheus]  sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="api"}[5m]))
C [Math]        $A / $B > 0.01            # ratio across two different backends

# Data-source-managed: a plain Prometheus rule file, evaluated by the ruler
groups:
  - name: api
    rules:
      - alert: HighErrorRate
        expr: sum(rate(http_5xx[5m])) / sum(rate(http_total[5m])) > 0.05
        for: 5m
        labels:   { severity: page }
        annotations: { runbook_url: "https://wiki/rb/api-5xx" }

Rule anatomy (Grafana-managed)

A: query   sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
         / sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
B: reduce  last(A)                  # collapse series to one number each
C: math    $B > 0.05               # the condition (boolean)
Evaluate every 1m  for 5m           # must be true 5m straight -> Firing

States: Normal → Pending (condition true, within for) → Firing. Plus NoData and Error states, each with a configurable behaviour (treat as OK / Alerting / keep last).

Routing & grouping

  • An instance walks the policy tree top-down; first matching node (by label matchers) handles it, unless "continue".
  • Group by labels (e.g. alertname, cluster) → one notification per group. Group wait (buffer new group), group interval (batch updates), repeat interval (re-notify still-firing).
  • Default policy is the catch-all root; add child policies per team/severity.
# notification policy tree (first match wins unless continue: true)
root:  group_by: [alertname, cluster]
       receiver: slack-alerts
       routes:
         - matchers: ['severity = page']
           receiver: pagerduty
           group_wait: 30s          # buffer a new group before first send
           group_interval: 5m       # batch further changes to that group
           repeat_interval: 4h      # re-page if still firing
         - matchers: ['team = data']
           receiver: slack-data

Good practice

  • Alert on symptoms / SLO burn, not every cause; keep for long enough to dodge blips.
  • Multi-dimensional rules (one rule, by (service)) beat one rule per service.
  • Always set summary, description, runbook_url; add a severity label for routing.
  • Decide NoData behaviour deliberately — "NoData = Alerting" catches dead exporters but is noisy on flaky scrapes.
  • Manage rules as code (provisioning / Terraform / the export YAML) for anything important.
# GOOD: symptom-based, multi-dimensional, actionable annotations
- alert: SLOBurnFast
  expr: (1 - slo:availability:ratio_rate5m{service=~".+"}) > (14.4 * 0.001)  # 2% budget/1h
  for: 5m
  labels: { severity: page }
  annotations:
