    summary: "{{ $labels.service }} burning error budget fast"
    runbook_url: "https://wiki/rb/{{ $labels.service }}"

# BAD: cause-based, per-host, no context -> pager noise
- alert: CPUHigh
  expr: node_cpu_usage > 0.8            # not user-visible; fires nightly on batch jobs
Cheat Sheet
  • Rule (queries + expressions + condition + every + for) → alert instances (one per dimension) → notification policy (routes by labels) → contact point (delivers).
  • States: Normal → Pending (for window) → Firing; plus NoData / Error (configurable).
  • Grafana-managed rule pipeline: Query → Reduce → Math/Threshold; any source, multi-source; state in Grafana DB.
  • Data-source-managed rule: PromQL/LogQL in the backend ruler; scales, managed as code.
  • Routing: label matchers, first match wins (unless "continue"); group by + group wait / group interval / repeat interval.
  • Silence = ad hoc label-matcher suppression; mute timing = recurring schedule.
  • Set summary/description/runbook_url + a severity label. Alert on symptoms/SLO burn, not causes. Multi-dim rules over per-target rules.
Q&A
What does the for duration do?
After the condition first becomes true the alert enters Pending; it only becomes Firing (and notifies) if the condition stays true continuously for the whole for period. It filters out brief spikes. It's separate from the evaluation interval (how often the rule runs).
Difference between Grafana-managed and data-source-managed alert rules?
Grafana-managed rules are evaluated by Grafana itself, can span any/multiple data sources, and support a multi-stage expression pipeline; their state lives in Grafana's database. Data-source-managed rules are Prometheus/Loki/Mimir ruler rules — single source, PromQL/LogQL only — that Grafana just provides a UI to edit; they evaluate and scale in that backend.
How do notification policies and contact points relate?
Contact points define how to notify (Slack channel, PagerDuty key, webhook). The notification policy tree defines which alerts go to which contact point, based on label matchers, plus grouping and timing. One contact point can be used by many policies.
What's the difference between a silence and a mute timing?
A silence is a one-off suppression: you specify label matchers and a start/end time (e.g. during a known maintenance). A mute timing is a reusable recurring schedule (e.g. "outside business hours", "every Saturday") that you attach to a notification policy so matching alerts don't page during those windows.
Why prefer one multi-dimensional rule over one rule per service?
A single rule with by (service) automatically produces an alert instance per service, including services added later, with one place to edit the logic and threshold. Per-service rules multiply maintenance, drift, and the chance of a new service having no alert.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What alert state comes between Normal and Firing?
Pending (while the condition holds but the for duration hasn't elapsed).
What object decides which contact point an alert goes to?
The notification policy tree (matching on instance labels).
Which labels are used for routing — labels or annotations?
Labels. Annotations are human-readable text only.

Intermediate core

An exporter dies and your "high error rate" alert goes quiet instead of firing. Why, and how do you catch dead targets?
When the exporter is down the query returns no series, so the error-rate condition is neither true nor false — the rule goes to NoData, and if NoData behaviour is "OK"/"Keep last state" nothing pages. Fixes: (1) Set the rule's NoData state to Alerting (accepting some noise on flaky scrapes, mitigated by for). (2) Better, add a dedicated up / absent alert: up{job="x"} == 0 or absent(http_requests_total{job="x"}), or a "target missing" rule, so target death is its own signal with its own routing. (3) Alert on scrape health globally (count(up == 0) by (job)). (4) For SLO-style rules, structure them so missing data counts against availability. Keep the "no data" alert lower severity/ticket unless the target is critical.
Design the notification policy tree for: platform team owns infra alerts, each product team owns its service alerts, sev1 pages 24/7 to PagerDuty, sev2 goes to Slack, everything muted for known maintenance.
Ensure rules set labels: team (platform | checkout | search | …), severity (sev1 | sev2 | sev3). Contact points: pagerduty-<team>, slack-<team>, plus a fallback slack-platform. Policy tree: root (default contact point = slack-platform, group by alertname,cluster,team, group wait 30s, group interval 5m, repeat 4h). Child policies (first match wins): (1) match team=platform → child with two grandchildren: severity=sev1→pagerduty-platform, else →slack-platform. (2) match team=checkout → severity=sev1→pagerduty-checkout, else→slack-checkout. (3) …one per team. Attach a mute timing "maintenance-window" (or use ad hoc silences with matchers like cluster=eu-1) at the appropriate node(s). Use severity=sev3 nodes routing to a low-noise channel or none. Set "continue" only where you deliberately want multi-delivery (e.g. also mirror sev1 to a war-room channel). Keep grouping labels consistent so a burst of related instances = one page.

Advanced deep

Implement multi-window, multi-burn-rate SLO alerting in Grafana for a 99.9% availability target. Explain the math and the rule setup.
Target 99.9% → error budget = 0.1% of requests over the SLO window (say 30 days). Burn rate = (error ratio over a window) / (budget ratio) = how many times faster than "allowed" you're spending budget; burn rate 1 exactly exhausts the budget in 30 days. Google SRE's recommended alerts fire when a fast and a slow window both exceed a threshold, to get fast detection without flapping: (1) Page: 2% of budget in 1h → burn rate ≥ 14.4 over 1h AND ≥ 14.4 over 5m. (2) Page: 5% in 6h → burn rate ≥ 6 over 6h AND ≥ 6 over 30m. (3) Ticket: 10% in 3d → burn rate ≥ 1 over 3d AND ≥ 1 over 6h. The short window confirms the burn is current (so you stop alerting quickly once it recovers); the long window confirms it's significant (not a blip). Setup: define recording rules for the error ratio at each window (job:slo_errors:ratio_rate5m, _rate30m, _rate1h, _rate6h, _rate3d) in Mimir/Prometheus so evaluation is cheap and consistent. Then Grafana alert rules (data-source-managed, so they scale and are code): rule "SLO fast burn" condition (job:slo_errors:ratio_rate1h > 14.4*0.001) and (job:slo_errors:ratio_rate5m > 14.4*0.001), for: 2m, labels severity=sev1, slo=availability; rule "SLO slow burn" with the 6h/30m pair at 6×, severity=sev1; rule "SLO budget ticket" with 3d/6h at 1×, severity=sev3. Annotations link the SLO dashboard and runbook. Multi-dimensional by (service). Route sev1 to PagerDuty, sev3 to a ticket queue. Add a companion dashboard: current burn rate gauges per window, remaining budget, and time-to-exhaustion projection. This gives you: quick paging on genuine fast burns, no paging on transient spikes, and a slow-burn ticket that catches a steady low-grade regression before the month's budget is gone.
How does Grafana alerting achieve high availability and avoid duplicate/lost notifications across multiple instances? What can still go wrong?
Grafana's unified alerting embeds a fork of Prometheus Alertmanager. In HA, the Grafana instances form a cluster over a gossip protocol (ha_peers, ha_listen_address, ha_advertise_address, or in k8s a headless service). Rule evaluation is distributed: with the "high availability" scheduler each instance evaluates all rules but the embedded Alertmanagers deduplicate — when an alert fires, the notification is sent by one instance; peers see the "notification log" (nflog) entry propagated via gossip and suppress their own send. Silences and notification state are also gossiped so a silence created on one node applies everywhere, and group wait/repeat interval timers are coordinated. State (alert instances, `for` progress) is persisted to the shared SQL DB and periodically to the Alertmanager's own store, so an instance restart doesn't reset pending timers or re-fire everything. What can still go wrong: (1) Gossip partition — if peers can't communicate, each cluster half dedups independently → duplicate notifications (better than lost). (2) Clock skew between instances can misalign group timers. (3) Shared DB outage — evaluation stalls; on recovery, a flush of state changes and possibly a burst of notifications; pending `for` timers may be affected. (4) Scaling the scheduler — every instance evaluating every rule doesn't scale to huge rule counts; that's why heavy setups push rules to the Mimir/Loki ruler (which shards evaluation) and use Grafana only as the Alertmanager/UI, or use an external Alertmanager (- alertmanagers config) shared by all. (5) Misconfigured HA (peers not actually connected — check the "Admin → Alerting → cluster" status) silently degrades to N independent Alertmanagers = N copies of every page. (6) Contact-point provider outages / rate limits are outside Grafana's dedup. Mitigations: verify cluster membership, run the DB HA, keep NTP tight, offload rule evaluation to backend rulers at scale, and consider a single external Alertmanager for a clean dedup domain.

Provisioning & Dashboards-as-Code

Click-ops doesn't survive a rebuild — define data sources, dashboards, and alerts as files.

Notes

File provisioning

On startup Grafana reads YAML from conf/provisioning/ (path set by GF_PATHS_PROVISIONING):

FolderDefines
datasources/Data source instances (type, url, access, auth, uid, isDefault, jsonData/secureJsonData).
dashboards/Providers that load dashboard JSON files from a directory (with foldersFromFilesStructure, updateIntervalSeconds, allowUiUpdates).
alerting/Alert rules, contact points, notification policies, templates, mute timings (unified alerting).
plugins/, access-control/App plugin config; RBAC roles & assignments.
  • Provisioned objects are read-only in the UI by default (allowUiUpdates: false) — the file is the source of truth; a delete from file removes the object (disableDeletion to guard).
  • Secrets: use secureJsonData + env var interpolation (${PROM_TOKEN}), never commit them.
# conf/provisioning/dashboards/team.yaml — a PROVIDER, not the dashboards
apiVersion: 1
providers:
  - name: team-dashboards
    folder: "Team A"
    type: file
    disableDeletion: true          # a missing file won't delete the dashboard
    allowUiUpdates: false          # UI edits are reverted on next reload
    updateIntervalSeconds: 30
    options:
      path: /var/lib/grafana/dashboards/team-a
      foldersFromFilesStructure: true

The dashboard JSON model

  • A dashboard is a JSON doc: uid, title, tags, templating.list (variables), panels[] (each with gridPos, targets[], fieldConfig, options), annotations.list, time, refresh, schemaVersion.
  • Export for sharing externally replaces concrete data sources with __inputs placeholders so it imports anywhere.
  • id is instance-local; uid is the portable identity — keep it stable in Git.
  • Bumping Grafana can bump schemaVersion and silently migrate the JSON — commit the migrated form.
# "Export for sharing externally" parameterises the data sources:
{
  "__inputs": [
    { "name": "DS_PROMETHEUS", "type": "datasource", "pluginId": "prometheus" }
  ],
  "__requires": [ { "type": "grafana", "id": "grafana", "version": "10.4.0" } ],
  "uid": "api-overview",             // keep stable in Git
  "schemaVersion": 39,              // bumped by upgrades -> commit the migrated file
  "panels": [ { "datasource": "${DS_PROMETHEUS}", ... } ]
}

Ways to manage dashboards as code

ToolApproach
Raw JSON + file provisioningStore .json in Git, mount into the provisioning dir. Simple; JSON is verbose and merge-hostile.
Jsonnet + grafonnet (or grafana-foundation-sdk)Generate JSON from concise, DRY code; libraries for panels/queries. Great for many similar dashboards.
Grafana Terraform providergrafana_dashboard, grafana_data_source, grafana_folder, grafana_rule_group, … via the HTTP API. Fits IaC pipelines; state-managed.
Grizzlykubectl-style CLI to push dashboards/datasources/rules from Jsonnet/YAML.
Git Sync / GitOps (newer Grafana)Grafana watches a Git repo of resources directly.
# grafonnet (Jsonnet): one function, many similar dashboards, no copy-paste JSON
local g = import 'g.libsonnet';
g.dashboard.new('API - ' + svc)
+ g.dashboard.withPanels([
    g.panel.timeSeries.new('Req/s')
    + g.panel.timeSeries.queryOptions.withTargets([
        prom.new('$ds', 'sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="%s"}[5m]))' % svc) ]),
  ])

# Terraform: state-managed, fits an IaC pipeline
resource "grafana_dashboard" "api" { config_json = file("dashboards/api.json") }

Library panels & reuse

Library panels are shared panel definitions referenced by many dashboards — edit once, propagates. In code, factor common panels/rows into Jsonnet functions or Terraform modules. Keep a house "dashboard library" (RED row, USE row, SLO header).

# library panel: stored once, referenced by libraryPanel.uid from many dashboards
"panels": [
  { "gridPos": {"h": 8, "w": 12, "x": 0, "y": 0},
    "libraryPanel": { "uid": "red-row-latency", "name": "RED - Latency p95" } }
]
# edit the library panel once -> every dashboard that embeds it updates

CI for dashboards

  • Lint JSON (schema, required tags, no hard-coded datasource names, panels have descriptions).
  • Validate PromQL/LogQL with promtool / cortextool.
  • Deploy on merge; provisioning picks up on the reload interval or a restart/API reload.
# CI pipeline for a dashboards repo
- run: jsonnet -m out/ dashboards.jsonnet                 # render
- run: |                                                   # lint
    for f in out/*.json; do
      jq -e '.uid and .schemaVersion' "$f" >/dev/null || exit 1
      ! grep -q '"datasource": *"[A-Za-z]' "$f"            # no hard-coded ds names
    done
- run: promtool check rules rules/*.yaml                   # validate PromQL
- run: curl -X POST $GRAFANA/api/admin/provisioning/dashboards/reload   # on merge
Cheat Sheet
  • File provisioning: YAML in conf/provisioning/{datasources,dashboards,alerting,plugins,access-control}/, read at startup / reload.
  • Provisioned = read-only in UI (unless allowUiUpdates: true); file is source of truth; disableDeletion to protect.
  • Pin data source uid in YAML so exported dashboards resolve across environments; secrets via secureJsonData + env interpolation.
  • Dashboard JSON: uid (portable id), templating.list, panels[] (gridPos/targets/fieldConfig), schemaVersion.
  • As-code options: raw JSON + provisioning, Jsonnet/grafonnet, Terraform provider, Grizzly, Git Sync.
  • Library panels for shared panels; Jsonnet functions / TF modules for shared rows.
  • CI: lint JSON, forbid hard-coded datasource names, validate queries, deploy on merge.
Q&A
What happens if you edit a provisioned dashboard in the UI?
By default you can't save — Grafana shows it as provisioned and read-only, and any change is lost on the next provisioning reload. Set allowUiUpdates: true in the provider to permit UI edits (then the file and the DB can diverge, which is usually undesirable).
Why pin data source UIDs in provisioning?
So a dashboard JSON that references datasource: {uid: "prometheus-main"} resolves in every environment. Without a fixed UID, each environment auto-generates a different one and imported dashboards break with "datasource not found".
What's the portable identifier for a dashboard — id or uid?
uid. The numeric id is assigned per Grafana instance and differs everywhere; the uid is chosen by you (or generated once) and is what URLs, links, and provisioning use.
Jsonnet/grafonnet vs raw JSON for dashboards — when is the extra tooling worth it?
When you have many dashboards that share structure (per-service RED dashboards, per-cluster views). Jsonnet lets you define a panel/row once as a function and stamp out dozens of dashboards, with real variables and imports. For a handful of bespoke dashboards, raw JSON in Git is simpler and the tooling overhead isn't justified.
How do provisioned alert rules relate to Prometheus rule files?
Grafana's alerting/ provisioning defines Grafana-managed rules (and contact points/policies) in Grafana's own YAML format. Prometheus/Mimir/Loki ruler rule files are separate and evaluated by those systems; Grafana can display and edit them if the data source supports rule management, but they're deployed through that system's own config, not Grafana provisioning.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Where does file-based provisioning config live?
In YAML files under conf/provisioning/ (datasources, dashboards, alerting, …).
Are provisioned dashboards editable in the UI by default?
No — they're read-only unless allowUiUpdates: true.
Which dashboard field is the stable, portable identity?
uid.

Intermediate core

Design a workflow where dashboards are authored in the Grafana UI but end up version-controlled and provisioned.
Give authors an "editable" workspace: a folder with a non-provisioned provider (or a separate dev Grafana) where they build and iterate freely. When happy, they export the dashboard JSON (via UI "Save JSON" / "Export", or the HTTP API / grafana-cli) and open a PR adding/updating the .json in the Git repo. CI: normalise the JSON (strip volatile fields like id, version, iteration; pin datasource to a UID or ${DS_*} input), lint it (required tags, descriptions, no ad-hoc datasource names), validate queries. On merge, a pipeline deploys the file into the provisioning directory of the real Grafana(s) (commit to a config repo, or terraform apply with the Grafana provider, or Grizzly push), where it becomes read-only. To change it, edit in dev, re-export, new PR. Optionally use a tool (e.g. a periodic job) that diffs live provisioned dashboards vs the repo and alerts on drift. For heavily-templated fleets, authors instead edit Jsonnet and CI renders JSON.
After a Grafana upgrade, your committed dashboard JSON produces a noisy diff on next export even though nobody changed it. What's happening and how do you handle it?
Grafana migrates dashboard JSON to the current schemaVersion on load — renaming/moving fields, converting deprecated panel options (e.g. old graph panel → timeseries, angular → react options, threshold format changes). So the version in Git (old schema) and what Grafana now emits (new schema) differ structurally without any human edit. Handling: (1) After the upgrade, deliberately re-export all dashboards once, review that the migration is semantically equivalent (render before/after), and commit the migrated JSON as a single "schema migration" PR. (2) Add a CI step that loads each dashboard through a matching Grafana version and normalises before diffing, so future diffs are meaningful. (3) Strip volatile fields (version, id, iteration) in a pre-commit hook. (4) Prefer Jsonnet/grafonnet or the Terraform provider, which target a schema and regenerate cleanly, reducing hand-managed JSON churn. (5) Pin the Grafana version across environments so dev and prod migrate identically.

Advanced deep

Design an end-to-end GitOps setup for a Grafana fleet (5 environments) covering data sources, dashboards, alerts, folders, and RBAC, with promotion and drift detection.
Repo layout: /lib (grafonnet + house panel/row/dashboard functions, alert-rule helpers), /dashboards (Jsonnet that imports lib and defines dashboards, parameterised by env), /datasources (YAML templates with ${...} for URLs/secrets and fixed uids), /alerting (rule groups, contact points, policies as YAML/Jsonnet), /rbac (folders, team→folder permissions, roles), /envs/<env>.libsonnet (per-env values: cluster names, datasource URLs, SLO targets, routing keys). Render: CI runs jsonnet to produce concrete JSON/YAML per env into an artifact. Deploy: choose one mechanism and stick to it — either (a) the Grafana Terraform provider (state per env, grafana_dashboard/grafana_folder/grafana_data_source/grafana_rule_group/grafana_team/grafana_folder_permission), or (b) commit rendered files into each env's provisioning directory (mounted via config repo / ConfigMaps) and let Grafana load them, or (c) Grizzly/Git Sync. Terraform gives drift detection for free (terraform plan); with provisioning, add a scheduled job that pulls live objects via the HTTP API and diffs against the rendered artifact, failing/alerting on unexpected drift (someone clicked "edit"). Set allowUiUpdates: false and disableDeletion appropriately; give teams editable personal folders outside GitOps. Promotion: changes land on main → auto-deploy to dev; a tag or PR-based promotion advances the same rendered artifact through staging → preprod → prod-eu → prod-us, only env values differing. Secrets come from the deploy pipeline's vault, injected at apply time, never in Git. Safety: CI validates every query (promtool/cortextool), checks dashboards have owners/tags, runs a "does it render" smoke test against a throwaway Grafana, and requires review for /alerting and /rbac changes (CODEOWNERS). Rollback = redeploy the previous artifact / terraform apply the prior commit. Net result: identical, reviewed observability config everywhere, no snowflake dashboards, and any manual change shows up as drift.
What fields must you strip or normalise when committing exported dashboard JSON, and why does each cause problems?
(1) id — instance-local numeric id; committing it causes "dashboard not found / id mismatch" on import elsewhere and needless diffs. Set to null. (2) version — increments on every save; pure diff noise and can trigger optimistic-concurrency conflicts on API import. Remove/zero it. (3) iteration / __requires / __inputs (unless doing an external-share export) — volatile timestamps / environment assumptions. (4) Concrete datasource references ("datasource": {"uid": "abc123"} where abc123 is env-specific) — replace with a fixed shared UID or a ${DS_PROM} template input so it resolves in every environment. (5) gnetId — ties it to a grafana.com published dashboard; drop for internal ones. (6) Absolute time ranges someone left set (e.g. a specific incident window) — reset to a relative default like now-6h. (7) refresh hard-coded to a very short interval — can hammer data sources fleet-wide; standardise. (8) timezone if you want it to follow the viewer. (9) Panel ids that collide after edits — renumber. (10) schemaVersion — don't hand-edit, but be aware it pins the migration state; keep it consistent with your Grafana version. (11) Any links with hard-coded hostnames. (12) Leftover library-panel inline copies vs references. A pre-commit normaliser (jq/script or a Jsonnet round-trip) that blanks id/version/iteration, rewrites datasource to inputs, and resets time/refresh keeps diffs meaningful and imports portable.

Auth, Orgs, Teams, Folders & RBAC

Who logs in, which org they land in, and what they can see and edit.

Notes

Authentication

  • Built-in: username/password in Grafana's DB. Fine for tiny setups; disable with disable_login_form once SSO is in.
  • OAuth / OIDC (Google, Azure AD, Okta, generic OIDC, GitHub, GitLab), SAML (Enterprise/Cloud), LDAP/AD. Map IdP groups → Grafana roles/teams/orgs with role_attribute_path / group mappings / team sync.
  • Proxy auth (auth.proxy): a reverse proxy (oauth2-proxy, mod_auth) sets a header Grafana trusts.
  • Anonymous access for public read-only dashboards (auth.anonymous, with an org + role).
  • Service accounts (replaced API keys): non-human identities with a role and tokens, for Terraform / CI / external callers.
# grafana.ini: generic OIDC + map an IdP claim to the Grafana role
[auth.generic_oauth]
enabled = true
auth_url   = https://idp.corp/authorize
token_url  = https://idp.corp/token
# JMESPath over the token: "grafana-admins" group -> Admin, else Viewer
role_attribute_path = contains(groups[*], 'grafana-admins') && 'Admin' || 'Viewer'

[auth]
disable_login_form = true          # force SSO once it works

Orgs vs the rest

An Organization is a hard tenancy boundary: separate users' role, dashboards, data sources, teams, alerting. A user can belong to multiple orgs with different roles. Grafana now steers you toward one org + folders + RBAC + teams instead; multi-org is clunky (data sources must be recreated per org, no cross-org dashboards) and semi-legacy. Use multi-org only for genuinely separate tenants.

# multi-org pain: a data source exists only inside ONE org
GET /api/datasources            # returns only the CURRENT org's sources
POST /api/user/using/3          # switch org, then re-create every data source here

# preferred model instead: one org, isolate with folders + team permissions
POST /api/folders  {"title": "Team A", "uid": "team-a"}
POST /api/folders/team-a/permissions  {"items":[{"teamId":7,"permission":2}]}  # 2 = Edit

Basic roles (per org)

RoleCan
ViewerView dashboards it has access to; no editing, no explore (unless enabled).
EditorCreate/edit dashboards & alerts, use Explore; not manage users/datasources/permissions.
Admin (org)Everything in the org: users, data sources, plugins, org settings.
Grafana Server AdminCross-org superuser: manage orgs and all users. Separate from org Admin.
Viewer   -> GET  /api/dashboards/uid/x           200
         -> POST /api/dashboards/db              403   (no edit)
Editor   -> POST /api/dashboards/db              200
         -> POST /api/datasources               403   (not infra)
Admin    -> POST /api/datasources               200   (within this org)
         -> POST /api/orgs                       403   (that's Server Admin only)
# Server Admin lives at /admin, is a per-USER flag, and is org-independent

Folders, dashboards & permission inheritance

  • Dashboards live in folders. Permissions set on a folder inherit to its dashboards (and, with nested folders, downward) unless overridden.
  • Grant permissions to a role, a team, or a user: View / Edit / Admin on that folder subtree.
  • Pattern: an "Editor" org role for most, but folder permissions that make team A Editor only on its folder and Viewer elsewhere. Or default everyone to Viewer and grant Edit per folder.
  • Alert rules and library panels are folder-scoped too.
# folder subtree: set once on the folder, inherited by every dashboard/alert inside
Folder "Payments"        Team Payments = Edit,  Org role Viewer = View
  |- dash "Txn latency"  (inherits: Payments Edit, others View)
  |- Folder "Payments/Reconciliation"
       |- dash "Ledger"  (inherits down; add "Team Finance = View" here to widen)
# override by setting an explicit permission on the child dashboard/subfolder

Teams & team sync

Teams group users so you assign folder/datasource permissions once. Team sync (Enterprise/Cloud) maps IdP groups to Grafana teams automatically on login, so membership follows your directory. Teams can also carry default preferences (home dashboard, theme).

# map IdP group -> Grafana team once; membership then follows the directory
[auth.saml]
[[auth.saml.group_mappings]]     # Enterprise team sync
group_dn  = "cn=payments,ou=groups,dc=corp"
org_id    = 1
grafana_team_id = 7
# on every login Grafana adds/removes the user from team 7 to match the IdP

Fine-grained RBAC (Enterprise/Cloud)

  • Beyond the 3 basic roles: granular permissions like dashboards:read, datasources:query, alert.rules:write, users:create, scoped to resources.
  • Built-in fixed roles (e.g. "Data source writer") + custom roles; assign to basic roles, teams, service accounts, or users.
  • Lets you say "this team can query datasource X but not edit it", "these people can manage alert rules but not dashboards".
# custom role: "can manage alert rules, cannot touch dashboards"
POST /api/access-control/roles
{
  "name": "custom:alert-manager",
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "alert.rules:read" },
    { "action": "alert.rules:write", "scope": "folders:uid:payments" }
  ]
}
POST /api/access-control/teams/7/roles  { "roleUid": "custom:alert-manager" }

Data source permissions

By default any org user can query any data source. Enterprise data source permissions restrict query access per team/role — important for multi-tenant setups where a shared Prometheus is scoped per team via headers/label enforcement.

# lock a data source so only one team can query it
POST /api/datasources/uid/prom-payments/permissions
{ "permission": "Query", "teamId": 7 }        # everyone else: 403 on query

# multi-tenant Prometheus: Grafana adds a tenant header per team
#   secureJsonData: { httpHeaderValue1: "payments" }
#   httpHeaderName1: "X-Scope-OrgID"          -> Mimir returns only that tenant's data
Cheat Sheet
  • Auth: built-in, OAuth/OIDC, SAML, LDAP/AD, proxy, anonymous. Map IdP groups → roles/teams via role_attribute_path / team sync.
  • Service accounts + tokens for CI/Terraform/external (API keys are deprecated).
  • Basic roles per org: Viewer < Editor < org Admin; plus cross-org Server Admin.
  • Org = hard tenant boundary (separate dashboards/datasources/users' roles) — now discouraged; prefer one org + folders + RBAC + teams.
  • Folder permissions inherit to dashboards/alerts/library panels; grant View/Edit/Admin to team / role / user.
  • Common pattern: everyone Viewer by default, Edit granted per team on their folder.
  • Fine-grained RBAC (Enterprise): granular actions (datasources:query, alert.rules:write…), custom roles, per-resource scope. Data source permissions restrict who can query a source.
Q&A
What's the difference between an Organization and a folder?
An org is a full tenancy boundary — its own users' roles, dashboards, data sources, teams, and alerting, with no sharing across orgs. A folder is just a grouping of dashboards within an org, used mainly for permission inheritance. Modern practice is one org with folders + RBAC rather than many orgs.
How does a user get Edit rights on only their team's dashboards?
Set their org role to Viewer (or Editor) and add a folder permission: their team gets "Edit" on the team's folder. Folder permissions inherit to all dashboards inside, so they can edit there and only view elsewhere.
What replaced API keys?
Service accounts. You create a service account with a role (and optionally RBAC permissions), then issue one or more tokens for it. Unlike old API keys, a service account is a first-class identity you can manage, disable, and audit.
What is team sync?
An Enterprise/Cloud feature that maps identity-provider groups to Grafana teams. On each login Grafana adjusts the user's team memberships to match their IdP groups, so folder/data-source permissions granted to teams stay in sync with your directory automatically.
By default, can a Viewer query any data source?
Yes — data source query access isn't restricted by default; any org user can run queries against any configured source (e.g. via Explore if enabled, or by editing a copy of a dashboard). Restricting per-team query access requires Enterprise data source permissions.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which basic role can use Explore and edit dashboards but not manage users?
Editor.
Where are folder permissions applied — per dashboard or inherited?
Set on the folder and inherited by the dashboards (and alerts/library panels) inside it.
What identity type should Terraform use to talk to Grafana?
A service account with a token (not a personal login, not a legacy API key).

Intermediate core

You use Okta SSO. New hires should land as Viewer, the SRE group as Editor on all folders, and the "grafana-admins" group as org Admin — no manual clicks. How?
Configure the generic OAuth/OIDC (or SAML) integration with Okta. Use role_attribute_path (a JMESPath over the token claims) to derive the org role, e.g. contains(groups[*], 'grafana-admins') && 'Admin' || contains(groups[*], 'sre') && 'Editor' || 'Viewer', and set role_attribute_strict = true so someone losing a group is downgraded. Set the default org and auto_assign_org_role = Viewer as a floor. For folder-level Editor rather than org-wide, instead keep everyone Viewer via role_attribute_path and use team sync: map Okta group sre → Grafana team SRE, then grant that team "Edit" on the relevant folders (or all folders). "grafana-admins" → org Admin via the role path. Result: role and team membership are recomputed from Okta claims on every login; offboarding in Okta removes access automatically.
A shared Prometheus holds all teams' metrics. How do you stop team A from querying team B's data in Grafana?
Grafana's basic model can't do row-level data security on a single data source, so combine: (1) Per-team data source instances, each provisioned to point at the Prometheus (or a Mimir tenant) with an enforced label matcher / tenant header — e.g. Mimir/Cortex X-Scope-OrgID: team-a, or a PromQL-enforcing proxy (prom-label-proxy) that injects namespace=~"team-a-.*" into every query. The team cannot edit this data source (provisioned, read-only). (2) Enterprise data source permissions: restrict query permission on prometheus-team-a to team A only, so B can't select it. (3) Folder RBAC so each team only sees its own dashboards (which reference only its own data source). (4) Disable the generic/shared Prometheus data source for non-admins, or remove it. (5) If truly strict isolation is required, separate Prometheus/Mimir tenants per team. The label-enforcing proxy + per-team scoped, permission-restricted data source is the usual pragmatic answer.

Advanced deep

Compare multi-org, folders+RBAC, and instance-per-tenant for isolating 50 customers in a Grafana you operate as a product. Recommend one.
Multi-org (single instance): each customer = one Grafana org. Pros: built-in separation of dashboards, users' roles, teams, alerting; one instance to run. Cons: data sources are not shared across orgs — you provision N copies; org switching UX is poor for your staff who need to see many; some features are org-unaware; RBAC and Cloud features are weaker across orgs; the org model is semi-legacy and gets less investment; noisy-neighbour on evaluation/rendering; a bug crossing the org boundary is a full breach. Folders + RBAC (single instance, single org): customer = top-level folder subtree + a team + scoped, permission-restricted data source(s). Pros: modern, well-supported path; fine-grained control; easy for your staff to work across customers; nested folders model hierarchy; dashboards-as-code straightforward. Cons: isolation is logical not physical — a misconfigured folder permission or a shared-data-source label-enforcement gap leaks data; alerting Alertmanager is shared (routing must be watertight); still one blast radius for an instance outage; you must be rigorous with provisioning and drift detection. Requires Enterprise/Cloud for data source permissions and fine-grained RBAC to be safe. Instance-per-tenant (container/namespace/Cloud stack per customer): Pros: hard isolation (separate process, DB, Alertmanager, data sources, upgrade cadence, blast radius); trivially explainable to security/compliance; per-tenant resource limits and billing. Cons: 50× the operational surface — upgrades, backups, cert rotation, monitoring-the-monitoring; higher cost; cross-tenant views for your ops team need aggregation tooling; slower to onboard unless fully automated. Recommendation: for a product with paying customers and any compliance story, instance-per-tenant, fully automated (Helm/Terraform per tenant, GitOps config, a control plane that provisions stacks) — the isolation guarantee is worth the automation investment, and Grafana Cloud's model is exactly this. If the customers are internal teams of one company (lower trust boundary) and you have Enterprise, folders + RBAC + per-team scoped data sources + team sync is the right trade-off: one instance, strong-enough logical isolation, far less ops. Avoid multi-org for new designs — it's the worst of both (logical isolation, legacy support, poor multi-tenant UX).
Walk through exactly how Grafana resolves whether a given user may view a specific dashboard, considering roles, folder inheritance, RBAC, and data source access.
On a dashboard load Grafana checks, roughly in this order: (1) Authn — is there a valid session / token? Which org is active for this user (from session; a user has a role per org)? (2) Org role — the user's basic role in that org (Viewer/Editor/Admin) is the baseline capability set. Server Admin is orthogonal (cross-org management, not dashboard content). (3) Dashboard/folder permissions — Grafana looks up the ACL for the dashboard: explicit permissions on the dashboard, else inherited from its folder (and, with nested folders, from ancestor folders), else the org-level default. Each ACL entry grants View/Edit/Admin to a role, a team the user is in, or the user directly; the highest matching permission wins. So a Viewer-role user can still be granted Edit on one folder; an Editor-role user can be restricted below default only if the instance is configured so that dashboards require explicit grants (there's a setting to make the general folder not world-viewable). (4) Fine-grained RBAC (Enterprise) — if enabled, the action dashboards:read scoped to that dashboard/folder UID must be satisfied by one of the user's assigned roles (basic-role-attached, team, service account, or custom). RBAC can grant or, with denial semantics in newer versions, further gate. (5) Rendering the panels — for each panel query, Grafana checks the user can query that data source: default-allow, unless Enterprise data source permissions restrict it to certain teams/roles; if denied, the panel errors while the rest of the dashboard still shows. (6) Provisioning doesn't affect view rights (only whether edits can be saved). (7) Team membership used above may have just been recomputed by team sync at login. Net: view is allowed iff (authenticated) AND (in an org with the dashboard) AND (max of applicable folder/dashboard ACL ≥ View, considering inheritance) AND (RBAC dashboards:read if enabled) — and individual panels additionally require data source query permission.

Explore, Correlations & Dashboard Design

Ad-hoc investigation, jumping between signals, and dashboards people can actually read.

Notes

Explore

  • A query-focused view with no panels to configure — type a query, see the result, iterate. For investigation, not monitoring.
  • Split view: two panes side by side (e.g. metrics left, logs right), time ranges linked or independent.
  • Query history and starred queries per user.
  • Data-source-specific helpers: log volume histogram + Logs for Loki; the metrics browser for Prometheus; trace view for Tempo; "Add to dashboard" to promote a query to a panel.
  • Requires the user to have Explore permission (Editor role, or `viewers_can_edit`/RBAC).
# Explore round-trip: iterate a query, then promote the keeper
1. {app="checkout"} |= "timeout"              # too noisy
2. {app="checkout"} |= "timeout" | json | duration > 2s   # narrowed
3. sum(count_over_time({app="checkout"} |= "timeout" [5m]))  # now a metric
4. "Add to dashboard" -> becomes a Time series panel on a new/existing dashboard
# split view: metrics query left, the same time range of logs right

Built-in cross-signal jumps

FeatureDoes
Trace to logsTempo data source config: from a span, open Loki filtered by the span's time & tags (e.g. pod, trace_id).
Trace to metricsFrom a span, run a templated PromQL (e.g. RED metrics for that service).
Logs to trace (derived fields)Loki config: regex a trace_id out of the line → link to Tempo.
ExemplarsPoints on a latency graph linking to a trace that produced that sample.
Data linksPanel/field links templated with values & labels → another dashboard / Explore / external tool.
CorrelationsInstance-level config: define "from results of query on source A, build a link to a query on source B" using field values as variables — adds a link on matching results across dashboards and Explore, no per-panel setup.
# Tempo data source config: span -> logs for the same pod & time
tracesToLogsV2:
  datasourceUid: loki
  tags: [{ key: 'pod', value: 'pod' }]
  query: '{pod="${__span.tags.pod}"} |= "${__span.traceId}"'

# Correlation (instance-wide): any result with a "service" field gains a link
source: prometheus     target: loki
target query: '{service="${service}"} | logfmt | level="error"'

Dashboard design principles

  • One dashboard answers one question ("is service X healthy?", "what's the DB doing?"). Don't build a 60-panel everything-wall.
  • Top-down: SLO / RED summary row first (stat + thresholds), then supporting detail, then deep-dive rows collapsed by default.
  • Consistency: same layout/units/colours across service dashboards (templated), so people build muscle memory.
  • Time alignment: every panel shares the dashboard time range; use annotations for deploys/incidents so spikes have context.
  • Legends: name series ({{label}}); hide legends on dense panels; use table legend with min/max/last for comparison.
  • Colour: red = bad consistently; don't rely on colour alone; cap series count (topk) so the graph is readable.
  • Performance: fewer panels, sane refresh, $__rate_interval, recording rules for heavy queries, collapse+lazy-load detail rows.
  • Text panel at the top: what this dashboard is for, who owns it, links to runbook & related dashboards.
# top-down layout, encoded in gridPos (y grows downward, 24-col wide)
row  "Health"      y=0   : 4x Stat (SLO, error %, p95, RPS)  thresholds green/red
row  "Traffic"     y=8   : Time series req/s by route, errors by code
row  "Dependencies" y=16 (collapsed:true) : DB, cache, queue depth   # lazy-loaded
# every service dashboard uses this SAME shape (templated) -> muscle memory

Annotations

Event overlays on time axes: manual (region-select → "add annotation"), from a query (ALERTS, a deploy metric, a CI webhook writing to the Grafana annotations API), or built-in "Alerting" annotations. Tag them and filter by tag.

# CI writes a deploy marker via the annotations API
curl -XPOST $GRAFANA/api/annotations -H "Authorization: Bearer $SA_TOKEN" -d '{
  "dashboardUID": "api-overview",
  "time": '$(date +%s000)',
  "tags": ["deploy", "api"],
  "text": "deploy v2.4.1 ('$GIT_SHA')"
}'
# dashboard annotation query:  tags = "deploy"   -> vertical lines on every panel
Cheat Sheet
  • Explore = ad-hoc querying, split view (metrics + logs), query history; "Add to dashboard" to promote. Not for standing monitoring.
  • Cross-signal: trace→logs/trace→metrics (Tempo config), logs→trace (Loki derived fields), exemplars on latency graphs, data links, Correlations (instance-wide result→link rules).
  • One dashboard = one question. Top-down: SLO/RED summary → detail → collapsed deep-dive.
  • Consistency (templated layout/units/colours); annotate deploys/incidents; name series with {{label}}; red = bad everywhere; topk to bound series.
  • Performance: fewer panels, sane refresh, $__rate_interval, recording rules, lazy-loaded rows.
  • Header text panel: purpose, owner, runbook + related-dashboard links.
Q&A
When do you use Explore instead of a dashboard?
During investigation — when you're iterating on queries, don't yet know what you're looking for, and want to pivot between metrics and logs quickly. Dashboards are for known, repeated views you monitor; Explore is the scratchpad. You can promote a good Explore query to a dashboard panel with "Add to dashboard".
What are Correlations?
Instance-level rules that say "given results from this query/data source, offer a link that runs that query on another data source, substituting field values". They add cross-signal navigation everywhere those results appear (dashboards and Explore) without configuring data links on each panel.
How does clicking a log line take you to its trace?
The Loki data source is configured with a derived field: a regex that extracts the trace ID from each line and renders it as a link to a Tempo (or other tracing) data source. Grafana opens the trace by that ID.
What's a good structure for a service dashboard?
A header text panel (purpose/owner/runbook), then a summary row with SLO/RED stat panels (rate, errors, p50/p95/p99 latency, saturation) coloured by threshold, then supporting time series (by endpoint, by dependency), then collapsed deep-dive rows (per-pod, GC, connection pools). Everything shares the time range; deploys are annotated.
Why annotate deployments on dashboards?
So that when a metric changes you can immediately see whether a release, config change, or feature-flag flip coincided with it. Annotations turn "something changed at 14:03" into "the 14:03 deploy caused this".
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which Grafana view has no panels and is meant for ad-hoc queries?
Explore.
What overlays deploy events on a time series panel?
Annotations.
Roughly how many questions should one dashboard try to answer?
One.

Intermediate core

A team's "service overview" dashboard has 45 panels, takes 8 seconds to load, and nobody can find anything. How do you rework it?
Split by audience/question: an at-a-glance health dashboard (5–8 panels: availability/SLO, error rate, p95 latency, traffic, saturation, recent deploys annotation) that answers "is it OK?" in two seconds, and separate drill-down dashboards (per endpoint, dependencies, runtime/GC, infra) linked from it via data links carrying the time range and variables. On the overview, collapse any remaining detail into rows that lazy-load. Cut query cost: $__rate_interval, recording rules for the heavy aggregations, sane Max data points, raise the min refresh, remove auto-refresh below 30s. Standardise units and add a header text panel with owner + runbook. Templating ($service, $env) so it's one dashboard for the whole fleet, not 45 panels for one service. Measure load time again; target < 2s.
Set up one-click navigation from a latency spike on a Grafana graph to the exact traces and logs behind it.
(1) Exemplars: ensure the app/exporter emits exemplars on the latency histogram and Prometheus/Mimir stores them; enable "Exemplars" on the panel's Prometheus query and configure the Prometheus data source with an exemplar link to the Tempo data source. Now the graph shows dots you click to open the slow request's trace. (2) Trace → logs: in the Tempo data source, configure "Trace to logs" pointing at Loki, mapping span tags (pod, namespace) and using the span's time window, so from the trace you jump to the surrounding logs. (3) Logs → trace: Loki derived field regex for trace_id → back to Tempo, for the reverse hop. (4) Optionally a panel data link "Open logs for this series" building a Loki Explore URL from the series labels + ${__url_time_range}, and a Correlation so the same jump works from any dashboard. Result: spike → exemplar → trace → logs, all time-scoped, in three clicks.

Advanced deep

Design a dashboard system for a 300-microservice org so that during an incident an on-call engineer can go from "something's wrong" to root-cause signal in under a minute.
Layered, templated, and linked: (1) Fleet / triage dashboard — one screen: per-service SLO burn-rate heatmap or table (red = burning), global error rate, global latency, deploy annotations across the org, active alerts panel (ALERTS{alertstate="firing"}). Sorted/filtered to surface the worst offenders. Every row links to… (2) Service dashboard (single templated definition, $service/$env/$region) — RED summary, dependency health (calls out to DBs/queues/other services with their error/latency), saturation (CPU/mem/pool/queue depth), recent deploys/flags, and a "top endpoints by error" table. Data links from every panel to logs (Loki, same selectors), traces (Tempo), and the specific drill-down. (3) Drill-down dashboards per concern (endpoint detail, DB, cache, JVM/GC, k8s pod). (4) Cross-signal wiring everywhere: exemplars on latency, trace→logs, logs→trace, Correlations so the same jumps exist from any panel. (5) Consistency: all service dashboards are the same Jsonnet-generated layout, so muscle memory works on any service; SLO thresholds pulled from a per-service config. (6) Context: deploy/incident annotations auto-fed from CI and the incident tool via the annotations API; a header panel per dashboard with owner + runbook + Slack channel. (7) Performance: recording rules for every summary metric (burn rate, RED per service) so the fleet dashboard is cheap even across 300 services; lazy-loaded detail rows; short but not silly refresh. (8) Alerts link back: every alert annotation includes dashboardUID/panelId so the page notification deep-links straight to the relevant service dashboard at the right time. The on-call flow: page → deep link to the service dashboard at incident time → RED + dependency row shows which dependency or endpoint is bad → click through to its traces/logs → root-cause signal. The fleet dashboard is the fallback when the page is vague ("elevated errors"). All of it is code, reviewed, and identical everywhere.
Annotations are useful but your Grafana DB's annotation table has grown to tens of millions of rows and is slowing everything down. Explain the causes and the fix.
Causes: (1) Alerting writes annotations on every state change — with many multi-dimensional rules and flapping alerts, that's a firehose (each instance transition = a row, plus one per rule evaluation in some configs). (2) Query-driven annotations configured with wide time ranges re-query often but the stored ones from region-select and API pile up. (3) CI/deploy pipelines POSTing an annotation per service per deploy, times hundreds of services times many deploys a day. (4) No retention configured, so rows accumulate forever. (5) The table is in the same DB as dashboards/users, so its bloat and the index maintenance slow unrelated queries; large SELECTs for dashboards with many annotation queries scan a lot. Fix: (a) Set retention: [annotations.alerting] max_age, [annotations.api] max_age, [annotations.dashboard] max_age (e.g. 90d) and max_annotations_to_keep caps; Grafana's cleanup job then trims. (b) Reduce alert-generated annotations: fewer, better rules; longer for; fix flapping; consider disabling alert state-history annotations if you have a separate alert history store (Grafana can use Loki for alert state history instead of the DB). (c) Rate-limit / dedupe deploy annotations — one per deploy with a tag, not per service; or store deploy events as a metric/log and render as an annotation query instead of stored rows. (d) Move Grafana's DB to a properly sized managed Postgres/MySQL with tuned autovacuum; ensure the annotation table's indexes (on epoch, dashboard_id, tags) are healthy; archive old rows. (e) Prefer annotation queries (compute overlays from an existing metric/log source at render time) over writing millions of stored annotations. (f) Monitor the table size and add it to capacity planning. Long term, treat "events" (deploys, incidents) as first-class data in a store built for it and surface them via queries, keeping the Grafana annotation table small.

Splunk Architecture

Forwarders collect, indexers store and search, search heads coordinate — and clustering makes each tier resilient.

Notes

The processing tiers

ComponentRole
Universal Forwarder (UF)Tiny agent on source hosts. Reads files/events, minimal processing, forwards raw to indexers. No search, no UI.
Heavy Forwarder (HF)Full Splunk with parsing enabled: can do index-time transforms, filtering, routing, and act as a syslog/HEC collection point. Heavier footprint.
Indexer (indexing tier)Parses incoming data into events, writes them to indexes (on disk as buckets), and runs the search work over its own data.
Search Head (SH)Runs the UI and REST API, parses SPL, dispatches the search to indexers, merges their partial results, does the final transforming/reporting commands.
Cluster/Deployment managersNon-data control nodes: Cluster Manager (indexer cluster), Deployer (SH cluster app bundles), Deployment Server (pushes config to forwarders), License Manager, Monitoring Console.
# on a Universal Forwarder host: point it at the indexers, tail a log
# $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/system/local/outputs.conf
[tcpout:primary]
server = idx1:9997, idx2:9997, idx3:9997      # S2S; forwarder auto load-balances

# inputs.conf
[monitor:///var/log/app/*.log]
sourcetype = app:json
index = app_prod
# UF forwards raw -> an indexer runs the parsing pipeline + stores + searches it

Index-time vs search-time

  • Parsing pipeline (on the first "full" Splunk to touch the data — an HF, or the indexer if UF): line breaking, timestamp extraction, host/source/sourcetype assignment, index-time field extraction (rare), routing/filtering.
  • Indexing: events written into buckets; the only index-time index is time plus a keyword index of the raw text (for fast TERM lookup).
  • Search-time: field extraction, lookups, calculated fields, tags, event types — applied when you search, from knowledge objects. Flexible, changeable after the fact (schema-on-read).
# INDEX-TIME (props.conf on the HF/indexer): fixed at ingest, reindex to change
[app:json]
TIME_PREFIX  = \"ts\":\"
MAX_TIMESTAMP_LOOKAHEAD = 25
LINE_BREAKER = ([\r\n]+)\{        # one JSON object per event
SHOULD_LINEMERGE = false

# SEARCH-TIME: add a field TODAY, it applies to data ingested YEARS ago
... | rex "latency=(?\d+)"   # ad-hoc, no reindex

Buckets & the data lifecycle

Events age through bucket states: hot (open, being written) → warm (rolled, read-only, still on fast storage) → cold (older, often cheaper storage) → frozen (deleted, or archived out). Controlled per index by size and time (maxHotBuckets, maxWarmDBCount, frozenTimePeriodInSecs, volume limits). Searchable retention = hot+warm+cold.

# indexes.conf — per-index lifecycle
[app_prod]
homePath   = volume:primary/app_prod/db      # hot + warm (fast disk)
coldPath   = volume:cold/app_prod/colddb     # cold (cheap disk)
frozenTimePeriodInSecs = 7776000             # 90 days -> then frozen
maxTotalDataSizeMB     = 500000              # size cap also rolls to frozen
coldToFrozenDir        = /archive/app_prod   # set = archive; unset = DELETE on freeze

Clustering

  • Indexer cluster: peers replicate buckets per replication factor (RF, e.g. 3 copies) and search factor (SF, e.g. 2 searchable copies). The Cluster Manager tracks peers and orchestrates fix-ups when one fails. Multi-site clustering pins copies per site for DR.
  • Search head cluster: 3+ SHs share config, saved searches, and scheduled-search load via a captain; the Deployer pushes app bundles. (Old "SH pooling" is deprecated.)
  • Forwarders load-balance across indexers (auto LB by time or volume) — no LB appliance needed for the S2S protocol.
# indexer-cluster peer — server.conf
[clustering]
mode = slave
manager_uri = https://cm.corp:8089
replication_factor = 3      # RF: 3 copies of every bucket exist
search_factor = 2           # SF: 2 of them carry the index files (searchable)
# lose a peer -> Cluster Manager re-replicates to restore RF/SF from survivors

Getting data in — entry points

Forwarders (files, Windows event logs, scripted/modular inputs), HEC (HTTP Event Collector — token-authenticated JSON/raw over HTTPS, for apps and cloud services), syslog into an HF/UF, and add-ons (TAs) that package inputs + parsing for a given technology.

# HEC: token-authenticated JSON over HTTPS, ideal for apps/serverless
curl -k https://hec.corp:8088/services/collector/event \
  -H "Authorization: Splunk 3f8a1c9d-...-b2" \
  -d '{"event": {"msg": "login ok", "user": "leo"}, "sourcetype": "app:auth", "index": "app_prod"}'

# inputs.conf on the HEC receiver
[http://app-auth]
token = 3f8a1c9d-...-b2
index = app_prod

Splunk Cloud vs Enterprise

Cloud is Splunk-operated: you get SHs and indexers as a service, use the Universal Forwarder / HEC / cloud data managers to send in, and install vetted apps. On-prem Enterprise you run every tier yourself.

# Cloud: you only operate the edge (forwarders/HEC) + author knowledge objects
UF outputs.conf -> [tcpout] server = inputs.<stack>.splunkcloud.com:9997
                   useACK = true                 # Cloud requires indexer ACK + TLS
# no indexes.conf / server.conf clustering to manage; apps must be Cloud-vetted

# Enterprise: the same data path, but YOU run indexes.conf, clustering, upgrades, capacity
Cheat Sheet
  • UF: light agent, forwards raw. HF: full Splunk, parses/filters/routes at index time. Indexer: parses + stores (buckets) + searches its data. Search head: parses SPL, fans out to indexers, merges, runs transforming commands.
  • Control nodes (no data): Cluster Manager, Deployer (SH cluster), Deployment Server (forwarder config), License Manager, Monitoring Console.
  • Index-time: line break, timestamp, host/source/sourcetype, keyword index. Search-time: field extraction, lookups, calc fields, tags, eventtypes (schema-on-read).
  • Bucket lifecycle: hot → warm → cold → frozen (frozen = deleted/archived). Searchable = hot+warm+cold.
  • Indexer cluster: Replication Factor (copies) + Search Factor (searchable copies), managed by Cluster Manager; multi-site for DR.
  • SH cluster: 3+ members, captain, Deployer pushes bundles.
  • Ingest: forwarders (S2S, auto load-balanced), HEC (HTTP token), syslog via HF, TAs/add-ons.
Q&A
Universal Forwarder vs Heavy Forwarder?
The UF is a stripped-down agent: it collects and forwards raw data with almost no processing, small footprint, no UI or search. The HF is a full Splunk instance with the parsing pipeline enabled, so it can extract timestamps, filter/route/transform events at index time, and terminate HEC/syslog — at a much larger resource cost. Use UFs on endpoints; use HFs where you need pre-index processing or a collection tier.
What's the difference between index-time and search-time fields?
Index-time processing happens once as data is ingested (line breaking, timestamp, host/source/sourcetype, the keyword index) and is baked in. Search-time extraction (regex field extractions, lookups, calculated fields, tags) is applied every time you search, from knowledge objects, and can be added or changed later without re-indexing — Splunk's schema-on-read model.
Describe the bucket lifecycle.
New events go into a hot bucket (writable). When it hits size/time limits it rolls to warm (read-only, fast disk). Older warm buckets roll to cold (typically cheaper disk). When they pass the retention limit they roll to frozen — by default deleted, or copied to an archive path if configured. Searches cover hot, warm, and cold.
What do Replication Factor and Search Factor mean in an indexer cluster?
RF is how many copies of each bucket exist across peers (fault tolerance for the raw data). SF is how many of those copies also have the index files needed to be searched (fault tolerance for search availability). SF ≤ RF. RF=3/SF=2 means 3 data copies, 2 immediately searchable.
What is HEC?
The HTTP Event Collector: an endpoint on indexers/HFs that accepts events over HTTPS with a token, as JSON or raw text. Applications, serverless functions, and cloud services push directly to it without a forwarder.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which component runs the SPL search UI and merges results?
The search head.
Which bucket state is currently being written to?
Hot.
Can you add a new field extraction without re-indexing data?
Yes — search-time extractions are applied at query time (schema-on-read).

Intermediate core

You need to drop 80% of a noisy sourcetype (health-check lines) before it's indexed to save license. Where and how?
Filtering must happen on a full Splunk instance in the parsing pipeline — either a Heavy Forwarder in front of the indexers, or the indexers themselves (not a UF, which doesn't parse). Configure props.conf to route the sourcetype through a transform: in transforms.conf, a stanza with REGEX = health.?check, DEST_KEY = queue, FORMAT = nullQueue; reference it from props.conf [sourcetype] TRANSFORMS-drop = drop_healthchecks. Events matching the regex are sent to the null queue and never indexed, so they don't count against license or storage. Keep the regex tight and test with a sample so you don't discard real errors. If only a HF tier can be changed, do it there; if data goes UF→indexer directly, apply it on the indexers.
A forwarder is configured with 6 indexers but 90% of its data lands on one. What's wrong?
Auto load balancing on the forwarder switches target indexers on an interval or volume boundary (autoLBFrequency, autoLBVolume). Common causes of skew: (1) The forwarder sends one very large file / a single long-lived TCP stream that isn't broken at an event boundary, so it sticks to one indexer until the file ends — enable forceTimebasedAutoLB (older) or ensure EVENT_BREAKER/EVENT_BREAKER_ENABLE is set for that sourcetype so LB can switch mid-stream. (2) Some indexers are listed but unreachable / blocked by firewall, so it falls back to the reachable one. (3) useACK plus a slow indexer causing backpressure and re-pinning. (4) DNS resolving all names to one host. (5) Very low event volume so it just doesn't switch often. Check splunkd.log on the forwarder for connection errors, verify all 6 are reachable on 9997, set event breakers, and consider indexer discovery (via the Cluster Manager) so the list stays correct.

Advanced deep

Design the Splunk topology for 5 TB/day ingest, 200 concurrent users, 30-day searchable retention plus 1-year archive, across two data centres for DR.
Ingest sizing: rule of thumb ~100–250 GB/day/indexer for mixed search load; 5 TB/day → roughly 20–40 indexers depending on hardware and search concurrency — size to the higher end because 200 users is heavy. Use reference-spec indexers (many cores, lots of RAM, fast NVMe for hot/warm). Indexer cluster: multi-site cluster spanning DC-A and DC-B, Cluster Manager in DC-A with a standby. Set site replication factor like origin:2, site1:2, site2:1, total:3 and site search factor origin:1, total:2 so each site can search locally and survive losing the other. This roughly doubles storage — budget for it. Storage tiering: hot/warm on NVMe sized for a few days; cold on cheaper bulk disk sized for the full 30 days × replication; frozenTimePeriodInSecs = 30 days with a coldToFrozenScript that copies buckets to object storage / an archive volume for the 1-year retention (restorable via thaw). Search tier: a search head cluster of ~6–10 members (200 concurrent users, scheduled searches, dashboards) with a Deployer; put SHC members in both DCs or keep primary in DC-A with DR members in DC-B. Dedicated SHs (or a separate small SHC) for heavy scheduled/ES workloads so ad-hoc users aren't starved. Collection tier: Universal Forwarders everywhere; a layer of Heavy Forwarders (or the indexers) for syslog and HEC, load-balanced, with useACK for delivery guarantees; Deployment Server(s) to manage forwarder configs (or Deployment Server + serverclasses, scaled out if > a few thousand forwarders); indexer discovery so forwarders learn the peer list from the Cluster Manager. Control plane: separate License Manager, Monitoring Console, Cluster Manager, Deployer, Deployment Server — none co-located with data. Capacity headroom: plan for N+1 indexers per site, burst ingest 2–3×, and search concurrency limits tuned. DR test: regularly fail the Cluster Manager over and kill a site to confirm RF/SF math holds and searches still complete.
Explain end to end what happens to a single log line from the moment a Universal Forwarder reads it to when it appears in search results.
(1) Input: the UF's file input monitors the path; a tailing processor reads new bytes, tracks position in the fishbucket (a checkpoint DB) so it doesn't re-read on restart. It assigns preliminary source (path), host (from inputs.conf/host default), and sourcetype (explicit or by rule). The UF does not parse into events — it forwards the raw stream (optionally with an EVENT_BREAKER hint so downstream/LB can split it) over the encrypted Splunk-to-Splunk (S2S) protocol on 9997 to an indexer chosen by auto load balancing. (2) On the indexer — parsing pipeline: the data enters the parsing queue. Line breaking splits the stream into events using LINE_BREAKER/SHOULD_LINEMERGE/BREAK_ONLY_BEFORE for that sourcetype. Timestamp extraction finds the event time via TIME_PREFIX/TIME_FORMAT/MAX_TIMESTAMP_LOOKAHEAD (or falls back to current time / file modtime), converting to epoch using TZ. props/transforms run: any index-time TRANSFORMS (routing to another index, nullQueue drops, host overrides, index-time field creation, sedcmd masking). (3) Indexing pipeline: the event's raw text is compressed into the current hot bucket of the target index (journal.gz), and Splunk updates the bucket's time index (tsidx) and the lexicon (keyword/segment index of tokens in the raw text) so keyword and TERM() searches are fast. If the index is clustered, the indexer streams copies to RF-1 peers; SF peers also build tsidx. An entry lands in the metadata (Hosts.data, Sources.data, SourceTypes.data). (4) Searchable: as soon as the event is written and fsync'd it's searchable on that peer (near real-time, typically sub-second to a few seconds). (5) Search: a user runs SPL on a search head; the SH parses it, determines the time range and required indexes, and dispatches the "remote" portion (everything up to the first non-streamable command) to all relevant indexers. Each indexer searches its buckets — time index narrows to candidate buckets, the lexicon narrows to candidate events, then raw events are read and search-time knowledge objects apply: field extractions (EXTRACT/REPORT/automatic KV), field aliases, calculated fields (EVAL-), lookups, tags, eventtypes. Partial results stream back to the SH, which runs the "reduce"/transforming commands (stats, sort, dedup, etc.), applies final formatting, and renders. In a clustered index the SH only asks one searchable copy of each bucket (the primary) to avoid duplicates. Total: raw line → forwarded → parsed into an event with time+metadata → compressed into a hot bucket with tsidx+lexicon (replicated) → immediately searchable → SH map/reduce with schema-on-read fields at query time.

Getting Data In

Inputs decide what to collect; props.conf / transforms.conf decide how it's parsed.

Notes

The four "default fields" — get them right at ingest

  • index — the storage bucket + the main access-control boundary. Choose per data category (retention, RBAC).
  • sourcetype — the format of the data (access_combined, cisco:asa, json). Drives all parsing config. The single most important field to set correctly.
  • source — where it came from (file path, input name).
  • host — the originating machine.
# set all four at the input (inputs.conf); everything downstream keys off them
[monitor:///var/log/nginx/access.log]
index      = web_prod          # retention + who can search it
sourcetype = access_combined   # a KNOWN sourcetype -> parsing config already exists
# source   -> defaults to the file path
# host     -> defaults to the forwarder's hostname (override with host_segment / host =)

Input types

InputUse
monitor://Tail files & directories (whitelist/blacklist, recursive, crcSalt for rotated logs).
WinEventLog://, WMI, perfmonWindows logs & metrics.
tcp:// / udp://Network inputs (syslog). Prefer a syslog daemon → file → monitor, or Splunk Connect for Syslog (SC4S), over raw udp://514.
HECToken-auth HTTPS JSON/raw from apps & cloud. Per-token index/sourcetype, ack option.
Scripted / modular inputsPull from APIs (packaged by Technology Add-ons: AWS, o365, etc.).
HTTP/file via Ingest Actions / Edge Processor / Ingest ProcessorNewer routing/masking/filtering before indexing.
# file tail, handling rotation
[monitor:///var/log/app]
whitelist   = \.log$
blacklist   = \.gz$
crcSalt     = <SOURCE>            # treat rotated same-name files as distinct

# raw syslog: don't listen on udp://514 directly — use SC4S -> file -> monitor
[udp://514]
sourcetype  = syslog
no_appending_timestamp = true

Key props.conf settings (per sourcetype)

[my:sourcetype]
SHOULD_LINEMERGE   = false          # true only for multiline w/o a clear break
LINE_BREAKER       = ([\r\n]+)      # regex; capture group = the break, is discarded
TIME_PREFIX        = ^\[            # where the timestamp starts
TIME_FORMAT        = %Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%3N%z
MAX_TIMESTAMP_LOOKAHEAD = 32        # don't scan the whole line for a date
TZ                 = UTC            # if the source has no offset
TRUNCATE           = 10000          # max event length in bytes
EVENT_BREAKER_ENABLE = true         # let forwarder LB split the stream
EVENT_BREAKER      = ([\r\n]+)
  • Line breaking and timestamps are ~90% of "GDI" problems. Bad line breaking → events merged/split; bad timestamps → data "in the future" or all at ingest time.
  • SHOULD_LINEMERGE=false + a correct LINE_BREAKER is faster and more predictable than the merge heuristics.

Where config must live

Index-time settings (line breaking, timestamps, index-time transforms) take effect on the first full Splunk instance that parses the data — the indexers, or an HF if one is in the path (not a UF). Search-time settings live on the search heads. Ship them in Technology Add-ons (TAs) to the right tier (indexer cluster via Cluster Manager, SHC via Deployer, forwarders via Deployment Server).

TA-nginx/
  default/
    props.conf        # LINE_BREAKER, TIME_FORMAT   -> deploy to INDEXERS (+ any HF)
    transforms.conf    # nullQueue / routing         -> INDEXERS
    inputs.conf        # [monitor://...]             -> FORWARDERS (Deployment Server)
    fields.conf        # EXTRACT-*, lookups          -> SEARCH HEADS
# same app, three tiers: CM pushes to the indexer cluster, Deployer to the SHC

Index-time transforms (transforms.conf)

[drop_debug]
REGEX = \sDEBUG\s
DEST_KEY = queue
FORMAT = nullQueue          # discard before indexing (license saving)

[route_to_security]
REGEX = sshd|sudo
DEST_KEY = _MetaData:Index
FORMAT = security           # send matching events to a different index

[mask_ccn]
REGEX = (\d{4}-){3}(\d{4})
DEST_KEY = _raw
FORMAT = XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-$2  # SEDCMD/transform masking of sensitive data

Onboarding checklist

  1. Pick index (retention + RBAC) and sourcetype (reuse a standard one or a TA's).
  2. Get a sample; verify event breaking and timestamp in "Add Data" preview.
  3. Set TZ if no offset; set MAX_TIMESTAMP_LOOKAHEAD.
  4. Confirm volume & license impact; add nullQueue filters for noise.
  5. Deploy the TA to indexers/HFs (index-time) and SHs (search-time).
  6. Validate: event count, no "line too long" / "outside MAX_DAYS_AGO", fields extract.
# step 6 validation searches, run after onboarding
index=web_prod earliest=-15m | stats count by sourcetype, host     # arriving?
index=web_prod | eval lag=_indextime-_time | stats avg(lag) p95(lag) # timestamps sane?
index=_internal source=*splunkd.log log_level=WARN "web_prod"       # breaking/time warnings
| search "outside the acceptable time window" OR "line longer than"
Cheat Sheet
  • Set the four defaults right: index (retention/RBAC), sourcetype (format — drives parsing), source, host.
  • Inputs: monitor:// (files), WinEventLog://, tcp/udp:// (prefer SC4S for syslog), HEC (app/cloud), modular inputs (API pulls via TAs).
  • props.conf essentials: SHOULD_LINEMERGE=false, LINE_BREAKER, TIME_PREFIX, TIME_FORMAT, MAX_TIMESTAMP_LOOKAHEAD, TZ, TRUNCATE, EVENT_BREAKER.
  • Line breaking + timestamps cause most GDI issues.
  • Index-time config runs on the first full Splunk (indexers or HF, not UF); search-time config on search heads. Ship via TAs to the right tier.
  • transforms.conf: FORMAT=nullQueue to drop, DEST_KEY=_MetaData:Index to route, DEST_KEY=_raw / SEDCMD to mask.
Q&A
Why is sourcetype the most important field at ingest?
Because nearly all parsing configuration — line breaking, timestamp extraction, search-time field extractions, lookups, tags — is keyed on sourcetype. Get it wrong (or let Splunk guess and create mylog-too_small) and events break badly and no fields extract. Assign a deliberate, consistent sourcetype, ideally one a Technology Add-on already understands.
Where do line-breaking and timestamp settings take effect?
On the first full Splunk instance in the data path that runs the parsing pipeline — the indexers, or a Heavy Forwarder if there is one. A Universal Forwarder doesn't parse, so putting these settings only on a UF does nothing.
How do you stop a noisy sourcetype from consuming license?
Route it to nullQueue with an index-time transform: a transforms.conf stanza matching the unwanted events with DEST_KEY = queue and FORMAT = nullQueue, referenced from props.conf via TRANSFORMS-x. Dropped events are never indexed and don't count against license. Apply on the HF/indexer tier.
What's the preferred way to ingest syslog?
Not raw udp://514 on an indexer (lossy, single point, no buffering). Use a dedicated syslog receiver — Splunk Connect for Syslog (SC4S) or rsyslog/syslog-ng writing to files that a forwarder monitors — which handles bursts, load balancing, and per-device sourcetyping.
An onboarded sourcetype shows all events timestamped at the ingest time. What happened?
Splunk couldn't find/parse a timestamp in the events, so it fell back to the time it received them. Fix the props.conf: set TIME_PREFIX to anchor where the timestamp is, TIME_FORMAT to match it exactly (including sub-seconds and offset), and MAX_TIMESTAMP_LOOKAHEAD big enough to reach it; set TZ if there's no offset in the data.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which default field controls how data is parsed?
sourcetype.
Which input type uses a token over HTTPS?
HEC (HTTP Event Collector).
Can a Universal Forwarder apply LINE_BREAKER settings?
No — it doesn't run the parsing pipeline; those apply on an HF or the indexers.

Intermediate core

A rotated log (app.log → app.log.1) is being re-indexed in full every night. Why, and how do you fix it?
Splunk tracks read position per file using a CRC of the first ~256 bytes plus the path (the "fishbucket"). If the rotation renames the file, or the first bytes are identical across days (a fixed header/banner), Splunk either sees a "new" file (path changed) or fails to distinguish it and re-reads. Fixes: (1) Monitor with a wildcard that covers the rotated names (monitor:///var/log/app.log*) so the renamed file is recognised as the same data continuing, and set followTail=0. (2) Add crcSalt = <SOURCE> so the full path is part of the identity (helps when many files share a header) — but note this makes a genuine rename look new, so it's a trade-off. (3) Increase initCrcLength if the first 256 bytes are a common header. (4) Best: configure the app to rotate by copytruncate or ensure the active file keeps its name and only archives are renamed, and only monitor the active name. (5) Check for the file being rewritten from the top (some loggers do), which always causes re-read.
You must mask Social Security numbers before they hit disk, and also send auth events to a restricted security index. Show the config approach.
Both are index-time transforms, deployed to the HF/indexer tier. Masking — either SEDCMD in props.conf: SEDCMD-mask_ssn = s/\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}/XXX-XX-XXXX/g; or a transforms.conf stanza writing DEST_KEY = _raw with a FORMAT that reconstructs the line with the number removed. This changes _raw before indexing so the SSN is never stored (irreversible — test carefully). Routing — transforms.conf: [to_security] REGEX = (sshd|sudo|authentication failure) DEST_KEY = _MetaData:Index FORMAT = security; reference from props.conf: [linux_secure] TRANSFORMS-route = to_security. Order matters — list masking before routing in TRANSFORMS- if the routing regex shouldn't see the raw SSN. Then set RBAC so only the security team's role has srchIndexesAllowed including security. Validate with a sample through "Add Data" / a test index first.

Advanced deep

Design a data onboarding standard for an org onboarding ~5 new sourcetypes a week, covering naming, config packaging, testing, and license governance.
Naming: a controlled vocabulary — indexes by data domain + retention tier (net_fw_90d, os_linux_30d, app_payments_1y), sourcetypes vendor:product:format (palo:pan:traffic, myco:orders:json), reusing CIM-compliant sourcetypes from official TAs wherever one exists. No auto-generated sourcetypes (disable [sourcetype]::learned drift; set explicit sourcetypes on every input). Config packaging: every onboarding is a versioned Technology Add-on in Git — inputs.conf (forwarder-side, deployed via Deployment Server serverclasses), props.conf/transforms.conf split into an index-time TA (to indexer cluster via Cluster Manager, and to HFs) and a search-time TA (to SHC via Deployer). No config edited directly on servers. CI lints the .conf (btool-style checks, regex compiles, no overlapping stanzas) and runs on a schedule. Testing: a staging Splunk with a dedicated onboarding index; the requester provides a representative sample (ideally 24h incl. edge cases — multiline stack traces, DST boundary, max-length lines); reviewer verifies in "Add Data" preview: correct event breaking, timestamp (incl. TZ and sub-second), truncation not triggering, all expected fields extracting, CIM mapping if applicable, and volume/EPS estimate. A checklist PR template. License governance: estimate daily GB before approval; require a nullQueue plan for known noise (health checks, debug); tag each index with an owner and a monthly GB budget; a daily report of ingest by index/sourcetype/host vs budget, alerting on >20% overage or a new unexpected sourcetype; use the license pool warnings and, on Cloud, the ingest/entitlement dashboards. Workflow: request (form) → TA PR → CI + staging validation → review → merge → Deployment Server / Cluster Manager / Deployer push → post-onboard validation search (count > 0, no parsing errors in index=_internal) → hand back a saved search + dashboard link. This keeps 5/week sustainable without snowflake configs or license surprises.
Explain how Splunk determines an event's timestamp, every setting involved, and the failure modes when data spans time zones and DST.
Order of precedence per event: (1) If DATETIME_CONFIG = CURRENT, use ingest time (no parsing). If = NONE, no timestamp processing at all. Otherwise use the datetime config (default /etc/datetime.xml patterns) plus sourcetype overrides. (2) Splunk looks for the timestamp starting at TIME_PREFIX (a regex; scanning begins right after the match) — without it, Splunk scans from the start of the event. (3) It reads up to MAX_TIMESTAMP_LOOKAHEAD characters (default 128) looking for something matching TIME_FORMAT (strptime spec). If TIME_FORMAT is unset, it tries the datetime.xml pattern library. (4) Time zone resolution: if TIME_FORMAT includes %z/%Z and the data has an offset, that wins. Else the TZ attribute for that sourcetype/host/source (an IANA name like America/New_York) is used. Else the forwarder/indexer's system TZ is assumed (a classic bug source). Per-host TZ can be set with [host::<h>] TZ = .... (5) Sanity clamps: events older than MAX_DAYS_AGO (default 2000) or newer than MAX_DAYS_HENCE (default 2) are rejected/clamped; MAX_DIFF_SECS_AGO/MAX_DIFF_SECS_HENCE flag events whose time is wildly off from the surrounding stream. Failure modes: (a) No offset + wrong assumed TZ — a log in US Eastern parsed on a UTC indexer lands 4–5h off; dashboards and correlation searches silently mis-bucket. Fix: explicit TZ. (b) DST transitions — if TZ is a fixed offset (TZ = GMT-5) rather than a zone name, half the year is wrong; always use the IANA zone so DST is handled. The "fall back" hour where local time repeats can also mis-order events — source data with an explicit offset avoids this. (c) Ambiguous formats — 02/03/04 (D/M/Y vs M/D/Y) parsed by the generic patterns can flip; pin TIME_FORMAT.
