Multi-tenancy: one tenant per team (or per cluster-team), with per-tenant limits (max global series, ingestion rate, query concurrency, max samples per query) so one team can't starve others; per-tenant retention overrides; usage/chargeback dashboards. Agents route each namespace's metrics to the owning team's tenant via relabeling the tenant header. Query & rules: central query frontend (with results caching and query sharding) behind Grafana; the ruler component runs recording rules (RED per service, SLO burn) and alerting rules per tenant, sharded — agents don't evaluate rules. Recording rules keep dashboard/alert queries cheap despite the fleet size. Alerting: central Alertmanager (HA pair/cluster) with per-team routing; a dead-man's-switch heartbeat per cluster so a whole cluster's collection going dark is detected. Meta-monitoring: monitor the agents themselves (remote_write queue length, dropped samples, shard balance, scrape_duration, up), the ingesters, and the compactor lag — ideally from a small independent Prometheus so the monitoring of the monitoring doesn't share fate. Cardinality governance: per-tenant series budgets + alerts on growth, edge relabel drops, and the shared-client-library standards. Rollout: everything via the Prometheus Operator / Helm / GitOps so 8 clusters are identical and adding cluster #9 is a config change.
Explain remote_write end to end: batching, sharding, the WAL, retries/backpressure, ordering, and the failure modes you must monitor.
Path: as samples are appended to the local TSDB (or agent-mode WAL), a remote_write component tails the WAL (write-ahead log) — it reads newly-written series and samples from WAL segments. This decouples scraping from sending: the scrape just writes locally; remote_write catches up from the WAL. Sharding: samples are distributed across N in-memory shards (queues), hashed by series, each shard with its own sender goroutine. The number of shards auto-scales between min_shards and max_shards based on the backlog (samples pending in the WAL vs sent) and throughput — if it's falling behind, add shards; if caught up, reduce. Batching: each shard accumulates up to max_samples_per_send (or flushes after batch_send_deadline), Snappy-compresses a protobuf WriteRequest, and POSTs it to the endpoint. Retries/backpressure: on 5xx or network error the batch is retried with backoff (min_backoff..max_backoff); on 429 it also backs off. If the endpoint stays slow/down, shard queues fill and the component stops reading new WAL as fast — the WAL grows on disk (bounded by local retention; if the outage outlasts WAL retention, samples are lost, oldest first). It does not block scraping (scrapes still write locally) until disk fills. Ordering: within a series, samples are sent in timestamp order; the receiver (Mimir/Cortex/Thanos receive) generally requires monotonically increasing timestamps per series and rejects out-of-order (there is now optional out-of-order ingestion support with a window). Across series there's no ordering guarantee. Exactly-once isn't guaranteed — a retry after a partial success can resend a batch; receivers dedupe by (series, timestamp) so it's idempotent in practice. HA dedup: two Prometheis with external_labels: {__replica__: a|b, cluster: x} both send; the receiver's HA tracker picks one replica as leader per (cluster) and drops the other's samples, failing over if the leader goes quiet. Failure modes to monitor: prometheus_remote_storage_samples_pending / _samples_in_total vs _samples_out_total (growing backlog = falling behind); prometheus_remote_storage_shards vs _shards_max (pinned at max = under-provisioned or endpoint slow); prometheus_remote_storage_samples_failed_total and _retried_total (endpoint errors); prometheus_remote_storage_samples_dropped_total and prometheus_remote_storage_exemplars_dropped_total (data loss — page on this); prometheus_wal_watcher_current_segment vs the WAL's newest segment (watcher lag); local disk usage (WAL growth during an outage); prometheus_remote_storage_highest_timestamp_in_seconds minus prometheus_remote_storage_queue_highest_sent_timestamp_seconds (send latency / lag in seconds — the most human-readable "how far behind are we"); and receiver-side 4xx (bad data, out-of-order, limit exceeded) vs 5xx (receiver unhealthy). Tuning levers: max_shards, max_samples_per_send, capacity (per-shard queue), batch_send_deadline, WAL retention (headroom for outages), and receiver-side ingestion limits. The key operational alert is "remote_write lag > X minutes" or "dropped samples > 0", because that's where you silently lose data.

Distributed Tracing

Follow one request as a tree of timed spans across every service it touches.

Notes

The model

  • A trace = all the work done for one logical request, identified by a trace_id.
  • A span = one unit of work (an HTTP handler, a DB query, a function): span_id, parent_span_id, name, start/end time, status, plus attributes (key/values), events (timestamped logs on the span), and links (to related spans in other traces).
  • Spans form a tree (or DAG with links); the root span is the entry point. A waterfall view shows each span's start offset and duration.
  • Span kind: server, client, producer, consumer, internal — tells the UI how to connect them.
# manual span around a business operation (OTel, Go)
ctx, span := tracer.Start(ctx, "charge_card", trace.WithSpanKind(trace.SpanKindClient))
defer span.End()
span.SetAttributes(attribute.String("psp", "stripe"), attribute.Int("amount_cents", 4999))

resp, err := stripe.Charge(ctx, ...)      // ctx carries trace_id + this span_id
if err != nil {
    span.RecordError(err)                 // -> a span event with the stack
    span.SetStatus(codes.Error, "declined")
}
// waterfall: charge_card is a child of the HTTP handler span, sibling of db.query

Context propagation

  • The trace_id + current span_id + trace flags travel with the request across process boundaries in headers: W3C traceparent/tracestate (the standard), or legacy B3.
  • Each service extracts the incoming context, starts a child span, injects the context into outbound calls (HTTP, gRPC, and message queues via message headers/attributes).
  • Instrumentation: auto (agents/SDK hooks for common frameworks and clients) + manual spans for business-meaningful operations. OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for APIs, SDKs, and the wire format (OTLP).
  • A gap in propagation = a broken trace (orphan spans, a new trace starting mid-request).
# W3C header carried on EVERY hop (HTTP, gRPC metadata, queue message headers)
traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
#            ver  trace_id (16 bytes)              parent span_id      flags(sampled)

# extract on the way in, inject on the way out
incoming := propagation.TraceContext{}.Extract(ctx, headerCarrier(r.Header))
child, span := tracer.Start(incoming, "handler")
propagation.TraceContext{}.Inject(child, headerCarrier(outReq.Header))   # or msg.Headers
# forget the inject on a queue publish -> consumer starts a NEW trace -> broken

Sampling

Head-basedTail-based
Decision whenAt the root, before the request runs (e.g. keep 1%)After the whole trace completes, at a collector
Can select on outcome?No — doesn't know yet if it'll error / be slowYes — keep all errors, all slow traces, sample the rest
CostCheap, stateless, consistent if propagatedCollector must buffer all spans of a trace; memory + complexity
ConsistencyPropagate the decision so all services agreeCentral, so naturally consistent

Common: low head sampling as a floor + tail sampling to always keep errors and outliers. Keep trace_id in logs so you can find a trace even when the request wasn't sampled (then only its logs exist).

# OTel Collector: low head-sample floor + tail rules that always keep the interesting ones
processors:
  probabilistic_sampler: { sampling_percentage: 2 }     # floor, applied at ingest
  tail_sampling:
    decision_wait: 10s
    policies:
      - { name: errors,     type: status_code, status_code: { status_codes: [ERROR] } }
      - { name: slow,       type: latency,     latency: { threshold_ms: 800 } }
      - { name: sample_rest, type: probabilistic, probabilistic: { sampling_percentage: 5 } }

What tracing answers

  • Where did the latency go? Which span dominates; serial vs parallel calls; N+1 query patterns; retries; queue wait time.
  • Which hop failed? The erroring span and its status/attributes, plus its events (exception stack).
  • Service dependency map — derived from span parent/child + kind across many traces.
  • RED metrics from spans ("span metrics" / metrics generated by the collector) — rate/error/duration per service+operation without separate instrumentation.
# TraceQL: find the traces that matter
{ resource.service.name = "checkout" && status = error }
{ span.db.system = "postgres" && duration > 500ms }        # slow DB spans
{ } | by(resource.service.name) | count() > 30              # fan-out / N+1

# span metrics the collector generates (spanmetrics connector) -> RED for free
traces_spanmetrics_calls_total{service="checkout", span_name="POST /pay", status_code="STATUS_CODE_ERROR"}
traces_spanmetrics_latency_bucket{service="checkout", le="0.5"}

Correlation

  • Exemplars: a latency histogram bucket carries an example trace_id → click a spike on a graph, open a slow trace.
  • Trace ↔ logs: logs include trace_id/span_id; span → its logs, log line → its trace.
  • Trace → profiles: link a span to a CPU profile of that time window.
# 1. graph shows a p99 spike; exemplar on the bucket carries a trace_id
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by(le)(rate(http_req_seconds_bucket[5m])))   # exemplars ON

# 2. open that trace -> the db.query span is 900ms of a 1.1s request

# 3. from the span, jump to its logs by the shared id
{app="checkout"} | json | trace_id="4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736"

Pitfalls

  • Missing propagation through async/queues, thread pools, batching — the common cause of broken traces.
  • Too many tiny spans (overhead, noise) vs too few (no detail). Span the meaningful boundaries.
  • High-cardinality attributes are fine on spans, but don't turn them into metric labels downstream.
  • Clock skew between hosts makes child spans appear to start before their parent — UIs clamp; keep NTP tight.
  • Sampling math: if you compute rates from sampled traces, weight by the sampling rate.
# async: the span ends when you enqueue, not when the work runs -> propagate explicitly
msg.Headers["traceparent"] = inject(ctx)          // carry context onto the message
// consumer:
ctx = extract(msg.Headers)
_, span := tracer.Start(ctx, "process", trace.WithLinks(trace.LinkFromContext(ctx)))

# rate from 2%-sampled traces must be scaled back up
sum(rate(traces_spanmetrics_calls_total[5m])) / 0.02     # true call rate
Cheat Sheet
  • Trace (one trace_id) = tree of spans (span_id + parent_span_id, name, start/dur, status, attributes, events, links). Root = entry point; waterfall = timeline view.
  • Span kind: server / client / producer / consumer / internal.
  • Context propagation via W3C traceparent/tracestate headers (or B3); extract → child span → inject into outbound calls incl. queue messages. OpenTelemetry + OTLP is the standard.
  • Head sampling: decide at root before outcome known (cheap, propagate the decision). Tail sampling: decide at collector after trace completes — keep all errors + slow, sample the rest (needs buffering).
  • Answers: where latency went, which hop failed, dependency map, RED-from-spans (span metrics).
  • Correlate: exemplars (graph → trace), trace_id in logs (trace ↔ logs), trace → profile.
  • Pitfalls: broken propagation through async/queues/threadpools; span granularity; clock skew; weight rates by sample rate.
Q&A
What's the difference between a trace and a span?
A trace is the whole request — everything done to serve one logical operation, tied together by a trace_id. A span is one timed step within it (a handler, a DB call), with its own ID, a parent pointer, timing, status, and attributes. Spans form a tree; the trace is the tree.
How does trace context move between services?
Via propagation headers — the W3C traceparent (and tracestate) header carries the trace ID, the caller's span ID, and sampling flags. Each service reads the incoming header, creates a child span, and writes the header onto its outbound requests (including onto message-queue records for async work).
Head-based vs tail-based sampling?
Head-based decides whether to keep a trace at the very start, before the request runs, so it can't preferentially keep errors or slow traces — but it's cheap and stateless. Tail-based decides at a collector after all the trace's spans arrive, so it can keep 100% of errors and slow outliers and sample the boring ones — at the cost of buffering every trace's spans in memory until it decides.
What are exemplars and how do they help?
Exemplars attach an example trace_id (and its value) to a histogram bucket sample. On a latency graph, a spike's data point links directly to a trace that experienced that latency — one click from "p99 jumped" to "here's a slow request's full breakdown".
Why do child spans sometimes appear to start before their parent?
Clock skew — the child's host clock is slightly ahead of the parent's. Timestamps come from each host independently, so a few milliseconds of NTP drift can invert the apparent order. Trace UIs usually clamp children within the parent's bounds; keeping NTP tight minimises it.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What identifies all the spans belonging to one request?
A shared trace_id.
Which HTTP header is the W3C standard for trace context?
traceparent (with tracestate for vendor data).
Which sampling type can guarantee you keep every error trace?
Tail-based sampling.

Intermediate core

A trace for a slow request shows the root span at 900 ms but the child spans only sum to 200 ms. What does that tell you and what next?
700 ms of the root span is unaccounted — time spent in the entry service that isn't inside any child span. Possible causes: (1) work not instrumented (JSON serialisation, business logic, in-process computation, template rendering) — add manual spans around the suspect code sections. (2) Waiting on something not spanned: acquiring a connection from a pool, a mutex/lock, thread-pool queue time before the handler ran, GC pauses — instrument pool checkout and add runtime/GC metrics; check if the gap is at the very start (queueing/admission) or middle (lock) or end (response write / slow client). (3) A downstream call whose client isn't instrumented, so its span is missing entirely — check outbound calls and library instrumentation coverage. (4) Blocking on a synchronous call to an external system without a client span. Next steps: add spans/events at the boundaries of the unaccounted region, look at CPU profile for that window (trace→profile link), check GC and pool-wait metrics for the pod at that timestamp, and compare to a fast trace to localise where the gap opens.
Requests that go through your message queue produce two disconnected traces instead of one. Why, and how do you fix it?
Context isn't propagated across the queue. The producer finishes its trace when it publishes; the consumer starts a brand-new trace when it picks the message up, because the traceparent wasn't carried on the message. Fix: on publish, inject the current trace context into the message's headers/attributes (most brokers support per-message headers; OTel messaging instrumentation does this automatically for supported clients). On consume, extract that context and start the processing span as a child (span kind consumer, with a link to the producer span if the relationship is fan-out/batch rather than 1:1). For batch consumers that pull many messages at once, use span links (one processing span linking to N producer spans) rather than forcing a single parent. Also propagate through any intermediate thread pool / executor inside the consumer (context must be captured and restored around the async hand-off), which is the other common break point. After this, the producer→queue→consumer path shows as one trace (or linked traces) with the queue wait time visible as the gap between publish and receive.

Advanced deep

Design a tracing setup for a 100-service platform at 500k req/s on a budget: instrumentation, sampling, collection, storage, and how you keep it useful.
Instrumentation: OpenTelemetry everywhere — auto-instrumentation (SDK/agent) for HTTP/gRPC servers & clients, DB drivers, queue clients, caches; plus a thin house wrapper that adds standard resource attributes (service.name, service.version, deployment.environment, k8s.*) and a few manual spans around business-critical operations. W3C propagation; ensure context flows through thread pools, async runtimes, and message headers (the usual break points) — CI check that a canary request stays one trace end to end. Sampling: two-stage. (1) Head sampling at the root at a low floor (e.g. 1–5%), decision propagated so all services agree — this bounds the span volume every service emits. (2) Tail sampling at a layer of OTel Collectors (the "gateway" tier): buffer spans by trace for a few seconds, then keep 100% of traces with an error span, 100% over a latency threshold (per-service p99-ish), a small % of the rest, and boost specific services/routes during incidents via config. Use consistent-probability sampling so rate math is recoverable (weight by 1/p). Keep trace_id in every log line so unsampled requests are still debuggable via logs. Collection: agent Collector as a DaemonSet/sidecar (receives OTLP from local pods, batches, adds k8s attributes, memory_limiter) → gateway Collector deployment (does tail sampling, which needs all of a trace's spans on one instance, so route by trace_id hash with the loadbalancing exporter) → storage. This tier also generates span metrics (RED per service/operation) and a service graph, so you get dashboards/alerts without extra instrumentation. Storage: a trace backend built for it — Grafana Tempo (object storage, cheap, trace-ID lookup + TraceQL), or Jaeger with a scalable backend, or a vendor. Retention short (7–14 days — traces age out of usefulness fast); object storage keeps cost low; index only what you query by (trace_id, service, duration, a few attributes) — Tempo's model of "cheap storage, search via metrics/logs then jump by trace_id" fits a budget. Keeping it useful: wire correlation — exemplars on latency histograms → traces; trace↔logs via trace_id; trace→profiles. Standard per-service dashboard includes a "slow traces" and "error traces" panel (from tail-sampled data). Alert on span-metric RED, not raw traces. Watch the collectors themselves (queue length, refused spans, sampling decisions, memory). Govern span attributes (no PII, bounded keys). Document the sampling policy so people know "your request may not have a trace, but it has logs with the trace_id". Net: low head floor keeps emission cheap; tail sampling keeps the interesting traces; span metrics give always-on RED; cheap object storage + short retention keeps the bill bounded; correlation makes the kept traces findable.
Tail-based sampling sounds strictly better than head-based. Explain its real operational costs and failure modes, and when head sampling is still the right choice.
How tail sampling works: a collector must hold all spans of a trace in memory until the trace is "complete" (a timeout after the last span, since there's no explicit end signal), then run policies (error, latency, rate, attribute-match, composite) to decide keep/drop. Costs / failure modes: (1) Memory — proportional to (traces in flight) × (spans per trace) × (span size) over the decision window; a latency spike or a slow downstream means traces stay open longer → buffer grows exactly when you're busiest; OOM drops traces silently. You must cap with num_traces/memory limits, which then drop traces under load — losing data when you most want it. (2) Span routing constraint — all spans of a trace must reach the same collector instance for the decision, so you need a load-balancing exporter that hashes by trace_id in front of the tail-sampling tier. That tier can't autoscale freely (rebalancing splits traces across instances → partial traces → wrong decisions); scaling events cause transient data loss/misdecisions. (3) Late spans — a span arriving after the decision window (slow service, retry, long-running job, clock issues) is dropped or creates an orphan; long traces (streaming, batch, websockets) don't fit the model well. (4) Latency to storage — traces are delayed by the decision window (seconds), so "live" trace search lags. (5) Complexity & cost — a stateful, carefully-sized tier to run and monitor (its own queue/refused/decision metrics), plus the compute to evaluate policies on every trace. (6) Consistency across a fleet — if some traces cross regions/clusters with separate collector pools, no single instance sees the whole trace; you either accept per-segment decisions or ship all spans to one global tier (bandwidth). (7) Rate math — non-probabilistic keep rules make "how many requests errored" from trace data non-trivial; you still need span-metrics for accurate RED. When head sampling is right: (a) very high volume where the tail-sampling buffer/compute cost is prohibitive — a low head rate is stateless and cheap and scales linearly. (b) When you primarily use traces for aggregate latency analysis / dependency mapping rather than catching individual rare errors (span-metrics + exemplars cover the "find a slow one" case). (c) Multi-region/multi-cluster where assembling whole traces centrally is too expensive. (d) Simplicity/reliability priorities — head sampling has no stateful tier to fail. (e) When errors are already well-covered by logs (with trace_id) and metrics, so you don't strictly need every error trace. Common pragmatic answer: both — a low head-sampling floor for baseline coverage and cheap scaling, plus a modest tail-sampling tier tuned to keep errors and slow outliers, sized and capped so that under extreme load it degrades to roughly head-sampling behaviour rather than falling over.

Incidents, Postmortems & Alert Fatigue

Respond in a structured way, learn without blame, and keep the pager survivable.

Notes

Incident response structure

  • Severity levels (SEV1–4 / P1–P4): defined by user impact and scope, not by how stressed anyone is. SEV1 = major outage / data loss / security; lower sevs = degraded / partial / single-tenant.
  • Roles: Incident Commander (coordinates, decides, doesn't fix), Ops/Responders (investigate & mitigate), Communications (stakeholders, status page), Scribe (timeline). One person can wear several hats on a small incident; separate them as it grows.
  • Mitigate before diagnose: stop the bleeding (roll back, fail over, disable the feature, scale, shed load) first; root cause can wait.
  • Comms cadence: regular updates even if "still investigating"; internal channel + external status page; declare start and all-clear explicitly.
  • Standard tooling: a declared incident opens a channel/bridge, a doc/timeline, and a tracking ticket automatically.
# /incident declare  -> automation spins up the scaffold
SEV2  checkout latency  IC=@leo  comms=@sara  scribe=@raj
  #inc-2026-08-29-checkout   (bridge)   doc: timeline.md   ticket: INC-482
  status page: "Investigating elevated checkout errors"   (update every 15m)

# order of operations
1. mitigate:  roll back deploy v2.4.1        <- stop the bleeding first
2. confirm:   error ratio back under 1%
3. THEN diagnose root cause
4. all-clear declared explicitly (not "seems fine now")

Key metrics

MetricMeaning
MTTDMean time to detect — incident start → someone/something notices. Improved by better symptom alerting & synthetics.
MTTAMean time to acknowledge — alert → a human owns it. Improved by routing/escalation.
MTTRMean time to recover/repair/resolve/mitigate (define which!). Improved by runbooks, safe rollbacks, practice.
MTBFMean time between failures — reliability of the system over time.

Time to mitigate (user impact ends) usually matters more than time to full resolution.

# one incident's timeline, in epoch terms
t0  09:02  bad deploy rolled out            <- incident START (impact begins)
t1  09:14  page fires                       MTTD  = 12 min
t2  09:16  on-call acks                     MTTA  = 2 min  (from page)
t3  09:23  rollback complete, errors normal MTT-mitigate = 21 min (from t0)  <- the one that matters
t4  11:40  faulty query fixed + deployed    MTTR (full) = 2h 38m

# track the distribution, not just the mean
histogram_quantile(0.9, sum by(le)(rate(incident_mitigate_seconds_bucket[90d])))

Blameless postmortems

  • Blameless: assume everyone acted reasonably with the information and tools they had. Ask "how did the system/process allow this?", not "who broke it". People must be safe to be honest, or you lose the facts.
  • Contents: summary & impact (users, duration, $ / SLO budget), a factual timeline (detection, key decisions, mitigation, resolution), root cause(s) and contributing factors, what went well / poorly / got lucky, and action items (each with an owner, a due date, and a priority; tracked to done).
  • Not just "the" root cause: complex failures have multiple contributing factors (a latent bug + a config change + a missing alert + a slow rollback). Use techniques like the 5 Whys carefully (it can tunnel on one chain) or a contributing-factors / causal-tree analysis.
  • Trigger criteria: every SEV1/2, any customer-visible outage, any near-miss worth learning from — agreed in advance, not discretionary after the fact.
  • Action items should reduce likelihood (fix the bug, add a guardrail), impact (graceful degradation, faster rollback), or detection (add the missing alert). Avoid "be more careful" items.
# postmortem skeleton (blameless)
## Impact:   42 min, ~18k failed checkouts, 31% of 30d error budget spent
## Timeline: factual, timestamped (see Key metrics)
## Contributing factors (NOT one root cause):
   - latent N+1 query, dormant for months
   - deploy skipped the staging soak step
   - no alert on DB connection-pool saturation
   - rollback took 9 min (manual steps)
## Action items (owner / due / priority):
   - [ ] add pool-saturation alert            @raj  2026-09-05  P1  (detection)
   - [ ] one-command rollback                 @leo  2026-09-12  P1  (impact)
   - [ ] fix the N+1                           @sara 2026-09-08  P2  (likelihood)
# NOT: "engineers should review queries more carefully"

Alert fatigue

  • Definition: so many low-value alerts that responders desensitise, delay, or ignore — and then miss the real one. It's a reliability risk, not just a morale issue.
  • Signals: high pages/shift, low actionability rate, routine silencing, alerts nobody owns, "we always get that one at night".
  • Fixes: symptom/SLO-based alerting; multi-window burn rate; for: durations; grouping & inhibition; delete never-actioned alerts; require owner + runbook for every alert; a weekly alert review that tunes or deletes; track pages/shift with a target.
  • On-call health: rotations large enough that a normal week is quiet; compensation; clean handoffs with an on-call log; a "you may fix noisy alerts on shift" mandate.
# weekly alert-review queries
topk(10, sum by (alertname) (increase(alertmanager_alerts_received_total[7d])))  # noisiest
# actionability per alert (needs a "did a human act?" signal, e.g. incident linkage)
sum by (alertname)(increase(page_led_to_action_total[30d]))
  / sum by (alertname)(increase(pages_total[30d]))
# rows near 0 -> tune the threshold, add for:, or DELETE the alert

Operational review loop

Weekly/biweekly: review incidents, page volume & actionability, action-item burn-down, SLO status, and recurring toil. Feeds prioritisation — reliability work competes with features via the error-budget policy.

# the weekly review dashboard, as queries
incidents_last_7d           = count(incident_start_timestamp > time() - 7*86400)
action_items_overdue        = count(action_item_due < time() and action_item_state != "done")
pages_per_shift_p90         = quantile_over_time(0.9, pages_per_shift[8w])
slo_budget_remaining        = 1 - (1 - sli:avail:ratio_rate30d) / (1 - 0.999)
# budget_remaining < 0.25  -> next sprint prioritises reliability items over features
Cheat Sheet
  • Severity by user impact/scope, not stress. Roles: Incident Commander (coordinates, doesn't fix), Responders, Comms, Scribe.
  • Mitigate before diagnose — roll back / fail over / disable feature / shed load first.
  • Regular comms cadence (internal + status page); explicit start & all-clear.
  • MTTD detect, MTTA acknowledge, MTTR recover (define it), MTBF between failures. Time-to-mitigate > time-to-full-resolution.
  • Blameless postmortem: how did the system allow this, not who. Summary+impact, factual timeline, contributing factors (not one root cause), action items with owner/date/priority tracked to done.
  • Trigger postmortems by pre-agreed criteria (every SEV1/2, customer-visible outage, notable near-miss).
  • Action items reduce likelihood / impact / detection — never "be more careful".
  • Alert fatigue = ignored pagers = missed incidents. Fix with symptom alerting, burn-rate, grouping, deletion, weekly review, quiet rotations.
Q&A
What does the Incident Commander do?
Coordinates the response — tracks what's known, assigns investigation/mitigation tasks, makes or brokers decisions (roll back? fail over? escalate?), manages comms cadence, and keeps the incident moving. The IC explicitly does not dig into the fix themselves; that's the responders' job. Separating coordination from hands-on-keyboard is what keeps a big incident from descending into chaos.
Why mitigate before diagnosing root cause?
Users are hurting now and the error budget is burning. A rollback, failover, feature-flag disable, or capacity bump often stops the impact in minutes, while root-causing can take hours. You buy time to investigate calmly. Diagnose fully afterward in the postmortem.
What makes a postmortem "blameless"?
It starts from the assumption that everyone involved made reasonable decisions given the information, time pressure, and tools they had, and it focuses on the systemic and process factors that allowed a mistake to become an incident — missing guardrails, confusing UIs, inadequate testing, slow rollback, absent alerts. Naming and blaming an individual destroys the psychological safety needed for people to report what actually happened, so you lose the ability to learn.
MTTR is ambiguous — why?
The "R" is used for repair, recovery, resolve, respond, and restore, and teams measure to different endpoints: end of user impact (mitigation), full service restoration, or closure of all follow-up. Time-to-mitigate is usually the number that matters to users. Always define which endpoint you mean before comparing MTTR across teams or over time.
Why is alert fatigue a reliability problem, not just a morale problem?
When most pages are non-actionable, responders learn to delay, batch, or ignore them — so when a genuine incident pages, it's acknowledged late or missed entirely, increasing MTTD/MTTA and thus impact. Noisy alerting directly degrades your ability to respond, on top of burning out the on-call.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Should the Incident Commander be the one fixing the problem?
No — the IC coordinates; responders investigate and mitigate.
What does MTTD measure?
Mean time to detect — from incident start to someone/something noticing.
What must every postmortem action item have?
An owner, a due date, and a priority — and it must be tracked to completion.

Intermediate core

A deploy at 14:00 caused a 40-minute partial outage. Sketch the postmortem's structure and two good vs two bad action items.
Structure: (1) Summary & impact: ~18% of checkout requests failed for 40 min (14:03–14:43), ~X orders lost, ~35% of the monthly error budget consumed, one SEV2. (2) Timeline (facts + timestamps): 14:00 deploy of vN; 14:03 error rate alert fires (fast-burn); 14:06 on-call acks; 14:09 IC declared, channel opened; 14:15 suspicion on the deploy; 14:22 rollback started; 14:31 rollback complete but caches still poisoned; 14:43 error rate normal; 14:50 all-clear. (3) Contributing factors: the bug (a null-handling regression on a code path only hit for guest checkout); it passed CI because tests lacked a guest-checkout case; canary was 5% for 2 min — too small/short to catch an 18%-of-a-subset failure; rollback took 9 min because it required a manual approval and a full redeploy; a poisoned cache extended impact 12 min past rollback. (4) What went well / poorly / lucky: alert & ack fast (good); rollback slow and cache handling unclear (poorly); lucky it was mid-afternoon with full staffing. (5) Action items. Good AIs: "Add guest-checkout path to the pre-merge integration suite" (owner, 1 wk, high) — reduces likelihood; "Make rollback one-click, no approval, target < 3 min; add a game-day to verify" (owner, 3 wks, high) — reduces impact; "Increase canary to 10% for 15 min with automatic error-rate abort" (owner, 2 wks, high) — reduces impact/detection; "Add cache-invalidation step to the rollback runbook and automate it" (owner, 1 wk, med). Bad AIs: "Engineers should review deploys more carefully" (not actionable, blames people); "Be more cautious with canaries" (vague, no owner/mechanism); "Add an alert for this specific null error" (over-fits the last incident instead of fixing the class); "Freeze deploys on Fridays" (cargo-cult, doesn't address the cause).
Leadership wants to track MTTR as a KPI and reward teams for lowering it. What are the risks and how do you set it up well?
Risks / gaming: (1) Definition drift — teams measure to the earliest defensible endpoint (mitigation, or even "alert cleared") to make the number small. (2) Under-declaring incidents — if it's not declared, it doesn't count; small outages get handled quietly and lessons are lost. (3) Severity deflation — classify SEV2s as SEV3 to keep them out of the tracked pool. (4) Discouraging thorough diagnosis — "mitigate and move on" without root cause to keep the clock short, so the same incident recurs. (5) Averaging hides the tail — a few very long incidents matter more than the mean; one team with rare-but-severe outages looks "better" than one with frequent minor ones. (6) It's a lagging, low-frequency metric — noisy quarter to quarter, easy to over-interpret. Doing it well: define endpoints precisely and publish them (time-to-detect, time-to-mitigate = user impact ends, time-to-resolve = service fully restored, time-to-close = action items done) and report all of them, not one blended MTTR. Use the distribution (median and p90), not just the mean, and pair with frequency (incident count / MTBF) and impact (user-minutes, budget burned) so a team can't win by hiding incidents. Make declaration criteria objective and audited. Treat the numbers as inputs to a conversation ("MTTM went up — why? rollback got slower?"), not a leaderboard with bonuses attached — rewarding the raw number is what drives the gaming. Complement with process metrics you actually want to improve: rollback time, canary coverage, action-item completion rate, alert actionability, and postmortem-on-time rate.

Advanced deep

Design an incident-management and learning program for a 300-engineer org: declaration, roles, comms, postmortems, action tracking, and how you keep it from becoming bureaucracy.
Declaration: anyone can declare; a single command (/incident) spins up a dedicated channel, a video bridge, an incident doc from a template, a tracking ticket, and pages the on-call IC pool. Objective severity rubric (user impact × scope × duration/uncertainty) posted in the channel; err toward declaring — a quick "actually fine, resolving" is cheap, a missed incident is not. Roles: a trained, rostered Incident Commander rotation separate from service on-call (so the IC isn't also the fixer); for SEV1 also assign Comms and Scribe; SEV3/4 can run with just the service on-call. IC training is a short course + shadowing. The IC runs the loop: assess → assign → decide (mitigate first) → communicate → repeat. Comms: internal updates on a fixed cadence (e.g. every 30 min for SEV1, or on state change) even if "no change"; external status page owned by Comms with pre-approved templates so legal/support don't gate each word; explicit "incident declared" and "resolved" markers; a stakeholder list per service. Postmortems: mandatory and pre-triggered for every SEV1/2 and any customer-visible outage; optional-but-encouraged for near-misses and SEV3s with a lesson. Blameless by policy and by facilitation (a trained facilitator for SEV1s, not the team that owns the service). Standard template: impact, timeline, contributing factors (plural), what went well/poorly/lucky, action items. Draft within 3 business days; review meeting within ~1 week, open to anyone, focused on systemic factors. Publish org-wide and searchable — other teams learn. Action tracking: every AI is a real ticket with owner, priority, and due date, linked from the postmortem; a dashboard tracks open incident AIs per team and their age; SEV1 AIs get a committed timeline and show up in the ops review; stale high-priority AIs escalate. Tie funding to it — the error-budget policy and the ops review are where reliability work gets prioritised against features. Anti-bureaucracy: keep the template short; SEV3/4 use a lightweight one-pager; automate everything mechanical (channel/doc/ticket creation, timeline capture from the channel, status-page prompts); don't require postmortems for trivial self-resolved blips; time-box the review meeting; measure the program by outcomes (repeat-incident rate, AI completion rate, MTTD/MTTM trend, on-call page load) not by paperwork volume; and periodically prune process steps nobody finds valuable. Feedback loop: a monthly reliability review aggregates incidents, page volume/actionability, AI burn-down, SLO status, and recurring toil into a prioritised list; themes (e.g. "deploys cause 40% of incidents") become funded initiatives. The goal is fast, calm response + honest learning + tracked follow-through, with the ceremony scaled to severity.
"Root cause" is a contested idea in incident analysis. Explain the critique, and what a mature postmortem practice does instead.
The critique (from resilience engineering / safety science — Woods, Cook, Dekker, Allspaw): (1) Complex systems fail in complex ways. A real incident is almost never one cause; it's a confluence — a latent bug that existed for months, plus a config change, plus a load spike, plus an alert that was missing, plus a rollback that was slow, plus the one engineer who knew the system being on holiday. Picking "the" root cause is choosing where to stop looking, and that choice is political and hindsight-biased. (2) Hindsight bias. After the fact, the path to failure looks obvious and the operators' "wrong" decisions look negligent. But they were acting on the information available then, under time pressure, with normal-looking signals. "They should have noticed X" ignores that X was one of fifty things and only looks salient now. (3) Counterfactual reasoning is a trap. "If only they had checked the dashboard" — you can always construct a counterfactual that would have prevented it; it doesn't tell you how to build a more robust system. (4) Human error as a cause is a dead end. "Operator error" is a starting point for investigation, not a conclusion — ask why the action made sense to them and why the system permitted it to cause harm. (5) Focusing on the failure ignores normal work. The same actions that "caused" this incident are how work gets done successfully every day; the system usually adapts around latent problems — understanding that adaptive capacity matters as much as the failure. What mature practice does instead: (a) Contributing factors, plural — enumerate the conditions that had to co-occur, technical and organisational, without ranking one as "the" cause. Tools: causal/contributing-factor trees, timelines annotated with "what did people know and believe at each point", and explicitly separating triggering event from the systemic conditions. (b) Second stories — for every "human error", the "second story" of why that was a reasonable action in context (bad tooling, misleading signal, unclear ownership, production pressure). (c) Multiple perspectives — interview the responders about their experience; the goal is to understand how the incident looked from inside, not to grade decisions. (d) Look at what went right — how was it detected, what made mitigation possible, where did the system or people successfully adapt; invest in those. (e) Action items across the three levers — reduce likelihood (fix bugs, add guardrails), reduce impact (graceful degradation, fast safe rollback, blast-radius limits), reduce detection time (the missing alert) — and also strengthen adaptive capacity (runbooks, game days, cross-training, better observability for the unknown-unknowns). (f) Blameless facilitation so the real narrative surfaces. (g) Accept that you're reducing risk, not eliminating a cause — the system will fail again differently, and the practice is continuous learning, not a search for the one fix. Some orgs rename the section "contributing factors" or "analysis" and ban the phrase "root cause" precisely to break the single-cause habit.

Issues, Types, Fields & Screens

Everything in Jira is an issue — and what an issue looks like is controlled by three layered schemes.

Notes

The issue is the atom

  • Every work item — story, bug, task, epic, sub-task, incident, change — is an issue with a key (PROJ-123), a type, a status, and a set of fields.
  • An issue belongs to exactly one project; its behaviour is governed by that project's schemes.
# the issue is the unit the REST API works in
GET /rest/api/3/issue/PROJ-123
{
  "key": "PROJ-123",
  "fields": {
    "project":   { "key": "PROJ" },        // exactly one
    "issuetype": { "name": "Story" },
    "status":    { "name": "In Progress" },
    "summary":   "Add fuzzy search",
    "customfield_10016": 5                  // Story Points (custom field id)
  }
}

Issue types

  • Standard types: Story, Task, Bug, plus Epic (a parent that groups stories). Sub-task is a special child type — always has a parent, can't exist alone, doesn't appear on the backlog independently.
  • The issue type scheme defines which types a project can use; the issue type screen scheme maps each type to the screens it shows.
  • Hierarchy levels (base): Sub-task < Standard (Story/Task/Bug) < Epic. Higher levels (Initiative…) need Advanced Roadmaps / Jira Premium.
# create a Story...
POST /rest/api/3/issue
{ "fields": { "project": {"key":"PROJ"}, "issuetype": {"name":"Story"},
              "summary": "Checkout revamp" } }
# -> { "key": "PROJ-140" }

# ...then a Sub-task MUST reference a parent
POST /rest/api/3/issue
{ "fields": { "project": {"key":"PROJ"}, "issuetype": {"name":"Sub-task"},
              "parent": {"key":"PROJ-140"}, "summary": "Wire the API" } }
# no parent -> 400 "parent is required"

Fields

CategoryExamples
System fieldsSummary, Description, Assignee, Reporter, Priority, Labels, Components, Fix Version/s, Affects Version/s, Due date, Environment.
Custom fieldsStory Points, Sprint, Epic Link (older) / Parent, Team, Acceptance Criteria, Severity, plus anything you add (text, select, user picker, cascading, number, date).
  • Components — project-scoped sub-parts (e.g. "API", "Billing"); can have a default assignee. Labels — free-form, global, no config.
  • Versions — project-scoped release markers; Fix Version = "shipped/planned in", Affects Version = "bug found in".
  • Custom fields are global objects — adding many, especially with unrestricted contexts, slows indexing and clutters every project. Reuse and scope with field contexts (per project / issue type).
# custom fields are referenced by id, not name
GET /rest/api/3/field
[ { "id": "customfield_10016", "name": "Story Points", "schema": {"type":"number"} },
  { "id": "customfield_10020", "name": "Sprint",       "schema": {"type":"array"} } ]

# scope one field to just two projects + issue type (a "context")
PUT /rest/api/3/field/customfield_10050/context/10001
{ "projectIds": ["10000","10004"], "issueTypeIds": ["10002"] }
# Fix Version vs Affects Version:  "fixVersions" = ships in,  "versions" = found in

Screens

  • A screen is an ordered list of fields. Three uses, wired by the screen scheme + issue type screen screen scheme: the Create screen, the Edit screen, the View screen, and additionally screens attached to workflow transitions (e.g. a "Resolve" screen that asks for Resolution + comment).
  • A field that isn't on any screen for an issue type is effectively hidden (still exists, still settable via API/automation).
  • Field configuration (scheme) controls per-field: required/optional, hidden/visible, description, default value, and renderer (wiki vs plain).
# the wiring: type -> screen scheme -> screen(s)
Issue Type Screen Scheme "PROJ"
  Bug   -> Screen Scheme "Bug SS"   -> Create: "Bug Create Screen"
                                       Edit/View: "Bug Screen"
  Story -> Screen Scheme "Default"  -> "Default Screen"
Workflow transition "Resolve Issue" -> Screen "Resolution Screen" (Resolution + comment)

# a field not on ANY screen for that type is still settable by API/automation,
# just invisible in the UI:
POST /rest/api/3/issue/PROJ-123  { "fields": { "customfield_10099": "set anyway" } }

Company- vs team-managed

  • Company-managed (classic): schemes are shared across projects, changed by Jira admins — consistency and scale, more governance.
  • Team-managed (next-gen): each project owns its own types/fields/workflow, configured by the project admin — fast and independent, but no cross-project scheme reuse and some features differ.
GET /rest/api/3/project/PROJ
{ "style": "classic" }     // company-managed: shares schemes, Jira-admin governed
{ "style": "next-gen" }    // team-managed:   own workflow/fields, project-admin owned

# consequence: a company-managed workflow edit propagates to every project on that
# scheme; a team-managed one changes only that project. Custom fields in team-managed
# projects are project-locked and don't appear in other projects' JQL/fields.
Cheat Sheet
  • Everything is an issue (PROJ-123): one project, a type, a status, fields.
  • Types: Story/Task/Bug (standard), Epic (parent), Sub-task (always has a parent, not on backlog alone). Allowed types = issue type scheme.
  • Fields: system (Summary, Assignee, Priority, Components, Fix Version…) + custom (Story Points, Sprint, Parent…). Custom fields are global — scope with contexts, don't over-create.
  • Components = project sub-parts (default assignee possible). Labels = global free-form. Fix Version = ships in; Affects Version = found in.
  • Screen = field list for Create / Edit / View / a transition. Not on a screen → hidden in UI. Field configuration sets required/hidden/default/renderer.
  • Company-managed = shared schemes, admin-governed. Team-managed = project owns its own config.
Q&A
What's special about a sub-task?
It's a child issue type that must have a parent, can't exist on its own, and doesn't appear independently on the backlog or as a standalone board card (it shows under its parent). It's for breaking one story into execution steps; it's not a way to model a real hierarchy of deliverables.
Difference between a Component and a Label?
Components are defined per project (an admin creates "API", "Frontend"…), can carry a default assignee and a component lead, and are structured. Labels are global, free-form text anyone can add, with no configuration — convenient but prone to typos and sprawl.
Fix Version vs Affects Version?
Affects Version records which release(s) a bug was found in; Fix Version records which release the work is planned for or was delivered in. Release reports and the "Releases" page are driven by Fix Version.
Why are unnecessary custom fields discouraged?
Custom fields are global objects. Each one adds to the Lucene index, appears in field pickers everywhere, and (with an unrestricted context) shows on every project's screens and JQL. Thousands of custom fields measurably slow indexing, search, and page loads. Reuse existing fields and restrict contexts to the projects/issue types that need them.
If a field isn't on the Edit screen, can it still be changed?
Yes — the field still exists and can be set by the REST API, automation rules, CSV import, or a workflow transition screen. It's just not editable in the normal issue UI. "Hidden" via field configuration is a stronger hide but still not a security control.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What controls which issue types a project can use?
The issue type scheme.
Which version field drives the Releases page?
Fix Version/s.
What is a screen, in Jira terms?
An ordered list of fields shown for a particular operation (Create, Edit, View, or a workflow transition).

Intermediate core

A team wants "Severity" required on the Create screen for Bugs only, not for other types, in one project only. Walk through the config.
(1) Create a custom field Severity (select list) if it doesn't exist; give it a context scoped to this project and issue type = Bug, with the option values. (2) Add Severity to the Create screen used by Bugs in this project — find the project's issue type screen scheme, see which screen scheme maps to Bug, and add the field to that screen scheme's Create screen (you may need a Bug-specific screen scheme so other types aren't affected). (3) In the project's field configuration scheme, find the field configuration applied to Bug, and mark Severity required there (create a Bug-specific field configuration if the current one is shared with other types). (4) Because contexts and field configurations are per project/issue type, other projects and other types are untouched. Team-managed projects skip most of this — you'd just add the field to the Bug type in that project's settings and mark it required. Test by creating a Bug (blocked without Severity) and a Story (no Severity field).
What breaks when you move an issue from a company-managed project to a team-managed one (or vice versa)?
Cross-type mismatches: the target project may not have the same issue type (mapped to a fallback), the same statuses (the move wizard forces a status mapping), or the same custom fields. Team-managed projects have their own field and status definitions, so a "Story Points" value from the company-managed field won't land in the team-managed project's separate Story Points field unless mapped — often data is dropped. Sprint history and Epic/parent links can be lost or need re-linking because sprints and epics are project-scoped in team-managed. Components and versions are project-scoped and won't carry. Workflow resolution and status semantics differ. Attachments, comments, and history move; structured metadata frequently doesn't. Best practice: avoid routine cross-style moves; if migrating, plan a field/status mapping, export first, and expect to re-apply sprint/epic associations.

Advanced deep

An instance with 400 projects has 3,000+ custom fields and search/indexing is slow. Design a rationalization program.
Measure: use the admin "Custom fields" view (or a marketplace app / the REST API) to pull, per field: type, number of contexts, whether context is "global" (all projects/all types), last used, screens it's on, and number of issues with a non-null value. Also check index size and reindex time trend. Categorize: (a) Duplicates — many "Story Points", "Sprint", "Team", "Root Cause", "Environment" fields created independently per project/team. (b) Unused — zero or near-zero populated issues, or not on any screen. (c) Over-scoped — a field only one team needs but with a global context, so it hits every project's screens/JQL. (d) Locked — app-managed fields (leave alone). Consolidate: pick one canonical field per concept; for duplicates, migrate values with a script/automation (copy old→new across affected issues), repoint screens and JQL/filters/dashboards/automation, then delete the duplicates. For unused fields, remove from screens, confirm no filter/board/automation/API references (search filters and gadgets by field), then delete. For over-scoped fields, replace the global context with project/issue-type-restricted contexts. Guardrails going forward: a request/approval process for new custom fields (justify why an existing one won't do), naming conventions, mandatory scoped contexts, a quarterly audit report, and admin-only field creation (remove that permission from project admins in company-managed). Execution safety: do it in waves, communicate to affected teams, snapshot filters/dashboards first, and schedule the big reindex in a maintenance window. Track index size and reindex time as the success metric, plus field count trending down.
Explain how Jira resolves what a user sees on an issue: the chain from project to the actual rendered Edit screen and a field's required/visible state.
The issue belongs to a project and has an issue type. Jira walks several scheme associations, all set at the project level: (1) Issue type scheme → is this type even allowed in the project. (2) Workflow scheme → maps the issue type to a workflow, which defines the issue's possible statuses and the transitions (and any transition screens). (3) Issue type screen scheme → maps the issue type to a screen scheme. (4) The screen scheme maps each operation (Create / Edit / View) to a specific screen; if an operation isn't mapped it falls back to the Default. (5) The screen is the ordered list of fields (tabs). A field must be (a) on this screen and (b) applicable to the project/type via its custom field context to appear at all. (6) The field configuration scheme maps the issue type to a field configuration, which per field sets: hidden vs visible (hidden wins over "on a screen"), required vs optional (enforced on Create/Edit/transition submit), the description text, the default value, and the renderer (wiki markup vs plain text). (7) Permission scheme and issue security scheme gate whether the user can see the issue and use Edit at all; field-level behaviour can be further constrained by workflow properties (e.g. jira.issue.editable=false in a status) or by validators on transitions. So the rendered Edit screen = (screen fields) − (hidden by field config) − (not in context) − (blocked by workflow status property), with "required" markers from the field configuration and additional required-ness possibly enforced by transition validators. Team-managed projects collapse most of this into the single project's own type/field/workflow settings, so the chain is shorter but the concepts (which fields, required, statuses) are the same.

Workflows, Statuses & Transitions

A workflow is a state machine for issues — and the Resolution field is the part everyone gets wrong.

Notes

Anatomy

  • A workflow = a set of statuses (states) + transitions (directed edges) an issue can take.
  • Statuses are global objects shared across workflows, each mapped to a status category: To Do (grey), In Progress (blue), Done (green). Boards and reports use the category, not the name.
  • The workflow scheme maps issue types → workflows for a project. Editing a workflow that's in use requires a draft → publish; changing which statuses exist may force a migration mapping for existing issues.
# the transitions available FROM the issue's current status
GET /rest/api/3/issue/PROJ-123/transitions
{ "transitions": [
    { "id": "31", "name": "Start work",  "to": { "name": "In Progress" } },
    { "id": "41", "name": "Ready for review", "to": { "name": "In Review" } }
] }
# execute one (by id, not by target status name)
POST /rest/api/3/issue/PROJ-123/transitions
{ "transition": { "id": "31" } }
# status category (To Do / In Progress / Done), not the name, drives boards + reports

Transitions have four hook points

HookRunsExamples
ConditionsBefore the transition is even offeredOnly assignee can transition; only if a sub-task is done; user in role.
ValidatorsOn submit, can block with an errorField required (Resolution, Fix Version); comment required; field has a value.
Post-functionsAfter the transition succeedsSet Resolution, clear Resolution, assign to reporter, update a field, fire an event, add a comment.
TriggersFired by dev-tool events"Branch created" → move to In Progress; "PR merged" → move to In Review.

A special transition from "Any status" (the All node) lets you go to a status from anywhere (e.g. a global "Close").

# one transition's hooks, in execution order
transition "Resolve Issue"  (-> Done)
  conditions:     user is assignee  AND  all sub-tasks are Done   # else button hidden
  validators:     "Resolution" field is required                  # else submit blocked
  post-functions: set Resolution = (from screen)
                  assign to Reporter
                  fire "Issue Resolved" event                     # -> notifications
  triggers:       (dev): "pull request merged" auto-fires this transition

Status vs Resolution — the classic trap

  • Status = where the issue is in the process ("In Progress", "Done").
  • Resolution = why it left the active process ("Done", "Won't Do", "Duplicate", "Cannot Reproduce"). A non-empty Resolution is what Jira treats as "this issue is resolved/closed".
  • Rule: a Set Resolution post-function (or a resolution screen) on every transition into a done status; a Clear Resolution post-function on every transition back out (Reopen). Forget the clear step and reopened issues stay "resolved" — they vanish from "open issues" filters, burndown, and notifications while sitting in an active status.
  • Never make Resolution a normal field on the Create/Edit screen — only set it via transitions.
# the bug: reopened issue still has a Resolution -> treated as closed
{ "status": { "name": "In Progress" }, "resolution": { "name": "Done" } }   # WRONG

# "Reopen" transition MUST carry a post-function:
post-function:  set Resolution = None      # or "Clear field value: Resolution"

# how it hides: these all filter on resolution, not status
JQL:  resolution = EMPTY          # "open issues" -> reopened-but-not-cleared vanish
burndown / "Complete sprint"  count issues by resolution, not status

Design guidance

  • Keep it small: To Do → In Progress → In Review → Done covers most teams. Every extra status is a board column and a place work stalls.
  • Map statuses to the right category so the board's Done column and "Complete sprint" behave.
  • Reuse a shared workflow across projects (company-managed) for consistent reporting; per-team workflows fragment cross-project metrics.
  • Prefer automation rules over heavy post-functions/scripted conditions for maintainability, unless you need the guarantee that it runs as part of the transition.
  • Avoid too many conditions that hide transitions — users get confused when the button they expect isn't there.
# GOOD: small, category-mapped
To Do(todo) -> In Progress(inprogress) -> In Review(inprogress) -> Done(done)
  + global "Any status -> Done"  (post-fn: set Resolution)
  + "Done -> In Progress"        (post-fn: clear Resolution)

# BAD: 11 statuses, 3 "blocked" variants, conditions hiding half the buttons
#   every extra status = a board column where work piles up + a reporting bucket
Cheat Sheet
  • Workflow = statuses + transitions (a state machine). Workflow scheme maps issue types → workflows per project.
  • Statuses are global; each has a category: To Do / In Progress / Done. Boards & reports use the category.
  • Transition hooks: conditions (show/hide), validators (block on submit), post-functions (act after), triggers (dev events).
  • Status = where in the process. Resolution = why it left the process; non-empty Resolution = "resolved".
  • Set Resolution on transitions into Done; Clear Resolution on Reopen — or reopened issues stay hidden from open-issue filters/burndown.
  • Never put Resolution on Create/Edit screens — only set via transitions.
  • Keep workflows small; reuse across projects for consistent metrics; prefer automation over scripted post-functions.
Q&A
What's the difference between Status and Resolution?
Status is the issue's position in the workflow ("In Progress", "Done"). Resolution explains why work stopped ("Done", "Won't Do", "Duplicate"). Jira considers an issue resolved when Resolution is non-empty, independent of the status name — which is why they must be kept in sync via transitions.
Why do "reopened" issues sometimes disappear from reports?
Because the Reopen transition moved the status back to an active state but didn't clear the Resolution. The issue still has Resolution = "Done", so filters like resolution = EMPTY, the sprint burndown, and "open issues" gadgets exclude it even though it's actively being worked. Add a Clear Resolution post-function to every transition out of a done status.
What runs in what order on a transition?
Conditions are evaluated first (they decide whether the transition button appears at all). On submit, validators run and can reject the transition with an error. If validators pass, the status changes and then post-functions execute (set/clear fields, assign, fire the event, re-index). Automation rules subscribed to the "issue transitioned" event run after.
How do you add a "Close" action available from any status?
Add a transition from the special "Any status" source to your Closed/Done status (a "global transition"). It shows on every status. Put a Set Resolution screen or post-function on it.
You edited a live workflow — why didn't it take effect?
Editing a workflow that's associated with a project creates a draft. You must publish the draft for it to apply. If your edit added/removed statuses, publishing prompts a status migration mapping so existing issues in removed statuses get moved.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What field does Jira use to decide an issue is "resolved"?
Resolution (non-empty = resolved).
Which transition hook can block a transition with an error message?
A validator.
What three categories can a status belong to?
To Do, In Progress, Done.

Intermediate core

Design the workflow config so Resolution is always correct, including reopen.
Statuses: To Do → In Progress → In Review → Done, plus a global "Won't Do". On the transition(s) into Done: a Resolution screen (so the user picks Done / Duplicate / etc.) or, for a simple team, a Set Resolution = Done post-function. On the "Won't Do" transition: Resolution screen or Set Resolution = Won't Do. On every transition whose destination is a non-Done status from a Done status — i.e. Reopen, or "Done → In Progress" — a Clear Resolution (Set Resolution = None) post-function, plus optionally reassign to the reporter and add a comment. Add a validator on the into-Done transitions requiring Resolution to be set. Keep Resolution off the Create and Edit screens entirely. Verify with JQL: status = Done AND resolution = EMPTY (should be zero) and statusCategory != Done AND resolution != EMPTY (should be zero).
A team wants issues to auto-move to "In Progress" when a branch is created and to "In Review" when a PR opens. Two ways to do this — compare.
Workflow triggers: on the target transition, add a trigger for "Branch created" / "Pull request created" (requires the Git provider integrated via the dev-tool connection). Pros: it's part of the workflow, runs as the transition (respecting conditions/validators/post-functions), no separate rule to maintain, works per project via the workflow scheme. Cons: configured per workflow (repeat for each), limited to the trigger types Jira ships, and only fires when the smart-commit/branch name references the issue key. Automation rules: a project or global rule with a "Branch created" / "Pull request created" trigger → "Transition issue to In Progress/In Review". Pros: centralized, easy to see/edit all rules in one place, can add conditions (only if currently in To Do), branch across multiple actions (assign, comment, notify), and reuse one global rule for many projects. Cons: runs after the event as a separate actor ("Automation for Jira"), so it can race with other rules, is subject to rule-execution limits/queues, and won't run if automation is disabled. Recommendation: automation rules for flexibility and central management, unless you specifically need the change to be enforced as part of the transition itself.

Advanced deep

50 teams each have a bespoke workflow; cross-team reporting (cycle time, throughput, "% done") is unreliable. Design a consolidation without a revolt.
Root problem: different status names, different numbers of stages, and inconsistent status category mapping mean board "Done" columns, sprint completion, and any cross-project JQL/report mean different things per team. Approach: (1) Define a small canonical workflow — e.g. Backlog (To Do) → Selected (To Do) → In Progress → In Review → Done, with correct categories — as the standard for company-managed projects. Allow one or two optional extra statuses (e.g. "Blocked", "In Test") from an approved list, each with a fixed category, so teams keep some flavour without fragmenting metrics. (2) Map every team's current statuses to the canonical set (a spreadsheet exercise with each team), being strict that anything representing "not started" is To Do, active work is In Progress, and shipped is Done — the category mapping is the non-negotiable part; names can vary a little if you must. (3) Migrate in waves: create the shared workflow + workflow scheme, associate it per project, run the status migration mapping, publish. Keep team boards working by adjusting column→status mappings. (4) Rebuild shared dashboards/filters on status category and standard fields, plus control-chart / cycle-time reports that now compare like-for-like. (5) Governance: new projects get the standard workflow by default; changes go through a review; team-managed projects are steered to the same status set via a template. (6) Change management: bring team leads in early, show them the broken cross-team reports as motivation, preserve their board experience, pilot with 3–5 friendly teams, provide a migration runbook, and give a deadline with support. The pitch is "you lose almost nothing on your board; the org gains trustworthy delivery metrics".
Post-functions vs automation vs app (ScriptRunner) for workflow logic: give the decision criteria, including ordering, reliability, and auditability.
Built-in post-functions / conditions / validators: run synchronously as part of the transition, in a defined order, before the user sees success. Use when the logic must be guaranteed atomic with the transition (set/clear Resolution, required-field validation, "block unless sub-tasks done"). Limits: the built-in set is basic (set a field, assign, fire event); ordering of post-functions matters and the "re-index"/"fire event" ones must stay in the right place; hard to see all of them across many workflows. Automation for Jira rules: run asynchronously after the event, as the "Automation" actor, from a central rule list. Use for cross-issue effects (update parent, create sub-tasks, sync fields), notifications, multi-step branching, scheduled jobs, and anything you want visible/editable in one place with an audit log per rule. Limits: eventual (a fraction of a second to seconds later, longer under load), subject to per-plan execution limits and queue throttling, can race with other rules and with the user's next action, silently skipped if automation is disabled or the rule errors, and loops need guarding. Not suitable when the change must be enforced before the transition completes. ScriptRunner / other apps (scripted post-functions, listeners, behaviours): run synchronously (scripted post-functions/validators) or on events (listeners), with full API access. Use for complex synchronous validation/mutation the built-ins can't express, dynamic field behaviour ("behaviours"), and bulk/admin scripting. Limits: code you own and must test; upgrades/Jira version changes can break scripts; performance risk if a script does slow work inside a transition; auditability depends on your logging discipline; another vendor dependency and cost; Cloud vs Data Center capabilities differ. Decision criteria: (1) Must it be atomic with the transition and block it? → validator/post-function (built-in if possible, ScriptRunner if the logic is complex). (2) Is it cross-issue, multi-step, or "nice to have if it runs a moment later"? → automation rule (best auditability and central management). (3) Does it need real code and can tolerate a marketplace dependency? → ScriptRunner, but keep scripts small, logged, and covered by a test project. (4) Prefer the least powerful tool that works for maintainability: config > automation > script. (5) Watch ordering: built-in post-functions have a fixed sequence you can reorder; automation and listeners fire after and among themselves in undefined order — don't have two mechanisms fighting over the same field.

Boards: Scrum vs Kanban

A board is a saved filter plus a column layout — not a container of issues.

Notes

What a board actually is

  • A board = a filter (the JQL that selects which issues appear) + configuration (columns, swimlanes, quick filters, card layout, estimation, working days).
  • Issues aren't "on" a board — they match the board's filter. One issue can appear on many boards; a board can span multiple projects if its filter does.
  • Columns map to one or more statuses. Moving a card between columns transitions the issue (if a valid transition exists). Statuses not mapped to any column are "hidden" from the board.
# a board's saved filter IS just a JQL query
GET /rest/agile/1.0/board/42/configuration
{ "filter": { "id": "10200" },
  "columnConfig": { "columns": [
    { "name": "To Do",       "statuses": [{ "id": "10000" }] },
    { "name": "In Progress", "statuses": [{ "id": "3" }, { "id": "10001" }] },   # 2 statuses -> 1 column
    { "name": "Done",        "statuses": [{ "id": "10002" }] } ] } }

# the filter behind it:
project = PROJ AND type != Sub-task ORDER BY Rank ASC   # missing "ORDER BY Rank" breaks drag-rank

Scrum vs Kanban board

Scrum boardKanban board
CadenceTime-boxed sprints; a Backlog screen to plan themContinuous flow; no sprints (optional "Kanban backlog" column)
Board showsOnly the active sprint's issuesEverything matching the filter, minus done older than N days
Key reportsBurndown, Sprint Report, VelocityCumulative Flow Diagram, Control Chart, Cycle time
WIP controlSprint scope (commitment)Column WIP limits
Best forPredictable planning cycles, forecasting with velocityOps/support, steady intake, continuous delivery

Both use the same underlying issues/workflow; the board type just changes planning UI and reports. You can switch, or run a "Scrumban" hybrid.

# SCRUM board shows only the active sprint
GET /rest/agile/1.0/board/42/sprint?state=active   -> { "values": [{ "id": 88 }] }
GET /rest/agile/1.0/sprint/88/issue                 # the board's cards

# KANBAN board shows the whole filter minus old done issues
# (config: "Kanban board sub-filter" e.g.  fixVersion in unreleasedVersions() OR
#          resolved >= -14d )
# and enforces flow via column WIP limits, not sprint scope

Board configuration knobs

  • Columns & statuses: add/remove columns, map statuses, set column WIP limits (min/max), set the "Done" column (drives sprint completion & the done-issue aging).
  • Swimlanes: horizontal grouping — by Epic, Assignee, Story (parent), Query (custom JQL rows, e.g. "Expedite"), or none. Query swimlanes are ordered top-down.
  • Quick filters: one-click JQL toggles ("Only my issues", "No sub-tasks", "Recently updated").
  • Card layout: which fields show on cards (up to a few extra), card colours (by priority / assignee / issue type / JQL).
  • Estimation: Story Points / original time / issue count; and the tracking unit for burndown.
  • Working days: for burndown day calculations.
  • Sub-task handling: whether the board shows parent+sub-tasks or rolls up.
# query swimlane: pull expedited work to the top, ordered
Swimlanes (type: Query):
  1. "Expedite"   ->  priority = Highest OR labels = expedite
  2. "Blocked"    ->  status = Blocked OR labels = blocked
  3. "Everything else"  ->  (auto)

# quick filters = one-click JQL toggles
"Only my issues"  ->  assignee = currentUser()
"No sub-tasks"    ->  type != Sub-task
# column WIP limit: In Progress max = 3  -> column turns red at 4

Common pitfalls

  • Filter too broad/narrow: cards missing = they don't match the filter, or their status isn't mapped to a column. Check the board's filter and column mapping first.
  • Board filter has no ORDER BY Rank: drag-to-rank on the backlog stops working; the filter must order by Rank.
  • Editing the board's filter affects everyone using that board; boards sharing a filter move together.
  • Only board admins (and the filter owner) can change config; a departed owner can orphan a board's filter.
# "my card vanished" — check in this order:
1. does it match the filter?   -> paste the board filter into Issue Search, add: AND key = PROJ-123
2. is its status mapped?       -> board config > Columns: is "In Review" under a column?
3. sprint board?              -> is the issue in the ACTIVE sprint?  (sprint field set?)
4. done-issue aging (Kanban) -> resolved > 14d ago drops off by default
# ownership: filter owner leaves -> reassign the filter, or the board silently breaks
Cheat Sheet
  • Board = saved filter + config (columns, swimlanes, quick filters, card layout, estimation). Issues match a board, aren't contained by it.
  • Columns → statuses; dragging a card transitions the issue. Unmapped statuses are hidden.
  • Scrum board: sprints + Backlog planning; shows active sprint; Burndown/Velocity/Sprint Report; WIP via sprint scope.
  • Kanban board: continuous flow, no sprints; CFD/Control Chart/cycle time; WIP via column limits.
  • Swimlanes: by Epic / Assignee / Story / Query / none. Quick filters = one-click JQL toggles.
  • Board filter must ORDER BY Rank for drag-ranking to work.
  • Same issues/workflow underneath — board type only changes planning UI + reports.
Q&A
What is a Jira board, technically?
A saved filter plus display configuration. The filter's JQL decides which issues show; the config defines columns (mapped to statuses), swimlanes, quick filters, card fields/colours, and estimation. Issues appear on any board whose filter they match.
A card isn't showing on the board even though the issue exists. First checks?
(1) Does the issue match the board's filter (project, type, any extra JQL clauses)? (2) Is the issue's status mapped to a column? Unmapped statuses are hidden. (3) On a Scrum board, is the issue in the active sprint? (4) Is a quick filter or swimlane hiding it? (5) On Kanban, is it a Done issue older than the board's "days" setting?
Scrum board vs Kanban board — when to choose which?
Scrum when work comes in planned batches and the team wants sprint commitments, velocity-based forecasting, and a regular cadence. Kanban when work arrives continuously (support, ops, platform), priorities shift often, and you care about flow metrics (cycle time, WIP) rather than sprint burndown.
What do column WIP limits do?
On a Kanban board (and optionally Scrum), you set a max (and min) number of issues for a column; Jira highlights the column red when exceeded. It's a visual nudge to finish work before starting more — Jira doesn't hard-block adding cards.
Why did backlog drag-and-drop ranking stop working?
The board's filter must end with ORDER BY Rank ASC. If someone changed the filter's sort (or it never had one), Jira can't persist manual rank order and drag-ranking is disabled. Re-add the Rank ordering to the saved filter.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What two things make up a board?
A saved filter (JQL) and its display configuration (columns, swimlanes, etc.).
Which board type has sprints?
Scrum.
What happens to the issue when you drag its card to another column?
Jira runs the workflow transition to the status that column maps to (if a valid transition exists).

Intermediate core

One team's work spans three projects. How do you give them a single board without merging the projects?
Create a saved filter with JQL like project in (ALPHA, BETA, GAMMA) AND (labels = team-orion OR component in (…)) ORDER BY Rank — whatever precisely identifies this team's issues across the three projects. Then create a board from that filter. Configure columns to map the union of statuses used across the three projects' workflows (they may differ — map each real status to the right column, and be careful about status category consistency so "Done" behaves). Set swimlanes by project or by epic if useful. Caveats: the three projects may have different workflows/fields, so transitions available from a card depend on that issue's own workflow; estimation should use a field all three populate (Story Points); sprint planning only works cleanly if the board is Scrum and all three projects share the sprint field (they do — Sprint is global in company-managed). Board admins are set separately from project admins. This is the standard "cross-project team board" pattern.
A support team's Kanban board is chaotic: everything's "In Progress", nothing finishes. What board-level changes help?
(1) Set WIP limits per column, especially on In Progress and In Review, sized to the team (e.g. ~1–1.5× headcount); the red overflow highlight forces the "stop starting, start finishing" conversation. (2) Split the "In Progress" column into meaningful stages (e.g. Analysis / Doing / Waiting-on-customer / In Review) so blocked vs active work is visible — and add a "Blocked" flag or a query swimlane for blocked items so they don't hide. (3) Add a dedicated "Expedite" query swimlane at the top for true urgent items, with its own (tiny) WIP limit, so urgent work doesn't just mean "everything's urgent". (4) Add quick filters ("Mine", "Waiting on others", "Older than 3 days") to surface stalled work. (5) Turn on the Control Chart and Cumulative Flow Diagram to make cycle time and where work piles up visible in retros. (6) Trim done-issue aging so the board isn't cluttered. The board changes won't fix the process alone, but WIP limits + explicit stages + blocked visibility are what make a flow problem impossible to ignore.

Advanced deep

Explain how the board, its filter, sprints, and rank interact — and the failure modes when multiple boards share a filter or a sprint spans boards.
Rank is a single global field (a lexicographic "LexoRank" string) per issue — there is one rank order across the whole instance, not per board. Every board that orders its filter by Rank shows issues in that same global order, filtered to its subset. Dragging to reorder on any board rewrites the global rank of the moved issue, so reordering on board A also reorders those issues relative to each other on board B. This is usually fine but surprising when two teams "own" overlapping issue sets. Sprints are objects with an ID, name, state (future/active/closed), and start/end dates; an issue's Sprint field can hold multiple sprint IDs (its history). A sprint is created from and associated with an "origin board", but issues carry the sprint value regardless of board.
