So an issue can be in Sprint 42 and appear on any board whose filter matches it — if two Scrum boards both match an issue that's in an active sprint, it shows in the active-sprint view of both, and completing the sprint from either board closes it for the issue everywhere. Failure modes: (1) Shared filter — two boards pointing at the same saved filter: editing the filter (or its ORDER BY) changes both; deleting/!editing column mappings is per-board but the filter is shared, so a filter change to fix board A can break board B's visible set. (2) Sprint started on the "wrong" board — a sprint's origin board determines which board's Backlog screen manages it; if the team plans on a different board, they can't start/complete that sprint there and see "no sprint" confusion. Keep one canonical board per team for sprint operations. (3) Overlapping board filters + sprints — an issue matching two teams' boards, put into team A's sprint, now clutters team B's active sprint and burndown; scope board filters so teams don't overlap, or use a component/team field in the filter. (4) Rank thrash — two teams re-ranking a shared pool fight each other; the fix is disjoint filters. (5) LexoRank rebalancing — when rank strings get too long, Jira runs a background rebalance; huge instances can see slow ranking during it. (6) Filter permissions — if the filter isn't shared with everyone who uses the board, they see an empty or partial board. Design rule: one board per team with a filter that cleanly partitions that team's work; do sprint operations only from that board; accept that Rank is global.
A director wants "one big board" showing all 12 teams' work for a portfolio view. Why is that usually the wrong tool, and what do you build instead?
Why a giant board is wrong: (1) A board is an execution tool — columns are workflow statuses, cards are individual issues, and it's tuned for a team moving work day to day. 12 teams' issues in one column list is unreadable and slow to render. (2) The 12 teams likely have different workflows, so status→column mapping is lossy or misleading. (3) Rank is global — a portfolio board that lets anyone drag-rank creates cross-team rank fights. (4) Sprints are per-team; an aggregate board can't show 12 concurrent sprints coherently. (5) The director doesn't need issue-level detail; they need epic/initiative status, delivery forecasts, and risks. What to build instead: (a) Advanced Roadmaps / Plans (Jira Premium) — a plan aggregating the 12 teams' boards/projects, showing the epic/initiative hierarchy on a timeline, capacity, dependencies, and scenario planning; this is the actual "portfolio view". (b) A dashboard with gadgets: epic progress (per team), created-vs-resolved, sprint health, cumulative flow, an "at risk" filter (e.g. due < endOfMonth() AND statusCategory != Done), and a two-dimensional filter statistics gadget (team × status). (c) A filter/JQL saved view at epic level: issuetype = Epic AND "Team[Dropdown]" in (…) ORDER BY due with status, % done (via linked issues or a progress field), target date. (d) If they insist on a board, make a read-mostly epic-level Kanban: filter issuetype in (Epic, Initiative), columns = a simple Not started / In progress / Done, swimlanes by team — a legible one-card-per-epic status wall, not 3,000 stories. The principle: boards are for teams executing; portfolios need roll-up (Plans), summary (dashboards), or an epic-level board, not a firehose.

Backlog, Sprints & Estimation

Turning an ordered list of work into time-boxed, forecastable delivery.

Notes

The backlog

  • The Backlog screen (Scrum boards) shows the ranked list of issues not in an active/future sprint, plus a section per planned sprint.
  • Ranking = drag to order (global Rank field); rank expresses priority sequence, not commitment.
  • Grooming / refinement: keep the top of the backlog small, clear, estimated, and dependency-free enough to pull into a sprint. Lower items can stay vague.
  • Bulk actions, inline create, and "send to top/bottom of sprint" speed planning.
# backlog = matches the board filter AND not in an active/future sprint, ordered by Rank
GET /rest/agile/1.0/board/42/backlog

# re-rank one issue (writes the global Rank field)
PUT /rest/agile/1.0/issue/rank
{ "issues": ["PROJ-140"], "rankBeforeIssue": "PROJ-118" }   # place it above PROJ-118

Sprints

  • Create a sprint (from the Backlog), drag issues in, set the goal, then Start sprint (name, duration, start/end). Only one active sprint per board by default (Jira allows parallel sprints as an option — use sparingly).
  • Complete sprint: incomplete issues go back to the backlog or a future sprint; the Sprint Report snapshots what was committed vs added vs completed.
  • Scope changes mid-sprint are recorded (scope creep line on the burndown).
POST /rest/agile/1.0/sprint
{ "name": "Sprint 24", "originBoardId": 42, "goal": "Ship checkout revamp" }
# -> { "id": 88, "state": "future" }

POST /rest/agile/1.0/backlog/issue           # pull issues in
{ "issues": ["PROJ-140","PROJ-141"] }        # (or /sprint/88/issue)

POST /rest/agile/1.0/sprint/88               # start it
{ "state": "active", "startDate": "...", "endDate": "..." }
# ...later: { "state": "closed" }  -> incomplete issues roll to backlog/next sprint

Estimation

MethodNotes
Story pointsRelative size (effort + complexity + uncertainty), often a modified Fibonacci scale (1,2,3,5,8,13). Not hours. Team-relative — not comparable across teams.
Time (original estimate)Hours/days. Concrete but tempts false precision and per-person accounting.
Issue countJust count stories; works if stories are sliced to similar size.
T-shirt / bucketsCoarse sizing for backlog items not yet ready.
  • The board's Estimation setting picks the field used for backlog/sprint totals and the burndown's Y axis.
  • Planning poker to estimate collaboratively and surface hidden assumptions.
  • Estimate stories, not sub-tasks (sub-tasks are execution breakdown; some teams put remaining time on sub-tasks for a separate task burndown).
# story points live in a custom field; the board's Estimation setting names it
POST /rest/api/3/issue/PROJ-140
{ "fields": { "customfield_10016": 5 } }        # 5 points  (Fibonacci-ish: 1,2,3,5,8,13)

# NOT hours: 5 points != 5 days. Relative size, team-local.
# sub-tasks: leave points empty; some teams put "remaining estimate" (time) here instead
{ "fields": { "timetracking": { "remainingEstimate": "4h" } } }

Velocity & capacity

  • Velocity = points completed per sprint (from the Velocity report). Use a rolling average of the last 3–5 sprints to forecast; don't treat it as a target or a performance metric.
  • Capacity planning: account for holidays, on-call, support rotation, meetings; commit below raw velocity when the sprint is short-staffed.
  • Only fully completed issues count toward velocity — a nearly-done 8-pointer scores 0 that sprint (don't split points on carry-over; re-estimate the remainder if needed).
# velocity = points COMPLETED per sprint (rolling avg, not a target)
Sprint 19: committed 34  completed 28
Sprint 20: committed 30  completed 31
Sprint 21: committed 32  completed 27
forecast = avg(28,31,27) = ~28.7 pts/sprint

# capacity this sprint: 5 devs x 8 days - (2 holidays + 5 on-call days) = 33 dev-days
#   -> commit ~24 pts (below velocity), not 34

Anti-patterns

  • Converting points to hours (defeats relative estimation).
  • Comparing velocity between teams or demanding it always increase (invites point inflation).
  • Committing to 100% of velocity every sprint (no slack for the unexpected).
  • Carrying the same story for 4 sprints — it's too big or blocked; split it.
  • Adding lots of scope mid-sprint without acknowledging the goal is at risk.
# the carry-over that should have been split
PROJ-155  "Payments overhaul"  13 pts
  Sprint 20: not done   Sprint 21: not done   Sprint 22: not done
# -> too big or blocked. Split into 3-5 pt slices, each independently shippable:
PROJ-155a  "Payments: read path"      5
PROJ-155b  "Payments: write path"     5
PROJ-155c  "Payments: reconciliation" 3
Cheat Sheet
  • Backlog = ranked list of issues not in a sprint. Rank = priority order (global field). Groom the top; leave the tail rough.
  • Sprint: create → add issues → set goal → Start (duration) → Complete (incomplete issues roll to backlog/next; Sprint Report snapshots committed vs done).
  • Estimation options: story points (relative, Fibonacci-ish, team-local, not hours), time, issue count, buckets. Board Estimation setting picks the burndown unit.
  • Estimate stories, not sub-tasks. Use planning poker.
  • Velocity = points completed/sprint; rolling avg of 3–5 to forecast; not a target, not cross-team comparable. Only fully-done issues count.
  • Capacity: subtract holidays/on-call/support; commit below velocity when short-staffed; keep slack.
  • Anti-patterns: points→hours, velocity as KPI, 100% commitment, 4-sprint carry-over, silent scope creep.
Q&A
What are story points and why not just use hours?
Story points estimate relative size — effort, complexity, and uncertainty combined — usually on a coarse Fibonacci-like scale. They're deliberately not hours because relative sizing is faster, more consistent across people, avoids false precision, and lets the team forecast via velocity without per-person time accounting. Converting them back to hours throws away all of that.
How is velocity calculated and how should it be used?
Velocity is the sum of estimates of issues completed in a sprint (shown in the Velocity report). Use a rolling average of the last few sprints to forecast how much the team can likely take on and roughly when a backlog will be done. It is not a productivity score, not a target to grow, and not comparable between teams (each team's points are its own scale).
A story was 90% done at sprint end. What happens to its points?
It counts as 0 toward that sprint's velocity — only completed issues count. It rolls to the next sprint (or backlog) with its estimate intact; teams generally re-estimate the remaining work rather than splitting the original points. Recurring carry-over is a signal the story is too big or blocked and should be split.
What's the difference between ranking and committing?
Ranking is ordering the backlog by priority — it says nothing about when work will be done. Committing is pulling issues into a sprint with the team's agreement that they'll aim to finish them by the sprint end. You rank the whole backlog; you commit only the top slice that fits capacity.
Why keep slack instead of committing to 100% of velocity?
Because real sprints have interruptions — production issues, urgent requests, sick days, underestimated stories. Committing to exactly the average velocity means any surprise blows the sprint goal. Teams typically commit somewhat below velocity (and adjust for known capacity gaps) so they can absorb the unexpected and still hit the goal.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Do story points represent hours?
No — they're a relative measure of size/complexity/uncertainty.
What counts toward a sprint's velocity?
Only issues fully completed in that sprint.
Where do incomplete issues go when you complete a sprint?
Back to the backlog or into a selected future sprint.

Intermediate core

A team's velocity is 40, 12, 45, 38, 41. How do you forecast, and what do you do about the outlier?
The 12 is an outlier — almost certainly a holiday sprint, a major incident, or a big release freeze. Investigate and, for forecasting, exclude it (or annotate why). Forecast from the remaining sprints: mean ≈ 41, range ~38–45, so plan around ~38–40 committed points per normal sprint (use the low end for commitments, the average for roadmap projections). To forecast a backlog of, say, 400 points: ~10–11 sprints, and present it as a range (9–12) not a single date. Adjust each sprint for known capacity (a person on leave, on-call load) rather than blindly using 40. Keep watching — if another low sprint appears, the "outlier" may be a pattern (chronic interruptions) worth fixing. Don't let the team chase "back to 45"; that just inflates estimates.
Product keeps injecting "urgent" work mid-sprint and the team never hits the sprint goal. What Jira mechanics and practices address this?
Make it visible: the burndown already shows a scope change line — review it every sprint retro and in sprint review with product, quantifying "we committed 38, 22 points of unplanned work was added, goal missed". The Sprint Report's "added during sprint" section does the same. Mechanics: (1) Reserve explicit capacity for unplanned work — commit to (velocity − historical injection average), effectively a buffer. (2) Use a distinct issue type or label ("Expedite"/"Unplanned") and a query swimlane at the top of the board so injected work is tracked and countable, not silently absorbed. (3) A rule that adding scope means removing equivalent scope ("one in, one out") — product chooses what drops. (4) For genuinely continuous interrupt work, consider moving that stream to a Kanban board with a WIP-limited expedite lane, and keep the Scrum sprint for planned work. (5) Protect the sprint goal as the real commitment (not the full issue list) so the team can still "succeed" by delivering the goal even if filler stories slip. Practice: agree an interrupt policy with product (what qualifies as sprint-breaking urgent vs "next sprint"), route non-urgent requests through backlog refinement, and if injection stays high, that's a prioritization/planning problem to escalate, not a team execution problem.

Advanced deep

Leadership wants to standardize story points across 15 teams so they can "add up capacity". Explain why that's flawed and what actually enables cross-team planning.
Why it's flawed: story points are deliberately relative to a team's own baseline — a team calibrates "a 3" against their reference stories, their codebase, their skills, their definition of done. Team A's 5 and Team B's 5 represent different amounts of work, and forcing a shared scale just moves the calibration problem without solving it (teams will drift back, or game the scale). Summing points across teams to get "org capacity" produces a number with no real meaning, and it invites the worst dynamics: point inflation, cross-team comparison as a performance cudgel, and estimation becoming a political exercise. Velocity is a per-team forecasting aid, not a currency. What actually enables cross-team / portfolio planning: (1) Plan at a coarser unit that is comparable — epics/features with T-shirt sizes or a rough sprint-count estimate per team, or "number of teams × number of sprints". (2) Use each team's own velocity to forecast that team's portion of a roadmap, then compose the timelines — Advanced Roadmaps / Plans does exactly this (per-team capacity from their velocity, rolled up with dependencies on a timeline). (3) Track throughput (features/epics completed per quarter per team) and cycle time for delivery-rate comparisons — these are unit-free and meaningful across teams. (4) For "can we take this on?", ask each team to forecast against their own backlog and velocity and report a confidence range, then aggregate the answers, not the points. (5) Keep story points as an internal team tool and explicitly tell leadership the org-level metrics are throughput, cycle time, epic burn-up, and forecast confidence — not summed points. The one legitimate standardization is a shared process (consistent definition of done, similar story-slicing guidance, refinement discipline) so each team's forecasts are individually trustworthy.

JQL: Searching & Filters

Jira Query Language — SQL-ish clauses over issue fields, powering filters, boards, dashboards, and automation.

Notes

Shape of a query

field OPERATOR value [AND|OR field OPERATOR value ...] [ORDER BY field ASC|DESC]

No SELECT — a JQL query is just the WHERE + ORDER BY. It always returns issues.

Operators

OperatorUse
= !=exact match / not
> >= < <=ordered fields (dates, numbers, priority, votes)
IN (a, b) / NOT INset membership
~ / !~text "contains" (indexed word match, not substring) — for summary, description, comment, text
IS EMPTY / IS NOT EMPTYnull check (use for resolution, fixVersion, custom fields)
WAS / WAS IN / WAS NOThistorical value of status/assignee/etc. (with AFTER, BEFORE, DURING, ON, BY)
CHANGEDfield changed (FROM, TO, AFTER, BY, DURING)
priority >= High                      # ordered field: High and Highest
component IN ("API", "Billing")
summary ~ "timeout"                   # indexed WORD match, not substring
fixVersion IS EMPTY
assignee WAS currentUser() DURING (-30d, now())      # historical value
status CHANGED TO Done AFTER startOfWeek()           # transition happened this week
labels != flaky                       # gotcha: this EXCLUDES issues with no labels at all
labels IS EMPTY OR labels != flaky    # ...include the unlabelled ones explicitly

Functions (value generators)

  • Dates: now(), startOfDay()/endOfDay(), startOfWeek(), startOfMonth(), and relative math: -1w, -3d, "-1w 2d". e.g. due <= endOfWeek(), created >= -14d.
  • People: currentUser(), membersOf("jira-developers").
  • Agile: sprint in openSprints(), sprint in closedSprints(), sprint in futureSprints().
  • Versions: fixVersion in releasedVersions(), unreleasedVersions(), earliestUnreleasedVersion(PROJ).
  • Links/hierarchy (varies by version/app): issuesInEpics(), parentEpic(), issueLinkType, linkedIssues("KEY", "blocks"), portfolioChildrenOf().
  • issueHistory() (recently viewed), votedIssues(), watchedIssues().
# functions produce values on the right-hand side
assignee = currentUser() AND sprint IN openSprints()
created >= startOfMonth(-1) AND created < startOfMonth()      # all of last month
reporter IN membersOf("support-team")
fixVersion = earliestUnreleasedVersion(WEB)
parent IN (PROJ-140) OR "Epic Link" = PROJ-140              # children of an epic
due <= endOfWeek() AND statusCategory != Done                # due this week, not done

Common recipes

project = PLAT AND statusCategory != Done AND assignee = currentUser() ORDER BY priority DESC, due ASC
project = WEB AND created >= -7d AND type = Bug
resolution = EMPTY AND updated <= -30d AND statusCategory = "In Progress"     # stale in-progress
status WAS "In Progress" BY jsmith DURING ("2024-01-01", "2024-03-31")
status CHANGED TO Done AFTER startOfMonth() AND assignee in membersOf("team-orion")
sprint in openSprints() AND type != Sub-task AND statusCategory != Done       # sprint scope remaining
project = SUP AND labels = escalation AND priority in (Highest, High) ORDER BY created ASC
filter = "Team Orion Base" AND due < now() AND statusCategory != Done          # compose saved filters

Saved filters

  • Save a query → a filter with an owner and share permissions (private / project / group / public). Boards, dashboard gadgets, and other filters (filter = "Name" ) reference it.
  • Subscriptions: email the filter results on a schedule (cron), to you or a group.
  • Permissions gotcha: a viewer only sees issues they have Browse permission on, and only sees the filter if it's shared with them. A board backed by a filter the team can't see shows empty.
  • An orphaned filter (owner deactivated) needs an admin to change the owner; boards/gadgets break meanwhile.
# save a query as a shared filter, then compose it elsewhere
POST /rest/api/3/filter
{ "name": "Team Orion Open", "jql": "project in (WEB,API) AND labels = team-orion AND resolution = EMPTY",
  "sharePermissions": [ { "type": "group", "group": { "name": "team-orion" } } ] }

# reference it by name from another query, a board, or a dashboard gadget
filter = "Team Orion Open" AND priority = Highest
# subscription: email results on a cron  ->  POST /rest/api/3/filter/{id}/... (or the UI)

Notes

  • ~ matches whole indexed words with stemming, not arbitrary substrings; wildcards text ~ "cust*" work, leading wildcards don't.
  • Custom field names with spaces or duplicates: quote them, or use cf[10021] by ID.
  • ORDER BY Rank is required on a board's filter for manual ranking.
  • JQL is also the language for automation conditions/branches and bulk-change selection.
summary ~ "custom*"      # OK: trailing wildcard on a text field
summary ~ "*tom"         # NO: leading wildcard not supported
"Story Points" >= 8      # quote field names with spaces...
cf[10016] >= 8           # ...or use cf[ID] (also disambiguates duplicate names)
... ORDER BY Rank        # required on a board filter for drag-to-rank to work
Cheat Sheet
  • JQL = field OP value [AND/OR ...] [ORDER BY ...]. No SELECT; always returns issues.
  • Ops: = != >… IN/NOT IN, ~/!~ (word contains), IS [NOT] EMPTY, WAS/WAS IN, CHANGED (with FROM/TO/AFTER/DURING/BY).
  • Functions: currentUser(), membersOf(), now()/startOfDay()/endOfWeek() + -1w, openSprints()/closedSprints(), releasedVersions()/unreleasedVersions(), linkedIssues().
  • Use statusCategory (To Do/In Progress/Done) for status-agnostic queries; resolution = EMPTY for "open".
  • Compose filters: filter = "Saved Name" AND .... Reference custom fields by cf[10010] if names collide.
  • Saved filter = query + owner + share scope; feeds boards, gadgets, subscriptions (scheduled email).
  • Viewer sees only issues they can Browse and filters shared with them; unshared filter → empty board.
Q&A
Why use statusCategory != Done instead of status not in (Done, Closed)?
Status names vary by project and workflow; statusCategory is one of three fixed values (To Do, In Progress, Done) that every status maps to. A query on the category works across all projects and survives someone renaming or adding statuses, so it's the portable way to say "not finished".
What does the ~ operator actually match?
It's a full-text "contains" against the Lucene index — it matches whole words (with stemming), not arbitrary substrings. summary ~ "login" matches "login failed" and "logins" but not "weblogins". Trailing wildcards (~ "log*") work; leading wildcards don't.
How do you find issues that were in "In Progress" at some point last month?
status WAS "In Progress" DURING (startOfMonth(-1), startOfMonth()). The WAS operator queries status history; DURING bounds the time window. You can add BY someuser to restrict to who made the change.
What is a saved filter and what can reference it?
A named, saved JQL query with an owner and share settings. Boards are built on a filter; dashboard gadgets take a filter; other JQL can embed one with filter = "Name"; and you can attach an email subscription to run it on a schedule. Sharing controls who can see and use it.
A colleague's board shows no issues for you but works for them. Likely cause?
Either the board's underlying filter isn't shared with you (so you can't see the board's query), or you lack Browse Project permission on the projects it covers (so the issues are invisible to you), or an issue security level hides them. Filter results are always intersected with the viewer's permissions.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which JQL keyword sorts results?
ORDER BY.
How do you query "assigned to me"?
assignee = currentUser().
How do you check a field has no value?
field IS EMPTY (e.g. resolution IS EMPTY).

Intermediate core

Write a query for "my team's bugs opened in the last 14 days that are still unresolved, worst priority first".
type = Bug AND created >= -14d AND resolution = EMPTY AND assignee in membersOf("team-orion") ORDER BY priority DESC, created ASC. Notes: created >= -14d is relative to now; resolution = EMPTY is the reliable "unresolved" check (don't rely on status names); membersOf("group") expands a group, or use a "Team" custom field: "Team[Dropdown]" = "Orion". Add project in (WEB, API) to scope. If "my team" is defined by component: component in (checkout, payments).
You need a dashboard gadget for "issues that have been reopened this quarter". How?
"Reopened" = the status went from a done state back to an active one, or the resolution was cleared. Best expression: status CHANGED FROM "Done" TO "In Progress" AFTER startOfMonth("-3M") — but status names vary, so if your workflow has a dedicated Reopen transition or a "Reopened" status use that: status CHANGED TO "Reopened" AFTER -90d. A more workflow-agnostic version: resolution CHANGED FROM "Done" TO EMPTY AFTER startOfDay(-90d) (works if your Reopen transition clears Resolution, which it should). Save it as a filter, then point a Filter Results gadget or a Two Dimensional Filter Statistics gadget (e.g. project vs assignee) at it. Consider adding project in (...) and type != Sub-task.

Advanced deep

A JQL-heavy instance is slow: board loads, gadget refreshes, and automation JQL conditions all lag. Diagnose and remediate.
Where time goes: Jira JQL runs against a Lucene index; slowness comes from expensive query shapes, index size (driven by issue count and custom field count), and fan-out (many boards/gadgets/subscriptions/automation rules all re-running similar queries). Diagnose: (1) Identify the worst queries — slow-query logging (Data Center), the /rest/api/2/search timings, or an app; look for common offenders. (2) Check index health/size and reindex time; a bloated custom-field set (thousands of fields, unrestricted contexts) inflates every query. (3) Count active filter subscriptions and their cron alignment (everything at the top of the hour = a stampede) and the number of automation rules with JQL conditions/branches firing per event. (4) Look for dashboards with many heavy gadgets shared org-wide. Query-level fixes: avoid ~ free-text scans where a structured field would do; avoid negation-only queries (NOT IN, !=, IS NOT EMPTY with no positive anchor) — always include a selective positive clause (project, type, a date bound) so Lucene can narrow first; avoid ORDER BY on unindexed/large custom fields; replace WAS/CHANGED history queries (they hit the changelog, expensive) with a status/label the workflow sets, or run them less often; bound time ranges (created >= -90d) instead of "all time"; reference filters (filter = X) so the DB/index can reuse, and keep the base filter tight. System-level fixes: rationalize custom fields (fewer fields, restricted contexts) — often the biggest lever; stagger subscription cron times; consolidate duplicate boards/gadgets; cap automation rule fan-out (scope rules to fewer projects, add cheap conditions before expensive JQL branches, use scheduled rules with a JQL that's bounded); archive or split very large projects; ensure the instance is sized (memory, index on fast disk) and the index is not fragmented; on Cloud, lean on the platform but still fix query shapes and field bloat. Governance: a review for new custom fields, a limit on dashboard gadget count, and periodic cleanup of unused filters/subscriptions/rules.
Explain the difference between WAS/CHANGED and normal field operators, what data source they use, and their limitations for reporting.
Normal operators (=, IN, ~, IS EMPTY, >…) test the issue's current field values, served from the Lucene index — fast, and what boards/most filters use. WAS / WAS IN / WAS NOT test whether a field ever held a value (optionally within DURING (d1,d2), BEFORE, AFTER, ON, or BY user). CHANGED tests whether a field transitioned (with FROM, TO, AFTER, BEFORE, DURING, BY). Both read the issue change history (the changelog / change items), not just the current index — so they're more expensive and only work for fields Jira records history on (status, assignee, resolution, priority, fixVersion, sprint, custom fields with history — but not comment text, and historically not all custom field types). Reporting limitations: (1) They answer "did X happen" / "was it ever Y", not "how long was it in state Y" — you can't get cycle time, time-in-status, or age-in-column from JQL alone; that needs the Control Chart, a time-in-status app, or exporting the changelog. (2) You can't ORDER BY or aggregate on historical values — JQL returns a flat issue list, so "average time to resolve by month" isn't a JQL query. (3) DURING windows are inclusive/edge-case-sensitive and time-zone dependent. (4) History is only as good as the changelog — bulk edits, imports, and some automation/API writes may not create the change items you expect, so WAS/CHANGED can miss transitions that happened via those paths. (5) Deleted statuses/users still appear in history but by ID/name and can be awkward to match. (6) Performance: on large instances, unbounded WAS/CHANGED queries are slow — always add a positive selective clause and a date bound. For real flow metrics, use the built-in agile reports (Control Chart, CFD, cycle time), a marketplace time-in-status app, or pipe the changelog to a data warehouse; use WAS/CHANGED for targeted questions like "issues a specific person moved to Done last sprint".

Epics, Stories, Sub-tasks & Hierarchy

How Jira models "big thing → smaller things", and where the model runs out.

Notes

The default three levels

LevelTypeRole
Epic (level 1)EpicA body of work delivered over multiple sprints; groups stories.
Standard (level 0)Story / Task / BugA sprint-sized deliverable; the unit of estimation and board flow.
Sub-task (level −1)Sub-taskExecution breakdown of one story; can't stand alone.
Initiative  PROJ-10   "Unified checkout"          (Premium only)
  Epic      PROJ-20   "Payments revamp"           parent = PROJ-10
    Story   PROJ-140  "Card read path"    5 pts   parent = PROJ-20
      Sub-task PROJ-141 "Wire the API"            parent = PROJ-140
    Story   PROJ-142  "Reconciliation"   3 pts   parent = PROJ-20
# GET /rest/api/3/issue/PROJ-20?fields=subtasks  ->  its stories (Cloud unified 'parent')

How the links work

  • Sub-task → parent: a hard containment. The sub-task's parent is its story; it moves/clones with it; it shows nested on the board and issue view.
  • Story → Epic: historically the "Epic Link" custom field (company-managed classic); newer Jira (and team-managed, and the unified data model) uses "Parent" for this too. Cloud has largely unified on parent for both story→epic and sub-task→story.
  • Issue links (blocks, is blocked by, relates to, duplicates, clones) are peer relationships, not hierarchy — they don't roll up progress and can cross projects.
# HIERARCHY: parent -> rolls up, drags children on move
POST /rest/api/3/issue/PROJ-141  { "fields": { "parent": { "key": "PROJ-140" } } }

# PEER LINK: no rollup, can cross projects, purely informational
POST /rest/api/3/issueLink
{ "type": { "name": "Blocks" },
  "inwardIssue":  { "key": "WEB-9" },
  "outwardIssue": { "key": "API-3" } }        # WEB-9 "is blocked by" API-3

Above the epic

  • Base Jira stops at Epic. Advanced Roadmaps (Premium) adds configurable higher levels — commonly Initiative above Epic, and you can add more (e.g. Theme). These use parent links up the chain.
  • Without Premium, people fake higher levels with issue links or labels — which don't roll up and are fragile.
# Premium: extra levels are real hierarchy, queryable
issuetype = Initiative AND statusCategory != Done
issueFunction in portfolioChildrenOf("issuetype = Initiative")   # (Structure/plugin flavour)

# Free workaround (fragile): a label per initiative
labels = "init-unified-checkout"     # no rollup, no timeline, breaks on typos

Rollup & progress

  • Epic progress on the board/roadmap = count (or estimate sum) of child issues by status category. Sub-task completion rolls into the story's progress bar.
  • Estimation lives at the story level. Epics aren't usually pointed (their size is the sum of their stories); sub-tasks aren't pointed (they'd double-count).
  • Cross-project epics: a story in project B can belong to an epic in project A (Cloud), but reporting and boards get messier — keep an epic's stories in one project where practical.
# epic progress = children grouped by status category (count OR estimate sum)
children of PROJ-20:
  Done        : 3 stories, 13 pts
  In Progress : 1 story,    5 pts
  To Do       : 2 stories,  8 pts
progress = 13 / (13+5+8) = 50% by points        # NOT: point the epic itself (double counts)

# JQL for the epic burn-up
"Epic Link" = PROJ-20 OR parent = PROJ-20

Practical guidance

  • Epic = a coherent outcome, 2–8 weeks, that you'd describe in one sentence to a stakeholder. If it never finishes, it's a label or a component, not an epic.
  • Story = independently valuable, fits in a sprint, testable. Use INVEST as a checklist.
  • Sub-task = "how", not "what". Use them for coordination within a story (design, backend, frontend, tests) — but don't over-decompose; many teams skip sub-tasks entirely.
  • Don't use sub-tasks to model separate deliverables (they can't be sprinted, ranked, or reported on independently, and moving the parent drags them along).
  • Keep hierarchy shallow: Initiative → Epic → Story → (maybe) Sub-task. Deeper "trees" via links become unmaintainable.
# EPIC: finishable outcome, one sentence
PROJ-20  "Let guests check out without an account"    ~5 weeks   -> good epic
PROJ-99  "Tech debt"                                  never ends -> should be a label

# STORY (INVEST): Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable
"As a guest I can pay with a saved card"   3 pts, fits a sprint, has acceptance criteria

# SUB-TASK = "how", within one story; many teams skip them entirely
PROJ-140 sub-tasks: [design, backend, frontend, e2e-tests]   # not separate deliverables
Cheat Sheet
  • Levels: Epic (1) → Story/Task/Bug (0) → Sub-task (−1). Premium adds Initiative+ above via Advanced Roadmaps.
  • Sub-task → parent = hard containment (moves/clones with parent, not on backlog alone). Story → Epic = "Epic Link" (classic) / parent (modern/Cloud).
  • Issue links (blocks / relates to / duplicates) = peer relationships, no rollup, can cross projects.
  • Estimate at the story level. Epic size = sum of stories; don't point epics or sub-tasks.
  • Epic progress = child issues by status category (count or estimate sum).
  • Epic = a finishable outcome (2–8 wks, one sentence). Never-ending → use a label/component. Story = INVEST. Sub-task = "how" not "what".
  • Don't model separate deliverables as sub-tasks (can't sprint/rank/report on them independently).
Q&A
What's the difference between a sub-task and an issue link?
A sub-task is a child in the hierarchy — it's owned by its parent story, contributes to its progress, moves and clones with it, and can't exist alone. An issue link (blocks, relates to, duplicates) is a peer relationship between two independent issues; it conveys dependency or relatedness but no ownership or rollup, and it can span projects.
How do you model something bigger than an epic?
With Jira Premium's Advanced Roadmaps, which adds configurable levels above Epic (typically "Initiative"), linked by the parent field. Without Premium there's no native level above Epic — teams approximate it with labels, components, or issue links, none of which roll up progress.
At which level do you put story points?
The story (standard issue) level. Epics are sized implicitly by the sum of their stories; sub-tasks aren't estimated because that would double-count the story's work. Some teams put remaining time on sub-tasks for a separate task-level burndown, but points stay on stories.
Why shouldn't you use sub-tasks to represent separate features?
Sub-tasks can't be added to a sprint independently, can't be ranked on the backlog, don't show as their own board cards in the normal flow, don't get their own epic link, and are dragged around whenever the parent moves or is cloned. Separate deliverables need to be standard issues (stories/tasks) so they can be planned, prioritised, and reported on individually.
What does an epic's progress bar actually measure?
The proportion of its child issues that are Done, either by count or by summed estimate depending on the view/config. Sub-task completion feeds into each story's own progress, which feeds the epic's. Issue-linked items are not counted.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What are the three default hierarchy levels?
Epic → Story/Task/Bug → Sub-task.
Does a "blocks" link create hierarchy?
No — it's a peer relationship with no rollup.
What's needed to have a level above Epic?
Jira Premium / Advanced Roadmaps (adds Initiative and configurable levels).

Intermediate core

A team has "epics" that have been open for 8 months and keep growing. What's wrong and how do you fix it?
Those aren't epics — an epic should represent a finishable outcome delivered over a few weeks to a couple of months. An 8-month ever-growing container is really a theme / product area / component (e.g. "Search", "Billing"). Fixes: (1) Convert the long-lived container to a component or label (or a Premium Initiative if you need rollup and roadmap placement). (2) Carve the actual work into real epics with clear done criteria and target releases ("Search: add filters", "Search: relevance v2"), each closable in 2–8 weeks. (3) Re-parent the existing stories to the new epics; close the old mega-epic. (4) Going forward, add a definition-of-done and a target version to every epic at creation, and review epics that have been open > N sprints in backlog refinement. Never-closing epics break epic burn-up, roadmap forecasting, and "what did we ship" reporting.
How would you represent a cross-team feature where the frontend work is in project WEB and the backend in project API?
Options: (1) One epic, stories in both projects (Cloud allows a story's parent epic to be in another project). Put the epic in whichever project "owns" the feature; create WEB stories and API stories under it. Rollup works, but each team's board (filtered to its project) only shows its slice, and estimation/velocity stay per team. Watch that both projects' workflows/statuses are compatible enough for a shared epic view. (2) An epic per project, linked ("WEB epic" relates to "API epic", or an Initiative above both in Premium). Cleaner per-team ownership and reporting; the coordination point is the Initiative or the link, and you track combined progress at that level. (3) Use issue links ("WEB-123 is blocked by API-456") for the actual dependencies regardless of epic structure, so sequencing is visible on both boards. Recommendation: if you have Premium, an Initiative containing one epic per project is the cleanest; otherwise two linked epics plus dependency links between the stories, and a shared filter/dashboard to see the whole feature.

Advanced deep

Design an issue hierarchy and linking convention for a 200-engineer org doing quarterly planning, so roadmaps roll up and teams stay autonomous.
Levels (Advanced Roadmaps / Premium): Theme (optional, strategic, annual) → Initiative (a quarter-ish cross-team outcome, owned by a PM/lead) → Epic (a single team's 2–8 week deliverable, owned by that team) → Story/Task/Bug (sprint-sized, team's board unit) → Sub-task (optional, team's choice, execution only). Each level links up via parent. Ownership rule: an Epic and everything under it lives in one team's project; Initiatives live in a shared "Portfolio" project and have child epics across many team projects. This keeps team boards/velocity/workflows fully autonomous while the portfolio rolls up. Dependencies: use issue links ("is blocked by" / "blocks") between the specific stories/epics that actually depend on each other — not hierarchy. Advanced Roadmaps visualises these on the timeline and flags scheduling conflicts. A convention: dependencies are declared at the epic level for planning and refined to story level during execution. Estimation: points at story level only; team velocity forecasts the team's epics; Advanced Roadmaps rolls epic estimates/dates up to Initiatives with per-team capacity. Initiatives get a coarse T-shirt size and a target quarter, not points. Fields/labels: a "Team" field (or component) on every issue for cross-project slicing; a "Target Version"/"Fix Version" per team for release tracking; an "Initiative" is the parent, not a label. Quarterly planning: PMs define/adjust Initiatives in the Portfolio project; teams break them into Epics on their own projects and rank them; Advanced Roadmaps produces the combined timeline with dependencies and capacity, and scenario planning for trade-offs. Reporting: portfolio dashboards on Initiative status (child epic rollup), epic burn-up per team, dependency risk (open "blocked by" links crossing team boundaries), and a "no parent" hygiene filter. Governance: every Epic must have a parent Initiative (or an explicit "keep the lights on" bucket) and a done definition; every Initiative has an owner and target quarter; a monthly review closes stale epics and re-parents orphans. The result: teams run their own boards, workflows, and sprints untouched; the hierarchy plus links give leadership a rolled-up, dependency-aware roadmap without forcing process uniformity.
Cloud unified "Epic Link" and sub-task parent into a single parent field. What broke or changed, and what should teams watch for?
Historically, company-managed classic Jira had two distinct mechanisms: a custom field "Epic Link" connected a story to its epic, while "Parent" connected a sub-task to its story. Team-managed projects and the newer unified data model use one parent field for both story→epic and sub-task→story. Consequences and things to watch: (1) JQL — queries and filters written against "Epic Link" = KEY or the issuesInEpics() / parentEpic() functions may need to become parent = KEY (or use the newer parent in (...)); Atlassian kept some backward-compatible aliases but not everywhere, and third-party gadgets/apps that hard-coded "Epic Link" can break. (2) Automation rules referencing the Epic Link field or smart values like {{issue.epic.key}} vs {{issue.parent.key}} — audit and update. (3) CSV import mappings and REST API payloads — the API moved from the Epic Link custom field ID to fields.parent; integration code and scripts need updating. (4) Reports/dashboards and saved filters grouping by "Epic Link" — recheck. (5) Naming confusion — "Parent" now means different things depending on the issue's level, so UI and training need to be clear (a story's parent is an epic; a sub-task's parent is a story). (6) Advanced Roadmaps already used parent up the chain, so higher levels are consistent, but mixed old/new projects in one plan can behave inconsistently during transition. (7) Marketplace apps — some lagged the change; verify epic-related app features still populate. Practical steps for a team: inventory all filters/gadgets/automation/integrations mentioning "Epic Link" or epic, test them after the change, update to parent, and update any internal docs/runbooks. Data itself isn't lost — the relationships carry over — but anything that queried or wrote the old field needs attention.

Agile Reports & Metrics

Burndown, velocity, cumulative flow, control chart — what each shows and how to misread it.

Notes

Scrum reports

ReportShowsRead it for
Sprint BurndownRemaining work (points or issue count) vs time, with a guideline to zero and a scope-change lineAre we on track? Is scope creeping? Late-sprint cliff = stories only closed at the end
Sprint ReportCommitted vs completed vs incomplete vs added/removed; per-issue outcomeRetro facts: what we said, what we did, what changed
Velocity ChartCommitted vs completed points per sprint (last ~7)Forecasting (rolling average); consistency of estimation
Epic Burndown / Burnup & Release BurndownProgress toward an epic or version over sprints, incl. scope addedWill this epic/release land? How much is scope growth vs delivery?
# healthy burndown: steady descent toward the guideline
pts | 34 *
    | 27  *. .          . = ideal guideline
    | 20    *   .        * = actual remaining
    |  8      *----+     +--+ = scope added mid-sprint (the scope-change line)
    |  0        *  +--*
    +--------------------- day 1 ........ 10
# late cliff (actual flat, then drops to 0 on day 10) = stories only closed at the end

Kanban / flow reports

ReportShows
Cumulative Flow Diagram (CFD)Stacked count of issues in each status category over time. Band width = WIP in that stage; band widening = a bottleneck; vertical distance between top and bottom = total WIP; horizontal distance ≈ approximate lead time.
Control ChartCycle time (or lead time) per completed issue, with a rolling average and standard-deviation band. Outliers = investigate. Trend down = flow improving.
Cycle time report (newer boards)Distribution / scatter of cycle times, often with percentiles (e.g. "85% of issues finish within 6 days").
# CFD read: a WIDENING band = the bottleneck stage
count
  |            ____ Done
  |         __/
  |     ___/______  In Review   <- this band keeps widening = review is the bottleneck
  |  __/__________  In Progress
  | /_____________  To Do
  +----------------------- time
# vertical gap (To Do top .. Done bottom) = total WIP;  horizontal gap ~ lead time

Definitions

  • Lead time: from request created (or committed) to delivered — the customer's wait.
  • Cycle time: from work started (entered In Progress) to done — the team's active time. Jira's Control Chart lets you pick the start/end statuses.
  • Throughput: issues completed per unit time.
  • WIP: items in progress at once. Little's Law: avg cycle time ≈ WIP / throughput — lower WIP → shorter cycle time.
# Little's Law, worked
WIP = 18 issues in progress
throughput = 6 issues/week
avg cycle time = 18 / 6 = 3 weeks

# cut WIP to 9 (same team, same throughput):
avg cycle time = 9 / 6 = 1.5 weeks     # nothing else changed - just stop starting

Gotchas / how these mislead

  • Burndown by issue count hides that remaining issues are the big ones; by points hides that points were re-estimated mid-sprint.
  • Velocity only counts fully-done issues; a flat line at 0 for a sprint usually means "everything carried over", not "no work".
  • Control Chart cycle time depends on the chosen start/end columns and is skewed by items that sat in a status over a weekend/holiday, or were reopened (a second trip through).
  • CFD needs the board's columns to match real workflow stages; a giant "In Progress" column with everything in it tells you nothing.
  • All of these break if the team games statuses (bulk-moving to Done at sprint end, skipping "In Review").
  • Comparing any of these across teams is invalid — different point scales, workflows, and DoD.
# the "0 velocity" that isn't zero work
Sprint 21: 6 stories, all 90% done, none CLOSED  ->  Velocity chart shows 0
# reality: ~25 pts of work happened; it all carried over

# cycle time skew: an issue reopened mid-flow
PROJ-88: In Progress (2d) -> Done -> reopened -> In Progress (3d) -> Done
# Control Chart may show ~5d or ~8d depending on start/end status choice + weekend span

What to actually watch

Trend, not absolute: is cycle time stable or drifting? Is WIP creeping up? Is scope-change on the burndown consistently large? Is velocity predictable (variance low) rather than "high"? Predictability beats magnitude.

# predictability > magnitude
Team A: velocity 40, 12, 55, 20, 48   avg 35, stdev ~17   -> can't plan
Team B: velocity 24, 26, 23, 25, 27   avg 25, stdev ~1.4  -> commit ~24, hit it

# the four trend questions, as things to chart over ~8 sprints:
cycle_time_p85   (flat or down = good)
avg_WIP          (creeping up = warning)
scope_change_pts (consistently >20% of commit = planning problem)
velocity_stdev   (low = predictable)
Cheat Sheet
  • Burndown: remaining work vs time + scope-change line. Late cliff = batch-closing at end.
  • Sprint Report: committed vs done vs incomplete vs added — retro facts.
  • Velocity: committed vs completed points/sprint; rolling avg to forecast; only fully-done counts.
  • CFD: band width = WIP per stage; widening band = bottleneck; top–bottom gap = total WIP; horizontal = ~lead time.
  • Control Chart: cycle time per issue + rolling avg ± stdev; pick start/end statuses; watch outliers & trend.
  • Lead time = created→done (customer wait). Cycle time = started→done (team active). Little's Law: cycle ≈ WIP / throughput.
  • Never compare metrics across teams. Value predictability (low variance) over big numbers.
Q&A
What does the scope-change line on a burndown tell you?
How much work was added to (or removed from) the sprint after it started. A burndown that isn't dropping might be fine if the flat part coincides with a jump in scope — the team is delivering but new work keeps arriving. Persistently large scope change means planning or interruption problems.
Lead time vs cycle time?
Lead time is the whole wait from when a request is created (or accepted) until it's delivered — what the requester experiences. Cycle time is the subset from when the team actually starts work (enters "In Progress") to done — the team's active handling time. Lead time includes backlog/queue time; cycle time doesn't.
How do you read a Cumulative Flow Diagram?
Each coloured band is a workflow stage; its vertical thickness at any date is how many issues are in that stage (WIP). A band that keeps widening over time is a bottleneck — work enters faster than it leaves. The vertical gap between the very top and bottom lines is total WIP; the horizontal gap between where a given quantity enters and exits approximates lead time. Parallel, roughly constant-width bands = healthy steady flow.
What does Little's Law imply for a team with long cycle times?
Cycle time ≈ WIP / throughput. If throughput (completion rate) is roughly fixed by capacity, the fastest lever to cut cycle time is to reduce WIP — start fewer things at once, enforce column limits, finish before starting. Adding more parallel work increases WIP and therefore cycle time.
Why can't you compare two teams' velocities?
Story points are calibrated to each team's own reference stories, skills, and codebase, and each team has its own workflow and definition of done. Team A's "20" and Team B's "20" represent different amounts of work, so the numbers aren't on the same scale. Compare a team only to its own history.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which report forecasts how much a team can take on next sprint?
The Velocity Chart (rolling average of completed points).
On a CFD, what does a widening band indicate?
A bottleneck at that stage — work is entering faster than it leaves.
Cycle time starts when an issue enters which status category?
In Progress (work actually started).

Intermediate core

A sprint burndown is flat for 8 days then drops straight to zero on the last day. What happened and what do you change?
Classic "big-bang" delivery: stories weren't being closed incrementally — either work was genuinely all finishing at once (stories too big / too interdependent), or the team wasn't updating statuses until the end, or everything piled up in "In Review" and got approved on the last day. Changes: (1) Slice stories smaller so several close every couple of days — target multiple items done by mid-sprint. (2) Enforce WIP limits and a "finish before you start" norm so work flows through Review instead of batching. (3) Make status updates a daily habit (or automate via PR/branch triggers) so the burndown reflects reality. (4) Watch the CFD — a fat "In Review" band confirms a review bottleneck; add reviewer capacity or a review SLA. (5) In the retro, check whether the sprint goal was actually met or just "everything got marked done". The flat-then-cliff shape means you have no early signal if the sprint is off track — that's the real risk to fix.
Leadership asks you to report "average cycle time" as a KPI and drive it down. What caveats do you raise and how do you set it up responsibly?
Caveats: (1) Cycle time depends entirely on the chosen start and end statuses — "In Progress→Done" vs "Committed→Released" give very different numbers; pick one and hold it constant. (2) The average is skewed by a few huge outliers; report the distribution and percentiles (median, 85th) instead — "85% of items finish within 6 days" is more honest and actionable. (3) It's gameable: split work into tiny issues, skip "In Review", or mark done early — so pair it with quality signals (reopen rate, escaped defects, review coverage). (4) Weekends/holidays and "waiting on customer" time inflate it — decide whether to use calendar or working days and whether to exclude explicit "blocked/waiting" statuses. (5) Reopened issues make two trips; decide how to count them. (6) Don't compare teams. Setup: define start = enters "In Progress", end = enters "Done", working days, exclude a "Blocked"/"Waiting" status if you have one; use the Control Chart / Cycle Time report per team; track the trend of the median and 85th percentile over rolling 4–8 weeks, not a single number; present alongside throughput and reopen rate so "faster" can't come at the cost of "worse". Frame it as a team-improvement signal in retros, not an individual or cross-team scorecard.

Advanced deep

Jira's built-in agile reports are limited (per-board, per-sprint, no cross-team roll-up, weak percentiles). Design a metrics pipeline that fixes this.
Source: extract issue data and, crucially, the changelog (status transitions with timestamps and author) via the Jira REST API (or Cloud's data connectors / a marketplace exporter) on a schedule. The changelog is what lets you compute time-in-status, cycle/lead time with any status boundaries, reopen counts, and flow efficiency — things JQL can't. Model: land it in a warehouse (BigQuery/Snowflake/Postgres) as fact tables: issue, issue_status_history (issue, from_status, to_status, entered_at, duration), sprint_membership, plus dimensions (team, project, type, epic, initiative). Derive per-issue metrics: lead time (created→first Done), cycle time (first In Progress→Done), time in each status, number of Done→reopen transitions, whether it left/re-entered the sprint. Metrics layer: compute rolling percentiles (p50/p85/p95) of cycle & lead time per team per week; throughput (Done count/week); WIP over time (from history, count issues In Progress on each day) and flow efficiency (active time / total time); scope-change and say/do ratio per sprint; aging WIP (oldest unfinished item per stage); dependency/blocked time. Roll up epics→initiatives for delivery forecasts (Monte Carlo on historical throughput for "when will these N items be done, with confidence bands" — far better than velocity math). Presentation: dashboards (Looker/Grafana/Power BI) with team-level trend views, a portfolio view of initiative burn-up + forecast, and a "flow health" scorecard (cycle time trend, WIP trend, aging items, reopen rate). Explicitly no cross-team leaderboards. Governance: consistent status→category mapping across teams (or a per-team config table so boundaries are comparable), document each metric's definition, refresh daily, and validate against Jira's own Control Chart for a couple of teams as a sanity check. This gives cross-team roll-ups, proper percentiles, forecasting, and historical flexibility that the built-in per-board reports can't.
Explain flow efficiency and aging work-in-progress, why they often reveal more than cycle time or velocity, and how to surface them in Jira.
Flow efficiency = active (working) time ÷ total elapsed time for an item, as a percentage. Most teams discover it's shockingly low — often 15–40% — meaning items spend the majority of their life waiting (in queue columns, blocked, waiting for review, waiting on another team, waiting for deploy). This is more revealing than cycle time alone because it tells you where the time goes: if flow efficiency is 20%, hiring faster developers or working harder barely moves cycle time — you have to attack the queues and hand-offs. It's more revealing than velocity because velocity can look fine while every item still takes 3 weeks wall-clock due to waiting. Aging WIP = for every currently-unfinished item, how long has it been in progress (or in its current status). A simple chart of "days in progress" per open item, or the oldest item per column, surfaces stuck work now, while you can still act — unlike cycle time, which only tells you about items that already finished (a lagging indicator). An item aging well past the team's 85th-percentile cycle time is a live risk: escalate, unblock, split, or swarm it. Surfacing in Jira: (1) Flow efficiency needs the changelog — classify each status as "active" or "queue/wait", then compute active vs total from status history (a marketplace time-in-status app, or the warehouse pipeline). Add explicit "Waiting"/"Blocked" statuses so wait time is measurable rather than hidden inside "In Progress". (2) Aging WIP: a board quick filter or a dashboard filter gadget like statusCategory = "In Progress" AND status CHANGED TO "In Progress" BEFORE -5d ORDER BY updated; or use a board with card-age indicators / a marketplace "aging" gadget; or the newer Jira board's built-in "days in column" on cards. Review aging items daily at standup ("what's our oldest item and what does it need?"), and review flow efficiency + queue widths (from the CFD) in retros. The combination — where time is lost (flow efficiency / CFD) plus what's stuck right now (aging WIP) — drives concrete process fixes (review SLA, reduce hand-offs, WIP limits) in a way that a single cycle-time or velocity number never does.

Automation Rules

No-code "when this, if that, do this" rules — the modern replacement for most workflow scripting.

Notes

Rule structure

TRIGGER  (what starts the rule)
  → CONDITION(s)   (gate: stop if not met)
  → BRANCH        (optional: operate on related issues)
      → CONDITION
      → ACTION(s)
  → ACTION(s)     (do the thing)

Triggers

  • Issue events: created, updated, transitioned, assigned, commented, field value changed, linked.
  • Scheduled: cron or interval, optionally with a JQL to act on a set of issues each run.
  • Dev events: branch created, commit created, PR created/merged/declined, build/deployment status.
  • Incoming webhook: external system calls a rule URL (with a payload & optional issue list).
  • Manual: a button on the issue ("Run rule"), SLA threshold (JSM), form submitted, on a schedule.
# scheduled trigger with a JQL (acts on each matched issue every run)
Trigger: Scheduled
  cron:  0 9 * * 1-5                       # weekdays 09:00
  JQL:   resolution = EMPTY AND updated <= -5d AND status = "In Progress"

# dev trigger
Trigger: Pull request merged
  -> Condition: {{pullRequest.destinationBranch}} equals "main"
  -> Action: Transition issue to "In Review"

Conditions & branches

  • Conditions: JQL condition, issue-fields condition, user condition, "related issues" condition (e.g. all sub-tasks are Done), advanced compare ({{smart value}} vs value).
  • Branches: re-scope the rest of the rule to related issues — sub-tasks, parent, epic, stories in epic, linked issues (by link type), or a JQL. Actions inside the branch run once per matched issue.
  • The "For current issue" vs branch distinction is the #1 source of bugs — forgetting a branch means you edit the trigger issue instead of the parent/children.
Trigger: Issue transitioned  (a sub-task -> Done)
  Branch: Parent                              # re-scope to the parent story
    Condition: {{issue.subtasks.size}} equals {{issue.subtasks.Done.size}}  # all done?
    Action:  Transition parent to "Done"
# WITHOUT the branch, "Transition to Done" would fire on the SUB-TASK (already Done) - no-op,
# and the parent never moves. The branch is the whole point.

Actions

Edit issue / transition / assign / comment / add or remove label / create issue / create sub-tasks / clone / link issues / send email / send Slack or Teams message / send web request (outbound REST) / log action / set entity property / re-fetch issue data / lookup issues ({{lookupIssues}}) / create variable.

# Action: Send web request (outbound REST) — e.g. ping an external system
POST https://hooks.corp/jira
headers:  Content-Type: application/json
body:     { "key": "{{issue.key}}", "status": "{{issue.status.name}}",
            "assignee": "{{issue.assignee.emailAddress}}" }

# Action: Edit issue
fields:   { "labels": ["auto-triaged"], "priority": { "name": "Highest" } }

Smart values

{{issue.key}}  {{issue.summary}}  {{issue.assignee.displayName}}
{{issue.fields.customfield_10021}}   {{issue.Story Points}}
{{now}}  {{now.plusBusinessDays(3)}}
{{issue.fixVersions.name}}           {{#if}}  {{/}}  {{^}} (else)
{{fieldChange.fromString}}  {{fieldChange.toString}}
{{webhookData.some.path}}  {{triggerIssue.key}}
{{lookupIssues.size}}  {{#lookupIssues}}{{key}} {{/}}
{{sprint.name}}  {{comment.body}}

Smart values support text functions, math, list iteration ({{#list}}…{{/}}), conditionals, and date math — a small templating language.

Common recipes

  • When all sub-tasks → Done, transition the parent to Done (trigger: sub-task transitioned; branch: parent; condition: all sub-tasks Done).
  • When a story moves to In Progress, set the assignee, add it to the active sprint, comment on the epic.
  • Scheduled: find issues updated <= -5d AND status = "In Progress" → comment "@assignee still active?" and add a "stale" label.
  • On PR merged → transition to In Review; on deployment to prod → transition to Done and set Fix Version.
  • Sync a field from parent to all children on change (branch: children; edit issue).
  • Auto-triage: on create, if summary ~ "outage" set priority Highest, assign to on-call, notify Slack.
# auto-triage rule, end to end
Trigger:   Issue created
Condition: {{issue.summary}} matches "(?i)outage|down|sev1"
Action:    Edit issue -> priority = Highest, labels += incident
Action:    Assign issue -> user from lookup: on-call schedule
Action:    Send Slack message -> #incidents
             "{{issue.key}} {{issue.summary}} — assigned {{issue.assignee.displayName}}"

Scope, limits & gotchas

  • Rules are single-project, multi-project, or global (admin). Broad scope + broad trigger = lots of executions.
  • Execution limits (Cloud): monthly rule-run quotas by plan; heavy rules get throttled/queued. Watch the audit log for failures and "no actions performed".
  • Loop protection: by default a rule's own edits don't re-trigger it; "Allow rule trigger" on an action can create loops — use carefully. Rule chaining (rule A's action triggers rule B) is allowed but can cascade.
  • Actor: actions run as the "Automation for Jira" app user (or a chosen actor) — needs permission on the target project; shows as that user in history and notifications.
  • Prefer automation over workflow post-functions/scripts for maintainability — unless you need the change to be atomic with a transition.
# the loop: an "Edit issue" action with "Allow rule trigger" ON, on an "Issue updated" rule
Trigger: Issue updated  ->  Action: Edit issue (set field)  [Allow rule trigger: ON]
#   edit fires "updated" -> rule runs -> edits -> "updated" -> ...  quota burned in minutes

# safe default: rule's own edits do NOT re-trigger it. Check the audit log:
Automation > Audit log  ->  status: SUCCESS | NO ACTIONS PERFORMED | SOME ERRORS
# actor = "Automation for Jira" (or chosen) must have Browse+Edit on the target project
Cheat Sheet
  • Rule = trigger → condition(s) → optional branch (related issues) → action(s).
  • Triggers: issue events, scheduled (+ JQL), dev events (PR/branch/deploy), incoming webhook, manual/SLA/form.
  • Branch re-scopes to sub-tasks / parent / epic / linked / JQL; actions run once per matched issue. Forgetting the branch = editing the wrong issue (the #1 bug).
  • Actions: edit/transition/assign/comment/label/create/clone/link/email/Slack/send web request/lookup issues.
  • Smart values: {{issue.key}}, {{issue.Story Points}}, {{now.plusBusinessDays(3)}}, {{fieldChange.toString}}, {{#lookupIssues}}…{{/}}, {{#if}}.
  • Scope: single / multi-project / global (admin). Cloud has monthly execution quotas; check the audit log.
  • Actions run as an actor (default "Automation for Jira") that needs permissions. Rule edits don't re-trigger unless you opt in (loop risk).
  • Prefer automation over post-functions/scripts unless the change must be atomic with a transition.
Q&A
What is a branch in an automation rule?
A step that changes which issue(s) the following conditions and actions apply to — from the trigger issue to related issues: its sub-tasks, its parent, its epic, stories in the epic, linked issues of a given type, or issues matching a JQL. Actions inside the branch execute once per matched related issue.
Why did my rule edit the wrong issue?
You almost certainly forgot a branch. Without one, every action operates on the issue that fired the trigger. To update the parent when a sub-task changes, you must add a "Branch: parent" step; to update children, "Branch: sub-tasks". This is the most common automation mistake.
How do you make a rule run over many issues on a schedule?
Use the Scheduled trigger with a cron/interval and tick "run a JQL search"; provide the JQL (e.g. stale issues). The rule then iterates the matching issues and runs the actions for each. Mind execution limits if the result set is large.
What are smart values?
A templating syntax ({{issue.key}}, {{now.plusDays(1)}}, {{fieldChange.toString}}…) for pulling data from the issue, the trigger, webhook payloads, and lookups into action fields — with text/date/math functions, list iteration, and conditionals. They're how you make actions dynamic.
Which user performs the actions, and why does it matter?
By default the "Automation for Jira" app account (you can override the actor per rule). That account must have permission on the target project or the action fails silently (check the audit log). It also appears as the author of comments, transitions, and notifications, which can confuse people or trip other rules that filter by user.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What are the three main parts of a rule?
Trigger, condition(s), action(s) — plus optional branches.
Where do you check why a rule didn't do anything?
The rule's audit log.
What smart value gives the current issue's key?
{{issue.key}}.

Intermediate core

Build the rule: when every sub-task of a story is Done, move the story to Done and comment on its epic.
Trigger: Issue transitioned — To status = Done, and restrict to issue type = Sub-task (add a "Issue fields condition: Issue Type is Sub-task" if the trigger can't). Branch: parent (the story). Condition inside the branch: "Related issues condition" → Sub-tasks → "all match" JQL statusCategory = Done (i.e. no sub-task is not-done). Also guard: parent's status is not already Done. Action (still in the parent branch): Transition issue to Done (choose the right transition; if none valid from current status, the rule logs an error — handle with a condition on the parent's current status). Then Branch: epic (parent of the story) → Action: Add comment — Story {{issue.parent.key}} completed: {{issue.parent.summary}} (or use a saved variable captured before the epic branch, since inside the epic branch {{issue}} is the epic). Edge cases: stories with zero sub-tasks (the "all done" condition is vacuously true — add "sub-tasks count > 0"); the transition not existing from certain statuses; and avoiding a loop if a Done transition itself fires other rules.
A global rule triggered on "issue updated" is hitting execution limits. How do you fix it?
"Issue updated" fires on every field change on every issue in every project — enormous volume. Fixes: (1) Use a more specific trigger — "Field value changed" for just the field you care about, or "Issue transitioned", or "Issue created". (2) Narrow the scope — make it a single- or multi-project rule instead of global, covering only projects that need it. (3) Add cheap early conditions — an issue-fields or JQL condition right after the trigger so the rule exits fast for non-matching issues (conditions are cheaper than actions but the run still counts; the bigger win is the specific trigger). (4) If it's really "react to any change of type X", consider a scheduled rule that batch-processes matching issues every N minutes instead of reacting in real time — far fewer executions. (5) Split into targeted per-project rules owned by those teams. (6) Check for rule chaining / loops inflating the count. (7) On Cloud, review the plan's monthly limit and the automation usage dashboard to see which rules dominate. General principle: the trigger should be as specific as possible; "issue updated" + global is an anti-pattern.

Advanced deep

An org has 400+ automation rules with lots of overlap, silent failures, and occasional loops. Design a cleanup and governance model.
Inventory: export all rules (REST API / the automation admin view). For each capture: scope (project/multi/global), trigger, actions, owner, last executed, success/failure counts, and monthly executions. Triage: (a) Dead — never executed in 90 days or always no-op → disable, then delete after a grace period. (b) Failing — audit log shows permission errors, invalid transitions, missing fields → fix or retire; the "Automation for Jira" actor needs project permissions everywhere it acts. (c) Overlapping — multiple rules reacting to the same trigger doing similar things (three rules all set assignee on create) → consolidate into one, or into a shared library rule. (d) Over-scoped — global rules that should be project rules; broad triggers ("issue updated") that should be specific → tighten. (e) Loop-prone — rules with "Allow rule trigger" on an edit action, or A→B→A chains → add guard conditions (only act if value differs), remove unnecessary re-trigger, document intended chains. Consolidate: define a small set of global rules for genuinely org-wide behaviour (SLA breach notifications, security-label handling), owned by the platform team; everything else is a project rule owned by that team. Use rule labels/naming conventions ([team] purpose) and put shared logic in fewer, well-documented rules. Governance going forward: (1) A request/review process for new global rules; project admins can create project rules freely but within guidance. (2) A monthly automation health dashboard: executions by rule, failure rate, quota usage, newly-failing rules → owners get alerted. (3) Naming + description standards; every rule states its purpose and owner. (4) A "no broad-trigger global rules" policy; prefer specific triggers and scheduled batch rules for bulk work. (5) Loop-safety checklist for reviewers. (6) Periodic (quarterly) prune of unused/failing rules. (7) Where a rule is really doing complex synchronous logic, evaluate whether it belongs as a workflow validator/post-function or an app instead. Execution: disable in waves with comms, keep an export to restore, and monitor the audit logs and quota after each wave.
Compare automation "send web request" + incoming webhooks against a real integration (app / middleware) for connecting Jira to other systems. When is each right?
Automation web request / webhook: a rule action POSTs JSON (built with smart values) to an external URL on some Jira event; an incoming-webhook trigger lets an external system push data into a rule (optionally with an issue list) which then edits issues. Pros: no code deployment, lives with your other rules, quick to build, good for simple one-directional notifications and light sync ("on transition to Done, notify our billing service"; "when CI calls this webhook, comment and transition"). Cons: (1) Reliability — limited ret/backoff on failed web requests, subject to automation execution quotas and throttling, and failures are only visible in the audit log (no alerting unless you build it). (2) Auth — you store a secret/token in the rule; limited to what headers/body you can template. (3) No state — can't easily do multi-step conversations, pagination, reconciliation, or dedupe; each run is stateless. (4) Payload limits and smart-value templating quirks for complex bodies. (5) Loose coupling to volume — a burst of events can hit quotas or rate-limit the target. (6) Hard to unit-test and version-control. Real integration (Marketplace app, or your own middleware / iPaaS like Workato/Zapier/n8n, or a service using the Jira REST API + registered webhooks): Pros: proper retries, dead-letter queues, backpressure, observability/alerting, secret management, stateful sync and reconciliation jobs, bidirectional field mapping with conflict handling, testing, and change management. Handles high volume and complex mappings. Cons: something to build/run/pay for; more moving parts; another deploy pipeline. When each: use automation web requests/webhooks for low-volume, low-stakes, mostly-notification or simple-trigger integrations where an occasional missed event is tolerable and you value speed and no-ops. Use a real integration when the sync is business-critical (billing, provisioning, compliance), high-volume, bidirectional, needs guaranteed delivery/reconciliation, involves complex mapping or many systems, or must be tested and audited. A common middle path: automation fires a webhook to your middleware, which owns the reliability, mapping, and state — keeping Jira-side config simple while getting production-grade delivery.

Projects, Schemes & Permissions

How Jira decides what a person can see and do — a stack of reusable schemes bolted onto each project.

Notes

Project styles

Company-managed (classic)Team-managed (next-gen)
ConfigShared schemes, changed by Jira adminsSelf-contained, changed by the project admin
ConsistencyHigh — many projects share one workflow/field/permission schemeLow — each project is its own island
Best forLarge orgs needing governance & cross-project reportingAutonomous teams wanting speed
GET /rest/api/3/project/PROJ?expand=permissions
{ "style": "classic",                       // company-managed
  "permissionScheme": { "id": 10000, "name": "Default software scheme" } }

# team-managed instead:
{ "style": "next-gen" }
# -> no shared schemes; PUT /rest/api/3/project/PROJ/role/{roleId}  edits ONLY this project

The scheme stack (company-managed)

Each project is associated with one of each:

  • Permission scheme — who can do each permission (Browse, Create, Edit, Transition, Assign, Administer, Delete, Manage Sprints…). Grants are to: a project role, a group, a user, "Reporter", "Assignee", "Project Lead", a user custom field, or "Anyone".
  • Notification scheme — who gets emailed on each event.
  • Issue type scheme + issue type screen scheme — allowed types & their screens.
  • Workflow scheme — type → workflow.
  • Field configuration scheme — type → field configuration (required/hidden/default).
  • Screen scheme — operation → screen.
  • Issue security scheme (optional) — per-issue visibility levels.
  • Priority / component / version — some project-scoped, some via scheme.
# one project's scheme bindings (all point to SHARED objects)
PROJ ->
  permissionScheme        = "Default software scheme"
  notificationScheme      = "Default notifications"
  workflowScheme          = "SW: Simplified Workflow Scheme"
  issueTypeScreenScheme   = "SW screen scheme"
  fieldConfigurationScheme = "Default"
  issueSecurityScheme     = (none)
# edit "Default software scheme" -> changes every project bound to it

Roles vs groups

  • Group = global membership list (e.g. jira-software-users), managed centrally; the same everywhere.
  • Project role = a named slot (Administrators, Developers, Users) whose members are set per project. Permission schemes grant to roles; each project decides who's in each role — so one shared permission scheme works for hundreds of projects.
  • Best practice: schemes grant to roles, not groups or users. Then onboarding a project = fill its role memberships; no scheme edits.
# permission scheme grants to a ROLE (reused by 100s of projects)
Permission "Assignable User"   -> role "Developers"
Permission "Administer Projects" -> role "Administrators"

# each project fills that role independently, no scheme edit
POST /rest/api/3/project/PROJ/role/10001      # 10001 = Developers
{ "group": ["team-orion-devs"] }
POST /rest/api/3/project/WEB/role/10001
{ "user": ["accountId:557058:abc"] }

Global permissions & application access

  • Application access: which groups get a Jira Software / JSM / JWM license seat (controls who can log in at all).
  • Global permissions: Administer Jira, Browse Users, Create Shared Objects, Manage Group Filter Subscriptions, Bulk Change.
  • Project permissions (from the permission scheme) are per project; Project admin can manage roles, components, versions, and (limited) some config, but not global schemes.
# three tiers, widest to narrowest
Application access:  group "jira-software-users" -> a license seat (can log in at all)
Global permission:   "Administer Jira" -> group "site-admins"
                     "Browse Users"    -> group "jira-software-users"
Project permission:  "Browse Projects" (scheme) -> role "Users" (per project)
# a user can hold a seat + Browse Users globally, yet see zero issues in a project
# whose permission scheme doesn't grant them Browse Projects

Issue-level security

  • An issue security scheme defines security levels (e.g. "Reporter & Devs only", "Managers"). Setting a level on an issue hides it from everyone not in that level, even if they have Browse Project.
  • Used for sensitive work (HR, security incidents, embargoed features). Default level can be set per project.
# issue security scheme
Level "Restricted"  members: role "Administrators", "Reporter", group "security-team"
Level "Normal"      members: role "Users"

# set the level on an issue -> anyone NOT in that level cannot see it, even with Browse Project
POST /rest/api/3/issue/HR-42  { "fields": { "security": { "id": "10100" } } }  # "Restricted"

# JQL respects it silently: "level = Restricted" returns nothing for outsiders

Gotchas

  • Editing a shared scheme affects every project using it — check the "used by" list first. Copy the scheme if you need a variant.
  • "I can't see the issue" is usually: no Browse permission, an issue security level, or (for a board) an unshared filter.
  • Team-managed projects have their own simplified permission model (roles + "who can access") — not the scheme stack; migrating between styles remaps everything.
  • Granting via group in a scheme is a common source of "why does this contractor have edit rights everywhere".
# "why can this contractor edit everything?"
Permission scheme "Default" -> "Edit Issues" granted to GROUP "jira-software-users"
# every licensed user is in that group -> edit rights on every project on this scheme
# fix: grant to role "Developers" instead, and manage role membership per project

# before editing a shared scheme, check the blast radius:
GET /rest/api/3/permissionscheme/10000   # then Settings > Issues > Permission Schemes
                                          # -> "Projects using this scheme" (often dozens)
Cheat Sheet
  • Company-managed: shared schemes, admin-governed, consistent. Team-managed: per-project config, autonomous, no scheme reuse.
  • Company-managed project = one each of: permission, notification, issue type (+ screen), workflow, field config, screen, optional issue security scheme.
  • Permission scheme grants each permission to: project role / group / user / Reporter / Assignee / Lead / user-field / Anyone.
  • Group = global list. Project role = per-project membership slot. Grant to roles, not groups/users — then onboarding = set role members, no scheme edits.
  • Application access = who gets a license/can log in. Global permissions = Administer Jira, Bulk Change, etc.
  • Issue security level hides an issue from anyone not in that level, overriding Browse Project.
  • Editing a shared scheme hits every project using it — check "used by", or copy first.
Q&A
Group vs project role — why prefer roles in permission schemes?
