The arms race favors attackers with effort. (2) Collisions / low specificity — many real users share a fingerprint (all current Chrome on Windows), and some legit non-browser clients (mobile apps, IoT, API SDKs, monitoring) have "unusual" fingerprints, so blocking on fingerprint alone causes false positives. (3) Drift — browsers change their ClientHello frequently (new ciphers, GREASE randomization, extension shuffling like Chrome's permutation), so fingerprint databases need constant updating and JA3 in particular is brittle to this (part of why JA4 exists). (4) TLS-terminating middleboxes / corporate proxies / VPN clients rewrite the handshake, so the fingerprint reflects the proxy, not the user — misclassifying enterprise users. (5) Shared CDNs/relays (iCloud Private Relay, other privacy proxies) normalize handshakes. (6) It says nothing about intent — a real browser automated by a human-in-the-loop or a legit accessibility tool looks fine. Practical use: treat the fingerprint as one weighted input to a scoring model alongside behavior, challenge outcomes, reputation, and rate — use it to raise friction (challenge) rather than hard-block, keep an allowlist for known-good non-browser clients (your mobile app's SDK, partners, monitoring), keep the fingerprint DB current, and expect to re-tune as browsers and evasion tooling evolve.

Measuring & Tuning CDN Performance

Hit ratio and offload are the levers; RUM tells you if users actually got faster.

Notes

The core metrics

MetricMeaning
Cache hit ratio (by requests & by bytes)hits / total. By-bytes matters for bandwidth cost; by-requests for origin RPS. They can differ a lot (few large misses).
Origin offload1 − (origin requests / total) — the fraction of load the CDN kept off origin.
Edge TTFB / response timeTime to first byte from the edge — hit vs miss split.
Origin latency (edge↔origin)How slow misses are; drives whether more caching or a closer origin helps.
Error ratesEdge 5xx, origin 5xx, timeouts — by PoP and by status.
Bandwidth & request volumeBy PoP/region, for cost and capacity.
# from CDN log analytics
hit_ratio_req  = sum(status="HIT") / count(*)                 # e.g. 0.97
hit_ratio_byte = sum(bytes where status="HIT") / sum(bytes)  # e.g. 0.82  (big files miss)
origin_offload = 1 - (count(origin_request) / count(*))       # 0.96

edge_ttfb_p50_hit  =  8ms
edge_ttfb_p50_miss = 140ms      # miss = a trip to origin -> caching / closer origin helps
error_rate_by_pop  =  ...        # a single PoP spiking = peering issue -> CDN ticket

RUM vs synthetic

  • RUM (Real User Monitoring): actual users' timings (Navigation Timing, Resource Timing, Core Web Vitals — LCP, INP, CLS, TTFB). Reflects real geo/device/network mix. Noisy; needs volume; can't test pre-launch.
  • Synthetic: scripted probes from fixed locations on a schedule. Reproducible, good for regression detection, alerting, and comparing providers/config — but a fixed set of clean nodes isn't your user population.
  • Use both: synthetic for control and alerting, RUM for truth about user experience and geo breakdown.
// RUM: collect real users' timings from the browser
const [nav] = performance.getEntriesByType("navigation");
new PerformanceObserver(l => {
  for (const e of l.getEntries()) beacon({ metric: e.name, value: e.value, geo: navigator.language });
}).observe({ type: "largest-contentful-paint", buffered: true });
beacon({ ttfb: nav.responseStart - nav.requestStart });   // truth, but noisy, needs volume

# synthetic: scripted, from fixed nodes, on a schedule -> reproducible, for alerting
$ webpagetest test https://shop.example --location "London:Chrome" --runs 5

Levers to improve it

  • Raise hit ratio: longer TTLs (s-maxage), immutable hashed assets, cache-key normalization (strip tracking params, don't Vary on high-cardinality), remove Set-Cookie from cacheable responses, micro-cache dynamic, add an origin shield, don't purge-all.
  • Speed up misses: origin shield near origin, warm keep-alive pool, closer/multi-region origin, faster origin, request collapsing, stale-while-revalidate so users don't wait on revalidation.
  • Reduce bytes: Brotli (better than gzip for text; precompress static at build for max level), modern image formats (WebP/AVIF) with content negotiation, responsive images, right-sizing, video codec/bitrate ladder, minification.
  • Protocol: HTTP/2 + HTTP/3, TLS 1.3, session resumption, OCSP stapling.
  • Prioritization & hints: Link: rel=preconnect/preload, 103 Early Hints (edge can send them), correct resource priorities.
  • Fewer round trips: bundle critical CSS, avoid redirect chains (each redirect = a round trip; do redirects at the edge, not origin), consolidate domains to reuse connections.
# raise hit ratio
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable   # hashed assets
cache_key.query_string.include = ["page","lang"]      # strip utm_*/fbclid
unset beresp.http.Set-Cookie for /static/*

# reduce bytes: precompress at build, negotiate image format
$ brotli -q 11 -k dist/*.js dist/*.css                # serve .br, fall back to gzip
Accept: image/avif -> serve .avif  (else .webp, else .jpg)

# fewer round trips: redirect AT THE EDGE, not origin (saves a full RTT)
if (req.url == "/old") return 301 "/new";

Diagnosing

  • Break down hit ratio by path/content-type — find the buckets dragging it down (usually HTML, or an API, or a fragmented asset path).
  • Look at top cache keys by request count and objects per URL to spot fragmentation.
  • Check X-Cache / cache-status headers on real responses; look for MISS, EXPIRED, BYPASS, STALE.
  • Correlate origin RPS spikes with deploys/purges (offload drops).
  • Per-PoP latency outliers → routing/peering issue → CDN ticket.
# hit ratio by content type -> find the bucket dragging it down
SELECT content_type, count(*) t, sum(cache_status='HIT')/count(*) hit_ratio
FROM cdn_logs GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY t DESC
#   text/css   0.99      <- fine
#   text/html  0.41      <- the problem: TTL too short, or Set-Cookie, or Vary

# check a real response's cache state
$ curl -sI https://cdn.example/page | grep -iE "x-cache|cache-status|age|vary"
x-cache: MISS
cache-status: "edge"; fwd=miss; key=...     # RFC 9211 Cache-Status
vary: cookie                                 # <- there's the reuse killer

Cost angle

CDN pricing is usually egress bytes + requests (sometimes per region tier, plus purges, edge-compute invocations, TLS, WAF). Higher hit ratio and smaller payloads cut both the CDN bill and origin egress. Watch region mix (some regions cost multiples of others).

# monthly bill drivers
egress_bytes  = sum(response_bytes)                 # x $/GB, tiered by region
requests      = count(*)                            # x $/10k
origin_egress = sum(bytes where cache_status!='HIT') # what still leaves YOUR cloud

# a 0.82 -> 0.92 byte-hit-ratio improvement on 100 TB/mo:
#   origin egress: 18 TB -> 8 TB  (~$900/mo saved at $0.09/GB)  + faster users
# APAC/LatAm egress can be 2-4x US/EU -> route + cache harder there
Cheat Sheet
  • Track: hit ratio (by requests & bytes), origin offload, edge TTFB (hit vs miss), origin latency, error rates by PoP, bandwidth/requests by region.
  • RUM = real users (CWV: LCP/INP/CLS/TTFB), truthful, noisy. Synthetic = scripted probes, reproducible, for alerting/regression/comparison. Use both.
  • Raise hit ratio: longer s-maxage, immutable hashed assets, cache-key normalization, no Set-Cookie on cacheable, micro-cache, origin shield, no purge-all.
  • Speed misses: shield near origin, keep-alive pool, closer origin, SWR, request collapsing.
  • Fewer bytes: Brotli (precompress), AVIF/WebP, responsive/right-sized images, minify, video bitrate ladder.
  • Protocol: h2+h3, TLS 1.3, resumption. Hints: preconnect/preload, 103 Early Hints. Kill redirect chains (do redirects at edge).
  • Diagnose by path/content-type; check X-Cache; top keys / objects-per-URL for fragmentation.
  • Cost = egress bytes + requests (+ purges/edge-compute/WAF); hit ratio & payload size cut both bill and origin egress.
Q&A
Why track hit ratio by bytes as well as by requests?
They answer different questions. By-requests hit ratio tells you how much request load (RPS) you kept off the origin. By-bytes tells you how much bandwidth you served from cache — which drives cost and can be very different if your misses happen to be large files (a 99% request hit ratio can still be a 70% byte hit ratio).
RUM vs synthetic monitoring — when do you use each?
Synthetic (scripted probes from fixed nodes) for reproducible regression detection, alerting, SLA checks, and comparing CDN configs/providers apples-to-apples. RUM for the real distribution of user experience across geographies, devices, and networks — the ground truth for "did users get faster", and for spotting a bad region you don't probe. Run both.
Your hit ratio is fine but real users in one region are slow. What do you check?
RUM/synthetic by region to confirm; then which PoP that region hits (cache-status/PoP headers), whether it's mostly MISS there (cold PoP, low traffic, fragmented key), the edge↔origin latency for those misses, and traceroutes for backhaul/peering issues (traffic leaving the region). Also protocol negotiation (are they getting h3?) and redirect chains. If it's routing/peering, open a CDN ticket with the evidence.
What's the fastest way to cut both CDN bill and origin load?
Raise the cache hit ratio (longer TTLs, key normalization, immutable hashed assets, micro-caching, origin shield) and shrink payloads (Brotli, AVIF/WebP, right-sized images, minification). More hits = fewer origin fetches and less origin egress; smaller responses = fewer billed bytes at the edge and from origin.
Why avoid redirect chains, and how does a CDN help?
Each redirect is a full request/response round trip before the user gets real content, and chains multiply it. Serving redirects (canonical host, http→https, locale) at the edge instead of the origin removes the origin round trip for the redirect, and collapsing multi-hop chains into a single redirect removes the rest.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does origin offload measure?
The fraction of total requests (or bytes) served from cache without hitting the origin.
Which monitoring type reflects your actual user population?
RUM (Real User Monitoring).
Which compression is generally better than gzip for text assets?
Brotli (especially precompressed at max level for static files).

Intermediate core

RUM shows p75 LCP regressed after a CDN config change, but synthetic tests look fine. How do you investigate?
Synthetic nodes are few, clean, and well-connected, so they can miss a regression that hits real users. Steps: (1) Segment the RUM — by geography, device, connection type, browser, page type, and new vs returning. LCP regressions usually localize (one region, mobile, a specific page). (2) Check what changed in the config: TTLs (lower → more misses → slower TTFB → later LCP), cache-key change causing fragmentation and cold PoPs, a new edge function on the viewer path adding latency to every request, protocol setting (h3 turned off?), compression change, an added redirect, image-format negotiation change, or an origin/shield change increasing miss latency. (3) Look at RUM sub-metrics: is TTFB up (caching/routing/edge-compute), or is it resource load time (compression, image size, priority), or render-blocking resources (Early Hints/preload removed)? (4) Compare hit ratio and edge TTFB by region before/after — a drop in a region with low traffic (objects evicted before reuse) points at TTL/key changes. (5) Reproduce with WebPageTest/synthetic from the affected geo and on a throttled mobile profile, not just the default nodes. (6) If it's an edge function, move it to the origin-request hook or scope it; if TTL, restore it; if key fragmentation, re-normalize. (7) Roll back the config change if you can't isolate it quickly, then bisect. RUM is the source of truth here — trust it over the green synthetic.
A video-heavy site has 98% request hit ratio but 65% byte hit ratio and a large CDN bill. What's going on and what do you do?
The misses are the big objects — likely large video segments or high-res assets that aren't caching well, so a small number of miss requests move a large share of the bytes (hence great request ratio, poor byte ratio) and you pay egress for all of it plus origin egress on the misses. Investigate: (1) Are segments cacheable? Check Cache-Control on segments (should be long TTL) and manifests (short); confirm the CDN caches them and that Range requests are cached (segmented/partial-object caching enabled) — if range responses bypass cache, every seek is a miss. (2) Cache-key fragmentation — signed-URL tokens or session params in the key make each user's segment a unique object; key on the path only and validate the token separately at the edge. (3) Long-tail content — a huge library where most titles are rarely watched means low reuse per PoP and eviction before a second view; a larger cache footprint / dedicated video config / mid-tier helps, or accept it. (4) Bitrate ladder — are you shipping 4K to phones? Tune the ABR ladder and per-device caps; use a more efficient codec (AV1/HEVC where supported) to cut bytes. (5) Origin shield so misses don't multiply origin egress across PoPs. (6) Region mix — check if expensive regions dominate; consider a multi-CDN or a cheaper provider for volume regions. (7) Right-size non-video assets (AVIF, responsive). The lever here is byte hit ratio and bytes-per-view, not request hit ratio.

Advanced deep

Design a CDN performance observability system: what to collect, from where, how to alert, and how to drive continuous improvement.
Data sources: (1) CDN logs (real-time streaming to your pipeline/SIEM/warehouse) — per request: cache status (HIT/MISS/EXPIRED/STALE/BYPASS), PoP, edge TTFB, origin latency (on miss), bytes, status, content-type, path, protocol (h2/h3), TLS version, and any surrogate keys. Sample high-volume, keep full fidelity for errors. (2) CDN analytics API — aggregate hit ratio, offload, bandwidth, request volume, error rates by PoP/region/host. (3) RUM — Navigation/Resource Timing + Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS, TTFB) with dimensions: geo, ASN, device, connection, browser, page type, cache status if exposed. (4) Synthetic — scripted journeys from many geos on realistic device/network profiles, on a schedule, plus on-deploy. (5) Origin metrics — RPS, latency, error rate, egress bytes (to correlate with offload). (6) Cost data — CDN billing by region/feature. Warehouse + dashboards: land logs and RUM in a columnar store; dashboards for hit ratio & offload (by path, content-type, PoP, over time), miss latency, edge/origin errors by PoP, byte vs request hit ratio, RUM CWV percentiles by geo/device, synthetic trends, and cost per region + cost per GB served. A "cache health" view: top cache keys by count, objects-per-URL (fragmentation), and paths with hit ratio below target. Alerting: hit ratio or offload drops > X% (catches TTL/key regressions, purge-all, deploys); origin RPS/error spike; edge 5xx by PoP; per-PoP p95 latency outlier vs its historical baseline (routing/peering); RUM p75 LCP/INP/TTFB regression by region; synthetic journey failure or latency regression; cost anomaly; cert expiry; purge lag; edge-function error rate/CPU. Route by severity; page on user-facing latency/error regressions, ticket on efficiency drops. Continuous improvement loop: a monthly review of hit ratio by bucket with owners for the worst; a "cache-key hygiene" check in CI for CDN config changes (no Vary: User-Agent, bounded query params); RUM-gated deploys (block or auto-rollback if CWV regresses); track offload %, byte hit ratio, p75 CWV by region, and cost/GB as North-Star metrics quarter over quarter; game-days for purge storms and PoP failures. Correlation: annotate all time-series with deploys, config changes, and purges so a metric move has an explanation. The system's job: know your real user latency by geo, know your offload and why it moves, and catch config regressions before users feel them.
You're asked to prove a CDN provider migration (or a config change) actually improved performance. Design the experiment and the analysis.
Goal: causal evidence that the change improved real user latency/reliability without regressing cost, not just "the dashboard looks greener". Method options, best first: (1) A/B split by traffic — if you can serve a percentage of real users via the new provider/config and the rest via the old (DNS-based split with a stable per-user assignment, or a multi-CDN steering layer, or a header/cookie the edge honors), run both concurrently for a representative period (≥ 1–2 weeks to cover weekday/weekend and a full traffic-geo cycle). This controls for time-of-day, seasonality, releases, and internet weather. Collect RUM for both cohorts with identical instrumentation: CWV (LCP, INP, CLS), TTFB, and errors, plus dimensions (geo, ASN, device, connection, page type). Also compare hit ratio, offload, origin load, and cost per cohort. (2) Interleaved / holdback — if a full A/B isn't possible, keep a holdback slice on the old config. (3) Before/after with a control — weakest: compare a window before and after, but use a control metric unaffected by the change (e.g. a page not served by the CDN, or a competitor benchmark) to subtract out background trends, and difference-in-differences the results. Analysis: compare distributions, not means — p50/p75/p95/p99 of TTFB and LCP per segment; use percentile bootstrap or Mann-Whitney for significance given RUM's heavy tails; check that the improvement holds per region (a global average can hide a big win in one region and a regression in another). Quantify effect size (e.g. "p75 LCP −180 ms in APAC, −40 ms in NA, no change EU") and business impact if you have it (conversion/bounce vs latency). Verify no regression in: error rate, hit ratio, byte hit ratio, origin egress, and cost (egress + requests + features, by region). Run synthetic from many geos in parallel as a corroborating, reproducible signal and for edge cases (h3 negotiation, TLS, cold-cache miss latency, redirect behavior). Guardrails: freeze unrelated releases during the test or annotate them; ensure the two configs are truly equivalent except the variable under test (same TTLs, compression, image policy); check assignment is unbiased (no geo/device skew between cohorts). Decision: adopt if the user-latency improvement is statistically significant, consistent across major regions, and cost-neutral-or-better; otherwise iterate or roll back. Document the deltas by segment so the decision is auditable.

Multi-CDN, Traffic Steering & Cost

Running two or more CDNs for resilience and performance — and the config-parity tax that comes with it.

Notes

Why multi-CDN

  • Resilience: a CDN provider does have global outages; a second provider removes that single point of failure.
  • Performance: no CDN is fastest everywhere — provider A may be best in APAC, B in South America. Steering per-region (or per-ASN) to the fastest picks up real latency wins.
  • Capacity / negotiation: spread load, avoid per-provider commit overages, use volume for pricing leverage.
  • Regional coverage: some providers have far better presence in specific markets (e.g. China needs a provider with ICP-licensed PoPs).
# RUM data that justifies the split (p75 TTFB by CDN by region)
region   cdn_a   cdn_b
NA        22ms    31ms      -> route NA to A
EU        18ms    19ms      -> either
APAC      140ms   45ms      -> route APAC to B
SA        90ms    60ms      -> route SA to B
# single provider = you eat the worst column somewhere; multi-CDN picks the min per row

Steering mechanisms

MethodHowNotes
DNS-based (managed DNS / traffic manager)Authoritative DNS returns CNAME/records pointing at CDN A or B based on geo, health, weight, or RUM dataMost common. Bound by DNS TTL (30–60s typical) — failover isn't instant; resolver behavior varies; needs low TTL + healthy resolvers.
RUM-based steeringA steering service collects real user timings per CDN per region/ASN and biases DNS answers toward the currently-fastestBest performance; needs a measurement beacon and a steering provider (e.g. specialist vendors). Reacts to real conditions.
Client-side / app-levelThe app picks a CDN hostname per asset, or measures and switches; or a manifest lists multiple CDNsFine control (per-object failover, e.g. video), more app complexity.
Anycast in front / a routing layerYour own edge (or a cloud LB) routes to a CDNAdds a hop; rare.
302 redirect steeringA lightweight decision endpoint redirects to the chosen CDNAdds a round trip; used for large downloads/video where the redirect cost is amortized.
# DNS-based steering: cdn.example is a CNAME the traffic manager rewrites
cdn.example.  30  IN  CNAME  cdn.example.a-cdn.net.     # APAC resolvers get b-cdn
#   TTL 30s -> failover is ~30-60s, not instant; keep TTL low, resolvers matter

# 302 steering for a big download (redirect cost amortised over a 2 GB file)
GET /download/app.dmg
  -> 302 Location: https://dl.b-cdn.net/download/app.dmg   # decision endpoint picks per client

# client-side manifest lists multiple CDNs for per-segment failover (video)
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:...
https://a-cdn.example/720p.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:...
https://b-cdn.example/720p.m3u8

The config-parity problem

  • Every CDN has its own config model, cache-key semantics, header handling, WAF, edge-compute runtime, purge API, and log format. Keeping two in sync is real work.
  • Manage as code (Terraform providers for each CDN, or a config-abstraction tool) so changes go to all providers together, reviewed, and tested.
  • Watch for behavioral differences: default cache TTLs, how each treats Vary/cookies/query strings, gzip vs brotli defaults, HTTP/3 support, error-page behavior, stale-while-revalidate support, header size limits.
  • Purge: a content change must purge all CDNs; surrogate-key support and semantics differ — abstract behind one purge service.
  • Edge compute: portable logic (or duplicated per runtime) — or keep edge logic minimal and provider-agnostic.
  • Certificates: each CDN needs a valid cert for your hostname — more issuance/renewal to automate.
# manage BOTH providers from one repo so config never drifts
resource "fastly_service_vcl"      "site" { ... cache key, TTLs, headers ... }
resource "cloudflare_ruleset"      "site" { ... same intent, different model ... }
# CI: apply to both, then run parity tests
$ for h in a-cdn b-cdn; do
    curl -sI https://$h.example/page | grep -iE "cache-control|vary|x-cache"
  done   # assert identical caching behaviour

# purge must fan out to every CDN, behind one abstraction
$ purgectl key prod-123     # -> Fastly purge + Cloudflare purge + ...

Health checking & failover

  • The steering layer probes each CDN (a canary object per CDN hostname) from multiple locations; on failure, shift traffic away within the DNS TTL.
  • Distinguish "CDN is down" from "origin is down" (both CDNs will fail if origin is down — don't flap between them).
  • Keep a tested runbook: force all traffic to one CDN, or bypass to origin, quickly.
# steering probes a canary per CDN from many locations
GET https://a-cdn.example/__canary   -> expect 200, body "ok", < 500ms
GET https://b-cdn.example/__canary   -> ...

# CDN-down vs origin-down: if BOTH canaries fail the same way -> origin issue, DON'T flap
if a_fail and b_fail:  page("origin"); hold steering
elif a_fail:           shift 100% -> B    (within DNS TTL)

# break-glass
$ steerctl pin --cdn b        # force everything to B
$ steerctl bypass --origin    # skip CDNs entirely

Cost model

  • Pricing = egress bytes (tiered, and by region — APAC/LatAm often 2–5× NA/EU) + requests + extras (purges, edge-compute invocations, WAF, TLS, real-time logs).
  • Multi-CDN lets you route volume regions to the cheaper provider there, and use commits/minimums across providers — but you now pay two platform minimums and double the ops.
  • Model total cost of ownership: bytes × per-region rate per provider + request costs + steering-service cost + engineering time for parity. Multi-CDN pays off for high volume, strict availability SLAs, or poor single-provider coverage in key markets; it's overhead for a small site.
# route volume by CHEAPEST provider per region, but mind the platform minimums
region  bytes/mo   a $/GB   b $/GB   -> route
NA      400 TB     0.02     0.03        A
EU      300 TB     0.02     0.02        split (fill both commits)
APAC    150 TB     0.12     0.08        B

tco = sum(region_bytes * chosen_rate)
    + a_platform_min + b_platform_min        # you now pay TWO
    + steering_service_fee
    + eng_time_for_config_parity
# break-even: only above ~tens of TB/mo, or when an SLA / market coverage forces it
Cheat Sheet
  • Why multi-CDN: provider-outage resilience, per-region best performance, capacity/pricing leverage, market coverage (e.g. China).
  • Steering: DNS-based (common, TTL-bound failover), RUM-based (steer to currently-fastest per region/ASN, best perf), client/app-level (per-object, e.g. video), 302 redirect (adds RTT, for large downloads).
  • DNS steering needs low TTL + reliance on resolver behavior; failover is seconds, not instant.
  • Config parity is the tax: different cache-key/header/Vary/WAF/edge-compute/purge/log semantics per CDN — manage as code (Terraform per provider), test, and abstract purge behind one service.
  • Health-check each CDN with a canary; distinguish "CDN down" vs "origin down" (don't flap); keep a break-glass runbook.
  • Cost = egress bytes (tiered, region-dependent: APAC/LatAm 2–5× NA/EU) + requests + extras. Multi-CDN = route volume to the cheap provider per region, but 2 platform minimums + double ops.
  • Worth it for high volume / strict SLA / weak single-provider coverage; overhead for small sites.
Q&A
What are the main reasons to run more than one CDN?
Resilience against a provider-wide outage (CDNs do go down globally), better performance by steering each region to whichever provider is fastest there, coverage in markets where one provider is weak (e.g. China), and load/pricing leverage across providers.
How does DNS-based steering fail over, and what's the catch?
The authoritative DNS (or a traffic-management service) health-checks each CDN and returns records pointing at a healthy one; on failure it stops handing out the bad CDN's records. The catch is DNS caching — clients and resolvers hold the old answer until the TTL expires, so failover takes as long as your TTL (plus some resolvers ignore low TTLs). It's seconds-to-minutes, not instant, and per-request failover isn't possible at the DNS layer.
What is RUM-based steering?
A steering service embeds a beacon that measures real users' latency to each CDN, aggregates it per region/ASN, and biases the DNS answers toward whichever CDN is currently performing best for that user population. It adapts to real-world routing and congestion rather than static geo rules.
What's the biggest ongoing cost of multi-CDN besides bandwidth?
Configuration parity. Each CDN has different cache-key rules, header/Vary/cookie handling, WAF, edge-compute runtime, purge API, TLS/cert management, and log format. Keeping behavior identical across providers — and testing every change against both — is significant engineering overhead, on top of two platform minimums and two sets of operational knowledge.
How do you avoid flapping between CDNs when the origin is down?
Distinguish CDN health from origin health in the steering layer's checks. If the origin is down, both CDNs return errors, so shifting traffic between them does nothing but add churn. Detect the "all CDNs failing" case and hold steady (or fail to a static/stale page) rather than oscillating.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What's the most common multi-CDN steering mechanism?
DNS-based steering (via a managed DNS / traffic-management service).
Why is DNS-based failover not instant?
Clients and resolvers cache the DNS answer until its TTL expires (and some ignore low TTLs).
Name the ongoing engineering cost unique to multi-CDN.
Config parity — keeping cache/WAF/purge/edge behavior identical across providers.

Intermediate core

You add a second CDN and hit ratio drops and origin load rises. Why, and how do you fix it?
You've split the cache: each CDN maintains its own independent cache, so traffic steered to CDN B misses on objects only CDN A has warmed (and vice versa), roughly doubling cold-cache misses to origin for popular content, and any per-CDN behavioral differences (default TTLs, cache-key handling) make it worse. Fixes: (1) Config parity — ensure both CDNs use the same TTLs, cache-key normalization, Vary/cookie handling, and honor your Cache-Control identically; manage as code so they can't drift. (2) Origin shield on both, ideally pointing at a shared shield tier or at least the same origin region, so misses from either CDN collapse against one origin and each CDN's shield stays warm. Some setups put a shared caching layer (your own, or one CDN acting as origin for the other) in front of the origin so both CDNs pull from a common warm cache. (3) Stable steering — steer by region/ASN with enough stickiness that a given population consistently uses one CDN (so its cache stays warm for them), rather than rapidly rebalancing. (4) Accept a modest hit-ratio cost as the price of resilience, but bound it: the shield + parity should keep origin load only slightly higher than single-CDN. (5) Pre-warm critical objects on both CDNs after deploys/purges. (6) Purge both CDNs together via one purge service so neither serves stale.
Design multi-CDN for a live-streaming platform where a provider outage during a big event is unacceptable.
Two (or three) CDNs chosen for strong live-video features and complementary regional strength. Steering: primarily client-side / manifest-level for the video path — the player gets a manifest listing segment base-URLs on multiple CDNs (or a steering response per DASH/HLS content-steering spec), measures throughput/errors per CDN in real time, and switches per-segment on failure or degradation. This gives sub-second, per-object failover that DNS can't. Use DNS/RUM-based steering for the page, API, and manifest hostnames as the coarse layer, with low TTLs. Origin: the packager/origin (or a mid-tier origin) is itself redundant and both CDNs pull from it (locked to both CDNs' egress + auth); consider an origin shield per CDN near the packager. Config parity: segment TTLs (long) and manifest TTLs (short, e.g. 1× segment duration), cache-key = path only (validate tokens at the edge, don't key on them), range/segment caching enabled, identical CORS and Cache-Control, on both — all as code. Token auth: signed URLs validated at each edge with a shared secret; same scheme both providers. Health & ops: canary segment per CDN probed from many geos; a real-time dashboard of per-CDN segment error rate, throughput, and rebuffer ratio from player beacons; a break-glass to force all clients to one CDN via the steering response. Distinguish origin-down (both fail — escalate to origin/packager) from CDN-down (steer away). Capacity: pre-negotiate burst capacity with both for the event, load-test, and run a game-day killing one CDN mid-stream to verify the player fails over without visible rebuffering. Cost: route steady-state volume by cheapest-per-region, but keep enough baseline on each so its cache is warm and failover doesn't cold-start. The key is per-segment client-side failover for the video itself, backed by coarse DNS steering and strict config/token parity.

Advanced deep

Build the decision framework for whether an org should adopt multi-CDN, single-CDN, or single-CDN + a fallback. Include the operating model if they go multi.
Assess along these axes: (1) Availability requirement — what's the cost of a multi-hour CDN outage? For a bank, a large e-commerce site during peak, or a live-events platform, it's severe → multi-CDN or at least a hot fallback. For a marketing site, a rare outage is tolerable → single-CDN. (2) Traffic volume — multi-CDN's platform minimums, steering-service cost, and parity engineering only amortize at scale (roughly: significant monthly egress, many TB+). Small volume → single. (3) Geographic distribution — if a large user share is in markets where your preferred CDN is weak (LatAm, India, China, Africa), a second provider strong there is a real performance and coverage win. (4) Performance sensitivity — latency-linked revenue (retail, media) benefits from RUM-steering to the fastest per region; internal tools don't. (5) Team capacity — multi-CDN needs config-as-code discipline, testing, and on-call familiarity with two platforms. (6) Content type — large-object/video benefits from client-side per-segment failover; a mostly-HTML site gets less from it. Options: (a) Single-CDN — simplest, best if volume/availability/coverage don't demand more; mitigate with good origin resilience, stale-if-error, and a documented "point DNS at origin / a static fallback" runbook. (b) Single-CDN + cold/warm fallback — a second CDN configured (as code) but carrying little/no traffic; DNS steering can shift to it on a verified outage within the TTL. Lower cost than true multi (minimal second-provider spend), covers the outage case, accepts a cold-cache period on failover. Good middle ground for most "availability matters" orgs. (c) Active-active multi-CDN — both carry meaningful traffic, RUM/DNS steering by region, client-side failover for critical paths. Best availability and performance, highest cost and complexity. Operating model if multi: config-as-code for every CDN (Terraform providers), one abstraction for purge (a service that fans out to all CDNs by surrogate key), minimal and provider-agnostic (or duplicated + tested) edge logic, a steering layer (managed DNS + RUM vendor) with health checks that separate CDN-vs-origin failure, automated cert issuance/renewal per CDN, a unified log pipeline normalizing each CDN's format, dashboards for per-CDN hit ratio/latency/errors/cost, quarterly parity audits, and regular game-days that kill one CDN. Define ownership (a platform/edge team), a change process that requires "tested on all providers", and a break-glass to pin traffic. Recommendation heuristic: default to single-CDN; move to single + warm fallback when a CDN outage would be a serious incident; move to active-active only when volume is high, latency is revenue-linked, or coverage in key markets requires it — and only if the team can sustain the parity discipline.
Explain how CDN egress pricing actually works and the levers to reduce a large bill, including the traps.
Pricing structure: the dominant charge is egress (data transfer out) bytes, priced per GB, almost always tiered (the more you send, the lower the marginal $/GB) and regionalized — delivery from/into North America and Europe is cheapest; Asia-Pacific, Latin America, Middle East, Africa, and India often cost 2–5× more per GB. You're billed by where the request is served (the PoP's region), not where your origin is. On top: HTTP/HTTPS request counts (per 10k), and metered extras — purge operations, edge-compute invocations + CPU time, WAF (per request or per rule), TLS (custom certs, sometimes per SNI), real-time log streaming, image optimization, and sometimes origin fetch bandwidth. Many contracts have a monthly minimum / commit with overage rates, and negotiated rates well below list at volume. Levers: (1) Raise byte hit ratio — every cache hit avoids origin-fetch bandwidth and, more importantly, the miss doesn't change egress but repeated misses for large objects do; mainly, higher offload lets you negotiate and reduces origin egress (your cloud provider also charges egress to the CDN — use the CDN's private interconnect / origin-shield to cut that). (2) Shrink bytes on the wire — Brotli for text (precompressed), AVIF/WebP and responsive/right-sized images (often the single biggest win), efficient video codecs and a sane bitrate ladder (don't ship 4K to phones), minification, remove unused assets. (3) Region routing — with multi-CDN, serve expensive regions via whichever provider is cheapest there; even single-CDN, check if a provider bills certain regions better. (4) Reduce requests — bundle where it still makes sense, HTTP caching so browsers don't re-request, avoid chatty polling, cut redirect chains. (5) Right-size extras — sample real-time logs, scope WAF/edge-compute to paths that need them, prefer tag purges over millions of URL purges, don't purge-all. (6) Commit tuning — size the commit to actual sustained volume; consolidate spend for a better tier; revisit rates annually. Traps: (1) Region mix surprise — a traffic shift toward APAC/LatAm can spike the bill even at flat total bytes; monitor cost per region, not just total. (2) Origin egress double-charge — forgetting that cache misses cost you cloud egress to the CDN; low hit ratio hurts twice. (3) Purge/edge-compute creep — automation that purges aggressively or an edge function on every request can quietly become a line item. (4) Image/video not actually optimized — assuming the CDN "handles it" when it's passing through originals. (5) Cache-key fragmentation inflating misses and thus origin egress. (6) Free-tier/committed regions not covering where your users actually are. (7) Real-time logs at full fidelity on high volume. Instrument cost by region/feature, correlate with traffic and config changes, and treat byte hit ratio + bytes-per-visit as cost KPIs.

VMs vs Containers & the Hypervisor

A VM virtualizes the hardware and runs a whole guest OS; a container virtualizes the OS and shares the host kernel.

Notes

The two stacks

What. A hypervisor slices real hardware into virtual machines; each VM boots its own kernel and OS. A container engine instead asks the single host kernel to give a process an isolated view (its own process tree, network, mounts) — no second kernel.

Why. Skipping the guest OS removes the thing that is slow to boot, large on disk, and expensive to patch. You get ~10× the density, images in MB instead of GB, and start-up in milliseconds — which is what makes autoscaling, CI, and "one process per container" practical.

# container: shares the host kernel, starts almost instantly
$ time docker run --rm alpine uname -r
6.8.0-40-generic            # <-- the HOST kernel version, not the image's
real    0m0.42s

# a VM boots a whole OS first
$ time (virsh start web01 && virsh-wait-ssh web01)
real    0m38.7s

Type-1 vs Type-2 hypervisors

What. Type-1 (bare-metal) runs directly on hardware: VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V, Xen, Linux KVM. Type-2 (hosted) runs as an application on a normal OS: VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, Parallels.

Why. Type-1 has less overhead and a smaller attack surface, so it runs production servers and clouds. Type-2 is for developer laptops where you already have a desktop OS.

# KVM (Type-1, built into the Linux kernel) present?
$ lsmod | grep kvm
kvm_intel             380928  0
kvm                  1146880  1 kvm_intel
$ virsh list --all
 Id   Name    State
 1    web01   running
 -    db01    shut off

Isolation strength

What. A VM boundary is enforced by the CPU (VT-x/AMD-V) and the hypervisor: separate kernel, virtual CPUs, virtual devices. A container boundary is enforced by the same kernel it is trying to contain — a kernel privilege-escalation bug can escape a container to the host.

Why. Run mutually distrusting or hostile workloads (a public "run my code" service, per-customer tenants) behind a VM or a micro-VM (AWS Firecracker, Kata Containers, Google gVisor's user-space kernel). Trusted internal microservices are fine in plain containers.

# plain container escape surface = the whole kernel syscall ABI
#   e.g. CVE-2022-0847 "Dirty Pipe", CVE-2019-5736 (runc host-binary overwrite)

# micro-VM: container image + workflow, but a real KVM boundary per pod
$ firecracker --config-file vm.json      # ~125 ms boot, ~5 MB overhead
# Kata / gVisor slot in as a Kubernetes RuntimeClass:
#   runtimeClassName: kata   # untrusted pods get a VM; trusted pods stay on runc

Density, speed & footprint

What / why. No guest kernel means a container's baseline cost is just its own processes.

                       VM                     Container
image size             1–20 GB               5–300 MB
start time             30–90 s               50–200 ms
memory floor           ~512 MB–1 GB           a few MB
per host               tens                   hundreds–thousands
patch the kernel       once per VM            once on the host

When to use which (and the hybrid)

  • VM: run a different OS/kernel, hard multi-tenant isolation, legacy apps, kernel modules, "lift and shift" whole machines.
  • Container: microservices, stateless web apps, CI jobs, dev environments, anything you deploy often and scale horizontally.
  • Hybrid (the norm in the cloud): cloud VMs (EC2, GCE) each run a container runtime; Kubernetes packs containers onto those VMs. Kata/Firecracker give you container ergonomics with a VM boundary for the untrusted bits.
# the real production stack, top to bottom
Pod (your containers)
  -> containerd / runc          # container runtime
  -> Linux kernel               # namespaces + cgroups
  -> guest OS on a cloud VM
  -> KVM hypervisor
  -> physical host in a datacentre
Cheat Sheet
  • VM = virtual hardware + full guest OS on a hypervisor; container = isolated process on the shared host kernel (namespaces + cgroups + rootfs).
  • Container advantages: MB images, ~100 ms start, ~10× density, patch the kernel once.
  • VM advantages: hardware-enforced isolation, run any OS/kernel, strong multi-tenant boundary.
  • Type-1 hypervisor = bare metal (ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM, Xen); Type-2 = hosted app (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation).
  • Container escape surface = the entire kernel; a kernel bug can break out. Distrusted workloads → VM or micro-VM (Firecracker, Kata, gVisor).
  • Common reality: containers inside cloud VMs — you get both layers.
  • "A container is a lightweight VM" is the wrong mental model — it's a fenced-off process.
Q&A
What does a container share with the host that a VM does not?
The kernel. Every container on a host runs its processes against that one kernel; there is no guest kernel. A VM has its own kernel isolated by the hypervisor and CPU virtualization extensions.
Why do containers start so much faster than VMs?
There is no OS to boot — no firmware, no bootloader, no kernel init, no systemd bringing up services. Starting a container is just clone()/exec() of a process with some namespaces and cgroup settings, so it's tens to a couple hundred milliseconds versus tens of seconds.
Can you run a Windows container on a Linux host (or vice versa)?
Not natively — the container uses the host kernel, so a Linux container needs a Linux kernel and a Windows container needs a Windows kernel. "Docker Desktop running Linux containers on Windows/macOS" works by running a small Linux VM and putting the containers inside it.
Is a container less secure than a VM?
The isolation boundary is weaker: a container is only as isolated as the kernel's namespace/cgroup/LSM implementation, and a kernel exploit escapes to the host and every other container. A VM boundary is enforced by hardware and a much smaller hypervisor. For hostile multi-tenant workloads you add a VM layer (Firecracker/Kata) or a user-space kernel (gVisor).
What is a micro-VM and why does it exist?
A stripped-down VM (e.g. AWS Firecracker) with no BIOS, minimal devices, and a fast boot (~100 ms), designed to wrap a single container/function. It gives you the container developer experience and packing density while keeping a real hypervisor boundary for isolation — used by AWS Lambda and Fargate.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

In one sentence, how does a container differ from a VM?
A VM virtualizes hardware and runs its own guest OS on a hypervisor; a container is an isolated process that shares the host's kernel, fenced off with namespaces and limited with cgroups.
Name a Type-1 and a Type-2 hypervisor.
Type-1 (bare-metal): VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V, Xen, Linux KVM. Type-2 (hosted): Oracle VirtualBox, VMware Workstation/Fusion, Parallels Desktop.
Roughly how big is a container image versus a VM image, and how fast does each start?
Container image: single-to-hundreds of MB, starts in ~50–200 ms. VM image: 1–20 GB, boots in ~30–90 s.

Intermediate core

A team says "just use containers, VMs are obsolete." Where would you push back?
Containers can't run a different kernel/OS, can't load kernel modules, and give a weaker isolation boundary. You still want VMs (or micro-VMs) for: hostile multi-tenant workloads (running arbitrary customer code), strict compliance/isolation requirements, workloads needing a specific or patched kernel, Windows workloads on Linux hosts, and "lift and shift" of legacy systems that assume a whole machine. In practice it's not either/or — containers run inside VMs in every cloud, so you get the density of containers and the boundary of VMs.
Why is "patch once" a real operational advantage of containers?
With VMs, a kernel CVE means patching and rebooting every guest — hundreds of OS instances, each with its own maintenance window. With containers, there is one kernel per host: patch and drain-reboot the host (or roll new host images) and every container on it is fixed. The container images still need their userspace packages patched, but the kernel — the largest and most security-critical component — is centralized.

Advanced deep

Design the isolation strategy for a platform that runs untrusted user-submitted code at scale (like a CI service or a serverless platform).
Plain containers are not enough — a single kernel LPE escapes to the host and every other tenant. Layered approach: (1) Wrap each job in a micro-VM — Firecracker or Kata Containers, one lightweight VM per job/function, so the boundary is KVM + a tiny device model, not the shared kernel. Expose it through a normal container/OCI interface (Kata plugs in as a Kubernetes RuntimeClass) so the rest of the platform is unchanged. Alternatively gVisor for a user-space kernel that intercepts syscalls — less overhead than a VM, more than runc, and it shrinks the host-kernel attack surface without full hardware virtualization. (2) Defence in depth inside the sandbox — seccomp allowlist to a minimal syscall set, drop all capabilities, no-new-privileges, read-only rootfs, non-root uid, tight cgroup limits (CPU, memory, PIDs, IO) to bound blast radius and prevent DoS, no host network (own netns, egress via a filtered proxy). (3) Host hardening — minimal host OS, up-to-date kernel with mitigations, one tenant per host or at least per VM, node auto-recycling, and no secrets/credentials on the node the sandbox can reach (no cloud metadata endpoint). (4) Blast-radius controls — short-lived nodes, per-job network policy, disk quotas, wall-clock timeouts, and monitoring for escape indicators. (5) Operational — keep the sandbox runtime (Firecracker/gVisor/kernel) patched aggressively; treat it as the crown-jewel dependency. Net: micro-VM per job for the hard boundary, plus full container hardening inside, plus disposable hosts — the model AWS Lambda/Fargate and modern CI runners use.

A Container Is Just a Process

There is no "container" object in the Linux kernel — it's an ordinary process with a private view of the system and its privileges trimmed.

Notes

No such thing as a "container" in the kernel

What. Linux has no container syscall or container struct. A container is a process (or process tree) started with: a set of namespaces (private view of PIDs, mounts, network, hostname, users, IPC), a cgroup (resource limits), a private root filesystem, and a reduced privilege set (dropped capabilities, a seccomp filter, an LSM profile).

Why it matters. Every "container" behaviour — "it has its own IP", "PID 1 inside is my app", "it can't see host files" — traces to one of those primitives. Debugging a container is debugging a process plus its namespaces.

# the same process, two views
# --- inside the container ---
/ # ps
PID   USER  COMMAND
1     root  nginx: master process       # thinks it is PID 1
/ # hostname
a1b2c3d4e5f6                             # its own UTS namespace

# --- on the host ---
$ ps -o pid,cmd -C nginx
   PID CMD
 48213 nginx: master process            # just PID 48213
$ sudo ls -l /proc/48213/ns             # the namespaces pinning it
lrwxrwxrwx net -> 'net:[4026533210]'
lrwxrwxrwx pid -> 'pid:[4026533207]'
lrwxrwxrwx mnt -> 'mnt:[4026533205]'

How a runtime starts one

What / how. A runtime like runc does roughly: clone() a child with the requested CLONE_NEW* flags → in the child, set up the mount namespace and pivot_root into the image's rootfs → apply the cgroup, seccomp filter and capability set → execve() the entrypoint.

# the essence, with shell tools (no Docker) -- see "Build a Container by Hand" for the full version
$ sudo unshare --pid --mount --net --uts --ipc --fork --mount-proc \
      chroot /var/lib/rootfs /bin/sh
/ # ps          # PID namespace: only our processes
/ # ip addr     # NET namespace: just lo, down
/ # hostname box ; hostname   # UTS namespace: private hostname
# add: cgroup for limits, capsh --drop=... for privileges, a seccomp profile

What is (and isn't) isolated

  • Isolated by namespaces: process list, mounts/filesystem view, network stack, hostname, users/UIDs, IPC objects, and the cgroup path itself.
  • Limited by cgroups: CPU time, memory, block IO, number of PIDs.
  • Shared with the host: the kernel (and thus the syscall ABI, kernel version, loaded modules), the system clock (unless the time namespace is used), and hardware.
  • Not isolated unless you ask: capabilities default to a set that still allows a lot; the seccomp profile must be supplied; without a user namespace, root in the container is root on the host.
# PID 1 pitfall: your app inherits init duties it may not perform
#   - reaping zombie children  -> use "docker run --init" or tini, or handle SIGCHLD
#   - forwarding SIGTERM       -> exec your app so it IS PID 1 and gets the signal
CMD ["node", "server.js"]        # exec form  -> node is PID 1, receives SIGTERM
CMD node server.js               # shell form -> /bin/sh is PID 1, may swallow signals

Why "it works on my machine" goes away

What / why. The image bundles the app and its entire userspace (libc, shared libraries, interpreter, tools, config) as immutable layers. The only thing not in the image is the kernel — and the syscall ABI is stable — so the same bytes run identically on any host with a new-enough kernel.

$ docker run --rm myapp cat /etc/os-release | head -1
PRETTY_NAME="Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm)"     # the image's userspace...
$ uname -r
6.8.0-40-generic                                  # ...on whatever kernel the host has
# reproducible: same image digest -> same files -> same behaviour, laptop or prod
Cheat Sheet
  • A container = process + namespaces + cgroup + rootfs + dropped privileges. No kernel "container" object.
  • Namespaces isolate what it sees; cgroups limit what it uses; rootfs confines its files; capabilities/seccomp/LSM restrict what it can do.
  • On the host it's a normal PID; inside, its PID namespace makes the entrypoint look like PID 1.
  • Shared with the host: the kernel, hardware, and (usually) the clock.
  • PID 1 duties: reap zombies (--init/tini) and forward SIGTERM (use exec form so your app is PID 1).
  • Portability comes from bundling the whole userspace as immutable layers; only the stable syscall ABI is external.
  • runc flow: clone(CLONE_NEW*) → mount ns + pivot_root → cgroup + seccomp + caps → execve(entrypoint).
Q&A
If you run ps aux on the host, do you see the container's processes?
Yes — they are ordinary host processes with host PIDs. Inside the container's PID namespace those same processes are renumbered starting at 1, and the container can only see its own subtree, but nothing hides them from the host.
What are the four ingredients that turn a process into a container?
Namespaces (isolated view of PIDs/mounts/network/hostname/users/IPC), cgroups (CPU/memory/IO/PID limits), a private root filesystem (chroot/pivot_root into the image), and reduced privileges (dropped capabilities + a seccomp syscall filter + an LSM profile like AppArmor/SELinux).
Why should your Dockerfile CMD/ENTRYPOINT use the exec form (JSON array)?
The exec form runs your binary directly as PID 1, so it receives SIGTERM on docker stop/pod termination and can shut down gracefully. The shell form runs /bin/sh -c "..." as PID 1, which often does not forward the signal to your app, so it gets SIGKILLed after the grace period.
What does a container not get its own copy of?
The kernel. All containers on a host execute against the same kernel, share its version and loaded modules and syscall ABI, and (unless the time namespace is in use) see the same clock. That shared kernel is also the security boundary.
Why is "works on my machine" less of a problem with containers?
The image is an immutable bundle of the application plus its entire userspace — libc, libraries, interpreter, CLI tools, default config — identified by a content digest. The same digest produces the same files everywhere, and the only external dependency is the stable kernel syscall interface.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Is there a "container" data structure in the Linux kernel?
No. "Container" is a userspace concept — the combination of namespaces, cgroups, a root filesystem, and privilege restrictions applied to a process. The kernel just sees processes.
Inside a container, what PID is your application usually running as, and why?
PID 1, because the container has its own PID namespace and the entrypoint is the first process in it. On the host it has some ordinary large PID.

Intermediate core

Your containerized app leaves zombie processes and doesn't stop cleanly on deploy. What's going on?
Two PID-1 problems. (1) Zombies: PID 1 is expected to wait() on orphaned children; if your app spawns subprocesses and doesn't reap them, they pile up as zombies. Fix: run a tiny init as PID 1 — docker run --init (uses tini), or tini/dumb-init as the entrypoint, or handle SIGCHLD yourself. (2) Doesn't stop cleanly: docker stop/Kubernetes sends SIGTERM to PID 1. If PID 1 is /bin/sh -c "myapp" (shell form CMD), the shell often doesn't forward the signal, so your app never gets it and is SIGKILLed after the grace period, aborting in-flight work. Fix: use the exec form (CMD ["myapp"]) so your app is PID 1, or use an init that forwards signals.
Walk through what runc does to start a container from an OCI bundle.
Given a bundle (a rootfs directory + a config.json): (1) create a new process with clone()/unshare() requesting the configured namespaces (CLONE_NEWPID, NEWNS, NEWNET, NEWUTS, NEWIPC, optionally NEWUSER, NEWCGROUP); (2) in the child, if a user namespace is used, set up the UID/GID mappings; (3) set the hostname (UTS ns), configure the network namespace (or let the runtime/CNI do it); (4) do the mount-namespace setup — bind/mount the configured mounts, then pivot_root into the image rootfs and mount a fresh /proc, /sys, /dev; (5) move the process into its cgroup and write the limits; (6) drop capabilities to the configured set, apply no_new_privs, install the seccomp BPF filter, apply the AppArmor/SELinux label; (7) execve() the configured entrypoint. The container is now that process running under all those restrictions.

Advanced deep

Given that a container is "just a process," how would you inspect and debug a misbehaving one on the host without exec'ing into it?
Treat it as a process plus namespaces. (1) Find the PID: docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' <id>, or crictl inspect, or ps with the cgroup. (2) Filesystem: /proc/<pid>/root/ is the container's rootfs as seen from the host — browse it directly; /proc/<pid>/cwd, /proc/<pid>/environ, /proc/<pid>/maps. (3) Enter selected namespaces with nsenter -t <pid> -n ip addr (just the netns to debug networking), -m for mounts, -p for the process view — you don't need any tools installed in the image because you bring the host's. (4) Resource state: read the cgroup files under /sys/fs/cgroup/<path>/ — memory.current, memory.events (OOM count), cpu.stat (throttling), pids.current. (5) Syscalls: strace -f -p <pid> from the host, or bpftrace/perf filtered by cgroup. (6) What's constraining it: /proc/<pid>/status shows CapEff (effective capabilities), Seccomp mode, and the namespace inode numbers (compare with lsns). (7) Kernel/host events: dmesg for OOM-killer messages and seccomp/audit denials, journalctl for the runtime's logs. This is also why "distroless" images are debuggable: the container has no shell, but the host does, and nsenter//proc/<pid>/root give you everything.

Linux Namespaces

Each namespace gives a process a private copy of one global kernel resource — the process tree, the network stack, the mount table, and so on.

Notes

What a namespace is

What. A namespace wraps a global kernel resource so that processes inside it see their own isolated instance of it. Change the resource inside, and only members of that namespace notice.

Why. This is the "isolation" half of containers. Give a process its own net namespace and it has its own IP, ports and firewall rules; its own pid namespace and it can't see or signal host processes; its own mnt namespace and it has a private filesystem tree.

# create namespaces for a shell, one flag per type
$ sudo unshare --pid --net --mount --uts --ipc --user --map-root-user \
      --fork --mount-proc /bin/bash

# inspect what any process is in
$ ls -l /proc/self/ns/
lrwxrwxrwx net -> 'net:[4026531840]'      # the number is the namespace's inode id
lrwxrwxrwx pid -> 'pid:[4026531836]'
$ lsns -t net                             # list network namespaces + their processes

The types, one by one

NamespaceIsolatesEffect inside
pidProcess IDs & the process treeFirst process is PID 1; only your subtree is visible; can't signal host PIDs.
mntThe mount tablePrivate set of mounts; pivot_root into the image rootfs; host mounts hidden.
netInterfaces, routes, iptables, sockets, portsStarts with only a down lo; you add a veth to reach the outside.
utsHostname & NIS domainsethostname() changes only this container's name.
ipcSystem V IPC, POSIX message queues, shared memoryOwn /dev/shm; can't attach to host shared-memory segments.
userUID/GID ranges & capability setsUID 0 inside maps to an unprivileged UID outside; root-in-container ≠ root-on-host.
cgroupThe cgroup filesystem root/proc/self/cgroup and /sys/fs/cgroup show a relative view, not the host path.
timeCLOCK_BOOTTIME / CLOCK_MONOTONIC offsetsContainer can present a different uptime (used for checkpoint/restore).

Creating, joining, and pinning them

How. Three syscalls. clone(CLONE_NEW*) starts a child in fresh namespaces. unshare(2) moves the calling process into new ones. setns(2) joins an existing namespace via an fd from /proc/<pid>/ns/<type> — this is exactly what docker exec and nsenter do.

# join a running container's network + pid namespace to debug it
$ PID=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' web)
$ sudo nsenter -t $PID -n -p ss -tlnp        # host's ss, container's sockets

# a namespace normally disappears when its last process exits;
# pin an empty one so it persists (how "ip netns" works):
$ sudo ip netns add blue
$ ls /var/run/netns/blue                       # a bind-mounted nsfs file keeps it alive
$ sudo ip netns exec blue ip link

The user namespace — the special one

What / why. It maps a range of UIDs/GIDs inside to a different range outside, and it is the only namespace an unprivileged user can create. Inside it you hold a full capability set (over that namespace's resources); outside, you are still unprivileged. This is the foundation of rootless containers: "root" in the container is really UID 100000 on the host, so a container breakout lands as a nobody.

# rootless: run a whole container as your user, no daemon, no sudo
$ podman unshare cat /proc/self/uid_map
         0       1000          1          # in-ns uid 0  -> host uid 1000
         1     100000      65536          # in-ns uid 1.. -> host 100000..

$ podman run --rm alpine id
uid=0(root) ...            # "root" inside
$ ps -o user,cmd -C sleep # ... but on the host it's owned by 'me' (or 100000)

Gotchas

  • A new net namespace has no connectivity — not even DNS — until you plumb a veth/bridge (the runtime or CNI does this).
  • unshare --pid needs --fork --mount-proc, otherwise ps still reads the host /proc.
  • Sharing a namespace is a feature: Kubernetes pods share net + ipc (+ optionally pid) so containers in a pod reach each other on localhost; docker run --net=container:web and --pid=host do the same manually.
  • User namespaces have historically been a source of kernel CVEs (lots of code becomes reachable by unprivileged users) — some hardened distros restrict them.
Cheat Sheet
  • Namespace = a process's private copy of one global kernel resource. Answers "what can it see?"
  • Types: pid (process tree), mnt (mounts), net (interfaces/ports/iptables), uts (hostname), ipc (SysV IPC/shm), user (UID/GID + caps), cgroup (cgroup root), time (boot/monotonic clock).
  • Syscalls: clone(CLONE_NEW*) new child, unshare(2) move self, setns(2) join existing (= docker exec/nsenter).
  • Pinned by /proc/<pid>/ns/*; survives via a bind-mount or open fd even with no process.
  • Namespaces isolate visibility; they don't limit resources (cgroups) or drop privilege (caps/seccomp) — except user, which remaps UIDs and is the basis of rootless.
  • Fresh net ns = only a down lo; needs a veth to reach anything.
  • unshare --pid also needs --fork --mount-proc to get a correct ps.
  • Pods deliberately share net+ipc so containers talk over localhost.
Q&A
Which namespace makes a container's entrypoint appear as PID 1?
The PID namespace. The first process created in a new PID namespace is numbered 1 and can only see processes in its own subtree; it also takes on init responsibilities (reaping orphans).
You create a fresh network namespace and can't ping anything. Why?
A new net namespace starts empty — just a loopback interface that is down. It has no route to the host or the internet until you create a veth pair, put one end in the namespace, attach the other to a bridge (or the host), bring them up, add a default route, and set up NAT. Container runtimes and CNI plugins do all of this for you.
How does docker exec get a shell "inside" a running container?
It calls setns(2) to join the target container's existing namespaces (mount, PID, net, IPC, UTS, and user if used), moves into its cgroup, applies the same seccomp/caps, then execve()s the requested command. nsenter -t <pid> -a is the manual equivalent.
What is special about the user namespace?
It remaps UIDs/GIDs (UID 0 inside → some high unprivileged UID outside) and is the only namespace an unprivileged process can create. It lets you have "root" inside a container without any real host privilege — the basis of rootless containers — but it also exposes more kernel code to unprivileged users, so it has a history of CVEs.
Do Kubernetes pod containers each get their own network namespace?
No — all containers in a pod share one network namespace (and IPC, and optionally PID). That's why they see each other on localhost and share the pod's single IP and port space, and why two containers in a pod can't both bind port 8080.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Name four Linux namespace types and what each isolates.
Any four of: pid (process IDs/tree), mnt (mount points), net (network interfaces, routes, ports, iptables), uts (hostname/domain), ipc (System V IPC and POSIX message queues), user (UID/GID mappings and capabilities), cgroup (the cgroup filesystem root view), time (boot/monotonic clock offsets).
Which command lists the namespaces on a system?
lsns (optionally lsns -t net for one type). You can also read /proc/<pid>/ns/ for a single process.

Intermediate core

Do namespaces limit how much CPU or memory a container can use?
No. Namespaces only control visibility — what processes, mounts, interfaces, etc. a process can see and act on. Resource limits (CPU shares/quota, memory ceilings, IO weight, PID count) are enforced by cgroups, a separate mechanism. A container with no cgroup limits can consume the whole host. The one namespace that also affects privilege is the user namespace, which remaps UIDs and scopes capabilities.
How do two containers in the same Kubernetes pod communicate, and what constraint does that create?
They share a network namespace (set up on the pod's "pause"/sandbox container), so they talk over localhost and share one IP. Constraint: they also share the port space — two containers in a pod cannot both listen on the same port — and network-level isolation between them is nil, so co-locating containers in a pod is a trust decision (it's meant for tightly-coupled helpers/sidecars, not arbitrary services).

Advanced deep

Explain how you would manually build the namespace isolation for a container using only shell tools, and where each step maps to what a runtime does.
(1) unshare the namespaces: unshare --user --map-root-user --pid --fork --mount --net --uts --ipc --cgroup /bin/bash. --fork is required with --pid so the shell's children are in the new PID ns; --map-root-user sets up a minimal uid_map/gid_map for the user ns. (2) mount namespace + rootfs: make mounts private (mount --make-rprivate /), bind-mount the image rootfs onto itself, mount --bind newroot newroot, cd newroot, pivot_root . old_root, then umount -l old_root; mount fresh proc, sysfs, devtmpfs/a minimal /dev. (3) UTS: hostname container01. (4) network: from the host, ip link add veth0 type veth peer name ceth0, ip link set ceth0 netns <pid>, attach veth0 to a bridge, assign addresses, bring links up, set a default route in the ns, add an iptables MASQUERADE rule for egress. (5) cgroup: mkdir /sys/fs/cgroup/mycontainer, write memory.max, cpu.max, pids.max, then echo <pid> > cgroup.procs. (6) privileges: capsh --drop=cap_sys_admin,cap_net_admin,... -- (or set the bounding/effective sets), prctl(PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS), install a seccomp BPF filter, apply an AppArmor/SELinux profile. (7) exec the entrypoint. Mapping: steps 1–4 are what runc's namespace/rootfs/network setup does from config.json; step 5 is the cgroup manager (systemd or cgroupfs driver); step 6 is the seccomp/capabilities/apparmorProfile fields; step 7 is process.args. Docker/containerd add image pull, layer/overlayfs assembly, and lifecycle/API on top.

Control Groups (cgroups v2)

Namespaces decide what a process can see; cgroups decide how much CPU, memory, IO and how many processes it can use.

Notes

What a cgroup is

What. A control group is a node in a filesystem tree (/sys/fs/cgroup/…) that a set of processes belongs to. Kernel controllers (cpu, memory, io, pids, hugetlb…) attached to that node account for and limit the resources those processes use.

Why. Without limits, one container can starve the host of memory (triggering the OOM killer on random victims), peg every CPU, or fork-bomb it. cgroups turn "best effort" into enforceable quotas and make usage measurable per container.

# where a process's cgroup is (v2 = one line, "0::<path>")
$ cat /proc/self/cgroup
0::/user.slice/user-1000.slice/session-3.scope

# a container's cgroup, from Docker
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-<id>.scope/memory.current
134217728
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-<id>.scope/memory.max
536870912                     # 512 MiB ceiling (from --memory 512m)

The controllers you'll touch

ControllerKey files (v2)Controls
cpucpu.max = "QUOTA PERIOD", cpu.weightHard cap (throttling) and relative share under contention.
memorymemory.max, memory.high, memory.current, memory.eventsHard OOM ceiling, soft throttle point, current use, OOM count.
ioio.max, io.weight, io.statPer-device bytes/s and IOPS caps; proportional weight.
pidspids.max, pids.currentMax processes/threads — stops fork bombs.
# create a cgroup, cap it, run something in it
$ sudo mkdir /sys/fs/cgroup/demo
$ echo '50000 100000' | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cpu.max   # 0.5 CPU (50ms per 100ms)
$ echo 128M          | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/memory.max
$ echo 100           | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/pids.max
$ echo $$            | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cgroup.procs  # move this shell in
$ yes > /dev/null &                                              # uses at most 50% of one core

Limits vs weights (requests)

What / why. cpu.max / memory.max are hard limits — the kernel throttles or OOM-kills at the ceiling. cpu.weight / io.weight are proportional shares that only matter under contention. Docker's --cpus sets cpu.max; --cpu-shares sets the weight. Kubernetes maps limits.cpu → cpu.max and requests.cpu → cpu.weight (and uses requests for scheduling + QoS class).

# Docker
$ docker run --cpus 1.5 --memory 512m --memory-swap 512m \
             --cpu-shares 512 --pids-limit 200 myapp
# --memory-swap == --memory  -> swap disabled for the container

# Kubernetes -> cgroup files
resources:
  requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi" }   # 250m -> cpu.weight ~= 10 ; scheduling
  limits:   { cpu: "1",    memory: "512Mi" }    # -> cpu.max "100000 100000", memory.max 512Mi

OOM and CPU throttling — the two things that bite

  • Memory: hit memory.max and the kernel first reclaims, then OOM-kills a process in that cgroup (usually your app, exit code 137). It does not touch the rest of the host. Check memory.events (oom_kill count) and dmesg.
  • CPU: hit cpu.max and the kernel throttles — runnable threads are stalled until the next period. Latency spikes, no crash. Check cpu.stat (nr_throttled, throttled_usec). A too-low CPU limit on a multi-threaded app or GC causes mysterious p99 latency.
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../cpu.stat
usage_usec 91230000
nr_periods 3120
nr_throttled 812                  # <-- throttled in ~26% of periods = limit too low
throttled_usec 4100000
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../memory.events
oom_kill 3                          # <-- 3 OOM kills; raise memory.max or fix the leak

v1 vs v2, and delegation

  • v1: one hierarchy per controller (/sys/fs/cgroup/memory, /cpu, …), a process could be in different cgroups per controller — messy. v2: one unified tree; controllers are enabled on a subtree via cgroup.subtree_control. Modern distros and Kubernetes default to v2.
  • Delegation: systemd owns the tree; containers get a sub-slice (system.slice/docker-*.scope, kubepods.slice/…). Rootless containers use systemd user delegation so an unprivileged user can set limits on their own subtree.
  • "No internal processes" rule (v2): a non-root cgroup can have member processes or child cgroups with controllers, not both.
Cheat Sheet
  • cgroup = a node in /sys/fs/cgroup that processes belong to; controllers account for + limit CPU, memory, IO, PIDs.
  • Namespaces = visibility; cgroups = resource limits. Different mechanisms.
  • Hard limits: cpu.max ("QUOTA PERIOD"), memory.max. Proportional shares (contention only): cpu.weight, io.weight.
  • Docker: --cpus→cpu.max, --cpu-shares→weight, --memory→memory.max, --pids-limit→pids.max.
  • K8s: limits→*.max; requests.cpu→cpu.weight + scheduling + QoS.
  • Over memory limit → OOM kill inside the cgroup (exit 137); check memory.events.
  • Over CPU limit → throttling, not a crash; check cpu.stat nr_throttled/throttled_usec.
  • cgroup v2 = single unified hierarchy (default now); v1 = per-controller trees.
Q&A
Namespaces vs cgroups — one line each.
Namespaces isolate what a process can see (PIDs, mounts, network, …). cgroups limit and account for what a process can use (CPU, memory, IO, PID count).
Your container is OOM-killed with exit code 137. What happened and what do you check?
It exceeded its cgroup memory.max; the kernel reclaimed what it could, then killed a process in that cgroup (137 = 128 + SIGKILL(9)). Check memory.events for the oom_kill count, memory.max vs your app's real working set, dmesg for the OOM report, and whether the JVM/Node heap is sized larger than the limit. Fix by raising the limit or fixing the leak/heap config — and know it did not affect other containers.
A CPU-limited container has fine average CPU but terrible p99 latency. Why?
CFS throttling. cpu.max is enforced per ~100 ms period; if the app (or its GC / thread pool) needs a burst that exceeds the quota, all its threads are frozen until the next period, adding tens of milliseconds of stall. Average usage stays under the limit but tail latency blows up. Check cpu.stat nr_throttled; fix by raising the limit, reducing quota-relative parallelism, or (K8s) using only requests without a tight limit for latency-sensitive workloads.
What's the difference between a CPU limit and a CPU request/share?
A limit (cpu.max) is a hard ceiling — the container is throttled once it hits the quota even if the host is idle. A request/share (cpu.weight) only matters under contention: it sets the proportion of CPU this cgroup gets relative to its siblings when they're all trying to run. An idle host lets a share-only container use everything.
What is cgroup v2 and why did it replace v1?
v1 had a separate hierarchy per controller, so a process could sit in different cgroups for cpu vs memory, making coordinated policy and delegation hard, and some features (like pressure-aware memory management) impossible. v2 is a single unified hierarchy where each process is in exactly one cgroup and controllers are toggled per subtree, enabling consistent policy, safe delegation to unprivileged users (rootless), and PSI/pressure metrics.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What do cgroups control that namespaces do not?
Resource usage — CPU time, memory, block IO bandwidth, and the number of processes/threads. Namespaces only control visibility/isolation.
Which Docker flags set the container's memory ceiling and process cap?
--memory (writes memory.max) and --pids-limit (writes pids.max). Also --cpus for a CPU cap.

Intermediate core

How do Kubernetes requests and limits map onto cgroup files, and how do they affect QoS?
limits.memory → memory.max (hard OOM ceiling). limits.cpu → cpu.max (CFS quota/period, causes throttling). requests.cpu → cpu.weight (proportional share under contention) and is what the scheduler sums against node allocatable to decide placement. requests.memory is used for scheduling and QoS but isn't a cgroup enforcement knob by itself. QoS class: Guaranteed if every container sets requests==limits for both CPU and memory; Burstable if at least one request is set but not equal to limits; BestEffort if nothing is set. Under node memory pressure the kubelet evicts BestEffort first, then Burstable exceeding requests, then Guaranteed last — and the OOM score adjustment follows the same ordering.
A container sets --memory 512m but no swap limit; what can still go wrong?
If the host has swap and --memory-swap isn't set equal to --memory, the container can spill to swap up to (memory + host swap), so it doesn't get OOM-killed at 512 MiB — it just thrashes, and every allocation-heavy operation becomes disk-slow, dragging down latency and the whole node's IO. Also, runtimes like the JVM or Node may read the host's total memory (on old cgroup-unaware versions) and size their heap to that, blowing past the limit and getting OOM-killed anyway. Fixes: set --memory-swap equal to --memory (disable container swap), use cgroup-aware runtimes / -XX:MaxRAMPercentage, and on Kubernetes note that swap is disabled by default for exactly this reason.

Advanced deep

Design resource governance for a shared multi-tenant node so one tenant can't degrade others, covering CPU, memory, IO, and PIDs.
CPU: give every workload a requests.cpu (→ cpu.weight) sized to its steady-state need so contention is shared fairly; set limits.cpu only where a hard cap is genuinely wanted (batch/abuse-prone), and be cautious with tight limits on latency-sensitive services because CFS throttling spikes tail latency — prefer weight + monitoring + a generous limit. Reserve capacity for the kubelet/system daemons (--kube-reserved, --system-reserved) so node agents never starve. Memory: always set limits.memory (→ memory.max) so a leak OOM-kills only that cgroup; set requests.memory equal to the limit for critical services (Guaranteed QoS) so they're evicted last; enable memory.high (soft limit) via the runtime where supported so a container is throttled/reclaimed before the hard OOM; disable swap (or set --memory-swap=--memory) to avoid thrash; keep node memory reservations for system components. IO: set io.weight per cgroup for proportional fairness on the shared disk; add io.max bytes/IOPS caps for known noisy neighbours (log-heavy, backup jobs); prefer separate/local NVMe for high-IO tenants; watch io.pressure (PSI). PIDs: set pids.max (K8s node-level --pod-max-pids or per-pod) to contain fork bombs and runaway thread creation. Isolation extras: one tenant per node pool where isolation must be strong (taints/tolerations + node affinity), or micro-VM runtime (Kata) for hostile tenants; NetworkPolicy so tenants can't reach each other; ResourceQuota + LimitRange per namespace so tenants can't over-request. Observability: alert on cpu.stat throttling ratio, memory.events OOM counts, PSI (cpu.pressure/memory.pressure/io.pressure) per cgroup, and eviction events; capacity-plan from actual usage vs requests. Net: weights for fair sharing, hard limits for blast-radius containment, node reservations for the system, PSI for early warning, and node-pool or micro-VM separation where the trust boundary demands it.

Image Layers & OverlayFS

An image is a stack of read-only tarballs; a running container adds one thin writable layer on top, merged into a single view by a union filesystem.

Notes

What an image layer is

What. Each Dockerfile instruction that changes the filesystem (FROM, RUN, COPY, ADD) produces a layer: a tar of the files that were added, changed or deleted relative to the layer below. An image is an ordered list of layer digests plus a config (env, entrypoint, …).

Why. Layers are content-addressed (sha256:…) and immutable, so: a layer is downloaded and stored once and reused by every image that shares it; a rebuild only re-ships the layers that actually changed; and starting N containers from an image copies nothing — they share the read-only layers.

$ docker history python:3.12-slim
IMAGE          CREATED BY                                      SIZE
<missing>      RUN pip install ...                             48MB
<missing>      COPY . /app                                     2.1MB
<missing>      ENV LANG=C.UTF-8                                0B      # metadata-only, no layer
<missing>      /bin/sh -c apt-get install -y libpq5            9.4MB
<missing>      (base debian layer)                             74MB

$ docker inspect --format '{{json .RootFS.Layers}}' myimage | jq
["sha256:8a1e...", "sha256:2f0b...", "sha256:9cc4..."]   # the ordered stack

How OverlayFS merges them

What / how. The runtime mount -t overlays the layers: the image layers are the read-only lowerdirs, a fresh empty directory is the writable upperdir, plus a workdir for atomic operations. The merged mount is what the container sees as /.

  • Read: overlay looks from the upper layer downward and returns the first copy of the path it finds.
  • Write / modify: copy-up — the file is copied from its lower layer into the upper layer, then written there. The lower layers are never touched.
