  • Delete: a whiteout (a character device 0:0, or an xattr) is created in the upper layer to mask the lower file. Deleting a directory uses an opaque marker.
# the actual mount for a running container (Docker, overlay2)
$ mount | grep overlay
overlay on /var/lib/docker/overlay2/<id>/merged type overlay
  (lowerdir=.../l/AAA:.../l/BBB:.../l/CCC,   # image layers, top-first
   upperdir=.../<id>/diff,                   # container's writable layer
   workdir=.../<id>/work)

# prove copy-up: edit a base-image file, see it appear in 'diff'
$ docker run -d --name c1 nginx
$ docker exec c1 sh -c 'echo hi >> /etc/nginx/nginx.conf'
$ ls /var/lib/docker/overlay2/<c1-id>/diff/etc/nginx/     # nginx.conf now here

Why this shapes how you write Dockerfiles

  • Order stable → volatile. Put rarely-changing steps (install OS packages, dependencies) before frequently-changing steps (COPY your source). A change invalidates that layer and every layer after it.
  • Cleanup must be in the same RUN. RUN apt-get install ... then a later RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists still ships the files — they're in the earlier layer; the later layer just adds whiteouts. Chain it: RUN apt-get install -y x && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*.
  • Big-file churn bloats the image. Modifying a 200 MB file in a later layer copies the whole 200 MB into that layer — the image now carries both versions.
  • Secrets leak across layers. COPY key . then RUN use-key && rm key — the key is still in the COPY layer forever. Use build secrets / multi-stage.
# BAD: source change busts the pip-install cache every build
COPY . /app
RUN pip install -r /app/requirements.txt

# GOOD: deps layer is cached until requirements.txt itself changes
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . /app

Storage drivers & where the layers live

  • overlay2 is the default on Linux (needs a kernel with overlayfs, most since 4.x). Alternatives: fuse-overlayfs (rootless), btrfs/zfs (CoW at the FS level), devicemapper (legacy), vfs (no CoW, full copy per layer — slow, testing only).
  • On disk (Docker): /var/lib/docker/overlay2/. Layers are dedup'd; docker system df shows real vs reclaimable; docker image prune / docker builder prune reclaim.
  • The writable layer dies with the container (docker rm). Anything that must survive goes in a volume or bind mount — which also skips copy-up and its write-amplification.
Cheat Sheet
  • Image = ordered list of content-addressed read-only layers (a diff tar each) + a config. Container adds one thin writable layer.
  • OverlayFS: lowerdir(s) = image layers, upperdir = container R/W, merged = what the container sees.
  • Read = first match top-down. Write = copy-up into upper. Delete = whiteout in upper.
  • Layers dedup'd & shared → fast pulls, small disk, near-zero-cost container start.
  • Changing a layer invalidates it and every layer after it → order Dockerfile stable→volatile; copy deps before source.
  • Clean up in the same RUN; a later rm only adds whiteouts, doesn't shrink the image.
  • Secrets in an early layer stay forever — use build secrets / multi-stage.
  • Default driver overlay2; rootless uses fuse-overlayfs. Writable layer is lost on rm — persist via volumes.
Q&A
Why can 50 containers from the same image start almost instantly and use little extra disk?
They all share the image's read-only layers via OverlayFS — nothing is copied at start. Each gets only a small empty upperdir for its writes. Disk grows only as each container actually modifies or creates files (copy-up).
You RUN apt-get install then in a later RUN delete the apt cache, but the image is still huge. Why?
The installed files and cache live in the earlier layer, which is immutable. The later RUN just adds whiteout entries that hide them in the merged view — the bytes are still shipped in the earlier layer. You must install and clean up in a single RUN ... && rm -rf ... so the cleanup is part of the same layer diff.
What is "copy-up" in OverlayFS?
When a process in the container modifies (or opens for write, or changes metadata on) a file that exists only in a read-only lower layer, overlay first copies the entire file up into the writable upper layer, then applies the change there. The lower copy is untouched. Modifying a large file therefore duplicates it into the container's writable layer.
Where does data written by a container go, and what happens to it on docker rm?
Into the container's writable upper layer (/var/lib/docker/overlay2/<id>/diff). It is deleted with the container. To persist data, mount a named volume or a bind mount at that path — those live outside the layer stack and survive container removal (and also avoid copy-up write-amplification).
Why does putting COPY . /app before RUN pip install hurt build times?
Any change to any source file changes the COPY layer's digest, which invalidates it and every subsequent layer — so pip install re-runs on every build. Copying just requirements.txt first lets the dependency layer stay cached until the dependency list itself changes.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

How many writable layers does a running container have?
One — a thin writable layer (the OverlayFS upperdir) on top of the image's read-only layers. It's discarded when the container is removed.
What makes two identical layers get stored only once?
Layers are content-addressed by a SHA-256 digest of their contents. Same contents → same digest → the store keeps one copy and every image/container that references that digest shares it.

Intermediate core

You added a secret in one COPY, used it, and deleted it in the next RUN. Is the image safe to publish?
No. The secret is baked into the COPY layer, which is immutable and part of the pushed image; the later RUN rm only whiteouts it in the merged view. Anyone can docker save the image, extract that layer's tar, and read the file. Safe options: BuildKit build secrets (RUN --mount=type=secret, never persisted to a layer), multi-stage builds where the secret only exists in a discarded builder stage, or injecting the secret at runtime instead of build time. If it's already published, rotate the secret — it must be considered compromised.
An image balloons to 3 GB after a step that just "updates a config file." Explain.
That "config file" is probably large (a model file, a bundled dataset, a database), and it lives in an earlier layer. Editing it in a later RUN/COPY triggers copy-up of the whole file into the new layer, so the image now contains both the original (in the old layer) and the modified copy (in the new layer). Same thing happens if a build step touches permissions/timestamps on a big directory tree. Fixes: generate the file in its final form in one layer, use a build arg/template so it's written once, keep large mutable data in a volume at runtime rather than the image, or flatten with a multi-stage COPY --from of just the final tree.

Advanced deep

Design the layer strategy for a large polyglot service image to maximize cache hits across builds and minimize pushed bytes.
Order by change frequency, coarse to fine: (1) base image pinned by digest; (2) OS packages (RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y ... && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* in one layer); (3) language runtime / toolchain if not in the base; (4) dependency manifests only (package.json+lockfile, requirements.txt/poetry.lock, go.mod/go.sum) then the dependency install — so deps re-resolve only when the lockfile changes; (5) application source; (6) build/compile step; (7) final config/entrypoint. Use BuildKit features: RUN --mount=type=cache for package-manager caches (npm/pip/go build cache) so the cache persists outside the image without bloating layers; --mount=type=secret for registry/credentials; parallel stages for independent language builds. Multi-stage: a fat builder stage (compilers, dev headers, test deps) and a slim runtime stage that COPY --from=builders only the artifacts + runtime deps onto a minimal base (distroless/alpine/scratch) — the builder layers are never pushed. Minimize pushed bytes: keep the runtime base tiny and stable (so it's already in the registry/nodes), split rarely- vs often-changing app assets into separate COPYs, avoid COPY . (use a tight .dockerignore and explicit paths so unrelated file changes don't bust the layer), and don't chmod -R/chown -R big trees in a late layer (copies them up). Cross-build cache: in CI, use --cache-from/--cache-to (registry or gha cache) so a fresh runner reuses layers; tag intermediate images. Verify: docker history/dive to spot fat or wasted layers and files duplicated across layers; measure "bytes changed per typical commit" and drive it toward just the source + build-output layers.

OCI, runc, containerd & the CRI

Open standards let any tool build an image any runtime can run, and let Kubernetes talk to any runtime through one interface.

Notes

Two OCI specs

What. The Open Container Initiative publishes standards so the ecosystem interoperates:

  • Image spec — the on-disk/registry format: a manifest (list of layer digests + config digest), a config (env, entrypoint, working dir, exposed ports), and the layer tarballs. Optionally a manifest list / image index for multi-arch.
  • Runtime spec — how to run a bundle: a rootfs/ directory plus a config.json describing namespaces, mounts, cgroup limits, capabilities, seccomp, the process to run.
  • Distribution spec — the registry HTTP API (/v2/…) for push/pull.
# an OCI image manifest (what a registry serves)
{ "schemaVersion": 2,
  "config": { "digest": "sha256:cfg...", "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.config.v1+json" },
  "layers": [
    { "digest": "sha256:l1...", "size": 3145728 },
    { "digest": "sha256:l2...", "size": 812   } ] }

# the runtime bundle runc actually consumes
bundle/
  config.json        # namespaces, mounts, cgroups, caps, seccomp, process.args
  rootfs/            # the merged filesystem

runc — the low-level runtime

What / why. runc is the reference OCI runtime: given a bundle, it does the clone() + namespaces + pivot_root + cgroups + seccomp + execve() dance from the "A Container Is Just a Process" topic, then exits. It is tiny and does one job. Alternatives that implement the same interface: crun (C, faster/lighter), runsc (gVisor, user-space kernel), kata-runtime (boots a micro-VM), youki (Rust).

# run an OCI bundle directly, no Docker, no containerd
$ mkdir -p bundle/rootfs
$ docker export $(docker create alpine) | tar -C bundle/rootfs -xf -
$ cd bundle && runc spec                 # generates a default config.json
$ sudo runc run demo                       # starts a shell in the container
$ sudo runc list ; sudo runc kill demo KILL ; sudo runc delete demo

containerd & the shim

What / why. containerd is the daemon that manages the container lifecycle: pulling images from registries, unpacking layers into an overlay snapshot, storing metadata, wiring up networking, and calling runc. Between containerd and runc sits a shim (one per container): it becomes the container's parent process and keeps the stdio and exit-status plumbing alive, so containerd (or dockerd) can be restarted or upgraded without killing running containers.

$ ctr images pull docker.io/library/redis:7-alpine
$ ctr run --rm -t docker.io/library/redis:7-alpine r1 redis-server --version
$ ctr containers ls ; ctr tasks ls
# process tree:  containerd --- containerd-shim-runc-v2 --- redis-server

The CRI — how Kubernetes stays runtime-agnostic

What / why. The Container Runtime Interface is a gRPC API the kubelet calls to create pod sandboxes and containers, pull images, stream logs/exec, and report status. Any runtime that implements CRI works: containerd (via its built-in CRI plugin) and CRI-O (a minimal runtime built specifically for Kubernetes) are the two in production. This is why "Kubernetes removed Docker" in 1.24 was a non-event — it removed the dockershim adapter; images and containerd underneath are unchanged.

# crictl = a CRI debugging CLI, works against containerd OR CRI-O
$ crictl ps                         # containers the kubelet started
$ crictl pods                       # pod sandboxes
$ crictl inspect <id> | jq '.info.runtimeSpec.linux.resources'
$ crictl logs <id> ; crictl exec -it <id> sh

# node config points the kubelet at the CRI socket
--container-runtime-endpoint=unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock

How the pieces line up

LayerJobExamples
OrchestratorSchedule, heal, scale across nodesKubernetes, Nomad
CRI runtime (high-level)Images, snapshots, lifecycle, CRI/APIcontainerd, CRI-O, (dockerd for the CLI)
ShimPer-container parent; decouple daemon restartscontainerd-shim-runc-v2
OCI runtime (low-level)clone/namespaces/cgroups/execverunc, crun, runsc (gVisor), kata-runtime
Cheat Sheet
  • OCI specs: image (manifest + config + layers), runtime (bundle = rootfs + config.json), distribution (registry API).
  • runc = reference low-level runtime: does the namespaces/cgroups/pivot_root/execve, then exits. Swappable: crun, runsc (gVisor), kata-runtime.
  • containerd = high-level runtime daemon: pull, unpack, snapshot, network, lifecycle, calls runc.
  • shim = one per container; becomes its parent so containerd/dockerd can restart without killing containers.
  • CRI = gRPC API the kubelet uses; implemented by containerd and CRI-O. "K8s removed Docker" = removed the dockershim adapter only.
  • Full stack: kubelet → (CRI) containerd → shim → runc → your process. Docker: docker CLI → dockerd → containerd → shim → runc.
  • Debug CLIs: ctr (containerd native), crictl (CRI, works with containerd or CRI-O), runc (bundles directly).
Q&A
What are the OCI image spec and OCI runtime spec?
The image spec defines the portable package format — a manifest listing content-addressed layer digests plus a config blob (env, entrypoint, …), served by registries. The runtime spec defines how to execute an unpacked image: a "bundle" of a rootfs/ directory and a config.json that specifies namespaces, mounts, cgroup limits, capabilities, seccomp and the process to run. Together they let any builder produce an image any compliant runtime can run.
What does runc do, and what does it not do?
runc takes an OCI bundle and creates the container process — sets up namespaces, mounts and pivot_root, applies the cgroup, seccomp filter and capability set, then execve()s the entrypoint — and then exits. It does not pull images, manage layers/snapshots, do networking beyond what's in config.json, keep any state, or provide an API. Those are containerd's job.
What is the container shim and why does it exist?
A small process (one per container) that containerd starts and that becomes the container's parent. It holds the container's stdio, keeps the pty open, and reports the exit code. Because it — not containerd — is the parent, you can restart or upgrade containerd (or dockerd) without every running container getting reparented to init or killed.
Did Kubernetes "remove Docker support," and what actually changed?
It removed dockershim — the built-in adapter that let the kubelet talk to the Docker daemon — in v1.24. The kubelet now speaks CRI directly to containerd or CRI-O. Since Docker already used containerd underneath, and images are OCI-standard, nodes and images are unaffected; you just don't run the Docker daemon on cluster nodes.
containerd vs CRI-O?
Both are CRI-compliant high-level runtimes for Kubernetes. containerd is a general-purpose runtime (also used by Docker and standalone via ctr/nerdctl) with a broad plugin ecosystem. CRI-O is deliberately minimal — it implements exactly the CRI and nothing else, tracks Kubernetes releases closely, and is the default in OpenShift. Functionally interchangeable for running pods.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Name the low-level and high-level runtime in a standard Kubernetes node.
Low-level (OCI) runtime: runc (or crun). High-level runtime: containerd (or CRI-O). The kubelet talks to the high-level one over the CRI gRPC API.
What is an "OCI bundle"?
A directory containing a rootfs/ (the container's filesystem) and a config.json (namespaces, mounts, cgroup limits, capabilities, seccomp, and the process to run). It's the input to an OCI runtime like runc.

Intermediate core

Trace a kubectl run nginx down to a running process.
API server persists a Pod to etcd → scheduler assigns it a node → that node's kubelet sees the Pod and calls the CRI: RunPodSandbox creates the pod's network namespace (via CNI) and a pause container; PullImage if needed; CreateContainer + StartContainer for nginx. containerd handles that: pulls the image from the registry (distribution spec), unpacks layers into an overlay snapshot, writes an OCI bundle (rootfs + config.json with the pod's namespaces, the container's cgroup limits from requests/limits, seccomp/caps), then starts a containerd-shim which invokes runc create/start. runc does clone() with the namespace flags, sets up mounts + pivot_root, applies cgroup/seccomp/caps, and execve("nginx"). runc exits; the shim stays as nginx's parent and streams logs/exit status back to containerd → kubelet → API server status.
How do you run "hostile" pods with a stronger boundary without changing the rest of the cluster?
Install an alternative OCI runtime that presents a stronger isolation boundary — Kata Containers (each pod in a lightweight KVM micro-VM) or gVisor (runsc, a user-space kernel that intercepts syscalls). Register it as a Kubernetes RuntimeClass (containerd/CRI-O config points a handler name at the runtime binary). Untrusted pods set spec.runtimeClassName: kata (or gvisor) and get the stronger sandbox; everything else keeps using runc. The CRI, kubelet, images, manifests and scheduling are unchanged — only the runtime handler differs — and you can use node labels/taints to place hostile pods on dedicated nodes as defence in depth.

Advanced deep

Why is the shim architecture important for daemon upgrades, and what breaks without it?
Without a shim, the container-manager daemon (dockerd/containerd) would be the direct parent of every container process. Consequences: (1) restarting or upgrading the daemon reparents all containers to PID 1 (init), losing the stdio pipes and the ability to collect exit codes — or, in the naive design, kills them; (2) the daemon must stay running to hold the pty and forward signals, so it can't be a stateless component; (3) a daemon crash orphans containers with no one to reap them or report status. The shim fixes this: containerd double-forks a tiny shim per container that becomes the container's parent, owns the pty/stdio fds, waits on the container, and exposes a small API (over a socket/FIFO) for containerd to reconnect to. So containerd can be stopped, upgraded, and restarted; on restart it re-discovers the shims and reattaches, and running containers never noticed. The shim also isolates faults (a bug handling one container's IO doesn't take down the daemon) and is where runtime-specific logic lives (there are shim implementations for runc, Kata, gVisor). The cost is one extra lightweight process per container (a few MB), which is why shims are written to be minimal.

Capabilities, seccomp, LSMs & Rootless

Namespaces and cgroups isolate and limit; this layer decides how much a container is actually allowed to do to the shared kernel.

Notes

Why "root in a container" is dangerous by default

What. Without a user namespace, UID 0 inside the container is UID 0 on the host. The container's root has a reduced default capability set, but that set still includes things like CAP_NET_RAW, CAP_SETUID, CAP_CHOWN, CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE — and any bind-mounted host path is writable as root.

Why it matters. A remote-code-execution bug in your app, running as root, plus a kernel LPE or a misconfigured mount, equals host compromise. Running as a non-root UID, dropping capabilities, and adding a user namespace each cut that path.

# default docker root: a trimmed but still potent capability set
$ docker run --rm alpine sh -c 'apk add -q libcap; capsh --print | grep Current'
Current: cap_chown,cap_dac_override,cap_fowner,cap_fsetid,cap_kill,cap_setgid,
         cap_setuid,cap_setpcap,cap_net_bind_service,cap_net_raw,cap_sys_chroot,
         cap_mknod,cap_audit_write,cap_setfcap

# the hardened baseline
$ docker run --rm \
    --user 10001:10001 \
    --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE \
    --security-opt no-new-privileges \
    --read-only --tmpfs /tmp \
    myapp

Linux capabilities

What. The kernel splits "root's power" into ~40 independent capabilities (CAP_NET_ADMIN = configure networking, CAP_SYS_ADMIN = the "kitchen sink", CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE = bind ports <1024, CAP_SYS_PTRACE = trace other processes, …). A process only holds the ones in its sets.

Why / how. Start from nothing and add back only what the workload needs. --cap-drop ALL then --cap-add the essentials; in Kubernetes it's securityContext.capabilities. Avoid --privileged (grants all capabilities, all devices, and lifts seccomp/AppArmor) — it's an isolation off-switch.

# Kubernetes: drop everything, add only what's required
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 10001
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
  capabilities:
    drop: ["ALL"]
    add:  ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]   # e.g. an app that must listen on :80
  seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }

seccomp — syscall filtering

What / why. A seccomp-bpf filter is a per-process allow/deny list over the ~350 syscalls. It shrinks the kernel attack surface: most containers never legitimately call keyctl, ptrace, mount, bpf, userfaultfd, kexec_load, … Docker's default profile blocks ~50 dangerous syscalls; Kubernetes needs seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault set explicitly (or a cluster default) to get it.

# see it working: the default profile blocks unshare(CLONE_NEWNS) etc.
$ docker run --rm alpine unshare -Urm sh
unshare: unshare failed: Operation not permitted        # seccomp said no

$ docker run --rm --security-opt seccomp=unconfined alpine unshare -Urm sh   # allowed (bad)

# a custom minimal profile (default action = errno, then allow a whitelist)
{ "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO",
  "syscalls": [ { "names": ["read","write","openat","close","futex","mmap","..."],
                  "action": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW" } ] }

LSMs — AppArmor & SELinux

What / why. A Linux Security Module adds mandatory access control on top of Unix permissions: a profile constrains which files a container can read/write, which mounts and capabilities it can use, and whether it can ptrace or send signals across labels. Docker applies a default docker-default AppArmor profile; Red Hat/OpenShift use SELinux with per-container MCS labels (each container gets a unique category pair, so container A can't touch container B's files even if permissions would allow it).

# confirm the profile is applied
$ docker run --rm alpine cat /proc/self/attr/current
docker-default (enforce)

# SELinux: bind mounts need a label or they're denied
$ docker run -v /data:/data:Z myapp     # :Z relabels /data with a private MCS label
                                        # :z shares the label between containers

Rootless containers

What / why. Run the entire container stack — daemon (or daemonless with Podman), runtime, and containers — as an unprivileged user, using a user namespace so in-container UID 0 maps to your host UID (or a subordinate range from /etc/subuid). A container breakout lands as a nobody, not as host root. Networking uses slirp4netns/pasta (user-mode) and storage uses fuse-overlayfs.

# Podman is rootless by default
$ id -u                      # 1000  (not root)
$ podman run -d -p 8080:80 nginx
$ podman unshare cat /proc/self/uid_map
     0   1000      1          # container root -> me
     1  100000  65536         # container uid 1..65535 -> my subuid range

# rootless Docker (opt-in)
$ dockerd-rootless-setuptool.sh install
$ export DOCKER_HOST=unix://$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/docker.sock

The hardening checklist

  • Non-root USER in the image; runAsNonRoot: true to enforce it.
  • --cap-drop ALL, add back the few you need. Never --privileged unless you truly are (a device driver, DinD).
  • no-new-privileges / allowPrivilegeEscalation: false (blocks setuid binaries from re-gaining privilege).
  • Seccomp RuntimeDefault (or tighter); AppArmor/SELinux enforcing.
  • --read-only rootfs + explicit tmpfs/volumes for the paths that must be writable.
  • Don't mount the Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) into a container — that's root-equivalent on the host.
  • Drop the cloud metadata endpoint from the container's network reach; don't pass host secrets via env.
  • Prefer rootless / user namespaces; for hostile workloads use a micro-VM runtime (Kata) or gVisor.
Cheat Sheet
  • Layers of restriction: user ns (remap UIDs) → capabilities (which root powers) → seccomp (which syscalls) → LSM (AppArmor/SELinux MAC) → the shared kernel.
  • Container root ≠ host root only if a user namespace is in use; otherwise it basically is host root minus a few caps.
  • --cap-drop ALL then add back essentials (e.g. NET_BIND_SERVICE). Never --privileged casually.
  • no-new-privileges / allowPrivilegeEscalation: false stops setuid re-escalation.
  • Seccomp RuntimeDefault blocks ~50 dangerous syscalls; Kubernetes needs it set explicitly.
  • LSM: AppArmor docker-default profile, or SELinux per-container MCS labels; bind mounts need :z/:Z under SELinux.
  • Rootless (Podman default, Docker opt-in): whole stack as an unprivileged user via user ns; breakout = nobody.
  • Never bind-mount /var/run/docker.sock into a container — it's host root.
Q&A
Is root inside a container the same as root on the host?
Without a user namespace, effectively yes — it's UID 0 on the host with a slightly reduced default capability set, and any bind-mounted host path is writable. With a user namespace, container UID 0 maps to an unprivileged host UID, so a breakout has no host privilege. Rootless containers always use a user namespace for this reason.
What does --privileged actually do, and why avoid it?
It grants all Linux capabilities, exposes all host devices, and disables the seccomp and AppArmor/SELinux profiles — essentially turning off the container's security controls. A privileged container can load kernel modules, reconfigure the host network, mount host filesystems, and trivially escape. Use it only for genuine cases (a device driver, Docker-in-Docker) and prefer targeted --cap-add / --device instead.
What is seccomp and what does the default profile buy you?
seccomp installs a BPF filter that allows or denies syscalls per-process. Docker's default profile denies ~50 syscalls that containers almost never need but attackers love — keyctl, ptrace (cross-process), mount, bpf, userfaultfd, kexec_load, various namespace/clone flags — shrinking the kernel attack surface with essentially no compatibility cost. In Kubernetes you must opt in with seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault (or a cluster-wide default).
How does SELinux keep two containers from touching each other's files?
Each container gets a unique MCS (Multi-Category Security) label — a pair of categories like s0:c123,c456. A process labelled with one set can only access files labelled with the same set, regardless of Unix permissions. So even if container A can read a world-readable file that container B wrote, the label mismatch denies it. Bind mounts need :z (shared label) or :Z (private label) to be accessible at all.
Why is mounting the Docker socket into a container a security problem?
/var/run/docker.sock is the Docker daemon's API, and the daemon runs as root. A process that can reach the socket can start a new container with --privileged, bind-mount /, and run any command as root on the host — it's equivalent to giving that container full host root. If a container needs to manage containers, use a scoped API proxy, a rootless daemon, or the Kubernetes API with RBAC instead.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Name three things you'd put in a container's securityContext to harden it.
runAsNonRoot: true / runAsUser, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, capabilities.drop: ["ALL"], readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault. Any three.
What does --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE achieve?
The container process holds no Linux capabilities except the one that lets it bind to ports below 1024. It can't do raw sockets, change file ownership, load modules, mount, ptrace others, etc. — minimal privilege for something that just needs to listen on :80/:443.

Intermediate core

An app "needs to run as root." How do you reduce the risk without changing the app?
(1) User namespace — run rootless (Podman, or Docker with userns-remap / rootless mode) so the app's UID 0 maps to an unprivileged host UID; a breakout is a nobody. (2) Drop capabilities to the minimum the app actually uses (--cap-drop ALL + a short --cap-add list found by testing, or by capsh/getpcaps tracing). (3) no-new-privileges so it can't re-escalate via a setuid binary. (4) --read-only root filesystem + tmpfs for /tmp//run. (5) Seccomp RuntimeDefault and an enforcing AppArmor/SELinux profile. (6) No host bind mounts (especially not the docker socket), no host network, block the metadata endpoint. (7) If it's genuinely untrusted, put it under a micro-VM runtime (Kata) via RuntimeClass. Often "needs root" really means "needs to bind :80" (grant just NET_BIND_SERVICE or use a high port + a proxy) or "needs to write somewhere" (a volume with the right ownership) — check before accepting the premise.
Explain the difference between capabilities, seccomp, and an LSM — do you need all three?
They restrict different things and overlap only partially, so yes, use all three (defence in depth). Capabilities gate privileged operations — a coarse allow-list of "root powers" (bind low ports, change ownership, admin the network, load modules). seccomp gates syscalls — finer-grained, it can block ptrace or keyctl entirely even for a process that has the relevant capability, shrinking the kernel's exposed API. LSMs (AppArmor/SELinux) do mandatory access control on resources — which files/paths, mounts, sockets, and cross-process operations are allowed, by label/profile, independent of DAC permissions and independent of syscalls. Example: capabilities might allow CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE, seccomp still allows open(), but the AppArmor profile denies writing to /etc/. A gap in one layer is often covered by another.

Advanced deep

Design container security controls for a platform running third-party workloads you don't fully trust, from image to runtime to node.
Supply chain / image: only run signed images (cosign + admission policy), from an allow-listed registry; scan every image (Trivy/Grype) and block on fixable HIGH/CRITICAL; generate and store an SBOM; base images minimal (distroless/alpine) and rebuilt on CVE. Admission: enforce Pod Security "restricted" (no privileged, no host namespaces, non-root, drop-ALL caps, seccomp RuntimeDefault, read-only rootfs) via Pod Security Admission or a policy engine (Kyverno/OPA Gatekeeper); deny hostPath, hostNetwork, hostPID, the docker socket, and privileged escalation; require resource limits and a runtimeClass for untrusted tenants. Runtime isolation: put untrusted pods under Kata Containers (per-pod micro-VM) or gVisor via RuntimeClass so a kernel exploit doesn't cross to the host; keep runc pods (trusted infra) on separate node pools (taints/tolerations + node affinity), one tenant per node pool where the threat model demands it. Inside the sandbox: non-root uid, all caps dropped, tight seccomp (custom profile per workload class), enforcing AppArmor/SELinux, read-only rootfs, no-new-privileges, cgroup limits on CPU/mem/PIDs/IO to bound DoS, user namespace on. Network: default-deny NetworkPolicy, per-tenant namespaces, egress via a filtering proxy, block link-local/metadata (169.254.169.254) at the CNI, mTLS between services (mesh). Node: minimal hardened host OS, current kernel with mitigations, no secrets on the node the workload can reach (disable/lock down the metadata service, use IRSA/Workload Identity scoped per pod), auto-recycle nodes, read-only where possible, host-level auditd/Falco for escape indicators (unexpected mount, ptrace, writes to /proc/sys, new caps). Blast radius: short-lived nodes, per-tenant ResourceQuota/LimitRange, per-namespace RBAC with no cross-namespace access, disk quotas, wall-clock timeouts. Detection & response: runtime security (Falco/Tetragon) alerting on the sandbox-escape signatures, centralized audit logs, and a playbook to cordon/drain/replace a node on suspicion. Net: verified minimal images, restrictive admission, a real isolation boundary (micro-VM) per untrusted workload, full in-sandbox hardening, default-deny networking, node-level least privilege and monitoring — assume the container will be compromised and make that not matter.

Container Networking Primitives

A fresh network namespace has nothing but a down loopback; a veth pair, a bridge and a NAT rule turn it into a container that can reach the world.

Notes

The empty network namespace

What / why. unshare --net (or a container's net namespace) starts with a single lo interface, and it's down. No routes, no DNS, no way out. Everything below is how you connect it.

$ sudo ip netns add c1
$ sudo ip netns exec c1 ip addr
1: lo: <LOOPBACK> state DOWN            # that's all there is
$ sudo ip netns exec c1 ping 8.8.8.8
connect: Network is unreachable

veth pairs — a virtual cable

What / why. A veth is a pair of interfaces acting like a patch cable: a frame sent into one end comes out the other. Put one end in the container's netns and leave the other on the host, and you have a link between the two.

$ sudo ip link add veth-c1 type veth peer name eth0-in
$ sudo ip link set eth0-in netns c1                   # one end into the container
$ sudo ip netns exec c1 ip addr add 172.18.0.2/16 dev eth0-in
$ sudo ip netns exec c1 ip link set eth0-in up
$ sudo ip netns exec c1 ip link set lo up
$ sudo ip link set veth-c1 up                          # host end up

A bridge — the virtual switch

What / why. To connect many containers, attach every container's host-side veth to a Linux bridge (a software L2 switch). Containers on the same bridge reach each other directly at layer 2 — no NAT, no routing. The bridge gets the gateway IP; it's the container's default route.

$ sudo ip link add br0 type bridge
$ sudo ip addr add 172.18.0.1/16 dev br0
$ sudo ip link set br0 up
$ sudo ip link set veth-c1 master br0                  # plug the veth into the switch
$ sudo ip netns exec c1 ip route add default via 172.18.0.1
$ sudo ip netns exec c1 ping 172.18.0.3                # another container on br0: works, no NAT

NAT — egress and port publishing

What / why. The container's 172.18.x.x address isn't routable on the real network. For egress, the host rewrites the source address on the way out (MASQUERADE). For ingress, -p 8080:80 installs a DNAT rule so traffic to the host's :8080 is redirected to the container's :80.

# egress: SNAT everything leaving the bridge subnet
$ sudo iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 172.18.0.0/16 ! -o br0 -j MASQUERADE
$ sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
$ sudo ip netns exec c1 ping 8.8.8.8                   # now works

# ingress: what "docker run -p 8080:80" adds
$ sudo iptables -t nat -A DOCKER ! -i br0 -p tcp --dport 8080 \
      -j DNAT --to-destination 172.18.0.2:80
$ curl localhost:8080                                   # reaches the container

DNS & service discovery

  • By default a container inherits the host's /etc/resolv.conf (or a runtime-provided resolver).
  • On a user-defined Docker bridge, the daemon runs an embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11 that resolves other containers by name — that's why docker compose lets web reach db by hostname.
  • Kubernetes runs cluster DNS (CoreDNS); Services get an A record like db.default.svc.cluster.local.
$ docker network create appnet
$ docker run -d --name db  --network appnet postgres
$ docker run --rm --network appnet alpine nslookup db
Server:  127.0.0.11
Address: 127.0.0.11:53
Name:    db
Address: 172.19.0.2

Network modes & CNI

ModeWhat it does
bridge (default)The setup above: private subnet, NAT egress, -p for ingress.
hostNo netns of its own — uses the host's stack directly. Fastest, zero isolation, port conflicts with the host.
noneJust lo. For fully offline/computational containers.
container:<id>Share another container's netns (how a K8s pod's containers share one IP).
overlayVXLAN tunnels between hosts so containers on different machines share an L2 segment (Swarm; K8s does the equivalent via CNI).

CNI (Container Network Interface) is the plugin standard Kubernetes uses: the kubelet calls a CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium, Flannel, AWS VPC CNI) with the pod's netns, and the plugin creates the veth/route/policy so the pod gets a cluster-routable IP. The primitives are the same — veth, bridge/routing, iptables/eBPF — just automated per pod.

Cheat Sheet
  • Fresh net namespace = a down lo and nothing else.
  • veth pair = virtual cable; one end in the container netns, other end on the host.
  • Linux bridge = virtual L2 switch; attach all container veths → they talk directly, no NAT.
  • MASQUERADE/SNAT = egress (rewrite source IP). DNAT = ingress; -p host:container installs it.
  • Container-to-container on the same bridge: plain L2, no NAT.
  • Embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11 on user-defined Docker networks resolves container names (why Compose service names work).
  • Modes: bridge (default), host (no isolation, fast), none (lo only), container:<id> (share netns = pod), overlay (VXLAN cross-host).
  • CNI automates veth/route/policy per pod; Kubernetes rule: every pod gets a routable IP, pod↔pod with no NAT.
Q&A
You put a process in a new network namespace and it has no connectivity. What's missing?
Everything except a down loopback. You need: a veth pair with one end moved into the namespace, IP addresses on both ends (or the host end on a bridge), the links brought up, a default route in the namespace pointing at the host/bridge, ip_forward enabled, and a MASQUERADE rule so the namespace's private IP is SNAT'd for egress. DNS (/etc/resolv.conf) too if you want name resolution.
What does -p 8080:80 actually do?
It adds a DNAT (destination NAT) rule in the host's nat table: packets arriving on the host's port 8080 have their destination rewritten to the container's IP:80 and are forwarded over the bridge. (Plus a matching rule so the container's replies are un-NAT'd.) It also usually adds a small userland proxy for loopback/edge cases.
How do containers on the same Docker user-defined network reach each other by name?
The Docker daemon runs an embedded DNS resolver, injected into each container as nameserver 127.0.0.11. It resolves container/service names on that network to their current IPs. On the default bridge network (legacy) this doesn't work — you needed --link; on any network you create with docker network create, it does. Compose creates such a network, so services resolve each other by service name.
What's the difference between --network host and the default bridge?
With host, the container does not get its own network namespace — it shares the host's interfaces, IP, ports and routing table. No veth, no bridge, no NAT: lowest latency and no port-mapping needed, but zero network isolation and the container's listeners collide with the host's. The default bridge gives the container a private IP on a NAT'd subnet, isolating it and requiring -p to expose ports.
What role does CNI play in Kubernetes networking?
CNI is the plugin interface between the kubelet and the network implementation. When a pod is created, the kubelet invokes the configured CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium, Flannel, cloud VPC CNI, …) with the pod's network namespace; the plugin sets up the veth, assigns an IP from the cluster/pod CIDR, adds routes (and, for policy-capable plugins, programs iptables/eBPF for NetworkPolicy). The result satisfies the Kubernetes model: every pod has a unique cluster-routable IP and any pod can reach any other pod without NAT.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What is a veth pair?
Two linked virtual network interfaces — whatever goes in one end comes out the other, like a virtual patch cable. Used to connect a container's network namespace to the host (or a bridge).
Do two containers on the same Docker bridge network need NAT to talk to each other?
No. They're on the same layer-2 segment (the bridge), so they communicate directly by IP with no NAT. NAT is only for egress to the outside world and for publishing ports inward.

Intermediate core

A container can reach the internet but not another container by name. Where do you look?
"Reaches the internet" means veth/bridge/route/NAT are fine. "Not by name" is DNS or network membership. Check: (1) are both containers on the same user-defined network? The default bridge has no embedded DNS. (2) Is the resolver 127.0.0.11 in the container's /etc/resolv.conf? (3) Does nslookup other-container 127.0.0.11 resolve? (4) Is the target container actually running and attached (docker network inspect)? (5) Is there a name vs alias mismatch (Compose service name vs container name)? (6) In Kubernetes: is CoreDNS healthy, is the Service created, is the pod's resolv.conf pointing at the cluster DNS ClusterIP, and is a NetworkPolicy blocking DNS (UDP/53 to kube-system)?
Why can't two containers in the same Kubernetes pod both listen on port 8080?
Containers in a pod share one network namespace (set up on the pod's pause/sandbox container), so they share a single IP and a single port space. Two processes — whether in the same container or different containers of the pod — can't both bind() the same port. They reach each other over localhost. If you need two services on 8080, they belong in separate pods.

Advanced deep

Compare bridge+NAT, overlay/VXLAN, and native-routing (e.g. cloud VPC CNI) container networking, and when you'd choose each.
Bridge + NAT (single host, or Docker default): container on a private subnet, SNAT for egress, DNAT for published ports. Simple, no dependency on the underlying network, works anywhere. Costs: NAT hides the real client IP, port-publishing is a bottleneck and a source of conflicts, and it doesn't span hosts. Good for local dev, single-node, or simple multi-container apps. Overlay / VXLAN (Flannel vxlan, Docker Swarm overlay, Calico VXLAN/IPIP, Cilium tunnel): pod/container traffic between hosts is encapsulated in UDP and tunnelled, so containers on different nodes share a flat address space regardless of the physical network. Pros: runs on any L3 network, no need to program the physical routers, easy to stand up. Cons: ~50 bytes of encapsulation overhead (MTU tuning, some throughput/CPU cost), and packet captures show the outer header not the pod IP. Good default for on-prem or mixed environments where you don't control routing. Native routing / no overlay (Calico BGP, Cilium native routing, AWS VPC CNI, GKE/Azure CNI): the pod IP is a real address in the datacenter/VPC and the network (BGP peers, or the cloud's SDN) routes to it directly — no encapsulation. Pros: line-rate, real source IPs end to end, security groups/flow logs see pod IPs, best for latency-sensitive and high-throughput workloads. Cons: consumes real IP space (VPC CNI can exhaust subnet IPs; needs prefix delegation), requires control of routing (BGP fabric) or a cloud CNI, and cross-cluster/hybrid gets harder. Choosing: managed cloud → that cloud's VPC CNI (native routing, integrates with security groups and load balancers) unless IP exhaustion pushes you to an overlay or Cilium with masquerade; on-prem with a plain L3 network → overlay (VXLAN) for simplicity, or Calico BGP if you can peer with the ToR switches and want native performance and real IPs; single host / dev → bridge+NAT. Cilium (eBPF) is increasingly the pick across all three because it replaces kube-proxy, does native routing or tunnel, and gives identity-based policy and observability.

Build a Container by Hand

Assemble a working container from a rootfs, unshare, pivot_root, a cgroup and capsh — no Docker, no runtime, just the kernel features.

Notes

Step 1 — get a root filesystem

What / why. The container needs its own /. Any minimal userspace works — a BusyBox or Alpine tarball, or export one from an existing image.

$ mkdir -p /tmp/box/rootfs
# option A: from an image
$ docker export $(docker create alpine:3.20) | tar -C /tmp/box/rootfs -xf -
# option B: debootstrap / an alpine-minirootfs tarball
$ ls /tmp/box/rootfs
bin  etc  lib  proc  sys  usr  var  ...

Step 2 — unshare the namespaces

What / why. Create the isolated views. --fork --mount-proc is needed so the child is really in the new PID namespace and gets a correct /proc.

$ sudo unshare \
    --uts --pid --mount --ipc --net --cgroup \
    --fork --mount-proc \
    -- /bin/bash            # we're now in fresh namespaces (still using the host rootfs)
# prove it:
# ps            -> only bash + ps
# hostname box  -> changes only here (UTS)
# ip addr       -> nothing but lo (NET)

Step 3 — switch into the rootfs with pivot_root

What / why. chroot is the quick version; pivot_root is what real runtimes use because it fully detaches the old root so the container can't escape back to it. Mount propagation must be made private first.

ROOT=/tmp/box/rootfs
mount --make-rprivate /                 # don't leak mounts back to the host
mount --bind "$ROOT" "$ROOT"           # pivot_root needs the new root to be a mount
mkdir -p "$ROOT/oldroot"
cd "$ROOT"
pivot_root . oldroot                    # new / is the rootfs; old / is at /oldroot
umount -l /oldroot && rmdir /oldroot    # cut the cord
mount -t proc  proc  /proc              # fresh /proc for the new PID namespace
mount -t sysfs sys   /sys
mount -t tmpfs tmp   /tmp
hostname box

Step 4 — put it in a cgroup

What / why. Namespaces don't limit anything. Add a cgroup v2 node with memory, CPU and PID caps and move the process into it.

# run these from the HOST shell, using the child's PID
CG=/sys/fs/cgroup/box
sudo mkdir -p "$CG"
echo '128M'          | sudo tee "$CG/memory.max"
echo '50000 100000'  | sudo tee "$CG/cpu.max"      # 0.5 CPU
echo '64'            | sudo tee "$CG/pids.max"
echo <child-pid>      | sudo tee "$CG/cgroup.procs"
# now: a fork bomb in the container hits pids.max; a memory hog is OOM-killed inside the cgroup

Step 5 — drop privileges

What / why. Strip capabilities, block re-escalation, and (ideally) install a seccomp filter and switch to a non-root UID.

# inside the container, before exec'ing the workload
capsh --drop=cap_sys_admin,cap_net_admin,cap_sys_module,cap_sys_ptrace,cap_sys_boot \
      --secbits=0x2f \
      --                                  # PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS via secbits/prctl
# then, ideally:
#   prctl(PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS, 1)
#   seccomp(SECCOMP_SET_MODE_FILTER, ...) with an allowlist
#   setgid(10001); setuid(10001)          # run as non-root
exec /bin/sh                              # the "entrypoint"

Step 6 — (optional) give it a network

What / why. The --net namespace is empty; wire a veth to a bridge for connectivity (see "Container Networking Primitives").

# from the host, PID = the container's PID
sudo ip link add veth0 type veth peer name ceth0
sudo ip link set ceth0 netns <PID>
sudo ip link set veth0 master br0 up
sudo nsenter -t <PID> -n ip addr add 172.20.0.2/24 dev ceth0
sudo nsenter -t <PID> -n ip link set ceth0 up
sudo nsenter -t <PID> -n ip route add default via 172.20.0.1

What you just proved

  • The shell is PID 1 — a PID namespace, nothing more.
  • ps can't see host processes; kill -9 <host-pid> fails — PID namespace isolation.
  • hostname changed only here — UTS namespace.
  • A memory hog is OOM-killed and the host is fine — the cgroup contained it.
  • capsh --print shows a reduced set — capabilities, not magic.
  • What a real runtime adds: image pull + overlayfs layer assembly (instead of a hand-made rootfs), a config.json instead of shell commands, a shim + API + lifecycle, and CNI instead of manual veth wiring.
Cheat Sheet
  • 1. rootfs: docker export a tarball, or a BusyBox/Alpine minirootfs.
  • 2. unshare: unshare --uts --pid --mount --ipc --net --cgroup --fork --mount-proc.
  • 3. pivot_root: mount --make-rprivate /; bind-mount the rootfs; pivot_root . oldroot; umount -l oldroot; mount fresh /proc, /sys, /tmp; hostname box.
  • 4. cgroup: mkdir /sys/fs/cgroup/box; write memory.max, cpu.max, pids.max; echo <pid> > cgroup.procs.
  • 5. drop: capsh --drop=..., no_new_privs, seccomp filter, setuid to non-root.
  • 6. network: veth pair, one end into the netns, other on a bridge, add addr + route.
  • This is exactly runc's job from config.json. Docker/containerd add image pull, overlayfs, shim, API, CNI.
Q&A
Why pivot_root instead of chroot?
chroot only changes the apparent root directory — the process still has a reference to the real root and, with enough privilege (or a second chroot), can climb back out. pivot_root moves the old root to a subdirectory which you then umount, so there is no remaining path to the host filesystem. Real runtimes use pivot_root (or MS_MOVE + chroot) for this reason.
Why does unshare --pid need --fork --mount-proc?
The PID namespace only takes effect for children of the calling process — unshare itself stays in the old namespace — so you need --fork to run the command as a child that's actually inside the new namespace. And ps reads /proc, which still shows the host's processes until you --mount-proc a fresh procfs for the new namespace.
After unshare, the container still limits nothing. Why, and what fixes it?
Namespaces are visibility isolation only. Without a cgroup, the process can use all the host's CPU and memory and fork without bound. Create a cgroup v2 node, write memory.max/cpu.max/pids.max, and move the PID into cgroup.procs.
In this hand-built container, is the shell "root"? Is that host root?
The shell runs as UID 0 because you started it with sudo and didn't add a user namespace — so yes, it is host root, just with fewer capabilities after capsh --drop. To make container-root not be host-root you'd add --user --map-root-user to unshare, creating a user namespace that maps in-container UID 0 to your unprivileged host UID.
What does a real runtime add on top of these six steps?
Image handling — pull from a registry, verify digests, assemble the read-only layers with OverlayFS instead of a hand-made rootfs; a declarative config.json (the OCI runtime spec) instead of ad-hoc shell; the seccomp profile, AppArmor/SELinux label, and full mount list; a shim for lifecycle and daemon-restart safety; a stable API; and CNI for networking instead of manual ip commands.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Name the minimum ingredients to turn a process into a container.
A root filesystem, a set of namespaces (at least mount + PID; usually also net, uts, ipc, and user), a cgroup for limits, and reduced privileges (dropped capabilities, no-new-privs, ideally seccomp). Then exec the workload.
What single command creates several namespaces and runs a shell inside them?
sudo unshare --uts --pid --mount --net --ipc --cgroup --fork --mount-proc /bin/bash

Intermediate core

Walk through building a minimal container for a static Go binary using only shell tools.
(1) rootfs: since the binary is static you barely need one — mkdir -p /tmp/box/rootfs/{proc,sys,tmp}, cp ./app /tmp/box/rootfs/app, maybe add /etc/ssl/certs for TLS and /etc/passwd. (2) namespaces: unshare --uts --pid --mount --ipc --net --cgroup --fork --mount-proc. (3) rootfs switch: mount --make-rprivate /, bind-mount the rootfs on itself, pivot_root into it, umount -l the old root, mount fresh proc/sysfs/tmpfs, set the hostname. (4) cgroup (from the host, using the child PID): mkdir /sys/fs/cgroup/box, write memory.max=64M, cpu.max='20000 100000', pids.max=16, echo <pid> > cgroup.procs. (5) privileges: capsh --drop=all --, set no_new_privs, install a tiny seccomp allowlist, setuid to a non-root uid (add the uid to /etc/passwd in the rootfs). (6) network: if it needs egress, create a veth pair, move one end into the netns, attach the other to a bridge, assign an address and default route, and add a MASQUERADE rule on the host. (7) exec /app. That's a functionally complete container; a Dockerfile with FROM scratch + COPY app / + a non-root USER produces the same thing with the runtime doing steps 2–7.
Your hand-built container's ps shows host processes even though you used --pid. Why?
Two likely causes. (1) You didn't pass --fork, so the command ran as unshare's own process, which stays in the parent PID namespace; only children enter the new one. (2) You didn't remount /proc — ps reads the procfs mounted at /proc, and until you mount -t proc proc /proc (or use --mount-proc, which requires --mount too) it's still the host's procfs showing every process. Fix: unshare --pid --mount --fork --mount-proc ....

Advanced deep

Map each part of an OCI config.json to the manual steps, and name what the manual approach still gets wrong that runc handles.
Mapping: process.args/env/cwd/user → the final exec and setuid/setgid; root.path → the rootfs you built + pivot_root; linux.namespaces → the unshare flags; mounts → the mount -t proc/sysfs/tmpfs and any bind mounts; linux.resources (memory/cpu/pids/io) → the cgroup files you wrote; process.capabilities (bounding/effective/permitted/inheritable/ambient) → capsh --drop; process.noNewPrivileges → the prctl; linux.seccomp → the seccomp filter; linux.uidMappings/gidMappings → --map-root-user/writing uid_map; hostname → hostname box; linux.maskedPaths/readonlyPaths → extra bind/remount tricks; linux.devices → mknod/bind of /dev/*. What the shell version gets wrong or omits: (1) it doesn't mask /proc/kcore, /proc/sys, /sys/firmware, /proc/sysrq-trigger etc. (runc's default maskedPaths/readonlyPaths) — leaving host-influencing knobs writable; (2) it usually skips a proper minimal /dev (null, zero, random, urandom, tty, pts) with correct modes, and the devices cgroup allow-list; (3) mount propagation edge cases — not making the parent mount private/slave correctly can leak container mounts to the host or vice versa; (4) it applies caps but not the full 5-set model, and often forgets ambient caps needed for non-root + file caps; (5) no seccomp by default (huge attack surface); (6) no AppArmor/SELinux label; (7) ordering/races — setting the cgroup from the host after the child starts is racy (the process runs briefly unconstrained); runc joins the cgroup before execve; (8) no cleanup/teardown of namespaces, cgroup, and network on exit; (9) no rootless plumbing (subuid/subgid, newuidmap). runc encodes all of this, tested against the OCI spec, which is why "just use runc" (or a runtime) is the right answer outside of learning exercises.

Docker Architecture: Client, Daemon, containerd

The docker command is a thin REST client; a root daemon does the work by driving containerd and runc.

Notes

Client / daemon split

What. docker is a CLI that talks the Docker Engine REST API to dockerd over /var/run/docker.sock (or a TCP endpoint). docker run, build, ps — all HTTP requests. The daemon holds all state.

Why it matters. The client can be remote (DOCKER_HOST=ssh://host, tcp://…). The daemon runs as root, so anyone who can reach the socket can start a privileged container and own the host — treat socket access as root.

$ docker version --format '{{.Client.Version}} / {{.Server.Version}}'
27.1.1 / 27.1.1

# it's just HTTP over a socket:
$ curl -s --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock http://localhost/v1.45/containers/json | jq '.[].Names'
$ docker context ls          # switch between local / remote daemons
$ DOCKER_HOST=ssh://build-01 docker ps

What the daemon delegates

  • containerd — container lifecycle, image pull/unpack, snapshots. Runs as a separate process; dockerd can restart without stopping containers because the shims hold them.
  • runc — the low-level OCI runtime that actually creates the process (namespaces, cgroups, execve).
  • BuildKit (buildkitd, in-process or standalone) — the modern build engine: parallel stages, cache mounts, build secrets.
$ pstree -p $(pgrep dockerd) | head
dockerd(1201)---containerd(1230)-+-containerd-shim(4501)---nginx(4522)
                                `-containerd-shim(4610)---redis-server(4631)
# stop dockerd -> containers keep running (shims + containerd survive)

Where the daemon keeps things

Path (default)Contents
/var/lib/docker/overlay2/Image layers + container writable layers.
/var/lib/docker/image/Image metadata, layer → digest maps.
/var/lib/docker/volumes/Named-volume data.
/var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/Config, and the *-json.log log file.
/etc/docker/daemon.jsonDaemon config: registries, log driver, storage driver, live-restore.
$ docker system df           # images / containers / volumes / build cache, reclaimable
$ docker info | grep -E 'Storage Driver|Cgroup|Runtime|Logging'
 Storage Driver: overlay2
 Cgroup Version: 2
 Default Runtime: runc
 Logging Driver: json-file

Rootless & alternatives

  • Rootless Docker — run dockerd as your user via a user namespace; a breakout has no host privilege. dockerd-rootless-setuptool.sh install.
  • Podman — daemonless and rootless by default; podman is CLI-compatible (alias docker=podman mostly works). No long-running root daemon to attack.
  • nerdctl — a Docker-compatible CLI directly on containerd.
$ dockerd-rootless-setuptool.sh install
$ export DOCKER_HOST=unix://$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/docker.sock
$ docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx        # no sudo, no root daemon
Cheat Sheet
  • docker CLI → REST API → dockerd (root) over /var/run/docker.sock. Client can be remote (DOCKER_HOST, docker context).
  • dockerd delegates to containerd (lifecycle/images) → shim (per container) → runc (OCI runtime). Also owns image store, BuildKit, networks, volumes.
  • Restarting dockerd doesn't kill containers — shims + containerd hold them (enable live-restore for full daemonless survival).
  • State: /var/lib/docker/ (overlay2 layers, volumes, container logs); config in /etc/docker/daemon.json.
  • docker system df / docker info to see storage, cgroup version, runtime, log driver.
  • Socket access == host root. Use rootless Docker or Podman (daemonless, rootless) to remove that.
Q&A
What happens when you run docker run nginx?
The CLI sends an HTTP request to dockerd over the Unix socket. dockerd (via containerd) pulls the image if absent, unpacks its layers into an overlay2 snapshot, sets up a network endpoint and any volumes, writes an OCI bundle, and asks containerd to start it — containerd spawns a shim which invokes runc to create the process (namespaces, cgroups, execve). Logs and status stream back through the shim to containerd to dockerd to your terminal.
Why can containers keep running while you restart the Docker daemon?
dockerd is not the container's parent — containerd and a per-container shim are. The shim owns the container's stdio and waits on it. So dockerd (and even containerd, with live-restore) can stop and start; on restart it reattaches to the existing shims and containers never noticed.
Why is mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container dangerous?
It's the API of a root daemon. A process with the socket can create a container with --privileged and -v /:/host, then run any command as root on the host. Giving a container the socket is equivalent to giving it host root.
Docker vs Podman — the architectural difference?
Docker has a long-running root daemon (dockerd) that all clients talk to. Podman is daemonless — the podman process forks conmon + crun/runc directly and exits — and rootless by default via user namespaces. Fewer moving parts, no privileged daemon as an attack surface or single point of failure; the trade-off is some features/ecosystem still assume the Docker daemon (though Podman offers a compatible API socket).
Where does a container's docker logs output actually come from?
With the default json-file log driver, the shim writes the container's stdout/stderr to /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log, and docker logs reads that file. Other drivers (journald, syslog, fluentd, awslogs) send it elsewhere — and then docker logs may not work locally.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Is the Docker CLI the thing that runs containers?
No. The CLI is a REST client; the dockerd daemon (root) does the work, delegating to containerd and runc. The CLI can even point at a remote daemon.
Name the process chain from dockerd to your container's process.
dockerd → containerd → containerd-shim (one per container) → runc (creates the process, then exits) → your process (child of the shim).

Intermediate core

A CI job needs to build images. Compare bind-mounting the docker socket, Docker-in-Docker, and a rootless/daemonless builder.
Bind-mount the host socket (-v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock): simplest and fastest (shares the host's cache), but the job has full host root and its builds run as siblings on the host daemon — a compromised or malicious job owns the runner. Only acceptable on fully trusted, single-tenant runners. Docker-in-Docker (docker:dind as a privileged sidecar): isolates the build daemon from the host, but the sidecar must be --privileged (its own security hole), the inner daemon has a cold cache each run (slow) unless you persist a volume, and nested overlayfs/storage quirks appear. Rootless/daemonless builder — BuildKit rootless, Buildah, Kaniko (builds in a container with no daemon at all), or img: no privileged daemon, no socket, runs as an unprivileged user, integrates with registry cache (--cache-from/--cache-to). This is the recommended approach for multi-tenant CI — Kaniko or BuildKit-rootless in a normal pod, pushing to a registry, with registry-backed layer cache for speed. Trade-off: some Dockerfile features (certain RUN mounts, exotic privileged steps) may need adjustment.
Kubernetes "removed Docker" — do your Docker-built images still run, and what changes on nodes?
Images still run — they're OCI-standard, and Docker builds them via BuildKit into the same format containerd consumes. What changed (v1.24): the kubelet no longer uses dockershim to talk to the Docker daemon; it talks CRI directly to containerd or CRI-O. On nodes that means you don't install/run the Docker daemon; you run containerd. Practical impacts: docker ps on a node won't show pods (use crictl); anything that shelled into the node's Docker daemon or used the docker socket for sidecars/logging must switch to CRI/containerd equivalents; image building moves off the node (to CI with BuildKit/Kaniko/Buildah). Developer laptops can keep using Docker to build and test.

Advanced deep

Design a hardened multi-user build/host setup: who can talk to which daemon, how builds are isolated, and how the cache is shared safely.
Threat model: developers and CI jobs are semi-trusted; a build must not be able to root the host or read another tenant's secrets/cache. No shared root daemon: don't expose /var/run/docker.sock to users or jobs, and don't run a shared privileged dockerd. Options: (a) per-user rootless Docker (each user's dockerd runs under their own user namespace, socket in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, no host privilege), or (b) daemonless builders — BuildKit-rootless / Buildah / Kaniko run as unprivileged pods/containers. Build isolation: each build runs in its own container/pod with dropped capabilities, seccomp, read-only host, tight cgroup limits, no host mounts, egress restricted to the package mirrors and the registry (block the metadata endpoint and internal services). For untrusted builds, run the builder under a micro-VM runtime (Kata) via RuntimeClass. Secrets: never bake into layers; use BuildKit --mount=type=secret (not persisted) for registry/creds; per-tenant service accounts scoped to their own registry namespace; short-lived tokens. Cache, shared safely: don't share a local layer cache directory between tenants (cache poisoning / info leak). Instead use registry-backed cache (--cache-to type=registry,ref=cache/<tenant> / --cache-from) with per-tenant cache repositories and RBAC, or BuildKit's gha/S3 cache scoped per tenant. Layers are content-addressed and immutable, so a shared read-only pull-through cache of public base images is fine; writable cache is per-tenant. Registry: push only to per-tenant namespaces, require image signing (cosign) and a scan gate before promotion, garbage-collect untagged. Runners: ephemeral (one job per VM/pod, then destroyed), no persistent credentials on disk, node auto-recycling. Audit: log every build (who, what Dockerfile digest, base images, output digest, pushed where) and every daemon/API call. Net: per-user rootless or daemonless builders, isolated build sandboxes with restricted egress, secrets via build-time mounts, and per-tenant registry-backed cache — so a build can be malicious and it still can't cross a tenant boundary or touch the host.

The Docker CLI: run, ps, exec, logs

A container moves through a small state machine — created, running, paused, exited, removed — and a handful of commands drive it.

Notes

docker run — the one you type most

What / how. Creates and starts a container from an image. The flags you actually reach for:

$ docker run \
    -d                       # detached (background); omit for foreground
    --name web               # stable name instead of a random one
    -p 8080:80               # publish host:container port
    -e LOG_LEVEL=debug       # env var  (or --env-file .env)
    -v data:/var/lib/app     # named volume  (or /host/path:/in/container for a bind mount)
    -w /app                  # working directory
    --restart unless-stopped # restart policy (no | on-failure[:N] | always | unless-stopped)
    --memory 512m --cpus 1   # cgroup limits
    --user 10001:10001       # run as non-root
    --rm                     # auto-remove when it exits
    myimage:1.4.2 ./start.sh --flag   # image  +  command/args (override CMD)

$ docker run -it --rm alpine sh        # -it = interactive TTY, for a shell

Inspecting what's there

$ docker ps                     # running containers
$ docker ps -a                  # + exited ones (still consuming disk)
$ docker ps --filter status=exited --format '{{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}'
$ docker inspect web            # full JSON: config, mounts, network, state
$ docker inspect -f '{{.State.Status}} {{.State.ExitCode}} {{.RestartCount}}' web
$ docker stats --no-stream      # live CPU / mem / net / block IO per container
$ docker top web                # processes inside (host PIDs)
$ docker port web               # published port mappings
$ docker diff web               # files changed in the writable layer

Getting inside & getting output

$ docker exec -it web sh                 # a new process in a RUNNING container
$ docker exec -u root web whoami        # as a different user
$ docker attach web                     # attach to PID 1's stdio (Ctrl-P Ctrl-Q to detach)

$ docker logs -f --tail 100 web         # stream stdout/stderr (json-file driver)
$ docker logs --since 10m --timestamps web
$ docker cp web:/app/report.csv .       # copy a file out (or in: ./x web:/app/x)

Why exec not attach: exec starts a fresh process (a debug shell) and leaves the app alone; attach connects to PID 1 — typing Ctrl-C there signals the app, and detaching cleanly needs the escape sequence.

Stopping & cleaning up

$ docker stop web              # SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after --time (default 10s)
$ docker kill web              # SIGKILL now  (or --signal SIGHUP to reload)
$ docker restart web
$ docker rm web               # remove a stopped container (-f to force-kill+remove)
$ docker rm -v web            # also remove its anonymous volumes

# bulk cleanup
$ docker container prune           # all stopped containers
$ docker system prune -a --volumes # stopped containers + unused images + networks + volumes + build cache
$ docker system df                 # what's reclaimable

Exit codes worth knowing

CodeMeaning
0Clean exit.
1–125The app exited with that code.
125The docker run itself failed (bad flag, image not found).
126Command found but not executable (permissions, wrong arch).
127Command not found in the image.
137128 + 9 = SIGKILL — usually OOM (check docker inspect → OOMKilled: true) or a stop timeout.
143128 + 15 = SIGTERM — stopped normally.
Cheat Sheet
  • run = create + start. Key flags: -d, --name, -p, -e/--env-file, -v, -w, --restart, --memory/--cpus, --user, --rm, -it.
  • ps (running), ps -a (+ exited), inspect (JSON), stats (live usage), top, port, diff.
  • exec -it <c> sh = debug shell (fresh process). attach = PID 1's stdio (careful).
  • logs -f --tail N --since 10m. cp c:/path . to extract files.
  • stop = SIGTERM then SIGKILL after 10s; kill = SIGKILL now; rm = delete stopped container.
  • Cleanup: container prune, image prune -a, system prune -a --volumes; system df.
  • Exit codes: 137 = SIGKILL/OOM, 143 = SIGTERM, 125 = docker run failed, 126/127 = command not executable / not found.
Q&A
What's the difference between docker exec and docker attach?
exec starts a new process inside a running container (e.g. a shell) — the main process is unaffected, and exiting the shell doesn't stop the container. attach connects your terminal to the container's PID 1 stdio; Ctrl-C sends SIGINT to the app, and you detach with the escape sequence (Ctrl-P Ctrl-Q) or you'll stop it.
Your container exits with code 137. What are the likely causes and how do you confirm?
137 = 128 + SIGKILL(9). Common causes: (1) OOM — hit the memory cgroup limit; confirm with docker inspect <c> --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}' and dmesg. (2) docker stop where the app ignored SIGTERM, so it got SIGKILL after the grace period — check that CMD is exec form and the app handles SIGTERM. (3) An external kill (orchestrator eviction, docker kill). Fix per cause: raise --memory / fix the leak, or handle SIGTERM and shut down within the grace window.
A stopped container still shows in docker ps -a and takes disk. Why, and how do you avoid it?
An exited container keeps its writable layer, config, and log file until removed — useful for post-mortem (docker logs, docker cp, docker diff). Use --rm on docker run for throwaway containers, run docker container prune periodically, and in production rely on the orchestrator or a cron to clean up.
How do you send a config-reload signal to a container instead of killing it?
docker kill --signal SIGHUP <container> (or SIGUSR1, etc.). docker kill without --signal sends SIGKILL. This is how you tell nginx/haproxy/etc. to reload without a restart.
Why does docker run myimage some-command behave differently from docker exec?
run creates a new container and some-command replaces the image's default CMD as PID 1. exec requires an already running container and adds a secondary process alongside PID 1. If the image's ENTRYPOINT is set, run's trailing args are appended to the ENTRYPOINT, not run standalone — use --entrypoint to override.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does docker run do that docker create doesn't?
create just prepares the container (writable layer, config) in the "created" state. run does create then start (and attaches unless -d).
How do you get a shell in a running container?
docker exec -it <container> sh (or bash if the image has it). -i keeps stdin open, -t allocates a TTY.

Intermediate core

A container keeps restarting. Walk through diagnosing it.
(1) docker ps -a — see the restart count and last status. (2) docker inspect <c> → .State (ExitCode, OOMKilled, Error, FinishedAt) and .HostConfig.RestartPolicy. (3) docker logs --tail 200 <c> — the app's own error (missing env var, can't reach the DB, bad config, port already in use, permission denied on a mounted path). (4) Exit code hints: 137 = OOM/killed (check memory limit, dmesg), 1/2 = app error, 126/127 = bad/missing command (wrong CMD, wrong arch image on the host), 139 = SIGSEGV. (5) Reproduce interactively: docker run -it --rm --entrypoint sh <image> and run the command by hand to see the failure. (6) Check mounts and env (docker inspect Mounts/Env) — a bind mount shadowing an image directory, or a volume with wrong ownership for the non-root user, is a classic. (7) If it's a healthcheck-driven restart (orchestrator), inspect the healthcheck command and timing. Fix the root cause, then set an appropriate restart policy (on-failure:5 rather than always so a crash loop is visible).
Why prefer docker exec over docker attach for debugging, and when is attach right?
exec spins up an independent process (a shell, or a one-off command) that you can enter and exit freely without touching the main process — ideal for poking around, checking files, running ps/netstat, tailing a file. attach wires your terminal straight to PID 1's stdin/stdout/stderr: Ctrl-C goes to the app (can kill it), and if you don't use the detach key sequence you stop the container on exit. attach is right when you specifically want to interact with the main process — e.g. a REPL container, or watching the exact stdout of a foreground app started with -d — and you know the detach sequence (Ctrl-P Ctrl-Q) or pass --sig-proxy=false.

Advanced deep

You can't exec into a "distroless" or scratch-based container to debug it — there's no shell. What are your options?
(1) From the host: get the PID (docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}') and use nsenter -t <pid> -a or specific namespaces (-n for network, -m for mounts) — you bring the host's tools, the container needs none. Browse its filesystem directly at /proc/<pid>/root/. Read cgroup state under /sys/fs/cgroup/. strace -f -p <pid>, lsof -p, ss -tnp filtered by the netns. (2) Debug/ephemeral container: docker debug <container> (newer Docker) or, in Kubernetes, kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container> attaches a temporary container sharing the target's namespaces so you get a shell + tools without modifying the image. (3) Sidecar: run a second container in the same pod/network/pid namespace (--pid=container:<id> --network=container:<id>) with a full toolbox image. (4) Copy tools in: docker cp a static busybox/gdb/ltrace binary into a writable path and exec it (only if there's a writable path and matching libc/arch). (5) Rebuild a debug variant: a Dockerfile target that adds a shell + tools on top of the same layers, run that image in the same environment. (6) Observe from outside: docker logs, docker stats, docker events, application metrics/traces, and a core dump analyzed offline. The distroless image stays minimal in production; debugging happens via the host or an ephemeral/sidecar container that borrows its namespaces.

Images, Tags, Digests & Registries

An image is a manifest pointing at a config blob and a set of layer blobs; a registry is content-addressed blob storage with an HTTP API.

Notes

Anatomy of an image

  • Manifest — a small JSON listing the config digest and the ordered layer digests (with sizes/media types).
  • Config — JSON with the runtime metadata: Env, Entrypoint, Cmd, WorkingDir, User, ExposedPorts, Labels, the layer diff_ids, and the build history.
  • Layers — gzipped tarballs of filesystem diffs.
  • Image index / manifest list — for multi-arch: maps os/arch → a per-platform manifest, so docker pull nginx gets the right build automatically.
$ docker buildx imagetools inspect nginx:1.27
Manifests:
  Platform: linux/amd64   Digest: sha256:aaa...
  Platform: linux/arm64   Digest: sha256:bbb...

$ docker inspect --format '{{json .Config.Env}}' nginx:1.27 | jq
$ docker manifest inspect nginx:1.27 | jq '.manifests[].platform'

Tags vs digests

What / why. myapp:1.4.2 is a human label a maintainer can move (today it points at digest A, tomorrow at B). myapp@sha256:9f2c… is the immutable content hash. For reproducible builds and supply-chain safety, pin base images by digest (or at least a specific version tag, never bare :latest).

# FROM with a digest -> byte-for-byte reproducible, immune to a re-pushed tag
FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:1e20f9b...c4

# see the digest of what you actually pulled
$ docker images --digests | grep myapp
myapp  1.4.2  sha256:9f2c...  a1b2c3   12MB
$ docker pull myapp@sha256:9f2c...        # deploy the exact bytes

Registries & the naming rules

A full reference is [registry[:port]/]namespace/repo[:tag|@digest]. If the registry is omitted, Docker assumes Docker Hub (docker.io) and prefixes library/ for official images.

alpine                     -> docker.io/library/alpine:latest
ghcr.io/acme/api:1.2       -> GitHub Container Registry
123456.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/api:1.2   -> AWS ECR
registry.internal:5000/team/svc@sha256:...        -> a private registry

$ docker login ghcr.io -u me                # writes creds to ~/.docker/config.json (or a helper)
$ docker tag myapp:1.4.2 ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.4.2
$ docker push ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.4.2
$ docker pull registry.internal:5000/team/svc:1.2

Push / pull mechanics

  • Pull: fetch the manifest → for each layer digest not already local, download the blob → verify its SHA → unpack. Shared base layers are skipped.
  • Push: for each layer, ask the registry "do you have sha256:…?" (a HEAD) → upload only the missing ones → then the config → then the manifest under the tag.
  • Rate limits: Docker Hub throttles anonymous/free pulls (per IP). In CI/clusters, authenticate, use a pull-through cache / mirror, or host base images in your own registry.
$ cat /etc/docker/daemon.json
{ "registry-mirrors": ["https://mirror.internal"] }     # pull-through cache for docker.io

# run a local registry (OCI distribution) for a lab / airgap
$ docker run -d -p 5000:5000 --name reg registry:2
$ docker tag alpine localhost:5000/alpine && docker push localhost:5000/alpine

Supply-chain hygiene

  • Sign images (Sigstore cosign sign) and verify at admission (Kyverno / Connaisseur / Ratify) so only trusted images run.
  • Scan for CVEs (Trivy, Grype, Docker Scout) in CI and block on fixable HIGH/CRITICAL.
  • SBOM — generate (syft) and attach so you can answer "which images contain log4j 2.14?".
  • Provenance / attestations — BuildKit can emit SLSA provenance recording how the image was built.
  • Garbage-collect the registry: delete untagged manifests, then run GC; keep a retention policy.
$ trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.4.2
$ cosign sign ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.4.2
$ cosign verify --key cosign.pub ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.4.2
$ syft ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.4.2 -o spdx-json > sbom.json
Cheat Sheet
  • Image = manifest (→ config digest + layer digests) + config (env/entrypoint/cmd/user/…) + layers (diff tarballs). Multi-arch via an image index.
  • Everything is content-addressed by sha256 → dedup, cache, integrity-checked pulls.
  • Tag = movable label; digest (@sha256:) = immutable. Pin bases by digest or a real version; never bare :latest.
  • Reference: [registry[:port]/]ns/repo[:tag|@digest]. No registry → docker.io/library/….
  • docker login / tag / push / pull. Creds in ~/.docker/config.json (or a credential helper).
  • Pull/push only transfer blobs the other side lacks (HEAD-then-upload). Hub rate-limits anon pulls — auth + a registry mirror in CI/clusters.
  • Supply chain: scan (Trivy/Grype), sign+verify (cosign), SBOM (syft), provenance; GC untagged manifests.
Q&A
What's the difference between an image tag and an image digest?
A tag (repo:1.4.2) is a mutable pointer — whoever controls the repo can re-push it to point at different bytes. A digest (repo@sha256:…) is the SHA-256 of the manifest and always refers to exactly the same image. Use digests (or immutable version tags) for anything you want to be reproducible or auditable.
