Why does docker pull of a slightly different version download only a fraction of the image?
Layers are content-addressed and shared. If the new image reuses the same base OS and dependency layers, those digests are already on the node, so Docker only downloads the layer(s) that actually changed (usually just your application layer). Same reason 20 images built FROM the same base cost little extra disk.
What is a manifest list / image index and why does docker pull alpine "just work" on both an M1 Mac and an x86 server?
The tag alpine points at an image index that maps each supported os/arch to a platform-specific manifest. The Docker client requests the entry matching the host's architecture, so the same command pulls the arm64 build on the Mac and the amd64 build on the server. docker buildx with --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 is how you produce one.
Your CI intermittently fails with "toomanyrequests: You have reached your pull rate limit." What do you do?
That's Docker Hub throttling anonymous/free pulls by IP. Fixes: authenticate the CI pull with a Hub account (higher limit), and better, mirror the base images you use into your own registry (ECR/GCR/GHCR/Harbor) or run a pull-through cache and point the daemon at it via registry-mirrors in daemon.json. Also pin bases so you're not re-pulling :latest constantly.
How do you make sure only trusted images run in your cluster?
Sign images at build time (cosign sign, keyless or with a KMS key) and enforce verification at admission — a policy engine (Kyverno, Gatekeeper, Connaisseur, Ratify) rejects any pod whose image isn't signed by an approved key, isn't from an allow-listed registry, or fails a scan/attestation check. Combine with immutable digests in manifests so the verified image is exactly what runs.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Where does docker pull redis pull from?
Docker Hub — docker.io/library/redis:latest. When no registry and no latest-alternative tag are given, Docker defaults to Hub and (for single-name images) the library/ namespace and the latest tag.
What are the three commands to publish a local image to a registry?
docker login <registry>, docker tag <local> <registry>/<ns>/<repo>:<tag>, docker push <registry>/<ns>/<repo>:<tag>.

Intermediate core

Design a tagging strategy for an application image used across dev, staging, and prod.
Immutable, meaningful tags: on every build, tag with the semantic version and the git SHA — myapp:1.4.2 and myapp:1.4.2-g8f3a1c9 (and the full digest is recorded). Never overwrite an existing version tag (enable registry tag immutability). Moving pointers for humans, not deploys: keep myapp:latest and myapp:1.4 / myapp:1 as convenience aliases updated by CI, but deploys reference the digest (or the exact 1.4.2), so a re-pushed alias can't silently change what's running. Environment promotion by digest, not rebuild: the artifact built once in CI is the same digest promoted dev → staging → prod (optionally with env-marker tags like myapp:prod pointing at the currently-live digest for observability). Pre-release: 1.5.0-rc.1, PR builds as pr-1234-g<sha> with a short retention policy. Base images: pin by digest in the Dockerfile; renovate/dependabot bumps them via PR. Registry hygiene: retention (keep last N of each minor, all released versions, expire PR/rc tags after X days), GC untagged manifests, and immutable tags so history is trustworthy. Net: build once, tag with version+SHA, deploy by digest, use moving tags only as human-facing aliases.
Explain what actually crosses the wire during docker push and why pushing a rebuilt image is usually fast.
The client computes each layer's digest and, for every layer, sends the registry a mount/HEAD check: "do you already have blob sha256:X (possibly cross-repo)?" The registry answers, and the client uploads (as a chunked/monolithic blob POST+PUT) only the layers the registry is missing. Then it uploads the config blob (also digest-checked) and finally PUTs the manifest under the tag. Because a rebuild that only changed application code produces the same base/OS/dependency layer digests as before, those are already in the registry and skipped — only the small application layer and the new config+manifest are uploaded. (Same mechanism makes cross-repository pushes cheap when repos share a base, if the registry supports cross-repo blob mount.)

Advanced deep

Design the image supply chain for a regulated org: build, sign, scan, store, verify, and respond to a new CVE in a base image.
Build: reproducible builds in isolated CI (BuildKit, pinned base by digest, no network beyond mirrors), emitting SLSA provenance attestations (how/where/from-what it was built) and an SBOM (syft, SPDX/CycloneDX) attached to the image. Deterministic where possible (fixed timestamps, sorted files). Scan: Trivy/Grype (and a second scanner for coverage) on the built image and its SBOM; fail the pipeline on fixable HIGH/CRITICAL; record results as an attestation. License scan too. Sign: cosign sign with a KMS/HSM-backed key or keyless (Fulcio/OIDC), signing the image digest and the provenance/SBOM/scan attestations. Store: private registry (Harbor/ECR/Artifactory) with immutable tags, RBAC per team/namespace, retention + GC, replication to prod regions, and a vulnerability-DB refresh + re-scan schedule. Promote: dev → staging → prod by digest only; a promotion step re-verifies signature + policy and adds an environment attestation. Verify at admission: cluster policy (Kyverno/Gatekeeper/Ratify) requires: image from an allow-listed registry, referenced by digest, cosign signature by an approved key, a passing scan attestation not older than N days, and a valid SBOM/provenance. Reject anything else; audit every decision. Runtime: continuous re-scan of running images against new CVE data; drift detection (running digest == approved digest); Falco/Tetragon for anomalies. New base CVE response: (1) query the SBOM store / registry metadata to list every image (and every running deployment) containing the vulnerable package/version — this is why SBOMs are mandatory; (2) rank by exposure (internet-facing, privileged, data-sensitive); (3) rebuild affected images from a patched base (automated: a base-bump PR triggers rebuilds of all dependents), re-scan, re-sign, re-attest; (4) roll out by digest through the normal promotion path, fastest for the highest-risk services, with a documented exception/mitigation (WAF rule, network policy) for anything that can't be patched immediately; (5) verify no vulnerable digest is still admitted (tighten the policy's max-CVE-age or add a specific block); (6) post-incident: measure time-to-detect and time-to-remediate, and check the base-image auto-bump automation caught it. Net: every image is signed, scanned, SBOM'd and provenance-tracked; only verified digests run; and the SBOM inventory turns "is CVE-X in our fleet?" into a query and an automated rebuild wave.

Writing Dockerfiles

A recipe of instructions; the filesystem-changing ones become layers, and the metadata ones set how the image runs.

Notes

The instruction set

InstructionWhat it does
FROM img[:tag|@digest] [AS name]Base image (and starts a build stage).
RUN cmdExecute a command at build time; commit the result as a layer.
COPY src dstCopy files from the build context (or --from=stage) into the image.
ADD src dstLike COPY, plus auto-extracts local tarballs and can fetch URLs. Prefer COPY.
ENV k=vEnvironment variable, present at build and run time.
ARG k[=default]Build-time variable (--build-arg); not in the running container.
WORKDIR /pathcd for following instructions and the container (creates the dir).
USER uid[:gid]UID for following RUNs and the container process.
EXPOSE portDocumentation/metadata only — does not publish anything.
ENTRYPOINT [..]The fixed executable; container args append to it.
CMD [..]Default command, or default args for ENTRYPOINT; overridden by docker run <img> ....
HEALTHCHECKA command Docker runs to mark the container healthy/unhealthy.
LABELKey/value metadata (maintainer, source, version).
VOLUME /pathDeclare a mount point (auto-creates an anonymous volume — often surprising; prefer explicit -v).

Shell form vs exec form

What / why. RUN cmd / CMD cmd (shell form) runs via /bin/sh -c — you get shell features (pipes, &&, variable expansion) but /bin/sh becomes PID 1 and may not forward signals. RUN ["cmd","arg"] / CMD ["cmd","arg"] (exec form, JSON array) execves directly — your process is PID 1 and gets SIGTERM. Use exec form for CMD/ENTRYPOINT; shell form is fine for RUN when you need shell operators.

CMD ["node", "server.js"]        # exec: node is PID 1, receives SIGTERM -> graceful stop
CMD node server.js               # shell: sh -c is PID 1, often eats the signal -> SIGKILL

RUN set -eux; \
    apt-get update; \
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libpq5; \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*  # cleanup in the SAME layer or it doesn't shrink the image

ENTRYPOINT + CMD together

What / why. A common pattern: ENTRYPOINT = the program, CMD = its default arguments. docker run img uses the default; docker run img --other-args replaces the args but keeps the program. An entrypoint.sh wrapper is the idiom for "do setup, then exec "$@"".

ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/app"]
CMD ["--config", "/etc/app/prod.yaml"]      # docker run img            -> app --config /etc/app/prod.yaml
                                            # docker run img --help     -> app --help
                                            # docker run --entrypoint sh img   -> a shell

# entrypoint.sh: run migrations, then hand off (exec so the app becomes PID 1)
#!/bin/sh
set -e
[ "$RUN_MIGRATIONS" = "1" ] && ./migrate
exec "$@"

ARG vs ENV, and build secrets

  • ARG is build-time only and visible in docker history — never pass secrets via --build-arg.
  • ENV persists into the running container — good for config defaults, bad for secrets (visible in inspect and to any process).
  • Real secrets: BuildKit RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc ... (mounted for that RUN, never written to a layer) or inject at runtime.
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:20-slim
ARG NODE_ENV=production
ENV NODE_ENV=$NODE_ENV
COPY package*.json ./
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc \
    npm ci --omit=dev            # .npmrc token used here, not baked into any layer
COPY . .
USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

$ DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build --secret id=npmrc,src=$HOME/.npmrc -t api:1.0 .

A solid baseline Dockerfile

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:...        # pinned base

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
WORKDIR /app

# deps first (cached until requirements.txt changes)
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
    pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# then source
COPY . .

RUN useradd -u 10001 -m app
USER 10001

EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c "import urllib.request,sys; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/healthz')" || exit 1
ENTRYPOINT ["gunicorn", "-b", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
CMD ["app:app"]

Common mistakes

  • COPY . . before installing deps → the dependency layer re-runs on every source change. Copy manifests first.
  • Cleaning up in a later RUN → the files are still in the earlier layer; chain && rm in the same RUN.
  • ADD for a URL or to unzip → use COPY; use explicit curl/tar so it's cached and auditable.
  • Shell-form CMD → no graceful shutdown. Missing USER → runs as root.
  • EXPOSE ≠ publish; you still need -p at run time.
  • No .dockerignore → a huge build context (.git, node_modules, dumps) and busted cache.
Cheat Sheet
  • Layer-making: FROM, RUN, COPY, ADD. Metadata-only: ENV ARG WORKDIR USER EXPOSE LABEL HEALTHCHECK ENTRYPOINT CMD.
  • Exec form (["a","b"]) for CMD/ENTRYPOINT → your process is PID 1, gets SIGTERM. Shell form only for RUN when you need &&/pipes.
  • Pattern: ENTRYPOINT = program, CMD = default args. entrypoint.sh ends with exec "$@".
  • ARG = build-time, in docker history (no secrets). ENV = build + run time. Secrets → RUN --mount=type=secret.
  • Order stable→volatile; copy dependency manifests before source; clean up in the same RUN.
  • Prefer COPY over ADD. EXPOSE documents, it doesn't publish. Set a non-root USER.
  • Always add a tight .dockerignore. Pin the base by digest or a real version.
Q&A
Which Dockerfile instructions create layers?
Only the ones that change the filesystem: FROM (brings in the base layers), RUN, COPY, ADD. ENV, ARG, WORKDIR, USER, EXPOSE, LABEL, ENTRYPOINT, CMD, HEALTHCHECK only update the image config (no layer), though they still create a cache checkpoint.
ENTRYPOINT vs CMD?
ENTRYPOINT is the executable that always runs; arguments you pass to docker run <img> ... are appended to it. CMD provides the default command (if there's no ENTRYPOINT) or the default arguments (if there is one), and is fully replaced by run-time args. Common idiom: ENTRYPOINT ["myapp"] + CMD ["--serve"]. Override the entrypoint itself with --entrypoint.
Why use the JSON-array (exec) form for CMD/ENTRYPOINT?
It execves the binary directly, so your program is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM on docker stop / pod termination, allowing graceful shutdown. The shell form (CMD myapp) runs /bin/sh -c "myapp"; sh is PID 1 and typically doesn't forward the signal, so your app is SIGKILLed after the grace period.
Is it safe to pass a token with --build-arg TOKEN=...?
No. ARG values are recorded in the image's build history and visible via docker history / docker inspect, and any layer that used the value may embed it. Use BuildKit build secrets (RUN --mount=type=secret,id=tok ... with --secret), which mount the secret only for that RUN and never persist it, or inject the credential at runtime.
Does EXPOSE 8080 make the port reachable?
No — it's metadata that documents which port the app listens on and is used by docker run -P (publish all exposed ports to random host ports) and by tools. To actually reach it you still need -p 8080:8080 (or a Compose/Kubernetes port mapping / Service).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Difference between COPY and ADD?
COPY just copies files/dirs from the build context. ADD also auto-extracts local tar archives and can download from a URL. Prefer COPY for clarity; use explicit curl/tar in a RUN when you need those behaviours.
How do you make a container run as a non-root user?
Create the user in the image (RUN useradd -u 10001 app or adduser) and add USER 10001 before the final CMD/ENTRYPOINT. Make sure any paths the app writes to are owned by that UID.

Intermediate core

Write (describe) an entrypoint script pattern that runs DB migrations then starts the app, and explain the exec "$@".
ENTRYPOINT ["/entrypoint.sh"], CMD ["gunicorn", "app:app"]. The script: #!/bin/sh, set -e, do preflight work (wait for the DB, run ./manage.py migrate if $RUN_MIGRATIONS, template a config file from env), then exec "$@". "$@" expands to the CMD (or whatever args were passed to docker run), and exec replaces the shell process with that command — so the app becomes PID 1, receives SIGTERM directly, and there's no leftover shell holding a PID. Without exec, the shell stays as PID 1, the app is its child, and signals/zombie-reaping behave badly. Keep migrations idempotent and consider running them as a separate init job in orchestrated environments so N replicas don't race.
A teammate's Dockerfile ends with RUN pip install ... then COPY . . then CMD python app.py. What would you change and why?
(1) Reorder for cache: COPY requirements.txt . then RUN pip install -r requirements.txt then COPY . . — so editing source doesn't reinstall dependencies every build. (2) Pin the base (FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:...), not bare python. (3) Non-root: add a user and USER. (4) Exec-form CMD: CMD ["python", "app.py"] so SIGTERM reaches Python (or better, run under gunicorn/uvicorn). (5) Slim it: --no-cache-dir, PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE, consider multi-stage if there are build deps. (6) .dockerignore for .git, __pycache__, tests, local venv. (7) Add HEALTHCHECK and EXPOSE. (8) If secrets are needed for install, use RUN --mount=type=secret, not ARG.

Advanced deep

Design Dockerfile conventions and a lint/CI gate for an org with dozens of services in many languages.
Golden base images: the platform team publishes and maintains a small set of hardened, pinned, regularly-rebuilt base images per language (distroless or slim), with a non-root user, CA certs, timezone data, and standard labels baked in; teams FROM those (by digest, bumped via automated PRs). Dockerfile conventions (documented + templated via docker init/cookiecutter): multi-stage (builder + minimal runtime), deps-before-source ordering, one RUN per logical step with cleanup, --mount=type=cache for package caches, --mount=type=secret for creds (never ARG), exec-form ENTRYPOINT/CMD with a tini/exec-"$@" entrypoint, explicit non-root USER, HEALTHCHECK, OCI LABELs (source repo, revision, version), and EXPOSE for docs. Lint gate in CI: hadolint with a shared config (fail on: unpinned FROM, apt-get without --no-install-recommends or without cache cleanup, ADD of remote URLs, sudo, missing USER, latest tags, pip/npm without pinning); plus dockerfile_lint/conftest policy for org-specific rules (must use golden base, must set USER < 1000 forbidden / must be >= 10000, must have labels, no secrets in ENV/ARG names matching a denylist). Build gate: BuildKit with provenance + SBOM; Trivy scan of the produced image (fail on fixable HIGH/CRIT); image size budget per service (warn/fail over threshold, checked with dive); verify the final image runs as non-root and its rootfs is minimal (no shell/package-manager in runtime stage unless whitelisted). Admission: cluster policy rejects images not built from a golden base digest, not signed, or failing scan. Maintenance: renovate bumps bases and pinned deps; a base-image change fan-out rebuilds dependents; a dashboard shows each service's base age, image size, CVE count, and non-root/rootfs compliance. Net: teams get a template and a golden base, CI enforces the conventions mechanically, and drift is visible — so "write a good Dockerfile" isn't left to memory.

The Build Cache, Context & .dockerignore

Each instruction is cached by a key derived from the instruction plus its inputs; the first miss invalidates every layer after it.

Notes

How the layer cache decides hit vs miss

  • The builder walks the Dockerfile instruction by instruction. For each, it computes a cache key from the previous layer's id plus this instruction.
  • RUN foo — key is just the literal command text (Docker does not know what foo did). Change a character → miss. apt-get update a week later still "hits" — hence the stale-package problem, solved by chaining update && install in one RUN.
  • COPY src dst / ADD — key includes a checksum of the copied files' contents (and mode/uid). Any changed byte → miss.
  • The first miss invalidates that layer and every layer after it.
$ docker build -t api .
 => CACHED [2/6] COPY requirements.txt .
 => CACHED [3/6] RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
 => [4/6] COPY . .                    # source changed -> miss here...
 => [5/6] RUN python -m compileall .  # ...so this reruns too

$ docker build --no-cache -t api .    # force a clean build
$ docker build --pull -t api .        # also re-check the base image tag

Ordering for maximum reuse

# rule: stable layers first, volatile layers last
FROM node:20-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./     # changes rarely
RUN npm ci                                  # cached until the lockfile changes
COPY . .                                    # changes every commit -> only this + below rebuild
RUN npm run build
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

The build context

What / why. docker build . sends the whole . directory (minus .dockerignore) to the daemon before the build starts — that's the "context". A fat context (a .git dir, node_modules, build outputs, DB dumps) is slow to transfer and makes COPY . checksums churn. BuildKit is lazier but a tight context still matters.

$ docker build .
Sending build context to Docker daemon  482MB      # <-- red flag, add .dockerignore

# .dockerignore  (glob syntax; ! to re-include)
.git
node_modules
dist
*.log
.env*
**/__pycache__
!package-lock.json

BuildKit: cache mounts, secrets, parallelism

What / why. BuildKit (default since Docker 23) builds stages in parallel, skips unused stages, and adds mounts that don't become layers:

  • RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip — a persistent package-manager cache outside the image; survives across builds without bloating a layer.
  • RUN --mount=type=secret,id=x — secret file for that RUN only.
  • RUN --mount=type=bind,from=ctx,source=...,target=... — read context files without a COPY layer.
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apt,sharing=locked \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/var/lib/apt,sharing=locked \
    apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends build-essential

RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/go-build \
    go build -o /out/app ./cmd/app

Sharing cache across machines (CI)

What / why. A fresh CI runner has an empty local cache. Export/import the cache to a registry or a CI cache backend so builds reuse layers.

$ docker buildx build \
    --cache-from type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/acme/api:buildcache \
    --cache-to   type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/acme/api:buildcache,mode=max \
    -t ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2 --push .

# GitHub Actions: --cache-from type=gha --cache-to type=gha,mode=max
# mode=max exports cache for ALL stages (incl. builder); mode=min only the final image
Cheat Sheet
  • Cache key: parent layer + instruction. RUN keys on the literal command; COPY/ADD on a checksum of the copied files.
  • First miss → that layer and all layers after it rebuild. Order stable → volatile: base, OS pkgs, deps, then source.
  • Copy dependency manifests (package.json, requirements.txt, go.mod) before the source so the install layer stays cached.
  • apt-get update alone can cache stale — chain update && install && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* in one RUN.
  • Build context = the whole dir sent to the daemon; trim it with .dockerignore (.git, node_modules, dist, *.log, .env*).
  • BuildKit: --mount=type=cache (persistent pkg cache, no layer), --mount=type=secret, parallel stages.
  • CI: --cache-from/--cache-to type=registry|gha,mode=max to reuse layers on fresh runners.
  • --no-cache full rebuild; --pull re-resolve the base tag.
Q&A
Why does changing one source file cause npm ci / pip install to run again?
Because COPY . . comes before the install step. Any file change busts the COPY layer, which invalidates every layer after it, including the install. Copy just the lockfile/manifest first and run the install, then COPY . . — now the install layer is reused until the dependency list itself changes.
You put RUN apt-get update and RUN apt-get install -y foo on separate lines. What's the bug?
The update layer can be a cache hit weeks later, so install runs against a stale package index — you get old versions or "package not found." Always chain them: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends foo && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*, so they invalidate together and the cache is cleaned in the same layer.
What is the "build context" and why does its size matter?
It's the directory you pass to docker build (usually .), which is packaged and sent to the daemon before the build runs. A large context (checked-in node_modules, .git history, artifacts) is slow to transfer, and its contents feed COPY . checksums so unrelated files churn the cache. A .dockerignore that excludes everything not needed for the build fixes both.
How do you get build-cache hits on a fresh CI runner that has no local Docker cache?
Use docker buildx with a remote cache: --cache-from and --cache-to pointing at a registry (type=registry,ref=...:buildcache,mode=max) or a CI-native backend (type=gha for GitHub Actions, S3, etc.). The runner imports previously-exported layers and only rebuilds what changed. mode=max also caches intermediate/builder stages, which matters for multi-stage builds.
What does RUN --mount=type=cache do that a normal layer doesn't?
It mounts a persistent directory (a package-manager cache like ~/.cache/pip, ~/.npm, the Go build cache) for the duration of that RUN only. The downloaded packages/objects persist across builds to speed re-installs, but they are not committed into the image layer, so the image stays small and the layer's cache key doesn't depend on the cache contents.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

If the first cache miss is at instruction 3 of 8, how many layers are rebuilt?
Six — instruction 3 and everything after it (3 through 8). Layers 1 and 2 are reused from cache.
What file trims the build context, and what would you typically put in it?
.dockerignore. Typical entries: .git, node_modules, dist/build, *.log, .env*, coverage, IDE folders, large local data — anything not needed to build the image.

Intermediate core

A multi-stage build's cache is never hit in CI even though the code didn't change. Diagnose.
Likely causes: (1) No shared cache — each CI runner starts empty; add --cache-from/--cache-to (registry or gha), and use mode=max so the builder stage is cached, not just the final image. (2) Context churn — COPY . with no/weak .dockerignore so CI-generated files (timestamps, .git, coverage) change the checksum every run; tighten it and COPY only what's needed. (3) Non-deterministic early instructions — an ARG that changes every build (a build number, CACHEBUST, date) placed before the expensive steps invalidates them; move build-varying args to the end. (4) Base image moves — FROM lang:latest plus --pull re-resolves to a new digest; pin by digest. (5) Different builder — classic builder vs BuildKit, or a fresh docker buildx instance per job with no persistent state; use a persistent builder or remote cache. (6) File mode/ownership differences between checkout on different runners (umask, CRLF) changing COPY checksums. Fix the biggest one first (usually remote cache + .dockerignore + pinned base).
How would you keep apt/pip/npm downloads fast across builds without bloating the image?
BuildKit cache mounts. For apt: RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apt,sharing=locked --mount=type=cache,target=/var/lib/apt,sharing=locked apt-get update && apt-get install -y ... and don't rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists (the cache mount handles it; without the mount you should remove it). For pip: --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip. For npm: --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm with npm ci --cache /root/.npm. For Go: cache /go/pkg/mod and /root/.cache/go-build. The downloaded artifacts live in the cache mount (persisted by the builder), so re-installs are fast, but nothing is committed into the layer — the final image only contains the installed packages, not the download cache. In CI, back the builder with a remote cache (--cache-to) so the cache mounts survive runner recycling too (BuildKit exports them with mode=max where supported).

Advanced deep

Design a build-cache strategy for a monorepo with 30 services so a change to one service rebuilds only what's affected, fast, on ephemeral runners.
Scope the context per service: build each image with its own directory (or a computed subset) as context, not the repo root, so an unrelated service's change doesn't churn COPY checksums. Use per-service .dockerignore or BuildKit --mount=type=bind to pull only needed paths. Shared base layers: a small number of golden base images per language, pinned by digest, already present in the registry/runner — every service FROMs one, so the OS/runtime layers are always cache hits. Dependency isolation: within each service Dockerfile, copy that service's lockfile(s) and install before copying source; for monorepo-shared libs, either pre-build them as an internal package/image and COPY --from, or use a workspace-aware install with only the relevant lockfile slice. Remote cache, per service: --cache-from/--cache-to type=registry,ref=cache/<service>,mode=max (or gha/S3), so a fresh runner imports that service's last layers; separate cache refs prevent cross-service cache thrash. Affected-only builds: a change-detection step (bazel/nx/turbo/pants, or a git-diff-to-service map, or hashing each service's input file set) decides which services actually changed — skip the rest entirely; also rebuild dependents when a shared lib changes. Determinism: pin bases and tool versions by digest, keep build-varying ARGs (build number, VCS ref) at the end or inject via LABEL only, normalize file modes on checkout. Parallelism: build independent services concurrently (matrix), each with its own buildx builder + cache ref; use mode=max so multi-stage builder layers are cached. Cache maintenance: TTL/size limits on cache refs, GC untagged, and a periodic "warm" build on main to keep caches fresh for feature branches. Net: per-service context + per-service remote cache + golden pinned bases + affected-graph detection means a one-service change transfers a small context, hits base + deps from cache, and rebuilds just that service's source/build layers, even on a runner that started with nothing.

Multi-Stage Builds & Minimal Images

Build with a fat toolchain image, then COPY --from only the artefact into a tiny runtime image — the build stage is never shipped.

Notes

The pattern

What / why. A single-stage image that compiles code ends up carrying the entire toolchain (compilers, headers, git, build caches) into production — hundreds of MB of attack surface you never run. Multi-stage: one FROM for building, another FROM for running, and COPY --from=<stage> to move just the output across.

# --- Go: 850 MB -> ~12 MB ---
FROM golang:1.22 AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod go mod download
COPY . .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/go-build \
    CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/app ./cmd/app

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot
COPY --from=builder /out/app /app
USER nonroot
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]

Choosing the runtime base

BaseSizeHasUse for
scratch0nothingFully static binaries (Go with CGO_ENABLED=0, Rust musl). Add CA certs + tzdata if needed.
gcr.io/distroless/*2–25 MBlibc, CA certs, tzdata; no shell/pkg-mgrCompiled apps, and language-specific variants for Java/Python/Node.
alpine~7 MBbusybox shell, apk, musl libcWhen you need a shell or a few packages; watch musl-vs-glibc quirks (DNS, some wheels).
debian:*-slim / ubuntu30–80 MBglibc, apt, coreutilsBroad compatibility, native extensions, when you can't fight musl.
# Node: build assets in a full image, run on a slim one
FROM node:20 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev

FROM node:20-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

More than two stages

  • A deps stage (just dependency resolution) that both a test stage and the final stage build on — deps resolve once.
  • Build for multiple targets from one Dockerfile with --target: --target test in CI, default (final) for release.
  • Copy artefacts from an external image with COPY --from=nginx:1.27 /etc/nginx/mime.types ./ — no need for that image to be a stage.
FROM python:3.12-slim AS base
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

FROM base AS test
COPY requirements-dev.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements-dev.txt
COPY . .
RUN pytest -q                       # docker build --target test .

FROM base AS final
COPY . .
RUN useradd -u 10001 app
USER 10001
CMD ["gunicorn", "-b", "0.0.0.0:8000", "app:app"]

What shrinking buys you

  • Smaller pulls — faster autoscaling, faster deploys, less registry egress.
  • Faster cold starts — less to unpack.
  • Fewer CVEs — no shell, no curl/wget, no package manager, no compilers means most scanner findings and most post-exploitation tools simply aren't present.
  • Clearer provenance — the runtime image contains only files you explicitly copied.
$ docker images
myapp   single-stage   1.24GB
myapp   multi-stage    18.4MB
$ trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL myapp:single-stage   # dozens of findings
$ trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL myapp:multi-stage    # usually 0-2

Gotchas

  • Missing runtime deps: distroless/scratch has no shell, so a HEALTHCHECK that calls curl won't work — use a tiny static health binary or the app's own --healthcheck. Missing CA certs → TLS failures; COPY --from=builder /etc/ssl/certs /etc/ssl/certs or use the -debian/:nonroot distroless variant.
  • Timezone: scratch has no /usr/share/zoneinfo; copy it or embed with the Go time/tzdata package.
  • Debugging: no shell to exec into — use kubectl debug/ephemeral containers or nsenter from the host (see the Containers skill).
  • musl vs glibc on Alpine: some Python wheels, glibc-only binaries, and NSS/DNS edge cases break — test, or use debian-slim.
  • mode=max on the build cache is needed to cache the builder stage in CI, or multi-stage loses its cache on fresh runners.
Cheat Sheet
  • Multi-stage: FROM toolchain AS builder → build → FROM tiny-runtime → COPY --from=builder /out/app /app. Only the last stage ships.
  • Runtime bases: scratch (static binaries only), distroless (libc + certs + tz, no shell), alpine (busybox + apk, musl), debian-slim (glibc + apt, most compatible).
  • Extra stages for deps (resolve once), test (--target test in CI), and cross-image copies (COPY --from=nginx:1.27 ...).
  • Wins: smaller pulls, faster cold start, drastically fewer CVEs, cleaner provenance (only files you copied).
  • Watch: CA certs, tzdata, no shell for HEALTHCHECK/debug, musl-vs-glibc breakage, and needing --cache-to mode=max to keep the builder cached in CI.
  • Go/Rust: CGO_ENABLED=0 + -ldflags="-s -w" → FROM scratch or distroless/static.
Q&A
What problem do multi-stage builds solve?
A single-stage build that compiles code ships the whole build toolchain — compilers, headers, git, package caches, source — in the production image: hundreds of MB and a large CVE/attack surface that never runs. Multi-stage lets you build in a fat image and then COPY --from just the resulting artefact into a minimal runtime image, so none of the build machinery is in what you deploy.
What's in a "distroless" image and what isn't?
It contains the language runtime / libc, CA certificates, timezone data, and a non-root user — enough to run a compiled app. It does not contain a shell, a package manager, curl/wget, coreutils, or build tools. That makes it small and hard to exploit, but you can't exec sh into it — debug via ephemeral containers or from the host.
When would you pick alpine over debian-slim or distroless?
Alpine when you need a shell and a couple of small packages and want to stay tiny, and your workload is known to be fine on musl libc. Prefer debian-slim when you have native extensions / glibc-only binaries / Python wheels that don't build for musl, or you've hit Alpine's DNS/NSS quirks. Prefer distroless when it's a compiled app that needs no shell — smallest and safest.
Your image built FROM scratch can't make HTTPS calls. Why?
scratch has no CA certificate bundle, so TLS verification fails with "certificate signed by unknown authority". Fix: COPY --from=builder /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt /etc/ssl/certs/ (after installing ca-certificates in the builder), or use distroless/static which includes them. Same class of issue: no /etc/passwd (add a USER numerically), no tzdata (copy /usr/share/zoneinfo or embed it).
In CI your multi-stage build stopped hitting cache for the compile step. Likely fix?
Add --cache-to type=registry,...,mode=max (and matching --cache-from). By default the exported cache only covers the final image's layers; mode=max also exports the intermediate/builder stages, so a fresh runner can reuse the expensive compile layers instead of rebuilding them.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which stage of a multi-stage build gets pushed to the registry?
Only the last stage (or the one selected with --target). Earlier stages exist only during the build as sources for COPY --from and for caching.
What does COPY --from=builder /out/app /app do?
Copies /out/app from the filesystem of the stage named builder into the current stage's image at /app. It's how the compiled artefact crosses from the build image to the runtime image.

Intermediate core

Convert a 1.2 GB single-stage Node image to a small multi-stage one — outline the Dockerfile.
Stage 1 (build): FROM node:20 AS build, WORKDIR /app, COPY package*.json ./, RUN npm ci, COPY . ., RUN npm run build, then RUN npm prune --omit=dev (or reinstall with --omit=dev) so node_modules has only production deps. Stage 2 (runtime): FROM node:20-slim (or a distroless Node image), WORKDIR /app, COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules, COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist (and package.json if needed), USER node, EXPOSE 3000, CMD ["node","dist/server.js"]. Extras: pin the base by digest, add a .dockerignore (node_modules, .git, dist from context), use --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm on the npm ci, add a HEALTHCHECK. Result: the compiler, dev dependencies, source, and npm cache are all left in the build stage; the runtime image is ~150–250 MB (or ~120 MB distroless) instead of 1.2 GB.
How do you run tests and build a release image from the same Dockerfile without shipping the test dependencies?
Use named stages with --target. A shared base stage installs production deps. A test stage does FROM base, adds dev/test deps, copies source, and RUNs the test suite (the build fails if tests fail). A final stage also does FROM base, copies source, sets the non-root user and CMD. CI runs docker build --target test . (builds through the test stage, running the suite) and, on success, docker build -t app:1.2.3 . (builds the default/final stage). The final image never includes pytest/jest/etc. because that stage doesn't inherit from test. With --cache-from/--cache-to mode=max the shared base layers are reused between the two builds.

Advanced deep

You must ship the smallest, most secure image for a Python service with native (C-extension) dependencies. Walk through the design and trade-offs.
Python + native extensions is the hard case because you can't just copy one static binary. Approach: multi-stage with a builder that has the compilers and dev headers, and a minimal runtime that has only the shared libraries the wheels link against. Builder: FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder (glibc, matches most wheels), install build-essential + the -dev packages for your native deps, create a venv (python -m venv /venv), pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt into it (with a --mount=type=cache for pip), and, if you want reproducibility/size, pip install from a pre-built wheelhouse. Runtime: options ranked by size/risk — (a) gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12 + COPY --from=builder /venv /venv and the app; smallest with no shell, but you must ensure every native lib the wheels need is present (distroless python includes libpython + common libs; extra libs like libpq, libjpeg, libxml2 may need copying from the builder's /usr/lib/...). (b) python:3.12-slim runtime + apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends just the runtime lib* packages (not the -dev ones) + the venv; larger (~80–120 MB) but robust and debuggable. (c) Alpine + musl only if all your wheels have musllinux builds or you're willing to compile them — often not worth the pain. Trade-offs: distroless gives the smallest CVE surface and size but "missing .so" errors are opaque and there's no shell to debug — mitigate by auditing with ldd in the builder (ldd /venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/**/*.so) and copying the exact libs, and by having a debug stage variant with a shell for local use. slim-runtime is bigger but "just works" and is easy to operate. Also: pin the base by digest, set PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE/PYTHONUNBUFFERED, run as non-root, --no-install-recommends, strip the venv (find -name '*.pyc' -delete, remove tests/`__pycache__`), consider pip install --compile then remove build metadata, scan with Trivy and iterate on findings, generate an SBOM, and load-test to confirm the native paths actually work under the minimal runtime. Recommendation: default to slim-runtime for operability; move to distroless once the lib set is proven, keeping a shelled debug stage.

Volumes, Bind Mounts & tmpfs

The container's writable layer is ephemeral and dies with the container; anything that must persist or be shared goes in a mount.

Notes

Ephemeral vs persistent

What / why. Files a container creates outside a mount land in its writable OverlayFS layer — deleted with docker rm, not shared, and slow for heavy writes (copy-up). Persist by mounting a volume or a bind mount; use tmpfs for scratch data that must never hit disk.

$ docker run --name c1 alpine sh -c 'echo hi > /data.txt'
$ docker rm c1
$ docker run --rm alpine cat /data.txt        # gone -- new container, fresh writable layer

Named volumes

What / why. Docker-managed storage under /var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/_data. Preferred for app data: portable across hosts via drivers, easy to back up, isolated from the host layout, and Docker pre-populates an empty volume with the image's existing content at that path (handy for config skeletons).

$ docker volume create pgdata
$ docker run -d --name db -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16
$ docker volume ls ; docker volume inspect pgdata
$ docker volume prune                 # remove volumes no container references

# back up / restore a volume
$ docker run --rm -v pgdata:/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine \
    tar czf /backup/pgdata.tgz -C /data .
$ docker run --rm -v pgnew:/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine \
    tar xzf /backup/pgdata.tgz -C /data

Bind mounts

What / why. Mount an exact host path into the container. Great for local dev (edit code on the host, see it live in the container) and for host artefacts (certs, /etc/localtime). Downsides: tied to the host's directory layout, host permissions/UID matter, and it's the vector for the classic footgun of mounting the docker socket or /.

$ docker run -d -p 8080:80 \
    -v "$PWD/src":/app/src:ro \        # :ro = read-only in the container
    -v /etc/localtime:/etc/localtime:ro \
    node:20 npm run dev

# new --mount syntax (explicit, preferred for scripts)
$ docker run --mount type=bind,src="$PWD/src",dst=/app/src,readonly node:20 ...
$ docker run --mount type=volume,src=pgdata,dst=/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16

tmpfs

What / why. An in-memory filesystem inside the container — fast, wiped on stop, never persisted. Use it for secrets you don't want on disk, session/scratch files, or when the rootfs is --read-only and you still need a writable /tmp.

$ docker run --rm --read-only \
    --tmpfs /tmp:rw,size=64m,mode=1777 \
    --tmpfs /run \
    myapp

-v vs --mount, and the shadowing rule

  • -v name:/path and --mount type=volume,src=name,dst=/path are equivalent; --mount is verbose but unambiguous (fails loudly if the source is missing, where -v would silently create a directory).
  • Mounting over a non-empty image directory hides the image's content for the life of the mount — a bind mount of an empty host dir onto /app/node_modules makes the container see nothing there. (An empty named volume, by contrast, gets seeded from the image on first use.)
  • Permissions: a bind-mounted host dir keeps its host ownership; if the container runs as UID 10001 and the dir is owned by your UID, writes fail. Fix with matching UIDs, chown, or an entrypoint that adjusts ownership.
# common dev trick: bind the source but keep the image's node_modules
$ docker run -v "$PWD":/app -v /app/node_modules node:20 ...
#   the anonymous volume on /app/node_modules "wins" over the bind for that subpath

Where this goes in orchestration

  • Compose: a top-level volumes: block + volumes: under each service; ./src:/app for binds.
  • Kubernetes: emptyDir ≈ anonymous volume, hostPath ≈ bind mount (discouraged), and PersistentVolumeClaim for real persistent storage — see the Kubernetes "Volumes, PV, PVC" topic.
  • Rule of thumb: stateless containers, state in a volume/PVC. Never rely on the writable layer for anything you'd miss.
Cheat Sheet
  • Writable layer = ephemeral (gone on rm), not shared, slow for heavy writes (copy-up). Persist → mount.
  • Named volume (-v name:/path): Docker-managed, portable, backup-friendly, seeded from the image if empty. Preferred for app data.
  • Bind mount (-v /host/path:/path[:ro]): exact host dir; dev live-reload, host artefacts; host UID/layout matters.
  • tmpfs (--tmpfs /tmp:size=64m): RAM-backed, wiped on stop, never on disk; secrets/scratch, and for --read-only rootfs.
  • --mount type=volume|bind|tmpfs,src=...,dst=... = explicit form; -v silently creates missing sources.
  • Mounting over a non-empty image dir hides its contents (bind or anonymous volume); an empty named volume is seeded from the image.
  • Backup a volume: docker run --rm -v vol:/data -v $PWD:/b alpine tar czf /b/vol.tgz -C /data .
  • Compose volumes:; Kubernetes emptyDir/hostPath/PVC. Keep containers stateless.
Q&A
What happens to data written inside a container (not in a mount) when the container is removed?
It's gone. Those files live in the container's writable OverlayFS layer, which is deleted with docker rm. They're also invisible to other containers and slow for large writes because of copy-up. Persist by mounting a volume or bind mount at that path.
Named volume vs bind mount — when do you use each?
Named volume for application state (databases, uploads, caches) — Docker manages it, it's portable across hosts (with a driver), easy to back up, and decoupled from the host's directory layout. Bind mount for development (live-editing source from the host) and for mounting specific host files into the container (TLS certs, /etc/localtime, config). Bind mounts couple you to the host path and its permissions.
You bind-mount an empty host folder onto /app/node_modules and the app can't find its dependencies. Why?
A mount overlays whatever was at that path in the image, so the image's installed node_modules is hidden by your empty host directory for the life of the mount. Fixes: don't bind that subpath (bind /app but add an anonymous volume on /app/node_modules so it keeps the image's copy), install deps into the volume, or use a named volume there (which gets seeded from the image content when first created, unlike a bind mount).
How do you give a container a writable /tmp while keeping its root filesystem read-only?
docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp:rw,size=64m,mode=1777 --tmpfs /run myapp. --read-only makes the rootfs immutable (great hardening), and the --tmpfs mounts give the few paths that genuinely need writes an in-memory, size-capped filesystem that's wiped on stop.
How do you back up a Docker volume?
Run a throwaway container that mounts both the volume and a host directory, and tar the volume into the host dir: docker run --rm -v myvol:/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine tar czf /backup/myvol.tgz -C /data .. Restore by extracting into a fresh volume the same way. For databases, prefer the DB's own dump tool (pg_dump, mysqldump) run against a paused/consistent state rather than a raw file copy.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which mount type survives docker rm of the container?
Named volumes and bind mounts survive — they live outside the container (in /var/lib/docker/volumes or on the host). The container's writable layer and tmpfs mounts do not.
What is a tmpfs mount good for?
Fast, in-memory, never-persisted storage — scratch/session files, secrets you don't want on disk, and providing writable paths (/tmp, /run) when the container root filesystem is read-only.

Intermediate core

A container running as a non-root user can't write to its bind-mounted data directory. How do you fix it properly?
The bind-mounted host directory keeps its host ownership/permissions, which don't match the container's non-root UID (e.g. 10001). Options, best first: (1) Match UIDs — create the container user with a UID that owns the host dir, or chown the host dir to the container's UID (sudo chown -R 10001:10001 ./data); document it. (2) Use a named volume instead of a bind — you control its initialization and can chown it once via an init container/entrypoint; it's also more portable. (3) Entrypoint fixup — start as root, chown the mount to the app UID, then exec gosu 10001 "$@" to drop privileges (adds a root moment at start). (4) On Linux with user namespaces / rootless, the mapping shifts UIDs — account for that. (5) SELinux hosts also need :z/:Z on the mount. Avoid the lazy fix of running the container as root just to write the file.
Why can heavy write workloads (a database) be slow if you leave their data in the container filesystem instead of a volume?
The container filesystem is an OverlayFS union: the image layers are read-only lower dirs and the container has one writable upper dir. The first time the container writes to (or even opens for write) a file that exists in a lower layer, OverlayFS does a copy-up — it copies the whole file into the upper dir before the write. For a database that constantly rewrites large data and WAL files, that's write amplification plus overlay metadata overhead, and every byte also counts against the container's writable-layer disk. A volume (or bind mount) is a plain directory on the host filesystem — no union, no copy-up — so writes go straight through at native speed, and the data persists and can be backed up. That's why every official database image documents a VOLUME for its data directory.

Advanced deep

Design storage for a stateful service (say Postgres) running in containers across a small fleet: persistence, backups, migration, and failure handling.
Persistence: never the writable layer — mount the data directory (/var/lib/postgresql/data) from durable storage. Single host: a named volume on a dedicated fast disk (NVMe), separate from the OS disk, with the volume driver pointed at that mount. Fleet: a networked/CSI volume (EBS, Ceph RBD, Longhorn, cloud disk) so the volume can re-attach to whichever node runs the container; in Kubernetes that's a PersistentVolumeClaim with a StorageClass, and the DB runs as a StatefulSet (stable name + its own PVC per replica). Set filesystem and mount options the DB wants (e.g. noatime), and size with headroom + alerting on usage. One writer: block storage is ReadWriteOnce — ensure only one Postgres instance mounts a given volume at a time (StatefulSet + fencing); don't put a DB on ReadWriteMany NFS. Backups: logical (pg_dump/pg_dumpall) on a schedule for portability + point-in-time via WAL archiving (archive_command to object storage) and periodic pg_basebackup; store off-node, encrypted, with retention and tested restores (a restore that's never run doesn't exist). Volume/disk snapshots are a fast complement but must be crash-consistent (snapshot the volume, or CHECKPOINT + filesystem freeze). Migration / node change: with a CSI/network volume, detach from the old node and attach to the new (the orchestrator does this on reschedule); with local disk, restore from backup/replica onto the new node. Keep the container image and PG major version pinned so a reschedule doesn't silently upgrade the on-disk format (major upgrades need pg_upgrade, a deliberate step). Failure handling: run a streaming replica (or use a managed HA operator — CloudNativePG, Patroni, Stolon) for automatic failover; health/liveness probes that don't kill a slow-recovering primary; PodDisruptionBudget so cluster maintenance doesn't take down the primary and its replica together; monitor replication lag, WAL archive success, disk %, checkpoint timing, and backup age; alerts on "no successful backup in 25h" and "replica lag > N". Data safety knobs: fsync=on, full_page_writes=on, appropriate wal_level; never --read-only the data mount; run the container non-root but with the data dir owned by the postgres UID. Net: durable re-attachable volume + StatefulSet semantics for single-writer, WAL-archiving + tested restores for recovery, and an HA operator + PDB + monitoring for availability — the container is disposable, the volume and the backups are the system of record.

Docker Networking & Port Publishing

User-defined bridge networks give containers private IPs, name-based DNS, and NAT to the outside — -p opens a door inward.

Notes

The built-in networks

NetworkBehaviour
bridge (default)Legacy default bridge docker0. Private subnet, NAT egress, -p for ingress. No name resolution (needed old --link).
user-defined bridge (docker network create)Same, plus an embedded DNS so containers resolve each other by name/alias, and better isolation between networks.
hostNo netns — shares the host's stack. No -p needed, no isolation, port conflicts with the host. Fastest.
noneOnly lo. For offline/compute containers.
macvlan / ipvlanContainer gets its own MAC/IP directly on the physical LAN — looks like a real host. For legacy apps that need L2 presence.
overlayVXLAN across hosts (Swarm). Containers on different machines share one L2 segment.
$ docker network create appnet
$ docker run -d --name db  --network appnet postgres:16
$ docker run -d --name web --network appnet -p 8080:80 myweb
$ docker run --rm --network appnet alpine ping -c1 db     # resolves via 127.0.0.11
$ docker network inspect appnet --format '{{range .Containers}}{{.Name}} {{.IPv4Address}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}'

Container-to-container

What / why. Put related containers on the same user-defined network and they reach each other by container name (or --network-alias) on the container port — no port publishing, no NAT. This is how Compose wires web → db. A container can join multiple networks (docker network connect) to bridge tiers.

# web talks to db directly; db is NOT exposed to the host at all
DB_HOST=db  DB_PORT=5432          # web's config -- just the service name

$ docker network connect backend web    # web now on frontend AND backend
$ docker network disconnect frontend db # db reachable only from the backend network

Publishing ports

-p 8080:80              # host 0.0.0.0:8080  ->  container :80   (DNAT)
-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80   # bind only to loopback -- not reachable from the LAN
-p 80                  # -> a random high host port (see: docker port <c>)
-P                     # publish every EXPOSEd port to random host ports
-p 5353:53/udp         # protocol-specific
  • -p 8080:80 installs an iptables DNAT rule + a small userland proxy for edge cases. Without -p, a port is unreachable from outside the container's network no matter what EXPOSE says.
  • Binding to 0.0.0.0 (the default) exposes it on every host interface — use 127.0.0.1: for local-only services.
  • Default-bridge published ports can bypass the host firewall (Docker inserts rules ahead of it) — a frequent surprise; use iptables integration settings or a user-defined network + explicit rules.

DNS & service discovery

  • On a user-defined network, each container's /etc/resolv.conf is nameserver 127.0.0.11 — Docker's embedded resolver, which knows the network's containers and forwards everything else to the host's resolvers.
  • --network-alias name lets several containers answer to the same name (round-robin) — a poor-man's load balance.
  • --dns, --dns-search, --add-host name:ip to override.
$ docker run --rm --network appnet alpine cat /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 127.0.0.11
$ docker run --rm --network appnet --add-host legacy:10.0.0.9 alpine getent hosts legacy

Debugging

$ docker exec web ss -tlnp                       # what's listening inside
$ docker exec web wget -qO- http://db:5432 || echo "no route/DNS"
$ docker network inspect appnet                  # subnet, gateway, connected containers
$ docker port web                                # published mappings
$ PID=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' web)
$ sudo nsenter -t $PID -n ip addr ; sudo nsenter -t $PID -n ip route   # from the host
$ sudo iptables -t nat -L DOCKER -n                # the DNAT rules -p created
Cheat Sheet
  • User-defined bridge (docker network create): private IPs + embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11 so containers reach each other by name. Prefer this over the legacy default bridge.
  • Same network → talk by container name on the container port, no -p, no NAT.
  • -p host:container = iptables DNAT inward. EXPOSE alone publishes nothing.
  • -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 for local-only; plain -p 8080:80 binds all interfaces.
  • Modes: host (no isolation, fast), none (lo only), macvlan/ipvlan (real LAN IP), overlay (cross-host VXLAN).
  • A container can join multiple networks (docker network connect/disconnect) to segment tiers.
  • Published ports may bypass the host firewall on the default bridge — a known gotcha.
  • Debug: docker network inspect, docker port, docker exec ss -tlnp, nsenter -t <pid> -n, iptables -t nat -L DOCKER.
Q&A
Why do containers on a user-defined network resolve each other by name, but not on the default bridge?
User-defined networks get Docker's embedded DNS server (injected as nameserver 127.0.0.11), which maps container names/aliases on that network to their IPs. The legacy default bridge network has no such DNS — historically you needed --link. Always create a network for multi-container apps (Compose does this automatically).
Does EXPOSE 8080 in the Dockerfile make the app reachable from my laptop?
No. EXPOSE is metadata. To reach it you must publish with -p 8080:8080 at run time (or -P to publish all exposed ports to random host ports, or a Compose/K8s mapping). Without publishing, the port is only reachable from other containers on the same Docker network.
What does -p 8080:80 actually change on the host?
Docker adds an iptables rule in the nat table's DOCKER chain: traffic arriving on the host's TCP 8080 has its destination rewritten (DNAT) to the container's IP:80 and is forwarded over the bridge; a companion rule un-NATs the return path. Docker also runs a small userland proxy to cover loopback and some edge cases. You can see it with iptables -t nat -L DOCKER -n.
How do you let two services talk to each other without exposing the database to the host?
Put both on a user-defined network and don't publish the database's port. The app connects to db:5432 (the container name), resolved by the embedded DNS, over the bridge — no -p for the DB, so it's unreachable from the host or LAN. Only the front-end service gets a -p. For tiered isolation, use two networks and connect the app to both.
When would you use --network host, and what's the risk?
When you need maximum network performance (no bridge/NAT hop), the app must see real client IPs without a proxy, or it needs to bind many ports / use protocols that don't NAT well. Risks: zero network isolation (the container shares the host's stack), its listeners collide with host services and other host-network containers, and any port it opens is immediately on the host — a firewall/exposure hazard. Prefer a user-defined bridge with explicit -p unless you have a specific reason.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What's the one command to create a network where containers can find each other by name?
docker network create <name> — a user-defined bridge with embedded DNS. Then run containers with --network <name>.
Which flag limits a published port to the local machine only?
Bind to loopback in the mapping: -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80. Plain -p 8080:80 binds 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces).

Intermediate core

Container A can't reach container B by name. Walk the diagnosis.
(1) Same network? docker inspect A and B → .NetworkSettings.Networks; if they're on different networks (or one is on the default bridge), fix with docker network connect or run both with --network appnet. (2) DNS reachable? docker exec A cat /etc/resolv.conf should show 127.0.0.11; docker exec A nslookup B. If DNS resolves but connection fails → it's a listener/port issue. (3) Is B listening on the expected port and interface? docker exec B ss -tlnp — it must bind 0.0.0.0 (or B's container IP), not 127.0.0.1 (loopback-only would be unreachable from A). (4) Right name? Container name vs --network-alias vs Compose service name; on the default bridge, name resolution simply doesn't exist. (5) Firewall/policy inside B's image, or a Docker userland-proxy quirk. (6) From the host: docker network inspect appnet to confirm both containers are attached with IPs, and nsenter -t <pidA> -n ping <B-ip> to test raw connectivity vs DNS. Usually it's "not on the same user-defined network" or "B binds 127.0.0.1".
Design the network topology for a web + API + database + cache stack so only what needs to be exposed is exposed.
Two (or three) user-defined bridge networks for tiering. frontend: the reverse proxy / web container, which is the only one with a published port (-p 443:443), plus the API. backend: the API, the database, and the cache — none published. The API is connected to both networks (docker network connect) so it bridges the proxy and the data tier; the database and cache are only on backend, so they're unreachable from the host or the internet and can only be hit by the API. Services address each other by name (api, db, redis). Bind the proxy's published port explicitly, terminate TLS there, and pass through. If you want the DB reachable for admin, add a separate admin network or a bastion container, not a host port. In Compose this is just multiple networks: entries with each service listing the networks it belongs to; the same shape maps to Kubernetes NetworkPolicies (default-deny + explicit allows: proxy→api, api→db, api→redis). Net: exactly one ingress point, data stores with no external attack surface, and lateral movement constrained to declared paths.

Advanced deep

Explain, end to end, what happens to a packet from the internet hitting -p 443:8443 on a container, and back.
Inbound: (1) A TCP SYN arrives on the host NIC destined for <host-ip>:443. (2) It enters netfilter; in the nat table's PREROUTING chain Docker's DOCKER chain has a rule matching ! -i <bridge> -p tcp --dport 443 -j DNAT --to 172.20.0.5:8443, so the destination is rewritten to the container's bridge IP and port, and conntrack records the original tuple. (3) Routing decision: the destination is now on the docker_gwbridge/user bridge subnet, so the packet is forwarded (host ip_forward=1) out the bridge interface. (4) FORWARD chain: Docker's DOCKER-USER and DOCKER chains must accept it (there's an ACCEPT for established/related and for the published mapping; DOCKER-USER is where you'd add your own filtering). (5) The bridge delivers the frame to the container's veth, it pops out eth0 inside the container's network namespace, and the app's socket bound to 0.0.0.0:8443 accepts it; PID is namespaced but it's a normal accept(). (Docker also has a userland docker-proxy process that can handle this path for hairpin/loopback and when kernel forwarding isn't usable.) Return: the app writes the response with source 172.20.0.5:8443, dest = the original client. It goes container → veth → bridge → host routing. conntrack matches the flow and reverse-NAT in POSTROUTING/reply direction rewrites the source back to <host-ip>:443 so the client sees a reply from the address it contacted. For egress the container initiates (not this flow), POSTROUTING has a MASQUERADE rule for the bridge subnet so its private IP is SNAT'd to the host IP. Key points to be able to state: PREROUTING DNAT in the DOCKER nat chain, kernel forwarding + FORWARD/DOCKER-USER accept, conntrack ties request and reply, reply-direction un-NAT, and the optional docker-proxy. That's also why the container sees the client's IP on a bridge network only if you preserve it (proxy protocol / X-Forwarded-For at L7), since L3 NAT keeps the client IP but many setups add an L7 proxy in front.

Docker Compose: Multi-Container Apps

One YAML file declares services, networks and volumes; docker compose up reconciles the whole stack.

Notes

The file

# compose.yaml  (the "version:" key is obsolete in the Compose Spec)
services:
  web:
    build: ./web                 # build from a Dockerfile...
    image: myorg/web:1.4         # ...and/or name the resulting image
    ports: ["8080:80"]
    environment:
      API_URL: http://api:8000
    depends_on:
      api: { condition: service_healthy }
    restart: unless-stopped

  api:
    build: ./api
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:secret@db:5432/app
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "wget", "-qO-", "http://localhost:8000/healthz"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
    depends_on:
      db: { condition: service_healthy }

  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
      POSTGRES_DB: app
    volumes: ["pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data"]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10

volumes:
  pgdata:

Everyday commands

$ docker compose up -d                 # build if needed, create net/volumes, start all
$ docker compose up -d --build         # force a rebuild
$ docker compose ps                    # status of the stack
$ docker compose logs -f api           # follow one service
$ docker compose exec api sh           # shell into a running service
$ docker compose run --rm api pytest   # one-off task container (own instance)
$ docker compose down                  # stop + remove containers + network
$ docker compose down -v               # ...also remove named volumes (data loss!)
$ docker compose config                # render the final merged config
$ docker compose watch                 # sync files / rebuild on change (dev)

Networking, DNS & depends_on

  • Compose creates a project network (<project>_default); every service is reachable at its service name on its container port. Add named networks: for tiering.
  • depends_on alone only controls start order, not readiness. Add condition: service_healthy (needs a healthcheck) so api waits for db to actually accept connections — otherwise the app must retry on its own.
  • ports: publishes to the host; expose: is intra-network only (and mostly redundant now).

Config, env & secrets

# .env  (auto-loaded; substitutes ${VAR} in compose.yaml)
TAG=1.4.2
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret

# compose.yaml
services:
  web:
    image: myorg/web:${TAG}
    env_file: [./web.env]         # bulk env into the container
    secrets: [db_password]        # mounted at /run/secrets/db_password (file, not env)
secrets:
  db_password:
    file: ./secrets/db_password.txt

Precedence (low→high): image ENV < Compose environment:/env_file: < shell env passed to compose < --env-file. Keep real secrets in secrets: (files) or a vault, not committed .env.

Profiles & override files

  • Multiple files merge: compose.yaml + compose.override.yaml (auto) + explicit -f base.yaml -f prod.yaml. Later files win; lists are replaced, maps are merged.
  • Profiles: tag optional services (profiles: ["debug"]); they start only with --profile debug or when named. Good for seeders, admin UIs, load generators.
  • develop.watch / docker compose watch: on file change, sync into the container or rebuild the image — fast inner loop without bind-mount permission headaches.
$ docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d
$ docker compose --profile debug up -d        # also starts profiled services
$ COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=staging docker compose up -d   # isolate a second copy of the stack

Scaling & limits

$ docker compose up -d --scale api=3       # 3 api replicas behind the service-name DNS (round-robin)
# per-service limits (Compose reads the non-Swarm keys):
services:
  api:
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:   { cpus: "1.0", memory: 512M }
        reservations: { cpus: "0.25", memory: 128M }
    cpus: 1.0            # legacy top-level keys also work
    mem_limit: 512m
Cheat Sheet
  • One compose.yaml: services:, top-level networks:, volumes:, secrets:. No version: key anymore.
  • Services reach each other by service name on the project network; ports: publishes to the host.
  • depends_on = start order only; add condition: service_healthy + a healthcheck for real readiness (or retry in the app).
  • up -d / up -d --build / ps / logs -f svc / exec svc sh / run --rm svc cmd / down / down -v (deletes volumes) / config.
  • .env auto-substitutes ${VAR}; env_file for bulk env; secrets: mounts files under /run/secrets/ — keep real secrets out of committed .env.
  • Compose files merge: base + auto compose.override.yaml + explicit -f; later wins. Profiles for optional services.
  • --scale svc=N for replicas (round-robin DNS); per-service deploy.resources.limits / cpus / mem_limit.
  • Compose = dev / CI / single host. Clusters → Kubernetes.
Q&A
How does the api service reach the db service in Compose?
By the service name as a hostname on the auto-created project network: db:5432. Compose runs an embedded DNS that resolves service names (and any aliases) to the current container IPs. No port publishing needed for intra-stack traffic.
Does depends_on: [db] guarantee the database is ready before the app starts?
No — by itself it only orders container start, not readiness; db's process may still be initializing. Add a healthcheck to db and depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } } to api, so Compose waits until the healthcheck passes. Even then, make the app resilient with connection retries — healthchecks can flap and orchestrators restart things.
What's the danger of docker compose down -v?
The -v removes the named volumes declared in the file — so your database data, uploads, etc. are deleted. Plain docker compose down keeps volumes (only removes containers and the network). Use -v deliberately for a clean reset, never habitually.
How do you keep dev and prod settings in one Compose project without duplicating everything?
Compose merges multiple files. Put shared definitions in compose.yaml; dev-only tweaks (bind-mounted source, debug ports, no restart policy) go in compose.override.yaml, which is applied automatically. For prod, an explicit docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up overrides with prod values (images instead of build, resource limits, real secrets, restart: always). Later files win; maps deep-merge, lists are replaced.
Compose --scale api=3 — how do requests get distributed, and what are the limits?
All three api containers register under the same service DNS name; the embedded resolver returns the set of IPs and clients pick one (effectively round-robin per DNS lookup). There's no real load balancer, health-aware routing, sticky sessions, or graceful draining — a crashed replica may still be handed out until DNS/its record updates. It's fine for local testing of concurrency; for production you want a proper LB/reverse proxy in front, or Kubernetes Services with EndpointSlices and readiness gating.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does docker compose up -d do?
Reads compose.yaml, builds images that need building, creates the project network and named volumes, and starts every service in the background, in dependency order.
Where do you declare a named volume shared by two services?
In the top-level volumes: block, then reference it under each service's volumes: list as name:/path/in/container.

Intermediate core

Your Compose app's API crashes on startup because the DB isn't ready. Give two fixes.
(1) Compose-level readiness gate: add a healthcheck to the db service (pg_isready / mysqladmin ping / a TCP check) and set depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } } on the API, so Compose only starts the API after the DB healthcheck passes. (2) App-level retry: make the API retry the DB connection with backoff on startup (most frameworks/ORMs support this, or a small wait-for-it/dockerize wrapper in the entrypoint) — this is the robust fix because it also survives DB restarts, failovers, and healthcheck flapping at runtime, not just first boot. Do both: the healthcheck makes local up clean, the retry makes it production-safe.
How would you run the same Compose stack twice on one machine (e.g. two feature branches) without conflicts?
Isolate the project name, which prefixes container names, the network, and volumes: COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=branch-a docker compose up -d and COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=branch-b ... (or -p branch-a). Each gets its own <project>_default network and its own volumes, so DNS names don't collide and data is separate. Then also avoid host port clashes: parameterize published ports via .env (WEB_PORT=8081 / 8082) or only publish through a shared reverse proxy that routes by hostname, or don't publish at all and reach services via docker compose exec / the project network. Watch for shared external resources (a fixed external network, a host bind-mount path, a fixed container_name) — remove hard-coded container_name and use relative bind paths so nothing is global.

Advanced deep

A team uses Compose for local dev and wants a smooth path to Kubernetes for production. Design that path and call out where Compose and K8s diverge.
Keep one source of truth for the app contract: the Dockerfile(s) and the set of services/ports/env/volumes. Use Compose for the inner loop (fast up, watch, bind-mounted source, seed data, test dependencies) and generate/maintain K8s manifests (or a Helm chart) for staging/prod, reviewed like code. Conversion: kompose convert or docker compose bridge gives a starting point (Deployment per service, Service per exposed port, PVC per named volume, ConfigMap/Secret from env), but treat it as scaffolding, not the deliverable. Where they diverge and what to do: (1) Networking — Compose service-name DNS → K8s Service + cluster DNS (svc.namespace.svc.cluster.local); Compose ports: host-publish → K8s Service type + Ingress; multiple Compose networks → NetworkPolicies. (2) Readiness — Compose depends_on/condition is start-time only; K8s has no ordering, so every service must have readiness/liveness probes and retry logic (which you should already have). (3) Storage — Compose named volume (single host) → PersistentVolumeClaim + StorageClass; a stateful service becomes a StatefulSet, not a Deployment; bind mounts of source don't translate (that was dev-only). (4) Config/secrets — .env/env_file → ConfigMap; secrets: files → Secret (+ encryption at rest / external secrets). (5) Scaling — --scale round-robin DNS → replicas + real kube-proxy load balancing + HPA; add PodDisruptionBudget. (6) Resources — deploy.resources → requests/limits (and now they drive scheduling + QoS + eviction). (7) Lifecycle — restart: policy → K8s restarts by default; add terminationGracePeriodSeconds + preStop hooks; jobs/one-offs (compose run) → Job/CronJob. (8) Build — Compose builds locally; K8s never builds — images come from a registry via CI, referenced by digest. Process: CI builds and pushes images (tag = version + SHA); the same image digest is deployed to dev-cluster → staging → prod via the chart; Compose in dev uses that same image (or build: for live code) so parity is high. Document the mapping so "add a service" means "add it to Compose and the chart." Net: Compose stays the developer experience, a reviewed Helm/manifest set is the deployable artifact, probes + retries + registry images + PVCs/StatefulSets bridge the semantic gaps.

CPU & Memory Limits

The --cpus, --memory and --pids-limit flags are a thin wrapper over cgroup v2 files — and the failure modes are OOM kills and CFS throttling.

Notes

The flags

FlagEffect
--cpus 1.5Hard cap: at most 1.5 CPU-seconds per wall second (CFS quota/period). Throttled beyond it.
--cpuset-cpus 0-3Pin to specific cores (NUMA / cache locality / isolating a noisy container).
--cpu-shares 512Relative weight (default 1024). Only matters under contention; an idle host ignores it.
--memory 512mHard ceiling. Kernel reclaims, then OOM-kills a process in the cgroup.
--memory-reservation 256mSoft target; the kernel pushes usage back toward it under host memory pressure.
--memory-swap 512mmemory + swap total. Set equal to --memory to disable swap for the container.
--oom-kill-disableDon't OOM-kill — the container hangs instead. Dangerous; needs a memory limit; almost never right.
--pids-limit 200Max processes/threads — contains fork bombs and runaway thread creation.
--blkio-weight / --device-read-bpsBlock-IO weight / bandwidth caps per device.
$ docker run -d --name api \
    --cpus 1.0 --memory 512m --memory-swap 512m \
    --pids-limit 200 --restart on-failure:3 \
    myorg/api:1.4

$ docker inspect api --format \
  '{{.HostConfig.NanoCpus}} {{.HostConfig.Memory}} {{.HostConfig.PidsLimit}}'
1000000000 536870912 200

Verifying and watching

$ docker stats --no-stream
NAME  CPU %   MEM USAGE / LIMIT    MEM %   PIDS
api   38.20%  190MiB / 512MiB     37.11%  22

# the real cgroup files (host)
$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-<id>.scope/cpu.max
100000 100000                        # --cpus 1.0
$ cat .../memory.current .../memory.max
199229440
536870912
$ cat .../cpu.stat | grep -E 'nr_throttled|throttled_usec'
nr_throttled 214                     # > 0 and rising -> cpu limit too low
$ cat .../memory.events | grep oom
oom_kill 0

OOM kill — exit 137

What / how. Container working set exceeds --memory → kernel reclaims caches, then invokes the OOM killer within that cgroup (the host and other containers are untouched). PID 1 dying = the container exits 137.

$ docker inspect api --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.ExitCode}}'
true 137
$ dmesg | tail
Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 4522 (java) total-vm:... anon-rss:...

# runtime heaps must respect the limit, or they OOM regardless:
JAVA:  -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0        # (modern JVMs are cgroup-aware)
NODE:  --max-old-space-size=384         # ~75% of a 512Mi limit
GO:    GOMEMLIMIT=460MiB                 # soft memory target, since Go 1.19

CPU throttling — the silent p99 killer

What / why. --cpus enforces a quota per ~100 ms period. If a burst (request handling, GC, a thread pool waking up) needs more than the quota, all the container's threads are frozen until the next period — tens of ms of stall. Average CPU stays under the limit; tail latency explodes.

# symptom: p50 fine, p99 terrible; cpu.stat shows throttling
nr_throttled 812 / nr_periods 3000     # throttled ~27% of periods
throttled_usec 4_100_000

# mitigations
#  - raise --cpus (or remove the hard cap for latency-sensitive services)
#  - reduce parallelism so the app can't demand more than the quota in a burst
#  - use --cpu-shares (weight) instead of a hard cap where the host has headroom
#  - pin with --cpuset-cpus to cut scheduler noise

Rules of thumb

  • Always set --memory in production — a leak then kills only that container, not the node.
  • Set --memory-swap equal to --memory (no swap) so you get a clean OOM instead of thrash.
  • Give runtimes a heap target relative to the limit (MaxRAMPercentage, --max-old-space-size, GOMEMLIMIT).
  • Be cautious with tight --cpus on latency-sensitive services — prefer weight + monitoring; use hard caps for batch/untrusted work.
  • Set --pids-limit to bound fork bombs.
  • Leave headroom on the host for the daemon and system — don't sum limits to 100% of the machine.
Cheat Sheet
  • --cpus N → cpu.max hard cap (throttled beyond). --cpu-shares → cpu.weight, contention only. --cpuset-cpus pins cores.
