  • --memory → memory.max hard ceiling; over it → OOM kill in the cgroup, exit 137. --memory-reservation = soft.
  • --memory-swap == --memory to disable container swap (avoid thrash; get a clean OOM).
  • --pids-limit caps processes/threads (fork-bomb guard). --device-read-bps etc. for IO.
  • Confirm: docker stats, docker inspect .State.OOMKilled/.ExitCode, cgroup files cpu.stat (nr_throttled), memory.events (oom_kill), dmesg.
  • Runtimes must be told the limit: JVM -XX:MaxRAMPercentage, Node --max-old-space-size, Go GOMEMLIMIT.
  • Tight CPU cap + bursty/multi-threaded app = CFS throttling = p99 latency spikes even with low average CPU.
  • Always limit memory in prod; leave host headroom; don't --oom-kill-disable.
Q&A
Container exits with 137 and OOMKilled: true. What do you do?
It hit --memory. Check the app's real working set (docker stats, a profiler) vs the limit; check dmesg for which process was killed. If the app is a JVM/Node/Go runtime, verify the heap is sized relative to the limit (-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75, --max-old-space-size, GOMEMLIMIT) — a heap larger than the container limit OOMs regardless. Then either raise the limit to fit the legitimate working set (plus headroom) or fix the leak. Note the kill was cgroup-scoped — other containers and the node were fine.
Average CPU is 40% of the limit but p99 latency is awful. Why?
CFS throttling. --cpus is enforced as a quota per 100 ms period; when a request (or GC pause, or thread-pool wakeup) needs a short burst above the quota, the kernel stalls all the container's runnable threads until the next period — adding tens of milliseconds. The average stays low because most periods don't hit the quota, but the tail is dominated by throttled periods. Confirm with cpu.stat (nr_throttled, throttled_usec). Fix: raise or remove the CPU cap for that service, cut parallelism so it can't demand more than the quota in a burst, or use a weight instead of a hard cap.
Why set --memory-swap equal to --memory?
By default --memory-swap is roughly memory + host swap, so a container over its memory limit can spill into swap instead of being OOM-killed — and then it just thrashes (every allocation becomes disk-slow, dragging down the whole node's IO) while appearing "alive." Setting them equal disables container swap, so exceeding the limit produces an immediate, clean OOM kill you can detect and act on. (Kubernetes disables pod swap by default for this reason.)
What's the difference between --cpus 1 and --cpu-shares 1024?
--cpus 1 is an absolute cap — the container never gets more than one CPU-second per second, even on a totally idle 32-core host (it will be throttled). --cpu-shares 1024 is a relative weight that only takes effect when CPUs are contended: a container with 1024 shares gets twice the CPU of one with 512 when they're both competing, but either can use the whole machine if it's otherwise idle. Use caps for hard multi-tenant quotas or batch jobs; use shares for fair sharing of a host with spare capacity.
What does --pids-limit protect against?
Runaway process/thread creation — a fork bomb, a bug spawning threads in a loop, a misconfigured worker pool. Without it, one container can exhaust the host's PID space and make the whole node unresponsive. Set it to a few times the container's normal thread count.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which Docker flag causes a container to be OOM-killed if it uses too much memory?
--memory (e.g. --memory 512m). It writes memory.max; exceeding it triggers the OOM killer inside that cgroup.
What exit code indicates a SIGKILL / OOM?
137 (128 + signal 9). Confirm OOM specifically with docker inspect <c> --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}'.

Intermediate core

A Java service is OOM-killed at a 1 GiB limit even though "it only needs 600 MB of heap." Explain.
The container's memory limit governs the whole process, not just the Java heap: heap + metaspace + thread stacks (each ~512 KB–1 MB × thread count) + JIT code cache + direct/native ByteBuffers (Netty, NIO) + GC structures + JVM/glibc overhead + any native libs. A 600 MB max heap easily becomes 900 MB–1.1 GB RSS, and older JVMs also ignored the cgroup and sized ergonomics from host RAM. Fixes: size the heap as a percentage of the container limit (-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 so it leaves room for non-heap), cap the other regions (-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize, -Xss, -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize, -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize), reduce thread pool sizes, use a modern cgroup-aware JVM, and set the container limit to the measured RSS under load plus ~20% headroom. Monitor memory.current vs limit and native memory tracking (-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary).
When should you NOT put a hard CPU limit on a container?
Latency-sensitive, bursty services (API servers, anything with a GC or a request-handling spike) where CFS throttling would turn a brief over-quota burst into a multi-period stall and wreck p99. For those, prefer a CPU request/share (so they get their fair slice under contention but can burst into idle capacity) plus monitoring of throttle metrics, and only add a generous limit as a safety ceiling. Hard caps are appropriate for batch jobs, untrusted/multi-tenant workloads where predictable isolation beats tail latency, and cost-controlled environments — and there you should still size the cap above the app's real burst need and watch nr_throttled.

Advanced deep

Design resource limits and monitoring for a mixed workload node running latency-sensitive services and batch jobs, so neither starves the other.
Classify workloads: (a) latency-critical online services, (b) throughput batch/async jobs, (c) system/daemons. CPU: give every workload a request (→ cpu.weight) sized to steady-state need so contention is shared proportionally; for online services set no hard --cpus cap (or a generous one well above burst) so they can use idle capacity and don't get CFS-throttled — rely on weight for fairness; for batch, set a real hard cap so it can't monopolize cores and give it a lower weight so online work preempts it under contention; optionally --cpuset-pin latency-critical services to dedicated cores and keep batch off those cores to remove scheduler/cache interference. Reserve cores/shares for system daemons (kubelet, containerd, node exporter) so they never starve. Memory: hard --memory on everything (leak containment); online services get request == limit (Guaranteed QoS → killed last, best OOM score); batch gets a modest limit and lower priority so it's evicted/killed first under node pressure; disable swap; set runtime heap targets relative to limits. IO/PIDs: io.weight favoring online services, hard io.max bytes/IOPS on batch (log/backup jobs are classic noisy neighbours), separate disks if possible; pids.max on everything. Node headroom: don't schedule to 100%; keep ~10–20% CPU/mem free for bursts and the system. Scheduling: use priority/preemption so a spike in online demand can evict batch pods; PodDisruptionBudgets protect the online tier during maintenance; taints/affinity to keep truly incompatible workloads on separate node pools when the interference can't be tuned away. Monitoring & alerting: per-cgroup CPU throttle ratio (nr_throttled/nr_periods, throttled_usec) — alert if online services throttle at all; memory.events OOM counts and memory.current/limit; PSI (cpu.pressure, memory.pressure, io.pressure) per cgroup and node-wide as an early-warning of contention; eviction events; online-service p99 latency correlated with node CPU/PSI; batch job throughput and queue depth. Loop: right-size requests from observed usage monthly; if online p99 degrades with node load, the batch weight/cap or the node's packing is wrong. Net: weights for fair sharing, hard caps only on batch/untrusted, memory limits everywhere, IO caps on noisy jobs, priority/preemption so online wins, node headroom, and PSI + throttle metrics as the signal that the balance slipped.

Hardening: Non-root, Caps, Read-only, Scanning

Assume the container will be compromised, then make that not matter: run unprivileged, drop everything, freeze the filesystem, and know what's inside.

Notes

Build-time

  • Minimal base pinned by digest (distroless / alpine / slim) — fewer packages = fewer CVEs and no shell/curl for an attacker to use.
  • Non-root USER with a high numeric UID; make writable paths owned by it. runAsNonRoot/USER 10001.
  • No secrets in layers — ARG is in docker history; a COPY key + later rm still ships the key. Use RUN --mount=type=secret or inject at runtime.
  • Drop setuid bits you don't need: RUN find / -perm /6000 -type f -exec chmod a-s {} + || true.
  • Multi-stage so compilers/dev deps never ship.
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot
COPY --chown=nonroot:nonroot --from=builder /out/app /app
USER nonroot
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]

Run-time flags

$ docker run -d \
    --user 10001:10001 \
    --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE \   # add back only what's needed
    --security-opt no-new-privileges \
    --read-only --tmpfs /tmp:rw,size=32m --tmpfs /run \
    --security-opt seccomp=/etc/docker/seccomp-strict.json \  # or leave default (already good)
    --memory 512m --cpus 1 --pids-limit 200 \
    --network appnet \                             # not --network host
    myorg/api:1.4
ControlWhy
--user / USERCompromise lands as an unprivileged UID, not container-root.
--cap-drop ALLRemoves the still-potent default caps (NET_RAW, SETUID, CHOWN, MKNOD…).
--security-opt no-new-privilegesA setuid binary inside can't regain privilege.
--read-only + --tmpfsAttacker can't drop tools/webshells on disk; only the explicit writable paths.
default seccomp + AppArmor~50 dangerous syscalls blocked; MAC on file/mount/ptrace. Don't disable them.
cgroup limitsBound DoS blast radius (CPU, memory, PIDs, IO).
user-defined network, no hostNetwork isolation; don't share the host stack.

Never do

  • --privileged (grants all caps + all devices + disables seccomp/AppArmor). Use targeted --cap-add/--device.
  • -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock — that's host root for the container.
  • -v /:/host, --pid=host, --network=host, --ipc=host unless you truly need them and understand the exposure.
  • Secrets in ENV / image / docker inspect-visible places. Use --secret, files under /run/secrets, or a vault.
  • Running as root "because the volume permissions are annoying" — fix ownership instead.

Scanning, signing, SBOM

# scan in CI, fail the build on fixable HIGH/CRITICAL
$ trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 myorg/api:1.4
$ grype myorg/api:1.4 --fail-on high              # second scanner for coverage

# sign the digest, verify at deploy/admission
$ cosign sign myorg/api@sha256:...
$ cosign verify --key cosign.pub myorg/api@sha256:...

# SBOM so "which images have libX < Y?" is a query, not an archaeology project
$ syft myorg/api:1.4 -o spdx-json > sbom.json
$ docker scout cves myorg/api:1.4                 # Docker's built-in analysis

Enforce at the cluster edge: an admission policy (Kyverno, Gatekeeper, Connaisseur, Ratify) that requires images to be from an allow-listed registry, referenced by digest, cosign-signed by an approved key, and carrying a fresh passing scan attestation.

Runtime detection

  • Falco / Tetragon — alert on escape indicators: a shell spawned in a container that shouldn't have one, mount/ptrace/setns calls, writes to /proc/sys, a new listening socket, package-manager execution, reads of /etc/shadow.
  • Drift detection: running image digest must equal the approved digest.
  • Ship container stdout/stderr and audit logs off-node; watch docker events / Kubernetes events.
Cheat Sheet
  • Top 3: non-root USER/--user, --cap-drop ALL (+ minimal --cap-add), never mount /var/run/docker.sock.
  • Build: minimal pinned base, multi-stage, non-root, no secrets in layers (RUN --mount=type=secret), drop unneeded setuid bits.
  • Run: --security-opt no-new-privileges, --read-only + --tmpfs, keep default seccomp + AppArmor, cgroup limits, user-defined network (not host).
  • Never: --privileged, host mounts of //socket, --pid/network/ipc=host casually, secrets in ENV.
  • Scan (Trivy/Grype/Scout) in CI, fail on fixable HIGH/CRIT; sign (cosign) + verify at admission; generate SBOM (syft).
  • Runtime: Falco/Tetragon for escape indicators; drift detection; logs/events off-node.
  • Hostile workloads → micro-VM runtime (Kata) / gVisor via RuntimeClass.
Q&A
What are the three highest-impact, lowest-effort container hardening steps?
(1) Run as a non-root user (USER in the image, enforced with --user/runAsNonRoot). (2) --cap-drop ALL and add back only the one or two capabilities the app truly needs. (3) Don't bind-mount the Docker socket (or the host root) into containers. Close behind: --read-only + tmpfs, no-new-privileges, and keeping the default seccomp/AppArmor profiles.
Why is --read-only a strong control?
Most post-exploitation steps write to disk — drop a reverse shell, a crypto miner, a modified binary, persistence. A read-only root filesystem blocks all of that; the app only gets the few writable paths you explicitly mount as tmpfs or volumes. It also catches "my app secretly writes to /" bugs early. Combine with a non-root user so even those writable paths are limited.
Where do secrets belong, and where do they not?
Not in ENV (visible via docker inspect, /proc/<pid>/environ, crash dumps, child processes), not in ARG/image layers (in docker history forever), not in the image at all. Use: BuildKit --mount=type=secret for build-time creds (never persisted), files mounted at runtime (--secret / Compose secrets: / K8s Secret volumes under /run/secrets), or a secrets manager the app fetches from at startup with a short-lived token. Rotate anything that ever leaked into a layer.
How do you make sure only vetted images run in production?
Shift-left + admission. In CI: scan (Trivy/Grype) and fail on fixable HIGH/CRITICAL, generate an SBOM, and cosign-sign the image digest. At deploy: an admission controller (Kyverno/Gatekeeper/Connaisseur/Ratify) rejects any pod whose image isn't from an allow-listed registry, isn't referenced by digest, lacks a valid signature by an approved key, or lacks a recent passing-scan attestation. Combine with drift detection so the running digest matches the approved one.
What does --privileged turn off, and what should you use instead?
It grants every Linux capability, exposes all host devices, and disables the seccomp and AppArmor/SELinux profiles — essentially removing the container's security boundary; such a container can trivially escape. Instead grant exactly what's needed: --cap-add SYS_ADMIN (or narrower), --device /dev/foo, a custom seccomp profile that allows the required syscalls, and for genuinely privileged needs (device drivers, DinD) isolate on dedicated nodes or a micro-VM runtime.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What single Dockerfile line most reduces the impact of an app RCE?
A non-root USER (with a matching numeric UID and correct ownership of writable paths), so code execution lands as an unprivileged user rather than container-root.
Name two tools that scan a container image for known vulnerabilities.
Trivy, Grype, Docker Scout, Clair, Snyk — any two.

Intermediate core

An image needs to bind port 80 and "won't work as non-root." How do you keep it unprivileged?
"Bind <1024" needs CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE, not root. Options: (1) run as non-root and grant just that capability — --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE, or in K8s securityContext.capabilities.add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"] with runAsNonRoot: true; on newer kernels you can also set the file capability on the binary (setcap 'cap_net_bind_service=+ep' /app) or the sysctl net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=0. (2) Have the app listen on a high port (8080) and map it — -p 80:8080 at the host, or a Service/Ingress in K8s — so nothing inside needs the capability at all. Option 2 is cleanest for orchestrated environments where a load balancer terminates :80/:443 anyway.
Your image is flagged for 40 CVEs by the scanner. How do you triage and reduce them?
(1) Separate signal from noise: filter to --ignore-unfixed (no patch exists yet — track, don't block) and to HIGH/CRITICAL; check whether the vulnerable package is actually reachable/used (a CVE in a dev tool that isn't in the runtime image, or a library path your code never calls). (2) Shrink the base: move to distroless/slim/alpine — most findings are in OS packages you don't need (shell, coreutils, perl, package manager); a multi-stage build that ships only the binary + minimal runtime often drops the count to near zero. (3) Update: rebuild FROM a freshly patched base (bump the pinned digest), apt-get upgrade the remaining needed packages in the build, bump application dependencies to patched versions (dependabot/renovate). (4) Remove packages pulled in transitively that you don't use. (5) Policy: set the CI gate to fail on fixable HIGH/CRITICAL only, with a documented, time-boxed exception process for the rest and a mitigation (WAF rule, network policy) where a fix isn't available. (6) Prevent regression: scheduled re-scans of running images against new CVE data, base-image auto-bump PRs, and an SBOM inventory so the next base CVE is a query + a rebuild wave, not a scramble.

Advanced deep

Write the container-security baseline (build, run, admission, runtime, response) you'd mandate org-wide, and how you'd roll it out without breaking every team.
Build baseline: golden pinned minimal bases maintained by the platform team; multi-stage; non-root USER (UID ≥ 10000); no secrets in ARG/ENV/layers (RUN --mount=type=secret only); drop unneeded setuid bits; OCI labels (source, revision); hadolint + a policy check in CI; Trivy/Grype scan failing on fixable HIGH/CRIT (with --ignore-unfixed tracked separately); SBOM (syft) and SLSA provenance attached; cosign-sign the digest. Run baseline (defaults, opt-out with justification): runAsNonRoot, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, capabilities.drop: ["ALL"], readOnlyRootFilesystem: true + explicit writable volumes/emptyDirs, seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault, resource requests+limits set, no host namespaces/hostPath/hostNetwork, no docker socket, egress restricted (default-deny NetworkPolicy + allow-list, block metadata endpoint), automountServiceAccountToken off unless needed. Admission: Pod Security Admission "restricted" enforced (audit first), plus Kyverno/Gatekeeper policies for image provenance (allow-listed registry, digest pinned, cosign-verified, recent passing-scan attestation), required labels, and the run-baseline fields; RuntimeClass=kata/gvisor required for workloads tagged untrusted. Runtime: Falco/Tetragon rules for escape indicators (unexpected shell, mount/ptrace/setns, /proc/sys writes, new listeners, /etc/shadow reads, package-manager exec), drift detection (running digest == approved), centralized audit + container logs, node auto-recycling, minimal hardened host OS, current kernel. Response: playbooks for "vulnerable base CVE" (SBOM query → ranked list → automated base-bump rebuild wave → deploy by digest → tighten admission max-CVE-age) and "suspected escape" (cordon/drain/replace node, snapshot for forensics, rotate any reachable credentials, review Falco timeline); measured MTTR. Rollout: (1) publish the standard + golden bases + Dockerfile templates + a self-serve docker init; (2) run all admission policies in audit/warn mode cluster-wide, produce a per-team compliance dashboard (which pods violate what); (3) fix the platform's own workloads first as reference; (4) office hours + PRs to help teams migrate (most failures are "add securityContext" and "add a writable emptyDir for /tmp"); (5) enforce in new namespaces first, then a deadline for existing ones with exceptions requiring sign-off and an expiry; (6) enforce the CI scan/sign gate on new images immediately, existing images by the deadline; (7) keep an escape hatch (a documented exception label with owner + reason + review date) so a genuinely special workload isn't blocked, and report on exception count trending down. Net: secure-by-default templates, audit-then-enforce admission, a compliance dashboard to make gaps visible, platform-led migration help, and a bounded exception process — so the baseline lands without a big-bang breakage.

Logging, Healthchecks, Tagging & CI Builds

The operational glue: logs to stdout, a real healthcheck, immutable tags, and a build-once/scan/sign/push pipeline.

Notes

Logging: stdout/stderr, structured

  • Log to stdout/stderr, not files inside the container. The runtime captures the streams; a log agent on the node ships them. Files in the container need a volume, rotation, and are lost on rm.
  • Structured (JSON) lines so the collector can index fields; include a level, timestamp, request id / trace id.
  • Log drivers (Docker): json-file (default; set max-size/max-file or a busy container fills the disk), local (compact binary), journald, syslog, fluentd, awslogs, gelf. Note: with a remote driver, docker logs may not work locally.
// /etc/docker/daemon.json  -- cap the default driver so it can't fill /
{ "log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": { "max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3" } }

// per container
$ docker run --log-driver json-file --log-opt max-size=10m --log-opt max-file=5 myapp
$ docker logs -f --tail 100 --since 10m --timestamps myapp

HEALTHCHECK

What / why. A command Docker runs periodically; the container is marked healthy/unhealthy. Orchestrators use it to gate traffic and trigger restarts. Check readiness (can it serve?), not just "process alive."

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=20s --retries=3 \
  CMD curl -fsS http://localhost:8000/healthz || exit 1
# distroless / no curl: ship a tiny static healthcheck binary, or use the app's own check
HEALTHCHECK CMD ["/app", "--health"]
  • --start-period gives slow starts grace (failures during it don't count).
  • Keep it cheap and dependency-light — a check that hits the DB flaps when the DB blips and causes restart storms.
  • Kubernetes ignores the Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK; it uses livenessProbe/readinessProbe/startupProbe instead (same idea, in the pod spec).

Restart policies & graceful stop

--restart no                 # default
--restart on-failure:5       # restart up to 5 times on non-zero exit  (best for surfacing crash loops)
--restart unless-stopped     # restart always, but not if you manually stopped it
--restart always             # restart forever (also on daemon start)
--stop-signal SIGTERM --stop-timeout 30   # SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 30s

Handle SIGTERM in the app: stop accepting new work, drain in-flight, close DB/connections, exit 0 — within the grace period. Exec-form CMD so PID 1 is your app. Add tini/--init if your app spawns children (zombie reaping).

Tagging strategy

  • Build once. Tag with version + git SHA (myorg/api:1.4.2, myorg/api:1.4.2-g8f3a1c); record the digest.
  • Deploy by digest (or exact version), never by a moving tag — so a re-pushed :latest can't silently change prod.
  • Keep :latest / :1.4 / :1 as human aliases updated by CI, and enable tag immutability on version tags in the registry.
  • Promote the same digest dev → staging → prod. Retention policy + GC untagged manifests.

CI build pipeline

# GitHub Actions sketch
- uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
- uses: docker/login-action@v3
  with: { registry: ghcr.io, username: ${{ github.actor }}, password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} }
- id: build
  uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
  with:
    context: .
    platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
    push: true
    tags: |
      ghcr.io/acme/api:${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
      ghcr.io/acme/api:sha-${{ github.sha }}
    cache-from: type=gha
    cache-to:   type=gha,mode=max
    provenance: true
    sbom: true
- run: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 ghcr.io/acme/api@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
- run: cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/acme/api@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
- run: echo "deploy digest ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}"   # -> update the manifest/chart

Housekeeping

$ docker system df                       # images / containers / volumes / build cache
$ docker image prune -a --filter "until=168h"
$ docker builder prune --keep-storage 10GB
$ docker system prune -af --volumes      # aggressive; careful with volumes
# on nodes: a cron / kubelet GC (imageGCHighThresholdPercent) to reclaim image space
Cheat Sheet
  • Logs to stdout/stderr, structured JSON with level + trace id. Cap json-file (max-size/max-file) or it fills the disk. Node agent ships them.
  • HEALTHCHECK = readiness check, cheap, with --start-period; distroless needs a static health binary. K8s uses probes in the pod spec instead.
  • Restart: on-failure:N surfaces crash loops; unless-stopped/always for daemons. Handle SIGTERM (drain, exit 0) within --stop-timeout; exec-form CMD; --init for zombie reaping.
  • Tag: build once, tag version + sha-<git>, deploy by digest, moving tags are aliases only, enable tag immutability, promote the same digest across envs.
  • CI: buildx (+ multi-arch), gha/registry cache mode=max, provenance + SBOM, scan & fail on fixable HIGH/CRIT, cosign sign the digest, deploy the digest.
  • Housekeeping: system df, image prune -a --filter until=, builder prune, node image GC.
Q&A
Why log to stdout/stderr instead of a file inside the container?
The container runtime captures the streams and a node-level agent ships them to your log store, with rotation handled outside the container. A file inside the container needs its own rotation, consumes the writable layer, is invisible to other tools, and is lost when the container is removed. "Log to stdout" is one of the twelve-factor rules for exactly this reason.
The disk on a node fills up with Docker logs. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
The default json-file log driver has no size limit, so a chatty container's <id>-json.log grows unbounded. Fix: set log-opts max-size and max-file globally in /etc/docker/daemon.json (or per container), or switch to the local driver (compact, rotated by default) or a remote driver. Then truncate the existing large files and restart affected containers.
What makes a good HEALTHCHECK, and what makes a bad one?
Good: cheap, fast, dependency-light, checks that the app can actually serve a request (e.g. an in-process /healthz that returns 200 when the HTTP server and essential local state are ready), with a --start-period so slow boots aren't penalized. Bad: expensive (heavy query), or checks external dependencies (DB, downstream API) — then a transient blip in a dependency marks every replica unhealthy and triggers a restart storm that makes the outage worse. Separate "can I serve?" (readiness) from "am I wedged?" (liveness) — K8s makes that explicit with separate probes.
Why deploy by image digest instead of by tag?
Tags are mutable pointers; myapp:1.4.2 could be re-pushed (by mistake or malice) to different bytes, and :latest changes constantly. A digest (myapp@sha256:…) is the content hash — it always refers to the exact image you built, tested, scanned, and signed. Deploying the digest gives you reproducibility, a real audit trail, and rollback to a known artifact, and it lets admission controllers verify the signature against a fixed target.
What should a container do on receiving SIGTERM?
Begin graceful shutdown: stop accepting new connections/messages, finish or safely abort in-flight work, flush buffers, close database and downstream connections, deregister from service discovery, then exit 0 — all within the stop grace period (default 10s Docker / 30s K8s; tune with --stop-timeout / terminationGracePeriodSeconds). It must be PID 1 to receive the signal, which means exec-form CMD/ENTRYPOINT. If it ignores SIGTERM it gets SIGKILL'd after the grace period, dropping in-flight requests.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Where should a containerized app write its logs?
To stdout/stderr. The runtime captures them and the platform's log collector ships them; nothing inside the container manages log files.
Which restart policy is best for catching a crash-looping service in development?
--restart on-failure:N — it stops retrying after N failures, so a crash loop surfaces instead of being hidden by infinite restarts like always.

Intermediate core

Design the CI pipeline that turns a git push into a deployable, trusted image.
(1) Checkout + metadata: compute version (git tag / semver) and short SHA. (2) Build once with buildx: multi-stage Dockerfile, --platform for the arches you run, pinned base by digest, --cache-from/--cache-to type=gha|registry,mode=max, --secret for any build creds, provenance: true and sbom: true. Tag with version and sha-<git>; capture the output digest. (3) Test: run unit/integration against the built image (or a --target test stage); optionally start it and hit /healthz. (4) Scan: Trivy/Grype on the digest, fail on fixable HIGH/CRITICAL (--ignore-unfixed tracked separately); record results as an attestation. (5) Sign: cosign sign the digest (keyless via OIDC or a KMS key); sign the SBOM/provenance/scan attestations too. (6) Push: to the registry with immutable version tags + the SHA tag; update moving aliases (:1.4, :latest) if used. (7) Promote: open a PR / trigger a deploy that updates the manifest/Helm values to the new digest for the target environment; higher environments are gated on the lower one succeeding. (8) Verify at deploy: admission policy re-checks signature + scan freshness + registry allow-list. Everything downstream references the one digest — no rebuilds per environment.
A rolling deploy drops a percentage of requests every time. What container-level things would you check?
(1) SIGTERM handling: is CMD exec-form so the app is PID 1 and receives the signal? Does the app actually drain (stop accepting, finish in-flight) rather than exit immediately? Is the grace period (terminationGracePeriodSeconds/--stop-timeout) long enough for the longest in-flight request? (2) Readiness vs traffic: is there a readiness probe (K8s) / good HEALTHCHECK so the new replica only gets traffic once it can serve, and the old one is removed from the LB before SIGTERM? A missing/too-lax readiness gate sends traffic to a not-yet-warm pod. (3) preStop hook / connection draining: add a small preStop sleep (or explicit deregister) so the load balancer/endpoints update propagates before the process starts shutting down — otherwise there's a window where the LB still routes to a terminating pod. (4) Keep-alive connections: long-lived HTTP/gRPC connections pinned to the old pod get cut on SIGKILL; the app should send GOAWAY / close idle connections on SIGTERM, and clients should retry idempotent requests. (5) Startup time: if pods take a while to be ready, use a startupProbe and raise maxSurge/lower maxUnavailable so capacity doesn't dip. (6) Slow dependencies: the new pod passing readiness but its warm caches/pools cold — add a warm-up step or readiness that reflects real capacity. The common root cause is "LB still routing during shutdown" + "app doesn't drain" — fix with preStop + readiness + graceful SIGTERM.

Advanced deep

Design end-to-end observability and lifecycle for containerized services across a fleet: logs, metrics, traces, health, and image lifecycle.
Logs: apps write structured JSON to stdout/stderr with a consistent schema (timestamp, level, service, version, trace_id, span_id, request_id, user/tenant where allowed). Node agent (Fluent Bit / Vector) tails the runtime's log files, adds pod/namespace/node/container labels, and ships to a store (Loki / Elasticsearch / a SaaS). Cap the runtime log driver so a chatty container can't fill the node; set retention + index policy centrally; sample debug logs. Metrics: Prometheus scrapes each service's /metrics (RED: rate, errors, duration per endpoint; plus queue depth, pool saturation, GC, and the resource-vs-limit ratios from cAdvisor/kube-state-metrics: CPU throttle %, memory working-set/limit, restarts, OOM count). Recording rules for SLIs; Grafana dashboards per service + a fleet overview; alerts on SLO burn rate, throttling on latency-critical services, OOM/restart spikes, and "backup/job age." Watch cardinality. Traces: OpenTelemetry SDK in every service, context propagated across HTTP/gRPC/queues; OTel Collector as a DaemonSet (+ gateway for tail sampling) exporting to Tempo/Jaeger; keep 100% of error and slow traces, sample the rest; exemplars link latency histograms to traces; trace_id in logs for correlation. Health: startupProbe (slow boot grace), readinessProbe (only real capacity gets traffic; reflects downstream reachability where appropriate), livenessProbe (only for genuine deadlock — cheap, no external deps, generous thresholds to avoid restart storms); preStop + adequate terminationGracePeriodSeconds + graceful SIGTERM for zero-drop deploys; PodDisruptionBudgets. Image lifecycle: build once in CI → test → scan (fail on fixable HIGH/CRIT) → SBOM + provenance → cosign sign the digest → push with immutable version + SHA tags. Deploy by digest, same digest promoted dev→staging→prod (GitOps: the manifest/chart in git is the source of truth, Argo/Flux reconciles). Admission verifies signature + scan freshness + registry allow-list + Pod Security. Continuous re-scan of running images against new CVE data; automated base-image bump PRs fan out rebuilds; drift detection (running digest == git digest); registry retention + GC; node image GC. Feedback loop: dashboards correlate deploy markers (from CI) with error/latency/restart changes for fast rollback; a monthly review right-sizes requests/limits from observed usage and prunes noisy alerts. Net: structured stdout logs + Prometheus RED + OTel traces all joined by trace_id, probes tuned so deploys don't drop traffic, and a build-once/sign/scan/deploy-by-digest GitOps pipeline with continuous CVE re-scanning — so you can see what every container is doing and always know exactly what's running and whether it's safe.

Cluster Architecture: Control Plane & Nodes

The control plane stores desired state and makes decisions; nodes run the workloads and report back.

Notes

Control-plane components

ComponentJob
kube-apiserverThe REST API front end. Authn/authz, admission, validation, and the only writer to etcd. Everything (kubectl, controllers, kubelet) goes through it.
etcdConsistent, replicated key-value store (Raft). Holds all cluster state — the source of truth. Losing quorum = the control plane is read-only/down.
kube-schedulerWatches for Pods with no node assigned; picks a node (filter feasible nodes, then score) and writes the binding.
kube-controller-managerRuns the built-in control loops: Deployment→ReplicaSet→Pod, node lifecycle, endpoints/EndpointSlices, jobs, service accounts, PV binding, …
cloud-controller-managerCloud-specific loops: provision LoadBalancers, attach volumes, label nodes with zone/instance-type, remove nodes deleted in the cloud.

Node components

ComponentJob
kubeletThe node agent. Watches the API for Pods bound to its node, tells the runtime (via CRI) to pull images and start containers, runs probes, mounts volumes, and reports Pod/node status back.
kube-proxyPrograms the node's iptables/IPVS (or eBPF, with Cilium) so ClusterIP/NodePort Service traffic is load-balanced to backend Pod IPs.
container runtimecontainerd or CRI-O, driven over the CRI gRPC API by the kubelet. See the Containers skill's "OCI, runc, containerd & the CRI".
$ kubectl get componentstatuses          # (deprecated) control-plane health
$ kubectl get nodes -o wide
NAME       STATUS   ROLES           VERSION   INTERNAL-IP    OS-IMAGE
cp-1       Ready    control-plane   v1.30.2   10.0.0.10      Ubuntu 22.04
node-1     Ready    <none>          v1.30.2   10.0.0.21      Ubuntu 22.04
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system        # apiserver, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager, coredns, kube-proxy, CNI

The request path: kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml

1. kubectl        -> POST /apis/apps/v1/.../deployments  to the API server
2. API server     -> authn (cert/token/OIDC) -> authz (RBAC) -> admission
                     (mutating: defaults, sidecars; validating: policy) -> validate schema
3. API server     -> write the Deployment object to etcd, return 201
4. deployment ctrl -> (watch) sees new Deployment -> creates a ReplicaSet
5. replicaset ctrl -> creates N Pod objects (nodeName empty)
6. scheduler      -> (watch) unscheduled Pods -> pick a node -> write Pod.spec.nodeName
7. kubelet(node)  -> (watch) Pods on my node -> CRI: pull image, create sandbox + containers
8. kubelet        -> run probes, write Pod status; endpoints ctrl updates EndpointSlices
9. kube-proxy     -> (watch) Services/EndpointSlices -> update node dataplane rules

Every step is a component watching the API server and writing back — the "level-triggered reconciliation" model. No component calls another directly.

HA & failure behaviour

  • etcd: run 3 or 5 members (odd, for quorum). Lose a minority → fine; lose quorum → API becomes read-only. Back it up (etcdctl snapshot save).
  • API server: stateless — run 2+ behind a load balancer.
  • scheduler / controller-manager: run 2+ but only one is active (leader election via a Lease); the standby takes over on failure.
  • Control plane down, nodes up: existing Pods keep running (the kubelet doesn't need the API to keep containers alive), but nothing new is scheduled, no self-healing, no rollouts, Services/Endpoints stop updating.
  • Managed Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS): the cloud runs and scales the control plane + etcd; you manage nodes and workloads.
Cheat Sheet
  • Control plane: kube-apiserver (front door, only etcd writer), etcd (Raft KV, source of truth), kube-scheduler (assign Pods to nodes), kube-controller-manager (built-in control loops), cloud-controller-manager (LBs, volumes, node cloud lifecycle).
  • Node: kubelet (runs Pods via CRI, probes, status), kube-proxy (Service dataplane rules), containerd/CRI-O (runtime).
  • Everything talks only to the API server; components watch it and write status back (level-triggered reconciliation).
  • Apply path: kubectl → apiserver (authn/authz/admission/validate) → etcd → deployment ctrl → RS ctrl → scheduler → kubelet → runtime; endpoints ctrl + kube-proxy wire networking.
  • HA: etcd 3/5 members (quorum), apiserver 2+ behind an LB, scheduler/controller-manager 2+ with leader election.
  • Control plane down, nodes up: running Pods survive; no scheduling/healing/rollouts/endpoint updates.
  • Managed K8s: cloud runs the control plane + etcd; you run nodes.
Q&A
What is the only component that writes to etcd, and why does that matter?
The API server. It centralizes authentication, authorization, admission control, validation, and versioning/conversion, so every write is consistently checked and audited, and other components never need etcd credentials or to agree on schema. It's also the single point to secure and to scale reads (with a watch cache).
What does the scheduler actually do?
It watches for Pods whose spec.nodeName is empty, runs a two-phase decision — filtering (which nodes are feasible: enough allocatable CPU/mem, taints tolerated, node selectors/affinity satisfied, volume zone matches, ports free) then scoring (spread, affinity preferences, least/most allocated, image locality) — picks the highest-scoring node, and writes a Binding that sets nodeName. It does not start containers; the kubelet on that node does.
The control plane is completely down. What still works and what doesn't?
Already-running Pods keep running — the kubelet manages containers locally and doesn't need the API server to keep them alive; kube-proxy keeps serving existing Service rules; DNS keeps resolving existing records. What stops: scheduling new Pods, restarting/rescheduling failed ones (self-healing), rollouts and scaling, ConfigMap/Secret updates propagating, Endpoint/EndpointSlice updates (so Services won't learn about new or dead Pods), kubectl, HPA, and admission. Recover etcd quorum / the API server and the controllers reconcile everything back.
Why run an odd number of etcd members?
etcd uses Raft, which needs a majority (quorum) to commit writes. With 2N+1 members you tolerate N failures; going from 3 to 4 members doesn't improve fault tolerance (still tolerates 1) but adds a member that can fail and increases write latency. So 3 (tolerate 1) or 5 (tolerate 2) — rarely more, because every write must be acknowledged by a majority.
What's the difference between kube-controller-manager and cloud-controller-manager?
kube-controller-manager runs the cloud-agnostic control loops: ReplicaSet/Deployment, Job, node lifecycle (marking NotReady, eviction timers), EndpointSlice, ServiceAccount tokens, PV/PVC binding, namespace cleanup, etc. cloud-controller-manager isolates the provider-specific parts: creating/deleting cloud load balancers for type: LoadBalancer Services, attaching/detaching cloud disks, labelling nodes with region/zone/instance-type, and removing Node objects for VMs that were deleted in the cloud. Splitting them lets Kubernetes core release independently of cloud integrations.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Name the control-plane components.
kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager, and (on cloud clusters) cloud-controller-manager. CoreDNS and kube-proxy are cluster add-ons rather than control-plane proper.
Which component on a worker node starts and supervises containers?
The kubelet — it reads Pod specs from the API server and drives the container runtime (containerd/CRI-O) over the CRI to pull images and run containers.

Intermediate core

Trace what happens between kubectl scale deploy/api --replicas=5 and 5 pods running.
(1) kubectl PATCHes the Deployment's spec.replicas to 5 via the API server (authn → RBAC authz → admission → validate) which writes it to etcd. (2) The deployment controller (watching Deployments) updates the current ReplicaSet's spec.replicas to 5. (3) The replicaset controller sees it owns 2 Pods but wants 5, and creates 3 new Pod objects (owner-referenced to the RS, nodeName empty). (4) The scheduler (watching unscheduled Pods) filters+scores nodes for each and writes a Binding setting spec.nodeName. (5) The kubelet on each chosen node (watching Pods for its node) calls the CRI to create the pod sandbox (network namespace via CNI, pause container), pull the image if needed, and start the containers; it runs the startup/readiness probes. (6) When a Pod becomes Ready, the EndpointSlice controller adds its IP to the Service's EndpointSlice; kube-proxy on every node updates its dataplane so the Service ClusterIP now load-balances across 5 backends. All of it is watch-driven reconciliation; kubectl's job ended at step 1.
How do you make the control plane highly available, and what's the failure behaviour of each part?
etcd: 3 or 5 members across failure domains; tolerates (N-1)/2 losses; losing quorum makes the API read-only until restored — take regular etcdctl snapshot save backups and test restore. kube-apiserver: stateless; run 2+ instances behind an L4 load balancer (or a VIP); clients/kubelets point at the LB; losing one is transparent. kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager: run 2+ replicas but they use leader election (a coordination Lease), so only one is active at a time; if the leader dies, a standby acquires the lease within the lease-duration and resumes reconciliation — brief pause in scheduling/healing, no data loss. cloud-controller-manager: same leader-election pattern. During any control-plane outage, existing workloads keep running (kubelet is autonomous); you lose scheduling, self-healing, rollouts, and endpoint updates until it's back. Managed offerings (EKS/GKE/AKS) do all of this for you and SLA the API endpoint.

Advanced deep

etcd is the bottleneck / at risk in a large cluster. Explain why, and how you'd design around it.
Why etcd is the pressure point: it's a single consistent store that every write must commit to a Raft majority (fsync on each member), and the API server keeps a watch cache backed by etcd watches. It scales poorly with: (1) object count & size — total DB size (default quota 2–8 GiB; hard cap ~8 GiB) and per-object churn; large ConfigMaps/Secrets, huge numbers of Pods/Events/Endpoints, CRDs with big status; (2) write rate — frequent status updates (node/pod heartbeats, controller re-writes, Events), each an fsync'd Raft round; (3) watch fan-out — many clients watching many resource types; (4) range reads that bypass the cache (large LISTs without pagination) hammering etcd directly; (5) latency sensitivity — slow disks (need low-latency SSD, dedicated, high IOPS) or cross-AZ RTT inflate every write; (6) compaction/defrag pauses. Design: run etcd on dedicated nodes with fast local NVMe, 3 or 5 members within a low-latency region (multi-AZ ok, not multi-region for the same cluster); tune --heartbeat-interval/--election-timeout for the RTT; enable auto-compaction and schedule periodic defrag (one member at a time) with alerting on DB size and etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration. Reduce load on the API server side: enable the watch cache and API Priority and Fairness to shed abusive traffic; make clients use paginated, resourceVersion-bounded LISTs and informers (shared watch) instead of polling; cut Event volume (shorter TTL, dedup) and move Events to a separate etcd if supported; keep Secrets/ConfigMaps small (mount large config from object storage or a CSI); avoid controllers that re-write status in hot loops; use EndpointSlices (not the monolithic Endpoints object) so a 5000-pod Service doesn't rewrite one giant object on every change; encrypt Secrets at rest with a KMS provider (adjust for the CPU cost). For extreme scale, shard by cluster — many smaller clusters federated by a management layer (Cluster API, fleet tooling) rather than one giant cluster — and/or move some CRDs to a separate API server + etcd (aggregated API). Also: separate the etcd used by the apiserver from any app that's tempted to use it directly (nothing should). Net: fast dedicated storage, small/odd membership, disciplined clients (informers + pagination + APF), low object churn (EndpointSlices, trimmed Events, small Secrets), scheduled compaction/defrag with monitoring, and horizontal sharding into multiple clusters before a single etcd is asked to hold too much.

Objects, the API & the Reconciliation Loop

You declare desired state in spec; controllers watch and drive the real world toward it, forever.

Notes

Every object has the same shape

apiVersion: apps/v1              # group/version -- which API and schema
kind: Deployment                # the resource type
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: shop
  labels: { app: api, tier: backend }
  annotations: { kubernetes.io/change-cause: "bump to 1.4.2" }
spec:                           # DESIRED state -- you write this
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
  template: { ... pod template ... }
status:                        # OBSERVED state -- controllers write this
  readyReplicas: 3
  conditions: [ { type: Available, status: "True" } ]
  • spec = what you want. status = what is. A controller's job is to make status match spec.
  • labels = queryable key/values used for grouping and selectors (a Service finds its Pods by label). annotations = non-identifying metadata for tools.
  • namespace = a soft boundary for names, RBAC, quotas, and network policy scope. Cluster-scoped objects (Node, PV, Namespace, ClusterRole, CRD) have none.

The reconciliation loop

What / why. Each controller runs: watch its resource (and related ones) → on any change (or a periodic resync) compute the diff between spec and reality → take the minimal action to close the gap → update status. It's level-triggered (acts on current state) not edge-triggered (acts on an event), so a missed event, a controller restart, or manual meddling all self-correct on the next pass. This is why Kubernetes "self-heals."

# see it heal
$ kubectl get pods -l app=api           # 3 running
$ kubectl delete pod api-7d9f-abcde
$ kubectl get pods -l app=api           # a replacement is already being created
# the ReplicaSet controller saw "have 2, want 3" and created one -- no event needed

Declarative vs imperative

ImperativeDeclarative (preferred)
kubectl create/run/scale/expose/set imagekubectl apply -f dir/ (or kustomize/Helm)
One-shot mutation; no record of intentManifests in git are the source of truth; apply computes a 3-way merge
Fine for quick fixes / debuggingReviewable, diffable, GitOps-able, rollback = revert the commit
$ kubectl apply -f k8s/            # create or update to match the files
$ kubectl diff  -f k8s/            # what would change
$ kubectl apply --server-side -f k8s/   # server-side apply: field ownership tracked per manager
$ kubectl get deploy api -o yaml  # full object incl. status & defaults
$ kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy   # schema docs from the API

API groups, versions & CRDs

  • Resources live in groups: core (v1 — Pod, Service, ConfigMap), apps/v1 (Deployment, StatefulSet), batch/v1 (Job), networking.k8s.io/v1 (Ingress, NetworkPolicy), rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1, …
  • Versions progress v1alpha1 → v1beta1 → v1; the API server stores one version and converts on the fly, so old manifests keep working until a version is removed.
  • CustomResourceDefinitions add your own kinds (e.g. Certificate, Kafka) that behave like built-ins — an operator then reconciles them (see the Helm/GitOps/Operators topic).
$ kubectl api-resources | head        # every kind, its group, namespaced?, short name
NAME          SHORTNAMES   APIVERSION   NAMESPACED   KIND
pods          po           v1           true         Pod
deployments   deploy       apps/v1      true         Deployment
$ kubectl api-versions
$ kubectl get crd

Object relationships & deletion

  • ownerReferences link children to parents (Pod ← ReplicaSet ← Deployment). Delete the parent → garbage collection deletes the children (foreground/background/orphan policy).
  • finalizers block deletion until a controller does cleanup (release a cloud LB, detach a volume); a stuck finalizer is a common "namespace won't delete" cause.
  • resourceVersion enables optimistic concurrency — an update with a stale version is rejected (409), so two writers don't clobber each other.
Cheat Sheet
  • Object = apiVersion + kind + metadata + spec (desired, you write) + status (observed, controller writes).
  • Labels group/select (Service→Pods); annotations = tool metadata; namespace scopes names/RBAC/quota (some kinds are cluster-scoped).
  • Reconciliation: watch → diff spec vs reality → minimal action → write status; level-triggered, so it self-heals and re-runs safely.
  • Prefer declarative kubectl apply -f (git = source of truth, kubectl diff, rollback = revert). Imperative for quick fixes/debug.
  • Groups/versions: core v1, apps/v1, batch/v1, networking.k8s.io/v1, …; alpha→beta→stable; server converts stored version.
  • CRDs add custom kinds; an operator reconciles them.
  • ownerReferences → cascading GC; finalizers block delete until cleanup; resourceVersion = optimistic locking.
  • Discovery: kubectl api-resources, kubectl explain <kind>.<path>, kubectl get -o yaml.
Q&A
What's the difference between spec and status?
spec is desired state that you (or a higher-level controller) author. status is observed state that the controlling component writes and continuously updates. A controller's entire job is a loop that makes status converge to spec. You almost never write status directly.
Why is "level-triggered" reconciliation important?
The controller acts on the current state, not on a stream of events. So if it misses an event (network blip, restart), or someone changes things out of band, or a create failed halfway — on the next sync it just re-computes "what is vs what should be" and fixes the difference. That's what gives Kubernetes self-healing and makes the same manifest safe to apply repeatedly (idempotent).
When would you use imperative commands vs kubectl apply?
Imperative (kubectl create, scale, set image, run, expose, delete) for quick, one-off actions — debugging, a hotfix, spinning up a throwaway pod, or generating a manifest skeleton with --dry-run=client -o yaml. Declarative apply -f for anything real: the manifests live in git, changes are reviewed and diffable, apply does a 3-way merge so it won't stomp fields it doesn't own, and rollback is reverting a commit. GitOps requires declarative.
Your namespace is stuck in Terminating. What's usually going on?
A resource in it has a finalizer whose controller isn't completing the cleanup (the controller is down, lacks permissions, or the external thing it must clean up is gone). Deletion blocks until every finalizer is removed. Diagnose with kubectl get <resource> -n <ns> -o yaml | grep finalizers; fix by restoring the controller, or (last resort, and risky) removing the finalizer manually so GC proceeds — accepting that the external cleanup didn't happen.
What are ownerReferences and what do they enable?
Metadata on a child object pointing at its parent (with UID, and controller: true for the managing one). They power cascading garbage collection: delete a Deployment and the GC controller deletes its ReplicaSet(s), which deletes the Pods. The deletion propagation policy (Foreground, Background, Orphan) controls ordering and whether children are kept.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What are the two halves of a Kubernetes object that describe "wanted" vs "actual"?
spec (desired state, authored by you) and status (actual state, maintained by the controller).
How does a Service know which Pods to send traffic to?
By label selector — the Service's spec.selector matches labels on Pods, and the endpoint controller keeps an EndpointSlice of the matching, ready Pod IPs.

Intermediate core

You kubectl edit a field on a live Deployment that's managed by GitOps. What happens, and why is that a problem?
Your edit is a write to the API server, so the controller reconciles to your new spec immediately — but the desired state in git is now out of sync with the cluster. With a GitOps tool (Argo CD/Flux) watching, one of two things happens: it flags the app as OutOfSync (drift detected), or, if auto-sync + self-heal is on, it reverts your change on the next reconcile back to what git says. Either way your fix is ephemeral and invisible to the team, and if it was load-bearing it'll vanish at the worst time. The right move: make the change in git via a PR (or, for a true emergency, edit live and immediately open the PR, and know the tool may revert you until it merges). This is exactly why declarative + git-as-source-of-truth matters: the cluster is a projection of the repo, not the other way round.
Explain what kubectl apply does that kubectl replace doesn't, and what "server-side apply" adds.
kubectl replace overwrites the whole object with your file — any field you didn't specify is removed, and it needs the current resourceVersion. kubectl apply does a three-way merge: it compares your new manifest, the previous manifest you applied (stored in the last-applied-configuration annotation), and the live object, so it only changes fields you actually manage and leaves alone fields set by other controllers (e.g. a HPA-managed replicas, defaulted values, injected sidecars). Server-side apply moves the merge into the API server and tracks field ownership per manager (kubectl, a controller, HPA) in metadata.managedFields; conflicts (two managers claiming the same field) are reported unless you --force-conflicts. It removes the fragile annotation, handles concurrent controllers cleanly, and is the model GitOps tools and controllers use.

Advanced deep

Design a custom controller/operator for a new resource kind: the API surface, the reconcile loop, and the failure/idempotency concerns.
API surface: define a CRD with a clear spec (only user intent — e.g. Database{engine, version, size, backupSchedule}) and a status (observed — phase, conditions[], observedGeneration, endpoints, lastBackupTime). Add an OpenAPI schema with validation + defaults, use a structural schema, set up conversion webhooks if you'll evolve versions, enable the status subresource (so status updates don't bump metadata.generation and RBAC can be split), add additionalPrinterColumns for kubectl get, and pick sensible shortNames/categories. Consider a validating/mutating admission webhook for cross-field rules the schema can't express. Reconcile loop (controller-runtime): watch the CR and the objects it creates (owned StatefulSet, Service, Secret, PVC, CronJob) with Owns(), plus Watches() for anything external you map back to a CR. On each reconcile for a key: fetch the CR (return if not found — it was deleted); if it has a deletion timestamp, run finalizer cleanup (delete cloud resources, deregister), then remove the finalizer; else ensure the finalizer is present. Then build the desired child objects from spec and CreateOrUpdate (or server-side apply) each, setting ownerReferences so GC cascades. Compute status from the observed children and patch the status subresource; set conditions (Ready, Progressing, Degraded) and observedGeneration. Return Result{RequeueAfter: ...} for periodic checks (backup age, health) and rely on watches for change-driven runs. Idempotency & correctness: the loop must be safe to run any number of times and from any starting state — always diff desired vs actual, never "do X once"; name child objects deterministically; use CreateOrUpdate/SSA not blind Create (handle AlreadyExists / conflicts by requeue). Make external calls idempotent (idempotency keys, "ensure exists" semantics) and record external IDs in status so a restart re-adopts rather than recreates. Use optimistic concurrency — on a 409 conflict, requeue and re-read, don't retry blindly. Rate-limit and use exponential backoff on the workqueue; make reconciles fast and bounded (don't block on long operations — kick them off, record progress in status, requeue). Failure handling: partial progress must be resumable (create Service failed after StatefulSet succeeded → next reconcile just creates the Service); set a Degraded condition + emit an Event on persistent errors; never leave the CR without a status update. Guard against thundering herd on operator restart (informer resync of thousands of CRs) with worker concurrency limits. Ops: leader election (one active operator), scoped RBAC (only the resources it manages), metrics (controller_runtime_reconcile_total, errors, queue depth, reconcile duration), structured logs keyed by CR namespace/name, and a clear upgrade story for the CRD schema. Net: a thin declarative CRD, a watch-driven loop that always reconciles desired-vs-actual with owner refs + finalizers + status conditions, idempotent create-or-update everywhere, optimistic-concurrency retries, and resumable partial progress — i.e. the same pattern the built-in controllers use, applied to your domain.

Pods: The Smallest Unit

A pod is one or more containers that are always co-scheduled and share a network namespace, IPC, and volumes.

Notes

What a pod is

What. The atomic deployable unit: a group of containers that always land on the same node, share one network namespace (one pod IP, one port space, reach each other on localhost), share IPC and any mounted volumes, and are started/stopped together. A hidden pause container holds the namespaces so app containers can restart without losing the pod's IP.

Why one-container-per-pod is the norm. Independent scaling, independent lifecycle, independent images. Multiple containers only when they're a single cohesive unit — an app + a tightly-coupled helper (log shipper, proxy, config reloader).

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: web, labels: { app: web } }
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: myorg/web@sha256:...
      ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
      resources:
        requests: { cpu: "100m", memory: "128Mi" }
        limits:   { cpu: "500m", memory: "256Mi" }
  restartPolicy: Always          # Always | OnFailure | Never (Never/OnFailure for Jobs)

Init containers & sidecars

  • Init containers run in order, to completion, before any app container starts. Use for: waiting on a dependency, running a migration, fetching config/secrets into a shared emptyDir, fixing volume permissions. A failing init container blocks the pod (retried per restartPolicy).
  • Sidecars run alongside the app for its whole life. Kubernetes 1.28+ has native sidecars — an init container with restartPolicy: Always that starts before app containers and is terminated after them (fixes the old "sidecar outlives/precedes the app" ordering pain).
spec:
  initContainers:
    - name: wait-db
      image: busybox
      command: ["sh","-c","until nc -z db 5432; do sleep 1; done"]
    - name: proxy               # native sidecar (1.28+)
      image: envoyproxy/envoy
      restartPolicy: Always      # <- makes this init container a sidecar
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: myorg/app

Probes — startup, readiness, liveness

ProbeFails →Use for
startupProbekill + restart the container (and pause the other probes until it passes)Slow-booting apps — give them time without a lax liveness threshold.
readinessProberemove the pod from Service endpoints (no traffic); container keeps running"Can I serve right now?" — warm caches, DB reachable, not overloaded.
livenessProbekill + restart the container"Am I wedged / deadlocked?" — only for unrecoverable states. Keep it cheap and dependency-free.
    startupProbe:   { httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }, failureThreshold: 30, periodSeconds: 2 }
    readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /ready,   port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 5 }
    livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 10, failureThreshold: 3 }
# probe types: httpGet | tcpSocket | exec | grpc

Common mistake: a liveness probe that checks a downstream dependency → when the DB blips, every replica is "unhealthy" and restarts, turning a blip into an outage. Liveness = self only; put dependency checks in readiness.

Pod lifecycle & termination

  • Phases: Pending → Running → Succeeded/Failed. Conditions: PodScheduled, Initialized, ContainersReady, Ready.
  • Restarts apply to containers within the pod (per restartPolicy), with exponential backoff — CrashLoopBackOff is the state, not an error itself.
  • Graceful termination: pod removed from endpoints → preStop hook runs → SIGTERM to PID 1 → wait up to terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30) → SIGKILL. Handle SIGTERM (drain, exit 0); add a small preStop sleep so the endpoint removal propagates before you stop serving.
    lifecycle:
      preStop: { exec: { command: ["sh","-c","sleep 5"] } }   # let LB/endpoints update first
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45

Pod-level settings you'll set

  • securityContext (pod + per-container): runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, fsGroup (volume ownership), seccompProfile, capabilities, readOnlyRootFilesystem.
  • nodeSelector / affinity / tolerations / topologySpreadConstraints — placement (see the Scheduling topic).
  • volumes + container volumeMounts (see the Storage topic).
  • serviceAccountName, automountServiceAccountToken: false if the pod doesn't call the API.
  • priorityClassName, hostAliases, dnsPolicy/dnsConfig.
Cheat Sheet
  • Pod = co-scheduled containers sharing net namespace (one IP, localhost), IPC, and volumes. A pause container holds the namespaces.
  • Usually 1 container/pod. Multi-container only for tightly-coupled helpers (proxy, log shipper, config reloader).
  • Init containers: run in order to completion before app containers (wait-for-dep, migrate, fetch config, fix perms).
  • Sidecars: 1.28+ native = init container with restartPolicy: Always; starts first, stops last.
  • Probes: startup (grace for slow boot), readiness (gate traffic, don't restart), liveness (restart if wedged; self-only, cheap). Types: httpGet/tcpSocket/exec/grpc.
  • Liveness checking a dependency = restart storm on a blip. Don't.
  • Termination: endpoint removal → preStop → SIGTERM → terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30) → SIGKILL. Handle SIGTERM; add a preStop sleep.
  • Don't create bare Pods — use a Deployment/StatefulSet/DaemonSet/Job so they're recreated and rolled.
Q&A
Why do containers in a pod reach each other on localhost?
They share one network namespace (set up on the pod's pause container), so they have the same IP and loopback interface and a single port space. Consequence: two containers in a pod can't both bind the same port, and there's no network isolation between them.
readiness vs liveness probe — when does each fire and what does it do?
Readiness: when it fails, the pod is removed from its Service's endpoints so it stops receiving traffic, but the container is not restarted — it's "temporarily can't serve" (warming up, overloaded, dependency briefly unavailable). Liveness: when it fails failureThreshold times, the kubelet kills and restarts the container — it's "this process is stuck and only a restart fixes it." Use readiness for anything transient; reserve liveness for genuine deadlocks and keep it cheap and self-contained.
What's the point of a startupProbe?
For apps that take a long, variable time to become ready (large caches, JVM warmup, DB migrations). Without it, you'd have to set the liveness probe's initialDelaySeconds/failureThreshold so high that it becomes useless at catching real hangs later. The startup probe runs first with its own generous budget; only once it passes do the liveness and readiness probes begin. If startup fails, the container is restarted.
Your pod won't terminate quickly / drops requests on rollout. What pod-spec things do you check?
(1) Does the app handle SIGTERM (drain and exit 0) and is it PID 1 (exec-form entrypoint)? (2) Is terminationGracePeriodSeconds long enough for the longest in-flight request? (3) Is there a preStop hook (a short sleep, or an explicit deregister) so the LB/EndpointSlice update propagates before the process starts shutting down — otherwise traffic still arrives at a terminating pod? (4) Is the readiness probe correct so new pods only get traffic when truly ready and old ones are pulled out first? (5) Long-lived connections (HTTP/2, gRPC, websockets) — does the server send GOAWAY / close idle conns on SIGTERM, and do clients retry idempotent calls?
When is a multi-container pod the right design, and when is it not?
Right when the containers form one unit that must share a lifecycle, node, network, or filesystem: an app + a service-mesh proxy sidecar, an app + a log/metrics shipper reading a shared emptyDir, an app + a config reloader, an adapter that reshapes the app's output. Wrong when you just want two things deployed together but they scale, fail, release, or get updated independently — those should be separate Deployments talking over a Service. Cramming a database and an app into one pod, or two unrelated microservices, loses independent scaling and rolling updates and couples their failure domains.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

How many IP addresses does a pod have?
One, shared by all its containers (they share the pod's network namespace). Services and other pods reach it at that single IP.
What runs first: init containers or app containers?
Init containers, in the order listed, each to completion, before any app container starts. If one fails it's retried and the pod stays Pending/Init.

Intermediate core

A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. Walk the diagnosis.
(1) kubectl describe pod <p> — Events (image pull error, failed mount, failed scheduling, OOMKilled, probe failures) and the container's Last State (exit code, reason, finished-at). (2) kubectl logs <p> -c <container> --previous — the crashed instance's stdout: config error, missing env var, can't reach a dependency, bad migration, panic. (3) Exit code: 137 = OOM/SIGKILL (check memory limit vs working set, describe shows OOMKilled), 1/2 = app error, 126/127 = command not executable/not found (wrong CMD or wrong-arch image), 139 = SIGSEGV. (4) If it's probe-driven: is the liveness probe too aggressive (short timeout, no startupProbe for a slow boot, checking a dependency)? That restarts a healthy-but-slow app in a loop. (5) Reproduce: kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=<same> --command -- sh and run the entrypoint by hand; or kubectl debug. (6) Check mounts/config: a ConfigMap/Secret key missing, a volume with wrong ownership for the non-root user, a bad args. (7) kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp -n <ns> for the cluster-side story. Fix the root cause; the backoff (10s, 20s, 40s… capped at 5m) clears once it stays up.
Explain the full graceful-termination sequence for a pod and where requests can be dropped.
When a pod is deleted (scale-down, rollout, eviction): (1) its deletionTimestamp is set and it's marked Terminating; (2) in parallel, the endpoint/EndpointSlice controller removes the pod's IP from Service endpoints, and the kubelet begins shutdown — these are not synchronized, so for a short window kube-proxy on some nodes may still route to the pod while it's stopping (drop risk #1); (3) the kubelet runs the preStop hook (if any) to completion; (4) it sends SIGTERM to each container's PID 1; (5) it waits up to terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30, minus the time preStop took); (6) any container still alive gets SIGKILL — in-flight requests on it are cut (drop risk #2); (7) the pod object is removed. Mitigations: a preStop sleep of a few seconds so endpoint removal propagates before the app stops accepting (covers #1); the app must catch SIGTERM, stop accepting new work, finish in-flight, close connections, and exit 0 within the grace period; set terminationGracePeriodSeconds ≥ longest request + preStop; for long-lived connections send GOAWAY/close-idle on SIGTERM and have clients retry idempotent requests; ensure readiness flips to not-ready immediately (some apps do this on SIGTERM) so nothing new is sent even before endpoint propagation.

Advanced deep

Design the probe + lifecycle configuration for a service with a 90s cold start, 200ms–30s request times, a warm in-memory cache, and a hard dependency on a database.
startupProbe: httpGet /healthz, periodSeconds: 3, failureThreshold: 40 (≈120s budget, comfortably over the 90s cold start) — container is restarted only if it never comes up; readiness/liveness are suspended until this passes so the slow boot isn't misread as a hang. readinessProbe: httpGet /ready, periodSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 3, successThreshold: 1. /ready should return 200 only when: the HTTP server is up, the cache is warmed to a usable level, and a lightweight DB check passes (a fast SELECT 1 with a short timeout — not a heavy query). This gates traffic during warmup and briefly pulls the pod out if the DB is unreachable, so requests fail fast elsewhere rather than piling up. livenessProbe: httpGet /livez, periodSeconds: 15, timeoutSeconds: 3, failureThreshold: 4 (≈60s before restart). /livez checks only the process itself — event loop responsive, no deadlock, worker threads not all stuck — and never touches the database, so a DB outage doesn't restart every replica (which would drop caches and stampede the DB on recovery). The generous threshold avoids restarting a pod that's merely slow under load. Lifecycle: terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45 (longest request 30s + margin + preStop); preStop: exec sleep 5 (or an endpoint-deregister call) so kube-proxy/EndpointSlice updates land before SIGTERM; app on SIGTERM: flip readiness to not-ready immediately, stop accepting new requests, let in-flight (up to 30s) finish, flush, close DB pool, exit 0. Rollout: maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 (or 25%) so capacity never dips during the slow rollout; PodDisruptionBudget minAvailable so node drains respect it. Cache: consider a warm-up job/preload on start and a readiness gate at, say, 70% cache fill rather than 100% so pods become useful sooner; expose cache-fill and DB-check latency as metrics and alert if readiness is flapping. Net: startupProbe absorbs the cold start, readiness reflects real serving capacity (incl. a cheap DB check), liveness is strictly self-scoped so a DB outage can't cause a restart storm, and preStop + grace period + SIGTERM draining make rollouts and node drains lossless.

Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets & Jobs

Pick the controller by what the workload needs: interchangeable replicas, stable identity, one-per-node, or run-to-completion.

Notes

Deployment — stateless apps

What / why. Manages a ReplicaSet (which manages Pods) and does rolling updates: on a template change it creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts pods over per the strategy, keeping old ReplicaSets (scaled to 0) for rollback. Pods are anonymous and interchangeable.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: api }
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 }   # never dip below 4 ready
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: api } }
    spec:
      containers: [{ name: api, image: myorg/api@sha256:... }]

$ kubectl rollout status  deploy/api
$ kubectl rollout history deploy/api
$ kubectl rollout undo    deploy/api --to-revision=3
$ kubectl set image deploy/api api=myorg/api:1.4.3      # triggers a rollout
  • maxSurge = extra pods allowed above replicas during the roll; maxUnavailable = how many can be down. 0/1 = zero-downtime but needs spare capacity.
  • type: Recreate = kill all, then start all (brief downtime) — for apps that can't run two versions at once.
  • revisionHistoryLimit, progressDeadlineSeconds (mark the rollout failed if stuck).

StatefulSet — stable identity & storage

What / why. For clustered/stateful software (databases, Kafka, Zookeeper, Elasticsearch). Each pod gets: a stable name (app-0, app-1…), a stable DNS record via a headless Service (app-0.app.ns.svc), and its own PersistentVolumeClaim from volumeClaimTemplates that survives pod rescheduling. Pods are created/updated/deleted in order (0, 1, 2 …).

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata: { name: pg }
spec:
  serviceName: pg          # the headless Service for stable DNS
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: pg } }
  template: { ... }
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata: { name: data }
      spec: { accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"], resources: { requests: { storage: 20Gi } },
              storageClassName: fast-ssd }
  updateStrategy: { type: RollingUpdate, rollingUpdate: { partition: 0 } }
  podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady    # or Parallel for faster, no-ordering start
  • Deleting a StatefulSet does not delete its PVCs (data is kept on purpose) — clean up manually.
  • partition: N in the update strategy = a canary: only pods with ordinal ≥ N are updated.
  • Scaling down removes highest ordinal first; the PVC stays for when you scale back up.

DaemonSet — one pod per node

What / why. Runs a copy on every node (or every node matching a selector/tolerating a taint) and adds one when a node joins. For node-level agents: CNI, kube-proxy, log collectors (Fluent Bit), node exporters, storage/CSI node plugins, security agents.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata: { name: fluent-bit }
spec:
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: fluent-bit } }
  template:
    spec:
      tolerations: [{ operator: Exists }]        # run on control-plane / tainted nodes too
      containers:
        - name: fluent-bit
          image: fluent/fluent-bit
          volumeMounts: [{ name: varlog, mountPath: /var/log, readOnly: true }]
      volumes: [{ name: varlog, hostPath: { path: /var/log } }]
  updateStrategy: { type: RollingUpdate, rollingUpdate: { maxUnavailable: 1 } }

Job & CronJob — run to completion

What / why. A Job runs pods until completions succeed, retrying failures up to backoffLimit. A CronJob creates a Job on a schedule.

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata: { name: migrate }
spec:
  completions: 1
  parallelism: 1
  backoffLimit: 4               # retries before the Job is marked Failed
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 600    # hard wall-clock cap
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600 # auto-delete the Job (and pods) 1h after finishing
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never       # Never or OnFailure (not Always)
      containers: [{ name: migrate, image: myorg/api, command: ["./migrate"] }]
---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata: { name: nightly-report }
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid            # Allow | Forbid | Replace
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 200
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  jobTemplate: { spec: { template: { spec: { restartPolicy: OnFailure, containers: [ ... ] } } } }
  • Indexed Jobs (completionMode: Indexed) give each pod a JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX — for sharded batch work.
  • CronJob concurrencyPolicy: Forbid skips a run if the previous is still going; Replace kills it.

Choosing

NeedUse
Stateless replicas, rolling updates, HPADeployment
Stable names, per-pod storage, ordered start (DBs, quorum systems)StatefulSet
Exactly one pod per node (agents)DaemonSet
Batch task that finishesJob
Scheduled batch taskCronJob
Leader-elected singleton serviceDeployment replicas: 1 + app-level leader election (not a StatefulSet unless it needs storage/identity)
Cheat Sheet
  • Deployment: stateless, interchangeable pods; owns a ReplicaSet; rolling update via maxSurge/maxUnavailable; rollout status/history/undo. Recreate for can't-coexist versions.
  • StatefulSet: stable pod names + stable DNS (needs a headless serviceName) + per-pod PVC (volumeClaimTemplates) + ordered ops. PVCs are kept on delete/scale-down. partition = canary.
  • DaemonSet: one pod per (matching, tolerating) node; auto-adds on new nodes; for CNI/kube-proxy/log/metrics/CSI/security agents.
  • Job: run to completions, retry to backoffLimit, restartPolicy: Never|OnFailure, activeDeadlineSeconds, ttlSecondsAfterFinished. Indexed for sharded work.
  • CronJob: schedule + jobTemplate; concurrencyPolicy: Allow|Forbid|Replace; history limits.
  • Singleton service = Deployment replicas:1 + app leader election, not a StatefulSet.
Q&A
Deployment vs StatefulSet — the core difference?
A Deployment's pods are anonymous and interchangeable — any replica can serve any request, they can be created/killed in any order, and they share nothing per-pod. A StatefulSet gives each pod a stable ordinal identity (app-0…), a stable DNS name, and its own PersistentVolumeClaim that follows that identity across rescheduling, and it creates/updates/deletes pods in order. Use StatefulSet only when the software needs that identity/storage/ordering (databases, quorum systems); otherwise Deployment.
What happens to storage when you delete a StatefulSet?
Nothing — the PVCs created from volumeClaimTemplates are deliberately not garbage-collected, so your data isn't lost when you delete or scale down the StatefulSet. You must delete the PVCs yourself when you actually want the data gone. (Newer versions add persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy to opt into deletion on scale-down/delete.)
How does a Deployment do a zero-downtime rollout?
On a pod-template change it creates a new ReplicaSet and, per the RollingUpdate strategy, scales the new one up and the old one down gradually. With maxUnavailable: 0 and maxSurge: 1 (or a percentage), it always keeps the desired number of ready pods — it adds a new ready pod before removing an old one. Readiness probes gate this: a new pod only counts (and gets traffic) once ready. If the rollout stalls past progressDeadlineSeconds it's marked failed; kubectl rollout undo scales the previous ReplicaSet back up.
