Why use a DaemonSet instead of a Deployment with N replicas for a log collector?
A log collector must run on every node to read that node's container logs / /var/log via a hostPath. A Deployment schedules N pods wherever the scheduler likes — you'd get some nodes with two collectors and some with none, and adding a node wouldn't add a collector. A DaemonSet guarantees exactly one per matching node and automatically places one on every node that joins (and can tolerate control-plane/taints to cover those too).
Your CronJob sometimes runs twice concurrently and corrupts data. Fix?
Set concurrencyPolicy: Forbid so a scheduled run is skipped while the previous Job is still active (or Replace to kill the old one, if that's safe). Also: make the job itself idempotent / use a lock so even a rare overlap (clock skew, a missed startingDeadlineSeconds window catching up) can't double-process; set activeDeadlineSeconds so a hung run can't block the next forever; and check that backoffLimit retries aren't re-running side effects.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which workload controller runs exactly one pod on every node?
DaemonSet.
What object does a Deployment create and manage?
A ReplicaSet (one per revision), which in turn manages the Pods. Rollbacks scale an old ReplicaSet back up.

Intermediate core

You need to run a 3-node Postgres cluster on Kubernetes. Which controller, and what specifically do you configure?
A StatefulSet (or, better, a Postgres operator that manages one). Configure: serviceName pointing at a headless Service (clusterIP: None) so each pod gets pg-0.pg.ns.svc etc. for peer discovery; volumeClaimTemplates with a ReadWriteOnce PVC per pod on a fast StorageClass, sized with headroom; replicas: 3; podManagementPolicy = OrderedReady (so pg-0 is primary-ready before replicas init) or Parallel if the operator handles ordering; updateStrategy: RollingUpdate with partition for canary upgrades; terminationGracePeriodSeconds long enough for a clean shutdown/checkpoint; a PodDisruptionBudget (minAvailable: 2) so node drains don't take primary+replica together; anti-affinity to spread the 3 pods across nodes/zones; readiness probe that reflects "accepting connections and (for replicas) not too far behind"; liveness probe that's process-only. Plus the non-StatefulSet parts: WAL archiving to object storage, a backup CronJob, monitoring of replication lag and disk, and an HA/failover mechanism (Patroni/operator) since a StatefulSet alone doesn't do leader election or promote a replica. Remember PVCs persist on delete — clean up deliberately.
A rollout is stuck — new pods aren't becoming ready and old ones aren't being removed. Diagnose.
kubectl rollout status deploy/x and kubectl describe deploy/x — look for ProgressDeadlineExceeded and the new ReplicaSet's replica counts. Then kubectl get pods -l app=x and describe/logs the new pods: (1) Readiness probe failing — new image's /ready path/port wrong, app crashing, config/secret missing, dependency unreachable; with maxUnavailable: 0 the rollout correctly refuses to remove old pods until new ones are ready, so it just sits (safe, by design). (2) Can't schedule — maxSurge needs spare capacity the cluster doesn't have (insufficient CPU/mem, no matching node for affinity/taints, PVC can't bind in the zone), pods stuck Pending. (3) ImagePullBackOff — bad tag/digest, registry auth, rate limit. (4) CrashLoopBackOff in the new version — check logs --previous. (5) A PodDisruptionBudget or admission policy blocking pod creation/deletion. Fix the pod-level cause, or kubectl rollout undo deploy/x to revert to the last good ReplicaSet while you investigate. The key insight: a "stuck" rolling update usually means the new pods can't become ready and the strategy is protecting availability by not proceeding.

Advanced deep

Design safe deployment strategies for three services: a stateless API (frequent deploys), a schema-changing monolith, and a stateful message broker.
Stateless API: Deployment with RollingUpdate, maxUnavailable: 0 / maxSurge: 25% for zero-downtime; strong readiness probe + preStop sleep + graceful SIGTERM so no requests drop; progressDeadlineSeconds to auto-fail stuck rolls; PDB (minAvailable) for node drains; deploy by image digest via GitOps. For extra safety on risky changes, do progressive delivery — Argo Rollouts / Flagger canary: shift 5% → 25% → 50% → 100% with automated analysis (error rate, p99, saturation) and automatic rollback on regression; or blue/green (two ReplicaSets, flip the Service selector after smoke tests) if you need instant switch + instant rollback. Feature-flag behavioural changes so deploy != release. Schema-changing monolith: the deployment strategy must accommodate the DB. Use expand/contract (parallel-change) migrations: (1) deploy a migration that only adds backward-compatible schema (new nullable columns, new tables) — run it as a pre-deploy Job or an init step, made idempotent and gated so N replicas don't race; (2) deploy app code that writes both old and new and reads new-with-fallback — now old and new app versions and old and new schema all coexist, so a normal RollingUpdate (or canary) is safe; (3) backfill data in a background Job; (4) after the new version is fully rolled and verified, deploy the "contract" migration that drops the old columns and the dual-write. Never combine a destructive migration with the same rollout that needs the old schema. If the app genuinely cannot run two versions at once against the DB, use strategy: Recreate in a maintenance window (accepting downtime) — but expand/contract usually avoids that. Keep migrations reversible or forward-fixable; test rollback of the app against the migrated schema. Stateful message broker (Kafka/RabbitMQ): StatefulSet with RollingUpdate + partition so you upgrade one broker at a time, highest ordinal first, waiting for it to rejoin the cluster and for under-replicated partitions to recover to zero before proceeding (an operator or a custom check between steps — the plain StatefulSet won't know about ISR). Set maxUnavailable: 1, a PDB of minAvailable: N-1, anti-affinity across nodes/zones, generous terminationGracePeriodSeconds for controlled shutdown (leader handoff, flush), and a readiness probe that only reports ready when the broker has caught up. Take a backup / verify replication before starting; do it in a low-traffic window; have a documented abort (halt at the current partition, don't roll forward). For major version jumps, follow the product's rolling-upgrade runbook (inter-broker protocol version pinning, etc.). Prefer a well-maintained operator that encodes all of this. Net: API — canary/blue-green with automated analysis and digest-based GitOps; monolith — expand/contract migrations so versions and schema coexist, then a normal roll; broker — one-at-a-time partitioned StatefulSet upgrade gated on cluster health, ideally via an operator.

Services, kube-proxy & Cluster DNS

Pods are ephemeral and get new IPs; a Service is a stable name + virtual IP that load-balances to the current set of matching pods.

Notes

Service types

TypeWhat you get
ClusterIP (default)A stable virtual IP + DNS name reachable only inside the cluster. The building block for everything else.
NodePortClusterIP + a port (30000–32767) opened on every node; external traffic to <anyNodeIP>:nodePort is forwarded to the Service.
LoadBalancerNodePort + the cloud-controller provisions an external L4 load balancer pointing at the NodePort on the nodes.
ExternalNameNo proxying — just a CNAME in cluster DNS to an external hostname (db.example.com).
Headless (clusterIP: None)No virtual IP; DNS returns the pod IPs directly (A records). For StatefulSets and clients that do their own load-balancing.
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: api, namespace: shop }
spec:
  selector: { app: api }
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80            # the Service port (what clients use)
      targetPort: 8080     # the container port (or a named port)
  # type: ClusterIP (default)
  # sessionAffinity: ClientIP   # sticky by source IP (crude)

Selector, EndpointSlices, and readiness

  • The Service's selector matches pod labels. The EndpointSlice controller keeps slices of the matching pods' IP:port — but only pods that are Ready (readiness probe passing). Failing readiness → pulled from the slice → no traffic.
  • EndpointSlices replaced the single monolithic Endpoints object so a 5000-pod Service doesn't rewrite one giant object on every pod change.
  • A Service with no selector + a manual EndpointSlice lets you point a Service name at an external IP (a DB outside the cluster).
$ kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=api
$ kubectl get svc api -o wide
NAME  TYPE       CLUSTER-IP     PORT(S)   SELECTOR
api   ClusterIP  10.96.14.201  80/TCP    app=api

kube-proxy modes

  • iptables (default): for each Service, rules that DNAT the ClusterIP to a random backend pod IP (equal probability). O(rules) grows with Services×endpoints; rule updates get slow at large scale.
  • IPVS: kernel L4 load balancer with real algorithms (rr, lc, sh) and O(1) lookups — better for thousands of Services.
  • eBPF (Cilium): replaces kube-proxy entirely; per-packet load balancing in eBPF, lower latency, no iptables blowup, and identity-aware policy.
# externalTrafficPolicy affects source IP + hop count for NodePort/LB
externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster   # (default) any node can forward; may add 1 hop; SNAT hides client IP
externalTrafficPolicy: Local     # only nodes with a local pod serve; preserves client IP; risk of imbalance
internalTrafficPolicy: Local     # in-cluster traffic prefers a same-node backend (latency)

Cluster DNS (CoreDNS)

  • Every Service gets <svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local → its ClusterIP. Named ports also get SRV records.
  • Pods' /etc/resolv.conf points at the CoreDNS ClusterIP with a search list (<ns>.svc.cluster.local, svc.cluster.local, cluster.local), so api resolves within the same namespace and api.other-ns across namespaces.
  • Headless Service: DNS returns all pod A records; StatefulSet pods also get pod-0.<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local.
  • dnsPolicy, dnsConfig (extra nameservers/searches), and the DNS cache (NodeLocal DNSCache) matter for perf; the classic ndots:5 issue causes extra lookups for external names.
$ kubectl run t --rm -it --image=busybox -- nslookup api.shop.svc.cluster.local
$ kubectl exec deploy/api -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 10.96.0.10
search shop.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
options ndots:5
Cheat Sheet
  • Service = stable virtual IP + DNS name; selector → EndpointSlices of Ready pod IPs.
  • Types: ClusterIP (in-cluster), NodePort (port on every node), LoadBalancer (cloud L4 LB), ExternalName (DNS CNAME), Headless (clusterIP: None → pod A records; for StatefulSets).
  • port = Service port clients use; targetPort = container port.
  • kube-proxy: iptables (default, random DNAT), IPVS (scales better), eBPF/Cilium (replaces kube-proxy).
  • externalTrafficPolicy: Local preserves client IP + avoids a hop but risks imbalance; Cluster spreads but SNATs.
  • DNS: <svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local; pods have a search list so api works same-ns, api.other-ns cross-ns. Watch ndots:5 for external lookups; use NodeLocal DNSCache.
  • Selector-less Service + manual EndpointSlice = point a Service name at an external endpoint.
Q&A
What is a ClusterIP and what listens on it?
A stable virtual IP allocated to a Service from the service CIDR. Nothing listens on it — it's not bound to any interface. Each node's kube-proxy (or the eBPF dataplane) installs rules that intercept packets destined for the ClusterIP:port and DNAT them to one of the Service's current backend pod IPs. Clients get a name and IP that don't change even as pods come and go.
How does a Service know a pod is a valid backend?
Two conditions: the pod's labels match the Service's selector, and the pod is Ready (its readiness probe passes, or it has no readiness probe). The EndpointSlice controller maintains slices of the IP:port of exactly those pods; kube-proxy load-balances across the slice. A pod failing readiness is removed from the slices, so it stops getting traffic without being killed.
Why did EndpointSlices replace the Endpoints object?
The old Endpoints object held all of a Service's backends in one resource. For a Service with thousands of pods, every pod add/remove/readiness-flip rewrote that whole object and pushed it to every node's kube-proxy — huge etcd write and network amplification, and it hit size limits (~1000 endpoints). EndpointSlices shard the backends into multiple small objects (default max 100 each), so a change touches one slice, scaling to very large Services. They also carry topology hints for topology-aware routing.
What does externalTrafficPolicy: Local do and what's the trade-off?
For NodePort/LoadBalancer Services, Local makes a node only forward external traffic to pods on that same node (and health-check as failed if it has none), so there's no second hop and the client's source IP is preserved (important for logging, allow-lists, geo). The trade-off: load is only balanced as evenly as pods are spread across nodes — a node with 3 pods and one with 1 get equal LB traffic, so the busy node's pods are hotter. Use it when you need real client IPs or minimal latency and you ensure even pod spread (topology spread constraints); otherwise Cluster (the default) spreads evenly but SNATs and may add a hop.
A pod can resolve api but not api.other-ns. Why might that be?
api resolves via the pod's DNS search list (<ns>.svc.cluster.local is tried first) — that only works for a Service in the same namespace. api.other-ns needs the full form to reach another namespace — it should resolve as api.other-ns.svc.cluster.local. If it doesn't: the Service may not exist in other-ns, a NetworkPolicy may be blocking DNS or cross-namespace traffic, CoreDNS may be unhealthy, or the pod's dnsPolicy/dnsConfig is overridden. Test with the FQDN directly and check CoreDNS logs.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which Service type gives you an external cloud load balancer?
type: LoadBalancer — the cloud-controller-manager provisions an L4 LB pointing at the Service's NodePort on the nodes.
What DNS name does a Service api in namespace shop get?
api.shop.svc.cluster.local (and api works from pods in shop, api.shop from other namespaces, via the search list).

Intermediate core

Traffic to a Service is being sent to a pod that's clearly broken. What's likely wrong?
The pod is still in the Service's EndpointSlices, which means Kubernetes thinks it's Ready. Causes: (1) No readiness probe — a pod with no readiness probe is "Ready" as soon as its containers start, regardless of whether the app can serve; add one. (2) Readiness probe too lax — it checks "port open" or "process up" (tcpSocket) rather than "can handle a real request"; make it an httpGet against a meaningful endpoint. (3) Probe checks the wrong thing — a static /healthz that returns 200 even when a critical dependency/pool is dead. (4) Slow to flip — periodSeconds/failureThreshold too high, so it takes minutes to mark the pod not-ready after it breaks; tighten them. (5) During termination, a window where the pod is shutting down but still in endpoints (no preStop delay). (6) The app isn't actually broken from K8s' view — it 500s on some routes but the probe path is fine; that's an app bug, not a Service bug. Fix the probe to reflect true serving capacity, and add preStop + graceful shutdown for the termination window.
How does a request from pod A to Service B actually get to a pod of B? Trace it.
(1) A's code connects to b.ns.svc.cluster.local:80. (2) A's resolver (from /etc/resolv.conf, pointing at the CoreDNS ClusterIP, with the search list) queries CoreDNS, which returns B's ClusterIP (e.g. 10.96.20.5). (3) A sends a packet to 10.96.20.5:80. It leaves A's veth and hits the node's networking stack. (4) On that node, kube-proxy has programmed rules for B's ClusterIP: in iptables mode, a chain that, with equal probability, DNATs the destination to one of B's Ready backend pod IPs (from B's EndpointSlices), e.g. 10.244.3.7:8080 (mapping port→targetPort); conntrack records the translation. In IPVS mode a virtual server does the same with a real LB algorithm; with Cilium, an eBPF program at the socket/tc layer does it per-packet. (5) The packet is now routed to the pod IP — same node (bridge/veth) or another node (via the CNI: overlay tunnel or native route). (6) It arrives at the backend pod, whose app is listening on 0.0.0.0:8080. (7) The reply goes back; conntrack reverse-translates the source from the pod IP back to the ClusterIP so A sees a reply from the address it contacted. If sessionAffinity: ClientIP is set, kube-proxy pins A to the same backend for a while. No component "proxies" in userspace (except legacy kube-proxy userspace mode); it's all kernel DNAT/conntrack or eBPF.

Advanced deep

A cluster with 8000 Services and 60000 endpoints has slow Service updates and high kube-proxy CPU. Diagnose and redesign.
Why: iptables-mode kube-proxy builds a chain per Service and per endpoint; a change triggers a full or large iptables ruleset regeneration and iptables-restore on every node. At 8000 Services / 60000 endpoints the ruleset is hundreds of thousands of rules; each rebuild is O(N), takes seconds, spikes CPU, and delays propagation of endpoint changes (so a scaled-up pod gets traffic late, a dead pod keeps getting traffic). Churn (deploys, HPA, node changes) multiplies it. DNS may also be a bottleneck (CoreDNS QPS, ndots:5). Redesign: (1) Switch kube-proxy to IPVS mode — it uses a hash table (O(1) lookups) and incremental updates instead of rebuilding a giant iptables blob; big CPU and latency win at this scale, with real LB algorithms. (2) Better: adopt Cilium (eBPF) and disable kube-proxy — Service load balancing runs in eBPF maps updated incrementally, no iptables Service rules at all, lower per-packet cost, plus identity-based policy and observability. (3) Ensure EndpointSlices are in use (default now) so endpoint changes touch one 100-entry slice, not a monolith; enable EndpointSlice topology / internalTrafficPolicy: Local where appropriate to cut cross-node hops. (4) Reduce churn: right-size HPA thresholds/stabilization so replica counts don't oscillate, use PDBs and surge settings to make rollouts smoother, and avoid thousands of tiny Services where a few with more endpoints would do. (5) DNS: deploy NodeLocal DNSCache (per-node caching resolver) to cut CoreDNS load and tail latency, scale CoreDNS (autoscaler), and fix ndots for workloads doing lots of external lookups (set dnsConfig.options ndots:1 or use FQDNs). (6) Consider splitting the cluster if 8000 Services reflects many independent tenants/teams — smaller clusters keep each dataplane manageable. (7) Monitor: kube-proxy sync duration (kubeproxy_sync_proxy_rules_duration_seconds), iptables rule count, CoreDNS latency/errors, and endpoint-propagation lag. Net: move off iptables-mode kube-proxy (IPVS, or Cilium/eBPF and drop kube-proxy), lean on EndpointSlices + topology routing, cut replica/Service churn, add NodeLocal DNSCache and scale CoreDNS, and shard the cluster if the Service count is really N tenants in a trench coat.

Ingress, Controllers & the Gateway API

One external entry point that routes HTTP(S) by host and path to many Services, terminates TLS, and does L7 features — run by a controller you install.

Notes

Ingress = rules; the controller = the proxy

What / why. A type: LoadBalancer Service per app means one cloud LB (and IP, and cost) each, and no L7 features. An Ingress is a set of L7 routing rules (by host and path) to Services. An ingress controller (ingress-nginx, Traefik, HAProxy, Envoy Gateway, or a cloud one like AWS ALB / GKE) watches Ingress objects and configures itself — it's the actual reverse proxy, fronted by a single LB.

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: shop
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt          # auto-provision the TLS cert
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts: [shop.example.com]
      secretName: shop-tls                                # a Secret of type kubernetes.io/tls
  rules:
    - host: shop.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /api
            pathType: Prefix
            backend: { service: { name: api, port: { number: 80 } } }
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend: { service: { name: web, port: { number: 80 } } }

What the controller does for you

  • Host + path routing, pathType (Exact, Prefix, ImplementationSpecific), default backend for unmatched requests.
  • TLS termination — reads a kubernetes.io/tls Secret; with cert-manager the cert is issued and renewed automatically (ACME/Let's Encrypt or an internal CA).
  • L7 features via annotations (controller-specific): rate limiting, auth (basic/oauth2/forward-auth), rewrites, redirects, CORS, request/response header manipulation, canary weighting, timeouts, body-size limits, WAF (ModSecurity).
  • Load balancing to pod IPs — most controllers bypass kube-proxy and send straight to EndpointSlice pod IPs (better balancing, keep-alive, sticky sessions).

Limits of Ingress (and why the Gateway API exists)

  • Ingress only really models HTTP host/path routing; everything else (TLS options, traffic splitting, header matching, gRPC, TCP/UDP) is done through non-portable annotations that differ per controller.
  • One Ingress = one team's concern, but there's no clean split between "platform owns the load balancer / TLS" and "app team owns their routes."
  • Gateway API (gateway.networking.k8s.io) is the successor: a role-oriented, expressive, portable spec.
# Gateway API: infra team owns GatewayClass + Gateway (listeners, TLS);
# app teams own HTTPRoute (attached to the Gateway)
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata: { name: prod, namespace: infra }
spec:
  gatewayClassName: envoy
  listeners:
    - name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
      port: 443
      tls: { certificateRefs: [{ name: wildcard-tls }] }
      allowedRoutes: { namespaces: { from: Selector, selector: { matchLabels: { ingress: "yes" } } } }
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata: { name: shop, namespace: shop }
spec:
  parentRefs: [{ name: prod, namespace: infra }]
  hostnames: ["shop.example.com"]
  rules:
    - matches: [{ path: { type: PathPrefix, value: /api }, headers: [{ name: x-canary, value: "1" }] }]
      backendRefs: [{ name: api-canary, port: 80, weight: 10 }, { name: api, port: 80, weight: 90 }]

Operational notes

  • The controller is a critical singleton path — run it as a Deployment with multiple replicas + PDB (or a DaemonSet), behind the LB; monitor its latency/error rate; roll it carefully.
  • ingressClassName (or the default class) decides which controller handles an Ingress — you can run several (e.g. internal vs external).
  • Client IP: the LB → controller → pod chain means the app must read X-Forwarded-For / proxy-protocol, and you should set the controller's trusted-proxy config.
  • Large clusters: watch for annotation sprawl and controller reload frequency (nginx reloads its config on Ingress changes).
Cheat Sheet
  • Ingress object = L7 routing rules (host + path → Service) + TLS refs. Does nothing without a controller.
  • Ingress controller = the actual reverse proxy (ingress-nginx / Traefik / Envoy / cloud ALB) behind one cloud LB, fronting many Services.
  • Features: host/path routing (pathType), TLS termination (kubernetes.io/tls Secret; cert-manager auto-issues/renews), and L7 extras via controller-specific annotations (rate limit, auth, rewrite, canary, WAF).
  • Most controllers route straight to pod IPs (EndpointSlices), bypassing kube-proxy.
  • Ingress is weak/non-portable beyond HTTP host/path → Gateway API: GatewayClass/Gateway (infra: listeners, TLS) + HTTPRoute/TCPRoute/GRPCRoute (app teams), portable, header/weight matching built in.
  • ingressClassName selects the controller; run internal + external classes as needed.
  • Run the controller HA (replicas + PDB), monitor it, and configure trusted proxies for real client IPs.
Q&A
You created an Ingress object but nothing is reachable. What's the first thing to check?
Whether an ingress controller is actually installed and running, and whether your Ingress's ingressClassName matches it. The Ingress object is just data; without a controller watching it (and a LoadBalancer/NodePort exposing that controller) it has no effect. Then check the controller's logs, that the referenced Services and their pods exist and are Ready, that the TLS Secret exists, and DNS points at the LB.
Why use an Ingress instead of a LoadBalancer Service per app?
Cost and capability. Each LoadBalancer Service provisions its own cloud L4 load balancer (and public IP, and monthly cost) and gives you no L7 features. One ingress controller behind a single LB can route hundreds of hostnames/paths to different Services, terminate TLS centrally (with automatic cert management), and add rate limiting, auth, redirects, header rewrites, canary splits, and WAF — all at layer 7.
How does TLS work with Ingress, and how do certs get renewed?
You reference a Secret of type kubernetes.io/tls (cert + key) in the Ingress's tls section; the controller loads it and terminates HTTPS at the edge, forwarding HTTP to the backend pods. For renewal, install cert-manager: an annotation (cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer) tells it to obtain a certificate for the Ingress's hosts via ACME (Let's Encrypt) — solving an HTTP-01 or DNS-01 challenge — and it writes/updates the Secret, reissuing before expiry automatically. The controller hot-reloads on the Secret change.
What problems does the Gateway API solve that Ingress doesn't?
(1) Portability — Ingress expresses only HTTP host/path; everything else is controller-specific annotations, so manifests don't move between controllers. Gateway API has first-class fields for header/method/query matching, traffic weighting, request mirroring, redirects, and separate TCPRoute/UDPRoute/GRPCRoute/TLSRoute. (2) Role separation — GatewayClass and Gateway (listeners, ports, TLS, which namespaces may attach) are owned by the platform/infra team; HTTPRoute objects are owned by app teams in their own namespaces and attach to a Gateway. (3) Extensibility — typed policy attachment instead of stringly-typed annotations. It's the intended long-term replacement; Ingress remains supported.
The app logs show every client IP as the ingress controller's pod IP. Fix?
The chain is cloud LB → controller → pod, each a proxy hop, so the L3 source becomes the previous hop. Solutions: the LB and controller pass the real client IP in X-Forwarded-For (or the PROXY protocol for L4); configure the controller's use-forwarded-headers / trusted-proxy CIDR list so it trusts and appends correctly, and have the app read X-Forwarded-For (leftmost untrusted entry). For NodePort/LoadBalancer Services fronting the controller, set externalTrafficPolicy: Local to preserve the client IP at the node hop (with the even-spread caveat). Don't trust X-Forwarded-For from untrusted sources — only from your known LB/controller.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Does an Ingress object route traffic by itself?
No. It's just routing rules. You must install an ingress controller (ingress-nginx, Traefik, Envoy Gateway, a cloud ALB controller, …) that reads Ingress objects and acts as the reverse proxy.
Where does an Ingress get its TLS certificate?
From a Secret of type kubernetes.io/tls (cert + private key) referenced in spec.tls[].secretName. cert-manager can create and renew that Secret automatically via ACME.

Intermediate core

Design external access for a cluster hosting 40 web apps across 12 domains with automatic HTTPS.
One (HA) ingress controller (e.g. ingress-nginx or Envoy Gateway) exposed by a single type: LoadBalancer Service — one cloud LB, one or a few public IPs. DNS: point each of the 12 domains (and their subdomains) at the LB (a wildcard where possible: *.apps.example.com); use external-dns to manage records from Ingress annotations. TLS: install cert-manager with a Let's Encrypt ClusterIssuer (DNS-01 for wildcards, HTTP-01 otherwise); each app's Ingress gets cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer and a tls block, so certs are issued and renewed automatically into per-app Secrets. Routing: each app team owns an Ingress (or HTTPRoute) in their namespace with their host + paths → their Service; use ingressClassName to pick the controller (add a second internal class + LB for admin/internal apps not on the public internet). Shared concerns at the controller: HTTP→HTTPS redirect, HSTS, sane timeouts and body-size limits, rate limiting, a WAF with per-Ingress opt-in tuning, and real client IP via forwarded headers / externalTrafficPolicy: Local. Isolation: NetworkPolicy so only the ingress-controller namespace can reach app pods on their ports; per-namespace resource quotas. Ops: controller as a Deployment with ≥3 replicas + PDB + anti-affinity, HPA on connections/CPU, dashboards for p99/error rate/reload frequency, and a staged rollout process for controller upgrades. For a cleaner platform/app split and portability, do the same with Gateway API: infra owns one Gateway with the HTTPS listener + wildcard cert; teams attach HTTPRoutes from their namespaces.
Ingress-nginx is reloading constantly and dropping connections during reloads. What's happening and how do you fix it?
ingress-nginx regenerates its nginx.conf and reloads whenever a watched object changes — Ingress specs, referenced Secrets, and (in some configs) Endpoints. With many apps and high pod churn (deploys, HPA scaling, node changes), that's frequent reloads; each reload spins up new worker processes and, under load, can drop in-flight connections or add latency. Fixes: (1) Enable dynamic endpoint updates (default in modern ingress-nginx via the Lua dataplane) so endpoint/pod changes update in memory without a config reload. (2) Reduce churn: right-size HPA (stabilization windows, sensible thresholds) so replica counts don't oscillate; smoother rollouts (surge settings, PDBs). (3) Tune worker-shutdown-timeout and enable graceful worker shutdown so old workers drain; ensure keep-alive and proxy-next-upstream retries are set. (4) Use fewer, larger Ingress objects instead of hundreds of tiny ones. (5) Run enough replicas that a reload on one doesn't matter, behind a health-checking LB. (6) Monitor reload count and success; alert on reload storms. (7) Consider a controller with a hot-reload/xDS dataplane (Envoy-based: Contour, Envoy Gateway) that updates config without process reloads.

Advanced deep

Compare Ingress, the Gateway API, and a service mesh for north-south and east-west traffic, and how you'd layer them.
Scope. Ingress / Gateway API = north-south (traffic entering the cluster): TLS termination at the edge, host/path routing to Services, edge auth, rate limiting, WAF. Service mesh (Istio, Linkerd, Cilium) = primarily east-west (pod-to-pod inside the cluster): automatic mTLS, identity-based authorization, retries/timeouts/circuit-breaking, traffic shifting for canaries, and L7 telemetry per service pair — via a sidecar proxy or an ambient/eBPF dataplane. Ingress vs Gateway API: Ingress is the older, minimal, HTTP-only, annotation-driven object — fine for simple "route these hostnames." Gateway API is the modern replacement: portable typed fields for header/method/weight matching, mirroring, redirects; separate route kinds for TCP/UDP/gRPC/TLS; and a role model (infra owns GatewayClass/Gateway with listeners + certs + which namespaces may attach; app teams own HTTPRoute in their namespaces). Prefer Gateway API for new platforms; meshes now expose their ingress gateways through it. Overlap: a mesh usually ships its own ingress gateway (an Envoy at the edge) that is your north-south entry point — so you don't necessarily run a separate ingress-nginx and a mesh gateway; use the mesh gateway (configured via Gateway API) for north-south and the mesh dataplane for east-west, unifying policy, mTLS, and telemetry end to end. Layering: (1) One edge: cloud L4 LB → the Gateway doing TLS, WAF, edge rate-limit, coarse routing to Services. (2) Inside: the mesh (if adopted) handles mTLS, per-service authz, resilience (retries with budgets, outlier detection, timeouts), and canary weighting — ideally the same traffic-split config drives edge and internal routing. (3) NetworkPolicy underneath for L3/4 default-deny as the backstop under the mesh's L7 policy. When you don't need a mesh: if you only need edge routing + TLS and a handful of services, Ingress/Gateway API + NetworkPolicy + app-level retries suffice; a mesh adds real operational cost (sidecar overhead or a new dataplane, upgrades, another proxy to debug). Adopt it when you specifically need cluster-wide mTLS, fine-grained service-to-service authz, uniform resilience/telemetry across many services, or progressive delivery — and consider ambient/eBPF meshes to cut the sidecar tax. Net: Gateway API (or Ingress) for the door, a mesh for the hallways, NetworkPolicy as the floor — and if you run a mesh, let its gateway be the door.

ConfigMaps & Secrets

Keep configuration out of the image; inject it as environment variables or mounted files at run time.

Notes

ConfigMap — non-secret config

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: { name: app-cfg }
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
  FEATURE_X: "true"
  app.yaml: |                # a whole file
    server:
      port: 8080
    cache: { ttl: 60 }
---
# consume it
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      envFrom: [{ configMapRef: { name: app-cfg } }]   # all keys -> env vars
      env:
        - name: LOG_LEVEL                               # or one key, maybe renamed
          valueFrom: { configMapKeyRef: { name: app-cfg, key: LOG_LEVEL } }
      volumeMounts: [{ name: cfg, mountPath: /etc/app }]  # keys become files
  volumes:
    - name: cfg
      configMap:
        name: app-cfg
        items: [{ key: app.yaml, path: app.yaml }]      # pick specific keys

Secret — sensitive config

  • Types: Opaque (arbitrary), kubernetes.io/tls (cert+key), kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson (registry pull creds), kubernetes.io/service-account-token.
  • Values are base64-encoded, not encrypted. Anyone with get secret RBAC (or etcd access) reads them. Enable encryption at rest (a KMS provider) and lock down RBAC.
  • Prefer file mounts over env vars for secrets: env is visible in kubectl describe pod-adjacent places, /proc/<pid>/environ, crash dumps, and is inherited by child processes.
$ kubectl create secret generic db-creds \
    --from-literal=username=app \
    --from-literal=password="$(openssl rand -base64 18)"

spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      env:
        - name: DB_PASSWORD
          valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: db-creds, key: password } }   # ok but see above
      volumeMounts: [{ name: creds, mountPath: /run/secrets/db, readOnly: true }]
  volumes:
    - name: creds
      secret: { secretName: db-creds, defaultMode: 0400 }
  imagePullSecrets: [{ name: regcred }]

env vars vs mounted files — the update behaviour

As env varsAs a mounted volume
When setAt container start — a snapshotWritten to the volume; kubelet refreshes it (~1 min sync) when the object changes
Change picked up?No — needs a pod restartThe file updates; whether the app uses the new value is up to the app (watch/reload, or SIGHUP)
Subpath mountsn/asubPath mounts do not auto-update — avoid for config you want live

To force pods to pick up a ConfigMap/Secret change: use an immutable, hashed name (app-cfg-8f3a1c) so changing config changes the pod template (Kustomize/Helm do this), or add a checksum annotation to the pod template so it rolls, or run a reloader (Stakater Reloader) that restarts the Deployment on change.

Better secret handling

  • Don't commit Secrets to git. Use Sealed Secrets (encrypt to a cluster-specific key, safe to commit) or SOPS + age/KMS.
  • External Secrets Operator / Vault Agent / CSI Secrets Store — the real secret lives in Vault / AWS Secrets Manager / GCP SM; the operator syncs it into a K8s Secret (or mounts it directly), with rotation.
  • Cloud IAM instead of static secrets — IRSA (EKS), Workload Identity (GKE), Managed Identity (AKS): the pod's ServiceAccount is federated to a cloud role, so it gets short-lived cloud credentials and there's no long-lived secret to leak.
  • immutable: true on a ConfigMap/Secret — can't be changed (only replaced), which reduces API-server watch load and prevents accidental edits.
# External Secrets Operator: K8s Secret is a projection of a Vault path
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata: { name: db-creds }
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef: { name: vault, kind: ClusterSecretStore }
  target: { name: db-creds }
  data:
    - secretKey: password
      remoteRef: { key: secret/data/prod/db, property: password }

Scoping & quotas

  • ConfigMaps/Secrets are namespaced — a pod can only reference ones in its own namespace.
  • Size limit ~1 MiB each (they're in etcd). Big config → mount from object storage or a CSI volume, not a ConfigMap.
  • Restrict who can read Secrets with RBAC (don't grant broad get/list secrets); consider a policy that blocks mounting the default ServiceAccount token unless needed.
Cheat Sheet
  • ConfigMap = non-secret key/values or whole files; Secret = same shape, base64-encoded (not encrypted), for sensitive data. Both namespaced, ~1 MiB max.
  • Consume: envFrom / env.valueFrom.configMapKeyRef|secretKeyRef (env vars), or a volume (keys become files).
  • env vars = snapshot at start (need restart to change). Mounted volume = auto-refreshes (~1 min) — but subPath mounts don't, and the app must actually reload.
  • Force a rollout on config change: hashed/immutable names, a pod-template checksum annotation, or a reloader.
  • Secrets: prefer file mounts over env; enable encryption at rest (KMS); tight RBAC on get secrets.
  • Don't commit raw Secrets: Sealed Secrets / SOPS. Sync from a manager: External Secrets Operator / CSI Secrets Store / Vault Agent.
  • Best: cloud workload identity (IRSA / Workload Identity / Managed Identity) — short-lived creds, no static secret.
  • immutable: true to lock a ConfigMap/Secret and cut watch load.
Q&A
Is data in a Kubernetes Secret encrypted?
Not by default — it's only base64-encoded, which is trivially reversible. It's stored in etcd as-is unless you configure encryption at rest (an EncryptionConfiguration with a KMS provider is recommended over the local aescbc key). Anyone with get secret RBAC in that namespace, or read access to etcd or an etcd backup, can read the value. So: encrypt at rest, restrict RBAC tightly, and prefer external managers / workload identity for high-value secrets.
You updated a ConfigMap but the running pods still use the old values. Why?
Almost certainly the config is consumed as environment variables, which are a one-time snapshot injected at container start — changing the ConfigMap doesn't touch running containers. Either restart the pods (rollout), or mount the ConfigMap as a volume (files auto-refresh within ~1 minute) and have the app watch the file / handle SIGHUP. Note a subPath volume mount also doesn't auto-update. To make config changes always trigger a safe rollout, name ConfigMaps with a content hash (Kustomize/Helm do this) or add a checksum annotation to the pod template.
Should secrets be injected as env vars or mounted files?
Prefer files (a secret volume with defaultMode: 0400, mounted read-only). Environment variables leak more easily: they show up in child processes' environments, in /proc/<pid>/environ, in crash dumps and some logging/APM tools, and in docker inspect-style output. Files can be permission-restricted, are read on demand, and don't propagate to subprocesses. Env vars are acceptable for low-sensitivity values or when a library only supports them.
How do you keep secrets out of git while still doing GitOps?
Options: (1) Sealed Secrets — a controller has a keypair; you kubeseal a Secret into a SealedSecret encrypted to the cluster's public key, which is safe to commit; the controller decrypts it in-cluster. (2) SOPS (with age or a cloud KMS) — encrypt just the values in a YAML file, commit that; a SOPS-aware tool (Flux has native support) decrypts at apply time. (3) External Secrets Operator / Vault / CSI Secrets Store — commit only a reference (which path in the manager); the real secret never touches git, and you get rotation. (4) Best where possible: workload identity so there's no static secret at all. Combine: reference-in-git for app secrets, workload identity for cloud API access.
What's the difference between envFrom and env with valueFrom?
envFrom: [{ configMapRef: { name: x } }] imports every key of ConfigMap/Secret x as an environment variable with the same name (optionally with a prefix). env: [{ name: FOO, valueFrom: { configMapKeyRef: { name: x, key: bar } } }] imports one key, and lets you rename it (key bar → env FOO). Use envFrom for bulk config, env.valueFrom when you need specific keys or different names or want to mix sources.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which object holds a database password — ConfigMap or Secret?
Secret (type Opaque). ConfigMap is for non-sensitive configuration.
If you mount a ConfigMap as a volume and then edit the ConfigMap, does the file in the pod change?
Yes — the kubelet refreshes the mounted file within about a minute. Whether the application reacts to the change depends on whether it re-reads the file (or is sent a reload signal). (A subPath mount is the exception — it does not update.)

Intermediate core

Design config + secret management for an app deployed to dev, staging, and prod via GitOps.
Non-secret config: a base ConfigMap in git plus per-environment overlays (Kustomize patches or Helm values-<env>.yaml). Generate ConfigMap names with a content hash (Kustomize configMapGenerator / Helm checksum annotation) so any change rolls the Deployment automatically. Mount as a volume for values you want hot-reloadable; env vars for the rest. Secrets: never raw in git. Choose one: Sealed Secrets (per-cluster key, encrypted manifests committed) or SOPS (values encrypted with a cloud KMS key per environment, Flux decrypts on apply) for app-managed secrets; or, better, External Secrets Operator pointing at a per-environment path in Vault/AWS SM/GCP SM, so git holds only the reference and the operator syncs + rotates. For cloud API access (S3, queues, DB IAM auth), use workload identity (IRSA / GKE Workload Identity / AKS) so there's no static secret at all — the pod's ServiceAccount is federated to a per-environment cloud role. Isolation: separate namespaces (or clusters) per environment; RBAC so only that environment's CI/operators can write its secrets; encryption at rest with a KMS provider; tight get secrets RBAC; block default SA token automount where unused. Promotion: the same app image digest flows dev→staging→prod; only the config/secret references differ per overlay, and secret values live in the per-environment manager. Rollout on change: hashed ConfigMap/Secret names or a reloader so a config bump is a normal, revertible deploy. Audit: every config change is a reviewed PR; secret access is logged by the manager; alert on unexpected secret reads.
A rotated secret in Vault isn't taking effect in the running pods. Walk through why and how to make rotation work end to end.
Rotation has to propagate through several layers, and any of them can be the stall. (1) Manager → K8s Secret: if you use External Secrets Operator, the K8s Secret only updates on its refreshInterval (or a webhook) — shorten the interval or trigger a manual sync; check the ExternalSecret's status/conditions and the operator logs (auth to Vault expired, path/property wrong). If you use the CSI Secrets Store driver, it only re-fetches on pod (re)start unless enableSecretRotation is on. (2) K8s Secret → pod: if consumed as env vars, the pod has a start-time snapshot — it will never see the new value without a restart. If consumed as a volume, the kubelet refreshes the file within ~1 minute (not subPath). (3) File → application: the app must re-read the file or accept a reload signal; many just read once at boot. Making it work: mount secrets as volumes (not env), have the app watch the file / support SIGHUP, and/or run a reloader (Stakater Reloader, or a pod-template checksum) so the Deployment does a rolling restart when the K8s Secret changes — combined with a short ExternalSecret refresh and connection-pool logic that re-authenticates gracefully (drain old connections, open new ones with the new credential). For databases, use a dual-credential rotation window (Vault dynamic secrets or two valid passwords) so there's no gap where neither works. Verify end to end: rotate in Vault → confirm ExternalSecret synced → confirm the K8s Secret's resourceVersion changed → confirm pods restarted / files updated → confirm new connections use the new credential and old ones drained.

Advanced deep

You're securing secrets for a large multi-team cluster. Design the model: storage, access, rotation, blast radius, and detection.
Source of truth: secrets live in a dedicated manager (Vault, or the cloud's Secrets Manager), not in etcd as the primary store and never raw in git. Per-team, per-environment paths with fine-grained policies. Kubernetes Secrets, where they exist, are short-lived projections synced by External Secrets Operator (or mounted via the CSI Secrets Store driver), with immutable where they don't rotate often. etcd: encryption at rest via a KMS provider (envelope encryption, key in a cloud KMS/HSM), key rotation procedure documented; encrypted etcd backups with restricted access. Access: RBAC that denies broad get/list secrets — grant per-namespace, per-name where feasible; separate the ability to create secrets (CI/operator SAs) from workloads that only need them mounted; disable default ServiceAccount token automount cluster-wide and opt in per workload; audit-log all secret reads. In the manager: policies scoped to a team's paths, authenticated via the pod's Kubernetes ServiceAccount (Vault k8s auth) or cloud workload identity — no shared static tokens. Prefer no static secret: workload identity (IRSA / GKE WI / AKS) for all cloud API access; Vault dynamic secrets for databases and cloud accounts (short-lived, auto-revoked); mTLS via a mesh for service-to-service auth instead of shared API keys. Rotation: everything time-bounded — dynamic DB creds with a TTL, cloud creds via STS, TLS via cert-manager. For unavoidable static secrets, automated rotation with a dual-credential overlap window and app logic to re-auth without downtime; alert on secrets older than policy. Blast radius: one team's secrets are unreachable from another (namespace + RBAC + manager policy + NetworkPolicy so pods can't reach another team's Vault path host); per-workload SAs so a compromised pod gets only its own secrets; short TTLs so a leaked credential expires fast; the ability to revoke a single credential/lease centrally. Detection: audit logs from the API server (secret gets) and the manager (path reads) shipped to a SIEM with alerts on anomalous access (a workload reading a path it never read, spike in reads, reads from an unexpected pod/IP); Falco/Tetragon rules for a container reading /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token unexpectedly or exfil patterns; secret-scanning in CI and on images to catch leaks into code/layers; canary/honeytoken secrets that alert if ever used. Break-glass: a documented, audited emergency-access path with just-in-time elevation and automatic expiry. Net: secrets in a real manager with per-team scoping and KMS-encrypted etcd, workload identity and dynamic secrets to minimize static credentials, tight RBAC + audited access, per-workload identities and short TTLs to bound blast radius, and SIEM + runtime rules + honeytokens for detection — assume a pod will be compromised and make it get only its own, soon-to-expire credentials.

Volumes, PV, PVC & StorageClasses

A pod asks for storage with a PersistentVolumeClaim; a StorageClass + provisioner turns that into a real disk automatically.

Notes

Ephemeral volumes

VolumeLifetime / use
emptyDirCreated empty when the pod starts, deleted when the pod is removed. Scratch space, cache, a shared dir between containers in a pod. medium: Memory = tmpfs.
configMap / secret / downwardAPI / projectedInject config, credentials, pod metadata, or a combined set as files.
hostPathMounts a path from the node. Powerful and dangerous — ties the pod to a node and can read/write host files. Only for node agents (DaemonSets).

Persistent storage: PV, PVC, StorageClass

  • PersistentVolume (PV) — a cluster-scoped resource representing a real volume (an EBS disk, a Ceph RBD image, an NFS export). Has a capacity, access modes, a reclaim policy, and either a static definition or a reference to the CSI driver.
  • PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) — namespaced; a request for storage (size, access mode, StorageClass). The pod references the PVC.
  • StorageClass — names a provisioner (a CSI driver) and parameters (disk type, IOPS, encryption, filesystem). A PVC that names a StorageClass triggers dynamic provisioning: the driver creates a matching PV + real disk, and the PVC is bound to it.
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata: { name: fast-ssd }
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
parameters: { type: gp3, iops: "5000", encrypted: "true" }
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer     # bind after a pod is scheduled -> right zone
reclaimPolicy: Delete                        # or Retain
allowVolumeExpansion: true
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: { name: data, namespace: shop }
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  storageClassName: fast-ssd
  resources: { requests: { storage: 20Gi } }
---
# pod uses it
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      volumeMounts: [{ name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/app }]
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: data }

Access modes

ModeMeaningTypical backend
ReadWriteOnce (RWO)Mounted read-write by one node (multiple pods on that node ok).Block storage (EBS, GCE PD, Ceph RBD) — the common case for databases.
ReadWriteMany (RWX)Read-write by many nodes at once.Shared filesystems (NFS, CephFS, EFS, Azure Files). Not all drivers support it.
ReadOnlyMany (ROX)Read-only by many nodes.Shared read datasets.
ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP)Exactly one pod, cluster-wide.Strict single-writer needs.

A pod requesting an RWO volume can only be scheduled where the volume can attach; two pods on different nodes can't share an RWO disk — that's why databases use StatefulSets (one PVC per pod), not a shared PVC.

Lifecycle knobs

  • reclaimPolicy: Delete (PVC deleted → PV and the cloud disk deleted — convenient, dangerous) or Retain (PV kept, must be cleaned up manually — safer for important data).
  • volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer — don't provision the disk until a pod using the PVC is scheduled, so the disk lands in the same zone as the pod (avoids "pod in zone A, disk in zone B, can't attach").
  • allowVolumeExpansion — edit the PVC's requests.storage upward; the CSI driver grows the disk and (online, usually) the filesystem. Shrinking is not supported.
  • Snapshots — VolumeSnapshot / VolumeSnapshotClass (CSI) to snapshot a PVC and restore into a new PVC.
  • StatefulSet volumeClaimTemplates create one PVC per pod (data-app-0…) that survives rescheduling; persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy controls deletion on scale-down/delete (default: keep).

CSI & the ecosystem

  • CSI (Container Storage Interface) is the plugin standard — drivers run as a controller Deployment (provision/attach/snapshot/expand) + a node DaemonSet (mount/format). Cloud disks, Ceph (Rook), Portworx, Longhorn, OpenEBS, NetApp, etc.
  • Generic ephemeral volumes — an inline PVC-like spec in the pod for per-pod scratch on a CSI backend (deleted with the pod).
  • Local persistent volumes — a node's local SSD as a PV (fast, but the data is pinned to that node; pod must reschedule there or lose it).
Cheat Sheet
  • Ephemeral: emptyDir (scratch/shared, dies with pod; medium: Memory = tmpfs), configMap/secret/downwardAPI/projected, hostPath (node path — agents only, dangerous).
  • PVC (namespaced, "I want storage") → StorageClass (names a CSI provisioner + params) → dynamic provisioning creates a PV + real disk, bound to the PVC. Pod references the PVC.
  • Access modes: RWO (one node — block storage, DBs), RWX (many nodes — NFS/CephFS/EFS), ROX, RWOP (one pod).
  • Two pods on different nodes can't share an RWO disk → databases use StatefulSet + volumeClaimTemplates (one PVC per pod).
  • volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer → disk provisioned in the pod's zone. reclaimPolicy: Retain → keep data on PVC delete. allowVolumeExpansion: true → grow (never shrink).
  • VolumeSnapshot for backup/restore. CSI = the driver standard (controller Deployment + node DaemonSet).
  • Local PV = fast but node-pinned; hostPath = node-pinned + host access.
Q&A
What's the relationship between a PVC, a PV, and a StorageClass?
A PVC is a namespaced request ("20 GiB, ReadWriteOnce, class fast-ssd"). A PV is a cluster-scoped object representing an actual volume. A StorageClass names a CSI provisioner and parameters. When a PVC names a StorageClass, the provisioner dynamically creates a PV (and the real disk) that satisfies the claim and binds them. Without dynamic provisioning, an admin pre-creates PVs and the control plane matches a PVC to a suitable one.
Why do stateful apps like databases use a StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates instead of a Deployment with one PVC?
Block storage is ReadWriteOnce — it can be attached to only one node at a time — so multiple replicas can't share one PVC. Each database replica needs its own persistent volume that follows its identity across rescheduling. volumeClaimTemplates gives each StatefulSet pod (db-0, db-1…) a dedicated PVC (data-db-0…) that isn't deleted when the pod moves or the StatefulSet is deleted, plus the stable network identity replicas need to find each other.
What does volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer solve?
The zone-mismatch problem. With Immediate binding, the disk is provisioned as soon as the PVC is created — possibly in a different availability zone than where the pod later gets scheduled, so the volume can't attach and the pod is stuck. WaitForFirstConsumer delays provisioning until a pod that uses the PVC is scheduled, so the CSI driver creates the disk in that pod's zone (and the scheduler also considers volume topology when placing the pod).
What happens to the cloud disk when you delete a PVC?
Depends on the PV's reclaimPolicy. Delete (common default for dynamic classes): deleting the PVC deletes the PV and the underlying cloud disk — data gone. Retain: the PV stays (in Released state) and the disk is kept; an admin must manually clean it up or re-bind it. For important data, set the class to Retain (or protect it with backups/snapshots and RBAC), because an accidental kubectl delete pvc with Delete policy is unrecoverable.
Can you shrink a PVC? Grow one?
Grow: yes, if the StorageClass has allowVolumeExpansion: true and the CSI driver supports it — increase the PVC's spec.resources.requests.storage and the driver expands the disk and filesystem (usually online). Shrink: no — Kubernetes and virtually all drivers don't support reducing a volume's size; you'd have to create a smaller PVC and copy the data.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which volume type is scratch space that disappears when the pod is deleted?
emptyDir. (With medium: Memory it's a tmpfs in RAM.)
What access mode does a typical cloud block disk (EBS/PD) support?
ReadWriteOnce (RWO) — mountable read-write by one node at a time. For many-node sharing you need a filesystem backend (NFS/EFS/CephFS) with ReadWriteMany.

Intermediate core

A pod is stuck Pending with "0/5 nodes available: pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims" — or "volume node affinity conflict". Diagnose.
Unbound PVC: kubectl describe pvc — is there a matching StorageClass? Is the class's provisioner (CSI driver) installed and healthy (kubectl get pods -n kube-system, driver logs)? Does the requested size/access mode have capacity/quota? For a static PV setup, is there an available PV matching size + access mode + class + selectors? For dynamic, check the provisioner logs for cloud API errors (permissions, quota, invalid params like an IOPS/type combo). Node affinity conflict: the volume was provisioned in one zone and the scheduler wants to place the pod in another. Fix by setting volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer on the StorageClass so the disk is created in the pod's zone (recreate the PVC if it's already bound wrong), and make sure the scheduler is topology-aware (CSI driver reports topology). Also check: node selectors/affinity/taints on the pod that eliminate the zone with the volume; a cluster with nodes only in zones the volume can't reach; or a manually created PV with a fixed nodeAffinity (local PV) whose node is cordoned/full.
Design storage for: (a) a Redis cache, (b) a Postgres primary+replica, (c) a shared uploads directory for 3 web replicas.
(a) Redis cache: it's a cache — often no persistence at all (emptyDir, or memory-backed). If you want warm restarts, a small RWO PVC per pod via a StatefulSet with AOF/RDB, on standard SSD, reclaimPolicy: Delete (losing it just means a cold cache). Anti-affinity across nodes. Don't over-engineer durability for a cache. (b) Postgres primary + replica: a StatefulSet (or, better, a Postgres operator) with volumeClaimTemplates — one RWO PVC per pod on a fast SSD StorageClass (gp3/pd-ssd, provisioned IOPS if needed), encrypted: true, volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer, reclaimPolicy: Retain (protect the data), allowVolumeExpansion: true, sized with headroom + disk-usage alerts. Spread pods across nodes/zones with anti-affinity; PDB minAvailable: 1. Streaming replication for the replica; WAL archiving to object storage and a backup CronJob (+ periodic VolumeSnapshot as a fast complement, but ensure crash-consistency). PVCs persist on delete — document cleanup. Single-writer is enforced by RWO + StatefulSet identity + the operator's failover logic (a plain StatefulSet won't promote a replica). (c) shared uploads for 3 web replicas: needs ReadWriteMany — a filesystem backend: cloud file service (EFS/Azure Files/Filestore) or CephFS/NFS via CSI, one RWX PVC mounted by all 3 pods. Be aware RWX filesystems have weaker performance and consistency semantics (locking, metadata latency) — for user uploads it's usually better to not use a shared filesystem at all: write uploads directly to object storage (S3/GCS) from the app, keeping the web pods stateless and horizontally scalable, and use a CDN in front. Reserve RWX for legacy apps that assume a POSIX shared dir.

Advanced deep

Design a backup, restore, and disaster-recovery strategy for stateful workloads on Kubernetes.
Layers of backup (defense in depth): (1) Application-consistent logical backups — pg_dump/mongodump/etc. plus continuous WAL/oplog archiving to object storage in another region, giving point-in-time recovery and portability across versions/platforms; run as CronJobs with monitoring on success and age ("no backup in 25h" alert). (2) Volume snapshots — CSI VolumeSnapshot on a schedule (a tool like Velero, Kanister, or the storage vendor's operator) for fast restore of a whole PVC; must be crash-consistent (quiesce/checkpoint the app or freeze the filesystem before snapshotting) — treat as a complement, not a substitute for logical backups. (3) Cluster-object backup — Velero (or GitOps as the source of truth) captures the Kubernetes resources (StatefulSets, PVCs, ConfigMaps, Secrets, CRs) so you can recreate the workload definition, not just the data. Store manifests in git (declarative) so "restore the app" = re-apply the repo. Restore procedure (documented + rehearsed — an untested restore doesn't exist): for a single PVC, restore a snapshot into a new PVC and point a new pod at it, or restore the logical dump into a fresh instance and replay WAL to the target time; for a whole namespace, Velero restore of objects + volumes, or GitOps re-apply + data restore. Test restore RTO/RPO quarterly with a real drill; measure and track. DR (region loss): cross-region replication — async storage/database replication to a standby cluster in another region (or restore-from-object-storage if RTO allows), backups and snapshots copied cross-region, DNS/global LB failover, and the cluster provisioned as code (Cluster API/Terraform + GitOps) so a new cluster in the DR region can be stood up fast. Decide RPO (how much data loss is acceptable → drives replication vs. periodic backup) and RTO (how fast → drives warm-standby vs. cold-restore) per workload and design to those. Safeguards: reclaimPolicy: Retain + RBAC + kubectl delete guardrails so a fat-fingered PVC delete isn't instant data loss; immutable/versioned backup bucket with object-lock to survive ransomware/accidental deletion; encrypted backups; least-privilege for the backup tool. Automation & visibility: dashboard of last-successful-backup age, snapshot count, replication lag, and last successful restore test per workload; alerts on any of them going stale. Net: logical backups + WAL for PITR, CSI snapshots for speed, Velero/GitOps for the K8s objects, cross-region copies + a code-provisioned DR cluster, RPO/RTO-driven replication choices, Retain + object-lock safeguards, and mandatory rehearsed restores.

Scheduling: Requests, Affinity, Taints

Requests decide where a pod fits and its QoS; affinity, anti-affinity, taints and spread constraints steer which node it lands on.

Notes

Requests & limits drive placement and QoS

  • The scheduler sums the CPU/memory requests of pods already on a node and only places a new pod where its requests still fit in allocatable (node capacity minus kube/system reserved).
  • Limits are enforcement ceilings (cgroups) — they don't affect scheduling, but a too-tight CPU limit causes throttling (see the Docker "resources" topic).
  • QoS class: Guaranteed (every container has requests==limits for CPU+mem), Burstable (some requests set), BestEffort (none). Under node memory pressure the kubelet evicts BestEffort → Burstable-over-requests → Guaranteed last, and OOM scores follow the same order.
resources:
  requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi" }   # scheduling + QoS + cpu.weight
  limits:   { cpu: "1",    memory: "512Mi" }    # cgroup ceiling (throttle / OOM)
# missing requests -> scheduler assumes ~0 -> node oversubscribed -> noisy neighbours + evictions

Steering placement

MechanismWhat it does
nodeSelectorSimplest: pod only on nodes with these labels (e.g. disktype: ssd).
Node affinityRicher node matching: requiredDuringScheduling (hard) or preferred (soft, weighted). Operators: In, NotIn, Exists, Gt, Lt.
Pod affinity / anti-affinityPlace near / away from other pods matching a label, within a topologyKey (node, zone). Anti-affinity spreads replicas; affinity co-locates chatty pods.
Taints & tolerationsA taint on a node repels pods unless they carry a matching toleration. Effects: NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, NoExecute (also evicts running pods).
Topology spread constraints"Keep pods evenly spread across zones/nodes within maxSkew." The modern, preferred way to do spreading.
nodeNameBypasses the scheduler entirely — pin to one node. Debug only.
# spread an app's replicas across zones, and don't stack two on a node
topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 1
    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
    whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
    labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
affinity:
  podAntiAffinity:
    requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
      - topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
        labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
  nodeAffinity:
    requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
      nodeSelectorTerms: [{ matchExpressions: [{ key: node.kubernetes.io/instance-type, operator: In, values: [c6i.xlarge] }] }]

Taints & tolerations in practice

# dedicate a node pool to GPU workloads
$ kubectl taint nodes gpu-1 nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule
# only pods that tolerate it (and want a GPU) land there:
tolerations:
  - key: nvidia.com/gpu
    operator: Exists
    effect: NoSchedule

# built-in taints the node controller adds:
#   node.kubernetes.io/not-ready, unreachable (NoExecute)  -> evict after tolerationSeconds
#   node.kubernetes.io/memory-pressure, disk-pressure, unschedulable
# control-plane nodes: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule

Priority, preemption & disruption

  • PriorityClass + priorityClassName: higher-priority pending pods can preempt (evict) lower-priority pods to fit. Use for critical infra vs batch; set preemptionPolicy: Never for "high priority but don't evict others."
  • PodDisruptionBudget (PDB): caps how many pods of a set can be voluntarily disrupted at once (minAvailable / maxUnavailable). Node drains (upgrades, autoscaler scale-down) respect it; involuntary events (a node dying) don't.
  • Descheduler (add-on): periodically evicts pods that violate current policy (node now over-utilised, anti-affinity broken after a scale event) so the scheduler can re-place them — the scheduler itself never moves a running pod.

Why pods stay Pending

$ kubectl describe pod api-xxxx
Events:
  Warning  FailedScheduling  0/6 nodes are available:
    3 Insufficient cpu,
    2 node(s) had untolerated taint {dedicated: gpu},
    1 node(s) didn't match pod topology spread constraints,
    ... (persistentvolumeclaim not bound / volume node affinity conflict).

Common causes: requests too big for any node, no node tolerates the required taint, anti-affinity/topology can't be satisfied (not enough distinct nodes/zones), PVC unbound or in the wrong zone, node selector matches nothing, or the cluster is simply full (needs the Cluster Autoscaler).

Cheat Sheet
  • Scheduler = filter (hard: fits requests, tolerates taints, matches required affinity, volume topology) → score (soft prefs, spread, utilisation) → bind nodeName.
  • requests = scheduling fit + QoS + cpu.weight. Missing requests → oversubscription. limits = cgroup ceiling only.
  • QoS: Guaranteed (req==lim) > Burstable > BestEffort for eviction survival + OOM score.
  • Steer: nodeSelector (simple), node affinity (rich, required/preferred), pod (anti-)affinity (near/away within a topologyKey), taints/tolerations (node repels unless tolerated; NoSchedule/PreferNoSchedule/NoExecute), topologySpreadConstraints (even spread, maxSkew).
  • Dedicated node pools = taint the nodes + toleration + node affinity on the pods.
  • PriorityClass → preemption of lower-priority pods. PDB caps voluntary disruption (drains, autoscaler). Descheduler re-balances (scheduler never moves running pods).
  • Pending? kubectl describe pod Events: Insufficient cpu/mem, untolerated taint, unsatisfiable affinity/spread, PVC unbound / zone conflict, or cluster full.
Q&A
What do CPU/memory requests actually do?
Two things. (1) Scheduling: the scheduler only places a pod on a node where the sum of all pods' requests still fits within the node's allocatable capacity — requests are the "reservation." (2) Runtime: requests.cpu becomes the cgroup cpu.weight (proportional share under contention) and, with requests.memory, determines the pod's QoS class, which drives eviction order and OOM-kill priority under node pressure. Limits, by contrast, only set the cgroup ceiling and don't influence scheduling.
How do you ensure the 3 replicas of a service land on 3 different nodes (and ideally 3 zones)?
Use topology spread constraints: one constraint with topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname and maxSkew: 1 (no two on a node), and another with topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone and maxSkew: 1 (spread across zones), both selecting the app's label, with whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule (or ScheduleAnyway if you'd rather run than block). The older way is podAntiAffinity with requiredDuringScheduling on the hostname topologyKey. You still need enough distinct nodes/zones for it to be satisfiable, or the extra replicas stay Pending (with hard constraints).
What's the difference between a taint and node affinity?
They point opposite ways. Node affinity is on the pod and says "I want to run on nodes like this" — it attracts. A taint is on the node and says "keep pods off me unless they explicitly tolerate this" — it repels. To dedicate a node pool you use both: taint the nodes so nothing schedules there by default, add a matching toleration to the pods that are allowed, and add node affinity so those pods also prefer/require that pool (otherwise a tolerating pod could still land elsewhere).
A node upgrade drains a node and your service briefly goes to zero replicas. How do you prevent that?
Add a PodDisruptionBudget for the service (minAvailable: 2 or maxUnavailable: 1). A drain is a voluntary disruption and honours the PDB — it evicts pods one at a time and blocks if evicting the next would violate the budget, waiting for a replacement to become Ready elsewhere first. Combine with spreading (so the drained node didn't hold all replicas), a rollout strategy with surge, and enough spare cluster capacity (or Cluster Autoscaler) so replacements can be scheduled. Note a PDB does not protect against a node crashing (involuntary).
When would you set a PriorityClass, and what's the risk?
To make sure critical pods (control-plane add-ons, ingress, monitoring, a latency-critical service) can always schedule — a higher-priority Pending pod can preempt (evict) lower-priority running pods to make room. Use it with low-priority classes on batch/best-effort work. Risks: preemption causes churn and can cascade (evicted pods re-schedule and maybe preempt others); a mis-set high priority on a large or crash-looping deployment can repeatedly evict everything else; and preemption ignores PDBs only as a last resort but still disrupts. Mitigations: reserve high priority for a small set, use preemptionPolicy: Never where you want priority ordering without eviction, and monitor preemption events.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which pod field does the scheduler use to decide if a pod fits on a node?
spec.containers[].resources.requests (CPU and memory). The scheduler sums requests of existing pods and checks the new pod's requests fit in the node's allocatable capacity.
What makes a pod land on a "tainted" node?
A matching toleration in the pod spec (key/value/effect). Without it, a node with a NoSchedule taint won't accept the pod.

Intermediate core

You have GPU nodes, general nodes, and a batch workload that should only use spare capacity. Design the scheduling.
GPU nodes: taint them nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule so only GPU workloads land there; GPU pods get a matching toleration and node affinity to the GPU instance-type label (so a tolerating-but-non-GPU pod doesn't sneak on), plus resources.limits["nvidia.com/gpu"]: 1 which the device plugin schedules against. Label + taint via the node pool config so new GPU nodes inherit it. General nodes: default; normal services use requests + topology spread across zones/nodes + PDBs. Batch "spare capacity only": give batch pods a low PriorityClass (below all online services) so when an online service needs room, the scheduler preempts batch pods; set batch resources.requests modest but real (so accounting is right) and a hard CPU limit so a batch job can't hog cores; add preemptionPolicy default (preemptable). Keep batch off the GPU nodes (no toleration) and optionally off a set of latency-critical nodes via another taint. Consider a dedicated "batch" node pool that the Cluster Autoscaler scales aggressively down to zero when idle, with batch pods node-affine to it, so batch runs on cheap/spot capacity and online workloads aren't disturbed at all. Add topologySpreadConstraints for the online services and a Descheduler to rebalance after autoscaler churn. Net: taints isolate GPU (and optionally latency-critical) pools; low priority makes batch yield to online work; a scale-to-zero spot node pool with node affinity gives batch "spare capacity" semantics without preemption noise.
Half your pods for one Deployment are Pending after a zone outage. Why, and how would you have designed to avoid it?
If you used topologySpreadConstraints (or anti-affinity) with whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule across topology.kubernetes.io/zone and one zone is gone, the constraint can't be satisfied for the pods that "should" be in the dead zone, so they stay Pending — the scheduler is doing what you told it. Also possible: the surviving zones don't have spare capacity (and the Cluster Autoscaler can't add nodes there fast/at all), or PVCs are pinned to the dead zone. Better design: (1) use whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway for zone spread (soft) so pods pack into surviving zones during an outage, while keeping hostname spread hard; or set minDomains and accept skew during degradation. (2) Run enough replicas and reserve enough headroom (or fast autoscaling with node pools in every zone) that N-1 zones can hold 100% of traffic. (3) Use nodeAffinity preferred (not required) for zone, and PodDisruptionBudgets so voluntary disruptions don't compound. (4) For stateful sets, replicate data across zones so losing one zone's PVCs isn't fatal. (5) Load-test the failover: shift all traffic to N-1 zones and confirm capacity + autoscaling keep up. The principle: spread for resilience in steady state, but make the constraint degrade gracefully (soft) so an outage doesn't turn "spread" into "refuse to run."

Advanced deep

Design node-pool topology, scheduling policy, and bin-packing strategy for a cluster running latency-critical services, batch jobs, GPU ML, and stateful databases, on a mix of on-demand and spot instances.
Node pools (each = a label + a taint so nothing lands there by accident): (a) system on-demand, small, for control-plane add-ons/ingress/monitoring (critical PriorityClass, PDBs); (b) online on-demand, right-sized instance types, for latency-critical services; (c) batch-spot, aggressive scale-to-zero, spot/preemptible, for batch/async; (d) gpu on-demand (or spot for interruptible training), tainted for GPU; (e) db on-demand, local-NVMe or high-IOPS EBS, tainted, one instance family, spread across zones. Scheduling policy: every workload has real requests. Online services: requests ~ p95 usage, generous or no CPU limit (avoid throttle), Guaranteed/Burstable QoS, topologySpreadConstraints hard on hostname + soft on zone, PDBs, high-ish PriorityClass, node affinity to online. Batch: node affinity to batch-spot, low PriorityClass (preemptable), hard CPU limits, tolerate spot-termination taint, checkpoint/resume so a spot reclaim isn't fatal, and a smaller terminationGracePeriod. GPU: toleration + node affinity to gpu, nvidia.com/gpu limits, MIG/time-slicing config if sharing; interruptible training on spot GPU with checkpointing, inference on on-demand GPU. Databases: node affinity + toleration for db, anti-affinity + zone spread so no two replicas share a node/zone, PDB minAvailable, Retain volumes, never on spot. Bin-packing: use the scheduler's NodeResourcesFit with a MostAllocated (bin-pack) score for the batch-spot pool (pack tight so the autoscaler can remove nodes) and LeastAllocated / balanced for the online and db pools (spread for headroom and failure isolation) — configure per-pool via a scheduler profile or scheduler-plugins, or run Karpenter which provisions right-sized nodes per pending-pod shape and consolidates. Autoscaling: Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter per pool with different aggressiveness (batch: scale to zero fast; online: keep warm headroom for spikes and zone failover; db: fixed or slow). Overprovisioning pods (low-priority pause pods) on the online pool to keep spare nodes warm for fast scale-out. Spot handling: node-termination handler to cordon+drain on the ~2-min notice, spread spot across instance types/zones to reduce correlated reclaim, only interruptible workloads on spot, PDBs respected during drain. Rebalancing: Descheduler (or Karpenter consolidation) to undo fragmentation after scale events, respecting PDBs and priorities. Guardrails: ResourceQuota/LimitRange per namespace, admission policy requiring requests + a PriorityClass + node affinity for anything on spot/gpu, and monitoring of Pending reasons, preemption rate, throttling on online services, spot reclaim rate, and node utilisation per pool. Net: isolate workload classes into tainted node pools, per-pool scheduling profiles (spread for online/db, bin-pack for batch), priority so batch yields to online, spot only for checkpointable work with drain handling, PDBs + zone spread for resilience, and Karpenter/Cluster-Autoscaler + Descheduler tuned per pool for cost without starving latency-critical services.

HPA, VPA & Cluster Autoscaler

HPA changes how many pods, VPA changes how big each pod, Cluster Autoscaler changes how many nodes.

Notes

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)

What / how. A controller that periodically reads a metric for a Deployment/StatefulSet's pods and sets replicas to keep the metric near a target: desired = ceil(current * currentMetric / targetMetric). CPU/memory come from metrics-server; custom/external metrics come from an adapter (Prometheus Adapter, KEDA, a cloud metrics adapter).

apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: { name: api }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: api }
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 30
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 65 } }
    - type: Pods                       # per-pod custom metric
      pods: { metric: { name: http_requests_per_second }, target: { type: AverageValue, averageValue: "200" } }
  behavior:
    scaleUp:   { stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0,   policies: [{ type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 30 }] }
    scaleDown: { stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300, policies: [{ type: Pods, value: 1, periodSeconds: 60 }] }
  • CPU-Utilization is a percentage of the pod's request — so HPA only works well if requests are set sensibly.
  • behavior: scale up fast, scale down slow (long stabilizationWindowSeconds) to avoid flapping.
  • Pick a metric that reflects load and is proportional to replicas — RPS or queue depth per pod beats CPU for IO-bound apps. KEDA adds event-source scalers (Kafka lag, SQS depth, cron, Prometheus queries) and scale-to-zero.

Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA)

What / why. Observes actual CPU/memory usage and recommends (or applies) better requests/limits. Modes: Off (recommendations only — the safe default), Initial (set on pod creation), Auto/Recreate (evict + recreate pods with new requests — disruptive; in-place resize is landing). Use for right-sizing, batch jobs, and single-replica/stateful workloads that can't scale out.

apiVersion: autoscaling.k8s.io/v1
kind: VerticalPodAutoscaler
metadata: { name: worker }
spec:
  targetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: worker }
  updatePolicy: { updateMode: "Off" }       # start here: read the recommendation, apply manually
  resourcePolicy:
    containerPolicies: [{ containerName: "*", minAllowed: { cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi },
