                          maxAllowed: { cpu: 2, memory: 2Gi } }]
$ kubectl describe vpa worker              # Recommendation: target / lowerBound / upperBound

Don't run HPA (on CPU/mem) and VPA in Auto on the same workload — HPA scales replicas based on utilisation-of-request while VPA changes the request, and they oscillate. HPA-on-custom-metrics + VPA is OK; so is VPA in Off/Initial.

Cluster Autoscaler (CA) / Karpenter

  • Cluster Autoscaler: watches for pods that are Pending because no node has room, and adds a node to a node group whose template would let them schedule; removes nodes that are under-utilised and whose pods can move elsewhere (respecting PDBs, local storage, and "do-not-evict" annotations). Works with cloud node groups / ASGs.
  • Karpenter (AWS, now broader): instead of fixed node groups, it looks at the exact resource shape of pending pods and provisions right-sized nodes (any instance type that fits, spot or on-demand), and consolidates — replacing/removing nodes to bin-pack cheaper. Faster and cheaper than CA in practice.
  • Scale-down is conservative: a node is removed only if it's been under-utilised for a while and every pod on it can be rescheduled without violating a PDB.
# make HPA + CA responsive: keep warm headroom with low-priority "pause" pods
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata: { name: overprovisioning }
value: -10
globalDefault: false
---
# a Deployment of pause containers at this priority reserves a node's worth of capacity;
# when real pods need room, they preempt the pause pods (instant), and CA adds a node behind.

Making it hang together

  • HPA needs somewhere to put new pods → run the Cluster Autoscaler (or Karpenter). Node provisioning takes 1–5 min, so keep warm headroom (overprovisioning pods, or CA --scale-down-utilization-threshold tuned) for fast spikes.
  • Set minReplicas for baseline + failover capacity; maxReplicas as a cost guardrail; PodDisruptionBudget so scale-down and node drains don't take a service to zero.
  • Metrics pipeline must be healthy: no metrics-server → HPA shows <unknown> and won't scale. Alert on HPA ScalingLimited / stuck at maxReplicas.
  • For event-driven and scale-to-zero (workers, consumers), use KEDA.
Cheat Sheet
  • HPA: sets replicas to keep a metric near target. desired = ceil(current * cur/target). CPU/mem via metrics-server; custom/external via an adapter or KEDA. CPU target is % of the request — set requests well.
  • HPA behavior: scale up fast (short/zero stabilization), down slow (300s) to stop flapping. Prefer a load-proportional metric (RPS / queue-per-pod) over CPU for IO-bound apps.
  • VPA: right-sizes requests/limits from observed usage. Modes: Off (recommend), Initial, Auto/Recreate (disruptive). For right-sizing, batch, single-replica/stateful.
  • Never HPA-on-CPU/mem + VPA-Auto on the same workload — they oscillate. HPA-on-custom-metrics + VPA is fine.
  • Cluster Autoscaler: adds a node when pods are Pending for lack of room; removes under-utilised nodes if their pods can move (PDB-aware). Karpenter: provisions right-sized nodes per pending-pod shape + consolidates — faster/cheaper.
  • HPA needs CA behind it. Node provisioning is 1–5 min → keep warm headroom (low-priority overprovisioning pods).
  • Guardrails: minReplicas (baseline + failover), maxReplicas (cost), PDBs (don't hit zero), healthy metrics pipeline (no metrics-server → HPA <unknown>).
  • Event-driven / scale-to-zero → KEDA.
Q&A
What are the three kinds of autoscaling and what does each change?
HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) changes the number of pod replicas based on a metric. VPA (Vertical Pod Autoscaler) changes each pod's CPU/memory requests/limits based on observed usage. Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter changes the number of nodes so pods have somewhere to run. HPA and CA are the common pair; VPA is for right-sizing and workloads that can't scale out.
Your HPA shows TARGETS: <unknown>/65% and never scales. Why?
The HPA can't read the metric. For CPU/memory targets that means metrics-server isn't installed or isn't healthy (check kubectl top pods — if that fails, so does the HPA). For custom/external metrics it means the metrics adapter (Prometheus Adapter, KEDA, cloud adapter) is missing or the metric name/labels don't match. Also check the pods have CPU requests set (Utilization is a percentage of request — no request, no percentage) and RBAC lets the HPA controller reach the metrics API.
Why shouldn't you run HPA and VPA together on the same Deployment?
If both act on CPU/memory they fight. HPA scales replicas to keep utilisation (usage ÷ request) near target; VPA changes the request based on usage. VPA lowers the request → utilisation appears higher → HPA adds replicas → per-pod load drops → VPA lowers the request again … oscillation, churn, and possibly cost blowout. Safe combinations: HPA on a custom metric (RPS, queue depth) that VPA doesn't touch, plus VPA for right-sizing; or VPA in Off/Initial mode (recommendations / set-once) alongside HPA.
HPA scales pods but they sit Pending for minutes. What's missing and how do you smooth it?
The Cluster Autoscaler (or Karpenter) — new pods need node capacity, and adding a cloud node takes 1–5 minutes (boot, join, image pull). Smooth it: (1) run CA/Karpenter and make sure the node group has headroom in max size and matching instance types; (2) keep warm spare capacity via low-priority "overprovisioning" pause pods that real pods preempt instantly, with CA adding a node behind them; (3) tune CA scale-down to be less eager so it doesn't remove the headroom; (4) set the HPA to scale up aggressively (short stabilization, 100%/30s policy) so it asks for capacity early; (5) pre-warm images (DaemonSet or node image with the app baked in) to cut pull time.
What metric should an HPA use for a latency-sensitive HTTP API, and why not just CPU?
Prefer a load-proportional metric: requests-per-second per pod, or in-flight requests / concurrency per pod, or (if there's a queue) queue depth per pod — targeted at a value that keeps p99 within SLO with headroom. CPU is a poor proxy for an IO-bound API: it can stay low while latency climbs because pods are waiting on downstreams, and CPU spikes from GC or batch work trigger scaling that doesn't help. If you must use CPU, target a conservative utilisation (e.g. 50–60%) so there's slack for bursts, and combine with a latency-based scaler (custom metric / KEDA Prometheus scaler on p95). Also scale up fast and down slow, and keep minReplicas high enough to absorb a sudden spike before new pods are ready.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does the HPA adjust?
The replica count of its target (Deployment/StatefulSet/ReplicaSet), to keep an observed metric near a target value.
What triggers the Cluster Autoscaler to add a node?
One or more pods that are Pending because no existing node has enough allocatable capacity (or matching topology) for them, and adding a node from a scalable node group would let them schedule.

Intermediate core

Design autoscaling for a queue-consumer worker fleet that should scale to zero when idle and burst on backlog.
Use KEDA with the appropriate queue scaler (Kafka lag, SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessages, RabbitMQ queue length, or a Prometheus query on backlog). A ScaledObject targets the worker Deployment with minReplicaCount: 0, maxReplicaCount: N, and a trigger like "messages per replica = 30" so desired replicas ≈ backlog / 30. KEDA activates from 0 when the metric crosses an activation threshold and, under the hood, creates a normal HPA for the >0 range. Configure cooldownPeriod (how long to wait before scaling back toward 0) and the HPA behavior to scale up fast, down slow, so a brief backlog dip doesn't kill all workers mid-batch. Pair with the Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter on a dedicated (possibly spot) node pool the workers are node-affine to, scaled to zero when there are no worker pods — so idle really means zero cost. Make workers idempotent and handle SIGTERM (finish or safely requeue the in-flight message) since scale-down and spot reclaim will kill them mid-work; use visibility-timeout / consumer-group semantics so a killed worker's message is redelivered. Add a small minReplicaCount (1–2) if cold-start latency on the first message matters, or accept the KEDA activation delay + node boot for true scale-to-zero. Monitor backlog age (not just depth), per-replica throughput, and scale events; alert if backlog age grows while at maxReplicaCount (need more max, bigger workers, or a downstream bottleneck).
Costs doubled after enabling autoscaling. Where do you look?
(1) maxReplicas too high + a bad metric — HPA scaling on CPU that spikes from GC/batch, or a per-pod target set too low, so it scales far beyond real need; check HPA events and the metric vs replica history. (2) Flapping — short scale-down stabilization causing scale up/down churn, each cycle possibly adding nodes; set a long scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds. (3) Cluster Autoscaler not scaling down — nodes stuck because pods can't move: no PDB headroom, pods with local storage / hostPath, restrictive anti-affinity, kube-system pods without PDBs, or the safe-to-evict: false annotation; also --scale-down-utilization-threshold too low. (4) Overprovisioning pods reserving more headroom than intended (wrong size/replica count). (5) Wrong instance types — CA node group uses expensive on-demand where spot or a smaller type would do; move to Karpenter for right-sized + spot + consolidation. (6) VPA in Auto bumping requests, which then reduces bin-packing density and forces more nodes. (7) Fragmentation — many partially-full nodes after scale events; add a Descheduler / Karpenter consolidation. (8) minReplicas raised for every service "to be safe." Fixes: right-size requests, choose load-proportional metrics with sane targets, cap maxReplicas, tune scale-down, ensure PDBs allow consolidation, use spot + Karpenter, and put a cost dashboard + alert (spend vs. request-utilisation) in place.

Advanced deep

Design an end-to-end autoscaling architecture for a platform with spiky user-facing services, steady internal APIs, batch pipelines, and cost pressure — covering metric choice, layering, headroom, and failure modes.
Layering: HPA (replicas) + Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter (nodes) as the core pair; VPA in Off/recommendation mode feeding a periodic right-sizing process (or Initial for batch); KEDA for event-driven and scale-to-zero. Per-workload class: user-facing spiky — HPA on a load-proportional custom metric (RPS or concurrency per pod, target set to hold p99 SLO with ~30–40% headroom), plus a secondary CPU cap so a pathological case still scales; aggressive scale-up behavior, conservative scale-down; high minReplicas for baseline + N-1 zone failover; PDBs. Steady internal APIs — HPA on CPU or RPS with modest headroom, low minReplicas, longer stabilization; VPA recommendations to right-size requests quarterly. Batch — KEDA (queue/cron) scale-to-zero on a dedicated spot node pool, low PriorityClass so it yields to online work, idempotent + SIGTERM-safe, VPA Initial to size each job. Nodes: Karpenter with multiple provisioners — on-demand for online/db (spread across zones, warm headroom), spot for batch and interruptible workers (diversified instance types, node-termination handler), consolidation on. Overprovisioning pause pods at negative priority sized to one node's worth per critical pool so spikes preempt instantly while a node is added (1–5 min). Headroom & speed: pre-pulled images (baked node image or a warming DaemonSet); HPA sync/stabilization tuned; CA/Karpenter given enough max and permissions; keep cluster utilisation target ~65–75% so there's slack. Cost controls: maxReplicas per HPA as a hard ceiling with an alert on "pinned at max"; spot + consolidation; scale-to-zero for anything that can; a dashboard of spend vs request-utilisation vs actual-utilisation per namespace, and an alert when they diverge; ResourceQuota/LimitRange per team; admission policy requiring requests + a PriorityClass. Failure modes to design for: (1) metrics pipeline down → HPA freezes at last count (acceptable) — monitor metrics-server/adapter health and alert; consider a fallback CPU metric. (2) Thundering scale-down after a spike → long scale-down stabilization + PDBs + descheduler discipline. (3) Node add too slow for the spike → overprovisioning pods + higher minReplicas + burst into idle capacity (no tight CPU limits on online). (4) HPA + VPA oscillation → never both on CPU/mem for the same workload. (5) Autoscaler can't scale down (stuck nodes) → PDBs on kube-system, no hostPath/local-storage on movable pods, safe-to-evict set correctly. (6) Spot mass-reclaim → instance diversification, only interruptible workloads on spot, on-demand fallback provisioner. (7) Zone outage → minReplicas and node headroom sized so N-1 zones carry 100%, soft zone spread so pods pack into survivors. (8) Cascading preemption from a mis-set priority → small high-priority set, monitor preemption rate. Validation: load-test each class to confirm scale-up keeps p99 within SLO and that a zone/spot-pool loss is survivable; chaos-test autoscaler behaviour. Net: HPA-on-load-metric + Karpenter with per-class provisioners, VPA for right-sizing not live control, KEDA for event/zero, overprovisioning + pre-pulled images for spike latency, hard max + spot + consolidation + a spend/utilisation dashboard for cost, and explicit handling for metrics outage, slow node add, oscillation, stuck scale-down, spot reclaim, and zone loss.

RBAC, Service Accounts & Pod Security

Who can call the API (RBAC + ServiceAccounts), and what a pod is allowed to do to the node/kernel (Pod Security + admission).

Notes

RBAC — who can call the API

  • Role (namespaced) / ClusterRole (cluster-wide) = a list of rules: apiGroups × resources × verbs (get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete…), optionally resourceNames.
  • RoleBinding (namespaced) / ClusterRoleBinding = grants a Role/ClusterRole to subjects: a User, a Group, or a ServiceAccount. A RoleBinding can reference a ClusterRole to reuse it in one namespace.
  • Rules are additive and purely allow — there are no deny rules; if nothing grants it, it's denied.
# read-only pods+logs in one namespace, for a CI service account
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata: { namespace: shop, name: pod-reader }
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
kind: RoleBinding
metadata: { namespace: shop, name: ci-can-read }
roleRef: { apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io, kind: Role, name: pod-reader }
subjects: [{ kind: ServiceAccount, name: ci, namespace: shop }]

$ kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:ci -n shop   # -> yes
$ kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:ci             # -> no

ServiceAccounts & pod identity

  • Every pod runs as a ServiceAccount (the namespace's default unless you set serviceAccountName). If the pod talks to the API, it uses that SA's token.
  • Modern tokens are bound, short-lived, audience-scoped projected volumes (auto-rotated) — not the old forever-Secret.
  • If a pod never calls the API, set automountServiceAccountToken: false (on the pod or the SA) so a compromised pod has no cluster credential.
  • Cloud identity federation: bind the SA to a cloud IAM role — IRSA (EKS), Workload Identity (GKE), Managed Identity (AKS) — so the pod gets short-lived cloud creds with no static secret.

Least privilege in practice

  • Don't grant cluster-admin to humans or CI. Start from a narrow Role and add verbs when something legitimately breaks.
  • Avoid wildcards (resources: ["*"], verbs: ["*"]). Beware secrets read, pods/exec, impersonate, escalate/bind, and create on pods (can mount any secret / run privileged) — those are effectively admin.
  • Prefer Groups for humans (mapped from your IdP via OIDC), ServiceAccounts for workloads and CI, each scoped to one namespace.
  • Audit with kubectl auth can-i --list, and tools like rbac-lookup, kubectl-who-can, rakkess.

Pod Security Standards & admission

LevelAllows
privilegedAnything — no restrictions.
baselineBlocks the worst: no privileged, no host namespaces, no hostPath (mostly), limited caps, no host ports (mostly).
restrictedHardened: runAsNonRoot, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, drop ALL caps (allow only NET_BIND_SERVICE), seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault, read-only rootfs encouraged, no host anything.
# Pod Security Admission: label the namespace with a level + mode
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: shop
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted      # reject non-compliant pods
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted          # kubectl warning
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted         # audit log entry
# a compliant securityContext:
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 10001
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }
  capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
  • Built-in Pod Security Admission covers the standard levels per namespace. For anything beyond that — require resource limits, block a registry, enforce labels, mandate a runtimeClass, restrict image tags — use a policy engine: Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper.
  • Admission has two phases: mutating (inject defaults, sidecars, labels) then validating (accept/reject). Policy engines run as validating (and optionally mutating) webhooks.
Cheat Sheet
  • Role/ClusterRole = rules (apiGroups×resources×verbs). RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding = grant a role to a User/Group/ServiceAccount. Additive, allow-only, no deny.
  • RoleBinding can bind a ClusterRole to scope a reusable role into one namespace.
  • Pods run as a ServiceAccount (namespace default unless set); token is bound + short-lived + projected. Set automountServiceAccountToken: false if unused.
  • Cloud creds without secrets: bind the SA via IRSA / GKE Workload Identity / AKS Managed Identity.
  • Dangerous grants: secrets get, pods/exec, pods create, impersonate, escalate/bind, wildcards — treat as admin.
  • Test: kubectl auth can-i <verb> <res> --as=system:serviceaccount:ns:sa; --list to enumerate.
  • Pod Security Standards: privileged / baseline / restricted; enforce via namespace labels (pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce|warn|audit).
  • Beyond PSA: Kyverno / OPA Gatekeeper for custom policy. Admission = mutating then validating webhooks.
Q&A
How do a Role and a RoleBinding relate?
A Role defines what may be done (verbs on resources) in a namespace. A RoleBinding defines who gets it — it links one or more subjects (User, Group, ServiceAccount) to a Role (or a ClusterRole, to reuse it namespace-scoped). Neither does anything alone; the binding is what activates the permissions for those subjects.
There are no deny rules in RBAC. How do you restrict something?
By not granting it. RBAC is purely additive allow-lists — a subject can do exactly the union of what all their bindings grant, and nothing else. To "restrict," you give narrow roles (specific verbs, specific resources, sometimes specific resourceNames) and never bind broad ones. If you need actual deny semantics (e.g. "no one may delete this namespace"), that's an admission policy (Kyverno/Gatekeeper) job, not RBAC.
Why is granting create on pods almost as powerful as cluster-admin?
Because a pod spec can mount any Secret in the namespace, run as root, use hostPath to read the node's filesystem, set hostNetwork/hostPID, or (if allowed) privileged: true — so whoever can create pods can craft one that exfiltrates every secret or escapes to the node. Same class of risk: pods/exec (run commands in existing pods), impersonate, and escalate/bind (grant yourself more RBAC). Pod Security Admission / policy engines are what actually constrain what those created pods may request.
A pod doesn't need to talk to the Kubernetes API. What should you configure and why?
Set automountServiceAccountToken: false (on the pod, or on its ServiceAccount so it applies to all pods using it). By default a projected SA token is mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/; if the pod is compromised, that token is a cluster credential an attacker can use (scoped to whatever RBAC the SA has — and the default SA often has more than you think, or can be a stepping stone). Removing the mount eliminates that credential entirely for workloads that don't need the API.
What's the difference between Pod Security Admission and Kyverno/Gatekeeper?
Pod Security Admission is built in and enforces the three fixed Pod Security Standards (privileged/baseline/restricted) per namespace via labels — it only constrains pod security fields and has no customization. Kyverno / OPA Gatekeeper are general admission-policy engines (webhooks) where you write arbitrary rules over any resource: require resource limits, forbid :latest tags, mandate certain labels/annotations, restrict registries, require a signed image, enforce a runtimeClass, auto-inject defaults (mutating), generate related objects, etc. Use PSA for the baseline and a policy engine for everything org-specific; they compose.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What identity does a pod use when it calls the Kubernetes API?
Its ServiceAccount (the namespace's default SA unless spec.serviceAccountName is set), via a projected, short-lived token mounted into the pod.
How do you check whether a service account can list secrets in a namespace?
kubectl auth can-i list secrets -n <ns> --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>. Add --list to enumerate everything the SA can do.

Intermediate core

Design RBAC for a multi-team cluster: platform team, per-team developers, per-team CI, and read-only auditors.
Namespaces per team (or per team+env) as the isolation unit. Platform team: a small group bound to cluster-admin (or a slightly reduced ClusterRole), gated behind SSO + MFA + audit, ideally with just-in-time elevation rather than standing access. Developers: an IdP group per team, mapped via OIDC to a Kubernetes Group, bound (RoleBinding in that team's namespace(s)) to a curated ClusterRole like edit minus dangerous verbs — typically allow CRUD on Deployments/Services/ConfigMaps/Ingress/HPA/PDB and pods/log, pods/exec only in non-prod (or behind break-glass in prod), deny direct Secret reads (use External Secrets / sealed), no RBAC/quota/namespace edits. CI: one ServiceAccount per team per environment, RoleBinding scoped to that namespace with exactly the verbs the pipeline needs (apply/patch on the app's kinds, get on rollout status), no cluster scope, token short-lived (or OIDC federation from the CI system so there's no long-lived token at all). Auditors: an IdP group bound to the built-in view ClusterRole via ClusterRoleBinding (read everything, all namespaces) — but note view historically could read Secrets in some versions; use a custom read-only ClusterRole that excludes secrets and */exec. Guardrails: admission policy (Kyverno) to prevent creating ClusterRoleBindings to cluster-admin, to require the edit-derived role not raw edit, and to block escalate/impersonate grants; ResourceQuota + LimitRange + NetworkPolicy per namespace; Pod Security Admission restricted enforced per namespace. Review: periodic rbac-lookup/kubectl-who-can reports, alert on new bindings to powerful roles, and everything as reviewed manifests in git.
A namespace is labelled pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted and a team's Deployment now fails to create pods. What are the likely violations and fixes?
restricted rejects a pod spec unless it: runs as non-root (runAsNonRoot: true and a non-zero runAsUser, or the image already has a non-root USER), sets allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, drops ALL capabilities (may re-add only NET_BIND_SERVICE), sets seccompProfile.type to RuntimeDefault (or Localhost), uses no host namespaces / host ports / hostPath, and mounts volumes only of allowed types. Typical failures: the image runs as root and there's no securityContext; a sidecar (Istio init, some agents) needs NET_ADMIN (needs an exception or a CNI-based mesh); a hostPath mount for logs (switch to a sidecar reading an emptyDir or node log agent as a DaemonSet in a privileged namespace); binding to port 80 (grant NET_BIND_SERVICE or use a high port). Fixes: add the compliant securityContext (pod + per-container), make the image non-root and fix file ownership, replace hostPath, and for genuinely privileged components run them in a dedicated namespace at baseline/privileged with tight RBAC and NetworkPolicy rather than loosening the whole app namespace. Use the warn/audit labels first to find all violations before flipping enforce.

Advanced deep

Design the full authn/authz/admission security posture for a shared production cluster, and how you'd roll it out to teams already running workloads.
Authn: humans via OIDC from the corporate IdP (short-lived tokens, MFA, groups carried as claims) — no static kubeconfigs, no shared admin cert; workloads via bound ServiceAccount tokens; CI via OIDC federation (GitHub/GitLab OIDC → short-lived K8s or cloud creds), not long-lived SA secrets. Disable anonymous auth; restrict the API server to a private endpoint + bastion/VPN. Authz (RBAC): namespace-per-team(-env); no standing cluster-admin for people (JIT elevation with expiry + audit); curated roles derived from edit/view minus dangerous verbs (no raw Secret reads, no exec in prod without break-glass, no RBAC/quota edits); per-team/per-env CI ServiceAccounts scoped to their namespace with least verbs; auditors on a custom read-only ClusterRole excluding secrets/exec. Regular automated RBAC diff/report; alert on new powerful bindings. Admission: enable API server audit logging (metadata+ for sensitive verbs) to a SIEM; Pod Security Admission enforce restricted per app namespace (privileged components isolated in their own namespaces); a policy engine (Kyverno) for org rules — require requests/limits + a PriorityClass; disallow :latest, unpinned/unsigned images, non-allow-listed registries; require images by digest + cosign verification (via Ratify/Kyverno + Sigstore); block hostPath/host namespaces/NodePort except where whitelisted; require a scan attestation not older than N days; auto-inject default securityContext, labels, and automountServiceAccountToken: false where possible (mutating); enforce NetworkPolicy presence (default-deny). RuntimeClass=kata/gvisor required for workloads tagged untrusted. Secrets: KMS encryption at rest; External Secrets / workload identity so raw secrets aren't in git or long-lived. Node/runtime: hardened minimal OS, current kernel, containerd, Falco/Tetragon for escape/anomaly detection, node auto-recycle, no cloud metadata access from pods (IMDSv2 hop limit / netpol), per-pod cloud identity. Rollout to running teams: (1) publish the standard + golden namespace template (with quota, limitrange, netpol, PSA labels, SA settings) + Dockerfile/manifest templates; (2) turn on audit logging and run all Kyverno policies + PSA in audit/warn mode cluster-wide; build a per-team compliance dashboard (which workloads violate which rule); (3) fix the platform's own workloads first as the reference implementation; (4) office hours + PRs to help teams remediate — most fixes are "add securityContext", "add resource requests", "pin the image", "add a NetworkPolicy"; (5) enforce in new namespaces immediately, and give existing namespaces a deadline with a documented, owner-attributed, time-boxed exception process; (6) enforce the CI image gates (scan/sign/registry) on new images now, existing by the deadline; (7) track exception count trending down and report to leadership. Keep a tested break-glass path (JIT cluster-admin with automatic expiry + alerting) so an incident isn't blocked by the very controls you added. Net: OIDC + short-lived tokens everywhere, least-privilege namespaced RBAC with JIT admin, PSA restricted + Kyverno for supply-chain/policy, KMS secrets + workload identity, runtime detection, and an audit-then-enforce rollout with a compliance dashboard, migration help, and a bounded exception process.

NetworkPolicies & Pod-to-Pod Firewalls

By default every pod can talk to every pod; a NetworkPolicy that selects a pod flips it to default-deny for the directions it specifies.

Notes

The default and the flip

  • No NetworkPolicy selects a pod → all ingress and egress allowed (the "flat network" default).
  • Any policy selects a pod → for the directions that policy lists (policyTypes: [Ingress] and/or [Egress]), traffic is denied unless an allow rule matches. Directions not listed stay open.
  • Policies are additive (union of allows) and namespaced. Rules select peers by podSelector, namespaceSelector, or ipBlock (CIDR + except), plus ports.
# default-deny ALL ingress + egress in a namespace (the recommended baseline)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: default-deny, namespace: shop }
spec:
  podSelector: {}                 # selects every pod in the namespace
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]  # ...with no rules -> deny both directions

Typical allow rules

# db: only accept 5432 from pods labelled app=api in this namespace
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: db-from-api, namespace: shop }
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: db } }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api } } }]
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
---
# api egress: allow DNS + the db + HTTPS to the internet, deny the rest
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: api-egress, namespace: shop }
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to: [{ namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system } },
             podSelector: { matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns } } }]
      ports: [{ protocol: UDP, port: 53 }, { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }]
    - to: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: db } } }]
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
    - to: [{ ipBlock: { cidr: 0.0.0.0/0, except: [10.0.0.0/8, 169.254.169.254/32] } }]
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 443 }]

Gotchas

  • Forgetting egress DNS — a default-deny-egress policy breaks name resolution; you must explicitly allow UDP/TCP 53 to CoreDNS. This is the #1 "why is nothing working" cause.
  • Cross-namespace needs namespaceSelector (label the namespace; kubernetes.io/metadata.name is auto-added). A bare podSelector only matches the policy's own namespace.
  • Ingress from outside the cluster — an ingress controller's traffic comes from the controller's pods (allow by their label/namespace), or from node IPs if hostNetwork; LoadBalancer/NodePort source may be a node IP after SNAT.
  • Return traffic is allowed automatically (stateful) — you don't need a matching reverse rule for replies.
  • No L7 — can't match HTTP paths, methods, or gRPC services. For that use a CNI with L7 policy (Cilium) or a service mesh.
  • Ports by name and endPort (ranges) are supported on recent versions/CNIs.

Beyond core NetworkPolicy

  • Cilium (CiliumNetworkPolicy) — identity-based (not IP-based) policy, L7 rules (HTTP method/path, Kafka topics, DNS names in egress), cluster-wide policies, and default-deny modes; eBPF enforcement.
  • Calico (GlobalNetworkPolicy, tiers, order, deny rules, host endpoints) — more expressive than core, including explicit deny and policy ordering.
  • Service mesh (Istio AuthorizationPolicy, Linkerd) — L7 authz on top of mTLS identity: "only web may GET /api/* on api." Complements L3/4 NetworkPolicy (defence in depth), doesn't replace it.
  • AdminNetworkPolicy (newer, cluster-scoped) — lets platform admins set guardrails that app-namespace policies can't override.
Cheat Sheet
  • Default: pod not selected by any policy = all traffic allowed. Selected by a policy = default-deny for the listed policyTypes, allow only what rules match.
  • Policies are additive, namespaced, L3/L4. Peers: podSelector, namespaceSelector, ipBlock (+ except), + ports.
  • Baseline: a podSelector: {} policy with policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress] and no rules = deny all in the namespace; then add explicit allows.
  • Always allow egress to CoreDNS (UDP/TCP 53) or a default-deny-egress breaks DNS — the classic trap.
  • Cross-namespace → namespaceSelector (namespaces are auto-labelled kubernetes.io/metadata.name). Return traffic is auto-allowed (stateful).
  • Needs an enforcing CNI (Calico/Cilium/Weave/cloud) — ignored otherwise. No L7 in core NetworkPolicy.
  • More power: Cilium (identity + L7 + DNS-name egress), Calico (global policy, deny, order), mesh AuthorizationPolicy (L7 on mTLS identity), AdminNetworkPolicy (cluster guardrails).
Q&A
What's the default network behaviour in a Kubernetes cluster, and how do you lock it down?
By default the pod network is flat — any pod can reach any other pod (and usually the internet) with no restriction. To lock it down you apply NetworkPolicies. The moment a policy selects a pod, that pod becomes default-deny for the specified directions (ingress/egress), permitting only traffic matching an allow rule. The recommended pattern is a namespace-wide default-deny (empty podSelector, both policyTypes, no rules) plus specific allow policies per app.
You applied a default-deny-egress policy and pods can't do anything. What did you forget?
DNS. A default-deny-egress policy blocks the pod's queries to CoreDNS, so every hostname lookup fails and nothing works — even though the app's actual dependencies might be allowed by IP. You must add an egress allow rule to the kube-system CoreDNS pods on UDP and TCP port 53. This is the single most common NetworkPolicy mistake.
Do NetworkPolicies work on any cluster?
No — the API objects always exist, but they're only enforced if your CNI plugin implements NetworkPolicy: Calico, Cilium, Weave Net, Antrea, and most cloud CNIs (with the policy add-on enabled) do; some minimal CNIs (plain Flannel, older kindnet) do not, and the policies are silently ignored. Always verify enforcement (apply a deny, confirm traffic is actually blocked) rather than assuming.
Can a NetworkPolicy block traffic based on HTTP path or method?
No. Core NetworkPolicy is layer 3/4 only — it matches on pod/namespace selectors, IP CIDRs, and TCP/UDP ports. For layer-7 rules ("allow GET /public/* but not POST /admin", or "only these gRPC methods") you need a CNI with L7 policy (Cilium's CiliumNetworkPolicy) or a service mesh's authorization policy (Istio AuthorizationPolicy), which enforce on mesh/proxy identity. Those layer on top of L3/4 NetworkPolicy, not instead of it.
How do you allow traffic from another namespace?
Use a namespaceSelector in the from/to block — a bare podSelector only matches pods in the policy's own namespace. Namespaces are automatically labelled kubernetes.io/metadata.name: <name>, so you can select an exact namespace, or add your own labels (e.g. tier: frontend) and select by those. You can combine namespaceSelector and podSelector in the same peer entry to mean "pods matching X in namespaces matching Y."
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

If no NetworkPolicy references a pod, what traffic can reach it?
All of it — any pod in the cluster can connect to it on any port. NetworkPolicy is opt-in; a pod is unrestricted until a policy selects it.
What must you always allow in a default-deny-egress namespace?
Egress to CoreDNS on UDP and TCP port 53 (in kube-system), or DNS resolution breaks for every pod.

Intermediate core

Design NetworkPolicies for a web -> api -> db -> cache stack with an ingress controller, default-deny everywhere.
In the app namespace, start with a default-deny policy (podSelector: {}, policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress], no rules). Then add per-tier allows: DNS — one policy selecting all pods (podSelector: {}) allowing egress to the kube-system CoreDNS pods on 53/UDP+TCP. web: ingress from the ingress-controller namespace/pods on 80/443; egress to api on its port. api: ingress from web on its port; egress to db (5432) and cache (6379), plus egress to any external APIs it calls (by ipBlock or, with Cilium, by DNS name), and 53 for DNS. db: ingress only from api on 5432; egress only DNS (and to a backup target if it pushes backups). cache: ingress only from api on 6379; egress only DNS. Ingress controller lives in its own namespace: label it, and reference it via namespaceSelector + podSelector in web's ingress rule; the controller's own egress policy allows it to reach the app namespaces' web pods. Block the metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254/32) in every egress ipBlock.except. Platform guardrail: an AdminNetworkPolicy (or Calico GlobalNetworkPolicy) denying all cross-namespace traffic except to shared services (DNS, monitoring, registry), which app policies can't override. Verify by applying and testing each blocked path (web -> db should fail; api -> db should work). Keep the policies in git next to the app manifests, and add a CI check that every app namespace has a default-deny.
An app worked fine, you added NetworkPolicies, and now intermittent failures appear only under load / only to some destinations. How do you debug?
Systematic isolation. (1) Confirm enforcement — which CNI, is NetworkPolicy actually enforced, which policies select the affected pods (kubectl describe netpol, or Cilium/Calico policy-trace tools). (2) DNS first — intermittent-under-load often means the DNS allow is missing or too narrow (only UDP not TCP 53; only one CoreDNS replica's label; NodeLocal DNSCache on a different path/IP that isn't allowed). kubectl exec and test nslookup vs direct-IP connect. (3) Egress scope — the app calls several external endpoints; your ipBlock allow covers some but not others, or the destination's IPs changed (CDN, cloud service) and your static CIDR is stale — switch to a DNS-name egress policy (Cilium) or a wider allow to a known egress proxy. (4) Cross-namespace / return path — a dependency moved namespaces, or a peer's egress policy (not your ingress) now blocks it; check both ends. (5) Ports — the app also uses a health/metrics port or a second protocol you didn't allow; probes from the kubelet (node IP) may be blocked (allow from the node CIDR or use hostNetwork-aware rules). (6) Load-related — ephemeral source ports are fine (return traffic is stateful), but conntrack table exhaustion or a CNI datapath limit under high connection churn can look like "policy drops"; check CNI/dropped-packet metrics and conntrack usage. (7) Use the CNI's flow logs / Hubble (Cilium) / Calico flow logs to see exactly which flows are denied and by which policy — that turns guesswork into a specific missing allow. Fix the specific rule, and add an observability panel for policy-denied flows so the next one is obvious.

Advanced deep

Design a zero-trust network posture for a multi-tenant cluster: segmentation, identity, egress control, L7 authz, and how it interacts with a service mesh.
Segmentation baseline: every tenant/app in its own namespace; a platform-owned AdminNetworkPolicy (or Calico GlobalNetworkPolicy tier) that denies all cross-namespace traffic by default and permits only shared infra (CoreDNS, monitoring scrape from the monitoring namespace, registry/artifact pulls, the ingress controller reaching app "web" pods). Each app namespace ships a default-deny (ingress + egress) plus explicit intra-app allows — enforced in CI (no namespace without a default-deny). Identity, not IP: use Cilium (eBPF) so policy is keyed on workload identity (derived from labels/ServiceAccount) rather than pod IPs, which churn — this also gives cluster-wide policies and works across nodes/overlays. Egress control: default-deny egress; allow DNS to CoreDNS; allow specific internal services by identity; for external destinations use DNS-aware egress (Cilium toFQDNs) or route all egress through a filtering egress gateway/proxy (allow-list of domains, TLS inspection where policy permits, logging) with a fixed source IP for partner allow-lists; block the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) everywhere and give pods scoped cloud identity instead. L7 authorization: put a service mesh (Istio, Linkerd, or Cilium's own L7) in place for mutual TLS between all pods (encrypt + cryptographically identify every connection) and L7 AuthorizationPolicy — "only web (verified SPIFFE identity) may call GET /api/v1/* on api", "only batch may publish to Kafka topic X". This is defence in depth on top of L3/4 NetworkPolicy, not a replacement: NetworkPolicy is the coarse floor that still applies to non-mesh traffic and infra, the mesh adds identity + encryption + L7. Interaction: keep them consistent — NetworkPolicy allows the ports the mesh needs (sidecar/xDS, mTLS), mesh AuthorizationPolicy expresses the fine-grained rules, and ideally generate both from one higher-level "service dependency" spec so they don't drift. Prefer an ambient / eBPF mesh to avoid the sidecar tax on a large multi-tenant cluster. Tenancy hardening: per-tenant NetworkPolicy that also blocks reaching other tenants' services and the API server (unless the workload needs it, then via a scoped SA), RBAC + ResourceQuota per namespace, and for hostile tenants a micro-VM runtime. Observability & enforcement: Hubble/Calico flow logs to a SIEM with alerts on denied flows and on new allowed flows (drift/lateral-movement detection); a CI policy check that new services declare their ingress/egress; periodic review of egress allow-lists; and chaos/verification tests that confirm tenant A genuinely cannot reach tenant B or the metadata endpoint. Guardrails app teams can't override: AdminNetworkPolicy for the cross-tenant deny and the metadata block; Kyverno to require a default-deny + mesh injection label per namespace. Net: namespace-per-tenant with a platform-enforced cross-tenant deny, identity-based (Cilium) L3/4 policy as the floor, default-deny egress with DNS-aware allow-lists or an egress proxy + metadata block, a mesh for mTLS + L7 authz on verified identity as the ceiling, both derived from one dependency spec, and flow-log-based detection of denied and newly-allowed traffic.

Logging, Metrics & Debugging Pods

Node agents ship container stdout to a log store; Prometheus scrapes metrics; kubectl describe/logs/debug and events are the first-line diagnostics.

Notes

Logging

  • Apps write structured JSON to stdout/stderr. The runtime writes it to a file on the node (/var/log/pods/…); a DaemonSet log agent (Fluent Bit, Vector, Promtail) tails those files, enriches with pod/namespace/node labels, and ships to a store (Loki, Elasticsearch, a SaaS).
  • kubectl logs only reads the current container's output; --previous for the last crashed instance; nothing after the pod is gone — hence the central store.
  • Don't run a per-pod logging sidecar unless you must (an app that can't log to stdout); it multiplies cost. Node-level collection is the norm.
$ kubectl logs deploy/api -c api --tail=200 -f --since=15m --timestamps
$ kubectl logs api-7d9f-abcde --previous          # the crashed instance
$ kubectl logs -l app=api --max-log-requests=10 --prefix   # across all pods of a label
$ stern api                                       # multi-pod tail (3rd-party)

Metrics

  • metrics-server — lightweight, in-memory, powers kubectl top and the HPA (CPU/mem). Not for dashboards/history.
  • Prometheus (usually via the kube-prometheus-stack / Prometheus Operator) — scrapes /metrics from apps, kube-state-metrics (object state: replicas, restarts, phases, PVC status), cAdvisor (per-container CPU/mem/throttle/OOM via the kubelet), and node-exporter. ServiceMonitor/PodMonitor CRs tell it what to scrape.
  • Dashboards in Grafana; alerts via PrometheusRule → Alertmanager. Traces via OpenTelemetry SDK → Collector → Tempo/Jaeger; correlate logs/metrics/traces by trace_id.
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata: { name: api, labels: { release: kube-prometheus-stack } }
spec:
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
  endpoints: [{ port: metrics, interval: 30s, path: /metrics }]

$ kubectl top pods -n shop --sort-by=memory
$ kubectl top nodes

Events & the first-line commands

$ kubectl get events -n shop --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -30
$ kubectl describe pod api-xxxx           # Events + container state + probes + mounts + node
$ kubectl get pod api-xxxx -o wide        # node, IP, restarts, age
$ kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase!=Running
$ kubectl rollout status deploy/api ; kubectl rollout history deploy/api
$ kubectl top pod api-xxxx --containers

Events are your friend but they expire (default TTL ~1h) — capture them (an event exporter to your log store) so a post-mortem hours later still has them.

Interactive debugging

# exec into a running container (needs a shell in the image)
$ kubectl exec -it api-xxxx -c api -- sh

# distroless / no shell: ephemeral debug container sharing the pod's namespaces
$ kubectl debug -it api-xxxx --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=api
# gives you curl, dig, tcpdump, ss, strace against the target's network + (with --target) pid ns

# debug a whole node
$ kubectl debug node/node-1 -it --image=busybox    # a pod with hostPath / for /host

# copy the pod with tweaks (add a shell, change command, drop the probe)
$ kubectl debug api-xxxx --copy-to=api-dbg --set-image=api=busybox -- sh

$ kubectl cp shop/api-xxxx:/app/heapdump.hprof ./heapdump.hprof   # pull an artefact
$ kubectl port-forward svc/api 8080:80                            # hit it locally

What to look at for common symptoms

SymptomCheck
Pendingdescribe pod Events: Insufficient cpu/mem, untolerated taint, unsatisfiable affinity/spread, PVC unbound / zone conflict, cluster full.
ImagePullBackOffEvents: bad tag/digest, registry auth (imagePullSecrets), rate limit, wrong architecture.
CrashLoopBackOfflogs --previous, exit code (137 OOM, 1/2 app error, 126/127 bad command), describe for OOMKilled / probe kills.
CreateContainerConfigErrorMissing ConfigMap/Secret key referenced by env/volume.
Ready but 500sApp logs, traces, downstream health; is the readiness probe meaningful?
OOMKilleddescribe (OOMKilled: true), kubectl top, cAdvisor container_memory_working_set_bytes vs limit, runtime heap config, dmesg on the node.
Node NotReadydescribe node conditions (MemoryPressure/DiskPressure/PIDPressure), kubelet + container-runtime logs (journalctl -u kubelet), CNI health.
Cheat Sheet
  • Logs: app → stdout/stderr (structured JSON) → runtime file on node → DaemonSet agent (Fluent Bit/Vector) → Loki/ES. kubectl logs is current-instance only; --previous for the crash; nothing persists after the pod.
  • Metrics: metrics-server (top + HPA, no history) vs Prometheus stack (kube-state-metrics = object state, cAdvisor = container resources/throttle/OOM, node-exporter). ServiceMonitor/PodMonitor to scrape; Grafana + Alertmanager.
  • First-line: kubectl describe pod (Events + state + probes + mounts), kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp (they expire — export them), get pods -o wide, rollout status/history, top pod --containers.
  • Interactive: exec -it; distroless → kubectl debug --image=netshoot --target=<c> (ephemeral container in the pod's namespaces); kubectl debug node/<n>; --copy-to to run a modified clone; cp / port-forward.
  • Symptom map: Pending → scheduling; ImagePullBackOff → tag/auth/arch; CrashLoopBackOff → logs --previous + exit code; ConfigError → missing CM/Secret key; OOMKilled → describe + top + heap config; Node NotReady → conditions + kubelet logs.
Q&A
Where do container logs go, and why do you need more than kubectl logs?
The container runtime writes each container's stdout/stderr to files on the node (/var/log/pods/…), and kubectl logs reads the current one (--previous for the last crashed one). But those files are rotated and deleted, and vanish when the pod is removed — no retention, no search across pods, no dashboards, no alerting, no correlation. So you run a node-level DaemonSet agent (Fluent Bit/Vector) that ships every container's logs, enriched with pod/namespace/labels, to a central store (Loki/Elasticsearch/SaaS) where you can query historically.
metrics-server vs Prometheus — what's each for?
metrics-server is a lightweight, in-memory aggregator of the kubelet's resource metrics — it powers kubectl top and the HPA (CPU/memory targets). It keeps no history and can't do custom metrics or alerting. Prometheus (usually the kube-prometheus-stack) is the real observability system: it scrapes and stores time series from app /metrics, kube-state-metrics (object state), cAdvisor (per-container CPU/mem/throttle/OOM), and node-exporter, and drives Grafana dashboards and Alertmanager alerts. You typically run both.
How do you debug a distroless pod that has no shell?
kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=<container> attaches an ephemeral container that shares the target's network (and, with --target, PID) namespaces, so you get curl/dig/tcpdump/ss/strace against the same network stack and process view without modifying the image. Other options: kubectl debug --copy-to=<name> --set-image=... to run a clone with a shell/different command, kubectl cp to pull artefacts, kubectl port-forward to reach it locally, or from the node use nsenter / /proc/<pid>/root (see the Containers skill).
A pod is CreateContainerConfigError. What does that mean?
The kubelet can't build the container's config because something it references doesn't exist — almost always a missing ConfigMap or Secret, or a missing key within one, referenced by an env.valueFrom, envFrom, or a projected/volume mount. kubectl describe pod names the exact missing object/key. Fix: create it (or fix the name/key), and note that if it's created after the pod, the pod recovers on its next sync / restart.
Kubernetes Events aren't showing the failure you're investigating from an hour ago. Why, and what's the fix?
Events have a TTL (default ~1 hour) and are stored in etcd, so old ones are garbage-collected. For post-mortems you need them persisted: run an event exporter (e.g. kubernetes-event-exporter, or Fluent Bit's kubernetes_events input) that watches the Events API and ships every event to your log store with timestamps, so you can look back days later. Also capture kubectl get events / describe output into the incident channel while debugging live.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

How do you see the logs of a container that already crashed and restarted?
kubectl logs <pod> -c <container> --previous — it returns the output of the previous (terminated) instance.
Which command shows a pod's Events, current container state, probes, and which node it's on?
kubectl describe pod <name>.

Intermediate core

A service's p99 latency spiked and some pods are restarting. Walk your investigation using kubectl + the observability stack.
(1) Scope: kubectl get pods -l app=svc -o wide — how many restarting, on which nodes, restart counts; kubectl rollout history — was there a recent deploy (correlate with the spike start in Grafana via a deploy annotation). (2) Restarts: kubectl describe pod → Last State / exit code / OOMKilled / probe failures; kubectl logs --previous for the crash reason. 137 → check memory: cAdvisor container_memory_working_set_bytes vs limit, and whether the deploy raised load or lowered the limit. Liveness-probe kills → is the probe too aggressive / checking a dependency? (3) Latency: Grafana RED dashboard — is it all pods or a subset (a bad node, a hot shard)? Error rate up too, or just latency? p99 vs p50 divergence points to tail causes: CPU throttling (cAdvisor container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods — limit too low?), GC pauses (runtime metrics), a slow downstream (traces: which span dominates), lock contention, or cache misses after the restarts dropped warm state. (4) Node: kubectl top nodes, node PSI / pressure conditions, noisy neighbour on the same node, disk IO. (5) Dependencies: is the DB/cache/downstream slow (its dashboards, traces), causing pile-up → readiness flaps → fewer endpoints → more load on the rest → more restarts (a feedback loop). (6) Mitigate: if a deploy caused it, kubectl rollout undo; if load-driven, scale up (HPA min, or manual) and check the autoscaler; if a single bad node, cordon+drain it; if CPU throttling, raise the limit. Then root-cause from logs/traces and add an alert for the leading indicator (throttle ratio, downstream latency, restart rate).
Design the logging + metrics + tracing stack for a 50-service cluster, including what to collect and how to keep costs sane.
Logs: apps emit structured JSON to stdout with a shared schema (ts, level, service, version, trace_id, span_id, request_id, tenant). Node DaemonSet (Fluent Bit or Vector) tails runtime logs, adds k8s metadata, drops or samples debug-level in prod, and ships to Loki (cheap object-storage backend, label-indexed) or an ELK/SaaS. Retention tiered: 7–14d hot for search, longer cold/compacted or to object storage for compliance. Control cost: keep label cardinality low (no request_id as a label), sample or drop noisy loggers, rate-limit per namespace, and alert on log-volume spikes. Also run an event exporter so k8s Events land in the log store. Metrics: kube-prometheus-stack — Prometheus (HA pair or Thanos/Mimir for long-term + global query) scraping via ServiceMonitor/PodMonitor: per-service RED (rate/errors/duration) from app /metrics, USE from node-exporter, object state from kube-state-metrics, container resources/throttle/OOM from cAdvisor. Recording rules for SLIs; Grafana dashboards (per-service + fleet); PrometheusRule → Alertmanager with routing by team/severity, alerting on SLO burn rate, restart/OOM spikes, throttling on latency-critical services, and pipeline health (metrics-server, scrape failures). Control cost/cardinality: cap labels, drop high-cardinality series with metricRelabelConfigs, use recording rules + downsampling (Thanos/Mimir), and set per-tenant series limits. Deploy NodeLocal DNSCache and scale CoreDNS (unrelated to obs cost but a common perf issue). Traces: OpenTelemetry SDK in every service, W3C context propagation across HTTP/gRPC/queues; OTel Collector as a DaemonSet (receive + batch + k8s attributes) feeding a gateway tier that does tail sampling — keep 100% of error and slow traces, sample the rest at a few %; export to Tempo/Jaeger (object-storage, cheap, trace-ID lookup + TraceQL). Generate span metrics (RED per service/operation) in the collector so you get always-on service graphs without extra instrumentation. Keep trace retention short (7–14d). Correlation: trace_id in every log line and as an exemplar on latency histograms, so one click goes metric → trace → logs. Ownership: the platform runs the stack; teams own their dashboards/alerts from templates; a monthly review prunes noisy alerts and right-sizes retention/sampling. Net: stdout+DaemonSet+Loki with sampling and low-cardinality labels, kube-prometheus-stack + Thanos/Mimir with cardinality controls and recording rules, OTel + tail-sampled Tempo + span metrics, all joined by trace_id — and cost kept down by sampling, low cardinality, tiered retention, and downsampling.

Advanced deep

A pod intermittently fails to reach a downstream service; it's not reproducible on demand. Design a debugging approach that captures the failure without a shell in the (distroless) image.
1. Frame it: is it DNS, TCP connect, TLS, or an application-level timeout? Look at the app's structured logs and traces first — the failing span's error and duration usually say (getaddrinfo failure vs connection refused vs deadline exceeded). Check whether failures cluster by source pod, destination pod, node, time, or load. 2. Always-on capture (so you don't need to catch it live): (a) app metrics — per-destination request rate/error/latency histograms and a counter by error type; (b) the CNI's flow logs / Cilium Hubble — records every flow and every dropped flow with the reason and the policy that dropped it; enable and dashboard denied-flow counts; (c) CoreDNS metrics + query logging (temporarily) for NXDOMAIN/SERVFAIL/latency; NodeLocal DNSCache metrics; (d) conntrack table usage on the nodes (exhaustion under connection churn looks exactly like random drops) and CNI datapath drop counters; (e) kube-proxy / IPVS metrics and EndpointSlice change rate (a flapping readiness on the destination removes it from endpoints intermittently). 3. Sidecar/ephemeral tooling without touching the image: run kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=<container> to get an ephemeral container sharing the pod's network namespace, and from there run a continuous probe loop (curl/nc to the destination every second, logging failures with timestamps) plus tcpdump -w /tmp/cap.pcap host <dest> so when it fails you have the packets; ss -s and ss -tanp to watch socket/conntrack state; dig in a loop to separate DNS from connect. Copy the pcap out with kubectl cp (from the ephemeral container's filesystem) or ship it to a volume. Alternatively deploy a small permanent "canary" pod with the same labels/policies/service account next to the workload, running the probe loop and exporting failure metrics. 4. Narrow the layer: if DNS — check the egress NetworkPolicy allows UDP and TCP 53 to all CoreDNS replicas (and NodeLocal if used), CoreDNS pod health/restarts, and ndots-driven lookup storms; if connect — check the destination's EndpointSlices during a failure (is it briefly empty?), the destination's readiness-probe flap, kube-proxy sync lag, and MTU/overlay issues (large-payload only?); if TLS — cert rotation, SNI, clock skew; if app timeout — the downstream's own latency/GC/pool-exhaustion under load. 5. Correlate: overlay the app-error timestamps with Hubble drops, CoreDNS errors, conntrack usage, EndpointSlice churn, and destination pod restarts — the one that lines up is the cause. 6. Fix + guard: e.g. add the missing DNS egress rule, raise conntrack limits / reduce connection churn with keep-alive pooling, fix the destination's readiness probe, or pin MTU; then add an alert on the leading signal (denied-flow count, conntrack %, DNS error rate, EndpointSlice-empty events) so the next occurrence is caught automatically. The theme: instrument the network path (Hubble/flow logs, DNS metrics, conntrack) for always-on evidence, and use ephemeral/canary containers for on-demand packet capture and continuous probing — the distroless image never needs a shell.

Helm, GitOps, Operators & CRDs

Package manifests with Helm, keep git as the source of truth with GitOps, and extend the API with CRDs + an operator.

Notes

Helm

  • A chart = templated manifests (templates/, Go templating), a values.yaml of defaults, Chart.yaml (name/version), and dependencies (charts/). helm install renders templates with merged values and applies them; the result is tracked as a release (revision history → helm rollback).
  • Environment differences via -f values-prod.yaml and --set. Hooks (pre-install, post-upgrade) run Jobs at lifecycle points. helm template renders without applying (great for GitOps and diffing).
  • Alternatives/complements: Kustomize (no templating — base + overlays + patches, built into kubectl -k), jsonnet, cdk8s (real code → YAML), or Helm charts rendered and then Kustomize-patched.
$ helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
$ helm install pg bitnami/postgresql -n data -f values-prod.yaml --version 15.5.1
$ helm upgrade --install api ./charts/api -n shop -f values-prod.yaml \
    --set image.tag=1.4.2 --atomic --timeout 5m       # --atomic: roll back if it fails
$ helm diff upgrade api ./charts/api -f values-prod.yaml    # (helm-diff plugin)
$ helm history api ; helm rollback api 3
$ helm template api ./charts/api -f values-prod.yaml | kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f -

GitOps (Argo CD / Flux)

  • Principle: the desired state of the cluster lives in a git repo (plain manifests, Kustomize, or Helm). A controller in the cluster continuously reconciles the cluster to match — applying changes, pruning removed resources, and reporting drift.
  • Benefits: every change is a reviewed PR (audit + rollback = git revert), the repo is the disaster-recovery source, no kubectl apply from laptops, and the cluster self-heals config drift.
  • Argo CD: an Application CR points at a repo path/chart + target cluster/namespace; a UI shows sync status and diffs; sync can be manual or automated with prune + selfHeal. Flux: a set of controllers (GitRepository, Kustomization, HelmRelease) — no central UI, more composable.
  • Image updates: a bot (Renovate, Argo CD Image Updater, Flux image automation) opens a PR bumping the image digest/tag in git; merge = deploy. App code and config both flow through git.
  • Secrets: not raw in git — Sealed Secrets, SOPS (Flux has native decryption), or External Secrets referencing a manager.
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata: { name: api, namespace: argocd }
spec:
  project: shop
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/acme/deploy
    path: apps/api/overlays/prod
    targetRevision: main
  destination: { server: https://kubernetes.default.svc, namespace: shop }
  syncPolicy:
    automated: { prune: true, selfHeal: true }
    syncOptions: [CreateNamespace=true]

CRDs & the Operator pattern

  • A CustomResourceDefinition registers a new kind (PostgresCluster, Certificate, Kafka) with an OpenAPI schema; it then behaves like a built-in resource (kubectl get, RBAC, watch).
  • An operator is a controller that watches that CR and encodes the operational runbook as code: provision the StatefulSet/Services/Secrets, handle failover and backups, do version upgrades, scale, and repair — the reconciliation loop from the "Objects & the API" topic, applied to a domain.
  • Common operators: cert-manager, Prometheus Operator, an ingress/gateway controller, database operators (CloudNativePG, Strimzi for Kafka), Crossplane (provision cloud infra via K8s CRs), external-secrets.
  • Build with Kubebuilder / Operator SDK / controller-runtime (Go), or Kopf (Python), or declaratively with the Operator Framework / Metacontroller for simpler cases.
# the whole "run me a Postgres HA cluster with backups" as one object
apiVersion: postgresql.cnpg.io/v1
kind: Cluster
metadata: { name: pg, namespace: data }
spec:
  instances: 3
  storage: { size: 50Gi, storageClass: fast-ssd }
  backup:
    barmanObjectStore: { destinationPath: s3://acme-pg-backups/pg, ... }
    retentionPolicy: "30d"
# the operator creates the StatefulSet, Services, PVCs, a primary + 2 replicas,
# manages failover, runs base backups + WAL archiving, and does minor-version upgrades.

Service meshes (where they fit)

A mesh (Istio, Linkerd, Cilium) is delivered as CRDs + an operator/control plane + a per-pod (sidecar or ambient/eBPF) dataplane. It adds mTLS between services, L7 authorization on verified identity, traffic shifting for canaries/blue-green, retries/timeouts/outlier-detection, and uniform L7 telemetry — layered on top of Services and NetworkPolicy. Adopt it when you need cluster-wide encryption/identity, fine-grained service-to-service authz, uniform resilience, or progressive delivery across many services; skip it (Services + Ingress + NetworkPolicy + app retries) if you don't — it's real operational overhead. Prefer ambient/eBPF meshes to avoid the sidecar cost.

Cheat Sheet
  • Helm: chart (templates + values.yaml + Chart.yaml + deps) → helm upgrade --install --atomic → a release with history (helm rollback). Per-env -f values-<env>.yaml. helm template to render for GitOps/diff. Kustomize = base + overlays + patches, no templating.
  • GitOps: git = desired state; Argo CD (Application CR + UI) or Flux (GitRepository/Kustomization/HelmRelease controllers) reconcile the cluster, prune removed resources, report/heal drift. Rollback = git revert. Image bumps via PR bots.
  • Secrets in GitOps: Sealed Secrets / SOPS / External Secrets — never raw.
  • CRD = new kind with a schema, acts like a built-in. Operator = a controller that reconciles the CR, encoding the ops runbook (provision, backup, failover, upgrade).
  • Build operators with Kubebuilder / Operator SDK / controller-runtime (Go) or Kopf (Python).
  • Examples: cert-manager, Prometheus Operator, CloudNativePG, Strimzi, Crossplane, external-secrets.
  • Service mesh = CRDs + control plane + dataplane; adds mTLS, L7 authz, traffic shifting, resilience, telemetry. Adopt only when you need those cluster-wide; prefer ambient/eBPF.
Q&A
What does Helm add over kubectl apply?
Templating (one chart, many environments via values), packaging + versioning + a repo to share charts, dependency management (subcharts), lifecycle hooks (pre/post install/upgrade Jobs), and release tracking with history so helm rollback reverts to a previous revision. The trade-off is Go-template complexity and a stateful "release" concept; Kustomize offers env-overlays without templating for teams that prefer that.
What is GitOps, in one sentence, and what are its main benefits?
The cluster's desired state lives in a git repo and an in-cluster controller continuously reconciles the cluster to match it. Benefits: every change is a reviewed, audited PR; rollback is git revert; the repo is the disaster-recovery source of truth; no ad-hoc kubectl apply from laptops; and configuration drift is detected and (optionally) auto-corrected.
How do image updates work in a GitOps setup — the controller doesn't watch the registry, does it?
By default no — the GitOps controller only reconciles what's in git. To deploy a new image you change the image tag/digest in git. That's usually automated: a bot (Renovate, Flux's image-automation controllers, Argo CD Image Updater) watches the registry, and when a new matching tag/digest appears it opens (or commits) a PR bumping the manifest; merging that PR is what triggers the deploy. This keeps git as the single source of truth and every deploy traceable to a commit.
What's the difference between a CRD and an operator?
A CRD is just a schema registration — it lets the API server store and serve a new kind of object (e.g. Certificate), with validation, RBAC, and kubectl support, but nothing acts on it. An operator is the controller that watches instances of that CR and does the work: it turns "I want a Postgres HA cluster with backups" into StatefulSets, Services, PVCs, failover logic, backup Jobs, and upgrade handling — encoding a human operator's runbook as a reconciliation loop. CRD = the noun; operator = the verb.
When should a team adopt a service mesh?
When they specifically need one or more of: automatic mTLS and workload identity across all services (compliance/zero-trust), fine-grained service-to-service authorization at L7, uniform resilience (retries with budgets, timeouts, circuit breaking, outlier detection) without per-app code, progressive delivery (traffic-percentage canaries/blue-green) across many services, or consistent L7 telemetry (golden signals per service pair). If they just need edge routing + TLS and a handful of services, Services + Ingress/Gateway API + NetworkPolicy + app-level retries is enough — a mesh is real operational cost (sidecar resource tax or a new dataplane, upgrades, another proxy to debug). Ambient/eBPF meshes reduce that cost and lower the adoption bar.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What is a Helm "release"?
A tracked, named installation of a chart into a cluster/namespace, with a revision history — so helm upgrade bumps the revision and helm rollback can revert to a previous one.
In GitOps, how do you roll back a bad change?
Revert the commit in git (git revert); the GitOps controller reconciles the cluster back to the previous state on its next sync.

Intermediate core

Design the repo structure and promotion flow for GitOps across dev, staging, and prod for ~20 services.
Repos: separate app repos (source + Dockerfile + CI) from one or more deploy (GitOps) repos so app developers don't need cluster access and deploy changes are reviewed by the right people. Structure (Kustomize or Helm): per service, a base/ with the common manifests and a overlays/{dev,staging,prod}/ with env-specific patches (replicas, resources, HPA bounds, ingress host, config); env-wide concerns (namespace, quota, network policy, PSA labels, shared config) in an env/<env>/ path. Each env has its own directory tree so a change to one env is an isolated diff. GitOps controller: Argo CD Application (or an ApplicationSet generating one per service/env) or Flux Kustomizations, one per (service, env), with automated sync + prune in dev/staging and manual sync (or auto with a gate) in prod. Promotion: CI builds one image, tags it version+SHA, and the image-automation bot opens a PR bumping the dev overlay's digest; merge → auto-deploy to dev. A promotion action (or a scheduled/PR-based step) copies that exact digest into the staging overlay → deploy + run e2e; then into prod overlay via a PR that requires approval (and optionally is time-windowed). The same digest flows through all three — no rebuilds. Secrets: per-env, via SOPS (Flux-native) or External Secrets pointing at a per-env path in the secrets manager; only references in git. Config drift & safety: prod selfHeal on (revert manual changes) with alerting when drift is detected; sync windows; PDBs + surge settings so auto-sync rollouts are safe; a "root" Application managing the others (app-of-apps) so bootstrapping a new cluster is one apply. Rollback: git revert the prod overlay PR. Observability: dashboards for sync status/health per service, alerts on OutOfSync/Degraded, and deploy markers into Grafana. Net: app repos vs deploy repo, base+overlays per service, one GitOps unit per (service,env), auto in dev/staging + gated in prod, promote by moving the same image digest through env directories via reviewed PRs, secrets by reference, selfHeal + PDBs + sync windows for safety.
Helm vs Kustomize — when would you pick each, and can you use both?
Helm shines for: distributing/consuming third-party software (a chart with a versioned repo, values contract, and upgrade path — e.g. ingress-nginx, kube-prometheus-stack, a database), packaging your own app for others to install with knobs, and needing lifecycle hooks or dependency subcharts. Cost: Go templating gets unreadable for complex logic, and the stateful "release" adds a moving part. Kustomize shines for: your own manifests where you want plain YAML you can read and kubectl-diff, environment variation via overlays/patches (strategic-merge or JSON patch), and no templating language — it's built into kubectl -k and is very GitOps-friendly. Cost: no parameters/loops, so lots of near-duplicate patches for very dynamic config, and no packaging/repo story. Both together (common): use Helm to pull and pin a third-party chart, render it with helm template (or via Flux's HelmRelease which supports postRenderers / Argo CD's Helm+Kustomize), then apply a Kustomize overlay on top to patch things the chart doesn't expose or to inject org-standard labels/policies. For your own apps, many teams standardize on Kustomize for readability and keep a tiny internal Helm chart only if they need parameterized generation. Decision rule: Helm for software you install, Kustomize for manifests you own — and compose them when a chart needs patching.

Advanced deep

You're replacing a fragile set of bash + kubectl runbooks for operating a stateful platform (say a Kafka fleet) with an operator. Design it: the CRD, the reconcile logic, upgrades, day-2 ops, and the risks.
Don't build first — evaluate mature operators (Strimzi for Kafka) before writing your own; only build if your requirements genuinely differ. If building: CRD design: a KafkaCluster spec expressing intent only — broker count, storage class/size, resources, version, listener/auth config, topic defaults, rack awareness; and a rich status — phase, per-broker readiness, under-replicated partition count, controller broker, in-progress operation, observedGeneration, and typed conditions (Ready, Progressing, Degraded). Structural OpenAPI schema with validation + defaults; enable the status subresource; add printer columns; consider a validating webhook for cross-field rules (can't shrink storage, version skew limits). Sub-resources for topics/users as their own CRDs (KafkaTopic, KafkaUser). Reconcile loop (controller-runtime): watch the CR and everything it owns (StatefulSet, headless Service, per-broker Service, ConfigMap, PVCs, PDB, Secrets, NetworkPolicy) with Owns(). Each pass: fetch CR; handle deletion via a finalizer (drain/decommission brokers cleanly, delete cloud resources, then remove the finalizer); ensure the finalizer + owner refs; build desired child objects from spec and CreateOrUpdate (server-side apply) with deterministic names; compute status from observed children + a Kafka admin client (ISR, offline partitions, controller). Return RequeueAfter for periodic health checks. Ordering/safety for stateful ops: the operator, not the StatefulSet, drives risky sequences — e.g. scale-up: add brokers, then trigger partition reassignment, wait for URP=0 before marking done; scale-down: reassign partitions off the target brokers first, verify, then remove; rolling upgrade: one broker at a time, highest ordinal first, respect the PDB, wait for the broker to rejoin and URP to return to 0 and (for major jumps) manage inter.broker.protocol.version and log.message.format.version in the documented two-phase way, with an abort that halts at the current broker. All operations idempotent and resumable (a restart mid-upgrade continues from observed state, never repeats a destructive step). Day-2: backups (offset/topic metadata + a MirrorMaker or tiered-storage strategy), certificate/credential rotation with overlap windows, config changes applied as a controlled rolling restart, topic/ACL management via the sub-CRDs, and metrics/alerts the operator itself emits (reconcile errors, operation duration, URP, offline partitions). Ops of the operator: leader election (one active), tightly scoped RBAC (only the kinds it manages), rate-limited workqueue with backoff, structured logs keyed by CR, Prometheus metrics (reconcile_total, errors, queue depth, duration), and a clear CRD-versioning/upgrade path (conversion webhooks). Risks: (1) the operator becomes a single point of failure for all clusters — a reconcile bug can roll-restart every Kafka at once; mitigate with canary CRs, a "paused"/maintenance annotation the operator honors, conservative concurrency, and staged operator upgrades. (2) It hides complexity — when it goes wrong, operators need to understand both Kafka and the operator; keep the manual runbook as a fallback and document how to take a cluster out of operator management. (3) Bad status → bad decisions; make the Kafka health checks robust and fail safe (don't proceed on unknown). (4) Version/skew handling is the hard part — test upgrade paths exhaustively in a lab. (5) Finalizer bugs can wedge deletions. (6) Reconcile storms on operator restart (informer resync of many CRs) — cap worker concurrency. Rollout: run the operator alongside the bash runbooks in read-only/observe mode first (it reports what it would do), then adopt one non-critical cluster, then expand, keeping the manual procedures until confidence is high. Net: a thin intent-only CRD + sub-CRDs, a watch-driven idempotent/resumable reconcile that drives risky stateful sequences itself (gated on Kafka health, PDB-aware, abortable), full day-2 automation, and heavy guardrails (canary CRs, pause annotation, staged operator upgrades, retained manual runbook) because the operator's blast radius is every cluster it manages.

gdb: The GNU Debugger

Stop a program anywhere, inspect and change its state, and walk the call stack — on a running process or a core dump.

Notes

Starting gdb and getting a backtrace

What. Load a program, run it, and when it stops (crash, breakpoint, signal) ask bt for the call stack. Why. 90% of debugging sessions are "where did it crash and with what arguments" — bt full answers both. Build with -g for symbols and line numbers; add -O0 so variables aren't optimised away and lines map 1:1.

$ gcc -g -O0 -o app app.c            # -g = debug info; -O0 = no optimisation while debugging
$ gdb ./app                          # or: gdb --args ./app --port 8080 file.txt
(gdb) run                            # start it; 'r' for short. args persist across runs
Program received signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.
0x0000555555555199 in parse (s=0x0) at app.c:42
42          return s[0];             # <-- the faulting line
(gdb) bt                             # backtrace: the call chain
#0  parse (s=0x0) at app.c:42
#1  0x00005555555551f0 in main () at app.c:11
(gdb) bt full                        # + every frame's local variables
(gdb) frame 1                        # hop to main's frame to inspect its state
(gdb) list                           # show source around the current line

# attach to something already running, or debug a core:
$ gdb -p $(pgrep myserver)           # attach to a live PID (needs ptrace permission)
$ gdb ./app core                     # post-mortem from a core dump

Breakpoints, watchpoints, catchpoints

What. A breakpoint stops at a location; a watchpoint stops when an expression's value changes; a catchpoint stops on an event (C++ throw, exec, a syscall). Why. Watchpoints find "who is corrupting this variable" without guessing; conditional breakpoints skip the 9,999 boring iterations and stop on the one that matters.

(gdb) break app.c:42                  # by file:line
(gdb) break parse                    # by function
(gdb) break parse if s == 0          # conditional: only when the guard is true
(gdb) tbreak main                    # temporary: auto-deleted after it hits once
(gdb) watch total                    # stop when 'total' changes (hardware watchpoint if possible)
(gdb) rwatch cfg.flags               # stop when it is READ
(gdb) catch throw                    # stop on any C++ exception being thrown
(gdb) catch syscall openat           # stop on a specific syscall
(gdb) info breakpoints               # list them, with hit counts
(gdb) condition 2 i > 1000           # add/replace a condition on breakpoint #2
(gdb) commands 2                     # run these gdb commands each time bp #2 hits
 > silent
 > printf "i=%d ptr=%p\n", i, ptr
 > continue
 > end
(gdb) delete 2      |  disable 2  |  ignore 2 50   # remove / mute / skip next 50 hits

Stepping and moving around the stack

What / how. Advance execution at source or instruction granularity, run out of the current function, or jump between stack frames to read their locals. Why. step descends into calls, next steps over them, finish runs the rest of the current function and prints its return value — the fast way to "let this call complete and show me what it gave back".

(gdb) next        # 'n' - execute one source line, stepping OVER calls
(gdb) step        # 's' - one source line, stepping INTO calls
(gdb) stepi       # 'si' - one machine instruction
(gdb) finish      # run until the current function returns; prints the return value
(gdb) until 58    # run until line 58 (handy to skip past a loop)
(gdb) continue    # 'c' - resume until the next stop
(gdb) return 0    # force the current function to return now with value 0

(gdb) bt                  # the frames
(gdb) frame 2  |  up  |  down   # select a frame by number / one out / one in
(gdb) info args          # the selected frame's parameters
(gdb) info locals        # its local variables
(gdb) info frame         # saved PC, caller, where args live

Inspecting and modifying data
