What. print evaluates any C/C++ expression (including calling functions); x dumps raw memory in a chosen format; set var writes into the inferior. Why. You can test a fix live — patch a variable, call a repair routine, or skip a bad branch — before touching the source.

(gdb) print cfg              # pretty-prints structs/containers (with pretty-printers)
(gdb) p/x flags             # hex; also /d /u /t(binary) /c /f /a(addr)
(gdb) p arr[3]              /  p *p@10        # 'p *ptr@N' = show N elements from ptr
(gdb) p (int)strlen(name)   # call a function in the inferior
(gdb) display total         # auto-print 'total' after every stop
(gdb) x/16xw &buf           # examine: 16 words, hex   (x/8xb bytes, x/s string, x/4i $pc)
(gdb) ptype cfg   |  whatis p   # type of an expression / a symbol
(gdb) info registers  |  p $rdi $rsi     # CPU registers / individual ones
(gdb) set var retries = 0   # change a live variable
(gdb) set $pc = &recover    # even redirect execution (advanced)

Core dumps and post-mortem debugging

What / why. A core dump is the process's memory image written at the moment it died. With the matching binary (same build, ideally with -g or separate debug info) you get a full backtrace of a crash that happened on a server hours ago — no reproduction needed.

$ ulimit -c unlimited                       # allow cores in this shell (or set a hard limit)
$ cat /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern         # where cores go; often piped to systemd-coredump
$ coredumpctl gdb myapp                      # systemd: opens the latest core in gdb
#   or, with a plain file:
$ gdb ./myapp /var/lib/coredump/core.myapp.1234

(gdb) bt                                     # the crash stack
(gdb) thread apply all bt                    # every thread's stack (deadlocks, races)
(gdb) info sharedlibrary                     # which .so's were loaded
(gdb) set solib-search-path /path/to/libs    # if libraries aren't found
# Debug info can live in a separate file: 'objcopy --only-keep-debug' + a .build-id link,
# or a distro's -dbg / debuginfod (set DEBUGINFOD_URLS to auto-download symbols).

Threads, forks, signals, remote, and scripting

What / why. Real programs fork, spawn threads, and take signals; gdb controls all of it. It also runs headless for CI (-batch), attaches over the network (gdbserver), and is fully scriptable via .gdbinit and a Python API.

# threads
(gdb) info threads                         # list; * marks the current
(gdb) thread 3                             # switch
(gdb) thread apply all bt                  # backtrace every thread (classic deadlock view)
(gdb) set scheduler-locking on             # while stepping, freeze the other threads

# forks & signals
(gdb) set follow-fork-mode child           # follow the child on fork() (default: parent)
(gdb) set detach-on-fork off               # keep BOTH under control
(gdb) handle SIGPIPE nostop noprint pass   # stop ignoring / spamming on a signal
(gdb) catch signal SIGABRT

# remote (embedded / container / another host)
target$  gdbserver :1234 ./app
host$    gdb ./app -ex 'target remote target-host:1234'

# non-interactive & scripted
$ gdb -q -batch -ex run -ex bt -ex quit --args ./app input   # crash + backtrace, then exit
$ gdb -x debug.gdb ./app                                      # run a command script
# ~/.gdbinit or ./.gdbinit: default settings, 'define' custom commands, load pretty-printers.
# TUI: 'gdb -tui' or (gdb) layout src   |   Reverse: (gdb) record; reverse-next / reverse-continue
Cheat Sheet
  • Build -g -O0. Start: gdb ./app, gdb --args ./app a b, gdb -p PID, gdb ./app core.
  • Crash triage: run → bt / bt full → frame N → info args/info locals.
  • Breakpoints: break f:line, break fn if cond, tbreak, watch v (change), rwatch (read), catch throw/catch syscall. info breakpoints, condition, commands, ignore.
  • Step: next (over), step (into), stepi, finish (out, shows return), until N, continue.
  • Data: p expr, p/x, p *ptr@N, p fn(args), display, x/16xw addr, ptype/whatis, info registers, set var x=….
  • Cores: ulimit -c unlimited, check /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern, coredumpctl gdb, need the matching binary + debug info (debuginfod).
  • Threads: info threads, thread N, thread apply all bt, set scheduler-locking on. Forks: set follow-fork-mode child.
  • Headless: gdb -q -batch -ex run -ex bt --args ./app. Remote: gdbserver :PORT ./app + target remote host:PORT. Scripts: .gdbinit, -x file.gdb, Python API.
Q&A
A release binary crashes but gdb shows <optimized out> for the variables you need. What now?
The compiler removed or coalesced them at -O2. Options: rebuild the translation unit with -g -O0 (or -Og, which keeps debuggability while optimising lightly) and reproduce; read the values from registers/stack with info registers and x/ using the disassembly (disassemble, layout asm) and the calling convention; or add targeted logging. For production, ship with -O2 -g and keep separate debug-info files so at least line numbers and the backtrace survive.
What's the difference between step and next, and between finish and until?
step enters function calls on the line; next executes them without stopping inside. finish runs until the current function returns and prints its return value; until (with no arg) runs until a line greater than the current is reached (so it exits a loop), and until N runs until line N. Use next to stay at your level, finish to get a call's result fast, until to escape a loop you don't care about.
How do you find which code is scribbling over a struct field?
A watchpoint: watch cfg.flags (hardware-assisted if the size/arch allow, so it's cheap). gdb stops the instant the value changes and bt shows the writer. If the address changes (the object is on the heap and re-allocated), set the watch after the object exists, or watch *(int*)0xADDR. For "corrupted much later" bugs, combine with AddressSanitizer or Valgrind, which flag the out-of-bounds write at its source.
gdb can't attach: "ptrace: Operation not permitted". Why?
The Yama LSM restricts ptrace to descendants by default (/proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope = 1). Fixes: run gdb as root or with CAP_SYS_PTRACE; start the target from within gdb instead of attaching; temporarily echo 0 | sudo tee /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope; or in containers add --cap-add=SYS_PTRACE and (often) --security-opt seccomp=unconfined.
The backtrace is full of ?? and wrong function names. What went wrong?
Symbol/binary mismatch or a corrupted stack. Check you loaded the exact binary that produced the core (same build id), that debug info matches (build-id, debuginfod, or the right -dbg package), and that shared-library paths resolve (info sharedlibrary, set solib-search-path). If the binary is right but the stack is garbage, you likely have stack corruption (buffer overflow, use-after-return) — switch to ASan/Valgrind to catch the overwrite.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which compiler flags do you add to debug comfortably with gdb, and why?
-g to emit DWARF debug info (line numbers, variable names, types) and -O0 so nothing is optimised away and each source line maps to a contiguous run of instructions. -Og is a middle ground for cases where -O0 is too slow or hides an optimisation-only bug.
Your program segfaults. Give the three gdb commands that usually pinpoint it.
run (reproduce under gdb — it stops at the fault), bt (the call stack and faulting line), then frame N + info locals/print to inspect the bad pointer or index in the relevant frame.

Intermediate core

A bug only appears on the 50,000th request. How do you stop exactly there without stepping 50,000 times?
A conditional breakpoint: break handle_request if req_id == 50000. If there's no handy counter, break on the function and use ignore <bpnum> 49999 to skip the first N hits, or attach a commands block that printfs state and continues while a guard is false. For "the Nth time some condition is true", keep a static counter or set a watch on the condition. If each iteration is expensive, prefer logging + a data breakpoint over interactive stepping.
Walk through post-mortem debugging of a crash that happened on a production server.
(1) Ensure cores are enabled and captured (ulimit -c, core_pattern/systemd-coredump) and that the service ships with -O2 -g or separate debug-info. (2) Get the core and the exact binary (match by build-id). (3) gdb ./app core (or coredumpctl gdb). (4) bt full for the crashing thread; thread apply all bt to see every thread (deadlock/race context). (5) Inspect the offending frame — frame N, print the pointer/index, p *obj, x/ around it; check $_siginfo for the fault address. (6) Resolve libraries (info sharedlibrary, set solib-search-path, debuginfod). (7) If the stack is corrupt, the crash is a symptom — reproduce under ASan/Valgrind to find the real overwrite. (8) Turn the finding into a regression test.

Advanced deep

Design a debugging strategy for an intermittent multi-threaded corruption that disappears under gdb ("heisenbug").
The probe changes timing, so lean on low-perturbation and record/replay tools. (1) Sanitizers first: build with -fsanitize=thread (TSan) to catch the data race directly, and separately -fsanitize=address for the memory error; these report the two racing accesses / the bad write with stacks, often without needing to "catch it live". (2) Deterministic replay: run under rr (rr record ./app then rr replay) — you get a gdb session you can run backwards (reverse-continue, reverse-next) from the failure to the cause, with identical timing every replay. gdb's own record works for smaller windows. (3) Hardware watchpoints on the corrupted address in the rr replay pinpoint the writer without slowing the original run. (4) Reduce nondeterminism to reproduce: pin to fewer cores (taskset), add scheduling stress (stress-ng, rr's chaos mode, or a sched_yield/usleep fuzz build), disable ASLR (setarch -R) for stable addresses. (5) Instrument, don't step: ring-buffer logging of the suspect operations with thread id + timestamp; a commands block on a breakpoint that logs and continues (no human in the loop, minimal stall); or a checksum/guard-page around the object (mprotect, or ASan's __asan_poison_memory_region) so the offending access faults immediately. (6) Post-mortem: if it does crash, thread apply all bt on the core plus the ring-buffer log usually shows the interleaving. (7) Once understood, add a TSan CI job and a stress test so it can't regress. Net: TSan/ASan to name the race, rr for reverse debugging with stable timing, watchpoints in replay to find the writer, and low-perturbation logging/guard pages instead of interactive stepping.

Valgrind: Memory & Thread Errors

Runs your program on a synthetic CPU and checks every memory access — leaks, invalid reads/writes, use of uninitialised values, bad frees — with no recompilation.

Notes

Memcheck: the errors it catches

What. Invalid reads/writes (out of bounds, after free, wrong stack frame), use of uninitialised values in a decision or syscall, free/delete mismatches, double frees, overlapping memcpy, and memory leaks at exit. Why. These are the bugs that either crash randomly much later or silently corrupt data; Memcheck flags them at the instruction that does the bad thing, with a stack trace.

$ gcc -g -O0 -o app app.c                 # -g for line numbers; -O1 max (higher can confuse it)
$ valgrind ./app                          # Memcheck is the default tool

==12345== Invalid write of size 4
==12345==    at 0x1091AA: store (app.c:14)      # <-- exact line
==12345==    by 0x1091E7: main (app.c:23)
==12345==  Address 0x4a8b064 is 0 bytes after a block of size 40 alloc'd
==12345==    at 0x484A2A3: malloc (vg_replace_malloc.c:381)
==12345==    by 0x109180: main (app.c:20)       # <-- where the too-small block came from

==12345== Conditional jump or move depends on uninitialised value(s)
==12345==    at 0x109233: main (app.c:29)       # you branched on garbage

==12345== HEAP SUMMARY:
==12345==     definitely lost: 40 bytes in 1 blocks

Leak checking and origin tracking

What / why. --leak-check=full lists every leaked block with the allocation stack; --show-leak-kinds=all also reports still reachable (referenced at exit — often fine) and indirectly lost. --track-origins=yes tells you where an uninitialised value was born (2× slower, worth it).

$ valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all --track-origins=yes \
           --error-exitcode=1 --log-file=vg.%p.txt ./app

# leak categories:
#   definitely lost  -> a real leak: no pointer to the block remains        (fix these)
#   indirectly lost  -> leaked only because its owner was leaked
#   possibly lost    -> only an interior pointer remains (custom allocators, some C++)
#   still reachable   -> pointer exists at exit; usually a global/cache, low priority

# make CI fail on any error/leak:
$ valgrind --leak-check=full --errors-for-leak-kinds=definite --error-exitcode=1 ./tests

Suppressions and reducing noise

What / why. Third-party libraries (glibc, OpenSSL, the dynamic loader, GUI toolkits) trip Memcheck for benign reasons. A suppression file silences specific known reports so real bugs stand out. Generate them, don't hand-write.

$ valgrind --gen-suppressions=all --log-file=vg.txt ./app    # prints a suppression per error
# paste the ones you trust into project.supp:
{
   glibc_dlopen_false_positive
   Memcheck:Leak
   fun:malloc
   ...
   obj:*/ld-*.so
}
$ valgrind --suppressions=project.supp --suppressions=/usr/lib/valgrind/default.supp ./app
# tip: also run with 'G_SLICE=always-malloc' / disable custom pools so the checker sees real malloc.

The other tools

What / why. Same framework, different instrumentation — select with --tool=.

# Cachegrind: cache-miss + branch-misprediction model (deterministic, good for A/B)
$ valgrind --tool=cachegrind --branch-sim=yes ./app
$ cg_annotate cachegrind.out.12345          # per-line I1/D1/LL misses

# Callgrind: call graph + instruction counts -> visualise in KCachegrind
$ valgrind --tool=callgrind --dump-instr=yes ./app
$ callgrind_annotate callgrind.out.12345 ; kcachegrind callgrind.out.12345

# Massif: heap usage over time (find the growth / the peak allocator)
$ valgrind --tool=massif --time-unit=B ./app
$ ms_print massif.out.12345      # ASCII graph + snapshots with allocation stacks

# Helgrind / DRD: data races, lock-order violations, misuse of pthreads/std::thread
$ valgrind --tool=helgrind ./app
$ valgrind --tool=drd --check-stack-var=yes ./app     # DRD: lower overhead, different heuristics

Valgrind vs compiler sanitizers

What / why. ASan/TSan/UBSan (-fsanitize=…) instrument at compile time: far faster (2–3×), so usable in CI on the whole suite and even some prod canaries. Valgrind needs no rebuild, catches uninitialised-read and leak cases ASan doesn't, and works on binaries you can't recompile — but it's slow and doesn't see custom-allocator internals well.

            Valgrind Memcheck            AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address)
recompile   no                          yes
slowdown    10-30x                      ~2x
uninit reads yes (killer feature)       no (that's MemorySanitizer, needs full rebuild)
leaks       yes                         yes (LeakSanitizer, on by default)
races       yes (Helgrind, slow)        yes (ThreadSanitizer, faster)  -- can't combine ASan+TSan
overflow detail  heap; limited stack    heap + stack + global, redzones, quarantine
use it when  can't rebuild; need uninit;  fast feedback; CI on every test; stack/global overflows
             one-off deep audit
Cheat Sheet
  • Default tool = Memcheck. Build -g (and no more than -O1). valgrind ./app.
  • Full run: valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all --track-origins=yes --error-exitcode=1 ./app.
  • Leak kinds: definitely lost (fix), indirectly lost, possibly lost (interior pointers), still reachable (usually OK).
  • Key errors: Invalid read/write of size N, Conditional jump depends on uninitialised value, Invalid free / mismatched free/delete, N bytes lost.
  • Noise: --gen-suppressions=all → curate a .supp file; pass with --suppressions=.
  • Other tools via --tool=: cachegrind (cache/branch model), callgrind (call graph → KCachegrind), massif (heap over time), helgrind/drd (data races, lock order).
  • CI: --error-exitcode=1 (+ --errors-for-leak-kinds=definite) so any finding fails the build; --log-file=vg.%p.txt.
  • ~10–30× slow, ~2× RAM. For fast/CI-wide checking prefer -fsanitize=address/thread/undefined; use Valgrind when you can't recompile or need uninitialised-read/leak detection.
Q&A
Memcheck reports "Conditional jump or move depends on uninitialised value(s)" but points at a line deep in a library. How do you find the real cause?
Re-run with --track-origins=yes — it adds a second stack showing where the uninitialised bytes were created (the malloc that wasn't zeroed, the struct field never set, the buffer passed to a syscall). The reported line is only where the tainted value was used; the origin is the bug. If it's genuinely inside a trusted library on defined-but-padded data, add a targeted suppression.
What's the difference between "definitely lost", "still reachable", and "possibly lost"?
Definitely lost: at exit, no pointer anywhere points into the block — a genuine leak, fix it. Still reachable: a pointer (often a global or singleton cache) still references it; the memory would be freed by the OS at exit anyway, so it's usually low priority (though it hides real leaks in long-running processes — clean up if you can). Possibly lost: only a pointer to the middle of the block remains — common with custom allocators, std::string small-buffer tricks, or pointer arithmetic; investigate but it's often benign.
Your program runs fine normally but Valgrind makes it 20× slower and it times out. What are your options?
Reduce the workload under Valgrind (smaller input, fewer iterations, a targeted test rather than the whole suite); raise timeouts in CI for the Valgrind job; use --tool=memcheck without --track-origins for a first pass; scope with client requests (VALGRIND_DO_LEAK_CHECK) around the region of interest; or switch to AddressSanitizer (~2×) for the CI-wide gate and keep Valgrind for periodic deep audits and for the uninitialised-read checks ASan lacks.
Can you run AddressSanitizer and Valgrind together? ASan and ThreadSanitizer?
Don't run ASan under Valgrind — ASan's shadow memory and interceptors confuse Memcheck and vice versa; pick one. ASan and TSan can't be combined in the same build (both own the allocator/shadow); build separate binaries. A typical matrix: one binary with -fsanitize=address,undefined, one with -fsanitize=thread, and an occasional plain-build Valgrind run for uninitialised values and leaks in third-party code.
Why does Valgrind sometimes miss a stack buffer overflow that AddressSanitizer catches?
Memcheck tracks addressability precisely for the heap (with red-zones around each malloc) but has limited visibility into stack and global layout — a small overrun into adjacent stack space may still be "addressable" from its point of view. ASan inserts red-zones around stack and global objects too and poisons them, so it flags those overflows. Use ASan for stack/global overflow coverage; use Memcheck for heap errors, uninitialised reads, and leaks without recompiling.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which Valgrind tool runs by default, and what does it check?
Memcheck. It validates every memory access: reads/writes must be to allocated, addressable memory; values used in branches or syscalls must be initialised; frees must match allocations and happen once; and it reports blocks still allocated (leaked) at exit.
What single option set do you use for a thorough leak report?
--leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all --track-origins=yes (and --error-exitcode=1 to fail CI). Build with -g so each leak has a source location.

Intermediate core

Your test suite is clean under Valgrind but a leak still grows in production over days. Why might Valgrind not see it?
Valgrind only checks the code paths your run exercises, and only reports what's outstanding at process exit. Reasons it can miss a prod leak: (1) the leaking path isn't hit by the tests (rare error handling, a specific request type, a config only used in prod); (2) it's classified as "still reachable" because a growing container/cache keeps a pointer — technically not "lost" but unbounded growth all the same; (3) it's not C heap at all — fd leaks, mmap regions, thread stacks, kernel-side buffers, or a language runtime's own allocator that Memcheck sees as one big block; (4) the process never exits, so run VALGRIND_DO_LEAK_CHECK periodically via the client request API. Fixes: add tests covering the prod path, run Valgrind against a soak/load test, track "still reachable" growth, and use Massif to see which allocation site grows over time.
How would you use Callgrind and Massif to investigate a service that's slow and memory-hungry under load?
Callgrind for CPU: run a representative workload under valgrind --tool=callgrind --dump-instr=yes --collect-jumps=yes, then open callgrind.out.* in KCachegrind. It gives an exact (deterministic) call graph with inclusive/exclusive instruction counts and, with --cache-sim=yes, modelled cache misses — so you see which functions and which call paths dominate, and whether the cost is compute or memory-stall. Because it's deterministic it's great for before/after comparisons of an optimisation. Caveat: it measures instructions/modelled cycles, not wall-clock, and the 20× slowdown changes contention — validate the win with a real profiler (perf) afterwards. Massif for memory: run valgrind --tool=massif --time-unit=B --detailed-freq=1, then ms_print. It shows heap size over "time" (bytes allocated) with periodic snapshots, each broken down by allocation call stack — so you see the peak, what's resident at the peak, and which call site is responsible for growth. Use it to distinguish "big transient buffers" from "steady leak/accumulation" and to find the specific allocation to pool, cap, or free earlier. Combine: Massif finds the allocation sites to fix, Callgrind confirms whether allocation/copy cost is also on the hot path.

Advanced deep

Design a memory-safety verification pipeline for a C/C++ codebase: what tools, at what stages, with what gates.
Layered, fast-to-slow. (1) Compile-time: -Wall -Wextra -Werror, -Wformat=2, -fstack-protector-strong, -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3; static analysis (clang-tidy, clang --analyze, Coverity/CodeQL) on every PR with a no-new-findings gate. (2) Per-PR dynamic: build the test suite three ways and run it in CI — -fsanitize=address,undefined (heap/stack/global overflow, UAF, UB) with -fno-sanitize-recover so any hit fails; -fsanitize=thread for the concurrent tests; if you can afford the full rebuild, an MSan build for uninitialised reads. All with -g -O1, symbolized stacks, and ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1:strict_string_checks=1:detect_stack_use_after_return=1. Gate: zero sanitizer errors. (3) Fuzzing: libFuzzer/AFL++ targets for every parser/deserialiser/protocol boundary, run in CI for a few minutes per PR and continuously (OSS-Fuzz style) on main; new crashes/ASan reports block or page. Corpus + regression tests from past bugs. (4) Nightly deep check: full suite (and a soak/load scenario) under Valgrind Memcheck with --leak-check=full --track-origins=yes --error-exitcode=1 and a curated suppressions file — catches uninitialised reads and leaks in third-party/uninstrumented code and doesn't need the sanitizer rebuild; plus Massif on the soak test with an alert if peak/steady heap regresses beyond a threshold. (5) Pre-release: Helgrind/DRD or a longer TSan run over concurrency-heavy scenarios; a Valgrind pass on the exact release artifact. (6) Production: ship with -O2 -g + separate debug-info and frame pointers; keep core dumps + coredumpctl/debuginfod so any crash gets a real backtrace; optional hardened allocator (scudo) or GWP-ASan sampling in canaries to catch rare heap bugs in the field at near-zero cost. Gates: PR blocked on static analysis, all sanitizer test runs, and fuzz-regression; merge to main blocked additionally on the nightly Valgrind/Massif being green (or an approved suppression/threshold change); release blocked on the concurrency and release-artifact passes. Hygiene: every fixed bug adds a regression test and, if found by fuzzing, a corpus entry; suppressions are reviewed and expire. Net: cheap compiler + static checks on every commit, ASan/TSan/UBSan + fuzzing per PR as the primary gate, Valgrind/Massif nightly for the gaps sanitizers leave, and crash-grade observability in production.

strace: System Call Tracing

Shows every system call a process makes — the arguments, the return value, the errno — so you can see exactly where it talks to the kernel and where it fails.

Notes

Running it: launch, attach, follow

What / how. Start a command under strace, or attach to a running PID with -p. -f follows fork/clone so you also trace children and threads. -o writes to a file (keeps strace's output off the program's stderr).

$ strace ./app arg1                       # trace a fresh run
$ strace -f -o trace.txt ./app            # follow children/threads, log to a file
$ strace -p 4242                          # attach to a running process (Ctrl-C detaches)
$ strace -f -p 4242 -e trace=network      # attach + only network syscalls
$ strace -ff -o out ./app                 # -ff: one file per PID -> out.4242, out.4243 ...

# common combo for "what is this daemon doing right now":
$ sudo strace -f -p $(pgrep -n nginx) -e trace=%file,%network -T -tt -s 200

Filtering: -e trace= and friends

What / why. Full traces are a firehose. -e trace= restricts to syscalls or predefined classes; this both cuts noise and cuts overhead. -e signal=, -e status=, and -P path narrow further.

$ strace -e trace=openat,read,write ./app        # explicit list
$ strace -e trace=%file ./app                    # class: anything that takes a filename
$ strace -e trace=%network ./app                 # socket/connect/bind/accept/send/recv
$ strace -e trace=%process ./app                 # fork/exec/exit/wait
$ strace -e trace=%memory ./app                  # mmap/mprotect/brk
$ strace -e trace=!futex,clock_nanosleep ./app   # everything EXCEPT these (noise removal)
$ strace -P /etc/myapp/config.yaml ./app         # only syscalls touching this exact path
$ strace -e signal=none ./app                    # hide signal lines
$ strace -e status=failed ./app                  # (newer strace) only calls that returned an error

Making the output useful: timing, strings, fds

What / why. Defaults truncate strings and hide time. These flags turn a raw trace into a readable diagnostic.

-t / -tt / -ttt     # wall-clock timestamp per line (-tt = with microseconds)
-r                  # relative time since the previous syscall (spot the long gaps)
-T                  # time spent IN each syscall  <0.000123>  (find the slow one)
-s 4096             # show up to 4096 bytes of string args (default 32 - too short)
-y                  # annotate fds with the file/socket they refer to:  read(3</etc/hosts>, ...)
-yy                 # + protocol/inode details for sockets
-v                  # unabbreviated structs (full stat/rlimit/... instead of "...")
-x / -xx            # non-printable bytes as hex
-k                  # print a user-space stack trace for each syscall (needs libunwind)
-i                  # instruction pointer at the time of the call

The summary mode: -c

What / why. -c suppresses the per-call log and prints a table at the end: call count, total time, average time, and error count per syscall. It's the fastest way to answer "is this process spending its time in the kernel, and doing what?".

$ strace -c -f ./app
% time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ----------------
 61.2    0.451203         220      2050        18 read
 24.7    0.182050          89      2044           write
  8.1    0.059700        1990        30           connect
  4.0    0.029410          14      2000       970 stat        # 970 failed stat() = a bad search path
------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ----------------
100.0    0.722363                  8600      1041 total
$ strace -c -w ./app        # -w: measure wall-clock time in syscalls (incl. time blocked), not CPU

What strace is for — the four questions it answers

  • "Why does it fail?" Find the failing syscall and its errno: openat(…"/etc/app.conf", O_RDONLY) = -1 ENOENT — wrong path. EACCES — permissions. ECONNREFUSED — nothing listening.
  • "Which files/hosts does it touch?" -e trace=%file / %network -y — discover the real config path, the library it loads, the endpoint it calls, without docs.
  • "Why is it slow / hung?" -T -r — a lone read(4…) or futex(…) or poll(…) taking 30s is your stall. -c -w shows if kernel time dominates.
  • "What's it doing at all?" Attach with -p to a wedged daemon — is it spinning on EAGAIN, stuck in accept(), or fork-bombing?
# classic one-liners
$ strace -f -e trace=%file ./app 2>&1 | grep -E 'ENOENT|EACCES'   # missing/denied files
$ strace -f -e trace=execve -e status=successful ./script.sh       # what did the script exec?
$ strace -p PID -e trace=%network -T -tt                           # live network activity + latency
$ strace -c -f -p PID                                              # then Ctrl-C for the summary
# NB strace slows the target a lot; on prod prefer 'perf trace', bpftrace, or a short sample.
Cheat Sheet
  • Run: strace ./app, attach: strace -p PID, children/threads: -f (or -ff -o pre for per-PID files), log: -o file.
  • Filter: -e trace=openat,connect, classes %file / %network / %process / %memory / %signal, negate with !; -P /path for one path; -e status=failed.
  • Readability: -tt (timestamps), -r (delta), -T (time in call), -s 4096 (string length), -y/-yy (fd → path/socket), -v (full structs), -k (stack).
  • Summary: -c (count/time/errors per syscall), -c -w (wall-clock, includes blocked time).
  • Failure hunt: strace -f -e trace=%file ./app 2>&1 | grep -E 'ENOENT|EACCES'.
  • Slow/hung: strace -p PID -T -r — look for the one syscall eating the time.
  • Sees the kernel boundary only — no pure-CPU work, no non-syscalling library calls (use ltrace / perf / gdb for those).
  • Heavy overhead (ptrace, 2 traps/call). On production prefer perf trace, bpftrace, or audit — or trace briefly.
Q&A
A program prints "cannot open config" and exits. How does strace pinpoint the cause in seconds?
strace -f -e trace=%file ./app and look at the openat/stat lines near the end. You'll see the exact paths it tried and the errno: ENOENT means it's looking somewhere you didn't expect (often a relative path, or $HOME/XDG_CONFIG_HOME not what you think); EACCES means the file exists but permissions/ownership/SELinux deny it; ELOOP/ENOTDIR point at a broken symlink or a path component that isn't a directory. The trace shows the search order, so you know exactly where to put the file or what to chmod.
Why does strace show nothing interesting for a CPU-bound program that's "stuck"?
Because it's not making syscalls — it's spinning in userspace (an infinite loop, a hot retry, heavy computation). strace only sees the kernel boundary. Switch tools: gdb -p PID then bt (where is it looping), perf top -p PID / perf record -p PID (which function burns CPU), or py-spy/async-profiler for managed runtimes. strace is the right tool only when the process is talking to (or waiting on) the kernel.
Your service is intermittently slow. strace -c shows most time in futex. What does that mean?
futex is the syscall behind mutexes/condvars/std::mutex/Go/Java locks — time there usually means lock contention (threads blocked waiting to acquire) or a condvar wait. Note -c (CPU time) undercounts blocked time; re-run with -c -w to see wall-clock time in syscalls, and -T -f to see how long individual futex calls block and which threads. Then move to a real profiler: perf lock, mutex/lock profiling in the runtime, or reduce critical-section size / sharding.
How do you trace a short-lived child process that a wrapper script spawns?
Use -f so strace follows fork/clone/execve into children, and -ff -o out so each PID gets its own file (out.1234) instead of interleaved output. To catch a specific program, add -e trace=execve to see every exec and its argv, or filter the per-PID files afterward. If the child re-execs quickly, strace -f -e trace=execve,exit_group ./wrapper.sh gives a clean map of the process tree.
Is it safe to strace a production process?
Cautiously. strace stops the target on every syscall (two ptrace traps each), so a syscall-heavy service can slow 10–100×, blowing latency SLOs and possibly tripping timeouts/health checks. If you must: attach briefly, filter hard (-e trace= a narrow set or one -P path), avoid -s large and -k, detach quickly (Ctrl-C on an attach leaves the process running). Better on prod: perf trace (much lower overhead), bpftrace/BCC scripts, or the audit subsystem — all can sample syscalls without freezing the process.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What exactly does strace show you?
Every system call the traced process makes — the call name, its arguments (decoded: paths, flags, struct contents), the return value, and the errno on failure — plus signals delivered. It's the process's conversation with the kernel.
Which flag lets strace follow into child processes and threads?
-f. Add -ff -o prefix to write a separate file per PID (prefix.PID) instead of interleaving everything.

Intermediate core

A binary you can't rebuild connects to the wrong database. How do you discover what host/port and config it's actually using?
strace -f -y -e trace=%file,%network -s 200 ./app. The %file lines with -y show every config/env file it opens and reads (so you find the real config path and can dump its contents from the trace with a big -s); the %network lines show connect() with the decoded sockaddr (IP:port), and -y/-yy annotate the socket fd. You'll also see getaddrinfo-driven DNS (connect to :53, reads of /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/hosts). Cross-reference the file it read just before the bad connect() — that's the config providing the wrong endpoint (or an env var: check the execve line's envp, or /proc/PID/environ).
Explain how you'd use strace to decide whether a slow request is CPU, disk, network, or lock contention.
Run strace -f -T -tt -c -w -p PID over a slow request (or wrap a single request). (1) Look at the -c -w summary: if total wall time in syscalls is a small fraction of the request time, the cost is userspace CPU — move to perf. (2) If time concentrates in read/pread/fsync on file fds (-y shows the paths) with large -T values, it's disk I/O — check iostat, the file, caching. (3) If it's recvfrom/read on a socket fd, or connect/poll/epoll_wait with long -T, it's network / a slow downstream — correlate the peer from the connect. (4) If it's futex (or SYS_futex waits) dominating wall time, it's lock contention — threads blocked on a mutex/condvar. (5) A tight loop of EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK on non-blocking I/O plus high CPU = a busy-poll bug. The per-line timestamps (-tt) and deltas let you see the exact gap where the latency accrues. Then switch to the matching specialist tool (perf, iostat, tcpdump, perf lock) to go deeper.

Advanced deep

strace helped in dev but is too invasive for the production incident you're now debugging. Design a low-overhead syscall-observability approach.
Why strace hurts: ptrace stops the tracee twice per syscall, serialises threads through the tracer, and can multiply latency 10–100× — unacceptable on a live SLO-bound service, and it can trip watchdogs. Alternatives, roughly in order: (1) perf trace — strace-like output built on perf events / eBPF, far lower overhead, supports --duration to show only slow calls, -p/--pid, and system-wide mode; good first reach. (2) bpftrace / BCC — write a tiny script that hooks the raw_syscalls:sys_enter/sys_exit tracepoints (or specific tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat etc.), aggregate in-kernel (count per syscall, latency histograms with @[probe] = hist(...), top files, error counts) and only emit summaries — near-zero overhead because nothing is stopped and data is reduced in the kernel. Examples: opensnoop, tcpconnect, funclatency, syscount, a per-syscall latency histogram scoped to the PID/cgroup. (3) Linux audit (auditd) with a targeted rule (e.g. watch a path, or a syscall for a specific uid) when you need durable, policy-grade logging rather than ad-hoc. (4) Existing telemetry: USE/RED metrics, the runtime's own tracing, and structured logs often already answer "which downstream is slow" without touching syscalls at all. (5) If you truly need strace-grade detail, do it on one canary instance taken out of rotation, or for a few seconds with a hard filter (-e trace= one or two calls, -P one path), then detach. Guardrails: scope every tool to the PID/cgroup, cap duration, prefer in-kernel aggregation over per-event userspace output, and know that even eBPF has some cost — test the probe's impact on a canary first. Deliverable: a small library of vetted bpftrace/perf-trace snippets (syscall latency histogram, failed-openat by path, slow connect by peer, futex-wait time per thread) that on-call can run safely, plus a runbook mapping symptoms to the right snippet.

ltrace: Library Call Tracing

Like strace, but one layer up: it logs the calls a program makes into shared libraries — malloc, strcpy, getenv, SSL_read — with their arguments and return values.

Notes

Basic use

What / how. Run a command under ltrace, or attach with -p. Each line is function(args) = return. -f follows children; -o logs to a file.

$ ltrace ./app
getenv("HOME")                          = "/home/leo"
malloc(1024)                            = 0x5555557592a0
snprintf("cfg=/home/leo/.apprc", 64, "cfg=%s/.apprc", "/home/leo") = 20
fopen("/home/leo/.apprc", "r")          = 0
+++ exited (status 1) +++               # fopen returned NULL -> config missing

$ ltrace -f -o lt.txt ./app arg        # follow forks, log to file
$ ltrace -p 4242                        # attach to a running process (Ctrl-C detaches)

Filtering which calls you see

What / why. -e selects functions by glob; -l selects by library. Combine to answer "what does this program ask OpenSSL / libc string functions to do".

$ ltrace -e 'malloc+free+realloc+calloc' ./app      # just the allocator
$ ltrace -e 'str*+mem*' ./app                       # string/memory family
$ ltrace -e '*@libcrypto.so*' ./app                 # everything from libcrypto
$ ltrace -l libssl.so.3 ./app                       # calls resolved to libssl
$ ltrace -e '-getenv' ./app                         # exclude a noisy call (leading '-')
$ ltrace -e 'malloc-@libfoo.so' ./app               # malloc, but not calls made from libfoo
$ ltrace -x 'internal_parse' ./app                  # -x: trace a non-PLT/static symbol by name

Output detail and the summary

-S              # ALSO show system calls (interleave strace-style lines: SYS_read(...)=...)
-T              # time spent in each call  <0.000042>
-t / -tt        # timestamp per line
-r              # relative time since previous line
-s 512          # max string length to print (default is short)
-C              # demangle C++ symbol names
-A 5            # array/struct elements to show
-n 2            # indent nested calls by 2 spaces (call-depth view)
-c              # SUMMARY only: count + time per function (like strace -c)

$ ltrace -c ./app
% time     seconds  usecs/call     calls      function
------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------------------
 47.1    0.010293          10      1024     memcpy
 22.0    0.004810           4      1200     malloc
 18.6    0.004070           4      1198     free
 ...
------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------------------
100.0    0.021850                  4700     total

Prototypes: why args sometimes print as hex

What / why. To show fopen("/etc/hosts", "r") instead of fopen(0x40201f, 0x402030), ltrace needs the function's signature. It ships prototype files (/usr/share/ltrace/*.conf or libc.so.conf etc.) for common libraries; for your own or obscure libraries, add a .conf entry or install the library's debug info.

# a custom prototype file:  ~/.ltrace.d/mylib.conf
int   mylib_open(string, uint);
void  mylib_free(addr);
$ ltrace -F ~/.ltrace.d/mylib.conf -e 'mylib_*' ./app
mylib_open("db.sqlite", 2)              = 3        # now decoded
# without the prototype you'd see:  mylib_open(0x4a1200, 2) = 3

When ltrace helps — and its limits

  • Use it for: reverse-engineering how a closed binary uses libc/crypto/DB client libs; watching malloc/free pairing and sizes without a rebuild; confirming which getenv/getpwnam/dlopen calls happen and with what; seeing the string passed to system()/exec*(); checking arguments to a library call you suspect is misused.
  • Limits: needs a dynamically linked ELF — a fully static binary has no PLT to trap, so ltrace sees little or nothing. Stripped binaries lose symbol names. Modern PIE + full RELRO + IFUNC and some libc versions break or partially break ltrace (it has historically lagged glibc changes). It only sees exported (PLT) calls by default — inlined or static-linked library code is invisible. Overhead is high (like strace). On many distros ltrace is less maintained than strace — if it misbehaves, fall back to strace -S-style reasoning, gdb breakpoints on the library functions (break malloc), or LD_PRELOAD shims.
# gdb fallback when ltrace won't cooperate:
$ gdb -q ./app -ex 'break malloc' -ex 'commands' -ex 'bt 2' -ex 'continue' -ex 'end' -ex run
# LD_PRELOAD fallback: a tiny wrapper that logs then calls the real symbol via dlsym(RTLD_NEXT).
Cheat Sheet
  • ltrace = library (PLT) call tracer. Line format: func(args) = ret. Run ltrace ./app or attach ltrace -p PID; -f children, -o file.
  • Filter: -e 'malloc+free', -e 'str*+mem*', -e '*@libssl.so*', exclude with leading -; by library -l libcrypto.so; static symbol -x name.
  • Detail: -S (also syscalls), -T (time/call), -tt (timestamps), -r (delta), -s N (string length), -C (demangle), -n N (indent nesting).
  • Summary: -c (count + time per function).
  • Args show as hex when there's no prototype — add a .conf (-F file) or install the lib's debug info.
  • Great for: how a closed binary uses libc/OpenSSL/DB libs, malloc/free auditing, args to system()/exec, getenv/dlopen discovery.
  • Limits: needs a dynamically linked, ideally non-stripped ELF; static binaries → nothing; PIE/RELRO/IFUNC and glibc changes can break it; only exported calls; high overhead; less maintained than strace.
  • Fallbacks: strace -S, gdb break malloc + commands, LD_PRELOAD shim.
Q&A
strace vs ltrace — when do you pick each?
strace for the kernel boundary: which files/sockets, why a syscall failed (errno), blocking/latency, process/signal behaviour — and it's robust on virtually any binary. ltrace for the library boundary: how the program uses libc/crypto/DB client libraries, allocation patterns, arguments to system()/exec, getenv/dlopen. Reach for strace first (more reliable); add ltrace when the question is specifically "what library calls, with what arguments". ltrace -S gives you both streams at once.
ltrace prints func(0x40120a, 0x7ffd...) = 0x55... instead of readable arguments. Why?
No prototype is available for that function, so ltrace can't tell that arg 1 is a char* to print as a string, etc. — it falls back to raw pointer/int values. Fix by providing a prototype: add the signature to a .conf file and pass -F file.conf, or install the library's -dev/debug package so ltrace can read the types. Standard libc/OpenSSL functions are usually decoded out of the box via the shipped config files.
You run ltrace on a Go (or Rust static) binary and see almost nothing. Why?
ltrace works by trapping calls through the PLT into shared libraries. A statically linked binary (typical for Go, and for Rust with musl) has no PLT calls to intercept — the library code is linked in directly — so there's nothing for ltrace to see. Go also makes raw syscalls itself, bypassing libc. Use strace for syscalls, gdb/perf for internal functions, or the language's own tooling (pprof, Go's runtime tracing).
How would you audit every malloc/free and spot a mismatch with ltrace?
ltrace -e 'malloc+calloc+realloc+free' -T -tt -o alloc.log ./app, then post-process: pair each malloc(sz) = 0xADDR with the later free(0xADDR). Addresses returned but never freed are leaks; a free(0xADDR) with no prior matching malloc (or a second free of the same address) is a double/invalid free. -c gives quick counts (if malloc+calloc count > free count, something leaks). This is a fast first look; for authoritative results use Valgrind Memcheck or ASan, which understand realloc, custom allocators, and report exact sites.
ltrace crashes the target or "detach: no such process" / doesn't attach on your distro. What now?
ltrace has historically had breakage against newer glibc/PIE/IFUNC and is less maintained than strace. Fallbacks that always work: set gdb breakpoints on the library functions (gdb -ex 'break SSL_write' -ex 'commands' -ex 'bt' -ex 'continue' -ex 'end' -ex run ./app); use an LD_PRELOAD shim that wraps the symbols (log args, then call dlsym(RTLD_NEXT, "sym")); or use strace -S plus reasoning about which libc call maps to which syscall. For allocation specifically, use Valgrind or a malloc-hook / MALLOC_TRACE/mtrace().
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does ltrace trace that strace does not?
Calls into shared libraries (functions resolved through the PLT) — malloc, strlen, getenv, SSL_read, etc. — with their arguments and return values. strace only sees system calls (the kernel boundary). ltrace -S shows both.
What kind of binary does ltrace work poorly or not at all on?
Statically linked binaries (no PLT to trap — e.g. Go, Rust+musl), and stripped binaries (no symbol names). Modern PIE + full RELRO + IFUNC and some glibc versions also degrade or break it.

Intermediate core

You suspect a third-party binary shells out to run a command with attacker-influenced input. How do you confirm and see the exact command?
Two complementary traces. ltrace: ltrace -f -s 4096 -e 'system+popen+exec*' ./app — shows the literal string passed to system()/popen() and the argv to execl/execv family calls, so you see the full command line and whether user input is interpolated unquoted. strace: strace -f -s 4096 -e trace=execve ./app — catches the actual execve(path, argv, envp) even if it's via posix_spawn or a direct syscall that ltrace misses, and shows the resolved path and full argument vector. Run both (or ltrace -S): ltrace tells you the API and the pre-shell string; strace's execve is the ground truth of what ran. If it's building a shell command from input, that's a command-injection finding.
A program is slow and you think it's the crypto library. How do you quantify that with ltrace, and what's the caveat?
ltrace -c -l libcrypto.so.3 -l libssl.so.3 ./app (or -e '*@libssl*') gives a per-function table: call counts and time attributed to each library call, so you can see e.g. RSA_private_decrypt or BN_mod_exp dominating, or an unexpected number of SSL_new/handshakes (connection churn). Add -T for per-call latency to catch a few very slow calls vs many cheap ones. Caveats: ltrace's own overhead is large and non-uniform, so the proportions are more trustworthy than absolute times; it only measures time in the traced (exported) calls, not work inlined or in sub-calls; and it can perturb timing enough to change behaviour (e.g. hide a race, or make I/O relatively cheaper). Confirm with a low-overhead profiler: perf record -g on the process and look at the libcrypto/libssl frames, or the library's own counters. Use ltrace to form the hypothesis ("it's doing 5,000 handshakes"), perf to prove the cost.

Advanced deep

ltrace is unreliable on your target. Design an LD_PRELOAD-based interposition layer to get the same information robustly, and note its limits.
Mechanism: build a shared object that defines the same symbols as the library functions you want to observe. Each wrapper: on first call, resolve the real function with dlsym(RTLD_NEXT, "name") (cache it); log the arguments (thread id, timestamp, decoded values); call the real function; log the return value/errno; return it. Load it with LD_PRELOAD=./hooks.so ./app so the dynamic loader binds the app's PLT entries to your wrappers instead of libc's. Use a lock-free ring buffer or per-thread buffers + a background flush to keep overhead and lock contention low; guard against reentrancy (a wrapper that itself calls a wrapped function — e.g. your logger calling malloc) with a thread-local "in hook" flag or by using raw syscalls / a preallocated arena in the logger. What it gets you: exact args/returns for the chosen functions, on any dynamically linked binary, with your own decoding (you know the prototypes), much lower and more predictable overhead than ltrace since only the functions you care about are intercepted, and you can add logic (count, sample, assert, inject faults for testing). Classic uses: allocation tracking (malloc/calloc/realloc/free with backtraces via backtrace()), fd/socket auditing, timing every SSL_* call, recording every getenv/open. Limits: only works for dynamically resolved calls — a statically linked binary, or calls the library makes internally to its own functions (not through the PLT), or direct syscalls (Go), are invisible; functions resolved via IFUNC or copied by the linker, and -Wl,-Bsymbolic/versioned-symbol cases, may not interpose; LD_PRELOAD is ignored for setuid/setgid binaries and can be stripped by secure-execution mode; symbol versioning means you may need dlvsym for the exact version; C++ mangled/overloaded symbols need care; and if the app also uses dlopen with RTLD_DEEPBIND your interposition is bypassed for that library. It's also invasive to set up per-function. When to prefer it: you need reliable, low-overhead, custom-decoded observation of a specific set of library calls on a binary you can run but not modify, and ltrace/gdb aren't cutting it — otherwise gdb breakpoints (break + scripted commands) or Valgrind (for allocation) are less work.

perf: The Linux Profiler

Samples the CPU thousands of times a second, or reads exact hardware counters, to show where cycles go — in your code and the kernel — with no recompilation.

Notes

perf stat: exact counts, not samples

What / why. Runs a command (or attaches) and reports precise totals for a set of events — cycles, instructions, cache misses, branch misses, context switches. No sampling, negligible perturbation. Use it first to answer "is this workload CPU-bound, memory-stalled, or branchy?" and to get IPC (instructions per cycle).

$ perf stat ./app                     # default event set + wall/user/sys time
 Performance counter stats for './app':
      1,842.11 msec task-clock       #    0.998 CPUs utilized
            37      context-switches
 6,271,004,882      cycles           #    3.404 GHz
 4,013,776,201      instructions     #    0.64  insn per cycle   <- low IPC = stalls
   812,004,113      branches         #  440.8 M/sec
    41,222,900      branch-misses    #    5.08% of all branches   <- high = mispredict cost
   1.845 seconds time elapsed

$ perf stat -d ./app                  # -d: add L1/LLC cache + TLB stats (repeat for more)
$ perf stat -r 10 ./app               # run 10x, show mean +- stddev  (benchmark mode)
$ perf stat -p 4242 -- sleep 5        # attach to a PID for 5 seconds
$ perf stat -a -I 1000 sleep 10       # whole machine, print every 1000 ms
$ perf stat -e cache-misses,cache-references,LLC-load-misses ./app   # pick your own events
$ perf stat -e '{cycles,instructions}:u' ./app   # a group, user-space only (:u ; :k = kernel)

perf record + perf report: the sampling profiler

What / how. perf record interrupts the CPU N times/second and saves the instruction pointer (and, with -g, the call stack) to perf.data. perf report then shows which functions the samples landed in — i.e. where wall time on-CPU is spent.

$ perf record -F 999 -g -- ./app arg          # 999 Hz, with call graphs, run this command
$ perf record -F 999 -g -p 4242 -- sleep 20   # profile a running process for 20s
$ perf record -F 999 -g -a -- sleep 10        # whole system for 10s
$ perf report                                 # interactive TUI (arrows, '+' to expand, 'a' annotate)
$ perf report --stdio --sort=overhead,symbol  # plain text
$ perf report -g graph,0.5,caller             # call graph, prune <0.5%, caller-oriented

# call-graph unwinding method matters:
--call-graph fp        # frame pointers - cheap & accurate IF built with -fno-omit-frame-pointer
--call-graph dwarf     # unwind from CFI - works without frame pointers, bigger perf.data, some skid
--call-graph dwarf,16384   # bump the stack dump size for deep stacks
--call-graph lbr       # hardware Last Branch Record - very cheap, limited depth, Intel

# report columns: 'Children' = inclusive (this fn + callees), 'Self' = exclusive (this fn only)
$ perf report --no-children        # show only self time (flat profile)

perf top: live profiling

What / why. A top-style, continuously-updating view of the hottest functions system-wide or for one process — the fastest way to answer "what is eating the CPU right now" on a box you just SSH'd into.

$ perf top                       # system-wide, hottest symbols, refreshing
$ perf top -p 4242 -g            # one process, with call graphs (press 'E' to expand)
$ perf top -e cache-misses       # sort by a different event
$ perf top --sort comm,dso       # group by process / shared object instead of symbol
$ perf top -K                    # hide kernel symbols  (-U hides userspace)
# lines like  16.20%  libc.so.6  [.] __memmove_avx_unaligned   -> a hot memcpy path

Events: perf list and what to count

What / why. perf can count hundreds of event sources. Knowing a few well is enough for most work.

$ perf list                      # everything available on this CPU/kernel
$ perf list 'cache*' 'sched:*'   # filter

# Hardware (PMU):   cycles  instructions  cache-references  cache-misses
#                   branches  branch-misses  ref-cycles  stalled-cycles-frontend/backend
#                   LLC-loads  LLC-load-misses  dTLB-load-misses  ...
# Software:         cpu-clock  task-clock  page-faults  context-switches
#                   cpu-migrations  minor-faults  major-faults
# Tracepoints:      sched:sched_switch  sched:sched_wakeup  block:block_rq_issue
#                   syscalls:sys_enter_openat  net:net_dev_xmit  kmem:kmalloc  ...
# Modifiers:        :u user  :k kernel  :h hypervisor  :G/:H guest/host  :p/:pp precise (less skid)
# Raw:              -e r04c5  (a PMU event by hex code from the vendor manual)

$ perf stat -e task-clock,context-switches,cpu-migrations,page-faults,\
cycles,instructions,branches,branch-misses ./app   # a solid default block

Flame graphs and perf script

What / why. perf report is a tree; a flame graph is a single picture of the whole profile — width = time, stack = depth — far easier to scan for the wide box that's the hotspot. perf script dumps raw samples for any custom post-processing.

# on-CPU flame graph (Brendan Gregg's FlameGraph scripts)
$ perf record -F 99 -g -- ./app
$ perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl | ./flamegraph.pl > cpu.svg
#   (newer perf: 'perf script report flamegraph' emits an HTML flame graph directly)

$ perf script                          # raw: timestamp, pid, event, full stack per sample
$ perf script -F comm,pid,tid,time,event,ip,sym   # choose columns
$ perf script | grep -c '^'            # sample count sanity check

# OFF-CPU time (blocked on I/O, locks, sleep) - not visible in a normal CPU profile:
$ perf record -e sched:sched_switch -e sched:sched_stat_sleep -g -- ./app
#   then build an off-cpu flame graph, or use bcc/bpftrace 'offcputime' which is simpler

The specialised subcommands

CommandWhat it answers
perf annotate SYMWhich instruction / source line inside a hot function costs — disassembly with sample %.
perf sched record + latency/timehistScheduler behaviour: run-queue latency, who preempted whom, wakeup-to-run delay (p99 latency bugs).
perf tracestrace-like syscall trace, far lower overhead; --duration 5 shows only slow calls, -s summary.
perf lock record + reportKernel lock contention: which lock, wait time, contention count.
perf mem record / perf c2cMemory access latency by address; c2c finds cache-line false sharing across cores.
perf probeAdd a dynamic tracepoint to any kernel or user function/line, capturing arguments — then record -e probe:....
$ perf annotate -s parse_row --stdio        # hot lines inside parse_row()
$ perf sched record -- ./app ; perf sched latency --sort max   # worst scheduling delays
$ perf trace -p 4242 --duration 10          # syscalls taking >10 ms on that PID
$ perf probe --add 'do_sys_openat2 filename:string'    # add a probe with an arg
$ perf record -e probe:do_sys_openat2 -aR sleep 5 ; perf script
$ perf probe --del '*'                       # clean up your probes afterwards

Setup, permissions, and gotchas

  • Install: perf ships in linux-tools-$(uname -r) / perf package — the version should match the running kernel or some features break.
  • Permissions: /proc/sys/kernel/perf_event_paranoid gates access — 3=nothing, 2=user-space only, 1=+kernel profiling, 0=+raw tracepoints, -1=everything. Lower it (sysctl kernel.perf_event_paranoid=1) or run as root/with CAP_PERFMON. kernel.kptr_restrict=0 to see kernel symbol addresses.
  • Call graphs need help: build the target (and ideally its libraries) with -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer, or use --call-graph dwarf (heavier) / lbr (Intel, shallow). Missing frames show as [unknown] or a broken tree.
  • JIT / managed runtimes: the JVM/Node/etc. need to emit a /tmp/perf-<pid>.map (e.g. -XX:+PreserveFramePointer + async-profiler, or --perf-basic-prof) or perf shows raw addresses for JITed code.
  • Containers: profile from the host (perf record -a or --pid=$(pidof ...)), or give the container CAP_PERFMON/SYS_ADMIN and a low paranoid setting; symbol files must be reachable.
  • VMs / cloud: hardware PMU counters are often unavailable or limited — cycles/instructions may be emulated or missing; perf stat falls back to cpu-clock. Bare metal for serious counter work.
  • Skid: the sampled IP can be a few instructions past the real one; use :pp (PEBS/precise) events for instruction-accurate attribution in perf annotate.
  • perf.data size: high -F + --call-graph dwarf + long runs = gigabytes; lower the frequency (99 Hz is plenty for a flame graph), shorten the window, or filter events.
# quick "profile this running service safely" recipe
$ sudo sysctl kernel.perf_event_paranoid=1
$ perf record -F 99 -g -p $(pgrep -n myservice) -- sleep 30
$ perf report --stdio --sort=overhead --percent-limit 1 | head -40
$ perf script report flamegraph          # or: perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > fg.svg
Cheat Sheet
  • perf stat ./app = exact counts (cycles, instructions, cache/branch misses) → IPC and stall analysis. -d detail, -r N repeat, -p PID, -a system, -I ms interval, -e events, :u/:k.
  • perf record -F 999 -g -- ./app then perf report = sampling CPU profile. -p PID, -a, --call-graph fp|dwarf|lbr.
  • perf report: Children = inclusive, Self = exclusive; --no-children for a flat profile; --stdio for text.
  • perf top -p PID -g = live hottest-functions view.
  • Events: perf list; HW cycles instructions cache-misses branch-misses LLC-load-misses; SW context-switches page-faults cpu-migrations; tracepoints sched:* syscalls:* block:*; modifiers :u :k :pp; groups {a,b}.
  • Flame graph: perf record -F 99 -g → perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > fg.svg (or perf script report flamegraph).
  • Subcommands: annotate (hot lines), sched (run-queue latency), trace (cheap strace), lock (contention), mem/c2c (false sharing), probe (dynamic tracepoints).
  • Setup: match linux-tools to the kernel; lower kernel.perf_event_paranoid; build target -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer; JIT needs perf-<pid>.map; VMs often lack the PMU.
  • Off-CPU (blocked on I/O/locks) is not in a normal CPU profile — use sched:sched_switch or bpftrace offcputime.
Q&A
When do you use perf stat versus perf record?
perf stat when you want exact totals for a few metrics and a verdict on the nature of the workload — IPC, cache-miss rate, branch-miss rate, context switches — with essentially zero perturbation; it's also the benchmarking tool (-r for mean±stddev). perf record when you want to know where in the code the time goes — it samples the instruction pointer and call stack so perf report/flame graphs can attribute cost to functions and call paths. Typical flow: perf stat to characterise, then perf record to localise.
Your flame graph is a flat wall of [unknown] frames. Why, and how do you fix it?
perf can't unwind the stack. Causes and fixes: (1) the binary/libraries were built with -fomit-frame-pointer (the default at -O2) so frame-pointer unwinding fails — rebuild the hot code with -fno-omit-frame-pointer, or record with --call-graph dwarf (uses CFI, works without frame pointers, at the cost of bigger perf.data and some skid), or --call-graph lbr on Intel. (2) No debug symbols — install the -dbg/debuginfo packages or build with -g. (3) JITed code (JVM/V8) with no /tmp/perf-<pid>.map — enable the runtime's perf map / use async-profiler. (4) perf_event_paranoid too high to read kernel symbols, or kptr_restrict hiding them.
The service's CPU usage is low but latency is bad. Will perf record find the problem?
Not on its own — a standard perf record samples on-CPU time, so if the threads are mostly blocked (waiting on I/O, a lock, a downstream, a sleep) they generate almost no samples and the profile looks empty or misleading. You need off-CPU analysis: record scheduler tracepoints (perf record -e sched:sched_switch -e sched:sched_stat_sleep -g) and build an off-CPU flame graph, use perf sched latency/timehist for run-queue and wakeup delays, perf lock for contention, or bpftrace/bcc offcputime which is the easiest. Combine on-CPU + off-CPU for the full latency picture.
What does a low "insn per cycle" (IPC) in perf stat tell you?
The CPU is spending cycles not retiring instructions — it's stalled. IPC around 0.2–0.6 on a modern core usually means memory stalls (cache/TLB misses — check cache-misses, LLC-load-misses, dTLB-load-misses, and stalled-cycles-backend) or heavy branch misprediction (branch-misses %, stalled-cycles-frontend). IPC around 2–4 means the core is busy doing useful work and the win is algorithmic (do less), not micro-architectural. So IPC steers you: low → fix data layout / access patterns / branches; high → reduce the work itself.
Is it safe to run perf on a production host?
Sampling with perf record -F 99 -g for a bounded window is typically 1–5% overhead and is a common production practice (Google/Netflix profile fleets this way). Keep it safe: use a modest frequency (99 Hz is enough for a flame graph), a short duration (-- sleep 30), scope to the PID or a cgroup rather than -a where possible, avoid --call-graph dwarf on very hot multi-threaded processes (large data + copy overhead — prefer fp or lbr), and watch perf.data disk usage. perf stat is essentially free. perf trace is much lighter than strace for syscall work. Avoid high-frequency tracepoint recording (e.g. every sched_switch system-wide) on a busy box unless briefly.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What's the difference between perf stat and perf record?
perf stat counts events exactly for the whole run (cycles, instructions, cache/branch misses, context switches) with near-zero overhead — it tells you the nature of the workload. perf record statistically samples the instruction pointer and call stacks into perf.data so perf report can tell you which functions the time is spent in.
Which flags give you a call-graph CPU profile of a running process for 20 seconds?
perf record -F 999 -g -p <pid> -- sleep 20, then perf report. -F sets sample frequency, -g captures call stacks, -p targets the PID, and the sleep bounds the duration.

Intermediate core

A function shows 30% "Children" but only 2% "Self" in perf report. What does that mean and where do you look next?
Children is inclusive time (the function plus everything it calls); Self is exclusive (samples that landed directly in that function's own instructions). 30% children / 2% self means the function itself is cheap but it's the gateway to expensive work — the cost is in its callees. Expand its subtree in the TUI (or perf report -g graph,0.5,caller, or a flame graph) to see which descendant carries the weight, then profile that function's self time with perf annotate to find the hot lines/instructions. If instead you'd seen high self and low children, the function's own loop/body is the hotspot and you annotate it directly. Use --no-children for a flat (self-only) view when the call graph is noisy.
You optimised a hot loop and wall time barely changed, though perf report still shows it as #1. How do you figure out what's really limiting it?
The sampling profile tells you where cycles are spent, not why they're wasted — move to counters and micro-arch analysis. (1) perf stat -d -d -d on the workload: look at IPC. If IPC is high (2+), the core is already busy and the loop is doing genuine work — the win is algorithmic (fewer iterations, better data structure), not tuning. If IPC is low, it's stalled. (2) Identify the stall: stalled-cycles-frontend vs stalled-cycles-backend; high cache-misses/LLC-load-misses/dTLB-load-misses → memory-bound (fix data layout, access order, prefetch, blocking, reduce working set); high branch-misses % → mispredicting (make branches predictable, branchless, sort input, use likely/unlikely). (3) perf annotate the loop with a precise event (-e cycles:pp or mem_load_retired.l3_miss:pp) to pin the exact instruction/line that stalls — often one load. (4) perf mem record / perf c2c if it's multi-threaded and the misses look like false sharing (two cores writing the same cache line). (5) Check you're not off-CPU for part of the "loop" (a syscall, page fault — perf trace, page-faults counter). (6) Consider the "roofline": compare achieved GFLOP/s and GB/s against the machine's peaks to see whether you're compute- or bandwidth-bound. The profile said "spend cycles here"; the counters say "because it waits on memory/branches", which is what tells you the fix.

Advanced deep

Design a continuous, fleet-wide profiling capability built on perf: what you collect, overhead control, symbolication, storage, and what perf alone can't give you.
Goal: always-on, low-overhead CPU (and ideally off-CPU) profiles from every service, queryable over time, so any regression or hotspot is one query away — the "continuous profiling" model. Collection: a node agent (or a modern eBPF profiler like Parca / Grafana Pyroscope, or perf in a loop) samples system-wide at a low frequency — ~19–49 Hz is plenty when aggregated over minutes across many hosts — with -g using frame pointers (mandate -fno-omit-frame-pointer in the org build, and for the base image/libc where possible) or LBR on Intel; avoid DWARF unwinding fleet-wide (CPU + data cost). Record in short rotating windows (e.g. 10–60s every few minutes) or use the eBPF approach that aggregates stacks in-kernel and never writes raw perf.data. Tag every profile with service, version, region, host, and the git build id. Add periodic perf stat snapshots (IPC, cache/branch misses, context-switches) as low-cardinality metrics. Optionally scheduled off-CPU captures (sched:sched_switch-based, sampled and time-boxed) for latency work. Overhead control: cap frequency; scope to cgroups/PIDs of interest rather than truly system-wide where possible; skip DWARF; time-box every capture; a global rate limiter and a kill switch; measure the agent's own CPU and alert if it exceeds a budget (<1%); back off automatically under high load. Symbolication: don't symbolicate on the production host — ship raw stacks (addresses + build ids + mapping info) and resolve offline against a symbol server (debuginfod, or an artifact store keyed by build id) so prod images can stay stripped. Handle JIT runtimes via their perf-map / async-profiler integration; handle containers/PIE via build-id + mmap records. Storage & query: fold stacks to collapsed form, store in a columnar/time-series backend designed for stack data (Parca/Pyroscope/FlameDB), with retention tiers (high-res days, downsampled months). Expose: flame graphs per service/version, diff flame graphs (this release vs last, this region vs that), top-functions trends, and "who regressed" alerts when a function's share jumps. Wire deploy markers in so a profile change lines up with a release. What perf alone doesn't give you: (1) why cycles are wasted — you still need perf stat counters / top-down analysis / perf c2c for the micro-arch story, run on demand on a repro host. (2) Reliable off-CPU / wall-clock latency attribution at fleet scale — needs scheduler tracing or eBPF offcputime, heavier and usually sampled/targeted. (3) Request-level context — perf stacks aren't tied to a trace id; you need distributed tracing (OTel) and correlation to answer "which endpoint/tenant". (4) Allocation profiling — use the runtime's heap profiler / bcc, not perf. (5) Managed-runtime semantics (GC pauses, JIT tiers) are better seen with async-profiler / runtime tooling. (6) Windows/other OS — perf is Linux-only. (7) It doesn't fix anything or rank by business impact — that's the human + the cost model. So: eBPF/perf continuous sampling with frame pointers for the always-on "where", on-demand perf stat/c2c/annotate for the "why", scheduler/off-CPU + tracing for latency, and a symbol server + diff-flamegraph UI + deploy markers so regressions surface automatically.

gcov: Code Coverage Analysis

Compile with coverage instrumentation, run the program (or the test suite), then see exactly which lines and branches executed — and which never did.

Notes

The build-run-report cycle

What / how. Add --coverage (shorthand for -fprofile-arcs -ftest-coverage when compiling, -lgcov when linking). Compile -O0 so lines map cleanly. Run the program; on normal exit it writes .gcda files next to the objects. Then run gcov on each source.

$ gcc -O0 -g --coverage -c calc.c -o calc.o        # emits calc.gcno now
$ gcc --coverage calc.o main.o -o app             # links libgcov
$ ./app                                            # or: run the whole test suite
#   -> writes calc.gcda, main.gcda  (execution counts)
$ gcov calc.c
File 'calc.c'
Lines executed:82.35% of 51
Creating 'calc.c.gcov'                              # annotated source

$ head calc.c.gcov
        -:    1:#include "calc.h"
        5:    7:int add(int a,int b){ return a+b; }   # executed 5 times
    #####:   12:int div(int a,int b){ return a/b; }   # ##### = NEVER executed
        -:   13:                                       # '-' = non-code line

Branch and function coverage

What / why. A line can be "covered" while a condition was only ever true. gcov -b adds per-branch taken/not-taken info; -c shows raw branch counts instead of percentages; -f gives a per-function summary. This is where you find the untested else, the error path that never fires, the && short-circuit you never exercised both ways.

$ gcov -b -c -f calc.c
Function 'div'
Lines executed:100.00% of 3
Branches executed:100.00% of 2
Taken at least once:50.00% of 2          # <-- one branch direction never taken
Calls executed:100.00% of 1

# in calc.c.gcov with -b:
        3:   15:  if (b == 0)
branch  0 taken 3 (fallthrough)
branch  1 taken 0                        # the "b == 0" error path is untested
    #####:   16:      return handle_div0();

Key gcov options

gcov SOURCE...            # produce SOURCE.gcov annotated files
  -b, --branch-probabilities   include branch taken/not-taken percentages
  -c, --branch-counts          show branch counts as absolute numbers, not %
  -f, --function-summaries     per-function line/branch/call coverage
  -a, --all-blocks             per basic-block counts (very detailed)
  -m, --demangled-names        demangle C++ names in the report
  -r, --relative-only          only report files with paths relative to the build dir
  -s DIR, --source-prefix DIR  strip this prefix from source paths
  -i, --json-format            machine-readable output (.gcov.json.gz) for tooling
  -o DIR                       where the .gcno/.gcda live (if not beside the source)
  -p, --preserve-paths         keep full path in the .gcov filename (avoids collisions)
  -u, --unconditional-branches include branches that are always taken
  -j, --json-format (older -i) ; -t, --stdout  print to stdout instead of a file

Readable reports: lcov and gcovr

What / why. Raw .gcov files are per-file text. lcov aggregates all .gcda into one .info database and genhtml renders a browsable, colour-coded report. gcovr (Python) does the same and also emits Cobertura XML / JSON / SonarQube formats that CI dashboards understand, plus a one-line summary with a fail-under threshold.

# lcov -> HTML
$ lcov --capture --directory . --output-file cov.info
$ lcov --remove cov.info '/usr/*' '*/tests/*' '*/third_party/*' --output-file cov.info
$ genhtml cov.info --output-directory cov-html     # open cov-html/index.html

# reset counters between test groups:
$ lcov --directory . --zerocounters        # or: find . -name '*.gcda' -delete

# gcovr -> CI
$ gcovr -r . --exclude tests --exclude-unreachable-branches \
        --xml-pretty -o coverage.xml --html-details coverage.html \
        --fail-under-line 80 --fail-under-branch 60      # non-zero exit if below

Gotchas and special cases

  • No .gcda written? The process must exit cleanly (return/exit()). A crash, _exit(), abort(), SIGKILL, or an infinite loop skips the atexit flush. Call __gcov_dump() (older: __gcov_flush()) before a known-fatal point, or install a signal handler that dumps then re-raises.
  • Long-running services: they never exit during a test. Send a signal that triggers __gcov_dump(), or build with -fprofile-update=atomic and dump periodically.
  • Counts accumulate across runs into the same .gcda — good for merging many test cases, but zero the counters (lcov --zerocounters / delete .gcda) when you want a clean measurement.
  • Remote/embedded target: the .gcda paths are baked in at compile time. Set GCOV_PREFIX=/tmp/cov and GCOV_PREFIX_STRIP=N on the target so files land in a writable place, then copy them back to the build tree for gcov.
  • Parallel tests: races on the same .gcda. Use -fprofile-update=atomic, or give each test process its own build/output dir and merge with lcov -a a.info -a b.info / gcov-tool merge.
  • Optimisation: coverage at -O2 is misleading (inlining, merged lines, dead-code elimination). Use a dedicated -O0 --coverage build for coverage; keep it separate from the perf build.
  • Coverage is necessary, not sufficient — 100% line coverage with weak assertions still misses bugs. Treat it as "what did we forget to test", not "the tests are good".
Cheat Sheet
  • Build: gcc -O0 -g --coverage ... (= -fprofile-arcs -ftest-coverage + link -lgcov). Compile emits .gcno; running emits .gcda.
  • Report one file: gcov file.c → file.c.gcov. Markers: ##### = never run, - = non-code, a number = hit count.
  • Branches/functions: gcov -b -c -f file.c — find untested else/error paths ("taken at least once" < 100%).
  • Useful flags: -m (demangle), -i/--json-format (tooling), -o DIR (where .gcno/.gcda are), -p (preserve paths), -s/-r (path trimming).
  • HTML: lcov --capture -d . -o cov.info → lcov --remove junk → genhtml cov.info -o html/.
  • CI: gcovr -r . --xml-pretty -o coverage.xml --fail-under-line 80 --fail-under-branch 60.
  • Reset between measurements: lcov --zerocounters -d . or find . -name '*.gcda' -delete. Counts otherwise accumulate.
  • No data: process must exit cleanly — crash/_exit/signal skips the flush; call __gcov_dump(). Remote: set GCOV_PREFIX/GCOV_PREFIX_STRIP. Parallel: -fprofile-update=atomic. Coverage build is -O0 and separate from the perf build.
Q&A
What's the difference between .gcno and .gcda files?
.gcno ("notes") is written by the compiler and describes the code structure — the basic blocks and the arcs (control-flow graph) — along with source line mappings. .gcda ("data") is written by the instrumented program at exit and holds the execution counts for those arcs. gcov combines the two: the .gcno says what the code is, the .gcda says how many times each part ran. Delete .gcno and rebuild if the source changed; delete .gcda to reset counts.
Line coverage is 95% but you still ship bugs in conditionals. What coverage metric helps and why?
Branch coverage (gcov -b, or condition/decision coverage). A line like if (a && b) do_x(); counts as "covered" the moment it executes once, even if b was always true and do_x()'s absence was never tested. Branch coverage requires each decision to go both ways; the report's "Taken at least once" < 100% flags the direction you never exercised — typically error handling, boundary cases, and the else you forgot. For safety-critical code go further to MC/DC (each condition independently affects the outcome).
Your test run produced no .gcda files. Give three reasons and fixes.
(1) The program didn't exit normally — it crashed, called _exit()/abort(), was SIGKILLed, or looped forever, so the atexit flush never ran. Fix: call __gcov_dump() before the fatal point, or a signal handler that dumps then re-raises; for long-running services, dump on a signal. (2) It ran in a different working directory or a read-only filesystem, so it couldn't write the .gcda next to the objects. Fix: run from the build dir, or set GCOV_PREFIX/GCOV_PREFIX_STRIP to redirect to a writable path. (3) The binary wasn't actually built with --coverage (or was relinked without -lgcov), or you're looking at a stale build. Fix: clean, rebuild with --coverage on both compile and link, verify .gcno exist.
How do you get coverage for a daemon that never exits during the test?
Trigger the profile dump without exiting: register a handler for a spare signal (e.g. SIGUSR2) that calls __gcov_dump() (and optionally __gcov_reset()), send it after the test scenario, then collect the .gcda. Alternatively build with -fprofile-update=atomic and periodically call the dump, or run the daemon under a test harness that sends SIGTERM and have a clean shutdown path that returns from main. Then lcov --capture as usual. For containers, mount a writable volume and point GCOV_PREFIX at it.
Can you measure coverage on an optimised (-O2) build? Should you?
You can — --coverage works at any -O — but the results are misleading: inlining attributes a callee's execution to the caller's lines, dead-code elimination removes lines so they show as non-code, and multiple source lines can collapse onto one block. For an honest line/branch map, use a dedicated -O0 --coverage build. The one time you'd measure at -O2 is profile-guided optimisation (-fprofile-use), where you deliberately want the optimiser's view — but that's optimisation, not test-coverage reporting.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which flag enables gcov instrumentation, and at which stages?
--coverage — on the compile step (it implies -fprofile-arcs -ftest-coverage, producing .gcno) and on the link step (it links libgcov). Build at -O0 for a clean line mapping.
In a .gcov file, what do ##### and - mean?
