Monitoring (WIDS/WIPS): dedicated sensors or AP scanning to alert on — rogue APs and evil twins (same SSID, different BSSID/vendor/cert), deauth/disassoc floods, WPS activity, karma/known-beacon attacks, unusual association patterns, and clients probing for corporate SSIDs off-site; auto-containment optional but tune carefully (containment is itself a deauth — legal/operational care). Feed alerts to the SOC, correlate with RADIUS auth logs (failed EAP, cert errors, impossible roaming). Endpoint side: MDM enforces the Wi-Fi profile (no manual SSID config, server-cert validation locked on, no "connect to open networks"), disables Wi-Fi Sense-style features, and removes saved open/PSK profiles. Validation: periodic authorised wireless assessments and continuous WIPS coverage checks; test that an evil-twin genuinely fails (client rejects the bad server cert) and that guest→corp isolation holds. Net: certificate-based WPA3-Enterprise with enforced mutual validation (no crackable/phishable secret), 802.11w against deauth, no WPS, strict role-based segmentation, per-device keys for the PSK-only stragglers, and WIDS/WIPS + RADIUS-log correlation so the attacks these tools perform either don't work or are detected immediately.

Sniffing & Traffic Analysis: tcpdump & tshark

Capture packets off the wire with a BPF filter, save to pcap, then slice and analyse — the same skill for debugging an outage and for understanding traffic during an authorised assessment.

Notes

tcpdump — capture with a BPF filter

What / why. The ubiquitous CLI sniffer. The filter expression is BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter), compiled and applied in the kernel so unmatched packets are dropped cheaply. Write to a pcap for real analysis; the terminal view is for a quick glance.

$ sudo tcpdump -D                                   # list capture interfaces
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -v host 10.0.0.5 and port 443
#   -i iface   -nn no name/port resolution   -v/-vv/-vvv verbosity   -e link-layer hdr   -X hex+ascii   -A ascii

# save to a rotating capture (don't fill the disk):
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w cap-%Y%m%d-%H%M%S.pcap -G 3600 -C 100 -W 24 -Z root 'tcp port 80 or tcp port 443'
#   -w file   -G seconds (time rotate)   -C MB (size rotate)   -W keep N files   -s 0 full packet (default now)

# read + re-filter a saved file:
$ tcpdump -r cap.pcap -nn 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn) != 0 and tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-ack) == 0'   # bare SYNs

# common BPF idioms:
#   host H   src/dst host H   net 10.0.0.0/24   port P   portrange 1000-2000
#   tcp / udp / icmp / arp     vlan 100     ether host AA:BB:..
#   'tcp[13] & 2 != 0'  (SYN set)     'icmp[icmptype] == icmp-echoreq'
#   not port 22   (exclude your own ssh session so the capture isn't recursive)

tshark — Wireshark on the command line

What / why. Wireshark's engine without the GUI: the same protocol dissectors, display filters (-Y), field extraction (-T fields -e ...), and the -z statistics that answer "who talked to whom, how much, how slow".

$ tshark -D ; tshark -i eth0 -f 'tcp port 443' -w cap.pcapng    # -f = capture (BPF) filter
$ tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y 'http.request' -T fields -e ip.src -e http.host -e http.request.uri
$ tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y 'dns' -T fields -e dns.qry.name -e dns.a | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
$ tshark -r cap.pcapng -q -z conv,tcp                 # TCP conversations (bytes, packets, duration)
$ tshark -r cap.pcapng -q -z io,stat,1                # throughput per second
$ tshark -r cap.pcapng -q -z endpoints,ip             # per-IP totals
$ tshark -r cap.pcapng -q -z http,tree                # HTTP request/response breakdown
$ tshark -r cap.pcapng -Y 'tcp.analysis.retransmission or tcp.analysis.zero_window'   # trouble
$ tshark -r cap.pcapng -z follow,tcp,ascii,3          # reassemble stream #3
# display-filter examples: ip.addr==10.0.0.5 && tcp.port==443 ; http.response.code>=500 ;
#   tls.handshake.type==1 (ClientHello) ; frame contains "password" ; tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0

Capture vs display filters, and getting the packets at all

  • Capture filter (tcpdump expr, tshark/dumpcap -f) is BPF, applied in-kernel before capture — keeps volume down but you can't recover what you filtered out. Use it to bound a long capture (host/port/protocol).
  • Display filter (Wireshark, tshark -Y) runs after capture on the dissected packets — far more expressive (any protocol field, comparisons, contains, matches), and you can change it repeatedly on the same pcap.
  • Seeing the traffic: you only capture what hits your NIC. For traffic between other hosts you need a switch SPAN/mirror port, a physical network TAP, an old hub, or to be on-path (a gateway, a proxy, or — in an authorised test — an ARP/MITM position). Wireless needs monitor mode (see the Wi-Fi topic).
  • Encryption: TLS/SSH payloads stay opaque. You can still see SNI (usually), cert details, timing, sizes, and endpoints. To read payloads you need the session keys (SSLKEYLOGFILE from a browser/curl you control) or a TLS-terminating proxy — only for endpoints you own/are authorised to intercept.

Where this is used — and the defensive side

  • Offensive / assessment: understanding protocols and data flows on an authorised engagement, catching credentials sent in cleartext (finding: "app uses HTTP Basic over plain HTTP"), confirming a MITM position works, extracting artefacts from a provided pcap in a CTF/DFIR exercise.
  • Defensive / ops (the bigger use): diagnosing latency/retransmits/resets, confirming a firewall rule, seeing what a mystery process talks to, malware C2 analysis from a pcap, and feeding IDS (Suricata/Zeek consume the same traffic).
  • Countering hostile sniffing: encrypt everything in transit (TLS 1.2+/1.3, SSH, IPsec/WireGuard, mTLS between services); switched networks with port security and dynamic ARP inspection / DHCP snooping to stop ARP-spoof MITM; 802.1X/NAC so an attacker can't just plug in; disable unused ports; segment; and monitor for NICs in promiscuous mode and for ARP anomalies.
  • Legal: capturing traffic you're not a party to, without authorisation, can be unlawful interception. Capture your own host freely; capture a network only with the owner's sign-off.
Cheat Sheet
  • tcpdump: tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -v <bpf>; save -w file; rotate -G secs -C MB -W count; read -r file; -A/-X for payload; exclude your SSH with not port 22.
  • BPF: host/src/dst host, net CIDR, port/portrange, tcp/udp/icmp/arp, vlan, flag tests (tcp[13] & 2 != 0 = SYN).
  • tshark: -f capture (BPF) filter, -Y display filter, -T fields -e f1 -e f2 extract, -r read, -w write.
  • tshark stats: -z conv,tcp, -z io,stat,1, -z endpoints,ip, -z http,tree, -z follow,tcp,ascii,N.
  • Display-filter examples: ip.addr==X, http.response.code>=500, tls.handshake.type==1, tcp.analysis.retransmission, frame contains "...".
  • Capture filter = kernel/BPF, pre-capture, cheap, irreversible. Display filter = post-capture, rich, re-runnable.
  • To see other hosts' traffic: SPAN/mirror port, TAP, hub, or on-path/MITM (authorised only). TLS payloads need keys (SSLKEYLOGFILE) or a terminating proxy.
  • Defence: encrypt in transit everywhere; switched net + port security + DAI + DHCP snooping + 802.1X; segment; watch for promiscuous NICs and ARP spoofing. Unauthorised interception can be illegal.
Q&A
What's the difference between a capture filter and a display filter?
A capture filter is a BPF expression compiled and run in the kernel as packets arrive — anything that doesn't match is never stored, so it keeps capture volume and CPU down, but you can't get filtered-out packets back. A display filter (Wireshark / tshark -Y) runs after capture against fully dissected packets, so it's far more expressive (any protocol field, string matching, comparisons) and you can change it as often as you like on the same file. Rule of thumb: capture filter to bound a long capture to the hosts/ports/protocol you care about; display filter to explore what you captured.
You run tcpdump on a switch port and only see broadcast traffic plus your own, not the conversation between two other servers. Why?
Switches forward unicast frames only to the port where the destination MAC lives — they don't flood every port like a hub. So your NIC never sees traffic between two other hosts. To capture it you need a SPAN/mirror port configured on the switch to copy those ports' traffic to yours, a physical network TAP inserted in the link, or to be on the traffic path (the default gateway, a proxy, or an authorised ARP-spoof/MITM position). Promiscuous mode on your NIC is necessary but not sufficient — the frames still have to arrive.
Can you read HTTPS content from a packet capture?
Not the payload, by default — it's encrypted under TLS. You can see: the TCP/IP endpoints, packet sizes and timing, the TLS handshake including the server certificate and usually the SNI hostname (unless Encrypted Client Hello is in use), and the negotiated version/cipher. To decrypt the payload you need the session secrets: set SSLKEYLOGFILE in a browser/curl you control and point Wireshark at it, or capture at a point where TLS is terminated (a reverse proxy you own). For third-party traffic you don't have keys for, the payload stays opaque — and intercepting it without authorisation would be unlawful anyway.
Which tshark option gives you a quick "top talkers" view from a pcap?
tshark -r cap.pcapng -q -z endpoints,ip for per-IP byte/packet totals, or -z conv,tcp (or conv,ip) for conversations ranked by volume with duration. -z io,stat,1 shows throughput over time. These are the CLI equivalents of Wireshark's Statistics → Conversations / Endpoints / IO Graph.
How do you keep a long tcpdump capture from filling the disk?
Use ring-buffer rotation: -w cap-%Y%m%d-%H%M%S.pcap -G 3600 (new file every hour) and/or -C 100 (new file every 100 MB), with -W 24 to keep only the last 24 files (older ones are overwritten). Add a tight capture filter so you're only storing the traffic you need, drop -s to a snap length if you only need headers, and consider writing to a dedicated volume. Monitor free space and have the capture stop or alert before the disk is critical.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What is BPF in the context of tcpdump?
Berkeley Packet Filter — the filter language for capture filters. The expression (e.g. tcp port 443 and host 10.0.0.5) is compiled to bytecode and run in the kernel so non-matching packets are discarded before they reach the tool.
Which flags save a capture to a file and read it back?
tcpdump -w file.pcap to write, tcpdump -r file.pcap to read (and you can apply a new BPF filter on read). Same -w/-r in tshark/dumpcap.

Intermediate core

You're given a 2 GB pcap from an incident and asked "what did the compromised host talk to, and was anything exfiltrated?". Walk through your tshark analysis.
(1) Orient: capinfos cap.pcapng for time range, packet count, link type. tshark -r cap -q -z endpoints,ip and -z conv,ip — who did the host (say 10.0.0.5) talk to, ranked by bytes, with direction and duration. Flag external IPs, especially high outbound byte counts. (2) Resolve destinations: tshark -r cap -Y 'dns' -T fields -e dns.qry.name -e dns.a to map IPs to names; look for DGA-looking domains, dynamic-DNS, newly-seen domains, and DNS with abnormally large TXT/NULL responses (DNS tunnelling). -z io,stat,60,'COUNT(dns)dns' for query-rate spikes. (3) C2 candidates: long-lived or beaconing connections — regular-interval small requests (-z io,stat per conversation, or export timestamps and look for fixed periods), connections to raw IPs on odd ports, TLS with self-signed or mismatched certs (-Y 'tls.handshake.type==11' and inspect the cert), HTTP with unusual User-Agents or URIs (-Y 'http.request' -T fields -e http.host -e http.user_agent -e http.request.uri). (4) Exfil: outbound transfers — large POST/PUT bodies (-Y 'http.request.method=="POST"' -T fields -e http.content_length), big uploads over FTP/SFTP/SMB, data-heavy DNS/ICMP (tunnelling), or steady large TLS flows to an unfamiliar endpoint; sum outbound bytes per external peer and compare to a baseline. Reassemble suspicious cleartext streams (-z follow,tcp,ascii,N) to see the actual content; for TLS you'll have sizes/timing only unless keys are available. (5) Lateral: internal-to-internal connections from the host on SMB/RDP/WinRM/SSH that are unusual for it. (6) Report: list of external contacts with classification (benign/unknown/malicious), the C2 indicator(s) and beacon interval, evidence of exfil (protocol, destination, approximate volume, timeframe), and IOCs (IPs, domains, JA3/certs, URIs) for blocking and threat hunting. Note what's inconclusive due to encryption.

Advanced deep

Design a network-visibility architecture for a production environment: where to capture, how to store, how to keep it useful and lawful.
Capture points: (1) Perimeter — TAPs (fail-open, or aggregating TAPs) on internet uplinks and DMZ links; (2) Core / inter-VLAN — SPAN or TAP on trunks between segments (east-west is where lateral movement hides); (3) Data-centre top-of-rack for server-to-server; (4) Cloud — VPC Traffic Mirroring / packet mirroring to sensors, plus flow logs everywhere as the always-on baseline; (5) Host-level — eBPF/agent-based flow + selective pcap on critical servers where you can't tap. Prefer TAPs over SPAN for fidelity (SPAN drops under load and reorders); use packet brokers to filter/dedupe/load-balance to the tools. What to run on the traffic: Zeek for connection/protocol logs (compact, queryable — the workhorse), Suricata for IDS/alerting, and a rolling full-packet capture (e.g. Arkime/Moloch, or Stenographer) with a retention window sized to budget (often 3–30 days) indexed by Zeek metadata so you can pivot from an alert to the packets. Flow logs / NetFlow kept much longer (months) for historical hunting. Storage: tiered — hot SSD for recent full pcap, cheaper disk/object for Zeek logs and flow, lifecycle policies; size for peak throughput × retention with headroom; compress; shard by sensor. Keeping it useful: normalise timestamps (PTP/NTP discipline on sensors), tag captures with sensor/segment, integrate with the SIEM so an alert links straight to the relevant Zeek session and pcap, maintain dissector/rule updates, and monitor the pipeline itself (drops at broker/sensor, disk, index lag). Decrypt where you legitimately can and it's worth it — TLS interception at the egress proxy for outbound (with clear policy and exclusions for banking/health/privacy categories), or key-log/keying material from your own servers for inbound — and accept metadata-only elsewhere; JA3/JA4 and cert fingerprints stay useful without decryption. Lawful & ethical: written policy and authorisation covering employee-traffic monitoring (notice/consent per jurisdiction — works councils in the EU, etc.), documented purpose (security/ops, not surveillance), minimisation (capture filters that exclude out-of-scope or highly sensitive flows, drop payloads where only metadata is needed), strict RBAC and audit on who can query captures and decrypt, retention limits enforced technically, and legal review for cross-border data. Access: analysts get read-only search; raw pcap export and decryption are privileged, logged actions. Validation: periodically test that a synthetic event is visible end-to-end (sensor → Zeek → SIEM → pcab retrievable), and that retention/rotation actually work. Net: TAP-first capture at perimeter + core + cloud-mirror, Zeek+Suricata+rolling full-packet with metadata indexing, tiered retention with long-lived flow logs, SIEM integration for alert-to-packet pivot, selective lawful decryption at controlled points, and a governance layer (authorisation, minimisation, RBAC, retention, audit) so the visibility is both effective and defensible.

Post-Exploitation Enumeration

You have a shell on an authorised target. Before anything else, answer: who am I, what can I do, what is this box, what can it reach — using built-in commands, quietly. Every enumeration step has a hardening mirror.

Notes

Identity & privileges — what can this account do?

What / why. First question after landing a shell. Am I root already? If not, what's my direct path up — sudo rights, group memberships (docker, lxd, disk, adm, sudo/wheel are all escalation-relevant), file capabilities, or a SUID binary.

$ whoami ; id                       # user, UID, GID, and supplementary groups (root = UID 0)
$ id -u ; groups                    # quick checks; group 'docker'/'lxd' often == root-equivalent
$ sudo -l                           # what may I run via sudo, and as whom, with/without a password
$ sudo -n true 2>&1                 # can I sudo without a password prompt?
$ getcap -r / 2>/dev/null           # file capabilities (cap_setuid+ep on a binary = privesc)
$ find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null      # SUID binaries (compare against GTFOBins)
$ find / -perm -2000 -type f 2>/dev/null      # SGID
$ cat /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/* 2>/dev/null
# defensive mirror: minimal sudo rules (no NOPASSWD, no wildcards, no shell-outs), audit group
# membership, drop unneeded SUID bits, use capabilities narrowly, monitor 'sudo -l' at scale.

System profile — what am I running on?

What / why. Kernel version and distro drive which local-privesc exploits apply; installed software and running services are the local attack surface; scheduled tasks are a classic escalation and persistence vector.

$ uname -a                          # kernel release + arch -> match against known local-privesc CVEs
$ cat /etc/os-release ; hostnamectl ; lsb_release -a 2>/dev/null
$ cat /proc/version ; arch ; getconf LONG_BIT
$ ps auxww                          # every process + full args (creds on command lines, root daemons)
$ ps -eo pid,user,cmd --sort=user
$ systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running   # or: service --status-all
$ cat /etc/crontab ; ls -la /etc/cron.* /var/spool/cron/crontabs 2>/dev/null   # writable script run by root?
$ dpkg -l 2>/dev/null | head ; rpm -qa 2>/dev/null | head   # installed packages/versions
$ mount ; cat /etc/fstab ; df -h                            # nfs/nosuid?, extra disks, creds in fstab
# defensive mirror: patch the kernel/packages (kills the CVE list), least-functionality (remove
# unused services), lock down cron script permissions, nosuid/nodev on data mounts, file-integrity
# monitoring on cron dirs and SUID files.

Network position — what can this box reach?

What / why. The compromised host is a pivot. Its listening services may expose more; its routes, ARP/neighbour table, and reachable hosts define the next hop; DNS and /etc/hosts reveal internal names.

$ ss -tulpen                        # listening TCP/UDP sockets + owning process + user (needs privs for -p)
$ ss -tanp                          # established connections (who is this box already talking to?)
$ lsof -i -P -n 2>/dev/null         # same idea via lsof: open network files / listeners
$ ip a ; ip r ; ip neigh           # interfaces, routing table, ARP/neighbour cache (nearby live hosts)
$ cat /etc/resolv.conf /etc/hosts   # internal DNS servers, hard-coded internal names
$ cat /proc/net/tcp 2>/dev/null     # listeners even without ss/netstat (hex, decode ports)
$ for i in $(seq 1 254); do (ping -c1 -W1 10.0.0.$i &>/dev/null && echo 10.0.0.$i up) & done; wait  # tiny sweep
# defensive mirror: host firewall default-deny (in AND out), network segmentation so a foothold
# can't scan/reach the estate, no secrets in resolv.conf/hosts, egress filtering to break C2/pivot,
# monitor east-west connection attempts and new listeners.

Credentials & sensitive files — the fast path onward

What / why. Reused credentials and forgotten secrets escalate or move laterally faster than any kernel exploit. Look in histories, config files, backups, environment, keys, and world-readable spots — without trampling data you're not authorised to touch.

$ cat ~/.bash_history ~/.zsh_history 2>/dev/null            # passwords typed on the CLI
$ env ; cat /proc/1/environ 2>/dev/null | tr '\0' '\n'      # secrets in environment
$ ls -la ~/.ssh ; cat ~/.ssh/id_* ~/.ssh/config ~/.ssh/authorized_keys 2>/dev/null
$ grep -RniE 'password|passwd|secret|api[_-]?key|token' /etc /opt /var/www 2>/dev/null | head
$ find / -name '*.kdbx' -o -name 'id_rsa' -o -name '*.pem' -o -name '.env' 2>/dev/null
$ cat /var/www/*/config*.php /opt/*/application.{properties,yml} 2>/dev/null    # DB creds in app config
$ find / -writable -type d 2>/dev/null | grep -vE '^/(proc|sys)' | head          # where can I write?
$ getent passwd ; ls -la /home/*                                                 # other users to target
# defensive mirror: secrets in a vault (not files/env/history), disable shell history for service
# accounts or scrub it, tight file perms on app config, unique creds per host/service (no reuse),
# SSH keys with passphrases + short-lived certs, DLP/AV on credential-file patterns, monitor mass
# 'grep -R' / reads of many config files by an unusual process.

Discipline & the defensive summary

  • Stay in scope: enumeration is fine; don't read customer data, don't run destructive commands, don't add persistence without written sign-off, and log every command with timestamps for the report.
  • Be quiet: prefer built-ins to uploaded scripts; avoid noisy sweeps on monitored networks; know that find / -perm -4000, mass grep -R, and ping sweeps are detectable.
  • Windows equivalents (for completeness): whoami /all, whoami /priv, net user/net localgroup administrators, systeminfo, tasklist /svc, netstat -ano, ipconfig /all, route print, schtasks /query, cmdkey /list, and Get-* PowerShell cmdlets.
  • The whole defensive point: least privilege (so the account can't do much), aggressive patching (so uname -a yields no exploit), no stray secrets (so credential hunting comes up empty), segmentation + egress filtering (so the pivot goes nowhere), and endpoint/audit logging (so all this enumeration lights up a dashboard). A well-run host makes a foothold a dead end.
Cheat Sheet
  • Identity/privs: whoami, id, sudo -l, groups (docker/lxd/disk/adm = danger), getcap -r / 2>/dev/null, find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null (SUID → GTFOBins).
  • System: uname -a + /etc/os-release (→ local-privesc CVEs), ps auxww, systemctl list-units --state=running, cat /etc/crontab + ls -la /etc/cron.*, mount/fstab.
  • Network: ss -tulpen / lsof -i -P -n (listeners + owner), ss -tanp (established), ip a/ip r/ip neigh, /etc/resolv.conf + /etc/hosts.
  • Creds/files: ~/.bash_history, env / /proc/1/environ, ~/.ssh/*, grep -RniE 'password|secret|api_key|token' /etc /opt /var/www, find / -name '*.env' -o -name 'id_rsa' -o -name '*.kdbx', find / -writable -type d.
  • Prefer built-ins over uploaded enum scripts (quieter). Watch for detectable actions: SUID hunts, mass grep, ping sweeps.
  • In scope only: no data access, no destructive commands, no persistence without sign-off; log everything.
  • Defensive mirror: least privilege + patch kernel/packages + secrets in a vault + segmentation & egress filtering + auditd/EDR alerting = foothold becomes a dead end.
Q&A
You land a shell. What are the first two commands and why?
id (and whoami) then sudo -l. id tells you your UID/GID and — crucially — supplementary groups: UID 0 means you're already root; membership in docker, lxd, disk, adm, or sudo/wheel is often a direct or near-direct path to root. sudo -l shows exactly which commands you can run as another user (often root), and whether a password is required — a misconfigured sudo rule (NOPASSWD, a wildcard, or a binary that can shell out) is the fastest, quietest escalation there is.
Why is uname -a one of the first things checked?
The kernel release and architecture determine which local privilege-escalation exploits could apply. An old kernel with a known LPE (Dirty COW, Dirty Pipe, OverlayFS bugs, nf_tables, etc.) can take a low-priv shell straight to root. Combined with /etc/os-release (distro + version pins the exact package set) you can shortlist candidate exploits before trying anything. The defensive corollary: a fully patched kernel makes this check yield nothing.
What's the difference between ss -tulpen and ss -tanp for enumeration?
ss -tulpen shows listening TCP/UDP sockets with the owning process and user (and extended info) — that's the box's local service attack surface, including services bound only to 127.0.0.1 that aren't reachable from outside but are reachable from your shell (a common privesc: a root-owned admin service on localhost). ss -tanp shows established connections — who this host is already talking to, which reveals internal peers, databases, and management hosts to target for lateral movement. You want both: what's listening here, and what this box connects to.
Where do you look for credentials that let you move on without an exploit?
Shell history (~/.bash_history, ~/.zsh_history — people paste passwords into commands), environment variables (env, /proc/<pid>/environ of running services), SSH material (~/.ssh/id_*, config, known_hosts for where keys are used), application config files (DB connection strings in config.php, application.properties, .env, web.config), backup files and archives, world-readable files in /opt//var, password managers (*.kdbx), cloud credential files (~/.aws/credentials), and CI/deploy scripts. A recursive grep for password|secret|token|api_key across /etc, /opt, and web roots is the fast sweep. Reused or over-scoped credentials found this way are frequently the actual root cause of a full compromise.
From a defender's side, how do you catch this enumeration activity?
It's high-signal if you're watching: (1) auditd / Sysmon-for-Linux / EDR rules for execution of recon commands (id, whoami, sudo -l, uname, ss, netstat, find ... -perm -4000, mass grep -R) especially by a web/app service account or from a process with an unusual parent (a shell spawned by nginx/php-fpm/java). (2) SUID/SGID enumeration and reads of many config files in a short window. (3) New listening sockets or outbound connections from a server that shouldn't initiate them (egress monitoring). (4) Internal port scans / ping sweeps from a host via NetFlow/Zeek. (5) Failed sudo and privilege-change events. (6) Uploaded enum tooling (linpeas/pspy) — file writes to /tmp + execution + world of recon syscalls. Correlate: "app account spawned a shell, then ran id/sudo -l/uname, then scanned the subnet" is a near-certain compromise. The controls that make it moot are still primary (least privilege, patching, no secrets, segmentation), but this activity should also page someone.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does id tell you that whoami doesn't?
whoami is just the username. id adds the numeric UID (0 = root), the primary GID, and — most usefully for enumeration — all supplementary group memberships (e.g. docker, sudo, adm, disk), several of which are escalation paths.
Which command lists listening ports and the process behind each?
ss -tulpen (or lsof -i -P -n, or legacy netstat -tulpen). The -p part (process/owner) needs sufficient privileges to see all processes.

Intermediate core

You have a low-priv shell as the www-data user on an authorised target. Give a structured 10-minute enumeration plan.
0–1 min — identity/privs: id, sudo -l (and sudo -n true), groups. If www-data is in docker/lxd or sudo lets it run something — escalate there and stop. 1–3 min — quick wins: getcap -r / 2>/dev/null, find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null (cross-ref GTFOBins), writable files/dirs in PATH and in cron dirs (ls -la /etc/cron*, cat /etc/crontab — a root cron running a www-data-writable script is instant root). 3–5 min — system: uname -a + /etc/os-release (shortlist kernel LPEs), ps auxww (root services, creds on cmdlines, an internal admin daemon), ss -tulpen (localhost-only root services this shell can reach). 5–7 min — app credentials: this is a web account, so cat /var/www/*/config*.*, .env, framework config → almost always DB creds; mysql -u.. -p.. / check for password reuse to a system user; look in /var/backups, deploy scripts, ~/.bash_history of any readable home. 7–9 min — pivot recon: ip a/r/neigh, /etc/hosts/resolv.conf, ss -tanp (what this box talks to — DB host, internal APIs), a light subnet ping loop if the network isn't heavily monitored. 9–10 min — decide: pick the most reliable, least-noisy path (usually: a sudo/cron/SUID misconfig, or reused DB/app creds → a real user → then kernel exploit only if needed), note everything with timestamps, and confirm the target is in scope before acting. Throughout: prefer built-ins, don't touch data, no persistence without sign-off.

Advanced deep

Design host hardening and detection so that a foothold as a service account yields nothing useful from enumeration and privilege escalation.
Least privilege & least functionality: service accounts are non-login (/usr/sbin/nologin), own only their own files, are in no privileged groups, have no sudo rights (or one tightly-scoped NOPASSWD to a single non-shell-capable binary at most), and run under systemd hardening (NoNewPrivileges, ProtectSystem=strict, PrivateTmp, ProtectHome, CapabilityBoundingSet= empty or minimal, SystemCallFilter, ReadOnlyPaths, RestrictAddressFamilies). Remove compilers, package managers where feasible, and unused SUID binaries (chmod u-s or dpkg-statoverride); mount /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm and data volumes noexec,nosuid,nodev. Patch aggressively: automated kernel and package updates with live-patching where possible — so uname -a maps to no known LPE. No stray secrets: all credentials from a secrets manager injected at runtime into memory/tmpfs, never in files, env dumped to logs, or images; disable shell history for service contexts; app config files readable only by the service user and containing references, not secrets; unique per-host credentials (no reuse), short-lived where possible. Filesystem: app code read-only to the service account; no world-writable dirs; cron/systemd-timer scripts owned by root and not writable by anyone else; file-integrity monitoring (AIDE/auditd watches) on SUID files, cron dirs, /etc, and app binaries. Network containment: host firewall default-deny inbound and outbound (allow only the exact peers/ports the service needs — DB, dependencies), so a foothold can't scan, pivot, or call out for C2/tooling; network segmentation and microsegmentation so even allowed traffic can't reach the crown jewels; no route to cloud metadata (or IMDSv2 with hop limit) so cloud creds aren't harvestable. Containerise / isolate where it fits: run the service in a container or micro-VM as non-root with dropped caps, read-only rootfs, seccomp — a shell inside is already boxed. Detection: auditd/Falco/EDR rules for (1) a shell or interpreter spawned by the service process (nginx/php-fpm/java → sh/bash/python), (2) recon command execution by the service account (id, sudo -l, uname, ss, find -perm -4000, mass grep -R), (3) reads of many config/credential files or of /etc/shadow, (4) new listeners or outbound connections from the host, (5) writes to /tmp followed by execution, (6) any successful privilege change. Ship to the SIEM, alert on the sequence, and cross-correlate with the app's own logs. Validate: periodically drop an authorised low-priv shell on a clone and confirm enumeration comes up empty and every step generated an alert. Net: non-login least-privilege service accounts under systemd sandboxing on patched, minimal hosts with no local secrets and default-deny egress, ideally containerised — plus behavioural detection on shell-spawns and recon commands so the (contained, unproductive) foothold still pages the SOC.

Terminal Toys: hollywood & cmatrix

Purely cosmetic screen effects — fake "hacker" dashboards and Matrix rain. Fun for a demo or a screensaver; they do nothing, and running one is not "hacking".

Notes

hollywood

What / why. A shell script (ships in a snap / some distro repos) that splits your terminal with byobu/tmux into panes each running a fast-scrolling real command (a compile, find, hexdump, tree, package lists) so it looks like a movie "hacking" montage. It's output theatre — nothing is being attacked, scanned, or cracked.

$ sudo apt install hollywood     # or: sudo snap install hollywood
$ hollywood                      # fills the terminal with fake-busy panes
$ hollywood 4                    # optional: target number of split "windows"
# quit: it's tmux/byobu underneath -> Ctrl-C in each pane, or close the terminal,
#       or  tmux kill-server  /  pkill hollywood
# needs byobu + tmux + a few coreutils; it just runs harmless commands loudly.

cmatrix

What / why. Renders the green "digital rain" from The Matrix in the terminal. A tiny C program using ncurses; classic use is a jokey screen-lock or a conference-booth background.

$ sudo apt install cmatrix
$ cmatrix                        # the falling characters
$ cmatrix -b                     # bold random characters
$ cmatrix -s                     # "screensaver" mode: any keypress exits
$ cmatrix -u 5                   # update delay 0-10 (higher = slower)
$ cmatrix -C red                 # colour: green(default)/red/blue/white/yellow/cyan/magenta/black
$ cmatrix -r                     # rainbow
# quit: press 'q' (or any key with -s). Ctrl-C also works.
# related toys: sl (steam locomotive), pipes.sh, cowsay, lolcat, asciiquarium, no more secrets (nms), genact.

Why this matters (a little)

  • Media literacy: "hacking" scenes in film/TV — and a lot of social-media "hacker" clips — are exactly this: cmatrix, hollywood, genact, or a scrolling nmap. Real offensive work is slow, quiet, and mostly reading output.
  • Harmless: no network activity, no privilege needs, no target — safe to run anywhere you're allowed to run software. The only "risk" is CPU/terminal noise and looking silly on a shared screen.
  • Don't confuse effort with effect: a busy-looking terminal proves nothing. Evidence in a real assessment is specific — a command, its output, a screenshot of the actual finding.
Cheat Sheet
  • hollywood: sudo snap install hollywood (or apt) → hollywood [N]. It's tmux/byobu running harmless commands in split panes. Quit: Ctrl-C / close terminal / pkill hollywood / tmux kill-server.
  • cmatrix: sudo apt install cmatrix → cmatrix. Flags: -s (any key exits), -b bold, -r rainbow, -C <colour>, -u 0..10 speed. Quit: q or Ctrl-C.
  • Both are cosmetic: no network, no target, no privileges. Not tools, not "hacking".
  • Other toys: sl, pipes.sh, cowsay/lolcat, asciiquarium, nms ("no more secrets"), genact.
  • Takeaway: on-screen busyness ≠ results. Real findings are specific commands + outputs + evidence.
Q&A
Does running hollywood or cmatrix do anything to a network or a target?
No. They only draw animation to your terminal and read a keypress to exit. There is no network traffic, no scanning, no exploitation — they're the equivalent of a screensaver. Anyone presenting one as "hacking" is doing nothing.
How do you exit each one?
cmatrix: press q (or any key if started with -s), or Ctrl-C. hollywood: it runs inside tmux/byobu, so Ctrl-C in each pane, close the terminal window, or from another shell pkill hollywood / tmux kill-server.
Why is it worth knowing these exist?
Media literacy. Most "hacker terminal" footage in films and viral clips is one of these (or a scrolling nmap/genact). Recognising the aesthetic keeps you from being impressed by — or fooled by — a screenshot of a busy green terminal. Real offensive security is methodical and mostly undramatic.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What category do hollywood and cmatrix belong to?
Terminal eye-candy / screen effects — cosmetic toys. They are not security tools and perform no offensive or defensive function.
What does cmatrix -s do?
Runs it in "screensaver" mode — it exits on any keypress rather than only on q.

Intermediate core

A "proof of hack" video shows a rapidly scrolling green terminal. How do you evaluate the claim?
Treat the visuals as meaningless and ask for concrete evidence. A scrolling terminal could be cmatrix, hollywood, genact, nms, a cat of a big file, or a legitimate but unremarkable command — the animation proves nothing. Real proof of a compromise is specific and reproducible: the exact target and scope authorisation, the vulnerability (CVE or class) and where it was, the request/payload used, the resulting access (a shell prompt showing id/hostname on the target, a specific file retrieved, a screenshot tied to the target's unique content), timestamps, and ideally steps to reproduce. If someone can't produce that and only has "look how fast the text goes", there's no substantiated claim.

Advanced deep

Why does the gap between "looks like hacking" and "is security work" matter for how organisations assess and hire security talent?
Because optics are a poor proxy for capability, and confusing them leads to bad decisions. Real offensive security is slow, methodical, heavily documentation-driven, and mostly consists of reading output, understanding a system's design, and reasoning about trust boundaries — not fast typing or busy screens. Consequences of getting this wrong: (1) Hiring/assessment — evaluate candidates on methodology (scoping, threat modelling, how they'd chain findings, how they'd report and remediate, ethics/authorisation judgement) and on hands-on labs with a written report, not on demos or jargon; a great pentester's deliverable is a clear risk-ranked report a dev team can act on. (2) Program metrics — measure security by outcomes (mean-time-to-remediate, exposed-service trend, detection coverage vs ATT&CK, findings that led to real fixes), not by activity theatre. (3) Culture — rewarding drama over rigour pushes people toward flashy one-off findings instead of the unglamorous work that actually reduces risk (patch pipelines, segmentation, secret management, detection engineering, secure defaults). (4) Defence — teams that expect attacks to "look dramatic" miss the real thing, which looks like a slightly unusual login or one odd process. The mature view: value the report, the reproducibility, the judgement, and the fix — and treat the green-terminal aesthetic as entertainment.
